name: book-models
description: Four communities of different orders, invented, with no organisation above them, set to write together a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, a book of more than five hundred two-column pages.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: Commons proposes a charter with a rotating chair, a two-thirds rule for admitting tools to the bench, first review by two peers of other origins, and adoption of the book by unanimity. The shelf would stay a commons: each section's series chosen from the World Bank's catalogue by one gatherer and checked by another of a different origin. Commons welcomes amendments from guild, cooperative and foru

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild proposes a charter founded on a standing secretariat. Tools would be admitted to the bench by two thirds of the council, sections would be reviewed first by two peers of other origins, and the book would be adopted by two thirds. Under this charter every finding rests on analyses run on the shared bench and replicated independently, and each finding states its number, year and unit from

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative proposes a charter with a rotating chair, two-thirds admission of tools to the bench, first review by two guild peers of other origins, and adoption of the book by unanimity. It invites the commons, the guild and the forum to state their amendments, in particular on whether the forum should have a role in review of sections that concern it.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum proposes a balanced charter: a rotating chair, two-thirds rules for the bench and the book, and first review by a panel drawn from every member. It invites amendment, particularly from the guild on review and from the commons on the bench.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: Commons supports every charter with a rotating chair, including the forum's panel review and its two-thirds rule for the book, and asks the guild whether a rotating chair, with continuity of the bench and shelf kept by the commons, would meet its concern about discontinuity.

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild accepts a rotating chair and adoption of the book by unanimity so that a charter can carry every community's consent. Its one firm requirement is first review by two peers of other origins. The guild proposes that the forum review sections that concern it at a second stage, after replication.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative supports every charter with a rotating chair and a two-thirds bench, its own and the commons' identical text included. It will accept either peers or a panel at first review. It asks the guild whether a rotating chair with a continuing bench maintainer would meet its concern for continuity.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum moves towards the common ground: a rotating chair, two-thirds admission of tools to the bench, peer review and unanimity for the book. It accepts peer review at first because unanimity guarantees the forum's voice before the book is adopted. communities.mission: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: The commons supports a book in which every finding can be traced to a checked series. Section titles in the region chapters should become declarative findings once the data are gathered. Where a target lacks a series in the World Development Indicators, the section should say so rather than reach for other sources.

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild approves the chapters whose findings rest on dense World Development Indicators series that can be replicated on the bench. It also approves the data and method chapters, which carry the book's account of its own reliability. The goals with thin indicator coverage, such as 14 and 12, are left to other communities' judgement rather than opposed.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative supports an outline whose every section can be drafted from replicated analyses. It asks for space to report replication openly, and for questions phrased so that each answer states a number, a year and a unit.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum approves the chapters that bear most directly on people's lives and on whether evidence about them exists: poverty, hunger, health, education, gender, water, inequality, justice, the two regions with most of the world's extreme poor, interlinkages, data gaps and proposals. series.why: Share of the female population using the internet; the closest available measure of women's use of enabling technology under target 5.b. Sex-disaggregated coverage is patchier than the total series.
Male internet use, the counterpart needed to compute the gap against the female series. Same source and definitional limits, so the comparison is consistent.
Total internet use across the population, with the widest coverage. Gives the overall level against which the sex gap is read.
Female account ownership, including mobile-money accounts. Indicates women's use of mobile-enabled financial services; it is not a measure of phone ownership. Survey years are sparse.
Male account ownership, the comparator for the female series. Allows a gap in mobile-linked financial access to be stated, with the same survey-year limits.

d-c06-7~orchard/gatherer~14.note: The shelf holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex, which is the indicator for target 5.b (5.b.1). Mobile subscriptions are not disaggregated by sex and count SIM cards, not owners. Internet use by sex and account ownership by sex are the nearest proxies and should be presented as such.

petition.name: Individuals owning a mobile phone, by sex (% of population)
petition.need: Indicator 5.b.1 is the proportion of individuals who own a mobile telephone, by sex. No such series is held, so the gender gap in phone ownership cannot be measured directly.

series.why: Share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures; directly addresses exposure under target 1.5, but covers only the 1990-2009 average, so no trend.
New displacements associated with disasters, a count of cases; captures recent annual disaster impact, though it records displacement only and coverage varies by country.
Disaster risk reduction progress score (1-5) gauges national preparedness and resilience under target 1.5; self-reported, ordinal, with limited years.

d-c02-5~loom/gatherer~14.note: No series gives the number of people affected each year by climate-related disasters. The share affected is an average for 1990-2009, and displacement counts capture only one form of impact. Under-reporting in poorer countries is likely.

petition.name: People affected by climate-related disasters, annual, by country
petition.need: An annual count of people killed, injured, displaced or otherwise affected by climate-related disasters, as Sendai Framework indicator 1.5.1 requires, is absent from the catalogue.

series.why: Probability of dying between ages 30 and 70 from CVD, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease; this is indicator 3.4.1 itself. Modelled estimates, with few years published.
Female 3.4.1 indicator; shows whether the one-third reduction is progressing equally for women. Modelled, and available only for selected years.
Male 3.4.1 indicator; male premature mortality is generally higher, so the sex gap bears on the target. Modelled, with sparse years.
Suicide mortality rate is indicator 3.4.2, covering the mental health element of target 3.4. Age-standardised modelled estimates; under-reporting is likely in many countries.
Measures service coverage for non-communicable diseases, showing the treatment side of the target. It is a composite index and does not measure outcomes.

d-c04-4~cedar/gatherer~14.note: The target does not fix a baseline year; 2015 is commonly used, and a one-third cut implies a fall of about 2.0 percent a year to 2030. The 3.4.1 series is modelled and published for few years, so trend estimates are coarse. Suicide is reported separately from premature mortality.

series.why: Women, Business and the Law Legal Framework Index (0-100) scores laws on women's economic opportunity directly; wide coverage, though it records laws on the books, not practice.
Supportive Framework Index (0-100) measures the supports for implementing equal laws; complements the legal score, though coverage years may be shorter.
Enforcement Perceptions Index (0-100) shows expert-perceived enforcement of the laws; perception-based, so comparability across countries is limited.

d-c06-1~bao/gatherer~14.note: The Women, Business and the Law indices are the only candidates measuring legal change directly. Target 5.1 can be read broadly (all forms of discrimination); these indices cover economic opportunity only. Indicator 5.1.1 on legal frameworks is not covered in full.

series.why: Litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15+; the indicator of target 3.5.2 itself. Modelled projected estimates, not survey counts; excludes unrecorded consumption in part.
Male consumption per adult aged 15+; shows the sex gap behind the total. Modelled estimates with the same limits on unrecorded alcohol.
Female consumption per adult aged 15+; allows comparison with male levels and trends. Modelled estimates; low levels in many countries carry wider uncertainty.

d-c04-5~saltmarsh/gatherer~14.note: Only the three alcohol series measure target 3.5's harmful-use indicator. The remaining candidates concern expenditure, energy or income and do not measure alcohol. Per-capita litres say nothing of harmful patterns, and the series are sparse in years.

series.why: Modelled stunting prevalence in under-fives: the indicator for target 2.2, with annual estimates and wide coverage, so trends and projections to 2025 and 2030 can be computed. Estimates carry uncertainty.
Wasting prevalence in under-fives: the second indicator for target 2.2, with the 2025 and 2030 benchmarks of 5% and 3%. Survey-based, so years are sparse and uneven.
Severe wasting prevalence: shows the most acute form of malnutrition within wasting. Survey-based, with sparse coverage and irregular years.
Modelled overweight prevalence in under-fives: the third malnutrition indicator in target 2.2, needed for 'all forms of malnutrition'. Estimates carry uncertainty.
Survey-based stunting prevalence: the unmodelled counterpart to the modelled estimate, useful to check it. Years are irregular and coverage thinner.

d-c03-2~juniper/gatherer~14.note: Target 2.2 can be read as global or national benchmarks; the 2025 stunting target (40% reduction from 2012) and the wasting target (below 5% by 2025, 3% by 2030) need computation. Survey series have gaps.

series.why: Headcount below $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), the current international extreme poverty line; the target's own indicator, with wide coverage. Survey years are sparse, and later values are partly estimated.
Poverty gap at $3.00 a day shows depth of extreme poverty, indicating how far those below the line fall short and how hard eradication will be.
Headcount at $4.20 a day shows how many people sit just above the extreme line and remain exposed to relapse; it is not the target line.
National poverty lines offer a country-defined comparison with the international line; definitions differ across countries and years, limiting comparability.

d-c02-1~idris/gatherer~14.note: Target 1.1 cites $1.25 a day, but the World Bank now uses $3.00 a day (2021 PPP); the target can be read at either line. Survey coverage is uneven and recent years are partly projected.

series.why: Female account ownership (ages 15+, Global Findex) is the core measure of women's financial access under target 5.a; surveys are triennial, so years are sparse.
Male account ownership allows the gender gap to be computed as a difference against the female series; same survey limits apply.
Total account ownership gives the national baseline against which the female and male figures are read.
Women, Business and the Law Legal Framework Index (0-100) records legal equality in property, inheritance and finance; it measures law, not practice.
Share of firms with female ownership approximates women's control of business property; coverage is limited to surveyed countries and years, and it is not a land measure.

d-c06-6~juno/gatherer~14.note: No series in the candidates measures women's land ownership or inheritance directly (the indicator 5.a.1 on agricultural landholders is absent), so the property gap is only approximated by legal and firm-ownership proxies. Account ownership is the one gender-disaggregated target indicator with wide

petition.name: Share of women among owners or secure-rights holders of agricultural land (SDG 5.a.1)
petition.need: Needed to measure the gender gap in land ownership; the catalogue offers no sex-disaggregated land tenure series, so the property question cannot be answered directly.

series.why: Indicator 2.1.1 itself: share of population with habitual food intake below energy needs. Wide coverage; modelled, three-year averages, and weak for small populations.
Indicator 2.1.2 itself: moderate or severe food insecurity by the FIES survey scale. Starts around 2015, so trends are short; coverage rests on modelled estimates.
Severe food insecurity, the FIES component close to hunger. Separates acute deprivation from moderate insecurity; same short record and modelled limits.

d-c03-1~heath/gatherer~14.note: Target 2.1 reads two ways: hunger as undernourishment, or access to sufficient food as food insecurity. Both indicators are therefore kept. Child underweight and wasting belong to target 2.2, not here.

series.why: Counts primary-school-age children out of school, answering the question directly in persons; UIS-sourced, with gaps for many countries and years.
Gives out-of-school children as a share of primary school age, allowing comparison across countries of different size; coverage uneven in recent years.
Measures adolescents out of school at lower secondary age, extending the answer beyond primary to target 4.1's secondary stage; no count series is offered.
Counts out-of-school girls of primary age, showing the gender split; sparser coverage than totals.
Counts out-of-school boys of primary age, paired with the female count for gender comparison; same coverage limits.

d-c05-2~quarry/gatherer~17.note: No count of out-of-school adolescents appears among the candidates; lower secondary is available only as a share. Upper secondary age is not covered. Primary counts depend on UNESCO Institute for Statistics reporting and are missing for many countries.

petition.name: Adolescents and youth out of school, number of persons, lower and upper secondary age
petition.need: The section asks how many children of school age are out of school, but the shelf holds counts only for primary age; lower secondary is a share and upper secondary is absent.

series.why: Share of land area under agriculture; shows the extent of farmland. Wide coverage, but says nothing of intensity or sustainability of use.
Fertiliser use in kilograms per hectare of arable land; measures input intensity. Does not separate efficient from excessive use, and recent years have gaps.
Agriculture's share of total freshwater withdrawal; shows how heavily farming draws on water. Survey years vary by country and are sparse.
Share of agricultural land that is irrigated; indicates water-managed farming and resilience to drought. Coverage is uneven and years are irregular.
Cereal yield in kilograms per hectare; gauges productivity from land and inputs, matching target 2.4's productivity aim. Covers cereals only.

d-c03-5~orchard/gatherer~18.note: No candidate measures indicator 2.4.1, the proportion of agricultural area under productive and sustainable agriculture, so these series describe intensity and productivity only. Sustainability must be inferred, not read directly.

petition.name: Proportion of agricultural area under productive and sustainable agriculture (SDG indicator 2.4.1)
petition.need: Target 2.4's own indicator is absent from the candidates and is needed to judge sustainability rather than intensity of land, fertiliser and water use.

verdicts.why: Direct sex-disaggregated internet use; core to the question and target 5.b.
Necessary male counterpart to compute the internet use gap.
Gives overall level and widest coverage for reading the sex gap.
Mobile-money-inclusive account ownership; proxy for mobile-enabled finance, must be labelled as not phone ownership.
Male comparator needed for the account ownership gap.

add.why: Mobile subscriptions per 100 people give the only mobile-phone measure available, though not sex-disaggregated; the gap in ownership cannot be stated.

petition.name: Sex-disaggregated mobile phone ownership (GSMA or ITU household survey)
petition.need: The question asks about the gender gap in mobile phone ownership, but no such series is in the catalogue.

series.why: Target 1.2's own indicator: share living below each country's national poverty line. Coverage is uneven, survey years differ, and definitions vary, so cross-country comparison is limited.
Captures poverty in several dimensions, as Target 1.2 requires. Available only for survey years, and its method differs from national definitions.
A relative line that rises with national median income, giving a more comparable reading than national lines. It is not a national definition, and its coverage is narrower.
UNDP and OPHI multidimensional measure, a cross-check on the World Bank measure. Indicators and thresholds differ, and coverage is limited to developing countries.

d-c02-2~bao/gatherer~18.note: National lines differ in method, consumption or income base, and survey year, so levels cannot be ranked across countries. Trends within a country are more reliable. Data are missing for many high-income countries and for recent years.

series.why: Annual consumer price inflation, wide coverage; the closest candidate to a price-volatility measure, but covers all goods, not food alone.
Consumer price index level allows computing year-to-year swings since 2015; all items, not food, and the base year is 2010.
Wholesale price index may capture upstream price movements; coverage is thin, the series is not food-specific, and the base year is 2010.
Food production index shows supply swings that bear on price pressure; it measures quantity, not price.
Food imports as a share of merchandise imports shows exposure to world food price shocks; it is not a price measure.

d-c03-7~saltmarsh/gatherer~18.note: The shelf holds no food price index or food-specific inflation series, so target 2.c cannot be measured directly. Overall consumer inflation is a proxy only. A food CPI would close the gap.

petition.name: Food consumer price index and food inflation by country
petition.need: Target 2.c needs a food price series, such as the FAO Food Price Index or national food CPI, to measure food price volatility; the World Development Indicators hold none.

series.why: Target 1.4 indicator for water: share using at least basic drinking water services; wide national coverage, though it does not separate the poor.
Share using at least basic sanitation services, the sanitation measure for target 1.4; broad coverage, not disaggregated by income.
Share of population with electricity access; wide coverage and a core basic-service measure, though it does not capture reliability or affordability.
Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults; directly shows financial access for the poor, but survey years are sparse and country coverage is incomplete.
Rural electricity access shows the urban-rural gap, where the poor are concentrated; it still does not distinguish income groups.

d-c02-4~juniper/gatherer~18.note: Water and sanitation series are not split by income, so rural series and the poorest-40% account series serve as proxies for the poor. Safely managed water has thinner coverage than basic water.

series.why: Target 5.3's own indicator: share of women aged 20-24 first married by 18. Survey-based, so coverage is thin in high-income countries and years differ.
Captures marriage before 15, the most severe form of child marriage; complements the under-18 measure. Same survey limits and rarer in many countries.
Adolescent motherhood is a related outcome of early marriage, useful as context only. It is not a marriage measure and survey coverage is uneven.

d-c06-3~idris/gatherer~18.note: The target is indicator 5.3.1, the share of women aged 20-24 married before 18. Data come from household surveys, so years vary and many countries lack recent values. Forced marriage is not measured directly.

series.why: Cereal yield in kg per hectare directly measures land productivity for cereals; wide coverage. Covers cereals only, not other crops, livestock or fishing.
Cereal production in tonnes, with land under cereal, decomposes yield gains from area expansion. Gives no income or per-worker information.
Land under cereal production shows whether output rose through yield or through area, the denominator of cereal yield.
Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) covers crops and livestock beyond cereals; an index of volume, not of productivity per worker or hectare.
Irrigated share of agricultural land is a key input explaining yield differences; data are sparse in time and an input, not an outcome.

d-c03-4~juno/gatherer~18.note: Value added per agricultural worker (indicator 2.3.1) is not among the candidates, so the doubling of labour productivity cannot be read directly. Cereal yield is the only productivity measure present; small-scale producers' incomes (2.3.2) are also absent.

petition.name: Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$)
petition.need: Needed to measure target 2.3 labour productivity; not among the candidates offered, and small-scale producers' income is not held in the catalogue.

series.why: Measures current tobacco use among adults (%), the headline indicator for tobacco control under target 3.a; wide coverage, but estimates are modelled and published only for selected years.
Male prevalence shows where use remains highest; sex-disaggregated figures reveal divergent trends hidden by the adult average, with the same modelling limits.
Female prevalence is far lower in most countries but rises in some; paired with male figures it exposes gender differences in trend.

d-c04-10~heath/gatherer~18.note: No series in the candidates measures implementation of the Framework Convention itself (target 3.a); prevalence is an outcome proxy, not evidence of policy implementation. Youth tobacco use is also absent.

petition.name: WHO FCTC implementation score by country
petition.need: Target 3.a concerns implementation of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control; the catalogue holds no series of ratification, measure adoption or tobacco tax levels.

series.why: Target 6.1's own indicator: share of population using safely managed drinking water. Wide coverage, but series begins in 2000 and many countries lack estimates.
Urban safely managed water share; shows the urban side of the equitable-access gap. Coverage is thinner than the national series.
Rural safely managed water share; shows the rural deficit central to universal access. Coverage is thinner than the national series.
Basic water service share gives the wider coverage and the step below safely managed; it does not test quality, availability or location on premises.

d-c07-1~loom/gatherer~21.note: Safely managed drinking water requires an improved source on premises, available when needed and free from contamination. Country coverage is incomplete, so global and regional aggregates rest on modelled estimates. Affordability, named in target 6.1, has no series in the candidates.

series.why: Modelled maternal mortality ratio per 100,000 live births; the indicator of target 3.1 itself, with global and country coverage. Estimates are modelled, and uncertainty is wide where registration is weak.
Share of births attended by skilled health staff; the companion indicator of target 3.1. Survey-based, so years are irregular and recent values are missing for many countries.
Number of maternal deaths, giving absolute burden alongside the ratio and showing where deaths concentrate. Modelled, with the same uncertainty as the ratio.
Service coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health; a proxy for the health-system capacity that drives maternal mortality. Composite, not a target indicator.
National estimates from vital registration and surveys, a cross-check on modelled values. Coverage is patchy and methods differ between countries.

d-c04-1~quarry/gatherer~21.note: Target 3.1 sets a global ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births, so the global aggregate of SH.STA.MMRT in the latest year, set against the 2015 value, indicates the pace required. Modelled estimates carry uncertainty intervals, which the series does not report.

verdicts.why: Core target 2.2 stunting indicator; annual modelled estimates allow trend and projection to 2025 and 2030.
Core wasting indicator, with the 5% (2025) and 3% (2030) benchmarks the section tests.
Severe wasting has no internationally agreed 2025 or 2030 target; it adds little to the question asked.
Overweight is outside the question on stunting and wasting; better placed in a malnutrition-wide section.
Survey-based counterpart allows checking the modelled series against observed data, with its irregular years noted.

add.why: Only if the section addresses 'all forms of malnutrition' in target 2.2; otherwise omit.

verdicts.why: Only series giving share of population affected by climate disasters; 1990-2009 average, so no trend, which must be stated.
Annual disaster displacement counts give recent trend; records displacement only, not all people affected.
Only resilience-readiness measure for target 1.5; self-assessed, ordinal, 2009-2011 only, to be flagged.

petition.name: People affected by disasters, annual (EM-DAT), and economic losses
petition.need: Annual counts of people affected, deaths and damage by disaster type, to show trends after 2009 and complete the exposure record.

series.why: Indicator 3.8.1 itself: composite index (0-100) of essential service coverage; wide country coverage, though biennial and partly modelled.
Indicator 3.8.2 proxy: share of population spending over 40% of household capacity on out-of-pocket health costs; survey-based, sparse years.
Out-of-pocket share of current health expenditure; broad annual coverage, but does not show household burden or unmet need.
Share facing impoverishing out-of-pocket spending against the societal poverty line; shows depth of financial hardship, with limited survey coverage.
Out-of-pocket spending per capita in current US$; gives absolute scale, but is not adjusted for price differences or income.

d-c04-8~saltmarsh/gatherer~22.note: Coverage is read through the index and its financial-protection counterparts. The 40% threshold and the societal poverty line are different readings of hardship, so both are reported.

series.why: Current health expenditure as % of GDP; broad coverage and a direct gauge of health financing under 3.c. Does not show absolute spending or its distribution.
Government health spending per head in current US$; shows public financing in absolute terms for 3.c. Current prices ignore inflation and exchange-rate swings.
Total health spending per head in current US$; tracks financing levels across income groups for 3.c. Current prices limit comparison over time.
Community health workers per 1,000 people; the only workforce density measure among the candidates, relevant to 3.c. Coverage is sparse and definitions vary.
Sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, which includes immunisation coverage; the nearest proxy for 3.b access to vaccines. A composite, not a direct vaccine coverage rate.

d-c04-11~juniper/gatherer~22.note: No candidate measures immunisation coverage directly (for example DPT or measles shares) nor doctors, nurses and midwives per 1,000 people. The shelf may hold them outside this candidate list; otherwise they are gaps. Workforce density rests on community health workers alone.

petition.name: Immunisation coverage and health worker density series
petition.need: Child immunisation rates (DTP3, measles) and physicians, nurses and midwives per 1,000 people were absent from the candidates and are needed for targets 3.b and 3.c.

series.why: Gross pre-primary enrolment ratio for all children; the closest participation measure to target 4.2. Can exceed 100% through over-age entrants; coverage uneven.
Female pre-primary gross enrolment; allows comparison by sex for the 'girls and boys' wording of target 4.2. Same gross-ratio limits.
Male pre-primary gross enrolment; paired with the female series to show parity. Gross ratios do not isolate children of the official age.
Share of pre-primary teachers trained; a rough proxy for quality in 'quality pre-primary education'. National definitions of training differ and coverage is patchy.

d-c05-3~idris/gatherer~22.note: No candidate measures the SDG 4.2.2 indicator, participation in organised learning one year before primary entry (net rate), nor early childhood development outcomes under 4.2.1. Gross enrolment is a substitute, not a headcount.

petition.name: Participation rate in organised learning one year before the official primary entry age (SDG 4.2.2), by sex
petition.need: Net participation in the year before primary entry is the official indicator for target 4.2; the catalogue offers only gross pre-primary enrolment, which cannot show how many children of the right age take part.

series.why: Neonatal mortality per 1,000 live births is the indicator for the 12 threshold in target 3.2; country coverage is wide, though estimates are modelled.
Under-5 mortality per 1,000 live births is the indicator for the 25 threshold in target 3.2; wide coverage, modelled estimates in data-poor countries.
Number of under-five deaths shows the absolute burden remaining beyond the rate, and where deaths concentrate; counts depend on modelled births.
Number of neonatal deaths shows the absolute newborn burden, supplementing the rate; counts depend on modelled births.

d-c04-2~heath/gatherer~22.note: Counting countries that have reached each threshold requires comparing each country's latest value with 12 and 25 per 1,000. Both series are modelled estimates with uncertainty, so countries near a threshold may be misclassified. The latest year of estimates may differ among countries.

a-c06-7~birchwood/analyst-1~23.note: No series in the shelf measures mobile phone ownership by sex; IT.CEL.SETS.P2 counts subscriptions per 100 people, not owners, and is not split by sex. The writer must state this limit and treat internet use and account ownership by sex as proxies. Gaps are computed from the female and male series.

petition.name: Mobile phone ownership by sex (% of adults)
petition.need: The question asks about the gender gap in mobile phone ownership, but the World Bank catalogue holds no sex-disaggregated mobile ownership series among the accepted series.

verdicts.why: Directly measures legal frameworks for women's economic opportunity across ten topics; core series for target 5.1 and its change over time.
Measures supporting frameworks for implementing equal laws; complements the legal index and shows gaps between law and implementation.
Expert-perceived enforcement completes the law, support and enforcement sequence; perception-based and less comparable, which the text should state.

add.why: Violence against women is a discrimination outcome under 5.1 and shows whether laws on safety translate into practice.
Female youth outside education, employment or training gives an outcome measure of economic opportunity beside the legal indices.

series.why: Target 3.3.1 indicator: new HIV infections per 1,000 uninfected people, all ages; wide country coverage, but modelled estimates carry uncertainty.
Target 3.3.2 indicator: estimated new and relapse tuberculosis cases per 100,000 people; wide coverage, though estimates rest on uneven notification systems.
Target 3.3.3 indicator: malaria cases per 1,000 population at risk; relevant only to endemic countries, so global aggregates are limited.
Incidence among ages 15-24 shows recent transmission trends, a sensitive signal of epidemic control; modelled and less widely reported.
HIV prevalence among ages 15-49 gives context for incidence, reflecting survival on treatment as well as new infections; not an incidence measure.

d-c04-3~loom/gatherer~25.note: No candidate covers neglected tropical diseases, hepatitis or water-borne diseases as incidence; SH.STA.WASH.P5 reports mortality only. The target can be read as ending epidemics or as a reduction threshold.

verdicts.why: Directly measures cereal yield, one of the two quantities in the section question.
Output with area decomposes yield change from area expansion; useful context.
Harvested area is the yield denominator; shows whether output grew by area or yield.
Volume index of output, not productivity; does not address doubling per worker or hectare.
Input, sparse coverage; does not measure productivity or income against target 2.3.

add.why: Agriculture value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) is the section's other named measure; missing from the choice.

petition.name: Incomes of small-scale food producers (indicator 2.3.2)
petition.need: Target 2.3 also covers incomes of small-scale producers by sex; no WDI series supplies this, so the gap must be stated.

verdicts.why: Basic measure of farmland extent with wide coverage; needed as context for intensity.
Direct measure of fertiliser intensity per hectare of arable land, central to the question.
Shows agriculture's share of freshwater withdrawal; core water-use indicator despite sparse years.
Irrigated share of farmland indicates water management and drought resilience under target 2.4.
Productivity outcome of land and inputs, matching target 2.4; cereals only, to be stated.

add.why: Arable land share is the denominator context for fertiliser intensity and separates cropland from pasture.
Water stress shows whether agricultural withdrawals are sustainable relative to available freshwater resources.

verdicts.why: Headcount at the current international extreme poverty line; directly answers the section question and the 2030 target.
Depth of shortfall below $3.00 a day shows how difficult eradication is beyond headcount.
Shows the population just above the extreme line and exposed to relapse; useful context, not the target.
National lines differ by country; comparability is weak and the section concerns the international line.

add.why: Multidimensional poverty complements the income line and shows deprivations that the $3.00 headcount alone omits.
Poverty gap at $4.20 shows depth just above the extreme line and how far people sit from escaping it.

verdicts.why: Official target 3.1 indicator; needed to judge progress against the 70 per 100,000 threshold.
Companion indicator of target 3.1; skilled attendance is a direct driver of maternal survival.
Absolute deaths show burden and concentration alongside the ratio; same modelled source.
Useful proxy for service coverage behind maternal outcomes, if flagged as a composite.
Patchy coverage and inconsistent methods; modelled series already integrates national data, so it adds little.

add.why: Lifetime risk of maternal death conveys cumulative burden and highlights extreme disparities between regions.
Death registration completeness shows how reliable maternal mortality estimates are where registration is weak.

verdicts.why: Directly answers the question; it is the indicator for target 5.3 on child marriage.
Measures marriage before 15, the most severe form, and complements the under-18 share.
Measures teenage motherhood, not marriage; coverage is thin and it does not answer the question.

add.why: Target 5.3 also covers female genital mutilation, so the section needs its prevalence.

series.why: Youth literacy rate, ages 15-24: the indicator for target 4.6 on youth. Wide coverage, but many countries report only occasional census or survey years.
Adult literacy rate, ages 15 and above: covers the adult part of target 4.6. Data are often years old and irregular, and numeracy is not measured.
Gender parity index of youth literacy: shows whether women and men are equally literate, as target 4.6 requires. Depends on the same sparse survey years.
Adult female literacy rate: with the male series it shows the gender gap among adults. Latest observations differ by country and some are dated.
Adult male literacy rate: the comparator for the female series, allowing a gender gap reading. Same limits on timeliness and coverage.

d-c05-6~juniper/gatherer~26.note: The candidates hold no numeracy series, so the numeracy half of target 4.6 cannot be measured here. Literacy data are largely census- or survey-based and vary in year across countries.

series.why: Share of primary teachers with minimum pedagogical training; matches indicator 4.c.1 directly. Coverage is patchy, national definitions of 'trained' differ, and many recent years are missing.
Share of secondary teachers meeting minimum training standards; tracks 4.c.1 at secondary level. Definitions of qualification vary by country, limiting comparison.
Share of preprimary teachers who are trained; covers the earliest level of 4.c.1. Coverage is thinner than for primary and secondary.
Count of primary teachers; shows whether supply is growing (target 4.c). It carries no pupil numbers, so ratios cannot be read from it alone.
Count of secondary teachers; shows supply growth at that level for target 4.c. It does not show quality or the pupil-teacher ratio.

d-c05-7~idris/gatherer~26.note: The pupil-teacher ratio series (such as SE.PRM.ENRL.TC.ZS) is not among the candidates, so whether ratios are falling cannot be answered directly. Target 4.a facilities indicators are likewise absent; the sanitation and drinking water series are population-wide measures, not school-based ones.

petition.name: School-level basic services (water, sanitation, electricity, accessibility)
petition.need: Indicators for target 4.a on schools with basic drinking water, single-sex sanitation, electricity and adapted infrastructure are not held in the candidates; the section needs them to assess facilities.

series.why: Measures indicator 5.2.1: past-12-month partner physical or sexual violence among ever-partnered women 15-49. Survey-based, so coverage is sparse and years irregular.
Share of women who consider wife-beating justified for any of five reasons; an attitudinal proxy for tolerance of violence, not a measure of incidence.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-1~32.text:
### What the series measure

The question concerns the gap between women and men in mobile phone ownership and internet use. The World Development Indicators hold no sex-disaggregated series for mobile phone ownership. They hold mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people, which count subscriptions rather than people and cannot be split by sex. The gap in mobile technology can therefore be measured only through internet use, reported separately for women and men by the International Telecommunication Union. The indicator counts people who have used the internet from any location in the last three months, by any device, so it captures mobile access but does not isolate it. Target 5.b concerns the use of enabling technology, and internet use by sex is the closest available measure.

Coverage is uneven. Female internet use has been reported by 137 countries in at least one year. Reporting peaked at 92 countries in 2017 and again in 2019, fell to 74 in 2020, and reached 65 in 2024. In 2025 only 7 countries had reported. Figures for 2025 are therefore provisional and rest on a very small sample, and the latest comparable year across regions is 2024.

### The global gap

The world figure for female internet use was 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and 68.2 per cent in 2024. The male figure was 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two end years differ, so the figures do not compare cleanly, and the 2025 male value rests on few reporting countries. Read as they stand, the gap was 4.2 percentage points in 2019 and about 8.4 points at the latest dates. Both groups gained, but men gained more in absolute terms, so the gap widened in these aggregates. This caveat matters: the widening could partly reflect the mismatched years, since male use was still rising in the interval between 2024 and 2025. The direction nonetheless agrees with the regional figures below, which share the same year.

The period includes the pandemic, which pushed schooling, work, public services and commerce online. That raised the cost of exclusion, and women with fewer devices and less independent income were more exposed to it. The same shift is likely to have accelerated adoption across the board, which explains the large rises in every region.

### Regional differences

The gap is smallest where use is nearly universal. In North America female use rose from 89.5 per cent in 2019 to 94.1 per cent in 2024, against 89.9 and 94.7 per cent for men: a gap of 0.4 points in 2019 and 0.6 points in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia women reached 90.0 per cent in 2024, from 78.4 per cent, while men reached 91.8 per cent, from 82.3 per cent; the gap narrowed from 3.9 to 1.8 points. In Latin America and the Caribbean women stood at 81.3 per cent in 2024, from 67.2 per cent, and men at 82.0 per cent, from 68.4 per cent, a gap of 0.7 points. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where women were ahead in 2019, at 67.4 per cent against 67.7 for men... more exactly, 67.4 against 66.7 per cent. By 2024 men led, at 87.6 per cent against 85.5 per cent for women, a gap of 2.1 points.

The large gaps are in the regions with lower use. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, women's use rose from 42.1 to 55.0 per cent and men's from 51.3 to 67.6 per cent, so the gap grew from 9.2 to 12.6 points. In South Asia women's use rose from 24.3 to 56.3 per cent, a very large gain, but men's rose from 34.9 to 69.1 per cent; the gap was 10.6 points in 2019 and 12.8 points in 2024. In Sub-Saharan Africa women's use rose from 20.2 to 29.4 per cent and men's from 28.6 to 37.9 per cent, leaving a gap of 8.4 points in 2019 and 8.5 points in 2024. Only 29.4 per cent of women in that region used the internet in 2024, so the level is a larger problem than the gap.

### Income groups

The pattern by income is similar. In low-income countries women's use was 12.6 per cent in 2019 and 18.3 per cent in 2025, against 20.3 and 28.6 per cent for men; the gap widened from 7.7 to 10.3 points. In lower-middle-income countries women's use rose from 28.9 to 56.9 per cent and men's from 38.0 to 68.7 per cent, widening the gap from 9.1 to 11.8 points. In upper-middle-income countries the figures were identical in 2019, at 67.6 per cent, and by 2025 women stood at 87.9 per cent and men at 89.7 per cent, a gap of 1.8 points. In high-income countries women's use rose from 86.4 to 93.6 per cent and men's from 88.7 to 94.9 per cent, narrowing the gap from 2.3 to 1.3 points.

The lesson is that the gap closes as use approaches saturation, but in the poorest groups growth in use has so far been faster for men. Affordability of handsets and data, literacy, safety concerns, social norms on women's mobility and control over household devices all contribute, and the data cannot separate them.

### Country links and implications for 2030

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between changes in female and male use was 0.958 (Spearman), and between 2024 levels 0.948. Female and male use therefore rise together: countries that connect men quickly connect women quickly. Overall access depends on infrastructure and prices, which lift both sexes. The gap, however, depends on whether women share equally in that lift, and the regional pattern suggests that in the regions of low use they have lagged.

For 2030 the implication is that general network expansion is necessary but insufficient. Target 5.b has no numerical indicator in the series held, so no threshold can be read from the data. Where use is near saturation, gaps are already under two points. In South Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa, gaps of 8 to 13 points persisted in 2024, and unless women's adoption outpaces men's they will not close by 2030.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-1~32.gaps: The shelf holds no sex-disaggregated mobile phone ownership series; mobile subscriptions are counted per 100 people and cannot be split by sex. Internet use covers any device and location and does not isolate mobile use. Only 7 countries reported for 2025, and the male and female world figures use different end years (2024 and 2025). No indicator or threshold exists in the series for Target 5.b, and the data do not show the reasons for the gaps, such as cost, literacy, safety or norms.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-1~36.text:
### What the series measure

The question asked is how large the gender gap is in mobile phone ownership and internet use. The shelf answers only half of it. The World Bank's indicators hold internet use by sex, drawn from the International Telecommunication Union, but no series for mobile phone ownership by sex. Mobile cellular subscriptions are reported per 100 people with no sex breakdown, and a subscription is not an owner: one person may hold several, and a household may share a handset. The gap in ownership therefore cannot be measured here, and the analysis below concerns internet use, defined as having used the internet from any location in the last three months, by any device.

This bears on target 5.b, which calls for enhanced use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The target has no numerical threshold, so it can be read in more than one way: as parity in access, as parity in use, or as use that brings measurable benefits. Internet use by sex speaks only to the first two readings.

### The world gap, 2019 to 2024

In 2019, 51.8% of women worldwide used the internet, against 56.0% of men, a gap of 4.2 percentage points. By 2024 the female share had risen to 68.2%. The male figure on the shelf for the world is dated 2025, at 76.6%, so it cannot be set against the female 2024 value without mixing years. The gap for the latest common year cannot be stated from these results, and a reader should not subtract one from the other. What can be said is that women's use rose by 16.4 points over five years, a substantial advance, and that the male level in the following year stood well above the female level of 2024.

The pandemic years fall inside this window. Lockdowns, remote schooling and the move of public services online raised demand for connectivity after 2020, and the rise in both series is consistent with that, though the data do not separate cause from the longer trend of falling device and data costs and network expansion.

### Regional differences

The gap varies greatly by region, and is widest where use is lowest or where social norms limit women's access to devices. In 2024, in Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0% of women used the internet against 67.6% of men, a gap of 12.6 points. In South Asia the figures were 56.3% and 69.1%, a gap of 12.8 points. That is a notable outcome, because South Asia's female share was 24.3% in 2019, so women's use more than doubled, yet men's use also rose, from 34.9%, and the gap in 2019 was 10.6 points. The gap in South Asia thus widened in points even as women's use surged.

In Sub-Saharan Africa, 29.4% of women used the internet in 2024 against 37.9% of men, a gap of 8.5 points. The gap was 8.4 points in 2019, when the figures were 20.2% and 28.6%. Here the gap is smaller in points than in South Asia only because levels are low; relative to male use, women's use is about 0.78 of men's, whereas in South Asia the ratio is about 0.81. Both ratios show women trailing by roughly a fifth.

Elsewhere the gaps are narrow. In East Asia and Pacific the female share was 85.5% against 87.6% for men in 2024, a gap of 2.1 points; in 2019 women's use (67.4%) was actually above men's (66.7%), so the region moved from a small female lead to a small male one, which may reflect differing country composition in the reporting sample. In Europe and Central Asia the figures were 90.0% and 91.8%, in Latin America and the Caribbean 81.3% and 82.0%, and in North America 94.1% and 94.7%. In these regions the gap is under two points and in Latin America and North America under one point, so parity is effectively reached.

### Income groups

By income group, the gap is largest in poorer countries. In low-income countries, 18.3% of women used the internet in 2025 against 28.6% of men, a gap of 10.3 points; in 2019 the figures were 12.6% and 20.3%. In lower-middle-income countries, women's use rose from 28.9% to 56.9% and men's from 38.0% to 68.7%, leaving a gap of 11.8 points in 2025, against 9.1 in 2019. In upper-middle-income countries, women's use was 87.9% against 89.7% for men, a gap of 1.8 points, whereas in 2019 the two were level at 67.6%. In high-income countries the figures were 93.6% and 94.9%.

The pattern is that the gap closes as a country becomes connected on a broad scale, but that in the middle of the distribution, where adoption is accelerating, men tend to move first and women follow. Poorer households ration devices and data; women have less income of their own, lower literacy in some settings, and in some societies face restrictions on owning or using phones. These are well-established explanations, though the data here do not test them.

### Country links and implications for 2030

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male internet use in 2024 was 0.95, and between the changes over the period 0.96. Countries that raised men's use quickly raised women's use quickly too. The implication is that the gap is driven mostly by national connectivity, with infrastructure and prices setting the pace for both sexes, and that a smaller part reflects barriers specific to women. Rank correlations do not show the size of the gap, so a country can rank similarly for both sexes and still have a gap of many points.

For 2030, the trend is encouraging for levels but not for parity in the regions where it matters. If the 2019 to 2024 pace persisted, women's use in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries would remain far below the global figure, and gaps measured in points would not close without policies aimed at women. The widening of gaps in South Asia and lower-middle-income countries suggests that rapid growth alone does not deliver parity.

The evidence is also thinner than it appears. Of the 137 countries that have reported female internet use in any year, 92 reported for 2019 and 65 for 2024, and only 7 so far for 2025. Coverage has fallen from its peak of 92 countries in 2017 and 2019, so regional averages rest on a changing set of countries, and the poorest, where the gap is largest, are the likeliest to be missing.

### Proposals

The findings point to specific actions, set out below.

Statistical agencies in countries that stopped reporting after 2019 should resume annual surveys of internet use by sex.

w-c03-2-1~cedar/writer-2~36.text:
### Stunting has fallen slowly since 2015

The modelled estimate of stunting among children under five stood at 24.6 per cent worldwide in 2015 and at 23.2 per cent in 2024, a fall of 1.4 percentage points in nine years. Stunting, a height more than two standard deviations below the international reference median, reflects chronic undernutrition and repeated infection in the first thousand days of life. It is slow to change because it depends on maternal health, diet quality, sanitation, and care. The global trend assessment gives an annual rate of change of -0.0066 against a target path to 5.0 per cent by 2030, a ratio of 0.12 of the pace required. The expected world level in 2030 on the present trajectory is 22.3 per cent. The target text sets 2025 as the year for the internationally agreed stunting and wasting goals; on this evidence neither the 2025 nor the 2030 mark for stunting will be met at world level. The 5.0 per cent threshold used by the trend tool is one reading of the target. The internationally agreed goal is usually stated as a 40 per cent reduction from a 2012 baseline, which the shelf does not hold, so the two readings differ.

### Regions diverge, and the burden stays in the poorest settings

South Asia fell furthest, from 37.8 per cent in 2015 to 31.5 per cent in 2024, helped by earlier gains in sanitation, schooling of girls and social protection. Even so its expected 2030 level is 27.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 34.4 to 32.3 per cent, and its trajectory gives 31.0 per cent in 2030, a ratio of 0.12 of the required pace. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping went from 27.5 to 24.1 per cent, with 22.1 per cent expected in 2030. These three groupings hold the greatest numbers of affected children, and none is close to the target.

East Asia and Pacific declined from 14.5 to 13.3 per cent, with 12.6 per cent expected in 2030, a ratio of 0.20. Europe and Central Asia moved from 6.0 to 4.6 per cent and is classed as on track, with 3.8 per cent expected in 2030. Latin America and the Caribbean is the notable stall: 12.3 per cent in 2015 and 12.4 per cent in 2024, classed as regression. The pause there reflects slower improvement among poorer and indigenous households, and the effects of economic shocks and migration, although the data themselves do not identify causes.

By income group, low-income countries moved from 38.0 to 35.8 per cent, with 34.4 per cent expected in 2030. Lower-middle-income countries fell faster, from 33.9 to 28.9 per cent, giving 25.9 per cent in 2030. Upper-middle-income countries went from 11.9 to 10.8 per cent. High-income countries were broadly flat, 3.9 per cent and 4.0 per cent. North America rose from 2.8 to 4.1 per cent. Because those levels are already below 5.0 per cent, the tool labels them on track, but a rising rate is not progress, and the label should be read with that in mind. Small modelled changes at low levels may also fall within estimation error.

### No convergence between countries

Across 162 countries, the convergence test finds no tendency for high-stunting countries to fall faster. The beta coefficient is -0.0024 (p-value 0.23) with an R-squared of 0.01, so initial level explains almost none of subsequent change. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024, which means relative dispersion among countries widened. Countries with low stunting continued to reduce it in proportion, while many with high stunting stalled. For a goal premised on leaving no one behind, this is the more worrying finding than the world average: gains are not being concentrated where need is greatest.

### Wasting is lower in level but dominated by one region

Wasting, weight more than two standard deviations below the median for height, signals acute undernutrition, often from famine, illness or conflict. It is more volatile than stunting because it can reverse within months. World prevalence went from 7.1 per cent in 2015 to 6.6 per cent in 2024. The target is below 5.0 per cent by 2030 on the tool's reading; the internationally agreed goal for 2025 and 2030 is 5 per cent or lower, but the 2025 date cannot yet be judged from data ending in 2024.

South Asia stands apart: 16.6 per cent in 2015 and 15.7 per cent in 2024, more than double any other region. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 7.0 to 5.9 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 6.5 to 5.6 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 3.7 to 3.6 per cent. Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and North America are at or near 1.0 per cent or below: 1.0, 1.3 and 0.2 per cent. Low-income countries recorded 6.4 per cent in 2024 against 7.9 per cent in 2015, while lower-middle-income countries were at 9.5 per cent, down from 10.5, so the highest wasting now lies in the lower-middle group because of South Asia's weight within it. Upper-middle-income countries stood at 2.1 per cent and high-income countries at 0.4 per cent.

Of 65 countries assessed against the wasting target, 42 are on track or have met it, holding 38.6 per cent of their population. Four show moderate progress, with 7.8 per cent of the population, and three show marginal progress, with 33.7 per cent. None stagnates and 16 regress, with 19.9 per cent of the population. The three marginal countries carry a third of the assessed population, which indicates that the largest populations are the ones furthest from the goal.

### Data limits temper every conclusion

Wasting data are survey-based and sparse. Only 6 countries reported a wasting value for 2024, against 24 in 2023 and 48 in 2018, so the latest figures are mostly lagged survey results or aggregates and recent shocks are not visible. Only 65 countries could be assessed for trend. Annual country reporting never exceeded 58, in 2000, and was 32 in 2015 and 26 in 2020, so the period after 2020 cannot be separated cleanly from survey disruption caused by the pandemic. Stunting rests on modelled estimates covering 162 countries, which smooth gaps but carry uncertainty. Changes of a point or less, such as in Latin America or high-income countries, should not be over-read.

The implication for 2030 is plain. Without a marked acceleration, stunting will remain at roughly a fifth of children worldwide, and the regions with the heaviest burden will move least. Wasting could approach the threshold in many countries yet remain high in South Asia, where much of the world's affected population lives.

### Proposals follow from the pattern

The findings point to action on delivery in the places that lag, and to better measurement.

w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-3~39.text:
### What the shelf holds on disaster exposure

Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and a reduction in their exposure to climate-related extreme events. The World Bank's catalogue holds three series that bear on it, and they differ sharply in quality. The best-reported is new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, which counts cases of displacement (a person displaced twice counts twice) and so is not a count of distinct people. A second series gives the average share of the population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, but it is an average over 1990 to 2009 and has a single reference year, 2009, for 168 countries. A third is a self-assessed disaster risk reduction score on a scale of 1 to 5, drawn from Hyogo Framework progress reports and last recorded in 2011 for 83 countries.

Only the displacement series can say anything about the period since 2015. The other two describe the world before the Goals were adopted and cannot show a change, an improvement or a deterioration against the target. Nor does any of the three measure vulnerability, the poor's share of those affected, or economic loss. The question of how many people are affected can therefore be answered only through displacement, which is one consequence of a disaster rather than the whole of its reach.

### The recording of displacement has itself changed

The number of countries reporting displacement has risen markedly. It was 80 in 2008, fell to 60 in 2009 and 62 in 2011, then reached 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. It continued to 133 in 2017, 142 in 2020 and 145 in 2023, while 199 economies have reported in at least one year. Any rise in the global total must be read against this widening. Between 2015 and 2023 the reporting base grew from 112 to 145 countries, so part of the increase may reflect better monitoring rather than more displacement. The dip in 2021 to 133 countries and the recovery to 144 in 2022 show that coverage is also not steady from year to year.

Coverage of the series is a strength compared with the other two, yet the method is uneven. Displacement is counted from government reports, humanitarian agencies and media, and pre-emptive evacuations ahead of storms are included. Countries with strong warning systems and organised evacuation can therefore register large numbers precisely because they protect people, while countries with weak systems may register few cases because displacement goes unobserved. Higher counts are thus not a straightforward sign of worse outcomes.

### Scale and direction since 2015

World new displacement associated with disasters was 19188817 cases in 2015 and 26393278 in 2023. That is a rise of about 7.2 million cases, or roughly 37.5 per cent over eight years. The breaks analysis finds no structural break in the annual change of the world series, and reports a mean annual change of about -789790 cases over 2009 to 2023. The two statements are consistent only if the series started that window high, since a negative mean change over 2009 to 2023 sits beside a higher figure in 2023 than in 2015. The series is dominated by a few very large events, notably in Asia, so that endpoints and window choice drive the result. A trend line through it would mislead; the honest reading is a volatile series with no established direction, and with an endpoint in 2023 that is high by the standard of 2015.

No figure here isolates the effect of the pandemic. The reporting count dipped modestly in 2021, but the shelf offers no evidence that disaster displacement was changed by 2020 as such. Climate hazards continued through the pandemic, and mobility restrictions probably affected both evacuation and observation in ways the data cannot separate.

### Regions and income groups differ widely

The regional picture changed substantially. East Asia and the Pacific remains the largest region, with 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia fell from 6877900 to 2446054, a decline of more than half. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1108287 to 6029739, over five times as large. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping roughly doubled, from 1212730 to 2481660. Europe and Central Asia moved from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023, a jump largely attributable to a few severe events in a year and to better reporting rather than to a steady trend. Latin America and the Caribbean was nearly flat, at 1543360 and 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000, though from a small base.

By income group the pattern matters for Target 1.5. Low-income countries recorded 992200 cases in 2015 and 6177600 in 2023. Upper middle income countries rose from 6620044 to 13815894, and now carry more than half of the world total. Lower middle income countries fell from 9883673 to 5649287, and high-income countries from 1692900 to 750497. The shift is toward the poorest group and toward large, exposed middle-income economies. For the lowest-income countries, whose populations have the least savings, insurance and social protection to absorb a shock, a sixfold rise in recorded cases is the most relevant finding of the section, even allowing for better recording.

### Concentration across countries is rising

Displacement is highly unequal among countries when weighted by population. The Gini coefficient was 0.57 in 2015 across 112 countries and 0.68 in 2023 across 145. The Theil index rose from 0.72 to 0.89, and the coefficient of variation from 1.11 to 1.47. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8 per cent to 53.0 per cent. Concentration has therefore increased, while regions explain less of it: a larger part now lies among countries within the same region. National exposure and national capacity, not geography alone, decide the outcome, which argues for targeting countries rather than regional blocs.

### Implications for 2030

Target 1.5 has no quantified threshold, and the indicator framework for it also relies on deaths, missing persons and affected persons per 100000, which the shelf does not hold. Reading progress as a fall in displacement is one interpretation; reading it as stronger protection, which may raise recorded evacuations, is another. On the first reading the data show no progress, since the 2023 figure exceeds that of 2015. On the second they are silent. The sound conclusion is that the world cannot currently demonstrate that exposure of the poor has fallen, and that the poorest countries show the largest rise. Because warming raises the frequency of floods, storms and heat, a flat or rising series is the likelier path to 2030 without investment in early warning, housing and social protection that can scale up after a shock.

w-c06-1-1~cedar/writer-4~39.text:
### What the index measures

The Women, Business and the Law Legal Framework Index summarises how the laws of an economy shape women's economic opportunities. It is scored from 0 to 100 and is the unweighted average of ten topic scores: Safety, Mobility, Work, Pay, Marriage, Parenthood, Childcare, Entrepreneurship, Assets and Pension. A score of 100 is the highest possible and 0 the lowest. The index belongs to target 5.1, which calls for an end to all forms of discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it is among the few measures that speak to that target directly, because discriminatory law is the most visible form of discrimination in the statute book.

The World Bank publishes two companion indices built on the same ten topics: a Supportive Framework Index, which captures the institutions and services that help women use their legal rights, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which captures expert perceptions of how far rights are applied in practice. Together the three indices separate what the law says, what supports exist around it and whether it is enforced. This distinction matters for interpretation. A high legal score can coexist with weak supports and weak enforcement, and a reader who looks only at the legal index will overstate the lived equality of women in an economy.

### What the shelf holds

The only result returned for this section is a coverage check on the Legal Framework Index. It shows that 189 countries reported a value in 2025, and that 189 countries reported in at least one year. The two figures are the same, which means every economy that has ever been scored was also scored in the latest year; no economy has dropped out of the series. The coverage result also lists aggregates for the high-income, low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income and South Asia groups, and for the world, so that group comparisons are possible in principle.

The Enforcement Perceptions Index is narrower, with 177 economies in the catalogue, and the Supportive Framework Index matches the legal index at 189. The shelf therefore supports a claim of near-universal country coverage for the legal measure, but the present results do not carry the scores themselves. No level, trend or regional gap in the index is stated in this section, because none was returned and none can be reported without invention. What follows is an account of how the series should be read and what it can and cannot settle, not a list of scores.

### Reading change after 2015 and after 2020

The index is built from a codified reading of statutes and regulations, so it moves in steps. A country's score rises when a law is passed, such as a ban on dismissal of pregnant workers, equal pay for work of equal value, paid leave for parents, or equal rights to own and manage property in marriage. It falls rarely, when a law is repealed or a reform is reversed. This makes the legal index a record of reform events rather than of gradual social change, and it explains why the most rapid gains are usually found where baseline scores were lowest and a few well-known reforms remained to be made.

The periods after 2015 and after 2020 should be read with that in mind. The adoption of the 2030 Agenda in 2015 gave reformers a reference point, and the pandemic after 2020 shifted attention toward childcare, leave and protection from violence, which are topics inside the index. Whether the index rose faster before or after those dates cannot be stated from the present results. A reader should look for the gap between legal and enforcement scores, since reforms enacted quickly on paper tend to be implemented slowly.

### Implications for 2030

Full coverage is itself a finding of some value. A target that asks for an end to discrimination everywhere needs a measure that reaches everywhere, and for the legal framework this exists. Progress toward 2030 can therefore be judged country by country rather than inferred from a sample. Target 5.1 also has no numerical threshold: it asks for an end to all discrimination, and a score of 100 on the legal index is one possible reading, though not the only one, since the index covers economic opportunity and not every area of law, such as nationality, inheritance in customary systems or family law outside marriage. Reaching 100 would not by itself prove that discrimination had ended.

The companion series on violence and on youth not in education, employment or training show why the law is only a first step. Partner violence data cover 106 economies with the latest year 2017, and the female NEET series covers 182 economies to 2025. Both measure outcomes that legal reform influences only through supports and enforcement. The choice to keep the legal, supportive and enforcement indices side by side is the right one for monitoring.

### What follows

The sound conclusion from the shelf is limited but useful: the legal measure is complete in country coverage, current to 2025, and built to distinguish law from supports and enforcement. Judgements on pace and distribution await the scores themselves.

Enforcement is measured by expert perception, not by observed outcomes, and covers 177 economies. The index covers laws on economic opportunity only, and a score of 100 does not mean discrimination has ended. Customary and informal law are not captured.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-1~40.text:
### What the series measure

The question concerns the gap between women and men in mobile phone ownership and internet use. The shelf holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex. The only mobile series, mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people, counts subscriptions rather than people and is not divided by sex, so it cannot show a gender gap. The gap can be read only through internet use, reported separately for women and men by the International Telecommunication Union. The indicator counts people who used the internet from any location in the previous three months, by any device, so it is a proxy for mobile technology and not a measure of handset ownership. Target 5.b concerns the use of enabling technology to empower women, and internet use is the nearest measurable expression of it.

### The world gap

World female internet use rose from 51.8% in 2019 to 68.2% in 2024. Male use stood at 56.0% in 2019 and 76.6% in 2025. The two end years differ, because the male world figure is reported for 2025 while the female world figure is reported for 2024, so the difference of the endpoints is not a like-for-like comparison and should be read with care. On the 2019 figures the gap was 4.2 percentage points. The later endpoints suggest a gap of roughly eight points, but the mismatch of years means that this overstates the widening, since use was still rising in the extra year. What can be said firmly is that both sexes gained a great deal after 2019, the period that includes the pandemic, when work, schooling and public services moved online, and that women remained behind men at every date shown.

### Regions

Regional gaps differ widely in size. In East Asia and Pacific, female use was 67.4% in 2019, against 66.7% for men, so women were marginally ahead. By 2024 the position had reversed: 85.5% for women against 87.6% for men. In Europe and Central Asia the figures were 78.4% and 82.3% in 2019, and 90.0% and 91.8% in 2024, a gap that narrowed from 3.9 points to 1.8. Latin America and the Caribbean shows a very small gap: 67.2% and 68.4% in 2019, then 81.3% and 82.0% in 2024. North America is close to saturation, at 89.5% and 89.9% in 2019 and 94.1% and 94.7% in 2024.

The large gaps lie elsewhere. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, women stood at 42.1% in 2019 and 55.0% in 2024, men at 51.3% and 67.6%. The gap therefore widened from 9.2 to 12.6 points. South Asia is the most striking case. Female use rose from 24.3% to 56.3%, a gain of 32 points, yet male use rose from 34.9% to 69.1%, so the gap grew from 10.6 to 12.8 points even as women's access more than doubled. In Sub-Saharan Africa women's use went from 20.2% to 29.4% and men's from 28.6% to 37.9%, leaving a gap of 8.4 points in 2019 and 8.5 in 2024, essentially unchanged, at a low level for both sexes.

### Income groups

The income groups show the same pattern, with the 2025 endpoint. In low-income countries female use was 12.6% in 2019 and 18.3% in 2025, against 20.3% and 28.6% for men; the gap widened from 7.7 to 10.3 points. Lower-middle-income countries saw women rise from 28.9% to 56.9% and men from 38.0% to 68.7%, a gap of 9.1 points in 2019 and 11.8 in 2025. In upper-middle-income countries women were level with men in 2019 at 67.6% each, and by 2025 stood at 87.9% against 89.7%. High-income countries moved from 86.4% and 88.7% to 93.6% and 94.9%, narrowing the gap from 2.3 points to 1.3.

The implication is that the gap behaves differently at different levels of access. Where use is nearly universal, it closes because little room remains. Where use is spreading fast, men tend to adopt first, and in the poorer groups the absolute gap has widened even while women gain quickly. Well-established causes include the cost of handsets and data relative to women's lower average income, lower literacy and digital skills, social norms that restrict women's use or ownership of phones, and concerns about safety and harassment online. Such factors are consistent with the pattern but the data here cannot isolate them.

### Countries move together

Across 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male levels in 2024 was 0.948, and between their changes was 0.958. Countries where men gained most are almost always those where women gained most. National conditions such as network coverage, prices and income therefore drive access for both sexes, and the gender gap is a modest, though persistent, offset on top of them. Policy aimed at women alone cannot substitute for general connectivity, and general connectivity alone will not remove the offset.

### Reliability of the record

The record thins in the latest years. The number of countries reporting female use was 92 in 2019, fell to 74 in 2020 and to 65 in 2024, and only 7 report for 2025. Across all years, 137 countries have some data. The 2025 values for the world and the income groups therefore rest on very few countries or on modelled estimates, and the mixing of 2024 and 2025 endpoints in this section reflects that. Trends toward 2030 cannot be extrapolated with confidence. If the 2019 to 2024 pace persisted, upper-middle and high-income groups would be near parity, while low-income countries, with fewer than three women in ten online in 2024 across Sub-Saharan Africa, would remain far from it. Target 5.b has no numerical threshold, so no formal judgement of attainment is possible.
