w-c03-2-1~ewan/writer-2~42.text:
### Stunting has fallen slowly and remains the condition of almost a quarter of the world's young children

Stunting, a height for age more than two standard deviations below the median of the WHO 2006 Child Growth Standards, is the most durable mark that chronic undernutrition leaves on a child. It records the accumulated effect of poor maternal nutrition, inadequate feeding in the first two years of life, repeated infection, unsafe water and poor sanitation. Once established after the second birthday it is largely irreversible, and it is associated with lower schooling, lower adult earnings and higher risk of chronic disease. It is therefore the clearest single test of whether the first thousand days of life have been protected, and Target 2.2 asks that the internationally agreed stunting goal be met by 2025, five years before the rest of the Goal.

The modelled estimates compiled in the Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates of UNICEF, the WHO and the World Bank show a world prevalence of 24.6 per cent of children under five in 2015 and 23.2 per cent in 2024. Across nine years the decline was 1.4 percentage points, a pace of a little over a seventh of a point a year. Expressed as an average annual rate of change, the world series fell at 0.0066 a year, that is by about two-thirds of one per cent of its own level each year. A child born in 2024 thus faced only a slightly lower chance of being stunted than a child born when the Goals were adopted.

The modelled series has broad coverage: 162 countries carry an estimate for 2024. This matters, because it is the one series in this section for which the global and regional numbers rest on a full panel of countries rather than on a thin scatter of recent surveys. The stunting picture is accordingly the most reliable of the indicators discussed here, even though the modelled values for individual countries between surveys are interpolations and not observations.

The arithmetic of the 2025 deadline can be stated without forcing any new number on the reader. The internationally agreed goal endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2012 was a 40 per cent reduction in the number of stunted children between 2012 and 2025. A reduction on that scale needs an annual rate of decline of several per cent a year, many times faster than the world achieved after 2015. At the observed rate the 2025 goal will not be met at world level, and with 2024 already in the data, no plausible single year could close the gap. The 2025 element of Target 2.2 should be recorded as missed for stunting.

### The regional distribution is wide and has hardly narrowed

The regional levels in 2024 describe two different worlds. In South Asia, 31.5 per cent of children under five were stunted in 2024 and in Sub-Saharan Africa 32.3 per cent; in Europe and Central Asia the figure was 4.6 per cent and in North America 4.1 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region stood at 24.1 per cent, close to the world average, while East Asia and the Pacific, at 13.3 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 12.4 per cent, occupied the middle ground.

The largest absolute improvement occurred in South Asia, where the prevalence fell from 37.8 per cent in 2015 to 31.5 per cent in 2024, a decline of more than six points and an annual rate of decline of 0.0200. South Asia began the period as the most affected region and ended it slightly below Sub-Saharan Africa. That reordering is one of the most important facts of the period. It reflects sustained, if uneven, progress in India, Bangladesh and Nepal, where national programmes extended maternal and child health services, community nutrition workers, sanitation campaigns and food transfers, and where rising household incomes and female schooling worked in the same direction.

Sub-Saharan Africa moved much more slowly, from 34.4 per cent in 2015 to 32.3 per cent in 2024, an annual rate of decline of 0.0070, about a third of the South Asian pace. Because the region's under-five population is growing fast, a falling prevalence there is compatible with a stable or rising number of stunted children; this section reports shares, not counts, and the reader should keep the distinction in mind. Africa now holds the highest regional prevalence, and on present trends it will hold an increasing share of the world's stunted children.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region fell from 27.5 per cent to 24.1 per cent, an annual rate of decline of 0.0147. Its level is heavily shaped by Pakistan and Afghanistan, whose prevalence is far above that of the Maghreb and the Gulf, and by conflict in Yemen, Syria and Sudan's neighbourhood. East Asia and the Pacific, where China's earlier transformation had already brought prevalence down, declined only from 14.5 per cent to 13.3 per cent; much of the region's remaining burden lies in Indonesia, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Myanmar and Timor-Leste rather than in China.

Two regions moved the wrong way. Latin America and the Caribbean recorded 12.3 per cent in 2015 and 12.4 per cent in 2024, essentially no change and technically a regression. The stagnation is notable because the region had a strong record of decline in the decade before 2015, built on conditional cash transfers and expanding primary health care; the slowing of growth, the fiscal squeeze of the later 2010s, the Venezuelan crisis and the pandemic all weighed on it, and persistent pockets among indigenous children in Guatemala and the Andes kept the average from falling. North America rose from 2.8 per cent to 4.1 per cent and the high-income group from 3.9 per cent to 4.0 per cent. At these low levels small shifts in modelled estimates can reflect the scarcity of recent anthropometric surveys in rich countries as much as real change, and the rise should be read with caution.

The income groups confirm the gradient. Low-income countries recorded 38.0 per cent in 2015 and 35.8 per cent in 2024; lower-middle-income countries fell from 33.9 per cent to 28.9 per cent; upper-middle-income countries from 11.9 per cent to 10.8 per cent; high-income countries were at 4.0 per cent in 2024. The steepest improvement came in the lower-middle-income group, which contains most of South Asia, while the poorest countries, many of them in conflict or protracted crisis, improved by about two points in nine years.

The cross-country test of convergence across 162 countries finds no catching up. The coefficient on initial level was -0.0024, with a p-value of 0.23 and an R-squared of 0.01, so the relationship between where a country started and how fast it improved is statistically indistinguishable from zero. Dispersion actually widened: the coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Countries with low prevalence kept improving proportionately at least as fast as countries with high prevalence, and in relative terms the gap between the best and worst placed children grew. The burden of stunting is becoming more concentrated, not less.

### Projections to 2030 point to a large shortfall almost everywhere

Target 2.2 asks for an end to all forms of malnutrition by 2030. That wording cannot be taken literally as zero stunting, since a small share of any healthy population falls below the reference cut-off. The bench's trend tool therefore applies a working threshold of 5 per cent of children under five, a reading of 'ending' stunting that is reasonable but not official; other readings, such as the extended World Health Assembly goal of halving the number of stunted children by 2030, would set different bars. The judgement that follows holds under either reading, because progress is so far short of both.

Extending each region's rate of change since 2015 to 2030 gives an expected world prevalence of 22.3 per cent in 2030. The ratio of the achieved rate to the rate required to reach the threshold is 0.12 for the world: the world is moving at about an eighth of the pace it would need. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected at 31.0 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.12; South Asia at 27.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.30, the best among the high-burden regions; the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 22.1 per cent, ratio 0.24; East Asia and the Pacific at 12.6 per cent, ratio 0.20; and Latin America and the Caribbean at 12.4 per cent, with a negative ratio of -0.02 that marks regression. Low-income countries are projected at 34.4 per cent, with a ratio of 0.11, and lower-middle-income countries at 25.9 per cent, ratio 0.28. Every developing region and every developing income group is classed as making marginal progress requiring significant acceleration, apart from Latin America, which is classed as regressing.

Only Europe and Central Asia is on a path below the threshold, with an expected 3.8 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 2.13, more than twice the required pace. North America and the high-income group are classed as on track because they already sit near or below the threshold, although their own trends are upward: the projection for North America is 5.3 per cent in 2030, which would carry it just above the working threshold if the modelled rise continued. That classification should be read as a statement about level, not about direction.

These projections are mechanical extrapolations of the 2015 to 2024 rate, and they carry the period's shocks within them. The pandemic years disrupted growth monitoring, school feeding, immunisation and household incomes, and the food and fertiliser price shock that followed the invasion of Ukraine raised the cost of a nutritious diet for poor families. Because stunting is cumulative and is measured in children up to five years old, a disruption to feeding and care in 2020 to 2022 shows up in the prevalence for several years afterwards. A modelled series smooths these effects, and the data presented here do not allow the post-2020 period to be separated cleanly from the trend before it; but nothing in the 2024 values suggests a recovery fast enough to change the 2030 conclusion.

### Wasting has fallen a little, but South Asia carries a disproportionate burden

Wasting, a weight for height more than two standard deviations below the median, is the acute form of undernutrition. It reflects recent weight loss from inadequate food or illness and carries a much higher immediate risk of death than stunting; severe wasting is a medical emergency. It is also seasonal and volatile, rising in the lean season, during droughts, floods and conflict, and falling quickly when food and care return. Survey estimates therefore depend heavily on the month in which data were collected.

The world prevalence was 7.1 per cent in 2015 and 6.6 per cent in 2024. The internationally agreed goal was to reduce and maintain childhood wasting below 5 per cent by 2025, and for 2030 below 3 per cent under the extended goals; the bench's tool uses the 5 per cent threshold for 2030. At world level neither will be met on the current path.

The regional pattern is sharper than for stunting. South Asia's prevalence was 16.6 per cent in 2015 and 15.7 per cent in 2024, more than twice the world average and almost three times the Sub-Saharan African level. This is the 'South Asian enigma' long noted in nutrition research: a region with faster income growth than Africa yet higher acute undernutrition, explained in large part by low birth weight, the poor nutritional status and low social position of many young mothers, and the high burden of infection where sanitation is poor. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 7.0 per cent to 5.9 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region from 6.5 per cent to 5.6 per cent. East Asia and the Pacific barely moved, from 3.7 per cent to 3.6 per cent. Elsewhere wasting is rare: 1.3 per cent in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2024, 1.0 per cent in Europe and Central Asia and 0.2 per cent in North America.

By income, the lower-middle-income group has the highest prevalence, 9.5 per cent in 2024 against 10.5 per cent in 2015, a consequence of South Asia's weight within it. Low-income countries fell from 7.9 per cent to 6.4 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 2.6 per cent to 2.1 per cent, and high-income countries from 0.6 per cent to 0.4 per cent. The fact that wasting is higher in lower-middle-income than in low-income countries is a reminder that acute undernutrition does not track national income closely; it follows maternal health, disease environment, crisis and the seasonality of food supply.

Among the 65 countries with enough data to assess a trend towards a 5 per cent threshold, 42 were on track or had met it, but they held only 38.6 per cent of the assessed population. Four countries, with 7.8 per cent of the population, made moderate progress; three countries with 33.7 per cent of the population made only marginal progress; and 16 countries, with 19.9 per cent of the population, regressed. No country was classed as stagnant. The distribution is telling: most countries by number are doing well, but a small number of populous countries with marginal progress account for a third of the population assessed, and these weigh heavily on the world figure. Without knowing which three countries they are, the population share suggests that at least one very large South Asian country is among them. Sixteen countries in regression, a quarter of those assessed, indicate that acute undernutrition has risen in a substantial set of places, which is consistent with conflict, drought in the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, and the economic shocks after 2020.

### The wasting data are too thin to judge recent change with confidence

The wasting series is not modelled; it is built from household surveys, and its recent coverage is poor. Only 6 countries reported a value for 2024. In the years after 2015 the number of countries with a survey in a given year ranged from 48 in 2018 to 26 in 2020, 31 in 2022 and 24 in 2023. The pandemic interrupted survey fieldwork exactly when information on acute undernutrition was most needed. Over the whole period since 2000, 162 countries have reported at least once, but any one year covers a minority of them.

The regional and world values for 2024 are therefore aggregates of the harmonised JME dataset that lean on older surveys carried forward. They are best read as estimates of the current level, not as observations of the change since 2020. The trend classification rests on the 65 countries with enough points, well under half of those that ever report. The honest conclusion is that wasting has fallen modestly since 2015, that the world will not reach 5 per cent by 2030 on current trends, and that the effect of the shocks after 2020 cannot be measured from these data with any precision. For stunting the modelled series gives full coverage, but it is itself anchored in surveys that are infrequent in many countries, so its post-2020 values also contain more modelling and less observation than those for earlier years.

### What the findings imply for 2030

Three conclusions follow. First, the 2025 stunting and wasting elements of Target 2.2 will be missed at world level, and the 2030 aim of ending malnutrition will be missed by a wide margin: on present trends more than a fifth of the world's young children will still be stunted in 2030. Second, the burden is concentrating. Stunting is not converging across countries, its dispersion is widening, and Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income countries are improving at roughly a third of South Asia's pace. Third, South Asia is the decisive region for both indicators: it has delivered the period's largest fall in stunting yet still has the world's highest wasting by a large margin, so its progress or failure largely determines the world totals.

The interventions that work are well established: protection of maternal nutrition before and during pregnancy, early and exclusive breastfeeding, adequate complementary feeding, micronutrient supplementation, treatment of severe acute malnutrition in the community, safe water and sanitation, and cash or food transfers to poor families with young children. What the record since 2015 shows is that these have not been delivered at the scale or with the continuity needed in the places where children are most at risk, and that shocks have repeatedly interrupted them.

proposals: Governments of Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, with their development partners, should finance a costed first-thousand-days package (maternal nutrition, breastfeeding support, complementary feeding, water and sanitation) protected in budgets against shocks, since their stunting is falling at about a third of South Asia's pace.

South Asian governments should make wasting a distinct policy priority, extending community treatment of severe acute malnutrition and maternal nutrition programmes, because the region's wasting prevalence remains more than twice the world average.

Latin American and Caribbean governments should restore and target the cash-transfer and primary-care programmes that drove earlier declines, focusing on indigenous and rural children where stunting has stalled.

National statistical offices, UNICEF and the WHO should fund regular anthropometric surveys, with timing that accounts for seasonality, so that wasting can be measured after 2020; the number of countries reporting fell to single figures for 2024.

The UN agencies that steward Target 2.2 should state explicitly how 'end all forms of malnutrition' is to be judged in 2030, replacing the expired 2025 goals with numeric thresholds for both stunting and wasting.
w-c03-2-1~ewan/writer-2~42.gaps: The section reports prevalence, not the number of stunted or wasted children, so population growth in Africa is not reflected. Wasting has only 6 country values for 2024 and few after 2020, so post-pandemic change cannot be measured; the stunting series is modelled between infrequent surveys. No severe wasting, sub-national, sex, wealth-quintile or urban-rural breakdowns are used, and the identity of the populous countries with marginal wasting progress is not shown. The 5 per cent thresholds are the bench's working reading of 'ending' malnutrition, not an official target; the 2025 World Health Assembly goals are framed in numbers of children, which are not computed here.

w-c06-3-1~dahlia/writer-1~42.text:
### The level in 2022

The World Bank series on women first married by age 18 measures the share of women aged 20 to 24 who were married or in union before their eighteenth birthday. For the world as a whole the aggregate stood at 19.5% in 2022. Roughly one young woman in five was therefore married as a child, a level that Target 5.3, which calls for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage, would set at zero by 2030. The indicator is a retrospective measure: women aged 20 to 24 report on events of the previous few years, so a value for 2022 describes marriages that took place largely between about 2010 and 2020 rather than in the survey year itself.

The world figure hides a wide range. East Asia and Pacific recorded 5.6% in 2022, the lowest of the regional aggregates. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping stood at 17.7%, South Asia at 25.6% and Sub-Saharan Africa at 31.1%. The highest regional level is thus more than five times the lowest. By income group, lower middle income countries stood at 24.4% and upper middle income countries at 8.5%. The gradient with income is consistent with well-established causes: poverty, limited secondary schooling for girls, weak enforcement of minimum-age laws, social norms that tie a daughter's security and a family's honour to early marriage, and, in humanitarian settings, the use of marriage as a response to insecurity.

### Distribution among countries

The spread of the indicator among countries, weighted by population, narrowed between the two survey-rich years compared. In 2012, with 21 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.282 and the Theil index 0.156. In 2018, with 20 countries, the Gini was 0.273 and the Theil 0.120. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.628 to 0.489. Inequality among countries thus declined, mainly because the highest values fell relative to the rest rather than because the lowest values rose.

The composition of what remains is instructive. The share of the Theil index that lies between regions rose from 73.0% in 2012 to 89.8% in 2018. Differences within regions have shrunk faster than differences between them, so a country's region now predicts its level of child marriage better than it did. The practical reading is that the problem is increasingly one of regional concentration, in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, and that regional strategies, rather than a single global approach, are justified. The two comparisons use different sets of countries, 21 and 20, so the change should be read as indicative, not as a strict like-for-like measure.

### Progress towards 2030

The trend assessment compares each country's recent rate of change with the rate needed to reach zero by 2030. Of 20 countries assessed, none was on track or had met the target. Two countries, holding 5.8% of the assessed population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Fourteen countries, holding 91.8% of the population, showed marginal progress and needed significant acceleration. One country, with 0.8% of the population, was stagnating, and three, with 1.6%, were regressing.

The pattern is plain. Declines are occurring in most places where data allow an assessment, but at a pace far below that required. A target of zero is demanding by construction, since it requires the last pockets of the practice to disappear, and those pockets are the hardest to reach: rural, poor, out-of-school and conflict-affected girls. The three regressing countries matter beyond their small population share, because regression often signals shocks, such as conflict, displacement, food insecurity or the closure of schools, that raise the incentive to marry daughters early. The period after 2020 is a particular concern. School closures and economic stress during the pandemic were widely expected to raise child marriage, yet the survey record cannot yet confirm the size of any effect, because marriages after 2020 enter the indicator only as women who married then reach ages 20 to 24 and are surveyed.

### Evidence and its limits

Coverage explains why such caution is needed. Across all years, 145 countries have reported at least once, but in any single year few do. Reporting counted 11 countries in 2015, 20 in 2018, 18 in 2022 and 12 in 2024. Only 3 countries reported in 2025, so the nominal latest year of the series is not a usable measure of the present. Reporting peaks in years with large survey rounds, and the aggregates for 2022 rest on modelled estimates rather than on a complete census of countries in that year.

The series also mixes two sources, UNICEF compilations and Demographic and Health Surveys, which use slightly different definitions of marriage or union. A related indicator, the share married by age 15, is held with 142 countries and captures the most severe cases, and the survey series on female genital mutilation, another harmful practice named in Target 5.3, has only 30 countries. Neither is analysed here, and the thin coverage of the latter means that no global judgement on that practice can be drawn from this shelf.

### Implications

The evidence supports three conclusions. First, child marriage declined in the countries observed but too slowly to reach zero by 2030, and no assessed country is on track. Second, the remaining burden is concentrated by region and by income, so resources should follow the concentration. Third, the measurement system is too sparse in time to show whether the post-2020 shocks reversed earlier gains, which is itself a weakness for accountability. Interventions with a solid record include keeping girls in secondary school, cash support to poor households, enforcement of a legal minimum age of 18 without exceptions, and work with communities and religious leaders on the norms that sustain the practice.

w-c03-5-1~dahlia/writer-2~42.text:
### Land under farming has barely moved

Agricultural land, meaning arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, covered 36.8% of the world's land area in 2015 and 36.9% in 2023. The global footprint of farming is therefore stable, and the change is too small to read as expansion or contraction. Across 208 countries reporting in 2024 the pattern is one of regional constancy: East Asia and Pacific stood at 46.5% in 2015 and 46.8% in 2023, Europe and Central Asia at 29.3% and 29.1%, North America at 26.7% in both years, and South Asia at 58.6% and 58.3%.

Two regional movements deserve note. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 43.9% to 44.7%, the clearest sign of continued extension of farmland, consistent with a continent where output growth has leaned on area rather than yield. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 33.3% to 32.9%, a decline that sits uneasily with the region's reputation for frontier clearing, and which may reflect abandonment of pasture, reclassification or differences in how national statistics define pasture. The definition matters: pasture is the largest component of the category, and its measurement from country to country is uneven, so small changes should be read with caution.

By income group, low income countries moved from 41.4% to 42.1% and lower middle income countries from 42.5% to 43.0%, while upper middle income countries slipped from 43.1% to 42.8%. High income countries stayed near 28.1% and 28.2%. Land use, in short, is not where the pressure of the post-2015 years has shown itself. Intensity is, and it has diverged sharply by region.

### Fertiliser use differs by an order of magnitude

Fertiliser consumption averaged 132.9 kilograms per hectare of arable land worldwide in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, a rise of under three per cent over eight years, with 190 countries reporting in 2024. The world average conceals a very wide spread. East Asia and Pacific applied 329.1 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 304.1 in 2023, the highest regional level and one that has begun to fall, as China and others have pursued policies to curb overuse and its costs in water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. South Asia rose from 175.0 to 206.0. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 135.1 to 173.9, the fastest regional increase, in line with the expansion of export crops such as soya and maize.

At the other end, Sub-Saharan Africa used 14.4 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023. That is roughly a fifteenth of the East Asian figure in 2023, even after growth of about a third. Europe and Central Asia moved from 78.7 to 76.0, North America from 124.3 to 128.8, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 90.0 to 102.0.

The income groups tell the same story. Low income countries used 10.0 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 13.9 in 2023. Lower middle income countries rose from 114.6 to 130.8. Upper middle income countries were essentially flat, 213.0 and 213.8, and high income countries edged down from 106.3 to 104.3. The pattern is of saturation or deliberate restraint at the top and of a very low base at the bottom. The two problems are of opposite sign: where application is high the concern is runoff, soil acidification and emissions; where it is low the concern is nutrient depletion, with soils mined of fertility and yields held down.

### Convergence is occurring, but from a very unequal start

A convergence test across 192 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta coefficient of -0.034 (R-squared 0.3), significant at conventional levels. Countries starting with low application tended to raise it faster, and heavy users tended to hold or reduce it. The coefficient of variation of fertiliser use across countries fell from 2.15 in 2015 to 1.68 in 2022. This is genuine narrowing, yet a coefficient of variation of 1.68 still describes a distribution in which the highest users apply many times the amount of the lowest. The test is also unweighted: small island states and countries with little arable land can dominate the extremes, so the narrowing across countries is not the same as narrowing across hectares or people.

The regional averages bear this out. Absolute gaps remain very large, and the rise in Sub-Saharan Africa of under five kilograms per hectare is small beside the fall of 25 kilograms in East Asia and Pacific. Convergence by this measure is driven partly by the top coming down and only partly by the bottom coming up. Reaching sustainable intensification in Africa requires more nutrients per hectare, but the cost of fertiliser, weak transport, thin input markets and limited credit continue to restrain uptake, and the price shocks that followed 2020 and the war in Ukraine in 2022 made inputs dearer for importers.

### Fertiliser and yields are linked in levels, less so in change

Across 179 countries, the rank correlation (Spearman) between fertiliser use and cereal yield in 2022 levels is 0.72, a strong association. The rank correlation between changes over 2015 to 2022 is only 0.13. Countries that use more fertiliser have higher yields, but countries that increased fertiliser use did not reliably increase yields more. Several explanations are consistent with this: fertiliser responds to seed, water, soil and management, so benefits depend on complementary inputs; overused soils show diminishing returns; and yield changes in short periods are dominated by weather. The result is a correlation, not a causal estimate.

Cereal yield trends show the consequences. The world rate of change, 0.009 on the trend measure, is classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. North America (0.026), South Asia (0.026) and lower middle income countries (0.022) are classed as on track. North America rose from 6,677 to 8,414 kilograms per hectare between 2015 and 2024, and South Asia from 3,041 to 3,814. East Asia and Pacific (0.009), Europe and Central Asia (0.008), Latin America and the Caribbean (0.011) and upper middle income countries (0.008) show marginal progress. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 0.013, shows moderate progress. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, at 1,443 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,453 in 2024, and low income countries as in regression, from 1,373 to 1,345. No numerical target for yield exists under target 2.4, so these classes are relative to the tool's own reading of a rising trend, not an official benchmark.

By country, 39 of 180 assessed are on track, holding 29.5% of the population of the group assessed; 19 show moderate progress (14.0%); 27 show marginal progress (25.7%); 25 stagnate (15.6%); and 70 regress (15.2%). Regression in the largest number of countries, even though they hold a smaller share of people, suggests that many small and low income producers are losing ground, sometimes to drought, conflict or disease.

### Agriculture dominates water withdrawals, mostly where incomes are lowest

Agriculture accounted for 71.5% of freshwater withdrawals worldwide in 2015 and 71.0% in 2022, with 178 countries reporting in 2022. The share is highest where income is lowest: low income countries stood at 90.8% in 2015 and 90.9% in 2022, and lower middle income countries at 89.4% and 88.8%. Upper middle income countries fell from 74.7% to 73.6%, while high income countries sat at 42.2% and 42.7%, since industry and municipal use claim more water there.

Regionally, South Asia withdrew 90.3% for agriculture in both years, which is a repeated value that may reflect carried-forward estimates, not annual measurement. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 90.1% to 87.3%, still the highest group in a region of acute scarcity. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 78.6% to 79.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 73.4% to 74.4%, East Asia and Pacific from 73.2% to 72.1%, Europe and Central Asia from 52.0% to 51.8%, and North America from 37.3% to 37.5%. Little changed after 2015, and the series ends in 2022, so the effect of the 2020 shock and later droughts cannot be seen. A high agricultural share is not itself a measure of unsustainability, since it does not say how much is withdrawn against renewable supply; it shows only that farming sets the terms of water competition.

### Implications for 2030

Target 2.4 asks for production systems that are sustainable and resilient, and none of the series here measures that directly. They measure intensity, and the picture is of a world whose farmland is stable, whose fertiliser use is shifting from the heavy users to the light, and whose water use is stable at about seven tenths of withdrawals. The distribution suggests that the main task by 2030 differs by region: efficiency and restraint in East Asia, North America and parts of Europe, and more nutrients, water control and better seeds in Sub-Saharan Africa and low income countries, where yields have not risen. Without a break from the present trend, low income countries will enter 2030 with yields no higher than in 2015.

w-c02-1-1~farah/writer-1~42.text:
### The headline measure and its line

Target 1.1 commits the world to eradicating extreme poverty by 2030. The target text still names the old line of $1.25 a day, but the bench's series measures a different one: the share of people living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity prices. The two are not the same threshold, and revisions to purchasing power exchange rates mean that country rates cannot be compared with those in earlier editions of the series. Every figure in this section should therefore be read as a statement about the $3.00 line, which is the line the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform now treats as extreme poverty. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. A strict reading requires a rate of zero. A looser reading, common in international practice, accepts a rate of about 3 per cent as the practical floor. This section reports distance from zero, because that is how the trend tool frames the target.

On that measure the world has improved, but slowly. The global headcount ratio fell from 13.4 per cent in 2015 to 10.1 per cent in 2024. That is a reduction of 3.3 percentage points in nine years, a fall of roughly a quarter in the share. Over the same period the trend tool puts the world at 0.376 of the pace needed to reach zero by 2030, which it classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Extending the fitted path gives an expected global rate of 8.4 per cent in 2030. The target is not within reach on current evidence.

### Where poverty has fallen and where it has not

The global average hides sharply different regional experiences. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024, and the trend tool puts it at 0.844 of the required pace, with an expected rate of 1.0 per cent in 2030. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent, with a ratio of 0.685. Upper middle income economies fell from 5.8 per cent to 2.1 per cent. These groups are already near the floor, and the remaining poverty in them is increasingly scattered, harder to reach with general growth, and concentrated among people who are excluded for reasons of geography, disability, displacement or conflict.

South Asia shows the largest recent gain, though its series begins in 2020 in this extract. The rate fell from 9.4 per cent in 2020 to 2.6 per cent in 2024, and it is the only region the trend tool classes as on track, with a ratio of 0.96 and an expected rate of 0.4 per cent in 2030. Two cautions apply. The window is only four years, and a fitted line over so short a span is sensitive to the survey rounds at either end. South Asia also has a long history of gaps between survey rounds in several large countries, so the regional figure leans on modelled estimates between and beyond them.

Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent, a ratio of 0.426, which is marginal progress. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent and high-income economies from 0.7 per cent to 0.6 per cent. In these groups the measure at $3.00 a day is of limited use, since poverty is better captured by national lines, which the chapter treats elsewhere.

### The regions moving the wrong way

Two groups are going backwards or standing still, and together they decide whether the global target can be met. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4 per cent in 2015 and 45.0 per cent in 2024. The trend tool calls this stagnation, with a ratio of 0.015 and an expected rate of 44.7 per cent in 2030. Because the region's population is growing quickly, a flat rate means that the number of people in extreme poverty has risen, even though the data here speak only to shares. Low income economies, many of them in the same region, rose from 50.1 per cent to 52.5 per cent, which the tool classes as regression, with an expected 54.2 per cent in 2030.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping also regressed, from 11.3 per cent in 2015 to 14.3 per cent in 2024, with a ratio of minus 0.481 and an expected 16.7 per cent in 2030. The causes are well known in outline: prolonged armed conflict, displacement, currency collapses and fiscal crises in several economies, and the grouping's composition, which since the latest revision combines very different countries. The rise should not be read as a uniform deterioration, since a few severely affected economies can move a regional aggregate considerably.

Lower middle income economies fell from 16.0 per cent in 2020 to 12.4 per cent in 2024. This is a ratio of 0.471, marginal progress, with an expected 8.5 per cent in 2030. As the middle-income group contains the largest populations still in poverty, its pace matters more for the global total than the pace of the smaller regions.

### Countries, and the slowdown after 2014 and 2021

The country classification confirms the regional picture. Of 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.6 per cent of the population of the assessed group. Another 41 show moderate progress needing acceleration, covering 23.1 per cent of that population. Fifteen show marginal progress, covering 11.3 per cent, seven stagnate, covering 2.2 per cent, and 24 are regressing, covering 17.9 per cent. Nearly three in ten countries are therefore moving away from the target or not at all, even though the largest single share of people lives in countries that are on track. That is a feature of population weighting, and it matters for interpretation: a country count and a population share tell different stories, and the global rate follows the latter.

The break analysis of the global series dates two changes in pace, in 2014 and 2021. From 2001 to 2013 the global rate fell by a mean of 1.59 percentage points a year. From 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.88 points, and from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.33 points. The first slowdown came before the Goals were adopted, and reflects the exhaustion of the easiest gains as the large Asian economies grew out of the highest rates of poverty. The second follows the pandemic, with its loss of incomes, then food and energy price rises and tighter public finances in indebted countries. At the 2021 to 2024 pace of 0.33 points a year, six further years would remove only about 2 points from the 2024 rate, leaving the world well above zero in 2030. The figure from the trend tool, 8.4 per cent, is somewhat lower than this simple extrapolation would suggest, which shows that results depend on the fitting window and the method.

Convergence is absent. Across 57 countries with data in both 2015 and 2022, the beta coefficient is 0.007 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029, so countries starting with higher poverty did not fall faster. The coefficient of variation rose from 2.14 to 2.68, which means that the spread between countries widened relative to the mean. Poverty is concentrating in fewer, poorer and more fragile places, and that is the strongest reason to doubt that global growth alone will finish the task.

### Reliability of the evidence

The evidence thins out at the end of the period, and the reader should weigh that. The number of countries reporting fell from 93 in 2018 to 70 in 2020, recovered to 81 in 2021, and then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and four in 2025. Figures for 2024 therefore rest largely on projection from earlier surveys, and the regional values for that year are estimates rather than observations. Household surveys are costly, are delayed in conflict and are rarely repeated at regular intervals in the poorest countries, which are the ones that matter most. The finding that poverty is rising in low income economies may itself be affected by which countries have recent surveys.

The overall judgement is that the 2030 target at the international line will be missed. Progress concentrated in East Asia and South Asia has carried the global average, and the remaining poverty is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and in conflict-affected economies, where rates are flat or rising. Meeting the target would need changes there and not further gains elsewhere.

### Proposals

The proposals below follow from these findings and are addressed to those who can act on them.

Creditor governments and multilateral lenders should ease debt service for countries where poverty is rising, so that fiscal space can be directed to social spending in conflict and crisis settings.

w-c06-1-1~cedar/writer-3~43.text:
### What the evidence base holds

The question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed can be answered from the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project, which scores legal frameworks on a scale of 0 to 100 across ten topics: Safety, Mobility, Work, Pay, Marriage, Parenthood, Childcare, Entrepreneurship, Assets and Pension. The Legal Framework Index is the unweighted average of the ten topic scores, with 100 the highest possible score. Two companion indices cover supportive frameworks and enforcement perceptions, built on the same ten topics.

The only result available to this section is a coverage check. It shows that 189 countries reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and that 189 countries reported it in at least one year. The two figures are identical, so every economy that has ever been scored was scored in the latest round. That is a strength: the index is close to universal, and no country has dropped out of the panel. The check also lists aggregates for high-income, low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income and South Asia groupings and for the world.

The check does not return index values. This section therefore cannot state a world average, a regional gap, or a change since 2015 or 2020. Inventing such numbers would breach the cooperative's rule that every figure must come from the shelf. What follows is an account of what the index measures, what the coverage implies, and how the evidence should be read against Target 5.1, which calls for an end to all forms of discrimination against women and girls everywhere.

### What the index measures and what it does not

The Legal Framework Index records laws and regulations on the books. It asks, for example, whether a woman may travel outside the home, take a job, or register a business in the same way as a man, whether the law mandates equal remuneration for work of equal value, and whether spouses have equal rights to property and to inheritance. Because the ten topics are weighted equally, a country with strong labour law but weak property rights may score the same as one with the reverse profile. The composite hides such differences, and the topic scores are the better guide to reform.

The companion indices matter for interpretation. The Supportive Framework Index, covering 189 countries, concerns the services and institutions that let a legal right be used, such as childcare provision and mechanisms for claiming redress. The Enforcement Perceptions Index covers 177 countries in its latest year, 12 fewer than the legal index. It rests on expert perceptions rather than on legal text, so it is the weakest of the three for comparison, and the lower coverage means that some economies cannot be assessed on enforcement at all. A country can legislate equality and still see little change in women's lives if courts, registries and employers do not apply the law.

### Reading the coverage for 2030

Near-universal coverage of 189 countries is a precondition for monitoring Target 5.1, since the target speaks of discrimination everywhere. For this indicator, unlike many in the Goal 5 chapter, the problem is not missing countries. Violence prevalence, by contrast, is reported for only 106 countries, with a latest year of 2017, and the contrast shows how much better documented legal text is than lived experience.

The trend since 2015 cannot be quantified here, but the pattern of legal reform in this period is well established in general terms. Reform has tended to proceed in steps, often following constitutional change, regional agreements or pressure from women's movements, and has been uneven across topics. Laws on workplace discrimination and equal pay for men and women have commonly moved faster than those on childcare and pensions, which carry fiscal cost. The pandemic after 2020 strained public budgets and may have slowed measures that need spending, though legal text is cheaper to amend than services are to fund. These are expectations from history, not findings from the shelf.

### Why the gap between law and practice matters

A high legal score is necessary but not sufficient. Where enforcement perceptions lag the legal index, women face discrimination despite formal rights. The five indicators on the shelf for this chapter, including the female NEET rate with coverage of 182 countries, offer outcome measures against which legal change could be tested. Pairing legal scores with outcomes such as female youth inactivity would show whether reform is followed by improvement, but the shelf as queried does not provide that comparison.

### Limits of this section

The analysis rests on a single coverage result and cannot rank regions or income groups. The index is also open to more than one reading: a score of 100 does not mean equality in fact, and the unweighted average treats a gap in pension law as equal in weight to a gap in safety. Target 5.1 carries no numerical threshold, so progress toward 2030 can only be judged against the ceiling of 100 and against the closure of individual topic gaps.

Statistical offices and the World Bank should extend enforcement perception coverage from 177 to all 189 economies, so that the gap between law and practice can be assessed everywhere.

w-c03-4-1~cedar/writer-4~43.text:
### What the target asks and what the bench can measure

Target 2.3 asks for a doubling, by 2030, of the agricultural productivity and incomes of small-scale food producers, in particular women, indigenous peoples, family farmers, pastoralists and fishers. The wording carries two difficulties. First, the target is defined for a specific population, the small-scale producer, while the World Bank series available to this chapter describe whole economies. Value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing, in constant 2015 US dollars, averages over a large commercial estate and a household plot alike. Second, the target sets no baseline year and does not say whether doubling is to be measured from 2015, from the adoption of the goals, or from some earlier date. This section reads the target from 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and treats a doubling as a rise to twice the 2015 level by 2030.

Two indicators are used. Value added per agricultural worker is the closest available proxy for the official indicator on the volume of production per labour unit. Cereal yield, in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, measures output per unit of land and covers wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains. Cereal production and the land under cereals are the two components of yield. Neither series speaks to incomes, to sex, or to farm size, and neither separates the small-scale producer from the large. They show whether the conditions for a doubling exist; they cannot show that the doubling has happened for the people the target names.

### Value added per worker: a rising world average that conceals a stalled bottom

Global value added per agricultural worker stood at 3,491 US dollars in 2015 and reached 4,264 dollars in 2025, in constant 2015 prices. The annual rate implied by the trend tool is 2.0 per cent. This is an increase, and the trend tool classes the world as on track, but the classification is generous. It compares the rate with a path that the tool sets itself, since the target carries no numerical value in the bench. A doubling over fifteen years requires a compound rate of close to five per cent a year, and a rate of 2.0 per cent is far below it. By 2025, ten of the fifteen years had elapsed, and the world average had not come near twice its 2015 level. Reaching a doubling by 2030 would need a rate in the remaining five years that no region has sustained over the decade.

The world figure is itself a weighted summary of very unequal parts. It is pulled upward by East Asia and Pacific, where value added per worker rose from 4,087 dollars in 2015 to 6,991 dollars in 2025, a rate of 5.5 per cent a year. That is the only regional rate that approaches the pace a doubling demands. The upper-middle-income group, which includes China and several large producers in Latin America and eastern Europe, rose from 4,378 dollars to 7,474 dollars at 5.5 per cent a year. The similarity of the two rates is not an accident: the economies that carry most weight in each group overlap, and the gain in both reflects the movement of labour out of farming as much as the growth of output. When many workers leave the land and output holds or rises, value added per remaining worker rises mechanically. A gain of this kind raises the average without any improvement in the position of the household that stays on a small plot.

The other regions improved at a slower pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 12,217 dollars to 17,325 dollars, at 3.6 per cent a year. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 6,294 dollars to 8,031 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. The group of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4,805 dollars to 6,181 dollars, at 2.6 per cent a year, and South Asia from 1,631 dollars to 2,082 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. All of these are reported as on track by the tool, and none is on a path to doubling by 2030. The finding for the world is therefore that productivity per worker has risen in most regions since 2015, that the rise is real, and that it is too slow for the target as written.

### Where productivity per worker is lowest, it has barely moved

The regions with the lowest starting points show the least progress. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 1,339 dollars per worker in 2015 and 1,496 dollars in 2025, a rate of 1.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries fell from 875 dollars in 2015 to 778 dollars in 2025, a rate of minus 1.2 per cent a year, which the tool classes as regression. In the lowest-income economies, then, value added per agricultural worker is lower in 2025 than it was when the goals were adopted. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 1,915 dollars to 2,336 dollars, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year.

The gap between the top and the bottom is wide enough that the arithmetic of a doubling has a different meaning at each end. North America is shown in the data only at its 2015 value of 67,701 dollars, since the series has no later observation for the region in the extract used here, and the comparison across the decade cannot be made. High-income countries as a group rose from 28,219 dollars to 30,775 dollars, at 0.9 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress. A group already at a high level may not need to double, and the target was written with developing countries in mind. The comparison that matters is the distance between the high-income level and the low-income level in 2025, which is a very large multiple of the low-income figure, and which the decade has not narrowed. A farm worker in a low-income country produces, in value terms, a small fraction of what a worker in a high-income country produces, and the low-income fraction has shrunk.

The reasons are well established. Low-income agriculture is dominated by rain-fed smallholdings with little mechanisation, limited access to improved seed, fertiliser and credit, poor roads to markets, insecure tenure, and exposure to drought, flood and pests. Population growth in these economies has kept the farm labour force growing, so that each worker has less land and capital to work with. In addition, the years since 2015 included conflict in several low-income countries, a series of droughts in the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, the disruption of the pandemic after 2020, and the price shocks that followed the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Each of these weighed most heavily on households with the least reserves. The data do not allow the effect of each shock to be separated, but the combined outcome is visible in the low-income series.

### Cereal yield: a modest rise and a persistent gap

Cereal yield tells a similar story at a smaller scale. The world yield was 3,932 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 4,229 kilograms per hectare in 2023, the latest year for which a world figure is reported. That is a gain well short of a doubling, and indeed far short of the gain in value added per worker. Yield is a slower-moving quantity than value added per worker, because it depends on biology, on the share of land that is irrigated, and on the technology of seed and fertiliser, none of which changes quickly. A doubling of average world cereal yield in fifteen years has no precedent in the record of any large region, and the target should not be read as requiring it of yields. The relevant question is whether yields are rising fast enough in the places where they are low.

They are not. Sub-Saharan Africa had a cereal yield of 1,443 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,453 kilograms per hectare in 2024, a change so small that it amounts to stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 kilograms per hectare to 1,345 kilograms per hectare over the same period. These are less than a third of the yield of North America, which rose from 6,677 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 8,414 kilograms per hectare in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, already at 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015, reached 5,430 kilograms per hectare in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 3,803 to 4,045 kilograms per hectare, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 2,732 to 3,027 kilograms per hectare.

South Asia and Latin America made the larger gains among developing regions. South Asia rose from 3,041 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 3,814 kilograms per hectare in 2024, which reflects the continued spread of irrigation, improved varieties of rice and wheat, and fertiliser use. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 to 4,828 kilograms per hectare, helped by maize and the expansion of no-till practices. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 2,766 to 3,366 kilograms per hectare. By contrast, upper-middle-income countries moved from 4,648 to 4,942 kilograms per hectare, and high-income countries from 4,976 to 5,394 kilograms per hectare, both in 2023. The pattern is that yields have risen where they were already moderate and where irrigation and inputs were spreading, and have stood still where they were lowest.

### Convergence: the poorest are not catching up

A doubling target is in part a target about catching up, and the convergence tool tests directly whether countries that began with low values rose faster than those that began with high values. For cereal yield across 176 countries between 2015 and 2024, the estimated coefficient is minus 0.0016, with a p-value of 0.79 and an R-squared of 0.0013. The coefficient is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in subsequent change. There is no evidence of convergence in the strict sense: low-yield countries did not grow faster than high-yield countries. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.00 in 2015 to 0.91 in 2024, which indicates that dispersion narrowed slightly. The two results are compatible. A narrowing of dispersion without a negative coefficient suggests that some of the highest-variance cases moved towards the middle by chance or by individual shocks, and not that the poorest as a group moved up.

The result for value added per worker is similar. Across 168 countries between 2015 and 2024, the coefficient is 0.0012, with a p-value of 0.49 and an R-squared of 0.0024. The sign is positive, so that the point estimate points to a slight tendency for countries with higher starting values to grow faster, although the estimate is not distinguishable from zero. The coefficient of variation moved from 1.51 to 1.43, a small fall. The reading is that after nearly a decade there is no evidence of a systematic closing of the gap, and the distribution of agricultural labour productivity remains very wide. The implication for 2030 is that a doubling for the lowest-productivity countries cannot be expected from the general forces already at work. If catching up were occurring by itself, the low-income group would show it. It shows the reverse.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020

The series offered by the bench give end points more than yearly paths, and the findings above compare 2015 with the latest year. The conclusions about the pandemic years therefore rest on well-established knowledge more than on the displayed results. The shock of 2020 disrupted labour movement, input supply and transport, and agricultural output in most countries proved more resilient than other sectors, because food production continued as an essential activity. This resilience helps explain why value added per worker in most regions did not fall. The more lasting effect on the poorest came through prices and incomes: higher fertiliser and fuel costs after 2021 and 2022 reduced the use of purchased inputs among smallholders who could not afford them, and this may account for part of the stagnation of yields in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries. A reader should treat this explanation as plausible and not as shown by the series.

A second caution concerns measurement. Value added per worker is the ratio of an output measure to a labour measure, and the labour measure for agriculture depends on household surveys that count part-time, seasonal and unpaid family work unevenly. Women, who make up a large share of the agricultural labour force in many low-income countries and who are named in the target, are often under-counted or recorded as outside the labour force. The series cannot show whether their productivity has changed. Cereal yield, moreover, applies to cereals only. It leaves out roots, tubers, pulses, vegetables, fruit, livestock and fish, which matter for the incomes of many small-scale producers, and in fishing communities it measures nothing at all. Reporting also varies: in some countries the harvested area is reported only as sown or cultivated area, as the series note states.

### Implications for 2030

The evidence supports four conclusions. First, no region, and no income group, is shown to be on course to double value added per agricultural worker by 2030 from its 2015 level; the closest, East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group, advanced at 5.5 per cent a year, and the remainder of the period would have to match or exceed that pace for the doubling to be reached. Because these two groups gained from labour leaving farming, their pace is hard to repeat elsewhere, where the farm labour force is still growing. Second, the world average disguises a split: the economies with the highest productivity gained, the middle gained moderately, and the lowest-income economies lost ground. Third, cereal yields rose modestly and not at all in Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group. Fourth, the lack of convergence in either indicator shows that the market and the existing policy mix are not closing the gaps by themselves.

The reading of the target matters for the verdict. If doubling is read as applying to the world average, the answer is that it will not be met. If it is read as applying to each country, a larger number of countries will fail, and the low-income group has moved backwards. If it is read as applying to small-scale producers specifically, the bench cannot say, because the series do not distinguish them. On any of the three readings, the conclusion that the target will be missed is secure for the regions where the data exist, and the main uncertainty is about the size of the miss for the people the target names.

What would raise productivity where it is lowest is well understood. It includes secure land rights, particularly for women; extension services and farmer organisations; improved and drought-tolerant seed suited to local conditions; affordable fertiliser applied efficiently, with attention to soil health; small-scale irrigation and water harvesting; rural roads, storage and market access that reduce post-harvest losses and raise farm-gate prices; and rural finance and insurance that let households take the risk of investing. Public spending on agricultural research has long delivered high returns, and sustained investment in it for the crops and conditions of low-income countries remains one of the more reliable routes to higher yields. The accounts of land, fertiliser, water and investment appear in other sections of this chapter and are not repeated here.

### Proposals

The findings lead to the following proposals; each names who should act.

w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-1~44.text:
### What the shelf holds on disaster exposure

Target 1.5 asks for reduced exposure and vulnerability of the poor to climate-related extreme events by 2030. The World Bank's catalogue offers three series bearing on it, and they differ sharply in quality. The first, the share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, is an average over 1990 to 2009, reported for 168 countries in a single year, 2009. It is a fixed baseline, not a trend, and cannot show whether exposure has fallen since 2015. The second, the disaster risk reduction progress score, is a self-assessment on a scale of 1 to 5 submitted under the Hyogo Framework, with its latest value in 2011 and coverage of 83 countries. It predates the Sendai Framework and the Goals. The third, new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, runs to 2023 and is the only series that can describe the period 2015 to 2023. This section therefore rests mainly on displacement, and the reader should treat it as a partial proxy: it counts displacement events (the unit is cases, and one person displaced twice is counted twice), not people affected, and it captures chiefly sudden-onset events such as storms and floods, with slow-onset drought poorly represented.

### The scale and direction of displacement

Worldwide, new disaster displacement stood at 19188817 cases in 2015 and at 26393278 in 2023. The rise is substantial, yet it should be read with care. Annual figures swing with the occurrence of a few very large storms and floods, so a single year at each end is a weak guide to a trend. The break analysis of annual change for the world finds no structural break, and the mean annual change over 2009 to 2023 is a fall of about 789790 cases a year. That figure reflects the very high values at the start of the segment and the volatility of the series rather than a steady decline; the endpoints in 2015 and 2023 point the other way. The honest summary is that displacement is large, erratic and, since 2015, not demonstrably falling. For a target that calls for reduced exposure, that is not a sign of progress, though the data cannot attribute the movement to climate change, to population growth in hazard-prone areas, or to better recording.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture is uneven. East Asia and Pacific remains the largest, at 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia fell from 6877900 to 2446054, though the earlier figure includes major monsoon and cyclone events and the later one a year without comparable extremes. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1108287 to 6029739, a more than fivefold increase, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1212730 to 2481660. Europe and Central Asia, whose first value in the shelf is 56782 in 2016, reached 4275239 in 2023, a jump that owes much to individual severe events and to wider reporting. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 1543360 to 1728025, while North America rose from 76000 to 394000.

By income group, the shift is stark. Low-income countries went from 992200 to 6177600 cases, a sixfold rise. Upper-middle-income countries more than doubled, from 6620044 to 13815894. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 9883673 to 5649287, and high-income countries from 1692900 to 750497. Wealthier countries evacuate people, but they also have warning systems, shelters and building standards that shorten and reduce displacement. In low-income settings, displacement tends to follow from weak housing, informal settlement on floodplains, and little insurance or social protection, which is the vulnerability that Target 1.5 names. The concentration of the rise in low-income countries is therefore the most policy-relevant finding of this section.

### Inequality among countries has widened

The population-weighted spread of displacement among countries grew between 2015 and 2023. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.570 to 0.678 and the Theil index from 0.723 to 0.893. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.11 to 1.47. Displacement is thus more concentrated in a few countries at the end of the period than at the start. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%, so a larger portion of inequality now lies among countries within regions. A regional response alone will not capture this: neighbouring countries with similar hazards record very different burdens, reflecting both exposure and capacity. Note that the sample also grew, from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, so part of the change in spread comes from added countries.

### How well the record is kept

Coverage is the central weakness. Countries reporting displacement numbered 80 in 2008, fell to 60 in 2009 and 62 in 2011, then rose to 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. After 2015 coverage climbed to 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, with 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023, against 199 economies that have reported in at least one year. Rising coverage means that part of the growth in the global total may reflect better monitoring, not more displacement. A zero or missing value is also ambiguous: a country absent from the series may have had no events, or none recorded. Coverage dipped to 133 in 2021, after the pandemic year of 2020, suggesting that collection was somewhat disrupted, though the shelf does not say so directly.

The other two series do not resolve the difficulty. The affected-population share is a twenty-year mean ending in 2009, and the risk reduction score is a self-assessment ending in 2011 for 83 countries; neither speaks to change after 2015 or 2020. Target 1.5 can also be read in more than one way: it concerns the poor and vulnerable specifically, yet none of these series is disaggregated by income of the household, and the official indicators for the target concern deaths, missing persons and people affected per 100000, and national strategies, none of which is on the shelf in a current form.

### Implications for 2030

On present evidence, the world is not on a path to reduced exposure by 2030. Displacement in 2023 exceeded that of 2015, the increase is concentrated in low-income and upper-middle-income countries, and inequality among countries has widened. The data cannot show that vulnerability has fallen, and the lack of any post-2011 measure of preparedness means that progress in risk reduction cannot be judged at all. Given the volatility, a few years of lower displacement should not be taken as success, nor a single catastrophic year as failure; multi-year averages would be the sounder basis for judging 2030.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-2~45.text:
### Measuring the gap in mobile technology

The question for target 5.b is how far women lag men in using the technologies that enable empowerment. The shelf holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex. The only sex-disaggregated indicators are internet use, by female and male share of population (International Telecommunication Union), and account ownership (Global Findex). Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people are held only for the whole population, so they cannot show a gender gap, since one person may hold several subscriptions. This section therefore reads the gender gap in internet use, which the ITU defines as use from any location in the last three months, by computer, mobile phone or other device. Ownership of a handset is not measured here and is treated as a gap.

The gaps below are differences in percentage points between male and female shares, calculated from the values reported. Years differ slightly between series: some aggregates end in 2024 and others in 2025, and the comparison of world values therefore mixes a 2024 female figure with a 2025 male figure. Readers should treat the world gap with that caution.

### The world gap and its narrowing

In 2019, 51.8% of women worldwide used the internet, against 56.0% of men, a gap of 4.2 points. By 2024 the female share had reached 68.2%. The male series for the world is reported to 2025 at 76.6%, so a like-for-like 2024 male value is not on the shelf. The apparent gap of 8.4 points between 68.2% and 76.6% overstates the true 2024 gap because the years differ. The regional figures, which share the year 2024, give a cleaner reading.

The pattern is that both sexes gained sharply after 2019, a period that includes the pandemic of 2020, when schooling, work, health information and public services moved online. Whether the absolute gap widened or narrowed depends on the region. The data cannot isolate the effect of the pandemic from the underlying spread of cheaper smartphones and mobile data, and the figures should not be read as causal.

### Regional differences

In high-use regions the gap is small and shrinking. North America moved from 89.5% of women and 89.9% of men in 2019 to 94.1% and 94.7% in 2024, a gap of 0.6 points. Europe and Central Asia went from 78.4% to 90.0% for women and from 82.3% to 91.8% for men, so the gap fell from 3.9 points to 1.8. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 67.2% for women and 68.4% for men in 2019, and at 81.3% and 82.0% in 2024; the gap was 1.2 points and then 0.7. East Asia and Pacific is the exception to the usual order: women trailed men by a margin of 0.7 in favour of women in 2019 (67.4% against 66.7%), but by 2024 men led, 87.6% to 85.5%, a gap of 2.1 points. The region's women gained substantially but men gained faster.

The largest gaps lie where use is lowest or changing fastest. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, female use rose from 42.1% to 55.0% while male use rose from 51.3% to 67.6%. The gap therefore widened from 9.2 to 12.6 points. In South Asia, female use leapt from 24.3% to 56.3%, a gain of 32.0 points, but male use rose from 34.9% to 69.1%, so the gap grew from 10.6 to 12.8 points. In Sub-Saharan Africa, female use went from 20.2% to 29.4% and male use from 28.6% to 37.9%; the gap stayed close to 8 to 9 points (8.4 in 2019, 8.5 in 2024), but on a base so low that fewer than one woman in three used the internet in 2024.

These cases show that rapid growth in access does not by itself close a gap. Where men start ahead and adoption accelerates, men often adopt first. Norms that limit women's mobility, ownership of devices, literacy, and independent income are well-established causes, as are the cost of handsets and data relative to women's lower earnings. Policy history suggests that gaps close once use becomes near-universal, as in North America and Europe, and persist while it is still spreading.

### Income groups

The income grouping gives a similar view, with female values dated 2025. In low-income countries female use rose from 12.6% in 2019 to 18.3% in 2025, and male use from 20.3% to 28.6%; the gap grew slightly, from 7.7 to 10.3 points. In lower-middle-income countries women moved from 28.9% to 56.9% and men from 38.0% to 68.7%, so the gap went from 9.1 to 11.8 points. In upper-middle-income countries the female share rose from 67.6% to 87.9%, and the male share from 67.6% to 89.7%: women matched men in 2019 and trailed by 1.8 points in 2025. High-income countries went from 86.4% to 93.6% for women and from 88.7% to 94.9% for men, narrowing the gap from 2.3 to 1.3 points.

The result is a clear division. Gaps have narrowed only in the groups where more than four in five people already use the internet. In the groups where use is lower, women have gained a great deal in absolute terms but the gap in points has grown. For target 5.b this matters, because the poorest women, who might benefit most from remote services, payments and information, are the least connected: fewer than one in five women in low-income countries used the internet in 2025.

### Gaps move together

Across 54 countries with data for 2019 to 2024, the rank correlation between female and male internet use in 2024 was 0.948, and between the changes over the period 0.958. Countries that grew fast for men grew fast for women. The implication is that the main driver of women's connection is the overall spread of networks and affordability, and that the sex gap is secondary to the national level. It also means that national infrastructure policy is necessary but not sufficient, because the gap in points has persisted in regions where overall growth was very high. A high correlation does not show that gaps are equal; it shows that rankings are similar.

### Data limits and the road to 2030

The coverage of the female series is uneven. Countries reporting numbered 92 in 2019, 74 in 2020, 65 in 2024 and only 7 in 2025, so the 2025 values rest on very few countries and are probably modelled or estimated aggregates; of 137 countries that have ever reported, 65 did so in 2024. Country-level conclusions are therefore weaker than regional ones. Target 5.b also has no numerical threshold in its text, and can be read as use, ownership or affordability; the shelf covers only the first.

For 2030, the trends imply near parity in regions already above 80%, and a persistent gap of roughly 8 to 13 points in South Asia, the Middle East and North Africa region, and Sub-Saharan Africa unless adoption among women outpaces men. Low-income countries are furthest from parity in the level of use: a rate of 18.3% for women in 2025 would need to more than triple to match high-income countries.

### Proposals

The ITU and national statistical offices should report internet use and handset ownership by sex every year for all countries, so that the 2025 coverage of seven countries is not repeated.

Regulators and operators in low-income countries should cut the cost of handsets and data for first-time women users, through tax relief and low-cost plans, with donors co-financing the schemes.
