w-c02-4-1~heath/writer-2~45.text:
### Water, sanitation and electricity reach most people, but not the poorest countries

Target 1.4 asks that all men and women, the poor and the vulnerable in particular, have equal access to basic services and to financial services. The World Development Indicators do not measure access by income within countries for water, sanitation or electricity. They measure it by country, and by income group of countries. Reading the poor through the poorest countries is therefore an inference, not a direct observation, and it should be held as such throughout this section.

On that reading, the global averages are encouraging. The share of the world's people using at least basic drinking water services rose from 88.1 per cent in 2015 to 91.5 per cent in 2024, and 202 countries reported in 2024. Access to electricity rose from 86.9 per cent to 91.9 per cent over the same years. These are gains of a few percentage points in nine years, and the remaining population is small in share but large in number and concentrated in a few places.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries carry the deficit

The distribution is sharply uneven. In drinking water, North America stood at 99.8 per cent in 2024 and high-income countries at 99.2 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa reached 67.5 per cent, up from 59.2 per cent in 2015. Low-income countries rose from 53.1 per cent to 60.3 per cent. Lower middle income countries moved from 85.2 per cent to 90.8 per cent and upper middle income countries from 92.6 per cent to 95.9 per cent. The gap between the poorest group and the richest was therefore about 46 points in 2015 and about 39 points in 2024: it narrowed, but remains very wide.

Electricity shows the same ordering with one striking exception. South Asia raised access from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, a transformation driven by large public programmes of grid extension and household connection. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, and low-income countries from 32.2 per cent to 48.8 per cent. Progress in points was real, yet in low-income countries about half the population still lacked electricity in 2024. Where populations grow quickly, connections must expand faster merely to keep the share constant, which helps explain why the gains in Africa are slower than the policy effort might suggest. Other regions are close to saturation: Europe and Central Asia stood at 99.9989 per cent in 2024 by the data's own precision, and North America at 100.0 per cent in both years.

Rural electricity gives a more encouraging picture of direction. Of 211 countries assessed, 161, holding 77.4 per cent of the assessed population, are on track or have met the target of full rural access by 2030. Another 23 countries (12.8 per cent of population) show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 10 (2.0 per cent) marginal progress. Seven countries (2.3 per cent) are stagnant and 10 (5.4 per cent) are regressing. The countries that are not on track are few but are those where conflict, fiscal weakness and sparse settlement make off-grid and mini-grid solutions the only practical route.

### Sanitation is the service furthest from the target

Basic sanitation is the weakest of the three. The trend assessment projects the world to reach 89.2 per cent by 2030 at the current rate, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 (46.6 per cent of population) are on track, 34 (17.7 per cent) show moderate progress, 54 (16.5 per cent) marginal progress, 37 (5.8 per cent) stagnation and 39 (13.4 per cent) regression. Nearly one fifth of the assessed population lives in countries that are stagnant or going backwards, a larger share than for water.

Regions differ widely. South Asia is on track, with a ratio of 1.11 and a projected 104.6 per cent for 2030 (a figure above 100 reflects extrapolation and cannot literally occur). East Asia and Pacific is also on track at 1.18, and upper middle income countries at 1.08. Lower middle income countries have a ratio of 0.75 and a projected 88.9 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan show a ratio of 0.48 and a projected 88.2 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.16 with a projected 42.0 per cent in 2030, and low-income countries a ratio of 0.10 with a projected 36.2 per cent, against 29.2 per cent in 2015 and 33.3 per cent in 2024. At this pace, two thirds of people in the poorest countries would still lack basic sanitation at the deadline. Sanitation requires household investment, land tenure, behaviour change and sewerage or faecal sludge systems, so it advances more slowly than services delivered by a utility or a single network.

A note on interpretation: North America is classed as regression, with a ratio of -1.03, yet its level is 99.5 per cent in 2024 against 99.7 per cent in 2015. The classification responds to the sign of a tiny change at a ceiling, and should not be read as a crisis. High-income countries, at 98.3 per cent in 2024, and Europe and Central Asia, at 97.4 per cent, are both classed as moderate progress with ratios of 0.55 and 0.69 for similar reasons: the last points are the hardest to close, and the target of 100 per cent is read literally.

### Rural water is converging slowly

Rural drinking water is where the poor are most likely to be found. Across 167 countries, rural access shows convergence between 2015 and 2024: the coefficient of initial level on subsequent growth is -0.0164 with R squared 0.27, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.27 to 0.23. Countries that started lower grew faster, so the spread narrowed. This is welcome, but the fall in dispersion is modest, and the trend assessment for water overall shows that 60 countries (33.9 per cent of population) are on track, 45 (33.8 per cent) show moderate progress, 55 (20.9 per cent) marginal progress, 17 (1.5 per cent) stagnation and 37 (9.9 per cent) regression. Regression in 37 countries is a warning that conflict, displacement, urban growth outrunning pipes and ageing systems can undo earlier gains.

### Financial accounts have expanded fastest

Account ownership among the poorest 40 per cent is the one indicator that speaks directly of the poor within countries. The world figure rose from 61.7 per cent in 2017 to 72.4 per cent in 2024. Low-income countries rose from 22.5 per cent to 37.3 per cent, the largest proportional gain, and lower middle income from 53.2 per cent to 63.4 per cent. Upper middle income reached 76.8 per cent and high income 92.8 per cent, up from 89.0 per cent. South Asia moved from 65.5 per cent to 73.3 per cent. The spread of mobile money and of digital payment of public transfers is the usual explanation, together with identity programmes.

Regional figures stop at 2021 because the latest survey round did not cover them in the regional aggregation. Within that window, Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 42.9 per cent to 67.9 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 64.1 per cent to 77.4 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 76.4 per cent to 86.3 per cent, and North America from 86.7 per cent to 92.1 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from 39.5 per cent to 46.1 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa from 32.0 per cent to 43.6 per cent, so these two regions remain the furthest behind. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and the 2017 to 2021 and 2017 to 2024 comparisons must not be mixed.

### What the pattern implies for 2030

The pattern is of services that arrive first where the state is capable and last where poverty is deepest. Since 2015 gains have been real, and the pandemic years of 2020 and after did not reverse the global averages, though the data cannot show whether the pace would otherwise have been faster. Full coverage by 2030 is out of reach for sanitation globally and for all three physical services in the low-income group. Electricity and water in most other regions are close to ceilings. The decisive question is therefore the final population in low-income and fragile countries, where the target is not likely to be met on current trends.

w-c04-1-1~farah/writer-2~45.text:
### The global ratio and the 2030 threshold

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled world ratio stood at 228.0 in 2015 and 197.0 in 2023, the latest year reported by all 194 countries. The decline is real, but the extrapolated trend gives an expected world ratio of 173.4 in 2030, far above the threshold. The trend tool classes the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and its ratio of achieved to required pace is 0.35. On present evidence the global target will be missed by a wide margin.

The arithmetic explains why. Reaching 70 from 197 in the seven years after 2023 would need a fall far steeper than any recent period delivered. The annual change in the world ratio averaged -8.4 points a year in 2001 to 2007 and -5.2 points a year in 2008 to 2019. The break analysis places a slowdown at 2008. Progress was already decelerating before 2015, so the post-2015 record continues a weakening trend rather than interrupting a strong one.

### Divergence between regions and income groups

The global figure conceals a very uneven distribution. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593.0 in 2015 to 448.0 in 2023, and its expected 2030 value is 350.5, five times the threshold. South Asia fell from 173.0 to 120.0, the largest proportional improvement among the large regions, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 and a progress ratio of 0.83. That region alone is classed as close to the target pace, though still needing acceleration.

By income, low-income countries moved from 491.0 to 346.0, with an expected 254.7 in 2030. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 291.0 to 235.0 and are expected to reach 194.9, a progress ratio of 0.44, the weakest of the groups with meaningful progress. Upper-middle-income countries went from 61.0 to 57.0, and high-income countries from 11.0 to 10.0. Both are already under 70, so the target is met there by this reading.

Several regions are classed as on track or met: East Asia and Pacific (70.0 to 66.0, expected 62.7), Europe and Central Asia (14.0 to 11.0), North America (17.0 to 16.0) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (54.0 to 47.0). These regions have little room left to fall under the global threshold; their status shows that the target has been achieved where it was nearly achieved already. Reaching it is not a measure of recent effort. North America's ratio, notably, barely moved, and a ratio of 16.0 remains high for a rich region, though the data here do not explain it.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception that moves the wrong way: 74.0 in 2015 and 77.0 in 2023, classed as regression, with 79.7 expected in 2030. The region sits just above the threshold and is drifting from it. Plausible causes, stated without figures, include the disruption of pandemic years, pressure on obstetric services and persistent inequality in access to care within countries, but the modelled series cannot separate them.

### Country classes and population coverage

Counting countries gives a more favourable picture than counting the ratio. Of 194 countries, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of those assessed. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress needing acceleration. Another 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress. One country stagnates and 7 regress, together under 1% of the population.

This means the global shortfall is not a failure of most countries; it is concentrated in a minority of high-burden ones, where ratios are many times the threshold. Because the global ratio is weighted by births, and births are concentrated where mortality is highest, the global figure is governed by those countries. Population-weighted shares of countries on track therefore overstate how far the world's mothers are covered.

### Inequality and convergence

The spread among countries has not narrowed in the weighted measures. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.63 in 2015 and 0.64 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.74 to 0.79. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.9% to 67.2%, so differences within regions account for slightly more of the inequality than before. The unweighted coefficient of variation fell from 1.50 to 1.41, and the convergence regression gives a beta of -0.0037 (p 0.0024) with an R-squared of only 0.05. Countries with higher starting ratios did decline somewhat faster in proportional terms, yet the relationship explains little, and weighted inequality still rose. Convergence is therefore weak and not general.

### The effect of 2020 to 2023

The break analysis finds the world ratio rising by 4 points in 2020 and by 31 points in 2021, then falling by 39 points in 2022 and 6 points in 2023. The pandemic plausibly raised maternal deaths through direct infection, strained health systems and interrupted care, and the later fall reflects recovery. These annual moves must be read with caution. The series is modelled, built from regressions on fertility, birth attendance, GDP and the share of maternal deaths among deaths of women, so sharp swings partly reflect revisions of inputs and the modelling method rather than observed counts. The 2023 value of 197.0 is nonetheless below the 2015 value of 228.0, so the pandemic reversed progress temporarily without cancelling it.

### What 2030 requires

The measured paths imply that the global target depends on sub-Saharan Africa and the lower-middle-income group, where most deaths and the largest gaps lie. The principal causes of maternal death, haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders and sepsis, are largely preventable with skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care, blood supply and quality postnatal follow-up. Family planning and the prevention of unsafe abortion also lower the ratio. Health-system investment, not only coverage of birth attendance, determines whether complications are treated in time. Other sections of the chapter treat these supports in detail; here the finding is that, at the pace of 2015 to 2023, the world reaches about 173 and not below 70.

### Data limits

The series covers all 194 countries in every year from 2000, but this completeness comes from modelling. Completeness of death registration with cause-of-death information was last reported in 2017 and covers 121 countries, so in many countries the ratio rests on estimates rather than counted deaths. The numbers are most reliable where registration is strong, which is where ratios are lowest.

w-c06-3-1~dahlia/writer-1~46.text:
### What the latest figures show

The World Bank's compilation of UNICEF and Demographic and Health Survey data puts the share of women aged 20 to 24 who were first married by age 18 at 19.5% for the world in 2022. That is roughly one young woman in five. The aggregate hides a wide range. East Asia and the Pacific stands at 5.6% in 2022, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping at 17.7%, South Asia at 25.6% and Sub-Saharan Africa at 31.1%. By income, lower middle income countries record 24.4% and upper middle income countries 8.5%.

The indicator is a retrospective measure. Women aged 20 to 24 are asked when they first married or entered a union, so the figure describes the experience of a cohort that was aged 15 to 17 some three to nine years before the survey. A value for 2022 therefore reflects conditions in the middle and late 2010s, and the effects of any policy adopted recently will appear only with a lag. This matters for judging what happened after 2015 and, above all, after 2020, when the figures available can say almost nothing about the pandemic period.

Target 5.3 asks for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage. The indicator captures only the first of these, and only for girls. Forced marriage of adult women is not measured, nor is marriage of boys. Marriage before 18 is also not the same as marriage in law: some countries set a minimum age of 18, others permit marriage at 16 with consent, and customary or religious unions may fall outside civil registration. The survey asks about union as well as formal marriage, which is a strength, but the thresholds of 15 and 18 are conventions rather than a single reading of the target.

### Why the regional pattern persists

The regional ordering follows well-known causes. Child marriage is most common where household poverty is deep, where schooling for girls ends early or is far from home, where dowry or bride-price arrangements make a daughter an economic burden or asset, and where norms tie family honour to a girl's chastity. Conflict, displacement and climate shocks raise the risk, because families turn to marriage as protection or as a source of income. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia combine several of these pressures, which explains why their rates are above the world level, while East Asia and the Pacific, with near-universal lower secondary schooling in many economies, is far below it.

The income gradient is steep but not mechanical. The gap between lower middle income and upper middle income countries is large, at 24.4% against 8.5%, yet policy choices within income groups matter. Countries that have raised the legal minimum age, kept girls in secondary school through stipends or fee abolition, and enforced registration of marriages have moved faster than their income would predict. The data on offer do not isolate these effects, and the reading here rests on established knowledge of causes rather than on a test within the series.

### Inequality among countries

The spread measures show how unevenly the practice is distributed. Among the 21 countries reporting in 2012 and weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.282 and the Theil index 0.156. By 2018, with 20 countries reporting, the Gini was 0.273 and the Theil index 0.120. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.628 to 0.489. Dispersion among countries narrowed, which is consistent with high-prevalence countries falling toward the rest.

The composition of the remaining inequality changed. Between regions, the share of the Theil index was 73.0% in 2012 and 89.8% in 2018. In other words, nearly nine tenths of the difference among the reporting countries in 2018 was a difference between regions, and little was a difference within them. Two cautions apply. The country sets in the two years are not identical, so part of the change may reflect who was surveyed. And the surveys are concentrated in lower income countries, so the spread describes inequality among surveyed countries, not among all countries. Even so, the finding suggests that regional approaches, rather than country-by-country exceptions, are the natural unit for action.

### Progress against the 2030 target

The trend assessment measures each country against a target of zero by 2030. Of 20 countries assessed, none is on track or has met the target, and that class holds 0.0% of their population. Two countries, with 5.8% of the assessed population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Fourteen countries, with 91.8% of the population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country, with 0.8%, is stagnating, and three countries, with 1.6%, are regressing.

The result is stark: almost the whole assessed population lives in countries whose present pace will not reach zero. A target of exactly zero is demanding, and a more lenient reading, such as a rate in single digits, would change the classification. Under any reading, however, the pace described is slow. The regressing countries deserve attention even though their share of population is small, because reversals often follow conflict, economic collapse or the closure of schools, and they signal where protection has failed.

The 2015 to 2020 and post-2020 periods cannot be separated cleanly. Schools closed widely in 2020 and 2021, household incomes fell, and child protection services were disrupted. Analysts widely expected a rise in early marriage as a result. The series cannot confirm or refute that expectation, since cohorts marrying in those years appear in surveys only later, and reporting for 2025 stands at three countries only.

### Data coverage and its limits

Coverage explains much of the uncertainty. The series holds 145 countries reporting in at least one year, yet in any single year the count is small: 21 in 2012, 11 in 2015, 20 in 2018, 12 in 2020, 18 in 2022, 12 in 2024 and 3 in 2025. Surveys arrive every three to five years in each country, so annual aggregates are built from different countries in different years. The world value of 19.5% is a modelled or composite estimate for 2022, and comparison of one year's aggregate with another's should be made cautiously.

The companion series on marriage before age 15 and on female genital mutilation, which share a legal and normative setting with child marriage, are not analysed in the results here. Female genital mutilation is reported by only 30 countries, with the latest year 2023, and is therefore a thin basis for global statements. Both practices are concentrated in particular regions and called for in the same target, yet they do not overlap fully, and a country with low child marriage may still have high cutting.

### Proposals

The findings point to action on schooling, law and measurement. Each proposal below names those responsible.

Donors and regional bodies should concentrate funds on the regions that account for nearly nine tenths of the remaining inequality between countries, and should give early attention to the countries where rates are rising.

National statistical offices, with UNICEF and the DHS Program, should field surveys on a regular cycle and publish the post-2020 cohorts promptly, so that the pandemic's effect on early marriage can be measured.

The trend classification covers 20 countries, not all 145. w-c04-4-1~farah/writer-1~46.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a reduction by one third in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator used here is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the age of 70 from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific rates and no other cause of death. The series reports 185 countries in 2021. The baseline year is read here as 2015, the year the goals took effect. The target can be read in more than one way, since the wording does not fix a baseline year. The trend tool applies a threshold of 12.57 per cent for 2030, which is two thirds of the world's 2015 value of 18.9 per cent.

The world figure stood at 18.9 per cent in 2015 and at 18.3 per cent in 2021. That is a fall of about 0.6 percentage points in six years, or roughly a thirtieth of the baseline value. A one-third reduction would require the figure to reach 12.6 per cent. The trend tool projects 17.5 per cent for 2030 on the current rate, and rates the world's progress as marginal, with a ratio of 0.22 of the pace required. The target will not be met at the global level on present evidence.

### Progress slowed after 2015

The break analysis places a structural break in the annual change of the world series at 2015. In the period from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was a fall of 0.26 percentage points. From 2015 to 2021 the mean annual change was a fall of only 0.09 percentage points. The decline therefore slowed to about a third of its earlier pace just as the goals began. The series ends in 2021, so the pandemic years fall inside the later segment, and the data cannot separate the effect of COVID-19 from a longer slowdown. The pandemic disrupted screening, diagnosis, and treatment of chronic conditions, and people with cardiovascular disease and diabetes were at higher risk of death from infection. Both effects may have held back the series, but the indicator excludes deaths from other causes, so only the indirect effects appear in it.

The slowdown also fits a wider pattern. Gains in cardiovascular mortality in wealthy countries, driven by blood pressure control, lower smoking and better acute care, have been large but are subject to diminishing returns. Rising obesity and diabetes push in the opposite direction. In low-income settings, hypertension and diabetes are frequently undiagnosed and untreated, and cancer is often found late.

### Regions diverge, and one is moving backwards

High-income countries fell from 13.8 per cent in 2015 to 12.8 per cent in 2021, and they are the only group the trend tool rates as on track, with an expected 11.4 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 1.93. Europe and Central Asia fell furthest in absolute terms, from 17.5 per cent to 15.7 per cent, with an expected 13.4 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.82. It is judged moderate progress needing acceleration. North America moved from 13.6 per cent to 13.3 per cent, with an expected 12.8 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.82, so it sits close to the threshold but has a slow rate of decline.

East Asia and Pacific fell from 17.8 per cent to 16.9 per cent, expecting 15.6 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.42. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 15.3 per cent to 14.7 per cent, expecting 13.9 per cent and a ratio of 0.50. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3 per cent to 20.7 per cent, expecting 18.5 per cent and a ratio of 0.39. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 21.9 per cent to 21.3 per cent, expecting 20.4 per cent and a ratio of 0.16.

South Asia is the one region where the indicator rose, from 22.1 per cent in 2015 to 22.9 per cent in 2021. The trend tool classes this as regression, with an expected 24.0 per cent in 2030. South Asia thus moved from a level close to that of Sub-Saharan Africa to the highest regional level in the data. Regional aggregates conceal national differences, and the figures should not be read as applying to every country in a group.

### Income groups show stagnation in the lower middle

By income, low-income countries fell from 24.0 per cent to 23.0 per cent, which leaves them with the highest level of any group and a ratio of 0.22 against the required pace. Lower middle income countries moved from 22.8 per cent to 22.8 per cent, an almost exactly flat result, and the trend tool labels it stagnation with a ratio of 0.004. This group contains very large populations, and its stagnation weighs heavily on the world figure. Upper middle income countries fell from 18.1 per cent to 17.1 per cent, with a ratio of 0.45. High-income countries stand lowest, as noted above.

The gap between the highest and lowest income groups remained large. In 2021 low-income countries had a figure about 10.2 percentage points above that of high-income countries. The ordering of the groups did not change between 2015 and 2021, and the lower middle income group lost ground relative to those above it.

### Inequality among countries is rising, not falling

The spread tool, weighting countries by population, finds a Gini coefficient of 0.15 in 2015 and 0.16 in 2021. The Theil index rose from 0.04 to 0.04 at the precision available, with values of 0.038 and 0.041. The share of Theil inequality lying between regions rose from 27.0 per cent to 33.1 per cent. Differences among regions are therefore a growing part of the total, consistent with the pattern of South Asia moving up while Europe and high-income countries moved down.

The convergence analysis shows no catching up. Across 185 countries, the coefficient of a regression of change on starting level is 0.0016, with a p-value of 0.70 and an R-squared of 0.001. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.36 to 0.38. Countries with high initial mortality did not improve faster than others, and the relation is statistically indistinguishable from none. A convergence of the kind seen in child mortality, where the worst-off countries gained fastest, is absent here.

### Health coverage for non-communicable diseases shows a weak link

The links tool compares changes in the indicator with the UHC service coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases, which rests on hypertension treatment, diabetes control and tobacco use. Across 184 countries the rank correlation of changes from 2015 to 2021 is 0.10, which is weak and positive, the wrong sign if better coverage were to lower mortality. The rank correlation of 2021 levels is -0.25, a moderate negative association: countries with higher coverage tend to have lower premature mortality. The level association is cross-sectional and also reflects income, so it does not show cause. The absence of a relation in changes suggests that over six years coverage gains did not translate into measurable mortality gains, perhaps because the effect lags, because tracer indicators capture only part of care, or because mortality moves through slow-changing risk factors.

### Implications for 2030

The target will be missed globally on present trends, and only high-income countries are on course. Reaching it would require an annual fall several times the 2015 to 2021 pace, and the later pace was already a third of the pace in 2001 to 2014. The most pressing concerns are South Asia, where the indicator is rising, and the lower middle income group, where it is flat. Because the indicator is a probability over forty years of life, it responds slowly to risk-factor change, and gains in this decade depend mainly on treatment of existing hypertension, diabetes and cancer.

Suicide mortality, the second part of the target's concern for mental health, is carried by series on rates per 100,000 population for both sexes and for males. No result on suicide was produced for this section, so no finding on it is given here.

proposals: Ministries of health in South Asia and lower middle income countries should make hypertension and diabetes detection and treatment in primary care a first call on budgets, since these two groups account for the stagnation and regression in the series.

The World Health Organization and development financiers should fund national cancer and chronic respiratory disease programmes in low-income countries, where mortality remains highest and gains are slowest.

Governments should strengthen tobacco, salt and sugar regulation, which acts on risk factors that move the indicator over a decade, and report coverage and outcomes together so that the weak link between them can be tested.
The World Health Organization should publish national estimates for 2022 onwards promptly so that the pandemic's effect can be separated from the longer slowdown.
w-c04-4-1~farah/writer-1~46.gaps: The series ends in 2021, so effects after the pandemic are not visible, and the pandemic cannot be separated from the earlier slowdown. The indicator is modelled by the World Health Organization and not directly observed in many countries. It covers four disease groups only, and excludes mental health, injuries and other conditions. Suicide series were on the shelf but no result on them was produced, so the mental health half of target 3.4 is not assessed here. The target's baseline year is not fixed in its wording, and the choice of 2015 is an assumption. The data give no separate results by sex in this section, and no results on causes, risk factors or quality of care.

w-c06-1-1~ewan/writer-1~47.text:
### The legal record now covers almost every economy, but the shelf holds only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that pays her pension at an earlier age and so on a shorter contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. That is why the measurement of laws has become one of the clearest windows on progress towards the target: it records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom.

The instrument used here is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life: safety from violence and harassment, freedom of movement, the right to work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, so a country that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left inheritance and property law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in any year. The two numbers being equal is itself informative. Nearly every member of the United Nations system is scored, and no economy that was once covered has dropped out. For a measure of national law, which can be read from statute books and does not depend on a household survey or an administrative register, such completeness is to be expected, and it contrasts sharply with the patchy coverage of the outcome indicators elsewhere in this chapter.

Coverage, however, is all that the bench has so far computed for this series. No level, regional average or change over time has been drawn from the shelf for this section, and the account that follows therefore does not state any score. That is a real limitation and it is stated plainly here rather than hidden: the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed can be answered in direction and in structure from the well-documented history of reform, but not yet in magnitude from the numbers this book is bound to use. What the coverage result does establish is that the answer, once computed, will rest on a full census of economies rather than a sample.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index, which the World Bank published for more than a decade and which was widely cited in the first years of the Goals, scored a narrower set of legal questions and gave most economies high marks once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds two domains that the earlier one largely omitted, safety and childcare, and it sits alongside two companion indices also held on the shelf: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts in each country judge the law to work in practice.

This matters for interpretation in three ways. First, scores under the new framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index, and any reader who remembers the older numbers should not set the new ones beside them as though they measured the same thing. Second, the inclusion of safety and childcare lowers the apparent standing of many economies that had been regarded as close to legal parity. Few countries legislate comprehensively against sexual harassment in public spaces and online, criminalise every form of domestic violence including economic and psychological abuse, and require or subsidise childcare services with quality standards. A country can therefore have abolished every explicit restriction on women's work and still be far from the top of the revised scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history is short. The coverage tool's report that the same 189 economies appear in any year and in 2025 is consistent with a series whose run is recent; whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, which this book uses as its baseline, has not been verified by the bench, and where it does not, a change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index at all.

The pairing of the three indices is the most important innovation for target 5.1. The target's own wording speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. A legal framework score records what the statute book says; the supportive framework score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give it effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The gap between the first and the other two is the gap between a promise and its delivery. It is widely understood from the project's own publications that this gap is large almost everywhere, and that the economies with the most complete laws are not always those whose institutions and courts carry them out. Measuring that gap country by country is the natural next computation for this section, and it is the subject of the petition attached to it.

### The direction of reform since 2015 is clear even where its size is not

The history of the past decade, as recorded in successive editions of the World Bank's reports and in national legislation, runs in one direction. Reforms that remove discrimination greatly outnumber those that introduce it. The most common changes have been of a recognisable kind. Many governments repealed rules that barred women from industrial jobs, night work, mining or work deemed arduous or dangerous, provisions that were originally framed as protection and that in practice excluded women from better-paid sectors. Many introduced or strengthened laws against sexual harassment at work, often with civil remedies or criminal penalties. A number mandated equal remuneration for work of equal value, rather than merely for identical work, which is the standard that addresses occupational segregation. Several equalised the ages at which men and women may retire with a full pension, or credited periods of childcare in pension calculations. Paid paternity leave, rare at the start of the period, spread steadily, and some countries introduced shared parental leave designed to reduce the penalty that employers attach to hiring women of childbearing age.

Reform in the domains of marriage and assets has been slower. Provisions that require a wife to obey her husband, that make the husband the legal head of household, that deny a woman the right to choose where to live or to obtain a passport on the same terms as a man, and that give daughters smaller shares of inheritance than sons are rooted in personal-status and family codes that are frequently tied to religious law or customary authority. Governments have proved more willing to change labour codes, which they see as instruments of economic policy, than family codes, which touch questions of identity and legitimacy. The result is a characteristic pattern: an economy may score well on work and pay while scoring poorly on marriage, mobility and assets, and the unweighted average conceals the fact that the remaining restrictions concentrate in the private sphere that governs a woman's ability to act independently in the first place.

The period after 2015 added two forces to this long trend. The Goals themselves gave governments a reference point and a reporting obligation; target 5.1 and its indicator placed legal frameworks on the agenda of every voluntary national review. And the evidence base widened. As economists documented the cost of women's exclusion from paid work to national income, finance ministries and development banks began to treat discriminatory law as a constraint on growth rather than a purely social question, and reform of the legal environment for women became a condition or an objective in a number of lending programmes. Reform waves in parts of the Middle East and North Africa and in sub-Saharan Africa during the late 2010s, including the removal of guardianship requirements for some legal acts and of bans on women's work in certain sectors, were among the most visible results.

### After 2020 the agenda broadened, and implementation became the binding constraint

The pandemic that began in 2020 tested the legal frameworks that had been built. It demonstrated that childcare is economic infrastructure: when schools and nurseries closed, the burden fell disproportionately on women, many of whom left paid work, and the absence of legal entitlements to care services or to flexible working arrangements was felt directly. It also coincided with a widely reported rise in domestic violence during lockdowns, which exposed the distance between laws that exist on paper and the shelters, hotlines, protection orders and police training that make them usable. The decision of the World Bank to add safety and childcare to the legal measure, and to pair it with indices of supportive frameworks and enforcement, can be read as a response to precisely these lessons.

The broad conclusion of the project's recent publications is that legislative reform did continue after 2020, though at a pace that varied sharply across regions and that has been insufficient to close the gap within the Goals' timetable. The more striking finding, and the one that the paired indices were built to reveal, is that the shortfall in implementation exceeds the shortfall in law. Many countries have passed statutes for which no regulations were issued, no budget allocated and no agency charged with enforcement. Equal pay laws without pay-transparency requirements or a labour inspectorate able to investigate complaints change little. Parental leave paid by employers rather than through social insurance gives employers a reason to avoid hiring women. Harassment laws without accessible complaint procedures or protection against retaliation are rarely invoked. The legal framework index is therefore an upper bound on the protection women actually enjoy, and progress measured by it alone will overstate progress towards target 5.1.

There has also been reversal. In a small number of countries, political change since 2020 has removed rights that had been granted, restricting women's movement, education and employment by decree. The coverage of the index includes such cases, and its census character is valuable here: an economy cannot leave the measure by ceasing to report, because the measure is constructed from its laws rather than from its statistics. The fact that 189 economies are scored in 2025, the same number as in any year, means that backsliding is recorded rather than lost.

### How regions and income groups differ, and what the distribution implies for 2030

The coverage tool identifies the aggregates for which the shelf can report the index: the world, the World Bank's high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups, and South Asia. Values for these aggregates have not yet been computed for this section, so their ordering cannot be stated with the book's numbers. The structure of the differences is nevertheless well established in the literature of the project and is worth setting out so that the reader knows what the computation should test.

High-income economies, above all those of the OECD, generally have the most complete legal frameworks, but none has reached full equality under the revised measure, largely because of gaps in childcare provision, in pension treatment of career breaks, and in the comprehensiveness of laws on violence. Upper-middle-income economies are heterogeneous: Latin America and the Caribbean and parts of Europe and Central Asia have undertaken extensive reform, while some resource-rich economies retain restrictive family law. The lowest scores are concentrated in the Middle East and North Africa and in South Asia, where personal-status codes still restrict mobility, marriage and inheritance, and in parts of sub-Saharan Africa where statutory and customary law coexist and the latter governs land and inheritance for much of the rural population. Sub-Saharan Africa has nevertheless been among the most active reforming regions, which is a reminder that the level of a score and its rate of change tell different stories.

The relation between income and law is real but loose. Low-income status does not prevent comprehensive legal reform, and several low-income and lower-middle-income economies have legal frameworks more equal than those of richer neighbours. Where income matters most is in the supportive and enforcement dimensions: courts, inspectorates, social-insurance systems that pay maternity and paternity benefits, and publicly funded childcare all cost money and administrative capacity. A plausible expectation, to be tested when the three indices are compared, is that the gap between law and its implementation is widest in low-income economies, so that the legal index flatters them more than it flatters richer countries.

For 2030 the implications are sober. Target 5.1 says all forms of discrimination, everywhere. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale, which under the revised measure no economy has done, and which at the historical pace of reform would take far longer than the years remaining. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform, which the record does show. The target can thus be read in more than one way, and the book's verdict depends on the reading: on the strict reading the target will be missed by a wide margin; on the directional reading it is being pursued, unevenly. What the distribution implies is that the remaining work is concentrated in particular domains rather than spread evenly. The labour-market provisions that were easiest to reform have largely been reformed in many places; what remains is family law, property and inheritance, comprehensive protection from violence, and the institutions of care. These are harder politically and costlier fiscally, and the pace of the past decade is unlikely to be sustained without deliberate effort. Because the indicators of violence, child marriage, decision-making and ownership treated in other sections of this chapter all depend in part on these remaining legal provisions, slow progress here will constrain progress there.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of this index. First, it scores the formal law of the largest business city in each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that apply to most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law governs marriage and land. Second, a perfect legal score is a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but far from a sufficient one. Social norms, the distribution of unpaid care, discrimination by employers that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much women's work all lie beyond the reach of a statute. The index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them.

With those cautions, the legal framework index remains the most complete instrument available for target 5.1, and its near-universal coverage of 189 economies makes it unusually suitable for a global account. The task for the remaining years is to convert that coverage into a measured record of change, by domain and by region, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every country.

claims.fact: c06-1.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Legislatures in economies that retain husband-headship, obedience, guardianship or unequal inheritance provisions in family and personal-status codes should repeal them before 2030, since these domains now hold most of the remaining legal discrimination.

Finance and labour ministries should attach regulations, budgets and an enforcing agency to every equality statute at the moment of its passage, including pay-transparency duties and an inspectorate empowered to act on equal-pay complaints.

Governments should finance maternity and paternity benefits through social insurance or general revenue rather than employer liability, and legislate for publicly supported childcare with quality standards, so that leave and care rights do not penalise the hiring of women.

The World Bank's Women, Business and the Law team should publish a back-cast of the revised legal framework index to 2015 and the subnational coverage of plural legal systems, so that change since the Goals' adoption can be measured on one consistent scale.

National statistical offices and voluntary national reviews should report the legal, supportive-framework and enforcement scores side by side, treating the gap between them as the headline measure of progress on target 5.1.

It is unverified whether the revised-methodology series on the shelf extends back to 2015; if not, change since the Goals' adoption cannot be measured with it, and the earlier index is not comparable. The companion Supportive Framework and Enforcement Perceptions indices were not analysed. The index scores formal law in the main business city and does not capture customary or religious law in rural areas, subnational variation in federal states, or women's actual use of legal rights; no series on the shelf measures court use, complaints filed or enforcement outcomes.

w-c03-5-1~cedar/writer-4~47.text:
### Land under farming has barely moved

Agricultural land, which the World Bank defines as arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, covered 36.8 per cent of the world's land area in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023. The global footprint of farming has therefore been essentially constant across the Goal period. Regional shifts are small. East Asia & Pacific rose from 46.5 per cent to 46.8 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 43.9 per cent to 44.7 per cent. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 33.3 per cent to 32.9 per cent, Europe & Central Asia from 29.3 per cent to 29.1 per cent, and South Asia from 58.6 per cent to 58.3 per cent. North America stayed near 26.7 per cent.

The income groups tell the same story. Low income countries moved from 41.4 per cent to 42.1 per cent, lower middle income countries from 42.5 per cent to 43.0 per cent, upper middle income countries from 43.1 per cent to 42.8 per cent, and high income countries from 28.1 per cent to 28.2 per cent. The pattern is a slight expansion where population and poverty are greatest and a slight contraction in upper middle income economies. Share of land is a coarse measure: it does not distinguish pasture from cropland, nor say whether land is degrading, and a stable share can conceal conversion of forest at one frontier offset by abandonment elsewhere. Target 2.4 asks for production systems that maintain ecosystems, so a flat footprint is compatible with progress but is not evidence of it.

### Fertiliser use differs by a factor of more than ten

Fertiliser consumption is the sharpest contrast in the section. The world averaged 132.9 kilograms of nutrients per hectare of arable land in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, a small rise. Behind this lie very different levels. East Asia & Pacific used 329.1 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 304.1 in 2023, the highest of any region and the only large one in clear decline. That fall is consistent with policy in the largest producers to limit nutrient overuse and its runoff, though the data alone do not identify the cause. South Asia rose from 175.0 to 206.0 kilograms, and Latin America & Caribbean from 135.1 to 173.9, the largest proportional gain among the large regions, reflecting expanding export cropping.

Sub-Saharan Africa applied 14.4 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023. Low income countries moved from 10.0 to 13.9. These are a small fraction of the world average, and the rise, though proportionally sizeable, leaves the gap vast. Low application reflects high input prices, weak distribution, thin credit and risk to smallholders, not a deliberate choice of sustainable practice; it goes with nutrient mining of soils and low yields. Other groups: lower middle income countries rose from 114.6 to 130.8; upper middle income countries were almost unchanged, from 213.0 to 213.8; high income countries slipped from 106.3 to 104.3. Europe & Central Asia moved from 78.7 to 76.0, North America from 124.3 to 128.8, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 90.0 to 102.0.

The sustainability reading therefore runs in opposite directions. Where application is above 300 kilograms, the concern is excess: nitrogen losses to water and air, and greenhouse gas emissions. Where it is below 20, the concern is too little: depleted soils and stagnant output. A single global target for fertiliser would mislead; the aim is better-matched application, which the per-hectare average cannot show.

### Dispersion in fertiliser use is narrowing

A convergence test across 192 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.034 (p-value effectively zero) with an R-squared of 0.3. Countries starting with high application tended to grow more slowly, or shrink, while low-use countries grew faster. The coefficient of variation fell from 2.15 in 2015 to 1.68 in 2022. Dispersion remains large, since a coefficient above 1.00 signals a distribution with a long upper tail, but it is narrowing. The pattern is partly arithmetic, as small bases grow fast from small absolute increments, and the test says nothing about whether the narrowing is desirable. Convergence driven by cuts at the top and gains at the bottom is the most favourable form; the regional levels above suggest both occurred, though unevenly.

### Water withdrawal is dominated by irrigation

Agriculture accounted for 71.5 per cent of total freshwater withdrawals worldwide in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. Reporting covered 178 countries in 2022. The share is highest where incomes are lowest and climates driest. Low income countries stood at 90.8 per cent in 2015 and 90.9 per cent in 2022; lower middle income countries at 89.4 and 88.8; upper middle income at 74.7 and 73.6; high income at 42.2 and 42.7. In low income economies farming is nearly the whole of water use because industry and municipal demand are small, so the figure reflects the structure of the economy rather than waste.

Regionally, South Asia stood at 90.3 per cent in both years, an identical figure that suggests the series was carried forward rather than newly measured, and it should be read with caution. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 90.1 to 87.3 per cent, possibly as desalination and urban demand grew. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 78.6 to 79.0, Latin America & Caribbean from 73.4 to 74.4, East Asia & Pacific from 73.2 to 72.1, Europe & Central Asia from 52.0 to 51.8, and North America from 37.3 to 37.5. The shifts are all within about three percentage points over seven years. The indicator is a share, so it cannot show whether absolute withdrawals are sustainable against renewable supply, which matters most in the driest regions.

### Intensity, yields and the 2030 outlook

Inputs matter because of what they yield. Across 179 countries from 2015 to 2022, the Spearman correlation between fertiliser use and cereal yield in 2022 levels was 0.72, a strong association. The correlation between changes over the period was only 0.13, weak. Countries that apply more have higher yields, but countries that increased use did not reliably raise yields faster. Soil, seed, water control, pest management and the starting level all intervene, and levels also reflect long history and climate. Fertiliser is not a sufficient route to productivity.

Cereal yield trends are uneven. The world rate was 0.009 on the tool's scale, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures pace against a notional improvement, and it is one reading among several. North America (8,414 kilograms per hectare in 2024), South Asia (3,814) and lower middle income countries (3,366) were classed on track. Sub-Saharan Africa was stagnant at 1,443 in 2015 and 1,453 in 2024, and low income countries regressed from 1,373 to 1,345. Of 180 countries assessed, 39 (29.5 per cent of their population) were on track, 19 (14.0 per cent) moderate, 27 (25.7 per cent) marginal, 25 (15.6 per cent) stagnant and 70 (15.2 per cent) regressing. Some regression may reflect weather in the end year.

For 2030, the evidence points to a split agenda. The poorest regions have low inputs, high dependence on irrigation withdrawal, stagnant yields and a slowly expanding agricultural footprint, so growth in output has leaned on land and not on intensity. Wealthier and fast-growing regions already use heavy inputs and must raise efficiency. The data after 2015 show no visible break after 2020 in the aggregate shares, which are too slow-moving to register shocks such as the pandemic or the fertiliser price spike of 2022.

w-c03-2-1~willow/writer-2~47.text:
### Stunting has eased slowly since 2015

Global stunting among children under five fell from 24.6% in 2015 to 23.2% in 2024, a fall of 1.4 percentage points in nine years. The modelled estimate is a prevalence, the share of children whose height for age is more than two standard deviations below the WHO 2006 median. A fall of this size is small against the task of the 2025 target, which the trend tool reads as 5.0% for stunting. The world trend tool classes the global path as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. At the observed rate the world would stand at 22.3% in 2030, far above 5.0%. The ratio of observed to required progress is 0.12.

The target text in Target 2.2 speaks of the internationally agreed 2025 goals, whereas the trend tool measures to 2030. Neither date will be met on this evidence. The target can also be read in more than one way: the internationally agreed thresholds are expressed in relative reductions, and a fixed 5.0% benchmark is a stricter reading for countries starting from high levels. Under either reading the global result falls short.

### Regions diverge, and the burden is concentrated

South Asia fell furthest, from 37.8% in 2015 to 31.5% in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 34.4% to 32.3%. Sub-Saharan Africa now has the highest regional prevalence, overtaking South Asia in relative terms. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group fell from 27.5% to 24.1%. East Asia and Pacific moved from 14.5% to 13.3%, and Europe and Central Asia from 6.0% to 4.6%. Latin America and the Caribbean was flat, 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, which the trend tool labels regression. North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%, and the high-income group from 3.9% to 4.0%. These low levels are close to the reference threshold, and small movements there reflect modelling and sampling noise as much as real change.

By income group, low-income countries moved from 38.0% to 35.8%, lower-middle-income countries from 33.9% to 28.9%, and upper-middle-income countries from 11.9% to 10.8%. Lower-middle-income countries made the largest gain, helped by large South Asian populations where sanitation, maternal schooling, social transfers and health services have improved over a long period. Low-income countries, where conflict, poverty and weak health systems are common, improved least. Every group other than Europe and Central Asia, and the high-income groups already near the benchmark, is classed as marginal progress or regression.

### Divergence, not convergence, across countries

Across 162 countries, the convergence test finds no tendency for high-stunting countries to improve faster. The beta coefficient is -0.002 with a p-value of 0.23 and an R-squared of 0.01, so initial level explains almost none of the change. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024, so dispersion across countries widened. Progress has been uneven, and a growing share of the remaining burden sits in a smaller set of countries that are poor, fragile or both. Stunting has deep roots in maternal health, early feeding, infection and poverty, so it moves slowly, and shocks such as the pandemic after 2020, food price rises and conflict can offset gains.

### Wasting is measured thinly but shows a similar gap

Global wasting, the share of children whose weight for height is more than two standard deviations below the median, fell from 7.1% in 2015 to 6.6% in 2024. The benchmark for wasting under the trend tool is 5.0% by 2030. South Asia stands far above all other regions, at 16.6% in 2015 and 15.7% in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 7.0% to 5.9%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 6.5% to 5.6%. East Asia and Pacific moved from 3.7% to 3.6%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.5% to 1.3%, and Europe and Central Asia from 1.5% to 1.0%. By income, low-income countries fell from 7.9% to 6.4%, lower-middle-income from 10.5% to 9.5%, upper-middle-income from 2.6% to 2.1%, and high-income from 0.6% to 0.4%.

Wasting is acute and can change within months with famine, illness or displacement, so annual survey values swing more than stunting. For this reason caution is needed in reading regional changes of under one point.

### Country trends and the reliability of the evidence

Of 65 countries assessed for wasting, 42 are on track or have met the target, holding 38.6% of the population of those assessed. Four, with 7.8%, show moderate progress needing acceleration, and three, with 33.7%, show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. None stagnate, and 16 are in regression, with 19.9% of the population. The three slow-moving countries carry a third of the assessed population, so a favourable count of countries hides a large unmet burden.

The assessment is incomplete. Only 65 of 162 countries could be assessed on wasting, and in 2024 only 6 countries reported a wasting value, compared with 32 in 2015 and 51 in 2014. Reporting has fallen to 24 countries in 2023 and 6 in 2024. Because wasting rests on household surveys, which occur every few years, the 2024 regional figures are modelled or carried from earlier surveys, and the 2024 value should be read as provisional. The stunting series reports 162 countries in 2024 but is also modelled in many cases.

### Implications for 2030

On present rates neither the 2025 nor the 2030 stunting target will be met at world level or in any developing region. Meeting 5.0% by 2030 from 23.2% would need a fall far faster than the 0.15 points a year seen since 2015. Wasting is closer but depends on South Asia, and on keeping the 16 regressing countries from sliding further. The policy levers are well established: maternal nutrition and adolescent health, breastfeeding support, complementary feeding, treatment of severe acute malnutrition, clean water and sanitation, and social protection that sustains food access in shocks.

w-c02-1-1~rowan/writer-1~47.text:
### The international line and the target

Target 1.1 as written refers to people living on less than $1.25 a day. That line has been revised several times since the goals were adopted, and the series on the shelf is measured at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices. The target can therefore be read in more than one way: as the eradication of poverty at the original line, or as its eradication at the current extreme line. This section uses the latter, with the target value set at zero by 2030. Eradication is also not defined as exactly zero in the source; a reading of 3 per cent or less is often used in international discussion, but the trend tool applied here tests against zero, which is the stricter reading. The conclusions below are therefore conservative in one respect and should be read with that in mind.

The world headcount ratio at $3.00 a day fell from 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 to 10.1 per cent in 2024. That is a fall of 3.3 percentage points over nine years. The trend tool gives a world rate of change of -0.03092 on its own scale, an expected value of 8.365 per cent in 2030, and a ratio of progress to required progress of 0.376, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. On present trends, the world would reach 2030 with roughly one person in twelve still below the line, not with none.

### Where poverty has fallen and where it has not

The aggregate conceals very different regional stories. East Asia and the Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Its ratio of progress is 0.844 and the expected 2030 value is 0.951 per cent, so the region is close to the lower bound of what a survey-based series can distinguish from zero. Europe and Central Asia moved from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent, with an expected 2030 value of 0.378 per cent. Upper middle income economies fell from 5.8 per cent to 2.1 per cent. These are the places where growth, wage employment and public transfers have worked together over decades, and where the remaining poor are increasingly a residual group that is harder to reach.

South Asia is the most striking improvement in the data, with a caveat. The series for the region begins in 2020 on the shelf, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The trend tool classes it as on track, with a ratio of 0.96 and an expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent. A fall of this size in four years is large, and part of it reflects the arrival of new survey rounds in large countries and the revision of earlier estimates, not only a real change in living standards. Because the window is short and starts after the pandemic shock, the on-track classification rests on thin evidence and should be treated as provisional.

Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent, with an expected 2030 value of 3.4436 per cent and a ratio of 0.426. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent and high-income economies from 0.7 per cent to 0.6 per cent. In these richer settings the measured shares are small, and the line is not the relevant yardstick for domestic policy; poverty is better captured by national lines, which another section of this chapter treats.

### Concentration in low-income and conflict-affected settings

The target will be decided in two groups. In Sub-Saharan Africa the headcount ratio was 45.4 per cent in 2015 and 45.0 per cent in 2024. The trend tool classes this as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.015 and an expected 2030 value of 44.7353 per cent. Population growth is high in the region, so an almost unchanged share means that the number of people below the line has risen. The share is a rate, and the data on the shelf do not give counts, so that statement rests on well-established demographic knowledge, not on a figure from this series.

Low-income countries as a group moved the wrong way, from 50.1 per cent in 2015 to 52.5 per cent in 2024. The trend tool classes this as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 54.1635 per cent. The group is defined by income and contains many states affected by conflict, weak revenue systems and dependence on rain-fed agriculture. Lower middle income economies fell from 16.0 per cent in 2020 to 12.4 per cent in 2024, with an expected 2030 value of 8.4601 per cent and a ratio of 0.471, which is marginal progress.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 11.3 per cent in 2015 to 14.3 per cent in 2024. Its expected 2030 value is 16.7305 per cent and the tool classes it as regression with a ratio of -0.481. Armed conflict, displacement and macroeconomic crises in several economies of the grouping are the established causes of such reversals. The regional grouping is also unusual in combining very different economies, so the aggregate should not be read as a uniform experience.

### Country classes and the pace of change

Across the 105 countries with enough data to be assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.6 per cent of the population of the assessed group. A further 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, holding 23.1 per cent. Another 15 show marginal progress, holding 11.3 per cent. Seven countries are stagnating, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.9 per cent of the assessed population. The weight of the on-track class is dominated by a few very populous countries, which is why the share of population is so much larger than the share of countries. Nearly a fifth of the assessed population lives in countries where poverty at this line is rising.

The breaks analysis of the world series locates changes in the pace of decline in 2014 and 2021. From 2001 to 2013 the mean annual change was -1.592 percentage points. From 2014 to 2018 it was -0.88, and from 2021 to 2024 it was -0.325. The pace of reduction has therefore slowed in each period. The goals were adopted just after the first slowdown, and the second reflects the pandemic, the subsequent inflation in food and energy prices and tighter fiscal space in many poorer economies. To reach zero from 10.1 per cent by 2030 would need roughly 1.7 percentage points a year, several times the latest pace.

Convergence is absent. Across 57 countries with data in both 2015 and 2022, the beta coefficient is 0.006583 with a p-value of 0.3958 and an R-squared of 0.0286. The coefficient of variation rose from 2.1437 to 2.6754. Countries with high initial poverty did not fall faster than the rest, and dispersion widened. This matches the regional picture: the remaining poverty is increasingly concentrated, and the aggregate gains of the largest economies do not carry over to the poorest.

### Data limits on the reading

Coverage shapes every finding. The number of countries reporting rose to 93 in 2018 and has fallen since, to 70 in 2020, 81 in 2021, 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and only 4 in 2025. The latest years are therefore largely modelled or projected values for aggregates, and survey gaps are widest in the places with the highest poverty, where surveys are costly and conflict makes them hard to run. Estimates for 2024 should be read as provisional. The 2030 values given here are linear extrapolations of past trends, not forecasts, and a sharp policy or economic change would alter them.

The world target is out of reach on present trends: 10.1 per cent in 2024, an expected 8.365 per cent in 2030, and a classification of marginal progress. Reaching it would require ending poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income and conflict-affected economies, where the share is stagnant or rising, not continuing the gains made in Asia.

w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-1~48.text:
### What the shelf holds on disaster exposure

Target 1.5 asks for reduced exposure and vulnerability of the poor to climate-related extreme events by 2030. The World Bank's catalogue offers three series bearing on it, and they differ sharply in vintage. The share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures is an average for 1990 to 2009, reported for 168 countries in a single year of record, 2009. The disaster risk reduction progress score, a self-assessment on a scale of 1 to 5, dates from 2011 and covers 83 countries. Only the series on new displacement associated with disasters, from the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, runs to 2023, and it is the only one that can speak to the period after 2015.

The two older series are therefore baselines, not trends. They cannot show whether exposure has fallen since the Sendai Framework replaced the Hyogo Framework, and they cannot show the effect of the pandemic years. The remainder of this section relies on displacement, which counts events of flight, not people: the unit is the number of cases, so one person displaced twice is counted twice.

### Displacement has risen since 2015

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19188817 cases in 2015 and 26393278 in 2023. That is a rise of roughly a third over eight years. Disaster displacement is highly episodic, driven by a few large storms, floods and monsoon seasons, so a pair of end years can mislead. The break analysis for the world series found no structural break in annual change. It reports a mean annual change of -789789.7 cases over 2009 to 2023, a negative figure that sits uneasily beside the rise since 2015. The two are reconcilable only because the series is volatile and the early years were unusually high; the mean over the whole segment is not a reliable guide to direction, and the endpoints comparison should be read with the same caution.

The movement cannot be separated from improved recording. The number of countries reporting new displacement was 80 in 2008, 60 in 2009 and 62 in 2011, rose to 118 in 2013, and reached 112 in 2015 and 145 in 2023. Part of any increase in the totals is therefore better observation, not more displacement. The world total is partly an aggregate over a changing set of countries, and a falling count in a country that stopped reporting is indistinguishable from a real fall.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional pattern is not uniform. East Asia and Pacific remained the largest contributor, at 8304660 in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia fell from 6877900 to 2446054, though one year's monsoon severity largely decides such a figure. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1108287 to 6029739, more than fivefold, a rise reflecting both flood and drought events and wider recording. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023, a jump that points to a particular large event or events and to the start of the record in 2016 rather than to a steady trend. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group rose from 1212730 to 2481660. Latin America and the Caribbean was nearly flat, at 1543360 and then 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000.

By income group the shift is more telling for Goal 1. Low-income countries recorded 992200 cases in 2015 and 6177600 in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 9883673 to 5649287, and upper-middle-income countries rose from 6620044 to 13815894. High-income countries fell from 1692900 to 750497. The poorest countries thus carry a growing share of recorded displacement, while the high-income group, with stronger early warning, shelter and building standards, recorded fewer cases. That pattern is consistent with the target's concern that exposure and vulnerability fall unevenly, but the figures are absolute counts. Without population denominators in the same series, a large country with a large count may be less exposed per person than a small one.

### Concentration has increased

Among countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of displacement was 0.570 in 2015 across 112 countries and 0.678 in 2023 across 145. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. Displacement is therefore more unequally distributed across countries in 2023 than in 2015, even though more countries report. The share of Theil inequality lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%, which means that a larger part of the disparity now lies among countries within the same region. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.11 to 1.47. For policy this means that regional averages hide the countries bearing the largest burdens, and that a few events in a few countries dominate the world total.

### What this implies for 2030

Target 1.5 has no numerical threshold in the text used here, and it can be read in more than one way: as a reduction in the number of people affected, in the share of the poor affected, or in losses relative to income. The data on the shelf allow none of these readings to be tested for the poor specifically. Displacement counts are not broken down by income of the displaced. The 1990 to 2009 exposure average is the only measure expressed as a share of population, and it ends six years before the goals began.

On the evidence of displacement alone, the direction since 2015 is upward, the poorest income group is carrying a rising count, and the distribution among countries has become more concentrated. Warming raises the frequency of the heavy rainfall, heat and drought events behind much of this, so a reversal by 2030 is unlikely without large gains in preparedness. Early warning, land-use planning, social protection that scales up after a shock, and insurance mechanisms are the established levers. Their effect is visible in the lower counts in high-income countries, which is suggestive and not proof, since hazard exposure also differs.

### Quality of the record

The record is weakest where it matters most. Reporting has improved, yet the baseline exposure series is dated, the progress score is a self-assessment by governments with no external check, and displacement data measure movement, not loss of livelihood, injury or death. Slow-onset events such as drought are poorly captured by displacement counts. Disaster-affected shares for the years after 2009 are absent from the shelf altogether.
