w-c05-7-1~heath/writer-1~48.text:
### Trained teachers in primary schools, 2015 to 2024

The supply of teachers who have received the minimum organised training required in their own country is the most direct measure the World Bank's indicators offer for target 4.c. The indicator has a ceiling of 100.0% in 2030, and it is a measure of the share trained, not of quality. Because each country sets its own minimum standard, a trained teacher in one system may have had far less preparation than in another. The figures below are therefore comparisons of trends within countries more than of absolute standards across them.

The world share of primary teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and 82.2% in 2024. That is a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. The trend tool classes this as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and its projection places the world at 83.4% in 2030, well short of full coverage. About one primary teacher in six therefore still lacks the minimum training, and on present course that will remain so.

The global figure is made up of very different regional movements. South Asia is the clear exception: its share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, and its projected value for 2030 is 99.3%, the only region classed as on track. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 66.2% in 2015 to 68.8% in 2022, the latest year the tool reports for the region, and is projected at 72.0% in 2030. Low-income countries moved from 65.8% to 69.2% over the same years, with a projection of 73.2%. Lower-middle-income countries went from 76.4% to 83.3% between 2015 and 2024, with a projection of 88.2%, which is moderate progress needing acceleration.

### Falling shares where the share was already high

A less expected result is that several regions moved backwards. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020. Latin America and the Caribbean slipped from 82.7% to 81.8% in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 83.9% to 80.5%. North America declined from 99.3% to 97.9%, and high-income countries as a group from 95.9% to 92.1%. All of these are classed as regression, and the projected 2030 values are 86.9%, 81.2%, 78.3%, 97.1% and 89.7% respectively.

These declines should be read carefully. Part of a fall in a high-income system can reflect the way teachers are counted rather than a deterioration in preparation: a country that admits staff on alternative or fast-track routes, or that hires to fill shortages during a period of expansion or retirement, may see the measured share fall even when pupils are taught as well as before. Teacher shortages in richer countries, driven by an ageing workforce, pay that competes poorly with other graduate careers and difficulty in retaining new entrants, are well documented, and they push systems to employ people before training is complete. The data cannot separate these explanations. The year-to-year reporting is also uneven, which matters below.

### Countries, not only regions

Across 129 countries assessed for primary education, 64 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 65.9% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 12 countries, with 4.2% of that population, show moderate progress, and 13, with 2.4%, show marginal progress. Four countries, with 1.2%, are stagnant. Regression affects 36 countries holding 26.3% of the population. More than a quarter of the assessed population therefore lives where the trained share is falling.

Secondary education shows a similar pattern with weaker coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 are on track, holding 61.5% of the population; 10 show moderate progress (2.1%); 14 marginal progress (7.7%); 7 stagnation (1.0%); and 36 regression (27.6%). The count of countries in regression is the same as for primary education, and the population share is slightly higher. Secondary teaching is more specialised, and expansion of enrolment since 2015 has required many new teachers, which is a likely cause of the weaker showing, although the series does not test it.

The classification should not be read as an even contest. A country already at 98% that slips slightly counts as regression, as does one at 50% that falls sharply. The class labels hide the difference in need. Policy attention belongs first with the systems where a large share of teachers is untrained, which are mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and among low-income countries.

### Convergence and inequality

Among 48 countries with data for both ends of the period, the convergence test returns a beta of -0.07 (p effectively zero, R-squared 0.34). The negative sign means that countries starting lower tended to gain more, so catching up is real. The coefficient of variation across these countries fell only from 0.17 in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024, a small narrowing. Convergence is therefore present but slow, and the countries furthest behind remain far from the others.

Population-weighted inequality among countries followed a different path. The Gini coefficient was 0.09 in 2015 and 0.07 in 2020, then 0.10 in 2024; the Theil index fell from 0.03 in 2015 to 0.01 in 2020. The number of reporting countries changed in each year, at 85, 93 and 79, so the three readings are not drawn from the same set of countries and should not be taken as a clean trend. Between-region differences accounted for 49.3% of the Theil index in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020, which says that about half of the inequality in this measure lies between regions, and half within them. The 2024 Theil value is not available.

### Teacher numbers and training are not linked

The count of primary teachers is available for 200 economies, and it does not explain the trained share. Across 48 countries, the Spearman correlation between changes in the number of teachers and changes in the trained share is -0.1, and between their 2024 levels it is 0.2. Both are weak. Hiring more teachers does not by itself raise the trained share, and in some cases rapid hiring may dilute it, as faster recruitment can outrun training capacity. Countries that add teachers quickly to bring class sizes down need to fund training places in step with the hiring, or the quantity gain will come at the cost of the quality indicator.

### What this means for 2030

On present trends the world will not reach full coverage of trained primary teachers, and the shortfall is concentrated in low-income countries and sub-Saharan Africa, where more than 30% of primary teachers lack training. South Asia shows that rapid improvement is possible within a decade where governments expand pre-service and in-service programmes at scale. The regressions in higher-income regions show that the gains cannot be assumed to hold once reached. Data timeliness is also a problem: only 13 countries reported in 2025, and several regional figures end in 2020 or 2022, so the picture after the pandemic is incomplete.

The analysis does not reach target 4.a, which concerns facilities, safety and inclusion. The series on the shelf cover teachers only, and no school-level measure of buildings, water, electricity or safety is analysed here.

proposals: Ministries of education in low-income countries and sub-Saharan Africa, with development partners, should fund pre-service and in-service training places in step with teacher recruitment, so that expansion does not dilute the trained share.
Governments in regions where the trained share is falling should publish how it is counted and review fast-track hiring, so that falls can be told apart from changes in definition.

The UNESCO Institute for Statistics should press countries to report promptly, as only 13 countries reported for 2025, and should publish the national minimum standard of training alongside each series.
South Asian ministries should share their methods of scaling teacher training with sub-Saharan African counterparts through regional cooperation under target 4.c.
w-c05-7-1~heath/writer-1~48.gaps: The indicator measures the share meeting each country's own minimum training standard, so levels are not comparable across countries and say nothing about teaching quality. Pupil-teacher ratios are not among the series analysed, so the question of falling ratios is not answered; only teacher counts and trained shares are shown. Secondary and pre-primary trained shares are covered only by country classification, not by regional levels. Several regional values end in 2020 or 2022, and country coverage varies by year, which limits trend comparisons. Nothing on school facilities, safety, disability access or gender sensitivity (target 4.a) is covered. Teacher pay, attrition and the content of training are absent.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-2~49.text:
### The gap in internet use

The World Development Indicators hold no series on mobile phone ownership by sex. The nearest measures are internet use by sex, drawn from the International Telecommunication Union, and the overall count of mobile subscriptions, which is not divided by sex. This section therefore reads Target 5.b through internet use, which the source defines as use in the last three months from any device, including a mobile phone. The reading is imperfect: use is not ownership, and a woman may use a phone that a relative owns.

On that measure, 68.2 per cent of women worldwide used the internet in 2024, against 51.8 per cent in 2019. The male series stands at 76.6 per cent in 2025, against 56.0 per cent in 2019. The male figure is for 2025 and the female world figure is for 2024, so the two are not strictly comparable at the world level. Seven countries reported in 2025, so the latest world values lean on estimates and modelling more than on fresh surveys. Comparisons of like years are safer at the regional level, where both series end in 2024.

### Regional differences

The gap is narrow where use is nearly universal and wide where it is not. In North America, 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia the figures were 90.0 and 91.8 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific they were 85.5 and 87.6 per cent, and in Latin America and the Caribbean 81.3 and 82.0 per cent. In these four regions the difference in 2024 was between 0.6 and 2.1 percentage points, so the gap is now small.

The picture changes in the regions where connection is still spreading. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women used the internet in 2024, against 67.6 per cent of men, a gap of 12.6 points. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 and 69.1 per cent, a gap of 12.8 points. In Sub-Saharan Africa they were 29.4 and 37.9 per cent, a gap of 8.5 points. The gap in Sub-Saharan Africa is smaller in points only because the base is low; women there are still far less likely than men to be online. A gap measured in points can mislead, because it shrinks as both levels approach zero or saturation. The ratio of female to male use gives a fairer guide: it is 0.78 in Sub-Saharan Africa, against 0.99 in North America.

### Change since 2019

The series are shown from 2019, which allows comparison of the years before and after the pandemic that began in 2020. Every region gained. South Asia shows the largest rise for women, from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, which is 32.0 points. Men there rose from 34.9 to 69.1 per cent, which is 34.2 points. The female gain was large but did not close the gap, which in points stayed close to 10 at the start and widened slightly to 12.8 by 2024. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the gap widened from 9.2 points in 2019 to 12.6 in 2024.

East Asia and Pacific is an unusual case. Women's use was 67.4 per cent in 2019, below the male 66.7 per cent only by a reading of the figures in the other direction: women were slightly ahead then, at 0.7 points, and behind by 2.1 points in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 20.2 to 29.4 per cent for women, a gain of 9.2 points, against 9.3 points for men, from 28.6 to 37.9 per cent. The gap there therefore did not narrow in absolute terms. Pandemic-era demand for remote work, schooling, payments and public services pulled people online, but the data do not show that it favoured women.

### Income groups

Income explains much of the pattern. In low-income countries, 18.3 per cent of women used the internet in 2025, against 28.6 per cent of men, up from 12.6 and 20.3 per cent in 2019. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 and 68.7 per cent in 2025, up from 28.9 and 38.0 per cent. In upper-middle-income countries, 87.9 per cent of women and 89.7 per cent of men used the internet, and in high-income countries 93.6 and 94.9 per cent. The upper-middle group is notable: in 2019 the two shares were equal at 67.6 per cent, and a gap of 1.8 points had opened by 2025. That reversal rests on aggregates and should be treated with caution.

The lower-middle group made the largest gains, with women's use rising by 28.0 points. Low-income countries have barely begun the transition: fewer than one woman in five used the internet in 2025. The causes are well known: the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, limited access to electricity, social norms that restrict women's mobility and control over devices, and concerns about harassment online.

### What the countries show

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, the female and male series move together very closely. The rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.948, and that of the changes since 2019 is 0.958. Countries where men connected quickly were nearly always countries where women connected quickly. This implies that the gap is set largely by national conditions, such as network coverage, prices and income, and that it is not a separate problem solved by separate means. It also implies that a country's overall growth in use does not guarantee a narrower gap: the correlation says nothing about whether the difference closes.

Coverage is a limit. The number of countries reporting female use rose from 1 in 2000 to 92 in 2019, and fell to 65 in 2024, with only 7 in 2025. In all, 137 countries have reported at some point. Many values in recent years are therefore estimated, and the poorest countries, where the gaps are largest, are the least likely to have surveys.

### Implications for 2030

Target 5.b has no numerical threshold in the data held here, and can be read as a call for greater use of enabling technology, or for parity of access. On the parity reading, high- and upper-middle-income regions are close to the target. Women in South Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and Sub-Saharan Africa are not. The pace of change after 2019 suggests that levels will continue to rise, but the gaps in points have stayed near their 2024 size in regions where growth was fastest. Without measures aimed at women, parity by 2030 is unlikely in those regions.

w-c04-2-1~willow/writer-3~50.text:
### Thresholds and the count of countries

Target 3.2 sets two numerical thresholds: neonatal mortality of no more than 12 per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality of no more than 25 per 1,000 live births. The bench's trend tool assessed 196 countries against each. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries are on track or have met the target, and those countries hold 72.4% of the assessed population. For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met it, with 74.7% of the population. The difference is modest, but the neonatal threshold is the harder one to approach.

The classification does not count only the countries already below the threshold. It also counts those whose recent rate of decline, projected to 2030, would take them below it. The phrase on track or target met therefore mixes two states. The reading is further qualified by the fact that a country far below the threshold needs no progress, while a country just above it needs a great deal. The data supplied here do not separate the two groups, so the number of countries that have already crossed the line cannot be stated from these results.

### Neonatal mortality: levels and direction

Global neonatal mortality fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024, which is still above the threshold of 12. The fall is slow: the world's fitted annual rate of change is about -0.0133, and the expected 2030 value of 15.9 leaves the world as a whole short of the threshold. The world ratio of 0.48 means that roughly half of the progress required has been achieved on the trend.

The regional spread is wide. North America moved from 3.9 to 3.6 and high-income countries from 3.2 to 2.8. Europe and Central Asia fell from 5.1 to 4.1, East Asia and Pacific from 8.3 to 6.7 and Latin America and the Caribbean from 10.0 to 8.3. All of these are below 12 and are classed as on track or met. South Asia is the notable success: neonatal mortality fell from 25.4 to 16.6, a fitted rate of about -0.0462, with an expected 2030 value of 12.5 and a ratio of 0.96. It is classed as on track, though its projected value lies marginally above 12 and the classification rests on the tolerance of the method.

The remaining regions are far behind. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 26.9 to 22.7, with an expected 2030 value of 20.3 and a ratio of 0.45. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 29.2 to 26.6, a rate of about -0.0103, which projects to 25.0 in 2030 and a ratio of 0.24. By income, low-income countries moved from 28.1 to 24.9 and lower-middle-income countries from 26.9 to 21.6. Upper-middle-income countries reached 6.8, well below the threshold.

### Under-five mortality: levels and direction

Under-five mortality worldwide fell from 42.9 per 1,000 in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024, against a threshold of 25. The world's fitted rate is about -0.0151, the expected 2030 value is 34.1 and the ratio is 0.49, so the world is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The global average is however dominated by a few very large populations at different points on the path, and it hides the fact that most countries are on track.

High-income countries fell from 5.8 to 5.1, and North America from 6.6 to 6.4, the slowest change of any region, but at a level so low that the target is not at issue. Europe and Central Asia fell from 9.6 to 7.8, East Asia and Pacific from 16.6 to 13.2, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 18.3 to 15.4. Upper-middle-income countries reached 13.1. South Asia fell from 42.6 to 26.8, the steepest rate of any group at about -0.0502; its expected 2030 value of 19.7 is below 25 and its ratio is 1.30.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 46.2 to 36.4, with an expected 2030 value of 31.1 and a ratio of 0.72, which is moderate progress. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 55.3 to 43.8, with an expected value of 37.5 and a ratio of 0.59. The gravest case is Sub-Saharan Africa, where the rate fell from 85.0 to 71.2, an expected 2030 value of 63.3 and a ratio of 0.36. Low-income countries fell from 84.9 to 68.8, with an expected value of 59.8 and a ratio of 0.42. Both would reach 2030 at more than twice the threshold.

### Countries off course

The remaining countries fall into four classes. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries (7.8% of the population) show moderate progress, 36 (11.9%) show marginal progress, 4 (2.1%) stagnate and 9 (5.7%) regress. For under-five mortality, 39 countries (16.1%) show moderate progress, 15 (4.0%) marginal progress, 3 (4.9%) stagnation and 4 (0.3%) regression. Neonatal mortality thus has many more countries making marginal progress, 36 against 15, and more that regress, 9 against 4. This is consistent with a well-known pattern: deaths in the first 28 days are less responsive than deaths later in childhood to the interventions that did most to lower under-five mortality, such as vaccination, malaria control and treatment of diarrhoea and pneumonia. Neonatal deaths depend on the quality of care at and around birth, skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care and care for small and sick newborns, which require a functioning health system rather than campaigns.

The stagnating three countries in the under-five class hold 4.9% of the population, a share far larger than their number suggests, which indicates that at least one populous country is in that class. Regression is concentrated in few and small populations, 0.3% for under-five mortality, and is typical of states affected by conflict, displacement or the breakdown of services. The data do not identify the countries in these classes.

### Before and after 2015 and 2020

The results compare 2015 with 2024 and do not give annual values, so a distinct break after 2020 cannot be measured here. It is known that the pandemic disrupted routine immunisation, antenatal and delivery care in many countries, and that conflict, food insecurity and cuts in aid have strained services since. Whether these produced reversals is not shown by the fitted rates, which average over nine years. The slower trends in the poorest regions are nonetheless consistent with a fragile health system that absorbs shocks poorly.

### Implications for 2030

The numbers support a two-part conclusion. The target is met or within reach for most countries, about two thirds of those assessed and nearly three quarters of the population. Yet the children at greatest risk live in the places that are not on course: Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income countries and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping. Because the share of world births in these places is rising while that elsewhere falls, the global average will move slowly and the world as a whole will miss both thresholds on current trends. South Asia shows that rapid change is possible at scale, as a result of expanded facility births, immunisation and better nutrition and sanitation, though its neonatal rate still sits near the threshold.

### Proposals

The results lead to the following proposals.

w-c04-2-1~willow/writer-3~50.gaps: The results give 2015 and 2024 only, so annual breaks after 2020 cannot be seen. The trend classes do not separate countries already below the thresholds from those projected to cross them, and they do not name the countries in each class. Rates are modelled estimates, uncertain where vital registration is weak. No series here covers causes of death, within-country inequality, stillbirths or the quality of care, and the classification depends on the method's tolerance, so that a value close to the line, as in South Asia's neonatal rate, can be read in more than one way.

w-c02-4-1~juniper/writer-3~50.text:
### Water, sanitation and electricity reach most people, but not the poorest countries

Target 1.4 asks that all men and women, the poor and the vulnerable above all, have equal access to basic services and financial services. The World Development Indicators do not measure access by income within countries for water, sanitation or electricity, so the poor are read here through country groups: low-income economies, Sub-Saharan Africa and rural populations. The picture is one of broad advance at the global level and a persistent deficit where poverty is deepest.

The share of the world's people using at least basic drinking water rose from 88.1 per cent in 2015 to 91.5 per cent in 2024, with 202 countries reporting in 2024. Access to electricity rose from 86.9 per cent to 91.9 per cent over the same years. These are gains of a few percentage points in nine years, and the global averages conceal the fact that the remaining gap is concentrated in a small number of places.

### Water: gains are largest where coverage was lowest, yet the gap remains wide

In high-income countries basic water coverage stood at 99.0 per cent in 2015 and 99.2 per cent in 2024, so there is little left to gain. Upper middle income countries moved from 92.6 per cent to 95.9 per cent, and lower middle income countries from 85.2 per cent to 90.8 per cent. Low-income countries rose from 53.1 per cent to 60.3 per cent, a gain of about seven points, but they remain almost forty points behind the high-income group.

Regionally, South Asia rose from 90.5 per cent to 95.9 per cent and East Asia and Pacific from 91.4 per cent to 95.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 97.6 per cent in 2024, and Europe and Central Asia 98.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping reached 92.9 per cent, from 90.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa climbed from 59.2 per cent to 67.5 per cent; it is the only region where about one person in three still lacks basic water. Population growth, weak utility finance and the cost of serving dispersed rural settlements explain much of this slow pace.

There is evidence of catching up among rural populations. Across 167 countries, the convergence estimate for rural basic water gives a coefficient of -0.0164 (R-squared 0.3), meaning that countries starting lower have tended to improve faster, and the coefficient of variation between countries fell from 0.27 in 2015 to 0.23 in 2024. Convergence is real but slow, and it leaves a tail of countries well short of universal coverage.

The trend assessment to 2030 is sobering. Of 214 countries assessed, 60, holding 33.9 per cent of the assessed population, are on track or have met the target of full coverage. A further 45 countries (33.8 per cent of population) show moderate progress needing acceleration, 55 (20.9 per cent) show marginal progress, 17 (1.5 per cent) stagnate and 37 (9.9 per cent) are regressing. Thus the target, read as 100 per cent coverage, will be missed by a majority of countries. Reading it as universal basic access is itself one interpretation; the indicator counts a source within a thirty-minute round trip as basic, which says nothing about safety.

### Sanitation: the weakest service, with stagnation at low incomes

Sanitation is further from the target. Using the trend tool, the world's expected coverage in 2030 is 89.2 per cent for basic sanitation, with a ratio of progress to required progress of 0.61, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. East Asia and Pacific rose from 83.7 per cent in 2015 to 94.8 per cent in 2024 and is on track, with a ratio of 1.18. South Asia is also on track, with a ratio of 1.11, and upper middle income countries have a ratio of 1.08.

The poorest groups fare worst. Low-income countries moved from 29.2 per cent to 33.3 per cent, a ratio of 0.10, classed as stagnation; their expected level in 2030 is 36.2 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.16 and an expected 42.0 per cent, so more than half of its people would still lack basic sanitation in 2030. Lower middle income countries advanced strongly, from 56.0 per cent to 73.9 per cent, but a ratio of 0.75 still falls short. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping, at 83.7 per cent in 2024, has a ratio of 0.48.

Among 213 countries assessed, 49 (46.6 per cent of population) are on track, 34 moderate, 54 marginal, 37 stagnant and 39 regressing, the last holding 13.4 per cent of the population. Regression in some countries, and a slight fall in North America from 99.7 per cent to 99.5 per cent, may reflect survey revisions and the definition of shared facilities as not basic, as well as population movements; the data cannot say which.

### Electricity: a South Asian success and a Sub-Saharan deficit

Electrification is the clearest success of the period. South Asia rose from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, the result of sustained public programmes of grid extension and, in places, off-grid solar. Lower middle income countries rose from 79.6 per cent to 91.4 per cent. East Asia and Pacific reached 98.6 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping 96.8 per cent. Europe and Central Asia stood at 100.0 per cent when rounded, and North America at 100.0 per cent in both years.

The deficit is now almost wholly African. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, and low-income countries from 32.2 per cent to 48.8 per cent. Though the gains of about sixteen points are large, nearly half of low-income populations remain without power. For rural electricity, 161 of 211 countries, holding 77.4 per cent of the assessed population, are on track or have met the target; 23 (12.8 per cent) show moderate progress, 10 (2.0 per cent) marginal progress, 7 (2.3 per cent) stagnate and 10 (5.4 per cent) regress. The global outlook is therefore far better for electricity than for sanitation, but the countries that are off track are the poorest and often fragile.

### Accounts: rapid growth, but a persistent gap for the poorest

Financial access is measured for the poorest 40 per cent of adults, which is a direct reading of the target's concern for the poor. Account ownership among them rose worldwide from 61.7 per cent in 2017 to 72.4 per cent in 2024, with 138 countries reporting in 2024. Low-income countries rose from 22.5 per cent to 37.3 per cent, the fastest proportional gain, helped by mobile money. Lower middle income countries rose from 53.2 per cent to 63.4 per cent, upper middle income from 62.5 per cent to 76.8 per cent, and high income from 89.0 per cent to 92.8 per cent. South Asia reached 73.3 per cent in 2024, from 65.5 per cent.

Regional series for several areas end in 2021 and are not comparable in year with the global figure. Between 2017 and 2021, East Asia and Pacific moved from 64.1 per cent to 77.4 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 76.4 per cent to 86.3 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 42.9 per cent to 67.9 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose only from 39.5 per cent to 46.1 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 32.0 per cent to 43.6 per cent. North America rose from 86.7 per cent to 92.1 per cent. No trend to target has been computed for accounts, and an account, once opened, may be dormant; ownership is not use.

### Implications for 2030

The period since 2015 shows that access grows fastest where public programmes are large and sustained, as in South Asia, and slowest where income, state capacity and settlement patterns hinder it. Sanitation is the service most likely to fail the target everywhere outside East and South Asia, and low-income countries will not close their gaps in water, sanitation or electricity at present rates. The data also show no clear break after 2020 within these annual series, though survey gaps during the pandemic mean that any such effect could be hidden.

w-c04-4-1~juniper/writer-4~50.text:
### What the target asks and what the indicator measures

Target 3.4 asks for a one third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates and no death from other causes. It is a conditional probability, not a count of deaths, so it is not distorted by population ageing in the way a crude death rate is. The series covers 185 countries in 2021. The target text does not fix a baseline year or a formula. This book reads the baseline as 2015, the year the goals were adopted, so that the world value of 18.9 % in 2015 implies a 2030 target of 12.57 %, a reduction of one third. A reader who took 2010 or 2000 as the baseline would obtain a different threshold, and this ambiguity should be borne in mind throughout.

The suicide rate, also named in the target through mental health, is a separate indicator with its own series. This section treats the mortality probability as the main measure and uses the health-service coverage index for non-communicable diseases as a point of comparison. Suicide data are held on the shelf, but no result on them was computed for this section, so no finding on suicide is claimed here.

### The world position in 2021

The world probability of premature death from the four disease groups was 18.9 % in 2015 and 18.3 % in 2021. That is a fall of roughly half a percentage point over six years. A one third reduction from 2015 would require a fall of about six points by 2030. At the observed pace the expected world value in 2030 is 17.5 %, which leaves the target far out of reach. The trend tool rates the world as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and its ratio of achieved to required progress is 0.22: about a fifth of the pace that the target demands.

The timing matters. A break test on the annual change in the world series places a break in 2015. Over 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was a fall of 0.26 percentage points a year. Over 2015 to 2021 it was a fall of 0.09 points a year, about a third of the earlier pace. Progress therefore slowed after the goals were adopted, not before. Part of the explanation lies in the pandemic years, when health systems diverted attention from hypertension, cancer screening and diabetes care, and when COVID-19 deaths fell disproportionately on people with these very conditions. Yet the break is dated to 2015, not 2020, so the pandemic cannot be the whole account. Slower gains in cardiovascular mortality in rich countries, a rising burden of diabetes and obesity, and the plateau of earlier gains from tobacco control and blood-pressure treatment are well-established contributors. The annual series ends in 2021, so any recovery after the pandemic is not yet visible.

### Regions and income groups

The regional picture is uneven. South Asia is the one region that moved in the wrong direction, from 22.1 % in 2015 to 22.9 % in 2021, and the trend tool classifies it as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 24.0 %. The lower middle income group, which contains much of South Asia, was flat: 22.8 % in 2015 and 22.8 % in 2021, a stagnation with a ratio of 0.00. This group holds a very large share of the world population, so its stagnation weighs heavily on the world figure.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 21.9 % to 21.3 %, and low-income countries from 24.0 % to 23.0 %. Low-income countries retain the highest risk of any group, and their expected 2030 value is 21.5 %, with a ratio of 0.22. Here the burden of non-communicable disease is rising in relative importance as infectious disease declines, but health systems built for acute infections are poorly equipped for long-term treatment of hypertension, diabetes or cancer. Measurement is also weaker in these countries, and many mortality estimates rest on modelled, not registered, deaths.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3 % to 20.7 %, a larger absolute fall than most regions, though the ratio of 0.39 still signals significant acceleration needed. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8 % to 16.9 %, with a ratio of 0.42. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 15.3 % to 14.7 %, with an expected 2030 value of 13.9 %. Upper middle income countries fell from 18.1 % to 17.1 %.

Europe and Central Asia made the largest regional gain, from 17.5 % to 15.7 %, and is classed as moderate progress with a ratio of 0.82. Its expected 2030 value of 13.4 % is above the regional target but not far from it. North America fell only from 13.6 % to 13.3 %, with an expected 2030 value of 12.8 %. High-income countries moved from 13.8 % to 12.8 %, and their expected 2030 value of 11.4 % lies below their own target; the trend tool rates them on track, with a ratio of 1.93. The only group on track is therefore the one that started with the lowest risk. A caution is needed: the ratio compares each group with a target set as a third off its own 2015 level, so on-track status for high-income countries as a group does not mean that every high-income country is on track, and the group figure hides national differences.

### Distribution among countries

The spread among countries is moderate but growing. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.152 in 2015 and 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index rose from 0.038 to 0.041. The share of the Theil inequality that lies between regions, as against within them, rose from 27.0 % to 33.1 %. Regions are thus becoming more distinct from one another, which fits the pattern above: Europe and high-income countries improving, South Asia and the lower middle income group standing still or worsening.

The convergence test confirms the absence of catching up. Across 185 countries, the coefficient from regressing change on the starting level is 0.0016 with a p-value of 0.70 and an R-squared of 0.001, which is statistically indistinguishable from zero. High-risk countries were not falling faster than low-risk ones, nor slower in any systematic way. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.360 to 0.380. For a target that is supposed to leave no one behind, this is the key finding: no mechanism of automatic convergence is operating, and the countries with the highest risk are not closing the distance.

### Treatment coverage and the limits of the link

The shelf also holds the service coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases, built from hypertension, diabetes and tobacco tracers. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between its level and the mortality probability in 2021 is -0.25: countries with better coverage tend to have lower premature mortality, as expected, but the association is weak. The rank correlation between changes in the two series from 2015 to 2021 is 0.10, essentially nil, and of the wrong sign for a simple causal story. Improvements in coverage have not been accompanied by detectable improvements in mortality over this short window.

Several explanations are consistent with this. Mortality from these diseases responds with a long lag to treatment and to prevention such as reduced tobacco use and salt intake, so six years is brief. The coverage index rests on only three tracers and omits cancer care and chronic respiratory disease, two of the four causes counted in the mortality measure. Coverage of a tracer, for instance having a diabetes diagnosis, is not the same as effective control. Finally, age structure and background risk differ between countries. The result should be read as a warning against assuming that service indices alone will deliver the target, not as evidence that treatment does not work.

### Implications for 2030

On present trends, the world will not come close to a one third reduction. Even the faster pace of 2001 to 2014, if resumed, would produce a world value near 14.4 % by 2030, which is still above 12.57 %; that figure is the authors' reading of the earlier pace and not a tool result. Reaching the target would thus require progress well above anything the series has recorded in this century. The central issues are the stagnant lower middle income group, regressing South Asia, and low-income countries that start with the highest risk. Priority should go to cheap and proven interventions: tobacco taxation, salt reduction, affordable blood-pressure and diabetes medicines delivered through primary care, and cervical and breast cancer screening and treatment.

### Proposals

See the list of proposals below, which follow from these findings.

w-c04-4-1~juniper/writer-4~50.gaps: The mortality series ends in 2021, so recovery after the pandemic cannot be seen. It is a modelled probability, not a count of registered deaths, and is weakest where registration is poor. It is not split by cause, so cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic respiratory disease cannot be separated, and it gives no breakdown by income, education or rural residence within countries. The target does not fix its baseline year, so the 2015 reading is a choice. Suicide and mental health well-being were not analysed here, and the coverage index covers only hypertension, diabetes and tobacco. The correlations do not establish cause.

w-c06-6-1~heath/writer-3~50.text:
### Account ownership as the measurable core of target 5.a

Target 5.a asks for equal rights to economic resources, including ownership and control of land and property, financial services, inheritance and natural resources. The World Bank's catalogue holds no series on land or property ownership by sex that the bench could read. The one dimension of the target that can be measured with a common instrument across many countries is access to financial services, captured by the Global Findex survey of account ownership among people aged 15 and over. An account here means one held at a bank or another financial institution, or the personal use of a mobile-money service in the previous 12 months. This section therefore reads the target through accounts, and says plainly where property is out of view.

Account ownership is not a proxy for property, but it matters in its own right. An account is the entry point to savings, credit, insurance and the receipt of wages and transfers without an intermediary. Where a woman cannot hold one, her earnings and social payments may pass through a male relative, and her capacity to invest in a business or to withstand a shock is reduced. Reading the account gap is therefore a reasonable way to gauge whether the economic resources named in the target reach women.

### The world gap narrowed, but did not close

Globally, 65.9 per cent of women aged 15 and over held an account in 2017, and 76.6 per cent did so in 2024. For men the figures were 72.8 per cent in 2017 and 80.9 per cent in 2024. The gap between men and women was therefore about 6.9 percentage points in 2017 and about 4.2 percentage points in 2024. Women gained roughly 10.7 percentage points over the seven years, men roughly 8.0 points, so the gap narrowed because women started lower and rose faster. The ratio of female to male ownership rose from 0.91 to 0.95, which shows a convergence that is real but incomplete.

These figures cover the period after 2015 only in part, since the series used here begin in 2017, and the interval includes the pandemic years after 2020. Digital payments, government-to-person transfers paid into accounts and the spread of mobile money during that period are generally understood to have widened access, and the gains recorded are consistent with that explanation. The data themselves do not separate these causes, and the survey rounds are spaced several years apart, so the timing of change within the interval cannot be read from them.

### Income groups: the gap is widest where ownership is lowest

The distribution by income level shows a persistent hierarchy. In low-income economies, 26.8 per cent of women held an account in 2017 and 40.6 per cent in 2024, against 37.3 per cent and 52.5 per cent of men. The gap was thus about 10.5 points in 2017 and about 11.9 points in 2024. In low-income economies the gap in points did not narrow; it widened slightly, even though women's ownership rose by about 13.8 points. Men's ownership rose faster in absolute terms, by about 15.2 points.

Lower-middle-income economies show a different pattern. Women's ownership rose from 55.6 per cent to 67.6 per cent, and men's from 64.4 per cent to 73.2 per cent, so the gap fell from about 8.8 points to about 5.6 points. In upper-middle-income economies women rose from 68.9 per cent to 82.5 per cent and men from 76.3 per cent to 85.6 per cent, narrowing the gap from about 7.4 points to about 3.2 points. In high-income economies the gap was already small: 92.1 per cent of women and 93.9 per cent of men in 2017, then 94.5 per cent and 95.3 per cent in 2024, a difference of under one point.

The lesson is that convergence occurred in the middle of the income distribution, while the poorest economies, where both levels are lowest, saw the gap persist. Growth in ownership alone does not close the difference; in low-income economies the expansion reached men first and in larger measure.

### Regions: the Middle East and North Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa lag

Regional figures for most regions end in 2021, the last survey year with regional estimates in this series, so they are not directly comparable with the 2024 income-group figures. South Asia is the exception, with 2024 values. Between 2017 and 2021, women's ownership in East Asia and Pacific rose from 71.2 per cent to 81.4 per cent, while men's rose from 75.7 per cent to 84.2 per cent; the gap fell from about 4.5 points to about 2.9 points. In Europe and Central Asia, women rose from 79.4 per cent to 88.0 per cent and men from 83.8 per cent to 91.2 per cent, a gap falling from about 4.3 to about 3.2 points.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest regional gain for women, from 52.1 per cent to 70.1 per cent, an increase of about 18.0 points, against about 18.3 points for men, from 58.7 per cent to 77.0 per cent. The gap therefore stayed close to 6.5 to 6.8 points. Rapid expansion lifted both sexes in step.

The widest regional gap is in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Women's ownership was 38.0 per cent in 2017 and 45.6 per cent in 2021, while men's was 56.8 per cent and 59.6 per cent. The gap was about 18.9 points in 2017 and about 14.0 points in 2021. It narrowed, yet remained the largest of any region, and fewer than half of women held an account in 2021. Legal restrictions on women's mobility, work and identification documents, as well as social norms, are widely cited as contributing to this pattern; the data here do not test those causes.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows a gap of about 11.5 points in 2017 and about 12.3 points in 2021: women's ownership rose from 36.9 per cent to 49.0 per cent, men's from 48.5 per cent to 61.4 per cent. Mobile money has driven much of the region's growth, and men appear to have adopted it somewhat faster. South Asia is more encouraging: women rose from 64.0 per cent in 2017 to 75.1 per cent in 2024, men from 74.7 per cent to 80.1 per cent, and the gap fell from about 10.7 points to about 5.0 points. Policies that open accounts for the whole population, together with biometric identification and direct benefit payments, are commonly credited with this change.

In North America, women's ownership was 93.4 per cent in 2017 and 97.1 per cent in 2021, while men's was 94.2 per cent and 93.8 per cent. Women thus overtook men by the later date. Such a reversal is small, and survey sampling error on both estimates should be borne in mind.

### What the trend classification implies for 2030

The trend assessment compares each country's path with a target of 100 per cent female account ownership by 2030. That target is a literal reading of universal access, and it is not written in target 5.a itself; the target speaks of equal rights, and an alternative reading would set the benchmark as parity with men rather than full coverage. Under the full-coverage reading, of 139 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 49.9 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. A further 41 countries, with 18.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 29, with 17.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries, with 3.2 per cent, are stagnant, and 33 countries, with 10.4 per cent, are regressing.

The count of regressing countries deserves attention. That 33 of 139 countries show a downward path, even though the world level rose, indicates that the global gain is concentrated. Since the Findex rounds are widely spaced and some countries have only a few observations, a regression label can reflect survey noise, a change in the mix of mobile-money use or a real fall in access. The classification should be taken as a flag for scrutiny, not as a verdict. The population shares show that nearly half of the assessed population lives in countries that are on track, largely because large economies with high ownership are among them, while the countries that are far behind are more numerous but smaller in population.

Taken together, the evidence suggests that universal female account ownership by 2030 is unlikely for the world as a whole: the 2024 level of 76.6 per cent leaves 23.4 points to cover in six years, whereas the 2017 to 2024 gain was about 10.7 points. Closing the gap with men is more plausible in the middle-income groups and in South Asia than in low-income economies, where the gap has not narrowed.

### Firms, legal frameworks and the limits of the evidence

The shelf holds further series that bear on the target but could not be read here at the level of detail needed. The Women, Business and the Law legal framework index, scored from 0 to 100 across ten topics including assets and entrepreneurship, covers 189 economies in 2025, which makes it a nearly complete record, and it is treated in the companion section on legal frameworks. The Enterprise Surveys series on firms with female participation in ownership and the Demographic and Health Surveys series on women's participation in household decisions, which covers 70 countries, were not examined in the results available. Neither is a measure of land or inheritance. For the central concern of the target, the ownership of land and housing by sex, no comparable series exists on the shelf.

w-c06-3-1~dahlia/writer-1~50.text:
### What the latest regional levels show

The World Bank series on women first married by age 18 measures the share of women aged 20 to 24 who were married or in union before their eighteenth birthday. For the world as a whole the figure was 19.5% in 2022. The global figure conceals a wide range. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 31.1% in 2022, South Asia at 25.6%, the grouping of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 17.7%, and East Asia and Pacific at 5.6%. By income, lower middle income countries stood at 24.4% and upper middle income countries at 8.5%.

These figures are the latest values the aggregate series holds, and the 2022 reading is the same for the start and end of the comparison made by the bench, so the levels alone say nothing about change. They do establish that the practice remains concentrated. A woman aged 20 to 24 in Sub-Saharan Africa was about five and a half times as likely to have married as a child as one in East Asia and Pacific, and the gap between lower and upper middle income countries is nearly threefold. Poverty, limited secondary schooling for girls, weak enforcement of minimum-age laws, customary practice and insecurity all feed early marriage; where girls stay in school and households are better off, the practice recedes.

### Progress against the 2030 target

Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage. Read literally, elimination means a value of zero by 2030, and the bench has applied that reading. It is one interpretation: the indicator counts marriage or union before 18, and the legal and social definitions of a union differ among countries, so zero is a demanding benchmark rather than a settled one.

Of the 20 countries with enough survey observations to be assessed, none was on track or had met the target, and none of their population fell in that class. Two countries, holding 5.8% of the assessed population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Fourteen countries, holding 91.8% of the population, showed marginal progress and needed significant acceleration. One country, with 0.8% of the population, was stagnant, and three countries, with 1.6%, were regressing. The weight of the assessment therefore lies in the large group where decline is real but far too slow. At present rates, elimination by 2030 is out of reach for every assessed country, and the question for policy is how quickly the decline can be hastened rather than whether the target will be met on time.

The assessed set is small against 145 countries that have reported at least once, so these shares describe the countries with repeated surveys and not the world. Countries with the heaviest burdens are not necessarily those with the most frequent surveys.

### Inequality among countries

Among the countries with data in both years, population-weighted inequality in the child marriage rate fell between 2012 and 2018. The Gini coefficient moved from 0.28 in 2012, with 21 countries, to 0.27 in 2018, with 20 countries. The Theil index fell from 0.16 to 0.12, and the coefficient of variation from 0.63 to 0.49. Countries have become somewhat more alike in their rates.

The composition of what remains is telling. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions rose from 73.0% in 2012 to 89.8% in 2018. Variation within regions has thus shrunk faster than variation between them, so the problem is increasingly defined by region: where a country lies now predicts its rate more than it did. Because the two years cover slightly different sets of countries, the comparison should be read as indicative. The finding still suggests that national laws, schooling and cash support have narrowed differences inside regions, while the regions of highest prevalence have not converged on the others.

### Surveys, the years after 2015 and after 2020

The data come from household surveys, mainly the Demographic and Health Surveys and UNICEF's Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys, and countries are surveyed every few years. The number reporting in a year has ranged from 5 in 2002 to 21 in 2012 and 20 in 2018. After 2015 the count was 11 in 2015, 16 in 2016, 11 in 2017, 20 in 2018 and 17 in 2019. In the pandemic years it was 12 in 2020, 13 in 2021 and 18 in 2022, then 17 in 2023, 12 in 2024 and only 3 in 2025. The 2025 figure is a sign of reporting lag rather than of any change in the practice.

This irregular rhythm limits what can be said about the effects of 2015 and of 2020. School closures, economic shocks and interrupted services during the pandemic were widely expected to raise early marriage, and the three regressing countries are consistent with that concern. The indicator, however, describes women aged 20 to 24, so it records marriages that took place several years earlier. A rise in marriages of girls in 2020 and 2021 would show up fully only in surveys of the middle and later 2020s. The present series therefore can neither confirm nor rule out a pandemic effect.

### Implications for 2030

The evidence supports three conclusions. Child marriage affects about one in five young women worldwide, and nearly one in three in Sub-Saharan Africa. Almost all assessed countries are moving in the right direction, but too slowly for the target as written. And the problem is increasingly regional, so effort has to be concentrated where prevalence is highest.

The measures with the best record are well established: keeping girls in secondary school, enforcing an unambiguous minimum marriage age of 18 without exceptions, registering births and marriages, supporting poor households so that marriage is not a means of relief, and working with communities and religious leaders. Because the indicator lags the behaviour it counts, results of action taken now will appear in the data late.

### Proposals

Governments in the regions of highest prevalence should set the legal minimum marriage age at 18 without exceptions for parental or judicial consent, and fund its enforcement through civil registration.

Ministries of education and their development partners should retain girls in secondary school through stipends, fee removal and safe transport, targeting districts where early marriage is most common.

National statistical offices and survey sponsors should schedule household surveys at fixed intervals so that every country reports at least every five years, and publish results promptly.

UNICEF and the World Bank should report the age 15 and age 18 indicators alongside a younger-cohort series, so that the effect of the pandemic years can be read sooner.

w-c04-1-1~farah/writer-1~50.text:
### The global ratio and the 2030 threshold

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled world ratio stood at 228.0 in 2015 and 197.0 in 2023. The decline is real but slow. Projecting the 2015-2023 trend to 2030 gives an expected ratio of 173.3 per 100,000 live births, far above the threshold. The trend tool classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and the ratio of achieved to required pace is 0.35. At the observed pace, roughly a third of the reduction needed is being delivered. The answer to the question posed is therefore no: on present evidence the global ratio is not on course for fewer than 70.

The figures are modelled estimates, not counts. The series is produced by a regression that draws on the share of maternal deaths among non-AIDS deaths in women aged 15-49, fertility, skilled birth attendance and income. Annual movements therefore partly reflect changes in model inputs and revisions, and should be read as estimates with wide uncertainty, particularly where vital registration is weak.

### Regional and income-group divergence

The global figure conceals a split between groups that have already met the threshold and groups that remain several multiples above it. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593.0 in 2015 to 448.0 in 2023, and its expected 2030 value is 350.5, five times the target. Its progress ratio is 0.46. South Asia made the largest proportional gain, from 173.0 to 120.0, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 and a ratio of 0.83: the nearest of the high-burden regions to the target, but still above it. Low-income economies fell from 491.0 to 346.0, expected 254.7 in 2030, while lower-middle-income economies fell from 291.0 to 235.0, expected 194.9, with a ratio of 0.44. That lower-middle-income group is slower than the low-income group in relative terms is notable. It contains large populations and countries with heavy absolute burdens of births, so its pace weighs heavily on the world total.

East Asia and Pacific, at 66.0 in 2023 against 70.0 in 2015, is classed as on track, as is the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping at 47.0, down from 54.0. Europe and Central Asia fell from 14.0 to 11.0, North America from 17.0 to 16.0, and high-income countries from 11.0 to 10.0. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61.0 to 57.0. These groups are below 70 already, so being on track means holding the level, not achieving a large reduction. Their slow absolute declines are floor effects: the remaining deaths are harder to avert, and in some high-income settings are affected by obesity, older maternal age and unequal access within countries.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception, rising from 74.0 to 77.0 and classed as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. The region is close to the threshold but moving away from it. Without discussing individual causes beyond what is well established, the region has high rates of caesarean birth and near-universal facility delivery, so the problem is more likely to lie in quality of care, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders, and inequality between and within countries than in access to a birth attendant. The pandemic period also fell heavily on the region.

### Countries and the distribution of risk

At country level the picture is more favourable than the world ratio suggests. Of 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 74.5% of the assessed population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of population, show moderate progress but need acceleration; 23 countries, with 8.4% of population, show marginal progress; one is stagnant; and 7, with 0.6% of population, are in regression. Most people live in countries that already meet the threshold, yet the world ratio remains high because the deaths are concentrated in the minority of countries with very high ratios and large numbers of births. A population-weighted share on track is thus a poor guide to where deaths occur.

Inequality among countries has not fallen. The population-weighted Gini coefficient of country ratios was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. Between-region differences accounted for 70.9% of the Theil index in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023, so the gap remains mainly regional, with a growing share arising within regions. The convergence test points the other way on a narrower measure: the coefficient of variation across countries fell from 1.500 to 1.410, and the convergence coefficient is -0.00372 (p 0.0024), though R squared is only 0.050. Countries with higher starting ratios tended to fall faster, but the relationship explains very little. Taken together, relative convergence is weak and the absolute gap between the worst-affected countries and the rest is still the dominant feature.

### Change after 2015 and after 2020

The break analysis of annual change in the world ratio identifies a slowdown in 2008 and disturbances from 2020. The mean annual change was -8.4 per 100,000 live births across 2001-2007 and -5.2 across 2008-2019. The pace of decline had therefore already slowed before the Goals began in 2015, and the 2015-2023 trend of -0.0181 a year in logarithmic terms is a continuation of that slower regime, not a new one. The Goals did not coincide with an acceleration.

The pandemic left a visible mark in the modelled series. The world ratio rose by 4.0 in 2020 and by 31.0 in 2021, then fell by 39.0 in 2022 and by 6.0 in 2023. Direct COVID-19 infection in pregnancy, disrupted antenatal and delivery services, and strained health systems are the well-established channels. The sharp reversal in 2022 means that the 2023 level of 197.0 sits below the 2015 level but above what an uninterrupted pre-2020 trend would have implied. Part of the swing may be an artefact of how the model treated pandemic-year inputs, and the size of the 2021 rise and 2022 fall should be read with that caution.

### What the trend implies for 2030

Meeting 70 by 2030 from 197.0 in 2023 requires a far steeper decline than anything observed in the series. The pace of 2001-2007, the fastest segment, would still leave the world ratio well above the threshold by 2030. Because the burden is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the ratio was 448.0, and in low-income and lower-middle-income economies, the global target will be decided there. Even if every region now classed as on track stays so, the world ratio cannot approach 70 unless these high-burden settings fall by a large proportion. Within the 2030 horizon, the realistic expectation is a substantial miss, with the gap widest for the poorest countries.

The determinants are well known: skilled attendance at birth, access to emergency obstetric care and blood, management of haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia and sepsis, family planning that reduces high-risk pregnancies, and a functioning referral system. Attendance by skilled staff is the series the shelf holds on one of these, and the UHC sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health is a broader gauge of service coverage. Attendance alone is not sufficient where facilities lack supplies, staff or transport, which is a reason the quality of care, not only its presence, belongs in the agenda.

### Measurement limits

The series reports for all 194 countries in every year from 2000 to 2023, but full coverage is a product of modelling, not of observation. The shelf's series on the completeness of death registration with cause-of-death information covers only 121 countries and ends in 2017, which shows how thin the directly observed base is. Where registration is incomplete, as it is across much of the high-burden world, ratios rest on surveys, sibling histories and covariates. The threshold of 70 can also be read in two ways: as a global ratio, as the target text states, or as a country-level standard, as the supplementary national target of no country above 140 is often cited. This section follows the global reading, and says so because the two lead to different verdicts on the 128 countries counted as on track.

w-c04-5-1~loom/writer-1~51.text:
### Global level and direction

Target 3.5 asks countries to strengthen the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including the harmful use of alcohol. The World Development Indicators carry one measure that bears on it: total alcohol consumption per person aged 15 or older, in litres of pure alcohol, published by the World Health Organization as projected estimates. The series sums recorded and unrecorded alcohol and adjusts for tourist consumption. The target has no numerical value, so progress can only be read as a direction of travel. The wording of the target also leaves open whether the aim is lower average consumption or lower harm, and the indicator captures only the first.

The world average fell from 5.9 litres in 2015 to 4.9 litres in 2020. That is a drop of about one litre in five years, and the trend tool classifies the world as on track, with a rate of -0.0363. Two cautions apply. The values are model-based projections, not annual surveys, so smooth movements partly reflect the method. The period also includes the pandemic year 2020, when closures of bars and restaurants, falling incomes and disrupted trade affected sales in ways that may not persist. Part of the fall may therefore be temporary.

### Regional differences

The regions start from very different levels. In 2020 Europe and Central Asia stood at 8.9 litres, down from 9.5 litres in 2015, and North America at 9.9 litres. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 0.3 litres, a level that reflects religious prohibition and legal restriction, and for which unrecorded consumption is hard to measure. The ordering is a matter of culture, law and price as much as of health policy.

The fastest decline was in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres to 4.5 litres, with a rate of -0.0657. South Asia fell from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, Latin America and the Caribbean from 6.5 litres to 5.8 litres, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 4.6 litres to 4.2 litres. All four are classed as on track. Europe and Central Asia, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, show moderate progress with acceleration needed. North America is the only region classed as regression: consumption rose from 9.5 litres to 9.9 litres, at a rate of 0.0075.

### Income groups

Alcohol consumption rises with income at the top and is flatter below. High-income economies fell from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a marginal decline that the tool says needs significant acceleration. Upper-middle-income economies fell sharply, from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres, the largest drop of any income group. Lower-middle-income economies fell from 3.9 litres to 3.3 litres. Low-income economies hardly moved, from 2.9 litres to 2.8 litres.

This pattern matters for interpretation. Declines in upper-middle-income economies are large enough to drive much of the global fall, given the weight of populous countries in that group. Low-income economies consume least but are the group where marketing by large producers, rising incomes and urbanisation have historically pushed consumption upward, and where regulation and treatment capacity are thinnest. A flat average there should not be read as safety.

### Countries and convergence

Among 183 countries assessed, 75 are on track, covering 60.4% of their population. A further 21 show moderate progress (11.0% of population) and 21 marginal progress (7.3%). Twelve are stagnant (3.1%), and 54 are in regression, covering 18.2% of their population. A decline in a majority of countries therefore coexists with a large minority where consumption is rising, and the regressing countries are numerous even though they hold under a fifth of people.

The countries are not converging. Across 181 countries, the regression of change on starting level gives a beta of -0.0059 with a p-value of 0.60 and an R-squared of 0.01, so the starting level does not predict the change. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.74 in 2020, a slight widening of dispersion. High consumers are not systematically cutting faster than low consumers, which means the global fall owes more to particular large countries than to a common pattern.

### Men and women

The male and female series move together. Across 185 countries the Spearman correlation of 2015-2020 changes is 0.99, and that of 2020 levels is 0.99. Countries where men drink more are those where women drink more, and where one falls the other falls. Because the two correlate so closely, the sex-disaggregated series add little independent information on direction; they would matter for levels, since men drink much more than women, but this section does not quote those levels. Policies that act on price, availability and marketing act on both sexes at once.

### Implications for 2030

On the measure available, the world is moving in the intended direction, and most regions and most countries by number are on track. Yet the fall rests on five projected years that include the pandemic, the high-income and low-income groups are moving slowly, and North America is moving the wrong way. If 2020 reflects a temporary shock, a rebound could erase part of the gain. Reading the result as success would be premature. Consumption per adult is also a poor proxy for harm: heavy episodic drinking, drink-driving and liver disease depend on how alcohol is consumed, not only on the average. Coverage is good, with 185 countries reporting in each year from 2000 to 2020 and 187 in some years, so the gap lies in the indicator's meaning, not in its reach.

w-c03-5-1~loom/writer-3~51.text:
### Land under farming has barely moved

Agricultural land, the sum of arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, covered 36.8 per cent of the world's land area in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023. The stability is the main finding: the extensive margin of farming has stopped growing at world level, and the 208 countries reporting in 2024 show no general wave of conversion or abandonment. The regional picture is similarly flat. South Asia remains the most heavily farmed region at 58.6 per cent in 2015 and 58.3 per cent in 2023. East Asia and Pacific stood at 46.5 per cent and then 46.8 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 43.9 per cent to 44.7 per cent, the largest gain among the regions, while Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 33.3 per cent to 32.9 per cent and Europe and Central Asia from 29.3 per cent to 29.1 per cent. North America held at about 26.7 per cent in both years.

By income group the shares are also close together: 41.4 per cent in low-income countries in 2015 and 42.1 per cent in 2023; 42.5 per cent and 43.0 per cent in lower middle income; 43.1 per cent and 42.8 per cent in upper middle income; and 28.1 per cent and 28.2 per cent in high income. The measure has a limit that matters for Target 2.4. It counts pasture alongside cropland, and it says nothing about the quality of the land, about degradation, or about whether land is managed to maintain ecosystems. A constant share can conceal soil loss in one place and recovery in another. The series is a measure of footprint, not of sustainability.

### Fertiliser use is uneven and converging slowly

Fertiliser consumption per hectare of arable land shows far wider differences than land use. The world average was 132.9 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, a small rise. Behind it lie very different levels. East Asia and Pacific applied 329.1 kilograms in 2015 and 304.1 in 2023, still the highest in the world, though falling, which is consistent with policy efforts in the largest producers to curb overuse and raise nutrient efficiency. South Asia rose from 175.0 to 206.0 kilograms. Latin America and the Caribbean rose sharply, from 135.1 to 173.9, reflecting the expansion of commercial grain and oilseed production. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 90.0 to 102.0. North America moved from 124.3 to 128.8, and Europe and Central Asia from 78.7 to 76.0.

Sub-Saharan Africa applied 14.4 kilograms in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023, about a fifteenth of the East Asian level in the latter year. The income groups tell the same story. Low-income countries used 10.0 kilograms in 2015 and 13.9 in 2023, against 114.6 and 130.8 in lower middle income, 213.0 and 213.8 in upper middle income, and 106.3 and 104.3 in high income. The poorest countries therefore gained in relative terms but remain at a level at which nutrient depletion, not pollution, is the central risk. Cost, weak input markets, poor transport and limited credit are the well-established explanations. At the other end, high application in some upper middle-income systems points to the opposite problem of runoff, water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from nitrogen.

Across 192 countries, fertiliser use shows convergence between 2015 and 2022. The convergence coefficient is -0.034 with R-squared of 0.3, and the coefficient of variation fell from 2.15 to 1.68. Countries starting with low application tended to raise it faster in proportional terms, and those with high application to hold or reduce it. The fall in dispersion is real but modest, and the explanatory power is limited: most of the variation between countries is not explained by starting level alone. Convergence of this kind is also ambiguous in terms of Target 2.4. Moving the lowest users up is desirable; moving the highest users down is desirable only if yields and soil health are protected.

### Agriculture dominates freshwater withdrawal

Agriculture accounted for 71.5 per cent of total freshwater withdrawals worldwide in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022, with 178 countries reporting in 2022. The share is much the same across the period, and the data are collected infrequently, so some country values are carried forward; South Asia's identical figure of 90.3 per cent in both years is an example and should be read as a lack of fresh observation rather than proof of no change. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 90.1 per cent in 2015 and 87.3 per cent in 2022, the largest fall, which probably reflects growing urban and industrial demand and desalination rather than less irrigation. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 78.6 to 79.0 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean from 73.4 to 74.4, and East Asia and Pacific from 73.2 to 72.1. Europe and Central Asia was near 52.0 per cent in both years and North America near 37 per cent.

The income gradient is steep. Low-income countries drew 90.8 per cent of their withdrawals for agriculture in 2015 and 90.9 per cent in 2022; lower middle income 89.4 and 88.8; upper middle income 74.7 and 73.6; high income 42.2 and 42.7. A high agricultural share is partly a sign of a small industrial and municipal economy and does not by itself indicate waste. The share also says nothing about the volume withdrawn, the pressure on renewable resources, or the efficiency of use. It cannot show whether withdrawals are sustainable, which is what Target 2.4 asks.

### Intensity and yield are linked in levels, not in change

Fertiliser and cereal yield are strongly associated in levels across 179 countries: the Spearman correlation of 2022 levels is 0.72. The association of changes between 2015 and 2022 is weak, at 0.13. Countries that use more fertiliser per hectare have higher yields, but countries that raised fertiliser use did not reliably raise yields faster. The reasons are well known: yield depends on seed, water control, pest management, soils and weather as well as nutrients, and returns to additional fertiliser diminish quickly once nutrient need is met. For low-use countries, the first increments tend to pay more than for high-use ones, but only where other conditions allow it.

Cereal yield trends confirm the divide. The world's rate of change was 0.009 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures pace against a generic standard and is an interpretive reading, not a legal commitment. North America, South Asia and the lower middle-income group were classed as on track, with rates of 0.026, 0.026 and 0.022. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan showed moderate progress at 0.013. East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, high income and upper middle income were all marginal, between 0.008 and 0.011. Sub-Saharan Africa stagnated at 0.001, and the low-income group regressed at -0.002; its yield was 1,373 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,345 in 2024, while North America reached 8,414 in 2024.

### Distribution of countries and implications for 2030

Among 180 countries assessed on cereal yield, 39 were on track or had met the standard, covering 29.5 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 19 showed moderate progress, with 14.0 per cent of population, and 27 marginal progress, with 25.7 per cent. Twenty-five stagnated, with 15.6 per cent, and 70 regressed, with 15.2 per cent. The count of regressing countries is large, but it covers a smaller share of people than the on-track group, so the failures are concentrated in many smaller or more fragile economies, where conflict, drought and weak input supply are common causes.

For 2030, the data suggest that production gains cannot come from more land, since the agricultural share is flat. They must come from yield, which means more nutrients where soils are depleted, and more efficient use where application is already heavy. Water offers little room: with about seven tenths of withdrawals already going to farming, further expansion of irrigation must come with efficiency and storage gains. The post-2015 and post-2020 periods show no visible break in these series, partly because they move slowly and partly because the latest water observations end in 2022. Nothing in the indicators measures resilience, ecosystem maintenance or adaptation, so the qualitative core of Target 2.4 cannot be judged from them.
