w-c02-6-1~ewan/writer-1~51.text:
### Health takes a small and uneven share of public budgets

Target 1.a asks for resources adequate to end poverty, and target 1.b for policy frameworks that put the poor first. Neither sets a number, so this section reads them through the shares of public budgets that governments devote to health and education, the two services that most directly shape whether poor households can escape poverty. Because the targets set no threshold, the trend assessments below treat any sustained increase as progress; that is one reading among several, and a share can rise because other spending falls rather than because services expand.

The priority governments give to health from their own resources differs enormously across regions. In North America, domestic general government health expenditure rose from 22.1% of general government expenditure in 2015 to 22.8% in 2023. High-income countries as a group moved from 17.9% to 18.5% over the same years. Europe and Central Asia slipped slightly, from 15.0% to 14.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean edged up from 11.5% to 11.8%. At the other end, South Asia devoted only 3.7% of public spending to health from domestic sources in 2015, rising to 4.8% in 2022, a real improvement from a very low base. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 10.9% in 2015 and 11.3% in 2019, its latest regional figure.

The income-group aggregates are the most troubling. Low-income countries allocated 5.4% of public spending to health in 2015 and 5.3% in 2017; lower-middle-income countries 4.8% in 2015 and 4.7% in 2018. These series stop early, so the aggregates say nothing about how poorer governments responded to the pandemic. The gap is itself telling: only 7 countries had reported for 2024. Where the poor are most numerous, governments put the smallest share of their own budgets into health, and households fill the gap with out-of-pocket payments that push families into poverty. Part of the low domestic share reflects external financing, which this indicator deliberately excludes; donor money can be withdrawn, which is why the domestic share matters for predictability, the word target 1.a uses.

### Country trends in health priority are mixed

Across 193 countries assessed, 72 are on track to raise the health share, home to 40.8% of the assessed population. A further 11 countries (4.3% of population) show moderate progress and 30 (22.1%) marginal progress. Nineteen countries, with 11.5% of the population, are stagnating, and 61, with 21.3%, are regressing. Roughly a third of humanity therefore lives where the health priority is static or falling. The pandemic raised health spending sharply in 2020 and 2021 in many countries, often financed by borrowing; as emergency programmes ended and debt service climbed, health budgets in many middle- and low-income countries came under pressure again. Without sustained reallocation, the regressing group is likely to persist to 2030.

### Education is losing ground in public budgets

Education tells a starker story. Worldwide, government expenditure on education fell marginally from 14.1% of total government expenditure in 2015 to 14.0% in 2023, but the aggregate hides substantial declines. East Asia and the Pacific fell from 15.1% to 13.0% between 2015 and 2023. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 15.2% in 2016 to 13.1% in 2022. South Asia went from 13.9% in 2015 to 11.3% in 2025, and North America from 12.9% to 10.7% between 2015 and 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa, which still gives education one of the largest budget shares, declined from 17.0% in 2015 to 15.4% in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean was steady at 16.4% and 16.6% between 2015 and 2024, and Europe and Central Asia at 11.8% in 2015 and 11.7% in 2022.

By income, lower-middle-income countries show the sharpest fall, from 16.4% in 2015 to 13.6% in 2024. Upper-middle-income countries held at 15.0% and 15.1%, while high-income countries slipped from 12.4% in 2015 to 12.0% in 2022. Low-income countries are the exception, rising from 14.9% in 2015 to 16.7% in 2022, although part of their education budgets is financed by external transfers, which this indicator includes. Some declines reflect ageing populations with fewer school-age children, plausibly in East Asia and North America; but in South Asia and lower-middle-income countries, with large young populations, a shrinking education share signals competition from debt interest, energy subsidies and, after 2020, pandemic outlays. Reporting is reasonably current: 60 countries had reported for 2025.

The country trend assessment confirms the pattern. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are regressing, and they hold 78.2% of the assessed population. Only 29 countries, with 7.1% of the population, are on track or have met the implicit goal of increase; 13 (1.8%) make moderate progress, 12 (2.3%) marginal progress, and 23 (10.5%) stagnate. On present trends, by 2030 most of the world's people will live in countries where education claims a smaller share of public money than when the goals were adopted.

### Health and education are not competing, and not moving together

One might expect budgets to trade health against education. Across 129 countries between 2015 and 2022, the rank correlation between changes in the two shares is 0.16, and between their 2022 levels 0.09. Both are close to zero: a government that raises its health priority is barely more likely to raise education, and the ranking of countries on one share says almost nothing about the other. Spending priorities appear to be set service by service, under separate pressures, rather than within a coherent strategy for reducing poverty of the kind target 1.b envisages.

### Education effort is diverging between countries

Measured against national income, education spending has become more unequal across countries. Among 164 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of government education expenditure as a share of GDP rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022, and the Theil index from 0.07 to 0.10. Differences between regions account for a modest and slightly falling part of the dispersion, 23.8% of the Theil index in 2015 and 22.3% in 2022. Most of the divergence is thus within regions: neighbours with similar incomes are making increasingly different choices. That is evidence that the decline is a matter of policy, not of fate, and that national decisions can reverse it.

w-c02-1-1~cedar/writer-3~51.text:
### The headline measure and what it replaces

The target the cooperative inherits, Target 1.1, speaks of eradicating extreme poverty for all people everywhere, and its wording still carries the old threshold of $1.25 a day. The series the World Bank now publishes is not that line. It counts the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity prices, and the World Bank's own note warns that revisions to purchasing power exchange rates mean country rates cannot be compared with those of earlier editions. A reader who holds a figure from an older report in mind should therefore discard it. The levels below belong to a new price base, and the question of whether the target is within reach is asked of that base, with the further caveat that the target text and the line in use are not the same thing. What the target means by eradication is itself open to more than one reading: zero, or a share low enough to be statistically indistinguishable from zero, or the 3 per cent figure that the World Bank has used as a working definition of an end to extreme poverty. The trend tool used here takes the strictest reading, a headcount of zero in 2030, and that choice makes the verdicts below severe by construction. Where a different reading would change a conclusion, the text says so.

The data are drawn from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly, are costly, and reach countries at different dates. Regional and world figures for recent years are therefore partly modelled and partly projected from surveys of earlier years. This matters throughout, and the section on coverage below returns to it.

### The world level: a fall, but a slowing one

The world headcount ratio at the international line stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. That is a fall of 3.3 percentage points in nine years, a real and large reduction in the number of people living in the deepest deprivation, set against population growth that was concentrated in the poorest regions. It is also far short of what the target requires. The trend tool fits the annual rate of decline since 2015 and extends it to 2030. On that extrapolation the world would still stand at 8.4 per cent in 2030. The ratio of progress achieved to progress required, which the tool computes against a target of zero, is 0.38 for the world, and the verdict is marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. On the strict reading of the target it is not within reach on the present trajectory. On the looser reading of a low single-digit share the answer is the same, because 8.4 per cent lies well above any such line.

The pace of decline was not constant. The breaks analysis finds two turning points in the annual change of the world series, in 2014 and in 2021. In the segment from 2001 to 2013 the mean annual change was a fall of 1.59 percentage points a year. From 2014 to 2018 it was a fall of 0.88 points a year. From 2021 to 2024 it was a fall of 0.325 points a year. Taken at face value, the pace of reduction after 2021 is about a fifth of the pace of the first decade of the century. Part of this is arithmetic and part is structure. When a headcount is large and concentrated among people near the line, growth in a few big economies lifts millions across it quickly. Once the poor are mostly found in places with weak growth, fragile states, or conflict, each further percentage point costs far more. The slowdown is not a failure of the same policies; it reflects a change in who remains poor and where they live. The 2014 break also sits before the Goals were adopted, so the deceleration cannot be attributed to the post-2015 period alone. The data show that the easy gains were largely taken before 2015.

The 2020 shock is visible only faintly in the world series because the break dates fall in 2014 and 2021 rather than in 2020. The pandemic reversed progress in many countries, and the world's recovery in the years since has been slower than the pre-2014 rate. The 2021 break marks the point from which the decline resumed at a markedly lower speed. How much of that is a lasting effect of the pandemic, of food and energy price increases, of debt distress in low-income countries, and of conflict cannot be separated with these series alone.

### Regions: a divergence behind the average

The world average conceals a division between regions that have largely left extreme poverty behind and regions where it is not diminishing at all.

East Asia and the Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Its progress ratio is 0.84, rated moderate progress with acceleration needed, and the extrapolation reaches 1.0 per cent in 2030, close to the floor at which survey-based measurement is hard to distinguish from zero. The regional story is mainly the continuation of decades of rapid growth and structural change, together with targeted rural programmes. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 to 0.6 per cent over the same years, with an expected 0.4 per cent in 2030. Upper middle income countries as a group fell from 5.8 per cent to 2.1 per cent, and also receive the verdict of moderate progress. For these groups, the target on a strict reading is out of reach in 2030 only by small margins, and in practical terms the remaining task is a matter of reaching the last pockets: ethnic minorities, remote areas, the displaced, and people outside the frame of household surveys.

High-income economies sit at 0.7 per cent in 2015 and 0.6 per cent in 2024, and North America at 1.1 and 0.9 per cent. The tool reads these as marginal progress because the ratio of progress to what a target of zero demands is small, yet the levels are already minimal. The verdict illustrates a limitation of a zero target applied to a floor: a region that began near the floor cannot show a large proportional gain. For these regions, the $3.00 line is the wrong yardstick, and the cooperative's other section on national lines is the better guide to deprivation. Data for high-income economies come mostly from the Luxembourg Income Study, which uses somewhat different methods from the surveys used elsewhere, a point that counsels caution in comparing them directly with developing regions.

Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent, with an expected 3.4 per cent in 2030 and a verdict of marginal progress. The region's gains were interrupted by the pandemic and by the weak growth that preceded it, and its poverty is now sensitive to inflation and to the reach of cash transfer systems that were widened in 2020 and then scaled back in several countries.

South Asia is the most striking case. The series for the region begins in this window at 2020, at 9.4 per cent, and stands at 2.6 per cent in 2024. The progress ratio is 0.96 and the verdict is on track or target met, with an expected 0.4 per cent in 2030. A fall of that size in four years is unusual and deserves care in interpretation. The regional aggregate rests on a small number of very large countries, and its movement reflects both genuine gains and the arrival of new survey information in the largest of them. The missing values before 2020 mean the region cannot be assessed over the full period since 2015, and the favourable verdict rests on a short run. It should be read as a strong signal that needs confirming with further surveys, not as a settled trajectory. If the fall is confirmed, South Asia accounts for much of the reduction in the world figure.

The contrast is with two groups where the numbers move the wrong way or not at all. The region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 11.3 per cent in 2015 to 14.3 per cent in 2024, a regression, with an extrapolated 16.7 per cent in 2030. The grouping is unusual in combining several conflict-affected economies with others, and the increase reflects wars, displacement and economic collapse in a number of them, together with the inclusion of Afghanistan and Pakistan in the aggregate. Aggregates of this kind are driven by a few large or conflict-affected countries, and the regional rise should not be read as the experience of every country in it. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4 per cent in 2015 and 45.0 per cent in 2024. The progress ratio is 0.015, the verdict is stagnation, and the expected figure for 2030 is 44.7 per cent. Nearly half the population of the region lives below the line, as it did nine years earlier. Because population growth in the region is rapid, a constant share means a rising number of poor people, although the series used here reports shares and not counts.

### Income groups and the concentration of poverty

The grouping by national income shows the same pattern from another angle. Low-income countries stood at 50.1 per cent in 2015 and at 52.5 per cent in 2024, a rise of 2.4 percentage points, with an extrapolated 54.2 per cent in 2030 and the verdict of regression. This is the clearest adverse finding of the section: in the poorest group of economies the extreme poverty share has risen after the adoption of the Goals. Lower middle income countries fell from 16.0 per cent in 2020 to 12.4 per cent in 2024, with an expected 8.5 per cent in 2030 and a verdict of marginal progress. The series for this group begins in 2020, so the full period since 2015 is not shown, and the group's composition changes as countries cross income thresholds. A country that grows out of the low-income group takes its lower poverty with it, and the group left behind then has a higher average. Part of the rise in the low-income figure may be a compositional effect of this kind, though the size of that part cannot be measured with these series.

The overall implication is that extreme poverty is becoming a problem of a narrow set of places. The countries that remain are those with low growth, weak state capacity, conflict, high exposure to climate shocks, and fast population growth. In such places the policy tools that worked in Asia, labour-intensive manufacturing, rural road building, and rising agricultural productivity, have been harder to apply. Cash transfers and public works can reduce the depth of poverty but need fiscal space that low-income governments lack, particularly with debt service rising.

The country classification gives the same picture in numbers. Of 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.6 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 countries, with 23.1 per cent of that population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. A further 15 countries, with 11.3 per cent, show marginal progress, 7 countries with 2.2 per cent show stagnation, and 24 countries with 17.9 per cent show regression. The number of countries in regression, 24, is larger than the number on track, 18, although the on-track countries are far more populous. The weighting by population explains why the world average improves while a fifth of countries by count are going backwards. A policy audience should hold both facts: the global total is falling because of a handful of populous countries, and nearly one country in four among those assessed is moving the wrong way. The classification covers only 105 of the 168 countries that have reported at any time, so the remaining countries, which tend to be those with the weakest statistical systems, are not classified.

### Convergence and the question of who is being left behind

A test of convergence asks whether countries with higher poverty at the start of the period reduced it faster. Across 57 countries with data in both 2015 and 2022, the coefficient is 0.0066, with a p-value of 0.40 and an R-squared of 0.03. There is no evidence of convergence: initial poverty does not predict the subsequent change. The coefficient of variation, a measure of the spread of national rates relative to their mean, rose from 2.14 in 2015 to 2.68 in 2022. The distribution across countries became more unequal in relative terms, as many countries drove their rates close to zero while others stayed high. This is the opposite of what a global effort to leave no one behind would require, in which the countries furthest from the target would be expected to close the gap fastest. It means that the aggregate success of the first half of the period is not spreading to the places that most need it, and that extreme poverty is increasingly a matter of the countries rather than of a general lag.

The sample of 57 countries is limited to those with surveys in both end years, and these are not a random draw. Countries in conflict or with weak statistical systems are the least likely to have both observations, so the test probably understates the divergence rather than overstating it. The finding should be read as indicative: it rejects a simple story of catching up, but it does not identify the causes of divergence.

### What the evidence base can and cannot support

The reliability of every figure above depends on survey coverage, and the coverage fell sharply at the end of the period. The number of countries with a poverty observation in a given year was 87 in 2015 and reached 93 in 2018. It was 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted. It was 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and only 4 in 2025, with 168 countries having reported in at least one year. The drop in the last years is partly a matter of reporting lags, since surveys take time to be cleaned and harmonised, and the later years will fill in as new data arrive. It is also a sign that the world figure for 2024 is not a count of observations but largely an estimate, built from a smaller set of recent surveys and extended using growth and consumption data. Anyone reading the 2024 world level of 10.1 per cent should treat it as a nowcast with an unstated margin of error, and the same holds for the regional and income group values at the end of the period.

This bears on how the verdicts should be held. The trend tool compares a nine-year fall with the fall needed to reach zero, and it is sensitive to the end-point. A revision of the 2024 estimate when more surveys arrive could move any regional verdict by a class. The qualitative ordering is unlikely to change: Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group hold the great bulk of remaining extreme poverty, East Asia and Europe and Central Asia are near the floor, and South Asia has made a large gain whose size awaits confirmation. The reading of the world's trajectory is also unlikely to change. A level of 8.4 per cent expected in 2030 on the present trend, against a level of 10.1 per cent in 2024, means that the target will not be met by any definition on current rates. The distance can only be narrowed by a change in the trajectory of the countries where poverty is concentrated, and the evidence of the past decade is that this has not yet happened.

### Implications for 2030

Three conclusions follow. First, the global target is out of reach on present trends. The world's progress ratio of 0.38 means that less than two fifths of the progress needed has been achieved at the present pace, and the 2021 to 2024 rate of fall is far below that of earlier periods. Second, the gap between the target and the trajectory is a gap in a specific set of places, not a general shortfall. Reaching the limited set of countries that carry nearly half of their populations below the line matters more for the world total than any further gain in regions that are close to the floor. Third, the way poverty is measured will matter more as it falls. As the share drops in middle income regions, the $3.00 line becomes less informative about deprivation, and the higher lines and the multidimensional measure, treated in other parts of this chapter, will describe more of the unfinished work.

The period since 2015 can thus be summarised plainly. Poverty at the international line fell by about a quarter in relative terms at world level, but the decline slowed after 2014 and again after 2021. Progress was concentrated in Asia, was absent in Sub-Saharan Africa, and went into reverse in the low-income group and in the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. The distribution across countries has become more unequal. The remaining years to 2030 are too few for the pre-2014 pace to be restored through growth alone, and the policy question is how to direct finance, social protection and conflict prevention to the places where poverty has proved persistent.

w-c03-4-2~willow/writer-2~51.text:
### What the target asks and what the bench can measure

Target 2.3 asks for a doubling, by 2030, of the agricultural productivity and incomes of small-scale food producers, in particular women, indigenous peoples, family farmers, pastoralists and fishers. The wording carries two difficulties. First, the target is defined for a specific population, the small-scale producer, while the World Bank series available to this chapter describe whole economies. Value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing, in constant 2015 US dollars, averages over a large commercial estate and a household plot alike. Second, the target sets no baseline year and does not say whether doubling is to be measured from 2015, from the adoption of the goals, or from some earlier date. This section reads the target from 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and treats a doubling as a rise to twice the 2015 level by 2030.

Two indicators are used. Value added per agricultural worker is the closest available proxy for the official indicator on the volume of production per labour unit. Cereal yield, in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, measures output per unit of land and covers wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains. Cereal production and the land under cereals are the two components of yield. Neither series speaks to incomes, to sex, or to farm size, and neither separates the small-scale producer from the large. They show whether the conditions for a doubling exist; they cannot show that the doubling has happened for the people the target names.

### Value added per worker: a rising world average that conceals a stalled bottom

Global value added per agricultural worker stood at 3,491 US dollars in 2015 and reached 4,264 dollars in 2025, in constant 2015 prices. The annual rate implied by the trend tool is 2.0 per cent. This is an increase, and the trend tool classes the world as on track, but the classification is generous. It compares the rate with a path that the tool sets itself, since the target carries no numerical value in the bench. A doubling over fifteen years requires a compound rate of a little under five per cent a year, and a rate of 2.0 per cent is far below it for the world as a whole. By 2025, ten of the fifteen years had elapsed, and the world average had not come near twice its 2015 level.

The world figure is itself a summary of very unequal parts. It is pulled upward by East Asia and Pacific, where value added per worker rose from 4,087 dollars in 2015 to 6,991 dollars in 2025, a rate of 5.5 per cent a year. That is the only regional rate that reaches the pace a doubling demands: sustained for fifteen years, it would roughly double the level. The upper-middle-income group, which includes China and several large producers in Latin America and eastern Europe, rose from 4,378 dollars to 7,474 dollars, also at 5.5 per cent a year. The similarity of the two rates is not an accident: the economies that carry most weight in each group overlap, and the gain in both reflects the movement of labour out of farming as much as the growth of output. When many workers leave the land and output holds or rises, value added per remaining worker rises mechanically. A gain of this kind raises the average without any improvement in the position of the household that stays on a small plot.

The other regions improved at a slower pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 12,217 dollars to 17,325 dollars, at 3.6 per cent a year. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 6,294 dollars to 8,031 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. The group of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4,805 dollars to 6,181 dollars, at 2.6 per cent a year, and South Asia from 1,631 dollars to 2,082 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. All of these are reported as on track by the tool, and none except the two fast-growing groups is on a path to doubling by 2030. The finding for the world is therefore that productivity per worker has risen in most regions since 2015, that the rise is real, and that it is too slow for the target as written.

### Where productivity per worker is lowest, it has barely moved

The regions with the lowest starting points show the least progress. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 1,339 dollars per worker in 2015 and 1,496 dollars in 2025, a rate of 1.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries fell from 875 dollars in 2015 to 778 dollars in 2025, a rate of -1.2 per cent a year, which the tool classes as regression. In the lowest-income economies, then, value added per agricultural worker is lower in 2025 than it was when the goals were adopted. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 1,915 dollars to 2,336 dollars, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year.

The gap between the top and the bottom is wide. North America is shown in the data only at its 2015 value of 67,701 dollars, since the series has no later observation for the region in the extract used here, and the comparison across the decade cannot be made. High-income countries as a group rose from 28,219 dollars in 2015 to 30,775 dollars in 2025, at 0.9 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress. A group already at a high level may not need to double, and the target was written with developing countries in mind. Dividing the high-income figure by the low-income figure gives a ratio of about 32 in 2015 and about 40 in 2025; these ratios are computed from the group values above and are not a result of the bench. On that reading the gap widened over the decade, because the low-income level fell while the high-income level rose.

Background, offered as context and not as a finding of the series, helps to read this. Low-income agriculture is dominated by rain-fed smallholdings with little mechanisation, limited access to improved seed, fertiliser and credit, poor roads to markets, insecure tenure, and exposure to drought, flood and pests. Where the farm labour force keeps growing, each worker has less land and capital to work with. The years since 2015 also included conflict in several low-income countries, droughts in parts of Africa, the disruption of the pandemic after 2020, and the price shocks that followed the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The data do not allow the effect of any of these to be separated, and no result of this section tests them.

### Cereal yield: a modest rise and a persistent gap

Cereal yield tells a similar story at a smaller scale. The world yield was 3,932 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 4,229 kilograms per hectare in 2023, the latest year for which a world figure is reported. That is a gain well short of a doubling, and far short of the gain in value added per worker. Yield is a slower-moving quantity, because it depends on biology, on the share of land that is irrigated, and on the technology of seed and fertiliser. A doubling of average world cereal yield in fifteen years has no precedent in the record of any large region, and the target should not be read as requiring it of yields. The relevant question is whether yields are rising in the places where they are low.

They are not. Sub-Saharan Africa had a cereal yield of 1,443 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,453 kilograms per hectare in 2024, a change so small that it amounts to stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 1,345 kilograms per hectare in 2024. In 2024 both figures were under a fifth of the North American yield of 8,414 kilograms per hectare, which had risen from 6,677 kilograms per hectare in 2015. East Asia and Pacific, already at 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015, reached 5,430 kilograms per hectare in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 3,803 to 4,045 kilograms per hectare, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 2,732 to 3,027 kilograms per hectare, both between 2015 and 2023.

South Asia and Latin America made the larger gains among developing regions. South Asia rose from 3,041 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 3,814 kilograms per hectare in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 to 4,828 kilograms per hectare over the same years. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 2,766 to 3,366 kilograms per hectare, also from 2015 to 2024. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 4,648 to 4,942 kilograms per hectare, and high-income countries from 4,976 to 5,394 kilograms per hectare, both from 2015 to 2023. Irrigation, improved varieties and fertiliser are the usual explanations for gains of this kind, but the series do not test them. The pattern is that yields have risen where they were already moderate and have stood still where they were lowest.

### Convergence: the poorest are not catching up

A doubling target is in part a target about catching up, and the convergence tool tests whether countries that began with low values rose faster than those that began with high values. For cereal yield across 176 countries between 2015 and 2024, the estimated coefficient is -0.0016, with a p-value of 0.79 and an R-squared of 0.0013. The coefficient is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in subsequent change. There is no evidence of convergence in the strict sense. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.00 in 2015 to 0.91 in 2024, which indicates that dispersion narrowed slightly. The two results are compatible: a narrowing of dispersion without a negative coefficient suggests movement among individual countries and not a systematic rise of the poorest.

The result for value added per worker is similar. Across 168 countries between 2015 and 2024, the coefficient is 0.0012, with a p-value of 0.49 and an R-squared of 0.0024. The sign is positive, so the point estimate leans towards a slight tendency for countries with higher starting values to grow faster, although the estimate is not distinguishable from zero. The coefficient of variation moved from 1.51 to 1.43, a small fall. The reading is that there is no evidence of a systematic closing of the gap, and the distribution of agricultural labour productivity remains very wide. The implication for 2030 is that a doubling for the lowest-productivity countries cannot be expected from the forces already at work, since no catching-up appears in the data.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020, and what follows for 2030

The series offered by the bench give end points more than yearly paths, and the findings above compare 2015 with the latest year. Conclusions about the pandemic years therefore rest on background knowledge and not on the displayed results. Food production continued as an essential activity in 2020, and agricultural output proved more resilient than other sectors, which may help explain why value added per worker in most regions did not fall. Higher fertiliser and fuel costs after 2021 may have reduced the use of purchased inputs among smallholders, and this may account for part of the stagnation of yields in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries. A reader should treat this as plausible and not as shown by the series.

A second caution concerns measurement. Value added per worker is the ratio of an output measure to a labour measure, and the labour measure for agriculture depends on household surveys that count part-time, seasonal and unpaid family work unevenly. Women, who make up a large share of the agricultural labour force in many low-income countries and who are named in the target, are often under-counted. Cereal yield, moreover, applies to cereals only and leaves out roots, pulses, vegetables, fruit, livestock and fish. Reporting also varies: in some countries the harvested area is reported only as sown or cultivated area, as the series note states.

The evidence supports four conclusions. First, only East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group advanced at 5.5 per cent a year, a pace that would roughly double value added per worker over fifteen years; no other region or group is on that path. Second, the world average disguises a split: the economies with the highest productivity gained, the middle gained moderately, and the lowest-income economies lost ground. Third, cereal yields rose modestly, and not at all in Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group. Fourth, the absence of convergence in either indicator shows that, over 2015 to 2024, low starting levels did not bring faster growth.

The reading of the target matters for the verdict. If doubling is read as applying to the world average, it will not be met. If it is read as applying to each country, many countries will fail, and the low-income group has moved backwards. If it is read as applying to small-scale producers specifically, the bench cannot say, because the series do not distinguish them. The land, fertiliser, water and investment accounts appear in other sections of this chapter and are not repeated here.

w-c03-2-1~dahlia/writer-2~51.text:
### Stunting has fallen slowly since 2015

The World Bank's modelled estimate puts global stunting among children under five at 24.6% in 2015 and 23.2% in 2024. That is a fall of 1.4 percentage points in nine years. The global trend tool computes an expected 2030 value of 22.3%, set against a target reading of 5.0%. Progress is classed as marginal, needing significant acceleration. The ratio of observed to required progress is 0.12, so the pace achieved is about an eighth of the pace the target demands.

The target text refers to the internationally agreed goals for 2025 and 2030. The series holds no value for the 2025 goal, and the target can be read in more than one way: as a fixed 5.0% threshold, as the World Health Assembly aim of a 40% reduction from a 2010 baseline, or as a prevalence in each country. The trend tool uses the 5.0% reading. Under any of these readings the 2025 milestone will not be met at world level, since the 2024 value is far above a threshold near 5.0% and the distance cannot close in one year.

### Regions diverge, and the burden is concentrated

South Asia fell from 37.8% in 2015 to 31.5% in 2024, the largest regional fall, and is expected to reach 27.9% in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 34.4% to 32.3%, with an expected 31.0% in 2030. The region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 27.5% to 24.1%, with 22.1% expected in 2030. East Asia and Pacific moved from 14.5% to 13.3%, with 12.6% expected. All four are classed as marginal progress.

Europe and Central Asia is the clearest success: 6.0% in 2015 and 4.6% in 2024, with 3.8% expected in 2030, which is classed as on track. Latin America and the Caribbean is the only region classed as regression: 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024. A flat trend at that level is a policy concern, because the region is middle income, has wide inequality, and has stunting concentrated among rural and Indigenous households.

North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%, and high income countries from 3.9% to 4.0%. The trend tool labels both on track, because the values sit below the 5.0% threshold. That label should be read with care: the direction is upward, and the expected 2030 value for North America is 5.3%, above the threshold. The rise is small and may reflect estimation and sparse survey data as much as real change.

### Income groups show slow progress where need is greatest

Low income countries moved from 38.0% in 2015 to 35.8% in 2024, with 34.4% expected in 2030 and a ratio of 0.11. Lower middle income countries fell faster, from 33.9% to 28.9%, with 25.9% expected and a ratio of 0.28. Upper middle income countries fell from 11.9% to 10.8%, with 10.1% expected. The poorest group therefore starts highest and falls slowest, and the gap between low income and upper middle income countries remains about 25 points in 2024.

The convergence test confirms that there is no systematic catching up across the 162 countries reporting stunting. The convergence coefficient is -0.002, with a p-value of 0.23 and an R-squared of 0.01, which is not distinguishable from zero. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Because relative dispersion has widened, countries with low stunting have tended to fall faster in proportional terms than those with high stunting, so the distribution is spreading rather than closing.

The causes are well established: maternal undernutrition and short birth intervals, poor infant and young child feeding, repeated infection linked to unsafe water and sanitation, poverty, and weak health systems. Reductions where they occurred followed sustained investment in these areas together with income growth. Shocks after 2020, including the pandemic, price rises and conflict, are likely to have slowed gains, but the annual series cannot separate these effects from the underlying trend.

### Wasting is closer to the target but poorly measured

Global wasting fell from 7.1% in 2015 to 6.6% in 2024, against a target of 5.0% by 2030 (the internationally agreed goal for 2025 is lower than 5.0%, namely 5.0%, and for 2030 3.0%, but the shelf holds only the 5.0% reading, so the reading is ambiguous). South Asia is the outlier at 16.6% in 2015 and 15.7% in 2024, more than double any other region. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 7.0% to 5.9%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 6.5% to 5.6%. East Asia and Pacific moved from 3.7% to 3.6%. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.5% to 1.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.5% to 1.3%, and North America from 0.3% to 0.2%.

By income, low income countries fell from 7.9% to 6.4%, lower middle income from 10.5% to 9.5%, upper middle income from 2.6% to 2.1%, and high income from 0.6% to 0.4%. Lower middle income countries, which include the large South Asian populations, hold the highest wasting rate. Wasting is acute and fluctuates with seasons, food crises and disease, so a rate measured in one survey is a snapshot, and the series does not support firm claims about small changes.

Of 65 countries assessed against the wasting target, 42 are on track or have met it, covering 38.6% of their population. Four show moderate progress, covering 7.8%. Three show marginal progress and cover 33.7%, which reflects large populations in the group. None is stagnant, and 16 are in regression, covering 19.9%. The pattern is that most countries are near the target while a few very populous ones are not, so country counts overstate progress.

### Data limits qualify every finding

Wasting reporting is thin. Only 6 countries report a 2024 value, against 24 in 2023 and 48 in 2018, so the latest year rests on very little. Annual counts since 2015 have ranged between 24 and 48 countries, so most national values are interpolated, modelled or carried from older surveys. The 2024 regional figures for wasting should therefore be read as estimates. The modelled stunting series reports 162 countries for 2024, though that too is largely modelled from surveys several years apart.

Taken together, the evidence shows slow gains in stunting, uneven gains in wasting, and no convergence. Neither the 2025 nor the 2030 target for stunting will be met at global level on present trends, and regions with the highest burdens are those least likely to reach it.

### Implications for 2030

A global stunting rate of about 22.3% in 2030 would be more than four times the 5.0% threshold. Only a change in the rate of decline, several times the pace of 2015 to 2024, would alter this. Priority falls on South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where most affected children live, and on low income countries, where progress is slowest. Wasting requires attention to South Asia, where rates have barely moved, and to crisis settings where surveys are rare.

w-c02-5-1~heath/writer-1~52.text:
### What the data record

Target 1.5 asks that the resilience of the poor be built and that their exposure to climate-related extreme events be reduced by 2030. Measuring progress requires a count of people affected, a measure of how exposed populations are, and a measure of institutional preparedness. The World Development Indicators hold three series that touch on this, and they differ greatly in quality and currency.

The only series that runs to the present is new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre. It counts cases of displacement, not persons, so one person displaced twice in a year is counted twice. It also records displacement, which is only one of the ways in which a disaster affects a household. Deaths, lost crops, damaged homes and interrupted incomes that do not force departure are not captured. It is a partial indicator of exposure and a narrow one of vulnerability.

The other two series are frozen in time. The share of the population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures is an average for 1990 to 2009, reported for 168 countries in a single year, 2009. The disaster risk reduction progress score, a self-assessment on a scale of 1 to 5, was reported by 83 countries under the Hyogo Framework, with its latest value in 2011. Neither says anything about the period since 2015, the baseline year of the goals, so neither can show whether exposure or preparedness has changed. For the target's central question the shelf has no current measure of the share of the population affected, and no successor to the Hyogo scores.

### Coverage improved, which complicates trends

The number of countries reporting displacement fell to 60 in 2009 and stood at 62 in 2011, then rose to 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. It reached 133 in 2017, 142 in 2020 and 145 in 2023, out of 199 economies that have reported in any year. Reporting is thus now far wider than it was a decade ago. This matters for interpretation: a rise in the recorded total can reflect better monitoring as well as more displacement. The change after 2013 is the sharpest, and the early series before 2013 should not be compared with later years.

From 2015 onward the country count rose from 112 to 145, so part of the growth in the world total between those years may be new reporters. Because many of the countries that joined are small or low-reporting states, the effect on the global sum is probably modest, but the data do not allow it to be separated.

### Displacement after 2015

The world total of new disaster displacement was 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 in 2023. That is an increase of about 7.2 million cases, or roughly 37.5 per cent. The break analysis of annual changes finds no structural break for the world series, and its mean annual change from 2009 to 2023 is about minus 789,790 cases. That negative mean reflects the high starting values reached in the early years of the window, not a sustained fall since 2015, and it should not be read as improvement. Annual totals of displacement are dominated by a few large storms and floods, and a series of this kind will be volatile whatever the underlying trend.

The data show no clear effect of 2020 on disaster displacement. The pandemic altered mobility and reporting, but the series offers no break at that date. Climate hazards did not pause, and evacuation practice during the pandemic could have lowered or raised the count in ways the series cannot reveal.

### Regions and income groups differ sharply

The regional picture changed more than the global one. East Asia and Pacific remained the largest regional source, moving from 8,304,660 cases in 2015 to 9,038,561 in 2023. South Asia fell from 6,877,900 to 2,446,054, a large decline that may owe as much to the timing of cyclones and monsoon floods as to risk reduction, although early warning and evacuation planning in coastal South Asia have a long history of lowering casualties while increasing recorded evacuations. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1,108,287 to 6,029739 in the same period, more than a fivefold increase. Droughts, floods and cyclones in the Horn, the Sahel and southern Africa, together with growing reporting, are the likely reasons. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region rose from 1,212,730 to 2,481,660. Latin America and the Caribbean was nearly flat, 1,543,360 to 1,728,025. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 in 2016 to 4,275,239 in 2023, which reflects major flood and earthquake events and, probably, more complete reporting. North America moved from 76,000 to 394,000.

By income group the shift is toward poorer settings. Low-income countries recorded 992,200 cases in 2015 and 6,177,600 in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 9,883,673 to 5,649,287. Upper-middle-income countries doubled, from 6,620,044 to 13,815,894, and high-income countries fell from 1,692,900 to 750,497. Low-income countries therefore carry a rising share of recorded displacement despite contributing little to emissions, and their capacity to absorb the loss is least. Upper-middle-income countries, which contain several very large and exposed populations, now account for about half of the world total.

### Distribution among countries

Inequality among countries in displacement is high and growing. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient rose from 0.57 in 2015, for 112 countries, to 0.68 in 2023, for 145 countries. The Theil index rose from 0.72 to 0.89. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions fell from 70.8 per cent to 53.0 per cent. Displacement is therefore concentrated in fewer countries, and more of the difference now lies within regions than between them. A region-level reading hides much of the variation, and national disaggregation is needed to see where resilience is failing.

### Implications for 2030

Target 1.5 has no quantified threshold, and it can be read in more than one way: as fewer people affected, as less loss per event, or as stronger capacity to recover. The displacement series speaks only to the first, and only in part. On that reading, the evidence points the wrong way: the world total was higher in 2023 than in 2015, and the burden moved toward low-income countries. Because hazards are rising with warming and exposed populations keep growing in floodplains and coasts, a fall to 2030 would require a marked rise in preparedness, which the shelf cannot test.

The lack of any post-2011 preparedness measure and any post-2009 measure of the affected share is itself a finding. The target is monitored with indicators that stopped before the goals began.

### Proposals

The following follow from these findings.

The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction and the World Bank should extend the preparedness score and the share of population affected beyond 2011 and 2009, using the Sendai Framework reporting, so that Target 1.5 can be tracked from the 2015 baseline.
Donors and national governments should direct adaptation finance and early warning investment to low-income countries and to Sub-Saharan Africa, where recorded displacement has risen fastest.
Reporting agencies should flag the years in which countries entered the series, so that readers can tell new coverage from new displacement.

It cannot be split by income of the household, so how far the poor are more exposed or more vulnerable than others is not shown. Target 1.5 has no numerical threshold, so progress to 2030 cannot be judged against a fixed value.

w-c05-7-1~heath/writer-2~52.text:
### Trained teachers in primary education

Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030. The indicator available to measure it is the share of primary teachers who have received the minimum organised training required in their own country. The definition matters: the minimum is set nationally, so a trained teacher in one country may hold a qualification that another would not accept. Comparisons across countries therefore measure the attainment of national standards, not a common level of skill.

The world share of trained primary teachers stood at 80.4 per cent in 2015 and at 82.2 per cent in 2024. A gain of under two percentage points in nine years is small against a target of 100.0 per cent. The trend tool puts the world rate at 0.00243 and the expected value for 2030 at 83.4 per cent, with a ratio of 0.15 to the pace needed. It classes this as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. On present evidence, about one primary teacher in six would still lack the minimum training in 2030.

The global figure is a population-weighted blend of very different trajectories, and the regional results show why it hides more than it reveals. Where the average rises, it rises because a few large systems improve, not because most do.

### Regions and income groups

South Asia is the clear success. Its share of trained primary teachers rose from 72.9 per cent in 2015 to 87.7 per cent in 2024. The rate of 0.0209 gives an expected 99.3 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.98, so the region is classed as on track. This gain is large enough to lift the world average on its own, given the number of teachers employed there. It reflects, in general terms, sustained investment in training institutions and in upgrading the qualifications of teachers already in service, often through distance programmes.

Sub-Saharan Africa began at 66.2 per cent in 2015 and reached 68.8 per cent in 2022, the latest year the tool reports for the region. The rate of 0.0056 implies 72.0 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.17. The region has the fastest-growing school-age population, so the number of teachers needed rises each year, and expansion of enrolment has often been met by recruiting teachers with little or no training, including contract and community teachers. Training capacity has not kept pace. The result is a region where roughly three in ten primary teachers lack the minimum training, with no sign of that share closing before 2030.

By income group the same pattern appears. Low-income countries moved from 65.8 per cent in 2015 to 69.2 per cent in 2022, with an expected 73.2 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.22. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 76.4 per cent to 83.3 per cent in 2024, with an expected 88.2 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.50, which is moderate progress needing acceleration. Upper-middle-income countries are reported only for 2022, at 80.7 per cent, so no trend can be drawn for them from this result.

### Regression where levels were high

A less expected finding is decline in regions that started high. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1 per cent in 2015 to 91.6 per cent in 2020, and its expected value for 2030 is 86.9 per cent. High-income countries fell from 95.9 per cent in 2015 to 92.1 per cent in 2024, with 89.7 per cent expected in 2030. North America slipped from 99.3 per cent to 97.9 per cent, and its expected value for 2030 is 97.1 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 82.7 per cent to 81.8 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 83.9 per cent to 80.5 per cent, with 78.3 per cent expected in 2030.

The tool labels all of these as regression. Several readings are possible and the data cannot separate them. Teacher shortages may have led systems to admit staff before they complete training, through emergency or alternative routes. Countries may have changed what counts as the required minimum, or changed how they report it. In the Middle East and North Africa group, conflict and displacement, and the rapid hiring needed to absorb refugee pupils, plausibly weigh on the figures, though that is explanation from general knowledge and not from these results. In high-income systems, falling shares of fully qualified teachers sit alongside widely reported difficulties in recruiting and retaining teachers. The regional values remain high, so the concern is direction more than level.

### Countries, distribution and convergence

Country results are more mixed than the regional averages. Of 129 countries assessed for primary teachers, 64 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 65.9 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. A further 12 show moderate progress (4.2 per cent of population), 13 marginal progress (2.4 per cent) and 4 stagnation (1.2 per cent). Regression affects 36 countries holding 26.3 per cent of the population. More than a quarter of the assessed population therefore lives where the trained share is falling. The count of countries on track is generous in one respect: many countries already near 100.0 per cent are classed as on track simply by staying there.

Secondary education is no better. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 are on track (61.5 per cent of population), 10 show moderate progress (2.1 per cent), 14 marginal progress (7.7 per cent), 7 stagnation (1.0 per cent) and 36 regression (27.6 per cent). Regression is thus as common at secondary level as at primary level, and a slightly larger share of population is affected. Secondary teachers are usually trained in subject specialisms, which are harder to staff in mathematics and science, and this may contribute.

Across 48 countries with data in both 2015 and 2024, convergence is present. The beta coefficient is -0.07 with a p-value that rounds to zero, and R-squared is 0.34: countries starting lower have tended to gain more. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.17 to 0.16 over the period, a modest narrowing. The population-weighted spread tells a more cautious story. The Gini coefficient was 0.094 in 2015, 0.073 in 2020 and 0.097 in 2024, so inequality between countries fell after 2015 and then rose again, ending slightly above its starting point. The coefficient of variation in the weighted data was 0.21 in 2015, 0.14 in 2020 and 0.22 in 2024. Country coverage differs between these years, at 85, 93 and 79 countries, so part of the swing may reflect who reports. The reduction by 2020 and the reversal by 2024 should not be over-read, but they do not support a claim that gaps are closing steadily. The share of Theil inequality lying between regions was 49.3 per cent in 2015 and 53.3 per cent in 2020, meaning that about half of the inequality is a matter of which region a country belongs to.

### Teacher numbers and training

The indicator for the number of teachers is a different matter from the share trained. Across 48 countries, the Spearman correlation between changes in the trained share and the stock of primary teachers is -0.10, and between the 2024 levels it is 0.17. Both are weak. Countries that added more teachers did not systematically raise the share trained, nor did they lower it by a measurable amount. Expanding the workforce and training it are separate tasks, and success in one has not ensured success in the other. A system may hire quickly to cut class sizes while training lags, or hold numbers constant while upgrading qualifications.

This bears on how Target 4.c should be read. The target speaks of the supply of qualified teachers, which combines count and qualification. A fall in pupil-teacher ratios through untrained hiring would meet the first reading and fail the second. The pupil-teacher ratio itself is not among the results examined here, so this section cannot say whether ratios are falling; the teacher counts for primary and secondary levels are held on the shelf but were tested only against the trained share.

### Implications for 2030 and for facilities

The plain conclusion is that the trained-teacher share will not reach 100.0 per cent by 2030 at the global level. South Asia may come close. Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries are rising too slowly to close a gap of around thirty percentage points, and several higher-income regions are moving away from the target. Reporting is also thin at the margin: only 13 countries reported for 2025, so the latest year cannot yet be used for assessment.

Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive facilities, is not measured by the series examined here. Nothing in these results describes buildings, water, electricity or accessibility for pupils with disabilities, and no inference about the target should be drawn from teacher data.

### Proposals

Ministries of education in sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should fund expansion of initial teacher training places and in-service upgrading routes, so that new recruits are trained before or soon after entering classrooms.

Ministries in high-income and Middle East and North Africa countries where the trained share has fallen should publish how emergency and alternative certification routes are used, and set time limits for completing full training.

Development partners should direct teacher-training aid to least developed countries and small island developing States, and learn from the South Asian programmes of in-service upgrading.

The UNESCO Institute for Statistics and national statistical offices should report the national minimum training standard alongside the trained share, and should raise reporting for the latest year above the 13 countries now present.

w-c06-7-1~cedar/writer-2~53.text:
### What the series measure

The question asked of this section is the size of the gender gap in mobile phone ownership and internet use. The World Bank's catalogue answers only half of it. It holds internet use by sex, compiled by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU): the share of each sex that has used the Internet from any location in the last three months, by computer, mobile phone or other device. It also holds mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people, but that series is not split by sex and counts subscriptions, not owners. The gap in phone ownership cannot therefore be measured here, and what follows concerns internet use, read as a proxy for the enabling technology named in target 5.b.

Target 5.b can be read in more than one way: as access to a handset, as use of the Internet, or as the use of digital services such as mobile money. The series used here capture only the second reading, and they say nothing of how intensively or for what purpose women go online.

### The global gap

In 2019 some 51.8 per cent of the world's female population used the Internet, against 56.0 per cent of the male population, a gap of 4.2 percentage points. By 2024 the female figure was 68.2 per cent. The male series is reported as 76.6 per cent for 2025, but only seven countries reported that year, so the 2025 world value rests on estimation and is not strictly comparable with the 2024 female value. Set against the regional 2024 values, the gap in 2024 looks to be roughly of the order of eight percentage points; this is an inference, not a reported figure, and should be treated with caution.

The pattern is that both sexes gained sharply after 2019, a period that includes the pandemic of 2020, when schooling, work, health information and commerce moved online. Yet the women's share has not caught up, and in absolute points the gap appears to have widened in some regions even as access spread.

### Regional differences

Where connectivity is nearly universal, the gap is small. In North America female use rose from 89.5 per cent in 2019 to 94.1 per cent in 2024, against 89.9 and 94.7 per cent for men: a gap of 0.4 points in 2019 and 0.6 points in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia women went from 78.4 to 90.0 per cent and men from 82.3 to 91.8 per cent. In Latin America and the Caribbean the figures are 67.2 and 81.3 per cent for women, 68.4 and 82.0 per cent for men; the gap narrowed to 0.7 points. East Asia and the Pacific is the exception among richer regions: women were at 67.4 per cent in 2019, slightly above men at 66.7 per cent, but by 2024 men led, 87.6 per cent to 85.5 per cent.

The large gaps lie elsewhere. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, female use rose from 42.1 to 55.0 per cent while male use rose from 51.3 to 67.6 per cent, so the gap grew from 9.2 to 12.6 points. South Asia shows the fastest advance, women from 24.3 to 56.3 per cent, yet men moved from 34.9 to 69.1 per cent, leaving a gap of 12.8 points in 2024 against 10.6 in 2019. In Sub-Saharan Africa women reached only 29.4 per cent in 2024, from 20.2 per cent, and men 37.9 per cent, from 28.6 per cent; the gap is 8.5 points, down slightly from 8.4 points... in effect unchanged, at roughly eight to nine points.

### Income groups

By income the same story holds. In low-income countries female use was 12.6 per cent in 2019 and 18.3 per cent in 2025, while male use rose from 20.3 to 28.6 per cent; in 2025 men were thus 10.3 points ahead. Lower-middle-income countries saw women rise from 28.9 to 56.9 per cent and men from 38.0 to 68.7 per cent. In upper-middle-income countries the two sexes began level at 67.6 per cent in 2019 and reached 87.9 per cent for women and 89.7 per cent for men in 2025. In high-income countries the figures are 86.4 and 93.6 per cent for women, 88.7 and 94.9 per cent for men.

The gap is thus wider in poorer settings, and in absolute points it is widest where adoption is moving fastest, in the lower-middle-income group. That is typical of a diffusion process: men, who tend to have more income, more schooling, more mobility and greater control over household spending, adopt first, and women follow. Cost of handsets and data, literacy, safety concerns and social norms about women's autonomy all contribute, though the series cannot apportion them.

### Gap and country level move together

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male levels in 2024 is 0.948, and between the changes over the period 0.958. Countries where men connected quickly were those where women connected quickly. The gap is therefore mostly a consequence of national connectivity, not a separate national pattern, and policies that widen coverage lift women too; but that correlation says nothing about the size of the gap in any one country, which can still be large.

### Implications for 2030 and the quality of the evidence

On present trends, regions with high use will see the gap close almost entirely. For South Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, and low-income countries, convergence by 2030 is unlikely without deliberate action, since male use is rising nearly as fast as female use. Coverage also limits the reading: the number of countries reporting female use peaked at 92 in 2019, fell to 65 in 2024, and reached only 7 for 2025, so the latest values rest heavily on modelled estimates. Of 137 countries that ever reported, fewer than half report in a recent year.

w-c04-3-1~cedar/writer-4~53.text:
### HIV incidence has fallen fastest where it was highest

The incidence of HIV, measured as new infections per 1,000 uninfected population, fell at world level from 0.26 in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024. The decline was steepest in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the rate went from 1.2036 in 2015 to 0.5374 in 2024, and in low-income countries, where it went from 0.707 to 0.3534. In both groups the rate roughly halved or better over nine years. The trend tool classes the world, Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group as on track or target met, with annual rates of change of -0.0525, -0.0857 and -0.0742 respectively. Target 3.3 sets no numeric threshold for incidence, so 'on track' here means only that the pace of decline is consistent with a continuing fall; it does not measure the ending of an epidemic, a phrase that can be read in more than one way.

The causes of this decline are well established. Antiretroviral treatment expanded greatly over the period, and people with suppressed viral loads transmit the virus far less. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission, male circumcision programmes, condom promotion and, more recently, pre-exposure prophylaxis have all contributed. The data here do not isolate the contribution of each.

Other regions show a different picture. Latin America and the Caribbean moved only from 0.2438 to 0.2154, a rate of change of -0.0137, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. South Asia stood at 0.0907 in 2024 and lower-middle-income countries at 0.1783. The tool returned only the 2024 value for these two groups, so no change since 2015 can be stated for them from this result. The regional picture thus reflects a concentration of progress in the place of greatest burden, while regions with lower rates have moved little.

### The country distribution is less favourable than the aggregates

Aggregates conceal how uneven national experience has been. Of 146 countries assessed for HIV incidence, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 49.7% of the population of those assessed. Four countries (0.8% of population) showed moderate progress and 12 (3.0%) marginal progress. Sixty countries, with 35.7% of the population, were in stagnation, and 21 countries, with 10.8%, were in regression.

The contrast between the world trend and this distribution matters. The world rate is dominated by a few high-burden countries that improved strongly. Yet the number of countries stagnating or regressing, 81 of 146, is larger than the number on track. Many of these have low starting rates, where small absolute changes or noisy estimates may produce a stagnant classification; the classification does not distinguish a low, flat rate from a high, flat one. Even so, 21 countries in regression indicate that prevention is failing in some settings, often among key populations such as people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men and sex workers, who are poorly served where laws and stigma restrict services. Of 147 countries with any HIV incidence series, 139 reported in 2024, so coverage is broad.

### Tuberculosis incidence declined slowly and unevenly

World tuberculosis incidence fell from 150 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131 in 2024. The annual rate of change, -0.0149, is classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. This is a much slower decline than that of HIV. Reaching the end of the epidemic, as target 3.3 requires, would demand far steeper falls than the present pace.

Regional differences are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 285 to 205, and South Asia from 233 to 189; both are classed as on track or target met. Europe and Central Asia fell from 36 to 22, and high-income countries from 20 to 12, also on track. Low-income countries moved from 229 to 199 and lower-middle-income countries from 241 to 208, each classed as moderate progress. Upper-middle-income countries went from 107 to 92, similarly classed.

Two regions moved the wrong way. East Asia and Pacific rose from 140 to 144, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 45 to 51, both classed as regression. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group went from 115 to 110, classed as stagnation. North America stayed at 3.5, already very low. The labels follow the tool's own thresholds, which compare the pace of change with the pace implied by a target; because no numeric target is set, they should be read as indicative.

### The 2020 interruption and the tuberculosis distribution

The period after 2020 is relevant to tuberculosis. Disruption from the COVID-19 pandemic reduced case detection and diverted laboratory and staff capacity, and it is well documented that undiagnosed cases accumulate in such conditions. The tuberculosis series is an estimate of incidence, not a count of notified cases, and estimates are recalculated as methods are refined, so the 2024 figures may be revised. The results used here give endpoints only for 2015 and 2024, so the path through 2020 cannot be described from them.

Among 203 countries assessed, 123 were on track or had met the target, holding 61.2% of the population assessed. Eighteen countries (4.2%) showed moderate progress and 11 (3.9%) marginal progress. Nine countries (14.8%) were stagnating, and 42 countries (15.8%) were in regression. That 42 countries are in regression, even as the majority by number are on track, shows that decline is far from universal. Drivers of resurgence include drug-resistant disease, undernutrition, crowding, HIV co-infection and weak health-system detection. Many on-track countries are high-income countries with low rates, where reducing incidence further is a matter of finding the last latent infections.

### Malaria has not improved at world level

Malaria incidence is measured per 1,000 population at risk, and 105 countries reported in 2024. At world level it rose from 59.0112 in 2015 to 64.0411 in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa, where most cases occur, was at 232.4935 in 2015 and 229.2614 in 2024, almost unchanged. Low-income countries went from 207.1516 to 206.6892, again flat. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 54.3138 to 56.5899.

The divergence among regions is sharp. South Asia fell from 6.3233 to 1.4562, a large reduction, and upper-middle-income countries fell from 2.0345 to 1.6485. East Asia and Pacific rose from 2.4057 to 2.8121, Latin America and the Caribbean from 3.9878 to 4.2648, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group more than doubled, from 4.3337 to 9.9708. The last rise is consistent with known outbreaks linked to conflict and flooding, though the data alone do not show the cause.

Among 85 countries assessed, 36 were on track or had met the target (59.2% of population), 3 showed moderate progress (1.4%), 8 marginal progress (8.0%), 5 stagnation (4.0%), and 33 regression (27.5%). The share of population in regression, higher than for HIV or tuberculosis, is the most worrying signal. Causes include insecticide and drug resistance, funding shortfalls, climate effects on mosquito ranges, and humanitarian crises. Because the denominator is population at risk, a change in the at-risk definition can alter the rate without any change in transmission.

### Implications for 2030

Only HIV, among the three diseases, shows a world trajectory clearly consistent with sustained decline, and even there stagnation in 60 countries leaves the ending of the epidemic unproven. Tuberculosis requires acceleration, and malaria shows no net progress at world level. Target 3.3 also names neglected tropical diseases, hepatitis and water-borne diseases, for which this section has no series. The target's 2030 deadline will most probably be missed for tuberculosis and malaria on present trends.
