w-c05-3-1~rowan/writer-2~53.text:
### The global level and its meaning

Pre-primary education is the stage at which organised learning begins, and Target 4.2 asks that all girls and boys have access to quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education so that they are ready for primary school. The indicator held on the shelf is the gross enrolment ratio, which divides total enrolment, regardless of age, by the population of the official pre-primary age group. It therefore measures participation, not quality, and it can exceed 100 per cent where older or younger children are enrolled. It is also not the same as the participation rate one year before primary entry that the Goal's own indicator uses, so the reading of the target here is necessarily indirect.

The world gross enrolment ratio was 56.0 per cent in 2015 and 60.9 per cent in 2020. About three children in five of the relevant age were therefore enrolled by 2020, a gain of nearly five percentage points in five years. The target sets no numerical threshold, and the trend tool accordingly classifies the world as making moderate progress but needing acceleration, at an annual rate of 0.0169 on its own scale. A universal ratio would require a far steeper climb than the one observed.

### Regional and income differences

The differences between regions are larger than the global movement. East Asia and Pacific rose from 74.8 per cent in 2015 to 83.2 per cent in 2020. Europe and Central Asia moved from 73.9 to 78.3 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 73.2 to 75.6 per cent. North America was almost unchanged, at 70.1 per cent in 2015 and 70.3 per cent in 2020. South Asia made the largest regional gain, from 54.2 to 62.0 per cent, a rise of nearly eight points.

The lowest ratios are in Sub-Saharan Africa, at 25.5 per cent in 2015 and 28.1 per cent in 2020, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 31.2 per cent and 33.8 per cent. In both regions fewer than a third of children of the age group were enrolled in 2020. Many families there bear the cost of early learning privately, public provision often begins at primary school, and the supply of classrooms and trained staff for young children has historically been a low priority against the pressure to expand primary places.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries rose from 17.4 per cent to 20.1 per cent, lower-middle-income countries from 52.7 to 58.5 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 70.4 to 77.9 per cent, and high-income countries from 81.8 to 83.8 per cent. In 2020 the gap between low-income and high-income countries was therefore 63.6 percentage points, and it had barely moved from the 64.4 points of 2015. Low-income countries gained about three points, similar in absolute size to what high-income countries gained, so the poorest group is not closing the gap in points even where its relative growth is quick.

### Trend classifications

The trend tool labels East Asia and Pacific, South Asia, low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups as on track, with rates of 0.0217, 0.0275, 0.0298, 0.0211 and 0.0205 respectively. The label for the low-income group needs care. A rate calculated relative to a starting level of 17.4 per cent looks fast, yet the group would remain far below universal enrolment in 2030 at that pace. The classification measures pace against an unspecified benchmark, since the target carries no figure, and should not be read as a statement that the goal will be met.

Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0196) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0165) are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Europe and Central Asia (0.0117) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0063) show marginal progress. High income (0.0047) and North America (0.0005) are classed as stagnant, which in the richest settings largely reflects ratios that are already high, or that are bounded by family choice and by the start of compulsory schooling.

Among 172 countries assessed, 57 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 38.4 per cent of the assessed population. A further 17 countries, with 7.0 per cent, show moderate progress, and 12 countries, with 2.8 per cent, marginal progress. Stagnation applies to 16 countries with 11.4 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded for 70 countries with 40.3 per cent of the population. That a large group of countries regressed, even as the world average rose, is partly an artefact of changing reporting, discussed below, and partly a real sign that gains are concentrated in a minority of populous countries.

### Distribution, convergence and the shape of the trend

Across countries, population-weighted inequality in enrolment fell. The Gini coefficient was 0.239 in 2015 across 164 countries and 0.178 in 2019 across 147 countries, and the Theil index fell from 0.117 to 0.065. The between-region share of the Theil index stayed close to half, at 48.1 per cent in 2015 and 48.5 per cent in 2019, so regional location still explains about half of all inequality in enrolment. The change in country sets between the two years limits the comparison.

Convergence is weak. Across 137 countries with data in both 2015 and 2019, the convergence coefficient was negative at -0.0174 (p 0.0157), meaning countries starting lower grew somewhat faster, but the R-squared was only 0.047, so initial level explains very little of the variation. The coefficient of variation declined from 0.482 to 0.452. Catch-up is therefore real but slow and highly uneven between countries.

The world series shows breaks in the pace of change in 2005 and 2014. The mean annual change was 0.68 points in 2001 to 2004, rose to 2.02 points in 2005 to 2013, and fell to 0.99 points in 2014 to 2020. The pace after 2014 was therefore less than half that of the preceding expansion. The slowdown is consistent with the exhaustion of easier gains, with the 2015 adoption of the Goals not producing a new acceleration, and with the interruption of 2020, though the data cannot separate these causes. At 0.99 points a year, the world ratio would reach roughly 70 per cent by 2030, well short of universality; this is a simple extrapolation and not a forecast.

### Data coverage after 2020

The record thins sharply at the end. The number of countries reporting enrolment was 164 in 2015, 147 in 2019 and 143 in 2020, then 71 in 2021 and only 4 in 2022. Of 199 countries that reported in any year, most therefore have no observation for the pandemic's second year, and almost none for 2022. Consequently the effect of school closures on young children, who were often the last to return and the most affected by lost provision, cannot be measured from this series. The regional figures end in 2020, and the large count of countries classed as regressing may reflect reporting gaps or pandemic disruption in part.

Trained teachers (as a share of pre-primary teachers) and the net intake rate in grade 1, which reaches only 2019, are held on the shelf as supporting indicators, but no results for them were produced for this section. Quality, which the target names explicitly, therefore cannot be assessed here beyond noting that enrolment is a necessary but not sufficient condition.

### Implications for 2030

The evidence points to a world in which participation in pre-primary education is rising but too slowly for any reading of Target 4.2 as universal access. The regions with the lowest enrolment, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, are growing at rates that leave them well below half of the age group in 2030 if the 2015 to 2020 pace continues. Progress depends on public financing of at least one year of free pre-primary provision, on training and retaining staff, and on timely data, since current reporting cannot show whether the post-2020 recovery has happened.

w-c06-3-1~ewan/writer-2~54.text:
### One woman in five still enters marriage as a child

Target 5.3 asks for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage by 2030. The indicator chosen to watch it is retrospective: it asks women aged 20 to 24 whether they were first married, or in a union, before their eighteenth birthday. The measure therefore describes marriages that took place roughly two to eight years before the survey, and a figure published for a given year reports decisions made in families during the preceding decade. That lag matters for any judgement about 2030, because a girl who will be counted in a survey at the end of the Goal period is today already in her teens.

On the World Bank's aggregate, 19.5 per cent of women aged 20 to 24 worldwide had been married by age 18 in 2022. Put plainly, about one young woman in five began married life as a child. The global figure conceals a wide regional spread. In Sub-Saharan Africa the share was 31.1 per cent in 2022, the highest of any region with an aggregate. South Asia followed at 25.6 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 17.7 per cent, close to the world average. East Asia and the Pacific, at 5.5 per cent, was far below every other reported region.

The income grouping tells a consistent story. Lower-middle-income countries recorded 24.4 per cent in 2022, nearly three times the 8.5 per cent of upper-middle-income countries. Child marriage is concentrated where household incomes are low, where girls leave school early, and where marriage payments and the economic logic of transferring a daughter to another household weigh heavily on parents. It is also concentrated where legal minimum ages are absent, contain exceptions for parental or judicial consent, or are not enforced in customary and religious unions. None of these causes is confined to one continent, but their combination is densest in the Sahel, parts of East and Central Africa and the northern plains of South Asia.

### South Asia's decline and Sub-Saharan Africa's weight

The regional ordering has changed over the past generation. South Asia once held the highest prevalence in the world; sustained expansion of girls' secondary schooling, falling fertility, conditional cash transfers tied to keeping daughters unmarried and in school, and stronger legal enforcement in the largest country of the region have pulled the region's share down. Sub-Saharan Africa has moved more slowly, and with its young and fast-growing population it holds a rising share of the world's child brides even where national rates are edging down. The 2022 figures, with Sub-Saharan Africa above South Asia, are the visible result of these two different speeds.

A regional aggregate is itself an estimate built from surveys taken in different years. Because the indicator is collected chiefly through Demographic and Health Surveys and Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys, each country contributes a reading only every few years, and the aggregates for 2022 fill the intervals by modelling. The regional levels should be read as the best available summary, not as the outcome of a single synchronised census.

### Inequality between countries is now mostly a regional matter

The spread of prevalence among the countries surveyed in a given year, weighted by population, narrowed between 2012 and 2018. The Gini coefficient fell from 0.28 to 0.27, a small change, but the Theil index fell more clearly, from 0.16 to 0.12, and the coefficient of variation from 0.63 to 0.49. The more striking change is in the decomposition of the Theil index: the share of inequality explained by differences between regions rose from 73.0 per cent in 2012 to 89.8 per cent in 2018. Countries within each region have grown more alike, while the gap between regions now accounts for almost all of the measured dispersion.

Two cautions apply. The 2012 calculation rests on 21 countries and the 2018 one on 20, and they are not the same countries, since each year's survey round covers a different set. Part of the apparent convergence may therefore reflect which countries happened to field surveys. Even so, the direction is plausible and policy-relevant: if child marriage is increasingly a regional phenomenon, the effort to end it is increasingly a matter for regional institutions, cross-border programmes and donors concentrated on two broad geographies, rather than for scattered national outliers.

### No country assessed is on course for elimination

The target is a level of zero by 2030, a demanding reading of 'eliminate'. A softer reading, such as elimination of marriage below 15 or a fall to negligible prevalence, would change the verdict for some countries, and the target text does not settle which is meant. Taken literally, the trend assessment is stark. Of the 20 countries with enough observations to fit a trend, none was on track or had met the target, so 0.0 per cent of the assessed population lives in a country on course. Two countries, holding 5.8 per cent of the assessed population, were making moderate progress that would need acceleration. Fourteen countries, holding 91.8 per cent of the assessed population, were making only marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. One country, with 0.8 per cent of the population, had stagnated, and three, with 1.6 per cent, had regressed.

The population shares are dominated by large countries, so the weight in the marginal-progress class tells us that the populous countries where most child marriages occur are declining, but far too slowly to approach zero within the Goal period. Historical declines in the countries that have reduced child marriage fastest have taken decades rather than years, and even the most successful have not reached elimination. A literal zero by 2030 is beyond reach almost everywhere; the practical question is how much the rate of decline can be raised.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020

The adoption of the Goals in 2015 coincided with an increase in attention: national action plans, the joint UNFPA and UNICEF global programme, and a wave of legal reforms raising the minimum age of marriage to 18 without exceptions in several countries. The retrospective nature of the indicator means that these reforms show up only slowly; a law passed in 2017 affects the girls who reach 20 to 24 in surveys of the mid-2020s. The data so far confirm a continued decline but no break in its pace large enough to move countries into the on-track class.

The period after 2020 carries a specific risk. School closures during the pandemic, loss of household income, interruption of protection services and, in some places, conflict and drought all raise the incentives families face to marry daughters early. Survey fieldwork was itself disrupted: 12 countries reported in 2020, against 17 in 2019, and only 3 had reported for 2025 at the time of writing. The effect of the pandemic on child marriage will be visible fully only when girls who were adolescents in 2020 and 2021 are surveyed in their early twenties, which places the evidence close to or after 2030.

### A thin evidential base

Across the whole period 145 countries have reported the indicator at least once, but in any single year the number is small: 11 in 2015, 20 in 2018, 18 in 2022. Most high-income countries do not report it at all, on the assumption that prevalence is negligible, an assumption that registration data in some of them do not fully support where informal or religious unions occur. The female genital mutilation series that completes target 5.3 is narrower still and is not analysed here. The conclusions above are therefore firm on direction and on the regional ordering, and cautious on exact levels and on country-level change since 2020.

proposals: Governments that still permit marriage below 18 through parental, judicial or customary exceptions should remove those exceptions and require registration of all unions, including religious and customary ones.

The African Union and regional economic communities in Sub-Saharan Africa, with donors, should fund keeping girls in secondary school through cash transfers and fee abolition, the measures associated with South Asia's faster decline.

UNICEF, the DHS Program and national statistical offices should restore survey rounds delayed after 2020 and add an annual marriage module to existing household surveys so that post-pandemic change is visible before 2030.
High-income countries should publish child-marriage prevalence from civil and population registers rather than assume it is negligible.
w-c06-3-1~ewan/writer-2~54.gaps: The indicator is retrospective and reflects marriages made up to eight years before each survey, so effects of post-2015 laws and of the pandemic are barely visible yet. Few countries report in any one year, most high-income countries never report, and 2025 has only three. The data do not separate formal marriage from informal union, do not record forced marriage or boys' early marriage, and give no within-country breakdown by wealth, residence or schooling here. Female genital mutilation, the other harmful practice in target 5.3, has coverage in only 30 countries and was not analysed. The literal target of zero is open to softer readings that the data cannot adjudicate.

w-c04-4-1~cedar/writer-1~54.text:
### What the target asks and how it is read

Target 3.4 calls for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The series used here is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, if current age-specific rates persisted and no other cause intervened. The target can be read in more than one way. The official indicator for 3.4.1 is this probability, and the baseline year is 2015, the year the goals took effect. The trend tool sets the target at 12.57 per cent by 2030, which is a third below the 2015 world level of 18.9 per cent. Other readings are possible, such as a one-third reduction from each country's own 2015 level. The regional results below use the world-derived threshold, so they measure distance to a single common line rather than to each region's own one-third reduction. The target also names mental health and well-being; the only mental health measure on the shelf is the suicide mortality rate, which this section treats with the care its crude form requires.

### The world level in 2015 and 2021

The world probability of premature death from the four disease groups was 18.9 per cent in 2015 and 18.3 per cent in 2021, a fall of about 0.6 percentage points in six years. A one-third reduction would require a fall to 12.6 per cent. The trend tool puts the world's expected 2030 value at 17.5 per cent on the pace observed since 2015, and the ratio of achieved to required progress is 0.22. The classification is marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. On present evidence, the world will not reach the target; it would reach roughly a fifth of the required reduction.

The break analysis shows why. The mean annual change in the world series was a fall of 0.26 percentage points a year across 2001 to 2014, and a fall of 0.09 points a year across 2015 to 2021. The tool detects a break at 2015. Progress therefore slowed by roughly two thirds just as the goals began. The 2021 endpoint also falls within the pandemic period, when health services were disrupted and COVID-19 deaths displaced and interacted with deaths from chronic disease; the series cannot separate these influences from a longer slowdown. Earlier gains came largely from falling cardiovascular mortality, through tobacco control, blood pressure treatment and better acute care. Such gains are not inexhaustible, and ageing, obesity and diabetes push in the other direction.

### Regions and income groups

The regional picture is uneven. High-income countries stood at 13.8 per cent in 2015 and 12.8 per cent in 2021, and are the only group classified as on track, with a ratio of 1.93 and an expected 2030 value of 11.4 per cent. North America fell from 13.6 per cent to 13.3 per cent, a slower decline, with an expected 2030 value of 12.8 per cent and a ratio of 0.82, so it is moderate progress needing acceleration. Europe and Central Asia moved from 17.5 per cent to 15.7 per cent, the largest regional fall, with a ratio of 0.82 and an expected 2030 value of 13.4 per cent.

East Asia and Pacific fell from 17.8 per cent to 16.9 per cent, with an expected 2030 value of 15.6 per cent and a ratio of 0.42. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 15.3 per cent to 14.7 per cent, with an expected 2030 value of 13.9 per cent and a ratio of 0.50. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3 per cent to 20.7 per cent, with a ratio of 0.39 and an expected 2030 value of 18.5 per cent.

The highest risks lie in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. South Asia is the one region where the measure rose, from 22.1 per cent in 2015 to 22.9 per cent in 2021, a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 24.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 21.9 per cent to 21.3 per cent, with a ratio of 0.16 and an expected 2030 value of 20.4 per cent. South Asia's size means its movement weighs heavily in the world figure, and it explains much of why the world ratio is lower than that of most other regions.

By income group, low-income countries fell from 24.0 per cent to 23.0 per cent, the highest level of any group, with a ratio of 0.22. Lower-middle-income countries went from 22.8 per cent to 22.8 per cent, effectively unchanged, with a ratio of 0.004, which the tool classes as stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries fell from 18.1 per cent to 17.1 per cent, with a ratio of 0.45. The lower-middle group is where much of the world's population lives, and its stagnation is the central fact of this section. The gap between low-income and high-income countries was about 10.2 percentage points in 2015 and about 10.2 points in 2021, so the absolute gap has not narrowed.

### Distribution and convergence

The spread among countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient was 0.152 in 2015 and 0.158 in 2021; the Theil index rose from 0.038 to 0.041. The share of the Theil inequality lying between regions, as opposed to within them, rose from 27.0 per cent to 33.1 per cent, so regional membership explains more of the difference between countries than before. This is consistent with the regional pattern above, in which Europe and high-income countries gained while South Asia lost ground.

The convergence test across 185 countries gives a beta of 0.0016 with a p-value of 0.70 and an R-squared of 0.001. Countries with higher starting levels did not fall faster, and countries with lower levels did not fall more slowly; there is no detectable convergence. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.36 to 0.38. Poorer, higher-risk countries are therefore not closing on the rest. Such a result implies that the goal's aim of leaving no one behind is not being met in this measure, and that world progress depends on where gains happen to occur.

### Treatment coverage and the limits of the link

The shelf holds the universal health coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases, built from hypertension, diabetes and tobacco tracer indicators. Across 184 countries, the rank correlation between changes in the two series from 2015 to 2021 is 0.098, which is weak and of the wrong sign for a simple story in which better coverage lowers mortality. The correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247: countries with higher coverage tend to have lower premature mortality, which is the expected direction, but the association is modest. Several factors explain this. Mortality responds to treatment with long lags, so six years of coverage change may not show up. The coverage index rests on only three tracers and measures contact with services rather than control of blood pressure or glucose, or access to cancer care. Countries with high coverage also differ in income, age structure and diet. The correlation does not establish cause in either direction.

### Suicide and mental health

The shelf holds crude suicide rates for the whole population and for males, but none of these figures was among the results supplied for this section, so no number is stated for them here. Because the rates are crude rather than age-adjusted, comparisons among countries with different age structures would mislead, and suicide is a poor proxy for the wider mental health and well-being the target names. Prevalence of depression and anxiety, service availability and self-harm are not covered.

### Implications for 2030

The world will not reach a one-third reduction by 2030 on present trends. High-income countries are on course to meet the world-derived threshold, but they hold a small share of the world's population. Where risk is highest, in low-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, the pace is a fraction of what is needed or is reversed. Reaching the target would require the world's annual decline to return to something like or above the pre-2015 pace and to be spread to the lower-middle-income group. The mix of interventions known to work is cheap by comparison with the burden: tobacco taxation, salt reduction, treatment of hypertension in primary care, and access to diabetes medicines, cervical cancer screening and vaccination against hepatitis B and human papillomavirus.

w-c06-5-1~willow/writer-1~54.text:
### What the shelf can and cannot say

The question put to this section is what share of women make their own decisions on health care and contraception. The indicator that answers it most directly is the proportion of women aged 15 to 49, married or in union, who decide for themselves on all three of: refusing sex with a husband or partner, using contraception, and their own health care. A woman counts only if she answers yes to all three components. The measure is strict by design, since a woman who controls two of the three is not counted.

The results available to this section do not contain the level of that indicator for any country or region. They contain only counts of reporting countries. The levels tool returned a figure, c06-5.r1, but its summary states only that 5 countries reported in 2024. A reader should therefore not expect a global share, a regional ranking or a trend in the share here. Any such number would be invented, and none is offered. What can be analysed with care is the structure of the evidence: how many countries report, in which years, and what that implies for judging target 5.6 by 2030.

### Coverage over time

Across the whole period from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries reported at least once. That is a modest number against the universe of countries, and it is concentrated among those that run Demographic and Health Surveys, which are mostly low and middle income countries. High income countries rarely appear, so the indicator is in practice a measure of the developing world, and no figure from it should be described as global.

The annual counts show the irregular rhythm of household surveys. In 2006 and 2007, 6 countries reported in each year; the count was 3 in 2008 and 4 in 2009, then 7 in 2010 and 7 in 2011. It rose to 12 in 2012, fell to 6 in 2013 and stood at 8 in 2014. The year 2015, the baseline of the Goals, had 5 reporting countries, and 2016 had 10. Counts of 6 in 2017 and 15 in 2018 followed, the highest in the series. The count then dropped to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020, recovered to 7 in 2021, and reached 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023. In 2024 it was 5.

These swings reflect survey cycles, not changes in women's autonomy. A country is surveyed every few years, so a year with few reports is not evidence of regression, and a year with many is not evidence of progress. The dip to 4 reporting countries in 2019 and again in 2020 coincides with the pandemic, when fieldwork was suspended or delayed in many places, and the recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is consistent with a backlog of surveys being completed. That inference rests on general knowledge of how fieldwork was disrupted, not on these counts alone.

### Why the latest year looks thin

The 5 countries reporting in 2024 should not be read as the current state of the world. Latest-year coverage is always low for survey-based series because publication lags fieldwork, and because countries are visited at intervals of several years. A comparison of 2024 with 2023 on country counts would mislead; only comparisons of the same countries across survey rounds can show change. The shelf results do not supply such pairs.

For the same reason, a before-and-after reading of 2015 or 2020 is not possible from these results. Counts before 2015 and after 2015 are of similar size, yet the countries may differ, so no change in the share can be inferred.

### Why the measure matters for target 5.6

Target 5.6 asks for universal access to sexual and reproductive health and rights as agreed at Cairo and Beijing. Rights in this sense are not delivered by clinics alone. A woman who cannot refuse sex, or who needs a husband's permission to use a method or to visit a clinic, cannot use services that exist. The decision-making indicator therefore captures the demand side of the target, and it complements measures of supply such as contraceptive use or antenatal attendance.

Well-established understanding suggests the main drivers of low autonomy are the age gap between spouses, early marriage, schooling, women's own earnings, norms that treat sex within marriage as an entitlement, and laws that require spousal consent. Progress tends to be slower where several of these coincide. The strict three-part construction also means that national shares are lower than shares for any single component, and that cross-country comparisons depend on how many women are married or in union, since unmarried women are outside the base.

### Reading the target in more than one way

The target can be read as a service goal or as a rights goal, and the indicator serves only the second. It also covers women married or in union, leaving out unmarried and adolescent women, whose decisions on sexual health are often most constrained. The related shelf series on unmet need, satisfied demand, antenatal care and attitudes to refusal of sex are not analysed in this section's results, and their findings cannot be reported here.

### Implications for 2030

With 81 countries having ever reported and only a few in any year, a global verdict on target 5.6 by 2030 cannot be reached from this evidence. The practical implication is that monitoring, not only outcomes, is the weak point. Without more frequent and wider reporting, a country could improve or deteriorate for several years before the data showed it.

proposals: National statistical offices and survey sponsors should field the decision-making module in every health survey round, so that each country reports at least once every five years.
The World Bank and the United Nations Population Fund should publish country-level values with survey years alongside the counts, so that change can be compared for the same countries across rounds.
Donors that fund household surveys should protect fieldwork schedules against shocks such as the pandemic and extend the module to unmarried women and adolescents.

w-c04-2-1~rowan/writer-1~54.text:
### The thresholds and the count of countries

Target 3.2 sets two numerical thresholds: neonatal mortality of no more than 12 per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality of no more than 25 per 1,000 live births. The World Bank series, drawn from the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, cover 196 countries in 2024. The trend tool classifies each country by whether its observed pace from 2015 would carry it to the threshold by 2030. The classification does not simply count countries already below the line; it counts countries that have met the target or are on course to meet it. That distinction matters, because the target can be read in two ways: as a floor every country must reach, or as a global average to be approached. The text of the target says all countries, and the analysis follows that reading.

For neonatal mortality, 130 of 196 countries are on track or have met the threshold, and they hold 72.4% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 17 countries, with 7.8% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 36 countries, with 11.9% of the population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Four countries, with 2.1% of the population, are stagnating, and 9 countries, with 5.7%, are regressing. In all, 66 countries are not on track.

For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met the threshold, with 74.7% of the population. Moderate progress is recorded for 39 countries (16.1%), marginal progress for 15 (4.0%), stagnation for 3 (4.9%) and regression for 4 (0.3%). In all, 61 countries are not on track. The under-five threshold is therefore marginally easier to reach in country count, though the neonatal threshold is the harder test of health-system quality, as explained below.

### Global levels and the pace since 2015

The world neonatal rate fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024. The world under-five rate fell from 42.9 to 37.4 per 1,000 over the same years. Both remain above their thresholds, and the global trend is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The fitted annual rate of change is -0.0133 for neonatal and -0.0151 for under-five mortality, in proportional terms. At those paces the world would reach about 15.9 neonatal deaths and 34.1 under-five deaths per 1,000 in 2030, against thresholds of 12.0 and 25.0. The ratio of achieved to required progress is 0.48 for neonatal and 0.49 for under-five mortality: the world is moving at roughly half the pace the target demands.

A global average hides a split. The world is held back by a minority of high-mortality countries that are also, in several regions, among the most populous. Meanwhile, most countries are already below or heading below the thresholds. The finding that nearly three quarters of the world's population live in countries on track coexists with a global rate that fails the test, because the average is weighted by births, and births are concentrated where mortality is highest.

### Regional differences

The regional picture is stark. In sub-Saharan Africa, neonatal mortality fell from 29.2 to 26.6 per 1,000 between 2015 and 2024, and under-five mortality from 85.0 to 71.2. Both are classed as marginal progress. The projected 2030 values are 25.0 for neonatal and 63.3 for under-five mortality, against thresholds of 12.0 and 25.0. The progress ratios are 0.24 and 0.36. Under-five mortality in the region is nearly three times the threshold in 2024.

South Asia is the region of greatest success. Neonatal mortality fell from 25.4 to 16.6 and under-five mortality from 42.6 to 26.8. The fitted paths give 12.5 and 19.7 in 2030, and the progress ratios are 0.96 for neonatal and 1.30 for under-five mortality. South Asia is classed as on track for both. The neonatal ratio is close to one, so the margin is thin: a small slowing would move the region out of that class. The gains owe much to expanded institutional delivery, immunisation and nutrition programmes, and falling fertility, though the data here do not separate these causes.

The region combining the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 26.9 to 22.7 for neonatal and from 46.2 to 36.4 for under-five mortality. Its neonatal trend is marginal (ratio 0.45) and its under-five trend moderate (ratio 0.72). The projected 2030 values are 20.3 and 31.1. Conflict and fragility in parts of the region, and the weight of high-mortality populations, explain much of the shortfall, although this is interpretation rather than a finding of the series.

East Asia and Pacific (6.7 and 13.2 in 2024), Europe and Central Asia (4.1 and 7.8), Latin America and the Caribbean (8.3 and 15.4) and North America (3.6 and 6.4) are all below both thresholds already and are classed as on track. North America's fall was slow, from 3.9 to 3.6 neonatal and from 6.6 to 6.4 under-five, because the rate was already low; at such levels, further gains are small and costly.

### Income groups and the neonatal share

By income, low-income countries recorded 24.9 neonatal and 68.8 under-five deaths per 1,000 in 2024, down from 28.1 and 84.9. Both trends are marginal, with ratios of 0.32 and 0.42, and expected 2030 values of 23.0 and 59.8. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.9 to 21.6 and from 55.3 to 43.8, with moderate progress (ratios 0.55 and 0.59) and expected 2030 values of 18.7 and 37.5. Upper-middle-income countries, at 6.8 and 13.1 in 2024, and high-income countries, at 2.8 and 5.1, are on track.

The gradient is steep: the low-income under-five rate is about 13 times the high-income rate. The gap in neonatal mortality is larger still in relative terms, roughly nine times. Neonatal deaths are a rising share of child deaths as overall mortality falls, because infectious causes after the first month respond to vaccines, sanitation and treatment faster than the risks of birth, prematurity and infection in the first days, which depend on skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care and neonatal units. In low-income countries, the neonatal rate fell by a much smaller proportion than in lower-middle-income countries, which suggests that the quality of care around birth is the binding constraint.

### Implications for 2030 and the effect of 2020

The series are annual estimates, so the pandemic years can be examined only through the trend classes, not as a separate break; the section's results do not isolate a post-2020 change. Modelled estimates in countries with weak vital registration are partly extrapolated, so year-to-year movements there should be read cautiously.

The implications are clear. Most countries will reach the thresholds, but the target is defined for all countries, and 66 countries on the neonatal measure and 61 on the under-five measure are not on track. The 9 countries with rising neonatal mortality and the 4 with rising under-five mortality are the most urgent cases. The population in stagnating countries is 4.9% for under-five mortality, a share far larger than their count of 3 countries implies, which indicates that at least one large country is among them. Reaching the thresholds in 2030 in sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries would require a pace several times the observed one.

### Proposals

The section's findings support the proposals below.

w-c02-4-1~farah/writer-1~54.text:
### Basic services reach most people, but not the poorest countries

Target 1.4 asks that all men and women, in particular the poor and the vulnerable, have access to basic services and to financial services. The series held on the shelf measure this by country and by region rather than by household income, so the poor appear here only through the places where they are concentrated: low-income countries, rural areas and the poorest 40% of the population in the account series. With that limit stated, the picture is one of broad progress since 2015 and a stubborn deficit at the bottom of the distribution.

The share of the world's people using at least basic drinking water services rose from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024, with 202 countries reporting in the latest year. Access to electricity rose from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same years, with 215 countries reporting. Both global figures conceal a wide spread. In high-income countries basic water coverage was 99.0% in 2015 and 99.2% in 2024, so little room for gain remained. In low-income countries it was 53.1% in 2015 and 60.3% in 2024. A gain of about seven percentage points over nine years leaves roughly four in ten people in those countries without basic water, a gap that cannot be closed by 2030 at that pace.

### Water: gains concentrated where coverage was already high

By region, basic water coverage in 2024 was 99.8% in North America, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia, 97.6% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 95.9% in South Asia and 95.3% in East Asia and the Pacific. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 92.9%, up from 90.0%. Sub-Saharan Africa reached 67.5%, up from 59.2% in 2015. South Asia gained the most among the large regions in absolute terms, 90.5% to 95.9%, which reflects sustained public programmes for piped and borehole supply. Sub-Saharan Africa gained about eight percentage points, but population growth has meant that the number of people without basic water has not fallen as quickly as the share.

The country-level trend classification shows how uneven the path to 2030 is. Of 214 countries assessed against a target of full coverage, 60 are on track or have met it, and they hold 33.9% of the assessed population. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 55 countries, with 20.9%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Seventeen countries, with 1.5% of the population, are stagnant, and 37 countries, with 9.9% of the population, are regressing. Regression in 37 countries is a notable finding: it means that in those places coverage is falling, probably because of conflict, displacement, rapid urban growth outrunning networks, or the decay of ageing systems. The definition matters here. Basic water means an improved source within a 30-minute round trip, so these figures say nothing about whether the water is safe, continuous or affordable.

Rural water access is converging. Across 167 countries, the convergence regression for rural basic water over 2015 to 2024 gives a beta of -0.0164 (p below 0.001, R2 0.272), and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Countries that began with lower rural coverage have tended to gain faster, so dispersion is narrowing. The R2 shows, however, that starting level explains only about a quarter of the variation in gains, and narrowing dispersion is not the same as reaching the target.

### Sanitation: the widest gap and the clearest divergence

Sanitation shows the sharpest contrasts. The trend tool puts the world as moderate progress needing acceleration, with an expected 2030 level of 89.2% and a ratio of actual to required progress of 0.61. East Asia and the Pacific, at 94.8% in 2024 (83.7% in 2015), is on track with a ratio of 1.18, as is South Asia, with a ratio of 1.11 and an expected 2030 level above full coverage, which the method treats as target met. Upper middle income countries are also on track, with a ratio of 1.08. South Asia's result reflects large national campaigns to end open defecation and to build household latrines.

Elsewhere the outlook is weaker. Lower middle income countries rose from 56.0% to 73.9% and are expected to reach 88.9% by 2030, a ratio of 0.75. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 85.6% to 90.3%, with an expected 93.7% in 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from 77.3% to 83.7%, a ratio of 0.48, classed as marginal progress. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.16 and an expected 2030 level of 42.0%. Low-income countries rose only from 29.2% in 2015 to 33.3% in 2024, with an expected 36.2% in 2030 and a ratio of 0.10, classed as stagnation. Two in three people in low-income countries therefore lack basic sanitation, and nothing in the trend suggests this will change materially by 2030.

High-income regions raise a different point. High income countries (97.5% to 98.3%) and Europe and Central Asia (95.7% to 97.4%) are classed as moderate progress, because their ratios, 0.55 and 0.69, are low relative to the requirement to reach 100%. North America is classed as regression, with a ratio of -1.03, as its level slipped from 99.7% to 99.5%. These are tiny movements near the ceiling, and they probably reflect small revisions and survey noise as much as real decline. The classification is mechanical: it compares the observed rate with the rate needed to reach 100.0% and cannot tell a trivial dip from a genuine loss. At country level, 49 of 213 countries are on track, holding 46.6% of the population; 34 show moderate progress (17.7%); 54 marginal progress (16.5%); 37 stagnation (5.8%); and 39 regression (13.4%). That 76 countries stagnate or regress on sanitation is a sign that policy attention and finance have not matched the scale of need, since sanitation, unlike electricity, rarely attracts private investment and depends on household behaviour and municipal budgets.

### Electricity: the largest gain, and a rural success

Electricity is the clearest success among the series. South Asia rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, a change driven largely by national connection drives in the most populous countries. Lower middle income countries rose from 79.6% to 91.4%. East Asia and the Pacific reached 98.6%, Latin America and the Caribbean 98.0%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 96.8%. Europe and Central Asia and North America are at or near universal access.

The remaining deficit is in Sub-Saharan Africa, where access rose from 39.2% to 55.1%, and in low-income countries, where it rose from 32.2% to 48.8%. Gains of about sixteen percentage points in each are large by historical standards, but nearly half of the population of low-income countries still lacks electricity. Falling costs of solar and off-grid systems are widening the means of reaching dispersed households, though whether such connections supply enough power for productive use is not captured by a binary access measure.

For rural areas, 161 of 211 countries assessed are on track or have met the target, holding 77.4% of the assessed population. Another 23 countries (12.8% of the population) show moderate progress, 10 (2.0%) marginal progress, 7 (2.3%) stagnation and 10 (5.4%) regression. Because the classification weights by population, the large on-track share reflects the big South Asian and East Asian gains, while the 17 countries in stagnation or regression are probably those where conflict or fragility prevents expansion.

### Financial accounts: rapid growth, with the poorest still behind

Ownership of an account at a financial institution or with a mobile money provider among the poorest 40% of adults rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024 worldwide, with 138 countries reporting in 2024. The regional series are available only to 2021 in this extract. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 42.9% to 67.9%, East Asia and the Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, Europe and Central Asia from 76.4% to 86.3%, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 32.0% to 43.6%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose only from 39.5% to 46.1%, and North America from 86.7% to 92.1%. South Asia reached 73.3% in 2024, from 65.5% in 2017. Mixed end years across regions mean that regional comparisons must be made with care.

By income group, low-income countries rose from 22.5% in 2017 to 37.3% in 2024, the fastest relative gain, while lower middle income countries went from 53.2% to 63.4% and upper middle income countries from 62.5% to 76.8%. High income countries moved from 89.0% to 92.8%. The gap between low-income and high-income countries among the poorest 40% therefore narrowed in absolute terms, from about 66 percentage points to about 56, yet more than six in ten poor adults in low-income countries still have no account. Mobile money, digital identity systems and the payment of social transfers into accounts account for much of the growth in Africa and South Asia. An account is only a first step: it does not measure use, savings, credit or the rights of women to control property, which target 1.4 also names.

### What the evidence implies for 2030

Three patterns follow. First, access is converging in the middle of the distribution and diverging at the bottom: low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa gain, but too slowly, especially in sanitation. Second, the years after 2020 are not visible as a break in these series. The data end in 2024 and annual movements are small, so any pandemic effect on services cannot be separated from the underlying trend, and the account series has survey rounds too sparse to show it. Third, the targets are read as full coverage, which is the strictest reading; if universal access were read as a high threshold, more countries would count as having met it. Under the strict reading, only electricity is close to being achieved, and sanitation and water in low-income countries are well out of reach.

proposals: National governments and development banks in low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa should prioritise sanitation finance, since the trend there is stagnation, and fund municipal operation and maintenance as well as construction.

Water authorities in the 37 countries where basic water coverage is falling should publish the causes of the decline and agree recovery plans with donors, with conflict-affected systems treated as a priority for humanitarian and development agencies jointly.
Electricity planners and funders should direct connection finance to the remaining low-income and fragile countries, combining grid extension with off-grid solar for dispersed rural households.
Central banks, regulators and mobile money providers should extend low-cost accounts and digital identity to the poorest adults, and pair them with the payment of public transfers into accounts.
The Joint Monitoring Programme and national statistical offices should report service quality and affordability alongside basic access, so that progress against target 1.4 reflects reliable services.
w-c02-4-1~farah/writer-1~54.gaps: The series report national or regional averages, not household income, so access among the poor is inferred from low-income countries, rural areas and the poorest 40% in the account series only. No series covers land ownership, inheritance, property rights or equal rights to economic resources, which target 1.4 also names. Safely managed water and sanitation, service continuity, affordability and electricity reliability are not measured here. The account data come from survey rounds with gaps, regional values stop at 2021 in this extract, and data for 2024 cover 138 countries. Sex-disaggregated figures for the poor are not on the shelf. Near-universal coverage figures are sensitive to survey noise, so small declines in rich regions should not be over-read.

w-c05-4-1~farah/writer-2~54.text:
### The global picture

Target 4.3 commits states to equal access for all women and men to affordable and quality technical, vocational and tertiary education by 2030. It sets no numerical threshold, so any reading of progress is a reading of direction and pace. The indicator available here, the gross enrolment ratio in tertiary education, counts all students regardless of age against the population of the age group that officially corresponds to the level. It measures participation, not affordability, quality or completion, and it can exceed 100 in systems with many older or repeat students.

The world gross tertiary enrolment ratio rose from 36.6 per cent in 2015 to 43.6 per cent in 2024. That is a gain of about seven percentage points in nine years. The trend tool classifies the world as making moderate progress but needing acceleration, with a rate of 0.0196 on its own scale. Growth reflects the expansion of secondary schooling in the 2000s, rising household demand for degrees, and the growth of private provision in many middle-income systems. The world figure is an average of very unequal parts, and the regional results show where the gain came from.

### Regional divergence

East Asia and Pacific rose from 44.3 per cent in 2015 to 63.3 per cent in 2024, the largest regional gain. Europe and Central Asia rose from 67.4 per cent to 84.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 48.4 per cent to 58.9 per cent. South Asia rose from 25.4 per cent to 32.8 per cent. All four are classed as on track or target met, with rates of 0.0406, 0.0260, 0.0221 and 0.0289 respectively. Policies behind these gains include the expansion of public and private universities, student loan and scholarship schemes, and in several countries deliberate national targets for enrolment.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping moved only from 27.3 per cent to 29.7 per cent, a rate of 0.0091, classed as marginal progress. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 8.8 per cent in 2015 to 9.3 per cent in 2021, a rate of 0.0080, also marginal. Its latest value is 2021, not 2024, so the recent years are unobserved. In a region where fewer than one person in ten of the relevant age group is enrolled, the demographic pressure of a growing youth cohort means that stagnant ratios imply a rapidly growing number of young people excluded from higher education. Constraints include the small number of secondary school completers, limited public funding per student and thin institutional capacity.

North America is the one region in regression. Its ratio fell from 86.8 per cent in 2015 to 79.0 per cent in 2024, a rate of -0.0104. A decline from a very high level is not the same kind of problem as stagnation at a low one. Plausible causes include falling enrolment in older cohorts, shifts toward shorter or non-degree pathways, demographic change and the effects of the pandemic years on adult and part-time study, though the data here cannot apportion these.

### Income groups

The income groups show the same pattern. Low-income countries moved from 8.9 per cent in 2015 to 9.3 per cent in 2021, marginal progress at a rate of 0.0077. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 21.7 per cent to 27.4 per cent by 2024 and are classed as on track, at 0.0264. Upper-middle-income countries rose from 46.6 per cent to 64.6 per cent, at 0.0368, the fastest of any income group. High-income countries rose from 76.2 per cent to 82.0 per cent, but at 0.0083 they are classed as marginal, because the measure of progress is relative to a ratio that is already high and the group includes countries whose enrolment fell.

The gap between low-income and upper-middle-income countries was about 37.8 percentage points in 2015 in the figures above, and by the latest years it exceeded 55 points. The two groups are measured in different end years, 2021 and 2024, so the comparison is indicative only. The direction is unambiguous: the middle of the distribution has pulled away from the bottom.

### Countries and convergence

Among 159 countries assessed, 75 are on track or have met the trend test, holding 69.8 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. A further 22 countries, with 11.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress needing acceleration. Sixteen countries, with 3.4 per cent, show marginal progress. Six, with 2.9 per cent, are stagnant. Forty countries, with 12.3 per cent, are in regression. The large on-track population share is driven by populous countries in Asia and the Americas; the count of 40 regressing countries is a reminder that falling enrolment is not confined to one region. Some declines may reflect revisions in population estimates or changes in reporting rather than real falls, and the data cannot separate them.

The convergence test across 82 countries with data for both 2015 and 2024 finds no catch-up. The beta coefficient is -0.00101 with a p-value of 0.901 and an R-squared of 0.000, meaning that initial level does not predict subsequent growth. The coefficient of variation fell only from 0.591 to 0.569. Countries with low enrolment are not, on average, growing faster than those with high enrolment. Without convergence, the world ratio can rise while the distribution stays as wide as before, which is what the evidence shows.

The link with gender parity is weak. Across the same 82 countries the rank correlation between changes in the tertiary gender parity index and changes in enrolment is -0.083, and between 2024 levels it is 0.176. Expanding enrolment therefore does not by itself move parity in either direction; the gender dimension is treated in its own section of the chapter.

### Implications for 2030 and data limits

If the global rate of about seven points per nine years continued, the world ratio in 2030 would be in the high forties, but that is an extrapolation, not a projection, and it is dominated by East and South Asia and Latin America. Regions with the lowest ratios would remain far from universal access at the 2030 horizon. For Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, the target cannot be read as met on any reading of equal access, since fewer than one in ten of the age group is enrolled.

Coverage constrains confidence. The number of countries reporting rose to 147 in 2015 and then eased to 133 in 2020, 125 in 2021, 126 in 2022 and 128 in 2023. It fell to 94 in 2024 and only 9 in 2025, so the latest years are incomplete and late revisions may change the picture. Regional aggregates for 2024 rest on fewer countries than those for 2015. Target 4.3 also covers technical and vocational education and affordability, which this indicator does not capture, and the post-2020 trajectory is only partly visible.

### Proposals

The findings point to action on access where it is lowest, on measurement and on the pace of expansion, as set out below.

w-c03-5-1~loom/writer-2~55.text:
### Land under farming has barely moved

Agricultural land, defined as arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, covered 36.8 per cent of the world's land area in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023. The footprint of farming is therefore stable at the global scale, and the first conclusion for Target 2.4 is that recent gains in food supply have not come from converting much additional land. The regional picture is similarly flat. South Asia has the largest share of land in agriculture, 58.6 per cent in 2015 and 58.3 per cent in 2023, which reflects dense populations and long-settled cropland. East Asia & Pacific stood at 46.5 per cent in 2015 and 46.8 per cent in 2023. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 43.9 per cent to 44.7 per cent, the clearest expansion among the regions, consistent with a continent in which output growth has leaned more on extending the cultivated area than on raising yields.

Europe & Central Asia fell from 29.3 per cent to 29.1 per cent, Latin America & Caribbean from 33.3 per cent to 32.9 per cent, and North America from 26.7 per cent to 26.7 per cent. By income group, low income countries moved from 41.4 per cent to 42.1 per cent, lower middle income from 42.5 per cent to 43.0 per cent, upper middle income from 43.1 per cent to 42.8 per cent, and high income from 28.1 per cent to 28.2 per cent. These changes are small, and the indicator cannot say whether the land is well managed, degraded, or recently converted from forest. Coverage is wide, with 208 countries reporting in 2024, but a share of land area is a blunt measure of intensity.

### Fertiliser use is high where yields are high

Fertiliser consumption measures plant nutrients applied per hectare of arable land. The world average was 132.9 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, a rise of under three per cent over eight years. Behind that stability lie divergent regional paths. East Asia & Pacific remains the most intensive region but declined from 329.1 to 304.1 kilograms per hectare, which fits policies in China that have sought to curb overapplication and its pollution costs. South Asia rose from 175.0 to 206.0. Latin America & Caribbean rose sharply, from 135.1 to 173.9, in step with the expansion of export-oriented grain and oilseed production.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region rose from 90.0 to 102.0, and North America from 124.3 to 128.8. Europe & Central Asia edged down from 78.7 to 76.0. Sub-Saharan Africa applied just 14.4 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023, a rise of about a third from a very low base but still a small fraction of the levels elsewhere. By income group the same gap appears: low income countries used 10.0 kilograms in 2015 and 13.9 in 2023, against 114.6 and 130.8 in lower middle income countries, 213.0 and 213.8 in upper middle income countries, and 106.3 and 104.3 in high income countries.

Two readings follow. At the top, high application does not mean sustainability; the upper middle income group sits at about double the high income level, and the nutrient losses to water and air that accompany surplus use work against the ecosystem language of Target 2.4. At the bottom, low application signals soil nutrient depletion, limited credit and weak input supply chains, and the target's productivity aim cannot be met without more nutrients in those places. The task is therefore not a single direction but a narrowing of the range.

### Application levels are converging

The convergence test across 192 countries over 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.0336 (R squared 0.28), significant at conventional levels. Countries starting with lower application grew faster in relative terms. The coefficient of variation fell from 2.15 in 2015 to 1.68 in 2022, so dispersion across countries narrowed. This is encouraging in that laggards are moving, but it is a statement about relative growth from small bases. A rise from 14 to 19 kilograms per hectare narrows ratios without closing an absolute gap of roughly ninety kilograms with the world average.

### Irrigation and the weight of water

Agriculture accounted for 71.5 per cent of total freshwater withdrawals worldwide in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022, from 178 countries reporting in 2022. The share is highest where water is scarcest or farming dominates the economy. South Asia stood at 90.3 per cent in both years, which is an identical reading and may reflect carried-forward estimates, since survey-based water accounts are updated infrequently. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region fell from 90.1 to 87.3 per cent, probably through growth in municipal and industrial demand and desalination rather than less irrigation. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 78.6 per cent and 79.0 per cent, Latin America & Caribbean at 73.4 and 74.4, East Asia & Pacific at 73.2 and 72.1, Europe & Central Asia at 52.0 and 51.8, and North America at 37.3 and 37.5.

The income gradient is steep. Low income countries drew 90.8 per cent of their withdrawals for agriculture in 2015 and 90.9 per cent in 2022; lower middle income 89.4 and 88.8; upper middle income 74.7 and 73.6; high income 42.2 and 42.7. As economies develop, other uses claim a larger part of water, but this ratio says nothing about stress. A high agricultural share can coexist with abundant supply, and a low share with severe depletion. The indicator measures withdrawals, not efficiency, groundwater depletion or the share of renewable resources used. Irrigated land (123 countries reporting) is on the shelf but no result is presented here, so the connection between irrigated area and withdrawals cannot be drawn from these findings.

### Inputs and yields

Cereal yield is the nearest outcome the shelf holds. Across 179 countries, the Spearman correlation between 2022 levels of fertiliser use and cereal yield is 0.72, a strong association. The correlation between changes over 2015 to 2022 is only 0.13. Countries that apply more fertiliser have higher yields, but countries that increased application did not reliably raise yields faster. Levels reflect long-run differences in soils, seeds, irrigation, mechanisation and income, while changes over a short window are noisy and depend on weather and prices. The result cautions against treating fertiliser as a lever on its own.

The yield trends bear this out. No numeric 2030 target exists for cereal yield, so the trend classes are relative judgements of pace. The world rate of 0.0092 is classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. North America (0.0260), South Asia (0.0255) and lower middle income countries (0.0221) are classed as on track. Latin America & Caribbean (0.0108) and East Asia & Pacific (0.0087) are marginal, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region (0.0129) shows moderate progress. Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0008) is in stagnation and low income countries (-0.0023) in regression, from 1,373 to 1,345 kilograms per hectare. Of 180 countries assessed, 39 are on track, covering 29.5 per cent of the population, and 70 are in regression, covering 15.2 per cent. A further 25 stagnate, covering 15.6 per cent, and 27 show marginal progress, covering 25.7 per cent.

### Implications for 2030

Land use is stable, fertiliser use is converging slowly, and water shares are fixed. The sustainable intensification that Target 2.4 describes requires changes at both ends of the distribution: more nutrients, better seeds and water control in low income and Sub-Saharan settings, and more efficient use where application is already heavy. The data cannot yet show whether the second kind of change is occurring, because they record quantities applied rather than losses. Changes after 2015 are modest, and the period includes the 2020 pandemic and the 2022 price shock in fertiliser markets, whose effects are not separable in these annual series. On the current trajectories, the countries in regression and stagnation, home to a large part of the world's food-insecure people, will not reach 2030 with materially higher yields.

proposals: National agriculture ministries in low income and Sub-Saharan African countries should prioritise input supply chains, soil testing and credit for fertiliser, paired with seed and water improvements, because application and yields remain far below other regions.

Governments of heavy-use countries, notably in East Asia and the upper middle income group, should continue to set nutrient-efficiency standards and reward precision application, so that high intensity does not erode ecosystems.

FAO and AQUASTAT should publish water statistics annually with flags for carried-forward values, and add a withdrawals-to-renewable-resources measure, so that agricultural water use can be judged against scarcity.
Development banks and donors should fund irrigation and water-management investment where agriculture draws about nine tenths of withdrawals, conditional on measured efficiency gains.
w-c03-5-1~loom/writer-2~55.gaps: The shelf holds no measure of nutrient losses, soil health, organic matter or fertiliser efficiency, so sustainability of intensity cannot be judged. Water data are withdrawals as a share of the total, not water stress, groundwater depletion or irrigation efficiency, and the identical South Asia values for 2015 and 2022 suggest infrequent updating. Irrigated land has only 123 reporting countries and is not analysed here. Cereal yield has no numeric 2030 target, so trend classes are relative. Pesticide use, resilience practices, climate adaptation and the 2020 and 2022 shocks cannot be separated in these annual series, and national averages hide differences inside countries.
