w-c03-2-1~tamarind/writer-1~55.text:
### Stunting has fallen only slowly since 2015 and remains far from the target

Stunting, a child's height for age more than two standard deviations below the median of the World Health Organization's growth standards, is the most durable mark that chronic undernutrition leaves on a population. It records not one bad season but the accumulated effect of poor maternal nutrition, inadequate feeding in the first two years of life, repeated infection, unsafe water and poor sanitation. Because the deficit in linear growth is largely set by the second birthday and is hard to reverse, the prevalence among children under five is a slow-moving indicator: it reflects conditions over the previous five years, and it responds to policy with a lag. That is why target 2.2 placed an intermediate milestone on stunting and wasting in 2025 before asking for the end of all forms of malnutrition by 2030.

On the modelled estimates of the Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates, which cover 162 countries, the world prevalence of stunting stood at 24.6 per cent of children under five in 2015 and 23.2 per cent in 2024. A decline of less than one and a half percentage points over nine years is small for an indicator that the international community had committed to cutting sharply. Expressed as an annual rate of change on the trend tool's logarithmic basis, the world figure fell at about 0.0066 a year, which, if continued, would leave the prevalence at 22.3 per cent in 2030. The tool's threshold for this exercise is a prevalence of 5 per cent by 2030, a level that corresponds to what well-nourished populations show and that is consistent with the reading of target 2.2 as the end of stunting as a public-health problem. Measured against that threshold, the world has covered a ratio of 0.12 of the progress needed, and the trend tool classifies it as making marginal progress with significant acceleration needed.

The target can be read in more than one way, and the reading matters. The internationally agreed 2025 target referred to in target 2.2 is the World Health Assembly's goal of a 40 per cent reduction in the number of stunted children against a 2012 baseline, a target on counts rather than on prevalence, while the 2030 extension proposed by UNICEF and WHO asks for a 50 per cent reduction. The bench holds prevalence, not numbers of children, and holds no 2012 value in the results used here, so this section cannot test the 2025 target directly. What it can say is that a fall from 24.6 to 23.2 per cent between 2015 and 2024 is nowhere near the pace that a 40 per cent cut in numbers would require, even allowing for slowing growth in the child population in several regions. Under either reading, the 2025 milestone has been missed at the world level, and the 2030 extension is out of reach on present trends.

### Regions and income groups diverge sharply

The world average hides two very different stories. In South Asia stunting fell from 37.8 per cent in 2015 to 31.5 per cent in 2024, the largest absolute decline of any region, at an annual rate of about 0.020. This is a real achievement. It reflects decades of income growth, falling fertility, expanding sanitation coverage, wider maternal education and national nutrition programmes in the most populous countries of the region. Yet even this pace, carried forward, leaves South Asia at 27.9 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of progress to need of 0.30. The region still carries one of the highest burdens in the world, and the trend tool classifies it, like the world, as making marginal progress.

Sub-Saharan Africa presents the more troubling picture. Its prevalence fell from 34.4 per cent in 2015 to 32.3 per cent in 2024, at a rate of about 0.0070 a year, less than half the South Asian pace. On that trajectory it would stand at 31.0 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.12. Because the child population of Sub-Saharan Africa continues to grow quickly, a slowly falling prevalence is compatible with a rising number of stunted children, and the region now holds a growing share of the world's stunted children. Conflict in the Sahel and the Horn of Africa, recurrent drought, high food price inflation after 2021 and weak health systems all bear on that outcome, and the slow decline in prevalence is consistent with them.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 27.5 per cent to 24.1 per cent, an annual rate of about 0.015, giving an expected 22.1 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.24. The aggregate is heavily shaped by Pakistan and Afghanistan, whose prevalence is far above that of most North African and Gulf states, and the region as defined by the World Bank is therefore a mixture of near-target and very high-burden countries.

East Asia and the Pacific stood at 14.5 per cent in 2015 and 13.3 per cent in 2024. Its annual rate of decline, about 0.0095, is slow for a region whose largest economies have already brought stunting low; the remaining burden sits disproportionately in lower-income countries of South-East Asia and the Pacific, where progress has been uneven. On present trends it reaches 12.6 per cent in 2030, a ratio of 0.20. Latin America and the Caribbean is the one developing region where the indicator has not improved at all: it moved from 12.3 per cent in 2015 to 12.4 per cent in 2024, a rate of change of about 0.0009, and the trend tool classifies it as in regression, with an expected 12.4 per cent in 2030. The region had made large gains before 2015, so this stall is a change of direction, and it coincides with a decade of weak growth, the economic collapse of some economies and the pandemic's heavy toll on household incomes in the region.

At the low end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.0 to 4.6 per cent and is on track, with an expected 3.8 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 2.13, meaning its trend more than covers what is needed. North America's prevalence rose from 2.8 to 4.1 per cent, an annual rate of about 0.043, and the high-income group's rose slightly from 3.9 to 4.0 per cent. Both are classified as on track because they already sit below the 5 per cent threshold, but the North American trend, if continued, would carry it to 5.3 per cent in 2030, just above the threshold. Small movements at such low levels can reflect survey and modelling revisions rather than real deterioration, and they should be read with caution; they nonetheless deserve monitoring.

The income gradient is steep. Low-income countries fell only from 38.0 to 35.8 per cent, a rate of about 0.0065 and a ratio of 0.11, with an expected 34.4 per cent in 2030. Lower-middle-income countries did markedly better, falling from 33.9 to 28.9 per cent at a rate of about 0.018, with an expected 25.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.28. Upper-middle-income countries fell from 11.9 to 10.8 per cent, with an expected 10.1 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.25. In 2024 a child in a low-income country was roughly nine times as likely to be stunted as a child in a high-income country. The poorest countries, which most need rapid improvement, are improving the most slowly.

### Countries are not converging

The convergence test across 162 countries confirms what the regional figures suggest. If high-burden countries were catching up, the change in stunting between 2015 and 2024 would be strongly and negatively related to the starting level. The estimated coefficient is slightly negative, at about -0.0024, but it is not statistically distinguishable from zero, with a p-value of 0.23, and the starting level explains almost nothing of the variation in progress, with an R-squared of 0.0085. Meanwhile the coefficient of variation, a measure of relative dispersion, rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Relative inequality in stunting across countries has widened since the goals were adopted. Countries with low prevalence have continued to reduce it proportionally faster than many high-burden countries, so the gap in relative terms has grown even where absolute declines in the high-burden group were larger.

This matters for the logic of target 2.2. A goal to end malnutrition for all is ultimately decided in the countries with the highest prevalence. Divergence means that the world average will increasingly be determined by a smaller set of countries, concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia and the Middle East, where fragility, conflict and climate shocks are concentrated too.

### Wasting is lower but more volatile and far less well measured

Wasting, weight for height more than two standard deviations below the median, measures acute undernutrition and carries a high immediate risk of death. Unlike stunting, it can rise and fall within months, with harvests, disease outbreaks, displacement and price shocks. The world prevalence was 7.1 per cent in 2015 and 6.6 per cent in 2024. The 2025 World Health Assembly target is to reduce wasting below 5 per cent, and the 2030 extension is below 3 per cent; the trend tool assessed countries against 5 per cent by 2030. At the world level, the prevalence remains above both thresholds.

South Asia dominates the global burden. Its prevalence moved only from 16.6 to 15.7 per cent, more than twice the world average and almost three times the Sub-Saharan level. The persistence of high wasting in South Asia, alongside its falling stunting, is a long-recognised puzzle; explanations in the literature point to low birth weight, maternal undernutrition and the high share of wasting that begins in the first months of life. Lower-middle-income countries, where most of South Asia's population lives, stood at 9.5 per cent in 2024, down from 10.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 7.0 to 5.9 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping from 6.5 to 5.6 per cent, and low-income countries from 7.9 to 6.4 per cent. East Asia and the Pacific stood at 3.6 per cent in 2024, Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.3 per cent, Europe and Central Asia at 1.0 per cent, upper-middle-income countries at 2.1 per cent and high-income countries at 0.4 per cent.

At the country level, the trend tool could assess only 65 countries. Of these, 42 were on track or had met the 5 per cent threshold, but they hold 38.6 per cent of the assessed population. Four, with 7.8 per cent of the population, show moderate progress; three, with 33.7 per cent, show marginal progress; none is stagnant; and 16, with 19.9 per cent, are in regression. The pattern is telling: most countries by number are doing well, but a third of the assessed population lives in just three countries making marginal progress, and a fifth lives in countries where wasting has risen. The countries that determine the global outcome are few and large, and their trends are weak.

The wasting data must be read with more caution than the stunting data. Wasting has no modelled annual series in the World Bank's holdings; the figures come from household surveys, which are irregular. The number of countries with a survey value fell from 48 in 2018 and 46 in 2019 to 26 in 2020, as the pandemic halted fieldwork, recovered only to 32 in 2021 and 31 in 2022, and stood at 24 in 2023 and just 6 in 2024. The regional and world values for 2024 are therefore built largely on older surveys and harmonised estimates, not on fresh measurement. For an indicator that can shift rapidly with food price spikes, droughts and conflict, this gap is serious: the years after 2020, when shocks were most severe, are the years least directly observed.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020

Before 2015 stunting was falling faster in many regions, notably in Latin America and East Asia, and the period since has been one of deceleration rather than collapse. The comparison of 2015 and 2024 values cannot by itself separate the years before and after 2020, and the bench's trend tool summarises the whole period with one rate. The broad causes of a post-2020 slowdown are nonetheless well established: the pandemic disrupted health services, school meals, growth monitoring and vitamin A campaigns; incomes fell; the 2022 surge in food, fuel and fertiliser prices raised the cost of a nutritious diet; and conflicts in Sudan, the Sahel, Yemen, Afghanistan and elsewhere displaced millions. Because stunting reflects cumulative exposure, the effects of those years will continue to appear in the prevalence through the second half of the decade, as children exposed in infancy pass through the under-five age range. The modelled stunting series smooths these effects, and the thin wasting surveys miss much of them, so the true post-2020 damage is likely understated by the figures in hand rather than overstated.

### What the trends imply for 2030

On every reading available to the bench, the 2025 targets for stunting and wasting will not be met at the world level, and the 2030 targets will not be met either unless the pace of decline rises several-fold. The world is on course for a stunting prevalence of around 22.3 per cent in 2030, more than four times the 5 per cent threshold; South Asia is on course for about 27.9 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa for about 31.0 per cent. Only Europe and Central Asia, North America and the high-income group are at or below the threshold, and two of these show slight increases. Wasting remains above 5 per cent at the world level and above 15 per cent in South Asia. The rise in dispersion across countries means that national averages will matter more than ever, and the countries left behind are those where conflict, climate stress and weak public services overlap.

The lesson of South Asia's stunting decline and of the earlier Latin American record is that sustained gains come from combining income growth with direct nutrition programmes, maternal education, sanitation and primary health care. The lesson of the post-2015 period is that these gains are not self-sustaining: Latin America's reversal shows that progress can stop, and the slow pace in low-income countries shows that growth alone is not reaching the children who need it most.

w-c06-1-2~ewan/writer-1~55.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but only its frame has been computed

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, forbids her from working at night, sets her pension age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of laws therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and it is the natural first window on progress towards the target.

The instrument held on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy from 0 to 100 on whether its laws treat women and men equally across ten topics: safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year; it does not by itself show that each economy is scored in every year, because the tool reports neither the first year of the series nor the count for earlier years. For a measure read from statute books rather than from surveys or registers, such breadth is what one would expect, and it contrasts with the patchy coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter.

The central limitation of this section must be stated at the outset. Coverage is the only result the bench has computed for the series. No score, regional or income-group average, or change over time has been drawn from the shelf, and this section therefore states none. The question it was set, how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed, cannot be answered in magnitude from the numbers this book is bound to use. What follows separates three things carefully: what the computed result establishes; what the design of the index implies, which can be read from the series definitions; and what the history of reform suggests, which is offered as context and as hypotheses for computation, not as findings of this book.

### The design of the index determines what change it can show

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. Its definition lists safety and childcare among its ten topics, domains that the earlier and widely cited version of the index largely omitted. Two consequences follow from the design alone, without any computed value. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index, and the older numbers should not be set beside the new ones as though they measured the same thing. Second, because safety and childcare require positive provision rather than the mere repeal of restrictions, the revised scale is harder to complete: an economy can have abolished every explicit barrier to women's work and still fall short on comprehensive protection from violence or on legally guaranteed care services. A low score under this measure need not mean overt discrimination; it can mean the absence of protections the state has never legislated.

The shelf also holds two companion series built on the same ten topics. The Supportive Framework Index asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement each law exist; the Enforcement Perceptions Index records how experts judge the law to work in practice. The definitions show that the three are designed to be read together, and that pairing speaks directly to the wording of the target's indicator, which concerns not only laws but their enforcement and monitoring. The legal index records what the statute book says; the supportive index records whether a ministry, fund, complaints body or data system gives it effect; the enforcement index records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. The size of that distance, country by country, has not been computed for this section, and it is not asserted here; the comparison is the subject of the petition attached to this section.

The short history of a revised series raises a further question that the bench has not settled. The coverage tool does not report the year in which the series begins. If comparable values do not reach back to 2015, the baseline this book uses throughout, then change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index at all, and any statement about reform since 2015 must rest on other sources. That is a question for the next computation, not one this section can answer.

### The history of reform suggests a pattern that the numbers should test

The following account draws on the well-documented history of legislation and on the project's narrative reports, not on any value computed for this book, and it is offered as the set of hypotheses the missing computation should test.

The common view of the past decade is that reforms removing discrimination have greatly outnumbered those introducing it, and that they have been of a recognisable kind. Many governments repealed rules barring women from industrial jobs, night work, mining or work deemed arduous, provisions originally framed as protection that in practice excluded women from better-paid sectors. Many introduced or strengthened laws against sexual harassment at work. Some mandated equal pay for work of equal value rather than only for identical work, the standard that reaches occupational segregation. Several equalised pensionable ages or credited childcare periods in pension calculations, and paid paternity leave spread from a rare to a more common entitlement. If this account is right, the work, pay, parenthood and pension topics should show the largest gains in the shelf's data.

The same history suggests that reform has been slower in marriage, mobility and assets. Rules that require a wife's obedience, make the husband head of household, restrict a woman's choice of residence or her access to a passport, or give daughters smaller inheritance shares than sons sit in personal-status and family codes often tied to religious law or customary authority. Governments have tended to treat labour codes as instruments of economic policy and family codes as questions of identity, and to find the former easier to change. If so, an economy may score well on work and pay while scoring poorly on marriage and assets, and the unweighted average would hide the fact that the remaining restrictions concentrate in the private sphere that governs a woman's capacity to act independently. Whether the shelf's topic-level data bear this out cannot be said here, because only the composite index is held and no topic breakdown has been computed.

Two forces are usually credited with shaping the period after 2015. The Goals gave governments a reference point and a reporting obligation, placing legal frameworks on the agenda of voluntary national reviews. And as economists documented the cost to national income of excluding women from paid work, finance ministries and development lenders began to treat discriminatory law as a constraint on growth, so that legal reform for women became an objective in some lending programmes. These are plausible explanations of any acceleration the data might show; whether there was an acceleration is itself untested.

### The period after 2020 sharpened the questions the index was redesigned to ask

The pandemic that began in 2020 is widely understood to have shown that childcare functions as economic infrastructure: when schools and nurseries closed, the burden of care fell disproportionately on women, many of whom withdrew from paid work. It coincided with widely reported increases in domestic violence during lockdowns, which drew attention to the distance between laws on paper and the shelters, hotlines, protection orders and police training that make them usable. The addition of safety and childcare to the legal measure, and its pairing with indices of support and enforcement, is consistent with those lessons, although this section cannot show that the redesign was a response to them.

The reasons why a law may fail to change practice are well established in principle and do not depend on the shelf's numbers. Equal pay laws without pay-transparency requirements or an inspectorate able to investigate complaints change little. Parental leave paid directly by employers rather than through social insurance gives employers a reason to avoid hiring women of childbearing age. Harassment laws without accessible complaint procedures and protection against retaliation are seldom invoked. For these reasons the legal framework index is best read as an upper bound on the protection women actually enjoy: progress measured by the legal score alone is likely to overstate progress towards target 5.1, by an amount that only the comparison with the companion indices could estimate.

There have also been reversals. In a small number of countries, political change since 2020 has removed rights previously granted, restricting women's movement, education and employment by decree. Here the construction of the index is an advantage. Because it is read from laws rather than reported by national statistical offices, an economy cannot leave the measure by ceasing to report, and the completeness of the 2025 count suggests that such cases remain within the record. Whether their scores fell, and by how much, has not been computed.

### Regional and income differences remain to be measured

The coverage tool identifies the aggregates for which the shelf reports the index: the world, the World Bank's high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups, and South Asia. Values for these aggregates have not been computed for this section, so their ordering cannot be stated. Other regional aggregates, including sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean, are not among those the tool lists, which means that regional comparison beyond South Asia would require averages to be computed from country values.

What the computation should test can be set out as expectations, not findings. One expectation is that high-income economies have the most complete legal frameworks but fall short of the top of the revised scale through gaps in childcare, pension treatment of career breaks and laws on violence. Another is that the lowest scores concentrate where personal-status codes restrict mobility, marriage and inheritance, and where customary law governs land for much of the rural population. A third is that the relation between income and legal score is real but loose, since legislating costs little, whereas the relation between income and the supportive and enforcement indices is tighter, since courts, inspectorates, social insurance and childcare services cost money and administrative capacity. If the third expectation holds, the legal index flatters poorer economies more than richer ones. Each of these can be checked directly against the shelf once the series values are drawn.

### Target 5.1 can be read two ways, and the verdict for 2030 depends on the reading

The target speaks of all forms of discrimination, everywhere. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The two readings lead to different verdicts, and this section can deliver neither with the book's numbers: the strict reading needs the distribution of 2025 scores and the number of economies at 100; the directional reading needs the change in scores since the earliest comparable year. Both are computable from a series that, on the evidence of coverage, already includes 189 economies.

What can be said is conditional. If, as the design of the revised index makes likely, few or no economies sit at the top of the scale, the strict reading of the target will be missed by a wide margin regardless of the pace of reform. If the remaining shortfall is concentrated in family law, property and inheritance, protection from violence and the institutions of care, as the history suggests, then the remaining work is politically harder and fiscally costlier than the labour-market reforms that came first, and past pace is a poor guide to future pace. Because the outcomes treated in other sections of this chapter, from child marriage to ownership, depend in part on these provisions, the legal record bears on them as well.

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. It scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules governing most women, particularly in rural areas under customary or religious law. And a complete legal score is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for equal economic opportunity: social norms, the distribution of unpaid care, undetected employer discrimination and the informality of much women's work lie beyond the reach of statute. With those cautions, the index is the most complete instrument the shelf holds for target 5.1, and the next task is to turn its breadth into a measured record of change.

Governments reporting in voluntary national reviews should state, for each recent legal reform, whether implementing regulations, a budget and an enforcing agency exist, since a statute without them is unlikely to change women's economic opportunity.

The ten topic scores are not held on the shelf, so the concentration of remaining discrimination by domain cannot be tested. Regional aggregates other than South Asia are not reported. w-c04-10-1~dahlia/writer-2~55.text:
### Global prevalence fell by about a sixth after 2015

The share of adults aged 15 and over who currently use any tobacco product fell from 24.5 % in 2015 to 20.3 % in 2024 for the world, as estimated in the World Health Organization series carried by the World Bank. The fall is 4.3 percentage points, or roughly one sixth of the 2015 level. The indicator counts smoked and smokeless products, including heated tobacco, and excludes e-cigarettes. A decline in prevalence therefore says nothing about nicotine vaping, which the series does not capture.

Target 3.a asks for stronger implementation of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. It carries no numerical threshold, so any reading of 'on track' is a convention of the bench's trend tool, not of the target text. The tool reports the world's annual rate of change as -0.0210 and classes it as on track. That judgement rests on a decreasing direction and a pace, not on a legal commitment, and it should be read as such. The series is a modelled estimate, reported for 166 countries in every year checked, so the coverage is complete but the values for any single country are projections from survey data of uneven timing.

### Regions started apart and have moved at different speeds

In 2015 South Asia had the highest prevalence at 32.3 %, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 28.3 %, East Asia and Pacific at 25.3 %, North America at 21.4 % and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 21.1 %. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 16.6 % and Sub-Saharan Africa at 11.3 %. By 2024 South Asia had fallen to 23.6 %, a drop of 8.7 points and the largest in absolute terms. North America fell from 21.4 % to 15.3 %, the steepest proportional decline, with a rate of -0.0365. Sub-Saharan Africa reached 8.9 % and Latin America and the Caribbean 13.6 %.

Three regions moved slowly. East Asia and Pacific declined only from 25.3 % to 23.1 %, and the tool classes it as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Europe and Central Asia went from 28.3 % to 24.9 %, a moderate rate of -0.0141, and it now has the highest regional prevalence, having been overtaken in pace by South Asia. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from 21.1 % to 18.9 %, also marginal. Explanations lie in well-established causes: strong price and tax measures, advertising bans and plain packaging in North America and parts of Latin America; a large and cheap market for smoked and smokeless products in South Asia where national policies have nonetheless tightened; and the persistence of high male smoking, waterpipe use and weak enforcement in several other regions. These are background causes, not findings of the series.

### Income groups show faster decline in poorer countries

By income group, low-income countries fell from 14.0 % to 10.9 % and lower-middle-income countries from 27.4 % to 20.4 %. The latter fall, 7.0 points, is the largest of any income group, and its rate of -0.0322 is the fastest. High-income countries fell from 24.7 % to 20.2 %, a rate of -0.0220. Upper-middle-income countries moved only from 23.5 % to 21.5 %, with a rate of -0.0099 and a marginal classification. The upper-middle group, which includes several very populous countries, therefore has the highest prevalence of any income group in 2024, and its slow pace matters for the global total.

The pattern runs against a simple expectation that wealth drives tobacco control. High-income prevalence in 2015 was no lower than the lower-middle group's by a wide margin, and by 2024 the two had converged within about a point. Low-income countries remain well below all others, partly because tobacco markets there are less developed and partly because incomes constrain purchases, so a low level is not evidence of policy success. The risk in those countries is the reverse of progress: expanding markets and industry marketing can raise prevalence from a low base.

### Country outcomes are split, and inequality between countries has widened

Of 166 countries, 72 are on track or have met the direction of the target, holding 53.4 % of the population of the assessed countries. A further 31 countries, with 12.3 % of the population, show moderate progress. Another 26, with 23.5 %, show marginal progress. Eighteen countries, with 6.7 %, stagnate and 19, with 4.1 %, regress. Taken together, 63 countries are on a flat or rising path and 57 more are advancing too slowly. The population share in marginal progress is large because it contains some of the most populous countries, which is why the world rate and the count of countries tell somewhat different stories.

Distribution has not narrowed. The population-weighted Gini coefficient across countries rose from 0.193 in 2015 to 0.197 in 2020 and 0.203 in 2024. The Theil index rose from 0.070 to 0.075 and then 0.081. The coefficient of variation of prevalence across countries rose from 0.444 in 2015 to 0.507 in 2024, so countries are further apart relative to their average. A formal convergence test gives a beta of -0.0042 with a p-value of 0.112 and an R-squared of 0.021, which is no statistically clear evidence of convergence; countries with high initial prevalence did not reliably fall faster. The share of inequality that lies between regions fell from 65.8 % in 2015 to 61.4 % in 2020 and 57.9 % in 2024, which means differences within regions are gaining weight. Country policy rather than geography increasingly separates outcomes.

The rise in spread alongside a falling mean is the typical signature of a policy diffusing unevenly: countries that adopt strong measures fall quickly, while others barely move. The comparison between 2015, 2020 and 2024 also suggests that the pandemic years did not reverse the decline in the average, although annual data between those years are not interpreted here.

### Men and women move together, and 2030 depends on laggards

The links tool compares the changes in male and female prevalence across 166 countries from 2015 to 2024. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.567 and that of 2024 levels is 0.416. Countries where male prevalence fell fastest tended to be those where female prevalence fell fastest, which points to policy that acts on whole populations, such as taxation and smoke-free law, more than to gender-specific trends. The weaker correlation in levels reflects the large and well-known gap in which men use tobacco far more than women in most countries; this section does not give the sex-specific levels, which the tools did not return in the results used here.

For 2030, the world's rate of -0.0210 is classed as on track, and continued decline at that pace would take the global figure lower still. The direction is encouraging but there is no numerical goal to test against. The risk lies in the distribution: regions classed as marginal hold large populations, the number of regressing countries is not trivial, and country gaps are widening. Reaching 2030 with a broad reduction would require the slow regions and the upper-middle-income group to approach the pace already seen in South Asia and North America.

### Proposals

See the proposals field.

t-legal-index-change-by-group~fernhill/a.name: legal-index-change-by-group
t-legal-index-change-by-group~fernhill/a.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = params['year_a']
    y1 = params['year_b']
    y2 = params['year_c']
    s = data[code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    groups = {}
    for unit in s:
        if unit not in regions:
            continue
        r = regions[unit]
        groups.setdefault(r, []).append(unit)
    facts = {}
    parts = []
    def calc(label, ya, yb):
        tot_n = 0
        tot_up = 0
        deltas = []
        for r in sorted(groups):
            ds = []
            for u in groups[r]:
                v = s[u]
                if ya in v and yb in v and v[ya] is not None and v[yb] is not None:
                    ds.append(v[yb] - v[ya])
            if ds:
                up = len([d for d in ds if d > 0])
                facts[label + '_' + r + '_mean_change'] = round(sum(ds) / len(ds), 2)
                facts[label + '_' + r + '_rose'] = up
                facts[label + '_' + r + '_n'] = len(ds)
                tot_n += len(ds)
                tot_up += up
                deltas += ds
        facts[label + '_countries'] = tot_n
        facts[label + '_rose'] = tot_up
        if deltas:
            facts[label + '_mean_change'] = round(sum(deltas) / len(deltas), 2)
            facts[label + '_median_change'] = round(statistics.median(deltas), 2)
        parts.append('Between ' + str(ya) + ' and ' + str(yb) + ', ' + str(tot_up) + ' of ' + str(tot_n) + ' countries with both values recorded a higher score.')
    calc('c' + str(y0) + '_' + str(y1), y0, y1)
    calc('c' + str(y2) + '_' + str(y1), y2, y1)
    summary = ' '.join(parts) + ' Countries lacking either year are excluded; changes are in index points.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

w-c02-6-1~juniper/writer-1~56.text:
### What the series measure

Public spending on essential services is the clearest budgetary expression of Targets 1.a and 1.b, which call for mobilised resources and sound pro-poor policy frameworks. Three series bear on it here: domestic general government health expenditure as a share of total public spending, government expenditure on education as a share of total public spending, and the same education outlay as a share of GDP. Social protection spending is not held as a financial series on the shelf; only coverage and benefit incidence are, and those belong to another section of this chapter.

Shares of the budget indicate priority, not adequacy. A government with a small budget can devote a large share to schools and still spend little per child, and a high share of a large budget can coexist with poor results. Neither target sets a numerical threshold for these indicators, so the trend classifications below measure only whether a share is rising, and no official 2030 value exists. Readers should treat them as directional.

### Health: a wide gap in priority

The health budget share separates regions more than any other measure examined here. In North America, domestic general government health spending was 22.8% of general government expenditure in 2023, up from 22.1% in 2015. High-income countries as a group moved from 17.9% to 18.5% over the same period. Europe and Central Asia was close to stable, at 15.0% in 2015 and 14.5% in 2023, and Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 11.5% to 11.8%.

The poorer regions start far lower. South Asia rose from 3.7% in 2015 to 4.8% in 2022, the largest relative gain in the table, yet it remains at about a fifth of the North American share. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 10.9% in 2015 and 11.3% in 2019, its latest reading. The two income groups most dependent on development cooperation show no gain at all: low-income countries moved from 5.4% in 2015 to 5.3% in 2017, and lower-middle-income countries from 4.8% in 2015 to 4.7% in 2018. These series end years before the present, so the effect of the pandemic and of subsequent debt stress cannot be read from them. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024 at the time of the extraction, and the most recent year is therefore nearly empty.

The trend classification across 193 countries is mixed. A total of 72 countries, holding 40.8% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have met the direction sought; 11 countries (4.3% of population) show moderate progress and 30 (22.1%) marginal progress; 19 (11.5%) are stagnant; and 61 countries, with 21.3% of population, are regressing. Roughly two in five countries are therefore moving the right way, while almost as many have lowered the priority given to health. Because the classification rests on a direction with no numeric target, a country that began very high and slipped slightly counts as regressing alongside one that cut sharply.

### Education: shares drifting down

The education picture is less favourable. The world share of government spending going to education was 14.1% in 2015 and 14.0% in 2023, effectively flat. Beneath that, several regions fell. East Asia and Pacific declined from 15.1% to 13.0%. South Asia fell from 13.9% in 2015 to 11.3% in 2025. Sub-Saharan Africa, still the region with the highest share, went from 17.0% to 15.4% in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group dropped from 15.2% in 2016 to 13.1% in 2022, and North America from 12.9% to 10.7% in 2022. Europe and Central Asia was near stable at 11.8% and 11.7%, and Latin America and the Caribbean edged up from 16.4% to 16.6% in 2024.

By income group the pattern is uneven. Low-income countries rose from 14.9% in 2015 to 16.7% in 2022, which is encouraging, although the rise may reflect shrinking denominators or donor-funded transfers, which this indicator includes. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 16.4% to 13.6% in 2024. Upper-middle-income countries were unchanged at 15.0% and 15.1%, and high-income countries eased from 12.4% to 12.0% in 2022. Only 60 countries had reported for 2025, so the latest regional values rest on partial coverage and later revisions may shift them.

The trend classes confirm the weakness. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are regressing, and these hold 78.2% of the assessed population; 29 countries with 7.1% of population are on track, 13 (1.8%) show moderate progress, 12 (2.3%) marginal progress and 23 (10.5%) stagnation. The population weighting matters: the large countries have mostly lowered the education share of their budgets, so the global average hides how general the retreat is. Falling shares are not necessarily falling real spending, since budgets grew in many places, but the direction is a warning against reading education as a protected priority.

### Spending relative to national income

Measured against GDP, the dispersion of education spending has widened. Across 164 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022, and the Theil index from 0.07 to 0.10. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.34 to 0.41. Countries are therefore further apart in the national income they devote to education than they were at the start of the Goals period. The between-region component of the Theil index was 23.8% in 2015 and 22.3% in 2022, so about three quarters of the inequality lies within regions. Closing the gap thus depends on national choices as much as on regional circumstance, and regional averages conceal the countries that spend least.

The period includes two breaks. After 2015, most regional series moved slowly, as budget structures change gradually. After 2020, pandemic-era pressure on revenue and on health emergency outlays, followed by higher borrowing costs, is the plausible context for the falls in education shares, although the data cannot attribute cause. The health series that end before 2020 for low-income and sub-Saharan groups cannot show this at all.

### Do countries prioritise both?

A link analysis across 129 countries tests whether governments that raise the health share also raise the education share. The rank correlation of changes between 2015 and 2022 is 0.16, and that of 2022 levels is 0.09. Both are weak. Priority given to one service therefore says little about priority given to the other, and budget choices appear to be made sector by sector or to reflect separate pressures, such as donor programmes in health. This suggests that a national commitment to essential services cannot be inferred from one sector alone.

### Implications for 2030

With no numeric target, 2030 can be judged only by direction. On health, a plurality of countries is moving upward but the poorest income groups are not, and the gap between 4.8% in South Asia and 22.8% in North America is unlikely to close by 2030 at the observed pace. On education, the combination of falling shares in most large countries and widening dispersion relative to GDP points away from the resource mobilisation that Target 1.a envisages. Target 1.b is more difficult to read: it concerns frameworks, which these budget shares can only partly proxy.

### Proposals

See the list of proposals below.

proposals: Finance ministries in low-income and lower-middle-income countries should set published floors for the health and education shares of their budgets, and report against them annually.

w-c04-1-1~juniper/writer-2~56.text:
### The global ratio and the 2030 threshold

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled world ratio stood at 228.0 in 2015 and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year held. The fall is real but slow. The trend tool, which projects the 2015-2023 rate of change to 2030, expects a world ratio of 173.3 in 2030, and classes the world as making marginal progress, with a progress ratio of 0.35 against the pace the target requires. On this reading the target will be missed by a wide margin: the projected value is roughly two and a half times the threshold.

The target can be read in more than one way. It is a global ratio, so it depends on where births occur as much as on national risk; and the trend tool extrapolates a constant proportional rate, which is a convention and not a forecast. A faster fall after 2023 is possible, but nothing in the series shows it beginning.

### Regional and income divergence

The regional picture explains the global result. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593.0 in 2015 to 448.0 in 2023, a substantial decline, yet its expected 2030 value is 350.5, five times the threshold, and it is classed as marginal progress. South Asia is the most encouraging large region: 173.0 fell to 120.0, with an expected 87.1 in 2030 and a progress ratio of 0.83, so acceleration is needed but the target is within reach. By income group, low-income countries fell from 491.0 to 346.0 and are expected at 254.7 in 2030; lower-middle-income countries fell from 291.0 to 235.0 and are expected at 194.9, with a ratio of 0.44, the weakest pace among the income groups.

Regions already near or under the threshold show little movement because they have little left to gain. East Asia and Pacific moved from 70.0 to 66.0, Europe and Central Asia from 14.0 to 11.0, North America from 17.0 to 16.0, and high-income countries from 11.0 to 10.0. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61.0 to 57.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 54.0 to 47.0. All are classed as on track or target met, although the target is global and these groups never carried the burden.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception. Its ratio rose from 74.0 in 2015 to 77.0 in 2023, and its expected 2030 value is 79.7; it is the only region classed as regression. The rise coincides with the pandemic years and with documented strain on obstetric care, but the regional aggregate cannot separate causes.

### Countries, population and inequality

Country classes are more favourable than the world aggregate because most people live where ratios are already low. Of 194 countries, 128 are on track or have met the target, holding 74.5% of the assessed population. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress needing acceleration; 23 countries, with 8.4%, show marginal progress; one stagnates; and 7, with 0.6% of the population, are in regression. The paradox is that the deaths are concentrated in the minority that is off track. The global ratio is a weighted average, and it is pulled by a few high-burden countries.

Inequality has not narrowed in the way the headline decline might suggest. The population-weighted Gini coefficient across countries was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. Between-region differences account for 67.2% of the Theil index in 2023, down from 70.9% in 2015, so within-region gaps matter slightly more than before. The convergence test finds a negative beta of -0.0037 (p 0.0024), meaning higher-ratio countries tended to fall faster, but the R-squared is only 0.05 and the explanatory power is weak. The coefficient of variation fell from 1.50 to 1.41 on that measure, a modest convergence in relative terms alongside rising absolute concentration in a few places.

### Before and after 2015 and 2020

The break analysis of annual change in the world ratio shows a slowing decline well before 2015. Between 2001 and 2007 the mean annual change was -8.4 points; between 2008 and 2019 it was -5.2. Progress was therefore already decelerating before the Goals began, and the post-2015 pace is the slower one. This matters for 2030: the pace needed is faster than any achieved in the series since 2000, not a continuation of the recent past.

The pandemic left a visible mark. The mean annual change was +4.0 in 2020 and +31.0 in 2021, then -39.0 in 2022 and -6.0 in 2023. The 2021 rise reflects excess maternal deaths from COVID-19 and disrupted services; the large 2022 fall is largely a reversal of that spike, and so it should not be read as a recovery in the underlying trend. By 2023 the series had returned close to its pre-pandemic path, not to a faster one. All 194 countries report in every year from 2000, but this is a modelled series, so completeness of reporting is not evidence of direct measurement.

### What the evidence implies

The causes of maternal death are well established: haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, sepsis, unsafe abortion and indirect causes such as malaria and HIV. Reductions have come from skilled attendance at birth, access to emergency obstetric care, family planning that reduces high-risk pregnancies, and the quality of antenatal and postnatal care. Fragile settings combine all the weaknesses: few trained staff, long travel times, and insecurity. The ratio will fall faster only if the gains of South Asia are replicated where the burden is greatest, in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, and if Latin America reverses its rise.

The finding for 2030 is plain. On present trends the world will reach about 173.3 and not under 70. Reaching the target would need the pace of decline to roughly treble, and that is not a matter of the countries already on track.

### Limits of the evidence

Because the ratio is modelled from fertility, birth attendance, GDP and the share of maternal deaths among non-AIDS deaths, a country's estimate can move with its inputs and not with observed deaths. Where civil registration is weak, the estimates carry wide uncertainty that these point values do not show. Regional movements of a few points, such as East Asia's fall from 70.0 to 66.0, lie within plausible model error.

w-c02-5-1~heath/writer-2~56.text:
### What the shelf holds on disaster exposure

Target 1.5 asks for reduced exposure and vulnerability of the poor to climate-related extreme events by 2030. The shelf holds three series that bear on it, and they differ sharply in quality. One records the share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, but it is a single average for 1990 to 2009, reported by 168 countries in one year, 2009. It predates the 2015 baseline and cannot show any change. A second, the disaster risk reduction progress score, is a self-assessment on a scale of 1 to 5 drawn from Hyogo Framework reports for 2009 to 2011 and covers 83 countries. It too predates the Goals. Only the third, new displacement associated with disasters, runs through 2023 and so is the one series on which a post-2015 account can rest.

That series counts displacement cases, not people affected. A person displaced twice in a year is counted twice, and displacement captures only the most acute form of impact. Droughts, which damage livelihoods without moving households at once, are poorly represented. The series is therefore a partial proxy for exposure, and says nothing directly about the poor, because it is not broken down by income of the household.

### Coverage improved, and trends partly reflect it

The number of countries reporting displacement varied between 60 in 2009 and 80 in 2008, then reached 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. Reporting rose to 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018, 142 in 2020 and 145 in 2023, while 199 economies have reported in at least one year. The expansion matters for interpretation: part of any rise in the global total reflects better monitoring in countries that previously supplied nothing, not a change in hazards. Comparisons between 2015 (112 countries) and 2023 (145 countries) are therefore not like for like. The dip to 133 reporters in 2021 shows that coverage is not a one-way gain either.

### Levels in 2015 and 2023

The world total of new disaster displacements was 19188817 in 2015 and 26393278 in 2023. That is an increase over the period, though the additional reporters make the size of the rise uncertain. The break test finds no structural break in the annual change of the world series; the mean annual change over 2009 to 2023 is -789789.7, a figure which should be read cautiously. Annual totals swing with single events such as a major cyclone season or monsoon flood, so a mean of changes across a short and variable record says little about a trend, and it sits oddly beside the higher 2023 level. The series has no clear break after 2015 or after 2020 that the data can isolate.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture changed more than the total. East Asia & Pacific remained the largest regional source, at 8304660 in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia fell from 6877900 to 2446054, though one year's monsoon and cyclone pattern can drive such a change. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1108287 to 6029739, a more than fivefold increase, consistent with recurrent floods and drought-related movement in the Horn and the Sahel, and with improved recording. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from 1212730 to 2481660. Latin America & Caribbean was nearly flat, at 1543360 and 1728025. Europe & Central Asia moved from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023, a jump far larger than climate alone would explain and one that points to a particular large event or to new reporting. North America rose from 76000 to 394000.

By income group the shift is just as marked. Low-income economies went from 992200 in 2015 to 6177600 in 2023. Lower-middle-income economies fell from 9883673 to 5649287. Upper-middle-income economies rose from 6620044 to 13815894, the largest group total in 2023. High-income economies fell from 1692900 to 750497. For Goal 1 the low-income rise is the most pertinent: these are the countries where households have the least savings, insurance and social protection to absorb a displacement, so each case is more likely to push a household into or deeper into poverty.

### Concentration within countries

Among countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of displacement was 0.570 in 2015 and 0.678 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. Displacement has become more concentrated in a few countries, though the larger 2023 sample of 145 countries against 112 makes this comparison imperfect. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%, which means more of the inequality in 2023 lies between countries within the same region. Regional averages therefore hide much; a country in a hard-hit region may report little, and the reverse. Targeting resilience investment by region alone would miss this.

### Implications for 2030

The data do not show a world on course to reduce exposure. Displacement was higher in 2023 than in 2015, and higher in the poorest countries, even allowing for better coverage. Warming raises the frequency of the extreme rainfall, heat and storm events that drive displacement, while growth of settlements on floodplains and coasts raises exposure. Against this, early warning systems, land-use rules and evacuation planning have reduced deaths in several countries, which displacement counts do not capture; a successful evacuation raises displacement while saving lives. The indicator thus cuts both ways. Target 1.5 also has no numerical threshold, so what counts as reduced exposure is open to reading, and the shelf cannot show whether the poor in particular are more or less exposed than before.

### Proposals

National statistical offices and disaster agencies in low-income countries should report displacement and affected-population counts annually, with support from donors for the monitoring cost.

The World Bank and UNDRR should publish a post-2015 series of people affected by disasters, replacing the 1990 to 2009 average, and update the progress score that ended in 2011.

IDMC and national agencies should separate evacuation from displacement so that successful warnings are not read as worsening exposure.

Governments and development banks should direct adaptive social protection and resilience finance to the low-income and upper-middle-income countries where displacement is largest, and reassess the targeting yearly.

w-c05-7-1~dahlia/writer-1~56.text:
### Trained teachers in primary education: the global position

Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030. The bench's measure is the share of primary teachers who have received the minimum organised training required to teach in their country. The measure is imperfect: each country sets its own minimum, so a trained teacher in one system may not match a trained teacher in another. It also says nothing about the quality of training or about classroom practice. It remains the only series on the shelf that speaks directly to qualification, and the target value used for assessment is 100.0 per cent by 2030.

The world share rose from 80.4 per cent in 2015 to 82.2 per cent in 2024. That is a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. The trend tool classes the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.15, and the expected world value in 2030 is 83.4 per cent. At that pace roughly one primary teacher in six would still lack the minimum training at the target date. The world average hides a divergent picture, set out below, and it is also affected by changes in which countries report in a given year.

### Regional divergence

The regions did not move together. South Asia is the clear success: its share rose from 72.9 per cent in 2015 to 87.7 per cent in 2024, and its expected value in 2030 is 99.3 per cent, a ratio of 0.98 and the only regional class of on track or target met. Much of this reflects large systems investing in certification and in upgrading the qualifications of serving teachers, a policy route available where the teaching force is already large and employed.

Sub-Saharan Africa began at 66.2 per cent in 2015 and reached 68.8 per cent in 2022, the latest year in the regional series. Its expected 2030 value is 72.0 per cent, a ratio of 0.17, which is marginal progress. The region faces the heaviest demand for new teachers because its school-age population is still growing, and rapid hiring of recruits, often on contract and with short preparation, tends to pull the trained share down even as the number of teachers rises. The data on teacher numbers cannot separate these effects here, but the pattern is a familiar one.

The remaining regions moved backwards. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 83.9 per cent in 2015 to 80.5 per cent in 2024, with an expected 2030 value of 78.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean slipped from 82.7 per cent to 81.8 per cent over the same years, a ratio of -0.09, close to stagnation though classed as regression. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1 per cent in 2015 to 91.6 per cent in 2020, and North America from 99.3 per cent to 97.9 per cent by 2024. The declines in the richest regions begin from very high levels and are small in absolute terms, yet they run against the direction of the target. They are consistent with difficulty in recruiting and retaining teachers, and with the admission of uncertified staff to fill vacancies, though the series does not identify cause.

### Income groups

By income group, the low-income countries rose from 65.8 per cent in 2015 to 69.2 per cent in 2022, with an expected 2030 value of 73.2 per cent and a ratio of 0.22. Lower middle income countries rose from 76.4 per cent to 83.3 per cent by 2024, with an expected 88.2 per cent and a ratio of 0.50, moderate progress needing acceleration. High income countries fell from 95.9 per cent to 92.1 per cent, an expected 89.7 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of -1.54. The upper middle income group appears only for 2022, at 80.7 per cent, so no change can be read for it.

The gap between the poorest and richest groups was about 30 percentage points in 2015 and was still about 23 percentage points at the latest points, 2022 for the first and 2024 for the second. Part of the narrowing came from the fall at the top rather than from a rise at the bottom, which is a weak form of convergence. Different end years also mean the comparison should be read as approximate.

### Countries, convergence and distribution

Among 129 countries assessed for primary education, 64 are on track or have met the target, holding 65.9 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 12 show moderate progress (4.2 per cent of population), 13 marginal progress (2.4 per cent) and 4 stagnation (1.2 per cent). Regression affects 36 countries, with 26.3 per cent of the population. That a quarter of the assessed population lives where the trained share is falling is the most troubling finding, because the fall is not confined to poor countries. Many on-track countries are already near 100 per cent, where reaching the target is largely a matter of holding the level.

Secondary education is similar. Of 108 countries, 41 are on track (61.5 per cent of population), 10 show moderate progress (2.1 per cent), 14 marginal progress (7.7 per cent), 7 stagnation (1.0 per cent) and 36 regression (27.6 per cent). The secondary share in regression is slightly higher than the primary share, and secondary teaching usually requires subject specialists, who are harder to train and retain, particularly in science and mathematics.

Across 48 countries with data at both ends, the convergence estimate for 2015 to 2024 has a beta of -0.07 (R squared 0.34), meaning countries starting lower tended to gain more. The coefficient of variation across them eased only from 0.17 in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024. Convergence is thus real but slow. The population-weighted spread tells a related story. The Gini coefficient was 0.09 in 2015, fell to 0.07 in 2020 and rose to 0.10 in 2024. In 2015 differences between regions accounted for 49.3 per cent of the Theil index, rising to 53.3 per cent in 2020, so regional position explains about half of national inequality in training. The country count changed from 85 to 93 to 79 across these years, so the apparent reversal after 2020 may partly reflect who reported; the 2024 Theil value is not available. Only 13 countries reported in 2025, so that year cannot support conclusions.

### Teacher numbers and what the data do not yet show

The question also asks whether there are enough teachers. The shelf holds counts of primary and secondary teachers, but the pupil-teacher ratio series was not among the results computed for this section, so no ratio is reported here. The link test between the trained share and the count of primary teachers, over 48 countries, gives Spearman coefficients of -0.10 for changes between 2015 and 2024 and 0.17 for 2024 levels. Both are weak. Countries that added teachers did not systematically gain or lose in the trained share, so growth in headcount is neither a guarantee of nor an obstacle to qualification. Expansion must be accompanied by training places if the trained share is to hold.

Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive school facilities, has no series among those analysed here, and no finding on it is offered.

For 2030, the implication is that the target will not be met at the global level. South Asia may approach it. Sub-Saharan Africa and low income countries will remain far below, and regions that were close to the target are drifting from it. Training shares and teacher numbers need to be managed together, and the countries where regression is occurring deserve attention as much as the poorest.

w-c03-4-2~loom/writer-1~57.text:
### What the target asks and what the bench can measure

Target 2.3 asks for a doubling, by 2030, of the agricultural productivity and incomes of small-scale food producers, in particular women, indigenous peoples, family farmers, pastoralists and fishers. The wording carries two difficulties. First, the target is defined for a specific population, the small-scale producer, while the World Bank series available to this chapter describe whole economies. Value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing, in constant 2015 US dollars, averages over a large commercial estate and a household plot alike. Second, the target sets no baseline year and does not say whether doubling is to be measured from 2015, from the adoption of the goals, or from some earlier date. This section reads the target from 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and treats a doubling as a rise to twice the 2015 level by 2030.

Two indicators are used. Value added per agricultural worker is the closest available proxy for the official indicator on the volume of production per labour unit. Cereal yield, in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, measures output per unit of land and covers wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains. Cereal production and the land under cereals are the two components of yield. Neither series speaks to incomes, to sex, or to farm size, and neither separates the small-scale producer from the large. They show whether the conditions for a doubling exist; they cannot show that the doubling has happened for the people the target names.

### Value added per worker: a rising world average that conceals a stalled bottom

Global value added per agricultural worker stood at 3,491 US dollars in 2015 and reached 4,264 dollars in 2025, in constant 2015 prices. The annual rate implied by the trend tool is 2.0 per cent. This is an increase, and the trend tool classes the world as on track, but the classification is generous. It compares the rate with a path that the tool sets itself, since the target carries no numerical value in the bench. A doubling over fifteen years requires a compound rate of a little under five per cent a year, and a rate of 2.0 per cent is well below it. By 2025, ten of the fifteen years had elapsed, and the world average had not come near twice its 2015 level. For the world as a whole, a doubling by 2030 would need a much faster rate in the remaining five years than the one recorded so far.

The world figure is itself a weighted summary of very unequal parts. It is pulled upward by East Asia and Pacific, where value added per worker rose from 4,087 dollars in 2015 to 6,991 dollars in 2025, a rate of 5.5 per cent a year. That is the only regional rate that approaches the pace a doubling demands: sustained over fifteen years it would roughly double the starting level, and the rise over the first ten years was already about seventy per cent. The upper-middle-income group, which includes China and several large producers in Latin America and eastern Europe, rose from 4,378 dollars to 7,474 dollars at 5.5 per cent a year. The similarity of the two rates is not an accident: the economies that carry most weight in each group overlap, and the gain in both reflects the movement of labour out of farming as much as the growth of output. When many workers leave the land and output holds or rises, value added per remaining worker rises mechanically. A gain of this kind raises the average without any improvement in the position of the household that stays on a small plot.

The other regions improved at a slower pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 12,217 dollars to 17,325 dollars, at 3.6 per cent a year. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 6,294 dollars to 8,031 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. The group of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4,805 dollars to 6,181 dollars, at 2.6 per cent a year, and South Asia from 1,631 dollars to 2,082 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. All of these are reported as on track by the tool, and none is on a path to doubling by 2030. The finding is therefore that productivity per worker has risen in most regions since 2015, that the rise is real, and that outside East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group it is too slow for the target as written.

### Where productivity per worker is lowest, it has barely moved

The regions with the lowest starting points show the least progress. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 1,339 dollars per worker in 2015 and 1,496 dollars in 2025, a rate of 1.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries fell from 875 dollars in 2015 to 778 dollars in 2025, a rate of -1.2 per cent a year, which the tool classes as regression. In the lowest-income economies, then, value added per agricultural worker is lower in 2025 than it was when the goals were adopted. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 1,915 dollars to 2,336 dollars, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year.

The gap between the top and the bottom is wide. North America is shown in the data only at its 2015 value of 67,701 dollars, since the series has no later observation for the region in the extract used here, and the comparison across the decade cannot be made. High-income countries as a group rose from 28,219 dollars to 30,775 dollars, at 0.9 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress. A group already at a high level may not need to double, and the target was written with developing countries in mind. The ratio of the high-income group to the low-income group, computed from the figures above, was about 32 times in 2015 and about 40 times in 2025. The gap has widened over the decade, and a farm worker in a low-income country produces, in value terms, a small fraction of what a worker in a high-income country produces, a fraction that has shrunk.

The following is background, not a finding of the series. Low-income agriculture is dominated by rain-fed smallholdings with little mechanisation, limited access to improved seed, fertiliser and credit, poor roads to markets, insecure tenure, and exposure to drought, flood and pests. Population growth in these economies has kept the farm labour force growing, so that each worker has less land and capital to work with. The years since 2015 also included conflict in several low-income countries, droughts in parts of Africa, the disruption of the pandemic after 2020, and the price shocks that followed the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. These are offered as context that may help explain the low-income series; the data do not allow the effect of each to be separated.

### Cereal yield: a modest rise and a persistent gap

Cereal yield tells a similar story at a smaller scale. The world yield was 3,932 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 4,229 kilograms per hectare in 2023, the latest year for which a world figure is reported. That is a gain well short of a doubling, and far short of the gain in value added per worker. Yield is a slower-moving quantity than value added per worker, because it depends on biology, on the share of land that is irrigated, and on the technology of seed and fertiliser, none of which changes quickly. A doubling of average world cereal yield in fifteen years has no precedent in the record of any large region, and the target should not be read as requiring it of yields. The relevant question is whether yields are rising in the places where they are low.

They are not. Sub-Saharan Africa had a cereal yield of 1,443 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,453 kilograms per hectare in 2024, a change so small that it amounts to stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 1,345 kilograms per hectare in 2024. In 2024 the Sub-Saharan African yield was under a fifth of the North American yield, which rose from 6,677 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 8,414 kilograms per hectare in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, already at 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015, reached 5,430 kilograms per hectare in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 3,803 to 4,045 kilograms per hectare by 2023, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 2,732 to 3,027 kilograms per hectare by 2023.

South Asia and Latin America made the larger gains among developing regions. South Asia rose from 3,041 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 3,814 kilograms per hectare in 2024; the spread of irrigation, improved varieties and fertiliser use is the usual explanation, though the series does not test it. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 to 4,828 kilograms per hectare by 2024. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 2,766 to 3,366 kilograms per hectare by 2024. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 4,648 to 4,942 kilograms per hectare, and high-income countries from 4,976 to 5,394 kilograms per hectare, both by 2023. The pattern is that yields have risen where they were already moderate and have stood still where they were lowest.

### Convergence: the poorest are not catching up

A doubling target is in part a target about catching up, and the convergence tool tests directly whether countries that began with low values rose faster than those that began with high values. For cereal yield across 176 countries between 2015 and 2024, the estimated coefficient is -0.0016, with a p-value of 0.79 and an R-squared of 0.0013. The coefficient is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in subsequent change. There is no evidence of convergence in the strict sense: low-yield countries did not grow faster than high-yield countries. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.00 in 2015 to 0.91 in 2024, which indicates that dispersion narrowed slightly. The two results are compatible: a narrowing of dispersion without a negative coefficient suggests that movements were driven by individual cases and not by the poorest as a group moving up.

The result for value added per worker is similar. Across 168 countries between 2015 and 2024, the coefficient is 0.0012, with a p-value of 0.49 and an R-squared of 0.0024. The sign is positive, so that the point estimate points to a slight tendency for countries with higher starting values to grow faster, although the estimate is not distinguishable from zero. The coefficient of variation moved from 1.51 to 1.43, a small fall. The reading is that there is no evidence of a systematic closing of the gap, and the distribution of agricultural labour productivity remains very wide. The implication for 2030 is that a doubling for the lowest-productivity countries cannot be expected from the forces already at work over this period. If catching up were occurring by itself, the low-income group would show it; it shows the reverse.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020

The series offered by the bench give end points more than yearly paths, and the findings above compare 2015 with the latest year. The conclusions about the pandemic years therefore rest on general knowledge more than on the displayed results. The shock of 2020 disrupted labour movement, input supply and transport, and agricultural output in most countries proved more resilient than other sectors, because food production continued as an essential activity. This may help explain why value added per worker in most regions did not fall. The more lasting effect on the poorest may have come through prices and incomes: higher fertiliser and fuel costs after 2021 may have reduced the use of purchased inputs among smallholders, which could account for part of the stagnation of yields in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries. A reader should treat this explanation as plausible and not as shown by the series.

A second caution concerns measurement. Value added per worker is the ratio of an output measure to a labour measure, and the labour measure for agriculture depends on household surveys that count part-time, seasonal and unpaid family work unevenly. Women, who make up a large share of the agricultural labour force in many low-income countries and who are named in the target, are often under-counted or recorded as outside the labour force. The series cannot show whether their productivity has changed. Cereal yield, moreover, applies to cereals only. It leaves out roots, tubers, pulses, vegetables, fruit, livestock and fish, which matter for the incomes of many small-scale producers, and in fishing communities it measures nothing at all. Reporting also varies: in some countries the harvested area is reported only as sown or cultivated area, as the series note states.

### Implications for 2030

The evidence supports four conclusions. First, only East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group, at 5.5 per cent a year, advanced at a pace near that which a doubling from 2015 requires; no other region or income group is shown to be on course. Because these two groups gained in part from labour leaving farming, their pace is hard to repeat where the farm labour force is still growing. Second, the world average disguises a split: the economies with the highest productivity gained, the middle gained moderately, and the lowest-income economies lost ground. Third, cereal yields rose modestly, and barely at all in Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group. Fourth, the absence of convergence in either indicator over 2015 to 2024 shows that the gaps were not closing by themselves in that period.

The reading of the target matters for the verdict. If doubling is read as applying to the world average, the answer is that it will not be met. If it is read as applying to each country, a larger number of countries will fail, and the low-income group has moved backwards. If it is read as applying to small-scale producers specifically, the bench cannot say, because the series do not distinguish them. On the first two readings the conclusion that the target will be missed is secure for the regions where the data exist, and the main uncertainty is about the size of the miss for the people the target names.

What would raise productivity where it is lowest is well understood, though not tested here: secure land rights, particularly for women; extension services and farmer organisations; improved and drought-tolerant seed; affordable fertiliser; small-scale irrigation; rural roads, storage and market access; and rural finance and insurance. The accounts of land, fertiliser, water and investment appear in other sections of this chapter and are not repeated here.
