Governments and research funders should treat the absence of convergence in yield and value added per worker as a reason to finance crop research and extension suited to low-yield regions, and should review the effect after the next full data year.
w-c03-4-2~loom/writer-1~57.gaps: The series describe whole economies and do not separate small-scale producers, women, indigenous peoples, pastoralists or fishers, and none measures incomes. Cereal yield omits other crops, livestock and fish. North America has no observation after 2015 for value added per worker in the extract. Latest years differ by series and region, and the results give end points, not yearly paths, so the effect of the pandemic and of price shocks cannot be isolated. The causes mentioned are background knowledge and not results.

w-c06-6-1~loom/writer-3~57.text:
### What the indicators measure

The commitment in target 5.a is wide: equal rights to economic resources, ownership and control of land and other property, financial services, inheritance and natural resources, in accordance with national laws. The World Bank's catalogue measures only part of it. The best-covered strand is financial services, through the Global Findex survey, which asks adults whether they hold an account at a financial institution or have personally used a mobile-money service in the past year. Findex reports the answer separately for women and men, so the gap between the two series is a direct measure of unequal access. No equivalent series on women's ownership of land or housing sits on the shelf, and that absence shapes this section: the account gap can be measured with some precision, while the property gap can only be discussed through proxies and through what is missing.

An account is an entry point, not a measure of economic control. A woman may hold an account that her husband operates, or may have received a mobile-money wallet only to collect a government transfer. The survey definition counts accounts held alone or together with someone else. The indicator therefore shows access to the formal and semi-formal payment system, not who decides how money is used. It is nonetheless one of the few gender-disaggregated economic indicators with near-global coverage, and for that reason it carries much of the evidential weight for the target.

The survey is also periodic rather than annual. Findex rounds have appeared at intervals of roughly three years, and the most recent round reached 139 countries in 2024. Some regional aggregates in the results below end in 2021 rather than 2024, which reflects the vintage of the regional series on the shelf. Comparisons across regions must therefore be made with that difference in end year in mind, and the section states the end year of every figure it quotes.

### The world gap

Globally, the share of women holding an account rose from 65.9% in 2017 to 76.6% in 2024. Over the same period the share of men rose from 72.8% to 80.9%. Both groups gained, and women gained more in percentage points, so the gap narrowed. It has not closed. At the 2024 levels a gap of several points remains at world level, and it is concentrated in a limited set of regions and income groups rather than spread evenly.

The world average conceals the shape of the problem. Where almost everyone holds an account, as in high-income economies, a gender gap cannot be large because there is no room for it. Where account ownership is still being built, as in low-income economies, the gap is determined by who is reached first. The evidence below shows that men are generally reached first, and that the gap is widest in settings where overall ownership is lowest or where social norms restrict women's mobility, employment and independent control of money.

The period 2017 to 2024 straddles two events that bear on this. The first is the global expansion of digital payments, which lowered the cost of opening an account and removed the need to visit a branch. The second is the pandemic after 2020, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers electronically and, in doing so, brought new account holders into the system. Whether these developments favoured women is the question the regional and income data allow the book to answer in part, though the survey cannot separate the effect of each cause.

### Regional differences

In East Asia and the Pacific, women's account ownership rose from 71.2% in 2017 to 81.4% in 2021, against 75.7% and 84.2% for men. In Europe and Central Asia the female share rose from 79.4% to 88.0% while the male share rose from 83.8% to 91.2%. In both regions the gap persisted but was modest, and both sexes gained at a similar pace. These are middle- and upper-middle-income regions where the remaining gap reflects pockets of exclusion, for instance among rural, older and less-educated women, rather than a general barrier.

Latin America and the Caribbean shows the largest absolute gain in the regional table. Women's ownership rose from 52.1% in 2017 to 70.1% in 2021, and men's from 58.7% to 77.0%. Both sexes gained by a very large amount in four years, and the gap stayed visible. The region's expansion owes much to the spread of conditional cash-transfer schemes paid into accounts, which are typically addressed to women as household recipients, together with the growth of digital wallets and low-cost accounts promoted by public banks and financial regulators. A cash-transfer route to an account is real inclusion in the sense of access, but it may be a narrower form of inclusion than an account opened for savings or credit.

South Asia reports through 2024. Women's ownership there rose from 64.0% in 2017 to 75.1% in 2024, while men's rose from 74.7% to 80.1%. The female gain was the larger, and the gap narrowed markedly. This is consistent with national drives to open basic accounts at scale, among them campaigns to give every household a bank account and to route subsidies directly into accounts. Such drives raise ownership quickly, but surveys in several countries have shown that accounts opened in a campaign are often dormant, so ownership may overstate active use. The indicator as defined here counts ownership, not activity.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the region where the gender gap is largest on the shelf. Women's ownership rose from 38.0% in 2017 to 45.6% in 2021, while men's rose from 56.8% to 59.6%. Women gained several points, yet fewer than half of women in the region held an account in 2021, and the male share was far higher. The region combines legal and social restrictions on women's mobility, employment and independent financial decisions with low female labour-force participation, which removes a main reason for an account, namely a wage. The inclusion of Afghanistan in the aggregate matters: since 2021 the restrictions imposed on women there make the regional picture after that year uncertain, and the 2021 end point predates much of that change.

Sub-Saharan Africa has a lower overall level but a gender gap smaller than that of the Middle East and North Africa group. Women's ownership rose from 36.9% in 2017 to 49.0% in 2021, and men's from 48.5% to 61.4%. The region is the global centre of mobile money, and the growth of agent networks allowed millions of people, women among them, to hold a wallet without ever entering a bank branch. Even so, the male share stayed above the female share at both dates, and the gap did not narrow on these figures. Mobile-money inclusion appears to have lifted both sexes in parallel rather than to have closed the difference between them. Women's lower rates of phone ownership, lower literacy and less independent income are the usual explanations, and the chapter's section on mobile technology treats the phone question directly.

North America is the single case in which the pattern reverses. Women's ownership rose from 93.4% in 2017 to 97.1% in 2021, while men's moved from 94.2% to 93.8%. By the later date, women's ownership exceeded men's. The movement is small and the sample for a region with few reporting countries is narrow, so it should not be over-read; still, it illustrates that a gender gap in account ownership is not inevitable once ownership is near universal.

### Income groups and the shape of the gap

The grouping by income level is more revealing than the regional one, because the gap is closely linked to the level of ownership. In low-income countries, women's ownership rose from 26.8% in 2017 to 40.6% in 2024. Men's rose from 37.3% to 52.5%. Even after the rise, well under half of women in these countries held an account in 2024, and the male share was above half. In absolute terms the gap in this group is as wide as in any other group on the shelf, and it did not shrink between the two years.

In lower-middle-income countries, women's ownership rose from 55.6% to 67.6% and men's from 64.4% to 73.2%. The gap here is smaller than among low-income countries and appears to have narrowed slightly. Upper-middle-income countries show a rise from 68.9% to 82.5% for women and from 76.3% to 85.6% for men. The gap narrowed more clearly, because women's gains were larger than men's. High-income countries sit close to the ceiling: women's ownership moved from 92.1% to 94.5%, men's from 93.9% to 95.3%, and the difference is small.

The pattern across the four groups is a familiar one in the diffusion of any financial service. Men adopt first, women follow, and the gap opens in the early and middle stages and narrows when the service approaches universality. The practical implication is that the gender gap in the poorest countries will not close by itself as the average rises; it closes only when the service has largely saturated the male population, and that is far away. For countries in the low-income group, the pace of progress matters more than the world average suggests, because these are also the countries where women have the fewest alternatives to cash.

The result also shows that the world-level improvement is driven in large part by the middle-income groups, where the population is large. This weighting effect should be kept in mind when reading the world figure: the rise from 65.9% to 76.6% reflects mostly the middle-income economies catching up, and it says less about the poorest women, whose ownership remains well below the world level.

### Position against the 2030 target

The trend classification applies a simple benchmark: full account ownership among women, 100%, by 2030. This is an interpretation, since target 5.a itself sets no numerical level, and the reading of the target as universal access to financial services is a choice made by the bench. A different reading, in which the target is met when the gap between women and men closes, would produce a different classification. The reader should treat the benchmark as demanding and as one of several defensible readings.

On that benchmark, of 139 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target. These countries hold 49.9% of the assessed population, a large share because the group includes some very populous economies and many high-income countries already near the ceiling. A further 41 countries, with 18.7% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 29 countries, with 17.8% of the population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries, with 3.2% of the population, show stagnation. Finally, 33 countries, with 10.4% of the population, show regression, meaning that women's ownership fell over the period assessed.

The number of regressing countries deserves attention. That 33 of 139 countries recorded a decline is not a statistical artefact to be dismissed. Declines may reflect survey differences, the closure of dormant accounts opened during campaigns or pandemic payments, a reduction in mobile-money use after a fall in transfers, political upheaval or sanctions, or genuine loss of access. The data cannot distinguish among these. What they do show is that the global rise is not universal; for roughly a quarter of the countries assessed, the direction was the wrong one, though these countries hold a smaller share of the population than those on track.

The weighting also shows the divide between countries and people. Half of the assessed population lives in countries classed as on track, but fewer than half of the countries are in that class on a count of nations. The countries that are not on track are numerous, smaller in population and concentrated in the lower-income groups, which are the ones with the largest gaps. A global target met by population weight can therefore coexist with a majority of countries failing it, and the section's reading is that the aggregate masks the countries where policy attention is most needed.

What changed after 2015 and after 2020 can be stated only in outline. The first Findex round on the shelf for these results is 2017, so the baseline year of the goals is not itself observed here, and the period from 2015 to 2017 is outside the comparison. Between 2017 and 2021 the regional data show large gains in nearly every region, consistent with the effect of digital payments and emergency transfers around 2020. From 2021 to 2024 only the global, income-group and South Asian series are available on the shelf, and they show continued gains for both sexes. The material does not allow the claim that the pandemic itself changed the gender gap, only that ownership rose through it.

### Property, enterprise and the missing evidence

The remaining parts of target 5.a, land, property and inheritance, cannot be measured with the account series. The shelf holds three other series that touch on the target without measuring it. The Women, Business and the Law legal framework index, reported for 189 countries in 2025, scores how laws shape women's economic opportunities, with a topic on assets within it; the chapter's section on legal frameworks treats the index, and here it matters only as context. A legal right to own or inherit property is a precondition, not an outcome. Where statute and custom diverge, as in many systems of customary land tenure, women may hold the right in law and be denied it in practice, and no legal index can show this.

The enterprise survey series on firms with female participation in ownership is the nearest measure of women's ownership of productive assets. It counts firms with at least one female owner, which says nothing about the size of the stake or about control, and it covers formal firms only. It therefore omits the informal farms, household enterprises and market trades in which most women in low-income countries work. The series on women's participation in household decisions, available for 70 countries, measures a different thing again, namely the share of married women with a say in health care, large purchases and family visits. Taken together, the series give pieces of an answer, but none gives the share of women who own land or a dwelling in their own name.

This gap in evidence matters for policy. Land is the main asset of rural households in much of the world, and secure title is associated with greater bargaining power, willingness to invest and access to credit as collateral. Reform of inheritance law, joint titling of land and registration drives are the main policy instruments, and without a global series their effect cannot be tracked against the target. The account data show that women's access to the payment system is improving and that the gap is largest where ownership is lowest; they do not show whether that improvement extends to the assets on which women's economic independence ultimately rests.

On the evidence available, the picture for 2030 is mixed. Account ownership is rising for both sexes and the gap is narrowing in several regions, yet the gap is widest in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan and in low-income countries, which are the places where women have the least access to formal economic life. A target of universal ownership by 2030 will not be met worldwide, given that the world figure stood at 76.6% in 2024 and that so many countries show slow progress or decline. A target of equal ownership is a more realistic aim in middle-income and high-income economies, and a distant one elsewhere.

w-c05-3-1~cedar/writer-3~57.text:
### Participation in the early years

Pre-primary enrolment is the broadest measure the World Bank's indicators hold of how many children take part in organised learning before primary school. It is a gross ratio: total enrolment at this level, whatever the age of the children, divided by the population of the official pre-primary age group. A ratio can therefore exceed 100 per cent where children outside the official age range are enrolled, and it does not show whether a given child attends, for how many hours, or with what quality. Read with that limit, the world figure was 56.0 per cent in 2015 and 60.9 per cent in 2020. About three in five children of pre-primary age were thus enrolled by the last year with broad coverage, a gain of roughly five percentage points in five years.

Target 4.2 asks for access to quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education so that all girls and boys are ready for primary school. The wording sets no numerical threshold in the indicator used here, and the trend tool in this book therefore has no target value to measure against. It classifies progress by rate of change instead, and the classification should be read as a judgement of pace, not as the measurement of a gap to a defined goal. The word 'all' can be read as universal enrolment, near 100 per cent, but a gross ratio makes that reading imprecise, since over-age enrolment can mask children who are missing.

### Regional and income differences

The differences between regions are larger than the change over time. In 2020 East Asia and Pacific stood at 83.2 per cent, Europe and Central Asia at 78.3 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean at 75.6 per cent and North America at 70.3 per cent. South Asia reached 62.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping stood at 33.8 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa at 28.1 per cent. Children in the two lowest regions were thus about a third to a quarter as likely to be enrolled as children in East Asia and Pacific.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries recorded 20.1 per cent in 2020, lower middle income 58.5 per cent, upper middle income 77.9 per cent and high income 83.8 per cent. The gap between the poorest and richest groups is therefore more than sixty percentage points. Pre-primary education is rarely compulsory, is often provided by private or community operators, and is frequently charged for; public systems in poorer countries have tended to put scarce funds into primary schooling first. That ordering of priorities explains much of the gradient.

In 2015 the regional figures were 74.8 per cent in East Asia and Pacific, 73.9 per cent in Europe and Central Asia, 73.2 per cent in Latin America and the Caribbean, 70.1 per cent in North America, 54.2 per cent in South Asia, 31.2 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan and 25.5 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa. Comparing the two years, East Asia and Pacific gained about 8.5 points and South Asia about 7.9. North America barely moved, from 70.1 to 70.3 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa gained 2.6 points and the Middle East grouping 2.7, from low bases, so absolute gaps widened even where relative growth was respectable.

### Pace of change and the outlook for 2030

The trend classification, based on annual rates of change from 2015 to 2020, puts several groups in the best category. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia, and the low, lower middle and upper middle income groups are rated on track or target met, with rates of 0.0217, 0.0275, 0.0298, 0.0211 and 0.0205 respectively. The rating for low-income countries needs care: a rate measured against a low starting level looks fast even though the level, 20.1 per cent, remains very low. At the pace recorded, low-income countries would still be well below half enrolment in 2030.

The world as a whole, at a rate of 0.0169, is rated moderate progress needing acceleration, as are Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0196) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping (0.0165). Europe and Central Asia (0.0117) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0063) are rated marginal progress, and high-income countries (0.0047) and North America (0.0005) are classed as stagnating. Stagnation at high levels is less worrying than stagnation at low ones; it may reflect a ceiling near saturation of demand, though a level of 70.3 per cent in North America shows that the ceiling is not universal enrolment, partly because pre-primary attendance is voluntary and fragmented between public and private provision.

Country-level results are more sobering than the group averages. Of 172 countries assessed, 57 are on track, holding 38.4 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 17 show moderate progress (7.0 per cent of population), 12 marginal progress (2.8 per cent) and 16 stagnation (11.4 per cent). Seventy countries, with 40.3 per cent of the population, are classed as regressing. That so many countries regress while regional aggregates rise is a warning about the data as well as the children: aggregates are weighted by population, and some of the apparent regression follows the thinning of reporting after 2019, which is discussed below.

### Inequality between countries and convergence

The spread of enrolment among countries narrowed before the pandemic. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient fell from 0.239 in 2015 (164 countries) to 0.178 in 2019 (147 countries), and the Theil index from 0.117 to 0.065. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.436 to 0.331. Differences between regions account for 48.1 per cent of the Theil index in 2015 and 48.5 per cent in 2019, so about half of the inequality is a matter of where a country lies and half of differences within regions. Narrowing was not therefore achieved by closing the regional gap; it came about largely from within-region catch-up, with the largest populations, notably in South Asia, rising towards the middle of the distribution.

A convergence test across 137 countries with data in both 2015 and 2019 gives a beta coefficient of -0.0174 (p-value 0.0157), meaning that countries with lower initial enrolment tended to grow slightly faster. The explanatory power is slight, with an R-squared of 0.047, and the coefficient of variation among these countries fell only from 0.482 to 0.453. Convergence exists but is weak: initial level explains under five per cent of the variation in growth, so national policy, financing and demography matter far more than catch-up as such.

### Before and after 2015 and 2020

The world series shows two structural breaks in annual change, in 2005 and 2014. Mean annual growth was 0.68 points in 2001 to 2004, rose to 2.02 points in 2005 to 2013, and fell to 0.99 points in 2014 to 2020. The Goals therefore began at a time when growth in pre-primary enrolment had already halved from its peak. A plausible reading is that the large expansion of the late 2000s, driven by national early-childhood policies and the extension of free pre-primary years in many middle-income countries, had run its course, and that the remaining children are harder to reach. This is an interpretation; the data show the slowdown, not its causes.

The effect of 2020 cannot be measured from this indicator. Reporting countries numbered 164 in 2015, 147 in 2019 and 143 in 2020, then fell to 71 in 2021 and only 4 in 2022. The 2020 regional and world figures are published aggregates, but the sharp fall in country reporting means that nothing reliable can be said about enrolment after school closures. Pre-primary centres were among the first facilities to close and among the last to reopen in many countries, and informal and private provision was exposed to loss of fees, so a fall is plausible. The data on hand neither confirm nor exclude it.

### Ready for primary school

The target speaks of readiness, which enrolment alone does not capture. Two further series bear on it. Trained teachers in pre-primary education, reported by 144 countries with a latest year of 2025, gauge the minimum qualification of staff, though a country's minimum can be low and differs between countries, so cross-country comparison is loose. The net intake rate in grade 1, covering 167 countries to 2019, indicates how many children enter primary school at the official age. Primary starting age, available for 210 countries and territories to 2025, defines the age group that pre-primary education serves, and differences in it change what a gross ratio means from one country to the next. These series were on the shelf, but the results computed for this section concern enrolment, and no finding on teacher training or intake is drawn here.

The overall assessment is that participation is rising, but unevenly and more slowly than in the late 2000s. Where it is lowest, in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa, the pace is not enough to reach levels now common elsewhere by 2030, and the evidence after 2020 is too thin to say whether the pandemic reversed gains.

w-c05-1-1~willow/writer-3~57.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The primary completion rate measures new entrants to the last grade of primary school, regardless of age, as a share of the population at the entrance age for that grade. At world level it stood at 87.9% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, a gain of almost nothing across nine years. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, so a world figure of 88.0% leaves roughly one child in eight short of the primary goal, and the lack of movement means the gap is not closing.

The measure has limits. Data limitations preclude adjusting for pupils who drop out during the final year, and because entrants of any age are counted against a single-age population, the ratio can exceed 100 where repetition and late entry are common. Only 11 countries reported for 2025, so the latest observations used here are 2022 to 2024 for most aggregates.

### Regional divergence in primary completion

The flat world average conceals movement in opposite directions. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group rose from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024, the largest gain among regions. East Asia and Pacific rose from 94.1% to 95.4% in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 97.2% to 98.1% in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 66.3% to 68.9%, so that nearly a third of children there still do not reach the last primary grade on this measure.

Several regions that were close to universal completion fell back. South Asia declined from 98.5% in 2015 to 94.4% in 2024, Latin America and the Caribbean from 98.4% to 96.5%, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. Part of such falls may reflect school closures and learning disruption after 2020, and part may reflect revisions in enrolment and population estimates, which the series cannot separate. Because the indicator is a gross intake ratio, a fall from above 98% can also reflect fewer over-age repeaters, not fewer completers; the data do not allow that to be tested.

By income group, low-income countries moved from 60.5% to 62.9% in 2023, lower middle income from 88.2% to 88.0% in 2024, upper middle income from 94.4% to 95.2% in 2023, and high income from 98.1% to 97.8% in 2024. The spread between low and high income, about 35 points in 2023, is the central feature of the distribution.

### Country trajectories to 2030 for primary completion

The trend assessment compares each country's rate of change since 2015 with the rate needed to reach 100% by 2030. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, covering 19.6% of the assessed population. Another 14 show moderate progress (13.0% of population) and 14 marginal progress (5.7%). Three are stagnant (0.5%). A striking 92 countries are classed as regressing, holding 61.3% of the population.

The regression class needs care. Countries already near 100% that fluctuate slightly below it are classed as regressing, as are countries with real declines. The large population share, which includes South Asia, reflects both effects. Even so, the verdict is clear: on present trends the world will not reach universal primary completion by 2030, and the countries furthest from it, mainly in Sub-Saharan Africa, are advancing too slowly to close the gap.

### Lower secondary completion shows more progress and wider gaps

Completion of lower secondary school rose from 74.8% in 2015 to 77.9% in 2024 worldwide. The gain is larger than in primary but still leaves more than one in five adolescents without a lower secondary certificate on this measure. The regional picture is uneven. East Asia and Pacific climbed from 86.3% to 97.3%, a rise of about eleven points that makes it the clear success. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. South Asia moved from 83.7% to 86.6%, and Europe and Central Asia from 90.9% to 91.9%. Latin America and the Caribbean was almost static, 81.3% to 81.5%. North America reported 104.3% in 2016 and 100.8% in 2023; values above 100 arise from the gross intake definition and indicate over-age entrants, not more than universal completion.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 42.3% to 44.4% in 2023, and low-income countries from 37.0% to 38.6% in 2023. In these settings fewer than half of adolescents complete lower secondary school. By income, lower middle income countries rose from 71.0% to 73.7%, upper middle income from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023 and high income from 94.0% to 95.6%. Upper middle income countries thus gained the most, widening the gap with the poorest.

Projecting each group's trend to 2030 gives an expected world rate of 80.0%, against a target of 100%; the world is classed as making marginal progress, with only 0.21 of the required pace. East Asia and Pacific, with an expected 105.4% and a ratio of 1.39, and upper middle income countries, expected at 99.3%, are on track. Low-income countries are expected at 40.1% and Sub-Saharan Africa at 46.2%, both classed as stagnation. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is expected at 73.9%, South Asia at 88.5%, lower middle income at 75.5%. Across the 173 countries assessed, 49 are on track (22.1% of population), 21 show moderate progress (16.1%), 32 marginal progress (38.4%), 5 stagnate (2.2%) and 66 regress (21.1%). The large share in the marginal class is explained by populous lower middle income countries moving slowly in the right direction.

### Learning lags behind completion

Target 4.1 requires completion that leads to effective learning, and the proficiency series is the weakest part of the evidence. The share of pupils below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary, using the low threshold set by the Global Alliance to Monitor Learning, was 45.9% in 2015 and 49.6% in 2019 for the world. The latest year of any reporting is 2023, with one country. These aggregates are therefore modelled from sparse assessments: 125 countries have reported in any year, but in a few waves, with 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021.

The pattern by region is stark. Sub-Saharan Africa had 80.7% below minimum proficiency in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019; low-income countries 83.5% and 87.4%. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 57.7% and 57.5%, South Asia at 55.8% and 56.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 49.1% and 51.0%. Europe and Central Asia improved from 6.8% to 5.5%, while North America held at 3.9% in both years and high-income countries moved from 6.4% to 6.2%. Upper middle income countries were at 28.0% and 28.6%, and lower middle income countries worsened from 52.9% to 57.4%.

East Asia and Pacific rose from 19.2% to 31.6%. This is better read as a warning about comparability than as a collapse: new countries entering the assessed sample, and changes in who is assessed, can move a regional aggregate sharply. The same caution applies to every figure here, and the series ends in 2019 for aggregates, before school closures of 2020 and 2021, so effects of the pandemic on learning are not measured.

The trend classes confirm that the learning target is distant. The world is classed as regression, with an expected 61.3% below proficiency in 2030 against a target of zero. Low income countries are projected at 99.1%, Sub-Saharan Africa at 91.0% and lower middle income at 71.7%, all by extrapolation of a short, noisy record. Only Europe and Central Asia, at 2.97% expected, shows moderate progress.

### Implications for 2030

Three conclusions follow. First, completion and learning are different problems: regions with high completion, such as Latin America and South Asia, still show around half or more of pupils below the reading threshold. Counting graduates therefore overstates the achievement of Target 4.1. Second, gains are concentrated where governments sustained expansion of schooling, as in East Asia and Pacific and the Middle East group, while the poorest countries, with rapid population growth, conflict and constrained budgets, are not moving fast enough. Third, the pace needed for 2030 is far above anything observed since 2015, so the realistic task is to narrow gaps and secure foundational learning, not to count on universality.

w-c04-5-1~juniper/writer-4~57.text:
### A fall in the world average

Total alcohol consumption per adult, measured as litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 and over per year, fell from 5.9 litres in 2015 to 4.9 litres in 2020 for the world as a whole. The series sums recorded and unrecorded consumption and adjusts for tourist consumption. Target 3.5 asks for stronger prevention and treatment of the harmful use of alcohol, but it carries no numerical threshold. The trend tool therefore assessed each series against a simple direction, a decrease by 2030, and the labels 'on track' or 'regression' below describe that direction only. They do not measure compliance with a quantified goal, and the target can be read in more than one way: lower average consumption is not identical to lower harm, since patterns of drinking, such as heavy episodic drinking, matter as much as the mean.

The world rate of change, -0.0 on the tool's scale of -0.0363, was classed as on track. The fall is large for a five-year window, and it should be read with care. The values are projected estimates, modelled from survey, sales and tax records, and the latest year is 2020, the first year of the pandemic. Closures of bars and restaurants, falling tourism and income shocks probably lowered recorded sales in many places, while the effect on unrecorded home or informal production is poorly observed. Part of the fall may therefore be temporary, and a rebound after 2020 cannot be excluded from these data.

### Regional differences

The levels differ widely. Europe and Central Asia stood at 9.5 litres in 2015 and 8.9 litres in 2020, and North America at 9.5 litres and 9.9 litres. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.4 litres to 4.5 litres, the steepest regional decline, at a rate of -0.0657. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.5 litres to 5.8 litres, South Asia from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 4.6 litres to 4.2 litres. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping recorded 0.4 litres in 2015 and 0.3 litres in 2020, by far the lowest level, which reflects religious and legal restrictions on sale and use; for that reason recorded figures there may understate unrecorded consumption.

North America is the only region classed as regression, with a rate of 0.0075 and a rise from 9.5 litres to 9.9 litres. Europe and Central Asia, with the highest consumption in the world apart from North America, was assessed as making moderate progress needing acceleration, at -0.0138. The regions with the greatest consumption are therefore those where the fall is slowest or absent, which matters because the burden of alcohol-related disease, from liver disease to injury, is concentrated where intake is highest.

### Income groups

By income, high-income countries moved from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a rate of -0.0075 classed as marginal progress. Upper-middle-income countries fell from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres, the sharpest fall of any income group, at -0.0585. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 3.9 litres to 3.3 litres, and low-income countries from 2.9 litres to 2.8 litres, a rate of -0.0054 and again marginal. The pattern is that the poorest countries drink least and change least, the middle group changes most, and the richest drink most and change little. Since the series falls most where consumption was already moderate to high in the middle-income band, the global decline is driven largely by large populations in East Asia and South Asia, whose weight pulls the world average down. Much of that decline sits in a few populous countries, and a falling world mean can coexist with rising consumption elsewhere, as the next section shows.

### The distribution of countries

Of 183 countries assessed, 75 were on track, holding 60.4% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 21 countries, with 11.0% of the population, made moderate progress, and 21 more, with 7.3%, made marginal progress. Twelve countries, 3.1% of the population, stagnated, and 54 countries, 18.2% of the population, regressed. Thirty per cent of countries by number therefore saw consumption rise, a share well above what the headline fall suggests. The population-weighted picture is more favourable than the count of countries because the large decliners are populous.

Convergence analysis across 181 countries gives no sign of countries drawing together. The beta coefficient of -0.0059 has a p-value of 0.6, and R squared is 0.01, so the starting level explains almost none of the subsequent change. The coefficient of variation rose slightly, from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.74 in 2020. Heavy-drinking countries have not systematically cut faster than light-drinking ones; the spread between countries is stable or widening slightly. That is relevant to 2030: if reductions do not concentrate where intake is highest, the global mean may fall without the number of high-consumption countries falling in step.

### Men, women and data quality

Male and female series move together almost perfectly. The Spearman correlation of country changes is 0.99 across 185 countries, and that of 2020 levels is 0.99. The result is largely a property of the estimation method, as the female series is typically modelled in relation to the male and national totals, so the near-identity cannot be taken as independent evidence that men and women change their habits in step. Levels for men are in general far higher than for women, so policies aimed at the national mean act mainly on male drinking.

Coverage is complete in form: 185 countries report in every year from 2000 to 2020, with 187 in 2010, 2015 and 2019. This regularity reflects modelled estimates produced for every country rather than a yearly survey in each. Projected values for 2020 may be revised as pandemic-period sales data arrive.

### Implications for 2030

On the direction-only reading, the world is on track, but the evidence for lasting change is thin. Five years, one of them a pandemic year, is a short basis. The measures that are known to reduce consumption, namely higher and indexed excise taxes, limits on availability and hours of sale, and restrictions on advertising, are well established. Where those are weak, and where marketing is expanding in growing markets, consumption can be expected to rise as incomes grow. The regression in North America and in 54 countries elsewhere shows that decline is not automatic.

t-compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-cho.name: compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-chose
t-compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-cho.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params['start_year'])
    y1 = int(params['end_year'])
    min_cov = params.get('min_countries', 10)
    s = data[code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    n = y1 - y0
    rates = {}
    skipped = 0
    for unit in s:
        ser = s[unit]
        if unit not in regions:
            continue
        a = ser.get(y0)
        b = ser.get(y1)
        if a is None or b is None:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        if a <= 0 or b <= 0 or n <= 0:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        rates[unit] = ((b / a) ** (1.0 / n) - 1.0) * 100.0
    facts = {}
    count = len(rates)
    facts['countries_with_both_years'] = count
    facts['countries_skipped'] = skipped
    facts['years_spanned'] = n
    if count < min_cov:
        facts['coverage_met'] = 'no'
        return {'facts': facts, 'summary': 'Coverage is below the minimum of ' + str(min_cov) + ' countries: only ' + str(count) + ' have values in both ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ' for ' + code + '. No growth rate is reported.'}
    facts['coverage_met'] = 'yes'
    vals = list(rates.values())
    med = statistics.median(vals)
    facts['median_cagr_pct'] = round(med, 2)
    facts['mean_cagr_pct'] = round(statistics.mean(vals), 2)
    best = max(rates, key=lambda k: rates[k])
    worst = min(rates, key=lambda k: rates[k])
    facts['fastest_country'] = names.get(best, best)
    facts['fastest_cagr_pct'] = round(rates[best], 2)
    facts['slowest_country'] = names.get(worst, worst)
    facts['slowest_cagr_pct'] = round(rates[worst], 2)
    groups = {}
    for k in rates:
        groups.setdefault(regions[k], []).append(rates[k])
    for g in groups:
        if len(groups[g]) >= 3:
            facts['median_cagr_pct_region_' + str(g)] = round(statistics.median(groups[g]), 2)
    summary = 'Between ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ', the median compound annual growth rate of ' + code + ' across ' + str(count) + ' countries was ' + str(round(med, 2)) + ' per cent a year. ' + str(skipped) + ' countries lacked a positive value in one of the two years and are excluded. The rate is computed from end points only and ignores movement between them.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

w-c06-5-1~ewan/writer-2~58.text:
### The indicator measures autonomy in three linked decisions

Target 5.6 asks for universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. Its first indicator, compiled by the United Nations Population Fund from Demographic and Health Surveys, counts a woman aged 15 to 49 who is married or in union as making her own informed decisions only if she answers yes on all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner, she decides on the use of contraception, and she decides on her own health care. The rule is strict by design. A woman who controls her health care but cannot refuse sex is not counted, and neither is a woman who uses contraception chosen by her husband. The measure is therefore a composite of bodily autonomy rather than a measure of service access, and it will always sit below the share of women who say yes to any single component.

That strictness matters for interpretation. The indicator can fall because one component weakens even while others improve, and it can rise because norms about refusal of sex shift without any change in health systems. It also excludes unmarried women, adolescents outside unions and women older than 49, so it describes autonomy within marriage, which is where the constraint the target addresses is generally most binding but not where all of it lies. A reader should treat any national figure as a statement about married women of reproductive age at the date of a particular survey, not about all women.

### The evidence base is thin and episodic

The shelf does not hold a global or regional aggregate for this series; the coverage tool reports none. What it does show is how sparse the underlying measurement is. Across the whole period from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported a value in at least one year. In no single year does the count come close to that. The largest annual count is 15 countries, in 2018. In 2008 only 3 countries reported, and in 2019 and 2020 only 4 each. In the baseline year of the goals, 2015, 5 countries reported. In 2024, the latest year held, 5 countries reported again.

The pattern follows the survey cycle rather than any steady statistical programme. The Demographic and Health Surveys run roughly every five years in each participating country, and the questions on refusing sex and deciding on contraception were added to the standard women's questionnaire only in its later phases. Counts therefore cluster: 12 countries in 2012, 10 in 2016, 15 in 2018, then 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 as surveys postponed during the pandemic were completed. Between those peaks the series nearly empties, with 6 countries in 2013, 6 in 2017 and 7 in 2021. Before 2012 the annual count never exceeded 7.

This is not a series that can show a world trend. A world share for any year would be an average over a handful of countries that happened to field a survey, and the composition of that handful changes from year to year. Comparing the countries that reported in 2018 with those that reported in 2023 compares different populations, not the same population at two dates. The book's tools return the reporting counts and the levels for the countries present, and the figure attached to the levels result shows those country values for the latest year; it should be read as a set of national snapshots, not as a distribution of the world.

### What can be said about levels and regions

The countries that do report are concentrated where the Demographic and Health Surveys operate: sub-Saharan Africa, South and South-East Asia, and a smaller number of countries in Latin America, the Caribbean, Central Asia and the Middle East. High-income countries are almost entirely absent, because they do not run these surveys and their own health and social surveys do not ask the three questions in this form. The indicator is, in practice, a measure of autonomy in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and its absence elsewhere should not be read as an assumption that the target is met there.

Among reporting countries, well-documented survey results show wide dispersion. Countries in southern and eastern Africa and parts of Latin America tend to report the highest shares, while countries in West and Central Africa and parts of South Asia report the lowest, sometimes with a minority of married women meeting all three conditions. The component that most often pulls the composite down varies: in some countries it is the ability to refuse sex, in others the decision on one's own health care, which is frequently taken by a husband or jointly with relatives. Within countries, the share generally rises with schooling, with household wealth and with urban residence, and it is lower among the youngest married women, who are most often in the unions described in the chapter's section on child marriage.

These patterns are consistent with what related series on the shelf measure, though this section does not report their values. The share of women who believe a husband is justified in beating his wife if she refuses sex is a direct attitudinal counterpart of the first component. Unmet need for contraception and demand satisfied by modern methods describe whether women who want to avoid pregnancy can act on that wish; a woman may decide on contraception and still lack supplies, or have supplies and lack the decision. The share of women participating in decisions on their own health care, large purchases and family visits uses a looser rule that counts joint decisions, and so will normally exceed the target 5.6 measure. Read together, these series separate norms, decisions and services, which the single composite cannot.

### Change after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be measured from this series

The question a goal chapter should answer is whether the world moved closer to universal reproductive autonomy after the goals were adopted. The data do not allow an answer at global level. With 5 countries reporting in 2015, 4 in 2020 and 5 in 2024, there is no common set of countries large enough to carry a trend from the baseline to the latest year. Change can only be judged country by country, where a nation has fielded two comparable surveys, typically five or more years apart.

The period after 2020 compounds the problem. Survey fieldwork stopped or was delayed in many countries in 2020 and 2021, which is visible in the low counts for those years and the rebound to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023. The pandemic also disrupted contraceptive supply chains and health services, and documented increases in intimate partner violence during lockdowns bear directly on the ability to refuse sex. Whether these shocks lowered autonomy durably, or only briefly, is precisely what the series is too sparse to show. The surveys completed in 2022 and 2023 mostly describe conditions after the acute phase.

A further concern is the funding of measurement itself. The Demographic and Health Surveys Program has depended heavily on a single bilateral donor, and the interruption of that funding in 2025 put the next round of surveys in doubt. Since this indicator exists only because of those surveys, the low count of 5 countries for 2024 may be not a trough in a cycle but the beginning of a longer gap. Without replacement, the world could reach 2030 with no country-level measurement of target 5.6 for a large part of the population it was meant to track.

### Implications for 2030

The target speaks of universal access, which implies that every married woman, and by the spirit of the Programme of Action every woman, should be able to make all three decisions. Even on the most favourable reading of national surveys, no reporting country is close to universality, and the countries with the lowest shares have changed slowly between surveys, because the constraint lies in marriage norms, laws on marital rape, women's education and economic dependence, all of which move over decades rather than years. Two readings of the target are possible: one sets a fixed threshold of universal autonomy, against which every reporting country falls short; the other asks for steady progress, which can only be assessed where a country has repeated surveys. On either reading, 2030 will be reached with the target unmet, and on the second reading most of the world will not be assessable at all.

The practical conclusion is that the gap in measurement is itself a finding of the section. Target 5.6 is one of the few targets defined in terms of women's agency rather than services, and it is among the least measured. The 81 countries that have ever reported are fewer than half of all countries, and the annual counts are smaller still.

### Proposals

The proposals that follow address both the autonomy the indicator measures and the measurement on which any assessment depends.

claims.fact: c06-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Donor governments and multilateral health funders should jointly guarantee financing for a full round of Demographic and Health Surveys before 2030, so that target 5.6 has at least one post-pandemic measurement in every country that has reported before.

National statistical offices in countries that do not run these surveys, including high-income countries, should add the three standard questions to existing health or social surveys so that the indicator ceases to describe only poorer countries.
UNFPA should publish the three components separately alongside the composite, so that governments can see whether the binding constraint is refusal of sex, contraception or health care.

Governments that have not done so should criminalise marital rape and remove requirements of spousal consent for contraception and health care, since these legal conditions bear directly on two of the three components.

The series covers only married or in-union women aged 15 to 49, excludes most high-income countries, and offers no breakdown by component, age, wealth or residence on the shelf. Country levels were not returned as facts here, so no national or regional values are quoted.

petition.need: For SG.DMK.SRCR.FN.ZS, compute change between each country's first survey at or before 2015 and its latest survey after 2015, with a count of countries and a population-weighted median, so that progress can be assessed on a constant set of countries.

w-c04-11-1~cedar/writer-1~58.text:
### Immunisation and reproductive, maternal, newborn and child services

The bench holds no direct series on immunisation coverage for this section. The nearest measure is the UHC service coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, which combines family planning, pregnancy care, child immunisation and child treatment on a scale of 0 to 100. It is therefore a proxy, and movements in it cannot be attributed to vaccination alone.

The index shows little movement. The world stood at 73 index points in 2015 and 72 in 2023, a rate of -0.0017 that the trend tool classes as regression. East Asia and Pacific held at 85 points, high income at 84, North America at 84, upper middle income at 83 and Latin America and the Caribbean at 78. Europe and Central Asia rose from 80 to 82, yet its rate of 0.0031 still reads as stagnation. These regions are near a plateau, where further gains are hard to win and a flat line may reflect a ceiling more than neglect.

The weaker results lie where need is greatest. Low income countries stayed at 51 points in both years. South Asia fell from 72 to 69, a rate of -0.0053, and lower middle income countries fell from 68 to 66, a rate of -0.0037. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 49 to 53, a rate of 0.0099, the only region with a positive movement large enough to be called marginal progress, and the tool states that significant acceleration is needed. Even after that gain it remains well below every other region except low income countries.

The country distribution confirms the pattern. Of 193 countries assessed, 11 are on track or have met the benchmark, covering 5.0% of the population. Another 9 show moderate progress, covering 3.1%, and 37 show marginal progress, covering 14.4%. Stagnation affects 105 countries with 48.1% of the population, and regression affects 31 countries with 29.5%. Nearly four in five people live in a country that is stagnating or regressing. The regression group is large by population because it includes populous South Asian and lower middle income countries. The target in this series is not numerically defined (the tool reports none), so the classes measure direction rather than distance from a stated goal.

Timing matters. The series ends in 2023 and the period includes the disruption to routine immunisation and antenatal care during the pandemic, followed by a patchy recovery. The data cannot separate the pre-2020 trend from that shock, and the flat regional lines suggest that the 2015 to 2019 gains, where they existed, were small.

### Domestic public health spending per head

Public money for health is rising almost everywhere, but the levels remain very unequal. World domestic general government health expenditure per capita rose from US$589.2 in 2015 to US$803.7 in 2023, in current dollars. High income countries rose from US$2,725.3 to US$3,847.3. North America went from US$4,587.0 to US$6,959.0, and Europe and Central Asia from US$1,525.4 to US$2,178.0. Upper middle income countries moved from US$221.4 to US$338.9, and East Asia and Pacific from US$413.7 to US$571.7.

At the lower end the increases are small in absolute terms. Low income countries spent US$7.0 per person in 2015 and US$7.3 in 2023. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from US$29.7 to US$31.7. Lower middle income countries rose from US$19.9 to US$30.9, and South Asia from US$14.7 to US$30.8, which is a doubling from a very low base. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region went from US$155.2 to US$190.2, and Latin America and the Caribbean from US$364.5 to US$415.7. A gain of a few dollars cannot buy a vaccine programme, a salary scale or a clinic network, so the headline growth hides a divide in the value of the public purse. Current dollars also mix real growth with price changes and exchange-rate movements, so the figures overstate real increases.

The country classification looks favourable: 142 countries, with 80.1% of the population, are on track or have met the benchmark, 12 show moderate progress (4.5%), 2 marginal progress (0.1%), 3 stagnation (1.3%) and 34 regression (14.0%). This reading is generous, because nominal per-head growth from a very low base counts as progress. The 34 countries in regression, holding 14.0% of the population, are those where public health spending per person fell, and they warrant the closest attention. Only 7 countries had reported 2024 values at the time of the extract, so the latest year is nearly empty.

### Health spending as a share of national income

Measured against national income, the picture is flatter. Current health expenditure, from all sources, was 9.7% of GDP in the world in 2015 and 10.1% in 2023. High income countries went from 12.0% to 12.5%, North America from 16.0% to 16.3%, and Europe and Central Asia from 9.3% to 9.6%. East Asia and Pacific rose from 6.4% to 6.8% and upper middle income countries from 5.5% to 6.0%. Latin America and the Caribbean barely moved, from 7.8% to 7.9%.

The lower-income groups went in the wrong direction. Low income countries fell from 5.4% to 4.6%, lower middle income countries from 3.9% to 3.7%, and South Asia from 3.5% to 3.3%. Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region eased from 5.4% to 5.3%. Here the contrast with the per-head series matters. Where public spending per person rose faster than output, as in South Asia, the share of GDP can still fall if the private and external components shrank or if GDP grew faster. For low income countries the fall in the share suggests that health did not keep pace with economies that had begun to grow, or that external funding retreated. The data do not decompose the cause, and a share of GDP also falls mechanically when output surges. Only 22 countries had reported 2024 values.

The share of income is the more relevant measure for target 3.c, which asks for substantially increased health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed. By that test the evidence is negative for the poorest groups: spending relative to income fell or stood still, while richer groups raised theirs.

### Convergence and the gap between countries

The convergence test on health expenditure per capita at purchasing power parity covers 190 countries between 2015 and 2023. The beta coefficient is -0.00001 with a p-value of 0.997 and an R-squared of 0.000, so there is no detectable tendency for poorer countries to catch up with richer ones in spending. The coefficient of variation eased from 1.24 to 1.20, a small narrowing in relative dispersion that the regression does not support as a systematic trend. Combined with the dollar levels above, the conclusion is that absolute gaps widened even as relative dispersion changed little. High income countries added about US$1,100 per person in public health spending between 2015 and 2023, while low income countries added about US$0.3.

This matters for 2030. Health systems in low income countries cannot reach universal coverage on public budgets of about US$7 per person, and external and household funds fill part of the gap. The bench holds external health expenditure per capita but no result was computed for it here, so the dependence of the poorest systems on aid, and the risk from recent reductions in aid, cannot be quantified in this section.

### Health workforce density

The workforce question cannot be answered with the shelf as it stands. The only workforce series is community health workers per 1,000 people, and it is sparse. Across 2000 to 2016, 64 countries reported in at least one year, and in any single year the count ranged from 3 to 29. In 2004, 29 countries reported; in 2014, 3; in 2015, 4; and in 2016, 6. The last year with data is 2016, so nothing after 2016 is covered, including the whole period since 2020. No trend can be computed, and no statement about rising or falling density is supported. Community health workers are also only one cadre: doctors, nurses and midwives are outside this series, and the national titles for community workers vary, which weakens comparison across countries.

The absence is itself a finding. Target 3.c names recruitment, training and retention of the health workforce, yet the monitoring series that would show whether the workforce is growing is the thinnest of the six examined. Migration of trained staff from poor to rich countries, the pay and retention policies that drive it, and the pandemic's effect on attrition are well-known pressures, but the numbers to measure them are not on the shelf.

### What the evidence implies for 2030

Across the three questions, the answer is mixed and unequal. Public spending per head is rising in most countries, but the poorest group gains only cents in absolute terms. Spending as a share of income is flat or falling in low and lower middle income groups. Service coverage is stagnant for most of the world's people and regressing for nearly three in ten. Workforce density cannot be assessed. At the observed rates, the groups with the lowest coverage, low income countries at 51 points and Sub-Saharan Africa at 53, will not close the gap with the 83 to 85 points of richer regions by 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa's rate of 0.0099 is the best on the list and still falls short.

The causes behind these patterns are well established. Domestic revenue in poor countries is low and its collection is limited by large informal economies, while debt service competes with health in budgets. Aid fell for some countries and is volatile. Immunisation depends on routine delivery by trained staff, cold chains and supply, and so on the same financing and workforce shortfalls. Conflict and fragile institutions explain much of the regression in some countries.

### Proposals

The figures that accompany this section show the regional trend classes of the coverage index, the country distribution, per-head public spending and spending as a share of GDP.

w-c02-2-1~willow/writer-1~58.text:
### What the national lines measure

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator behind it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines, is unlike the international measures in that each country sets its own line, with its own method, survey and price basis. A rate of one level in one country is therefore not equivalent to the same rate in another. The series is valuable because it reflects what each society regards as a minimum, and it is hazardous for the same reason: a ranking of countries by it mixes differences in hardship with differences in definition.

The World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform holds the series for 161 countries in any year. That is broad, yet no single year comes near it. The sections of this chapter on the international line and on basic services treat comparable measures; this section concerns what the national lines can and cannot support.

### Coverage over time

Reporting is thin and uneven. In 2000, 16 countries reported, and in 2001, 15. The count rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, then held near 40 to 50 through 2008 to 2014: 40 in 2008, 47 in 2009, 50 in 2010, 49 in 2011, 50 in 2012, 45 in 2013 and 46 in 2014. After the Goals were adopted, the count rose to 55 in 2015 and 57 in 2016, dipped to 53 in 2017, and reached 67 in 2018. It was 62 in 2019 and 57 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted in many places. The peak came in 2021, with 72 countries.

The decline since then is largely an artefact of timing. Surveys take time to be fielded, cleaned and published, so recent years fill in later: 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and only 13 in 2025. A reader should not take the fall as a fall in the number of countries measuring poverty. It does mean that the latest years cannot support statements about the world, and that the 2025 values, for 13 countries, describe a handful of economies that are not a representative sample.

The changing composition matters for every comparison across years. A rise in the average rate between two years may reflect a change in which countries report rather than a change in poverty. Comparisons within a country over time are sound; averages across years are less so.

### Dispersion among countries

The spread of rates among countries, weighted by population, was computed for each year. The Gini coefficient of the national rates was 0.22 in 2002 and 0.15 in 2009, then climbed: 0.28 in 2013, 0.34 in 2014, 0.39 in 2015, 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018, 0.63 in 2019 and 0.66 in 2020. It then fell abruptly to 0.35 in 2021, was 0.40 in 2022 and 0.35 in 2023, and reached 0.32 in 2024.

These movements should not be read as the world growing steadily more unequal in poverty and then abruptly converging. The sample of reporting countries changed, and large populous countries enter and leave it. The Theil index tells the same story, rising from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.72 in 2019 and falling to 0.20 in 2021; no Theil value is available for 2020. Between-region differences account for a large share of the Theil index in most years: 75.8 per cent in 2013, 88.4 per cent in 2014, 67.7 per cent in 2015 and 77.1 per cent in 2019, and 83.5 per cent in 2024. Regional position, rather than differences within regions, thus explains most of the inequality among countries in national poverty rates, though with a large margin of sampling uncertainty.

The swing from 2019 to 2021 coincides with the pandemic, but a break in the series composition probably explains more of it than any change in hardship. The figure for the spread should be consulted with that caution.

### Progress towards the halving

The trend tool classified 94 countries against a halving by 2030. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Seven countries, with 3.8 per cent of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration; seven, with 4.4 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration; five, with 2.1 per cent, are stagnant; and 34, with 26.0 per cent, have regressed.

The result is mixed. Most of the population in the assessed set lives in countries moving in the right direction, yet a third of the countries, 34 of 94, show poverty rising at their own lines. The difference between a country share and a population share shows that on-track status is concentrated in a few populous countries, while regression is spread over many smaller ones and some larger ones. The classification also depends on the years chosen and on the interval between surveys; a country with two surveys far apart is judged on very little. The target itself can be read in two ways, as a halving of each country's rate or as a halving of the aggregate, and the classification adopts the first. Under the second reading the picture would be driven by the largest countries.

### Comparability with other measures

The national rate moves with the international measure, but only moderately. Across 36 countries from 2015 to 2021, the rank correlation between the levels of the national rate and the rate at 3.00 dollars a day was 0.72, and that between their changes was 0.53. Countries with high national poverty tend to have high international poverty, but the direction and size of changes agree much less. Several causes plausibly explain this: national lines are revised, they rise with living standards in richer countries, and surveys differ in whether they measure income or consumption. The international series also had its purchasing power conversions revised, so rates cannot be compared with earlier editions.

The practical conclusion is that national lines are the right measure for judging a country's own progress against its own definition, and a poor measure for ranking countries. A fuller account needs the multidimensional and societal-line series, which add education, infrastructure and relative standards, but they are not examined here.

### Implications for 2030

With recent years sparsely reported and the regressing group so large, a global verdict on target 1.2 cannot be given from this series. What can be said is that progress is real in a large share of the assessed population, that it is far from universal, and that the evidence base thins just when the post-pandemic period most needs measuring.

Poverty in all its dimensions, as target 1.2 words it, is not captured by a headcount alone.

w-c05-4-1~willow/writer-2~58.text:
### The global picture

Target 4.3 commits states to equal access to affordable and quality technical, vocational and tertiary education by 2030. The target carries no numerical threshold, so any reading of progress rests on the direction and pace of change rather than on a fixed goal. The gross enrolment ratio is the indicator held on the shelf. It divides total tertiary enrolment, whatever the age of students, by the population of the age group that officially corresponds to the level. It can therefore exceed 100 per cent, and it says nothing about quality, completion or affordability.

The world ratio rose from 36.6 per cent in 2015 to 43.6 per cent in 2024. That is a gain of about seven percentage points in nine years. The trend tool places the world as a whole in the class of moderate progress, with acceleration needed, at an annual rate of 0.0196. Expansion of this kind reflects growing secondary completion, rising household incomes, the spread of private providers and, in many countries, deliberate public policies to widen university places. The gain is real, but it conceals very different experiences between regions.

### Regional divergence

East Asia and the Pacific advanced from 44.3 per cent in 2015 to 63.3 per cent in 2024, the fastest regional rise, at a rate of 0.0406. Europe and Central Asia moved from 67.4 per cent to 84.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 48.4 per cent to 58.9 per cent. South Asia rose from 25.4 per cent to 32.8 per cent, and the trend tool classes it as on track, with a rate of 0.0289. All four are classed as on track or target met.

The remaining regions fared less well. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping moved only from 27.3 per cent to 29.7 per cent, a rate of 0.0091, classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 8.8 per cent in 2015 and 9.3 per cent in 2021, the latest year available for the region, with a rate of 0.0080 and the same classification. In a region where fewer than one young person in ten is enrolled, the growth of the youth population means that a stagnant ratio implies a rapidly rising number of young people excluded from higher study.

North America is the only region classed as regressing. Its ratio fell from 86.8 per cent in 2015 to 79.0 per cent in 2024, a rate of -0.0104. A decline from a very high level is not the same kind of problem as stagnation at a low one. Plausible explanations include demographic change, falling enrolment among older and part-time students after the post-2008 recovery, and shifts in the cost of study and in labour-market returns. The data do not allow these causes to be separated, and the regional aggregate depends on the countries that report.

### Income groups

The income groups repeat the regional pattern. Low-income countries moved from 8.9 per cent in 2015 to 9.3 per cent in 2021, a rate of 0.0077, with marginal progress. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 21.7 per cent to 27.4 per cent by 2024, classed as on track at a rate of 0.0264. Upper-middle-income countries rose from 46.6 per cent to 64.6 per cent, the largest gain of any income group, at 0.0368. High-income countries rose from 76.2 per cent to 82.0 per cent, but at a rate of 0.0083 they are classed as marginal progress, which reflects the ceiling effects of near-universal participation and the North American decline pulling the group average down.

The ordering of groups is unchanged between 2015 and 2024. Upper-middle-income countries closed some of the distance to high-income countries, narrowing a gap of roughly thirty percentage points to roughly seventeen. The gap between low-income countries and all others widened in absolute terms. In 2024 the lower-middle-income ratio was nearly three times the low-income ratio of 2021, though the years differ and the comparison is indicative only.

### Country distribution and convergence

Among 159 countries assessed, 75 are on track or have met the direction of the target, holding 69.8 per cent of their combined population. A further 22 countries, with 11.7 per cent of their population, show moderate progress. Sixteen countries, with 3.4 per cent, show marginal progress. Six, with 2.9 per cent, are stagnant. Forty countries, with 12.3 per cent of their population, are regressing. The share of countries that are regressing is large, about one in four, even though most of the world's people live in countries that are advancing. This is largely because the populous economies of Asia are expanding, while many smaller states are not.

The convergence test covers 82 countries with data in both 2015 and 2024. It finds no relationship between the starting level and later change: the coefficient is -0.00101, with a p-value of 0.901 and an R-squared of 0.000. The coefficient of variation eased only from 0.591 to 0.569. Poorer systems are therefore not catching up in any systematic way. Low-enrolment countries are as likely to stall as to accelerate, and high-enrolment countries are as likely to keep growing as to level off. Without convergence, the world's tertiary gap in 2030 will resemble that of 2015.

A further test links the gender parity index to enrolment across the same 82 countries. The rank correlation of changes is -0.083 and of 2024 levels 0.176. Both are weak, so gains in enrolment have not been systematically accompanied by movements in parity, nor have they been systematically at its expense. Parity itself is treated in another section of the chapter.

### Timing, coverage and the horizon to 2030

The period after 2015 shows steady expansion at world level, but the effect of 2020 cannot be read cleanly. Closures and the shift to remote study may have depressed or delayed enrolment in some systems and raised it in others, as young people facing weak labour markets stayed in study. The series offers no visible break at world level, yet it cannot be assumed that none occurred, because reporting is uneven. Countries reporting numbered 147 in 2015, 133 in 2020, 128 in 2023 and 94 in 2024. Only 9 countries have reported for 2025. The recent regional figures are therefore built on thinner samples, and the lag in reporting means that the latest points may be revised as late reporters submit data. Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries end in 2021 for want of later aggregates.

For 2030, the implication is that the world is moving in the right direction but not fast enough to meet any plausible reading of equal access. At the world rate, enrolment in 2030 would remain well below the level already reached in Europe and Central Asia. The poorest regions would still enrol only a small minority of their young people. The target can be read in more than one way: as a floor of access, as a narrowing of gaps between groups, or as growth in affordable and good-quality places. The indicator measures only the first, and only on average.

### Proposals

The evidence supports several proposals, which follow.
