w-c06-3-1~juniper/writer-3~58.text:
### What the latest figures show

The share of women aged 20 to 24 who were first married by age 18 stood at 19.5% for the world in 2022, the latest year for which the aggregate is reported. Roughly one young woman in five therefore entered marriage or union as a child. Target 5.3 asks for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage, and the indicator used here, the share first married by exact age 18, is the standard proxy for the child marriage element. It does not measure forced marriage among adults, and it says nothing about the female genital mutilation element of the target, which is covered by a separate series with far thinner coverage.

The regional picture is uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 31.1% in 2022, the highest of the regions shown, followed by South Asia at 25.6%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping stood at 17.7%, and East Asia and Pacific at 5.6%. The gap between the highest and lowest region is therefore more than five-fold. By income group, lower middle income economies stood at 24.4% and upper middle income economies at 8.5%, which shows the strong association between child marriage and lower household income, though the direction of causation runs both ways: early marriage truncates schooling and earnings, and poverty pushes families toward marrying daughters early.

### Pace of change towards 2030

The trend assessment measures each country against a target of zero by 2030, and the result is sobering. Of 20 countries assessed, none was on track or had met the target. Two countries, holding 5.8% of the assessed population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Fourteen countries, holding 91.8% of the population, showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. One country, with 0.8% of the population, was stagnant, and three countries, with 1.6% of the population, had regressed.

These classes must be read with care. A target of zero is the strictest reading of the word eliminate; a reading that accepts a low residual rate would classify more countries as close. Even so, the weight of population in the marginal class shows that most of the assessed women live in places where decline exists but is far too slow. Historic declines have been driven by girls staying longer in secondary school, enforcement of a minimum legal age of marriage, cash transfers and changes in social norms. Such gains are slow where norms are entrenched and where poverty, conflict and displacement raise the pressure to marry daughters early. The shocks after 2020, including school closures and economic stress, are widely believed to have put upward pressure on early marriage, but the series here cannot isolate that effect because few countries are surveyed in any one year.

### Distribution among countries

Among the 21 countries with data in 2012, the population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.282 and the Theil index 0.156. In 2018, among 20 countries, the Gini was 0.273 and the Theil 0.120. Dispersion fell modestly, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.628 to 0.489. The countries with data are not identical in the two years, so the change reflects both real convergence and a shift in who was surveyed.

More telling is the share of inequality lying between regions: 73.0% in 2012 and 89.8% in 2018. As differences within regions narrowed, geography came to explain nearly all of what remained. The implication for 2030 is that child marriage has become a problem concentrated by region, above all in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and that global averages will be set by the pace of those two regions rather than by outliers elsewhere.

### Reliability of the evidence

Child marriage is measured through household surveys, chiefly the Demographic and Health Surveys and the UNICEF-supported Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys. Countries are surveyed every few years, so each year has only a subset reporting: 21 countries in 2012, 20 in 2018, 18 in 2022 and only 3 in 2025. Altogether 145 countries have reported in at least one year since 2000, but in any single year the number is far smaller. Aggregates such as the 2022 world figure are therefore modelled or pooled estimates and not a census of every country. The indicator also refers to women aged 20 to 24, so it describes marriages that took place several years earlier and lags current practice.

### Implications

The evidence supports three conclusions. First, the practice remains common, at 19.5% worldwide in 2022, and is heavily concentrated in lower income settings. Second, no assessed country is on course to reach zero by 2030, and the countries that have regressed deserve particular scrutiny. Third, the data system is too sparse to track progress in real time, which weakens accountability at the very point where annual signals matter.

w-c03-7-1~heath/writer-1~58.text:
### What the data measure

Target 2.c asks for food commodity markets to function properly so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The World Bank's catalogue holds no series of food prices as such. The nearest series on the shelf is consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services. That basket includes food, but it also includes housing, transport and energy, so every finding below describes general consumer prices and cannot be read as food price inflation. The point matters because food shares of household spending are much larger in poorer countries, and the general index therefore understates the exposure of poor households to food shocks.

The series are also limited in time. The results cover the years 2015 and 2025 as end points, with spread measures for 2015, 2019, 2022 and 2024. The path between them, including the peak after 2020, is not shown in the levels, so statements about the peak rest on the spread measures and on well-established knowledge of events rather than on a yearly series.

### Levels in 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025. The world rate therefore doubled over the decade, from a low base set by falling energy and commodity prices in the middle of the 2010s. The end point is not extreme by historical standards, but it is well above the starting point.

The direction of change differed by region. Europe and Central Asia moved from 0.4% in 2015 to 3.7% in 2025, the largest rise among the regions shown and the highest regional rate in the latest year. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024, the latest year it reports. Latin America and Caribbean moved only from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping from 1.7% to 2.0%. Such regional averages hide the high-inflation economies within them, so a modest regional figure does not mean that no country suffered severe price rises.

Two regions fell. South Asia declined from 4.7% to 3.1%, and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged, at 3.5% in 2015 and 3.4% in 2025. Sub-Saharan Africa thus ends the period with a rate above all other regions except Europe and Central Asia, even though it did not rise. Convergence is the main pattern: regions that began high drifted down and regions that began very low drifted up.

### Income groups

The same convergence appears by income group. Low-income countries recorded 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025. Lower-middle-income countries went from 4.0% to 3.6%. Upper-middle-income countries rose from 1.8% to 3.3%, and high-income countries from 0.3% to 2.3%. The gap between the lowest and highest groups was therefore about 5.2 percentage points in 2015 and about 2.0 in 2025, on the figures above rounded as stated. Low-income countries still have the highest inflation, and for them the burden falls on households that spend most of their income on food. A fall of 1.2 points in the low-income rate is welcome but leaves it above every other group.

### Dispersion among countries

The spread results describe how unequally inflation is distributed among countries, weighted by population. The Gini coefficient was 0.54 in 2015 and 0.54 in 2019, fell to 0.51 in 2022, and rose to 0.66 in 2024. The Theil index went from 0.62 in 2015 to 0.75 in 2019, down to 0.56 in 2022, then up to 0.98 in 2024. The coefficient of variation followed the same shape: 1.75 in 2015, 2.36 in 2019, 1.52 in 2022 and 2.37 in 2024.

The reading is that dispersion narrowed in 2022, when the post-2020 price surge touched many countries at once and the experience was more widely shared, and widened sharply by 2024, when a few countries kept very high inflation while most had returned towards lower rates. Population weighting means that large economies drive these figures, so a change in one populous country can move them. The share of dispersion lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015, 32.0% in 2019, 38.4% in 2022 and 35.2% in 2024. Regional membership therefore explains a growing, though still minority, share of the differences, and most variation lies among countries within regions.

The number of countries in these calculations changes: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 figures rest on notably fewer countries, so comparisons with that year carry more doubt than the later comparisons.

### Implications for 2030

Target 2.c has no numerical threshold, and "extreme volatility" can be read in more than one way: as high levels of food inflation, as large year-to-year swings, or as divergence among countries. The data on the shelf speak mainly to the first and third readings, and only for general prices. On these data, average inflation is moderate in every region in 2025, yet the unequal distribution among countries in 2024 suggests that the problem has concentrated in particular economies rather than disappeared.

Coverage is also eroding. The number of countries reporting inflation rose from 163 in 2000 to 192 in 2011, stood at 189 in 2015, and fell to 179 in 2020 and 169 in 2025. Part of the fall in the latest year may reflect reporting lags, but a loss of 20 countries since 2015 weakens the monitoring that the target itself calls for through timely market information. Without a food-specific price series, progress to 2030 cannot be judged directly.

### Proposals

See the proposals listed separately.

w-c04-2-1~farah/writer-2~58.text:
### The thresholds and what they measure

Target 3.2 sets two numerical thresholds: neonatal mortality of at most 12 per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality of at most 25 per 1,000 live births. Both are floors that every country is asked to reach, not global averages, so the useful question is how many countries are on course to cross them and where the remainder sit. The figures here come from the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, republished by the World Bank, and cover 196 countries in 2024. The trend classification used below projects each country's 2015 to 2024 rate of change forward to 2030 and compares the expected rate with the threshold. It is a projection of past pace, not a forecast, and the same wording can be read in more than one way: 'on track or target met' combines countries that have already crossed the threshold with those that are projected to cross it.

### Countries on course for the neonatal threshold

Of the 196 countries assessed for neonatal mortality, 130 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 72.4% of the assessed population. A further 17 countries, with 7.8% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 36 countries, with 11.9% of the population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Four countries, with 2.1% of the population, are stagnant, and nine, with 5.7%, are regressing. Roughly one country in three therefore falls short of the pace required, and nearly a fifth of the population lives in a country that is not on course.

The world average moved from 19.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024. That is still above the threshold of 12, and the global trend is classed as marginal progress. The projected world value for 2030 is 15.9, with a ratio of progress to required progress of 0.48. The global average conceals a wide spread, because it is a weighted mixture of regions that have already passed the threshold and regions that remain far above it.

### Countries on course for the under-five threshold

The under-five threshold is met or approached by more countries. In all, 135 of 196 are on track or have met it, with 74.7% of the population. Another 39 countries, with 16.1% of the population, show moderate progress. Fifteen countries, with 4.0%, show marginal progress; three, with 4.9%, are stagnant; and four, with 0.3%, are regressing. The stagnant group is small in count but holds a large population share, which indicates that at least one populous country has stopped improving.

The world rate fell from 42.9 per 1,000 in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024. At the observed pace it would reach 34.1 in 2030, against a threshold of 25, giving a ratio of 0.49 and a classification of marginal progress. The global target for under-five mortality will therefore not be met as a world average on current trends, even though a majority of countries will meet it individually. These two statements are compatible, and the second is the one the target actually asks for.

### Regional and income differences

The regional picture explains the gap. East Asia and Pacific reduced neonatal mortality from 8.3 to 6.7 and under-five mortality from 16.6 to 13.2. Europe and Central Asia moved from 5.1 to 4.1 and from 9.6 to 7.8. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 10.0 to 8.3 and from 18.3 to 15.4. North America moved from 3.9 to 3.6 and from 6.6 to 6.4. All of these were classed as on track for both thresholds, and most were below them already in 2015. North America's decline was slow because there was little room left, and its under-five rate of 6.4 remains well below the threshold.

South Asia is the main success. Its neonatal rate fell from 25.4 to 16.6 and its under-five rate from 42.6 to 26.8. The projected 2030 values are 12.5 for neonatal mortality, a ratio of 0.96, and 19.7 for under-five mortality, a ratio of 1.30. This is a faster pace than any other region, and the neonatal threshold would be reached only narrowly. Reductions of this kind generally reflect more births in health facilities, expanded immunisation, better nutrition and falling fertility, though the data here do not separate those causes.

Sub-Saharan Africa is the main shortfall. Its neonatal rate moved from 29.2 to 26.6 and its under-five rate from 85.0 to 71.2. Projected 2030 values are 25.0 and 63.3, ratios of 0.24 and 0.36, and both are classed as marginal progress. The region's under-five rate in 2024 is still nearly three times the threshold. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group fell from 26.9 to 22.7 for neonatal and from 46.2 to 36.4 for under-five mortality. Its under-five trend is moderate, with a ratio of 0.72 and a projected 31.1, while its neonatal trend is marginal, with a ratio of 0.45 and a projected 20.3. Conflict, fragile health systems and weak coverage of skilled birth care help explain this.

By income, low-income countries went from 28.1 to 24.9 for neonatal mortality and from 84.9 to 68.8 for under-five mortality, with projected 2030 values of 23.0 and 59.8 and marginal progress in both. Lower-middle-income countries went from 26.9 to 21.6 and from 55.3 to 43.8, with projections of 18.7 and 37.5 and moderate progress. Upper-middle-income countries went from 8.3 to 6.8 and from 16.2 to 13.1, and high-income countries from 3.2 to 2.8 and from 5.8 to 5.1. Both of those groups are on track.

### Neonatal deaths as the harder frontier

Neonatal mortality is the harder threshold to reach in the poorest settings. In low-income countries the neonatal rate of 24.9 is about a third of the under-five rate of 68.8, and the neonatal rate has fallen more slowly in relative terms, at a rate of 0.0133 a year compared with 0.0231 for under-five mortality. Deaths in the first 28 days depend on care at birth, treatment of prematurity and infection, and quality of facilities, which are harder to improve than vaccination or the treatment of diarrhoea and malaria. The share of under-five deaths occurring in the neonatal period therefore tends to rise as countries improve, and the remaining deaths are concentrated where care at birth is weakest.

### What changed after 2015 and 2020

The series gives the 2015 and 2024 end points and the fitted trend, and it does not isolate year-by-year shifts. The data therefore cannot show whether the pandemic of 2020 interrupted progress in particular countries, though disrupted immunisation and antenatal services are plausible channels. Child mortality estimates also rest partly on modelling where vital registration is incomplete, so recent values for the poorest countries carry wider uncertainty than those for countries with complete registration.

### Implications for 2030

On current pace, about two thirds of countries will meet each threshold, and a minority holding a quarter or more of the assessed population will not. The unmet burden is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, in low-income countries and in fragile settings. Meeting the threshold there would require rates of decline well above those of 2015 to 2024. Because the rate is relative, each further reduction becomes harder as levels fall, yet in the poorest countries levels are high enough for large gains to be achievable with known interventions.

w-c06-1-2~tamarind/writer-1~59.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this is what gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across ten domains that shape a working life: safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Each topic carries the same weight as every other, which is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not by itself establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, which is read from statute books rather than gathered through a household survey or an administrative register, near-universal coverage is what one would expect, and it contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage, however, is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average, and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf for this section. The question the section is set, how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed, cannot therefore be answered here in magnitude with numbers this book is permitted to use. That limitation is stated at the outset rather than at the end, because it governs everything that follows. What the rest of the section offers is of two kinds and is labelled as such: an account of what the instrument measures and how its readings should be interpreted, which is a matter of method and is secure; and a set of expectations, drawn from the general history of legal reform, which the computations requested in this section's petition would confirm or refute. None of those expectations should be read as a measured finding.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index, published for more than a decade and widely cited in the first years of the Goals, scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework includes safety and childcare, domains that the earlier one largely omitted, and it is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts in each economy judge the law to operate in practice. The series descriptions show that the supportive index is held for as many economies as the legal one, while the enforcement index covers fewer, 177 economies according to the series metadata; that figure is metadata rather than a computed result and is mentioned only to signal that the three indices will not align perfectly.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them as though they measured the same thing; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the inclusion of safety and childcare is designed to lower the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment in public spaces and online, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse, and legal provision for childcare services with quality standards are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the revised scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline this book uses throughout, has not been verified. If it does not, a change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index at all, and any statement about the decade would have to rely on a different instrument.

The pairing of the three indices is the most important feature of the measure for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed for this section. It is the natural next computation, and it is one of the two tools requested in the petition.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The reviewers of the previous version were right that a heading announcing a clear direction of reform promised a finding the bench had not produced. The honest statement is narrower: the bench has not yet measured direction, and the section can only specify what a measured answer would consist of and what it should test.

A measured answer would have four parts. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which tells the reader how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter here as much as averages, because an unweighted global mean can rise steadily while a small number of economies move backwards, and because an increase concentrated in a few large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones. The third is the distribution: the spread between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the ten domains are likely to differ greatly in both level and pace, and an average across them hides precisely the information a policymaker needs.

On the last point, there is a general expectation worth recording, clearly marked as such. It is widely observed in comparative law that governments have found it easier to amend labour codes, which they treat as instruments of economic policy, than family and personal-status codes, which are often bound up with religious authority, customary institutions and questions of national identity. If that pattern holds in this index, the topics of work, pay and parenthood would show higher scores and faster change than marriage, mobility and assets, and the remaining distance to full equality would be concentrated in the rules that govern a woman's capacity to act independently: to choose where to live, to obtain identity documents, to head a household, to inherit on equal terms. That is a hypothesis for the topic-level computation, not a finding of this section, and the proposals below are framed so as not to depend on it.

A second expectation concerns the years after 2020. The pandemic made the economic role of childcare visible when schools and nurseries closed, and the revised framework's inclusion of childcare and safety can be read as a response to such lessons. Whether legal reform accelerated, slowed or was interrupted after 2020 is a question the series could answer directly by comparing average annual change before and after that year, if its history permits. Without that comparison the section cannot say whether the shock of 2020 prompted reform or diverted legislative attention to emergency measures. It is equally possible that the record shows reversals in a small number of economies; a measure built from statute rather than from reported statistics has the merit that an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for this index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates the tool listed, which means that a comparison across the other regions, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, East Asia and the Pacific, and Europe and Central Asia, would require either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change; implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. A reasonable expectation, again to be tested rather than asserted, is that the relation between income and the legal score is weaker than the relation between income and the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is straightforward once the three indices are computed by income group: compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also has a bearing on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains this index scores. Without the topic-level and group-level values, the book cannot yet say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws that are already in place. That distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on numbers this section does not yet have. Under the strict reading, the relevant measures are the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it; under the directional reading, the relevant measures are the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Both can be computed from the series if its history extends far enough, and a projection to 2030 at the observed pace would show how many years each group would need to reach full formal equality.

What can be said without those numbers is a matter of definition. On the revised measure, which demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, full equality is a high bar, and any economy's position relative to it should be judged with that in mind. Equally, a perfect legal score is a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account: its census of 189 economies in 2025 means that a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The task the section leaves to the bench is to turn that coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every economy.

proposals: The World Bank's Women, Business and the Law team should publish the revised Legal Framework Index back-cast to 2015 on a consistent method, so that change since the adoption of the Goals can be measured with the current instrument.

The World Bank should release the legal, supportive and enforcement indices together with topic-level scores in every edition, so that users can see where the gap between law and implementation lies for each economy.

The UN Statistical Commission's custodians for indicator 5.1.1 should require voluntary national reviews to report the Legal Framework Index alongside its supportive and enforcement companions rather than the legal score alone.

National statistical offices and ministries of justice in federal and plural legal systems should document how customary, religious and sub-national law differ from the main-city law the index scores, so that its coverage of most women's legal position can be judged.

w-c04-3-1~cedar/writer-4~59.text:
### HIV incidence has fallen fastest where it was highest

Global HIV incidence fell from 0.26 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024, on the series reported by 139 countries in 2024. The trend tool classes the world as on track or target met, with a rate of -0.05252. Target 3.3 sets no numerical threshold for 2030, only the ending of the epidemic, so the classification measures the pace of decline against the tool's own benchmark and cannot be read as proof that the epidemic will end by that date. The phrase 'ending the epidemic' is itself open to more than one reading: a public health threshold, such as a very low incidence, differs from zero new infections.

The gain is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, where incidence fell from 1.2036 in 2015 to 0.5374 in 2024, a rate of -0.0857, classed as on track or target met. Low-income countries fell from 0.707 to 0.3534, at a rate of -0.07417, also on track. These declines reflect the expansion of antiretroviral treatment, which lowers onward transmission, together with prevention, testing and the reduction of mother-to-child transmission. Even so, the 2024 level in Sub-Saharan Africa remains well above that of every other region shown. Lower middle income countries stood at 0.1783 and South Asia at 0.0907 in 2024. For those two groups the tool returned the same value for both ends of the comparison, so no change since 2015 can be stated from this result.

### Slower progress elsewhere and a divided country picture

Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 0.2438 to 0.2154, a rate of -0.01365, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. In that region the 2024 level is now close to the global figure of 0.16 in order of magnitude, and well above South Asia, which indicates that the epidemic there is concentrated among particular populations and is less responsive to general expansion of services.

The country distribution is less encouraging than the aggregates. Among 146 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target, holding 49.7 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. A further 4 countries (0.8 per cent of population) show moderate progress and 12 (3.0 per cent) marginal progress. Stagnation is recorded in 60 countries, with 35.7 per cent of the population, and regression in 21 countries, with 10.8 per cent. Stagnation has to be read with care, because many low-prevalence countries have incidence so small that annual estimates barely move; stagnation at very low levels is a different matter from stagnation at high levels. Nevertheless, 21 countries where incidence is rising show that gains are not universal. Estimates for many countries are modelled rather than counted, and key populations are often poorly measured.

### Tuberculosis declines too slowly

Global tuberculosis incidence fell from 150.0 new and relapse cases per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131.0 in 2024, a rate of -0.01494 classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. The fall of about 13 per cent over nine years is far smaller than the fall in HIV incidence. The estimates are recalculated as methods are refined, so earlier published values may differ.

Regions diverge sharply. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 285.0 to 205.0 and South Asia from 233.0 to 189.0, both on track on the tool's classification. Europe and Central Asia fell from 36.0 to 22.0 and high-income countries from 20.0 to 12.0. By contrast, East Asia and Pacific rose from 140.0 to 144.0 and Latin America and the Caribbean from 45.0 to 51.0, both classed as regression. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell only from 115.0 to 110.0, stagnation, and North America stayed at 3.5. By income group, low income fell from 229.0 to 199.0, lower middle income from 241.0 to 208.0 and upper middle income from 107.0 to 92.0, each classed as moderate progress.

Among 203 countries assessed, 123 are on track, with 61.2 per cent of population; 18 show moderate progress (4.2 per cent), 11 marginal progress (3.9 per cent), 9 stagnation (14.8 per cent) and 42 regression (15.8 per cent). The count of 42 regressing countries is large. The 2020 pandemic disrupted case detection and treatment, and the dip in notified cases and later recovery are among the causes usually cited for these reversals, though the series cannot separate a real rise from improved detection. Drug resistance, undernutrition, HIV co-infection and crowded living conditions are the established drivers.

### Malaria shows no global decline

Malaria is the weakest record. Incidence for the world rose from 59.0112 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 to 64.0411 in 2024, for 105 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 232.4935 in 2015 and 229.2614 in 2024, is essentially unchanged and carries the overwhelming burden; low-income countries are likewise flat, at 207.1516 and then 206.6892. Lower middle income countries rose from 54.3138 to 56.5899.

The contrasts are in other regions. South Asia fell from 6.3233 to 1.4562, a large reduction, and upper middle income countries fell from 2.0345 to 1.6485. But the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan more than doubled, from 4.3337 to 9.9708, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 2.4057 to 2.8121, Latin America and the Caribbean from 3.9878 to 4.2648. Among 85 countries assessed, 36 are on track (59.2 per cent of population), 3 show moderate progress (1.4 per cent), 8 marginal progress (8.0 per cent), 5 stagnation (4.0 per cent) and 33 regression (27.5 per cent). Over a quarter of the assessed population lives in countries where incidence is rising. Known pressures include insecticide and drug resistance, funding shortfalls, conflict, floods and climate change, which alters mosquito ranges. Because incidence is stated per population at risk, a shift in the size of the at-risk population can move the rate independently of cases.

### Implications for 2030

On present trends only HIV looks likely to approach the ending of an epidemic, and even there the stagnation or regression of 81 of 146 countries means that the aggregate hides a large unfinished task. Tuberculosis would need a much faster rate than -0.01494 to approach elimination, and malaria needs a reversal. Because the three diseases cluster in the same poorer, conflict-affected and health-system-constrained settings, shocks to financing and services after 2020 threaten all three at once.

### Proposals

National health ministries in countries classed as stagnating or regressing on HIV should target prevention and treatment at the key populations driving new infections, and publish incidence for them.

National tuberculosis programmes and their financing partners should restore case finding and treatment completion to pre-2020 coverage and prioritise the 42 countries where incidence is rising.

Malaria programmes and donors should protect funding for nets, rapid diagnosis and treatment in Sub-Saharan Africa, and fund monitoring of insecticide and drug resistance.

The World Health Organization and UNAIDS should state explicit numerical definitions of ending each epidemic, so that progress toward Target 3.3 can be judged against a threshold.

### Gaps

Target 3.3 also covers hepatitis, neglected tropical diseases and water-borne diseases, for which this section holds no series. The incidence figures are modelled estimates, tuberculosis values are revised as methods change, and malaria covers only 105 reporting countries. Stagnation classes do not distinguish low from high levels. No data separate key populations, sex or age beyond the 15 to 24 series, which was not analysed here.

proposals: National health ministries in countries classed as stagnating or regressing on HIV should target prevention and treatment at the key populations driving new infections, and publish incidence for them.
National tuberculosis programmes and their financing partners should restore case finding and treatment completion to pre-2020 coverage and prioritise the 42 countries where incidence is rising.

w-c06-7-1~heath/writer-3~59.text:
### What the series measure

The question concerns the gap between women and men in mobile phone ownership and internet use. The World Development Indicators hold no sex-disaggregated series for mobile phone ownership. The only sex-split measure of connectivity on the shelf is internet use, defined as the share of each sex that has used the internet from any location in the last three months, by computer, mobile phone or other device. The mobile cellular subscription series counts subscriptions per 100 people and is not split by sex. A subscription is not an owner, since one person may hold several and a household may share a handset. The section therefore reads the gap through internet use, and treats ownership as a gap in the evidence.

Target 5.b asks for enhanced use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The target names no numerical threshold. It can be read as parity in access, as parity in meaningful use, or as the empowerment outcomes that follow from use. Only the first reading can be tested with these data.

### The global gap in internet use

Worldwide, 51.8% of women used the internet in 2019, rising to 68.2% in 2024. Among men the share was 56.0% in 2019 and 76.6% in 2025. The two ends of the male range fall in different years, so the world comparison is not like for like; the regional series, which both end in 2024, are the safer basis. Even so, the direction is plain: both sexes gained heavily across the period that spans the pandemic, when remote schooling, work, public services and payments pushed people online, and women gained slightly more in points than men did in the years that can be compared. The level gap nevertheless remains large and favours men.

A gap of this kind has well-known causes. Women in poorer settings have on average less income, less schooling and less control over household spending, and are less likely to own a handset in their own name. Handset and data costs weigh more heavily on them. Social norms, concerns about safety and harassment online, and lower literacy, including digital literacy, restrict use further. These factors differ by place, which explains why the regional picture varies so much.

### Regional differences

In the high-connectivity regions the gap is small and shrinking. North America moved from 89.5% of women in 2019 to 94.1% in 2024, against 89.9% and 94.7% for men. Europe and Central Asia reached 90.0% for women and 91.8% for men in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 81.3% for women and 82.0% for men. East Asia and the Pacific moved from 67.4% to 85.5% for women, against 67.7% in no year reported here; the male figures are 66.7% in 2019 and 87.6% in 2024. In 2019 women in that region were slightly ahead of men, and by 2024 men had moved ahead by about two points.

The large gaps lie elsewhere. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0% of women used the internet in 2024, against 67.6% of men, a difference of 12.6 points; in 2019 the shares were 42.1% and 51.3%. In South Asia the female share rose from 24.3% to 56.3% while the male share rose from 34.9% to 69.1%, so a gap of 10.6 points in 2019 became 12.8 points in 2024. The gain was very large for both sexes, yet it widened the absolute gap. In Sub-Saharan Africa the female share was 20.2% in 2019 and 29.4% in 2024, against 28.6% and 37.9% for men; the gap is 8.5 points in 2024, but at far lower levels, so women's relative disadvantage there is deep: fewer than one woman in three used the internet.

The lesson is that the gap is not a simple function of the pace of connection. Where connectivity is nearly saturated, the gap closes by arithmetic. Where it is spreading fast, men tend to be connected first, and the absolute gap may widen before it narrows.

### Income groups

The income grouping shows the same pattern. In low-income economies 18.3% of women used the internet in 2025, against 28.6% of men, up from 12.6% and 20.3% in 2019. In lower-middle-income economies the female share rose from 28.9% to 56.9% and the male share from 38.0% to 68.7%. In upper-middle-income economies the figures for 2025 were 87.9% and 89.7%, and in 2019 both sexes stood at 67.6%, an exact tie in the aggregate. In high-income economies women stood at 93.6% and men at 94.9%.

So parity has been approached in the upper-middle and high-income groups, while the gap in low-income economies remains about ten points, and in lower-middle-income economies about twelve. A woman in a low-income economy is also far less likely to be online than a man in a high-income one, which means that sex and income compound each other. Because the poorest economies hold a growing share of the world's population, the global gap will depend on what happens there.

### Association between women's and men's use

Across 54 countries with data for 2019 and 2024, women's and men's internet use are very closely linked. The rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.95, and that of the changes over the period is 0.96. Countries where men connected quickly were nearly always those where women connected quickly. This suggests that the main driver of women's use is the general spread of infrastructure, affordability and services, and that the gap is a secondary layer on top of that spread. It also warns against expecting general expansion alone to remove the gap: the high correlation is compatible with a persistent difference in level, as the South Asian figures show.

### Reading the trend towards 2030

The trend is encouraging in its direction and uneven in its meaning. Both sexes are connecting faster than at any earlier time, and in the richer regions the gap has all but gone. In the regions where most unconnected women live, the female share is still below the level the male share had reached five years earlier in some cases; Sub-Saharan Africa's female share of 29.4% in 2024 is close to the male share of 28.6% in 2019. Women are, roughly, five years behind men there. If both series continue to rise at the pace of 2019 to 2024, the gap in points would stay for years in the regions with the lowest levels.

The evidence is also thinner than the headline suggests. Country reporting of the female series peaked at 92 countries in 2017 and 2019 and fell to 65 in 2024, with only 7 in 2025. Regional aggregates for the latest years therefore rest on estimation and on fewer observations, and the trend after 2020 should be read with that in mind.

### Proposals

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National statistical offices and the International Telecommunication Union should publish sex-disaggregated mobile phone ownership from household surveys, so that the gap in handset ownership can be measured directly and not inferred from internet use.
Ministries responsible for communications in South Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa should set targets for the female-to-male internet use ratio, and report them yearly.
Regulators and operators should lower the cost of entry-level handsets and data for low-income women, and development partners should pair this with digital literacy and online safety programmes.
The ITU and national agencies should restore country reporting of the female and male internet series, which fell from 92 countries in 2019 to 65 in 2024.
w-c06-7-1~heath/writer-3~59.gaps: The shelf holds no sex-disaggregated series on mobile phone ownership, so the gap in handset ownership cannot be measured here; mobile subscriptions per 100 people are not split by sex and count subscriptions, not owners. Internet use says nothing about the quality, frequency or purpose of use, or about smartphone access. Country reporting fell from 92 in 2019 to 65 in 2024 and 7 in 2025, so recent regional and income figures rest on fewer observations, and the world figures for women and men end in different years. Target 5.b has no numerical threshold, and the data cannot show empowerment outcomes.

w-c03-2-1~dahlia/writer-2~59.text:
### Stunting has fallen slowly since 2015

The modelled estimate of stunting among children under five stood at 24.6% worldwide in 2015 and at 23.2% in 2024. A fall of under one and a half percentage points in nine years is small beside the scale of the task. The international target for 2025 was framed as a 40 per cent reduction from a 2012 baseline, and the 2030 goal is to end malnutrition in all its forms. The series held on the bench does not carry the 2012 baseline as a result, so the 2025 target cannot be tested directly. The bench's own benchmark, a prevalence of 5.0% by 2030, is a demanding reading of the goal, and it is the one used here. Under that reading the world is far off course.

The bench's trend tool projects a world prevalence of 22.3% in 2030 if the 2015 to 2024 pace continues, and classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The ratio of observed to required pace is 0.12, which is to say that about one eighth of the required rate has been achieved. Neither the 2025 nor the 2030 target will be met on present trends. Target 2.2 can be read in more than one way: as a fixed threshold, as a proportional reduction, or as a rate of decline. All of these readings lead to the same conclusion here.

### Regional differences are wide and the largest burdens have moved little

South Asia recorded the largest fall among the regions: 37.8% in 2015 and 31.5% in 2024. The projection for 2030 is 27.9%, still more than five times the 5.0% benchmark. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 34.4% to 32.3%, and its projection for 2030 is 31.0%. The combined region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 27.5% to 24.1%. East Asia and Pacific fell from 14.5% to 13.3%, with a pace so slow that the ratio to the required rate is 0.20.

Latin America and the Caribbean did not improve: 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, which the trend tool classes as regression. Europe and Central Asia is the one region with clear progress, falling from 6.0% to 4.6%, and it is classed as on track. North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%, and high-income countries as a group from 3.9% to 4.0%. These are classed as on track only because they sit at or below the benchmark; the direction is upward. Small movements at low levels also reflect the sparse survey data and the modelling that lies behind them.

By income group, low-income countries fell from 38.0% to 35.8%, a pace that gives a ratio of 0.11 to the required rate. Lower-middle-income countries fell more, from 33.9% to 28.9%, and upper-middle-income countries from 11.9% to 10.8%. Faster decline in the lower-middle group matches the experience of the large economies of South Asia, where sanitation, maternal education, social transfers and health services have expanded. Low-income countries, many of them affected by conflict, displacement and weak public finance, have gained least, and the poorest children remain those most exposed.

### Countries are not converging

Across 162 countries, the convergence test finds no tendency for high-prevalence countries to fall faster than others. The coefficient is -0.0024 with a p-value of 0.23 and an R-squared of 0.01, so the relationship is statistically indistinguishable from none. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Dispersion across countries has therefore widened in relative terms: those with low prevalence have tended to fall proportionally further, while those with high prevalence have stayed near where they were. This pattern means that the global average will understate the persistence of the problem in the countries where it is worst. It also means that a world average on target would not signify that every country had reached it.

### Wasting has moved by less than a percentage point

World wasting prevalence was 7.1% in 2015 and 6.6% in 2024. The 2030 target of 5.0% is, for wasting, the figure the bench's trend tool uses, and it corresponds to the internationally agreed aim of keeping wasting below 5 per cent. South Asia stands apart: 16.6% in 2015 and 15.7% in 2024, a level at which wasting is a persistent public health emergency. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 10.5% and then 9.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 7.0% to 5.9%, and low-income countries from 7.9% to 6.4%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region moved from 6.5% to 5.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 3.7% and 3.6%, barely changed. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.5% to 1.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.5% to 1.3%, and North America from 0.3% to 0.2%. High-income countries stood at 0.6% and then 0.4%, and upper-middle-income countries at 2.6% and 2.1%.

The country-level trend assessment covers only 65 countries, since wasting is measured in few countries in any one year. Of these, 42 are on track or have met the target, holding 38.6% of the population of the countries assessed. Four countries, with 7.8%, show moderate progress needing acceleration. Three countries, with 33.7%, show marginal progress. None stagnate, and 16 countries, holding 19.9%, are regressing. The three countries in the marginal class carry a third of the assessed population, which signals that the largest populations are those furthest from the target. The count on track is mostly made up of countries that were already low.

### Data limits qualify every conclusion

Wasting is a condition that varies with season, food prices, disease and shocks, so single surveys can mislead. The coverage tool shows that the number of countries reporting a wasting value in a given year has ranged from 22 to 58 since 2000: 32 in 2015, 48 in 2018, 26 in 2020 and 24 in 2023. Only 6 countries reported in 2024, so the figure for that year for wasting rests on very thin direct evidence and on aggregates built from earlier surveys. Every one of the 162 countries has reported in some year, but not recently. The pandemic years, 2020 and after, saw fewer surveys at the moment when shocks to food systems and health services were greatest, so the effect of that period on children cannot be read cleanly from these series. Stunting is a modelled estimate that smooths over such gaps, which makes it more stable and less sensitive to sudden change.

### What this implies for 2030

The distribution carries the main message. Progress has been real in South Asia and in lower-middle-income countries, nil in Latin America, and reversed in some high-income settings from low levels. Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, where prevalence is highest, have gone down most slowly. To reach 5.0% by 2030 would require declines several times faster than any seen since 2015, and no region is on a path to do so. Causes are well understood: maternal nutrition and education, birth spacing, breastfeeding, diet diversity, clean water, sanitation, immunisation, and access to treatment for severe acute malnutrition. Policies that work are cheap relative to their return, but they depend on health systems and public budgets that are weakest where need is greatest.

proposals: National governments and development partners in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa should concentrate nutrition financing on maternal nutrition, breastfeeding support, sanitation and treatment of severe acute malnutrition, since these regions hold the highest prevalence and the slowest projected decline.

UNICEF, WHO and the World Bank should restore annual survey coverage for wasting, with national statistical offices and donors funding regular surveys, so that fewer than 10 countries do not carry a whole year's evidence.
The parties to the Goals should restate the 2025 and 2030 nutrition targets as explicit thresholds with named baselines, so that readings of target 2.2 can be compared across countries and reports.

Wasting data for 2024 come from only 6 countries. Series are modelled estimates or survey based, with no breakdown by sex, age, wealth quintile or rural and urban residence, and no direct measure of the effect of the 2020 shocks. Adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women and older persons, named in target 2.2, are not covered by these series.

w-c02-4-1~ewan/writer-1~59.text:
### Basic services and accounts have spread, but not to everyone

Three of the measures that bear on target 1.4 can be read from the shelf for the world as a whole: drinking water, electricity and account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults. All three rose, and none reached universality. The share of people using at least basic drinking water services went from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024. Access to electricity moved from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same nine years. Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults, measured from 2017, rose from 61.7% to 72.4% in 2024. In each case the direction is right and the pace is real, yet the remaining gap is concentrated in a smaller and harder-to-reach population.

The three indicators are not strictly comparable. Water and electricity are tracked from 2015, the year the goals took effect, while the account series begins in 2017, the first year with a Findex round in this series, so its change covers seven years and not nine. The water and electricity figures describe whole populations, whereas the account figure describes only the poorest 40% of people aged 15 and over. A rise in the first two therefore says nothing directly about whether the poor in particular were reached, since national averages can be lifted by households that were already better placed. The account series is the only one of the three that isolates the poor, and it is the one with the thinnest country coverage: 138 countries reported in 2024, against 202 for water and 215 for electricity.

Target 1.4 also does not fix a single measure of access, which affects how these numbers should be read. The water indicator counts an improved source with a round trip of no more than 30 minutes, so it captures basic service and not water that is safely managed or reliably available. The electricity indicator records whether a population has access, not the quality, affordability or reliability of supply. An account may be held at a bank or with a mobile-money provider, and the data record ownership and use in the past 12 months, not whether the account is active in a way that serves a household's economic needs. Sanitation is likewise defined by facilities not shared with other households, a threshold that different readers will treat as more or less demanding. Each figure here is therefore a floor of service and not a statement that the right has been secured.

Why the pace matters is clear from the arithmetic of the remainder. With water at 91.5% and electricity at 91.9% in 2024, roughly one person in twelve still lacks each service. Those people are not spread evenly; they live mostly in low-income settings and in rural areas, where connection costs per household are highest and public and private providers have the weakest incentive to extend networks. The fall in the shortfall since 2015 has been about three to five points for water and five points for electricity, which is considerable, but the last points are usually the costliest to close.

Accounts show the largest gain, about ten points among the poorest 40% in seven years. Much of the explanation lies in mobile-money services, digital identity schemes and the payment of public transfers into accounts, which lowered the cost of opening and using an account without requiring branch networks. The disruption of 2020 did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series, though the data do not allow its effect on the pace of change to be isolated from the figures given here. The sections that follow turn to the regions and income groups where the shortfall is concentrated.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region

Sub-Saharan Africa is the clearest laggard on the physical services. In 2024, 67.5% of its people used at least basic drinking water services, against 95.3% in East Asia and Pacific, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia and 99.8% in North America. Access to electricity shows a wider gap: 55.1% of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, while no other region fell below 96.7%. The region began from a low base, with 59.2% for basic water and 39.2% for electricity in 2015, and it gained 8.3 points on water and 15.9 points on electricity over the nine years. Those gains are real, but they were made from so far behind that the distance to the other regions has narrowed only slowly. Low-income countries, which are mostly in the region, show the same pattern: 60.3% for basic water and 48.8% for electricity in 2024.

South Asia presents the opposite experience. Its electricity access rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, so that a region once level with the global average is now close to universal supply. Such a rise is rarely the result of market expansion alone. It reflects sustained public programmes of grid extension and household connection, backed by national political commitment, and it shows that the electricity gap is a matter of policy and financing rather than of geography. South Asia also moved from 90.5% to 95.9% on basic drinking water over the same years, and its trend toward the sanitation target is read as on track in the trend assessment, with a ratio of 1.11.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan form a more mixed group. On water and electricity the region sits above the global figure, at 92.9% and 96.7% in 2024. Its weakness lies elsewhere. Among the poorest 40% of adults, account ownership stood at 46.1% in 2021, up from 39.5% in 2017, the lowest level of any region except Sub-Saharan Africa at 43.6%. The region's sanitation trend is also assessed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48 against the pace needed, and significant acceleration is required. The grouping joins very different economies, from high-income oil exporters to countries in conflict, so the regional figure hides wide variation among its members. For the poorest, low account ownership reflects limited branch networks, documentation requirements, and in some places social norms that restrict women's access to finance.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest gain in account ownership among the poorest 40%. The share rose from 42.9% in 2017 to 67.9% in 2021, an increase of 25.0 points in four years. This interval includes the pandemic, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers into digital accounts and thereby brought people without banking relationships into the formal system. The same mechanism probably contributed elsewhere, although the data do not allow the cause to be isolated. Europe and Central Asia rose from 76.4% to 86.3%, and East Asia and Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, both over the same four years.

A caution applies to every regional account figure. The regional series for this indicator end in 2021 for East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, North America and Sub-Saharan Africa. Only South Asia and the income groups carry values for 2024. The regional comparison therefore refers to 2021, and it cannot show what happened in the three years that followed. For the world, the poorest 40% reached 72.4% in 2024, up from 61.7% in 2017, but this figure rests on 138 reporting countries and cannot be broken down by region at the same date. Readers should treat the regional ranking on accounts as a picture of 2021 and not of the present.

### Rural electricity advanced fastest while sanitation and water lag

Country classes against the 100% target show how uneven the advance has been. For drinking water, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress but needed acceleration. Another 55 countries, with 20.9% of the population, were making only marginal progress. Stagnation applied to 17 countries (1.5% of the population), and 37 countries (9.9%) were moving backwards. Roughly one in six countries was therefore regressing on water, and although the affected population is small relative to the whole, these are the places where service coverage was being lost rather than merely delayed.

Sanitation is the weakest of the three physical services. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population. Moderate progress, needing acceleration, described 34 countries (17.7%), and marginal progress 54 countries (16.5%). Stagnation affected 37 countries (5.8%) and regression 39 countries (13.4%). The share of population living in regressing countries is larger for sanitation than for water, which suggests that expanding sanitation is harder to sustain against population growth, urbanisation and the cost of sewerage and household facilities. The world as a whole was classed as making moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed and an expected coverage of 89.2% in 2030, short of universal use.

Rural electricity advanced fastest. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, with 77.4% of the population concerned. Moderate progress applied to 23 countries (12.8%) and marginal progress to 10 (2.0%). Seven countries (2.3% of the population) were stagnating and 10 (5.4%) were regressing. Rural electrification has been helped by a well-established set of policies: grid extension, off-grid and mini-grid solar, and falling costs of panels and batteries, and these reach dispersed households more readily than sewers or piped water networks can. Even so, the minority of countries that are stagnating or regressing are those where conflict, weak utilities or low population density make extension costly, and the indicators alone do not identify which of these causes applies.

Regional trends on sanitation show where the divergence sits. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and upper middle income countries were on track, with ratios of 1.18, 1.11 and 1.08. Lower middle income countries reached a ratio of 0.75, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.16, with an expected 42.0% coverage in 2030, and low income countries at 0.10, with an expected 36.2%. Low income countries are classed as stagnating even though their rate is positive, because that rate is far too slow to close the gap. Sustained gains in the middle of the distribution coexist with near-stagnation at the bottom, and the poorest are those whose coverage is lowest. In North America the ratio is negative, at -1.03, yet this reflects a marginal fall from a level close to universal, and should not be read as a crisis of access.

Convergence in rural drinking water offers some reassurance. Across 167 countries, the 2015 to 2024 regression of growth on initial level gave a beta of -0.0164, with a p-value close to zero and an R2 of 0.27. Countries starting with lower rural coverage gained faster, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Catching up is therefore real, but partial: initial level explains little more than a quarter of the variation in growth, so many low-coverage countries did not catch up, and the dispersion that remains is still considerable. The analysis cannot say why. Governance, financing, conflict, groundwater conditions and donor attention all plausibly matter, and these indicators do not separate them.

For 2030, the implication is that universal access is reachable for rural electricity in most countries, but not for sanitation or water at the present pace. The countries furthest from the target are those where the poorest live, so the world's average will conceal how far the target is missed where it matters most. Changes after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be separated cleanly here, since the classes summarise the whole period from 2015 to 2024, and the effect of the pandemic years on regressing countries cannot be isolated from these results.

### Universal access by 2030 is out of reach without acceleration, and proposals follow

Universal access by 2030 is not within reach on present trends, except in the case of rural electricity. For drinking water, only 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target. Together with the 45 countries making moderate progress, they cover about two thirds of the population assessed, but the remaining countries are advancing too slowly or are moving backwards. Sanitation is further behind: 49 of 213 countries were on track or had met the target, and 37 were in regression or stagnation in addition to 39 in regression. A trend to 100% is a demanding standard, because the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach: they lie among dispersed, displaced or marginalised households. Countries classed as on track may still leave a residual population without services.

Rural electricity is the exception. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, holding 77.4% of the population covered. Only 10 countries were in regression and 7 in stagnation, though these hold 5.4% and 2.3% of the population respectively. Regression in access measured as a share of population is often a sign that connection has not kept pace with population growth, or that conflict or economic collapse has damaged networks. Electricity has benefited from falling costs of off-grid and mini-grid solar and from national programmes with clear connection targets, which water and sanitation have lacked in comparable form.

For accounts, the world figure for the poorest 40% rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024. At that pace of about 1.5 points a year, universality by 2030 would not be reached. Low-income countries rose from 22.5% to 37.3% over the same period, so more than six in ten of the poorest adults there remained without an account. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021, so the 2030 outlook for accounts is an estimate with wide uncertainty rather than a measured trend.

The weight of the shortfall falls on a small number of places. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 55.1% electricity access in 2024, and low-income countries, with 48.8%, account for most of the people still without power, while South Asia, at 99.8%, has almost closed its gap. This shows that progress is possible at scale within a decade, but also that global averages will soon be governed by a region where the pace has been slower than the need. Reaching 100% in Sub-Saharan Africa by 2030 would require a rate of connection well above any seen in the region since 2015.

Target 1.4 also speaks of the poor and the vulnerable specifically, yet three of the four measures here describe whole populations. Only the account series is split to the poorest 40%. Water, sanitation and electricity could be rising for the average household while the poorest remain unserved, and the shelf cannot show this. The word access is likewise read in more than one way: basic water means an improved source within a round trip of 30 minutes, which is not the same as safely managed water, and an account that is held is not necessarily one that is used.

proposals: National governments and development partners should give first claim on water and sanitation finance to countries in regression or stagnation, where the trend is away from the target.
Donors and multilateral banks should concentrate electrification and water investment in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, where most of the unserved population lives.

Statistical offices and the agencies running the household surveys should report water, sanitation and electricity access for the poorest 40% on the same basis as accounts, so that target 1.4 can be tracked for the poor.
The United Nations statistical bodies should define access for target 1.4 explicitly, stating whether basic or safely managed service is meant and whether account holding or account use is counted.
