w-c02-1-1~juniper/writer-1~60.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 commits the world to eradicating extreme poverty by 2030, and its wording cites a line of $1.25 a day. That figure belongs to an older price base. The series available to this book, drawn from the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform, counts people living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Revisions to purchasing power exchange rates have raised the nominal line while aiming to preserve roughly the same real standard of deprivation. The target therefore has to be read through the updated line, and this is one of several reasonable readings. Eradication is also not defined numerically in the target text. The World Bank's own working goal for 2030 is a headcount of 3 per cent, which is a convention rather than a literal zero, and a strict reading of eradication would be harder to meet than that convention.

On this measure, the world headcount stood at 13.4% of the population in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 it had fallen to 10.1%. The decline is 3.3 percentage points over nine years, an average of a little over a third of a point a year. That is real progress, yet it is modest set against a target that requires the figure to approach zero within six further years. Earlier editions of the same series used lower lines and earlier price bases, so rates quoted in older reports cannot be compared with these. Country rates in particular have shifted with each revision.

The 2024 value should be treated with caution because it rests on thin coverage. Poverty headcounts are not observed continuously. They are estimated from household surveys, which are fielded every few years, are published with a lag, and are then aligned to common reference years. The number of countries with a reported value shows the pattern. It was 87 in 2015, 93 in 2018, and 81 in 2021, before falling to 70 in 2020's neighbours of 73 in 2022 and 60 in 2023. In 2024 only 26 countries report a value, and in 2025 only 4 do. Across the whole series, 168 countries report in at least one year.

The fall in reporting is a feature of how the data are produced, not evidence that poverty has disappeared in the missing countries. Recent years are filled in for the aggregates by projecting from earlier surveys and from national accounts growth, so the 2024 world figure is closer to a nowcast than to a count. The 2015 figure, by contrast, rests on a far larger body of survey evidence. Comparing the two therefore sets a measured value against a partly modelled one. The comparison is still informative about direction and rough scale, but the second decimal place should not be read as precise.

The pandemic compounds the difficulty. Survey fieldwork was disrupted in 2020, when 70 countries reported, down from 78 in 2019, and the countries that were hardest to survey are often those where poverty is deepest and conflict or weak statistical capacity is present. Missing observations are therefore unlikely to be random. If they are concentrated among poorer and more fragile states, the world figure may understate the true headcount, though the direction and size of any bias cannot be established from this series. The sections that follow set the global number against its regional and income group detail, where the weaknesses of the aggregate become clearer.

### Regions and income groups diverge sharply

Averages conceal the main feature of the data: extreme poverty at $3.00 a day is now concentrated in a few places, and the gap between those places and the rest has widened since 2015. The world figure fell from 13.4% in 2015 to 10.1% in 2024, yet that fall was produced by a small number of regions. Others barely moved, and two went backwards.

East Asia and Pacific shows the largest sustained gain among the regions with a full series from 2015. Its headcount fell from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. The cause is well known: decades of rapid growth in wages and employment, structural movement of labour out of agriculture, and public investment in rural infrastructure. The trend computation places the region at a ratio of 0.84 of the progress needed to reach zero by 2030, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Its expected level in 2030 is 0.951%, so the target would be narrowly missed on the present rate, though the remaining population is small. Europe and Central Asia follows a similar pattern at a lower level, falling from 1.2% in 2015 to 0.6% in 2024, with a ratio of 0.69. Remaining poverty in such low-rate regions is hard to remove, because it tends to lie in marginal groups and in areas that growth does not reach.

South Asia requires a caution. Its series is reported at 9.4% in 2020 and 2.6% in 2024, and no value for 2015 appears in the results. The series therefore begins five years after the others, and the comparison with 2015 cannot be made. The reason is a break in survey coverage: household surveys in the region's largest economy were not available for much of the period, so regional estimates for intervening years rest on interpolation and on newer survey rounds. A fall of this size over four years is large, and part of it may reflect the change in data sources rather than a change in living standards alone. The trend tool, which fits the short series, reports the region as on track, with a ratio of 0.96 and an expected 2030 level of 0.378%. That reading should be treated as provisional until the break is resolved. Because South Asia holds a large share of the world's population, its revised level affects the global figure as well.

Latin America and the Caribbean fell more slowly, from 6.0% in 2015 to 4.3% in 2024. The ratio of 0.43 marks marginal progress, and the expected 2030 level is 3.4%. The region's progress was interrupted by the economic shock of 2020 and by weak growth in the years that followed, and its high inequality means that growth reduces poverty less than elsewhere. North America moved from 1.1% to 0.9% and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. These are very small changes, and the ratios of 0.28 and 0.23 reflect how little room remains rather than failure in any ordinary sense. At that level, poverty at $3.00 a day is a question of coverage by the lowest incomes and not of national output.

The sharpest divergence lies in the other two groups of regions. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, a change too small to separate from survey noise. The trend tool classes it as stagnation, with an expected 2030 level of 44.7%. Population growth in the region is rapid, so a stable rate means a rising number of people in poverty, though that count lies outside the series examined here. Slow productivity growth in agriculture, limited creation of formal jobs, conflict, debt burdens and repeated climate and price shocks all help to explain why growth has not translated into lower poverty.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the region where poverty rose most among those with complete series, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024. The trend is classed as regression, with an expected 2030 level of 16.7%. The grouping combines very different economies, so the aggregate hides the cause: protracted conflict, displacement and economic collapse in several countries are the usual explanations, and the inclusion of Afghanistan and Pakistan in the group means that recent crises there weigh on the figure. Coverage of surveys in conflict settings is also poor, and the true level may be higher than reported.

Income groups repeat the pattern and sharpen it. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% in 2015 to 2.1% in 2024, with a ratio of 0.82. Lower middle income countries are reported at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024, a series that again begins in 2020, with an expected 2030 level of 8.5% and a ratio of 0.47. Low income countries went from 50.1% to 52.5%, a regression, with an expected 2030 level of 54.2%. The ordering is clear: the poorer the group, the slower the progress, and for the poorest the rate has risen. Poverty reduction since 2015 has therefore been strongest where it was already least widespread.

For 2030 this means that the world total depends increasingly on two conditions: low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries, where the headcount has not fallen, and the reliability of the South Asian estimate. Where poverty is highest, the series show no decline to extend, and the target cannot be reached by continuing the existing pattern.

### Progress slowed after 2013 and countries are not converging

The annual change in the world headcount at $3.00 a day does not move at a constant pace. A break analysis of the world series finds two shifts, in 2014 and in 2021. Before the first break, from 2001 to 2013, the headcount fell by a mean of 1.6 percentage points a year. Between 2014 and 2018 the mean fall was 0.9 points a year, a little over half the earlier pace. From 2021 to 2024 it was 0.3 points a year, roughly a fifth of the pace of the early 2000s. The break years matter as much as the means. The first slowdown begins a year before the Goals were adopted, so it cannot be attributed to the post-2015 period. The second coincides with the recovery from the pandemic, when the rapid gains that followed the 2020 shock gave way to a much slower decline.

The reason for the slowdown is partly arithmetic. When the headcount is high, a given rate of income growth lifts many people over the line at once. As the share falls, those who remain are fewer, poorer and harder to reach, and they are concentrated in places with weak growth, fragile institutions or conflict. A slower decline is therefore expected even if policy effort holds constant. The data do not show how much of the slowdown is arithmetic and how much reflects weaker growth, since the break analysis describes the shape of the series and does not apportion it among causes. Well-established history points to several candidates: the end of the commodity boom of the early 2010s, the slowdown in global trade, rising food and energy prices, the pandemic, and a rise in conflict in several low-income countries. The tools used here cannot rank them.

The second finding concerns whether poorer countries are catching up. A convergence test across 57 countries with data for both 2015 and 2022 regresses the change in the headcount on its starting level. The coefficient is 0.007, with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.03. The coefficient is not distinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains about 3% of the variation in subsequent change. Countries that began with higher poverty did not fall faster than the others. If convergence were operating, high-poverty countries would show larger declines and the coefficient would be clearly negative in this specification. It is neither.

Dispersion points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.14 in 2015 to 2.68 in 2022. The countries are therefore more unequal in their poverty rates at the end of the period than at the start. This follows from the pattern already described: many countries with low rates reduced them towards zero, while a smaller number with high rates changed little. Because the coefficient of variation is relative to the mean, falling averages can raise it even when high-poverty countries are not worsening in absolute terms. The rise should be read as a widening of relative differences and not, by itself, as proof that any country has become poorer.

These results rest on a sample with uneven coverage. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are not fielded every year in every country. The number of countries reporting fell from 87 in 2015 to 81 in 2021 and 73 in 2022. It dropped to 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Of 168 countries reporting in any year, the recent years are thin, so the means for 2021 to 2024 rest on a shrinking and possibly unrepresentative group. Much of the later data are likely to be estimates and projections for countries without a recent survey, and the series as supplied does not say which values are which. The final segment of the break analysis is therefore the least secure, and the 57-country convergence sample covers about a third of those reporting in any year. Countries with surveys in both years are more likely to be stable and well-resourced, which may understate the persistence of poverty in conflict-affected states.

For 2030, the implication is direct even before projections are made. A mean decline of 0.3 points a year is far below the pace that eradication would require from a level above 10%, and the absence of convergence means that no catching-up dynamic can be expected to accelerate it. The causal reading remains limited: the patterns documented here are associations in a changing and incompletely observed sample, and they do not identify which policies or shocks produced them.

### The 2030 target is out of reach on current trends, and proposals follow

Country-level results confirm what the regional figures suggest: the 2030 target will not be met on current trends. Of 105 countries assessed against a target of zero by 2030, 18 are on track or have met it, and these hold 45.6% of the population of the assessed countries. The large population share reflects the weight of a few populous economies, South Asia among them, whose headcount fell steeply after 2020. A further 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 23.1% of the population. Another 15 show marginal progress and would need significant acceleration, covering 11.3%. Seven countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the population, and 24 are regressing, with 17.9%. The regressing group is the most troubling, since in these countries the headcount at $3.00 a day is rising rather than falling.

The regional projections show how far even the best performers fall from zero. East Asia and Pacific, the region with the largest sustained gain, is projected at 0.951% in 2030, down from 2.0% in 2024. Europe and Central Asia is projected at 0.378%, and upper middle income countries at 1.067%. South Asia is classed as on track, with an expected 0.378% in 2030, although its series begins only in 2020 and the short span makes that projection fragile. For the world as a whole, the expected headcount in 2030 is 8.365%, against 10.1% in 2024. The ratio of progress achieved to progress required is 0.376, which the method classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. At the pace recorded, less than two fifths of the required decline would be delivered.

The weakest results lie where poverty is deepest. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a headcount of 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, and an expected 44.735% in 2030. Low-income countries are classed as regressing: 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, with an expected 54.164% in 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping is also regressing, from 11.3% to 14.3% over the same period, with 16.731% expected in 2030. Conflict, fragile institutions, weak growth and rapid population increase are well-established causes of such outcomes. Because these regions hold a growing share of the world's poor, the global figure will be set increasingly by them, and gains elsewhere cannot offset their stagnation.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Read literally, eradication means a headcount of zero, and no region reaches it on current trends. Read as the working threshold often used in international monitoring, a headcount below 3%, the picture differs: East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, upper middle income countries and, on its short series, South Asia would fall below that mark, while the world, Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries would not. The book reports both readings, because the choice changes the verdict for several regions but not the verdict for the world or for the poorest places.

The evidence also carries limits that bear on 2030. Survey coverage has weakened at the end of the series. Countries reporting numbered 93 in 2018 and 87 in 2015, but 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and only 4 in 2025. Figures for 2024 therefore rest partly on estimates and projections from earlier surveys, and the figure for 2025 is not usable. Poverty counts depend on household surveys that take years to field and process, so the latest values may be revised once new surveys arrive. Revisions to purchasing power parities also prevent comparison with earlier editions of the series. The projections above are linear extrapolations of past rates; they describe where present trends lead, not what policy could achieve.

The conclusion is plain. Extreme poverty at $3.00 a day has fallen since 2015 but not fast enough, and the remaining burden is concentrated in places where it is not falling at all. The proposals below follow from that finding.

proposals: Governments of low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries, with their development partners and multilateral lenders, should concentrate poverty-reduction finance and programmes on these places, since they hold the stagnating and regressing headcounts that will decide the global result.

National statistical offices, supported by the World Bank and bilateral donors, should restore the frequency of household surveys so that 2024 and 2025 figures can be checked against fresh data rather than projections.

The bodies that monitor Target 1.1, including the World Bank and the United Nations statistical system, should report progress against both readings of the target, a headcount of zero and a headcount below 3%, and state which is used.

w-c04-4-1~juniper/writer-2~60.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.6% for the world by 2030. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, which is a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The measure is also a ceiling on what can be learned. The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year or two after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 divides into three groups: regions where the probability of premature death from the four main non-communicable diseases fell appreciably, regions where it hardly changed, and one region where it rose. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall among the regions, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, a respectable decline that nonetheless leaves the region with a probability well above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021.

The small movers are the two Americas. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America already began from the lowest regional level, so a modest fall is less surprising there, but the pace is far from the one-third reduction that Target 3.4 describes. Established knowledge points to causes that are familiar: gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking rates have been offset in part by obesity, diabetes and, in some countries, the effects of drug overdose and unequal access to treatment on adult mortality. In Latin America and the Caribbean, rising metabolic risk and fragmented primary care in many health systems plausibly work against faster progress.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, which made it the region with the highest level in 2021, having been marginally below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group in 2015. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates in the 30 to 70 range did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends, which is consistent with high rates of hypertension, diabetes and air-pollution-related respiratory disease, together with late diagnosis and heavy out-of-pocket costs for long-term treatment. The period also includes the pandemic years, when disruption to screening and chronic care, and the effect of infection on people with existing conditions, may have pushed the 2021 figure upward; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves the level close to the South Asian one. The extract supplied for the region is truncated, so the regional series should be read from the full database before any statement about its pace is relied upon. Measurement is also a concern in this region, where death registration is incomplete and the estimates lean heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, which is to say almost no change. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. The two richer groups therefore improved by about one percentage point each, while the lower-middle group, which contains South Asia's large populations, stood still. The gap between the low-income and high-income groups remained roughly ten percentage points in 2021.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability bounded by the experience of all adults, but the direction is towards greater inequality, not less. The share of the Theil index lying between regions, as opposed to within them, grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than it did in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences, and that the regions pulling away from the rest, in both directions, are shaping the global picture.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.2619 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.08728 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. The ratio of the two is 0.33. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted, not towards it.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. Established knowledge points to several plausible contributors that the data here do not separate: the earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from improved treatment of heart disease, and such gains are subject to diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The final years of the window, 2020 and 2021, also coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions and may have raised deaths from these causes among people infected with the virus. The series does not allow those effects to be isolated from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.00156 with a p-value of 0.697 and an R-squared of 0.0011. The coefficient is positive but statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation across the 185 countries rose from 0.360 in 2015 to 0.380 in 2021. Relative spread between countries widened slightly. Because the indicator is a probability expressed as a share, a given absolute fall is a larger proportional fall in a country with a low level, so a widening coefficient of variation is consistent with low-level countries improving proportionally faster, or with high-level countries stagnating or worsening. Either reading means the distribution did not tighten. For a target defined in relative terms, this matters: a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and the data show no sign that such countries are receiving it.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.098, and the Kendall coefficient is 0.0706. Both are weak. Moreover, the positive sign is the wrong direction for a simple expectation: better coverage would be expected to accompany larger falls in mortality, which in this coding would produce a negative correlation of changes. The association is close to nil, and it provides no support for the view that countries with larger coverage gains saw larger mortality gains over this short window.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.247 by the Spearman measure, and -0.1713 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is moderate in size, but it describes a cross-section, in which income, age structure, the health system as a whole and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together. It cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented in them. The mortality series is modelled by the World Health Organization from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths can be read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021 and the trend projection reaches 17.5% in 2030, so the global ratio of progress is 0.22. A ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target; 0.22 means roughly a fifth of that pace. At the observed rate, the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction, and the gap to be closed in the remaining years is larger than the distance covered since 2015.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, is the nearest of the regions to the required pace, with an expected value of 13.4% in 2030. Its path is moderate progress, and the target would still be missed without acceleration. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6% in 2030, which is marginal progress and leaves a wide gap. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030. The same classification should be read with care, since high-income countries began from a lower level, and the target value of 12.57% is itself computed from one baseline.

That last point is an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions at 22% or more would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above follows the first. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected 24.0% in 2030, higher than its 22.9% in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.00 and an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest, and the gap between income groups, already wide in 2021, is on course to persist or widen.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none, and the correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment, chronic respiratory care or the quality of care. A weak link therefore does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the coverage measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality, named in the section's title, cannot be treated here. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. The omission is a gap in this account, not evidence that the matter is minor. Mental health is part of the wording of target 3.4, and the indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover it.

The proposals follow from these findings. Health ministries in countries with weak coverage should give priority to hypertension detection and treatment and to tobacco control, since these are the tracer areas where the sub-index is lowest and where prevention acts most cheaply on cardiovascular death. The World Health Organization and national statistical offices should publish the premature mortality indicator by country each year, so that stagnation, as in lower middle income countries, and regression, as in South Asia, are seen while correction is possible. The same bodies should report suicide mortality alongside it, by sex, so that both parts of target 3.4 are followed together. The United Nations bodies that guide the goals should state the baseline, global or regional, from which the one-third reduction is judged.

w-c03-5-1~heath/writer-2~60.text:
### Farming's footprint on land, fertiliser and water is large and nearly static

Farming occupies a little over a third of the world's land. Agricultural land, which combines arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, stood at 36.8 per cent of land area in 2015 and at 36.9 per cent in 2023. The change is about a tenth of a percentage point over eight years, which is small enough to be read as stability. The series is reported by 208 countries in 2024, so the global figure rests on near-complete coverage. A stable share does not show that pressure on land is unchanged, since the share says nothing about which land is farmed, how degraded it is, or whether forest and wetland were converted while abandoned land reverted elsewhere.

Fertiliser use shows a modest rise. Consumption was 132.9 kilograms per hectare of arable land in 2015 and 136.5 kilograms in 2023, an increase of about three and a half kilograms. The measure counts nitrogenous, potash and phosphate nutrients and excludes manures, so it understates total nutrient application where animal and plant manures are widely used. The world average also conceals a very wide spread between countries, which the next part examines. Here it is enough to note that a flat global mean can coexist with rising use in some places and falling use in others, each with different consequences. Too little fertiliser leaves yields and soils depleted. Too much brings nutrient runoff, water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Water use follows the same pattern. Agriculture accounted for 71.5 per cent of total freshwater withdrawal in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. Roughly seven of every ten units of freshwater taken from rivers, lakes and aquifers go to farming, and that share barely moved across the period. The series is reported by 178 countries in 2022, and the latest year is earlier than for land and fertiliser, so any change after 2022 cannot be observed. A fall of about half a percentage point may reflect growth in industrial and municipal withdrawals as much as any saving in the field. The share also measures the distribution of use between sectors, not the volume withdrawn or whether withdrawals are sustainable.

These three series are measures of intensity and footprint, not of sustainability. Target 2.4 asks for sustainable food production systems and resilient agricultural practices that raise productivity while maintaining ecosystems, and it sets no numerical threshold and no base year. It can be read in more than one way. One reading treats it as a call to produce more on the same land with fewer inputs. Another treats it as a call to restore ecosystems even at some cost to output. A third stresses adaptation to drought and flooding, which none of these series captures. Because the target is open, a figure such as 36.9 per cent of land cannot be judged on or off track. It can only be described and compared over time and across places.

Two points follow from the global picture. First, the period since 2015 shows no sharp break in any of the three measures, and the available years do not reveal a clear shift attributable to the disruption after 2020. Second, a near-static aggregate is the starting point, not the conclusion. The questions of where intensity is high, where it is rising and where it is too low for food security are matters of regional and national difference.

### Regions differ most in fertiliser, and least in the share of land farmed

Regional differences are widest in fertiliser use and narrowest in the share of land that is farmed. In 2015, East Asia and Pacific applied 329.1 kilograms of nutrients per hectare of arable land, the highest of any region. By 2023 the figure had fallen to 304.1. Sub-Saharan Africa sat at the opposite end, with 14.4 kilograms in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023. The gap between the two regions therefore remained above 280 kilograms per hectare, even though the African figure rose by about a third and the Asian figure fell. The fall in East Asia and Pacific is consistent with policies in the largest producers that discourage over-application and promote balanced nutrient use, while the African level reflects the cost of fertiliser, weak distribution and limited credit for smallholders rather than a deliberate choice of low-input farming.

Other regions moved upward. South Asia rose from 175.0 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 206.0 in 2023, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 135.1 to 173.9, the largest relative rise among the larger regions. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 90.0 to 102.0. North America changed little, from 124.3 to 128.8, and Europe and Central Asia drifted down from 78.7 to 76.0. The world average, at 132.9 in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, therefore conceals two opposing movements: a decline in the heaviest-using region and increases in most others. Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income countries rose from 10.0 to 13.9 and lower-middle-income countries from 114.6 to 130.8, while upper-middle-income countries were almost flat at 213.0 and 213.8, and high-income countries eased from 106.3 to 104.3. Low-income countries still use roughly one fifteenth of the amount used in upper-middle-income countries per hectare, which bears directly on the productivity aims of target 2.4.

The share of land in agriculture varies much less between regions, and it hardly moved after 2015. East Asia and Pacific stood at 46.5 per cent in 2015 and 46.8 in 2023, Sub-Saharan Africa at 43.9 and 44.7, and South Asia at 58.6 and 58.3. North America held at about 26.7 per cent in both years. Latin America and the Caribbean slipped from 33.3 to 32.9 per cent. These shares are shaped by climate, terrain and history, so they change slowly, and the small shifts are not evidence of a policy effect. Sub-Saharan Africa is the one region where farmland grew appreciably, which fits a pattern in which output has been raised by expanding cultivated area more than by raising inputs per hectare.

Water use for farming differs by region in a way that follows aridity and the dependence on irrigation. In 2022, agriculture accounted for 90.3 per cent of freshwater withdrawals in South Asia and 87.3 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, which had been 90.1 per cent in 2015. North America stood at 37.5 per cent and Europe and Central Asia at 51.8, where industry and municipal supply take larger shares. The South Asian value is identical in 2015 and 2022, at 90.3 per cent. Withdrawal shares in this series come from national surveys that are updated irregularly, and an unchanged value to four decimals more probably reflects a carried-forward estimate than genuine stability. The figure should be read as a level, not as evidence that the balance of use did not shift. For 2030, the regional spread points to different tasks: restraint and efficiency in the heavily fertilised and water-stressed regions, and access to inputs where use remains very low.

### Yields rose slowly and country outcomes diverged

Cereal yields rose slowly across most of the world after 2015, and the pace differed sharply between regions and countries. The world rate of change is given as 0.9 per cent a year, a figure the tool classes as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 5,430 in 2023, a rate of 0.9 per cent a year. Europe and Central Asia moved from 3,803 to 4,045 over the same years, at 0.8 per cent a year. High-income economies rose from 4,976 to 5,394, at 1.0 per cent a year. All three fall in the marginal class. Upper middle income countries also sit there, at 0.8 per cent a year. These are regions with already high yields, where the room for further gain is narrower and the gains come from breeding, management and precision rather than from added inputs.

The classification needs careful reading. No target value for cereal yield is set in the targets of Goal 2, and target 2.4 speaks of productivity and resilience without a number. The tool therefore judges each series against the rate of a rising trend, not against a fixed goal. A class such as marginal progress is a judgement of pace relative to that trend, and a different reference rate would shift some regions between classes. The labels should be taken as a comparison between places, not as a verdict on whether any region has met an official threshold.

The lower-yield regions show the widest spread of outcomes. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 in 2015 to 4,828 in 2024, at 1.1 per cent a year, still classed as marginal. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached a moderate class at 1.3 per cent a year, with yields going from 2,732 to 3,027 by 2023. South Asia, by contrast, rose from 3,041 to 3,814 by 2024, a rate of 2.6 per cent a year, and North America from 6,677 to 8,414, at 2.6 per cent. Lower middle income countries went from 2,766 to 3,366, at 2.2 per cent. These three groups are the ones classed as on track or target met. South Asia and lower middle income countries gained from wider irrigation, improved seed and expanded input use, while North America gained from an already high base and favourable recent seasons, so the same label stands for different causes.

The weakest results lie where yields are lowest and the need is greatest. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 1,443 to 1,453 kilograms per hectare between 2015 and 2024, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which is stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 to 1,345, a rate of minus 0.2 per cent a year, classed as regression. A yield in these groups is less than a third of that in North America in 2024. Rain-fed farming, thin use of improved seed, limited credit, weak roads and exposure to drought and conflict all weigh on these outcomes, and the period since 2020 added shocks to input costs and supply chains. Because yield is measured per hectare harvested, a rise in cropped area onto poorer land can also hold the average down.

The country tallies confirm that the divergence is wide. Of 180 countries assessed, 39 are on track or have met the trend, and they hold 29.5 per cent of the population covered. Another 19 countries show moderate progress, with 14.0 per cent of the population. A further 27 show marginal progress, with 25.7 per cent, a large share because this class includes populous middle-income economies. Stagnation applies to 25 countries and 15.6 per cent of the population. Regression applies to 70 countries, the largest count of any class, though these hold only 15.2 per cent of the population, which says that the falling yields are mostly in smaller countries.

Two readings follow. By population, most people live where yields are either improving at a fair pace or creeping up, so global averages hide the problem. By country count, however, the commonest outcome is decline, and 95 countries are stagnant or falling in yield. Year-to-year weather can drive a drop between two chosen end years, so some of the 70 may reflect a poor season at the end of the window and not a lasting fall. The trend over 2015 to 2024 is a short window for crops that swing with rainfall, and the result should be treated with that caution. For 2030, the pattern implies that global yield growth will stay modest unless the stagnant and regressing countries change course, and these are the places where food insecurity is concentrated.

### Fertiliser use is converging, but it explains yield levels more than yield change

Fertiliser use has been converging. Across 192 countries, the coefficient of variation of fertiliser consumption per hectare of arable land fell from 2.2 in 2015 to 1.7 in 2022. Countries that began with low application rates tended to increase them faster than countries that began with high rates, and the convergence coefficient of -0.034 is statistically distinguishable from zero (p below 0.001). The model explains 27.5 per cent of the variation in country growth, so the starting level is an important influence but far from the only one. Convergence of this kind reflects two movements at once: a rise from low bases in parts of Africa and South Asia, and a levelling off or decline in some of the most intensive systems, where fertiliser prices, nutrient regulation and efficiency gains have reduced application per hectare.

Convergence in inputs does not mean convergence in outcomes. Across 179 countries, the Spearman rank correlation between fertiliser use and cereal yield in 2022 is 0.72. Countries that apply more nutrients per hectare are, with few exceptions, the countries that harvest more grain per hectare. The relationship between changes is much weaker. The Spearman correlation between the change in fertiliser use and the change in cereal yield from 2015 to 2022 is 0.13, and the Kendall coefficient is 0.10. A country that raised its application rate was only slightly more likely to see yields rise faster than others.

The contrast has a plain reading. High input goes with high yield because intensive systems combine fertiliser with improved seed, irrigation, mechanisation, extension services and reliable markets. Extra input applied alone, in the absence of those complements, does not reliably raise yields. Weather in individual years, soil degradation, pest pressure and the response curve of crops, which flattens at high rates, also weaken the link in changes over a short window of seven years. Where soils are depleted and application is very low, additional nutrients can raise yields substantially, yet the data here do not isolate such cases.

The correlations also do not establish cause. Wealthier countries with better institutions both use more fertiliser and obtain higher yields, and climate and soil quality shape both. The rank measures used here describe association only, and the measure of changes covers a period that includes the disruption to fertiliser prices and supply after 2020, which affected countries unevenly. For 2030, the finding cautions against treating higher fertiliser use as a target in itself. Target 2.4 calls for productive and sustainable systems, and the evidence suggests that gains depend on how nutrients are used, not only on how much is applied.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.4 asks for production systems that raise productivity while maintaining ecosystems, and the evidence in this section shows that the two halves of that wording are moving unevenly. Fertiliser intensity is not falling where it is already high. In East Asia and Pacific it declined from 329.1 kilograms per hectare of arable land in 2015 to 304.1 in 2023, yet remained more than twice the world figure of 136.5 kilograms. In the upper middle income group it was 213.0 in 2015 and 213.8 in 2023, effectively unchanged, and in the high income group it eased only from 106.3 to 104.3. Where use is low it is rising: Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 14.4 to 19.3 kilograms and the low income group from 10.0 to 13.9. These increases begin from so small a base that they leave the continent far from the application levels seen elsewhere.

The yield record offers little reassurance. Of 180 countries assessed on cereal yield, 39 were on track or had met the target, holding 29.5 per cent of the assessed population, while 70 were in regression, holding 15.2 per cent. A further 25 were stagnant and 27 showed only marginal progress. Fertiliser levels track yield levels closely across 179 countries (Spearman 0.72 for 2022 levels), but changes in fertiliser track changes in yield only weakly (0.13 for 2015 to 2022). More nutrients are therefore not a reliable route to faster gains; soils, seed, water control, markets and extension services decide what a kilogram of fertiliser yields.

Water shows the least movement. Agriculture took 71.5 per cent of freshwater withdrawals in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. South Asia stayed at 90.3 per cent in both years, which is consistent with a series that is carried forward rather than newly measured, and the low income group remained near 90.9 per cent. Withdrawal share says nothing about whether extraction is sustainable, so the data cannot show whether the ecosystem clause of the target is being met. For 2030, the likely outcome is intensity that stays high in the leading regions, grows slowly in the low-input regions, and yields that remain short of the pace required.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c03-1-1~rowan/writer-1~60.text:
### Global prevalence of undernourishment and food insecurity

The world picture for target 2.1 is set by two indicators from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and they tell different stories. The prevalence of undernourishment stood at 8.0 per cent of the global population in 2015 and at 8.1 per cent in 2024. Over nine years, the first seven of them under the Sustainable Development Goals, the share of people whose habitual food intake cannot supply the dietary energy needed for a normal, active and healthy life did not fall. It was, to the precision the series allows, unchanged. The 2024 figure rests on reports from 165 countries, so the world value is built on near-complete coverage.

The second indicator, the prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity, moved sharply. It rose from 21.4 per cent in 2015 to 28.0 per cent in 2024. This indicator counts people living in households where at least one adult reported, at times during the year, eating poor-quality diets and possibly cutting the quantity of food. It is far broader than undernourishment, and its level is correspondingly higher: in 2024 more than one person in four lived in such a household, against roughly one in twelve classed as undernourished. The 2024 value rests on 135 reporting countries, fewer than for undernourishment, so the world aggregate depends more on modelled estimates for countries without a survey.

The two measures should not be read as duplicates or as rivals. Undernourishment is a modelled estimate. It compares the food available in a country, and how unequally it is distributed, with a minimum energy requirement. It responds to supply, trade and income distribution, and it captures chronic shortfalls in calories. Food insecurity is experience-based. It comes from survey questions about worry, compromised diet quality and reduced portions, so it registers the effect of price shocks, lost income and disrupted markets on households, including those who still reach the energy minimum but eat badly or anxiously. A flat undernourishment line beside a rising food insecurity line is therefore coherent. Calorie shortfall has stayed steady, while access to an adequate and varied diet has worsened for a much larger group. The period contained the disruption of 2020 and the food and energy price rises that followed, shocks of the kind the experience-based measure is designed to detect.

The yardstick for progress needs care. Target 2.1 calls for an end to hunger and for access by all people to safe, nutritious and sufficient food all year round, and it states no number. The convention adopted here reads the end of hunger as undernourishment at or below 2.5 per cent, which is also the lowest value the FAO series reports; the series note says that a value of 2.5 may signify a prevalence below that level. Against that reading, the world in 2024 stands at more than three times the threshold. The target also names no threshold for food insecurity, although its wording on access for all points towards it. Any figure set for that indicator, whether zero or a reduction from a baseline, would be an interpretation by the reader and not a value fixed by the target. The prevalence of undernourishment is therefore treated as the primary measure of the target, and food insecurity as the wider measure of access and sufficiency.

The finding matters for what follows. With undernourishment unchanged and food insecurity higher, the world has not moved towards the end of hunger since 2015, and on the broader measure it has moved away. The sections that follow show where the burden lies and how reliable the figures are.

### Regional and income-group differences

Regional averages conceal a split between a few regions that have moved towards the target and several that have moved away from it. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest prevalence of undernourishment among the regions in both years, rising from 18.4 per cent in 2015 to 22.3 per cent in 2024. The trend tool classes this as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 25.4 per cent against a target of 2.5 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved in the same direction from a lower base, from 9.6 per cent to 12.3 per cent, and the tool projects 14.6 per cent in 2030. Conflict, displacement, currency crises and dependence on imported grain are well-established drivers of such deteriorations, and they cluster in these two regions.

The regions that improved did so from different starting points. South Asia fell from 12.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent, the largest decline among the regions in absolute terms, yet the tool reads this as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, since the expected 2030 value of 7.9 per cent remains well above 2.5 per cent. East Asia and Pacific fell from 4.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent and is the closest of the improving regions to the target, with an expected 2030 value of 2.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean eased only from 5.5 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Europe and Central Asia edged up from 2.8 per cent to 2.9 per cent, and North America remained at 2.5 per cent. Because the published figure is reported as 2.5 where the true prevalence may be lower, North America's flat line signals a floor in the data, not an absence of change.

Income groups show the same gradient more sharply. Low-income countries recorded 24.1 per cent in 2015 and 27.3 per cent in 2024, a regression in the tool's reading. Lower-middle-income countries were almost unchanged, at 12.5 per cent and then 12.1 per cent, which the tool classes as stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries fell from 4.3 per cent to 4.0 per cent, and high-income countries from 2.6 per cent to 2.6 per cent at one decimal place, close to the floor. Hunger is therefore concentrated in the poorest economies, and it is there that the global average is being held up. The world figure of 8.1 per cent in 2024 is the product of improvement in the large populations of South Asia and East Asia offsetting deterioration in Africa and the Middle East, not of broad advance.

The measure of food insecurity, which captures experience of reduced diet quality or quantity and not habitual energy supply, shows a harsher picture. Among low-income countries it reached 65.4 per cent in 2024, up from 55.1 per cent in 2015, so that roughly two in three people lived in moderately or severely food insecure households. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 29.2 per cent to 41.8 per cent, a much steeper deterioration than their flat undernourishment figure suggests. Upper-middle-income countries held at 12.8 per cent and then 12.6 per cent, and high-income countries at 8.2 per cent and then 7.9 per cent. The gap between the two indicators widens as income falls.

South Asia illustrates why both indicators are needed. Undernourishment fell there from 12.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent, while moderate or severe food insecurity rose from 28.0 per cent to 36.7 per cent. The two can diverge because one is modelled from national food supply and distribution, whereas the other is reported by households and responds quickly to price rises, income losses and the strains after 2020, including inflation in staple foods. A region can have enough calories in aggregate and still contain many households that cannot afford a regular, adequate diet. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan show the sharpest case on the household measure, rising from 27.6 per cent to 40.1 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 23.7 per cent to 25.2 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 8.5 per cent to 8.8 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 10.3 per cent to 10.4 per cent, and North America from 10.3 per cent to 10.7 per cent.

For 2030, the implication is that the target will not be met by regional averages moving at their present pace, and that the poorest countries are moving away from it. Only North America is classed as on track, and it is already at the reporting floor.

### Country trajectories and the quality of the data

The country classifications make the global averages easier to read. For undernourishment, the trend tool assessed 168 countries against the target of 2.5 per cent by 2030. Of these, 68 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 41.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 24 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 17 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries are stagnant. Regression affects 53 countries, which hold 20.9 per cent of the population. The classes therefore divide almost evenly in number between countries that are moving towards the target and countries that are not, and the population weights show where the burden lies. The marginal-progress class is small in number but holds 26.5 per cent of the population, so a few very populous countries are improving too slowly to reach the target. Their pace matters more for the 2030 outcome than the count of countries suggests.

The finding that 68 countries are on track or have met the target needs a caveat about the indicator. The FAO reports prevalence values below 2.5 per cent as 2.5, so a country that has already met the target cannot be told apart from one sitting at the threshold. Many of the countries in the on-track class are likely to be middle- and high-income countries that began near the target and have stayed there. Their classification reflects the absence of a problem rather than a gain made since 2015. The class is therefore a weaker sign of progress than its size implies, and it should not be set against the regressing countries as if both groups had moved a similar distance.

Food insecurity gives a harsher picture. The tool assessed 157 countries for moderate or severe food insecurity. Regression is the largest class: 81 countries, holding 60.5 per cent of the population. Only 40 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 28.9 per cent of the population. Three countries show moderate progress, covering 4.5 per cent of the population, and six show marginal progress, covering 2.8 per cent. Stagnation affects 27 countries and 3.3 per cent of the population. The gap between the two indicators is large. Undernourishment, which is estimated from national food balance sheets and a model of how food is distributed, has held roughly steady. Food insecurity, which is measured from what households report about their own experience, has worsened in most of the world's people. Households can report hardship before the national supply of calories changes, and rising food prices, reduced incomes and the shocks of 2020 and after are the kind of pressure that survey-based measures capture first.

The reading of the food insecurity classes rests on a methodological limit. The indicator has no numeric target under the Goals. The trend tool therefore had to judge direction only, with a decrease taken as the aim, and it could not measure distance to a defined value. The classes mean that a country is moving up or down, or is flat. They do not mean that a country is near or far from an agreed end point. A country counted as on track has a falling prevalence, and that may still be a high prevalence. The target can also be read in more than one way: target 2.1 speaks of ending hunger and securing access to sufficient food all year round, which could be read as zero, as a low threshold such as that used for undernourishment, or as a reduction relative to a baseline. The classification is sensitive to that reading, and no single reading has been privileged here.

Coverage is the second limit. The number of countries reporting food insecurity was 99 in 2015 and 100 in 2016. It rose to 115 in 2017, 122 in 2018 and 136 in 2019, then to 144 in 2020, 146 in 2021 and 148 in 2022. It fell back to 135 in 2023 and again in 2024. In all, 157 countries reported in at least one year. The early years rest on about two thirds of the countries that later report, so a comparison between 2015 and a later year may reflect a change in who is counted rather than a change in conditions. The trend tool compares each country with its own record, which reduces this problem, but the regional and global averages are less secure. Countries that joined the survey later may differ systematically from those that reported from the start, since national surveys tend to arrive first where statistical capacity and funding are stronger.

The fall to 135 countries in 2023 and 2024 weakens the latest years in the same way. Some of the decline may reflect reporting delays that later revisions will fill, but that cannot be established from the series as it stands. The most recent estimates are therefore the least settled. For 2030, the lesson is that a monitoring system whose coverage grows and then shrinks cannot give a firm account of how far the world is from the target. The direction of the findings is consistent across the indicators and the classes, but the exact counts should be read as approximate.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The measured rates do not point towards the target. The trend tool classes the world as a whole as regression for undernourishment, with an expected 2030 value of 8.2 per cent against a target of 2.5 per cent. The ratio of progress to the progress required is -0.03, which is to say the global line is flat and slightly inclined the wrong way. Target 2.1 asks for an end to hunger by 2030, and at present rates the world would arrive at the end of the period with roughly the prevalence it had at the start.

The regression is concentrated in a few places. Low-income countries are expected to reach 29.7 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of -0.26. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.4 per cent, with a ratio of -0.44. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region is expected to reach 14.6 per cent, with a ratio of -0.71, the steepest deterioration among the regions in relation to its distance from the target. The causes are well established: armed conflict, displacement, repeated drought and flood, currency weakness that raises import costs, and the price shocks that followed 2020 weigh most on economies that import food and hold few reserves. Europe and Central Asia also shows regression, but from a low base, with an expected 2030 value of 3.1 per cent.

Progress elsewhere is real but insufficient. South Asia is expected to reach 7.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.46, and East Asia and Pacific 2.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.79. High-income countries are expected to reach 2.5 per cent, close to the floor at which the indicator is reported, and North America sits at that floor. Because the FAO note states that a value of 2.5 may signify a prevalence below 2.5 per cent, countries at the floor cannot be distinguished from one another, and a target of 2.5 per cent is in effect a target of reaching the reporting limit. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnant, with an expected 11.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean as marginal, at 4.9 per cent. Even the regions that improve would need to speed up to reach the target.

The country classes confirm the concentration. Of 168 countries, 53 are in regression and hold 20.9 per cent of the assessed population, while 68 are on track or have met the target. The success of many small or already well-fed countries therefore masks the difficulty of the places where hunger is deepest.

Food insecurity adds a harder reading. Among 157 countries assessed for moderate or severe food insecurity, 81 are in regression and hold 60.5 per cent of the assessed population, and 40 are on track, holding 28.9 per cent. Regression covers a far larger share of people than it does for undernourishment, where it covers 20.9 per cent. Food insecurity has therefore worsened in places where undernourishment has eased, which suggests that access, affordability and diet quality have deteriorated even where average energy supply has held. This matters for 2030, because a country can look close to the undernourishment target while a large share of its households still skip meals or eat poor diets. The food insecurity indicator also carries no numeric target, so the classification measures only the direction of change and not the distance to a goal, and the tool cannot say how far any country is from success.

The data base is improving and still uneven. The number of countries reporting food insecurity rose from 99 in 2015 to 148 in 2022, then fell to 135 in 2023 and 2024. Part of the apparent worsening may reflect changes in which countries report, because early coverage was thinner, and the fall in reporting after 2022 weakens the picture for the years that matter most for judging recovery after 2020.

In sum, the aim of ending hunger by 2030 will not be met on present rates, and the shortfall is a matter of where resources and attention are directed. The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c02-5-1~dahlia/writer-1~60.text:
### Disaster displacement is the measure that exists, and it is rising

The only series in the bench that records recent exposure to climate-related disasters is the count of new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre. It stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and at 26,393,278 in 2023. The world total therefore rose over the eight years, by a little more than a third, and it did so in the period that target 1.5 covers, which asks countries to reduce the exposure and vulnerability of the poor and of people in vulnerable situations to climate-related extreme events by 2030.

The unit needs care. The series counts cases of new displacement, not persons. A household that flees a flood in March and a cyclone in September enters the count twice, and a person who returns home and is displaced again is counted again. The figure is also not a count of people affected: those whose crops fail in a drought, whose homes are damaged but who stay, or who lose income without moving do not appear. Displacement measures the part of exposure that is severe enough to force people from their homes and that is visible to the agencies which report it. It is a floor under the scale of exposure, not an estimate of it.

The measure also records hazards beyond those that the target names strictly as climate-related. Storms, floods, wildfires and droughts are included, as are geophysical events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, depending on how events are classified. The series therefore cannot be read as a pure signal of climate change. Part of any rise reflects more people living in harm's way, in coastal cities and river plains, and part reflects better monitoring and reporting. A single large event can move a national figure, and through it a regional one, by millions in one year.

The analysis of breaks in the annual change of the world total finds none. Over 2009 to 2023 the mean annual change is negative, at about 789,790 cases a year, which sits oddly beside the higher 2023 figure than 2015. The reading is that the series is dominated by large swings from year to year, so that the endpoints, and the mean of changes taken from a high early year, tell different stories. Neither 2015 nor 2020 marks a statistical rupture. The rise from 2015 to 2023 should be taken as a movement within a volatile record, not as a trend established against that volatility.

This matters for 2030 because the target has no quantified threshold, and the only indicator that tracks exposure directly has no baseline that fixes what reduction would mean. A target that asks for reduced exposure can be read as fewer displacements in absolute terms or as fewer relative to population at risk; the data support the first reading only, and by that reading the world is, on the endpoints, moving away from the target.

### Coverage has widened, but the wider measure of exposure is a single historical period

The number of countries that report disaster displacement has grown steadily, and this complicates any reading of the rising total. In 2008, 80 countries reported. The count fell to 60 in 2009, recovered to 73 in 2010, dipped again to 62 in 2011 and reached 79 in 2012. It then jumped to 118 in 2013, slipped to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. After 2015 it rose almost every year, reaching 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020. It stood at 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across the whole series, 199 countries and territories have reported in at least one year, so even the latest year leaves some of them without a figure.

This matters for interpretation. A world total built from 112 countries in 2015 and 145 in 2023 is not a sum over the same set of countries. Part of the rise in displacement may reflect better recording, wider monitoring and the entry of countries that were previously silent, rather than a larger number of people forced from their homes. The data as given cannot separate the two effects. A like-for-like comparison over countries reporting in both years would be needed, and the figures here do not provide one. The lower counts of 2009 and 2011 also show that early coverage was uneven, which argues against reading the years before 2013 as a baseline.

The wider measure of exposure is weaker still. The share of the population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures is an annual average for 1990 to 2009, compiled from the EM-DAT disaster database. It is reported for 168 countries in a single year, 2009, with no regional or world aggregates and no later update. It therefore describes the two decades before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. It carries no trend, no value for 2015 and none for 2020, and it cannot show whether exposure has changed since the goals began.

The question of how many people are affected by climate-related disasters therefore cannot be answered from these data. Displacement counts cases of movement, not persons, since one person may be displaced more than once in a year. The historical average gives a share of the population but belongs to a past period. Neither series measures people affected in the sense that target 1.5 implies, and no series on the shelf measures the exposure of the poor in particular.

### Regions differ sharply and the inequality among countries has grown

Regional totals of new disaster displacement diverge widely, and the direction of change differs from one region to the next. East Asia and Pacific remains the largest single contributor. Its count moved from 8,304,660 cases in 2015 to 9,038,561 in 2023, a modest rise that leaves the region with the highest absolute burden in the series. The region is exposed to typhoons, monsoon floods and seismic hazards alike, and it holds very large populations along coasts and river deltas. Only part of that exposure is climate-related, since displacement by earthquakes and volcanic activity is counted in the same series.

South Asia moved in the opposite direction. Its count fell from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 in 2023. A fall of this size should not be read as a lasting gain in resilience. Displacement counts in the region depend heavily on whether a single large cyclone or flood season strikes populated areas in a given year, and early warning and evacuation, which have improved in several countries, can raise recorded displacement as well as save lives, because evacuations are counted as displacement. Two endpoints cannot separate these influences.

The largest proportional rise is in Europe and Central Asia, from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 in 2023. Part of this is likely to reflect wider reporting and a small starting base, and part genuine events, but the data cannot apportion the two. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan roughly doubled, from 1,212,730 to 2,481,660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 to 1,728,025. North America rose from 76,000 to 394,000, a fivefold increase from a low base that is small beside the Asian totals.

The spread among countries has widened. Weighting countries by population, the Gini coefficient of new displacement rose from 0.570 in 2015 to 0.678 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. Both measures say that displacement has become more concentrated in a few countries. The number of countries in the comparison also grew, from 112 to 145, so part of the change may follow from wider coverage rather than from a change in the underlying events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. In 2015 most of the inequality was a matter of which region a country belongs to. By 2023 almost half lay among countries within the same regions. Regional averages therefore describe the pattern less well than they once did, and targeting of resilience support by region alone would miss many of the most exposed countries. For 2030, the implication is that national and subnational monitoring will matter more than regional aggregates, and that a single global total conceals sharply different trajectories.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The trend in the world series should be read with caution. The test for structural breaks in the annual change of world displacement found none. The mean annual change over 2009 to 2023 was -789,790 cases, a negative figure that sits oddly beside the rise already described between 2015 and 2023. The two readings do not contradict each other: the mean is taken over a window that begins in a year when only 60 countries reported, and it reflects a few very large swings rather than a settled direction. Displacement counts follow the occurrence of major storms, floods and earthquakes, so a single severe season can dominate a year. A series of this kind cannot support a statement that exposure is falling or rising steadily, and no break marks 2015 or 2020 as a turning point.

The implication for 2030 is therefore limited. Target 1.5 sets no quantified level. It asks for resilience to be built and for exposure and vulnerability to be reduced, but it names no number of people, no share of population and no date before 2030 at which progress is to be checked. Without a threshold, no trajectory can be judged on or off course. The target can also be read in more than one way: as a fall in the number of people affected, as a fall in the share of the poor among those affected, or as a rise in the capacity to absorb losses. The displacement series speaks to the first reading only, and imperfectly, because it counts movements and not the poor.

The widening of reporting adds a further caution. Coverage rose from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, out of 199 that have reported in any year. Some of the increase in counts may reflect better recording, not greater harm. Inequality among countries also grew over the same years, with the Gini coefficient moving from 0.57 to 0.68, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. Disparity within regions is now a larger part of the picture, which a regional average conceals.

The broader measure of exposure, the share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, ends in 2009 and cannot be set beside recent years. The disaster risk reduction score, from self-assessments for 83 countries ending in 2011, is likewise too old and too subjective to show what has changed since 2015.

The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre and the World Bank should publish the displacement series together with a note on the countries reporting each year, so that rising counts are not mistaken for rising harm.
Regional bodies and the authors of future goal reviews should track disparity among countries within each region, since the between-region share of inequality has fallen.
The parties to the Sendai Framework should set a quantified level for target 1.5, so that progress to 2030 can be judged against a threshold.
