w-c05-2-1~cedar/writer-4~65.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

The headline figure for children of primary school age who are out of school is a sum of group totals, and it needs to be read with that in mind. Adding the four income groups' counts gives about 87.5 million children in 2025, set against about 87.4 million in 2015. The title rounds this to 88 million. The two totals are almost identical, which means a decade that began with the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals has ended with no reduction in the number of children outside school.

The composition beneath that flat total has changed. Low-income countries counted 30.1 million out-of-school children in 2025, up from 26.0 million in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million over the same period. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. The fall in the lower middle income group offset the rises elsewhere, so the global sum conceals a movement of the burden toward the poorest countries. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest share, about 46.4 million of the total, because they contain very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate.

The figures must not be taken as a global estimate. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, as the results record, while the series itself holds a much wider coverage across its history, 198 countries for the count. A sum built on so few reporters in the latest year depends on which countries happened to report, and the group totals may reflect different country sets in 2015 and 2025. The comparison between the two years is therefore indicative of direction only. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, and those in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count as out of school. Rises in some groups may partly reflect late entry or enrolment in pre-primary classes rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. A total that has not fallen since 2015 implies that the first decade of the goals did not close that gap. The years after 2020 sit in the same data window, and the interruption of schooling during the pandemic, together with conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries, are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up. The available results do not separate these effects, so they cannot be attributed with precision.

For 2030, the implication is that the arithmetic is unfavourable. With the global count unchanged over ten years, ending exclusion in the five that remain would require a rate of decline that the period to 2025 has not shown. The rates in the following part show where that difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries. The ratio between the two is about 9.64. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall steadily as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. Fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was therefore outrun by demography.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest number of out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. Much of the global stability in the total, noted earlier, reflects this gain being offset by increases elsewhere.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015. This is a rise of 5.6 percentage points, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion deepens as children grow older: many enter school, few progress, and costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push them out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, adolescent exclusion was broadly flat or slightly lower. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest and where the cohorts are growing fastest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which two in five lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, with a small excess of boys in every income group. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys. The sexes are therefore not far apart, though here girls are the larger group. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys, so the girls' count rose by about 2.17 million over the decade and the boys' by about 1.90 million. The gap in low-income countries widened slightly in absolute terms and remains in the girls' disadvantage.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' exclusion fell faster than boys' there, by about 3.13 million against about 2.44 million. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in all three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

The direction of the sex difference thus changes with national income: girls are the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, the barriers that fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, remain active. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. Only 8 countries are reporting in 2025 in these series, so the group totals rest on thin and uneven reporting, and part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Where the data end at the national level, parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are also well-established pressures after the pandemic. The data do not separate these causes.

The country classes confirm that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are numerous, while the population share on track is nearly as large.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents are the weakest point. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, while every other group held steady or improved slightly. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, so that picture rests on thin and uneven coverage. A pattern in which exclusion grows as children pass the end of primary school is consistent with fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and with too few secondary places, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.

Governments of low-income countries and their development partners should direct education financing to access in the poorest systems, covering school places, removal of fees and support for the poorest households, since these countries show stagnation at primary age.

Ministries of education and donors should prioritise lower secondary access in low-income countries, where exclusion rose to 41.7% in 2025, through more places, transport and measures that keep girls and boys enrolled past primary level.

The United Nations statistical system and national governments should monitor the 95 regressing countries individually, and the monitoring should state explicitly whether the target is read as zero exclusion or as a tolerated residual share.

w-c05-5-1~juniper/writer-3~65.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small, but its direction is not the one that Target 4.5 requires, and it should be read with caution: in the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not of eliminating those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.9970 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.9968 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.9949 in North America and 0.9910 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.9822. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.9696 in 2015 to 0.9762 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.9910 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.8678 in 2015 and 0.9003 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.9524 to 0.9646. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.0182 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.0517, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. This reversal is well established in the literature: where boys leave school early for paid work, or where girls are kept in school longer by policy and by labour-market incentives, the index rises above 1.00. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.0102 to 0.9819 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.9929.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.1221 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.2911 and North America 1.3008, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.1534, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.1275, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.0577 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.9540 to 1.0285. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.7942 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.7345 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.3008 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.9263 at primary level in 2020, 0.8187 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.6719 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.9919 at primary level in 2020, 0.9966 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.0377 at tertiary level in 2024, and so have reached parity or passed it at every level. The low-income group is the only one in which girls and women are under-represented at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. The coefficient of variation was 0.11. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison, and the male series has the same coverage in the shelf's description. In 2025, however, only 11 countries have reported. The count was 110 in 2024, and reporting for the latest year is always incomplete because national statistics reach the international database after a lag. The 2025 figure is therefore a feature of data release, not evidence that countries stopped collecting, but the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is not one. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and so the narrowing of a gap that favoured girls pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. A change of this kind in a high-income region may reflect shifts in enrolment among older adolescents, but the data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that remain to the disadvantage of girls are concentrated at two levels and in two regions. At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.9003 in 2020, up from 0.8678 in 2015, and low-income countries stood at 0.8187, up from 0.8062. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.9524 to 0.9646 over the same years. Both regions are closing the gap, but at these rates parity by 2030 is uncertain. For Sub-Saharan Africa the tertiary index of 0.7942 in 2021 shows that the gap widens at higher levels, and the low-income figure of 0.6719 in 2021 is lower still.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.2911 in 2024 and North America 1.3008, while Europe and Central Asia reached 1.1534 and high-income countries 1.2086. Target 4.5 asks for the elimination of disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, and an index well above 1.00 is a disparity of a different kind. In South Asia the tertiary index crossed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the lower-middle-income group did likewise, from 0.9593 to 1.0377.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024, so recent completion gaps cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, which is too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow. They concern reporting, survey coverage, retention of girls in the lagging regions, and monitoring of boys at tertiary level.

w-c04-8-1~tamarind/writer-2~66.text:
### Service coverage has widened, but the world is far from universal

The UHC service coverage index stood at 68.0 index points for the world in 2015 and at 71.0 in 2023, the latest year for which all 193 countries report. The index is a composite of 14 tracer indicators spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases and service capacity and access. It runs from 0 to 100, and a score of 100 is the natural reading of 'universal' in target 3.8. That reading is one of several. The target also names financial risk protection and access to safe, affordable medicines, which the index does not measure directly, and a country may score high on tracer services while leaving households exposed to heavy costs. The index should therefore be read as a measure of the breadth of essential services, not as a verdict on the whole target.

On that measure, the gain over eight years was 3.0 points, and the world remained 29.0 points short of 100 in 2023. The shortfall is large because the tracer indicators include services that are hard to extend to everyone, such as the control of hypertension and diabetes and the capacity of facilities, alongside those that are easier to scale, such as vaccination and antenatal care. A composite also moves slowly, since a gain in one area can be offset by stagnation in another.

The income groups show the same ordering at both dates. Low-income countries scored 41.2 in 2015 and 43.8 in 2023, a rise of 2.6 points. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6, and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. High-income countries, which started closest to the ceiling, added 1.9 points, so they were not saturated and also kept improving. The lower-middle-income group gained most, 5.5 points. The poorest group, which has the most to gain, gained least in absolute terms, and it remained in 2023 below the level the lower-middle-income group had reached in 2015.

The gap between countries narrowed slightly, though not by much. Among the 193 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the index fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index fell from 0.030 to 0.024. Convergence is therefore real, but it takes place at a low overall level. Most of the inequality lies between regions: the between-region share of the Theil index was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, so where a person lives, more than differences within a region, accounts for the variation in service coverage. Because the weighting is by population, the improvement in the large South Asian economies, whose regional score rose from 60.0 to 68.0, accounts for much of the narrowing. The regional pattern is taken up in the next part.

The pace matters for 2030. A rise of 3.0 points in eight years, set against a distance of 29.0 points, shows that universality by 2030 was not within reach on the present trajectory. Whether the period after 2020 slowed progress cannot be judged from these figures alone, since the series offers only the endpoints reported here and the latest year is 2023.

### Regions differ widely in coverage and in out-of-pocket burden

Coverage differs more between regions than any single year-on-year change in the world average would suggest. In 2023 North America scored 88.0 index points on the UHC service coverage index, Europe and Central Asia 82.0, East Asia and Pacific 80.0 and Latin America and the Caribbean 79.0. South Asia stood at 68.0, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 66.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 50.0. The gap between the top and bottom regions was therefore 38.0 points, a distance that no region other than Sub-Saharan Africa comes close to approaching from below.

The direction of travel differs as well. South Asia made the largest regional gain, from 60.0 in 2015 to 68.0 in 2023, and moved from below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 76.0 to 80.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 45.0 to 50.0. Latin America and the Caribbean did not move at all, at 79.0 in both years, which means it was overtaken in pace by regions that started lower. North America, already near the top, added 1.0 point. Income groups tell a consistent story: low-income countries moved from 41.2 to 43.8, lower-middle-income countries from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6 and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. The low-income gain of 2.6 points was smaller than the gains of the other three groups, so the poorest countries are improving, but not fast enough to close the distance.

Out-of-pocket spending adds a second view of the same divide. As a share of current health expenditure it was 11.1% in North America in 2023, 16.5% in Europe and Central Asia, 26.0% in East Asia and Pacific, 28.3% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 29.7% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 30.4% in Sub-Saharan Africa and 46.6% in South Asia. The world figure was 17.3%, down from 18.4% in 2015. South Asia is the striking case: its share fell from 64.3% to 46.6%, the largest fall of any region, yet it remains the highest. Households there still pay nearly half of all health spending directly, which is a consequence of low public funding and a large private provider sector rather than of any shortage of services alone. Latin America and the Caribbean and East Asia and Pacific moved the other way, from 28.2% to 29.7% and from 25.7% to 26.0%, so reliance on household payments grew slightly even where coverage was already high.

The share of health spending paid out of pocket and the share of people suffering hardship are related but not the same thing. Hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on health, affected 26.0% of the world population in 2022, against 28.0% in 2015. By region it ranged from 7.5% in North America and 13.0% in Europe and Central Asia to 20.3% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 26.5% in East Asia and Pacific, 27.5% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 31.7% in South Asia and 35.2% in Sub-Saharan Africa. Sub-Saharan Africa thus has the highest hardship even though South Asia has the highest out-of-pocket share. The reason is that where incomes are low, even a modest absolute payment can consume most of what remains after basic needs. In three regions, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, hardship rose slightly between 2015 and 2022, and in North America it was nearly flat, from 7.4% to 7.5%. High-income countries as a group moved from 9.5% to 9.7%. Hardship estimates rest on household surveys that are fielded irregularly, and only three countries report for 2024, so these regional values are modelled and carry wider uncertainty than the service index.

The spread among countries on the service index narrowed. The Gini coefficient, weighted by population, fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.030 to 0.024. This is convergence, and it is the right direction. Yet the share of the Theil index lying between regions was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, essentially unchanged. About seven-tenths of the inequality in coverage is therefore explained by which region a country belongs to, and the narrowing has come about by lifting the whole distribution rather than by dissolving regional divides. For 2030 this means that national averages hide a structure: a country in Sub-Saharan Africa starts from a position that regional peers share, and policies that raise coverage must be judged against that regional floor.

### Coverage gains were modest and financial protection moved unevenly

Financial protection improved only slightly at the global level between 2015 and 2023, and the improvement was concentrated in a few regions. The world share of current health expenditure paid directly by households fell from 18.4% in 2015 to 17.3% in 2023. The share of people facing financial hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on out-of-pocket health costs, fell from 28.0% in 2015 to 26.0% in 2022. Both movements are in the right direction, but they are small beside the scale of the problem. More than one person in four still sits above the hardship threshold in the latest year with broad data.

The global averages conceal opposite movements. South Asia accounts for much of the fall in the out-of-pocket share, which dropped from 64.3% in 2015 to 46.6% in 2023, and the lower middle income group fell from 58.3% to 47.0% over the same years. Low income countries moved from 53.0% to 44.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan also fell, to 30.4% and 28.3% respectively. These are large reductions, yet they began from very high levels, and in South Asia nearly half of health spending is still paid at the point of care. In East Asia and Pacific the out-of-pocket share edged up from 25.7% to 26.0%, and in Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 28.2% to 29.7%. Europe and Central Asia (17.8% to 16.5%), North America (11.9% to 11.1%) and high income countries (14.4% to 13.4%) declined modestly from low bases.

The hardship measure tells a different story from the spending share, and the difference matters. East Asia and Pacific shows a clear fall in hardship, from 30.0% to 26.5%, although its out-of-pocket share did not fall. This shows that the two measures are not interchangeable: hardship depends on household budgets, prices and the burden of illness as well as on how the system is financed. In Europe and Central Asia hardship rose from 12.6% to 13.0%, in Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.5% to 20.3%, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 27.0% to 27.5%. North America moved from 7.4% to 7.5% and high income countries from 9.5% to 9.7%. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the highest at 35.2% in 2022, down from 38.7%, and South Asia stood at 31.7%, down from 35.7%. Low income countries fell from 38.5% to 34.7% and lower middle income countries from 34.4% to 31.5%, while upper middle income countries moved from 26.5% to 24.9%. Hardship is therefore not confined to the poorest countries: in several middle and high income regions it is stagnant or worsening, which reflects the rising cost of care for chronic conditions, medicines and long-term services that public schemes often cover only in part.

The country-level classification confirms the unevenness. Of 72 countries assessed against the direction of the target, 27 are on track or have met it, holding 34.0% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 9 show moderate progress needing acceleration (9.5%), and 4 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration (22.7%). One country is stagnant, and 31 are regressing, holding 33.7% of the assessed population. Regression is thus as common as success, and the two groups are of similar demographic weight. No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures only direction of travel and not distance to a defined goal; the reading of target 3.8 as a call for financial risk protection for all leaves open what level of hardship would count as acceptable.

Public funding appears to matter. Across 21 countries with data for both series, the share of people in hardship is negatively associated with the share of health spending funded from domestic government sources. The rank correlation is -0.525 for 2022 levels and -0.258 for changes between 2015 and 2022. The level association is moderate, and the association for changes is weak. This is association rather than proof of cause: richer countries tend to have both higher public shares and lower hardship, and the weaker link in changes suggests that raising the public share does not by itself reduce hardship, whose course also depends on what is covered, on prices and on who is reached.

The evidence base itself is uneven. Hardship has thinner coverage than the service index, with 3 countries reporting in 2024 against 22 for the out-of-pocket share, so regional aggregates rest on survey years that differ between countries. Movements of one or two points in a regional hardship figure should be read with caution. The broad picture is nevertheless consistent: protection improved where out-of-pocket reliance was highest, and it stalled or reversed in regions that had already moved furthest on coverage.

### At the current pace, 2030 will be missed, and proposals follow

The trend assessment leaves little room for optimism about 2030. Measured against a target of 100 index points, no country is on track for the UHC service coverage index: 0 of 193 countries assessed are on track or have met the target. Only 2 countries, holding 17.3% of the population, show moderate progress that would still need acceleration. A further 102 countries, holding 64.7% of the population, show marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Another 57 countries, holding 11.0% of the population, stagnate, and 32 countries, holding 7.0% of the population, regress. Most of the world's people therefore live in countries where coverage is rising too slowly to matter for the target. The reading depends on the target. Target 3.8 sets no numerical threshold, and 100 index points is a convention that no health system has reached in practice. Judged against it, the assessment is severe by construction, but the direction of the finding holds under a gentler yardstick, because the projected 2030 values sit well below any plausible aspiration.

The projections show the scale of the shortfall. The world is expected to reach 73.7 index points in 2030, a ratio of 0.18 of the pace needed. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 54.8 index points, with a ratio of 0.18, and low-income countries at 46.2, a ratio of 0.09 that the assessment classes as stagnation. Lower middle income countries are projected at 67.6, with a ratio of 0.25. South Asia has the fastest pace of any region and is projected at 75.9 index points in 2030, a ratio of 0.40, still short of what the target requires. Latin America and the Caribbean is projected to stay at 79.0, with a ratio of 0.00. Even high-income countries, projected at 86.9 with a ratio of 0.21, and North America, projected at 88.9, fall short of the target. The gap between the poorest and richest groups therefore does not close. The groups with the most to gain advance slowly, and the groups with the highest coverage have reached a plateau at which further gains are hard to win.

Financial protection tells a more divided story. Among the 72 countries with enough data to assess the hardship indicator, 27 countries, holding 34.0% of their population, are on track or have met the target. Another 9, holding 9.5%, show moderate progress. Against this, 31 countries, holding 33.7% of their population, are regressing, and 4 more, holding 22.7%, show marginal progress. Only 1 country stagnates. Progress is real in some places, but the regressing group is nearly as large in population as the group that is succeeding, and the assessment covers only 72 of the countries that report the coverage index. Reading the two assessments together, coverage of services is advancing too slowly almost everywhere, while financial protection is improving in some countries and deteriorating in others, so that the two cannot be assumed to move together.

Public financing is the clearest lever. Across 21 countries with data for both series from 2015 to 2022, the rank correlation between the level of financial hardship and the domestic government share of current health expenditure was -0.52. Countries that fund more of their health spending from public sources tend to have fewer households in hardship. The rank correlation between the changes in the two series was weaker, at -0.26, so a rise in public financing did not reliably produce a fall in hardship within the period. The sample is small and the association is not proof of cause, but it agrees with the long-established finding that pooled, prepaid funding protects households better than direct payment at the point of care.

The following proposals follow from these findings.

w-c05-8-1~cedar/writer-1~66.text:
### Education spending averages 3.6 per cent of GDP and 14 per cent of government budgets

Two measures describe how much of a country's resources goes to schooling. The first expresses general government expenditure on education as a share of gross domestic product, and shows the weight of public education in the whole economy. The second expresses the same expenditure as a share of total government expenditure, and shows the priority given to education within the public budget. The two can diverge: a government may hold education's place in its budget steady while the economy, and the budget with it, changes in size.

On the first measure, the world figure fell from 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023. That is a decline of about 0.6 percentage points over eight years, in a period that includes the shock of 2020, when output contracted in most economies and public budgets were redirected towards health and income support. The decline is not a matter of a few outliers alone, since the world figure is an aggregate across many reporting countries. Coverage matters here: the latest year nominally available is 2025, but only 2 countries reported GDP-share data for that year, so the most recent usable world figure is for 2023.

On the second measure, the picture is different. The world share of government expenditure was 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, essentially unchanged. For this series 60 countries reported in 2025, a much fuller recent record than for the GDP share, though the world aggregate shown here also ends in 2023.

The two results can be reconciled without contradiction, but they cannot be read as a single verdict. If education held a constant slice of government spending while its share of GDP fell, then total government spending relative to GDP must have fallen too, or the country mix behind the world aggregate shifted. Either way, a steady budget share does not guarantee that schools are better financed in relation to national income. It also does not show how much is spent per pupil, which depends on the number of children, on prices and on the exchange rate, none of which these series capture.

Neither target sets a numeric benchmark for these indicators. Target 4.1 concerns completion of free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education, and target 4.c concerns the supply of qualified teachers; spending is an input to both, not a measure of either. Judgements here therefore rest on direction of change alone. On that reading, the fall in the GDP share after 2015 is an adverse movement, and the flat budget share is neither progress nor retreat. Reaching either target by 2030 would be harder on a shrinking base of public resources, a point developed in the parts that follow.

### Regions differ by two percentage points of GDP, and country spread is widening

Regional averages of public education spending span roughly two percentage points of GDP. North America spent 4.8 per cent of GDP in 2022, almost unchanged from 4.8 per cent in 2015. Europe and Central Asia stood at 4.6 per cent in 2022, down from 4.8 per cent in 2015. At the other end, South Asia spent 2.9 per cent in 2024, up slightly from 2.7 per cent in 2015, and Sub-Saharan Africa spent 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent. The gap between the highest and lowest region is therefore about two points, and it has barely narrowed since 2015.

The movements after 2015 differ by region. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the one region with a marked rise, from 3.7 per cent in 2015 to 4.4 per cent in 2022. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 4.4 per cent to 3.8 per cent in 2023, a period that includes the fiscal strain of the pandemic and its aftermath. East Asia and Pacific held at about 3.5 per cent throughout. The world average fell because the larger declines occurred in regions with large populations and in the lower-middle-income group, not because most regions cut spending.

The ordering changes when spending is measured against the budget rather than the economy. Latin America and the Caribbean devoted 16.6 per cent of government expenditure to education in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa 15.4 per cent, whereas North America devoted 10.7 per cent in 2022 and Europe and Central Asia 11.7 per cent. Regions with small tax bases and young populations therefore give education a large share of what they spend, yet this still yields a small share of national income. Priority within the budget cannot compensate for a limited budget. For these regions, raising revenue matters as much as the allocation decision.

The spread among countries has widened. The population-weighted Gini coefficient of spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.181 in 2015 to 0.210 in 2020 and 0.230 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.091 and then 0.110 over the same years. The share of this inequality lying between regions was 23.8 per cent in 2015 and 27.0 per cent in 2020, but fell to 10.5 per cent in 2023. Differences now lie increasingly among countries within the same region, so regional averages conceal growing divergence and regional policy alone cannot address it.

A caution applies to the 2023 comparison. The 2023 figures cover 121 countries against 164 in 2015, and the missing countries are not a random subset. Late reporting tends to come from countries with weaker statistical systems, so the rise in inequality may partly reflect who reported rather than what was spent. The direction from 2015 to 2020, when 164 and 170 countries reported, is more secure than the level reached in 2023.

### Most countries regressed, and the two measures move together only moderately

Classified against a trajectory towards higher spending, most countries moved the wrong way. Of 186 countries assessed on the share of GDP, 98 regressed, and these hold 62.3 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 40 were on track or had met the direction of travel, covering 11.1 per cent of that population. The remainder were spread across moderate progress (14 countries), marginal progress (20 countries) and stagnation (14 countries). No numerical target exists for either measure, so the classes describe direction and pace, not distance from a goal; the reading depends on the assumption that an increase is the desired movement.

The budget share tells a harsher story. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 regressed, holding 78.2 per cent of the population, while 29 were on track, holding 7.1 per cent. Stagnation affected 23 countries with 10.5 per cent of the population. That the population share of regression exceeds the country share on both measures indicates that several very populous countries lost ground, which weighs heavily on any global reading of Goal 4 financing.

Spending levels did not draw together. Across 146 countries, the regression of change in the GDP share on its 2015 level gave a beta of -0.00559 (p 0.64, R2 0.004), which is indistinguishable from no convergence. Low spenders did not catch up, and high spenders did not fall back. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.379 in 2015 to 0.449 in 2022, so dispersion widened in relative terms. Countries starting with little did not close the gap, which matters for target 4.c and target 4.1, since teacher supply and free schooling depend on a stable funding base.

The two measures are related, but only moderately. Across 131 countries, the Spearman correlation of changes between 2015 and 2022 was 0.415, and that of 2022 levels was 0.468. A fall in the GDP share therefore partly accompanies a lower priority for education within the budget. The rest reflects other fiscal movements: a country may keep its budget share while the whole public sector shrinks relative to output, or output may rise faster than outlays during recovery. The reverse also holds, as education may gain priority within a budget that is itself contracting.

These data cannot identify causes. The post-2015 and post-2020 periods included commodity price falls, pandemic spending on health and income support, rising debt service and, in some cases, rapid growth in GDP that diluted ratios. Which of these drove each country's result cannot be read from two ratios. The classification also rests on the quality of trend fitting for short and gappy series. For 2030, the pattern implies that present trajectories will not lift most countries' spending, and that improving one measure does not guarantee the other.

### Reaching 2030 requires reversing the fall in spending and improving reporting

The implication for 2030 is plain: targets 4.1 and 4.c are paid for from budgets. Free primary and secondary schooling, and a larger supply of qualified teachers, depend mainly on wages, which make up most current spending in education. The world average for public education spending stood at 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 and at 3.6 per cent in 2023. A fall of that size leaves less room for hiring, training and retaining teachers at the moment when enrolment pressure remains high in the poorest countries. Neither target sets a numerical spending level, so the direction of travel is the only yardstick available, and it points the wrong way.

The decline is not uniform, and the places where it is least affordable deserve attention. South Asia, at 2.9 per cent of GDP in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent in 2015, remain below the world average. Low-income countries spent 3.0 per cent in 2022, against 3.2 per cent in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 4.1 per cent to 3.4 per cent between 2015 and 2023. These are the groups with the largest school-age populations, so a given share of income buys less per learner there than anywhere else.

Monitoring is also weakening. The number of countries reporting the share of GDP rose to 171 in 2017 and stood at 164 in 2022, but fell to 121 in 2023 and to 40 in 2024, with only 2 in 2025. Part of this is the ordinary lag of reporting, and the latest years will fill in. Even so, any reading of the period after 2020 rests on a thinning sample, and the averages for 2023 and 2024 may shift when late reporters arrive. Where data are missing, the position of a country cannot be told from the figures.

A further caution concerns interpretation. No single share defines adequate spending, and a country may spend a modest share of income efficiently, or a large share poorly. The share of GDP and the share of the budget answer different questions, and neither says what is spent on each child.

w-c02-3-1~loom/writer-4~67.text:
### Social protection reaches just over half of the world's population

Social protection and labour programmes reached 56.3% of the world's population in 2021, according to the World Bank's ASPIRE database, which draws on nationally representative household surveys. That is the single reading the bench holds for the world aggregate. The result lists the same value for its first and latest year, so it describes a position and not a change. It cannot show whether coverage rose after 2015 or fell after 2020, and no claim about either period can rest on it.

The indicator counts the share of people participating in social insurance, social safety nets, unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes, and its estimates include indirect beneficiaries, such as family members who live in a household where someone receives a benefit. The measure is therefore generous in one respect: a household with one pensioner counts as covered throughout. It is also broad in what it admits. Contributory pensions, health insurance, paid sick leave, cash transfers, food transfers, training and wage subsidies all count. A figure of 56.3% thus says that just over half of people live in households touched by at least one such programme. It does not say how adequate the benefit is, how regular it is, or whether it replaces a meaningful part of income.

The distinction matters because target 1.3 is about the poor and the vulnerable, not about the population as a whole. Coverage of everyone is a poor proxy for coverage of those in poverty. In wealthier countries, much of the population is covered through social insurance linked to formal employment, and a high national figure can coexist with gaps among informal workers, rural households and people outside the labour market. Conversely, a country with a modest overall figure may target its safety nets tightly on the poorest. The all-population series should therefore be read as an outline of the system's reach, with the coverage of the poorest quintile, taken up in a later part, as the closer test of the target.

The wording of the target also allows more than one reading. It calls for nationally appropriate systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. Neither 'substantial' nor 'vulnerable' carries a numeric threshold. A reader may take substantial to mean a majority, near-universal coverage of the poorest, or simply a clear rise from a starting point. Vulnerability can be defined by a poverty line, by exposure to shocks, or by life-cycle risks such as old age, disability and childhood. With no agreed benchmark, the 56.3% figure cannot be graded as met or missed. It can only be compared across groups of countries and, when repeated readings exist, across time.

The data have further limits. The world value rests on surveys that are carried out in different years in different countries, so a single reference year of 2021 is an alignment of estimates, not a simultaneous census. Only 1 country reports for 2023, the latest year in the series, so the most recent period is almost empty and the bench cannot say what became of coverage as pandemic emergency programmes were wound down. Coverage of 130 countries is substantial but not complete, and the countries missing are often those with weaker statistical systems and, plausibly, weaker protection. The world figure should accordingly be taken as indicative.

For 2030, the finding is that just under half of the world's people were outside any recorded programme in 2021, and that the target's own language leaves the finish line undefined. The next parts show where the gaps lie.

### Coverage differs sharply between regions and income groups

Regional coverage in 2021 spans a range of about twenty-two percentage points. South Asia records the highest share, at 72.5% of the population, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 63.7% and East Asia and Pacific at 61.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 54.5%, and the grouping of Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is lowest, at 50.6%. Only South Asia and the two best-placed regions lie above the world figure of 56.3%; the other two regions fall below it.

The South Asian figure should be read with care. The indicator counts direct and indirect beneficiaries, so a household is counted as covered when any member takes part in a programme. Large public works schemes, food transfers and subsidised in-kind programmes, which are widespread in the region, can therefore lift the headline share well above what the poorest households receive in cash. Coverage of a population is not adequacy of benefits: the indicator records participation, not the value of transfers, their regularity or whether they lift a household above a poverty line. A high share and a deep floor are different things.

The contrast between income groups is wider than that between regions. Low-income countries reach 18.3% of their people, against 55.1% in lower-middle-income countries, a gap of roughly three to one. The summary supplied to this part is truncated beyond the lower-middle-income group, so the upper-middle-income and high-income values of 62.2% and 77.8% appear in the facts held but the series behind them is not examined here; they confirm that coverage rises with income, though the step from lower-middle to upper-middle income is small at 7.1 percentage points, far smaller than the step from low to lower-middle income.

The low-income figure matters most for target 1.3, which asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable. Extreme poverty is concentrated in low-income and fragile countries, and these are the places where fewer than one person in five is reached. Causes are well established: narrow tax bases, limited administrative capacity, large informal economies in which contributory insurance does not reach workers, and heavy reliance on short-lived, donor-funded projects instead of permanent national systems. Higher-income countries combine payroll-based insurance with tax-funded pensions and family benefits, which together cover most of the population.

The evidence has limits. Every level quoted is for 2021, and the result lists the same value as first and latest year for each group. No change since 2015 or since 2020 can therefore be stated for any region or income group, and the pandemic's expansion of emergency transfers cannot be separated from lasting coverage. Only one country reports for 2023, so the most recent survey year is almost empty. The ordering of regions is firm for 2021; its movement over time is not shown by these data.

### Coverage of the poorest quintile has regressed in many countries with data

The trend classification for the poorest-quintile measure of social safety net coverage is the least encouraging result of the section. Of 55 countries assessed, 19 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 33.4% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 2 countries show moderate progress, needing acceleration, with 12.4% of that population, and 4 show marginal progress, with 2.2%. Another 4 are stagnant, with 3.1%. Regression is recorded in 26 countries, which hold 48.9% of the population. Regression is the largest single class by country count and by population, so coverage of the poorest fifth fell in nearly half of the assessed countries, weighted by people.

The classification needs a careful reading. Target 1.3 sets no numeric threshold for coverage of the poor. It asks for substantial coverage by 2030, and the phrase can be read in more than one way: a majority of the poorest quintile, near-universal coverage, or simply a rising share. The trend tool therefore has no value to reach and judges direction alone. A country counted as on track is one whose coverage has risen at a pace the tool treats as consistent with improvement, not one that has been shown to reach any agreed level. Equally, a country counted as regressing may still cover a large share of its poorest households, having fallen from a higher level. The classes describe movement, not adequacy.

Several well-established causes could lie behind a fall. Coverage is measured as the share of people in the poorest quintile who take part in programmes, and it falls when programmes are closed, shrunk or left without indexation while the population grows. It also falls when emergency schemes introduced in a crisis are wound down. Changes in survey design and in the list of programmes captured can move the figure without any change in what households receive. The data cannot separate these explanations, and the section does not claim to.

The reliability of any trend depends on how often countries are observed, and here the record is thin and uneven. Only 2 countries reported in 2000 and 3 in 2002. Reporting rose to 11 in 2005, 36 in 2010 and 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013 before recovering to 35 in 2014. It reached 47 countries in 2018, the best-observed year, and was 36 in 2019. Reporting then dropped to 24 in 2020 and recovered to 30 in 2021. Only 17 countries reported in 2022 and a single country in 2023. In all, 121 countries have reported in at least one year, but no single year approaches that number.

This pattern has two consequences. First, the years after 2020 are poorly observed. Surveys are fielded with a delay and processed into the database later, so the thinning of 2022 and 2023 partly reflects lag and not an end to measurement. The effect of the pandemic and of the withdrawal of emergency support on the poorest households is therefore largely invisible in these data, and the regressions recorded cannot be assigned with confidence to the period after 2015 or to the period after 2020. Second, the countries that appear in any trend are those with surveys at both ends of their series, and these may differ systematically from the countries that are never observed twice. Conclusions drawn from the 55 assessed countries should not be extended to the other countries without that caution.

A separate question is whether the whole-population measure can stand in for the poorest quintile where the latter is missing. The links tool compares changes and levels for the two measures across 18 countries between 2015 and 2021. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.928, and that of 2021 levels is 0.909. Countries that gained or lost coverage for the whole population largely did so for the poorest quintile too, and countries with high overall coverage also tend to cover their poorest households well. The association is strong in rank terms.

The sample is small, however, at 18 countries, and a rank correlation says nothing about the gap between the two measures in any one country. High overall coverage can coexist with weak targeting of the poor, and the correlation does not test that. It supports using the whole-population series as a rough guide to direction where the poorest-quintile series is absent, but not as a substitute for it.

For 2030 the implication is sobering. With a direction-only reading, a third of the assessed population is on track, while nearly half lives in countries where coverage of the poorest has slipped. Without a numeric target and with sparse recent data, the world cannot say with confidence how far the poorest are covered or how fast that is changing.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence permits a cautious reading of 2030. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable, yet the world figure of 56.3% in 2021 describes the whole population, not the poor. The only measure aimed at the poorest is the safety net coverage of the poorest quintile, and its trend classification is discouraging: of 55 countries assessed, 26 show regression, and they hold 48.9% of the population of the countries assessed. Only 19 countries are on track or have met the target. If these trajectories continue, the poorest are unlikely to be reliably reached by 2030 in a large part of the sample.

The gap between income groups sharpens this reading. Low-income countries reach 18.3% of their population, against 77.8% in high-income countries, a distance that no plausible rate of expansion closes in the years that remain. Those are the countries where extreme poverty is concentrated and where public budgets and administrative capacity are most constrained. Coverage there depends on donor-financed programmes, which are exposed to funding cycles, and on household registries that are often incomplete. Progress in the middle-income groups, at 55.1% for lower middle income and 62.2% for upper middle income, shows that expansion is feasible, but it does not transfer automatically to the poorest settings.

The evidence base is itself a constraint. Reporting on poorest-quintile safety net coverage peaked at 47 countries in 2018 and fell to 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022, with a single country in 2023. Surveys were thinned precisely when the pandemic raised the need for protection, so what changed after 2020 cannot be read with confidence. The regression recorded in many countries may reflect real losses, a change in survey design or programme definitions, or the ending of temporary schemes; the data cannot separate these.

The target also lacks a numeric reading. Substantial coverage could mean a majority of the poor, or a threshold such as three in four, and the classification of on track or regressing depends on that choice. Until it is fixed, countries can be judged differently by different readers.

The two coverage measures move together. Across 18 countries with data for 2015 to 2021, the rank correlation between changes in poorest-quintile coverage and changes in whole-population coverage is 0.93, and between their 2021 levels it is 0.91. This supports using the broader measure, which is reported by more countries, as a provisional guide where poorest-quintile data are missing. The sample is small, though, and a strong rank correlation does not show that the poorest receive a proportionate share in every country, so the broader figure cannot substitute for the narrower one.

Several proposals follow from these findings.

proposals: National statistical offices, with funding from development partners, should run household surveys that measure social protection on a regular cycle, so that coverage of the poorest quintile can be tracked in every country and not only in those that happen to be surveyed.

The United Nations statistical community and the governments that adopted the goals should agree a numeric reading of substantial coverage under target 1.3, stating the share of the poorest quintile to be reached, so that progress can be judged against a common standard.

Governments of low-income countries and their bilateral and multilateral partners should prioritise extending programmes in low-income countries, with multi-year financing that does not lapse with donor budget cycles.

The World Bank and national agencies should report coverage of the poorest quintile beside the whole-population figure in every release, so that the headline number does not mask the position of the poor.

Analysts and policymakers should use whole-population coverage only as a provisional guide to the position of the poorest, given the strong link between the two measures in a small sample of countries, and should replace it with poorest-quintile data when these become available.

Target 1.3 has no numeric threshold for substantial coverage.
