w-c08-5-1~cedar/writer-3~68.text:
### Private investment in energy infrastructure is concentrated in middle-income economies

Investment in energy with private participation is the one series on the shelf that measures money committed to energy infrastructure in developing countries. It records commitments to projects that have reached financial closure in low- and middle-income countries, where private parties carry operating risk. It therefore speaks to target 7.b, which calls for expanded infrastructure and upgraded technology, and only indirectly to target 7.a, since it says nothing of research, technology transfer or public cooperation. The figures are in current US dollars and are not adjusted for inflation, so a rise over nine years is partly a rise in prices. In 2024, 46 countries reported, a small part of the developing world, and years with no reported project are indistinguishable from years with no data.

The flows are concentrated in upper middle income economies. Their private energy investment rose from US$31.0 billion in 2015 to US$58.4 billion in 2024, so that the group's commitments nearly doubled in nominal terms. Lower middle income economies stood at US$7.4 billion in 2015 and US$7.9 billion in 2024, a gain too small to survive inflation. In real terms, the group's private energy investment has probably fallen. In 2024 the upper middle income group attracted about seven times what the lower middle income group did, a gap that widens the further down the income scale one looks. The series provides no separate reading for low-income countries in the results drawn here, which is itself a sign of how thin the private pipeline is where access needs are greatest.

Regional paths diverge. Latin America and the Caribbean, a region with deep capital markets, established auction systems and a long record of private power concessions, fell from US$11.9 billion in 2015 to US$8.4 billion in 2024. South Asia moved the other way, from US$2.4 billion to US$3.4 billion, though from a base far below its need. Project-based commitments are lumpy: a few large transactions can move a regional total sharply from year to year, so comparing two single years, as here, overstates the clarity of the trend. Neither endpoint should be read as a steady trajectory.

The implication for 2030 is that private capital follows creditworthiness and market size rather than need. Unless public finance and concessional lending reduce risk in lower-income markets, the middle-income concentration seen in 2024 is likely to persist, and the infrastructure behind electricity access will depend on public budgets and aid where private investors do not go. Later parts take up generation and aid flows.

### Regions and income groups differ sharply in capital flows and in renewable generation

Regional and income-group comparisons show that capital and clean generation do not move together. Among regions, Latin America and the Caribbean recorded a fall in private energy investment from US$11.87 billion in 2015 to US$8.40 billion in 2024. South Asia moved the other way, from US$2.39 billion to US$3.45 billion. The Latin American decline is not a sign of retreat from renewables; the region already generates a comparatively large share of its electricity from non-hydro renewable sources, and earlier auction-led waves of investment may have front-loaded commitments. Because the series records commitments at financial closure in a given year, it is lumpy, and two end-point years cannot distinguish a lasting trend from a few large projects.

The income groups show the starkest contrast. Upper middle income countries rose from US$31.02 billion in 2015 to US$58.39 billion in 2024, almost doubling. Lower middle income countries moved from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion, which is a small change in current dollars and therefore a decline once inflation is considered. The series is reported for 46 countries in 2024, so the totals rest on a narrow base of reporters. The group that holds the greatest backlog of unserved households and the weakest grids attracts the smallest private flows.

Non-hydro renewable electricity tells a similar story. The world share rose from 6.6% in 2015 to 12.4% in 2021. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 6.9% to 15.1%, and East Asia and Pacific from 4.8% to 12.0%, both ending above the world average. South Asia rose from 4.6% to 8.5%, still below the world level. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 2.1% to 4.3%, roughly doubling from a low base. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached only 2.9% in 2021, up from 0.6%, a reflection of large fossil fuel endowments and long-established thermal fleets.

By income group, the divergence is sharper still. Upper middle income countries rose from 4.6% to 11.9%, and lower middle income countries from 4.1% to 7.3%. Low income countries fell from 0.7% to 0.5%, the only group to lose ground. For these economies, shares are small enough that a single plant, or a change in total output, can shift the figure, but the direction is clear: the poorest countries are not yet sharing in the solar and wind expansion seen elsewhere. The comparison with high income countries, at 14.1% in 2021, shows that several middle-income regions have nearly closed the gap, while low income countries sit far below it.

The implication for 2030 is that progress is concentrated where capital is already plentiful and institutions are able to contract with private developers. Reaching the poorest countries is likely to need concessional finance and public risk-sharing, since private commitments alone have not flowed there. The latest renewable-share data end in 2021, so effects of the post-2020 recovery and of recent cost declines in solar cannot be read from this series.

### Renewable shares have grown, but the gaps between countries have not closed

Renewable electricity from sources other than hydropower has risen in almost every region since 2015, yet the broader measure of renewable final energy consumption tells a more uneven story. Between 2015 and 2021 the world share of non-hydroelectric renewables in electricity production rose from 6.6% to 12.4%, a trend rate of 0.11 percentage points a year in the tool's reckoning. East Asia and Pacific rose from 4.8% to 12.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 6.9% to 15.1%, and upper middle income countries from 4.6% to 11.9%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 2.1% to 4.3% and South Asia from 4.6% to 8.5%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan started from 0.6% and reached 2.9%, the fastest rate of any group, but from a very low base. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 0.7% to 0.5%, the only group classed as in regression.

The measure of renewable energy in final consumption must be read differently. The low-income share fell from 77.0% in 2015 to 74.6% in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 70.3% in 2020, up from 68.0%. These very high shares do not signal a clean energy system. They mainly reflect traditional biomass, chiefly wood and charcoal burned for cooking, which the indicator counts as renewable. A falling share in a poor country can therefore accompany a shift towards modern fuels, and a rising share elsewhere can reflect genuine growth in solar, wind and other modern sources. The two series should be read together, and the low-income decline is a point of interpretation, not proof of lost ground in clean energy.

The rates in final consumption are slow in the regions that matter most for access. Lower middle income countries moved from 41.7% to 43.3%, South Asia from 34.9% to 36.9%, and Sub-Saharan Africa as noted, each classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan was classed as moderate progress, from 7.1% to 7.5%. High income countries and North America, at 12.8% and 12.5% in 2020, were classed as on track, as were East Asia and Pacific and Europe and Central Asia.

A caution applies to every such label. Target 7.b carries no numerical value, so the classification of on track means only that the trend is rising, not that any threshold will be met by 2030. The labels also say nothing about whether the pace suffices for universal access.

Across 208 countries, the data show no catching up in renewable electricity. The convergence coefficient was -0.004 (p 0.882, R2 0.001), so a country's starting share did not predict its subsequent gain. Dispersion nonetheless narrowed, with the coefficient of variation falling from 1.71 in 2015 to 1.36 in 2021. The two results are compatible: the spread shrank because the world average rose and several large economies expanded quickly, not because poorer or lower-share countries closed on leaders. For 2030, the implication is that growth is broad but not self-correcting, and the lagging low-income group will not converge without deliberate financing.

### International support is under-measured, and 2030 depends on financing the lagging regions

Target 7.a asks for enhanced international cooperation on clean energy research and technology, and the shelf measures it poorly. The only series bearing on it is net official development assistance to the least developed countries, reported by 32 countries in 2023. That series counts concessional grants and loans for every purpose, from health and schooling to governance. It does not isolate what was spent on clean energy research, technology transfer or infrastructure. No figure for energy-specific cooperation can therefore be stated, and the reading of 7.a rests on an indicator that cannot answer the question put to it. The figure attached to this result shows the aggregate flow only.

The other results explain why the gap in measurement matters. Private capital is committed mainly where markets are deep. Upper middle income countries drew about US$58.39 billion in 2024, up from about US$31.02 billion in 2015, while lower middle income countries moved only from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion. Low-income countries, and the least developed countries that ODA is meant to serve, are thinly represented in the private flows. Concessional public money is the instrument best suited to fill that space, yet the evidence cannot show whether it is going there for energy.

The convergence result gives a further warning for 2030. Across 208 countries between 2015 and 2021, the beta coefficient for non-hydroelectric renewable shares was -0.004 (p-value 0.882) with an R squared of 0.001. Starting position therefore explained almost nothing of subsequent growth: laggards did not catch up systematically, and leaders did not pull away in any regular pattern. The coefficient of variation fell from 1.712 to 1.358, so dispersion narrowed somewhat, but without the steady closing that a convergence process would show. Reaching 2030 with lagging regions included will not happen by default. It requires deliberate finance directed to countries that private investors pass over, and a way of seeing whether that finance arrives.

Target 7.b compounds the difficulty, because it carries no numerical benchmark. Expanding infrastructure and upgrading technology for least developed countries, small island developing States and landlocked developing countries can be read in several ways, and progress cannot be judged as on or off course without a threshold.

proposals: Donor governments and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report clean energy research, technology and infrastructure cooperation as a separate flow to each least developed country, so that target 7.a can be measured directly.

Multilateral development banks and bilateral donors should direct concessional public finance to low-income and lower middle income countries, where private capital is thin, rather than relying on private participation to reach them.

The International Energy Agency and the World Bank should publish non-biomass renewable shares separately from total renewable consumption, so that progress in modern clean supply is not masked by traditional biomass.

The United Nations Statistical Commission and member states should set a numerical benchmark for target 7.b, such as per-capita generating capacity in least developed countries, against which progress can be judged.

Installed generating capacity, grid investment and public energy finance are not held, and target 7.b has no numerical threshold.

w-c03-3-2~dahlia/writer-1~68.text:
### Child overweight and anaemia in women stand at 5.5 per cent and 30.7 per cent

Two indicators of malnutrition other than stunting and wasting are measured here: overweight among children under five, and anaemia among women of reproductive age. Target 2.2 names all forms of malnutrition and the nutritional needs of adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, yet its numerical benchmarks cover only stunting and wasting. The two indicators therefore describe parts of the target that carry no quantified goal in the wording given. The overweight series is scored in this section against a reference value of 3.0 per cent by 2030, which is a working benchmark of the bench's trend tool and not a value written into the target. The anaemia series has no benchmark at all.

In 2024 the world prevalence of child overweight, defined as weight for height more than two standard deviations above the WHO 2006 median, was 5.5 per cent of children under five, up from 5.2 per cent in 2015. The rise is small, at about 0.3 percentage points over nine years, but it runs against the direction the target implies. The estimate rests on 163 countries reporting in 2024. It is a modelled estimate, so year-to-year movements are smoothed and partly reflect the model rather than fresh surveys, especially in countries that are surveyed only every few years.

Anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 is far more common. In 2023 the world prevalence was 30.7 per cent, against 28.0 per cent in 2015, an increase of about 2.7 percentage points. The measure combines non-pregnant women with haemoglobin below 12 g/dL and pregnant women below 11 g/dL, and 192 countries are covered. Nearly one woman in three of reproductive age is therefore anaemic, a share that is large but not a majority. The condition matters for maternal health, for birth outcomes and for the nutrition of the next generation of children.

Both series worsened after 2015, and neither has an internationally agreed target value within the goal framework used here. A rise in child overweight is not necessarily a failure of the same kind as a rise in anaemia, since the two reflect different diets and health conditions. Even so, the direction of both indicators is adverse. Haemoglobin measurement also depends on altitude, smoking and survey method, and country estimates are modelled where surveys are scarce. The levels reported here should be read as well-founded orders of magnitude, not as exact counts. For 2030, the starting point is a world in which both burdens are larger than at the outset of the agenda.

### Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower

Regional levels of the two burdens run in opposite directions. Child overweight is lowest in South Asia, at 3.4 per cent of children under five in 2024, and highest in North America, at 9.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 8.8 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 7.8 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa records 3.8 per cent. Anaemia among women aged 15 to 49 reverses the order: North America has the lowest prevalence, 14.9 per cent in 2023, and South Asia the highest, 51.1 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 36.7 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 35.2 per cent, whereas East Asia and the Pacific, at 18.7 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 20.0 per cent, lie near the lower end.

The pattern by income group repeats the regional one. Overweight is 3.5 per cent in low-income countries and 4.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 8.6 per cent in upper-middle-income and 8.4 per cent in high-income countries. Anaemia is 35.6 per cent in low-income and 46.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 19.8 per cent in upper-middle-income and 17.3 per cent in high-income countries. Child overweight is thus highest where anaemia is lowest, and the reverse holds in the poorest regions. This does not mean that the two conditions exclude one another within a country or a household; regional averages cannot show whether both occur together. Lower overweight in the poorest groups should not be read as a sign of better nutrition, since anaemia there remains heavy.

In relative terms the regional gap is wider for anaemia than for overweight. The highest regional anaemia prevalence is more than three times the lowest, at a ratio of 3.43, while the highest regional overweight prevalence is 2.92 times the lowest. Among 192 countries, weighted by population, the between-region share of the Theil index was 77.9 per cent in 2023, up from 74.1 per cent in 2015, so geography accounts for most of the inequality in anaemia. The Gini coefficient fell from 0.287 to 0.272 over the same years. Differences among countries have narrowed slightly overall, yet what remains is increasingly a matter of the region to which a country belongs. Neighbouring countries tend to share their fortunes, which points to regional conditions as well as national policy; the results themselves do not identify the causes.

### Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere

The trend classes show that movement on both indicators has mostly been in the wrong direction since 2015. Child overweight is assessed against a benchmark of 3.0 per cent by 2030, a figure adopted for this book and not written into Target 2.2. Of the 163 countries assessed, 92, holding 66.6 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, meaning that prevalence is rising where the benchmark requires it to fall. Only 33 countries, with 21.3 per cent of the population, are on track or have already met the benchmark. A further 10 countries (2.0 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 20 (7.5 per cent) show marginal progress and 8 (2.6 per cent) are stagnant. A stricter or looser line would change how many countries count as on track, but the direction of travel does not depend on the line.

Regionally, regression is the common pattern. East Asia and Pacific, high-income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are all classed as regressing, as are the low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups. The annual rates of change are small, 0.0153 for East Asia and Pacific and 0.0165 for Latin America and the Caribbean, but they point upward in each case. South Asia shows the fastest rise, at 0.0518, from a low base, so the increase is not confined to richer economies. The regression ratios compare the observed rate with the rate the benchmark requires. They are large in magnitude for low-income and lower-middle-income countries, at -6.09 and -2.37, and smaller for high-income countries, at -0.36. Europe and Central Asia is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.11, and its expected prevalence of 7.32 per cent in 2030 remains far above 3.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the only region with moderate progress, a ratio of 0.67, and its expected 2030 level of 4.36 per cent would still be above the benchmark. At the world level the ratio is -0.21, a regression, with 5.67 per cent expected in 2030.

Anaemia among women of reproductive age shows a more uniform picture. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are regressing. Only 2 countries (1.7 per cent of the population) are on track, 1 shows moderate progress, 9 show marginal progress and 18 are stagnant. Every region and income group is classed as regressing. The world rate of change is 0.0115. Rates are highest in North America, at 0.0359, and in high-income countries, at 0.0239, and lowest in East Asia and Pacific, at 0.0023. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.0202, also rises faster than South Asia, at 0.0070, so the fastest rises are not simply those of the highest-prevalence regions; they are concentrated among regions with lower prevalence. No target value is set for anaemia in this assessment, so the classes measure only whether prevalence is falling.

The spread across countries narrowed slightly. The Theil index fell from 0.130 in 2015 to 0.116 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index rose from 74.1 per cent to 77.9 per cent, so what inequality remains is increasingly a matter of which region a country belongs to. The narrowing does not signal improvement, since prevalence rose in nearly every country. These data identify no causes. Changing diets, shifts in the measurement of haemoglobin and modelled estimates for countries with sparse surveys could each contribute, and none can be separated here. A rise across nearly every country justifies caution about attributing the result to any single national policy.

### The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course

Change and level tell different stories about the two burdens. Across 162 countries, the rank correlation between changes in child overweight and changes in women's anaemia over 2015 to 2023 is -0.030, which is indistinguishable from none. Countries where overweight rose faster were no more and no less likely to see anaemia rise. The correlation of 2023 levels is -0.469, a moderate negative association: countries with higher child overweight tend to have lower anaemia among women. This is a statistical association between levels only. The results do not show why it arises, and they give no sign that one burden displaces the other. Because the two do not move together, a response designed for one cannot be assumed to reach the other.

The outlook for 2030 follows from the trend classes. For child overweight, the world is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -0.207 against the benchmark of 3.0 per cent and an expected 2030 prevalence of 5.7 per cent. North America is expected to reach 10.8 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 9.7 per cent, while high-income countries are expected to reach 9.1 per cent. South Asia has the lowest level but the fastest rise, at a rate of 0.052, and is expected to reach 4.6 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 4.3 per cent, below the world figure but still a regression. Only the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows moderate progress, with an expected 4.4 per cent, and even there the benchmark is not met on the current course.

For anaemia, no numerical target is set, so the classes measure only the direction of travel. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, and only 2 are on track against the benchmark applied. Because that benchmark is not an agreed one, these classes describe direction, not failure against a commitment. The direction is nonetheless adverse. Both findings rest on modelled estimates, which are revised and which smooth over years in which surveys were absent.

The findings support four proposals, set out below. They are drawn from the results above, and the data that would test them are noted under the gaps.

w-c04-4-2~farah/writer-1~68.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.6% for the world by 2030. The same reading is applied to every region and income group, so the regional verdicts that follow in this section rest on that single convention. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool, a linear extrapolation of the 2015-2021 pace, places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, which is a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 divides into three groups: regions where the probability of premature death from the four main non-communicable diseases fell appreciably, regions where it hardly changed, and one region where it rose. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, a respectable decline that still leaves the region above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021. Extended along its own linear path, the region would stand at 18.5% in 2030, against the target value for the world of 12.57%. The trend tool places it at a ratio of 0.39 of the pace the target requires.

The small movers are the two Americas. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America began from the lowest regional level, so a modest fall is less surprising there, yet its pace reaches a ratio of 0.82 of that required, while Latin America and the Caribbean reaches 0.50. Linear extension gives 13.9% for the latter in 2030. Outside the data, it is widely understood that gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking have been offset in part by obesity and diabetes, and by unequal access to treatment; these causes are not measured by the results used here.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, and its pace ratio is negative, at -0.20, which the trend tool labels regression. Linear extension would place the region at 24.0% in 2030. Among regions it had the highest level in 2021, though low-income countries as an income group stood slightly higher, at 23.0%. In 2015 it was marginally below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates between 30 and 70 did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends. Established knowledge points to hypertension, diabetes, air pollution and the cost of long-term treatment as plausible contributors. The period includes the pandemic years, when disrupted screening and chronic care may have raised the 2021 figure; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves its level close to the South Asian one. Its pace ratio is 0.16, and linear extension gives 20.4% in 2030. Measurement is a concern here, since death registration is incomplete and the estimates rely heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, a ratio of 0.22, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, a ratio of 0.00, which is stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. High-income countries alone are classed as on track, with a ratio of 1.93 and a linear value of 11.4% in 2030, which would lie below the target value. The two richer groups improved by about one percentage point each, while the lower-middle group, which contains South Asia's large populations, stood still. The gap between the low-income and high-income groups remained roughly ten percentage points in 2021.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability that all adults experience, but the direction is towards greater inequality. The share of the Theil index lying between regions grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences. All trend readings here are linear extensions of the 2015 to 2021 change, and the target value is derived from the 2015 world baseline applied as a common benchmark, so regional ratios should be read as indications, not forecasts.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.26 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.09 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. The following explanations rest on general knowledge, not on any result of this section, and the data do not separate them. Earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from better treatment of heart disease, and such gains meet diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The years 2020 and 2021 coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions. The series cannot isolate these effects from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.00156 with a p-value of 0.6965 and an R-squared of 0.0011. The coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measures point the same way, though they are not the same statistic. The convergence test reports a coefficient of variation of 0.3596 in 2015 and 0.3798 in 2021, computed across countries without population weights. The spread tool, which weights countries by population, reports a coefficient of variation of 0.2713 in 2015 and 0.2819 in 2021. The levels differ because of the weighting, but both rise. The population-weighted Gini coefficient moved from 0.1519 to 0.1582, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 27.0% to 33.1%. Relative spread widened slightly, and a growing part of it lies between regions, not within them. For a target defined in relative terms this matters, because a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and no systematic acceleration in such countries appears in the convergence result.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.0981 and the Kendall coefficient is 0.0706. Both are weak. Both changes are taken as end value minus start value, so a rise in coverage and a fall in mortality carry opposite signs. If coverage gains went with larger mortality falls, the correlation would be negative. The weak positive value gives no support for that expectation over this short window, though it is too small to show the opposite either.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.2467 by the Spearman measure and -0.1713 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is modest in size, and it is described here as modest throughout, being larger than the correlation of changes but far from strong. It describes a cross-section in which income, age structure, the wider health system and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together, and it cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented. The mortality series is modelled by the World Health Organization from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths can be read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021 and the trend projection, a linear extrapolation of the 2015 to 2021 pace, reaches 17.5% in 2030, so the global ratio of progress is 0.22. A ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target; 0.22 means roughly a fifth of that pace. At the observed rate the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction, and the gap still to be closed is larger than the distance covered since 2015.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, is the nearest of the regions to the required pace, with an expected value of 13.4% in 2030. North America, at 0.82 in the classification, is expected to reach 12.8%, close to the threshold because it began from a low level. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6%, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.50, 13.9%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 0.39, is expected to reach 18.5%, which is marginal progress. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030. That classification should be read with care, since high-income countries began from a lower level, and the target value of 12.57% is itself computed from one baseline.

That is an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions at 22% or more would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above applies the global reading to every region. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected 24.0% in 2030, higher than its 22.9% in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.00 and an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22 and an expected 21.5%. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest, and the gap between income groups is on course to persist.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none. The correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment, chronic respiratory care or the quality of care. A weak link therefore does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the coverage measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality, named in the section's title, cannot be treated here. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. The omission is a gap in this account, not evidence that the matter is minor. Mental health is part of the wording of target 3.4, and the indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover it.

The proposals follow from these findings. They rest partly on established knowledge about prevention, not on a result of this section.

w-c04-1-2~cedar/writer-4~69.text:
### The global ratio fell from 228 to 197 and remains far above 70

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled estimate for the world stood at 228.0 in 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year available. That is a fall of 31 points over eight years, or about 3.9 points a year on average. The ratio in 2023 is still nearly three times the target value.

The arithmetic of the gap is plain. From 197.0 in 2023, a ratio below 70 by 2030 would require a reduction of more than 127 points in seven years, or over 18 points a year. That is between four and five times the average annual fall observed since 2015, about 4.6 times on these figures. The distance does not shrink by small adjustments to the pace; it would require a different trajectory altogether. The trend tool, which extrapolates the rate observed since 2015, expects a world ratio of 173.4 in 2030, and classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The comparison of required and observed pace is made on rounded published figures, and the exact required pace depends on the unrounded estimates.

The target is worded as a global ratio, not as a national one. A global ratio is a weighted outcome: it is pulled down by countries with very low ratios and pulled up by countries with very high ratios, weighted by the number of live births. Because births are concentrated in regions where the ratio is highest, the world figure is governed far more by those regions than by the many countries already below 70. Reading the target as global means that a country-by-country reading is a separate question, which the later parts of this section address. A reading in which every country must fall below 70 would be stricter still, and the wording of the target does not require it.

The quality of the series needs stating plainly. Coverage is not the weakness: the modelled ratio is reported for all 194 countries in every year from 2000 to 2023, so no country drops out of the comparison and no year has gaps. That completeness is however a product of modelling rather than of observation. The estimates are produced by a regression model that draws on the share of maternal deaths among deaths of women aged 15 to 49, fertility, skilled birth attendance and national income. Where civil registration of deaths with causes is incomplete, as it is in many of the countries with the highest ratios, the estimate leans on those covariates rather than on counted deaths. The figures therefore carry uncertainty that the single published value does not display, and a change of a few points between years should not be read as a firm observation.

This uncertainty does not rescue the target. A fall of 31 points is small beside a shortfall of more than 127, and no plausible revision of the model would close a gap of that size. What the uncertainty does affect is the confidence with which any single country or short period can be judged. For the world as a whole, the finding is robust: the ratio is falling, it is falling slowly, and 2030 will arrive with it well above 70 unless the pace changes sharply.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of forty

The spread between regions is wider than any global average suggests. In 2023 the modelled ratio for Sub-Saharan Africa was 448 deaths per 100,000 live births, against 11 for Europe and Central Asia. The gap between those two regions is a factor of about forty, and it is the clearest sign that Target 3.1 is a global average assembled from very unequal parts. Where a woman gives birth, and in which health system, still decides the risk she faces more than any other single circumstance.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593 in 2015 to 448 in 2023, a fall of 145 points, and carries by far the highest ratio of any region. South Asia fell from 173 to 120, a fall of 53 points, and its fall in proportion is the larger of the two. Both remain well above 70. The trend tool reads South Asia as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 against a target of 70, so the shortfall there is modest in scale and could be closed with acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is read as making marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 350.5, about five times the target. Its ratio of progress to the pace required is 0.46, against 0.83 for South Asia. Closing the global gap depends overwhelmingly on the first of these two regions.

Several regions already lie below the threshold. Europe and Central Asia stood at 11 in 2023, down from 14 in 2015, and North America at 16, down from 17. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 54 to 47, and its expected 2030 value is 41.6. These regions are classed as on track, though for the wealthiest the ratio is already so low that further gains are small in absolute terms. East Asia and Pacific fell from 70 to 66, so it sits just below the target. Its expected 2030 value of 62.7 leaves little margin, and the classification rests on a gentle slope rather than on a secure lead.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among regions. Its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is the only region classed as in regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. A region of middle-income countries, with high rates of facility birth, has moved away from the target. Well-established explanations include the disruption of health services during the pandemic years, persistent inequality between urban and rural or Indigenous populations, and the weight of unsafe abortion and hypertensive disorders. The data used here cannot apportion the rise among these causes. It matters because the region was close to the threshold and has moved the wrong way.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 491 in 2015 to 346 in 2023, and are read as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 254.7. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 291 to 235 and are read as making only marginal progress, with an expected value of 194.9 and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.43. That is a slower proportional fall than in the poorest group, and it concerns a larger number of births. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61 to 57, with an expected 2030 value of 53.7, and high-income countries from 11 to 10. The two upper groups are already below 70, so the whole of the remaining distance lies in the lower two.

Country classes confirm that the picture is mixed rather than uniformly poor. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of the classified countries. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country is in stagnation and 7 are in regression, together under 1% of the population. The majority of people live in countries that will reach the target, yet the global average is held up by a minority of countries with very high ratios and large numbers of births. For 2030 this means that the global result will be settled by a few dozen countries, mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and not by the many already at or near the threshold.

### Progress slowed after 2008 and the pandemic years disturbed the series

The series shows that progress was already slowing before the goals were adopted. The breaks analysis identifies a change of regime in 2008. In the segment from 2001 to 2007, the global ratio fell by a mean of 8.4 points a year. In the segment from 2008 to 2019, the mean annual fall was 5.2 points. The pace of decline therefore dropped by about 38% before 2015, and the adoption of the goals did not restore the earlier speed. The measured fall of the post-2015 years continues the slower trend and is not a recovery from it. Well-established explanations include the exhaustion of the easiest gains, such as the expansion of skilled attendance at birth in countries that started from low coverage, and the harder task of reaching the remaining deaths, which are concentrated among women in poor, rural and conflict-affected settings where emergency obstetric care is least available.

The pandemic years then disturbed the series. The annual change was an increase of 4 points in 2020 and an increase of 31 points in 2021. The change reversed to a fall of 39 points in 2022, and the fall in 2023 was 6 points. The pattern is consistent with a shock and a recovery: disrupted maternity services, diversion of health staff and direct deaths from infection in pregnancy are all plausible contributors to the rise, and the return of services would explain the fall. The analysis cannot establish this cause. The ratio is a modelled estimate, built by regression from covariates such as fertility, birth attendance and income, and is not a count of registered deaths. A sharp one-year rise followed by a sharp one-year fall may partly reflect the way the model treats pandemic-era inputs and the revision of estimates. The breaks detected in 2020 to 2023 are single-year segments and should be read as flags, not as stable trends. The 2022 fall should therefore be treated as a modelled rebound and not as a durable gain.

The spread among countries has not narrowed in population-weighted terms. The Gini coefficient of the ratio across 194 countries was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 70.9% in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023, so most inequality is still a matter of regional membership, though the within-region component has grown a little.

Convergence is weak. A regression of change on the starting level across the 194 countries gives a coefficient of -0.00372 with a p-value of 0.0024, but an R-squared of only 0.050. Countries with higher ratios in 2015 tended to fall slightly faster, the direction needed for catching up, yet the starting level explains about 5% of the variation in change. Most of what separates fast improvers from slow ones lies in policy, conflict, financing and the strength of health systems. The convergence analysis, which counts countries equally, gives a coefficient of variation falling from 1.500 to 1.410, a modest narrowing. The population-weighted spread measures rose, and the two views differ because large countries with high ratios have not improved as quickly as the many small ones. For 2030, neither the slowed trend before 2015 nor the weak catching up since offers grounds for expecting the pace to rise. The target depends on a faster fall where the ratio is highest, and the record to 2023 shows no sign that this is under way.

### At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed, and proposals follow

Extending the recent pace to 2030 gives a global ratio of about 173.4 per 100,000 live births, against a target of 70. The trend tool places the world in the class of marginal progress, with a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.35. Reaching the target from the 2023 level of 197.0 would require a fall of about 127 points in seven years, or about 18 points a year, against an average fall of about 3.9 points a year since 2015. The required pace is therefore between four and five times the pace of the past eight years. The target cannot be met by continuing present practice. It would take a change in the scale and the targeting of effort.

The country classification shows where the shortfall lies. In 128 of the 194 countries assessed, the ratio is on track or the target is already met, and these countries hold 74.5% of the classified population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 23 countries, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country stagnates and seven regress, together holding well under 1% of the population. Roughly a quarter of the classified population therefore lives in countries that will miss the target without faster change. A majority of countries being on track does not imply that the global ratio will reach 70, because the global figure is governed by the few places where ratios are very high and births are numerous.

The regional projections confirm this. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 448 in 2023, would reach about 350.5 in 2030 at its present rate, with a ratio of progress of 0.46. South Asia, at 120 in 2023, would reach about 87.1, with a ratio of 0.83, the closest of the regions needing acceleration. Among income groups, low-income countries would reach about 254.7 and lower-middle-income countries about 194.9, with ratios of 0.56 and 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries, at 57 in 2023 and projected at about 53.7 in 2030, and high-income countries, at 10, are on track. East Asia and Pacific, at 66, is also classed as on track, although the margin is narrow, with a projection of about 62.7 in 2030. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the better-placed regions: its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and the trend tool classes it as regression, with a projection of about 79.7 in 2030.

Inequality among countries has not narrowed in the population-weighted measures. The Gini coefficient of country ratios rose from 0.628 in 2015 to 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.739 to 0.793. Differences between regions still account for 67.2% of the Theil index in 2023, down from 71.0% in 2015 (0.7095 before rounding), so the burden remains largely a matter of which region a woman lives in, though within-region differences are gaining weight. The convergence test across the 194 countries, unweighted, finds a small negative coefficient of -0.0037, with an R-squared of only 0.05, so catching-up among countries is weak.

The ratios are modelled estimates, and in many high-burden countries they rest on little direct counting. Any projection to 2030 inherits that uncertainty, and the classification of a single country near the margin should be read with caution.

w-c04-9-1~willow/writer-2~69.text:
### The global picture rests on rates, not counts

The question posed for this section asks for a number of deaths. The evidence retrieved cannot supply one. The only result available is a rate: deaths attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene per 100,000 population, for 2019, across 183 countries. A rate is a count divided by population, so it cannot be turned back into a count without population figures that this result does not carry. No absolute total of deaths from unsafe water appears in the retrieved material, and none is offered here.

The position for air pollution is weaker still. The shelf holds a series on the mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, age-standardised, as well as a series on mean annual exposure to fine particulate matter. Neither was retrieved as a result for this section. Nothing is therefore stated about how many people die from air pollution, how fast the rate is falling, or which regions carry most of it. Any statement on those points would rest on no evidence in hand, and the section declines to make one.

This limit bears on how Target 3.9 is read. The target calls for a substantial reduction in the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and from air, water and soil pollution. The wording can be read as a count, in which case population growth works against progress even when conditions improve, or as a rate, in which case a falling risk counts as success even if the number of deaths stays high. The wording does not settle the matter. The indicator series the World Bank reports measures a rate, and it is the rate that the evidence here can describe. A reader should take any later statement about progress in this section as a statement about risk per head of population, not about the total toll.

The one result that exists does show how unevenly that risk is spread. Across the 183 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the unsafe-water mortality rate in 2019 is 0.53, and the coefficient of variation is 1.03. A coefficient of variation above one means that the spread of national rates is wider than their average, which is the signature of a distribution with a long tail of countries where the risk is far above the norm. The next part examines where that tail lies and how much of the inequality is a matter of region.

### Regions explain most of the inequality between countries

The spread of the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate across the 183 countries covered in 2019 is wide. The Gini coefficient is 0.535 and the Theil index is 0.502. Both measures are computed with countries weighted by population, so the result describes how the rate is distributed among people rather than among states. A populous country with a high rate therefore pulls the figures upward more than a small one would. The coefficient of variation is 1.03, which means the standard deviation of the rate is slightly larger than its mean. That pattern is typical of a distribution in which a minority of countries carry rates far above the rest.

The most informative figure is the between-region share of the Theil index, 75.2%. Three quarters of the measured inequality is therefore accounted for by differences between regions, and only about a quarter by differences among countries inside the same region. Where a country lies is a stronger predictor of its mortality from unsafe water and sanitation than anything that distinguishes it from its neighbours. This is consistent with well-established knowledge of the causes. Deaths from diarrhoeal disease, intestinal worm infections and malnutrition linked to poor hygiene depend on piped water, sewerage, treatment services, nutrition and primary care, and these are shared in broad terms by countries at similar stages of development and in similar climates. Regional patterns of income, public investment and health-system reach are therefore reflected closely in the rate.

The finding matters for how action is organised. If most of the gap lies between regions, then closing it depends on raising the level of whole regions, through regional financing, shared infrastructure programmes and commitments that cover many countries at once, rather than on correcting a few outliers within each region. The remaining quarter is not trivial, though. It signals that some countries do markedly better or worse than their regional setting would predict, and those cases are worth examining for policies that can be copied.

The limits of the result should be stated plainly. The decomposition reports a share, not a ranking, so it does not name the regions or countries with the highest rates, nor does it show which regions contribute most to the between-region component. It covers a single year, 2019, and so says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed since 2015 or been affected by events after 2020. The inequality measures also rest on modelled estimates rather than complete death registration, which in many low-income countries is partial. Readers should treat the figures as a robust indication of structure rather than a precise count of deaths.

### Change since 2015 cannot be measured from one year

The single observation for 2019 describes a position, not a movement. Target 3.9 calls for a substantial reduction in deaths from pollution and contamination by 2030, and a reduction can only be shown by comparing at least two points in time. The result retrieved for this section holds one year, 2019, for 183 countries. No statement is therefore made here on whether mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene fell after 2015, nor on how the years after 2020 compare with those before. The bench's tools return no earlier or later reading for this indicator, and an inference from a single cross-section would be a guess presented as a finding.

Three kinds of evidence would be needed to turn the position into a trend. The first is a series of annual rates from 2015 onward, ideally from 2000, so that a pre-2015 trajectory exists against which the post-2015 period can be judged. The shelf lists the indicator with 2019 as its latest year, which means that the period of the pandemic and its disruption to health services, to water programmes and to household incomes is not observed at all. The second is a count of deaths. A rate can fall while the number of deaths stays level or rises if populations grow, and the reverse is also possible, so the two answer different questions. The third is an air pollution indicator read alongside the water measure. The shelf holds a rate of deaths attributed to household and ambient air pollution and a measure of mean exposure to fine particles, but neither was returned as a result for this section, so the two halves of the question on pollution and unsafe water cannot be set side by side here.

Caution is also due on causes. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2%, and the Gini coefficient is 0.535. These figures show that the rate is unequally distributed and that regional grouping accounts for most of that inequality. They do not show why. It is well established that water and sanitation infrastructure, income, the quality of primary health care and the treatment of diarrhoeal disease all bear on such deaths, but the spread of one year's rates cannot separate these influences from one another or from the age structure of populations, from climate, or from conflict. Attributing the pattern to water infrastructure or to national income on this evidence alone would go beyond what was measured. The coefficient of variation, 1.03, confirms the dispersion without explaining it.

For 2030 the consequence is that progress on this part of target 3.9 cannot at present be judged from the evidence in hand. The target also does not define what "substantially" means, and it can be read against a baseline of 2015, of 2000 or of the latest available year. Until a series spanning those years is assembled, any statement on whether the goal is on course would be unsupported.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 3.9 asks for a substantial reduction by 2030, and the 2019 evidence shows where that reduction has to happen. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2% across 183 countries. Three quarters of the inequality in mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene therefore lies between regions rather than within them. Progress on the target depends on the regions where rates are highest. Because the Gini coefficient of 0.54 and a coefficient of variation of 1.03 describe a distribution with a long upper tail, a global average would be pulled down by regions with low rates and would conceal the places where most of the avoidable deaths occur.

This has a practical consequence for how 2030 is judged. A global rate can fall while the highest-rate regions barely move, if the improvement is concentrated where rates were already low. Such a result would satisfy a global reading of the target and fail the people the target is meant to reach. The target text does not say whether reduction is to be assessed in numbers of deaths or in rates, and it sets no baseline or percentage. Both readings are defensible, and they can diverge where populations are growing quickly, which is often where rates are highest. Where the rate falls but the population grows, the count may fall little or rise.

The data held for this section limit what can be concluded. Only one year, 2019, was analysed, so no trend since 2015 or 2020 is claimed here. The air pollution mortality series and the unintentional poisoning series are on the shelf but were not analysed for this section, although Target 3.9 covers air, water and soil pollution and hazardous chemicals together. The conclusions above concern one of those components only.
proposals: The World Health Organization and national statistical offices should report the mortality rate and the count of deaths together, so that population growth does not hide or exaggerate progress on Target 3.9.

The custodians of the Sustainable Development Goal indicator framework should add the air pollution mortality series to the assessment of Target 3.9, so that water, sanitation and air are read together.
The World Health Organization should publish regional breakdowns of attributed mortality alongside national figures, since 75.2% of the 2019 inequality lies between regions.

The United Nations regional commissions and national governments should set regional milestones for 2030, each tied to the 2019 inequality figures (a Gini of 0.54 and a between-region Theil share of 75.2%), so that the highest-rate regions are held to account.
w-c04-9-1~willow/writer-2~69.gaps: Only 2019 was analysed for the water, sanitation and hygiene rate, so no change since 2015 or 2020 can be stated. Counts of deaths were not retrieved. The air pollution and poisoning series were not analysed here, and soil contamination has no series on the shelf. The target sets no numerical baseline, so 'substantially reduce' can be read in more than one way.

w-c02-5-2~juniper/writer-2~69.text:
### Disaster displacement is the measure that exists, and it is rising

The only series in the bench that records recent exposure to climate-related disasters is the count of new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre. It stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and at 26,393,278 in 2023. The world total therefore rose over the eight years, by a little more than a third, and it did so in the period that target 1.5 covers, which asks countries to reduce the exposure and vulnerability of the poor and of people in vulnerable situations to climate-related extreme events by 2030.

The unit needs care. The series counts cases of new displacement, not persons. A household that flees a flood in March and a cyclone in September enters the count twice, and a person who returns home and is displaced again is counted again. The figure is also not a count of people affected: those whose crops fail in a drought, whose homes are damaged but who stay, or who lose income without moving do not appear. Displacement measures the part of exposure that is severe enough to force people from their homes and that is visible to the agencies which report it. It is a floor under the scale of exposure, not an estimate of it.

The measure also records hazards beyond those that the target names strictly as climate-related. Storms, floods, wildfires and droughts are included, as are geophysical events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, depending on how events are classified. The series therefore cannot be read as a pure signal of climate change. Part of any rise reflects more people living in harm's way, in coastal cities and river plains, and part reflects better monitoring and reporting. A single large event can move a national figure, and through it a regional one, by millions in one year.

The analysis of breaks in the annual change of the world total finds none. Over 2009 to 2023 the mean annual change is negative, at about 789,790 cases a year, which sits oddly beside the higher 2023 figure than 2015. The reading is that the series is dominated by large swings from year to year, so that the endpoints, and the mean of changes taken from a high early year, tell different stories. Neither 2015 nor 2020 marks a statistical rupture. The rise from 2015 to 2023 should be taken as a movement within a volatile record, not as a trend established against that volatility.

This matters for 2030 because the target has no quantified threshold, and the only indicator that tracks exposure directly has no baseline that fixes what reduction would mean. A target that asks for reduced exposure can be read as fewer displacements in absolute terms or as fewer relative to population at risk. The data allow only the first reading to be tested. By that reading the endpoints point away from the target, but given the volatility of the record this is an indication, not a settled finding.

### Coverage has widened, but the wider measure of exposure is a single historical period

The number of countries that report disaster displacement has grown over the period, though not without interruption, and this complicates any reading of the rising total. In 2008, 80 countries reported. The count fell to 60 in 2009, recovered to 73 in 2010, dipped again to 62 in 2011 and reached 79 in 2012. It then jumped to 118 in 2013, slipped to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. After 2015 it rose in most years, reaching 133 in 2017 and 141 in 2018, but it fell to 136 in 2019 and to 133 in 2021 after standing at 142 in 2020. It stood at 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across the whole series, 199 countries and territories have reported in at least one year, so even the latest year leaves some of them without a figure.

This matters for interpretation. A world total built from 112 countries in 2015 and 145 in 2023 is not a sum over the same set of countries. Part of the rise in displacement may reflect better recording, wider monitoring and the entry of countries that were previously silent, rather than a larger number of people forced from their homes. The data as given cannot separate the two effects. A like-for-like comparison over countries reporting in both years would be needed, and the figures here do not provide one. The lower counts of 2009 and 2011 also show that early coverage was uneven, which argues against reading the years before 2013 as a baseline.

The wider measure of exposure is weaker still. The share of the population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures is an annual average for 1990 to 2009, compiled from the EM-DAT disaster database. It is reported for 168 countries in a single year, 2009, with no regional or world aggregates and no later update. It therefore describes the two decades before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. It carries no trend, no value for 2015 and none for 2020, and it cannot show whether exposure has changed since the goals began.

The question of how many people are affected by climate-related disasters therefore cannot be answered from these data. Displacement counts cases of movement, not persons, since one person may be displaced more than once in a year. The historical average gives a share of the population but belongs to a past period. Neither series measures people affected in the sense that target 1.5 implies, and no series on the shelf measures the exposure of the poor in particular.

### Regions differ sharply and the inequality among countries has grown

Regional totals of new disaster displacement diverge widely, and the direction of change differs from one region to the next. East Asia and Pacific remains the largest single contributor. Its count moved from 8,304,660 cases in 2015 to 9,038,561 in 2023, a modest rise that leaves the region with the highest absolute burden in the series. The region is exposed to typhoons, monsoon floods and seismic hazards alike, and it holds very large populations along coasts and river deltas. Only part of that exposure is climate-related, since displacement by earthquakes and volcanic activity is counted in the same series.

South Asia moved in the opposite direction. Its count fell from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 in 2023. A fall of this size should not be read as a lasting gain in resilience. Displacement counts in the region depend heavily on whether a single large cyclone or flood season strikes populated areas in a given year, and evacuations are counted as displacement, so improved early warning could raise recorded displacement as well as save lives. Two endpoints cannot separate these influences.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 in 2023, a rise of more than fivefold that is the largest among the regions compared over the same years. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 in 2023, a larger multiple, but from a small base and a later starting year, so the two are not strictly comparable. Part of these rises is likely to reflect wider reporting and part genuine events, but the data cannot apportion the two. Between 2015 and 2023 the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan roughly doubled, from 1,212,730 to 2,481,660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 to 1,728,025. North America rose from 76,000 to 394,000, a fivefold increase from a low base that is small beside the Asian totals.

The spread among countries has widened. Weighting countries by population, the Gini coefficient of new displacement rose from 0.570 in 2015 to 0.678 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. Both measures say that displacement has become more concentrated in a few countries. The number of countries in the comparison also grew, from 112 to 145, so part of the change may follow from wider coverage rather than from a change in the underlying events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. In 2015 most of the inequality was a matter of which region a country belongs to. By 2023 almost half lay among countries within the same regions. Regional averages therefore describe the pattern less well than they once did, and targeting of resilience support by region alone would miss many of the most exposed countries. For 2030, the implication is that national and subnational monitoring will matter more than regional aggregates, and that a single global total conceals sharply different trajectories.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The trend in the world series should be read with caution. The test for structural breaks in the annual change of world displacement found none, and the mean annual change over 2009 to 2023 was -789,790 cases. That negative figure sits oddly beside the rise between 2015 and 2023, and the two readings are not reconciled by the data alone. Displacement counts follow the occurrence of major storms, floods and earthquakes, so a single severe season can dominate a year. A series of this kind cannot support a statement that exposure is rising or falling steadily, and no break marks 2015 or 2020 as a turning point.

The implication for 2030 is therefore limited. Target 1.5 sets no quantified level. It asks for resilience to be built and for exposure and vulnerability to be reduced, but it names no number of people, no share of population and no date before 2030 at which progress is to be checked. Without a threshold, no trajectory can be judged on or off course. The target can also be read in more than one way: as a fall in the number of people affected, as a fall in the share of the poor among those affected, or as a rise in the capacity to absorb losses. The displacement series speaks to the first reading only, and imperfectly, because it counts movements and not the poor. Between 2015 and 2023 the count rose, but the volatility of the series and the change in reporting mean that this rise is an indication and not proof of movement away from the target.

The widening of reporting adds a further caution. Coverage rose from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, out of 199 that have reported in any year, although it dipped in 2019 and 2021. Some of the increase in counts may reflect better recording, not greater harm. Inequality among countries also grew over the same years, with the Gini coefficient moving from 0.57 to 0.68, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. Disparity within regions is now a larger part of the picture, which a regional average conceals.

The broader measure of exposure, the share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, ends in 2009 and cannot be set beside recent years. The disaster risk reduction score, from self-assessments for 83 countries ending in 2011, is likewise too old and too subjective to show what has changed since 2015.
