w-c03-7-2~farah/writer-2~70.text:
### Consumer price inflation stands in for food prices

Target 2.c asks for measures that keep food commodity markets and their derivatives working properly and that give timely access to market information, including on food reserves, so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The target names no numerical threshold and no price index. Its indicator in the global framework is a food price anomalies measure, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold among the series available to this book. Volatility is therefore not measured here directly, and every statement in this section about prices is an indirect reading.

The nearest series is headline consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services for the average consumer. Food is one component of that basket, and its weight varies widely: it is large in low-income households and economies, and small in high-income ones. Headline inflation also contains energy, housing, transport and services, so a rise in the headline rate can follow a fuel shock, a currency depreciation or a rent adjustment with food prices barely moving. The series is read here as a signal of pressure on household budgets, not as a record of food price swings.

The series also has limits as a measure of volatility. The results available to this section give levels at 2015 and 2025 and measures of dispersion among countries in four selected years. They do not give the year-to-year path, which is what volatility requires. What follows describes the price environment and its unevenness, and does not claim to measure instability over time.

Coverage shapes what can be said. In 2015, 189 countries reported consumer price inflation, and the same number reported in 2016. The count then drifted down, to 185 in 2017, 179 in 2020, 176 in 2024 and 169 in 2025. Across all years 193 countries reported at least once, so some economies have gaps in particular years. The data do not show which economies dropped out, and the reasons for interrupted reporting cannot be read from them. The latest year, 2025, is the thinnest and may be revised as late submissions arrive. Comparisons across the period therefore rest on a changing set of countries, and the parts that follow rely mainly on regional and world aggregates, which are less sensitive to the loss of single reporters.

### World inflation doubled between 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025, a little more than double the earlier rate. Both figures are annual percentage changes in the cost of a general basket of goods and services, so they describe the price level that households face and not the price of food alone. Food is a large part of that basket in poorer economies and a smaller part in richer ones.

The two endpoints conceal the path between them. A comparison of 2015 with 2025 does not show how far inflation fell or rose in the years between, and it should not be read as a steady climb. The period contains the weak price environment of the middle 2010s, the disruption of 2020 and the supply shocks that followed, and an endpoint comparison cannot separate these. Volatility concerns movement from year to year, and the result used here reports levels at two dates only. It therefore shows that the world rate ended the period well above where it began, and it does not measure how much the rate moved in between.

Low-income countries show a different pattern from the world as a whole. Their inflation was 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025, so it fell over the decade while the world rate rose. Lower middle income countries also eased, from 4.0% to 3.6%, whereas upper middle income countries rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high income countries from 0.3% to 2.3%. That fall in the poorest group should not be taken as relief. Low-income countries began from the highest rate of any income group in 2015, and they remain above the world rate in 2025. Households there spend the largest share of their budgets on food, so a given rate of general inflation weighs more heavily on them than on households in richer groups. Coverage also changed: 169 countries reported in 2025, against 189 in 2015, so part of the comparison rests on a smaller set of countries at the later date.

The finding matters for Goal 2 because food access depends on what a household can buy with its income, and persistent price growth erodes that. Yet the series cannot show whether food prices moved more or less than prices generally, nor whether any rise came from commodity markets, exchange rates, energy costs or domestic policy. Those causes bear on whether the measures named in target 2.c are working, and the data used here do not distinguish among them.

### Regions began far apart and converged at a higher level

The regional picture in 2015 was one of wide separation. South Asia recorded consumer price inflation of 4.7% and Sub-Saharan Africa 3.5%, while Europe and Central Asia stood at 0.4% and North America at 0.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.8%, was also among the regions with very low rates. Latin America and the Caribbean (1.9%) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (1.7%) sat between the two groups. Income groups showed the same ordering: low-income economies stood at 5.5% and high-income economies at 0.3%.

By 2025 the gap between the highest and lowest regional rates had narrowed, though the order of the regions had changed. South Asia fell to 3.1%, a decline of about 1.6 percentage points, and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged at 3.4%, against 3.5% in 2015. Europe and Central Asia moved furthest in the opposite direction, rising from 0.4% to 3.7%, which made it the region with the highest rate in the latest year, narrowly ahead of Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1.7% to 2.0%. Movements in these three were modest, and all three ended 2025 at about 2%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024; its latest observation is for 2024, not 2025, so it is not strictly comparable in date with the other regions.

Income groups tell a similar story. Low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower-middle-income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while upper-middle-income economies rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high-income economies from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing therefore came partly from falls at the top and mostly from rises at the bottom of the 2015 distribution. Energy and food price shocks after 2020 are well-established drivers of the rises in importing regions, but these series cannot show how far each region's movement was due to them.

The pattern matters for Target 2.c because the regional spread now conceals a change of rank: the region with the lowest inflation in 2015 had the highest in 2025. Sub-Saharan Africa's flat line may hide large differences between countries, and a regional aggregate cannot show how often households met sharp price spikes within single years. For 2030, exposure to price shocks has become more evenly spread across regions, and no region now enjoys the near-zero inflation seen in 2015.

### Dispersion among countries widened after 2022

The spread of annual consumer price inflation among countries, weighted by population, was almost unchanged between 2015 and 2019 on the Gini measure, at 0.538 in 2015 and 0.538 in 2019. It narrowed to 0.511 in 2022, the year in which price pressures were felt in most economies at once, and then rose sharply to 0.660 in 2024. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the upper end of the distribution, gives a similar picture: 0.621 in 2015, 0.751 in 2019, 0.559 in 2022 and 0.982 in 2024. The 2024 values are the highest of the four years examined on both measures.

The composition of the inequality matters for interpretation. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015, 32.0% in 2019 and 38.4% in 2022, which fits a period in which regional averages moved apart before the 2024 observation. In 2024 the between-region share fell to 35.2%, so that most of the Theil index lay within regions. The rise in dispersion after 2022 is therefore mainly a divergence among countries of the same region, not a return of the regional gaps of 2015. Some economies may have brought inflation down as monetary tightening and falling energy costs worked through, while others continued to face currency depreciation, fiscal strain or conflict. The results do not identify which countries fall in which group, so this explanation rests on well-established patterns and not on the series itself. A regional average conceals the divergence, and a policy aimed at a region as a whole could miss the countries where food price stress is most acute.

Three cautions apply. First, the number of countries in the calculation differs by year: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 sample is much smaller than the 189 countries that reported inflation that year, so part of the comparison with later years reflects who is included and not only how prices moved. Second, population weighting gives large economies great influence, and a change in one of them can shift the result. Third, the measure is of general consumer prices, so it is an indirect guide to uneven exposure to food price volatility. For 2030, the widening within regions suggests that the risk of extreme price swings will be concentrated in a minority of countries, and that monitoring needs to be national in its detail.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.c cannot be scored from these data. It sets no numerical threshold and can be read in two ways: as the proper functioning of commodity markets and the availability of market information, or as the narrower outcome of limited price volatility. The series available touch only the second reading, and only indirectly, through general consumer prices. World inflation of 1.4% in 2015 and 3.0% in 2025 is consistent with greater price pressure on households. It says nothing about whether markets, derivatives or reserve reporting function better or worse than before, and the two endpoint values do not describe the path between them.

The outlook for 2030 is therefore uncertain in direction. Regional rates in 2015 ran from 0.4% in Europe and Central Asia to 4.7% in South Asia. By 2025 the range was narrower, from 2.0% in East Asia and Pacific to 3.7% in Europe and Central Asia, which moved from the lowest rate to the highest. Among income groups, low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower middle income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while high-income economies rose from 0.3% to 2.3%. The ranking of regions was thus reshuffled as well as compressed. Dispersion among countries points the other way: the population-weighted Gini measure stood at 0.660 in 2024, against 0.511 in 2022, so a narrower spread of group averages sits beside a wider spread of country experience. The data do not show which countries make up the upper tail, and the rates cited here are general consumer prices, not food prices.

Coverage bears on any monitoring to 2030. Countries reporting inflation numbered 189 in 2015 and 169 in 2025, and the data do not say whether the fall in 2025 is permanent or reflects later reporting. The proposals below follow from these limits: they aim to replace a proxy with measures that match the wording of the target, and to keep watch on the countries at the upper end of the distribution.

proposals: The World Bank and the IMF should publish a monthly food consumer price series by country alongside the general index, so that food price volatility can be measured directly against target 2.c.
National statistical offices in countries at the upper end of the inflation distribution should report food price data on time, and development partners should fund this work.
The FAO and the agencies responsible for the framework indicator on food price anomalies should release it in the World Bank catalogue, with country values, so that the target can be scored.
w-c03-7-2~farah/writer-2~70.gaps: The catalogue holds no food price index, no food price anomalies series and no data on reserves, derivatives markets or market information, so target 2.c cannot be measured directly. Year-by-year volatility between 2015 and 2025 is not examined here, and the countries in the upper tail of inflation are not identified.

w-c04-11-2~tamarind/writer-1~71.text:
### Immunisation and maternal and child services are largely flat at the global level

The nearest measure the shelf holds for immunisation and related services is the universal health coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health. It combines four tracer indicators: family planning, pregnancy care, child immunisation and child treatment, and it is scored from 0 to 100 index points. It is not a direct measure of vaccine coverage, because immunisation is only one of the four components. A movement in the index may therefore reflect changes in family planning or in the treatment of childhood illness rather than in vaccination. The reading offered here is of service coverage in general, with immunisation as one part of it.

Target 3.b can be read in more than one way. It concerns research and development, access to affordable essential medicines and vaccines, and the terms of the Doha Declaration. Coverage of services is an outcome of access, not a measure of research effort or of the price of medicines. The index speaks to access only in part, and the other elements of the target are not captured by any series held here.

At the global level the trend classification is regression, at a rate of -0.0017. The index values behind the regional classes are not carried among the facts of this section, so levels are not quoted here; only the classes and rates are. The change is small. Its significance lies in what it fails to show: there is no sign of the steady gain that a fifteen-year agenda implies, and a world expected to advance towards fuller coverage has, on this measure, slipped slightly.

Most regions are flat. East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, high income countries, North America, upper middle income countries and low income countries are all classified as stagnating, each with a rate of zero. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also stagnant. Europe & Central Asia shows a small positive rate of 0.0031, which is still classed as stagnation. Stagnation at high levels is less troubling than stagnation at low ones, since there is less room for gain, yet it means that remaining gaps are not closing. Low income countries remain far below every other group on the index, and a rate of zero offers no sign that this distance is narrowing.

The worst movements are in the middle of the income range. The lower middle income group has a rate of -0.0037 and South Asia a rate of -0.0053, and both are classed as regression. Disruption to routine services during the pandemic after 2020 is a recognised cause of lost coverage in many countries, and populous countries weigh heavily in group averages. The results do not separate the period before 2020 from the period after, so the share of the fall due to the pandemic cannot be stated. Sub-Saharan Africa is the only region with a clear gain, at a rate of 0.0099, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. The gain is real but begins from a low base.

The country classification confirms the pattern. Of 193 countries assessed, 11 are on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population. Another 9, with 3.1 per cent, show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 37, with 14.4 per cent, show marginal progress. Stagnation covers 105 countries and 48.1 per cent of the population, and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. The index carries no fixed 2030 target, so these classes rest on the direction of travel, not on a stated goal; 'on track' here means a rising trend, not a target met. Taken together, stagnation and regression cover 77.6 per cent of the population, which makes a general recovery in service coverage by 2030 unlikely without a clear change of course.

### Health spending has risen in dollar terms but barely as a share of output

Domestic general government health expenditure per capita rose from 589.2 current US dollars in 2015 to 803.7 in 2023 for the world as a whole. The series is in current dollars and is not adjusted for inflation or for population structure, so part of the rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger volume of care. The movement also says nothing about how the money was used.

Measured against output, the picture is much flatter. Current health expenditure was 9.7 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2023. Spending has therefore grown roughly in step with the economies that carry it. A rising dollar figure alongside a stable share means that health has held its place in national budgets and household outlays but has not gained priority. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, and a global share that moves by less than half a percentage point over eight years cannot be read as that kind of increase. The share also includes private and external spending, while the per capita series covers only domestic government spending, so the two measure different things and are not directly comparable.

The global average conceals a division by income. In high income countries the share of GDP rose from 12.0 per cent to 12.5 per cent, and in upper middle income countries from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent. In lower middle income countries it fell from 3.9 per cent to 3.7 per cent, and in low income countries from 5.4 per cent to 4.6 per cent. The fall among the poorest runs against the direction target 3.c requires. The data do not show why it fell. Faster growth elsewhere in the economy, reduced external funding, debt pressure and conflict are all plausible contributors, but none can be separated here.

Regional shares tell a similar story. North America stood at 16.0 per cent in 2015 and 16.3 per cent in 2023. South Asia declined from 3.5 per cent to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent in both years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 5.4 per cent to 5.3 per cent. Only East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean moved up, and by small margins.

The period after 2020 matters for interpretation. The pandemic raised health spending in many countries and depressed GDP in the same years, which lifts the share temporarily. The 2023 values are therefore not a clean continuation of the pre-2020 path. Coverage of the latest year is also thin: only 22 countries reported the share for 2024, and only 7 reported domestic government spending per capita, so 2023 is the last year that supports regional comparison.

For 2030, a financing share that has hardly moved offers little ground for expecting a step change. Without a deliberate rise in public priority, the countries with the least spending will remain far from the resources that basic services need.

### Regions and countries differ by orders of magnitude

North America spent 6,959.0 current US dollars per head of domestic government money on health in 2023, against 30.8 dollars in South Asia and 31.7 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa. The ratio between the top and the bottom is therefore above 200 to one. Europe and Central Asia stood at 2,178.0 dollars, East Asia and Pacific at 571.7 dollars, Latin America and the Caribbean at 415.7 dollars, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 190.2 dollars. By income group the gradient is as steep: high-income countries spent 3,847.3 dollars, upper middle income countries 338.9 dollars, lower middle income countries 30.9 dollars and low-income countries 7.3 dollars. These are current dollars at market exchange rates, so they understate what a dollar buys in poorer countries, where wages and many services cost less. Even so, no plausible adjustment closes a gap of this size.

The movement since 2015 widens the distance in absolute terms. North America started from 4,587.0 dollars and gained roughly 2,372 dollars per head by 2023, while Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 29.7 to 31.7 dollars and low-income countries from 7.0 to 7.3 dollars. South Asia is the exception among the poorer regions: its figure roughly doubled, from 14.7 to 30.8 dollars, though from a very small base. The pattern is one of growth proportional to the starting level in the richer groups and near-stillness at the bottom. Rapid population growth in low-income countries also means that a flat per-capita figure can conceal a rising national outlay that merely keeps pace with numbers of people.

The share of output spent on health gives a less favourable picture for the poorest. Low-income countries fell from 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 4.6 per cent in 2023, and lower middle income countries from 3.9 to 3.7 per cent. High-income countries rose from 12.0 to 12.5 per cent and upper middle income countries from 5.5 to 6.0 per cent. South Asia slipped from 3.5 to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed. On this measure the poorest groups moved the other way. The results do not identify the reasons. Weak tax bases, debt service and the strain of the pandemic and later price rises on public budgets are commonly cited, but none is tested here. Because the indicator covers all current health spending, a fall also means that private and external money did not offset the shortfall in the poorest groups. The latest year is thinly reported: only 7 countries had a 2024 value for domestic government spending per head and 22 for the share of GDP, so the regional figures for 2023 rest on estimates that may be revised.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the regional averages. For domestic government health spending per head, 142 of the 193 countries assessed were classed as on track, holding 80.1 per cent of their combined population. No target value is set for this series, so the classes describe direction and pace of change in current dollars, not distance from a goal, and they do not show that the financing aim of target 3.c has been met. A further 12 countries showed moderate progress, and 34 were in regression, holding 14.0 per cent of the population. Rising dollar spending in most countries therefore coexists with a sizeable minority of countries, and of people, where it fell.

The service coverage sub-index is flatter. Only 11 of the 193 countries were on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population, while stagnation covered 105 countries and 48.1 per cent and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. Nearly four in five people live in a country where coverage of these services stood still or fell. The regression class is large in population because it includes South Asia and the lower middle income group, where the regional indices fell. The two series are not linked in these results, so they cannot show why rising spending in many countries sits beside flat coverage; delivery, workforce and reach of services are plausible candidates, but the data do not test them.

### Spending has not converged and the workforce cannot be measured well

Spending per head at purchasing power parity shows no sign of countries drawing together. Across 190 countries, the regression of growth in current health expenditure per capita (international dollars) between 2015 and 2023 on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00001, with a p-value of 0.997 and an R-squared of 0.0. Countries that began with low spending did not grow faster than those that began high, and the starting level explains none of the variation in growth. The coefficient of variation, a measure of relative dispersion, moved from 1.24 in 2015 to 1.20 in 2023. That change is small and is not backed by a convergence relationship, so it should be read as little more than stability in the spread.

The result matters for target 3.c, which calls for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed countries and small island developing States. Convergence would be the sign that the gap in resources was narrowing. Its absence means that the large differences in spending described earlier in this section are being carried into the final years of the agenda. Health budgets depend on national income, on the capacity of governments to raise revenue and on debt service burdens, and these did not obviously change in a way that favoured poorer countries during the period; this is background knowledge and not a result of the test. The shocks of 2020 fell on all budgets, but countries with more fiscal room could more easily sustain health spending. The test here is across countries and does not separate these channels, and it covers 2015 to 2023 only, so any later change is not captured.

The health workforce is harder still to assess. The shelf holds one series on community health workers per 1,000 people, and it is thin. Only 64 countries report in any year of the series. The number reporting in a single year ranges from 3 in 2002 and 3 in 2014 to 29 in 2004 and 21 in 2008. After 2010 the count never exceeds 13: 6 in 2011, 7 in 2012, 6 in 2013, 3 in 2014, 4 in 2015 and 6 in 2016. The latest year in the series is 2016, so nothing is recorded for the period after 2015 beyond those few reporters, and nothing after 2020.

With so few reporters, and with a different set of countries in each year, a change in the average could not be told from a change in who reports. No trend in workforce density, upward or downward, can be asserted, and no judgement can be made on whether the recruitment and retention called for in target 3.c is occurring. Community health workers are also defined differently from country to country, under varied national titles, which weakens comparison even where data exist. The series also says nothing of doctors, nurses or midwives. The honest finding is that spending can be measured and has not converged, whereas the workforce, the input on which services most depend, cannot be measured well enough to be followed towards 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Targets 3.b and 3.c ask for more vaccines and medicines for developing countries, and for substantially more health financing and workforce. The shelf supports only a partial reading. The financing evidence is a direction-of-travel test on current dollars, with no target attached, so it cannot show that the financing half of 3.c has been met. It shows that 142 of 193 countries, holding 80.1% of the assessed population, are rising in domestic government health spending per head. That majority is dominated by countries that already spend most. A further 34 countries, with 14.0% of the population, show regression, and these are the systems where the target is most at risk.

For 3.b the shelf holds only the composite reproductive, maternal, newborn and child index, which is not a measure of vaccine coverage or of access to medicines. Read as a proxy, it is discouraging. Only 11 countries, with 5.0% of the population, are on track, while 105, with 48.1%, are stagnating and 31, with 29.5%, are regressing. Together, stagnation and regression cover 77.6% of the assessed population. The index is consistent with disrupted routine services after 2020, but it cannot attribute the pattern to vaccines, and it cannot be linked to spending with the series held. If present trends hold, most of the world's population will reach 2030 with coverage no better than today.

The share of output devoted to health shows that dollar growth alone is not sufficient. Low-income countries fell from 5.4% of GDP in 2015 to 4.6% in 2023, while high-income countries rose from 12.0% to 12.5%. South Asia's share slipped from 3.5% to 3.3%, even though its per-head public spending rose from a very low base. Spending therefore grew in absolute terms nearly everywhere, but did not keep pace with output where need is greatest. Why is a matter for national studies: tax capacity, debt service, competing pressures after 2020 and the pattern of external aid are the usual explanations, and none can be tested with these series. Without a deliberate shift, the gap in 2030 is likely to be wider than in 2015.

The workforce half of 3.c cannot be judged. Community health workers were reported by only 64 countries in any year, by no more than 29 in any single year, and by just 6 countries in 2016, the last year of record. A target to recruit and retain workers cannot be monitored from a series that thin. Estimates for 2024 also rest on 7 reporting countries for domestic government spending and 22 for spending as a share of GDP, so the latest picture is provisional.

w-c06-1-3~tamarind/writer-4~71.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Equal weight for every topic is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is to be expected. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf, so the direction and size of change in laws affecting women's economic opportunity cannot be stated here. The remaining parts of the section therefore describe what the index measures and how its readings should be interpreted, and set out what a measured record would have to contain. They make no claim about magnitude.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds safety and childcare, domains the earlier one largely omitted, and it is accompanied by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the inclusion of safety and childcare lowers the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse, and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the revised scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether comparable values exist back to 2015, the baseline this book uses throughout, has not been verified. If they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and any statement about the decade would need a different instrument.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. The only result computed so far is coverage: the legal index is reported by 189 economies in 2025, and 189 economies report in at least one year. That distance between promise and delivery has not yet been computed, and it is the natural next step for this section.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

A measured answer to the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed would consist of four parts, none of which the bench has yet computed. Only the coverage of the Legal Framework Index has been established: 189 economies reported in 2025, and 189 reported in at least one year. That establishes the frame within which a measured answer could be built, and nothing more.

The first part is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and because a few large reforms look the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones. The third is the distribution: the spread between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker most needs to see.

Two comparisons would give the record its meaning for 2030. The first sets average annual change before 2020 against change after it, if the history of the series permits, and so shows whether the pandemic prompted reform or diverted legislative attention. The second compares the topics of work, pay and parenthood with those governing marriage, mobility and assets. Comparative experience suggests that labour codes are amended more readily than family and personal-status codes, but this is background knowledge and not a result of this section.

One feature of the measure favours the exercise. Because the index is built from statute and not from reported statistics, an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report. Any backsliding would appear in the scores and not as a gap in the data, which makes a computed record of direction more trustworthy than most series in this chapter.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for this index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates listed, so a comparison across the other regions would need either further aggregates or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change; implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. If the legal score rises less steeply with income than the supportive and enforcement scores, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Until group-level values exist, the book cannot say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. That distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values the bench has not yet computed. Under the strict reading, the relevant measures are the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they are the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change.

What can be said now is limited to definition and coverage. The Legal Framework Index was reported by 189 economies in 2025, and the same 189 reported in at least one year, so the frame for either reading is complete. On a measure that demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, full equality is a high bar, and any economy's position should be judged with that in mind. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companion series and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

The legal index is well suited to a global account because its coverage is close to a census: 189 economies reported in 2025, and 189 reported in at least one year. A measured answer, once computed, will therefore rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. What the bench has established is that frame and nothing further. The question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed remains open in this section, because no level, change or comparison has been computed. The task left to the bench is to turn the coverage into a record of levels, changes since 2015 and since 2020, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice becomes visible for every economy.

Enforcement is measured through perceptions, and the data do not show actual outcomes in courts or administrations. Regional aggregates are limited to South Asia among the geographic regions listed.

w-c02-6-2~cedar/writer-2~71.text:
### Health and education budgets claim stable but modest shares of spending

Government budgets show a stable but modest commitment to the services that bear most directly on poverty. Education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in the world in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, a fall of about 0.1 of a percentage point over eight years. The world figure is nearly flat, but regional movements beneath it differ. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, while Latin America and the Caribbean held at 16.4 per cent in 2015 and 16.6 per cent in 2024. Low-income countries moved against the general direction, from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022. Reporting for 2025 is partial, with 60 countries, so the latest observations describe a subset and not the world.

Health is harder to summarise. The series, domestic general government health expenditure as a share of general government expenditure, is reported here by region and income group, and no world figure is given. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024, so the final year supports no statement. The most recent usable readings fall between 2017 and 2023, depending on the group, and comparisons across groups therefore mix end years. They indicate direction and scale and are not a common-year ranking.

Social protection is the third service named in the section's question, and no result for its share of public spending is available in this bench. The coverage and benefit-incidence series describe who is reached, not how much governments spend, and they are treated in another section of the chapter. The absence should not be read as a low or a high figure.

The targets add a further limit. Target 1.a calls for significant mobilisation of resources and for adequate and predictable means, and target 1.b calls for sound policy frameworks that support accelerated investment in poverty eradication. Neither sets a threshold, a base year or a required share of spending, and the series held here measure domestic budgets, not development cooperation, so target 1.a is only partly addressed. Any classification of progress therefore rests on direction alone: a rising share is read as movement towards the target. That reading is open to challenge, since a share can fall while the absolute amount rises with growth, and can rise because other spending is cut.

### Regions and income groups differ widely in health priority

Health receives very different priority across regions and income groups. North America devoted 22.1 per cent of general government expenditure to health from domestic sources in 2015 and 22.8 per cent in 2023, the highest share of any region reported. Europe and Central Asia stood at 15.0 per cent in 2015 and 14.5 per cent in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 11.5 per cent to 11.8 per cent over the same years. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2019, the last year in its series. South Asia began far lower, at 3.7 per cent in 2015, and reached 4.8 per cent in 2022. That is the largest proportional gain among the regions shown, yet the region still allocates less than a third of the share of Europe and Central Asia in 2023.

The income groups repeat the pattern. High-income economies assigned 17.9 per cent in 2015 and 18.5 per cent in 2023. Low-income economies assigned 5.4 per cent in 2015 and 5.3 per cent in 2017, and lower-middle-income economies 4.8 per cent in 2015 and 4.7 per cent in 2018. Comparing 2015 alone, the high-income share is about 3.3 times the low-income share and about 3.7 times the lower-middle-income share. These ratios apply to shares only, before account is taken of the far smaller budgets to which they are applied. A poor country that gives a small share of a small budget to health leaves households to meet the difference from their own pockets, which is a recognised route into impoverishment.

These comparisons carry a caveat. The series do not end in the same year: the low-income and lower-middle-income series stop in 2017 and 2018, and the Sub-Saharan African series in 2019, so none of them can show what followed the pandemic of 2020 or the debt pressures that came after. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024 at the time of the data, so the latest year is not yet a basis for comparison. A gap measured in earlier years for the poorest groups may since have narrowed or widened, and the data cannot say which.

Education shares show a different ordering, though not a clean one. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 15.4 per cent in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 16.6 per cent in 2024, give education the largest shares of their budgets among the regions listed, while North America gave 10.7 per cent in 2022, down from 12.9 per cent in 2015. Low-income economies raised their education share from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, a period in which their health share did not move. Poorer groups thus tend to put more of their budgets into schooling than into health, and richer groups the reverse. The share is a measure of priority, not of adequacy, because a large share of a small budget may still buy little per pupil.

### Education shares fell in most countries while inequality in spending widened

Since 2015 the education share of public budgets has weakened in most countries. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are classed as in regression, and these hold 78.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 29 countries, with 7.1 per cent of that population, are on track or have met the direction of travel. A further 13 countries (1.8 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 12 (2.3 per cent) marginal progress and 23 (10.5 per cent) stagnation. No numerical target exists for these indicators, so the classes measure movement towards an increase and not distance from an agreed level. An increase is itself only one reading of progress, since a falling share can accompany rising total budgets or a growing economy.

The population weighting explains why the picture is so unfavourable, for the regressing group includes populous regions. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent of government expenditure in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, and South Asia from 13.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2025. North America also declined, from 12.9 per cent in 2015 to 10.7 per cent in 2022. The movement was not universal. Low-income countries rose from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, and Latin America and the Caribbean edged up from 16.4 per cent to 16.6 per cent in 2024. Competing claims on budgets, such as debt service, pensions and health, and the fiscal pressure that followed the pandemic after 2020, are commonly cited pressures on education shares, although these data do not identify which of them operated in any given country.

Spending relative to national income shows a different problem, that of divergence. Across 164 countries, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of education spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.101, an increase of more than half. The between-region share of that Theil index moved from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent. Regional differences therefore account for under a quarter of the inequality in both years, and the widening came mainly from differences among countries within regions. Regional averages thus conceal the divergence, and policies aimed at whole regions would miss most of it.

Health presents a more favourable record. Of 193 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the direction of travel, holding 40.8 per cent of their population, while 61 are in regression, holding 21.3 per cent. Another 30 countries (22.1 per cent of the population) show marginal progress, 19 (11.5 per cent) stagnation and 11 (4.3 per cent) moderate progress. The series cannot show whether the pandemic raised the priority of health budgets, though that is a plausible contributor.

The two shares do not move together. The Spearman correlation between changes in the health share and the education share across 129 countries over 2015 to 2022 is 0.16, and between their levels in the later year of that span 0.09. Countries that raised one share were therefore hardly more likely to raise the other, and no common cause is shown. Neither is a trade-off. Governments appear to set the two priorities largely independently, so the weakening of education shares needs its own explanation in each country.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Spending shares carry no numerical target under targets 1.a and 1.b, so progress can be judged only by direction. The trend classes ask whether a share is rising, which is a weak test: a country may be on track while spending too little, and another in regression while spending generously. The classes are signals of priority, not verdicts on adequacy. The target wording can also be read as concerning domestic budgets, development cooperation, or both. The series examined cover domestic budgets only, so nothing here speaks to external resources under target 1.a.

On this reading health is nearer to progress than education. For the domestic health share, 72 of 193 countries assessed are on track, holding 40.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, while regression affects 61 countries with 21.3 per cent. Whether any rise after 2020 reflects emergency responses to the pandemic cannot be shown by these results, and whether health budgets persist under fiscal pressure is not settled by the data. For education the pattern is the reverse: 110 of 187 countries are in regression, with 78.2 per cent of the population, against 29 on track with 7.1 per cent. Because the regression class holds most of the population, the direction of education budgets matters for most of the world's children, though the results do not identify which countries drive it.

The outlook for 2030 is uneven. Health shares may keep rising in a large group of countries, but 21.3 per cent of the population lives where they are falling. Education shares are falling where most people live, and the pattern is not uniform: the low-income group rose from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, so falling shares are not confined to poorer countries. Spending as a share of GDP became more unequal, as the Theil index rose from 0.065 in 2015 to 0.101 in 2022. The between-region share eased from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent, which implies that the widening occurred mostly within regions.

Two limits qualify every reading. Spending data for low-income countries often end years before the latest reporting year, so recent shifts there are unseen. Social protection spending is not covered by the spending series examined, and its coverage and targeting are treated in other sections of this chapter.

w-c04-5-2~heath/writer-2~71.text:
### Global consumption fell between 2015 and 2020

Global alcohol consumption per adult fell over the first five years of the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization estimate, carried in the World Development Indicators, puts total consumption at 5.9 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 and over in 2015. By 2020 it stood at 4.9 litres. The fall is about 1.0 litre, or roughly one sixth of the 2015 level, in five years. The measure sums recorded sales and an estimate of unrecorded alcohol, such as home production and informal trade, and is adjusted for tourist consumption.

Target 3.5 calls for strengthening the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including the harmful use of alcohol. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline year. The target can therefore be read in more than one way. One reading takes the wording to concern harm, which per capita volume captures only in part, since the same average can conceal heavy episodic drinking in a minority. Another reading treats volume as the best available proxy and counts a sustained decline as progress. This book adopts the second reading, because volume is the only alcohol series the shelf holds, and it states that choice openly. On that reading the world moved in the intended direction after 2015.

The series needs careful handling. The figures are projected estimates, not counts from a survey of drinkers in each year. Statisticians model them from sales, tax records, production data and occasional surveys, and then project forward where observations are thin. A smooth global path is therefore partly a product of the method, and a single year should not be read as a precise count. The final year, 2020, coincides with the first months of the pandemic, when closures of bars and restaurants, lost tourism and shifts in household purchasing altered both drinking and its measurement. Whether the 2020 figure reflects lasting change or a temporary disturbance cannot be settled from this series alone.

Coverage is nearly complete. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2020, 187 countries report in at least one year, and 185 report in 2020. The few countries that drop out in some years do not alter the global picture materially, though the estimates for those places are less secure. The world figure is thus a broad measure, and the sections that follow turn to the regions, income groups and countries that lie behind it.

### Regions differ widely in level and in direction

Regional levels span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia and North America sit at the top. Consumption in Europe and Central Asia was 8.9 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2020, down from 9.5 litres in 2015. North America stood at 9.9 litres in 2020, up from 9.5 litres. Among the regions reported, North America is the only one in which the estimate rose. Its rate of 0.0075 is classed as regression, while every other region shows a negative rate. Latin America and the Caribbean lies in the middle band, at 5.8 litres in 2020 against 6.5 litres in 2015. At the bottom, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan record about 0.3 litres in both years, 0.4 litres in 2015 and 0.3 litres in 2020. That level reflects widespread abstention and legal restriction. It is also a region in which unrecorded consumption is hardest to measure, so the level should be read with caution.

The largest regional fall is in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020. Its rate of -0.0657 is the steepest of any region and is classed as on track or target met. South Asia fell from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, at a rate of -0.0360, also classed on track. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0216, is placed in the same class. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0138, is classed as moderate progress, but acceleration needed. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0181, receives the same class even though its level is so low. These classes need a caveat. The Goals set no numerical target for alcohol under target 3.5, which asks only for strengthened prevention and treatment of harmful use. The classification therefore measures the direction and speed of change, and does not show whether a region has reached a safe or desired level.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 4.6 litres in 2015 to 4.2 litres in 2020, at a rate of -0.0211, classed on track. That is a fall of about half a litre, much smaller than in East Asia and Pacific, where consumption fell by almost two litres.

The income groups show a similar divergence. High-income economies fell only from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, at a rate of -0.0075, classed as marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed. They remain the heaviest-drinking group. Low-income economies, at 2.9 litres in 2015 and 2.8 litres in 2020, moved even less, at -0.0054, and are classed in the same way. Upper-middle-income economies fell from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres, at -0.0585, and lower-middle-income economies from 3.9 litres to 3.3 litres, at -0.0340; both are classed on track. The largest reductions therefore came in the middle-income groups, while the highest-consuming group fell slowly and the lowest-consuming group barely moved. The period also spans 2020, when closure of bars and restricted travel altered recorded sales, and the projected estimates for that year rest partly on modelling, so part of the fall may not persist.

### Country trajectories split between steep falls and regression

The trend classification covers 183 countries and rates each by its course towards a lower level of consumption. Target 3.5 sets no numerical goal for alcohol, so the classes measure direction and pace against a decrease by 2030, not distance from a stated threshold. That is one of several possible readings and applies throughout.

The country picture is divided. In 75 countries, holding 60.4% of the population of those assessed, consumption is on track or the target is met. A further 21 countries, with 11.0% of their population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 21, with 7.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. In 12 countries, with 3.1%, consumption stagnates. In 54 countries, with 18.2%, it is in regression, meaning that consumption per adult is rising.

The two ways of counting give different weights. By number of countries, 75 of 183 are on track, well under half, while 54 are in regression, about three in ten. By population, the on-track class holds 60.4% and the regression class 18.2%. The gap between the two views shows that the on-track group includes populous countries, and that the regressing group is made up largely of smaller ones. The country-level data are not tabulated here, so which countries these are is not stated. The 60.4% is therefore a statement about people, not a sign that most countries are succeeding.

The reasons for regression are not measured in these results. Well-established experience suggests that rising incomes, urbanisation, commercial marketing and weak taxation or licensing of alcohol have raised consumption in many middle-income settings, while taxes, limits on availability and restrictions on advertising have helped to lower it where drinking is high. Countries that begin from very low levels, often for cultural or religious reasons, can register regression from a small base, so the class does not always signal a harmful level.

Coverage is nearly complete. Between 185 and 187 countries report in every year from 2000 to 2020, and 187 report in at least one year. The estimates are projected by the World Health Organization from survey and sales data, not counted directly, so country-level movements, above all for 2020, partly reflect modelling and not observed change. The classification should be read as an indication of direction, not as a precise ranking.

### Change was not convergent and moved alike for men and women

Change between 2015 and 2020 was not convergent. Across 181 countries, a regression of five-year change on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00589, with a p-value of 0.603 and an R-squared of 0.012. The sign is negative, which would mean that countries with higher consumption fell slightly faster, but the coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the starting level explains about 1.2% of the variation in change. High-consumption countries did not systematically close the gap with low-consumption ones.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of consumption across countries rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.74 in 2020. The spread of national levels relative to their mean therefore widened slightly. Because the global average fell while dispersion rose, reductions were uneven in proportion: some countries fell sharply, some barely moved, and some rose. The difference between the two coefficients is small, and a movement of two hundredths in a five-year window should not be read as a settled trend.

The second result concerns the sexes. Across 185 countries, the changes in male and female consumption between 2015 and 2020 are almost perfectly rank-correlated, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.99 and a Kendall coefficient of 0.94. The 2020 levels are nearly as closely aligned, at 0.99 and 0.92. Countries in which men reduced consumption most are, almost without exception, those in which women did so as well. Rank correlation says nothing about the absolute gap between men and women, which is large in nearly every country; it says only that the ordering of countries is shared.

Such a close match is consistent with drivers operating at national level rather than in behaviour specific to either sex. Taxation and pricing, limits on availability and marketing, and social norms act on whole populations, although the results do not test any of these. The method also contributes. The figures are projected estimates, built from national sales, survey and modelling inputs, and the same adjustments to a country's total are likely to carry through to both sex-specific series. Part of the correlation may therefore be an artefact of estimation rather than a finding about behaviour.

No causal claim follows from these results. The window is five years and covers the disruption of 2020, and the lack of convergence describes the data rather than judging any policy. What can be said is that the starting level did not organise the change, and that the sex of the drinker did not alter a country's place in the ordering.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to a world moving in the right direction on alcohol, though not evenly. The world rate of -0.0363 is classed as on track or target met, yet it leans on large falls in East Asia and Pacific, where consumption went from 6.4 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020, and in upper middle income countries, where it went from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres. In high-income countries the fall was from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a rate of -0.0075 classed as marginal progress, and North America moved the other way, from 9.5 litres to 9.9 litres. Target 3.5 sets no numerical threshold, so every class here describes direction and pace against a decrease. Whether the gap between regions narrows or widens by 2030 cannot be read from two observation points, and the 2030 horizon lies ten years after the last observation in 2020.

The country picture shows the same division, and it should be read together with the population shares. Consumption is regressing in 54 countries holding 18.2% of the assessed population, and 12 more are stagnant. Population weighting is why the 75 countries on track account for 60.4% of that population: they are fewer than half of the 183 assessed, but they include populous ones. The global verdict therefore depends on a limited set of large countries, and the results alone do not name them. A global verdict of progress can coexist with widespread failure elsewhere.

The absence of convergence matters for 2030. With a coefficient of -0.00589 and a p-value of 0.603, nothing in the data suggests that high-consumption countries are catching down unaided. Falls are more likely to follow national policy choices, such as taxation, availability controls and marketing rules, than a general pull towards a common level, though the results do not test these causes. Low-income countries, where consumption is lowest at 2.8 litres in 2020, show only marginal progress, and the data cannot say whether rising incomes will push consumption upward there. Projected estimates carry uncertainty, and the 2020 value may reflect pandemic disruption to trade and sales.

w-c06-3-2~rowan/writer-2~71.text:
### The global level in 2022

In 2022, 19.5% of women aged 20-24 worldwide had been first married by age 18. The indicator, which the World Bank carries from UNICEF and the Demographic and Health Surveys, counts women in that age band who were married or in union before their eighteenth birthday. The age band is chosen deliberately: women aged 20-24 have all passed the threshold, so the share records a completed experience rather than a risk still running, and it reflects marriages that took place in roughly the preceding decade, a general property of the age band and not a result drawn from the data here. Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage, and this share is the measure by which progress towards it is read.

The world figure should be read as a modelled estimate, not as a count. No agency surveys every woman in every country each year. Household surveys are fielded in a given country once every few years, and the aggregate is built from those surveys, carried forward and combined with population weights. The value for 2022 therefore describes the best available picture of that year, and it rests on a much smaller set of direct observations than the single number suggests. The world aggregate is reported for 2022 only, so no change over time can be drawn from it, and any claim about movement since 2015 or since 2020 has to be made from other evidence. The absence of a second year is a limit of the data and does not indicate stagnation.

The sparseness is visible in the reporting itself. Over the whole series, 145 countries have reported a value in at least one year, yet in any single year only a fraction of them do. The most recent year, 2025, holds observations from just 3 countries, which is too few to say anything about the present beyond what the aggregates carry. The latest year with a full set of aggregates is 2022, and it is the reference point for the rest of this section.

The figure matters because early marriage is closely tied to the other outcomes of this chapter. Well-established research links marriage before 18 to earlier school leaving, earlier childbearing and greater exposure to violence at home, and to less say over a woman's own health and finances; these links come from outside knowledge, not from the results reported here. A level of 19.5% means that about one young woman in five began adult life in that position. The sections that follow set this global value against regional and income differences, the spread among countries, and the pace required to reach 2030.

### Regional and income differences

Regional averages for 2022 show a wide spread behind the world figure of 19.5%. East Asia and Pacific stands lowest, at 5.6% of women aged 20-24 first married by age 18. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan follow at 17.7%, a little below the world level. South Asia reaches 25.6%, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest at 31.1%. Sub-Saharan Africa's share is therefore more than five times that of East Asia and Pacific, a ratio of 5.60 derived from the two regional values.

The regional grouping used here is not the one found in every United Nations or World Bank publication. It joins the Middle East and North Africa with Afghanistan and Pakistan, two countries that other conventions place in South Asia. A comparison with figures published under a different grouping may therefore differ, and the South Asian and Middle Eastern values should be read as belonging to this arrangement only. Regional values are also summaries of countries with very different populations and survey dates, so a single regional share can hide sharp contrasts within it.

Income groups tell a similar story. Lower middle income economies stand at 24.4%, against 8.5% for upper middle income economies, a ratio of 2.89 derived from those two values. Child marriage is thus markedly less common in the upper middle income group. The results do not explain the gradient. Outside the data, it is widely held that poverty, limited schooling for girls, rural residence and weak enforcement of minimum-age laws sustain early marriage, while longer schooling and wider paid work for women delay it; this is background knowledge, not a finding of these results. Income is not the whole account, since South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa may differ in norms, in the role of dowry and bride price, and in the reach of legal reform.

No figure for high income or low income economies is shown in these results. The absence matters: the gradient across the full income range cannot be stated from this evidence, and nothing here shows where the practice is most concentrated among the poorest countries. The comparison offered covers the middle of the income distribution only.

### Inequality among countries and the thin evidence

Inequality among countries in the share of women first married by age 18 appears to have narrowed between 2012 and 2018, though the evidence for the comparison is thin. The population-weighted Gini coefficient across reporting countries stood at 0.282 in 2012, when 21 countries had data, and at 0.273 in 2018, when 20 did. The Theil index fell further, from 0.156 to 0.120. The coefficient of variation, which is more sensitive to the highest values, fell from 0.63 to 0.49. All three measures point the same way: countries with data were closer together in 2018 than in 2012.

The composition of the remaining inequality changed more than its size. The share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 73.0% in 2012 to 89.8% in 2018. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the total, and what separates the countries with data is increasingly the region in which they sit. The pattern could arise in several ways, and these results do not show which applies. If it holds beyond the countries surveyed, regional programmes and regional political commitments would matter more, but two different country sets cannot establish that, and a global average may conceal a divide that is largely geographic.

These readings must be held loosely, because the surveys that feed the indicator are irregular. Household surveys are fielded in each country every few years, so the set of countries reporting changes from one year to the next. Counts range from 5 countries in 2002 and 6 in 2001 to 21 in 2012 and 20 in 2018. Since 2015 the count has run from 11 in 2015 and 2017 to 18 in 2022, with 12 in 2020 and 12 in 2024. In 2025 only 3 countries report, which leaves that year unusable for any comparison. In all, 145 countries have a value in at least one year, but no more than 21 have a value in any single one.

The 2012 and 2018 comparison therefore rests on two different sets of countries, and a fall in the Gini or Theil index may reflect who was surveyed as much as what changed. Neither year allows a clean reading of the effect of the 2015 adoption of the goals or of the disruption after 2020, since the years in between draw on still other country sets. The inequality findings show a plausible direction of travel, not a measured trajectory, and they cannot be extended to countries that were not surveyed.

### Pace against the 2030 target

Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of harmful practices, including child, early and forced marriage, but its text names no numerical threshold. The most direct reading is a rate of zero by 2030. Others are possible: a large fall from a baseline, or convergence on the level of the best-performing regions. The trend assessment adopts the first reading, a target of 0.0% by 2030, and measures each country's recent pace against the pace that reading requires.

Of the 20 countries with enough observations to be classified, none is on track or has met the target. Two show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed there too; they hold 5.8% of the population of the assessed countries. Fourteen show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, and these hold 91.8% of that population. One country is stagnant, and three are regressing. The assessed countries are therefore overwhelmingly ones in which the share is falling too slowly to reach zero, and the few that are moving in the wrong direction are small in population terms.

The classification covers 20 countries out of 145 that have reported at some point. Countries are classed only where repeated surveys allow a trend to be drawn, and survey rounds arrive unevenly: 11 countries reported in 2015, 12 in 2020 and 3 in 2025. The 2025 count is very low, and the data do not show why; it may reflect surveys not yet published, but that cannot be confirmed from these results. For this reason the pace assessment cannot say how the practice changed after 2015 or after 2020 for most countries. Whether the disruption of schooling, health services and household incomes during the pandemic raised early marriage cannot be settled by the thin post-2020 series, though the mechanisms are widely noted in outside literature.

What this implies for 2030 is plain. With 91.8% of the assessed population in the marginal class, the world will not reach zero by 2030 on current trends. The regional levels shown earlier, 25.6% in South Asia and 31.1% in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2022, indicate where most of the remaining gap lies. Outside the results, experience in many countries links falls in marriage before 18 to longer schooling for girls, enforcement of a minimum legal age, and rising household incomes. These change slowly, and acceleration of the scale required would need all three to improve at once.

The proposals that follow from these findings are set out below.
