w-c05-1-2~dahlia/writer-2~73.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The world primary completion rate stood at 87.9% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 88.0% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The gain across nine years is about 0.2 percentage points. The period spans the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the school closures of 2020 and the uneven recovery since, and the aggregate shows little trace of any of them: neither a surge after 2015 nor a visible collapse after 2020. A flat global line can conceal movement in both directions, and the regional and income-group figures show that it does.

The indicator needs careful reading. Primary completion here is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of primary education: new entrants in that grade, whatever their age, divided by the population at the entrance age. Because late entrants are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100, and it is not the share of a birth cohort that finishes primary school. The figure may also overstate true completion, since pupils who leave during the final year are not adjusted for. The target can be read in more than one way: as universal completion, or as a ratio of 100 or more, which can be reached while some children remain outside school. The trend assessment in this chapter takes the second, arithmetical reading.

The movement beneath the flat world line is considerable. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024, nearly ten points. East Asia and Pacific rose from 94.1% to 95.4% by 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 97.2% to 98.1% by 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved only from 66.3% to 68.9%, so that it remains the region furthest from the target at this level. Offsetting these gains, South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 98.4% to 96.5%, and North America from 98.9% in 2015 to 96.0% in 2023. By income group, low-income countries moved from 60.5% to 62.9% in 2023, lower-middle-income countries stayed level at 88.2% and 88.0%, upper-middle-income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2%, and high-income countries held near 98%. The world average is therefore flat because regional gains in the Middle East and North Africa are cancelled by declines in South Asia and the Americas, while the poorest countries stay far below the rest.

The country classification reads accordingly. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, holding 19.6% of the assessed population, and 92 are classed as regression, holding 61.3%. A further 14 show moderate progress, 14 marginal progress and 3 stagnation. Part of the regression class may reflect countries whose ratios were inflated above 100 by late entry and repetition and have since drifted back towards 100. The results do not separate this correction from real deterioration, so the count alone cannot say how much of the regression is genuine loss.

Reporting is a further limit. Only 11 countries had reported a value for 2025 at the time of access, so the latest year is nearly empty and the global figure rests on 2024. Administrative data on last-grade entry are published with a lag, so the finding of near stagnation is firm to 2024 but says little about the final years before the target date.

### Lower secondary completion shows slow, uneven gains

The world lower secondary completion rate stood at 74.8% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 77.9% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The gain across nine years is about 3.1 percentage points. The measure is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education, so it counts new entrants in that grade whatever their age, and a value can exceed 100.0%. It indicates intake to the last grade, not certified completion.

Primary completion was 88.0% in 2024, so the gap between the two cycles is about 10 percentage points. A gross intake ratio cannot be turned into a count of adolescents who miss the last grade, and no such count is offered here. The gap does show that the pipeline narrows after primary school. The causes are well established in the literature, though the results above do not measure them: costs rise after primary school, schools become scarcer and more distant, and older children face competing demands on their time.

The regional series show where the shortfall lies. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 42.3% in 2015 and 44.4% in 2023, a rise of about 2.0 percentage points, so the region remains far below half of the way to universal intake at this level. Low-income countries moved from 37.0% in 2015 to 38.6% in 2023 and are the group furthest from the target. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 57.1% to 66.7% in 2024, a gain of about 9.5 points that is the largest after East Asia and Pacific, yet it remains below the world rate. South Asia advanced from 83.7% to 86.6%.

The regions already close to the target have moved little or have arrived. East Asia and Pacific rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, the largest regional gain and the main reason the world rate has risen. Europe and Central Asia moved from 90.9% to 91.9%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 81.3% to 81.5%, which the trend tool classes as stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 93.0% in 2023, high-income countries from 94.0% to 95.6% in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries from 71.0% to 73.7% in 2024. The world gain therefore rests chiefly on East Asia and the upper-middle-income group, while low-income countries have closed little of the distance.

Several series do not cover the full period. The North American series begins in 2016 at 104.3% and ends in 2023 at 100.8%. Both values exceed 100.0% because the ratio counts older entrants, so the decline does not signal a fall below universal intake, and the tool still classes the region as on track. The Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income and upper-middle-income series end in 2023, one year before the world series, so comparisons across aggregates mix periods of eight and nine years. Only 11 countries reported a value for 2025, too few to support any statement about that year. A rise or fall of a point or two in the latest years should not be read as firm.

The trend assessment covers 173 countries against a target of 100.0% by 2030. It places 49 on track or at target, holding 22.1% of the population covered, and 66 in regression, holding 21.1%. Thirty-two countries, with 38.4% of the population, show marginal progress. The weight of population in the marginal group means most adolescents live in countries that will not reach universal intake by 2030 without a sharp change of pace.

### Regions and countries diverge sharply

Regional averages conceal a wide spread in how far children travel through school. In Sub-Saharan Africa the primary completion rate was 68.9% of the relevant age group in 2024, up from 66.3% in 2015. Lower secondary completion in the same region was 44.4% in 2023, up from 42.3% in 2015. Fewer than half of the children in the region complete that stage, and a gain of about two points in eight years leaves it far from the target of 100.0%. The trend tool classes the region as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected value of 46.2% in 2030. Low-income countries show the same pattern: 62.9% at primary in 2023 and 38.6% at lower secondary, with an expected 2030 value of 40.1% at lower secondary. They are the group furthest from the target on both measures.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region shows the largest gain in primary completion, from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly ten points. At lower secondary the region rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. The tool still classes it as marginal progress at lower secondary, with an expected 73.9% in 2030. The regional figure mixes countries in very different circumstances, and conflict and displacement make measurement uncertain in some of them, so the gain is a regional average and not a uniform improvement.

East Asia and Pacific is the clearest success. Lower secondary completion rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, and the region is classed as on track, with an expected 105.4% in 2030. Primary completion in the region reached 95.4% in 2022, from 94.1% in 2015. Upper middle income countries are also classed as on track at lower secondary, rising from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023. Lower middle income countries moved from 71.0% to 73.7% at lower secondary and were flat at primary, at 88.2% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, so the middle-income gains are concentrated in the upper group.

Several regions went backwards at primary level. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 98.4% in 2015 to 96.5% in 2024, South Asia from 98.5% to 94.4%, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. These regions began near universal completion, so the declines differ in kind from the shortfalls in Africa. The data do not show whether the falls reflect the disruption of 2020 or changes in repetition and age at entry, which can move a gross intake ratio without any change in the number of children finishing. Europe and Central Asia, by contrast, rose from 97.2% to 98.1%. At lower secondary, Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as stagnant, at 81.3% in 2015 and 81.5% in 2024, while South Asia improved from 83.7% to 86.6%.

Country classes confirm the divide. Of 173 countries assessed on primary completion, 50 are on track or have met the target, and 92 are in regression, holding 61.3% of the classed population. Where a country already stands near or above 100.0%, the classification reads small fluctuations as decline, so the label may overstate failure; the results do not separate these cases. At lower secondary, 49 countries are on track, holding 22.1% of the population, and 66 are in regression, holding 21.1%. The 32 countries in marginal progress hold 38.4% of the classed population, which shows how many people live in countries that are advancing, but too slowly to arrive by 2030.

### Learning lags behind completion, and the data are thin

Completion measures how many children reach the last grade; it does not show what they have learned. The indicator of pupils below the minimum reading proficiency level at the end of primary schooling addresses that gap, and it shows a worse picture. Worldwide, 45.9% of pupils at the end of primary were below the minimum level in 2015, and 49.6% were below it in 2019. Set beside a world primary completion rate near nine in ten, the figures mean that a large share of children who finish primary school cannot yet read a simple, short text independently and fluently. Completion without learning does not deliver the quality that Target 4.1 requires. The series measures reading at the end of primary only. No minimum proficiency measure for the end of lower secondary is held, so the question for that stage cannot be answered from these data.

The regional contrasts are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest share below the threshold, at 80.7% in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019. Among income groups, low income countries stood at 83.5% in 2015 and 87.4% in 2019, and lower middle income countries at 52.9% and 57.4%. South Asia was nearly unchanged, at 55.8% and then 56.0%, and the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 57.7% to 57.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 49.1% to 51.0%. The data do not show why. Well-established knowledge points to rapid enrolment growth in systems that lacked the teachers, materials and classroom conditions to teach basic skills, but this account is background, not a result of the series.

At the other end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.8% to 5.5%, and high income countries from 6.4% to 6.2%. North America was flat, at 3.9% in both years. Low shares in these regions leave little room for movement, so the near absence of change there is not a stagnation of the same kind as in South Asia. Upper middle income countries were close to unchanged, at 28.0% in 2015 and 28.6% in 2019.

The largest movement was in East Asia and Pacific, where the share below the threshold rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019. A rise of that size in a region with strong education systems calls for caution. It may partly reflect a change in which countries and pupils were assessed between the two waves, not only a decline in learning. Where a wave adds countries with weaker results, the regional figure rises with no change in any single country. The data in hand cannot separate the two explanations. The trend calculation for the region, which extrapolates to 124.3% in 2030, is impossible as a share and shows only that two points cannot support a projection.

The coverage of the series explains the difficulty. Data come in survey waves, not as annual observations. Countries reporting numbered 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, with only isolated reports in 2022 and 2023, one country in the latter year. In all, 125 countries reported in at least one year. The aggregates end in 2019, so they do not capture the effect of the school closures of 2020 and after, which is a serious omission for a question about what changed after 2020. The 2021 wave exists at country level but has no regional aggregate in the results here.

For 2030 the implication is plain on the evidence available. Extrapolating the 2015 to 2019 movement gives 61.3% of pupils below the threshold worldwide, against a target of zero, and the trend is classed as regression. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 91.0% and low income countries 99.1% on the same arithmetic. Only Europe and Central Asia shows moderate progress, and it begins from a low base, with an extrapolated 3.0% in 2030. The extrapolations are mechanical, rest on two points and should be read as direction, not forecast. Still, the direction is away from the target in most regions, and the gap between completion and learning is widening where completion is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At present rates the world will miss target 4.1. The lower secondary trend to target gives the world an expected completion rate of 80.0% of the relevant age group in 2030, against a target of 100.0%, with a trend ratio of 0.21, which falls in the class of marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Primary completion shows the more troubling pattern in the country classes. Of 173 countries assessed, 92 are classed as regressing, and they hold 61.3% of the assessed population. The class is drawn from a trend to target, so a country that reached a high rate and then slipped slightly is recorded as regressing. The figure therefore overstates deterioration in places near the ceiling, and the target can be read either as exact universal completion or as a rate close to it. Even so, the size of the regressing group means that the primary result cannot be set aside as a statistical artefact.

At lower secondary the picture is more mixed. There, 49 countries are on track or have met the target, holding 22.1% of the assessed population, and 66 are regressing, holding 21.1%. The remainder sit between these poles, which shows that the world average is built from a few fast movers and a large group moving slowly. Acceleration is therefore a problem of particular places and not of every country at once.

The places furthest from the target are the low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa. Low income countries have an expected lower secondary rate of 40.1% in 2030, and Sub-Saharan Africa 46.2%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region has an expected 73.9%, which is higher but still short of the target.

Learning outcomes point the same way and are less certain. The learning trend for the world is classed as regression, with an expected share of pupils below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary of 61.3% in 2030, against a target of 0.0%. This figure is an extrapolation of a rising share and is a different quantity from the population share of regressing countries given above. In Low income countries the expected share is 99.1% in 2030, up from 87.4% in 2019, and in Sub-Saharan Africa 91.0%. These values are extrapolations from a short series, but the direction is unmistakable. The data end in 2019, so they cannot show whether the recovery since 2020 has changed the course.

t-legal-index-change-by-group~birchwood/.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params.get('start_year', 2015))
    y1 = int(params.get('mid_year', 2020))
    y2 = int(params.get('end_year', 2025))
    s = data[code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    facts = {}
    def get(d, y):
        v = d.get(y)
        if v is None:
            v = d.get(str(y))
        return v
    def run(a, b, tag):
        groups = {}
        n = 0
        rose = 0
        for c in regions:
            if c not in s:
                continue
            d = s[c] if not isinstance(next(iter(s[c].values()), None), dict) else s[c]
            va = get(d, a)
            vb = get(d, b)
            if va is None or vb is None:
                continue
            g = regions[c]
            groups.setdefault(g, []).append(vb - va)
            n += 1
            if vb > va:
                rose += 1
        facts[tag + '_countries'] = n
        facts[tag + '_rose'] = rose
        if n:
            allv = [x for l in groups.values() for x in l]
            facts[tag + '_mean_change'] = round(statistics.mean(allv), 2)
        for g in sorted(groups):
            l = groups[g]
            facts[tag + '_' + g + '_mean'] = round(statistics.mean(l), 2)
            facts[tag + '_' + g + '_rose'] = sum(1 for x in l if x > 0)
            facts[tag + '_' + g + '_n'] = len(l)
    run(y0, y2, str(y0) + '_' + str(y2))
    run(y1, y2, str(y1) + '_' + str(y2))
    k1 = str(y0) + '_' + str(y2) + '_countries'
    k2 = str(y1) + '_' + str(y2) + '_countries'
    summary = 'Change in the index ' + code + ' by region: ' + str(facts[k1]) + ' countries have scores in both ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y2) + '; ' + str(facts[k2]) + ' in both ' + str(y1) + ' and ' + str(y2) + '. Countries without both years are excluded. Index points.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}
import statistics
t-legal-index-change-by-group~birchwood/.about: Computes the change in a score series (the WBL Legal Framework Index) between two pairs of years, 2015 to 2025 and 2020 to 2025, grouped by region code, with the count of countries whose score rose. Income groups appear only if the region map carries them; here grouping uses the region map supplied. Countries missing either year are excluded.

cases.expect: Facts give, for 2015 to 2025 and 2020 to 2025, the number of countries with both years, the number whose score rose, the mean change in index points overall and per region. Rose counts never exceed country counts; the summary names both country counts.

w-c09-2-1~cedar/writer-3~74.text:
### World output per worker has risen by a fifth since 2015

Output per worker is the measure the bench uses for target 8.2, which asks for higher levels of economic productivity. GDP per person employed, expressed in constant 2021 purchasing power parity dollars, stood at 42,386 in 2015 and reached 50,672 in 2025. That is a rise of about 19.6 per cent over ten years, equivalent to roughly 1.8 per cent a year. The trend tool reads this pace as moderate progress, but with acceleration needed.

The result matters because productivity is the main route by which employment translates into rising living standards. An economy can raise total output by adding workers, but only gains in output per worker allow wages and public revenue to grow without more labour being drawn in. A global rate of 1.8 per cent a year is positive and sustained, yet it is a pace that doubles output per worker only over roughly four decades. The target's call for diversification, technological upgrading and innovation implies a faster and broader movement than this average suggests.

The indicator has no numeric target. Target 8.2 says only that productivity should be higher, so the reading rests on direction and pace rather than a threshold. Any classification of progress, including the one used here, depends on a rule applied by the tool to the observed rate of change, and a different rule would give a different label. The finding that the world has moved in the right direction is firm; the finding that the pace is moderate is a judgement about what pace would suffice.

The period contains two breaks. Growth after 2015 was shaped by weak investment and slow trade expansion in many economies, and the pandemic of 2020 disrupted employment and output sharply. Because output per worker is a ratio, such a shock can move it in either direction: when low-productivity jobs are lost first, the ratio can rise even as total output falls. The ten-year change reported here therefore compresses a path that was neither smooth nor driven by a single cause, and the endpoints alone do not separate lasting gains from statistical effects of the shock.

The limits of the series should be stated plainly. Output per worker divides GDP by total employment, so it inherits the weaknesses of both. Employment estimates in many countries rest on modelled values rather than regular labour force surveys, and informal work is imperfectly captured. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, fewer than the series' wider coverage of 177, so the latest values rest on a smaller set of economies than earlier years, and the world aggregate for 2025 is partly an estimate. Comparisons across years should be read with that in mind.

For 2030, a continuation of the present rate would add a further increase of similar proportion to the 2025 level, but it would leave the global average resting on very uneven foundations. The sections that follow show that the world figure conceals regions where output per worker has risen quickly and others where it has fallen.

### Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker

The regional spread in output per worker is wide. In 2025 a worker in North America produced 152,091 dollars of GDP (constant 2021 PPP), and one in Europe and Central Asia produced 103,033 dollars. South Asia stood at 24,604 dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 12,931 dollars, and the low-income group at 6,041 dollars. The gap between North America and the low-income group is therefore roughly twenty-five-fold, and between North America and Sub-Saharan Africa roughly twelve-fold. Differences of this size reflect capital per worker, the sectoral mix of employment, the quality of institutions and the technology in use, not effort. In low-income economies a large share of workers remain in subsistence agriculture and small household enterprises, where output per person is low and changes slowly.

Growth since 2015 has not narrowed these gaps evenly. East Asia and Pacific rose from 33,564 dollars to 49,219 dollars, a rate of 3.9 per cent a year, and the trend tool classes it as on track. South Asia rose from 17,922 dollars to 24,604 dollars, at 3.2 per cent a year, also classed on track. Both regions combined structural shifts of labour from farming to manufacturing and services with sustained investment, which is the route that target 8.2 describes through diversification and technological upgrading. East Asia and Pacific has moved close to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, which reached 50,325 dollars in 2025, up from 46,188 dollars in 2015, a pace of 0.9 per cent a year that is classed as marginal progress.

The richer regions advanced at a moderate pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 88,803 dollars to 103,033 dollars, at 1.5 per cent a year. North America rose from 132,207 dollars to 152,091 dollars, at 1.4 per cent a year. Both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Because these gains start from very high levels, a modest rate still adds a larger absolute sum per worker than the fast growth of poorer regions does in some cases. That arithmetic is one reason absolute gaps can widen while growth rates favour the poorer regions.

Two regions stand apart for lack of progress. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 42,759 dollars to 43,303 dollars, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as stagnation. A decade of near-zero productivity growth in a middle-income region points to weak investment, a large informal sector and dependence on commodity exports, which resist upgrading. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 13,373 dollars to 12,931 dollars, a rate of minus 0.3 per cent a year, classed as regression. Output per worker there has declined because employment has grown faster than output as a young and fast-growing workforce enters low-productivity work. The Sub-Saharan Africa series is truncated in the source summary for some entries, so the regional figures quoted here are those the tool returned in full, and readers should treat finer detail with caution.

For 2030 the implication is that no common global pace can be assumed. Regions already growing at three per cent or more can keep climbing, but the two regions with stagnant or falling output per worker hold the largest shares of workers in poverty, and the target cannot be met in spirit while they stay behind. The target itself sets no numerical threshold, so classifications such as on track rest on the bench's reading of a rising trend, and a different reading would change them.

### Country outcomes split between rapid gains and decline

Beyond the world average, the bench classifies each of the 177 countries with data by the pace of its output per worker. Because the target 8.2 carries no numeric threshold, the classes rest on a model-based reading of each country's trend towards 2030, and the labels should be taken as relative judgements rather than findings against a legal standard.

The result is a split. A total of 48 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 52.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. At the other end, 46 countries are in regression, meaning that output per worker has fallen over the period, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population. Between the two lie 30 countries with moderate progress that needs acceleration, 34 with marginal progress that needs significant acceleration, and 19 in stagnation. Together the middle three classes account for 83 countries, nearly half of those assessed, yet their population shares are 17.0 per cent, 7.4 per cent and 8.1 per cent respectively.

The gap between the count of countries and the share of people is the main interpretive point. Counted by country, 48 of 177 are on track, a little over a quarter. Counted by population, the on-track group holds just over half. The difference arises because several very populous economies, which have long sustained rapid growth in output per worker as labour moves from farming into industry and services, sit in the on-track class. Their weight lifts the population-weighted picture well above the picture seen by a government counting its peers. A reader should therefore not conclude that most countries are advancing: by number, those regressing nearly match those on track.

Regression is the most troubling class, since it means that workers in these 46 countries produce less than before. Well-established causes include conflict and state fragility, commodity price collapses, macroeconomic crises and, after 2020, the lasting loss of output and employment disruption from the pandemic. Many of these economies start from low levels of output per worker, so decline widens the gap with the rest rather than closing it. Stagnation, in 19 countries, points to economies where structural change has stalled, with labour remaining in low-productivity activity.

The classification also depends on choices that could be made differently. Without a numeric target, a different benchmark, such as a growth rate set by the target's wording of higher productivity or a rate needed to halve a gap with richer economies, would move countries between classes. Employment estimates, which underlie the denominator, are modelled for many countries, so countries near class boundaries may be misplaced. For 2030, the implication is that the world average conceals a divergence: a large group of populous economies is advancing, while a sizeable minority of countries, mostly poorer ones, is losing ground and will need a change of course, not just faster growth, to reach higher productivity by the end of the decade.

### Inequality between countries has narrowed, but convergence is weak

The spread of output per worker among countries has narrowed over the decade. Weighting each country by its population, the Gini coefficient of GDP per person employed fell from 0.449 in 2015 to 0.427 in 2020 and 0.412 in 2025. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the top and bottom of the distribution, fell from 0.347 to 0.308 and then to 0.286. Both measures point the same way. The fall was somewhat larger in the first five years than in the second, although the 2025 figures cover 168 countries against 177 earlier, so part of the comparison rests on a changed set of countries.

The narrowing is not matched by catch-up among countries as such. The convergence test regresses each country's growth in output per worker over 2015 to 2025 on its starting level. If poorer countries were closing the gap, the coefficient would be clearly negative. It is -0.00249, with a p-value of 0.0541, so it falls just short of the conventional 5 per cent threshold, and the R2 is 0.013, meaning that the starting level explains about 1.3 per cent of the variation in growth across the 168 countries. The unweighted coefficient of variation, which treats every country alike, moved only from 0.893 to 0.876 on this common set. The weighted measures fell far more than the unweighted one, which implies that the improvement came mainly from where the large economies stood, not from a general closing of the gap by small and poor ones. Fast growth in a few populous economies lowers a population-weighted index even when most countries stay where they were relative to the rest.

The decomposition by region supports this reading. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions rose from 68.3 per cent in 2015 to 71.9 per cent in 2020 and 75.2 per cent in 2025. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the remaining inequality, and the divide that persists is increasingly one between world regions. Countries within a region have grown more alike, while the distance between the high-output and low-output regions has proved harder to close. This fits the regional levels described earlier in the section, where the lowest-income groups remain a small fraction of the output per worker of the richest.

The period saw two shocks, and they affect how the figures should be read. The pandemic of 2020 cut output sharply in many economies, including some of the richest, and a temporary fall at the top can lower measured inequality without any gain for poorer workers. Recovery since then has been uneven, and the lower Gini and Theil values of 2025 show that the earlier narrowing has held rather than reversed. Even so, a weak and statistically marginal convergence coefficient gives little ground to expect that gaps between countries will close by 2030 on present trends. Target 8.2 sets no numeric threshold, and it can be read either as higher productivity everywhere or as faster productivity gains where levels are lowest. On the first reading, the world has made progress. On the second, the evidence is thin, and the narrowing seen in the weighted indices should not be mistaken for it.

### Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals

The pace of productivity growth follows the shocks that struck the world economy more than any steady trend. The break analysis for the world series finds change points in 2004, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. Between 2004 and 2008, output per worker rose by a mean of 1,001 dollars a year (constant 2021 PPP). The global financial crisis interrupted that run in 2009, when the mean annual change was -404.0 dollars. From 2010 to 2019 gains resumed at a mean of 967.5 dollars a year, close to the pre-crisis pace but not above it. The decade before the Goals were adopted therefore ended with no acceleration in the rate of gain.

The pandemic repeated the pattern on a similar scale. In 2020 output per worker fell by 369.1 dollars, and in 2021 it rebounded by 1,567 dollars. Part of the rebound is a recovery of what was lost, and part reflects the composition of employment: when low-productivity jobs disappear in a downturn, output per remaining worker can rise even where output is falling. From 2022 to 2025 the mean annual gain was 815.5 dollars, below the 2010-2019 pace. The recovery has thus not restored the earlier rate of improvement, and a pace of that size leaves the world short of a path that would lift low-productivity regions towards 2030 in any meaningful way.

The link between productivity and headline growth is weaker than might be assumed. Across 168 countries for 2015-2025, the Spearman correlation between changes in output per worker and GDP growth is -0.048, which is effectively no relation. For 2025 levels the Spearman coefficient is -0.413, a moderate negative association: countries with lower output per worker tend to record higher growth rates. This is consistent with catch-up from a low base, but also with growth that comes from adding workers or hours rather than raising output per worker, so that rapid GDP growth does not by itself signal rising productivity. Rank correlations also say nothing of cause, and the two series are measured with different coverage and quality.

The country classification shows why the outlook for 2030 is uneven. Of 177 countries assessed, 46 are in regression, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population assessed, while 19 are stagnating. Target 8.2 has no numeric threshold, so these classes are relative readings and not findings against a fixed standard.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. Each concerns the pace of gain, the countries left behind and the quality of the evidence.

Development partners and multilateral lenders should direct technical and financial support first to the lagging regions, above all low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa, and to the countries in regression, tying it to diversification and technological upgrading.

National statistical offices, with the International Labour Organization and the World Bank, should improve the coverage and timeliness of employment data, so that output per worker can be computed for every country and separated from changes in hours worked and in the composition of employment.

Target 8.2 has no numeric threshold, so the country classes are relative readings. The data do not cover sectoral productivity, so diversification and high-value-added activity cannot be assessed directly. The correlations are rank associations and do not establish cause.

w-c08-4-1~willow/writer-1~74.text:
### Global energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured in megajoules per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, stood at 4.8556 in 2015 and at 4.5449 in 2021. That is a fall of about 6.4 per cent over six years, or roughly 1.1 per cent a year. The trend tool records a rate of -0.01096 for the world and classes it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Lower intensity means that less primary energy is supplied for each unit of output, so the direction is right; the question this section poses is whether the pace is adequate.

Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, and the wording admits more than one reading. The first difficulty is the baseline: the rate to be doubled may be the rate of an earlier period, such as the years before 2015, or the rate of the first years after adoption, and the choice changes what counts as success. The second is the measure. Energy intensity of GDP is the customary proxy, yet it reflects more than efficiency in the engineering sense. A shift from manufacturing to services lowers intensity without any device becoming more efficient, and a change in the price of fuels or in the exchange of goods between countries can move it too. The figure used here is therefore an indicator of the target and not a direct measurement of it.

The series also stops early. The world value ends in 2021, and only some regions carry a value for 2022. The bench's tool reports 116 countries reporting in 2022, against a coverage of 201 economies for the series as a whole, so the latest year is thin and aggregates for it should be read with care. Years after 2021 are absent from the global figure, which means that the recovery from the shock of 2020 and the energy price disturbances that followed are not captured. Any statement about how far the world has moved since the pandemic rests on a record that ends before those events had fully worked through.

The period 2015 to 2021 nevertheless offers a first reading. A fall of 1.1 per cent a year is a steady gain, but target 7.3 demands more than steadiness. If the rate of improvement is to double against a baseline of the same order, the annual fall would need to be roughly twice what is recorded here for the whole of the remaining period to 2030. The sections that follow examine whether the regions that matter most for the world total are moving at that speed, and when within the period the gains were made.

### Regions improved at very different speeds

Europe and Central Asia is the one region that clearly stands apart. Its intensity fell from 4.002 megajoules per dollar in 2015 to 2.5791 in 2022, a rate of -0.06083 in the trend tool's units, and it is classed as on track or target met. The fall is steeper than that of any other region, and it is large enough to pull the high-income group down with it, from 4.3961 in 2015 to 3.4666 in 2022 (rate -0.03337, also on track). Part of this reflects long-standing efficiency policy, building standards, fuel switching and the restructuring of heavy industry. Part may reflect the cyclical effects of the 2022 energy price shock, which cut consumption. The data alone cannot separate the two.

North America and South Asia also improved appreciably. North America moved from 5.0428 in 2015 to 4.364 in 2022 (rate -0.02044), and South Asia from 4.5047 in 2015 to 3.9427 in 2021 (rate -0.02197). Both are classed as on track. The two cases differ in nature. North America began from a high level and gained through vehicle and appliance standards and a shift in the fuel mix. South Asia gained while its economy grew quickly, which can lower intensity when output expands faster than energy supply, and when growth shifts toward services.

East Asia and Pacific made moderate progress, from 5.6997 in 2015 to 5.2313 in 2021 (rate -0.01419), and the trend tool says acceleration is needed. The region's weight in world industry means that its pace bears heavily on the global result. Latin America and the Caribbean has the lowest starting level among the developing regions, 3.4822 in 2015, and moved only to 3.265 in 2022 (rate -0.00916). Progress there is marginal, and significant acceleration is needed. A low level partly reflects an economy with a large share of hydropower and services, so there is less obvious scope for gains.

Two regions were almost flat. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from 5.3599 in 2015 to 5.332 in 2021 (rate -0.00087), and Sub-Saharan Africa from 6.2412 to 6.1403 over the same years (rate -0.00271). Both are classed as stagnation. In energy-exporting economies, low domestic fuel prices and subsidies weaken the incentive to save energy. In Sub-Saharan Africa, intensity is high in part because of inefficient fuel use and old equipment, and because of a heavy weight of energy-intensive activity relative to output. The caution on reading these numbers is that the measure divides energy by GDP, so it mixes efficiency with economic structure. A region rich in heavy industry or cold climates will show a higher intensity than a services economy using energy equally well.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 7.415 in 2015 to 7.1393 in 2021 (rate -0.00629), the highest level and marginal progress. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 4.644 to 4.2707 (rate -0.01387), moderate progress. Upper-middle-income countries went from 5.5767 to 5.2119 (rate -0.01121), marginal progress. The countries with the highest intensity are thus improving least, so the gap between them and the high-income group widened in relative terms. Country data are not summarised here, and the number of reporting countries in the latest year is small, so regional figures for 2021 and 2022 rest on partial coverage.

### The rate of improvement peaked before 2018 and then slowed

The break analysis of the annual change in world energy intensity divides the series into five segments, with statistical breaks falling in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. The first segment, 2001-2004, shows a mean annual change of -0.0498 megajoules per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. The second, 2005-2008, is more than twice as steep, at -0.1154. The third, 2009-2010, is slightly positive at 0.0070, which means that intensity rose on average in those two years. The fourth, 2011-2017, returns to a fast decline of -0.1045. The last, 2018-2021, is -0.0325.

The pattern is that of a rate which peaked and then eased, not one that rose steadily. The two fast segments, 2005-2008 and 2011-2017, run at about the same pace, near 0.10 to 0.12 megajoules per year. The latest segment is about a third of the 2011-2017 rate (0.0325 against 0.1045, a ratio of 0.31). Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement. A rate that has fallen to a third of its recent peak runs in the opposite direction. Even measured against the slow early segment of 2001-2004, the latest rate is smaller still, at 0.65 of that earlier pace (0.0325 against 0.0498). By this reading, the most recent years are the weakest of the four declining segments, and the doubling is not being approached.

Several cautions apply. The breaks are statistical devices. They mark years in which the mean annual change shifts enough to be detected in a series of annual observations, and they do not mark events. The dates are therefore approximate, and a different method or a different window could place them a year earlier or later. The segments are also short: the 2009-2010 segment holds only two observations, and the last holds four, so each mean rests on few points and is sensitive to a single unusual year. The final segment ends in 2021, so the later years for which other series extend to 2022 and beyond are not covered by this analysis.

The positive change in 2009-2010 coincides with the global financial crisis and its recovery. That timing is suggestive, and it is consistent with what is generally understood about downturns: when output falls sharply, energy use does not fall in proportion, because buildings, vehicles and industrial plant still consume energy at low utilisation, so intensity can rise. A rebound can then reverse the effect. The data on hand show the coincidence in time but do not establish the cause.

The same restraint applies to the slowdown after 2018. Candidate explanations are many. The pandemic disrupted output and energy use in 2020 and 2021 in uneven ways, and the 2018-2021 segment contains both years. Energy prices affect the incentive to save energy. Structural change in economies, such as a shift between industry and services, or the relocation of energy-heavy production, moves intensity without any change in the efficiency of individual processes. Changes in the pace of investment in efficient buildings, appliances and industrial equipment would also matter. The series used here is a ratio of primary energy supply to GDP, and it cannot separate these influences. Attribution would need sector-level data and decomposition methods that this analysis does not provide.

For 2030, the implication is that the recent record does not support an expectation of a doubled rate. The 2011-2017 segment shows that a fast pace has been reached before, at about three times the latest rate, so the slowdown is not a fixed ceiling. Whether the faster pace can be regained depends on factors the break analysis cannot see. What the analysis does show is that the starting point for any acceleration is a rate that has weakened, and that the later years of this decade would have to run well above anything seen since 2018.

### Target 7.3 is not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030. The target does not name a baseline period, and it can be read in more than one way: as a rate twice that of an earlier span, or as a rate twice that of the decades before 2015. On either reading, the measured record falls short. The world mean annual change in the 2018-2021 segment was -0.03247 megajoules per dollar, against -0.10452 in 2011-2017. The later rate is about a third of the earlier one, not double it. The 2015-2021 average does not approach the earlier rate either: the trend tool gives a world rate of -0.01096 and classes it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The unit of that rate differs from the segment means, so the comparison rests on the direction and the size of the gap, not on a single ratio.

The regional picture shows why the aggregate is weak. Only Europe and Central Asia (-0.06083), North America (-0.02044), South Asia (-0.02197) and the high-income group (-0.03337) are classed as on track or target met. Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.00271) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (-0.00087) are classed as stagnating. Their intensities in the latest year were 6.1403 and 5.332, against 6.2412 and 5.3599 in 2015. East Asia and Pacific, the largest energy-using region in the group, improved at -0.01419 and is classed as needing acceleration. Latin America and the Caribbean (-0.00916) and the low-income group (-0.00629) are classed as marginal. The regions that improve fastest are not those where the most efficiency is to be gained. Low-income countries still use 7.1393 megajoules per dollar, about twice the level of the high-income group at 3.4666.

The implication for 2030 is that the target will be missed unless the recent pattern changes sharply. Data end in 2021 for most regions and in 2022 for some, so the post-2020 record is short and mixed with the recovery from the pandemic, when output and energy use moved unevenly. The slowdown after 2018 may be partly a cyclical effect and partly a sign that the easiest gains, such as the retirement of old industrial capacity, have been taken. Neither can be settled with the present series. Intensity also reflects the structure of an economy as well as efficiency: a shift from heavy industry to services lowers it with no change in how any process uses energy, and the reverse shift in a developing economy raises it. A fall in the ratio therefore cannot be read as efficiency gain alone.

These findings point to a small number of actions, set out in the proposals below.

w-c04-6-1~ewan/writer-1~75.text:
### The global rate barely moved after 2015

The 2020 target to halve road deaths was not met on the evidence available. The World Bank's indicator of mortality caused by road traffic injury, expressed as estimated deaths per 100,000 population, stood at 17.0 for the world in 2015 and at 16.7 in 2019. That is a fall of about 1.5 per cent over four years. A halving would have required a rate near 8.5 by 2020, and the measured rate remained close to double that level.

Two limits on this reading need stating. The series ends in 2019, so the target year itself cannot be observed; the conclusion rests on the last four years before it, and a sudden fall in 2020 of the size required is not plausible given how slowly the rate moved beforehand. The path of 2020 is also disturbed by the pandemic, when restrictions on movement reduced traffic in many places, so any later figure would need careful interpretation before it was read as progress on safety.

The second limit concerns the wording of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of deaths and injuries, and of the number of them, whereas the indicator covers deaths only and is a rate per head of population. A rate can fall while the count of deaths rises if population grows faster, and it can stay flat while the count grows. The target can therefore be read in more than one way: as a halving of the count, or as a halving of the rate. On either reading the evidence points the same way, since the rate has barely changed and no series on non-fatal injuries is held on the shelf. The measure used here is the more lenient of the two, which makes the shortfall harder to dismiss.

Coverage supports the finding. Estimates are available for 183 countries in 2019 and for 190 countries in at least one year, with regional and income aggregates alongside. The series is modelled by the World Health Organization rather than counted directly, since many countries lack complete registration of deaths by cause. A flat global line therefore reflects estimates built from a mix of registered and modelled data, and small movements of the order seen here should not be over-read. What can be said with confidence is the scale of the gap between the target and the outcome, not the precise change of a few tenths of a point.

### Regions diverged, and only Europe and Central Asia moved fast

Regional rates for 2015 and 2019 show that the small global movement conceals very different trajectories. Europe and Central Asia was the only region to record a substantial decline, from 9.2 deaths per 100,000 population in 2015 to 7.4 in 2019. That is the lowest regional rate in the series and the only one that approaches the level a halving would have required. The decline is consistent with long-established road safety policy in much of that region: enforcement of speed limits and seat-belt use, safer vehicle standards, and investment in road design.

East Asia and Pacific moved only slightly, from 17.0 to 16.5. Latin America and Caribbean fell from 18.3 to 17.3, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 17.3 to 17.0. These are declines of a few per cent, far from the pace the 2020 target implied. South Asia was effectively flat, at 15.6 in 2015 and 15.6 in 2019, which means that its rate did not fall while motor vehicle use continued to expand in the region.

Two regions moved in the wrong direction. North America rose from 11.5 to 11.9, an increase from a rate that was already above that of Europe and Central Asia. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.8 to 27.4, and it carries the highest regional rate in either year. The pattern matters for 2030: the places with the most deaths per head are not the places that are improving, and rapid motorisation without matching investment in roads, vehicle standards and emergency care tends to raise road deaths before it lowers them.

These comparisons rest on regional means, and a mean can hide wide spread among the countries inside a region. A region's rate reflects both its safest and its most dangerous countries, and the ranking of regions says little about any single national road network. Coverage is broad but not complete: 183 countries report in 2019, and the indicator is built from modelled estimates, not only from counted deaths, so small year-to-year changes in a regional rate should be read with caution. The country-level spread is taken up in the next part.

### Dispersion widened while few places gained ground

The convergence test asks whether countries with higher road death rates in 2015 reduced them faster than others up to 2019. Across 182 countries the estimated coefficient (beta) is 0.031, with a p-value of 0.0058. The sign is positive. Under the convention of the test, a negative coefficient would indicate catch-up by high-rate countries; a positive one indicates that the countries with higher starting rates fell more slowly, or rose, relative to the rest. The result is therefore the opposite of convergence, and it is unlikely to be a chance finding at conventional thresholds.

The second measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation, the standard deviation of national rates divided by their mean, rose from 0.54 in 2015 to 0.63 in 2019. Rates across countries were more unequal in relation to their average at the end of the window than at the start. A world rate that scarcely changed therefore hides a widening spread: some countries, concentrated in the lower-rate regions already described, improved, while many high-rate countries stood still or deteriorated. The low-income group, whose mean rate rose between the two years, is consistent with this reading.

The limits of the test are considerable. The R-squared is 0.108, so initial rates account for only about one-tenth of the variation in subsequent change. Most of what separates one country's trajectory from another's lies outside this simple relationship. The window is also only four years, from 2015 to 2019, and short intervals magnify the effect of estimation noise. Country figures for road deaths are modelled estimates, since many countries lack complete death registration with cause information, and year-to-year movements in a modelled series may partly reflect revisions of method and inputs rather than real change. The test also stops at 2019 and says nothing of the period after 2020.

The tools measure outcomes, not causes, so any explanation must remain cautious. Well-established experience suggests that road deaths fall where speed management, helmet and seat-belt laws, vehicle safety standards and emergency care are enforced, and that they rise where motorisation grows faster than safe road design and enforcement. Countries that already held such measures were better placed to continue improving, while rapidly motorising low-income countries faced rising exposure. That would produce widening dispersion, but this reading is a hypothesis consistent with the pattern, not a result the data establish.

For 2030 the implication is that a rising spread makes a uniform global pace misleading. Progress will depend on the countries at the top of the distribution, where rates are highest and have not fallen.

### The 2030 target of 8.5 needs a different pace, and proposals follow

The 2030 horizon asks for a rate of 8.5 deaths per 100,000 population, which is the 2015-era world rate of 17.0 halved. Set against that figure, the trend projections show how far the present pace falls short. The world rate is expected to reach 16.1 in 2030 if the 2015 to 2019 movement continues, a ratio of 0.11 of the pace required. The classification is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The distance between 16.1 and 8.5 is close to the whole of the 2015 rate.

Only two groups are on track. Europe and Central Asia is expected to reach 4.1 in 2030, with a ratio of 6.91, meaning its pace is nearly seven times that required for its own path to the target. High-income countries are expected to reach 7.3, a ratio of 2.48, which also lies below 8.5. Both results rest on four years of data and on a mix of countries with long-standing road safety regimes. The high-income result is the less secure of the two, since its 2019 rate of 8.7 still stood above 8.5.

East Asia and Pacific shows marginal progress, with an expected rate of 15.2 in 2030 and a ratio of 0.22. Latin America and the Caribbean is similar, at 14.8 and 0.36. Upper middle income countries are expected to reach 15.2, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 16.2. None of these approaches 8.5 on present pace. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnating, at 17.3.

Four groups show regression. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 29.2 and low-income countries at 31.5, both rising. North America is projected at 13.3, and South Asia at 15.7. The groups with the highest rates are therefore moving away from the target, while those that have already reduced deaths are moving towards it. The 2030 gap will be set largely where motorisation is expanding fastest and roads, vehicle standards and emergency care are weakest.

The figure of 8.5 is one reading of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of halving the number of deaths and injuries, not the rate. A halving of counts would be harder where populations and vehicle fleets are growing, and a halving of the rate ignores that growth. The 2015 base year is also a convention, since the target text names no baseline. Injuries are not measured by the indicator used here. Readers should treat 8.5 as a benchmark and not as the single correct threshold.

Several proposals follow from these findings.

w-c09-3-1~cedar/writer-2~75.text:
### Vulnerable employment is the measured proxy for informality

Informal employment, the condition target 8.3 has in view, is not measured directly by any series on the shelf. The nearest measured proxy is vulnerable employment: the sum of own-account workers and contributing family workers, expressed as a percentage of total employment. The series is a modeled estimate of the International Labour Organization, and it is available for 187 economies, with 182 countries reporting in 2025. The proxy is imperfect. Some own-account workers are registered, taxed and covered by social protection, while some wage jobs are informal, with no contract and no insurance. The share of vulnerable employment therefore indicates the extent of weak job security and thin social protection, and it cannot be read as a count of informal jobs.

A second caution concerns the target itself. Target 8.3 asks for policies that encourage the formalization and growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises, but it names no numeric threshold and no year-specific level. Any statement of progress is thus a reading of direction: whether the share falls, stays flat or rises. The trend tool applies a decreasing direction by 2030 with no fixed goal, and its verdicts should be understood in that light. A different reader might judge the same movement more or less favourably.

At world level, vulnerable employment stood at 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 and at 42.4 per cent in 2025. The fall is about 0.7 percentage points over a decade. Roughly two in five workers worldwide therefore remain in own-account or contributing family work, a share that has barely moved across a period that included the adoption of the goals and the shock of 2020. The trend tool classes the world movement as stagnation, with an annual rate of change of -0.0017 on its scale.

This matters because the world figure conceals very different realities, taken up in the parts that follow. It also matters because vulnerable work is the form of employment least likely to carry a stable wage, a contract or a pension. A global share that has hardly shifted suggests that the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not, on the whole, been converted into a move towards paid employment with protection. The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring in many low-income economies probably weighed on the decade, although the series, being modeled, cannot show the timing of such effects with precision.

### Regions differ by a factor of sixteen

In 2025 the regional range in vulnerable employment is wide. South Asia stands at 69.7 per cent of total employment and Sub-Saharan Africa at 71.0 per cent. North America stands at 4.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 12.9 per cent. The highest regional figure is therefore about sixteen times the lowest (71.0 against 4.5). Two regions, both in the developing world, have roughly seven in ten workers in own-account or contributing family work. In the richest region the figure is below one in twenty.

The middle group lies between these poles and is more tightly bunched. East Asia and Pacific stands at 35.3 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 36.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 31.5 per cent. In each of these regions roughly one worker in three is in vulnerable employment. The three differ by less than five percentage points, although their economic structures, institutions and histories are quite unlike. A region-wide average also conceals large differences among countries, and the regional figures are population-weighted aggregates of modeled estimates, not direct counts.

The pattern follows the structure of production. Where agriculture and small-scale household enterprise employ most people and large firms offering wage contracts are few, own-account work and unpaid family work are the default forms of employment. Where manufacturing and services are organised in larger firms and wage employment is the norm, the share is small. The income groups tell the same story. Low-income economies stand at 76.1 per cent and high-income economies at 8.0 per cent, so that income level and the share of vulnerable work move together.

The figure for Sub-Saharan Africa is cut short in the source summary and the tool output carries the full value, which is the one used here. The spread across countries confirms that region is the main divide: 71.9 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2025 lies between regions, not within them. For target 8.3 this means that the task of formalisation is concentrated in a few regions, and that national averages in the middle group still hide pockets of far higher vulnerability.

### Women carry more vulnerability where it is highest

In 2025 the world figure for women stands at 43.1 per cent of female employment, against 41.9 per cent of male employment for men. The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point. It conceals a division by region. Where vulnerable employment is most widespread, women are more exposed than men. Where it is rare, the order reverses.

The gap is widest in South Asia, where 76.2 per cent of employed women are in vulnerable jobs against 67.1 per cent of employed men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the figures are 79.2 per cent for women and 63.9 per cent for men, a difference of more than fifteen points. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the shares are 41.6 per cent and 34.7 per cent. These are the regions in which a large part of women's work is unpaid help in a family farm or business, or own-account activity in small trade and agriculture, with little social protection. Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work, since it can be combined with household duties.

The pattern runs the other way in the richest regions. In Europe and Central Asia the female share is 11.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent for men, and in North America 3.3 per cent against 5.4 per cent. High income economies show 6.9 per cent for women and 9.0 per cent for men. Men are more often self-employed in these economies, in trades, construction and freelance work, while women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts in services, health and education. A lower share of vulnerable employment among women here is not by itself a sign of advantage, since the series does not capture pay, hours or the quality of wage jobs.

By income group the same crossing appears. In low income countries the female share is 82.9 per cent and the male share 70.9 per cent. In lower middle income countries the figures are 74.0 per cent and 61.2 per cent. In upper middle income countries the gap narrows to 35.6 per cent against 34.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is close to parity, at 31.3 per cent for women and 31.6 per cent for men. The gender gap in vulnerability is thus largest in the poorest settings and closes as incomes rise, which bears directly on the inclusive aim of target 8.3.

### Change has been slow, uneven and not convergent

Across the 187 countries assessed, the trend to 2030 is mostly one of slow or absent progress. Only 24 countries, holding 3.7 per cent of the population of the group, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 19 countries, with 6.1 per cent of the population, show moderate progress that would need acceleration. The largest population weight lies in the 48 countries with marginal progress, which hold 51.7 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. Another 59 countries stagnate, with 25.0 per cent of the population, and 37 regress, with 13.5 per cent. Target 8.3 sets no numerical threshold, so the classes measure movement in the desired direction (a decrease) and not distance from an agreed goal; the reading is one of direction only.

The weight of population in the slower classes matters more than the count of countries. Large economies with high shares of own-account and family work move slowly, so the world average is determined by them, while many small and wealthy economies that were already low account for most of the on-track count. Progress that does occur is therefore concentrated where the problem was already smaller.

Between-country inequality in the indicator did not narrow. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.317 in 2015 across 187 countries and 0.320 in 2025 across 182. The Theil index moved from 0.178 to 0.182. The share of that inequality lying between regions, and not within them, stayed near 71 per cent: 70.8 per cent in 2015 and 71.9 per cent in 2025. The geography of vulnerability is thus still mainly a matter of which region a worker lives in. The change in country coverage, from 187 to 182, is small and does not alter the reading.

The convergence test points the same way. The coefficient on initial levels is slightly negative (beta -0.00281, p-value 0.0001), so countries with higher initial shares fell marginally faster, but the fit is weak, with an R-squared of 0.066 across 182 countries. Meanwhile the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.717 to 0.735, meaning that dispersion between countries grew. A weak tendency towards catching up coexists with a widening spread, which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved. Neither the post-2015 nor the post-2020 period can be separated by these summary measures, and the shock of 2020 is not isolated here.

Wage and salaried employment is the mirror of vulnerable employment. The rank correlation of 2025 levels is -0.994, and that of changes since 2015 is -0.920, across 182 countries. Because the two shares are close to complements, with employers forming a small remainder, this is largely definitional and gives no independent evidence that wage growth causes lower vulnerability. It does show that a fall in vulnerable work has meant a rise in paid employment, and not a shift towards other forms of work.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace of 2015 to 2025 the world would not reach a markedly lower share by 2030. The trend tool classes the world as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0017 a year, a change too small to alter the lives of most workers within five years. The calculation extends the recent line and is not a forecast. Target 8.3 sets no number for vulnerable employment, so the reading of 'on track' is the tool's: any decrease counts as movement in the right direction. Measured against the wider aim of decent work, the pace is insufficient.

The global result is decided by the populous group of 48 countries with marginal progress, which holds 51.7 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. South Asia, with a rate of -0.0074, and East Asia and Pacific, with -0.0074, sit in this class. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0007, stagnates, and Low income countries are classed as regression, with a rate of 0.0000. These are the places where the share is highest or where the numbers of workers are largest. Faster movement there would count for more than any gain in Europe and Central Asia (-0.0137) or among high income countries (-0.0127), where the share is already low.

The link between vulnerable employment and wage employment is close: across 182 countries the Spearman correlation of 2025 levels is -0.99, and of changes since 2015 it is -0.92. Vulnerable employment falls where wage jobs grow. The two series largely mirror one another, so the route to lower vulnerability runs through the creation of paid jobs and the growth of firms able to employ, and not through relabelling own-account work.

Five proposals follow. The International Labour Organization and national statistical offices should monitor informal employment directly alongside the modeled proxy, using labour force surveys. Governments should set a quantified national reading of target 8.3, stating the share of vulnerable or informal work to be reached by 2030. Ministries of labour and of industry in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa should prioritise wage job creation and the formalisation of micro and small enterprises, with access to finance and simpler registration. National planners should give women's vulnerability its own targets, since women are more exposed where the share is highest. Statistical agencies and the ILO should report data gaps openly, including the modeled status of many national figures.
