w-c06-1-3~dahlia/writer-1~76.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Equal weighting is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through a household survey, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change since 2015 or 2020 has been drawn from the shelf, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot be answered in magnitude here. The remainder of this section therefore sets out how the index should be read and what a measured answer would require, and offers no estimate of change.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds safety and childcare, domains the earlier one largely omitted, and it is accompanied by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice. The only computed result for this section is the coverage of the legal index, which reports for 189 economies in 2025 and for 189 in any year. The companion series are described as covering a similar but not identical set of economies, so the three indices will not align perfectly.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them as though they measured the same thing; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the inclusion of safety and childcare lowers the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse, and legal provision for childcare with quality standards are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether comparable values exist back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been verified. If they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and any statement about the decade would need a different instrument.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because its indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed here, and it is the natural next measurement for this section.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

A measured answer to how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed would have four parts. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and because a handful of large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones.

The third part is the distribution: the spread between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index differ in level and pace, and an average across them hides the information a policymaker most needs. Of these four parts, the bench has so far produced only the coverage count: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and 189 reported it in at least one year. Level, change, distribution and topic scores remain to be computed, and this section does not claim a direction of reform.

Two patterns are worth testing, and both are stated as expectations rather than findings. Comparative law suggests that labour codes, treated as instruments of economic policy, are easier to amend than family and personal-status codes, which are bound up with religious authority and custom. If that holds, the remaining distance to equality would lie in the rules governing a woman's capacity to act independently: where she lives, what documents she can hold, whether she heads a household and how she inherits. The second expectation concerns the period after 2020, when school and nursery closures made childcare visible as an economic institution. Comparing average annual change before and after 2020 would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or paused. Because the measure is built from statute and not from reported statistics, an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores themselves.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool lists the aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. South Asia is the only geographic region among the listed aggregates. A comparison across the other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison matters because formal law costs little to change, whereas implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, maternity and paternity benefit schemes, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. If the relation between income and the legal score is weaker than the relation between income and the supportive and enforcement scores, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking built on it would misdirect attention. This is a hypothesis, not a finding. The test is to compare, for each income group, the gap between the legal score and each companion score.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, reproductive decisions and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on provisions in the domains the index scores. Until group-level values exist, the book cannot say whether the economies with the worst outcomes are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation. What the record does establish is its breadth: 189 economies reported the index in 2025, and 189 reported in at least one year.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading. The shelf lets either be tested for 189 economies in 2025, the full set that reports the Legal Framework Index, but the bench has so far computed only that coverage, not the levels or changes.

Under the strict reading, the relevant measures are the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they are the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. A projection to 2030 at the observed pace would show how many years each income group would need to reach full formal equality.

What can be said now concerns definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar and any economy's position should be judged against it. A perfect legal score is also necessary for equality of economic opportunity but not sufficient. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account: its census of 189 economies in 2025 means that a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The task the section leaves to the bench is to turn that coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every economy.

w-c07-4-1~farah/writer-2~76.text:
### Water quality is measured mainly through sanitation and ecosystem proxies

Target 6.3 calls for halving the proportion of untreated wastewater, and Target 6.6 for the protection and restoration of water-related ecosystems, including mountains, forests, wetlands, rivers, aquifers and lakes. Neither can be measured directly with the series on the shelf of the World Bank's World Development Indicators. No series on the share of wastewater treated, on ambient water quality in rivers, lakes and aquifers, or on the condition of wetlands is held. Any reading of these two targets is therefore indirect, and the conclusions drawn from it carry less weight than those for drinking water or sanitation access.

Three kinds of proxy are available. Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using a private facility whose excreta are safely disposed of or treated, is the nearest stand-in for Target 6.3, because untreated human waste is among the main sources of pollution in surface and ground water. Terrestrial protected areas and forest area stand in for Target 6.6, since protected catchments and forested slopes shape the quality and regularity of the water that flows from them. Marine protected areas, water stress and the mortality rate attributed to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene supply context. Each is a proxy in the strict sense. Sanitation safely managed at the household says nothing about industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, which Target 6.3 also names. A land area under protection is a legal designation, not a measure of the health of a river or wetland, and forest area records tree cover without distinguishing natural stands from plantations.

The sanitation series is also the thinnest of its kind among the household indicators, though its coverage is stable. Countries reporting numbered 137 in 2000, 146 in 2016, the highest count in the series, and 141 in 2024. The count therefore fell by five countries between 2016 and 2024, a drift that began after 2019 and deepened after 2020, when disruption to household surveys and to national statistical offices was widespread. A total of 146 countries reported in at least one year, so some economies are never covered at all. Regional and income-group figures are modelled aggregates, and they rest on fewer observations in the places where sanitation is weakest. The estimates that follow should be read with that limitation in mind.

### Safely managed sanitation rose from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent between 2015 and 2024

Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using improved facilities that are not shared and from which excreta are safely disposed of, stood at 48.4 per cent of the world population in 2015 and at 58.5 per cent in 2024. The gain of about ten percentage points over nine years is substantial, and the series covers 141 countries reporting in 2024, so the global figure rests on a broad base rather than a handful of observations.

What this proxy says about Target 6.3 is limited, and the limit matters. The indicator follows excreta through the whole chain of containment, emptying, transport and treatment or disposal, so a rise in it means that more households are served by systems that do not leave waste in streets, fields and watercourses. That is a reasonable stand-in for pressure on water quality from human waste. It does not measure the share of wastewater that is treated, nor industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, and it says nothing about the condition of the rivers, lakes and aquifers that receive the discharge. A country may serve its households well and still pollute its waters from other sources. The rise from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent should therefore be read as evidence of progress on one component of Target 6.3, not as a measure of the target.

A second caution concerns the classification of progress. Target 6.3 carries no numeric threshold in the bench's trend tool: it asks for the proportion of untreated wastewater to be halved, a relative aim that cannot be applied to this proxy without an agreed baseline. The classes returned by the trend method, such as on track or target met, are therefore a judgement about the pace of change, set against the tool's own projection to 2030, and not a comparison with a fixed goal. On that basis the world is classed as on track or target met, with an annual rate of change of 0.0213 in the tool's units. Because the method rewards steady movement and not attainment of a stated level, a region can be classed as on track while a large share of its people still lack safe sanitation. The classes are best read together with the levels, which the following parts set out region by region.

The year of the data also bears on interpretation. The series runs to 2024, so it spans both the period after 2015, when the goals were adopted, and the disruption after 2020. The global rate shows no sign of a break in that disruption at the aggregate level, though the annual values behind the aggregates are partly modelled from sparse household surveys and censuses, and a short-lived shock could be smoothed away. For 2030, the figures imply continued gains, yet not universal coverage: at the pace recorded, the world would remain well short of full safe sanitation.

### Regions differ widely, and the gap between them explains most inequality

The contrast between regions is the plainest feature of the series. In 2024 North America stood at 95.4 per cent of its population using safely managed sanitation, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 25.9 per cent. Europe and Central Asia, at 80.2 per cent, and the high-income group, at 84.4 per cent, sit well above the world figure of 58.5 per cent. Between these poles lie East Asia and Pacific at 63.6 per cent, South Asia at 60.1 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 54.4 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 51.2 per cent. A person born in the best-served region is almost four times as likely to use a safely managed service as one born in the worst-served.

The pace of change differs as much as the level. South Asia rose from 40.8 per cent in 2015 to 60.1 per cent in 2024, the largest gain of any region, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 49.0 per cent to 63.6 per cent. Both are classed as on track in the trend analysis, as are the lower-middle-income group, which moved from 38.3 per cent to 51.9 per cent, and the upper-middle-income group, which moved from 49.1 per cent to 62.4 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean advanced more slowly, from 43.2 per cent to 51.2 per cent, and is judged to need acceleration. At the top, North America moved only from 95.2 per cent to 95.4 per cent, and the high-income group from 80.7 per cent to 84.4 per cent, which the analysis reads as stagnation. Europe and Central Asia, at a high level, shows marginal progress. Near-stagnation at a high level is partly a ceiling effect, since the last few points are the costliest to reach, and it does not carry the same concern as stagnation at a low level.

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group show a more troubling pattern. The region rose only from 21.6 per cent to 25.9 per cent, and low-income countries from 21.6 per cent to 26.9 per cent. The trend tool labels both on track, but this reflects the way the rate is read against a target that the tool leaves undefined, not any prospect of universal coverage. At these rates, three quarters of the region's population would still lack safely managed sanitation in 2030. Where a target can be read in more than one way, the label should not be taken as a verdict.

Spread among countries narrowed over the period. The population-weighted Gini coefficient fell from 0.261 across 145 countries in 2015 to 0.208 across 141 countries in 2024, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.484 to 0.382. Differences between regions account for 59.6 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2024, so most of the remaining disparity lies in where a country is located and not in variation within regions. The change in the country set between the two years is a caveat on the comparison. Convergence across 140 countries is weak: the beta coefficient is -0.00364 with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R squared of 0.018, so initial level explains very little of later gains. The narrowing owes more to the large populous gainers in Asia than to a systematic catching up by the poorest.

### Ecosystem indicators show stagnation and regression in many countries

Beyond sanitation, the shelf offers only land-based proxies for the condition of water-related ecosystems, and these show little sign of the protection and restoration that Target 6.6 set for 2020. The classification of country trends for terrestrial protected areas is divided. Of 211 countries assessed, 71 are on track or have met the target, covering 34.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Against that, 54 countries are classed as regressing, and these hold 33.0 per cent of the population. A further 45 stagnate and 27 show only marginal progress. Protected land is a coarse proxy, since a designated area need not contain a wetland or a river headwater, and the series records designation rather than the quality of management. The regression class also needs careful reading, because the shelf sets no numeric target for the indicator and a decline may reflect boundary revisions or reclassification as well as loss of protection.

The sanitation classes, drawn from the same trend tool, show a similar spread. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target and 42 stagnate, while 25 regress. The regressing countries hold 6.8 per cent of the population assessed, a small share but a signal that gains in the global figure are not universal. These classes matter for water quality because untreated excreta remain a leading source of pollution in rivers, lakes and aquifers, so stagnation in sanitation is also stagnation in the protection of freshwater.

Forest area, which regulates flows, filters runoff and shelters headwaters, is stagnant in most regions. East Asia and Pacific moved from 26.98 to 27.26 per cent of land area between 2015 and 2023, and South Asia is classed as stagnating despite a rising rate. The losses are concentrated where pressure on land is greatest. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 47.18 to 46.11 per cent over the same years, and low income countries from 20.98 to 19.86 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa and the lower middle income group are also classed as regressing, and the world as a whole is classed as regressing, at a rate of -0.0011. The drivers are well established: conversion of forest to farmland and pasture, fuel wood collection and infrastructure expansion, set against uneven enforcement of protection.

The central limit is that rivers, wetlands, lakes and aquifers have no series on the shelf. Target 6.6 therefore cannot be fully assessed, and the deadline of 2020 has passed without a measured verdict. What the proxies do show is that no region combines gains in forest, protected land and sanitation, which gives no ground for assuming that unmeasured freshwater ecosystems have improved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Convergence in safely managed sanitation is weak. Across 140 countries between 2015 and 2024 the estimated beta is -0.00364, with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R-squared of 0.018. The negative sign points to a slight tendency for countries with lower starting levels to gain faster, but the relationship is at best marginal by conventional thresholds and explains almost none of the variation between countries. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.549 in 2015 to 0.501 in 2024, a narrowing too small to close the gap between regions before 2030. Current trends therefore leave Sub-Saharan Africa far behind, while the countries already on track continue to advance.

The classification of country trends shows where the burden lies. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target, yet a further 42 are stagnating and 25 are regressing. Countries on track hold 59.6 per cent of the population of those assessed, so the global average is carried largely by a few populous countries. Forest area tells a similar story: the world trend is regression, at a rate of -0.0011, and Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.00636) and low-income countries (-0.00682) lose forest fastest. These are the settings where water-related ecosystems and sanitation are least protected and least measured.

Three proposals follow. First, national statistical offices, the UN custodian agencies and the World Bank should add the share of wastewater treated and the extent of freshwater ecosystems to the core indicator set, so that Targets 6.3 and 6.6 can be read directly rather than through proxies. Second, governments and development financiers should direct sanitation investment to the 42 stagnating and 25 regressing countries, rather than to those already on track. Third, forest-rich countries with the steepest losses, with the support of climate and conservation funds, should protect forests where losses concentrate, since catchment forests regulate water quality and flow. Finally, reports on the goals should state plainly where data are missing, and not fill the gaps with unsupported estimates.

w-c05-2-2~loom/writer-1~77.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

The headline figure for children of primary school age who are out of school is a sum of group totals, and it needs to be read with that in mind. Adding the four income groups' counts gives about 87.8 million children in 2025, set against about 87.4 million in 2015. The title rounds this to 88 million. The two totals are almost identical, which means a decade that began with the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals has ended with no reduction in the number of children outside school.

The composition beneath that flat total has changed. Low-income countries counted 30.1 million out-of-school children in 2025, up from 26.0 million in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million over the same period. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. The fall in the lower middle income group offset the rises elsewhere, so the global sum conceals a movement of the burden toward the poorest countries. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest share, about 46.4 million of the total, because they contain very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate.

The figures must not be taken as a global estimate. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, as the results record, while the series itself holds a much wider coverage across its history, 198 countries for the count. A sum built on so few reporters in the latest year depends on which countries happened to report, and the group totals may reflect different country sets in 2015 and 2025. The comparison between the two years is therefore indicative of direction only. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, and those in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count as out of school. Rises in some groups may partly reflect late entry or enrolment in pre-primary classes rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. A total that has not fallen since 2015 implies that the first decade of the goals did not close that gap. The years after 2020 sit in the same data window, and the interruption of schooling during the pandemic, together with conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries, are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up. The available results do not separate these effects, so they cannot be attributed with precision.

For 2030, the implication is that the arithmetic is unfavourable. With the global count unchanged over ten years, ending exclusion in the five years that remain would require a rate of decline that the period to 2025 has not shown. The rates in the following part show where that difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries, roughly ten times the rate. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall steadily as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. A plausible explanation, not tested by these series, is that fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was outrun by the growth in the number of children.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest number of out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. Much of the global stability in the total, noted earlier, reflects this gain being offset by increases elsewhere.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015. This is a rise of 5.6 percentage points, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion deepens as children grow older. Likely reasons, which the data do not test, are that many enter school but few progress, and that costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push adolescents out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, adolescent exclusion was broadly flat or slightly lower. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which 41.7% of lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, but the direction of the small difference depends on national income. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys, so girls are the larger group there. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys. The girls' count therefore rose by about 2.17 million over the decade and the boys' by about 1.90 million, and the gap in low-income countries widened slightly in absolute terms, to the girls' disadvantage.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' exclusion fell faster than boys' there, by about 3.13 million against about 2.44 million. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in these three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

Girls are thus the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, barriers that plausibly fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, may remain active, though these results do not test such causes. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. The sex-disaggregated series draw on 8 countries reporting in 2025, whereas the totals by income group draw on 12, so the two sets should not be compared directly. Part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are plausible pressures after the pandemic, though these are explanations the data do not test and cannot separate.

The country classes show that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are the most numerous, and their 34.4% of the population is close to the 34.9% share that is on track or has met the target.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. The group levels rest on 12 reporting countries in 2025, a small base for four income groups. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents are the weakest point. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, while every other group held steady or improved slightly. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, so that picture rests on thin and uneven coverage. A pattern in which exclusion grows as children pass the end of primary school is consistent with fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and with too few secondary places, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.

The international community should set and publish an explicit reading of target 4.1, including any tolerated residual share, so that progress is measured the same way across countries.

w-c05-5-2~cedar/writer-4~77.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small and should be read with caution. In the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. The fall is not a loss for girls: it largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, since South Asia moved from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020 and lower middle income countries from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.997 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.997 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.995 in North America and 0.991 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.982. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.970 in 2015 to 0.976 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.956 to 0.958. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.061 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.868 in 2015 and 0.900 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.952 to 0.965. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.018 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.052, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. The data do not show why. One hypothesis, which these series cannot test, is that boys leave school early for paid work in some settings. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.010 to 0.982 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.993.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.122 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 and North America 1.301, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.153, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.128, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.058 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.954 to 1.029. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.794 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.735 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.301 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.992 at primary level in 2020, 0.997 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.038 at tertiary level in 2024, close to parity at the first two levels and above it at the third. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure. The spread is also reported only for 2015, so these data cannot show whether dispersion has narrowed since.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison, and the male series has the same coverage in the shelf's description. In 2025, however, only 11 countries have reported. The count was 110 in 2024, and reporting for the latest year is always incomplete because national statistics reach the international database after a lag. The 2025 figure is therefore a feature of data release, not evidence that countries stopped collecting, but the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is largely a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for them. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and this pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. The data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that remain to the disadvantage of girls are concentrated at the secondary and tertiary levels and in two regions. At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.900 in 2020, up from 0.868 in 2015, and low-income countries stood at 0.819, up from 0.806. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.952 to 0.965 over the same years. Both regions are closing the gap, but at these rates parity by 2030 is uncertain. For Sub-Saharan Africa the tertiary index of 0.794 in 2021 shows that the gap widens at higher levels, and the low-income figure of 0.672 in 2021 is lower still. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.103 in 2015 to 1.122 in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 in 2024 and North America 1.301, while Europe and Central Asia reached 1.153 and high-income countries 1.209. Target 4.5 asks for the elimination of disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, so an index well above 1.00 is a disparity of a different kind. In South Asia the tertiary index crossed parity, from 0.954 to 1.029, and the lower-middle-income group did likewise, from 0.959 to 1.038. The fall in the world primary index, from 0.999 in 2015 to 0.983 in 2020, largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for girls.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024, so recent completion gaps cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, which is too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow, each tied to a finding above. They concern reporting, survey coverage, retention of girls in the lagging regions, and monitoring of boys at tertiary level.

w-c06-5-2~farah/writer-1~77.text:
### The indicator and what it measures

Target 5.6 commits governments to universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The principal measure of progress in this section is the share of married or partnered women aged 15 to 49 who make their own informed decisions regarding sexual relations, contraceptive use and reproductive health care. It is compiled by the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Statistics Division, mainly from Demographic and Health Surveys, and reported in the World Bank's World Development Indicators as a percentage of those women.

The indicator is a composite, and its base is women who are married or in a union, not all women of that age. A woman counts as deciding for herself only if she answers yes to all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner if she does not want it; she decides on the use of contraception; and she decides on her own health care. A woman who answers yes to two of the three is not counted. The measure is therefore strict, and its level is bound to be lower than the level for any single component. Unmarried women are left out, so the series describes one part of the female population.

The reading of own decisions is not fixed across surveys. Each component rests on a question put to the respondent, and the wording, the response options and the interpretation of a joint decision with a partner can differ between survey rounds and between countries. A woman who decides jointly with her husband after discussion may be recorded differently from one whose husband decides alone, and cultural norms shape how women describe such arrangements. Answers on refusing sex are also sensitive to the setting of the interview. Differences between countries, or between years in one country, may thus partly reflect measurement and not only a change in women's autonomy.

The retrieved results for this section report how many countries supply the indicator, not the share values themselves. In 2024 the count was 5 countries, and across 2006 to 2024 a total of 81 countries have reported at least once. The share of women who decide for themselves is therefore not stated here for any country or year, and the question this section asks cannot be answered with a figure from these results. The indicator is also not the only evidence the shelf holds on target 5.6. Related series cover a wider set of household decisions, demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods, unmet need for contraception, attitudes towards refusing sex and prenatal care. They measure different things and are cited in the parts that follow only where they help to interpret the composite.

### Thin coverage limits any global picture

Only 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions in 2024, the latest year in the series. The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries but no share values for those five, so the share of women who make their own decisions on health care and contraception cannot be stated for any country or year in this section. No aggregate is published for the indicator in any year, so the World Bank's catalogue gives no regional or world share either. The question is therefore answered only in part: no global figure exists, and the national readings are not in the material available to this part.

The 2024 count rests on the survey calendar rather than on any change in the underlying behaviour. Demographic and Health Surveys are fielded country by country, usually at intervals of several years, and a country appears in a given year only if a survey was completed and processed. A year with few reporting countries is a year in which few surveys were released, not evidence that decision-making has become less common or less measured. The 5 countries of 2024 are an accident of timing, and they are not a sample drawn to represent any region or income group.

For that reason the 2024 levels result supports only a handful of national readings. Each can describe the country it belongs to. None can be averaged into a regional picture, and none should be read as typical of countries with similar incomes or located in the same region. Averaging five values drawn from whichever surveys happened to conclude would mix countries whose populations, laws and health systems differ widely, and would give a number that describes no real population.

The wider record shows how uneven the coverage is. Across all years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. Yet the number reporting in a single year has ranged from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018. Even in the best year, 15 countries is a small part of the 81 that have a measured value at some point, and the set of reporting countries changes from year to year. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years would therefore reflect a change in who reported as much as any change in women's autonomy.

The constraint matters for the 2030 agenda. Target 5.6 is to be judged on whether access and rights are universal, and a measure reported by only 3 to 15 countries in any year cannot show whether the target is being reached. The indicator is also confined to women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in union, and it counts a woman only if she answers yes to all three components: refusing sex, using contraception and seeking health care. Women outside unions, and countries without a recent survey, are absent from the evidence, and the composite cannot separate decisions on health care from decisions on contraception. The thin coverage is itself a finding: monitoring of this target depends on a few countries per year.

### Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data

Reporting by year shows why regions and countries cannot be compared on current data. The number of countries reporting the indicator ranged from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018. Between those years, the count moved among 4 in 2009, 7 in 2010, 12 in 2012, 6 in 2013 and 10 in 2016. Each year's reading therefore describes a different group of countries, and a change in a year's picture may reflect who was surveyed rather than any change in women's lives.

The pattern follows the survey cycle. Demographic and Health Surveys visit a country every few years, and the countries reached in one year are seldom those reached in the next. A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2018 and 2019, cannot be set side by side. Regional groupings fare no better, because a region may be represented by one or two countries in one year and by none in another. Without a published aggregate, no regional average exists to correct for this, and constructing one from such uneven entries would imply a precision the data do not hold.

Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once, yet in 2024 only 5 reported. A country's most recent reading may therefore be several years old, and comparing latest values across countries mixes survey years that may be a decade apart. Over that span, access to services, schooling and social norms can shift, so the gap between two countries' values may be partly a gap in dates.

The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries and no share values, so no country's reading for 2024 is stated here, and the question of the share of women who decide for themselves is unanswered for that year. Differences between countries could be described only where the same survey design and indicator definition apply, since the measure counts a woman only if she decides on all three areas: refusing sex, using contraception and her own health care. The base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so women outside unions are not covered. The 5 countries reporting in 2024 are too few to support any ranking or regional statement, and none is made.

### Reporting has changed little since 2015

Reporting on women's own informed decisions has swung widely since the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, without a trend. In 2015, 5 countries reported the indicator. The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached a peak of 15 in 2018, then fell to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020. It recovered to 7 in 2021, 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023, before dropping to 5 in 2024. Across the years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once.

This pattern follows the survey cycle and not women's circumstances. Household surveys are fielded in a country every few years, and each round is processed and compiled some time afterwards. A year with many reporting countries is one in which many survey rounds happened to be completed and published; a year with few is one in which fewer did. The low count in 2024 is likely to reflect publication lag in part, so that later releases may add countries to recent years. The data do not show this, and it should be treated as an expectation and not a finding.

The count of 4 countries in 2020 coincides with the onset of the pandemic, which interrupted fieldwork in many countries from that year. The count of 4 in 2019 precedes the pandemic, and the series alone cannot separate the effect of disruption from the ordinary variation of survey timing. The recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is consistent with fieldwork resuming, but it too is a count of surveys and not a measure of change.

The consequence is that no before-and-after comparison around 2015 or 2020 can be drawn from this series. Each year's group of reporting countries differs from the last, so a rise or fall in any average would reflect who was surveyed. The retrieved results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, so a trend in women's decision-making since 2015 cannot be stated from these data, and the 2030 horizon cannot be assessed against a baseline that does not exist in comparable form.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 5.6 cannot be judged as on track or off track with the data now held. The indicator on women's own informed decisions has no aggregate in any year, and the number of countries reporting in a given year has swung between 3 in 2008 and 15 in 2018. Only 5 countries reported in 2024, the latest year. Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. The retrieved results give the count of reporting countries and no share values, so the question of what share of women make their own decisions has no figure to answer it here. A trend needs the same countries measured at intervals, and the shelf does not offer that. Whether a country has moved towards 2030 therefore cannot be told from a comparison of one year's reporters with another's.

The reading of the target adds a second difficulty. Target 5.6 speaks of universal access and of reproductive rights, which no single survey question captures. The indicator requires a woman to answer yes to all three components: refusing sex, choosing contraception and deciding on her own health care. Its base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so unmarried women and adolescents fall outside it. A rise or fall in the share could reflect a change in any of the three components, and the series alone does not say which.

The proposals below follow from these findings. They aim to make the next five years of reporting usable for judging the target, since the period to 2030 is short and surveys are slow to field.

t-numbers-affected-from-prevalence~saltm.name: numbers-affected-from-prevalence
t-numbers-affected-from-prevalence~saltm.code:
def tool(data, params):
    pcode = params['prev_code']
    popcode = params['pop_code']
    base = int(params['base_year'])
    y1 = int(params['year_a'])
    y2 = int(params['year_b'])
    red1 = params['reduction_a']
    red2 = params['reduction_b']
    prev = data[pcode]
    pop = data[popcode]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    def latest(d, y, window):
        for k in range(window + 1):
            if (y - k) in d:
                return d[y - k]
        return None
    win = int(params['window'])
    tot = {}
    reg = {}
    used = []
    for c in regions:
        if c not in prev or c not in pop:
            continue
        p = None
        for u in prev[c]:
            p = latest(prev[c][u], base, win)
            break
        n = None
        for u in pop[c]:
            n = latest(pop[c][u], base, win)
            break
        if p is None or n is None:
            continue
        cnt = p / 100.0 * n
        tot[c] = cnt
        r = regions[c]
        reg[r] = reg.get(r, 0) + cnt
        used.append(c)
    total = sum(tot.values())
    facts = {}
    facts['countries_with_data'] = len(used)
    facts['baseline_year'] = base
    facts['baseline_count_total'] = round(total)
    facts['target_a_year'] = y1
    facts['target_a_count'] = round(total * (1 - red1 / 100.0))
    facts['target_b_year'] = y2
    facts['target_b_count'] = round(total * (1 - red2 / 100.0))
    if used:
        ranked = sorted(used, key=lambda c: -tot[c])
        top = ranked[:5]
        facts['top5_share_pct'] = round(100.0 * sum(tot[c] for c in top) / total, 1) if total else 0
        facts['largest_country'] = names.get(ranked[0], ranked[0])
        facts['largest_count'] = round(tot[ranked[0]])
    for r in reg:
        facts['region_' + r] = round(reg[r])
    summary = ('Counts are prevalence (' + pcode + ') multiplied by population (' + popcode + ') for ' + str(len(used)) + ' countries, using the latest value within ' + str(win) + ' years up to ' + str(base) + '. The baseline total is ' + str(round(total)) + ' children. A ' + str(red1) + '% cut gives ' + str(round(total * (1 - red1 / 100.0))) + ' by ' + str(y1) + '; a ' + str(red2) + '% cut gives ' + str(round(total * (1 - red2 / 100.0))) + ' by ' + str(y2) + '. Countries without survey data are omitted, so the total understates the global count; the target wording admits more than one reading of the baseline.')
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}
