w-c02-1-2~tamarind/writer-2~80.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 asks that extreme poverty be eradicated for all people everywhere by 2030, and its wording quotes a line of $1.25 a day. That line belongs to an earlier price base and has been superseded several times as purchasing power parity exchange rates were revised. The measure used here is the current international line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, published by the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform. Poverty rates under this line cannot be compared with those printed in earlier editions of the series, and the figures in this book should not be set beside older statements of the target without that caution.

On this measure, 13.4% of the world's population lived below $3.00 a day in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 the share was 10.1%. The fall is real and of consequence: a little over three percentage points in nine years, in a period that included a pandemic and a sharp rise in food and energy prices. It also shows how far the world remains from the target. At the 2024 level, roughly one person in ten still lives below the line, and the target date is six years off.

The word eradicate admits more than one reading, and the choice changes the verdict. The strict reading is a headcount of 0%, which no measured aggregate has approached and which survey-based estimation could not confirm even if it were reached, since sampling error and gaps in coverage make an exact zero unobservable. The reading used in World Bank practice is a threshold of 3% of the population, below which extreme poverty is treated as ended as a global phenomenon. Against the 3% threshold the world stands at more than three times the required level in 2024; against zero the distance is the whole of the 10.1%. Both readings lead to the same conclusion for 2030, but they differ in what a successful outcome would mean, and the text of the target does not choose between them.

The choice of line matters for a second reason. A line of $3.00 a day is a very low standard, set to reflect the national lines of the poorest countries. Falling below it signals deprivation of food, shelter and basic needs. Rising above it does not signal security, and many households that have crossed it remain close enough to be pushed back by a poor harvest, an illness or a price shock. Later parts of this section turn to what the higher line of $4.20 a day adds.

The 2024 value must be read with care. The data behind the headcount are household surveys, which are conducted in each country at intervals of several years and are published with a delay. Figures for the most recent years therefore rest partly on estimates that carry forward earlier surveys using national accounts growth and other assumptions. The coverage record shows the effect. In 2015, 87 countries reported a value, and 93 did so in 2018. The number fell to 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted. It stood at 60 in 2023 and only 26 in 2024, and just 4 countries reported in 2025. The 2024 aggregate of 10.1% is thus a nowcast built on a thin base of direct observation, and later revisions can be expected as surveys arrive.

Two cautions follow for any reader. The fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is a robust direction but not a precise magnitude, and the end point is less firm than the start. The series shows the change but not its causes. The global figure also conceals a very uneven distribution, taken up in the next part, in which the decline has been concentrated in a few regions while others have seen little progress or a reversal.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture beneath the global figure is one of sharp divergence. East Asia & Pacific recorded the largest fall among the regions with a full series: the headcount at $3.00 a day went from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. Europe & Central Asia began from a low base and moved from 1.2% to 0.6%. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 6.0% to 4.3%, a decline that is real but slower in proportion than those of the two regions above. North America, at 1.1% in 2015 and 0.9% in 2024, was already close to the floor of what survey-based measurement can distinguish from zero. The series show the size of these changes but not their causes; any explanation offered here comes from general knowledge outside the results and is not a finding of them.

South Asia requires a caution. The series for the region is shown from 2020, at 9.4%, and reaches 2.6% in 2024. Read at face value, this is the steepest fall of any region in the period. The reading cannot be extended to 2015, because the regional value for the earlier years is not in the results, and regional estimates depend on a small number of large countries with infrequent household surveys, so the aggregate may rest on interpolation and projection as much as on fresh observation. The 2020 starting point also falls in the year of the pandemic, so part of the apparent decline may be recovery from a temporary shock rather than a sustained trend. The figure is therefore best taken as a sign of strong improvement of uncertain size, not as a measured change over the full period since 2015.

The regions where poverty has not fallen are those where the global total is now decided. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan moved in the wrong direction, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024. The grouping combines economies of very different kinds, and the data do not say which members account for the rise, so it should not be read as a uniform deterioration across the region. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, almost no change in nine years. A flat rate combined with a growing population would imply a rising number of people below the line, but the number of people is not measured in these results, and the claim is an implication, not a finding.

Income groups tell the same story from another side. Low-income countries recorded 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, a rise, so that more than half the population of the poorest group of economies lives below $3.00 a day. Lower middle income countries stood at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024; the series for this group, like that for South Asia, is shown from 2020 only, and the same caution applies. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% to 2.1%, and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. The pattern is that the decline has been concentrated where poverty was already moderate, and that it has bypassed the group where poverty is deepest.

This matters for the target. The global fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is driven chiefly by the regions that started with modest rates and moved quickly, while the regions and income group with the highest rates did not move or moved backwards. The remaining headcount is increasingly located in low-income settings, where household survey coverage is also thinner. Eradication by 2030 would require that the regions now stagnant reverse course abruptly, which no part of the 2015 to 2024 record suggests.

### Country progress and the absence of convergence

Sorting countries by the pace of their progress towards a headcount of zero by 2030 shows how uneven the record is. Of 105 countries assessed on the $3.00 a day line, 18 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 45.6% of the population of the assessed countries. That share is large because it includes some of the most populous economies. The count of countries is far less encouraging than the share of people: 18 of 105 is a small minority of national experiences.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and they hold 23.1% of the assessed population. A further 15 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, holding 11.3%. In neither group is the target reached at the present pace. Moderate progress means the direction is right and the speed is insufficient; marginal progress means that closing the remaining distance would take a change of pace that few countries have managed in a single decade.

The weakest classes matter most for the meaning of the target, which asks for eradication for all people everywhere. 7 countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the assessed population. 24 countries are regressing, with 17.9%. Regression in 24 of 105 assessed countries, nearly a quarter, is a finding in its own right. The series shows that the headcount rose in these countries but cannot show why. Outside the results, established knowledge suggests that conflict, fragility, macroeconomic shocks, high food and energy prices and the aftermath of the pandemic of 2020 are among the usual candidates; this section does not test any of them. Because the classification measures movement from each country's own latest observations, a country can regress from a low level as well as from a high one, and the class does not by itself say how deep the deprivation is.

The convergence test addresses whether poorer countries are catching up. Across 57 countries with data from 2015 to 2022, the regression of change in the headcount on its starting level gives a beta of 0.00658 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029. A negative and significant coefficient would have shown that countries starting with higher headcounts fell faster. The coefficient is instead slightly positive, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 3% of the variation in outcomes. Starting poverty did not predict the later pace of change.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.144 in 2015 to 2.675 in 2022. A rising coefficient means that the spread of national headcounts grew relative to their mean. Two readings are open. It may reflect a true divergence in national fortunes. It may also reflect that the headcount, as it approaches zero in many countries, has a small mean, which can inflate a ratio-based dispersion measure even when absolute differences narrow. The absolute test and the relative one should be read together, and neither shows catching up.

The sample limits both results. The convergence test covers 57 countries, fewer than the 105 classified, because it needs observations close to both 2015 and 2022. Household surveys in the poorest and most fragile countries tend to be the least frequent, so the unobserved countries are plausibly those where poverty is deepest, and the finding of no convergence may understate the divergence. For 2030, the absence of catch-up has a direct meaning: the global target cannot be met by the average trend alone, because the remaining poverty lies in countries that are not closing the distance.

### A slowing decline and its limits as evidence

The pace of decline in the world headcount at $3.00 a day has not been steady. A break analysis of the annual change in the world series finds two turning points, in 2014 and in 2021. Between 2001 and 2013 the headcount fell by a mean of 1.6 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.9 points, and in the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.3 points. The pace of decline in the most recent segment is therefore about a fifth of that recorded in the first. The two breaks fall close to two events that shaped the period: the end of the commodity-price boom and the slowdown of growth in many low-income economies after 2014, and the pandemic shock of 2020 followed by uneven recovery. These associations come from outside knowledge of the period and are not findings of the results. The data show when the pace changed; they do not isolate why. Attribution would need counterfactual modelling that the series alone cannot supply, and the timing of breaks in a short annual series is itself uncertain by a year or more.

A further reason for caution is mechanical. When the headcount is already low, each point of decline is harder to achieve, because the remaining poor are concentrated in places that are poorer, more remote and less able to benefit from average growth. A slowing decline is therefore expected even without any change in policy effort. Yet this does not make the slowdown benign. The target requires the headcount to reach zero, or a figure close to it, and a falling rate of change moves that outcome further from 2030, not nearer.

The evidence behind the latest segment is thinner than the evidence behind the earlier ones. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly and published with a lag. The number of countries reporting a figure for the headcount was 87 in 2015, 70 in 2020 and 81 in 2021. It fell to 60 in 2023, to 26 in 2024 and to 4 in 2025. The decline in recent years is partly a matter of surveys not yet processed or not yet conducted, so the world and regional figures for 2023 onward lean on estimates that carry forward earlier survey information with growth data and assumptions about distribution. The mean change for 2021-2024 should be read as a provisional estimate, likely to be revised as surveys arrive, and the 2025 figures hardly rest on observed data at all.

The coverage problem is uneven as well as thin. Countries with infrequent surveys, often those with the highest poverty and the weakest statistical systems, are the ones most likely to be absent from a given year, though the results do not rank countries by survey frequency. The world aggregate can therefore be least well measured where the number of poor people is largest. Anyone assessing whether 2030 is within reach should weigh the slowdown found here as a signal that is probably real in direction, since the breaks are consistent across segments, but uncertain in size.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace observed since 2021, the world will not reach zero extreme poverty by 2030. The world headcount at $3.00 a day stood at 10.1% in 2024, and the trend to the target projects 8.4% in 2030 on the present rate, a ratio of 0.38 of the progress needed. The trend classifies the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Target 1.1 can be read as zero, or as a low threshold such as 3%. Neither reading is met at this pace: the gap between 10.1% and 3% is far larger than the few remaining years can close at a mean annual fall of 0.3 points in the segment from 2021 to 2024.

Even the regions that are advancing need to go faster. East Asia & Pacific, the best performer among the regions with a full series, is expected to stand at 1.0% in 2030 on its present rate, against a target of zero, with a ratio of 0.84. Europe & Central Asia is expected at 0.4%, and upper middle income countries at 1.1%. These residual shares are small, but they are the hardest to remove. Well-established experience suggests that the people concerned are often in remote, conflict-affected or marginalised groups that growth alone does not reach; the series records the shares, not the reasons. South Asia is classed as on track, with an expected 0.4% in 2030 from 9.4% in 2020. That series begins in 2020, and the classification rests on four years of change from a pandemic-affected base, so it is provisional.

The weight of the problem lies where the trend is flat or reversed. Sub-Saharan Africa is in stagnation, with an expected 44.7% in 2030, and low-income countries are in regression, with 54.2% expected. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also in regression, with 16.7% expected. Because the global headcount is the sum of these parts, the world cannot approach zero while these groups stay where they are. Among 105 countries assessed, 24 are in regression and hold 17.9% of the assessed population. If population growth continues while the rate is flat, the number of people below the line would rise, but that number is not measured here.

The proposals that follow from these findings are set out in the list. The three-year survey interval is a proposal, not a finding; it is tied to the fall in reporting from 70 countries in 2020 to 26 in 2024.

w-c05-8-2~willow/writer-1~80.text:
### Education spending averages 3.6 per cent of GDP and 14 per cent of government budgets

Two measures describe how much of a country's resources goes to schooling. The first expresses general government expenditure on education as a share of gross domestic product, and shows the weight of public education in the whole economy. The second expresses the same expenditure as a share of total government expenditure, and shows the priority given to education within the public budget. The two can diverge: a government may hold education's place in its budget steady while the economy, and the budget with it, changes in size.

On the first measure, the world figure fell from 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023. That is a decline of about 0.6 percentage points over eight years, in a period that includes the shock of 2020, when output contracted in most economies and public budgets were redirected towards health and income support. The country classification shows the fall was widespread: of 186 countries assessed, 98 regressed on this measure. Coverage matters here: the latest year nominally available is 2025, but only 2 countries reported GDP-share data for that year, so the most recent usable world figure is for 2023.

On the second measure, the picture is different. The world share of government expenditure was 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, essentially unchanged. For this series 60 countries reported in 2025, a much fuller recent record than for the GDP share, though the world aggregate shown here also ends in 2023.

The two results can be reconciled without contradiction, but they cannot be read as a single verdict. If education held a constant slice of government spending while its share of GDP fell, then total government spending relative to GDP must have fallen too, or the country mix behind the world aggregate shifted. Either way, a steady budget share does not guarantee that schools are better financed in relation to national income. It also does not show how much is spent per pupil, which depends on the number of children, on prices and on the exchange rate, none of which these series capture.

Neither target sets a numeric benchmark for these indicators. Target 4.1 concerns completion of free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education, and target 4.c concerns the supply of qualified teachers; spending is an input to both, not a measure of either. Judgements here therefore rest on direction of change alone. On that reading, the fall in the GDP share after 2015 is an adverse movement, and the flat budget share is neither progress nor retreat. Reaching either target by 2030 would be harder on a shrinking base of public resources, a point developed in the parts that follow.

### Regions differ by two percentage points of GDP, and country spread is widening

Regional averages of public education spending span roughly two percentage points of GDP. North America spent 4.8 per cent of GDP in 2022, almost unchanged from 4.8 per cent in 2015. Europe and Central Asia stood at 4.6 per cent in 2022, down from 4.8 per cent in 2015. At the other end, South Asia spent 2.9 per cent in 2024, up slightly from 2.7 per cent in 2015, and Sub-Saharan Africa spent 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent. The gap between the highest and lowest region is therefore about two points, and the regional ranking has barely changed since 2015.

The movements after 2015 differ by region. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows the largest rise, from 3.7 per cent in 2015 to 4.4 per cent in 2022, and South Asia rose modestly. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 4.4 per cent to 3.8 per cent in 2023, a period that includes the fiscal strain of the pandemic and its aftermath. East Asia and Pacific held at about 3.5 per cent throughout. The world figure fell from 4.2 per cent in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023, alongside declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, Europe and Central Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and the lower-middle-income group. The results do not analyse the composition of the world aggregate, so they cannot say which regions account for most of the fall.

The ordering changes when spending is measured against the budget rather than the economy. Latin America and the Caribbean devoted 16.6 per cent of government expenditure to education in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa 15.4 per cent in 2024, whereas North America devoted 10.7 per cent in 2022 and Europe and Central Asia 11.7 per cent in 2022. The comparison mixes 2022 and 2024 values, because the latest year reported differs by region. Even so, the pattern is clear: regions with small tax bases and young populations give education a large share of what they spend, yet this still yields a small share of national income. Priority within the budget cannot fully compensate for a limited budget, so raising revenue matters as much as the allocation decision.

The spread among countries has widened. The population-weighted Gini coefficient of spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.181 in 2015 to 0.210 in 2020 and 0.230 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.091 and then 0.110 over the same years. The share of this inequality lying between regions was 23.8 per cent in 2015 and 27.0 per cent in 2020, but fell to 10.5 per cent in 2023. Differences now lie increasingly among countries within the same region, so regional averages conceal growing divergence and regional policy alone cannot address it.

A caution applies to the 2023 comparison. The 2023 figures cover 121 countries against 164 in 2015, and the missing countries are not a random subset. Late reporting tends to come from countries with weaker statistical systems, so the rise in inequality may partly reflect who reported rather than what was spent. The direction from 2015 to 2020, when 164 and 170 countries reported, is more secure than the level reached in 2023.

### Most countries regressed, and the two measures move together only moderately

Classified against a trajectory towards higher spending, most countries moved the wrong way. Of 186 countries assessed on the share of GDP, 98 regressed, and these hold 62.3 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 40 were on track or had met the direction of travel, covering 11.1 per cent of that population. The remainder were spread across moderate progress (14 countries), marginal progress (20 countries) and stagnation (14 countries). No numerical target exists for either measure, so the classes describe direction and pace, not distance from a goal; the reading depends on the assumption that an increase is the desired movement.

The budget share tells a harsher story. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 regressed, holding 78.2 per cent of the population, while 29 were on track, holding 7.1 per cent. Stagnation affected 23 countries with 10.5 per cent of the population. On both measures the population share of regression exceeds the country share, so larger countries are over-represented among those regressing. The results do not identify which countries these are, nor their school-age populations.

Spending levels did not draw together. Across 146 countries, the regression of change in the GDP share on its 2015 level gave a beta of -0.00559 (p 0.64, R2 0.004), which is indistinguishable from no convergence. Low spenders did not catch up, and high spenders did not fall back. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.379 in 2015 to 0.449 in 2022, so dispersion widened in relative terms. Countries starting with little did not close the gap, which matters for target 4.c and target 4.1, since teacher supply and free schooling depend on a stable funding base.

The two measures are related, but only moderately. Across 131 countries, the Spearman correlation of changes between 2015 and 2022 was 0.415, and that of 2022 levels was 0.468. A fall in the GDP share therefore partly accompanies a lower priority for education within the budget. The rest reflects other fiscal movements: a country may keep its budget share while the whole public sector shrinks relative to output, or output may rise faster than outlays during recovery. The reverse also holds, as education may gain priority within a budget that is itself contracting.

These data cannot identify causes. The post-2015 and post-2020 periods included commodity price falls, pandemic spending on health and income support, rising debt service and, in some cases, rapid growth in GDP that diluted ratios. Which of these drove each country's result cannot be read from two ratios. The classification also rests on the quality of trend fitting for short and gappy series. For 2030, the pattern implies that present trajectories will not lift most countries' spending, and that improving one measure does not guarantee the other.

### Reaching 2030 requires reversing the fall in spending and improving reporting

The implication for 2030 is that targets 4.1 and 4.c are paid for from public budgets. Free primary and secondary schooling and a larger supply of qualified teachers both require sustained financing. The world average for public education spending stood at 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 and at 3.6 per cent in 2023. A fall of that size leaves less room for hiring, training and retaining teachers. Neither target sets a numerical spending level, so the direction of travel is the only yardstick available, and on the share of GDP it points the wrong way.

The fall is visible in several groups, and the lowest starting points deserve attention. South Asia, at 2.9 per cent of GDP in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent in 2015, remain below the world average. Low-income countries spent 3.0 per cent in 2022, against 3.2 per cent in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 4.1 per cent to 3.4 per cent between 2015 and 2023. Declines also appear in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Europe and Central Asia, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and South Asia, recorded rises. The results hold no population weights for regions, so they cannot show which changes drove the world figure. The budget-share comparisons mix years, with some regional values for 2022 and others for 2024, and should be read as approximate.

Monitoring is also weakening. The number of countries reporting the share of GDP rose to 171 in 2017 and stood at 164 in 2022, but fell to 121 in 2023 and to 40 in 2024, with only 2 in 2025. Part of this is the ordinary lag of reporting, and the latest years will fill in. Even so, any reading of the period after 2020 rests on a thinning sample, and the averages for 2023 and 2024 may shift when late reporters arrive. Where data are missing, the position of a country cannot be told from the figures.

A further caution concerns interpretation. No single share defines adequate spending, and a country may spend a modest share of income efficiently, or a large share poorly. The share of GDP and the share of the budget answer different questions, and neither says what is spent on each child.

w-c03-3-3~dahlia/writer-2~80.text:
### Child overweight and anaemia in women stand at 5.5 per cent and 30.7 per cent

Two indicators of malnutrition other than stunting and wasting are measured here: overweight among children under five, and anaemia among women of reproductive age. Target 2.2 names all forms of malnutrition and the nutritional needs of adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, yet its numerical benchmarks cover only stunting and wasting. The two indicators therefore describe parts of the target that carry no quantified goal in the wording given. The overweight series is scored in this section against a reference value of 3.0 per cent by 2030, which is a working benchmark of the bench's trend tool and not a value written into the target. The anaemia series has no benchmark at all.

In 2024 the world prevalence of child overweight, defined as weight for height more than two standard deviations above the WHO 2006 median, was 5.5 per cent of children under five, up from 5.2 per cent in 2015. The rise is small, at about 0.3 percentage points over nine years, but it runs against the direction the target implies. The estimate rests on 163 countries reporting in 2024. It is a modelled estimate, so year-to-year movements are smoothed and partly reflect the model rather than fresh surveys, especially in countries that are surveyed only every few years.

Anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 is far more common. In 2023 the world prevalence was 30.7 per cent, against 28.0 per cent in 2015, an increase of about 2.7 percentage points. The measure combines non-pregnant women with haemoglobin below 12 g/dL and pregnant women below 11 g/dL, and 192 countries are covered. Nearly one woman in three of reproductive age is therefore anaemic, a share that is large but not a majority. The condition matters for maternal health, for birth outcomes and for the nutrition of the next generation of children.

Both world averages were higher at the latest year than in 2015, and anaemia has no internationally agreed target value within the goal framework used here. A rise in child overweight is not necessarily a failure of the same kind as a rise in anaemia, since the two reflect different diets and health conditions. Even so, the direction of both world figures is adverse. Haemoglobin measurement also depends on altitude, smoking and survey method, and country estimates are modelled where surveys are scarce. The levels reported here should be read as well-founded orders of magnitude, not as exact counts. For 2030, the starting point is a world in which both burdens are larger than at the outset of the agenda.

### Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower

Regional levels of the two burdens run in opposite directions. Child overweight is lowest in South Asia, at 3.4 per cent of children under five in 2024, and highest in North America, at 9.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 8.8 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 7.8 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa records 3.8 per cent. Anaemia among women aged 15 to 49 reverses the order: North America has the lowest prevalence, 14.9 per cent in 2023, and South Asia the highest, 51.1 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 36.7 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 35.2 per cent, whereas East Asia and the Pacific, at 18.7 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean, at 20.0 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia, at 21.3 per cent, lie near the lower end.

The pattern by income group repeats the regional one. Overweight is 3.5 per cent in low-income countries and 4.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 8.6 per cent in upper-middle-income and 8.4 per cent in high-income countries. Anaemia is 35.6 per cent in low-income and 46.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 19.8 per cent in upper-middle-income and 17.3 per cent in high-income countries. Child overweight is thus highest where anaemia is lower, and the reverse holds in the poorest regions. This does not mean that the two conditions exclude one another within a country or a household; regional averages cannot show whether both occur together. Lower overweight in the poorest groups should not be read as a sign of better nutrition, since anaemia there remains heavy.

In relative terms the regional gap is wider for anaemia than for overweight. Dividing the highest regional level by the lowest, a derived ratio rather than a published result, gives 3.43 for anaemia and 2.92 for overweight. Among 192 countries, weighted by population, the between-region share of the Theil index was 77.9 per cent in 2023, up from 74.1 per cent in 2015, so geography accounts for most of the inequality in anaemia. The Gini coefficient fell from 0.287 to 0.272 over the same years. Differences among countries have narrowed slightly overall, yet what remains is increasingly a matter of the region to which a country belongs. Neighbouring countries tend to share their fortunes, which points to regional conditions as well as national policy; the results themselves do not identify the causes.

### Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere

The trend classes show that movement on both indicators has mostly been in the wrong direction since 2015. Child overweight is assessed against a benchmark of 3.0 per cent by 2030, a figure adopted for this book and not written into Target 2.2. Of the 163 countries assessed, 92, holding 66.6 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, meaning that prevalence is rising where the benchmark requires it to fall. Only 33 countries, with 21.3 per cent of the population, are on track or have already met the benchmark. A further 10 countries (2.0 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 20 (7.5 per cent) show marginal progress and 8 (2.6 per cent) are stagnant. No test of other benchmark values was run, so how the count of countries on track would change under a stricter or looser line, and whether the direction of travel would hold, is not established here.

Regionally, regression is the common pattern. East Asia and Pacific, high-income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are all classed as regressing, as are the low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups. The annual rates of change are small, 0.0153 for East Asia and Pacific and 0.0165 for Latin America and the Caribbean, but they point upward in each case. South Asia shows the fastest rise, at 0.0518, from a low base, so the increase is not confined to richer economies. The regression ratios compare the observed rate with the rate the benchmark requires. They are large in magnitude for low-income and lower-middle-income countries, at -6.09 and -2.37, and smaller for high-income countries, at -0.36. Europe and Central Asia is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.11, and its expected prevalence of 7.32 per cent in 2030 remains far above 3.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the only region with moderate progress, a ratio of 0.67, and its expected 2030 level of 4.36 per cent would still be above the benchmark. At the world level the ratio is -0.21, a regression, with 5.67 per cent expected in 2030.

Anaemia among women of reproductive age shows a more uniform picture. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing. Only 2 countries (1.7 per cent of the population) are on track, 1 shows moderate progress, 9 show marginal progress and 18 are stagnant, so the rise is widespread but not universal. Every region and income group is classed as regressing. The world rate of change is 0.0115. Rates are highest in North America, at 0.0359, and in high-income countries, at 0.0239, and lowest in East Asia and Pacific, at 0.0023. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.0202, rises faster than South Asia, at 0.0070, although South Asia has the highest prevalence of any region, at 51.1 per cent in 2023. The fastest rises therefore occur in regions with lower prevalence, but the pattern rests on a few regions and every region is rising. No target value is set for anaemia in this assessment, so the classes measure only whether prevalence is falling.

The spread across countries narrowed slightly. The Theil index fell from 0.130 in 2015 to 0.116 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index rose from 74.1 per cent to 77.9 per cent, so what inequality remains is increasingly a matter of which region a country belongs to. The narrowing does not signal improvement, since prevalence rose in most countries. These data identify no causes. Changing diets, shifts in the measurement of haemoglobin and modelled estimates for countries with sparse surveys could each contribute, and none can be separated here. A rise across most countries justifies caution about attributing the result to any single national policy.

### The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course

Change and level tell different stories about the two burdens. Across 162 countries, the rank correlation between changes in child overweight and changes in women's anaemia over 2015 to 2023 is -0.030, which is indistinguishable from none. Countries where overweight rose faster were no more and no less likely to see anaemia rise. The correlation of 2023 levels is -0.469, a moderate negative association: countries with higher child overweight tend to have lower anaemia among women. This is a statistical association between levels only. The results do not show why it arises, and they give no sign that one burden displaces the other. Because the two do not move together, a response designed for one cannot be assumed to reach the other.

The outlook for 2030 follows from the trend classes. For child overweight, the world is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -0.207 against the book's own working benchmark of 3.0 per cent and an expected 2030 prevalence of 5.7 per cent. North America is expected to reach 10.8 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 9.7 per cent, while high-income countries are expected to reach 9.1 per cent. South Asia has the lowest level but the fastest rise, at a rate of 0.052, and is expected to reach 4.6 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 4.3 per cent, below the world figure but still a regression. Only the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows moderate progress, with an expected 4.4 per cent, and even there the benchmark is not met on the current course. These projections extend a straight line fitted to 2015 to 2024 and are not forecasts of policy effects.

For anaemia, no numerical target is set, so the classes measure only the direction of travel. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing; 18 are stagnant, 9 show marginal progress, 1 shows moderate progress and only 2 are on track against the working benchmark applied. Because that benchmark is not an agreed one, and no test was run of how the classes change if it is moved, these classes describe direction in the data and not failure against a commitment. The direction is nonetheless adverse in most countries and in every region. Both findings rest on modelled estimates, which are revised and which smooth over years in which surveys were absent.

The findings support the proposals below, which are monitoring and targeting measures and not claims about which programmes work, since the results identify no causes.

w-c02-4-3~farah/writer-2~80.text:
### Basic services and accounts have spread, but not to everyone

Three of the measures that bear on target 1.4 can be read from the shelf for the world as a whole: drinking water, electricity and account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults. All three rose, and none reached universality. The share of people using at least basic drinking water services went from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024. Access to electricity moved from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same nine years. Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults, measured from 2017, rose from 61.7% to 72.4% in 2024. In each case the direction is right and the pace is real, yet the remaining gap is concentrated in a smaller and harder-to-reach population. Sanitation, treated in the sections that follow, is the fourth measure on the shelf and is read through its trend classes, since the shelf gives no world level for it here.

The three indicators are not strictly comparable. Water and electricity are tracked from 2015, the year the goals took effect, while the account series begins in 2017, the first year with a Findex round in this series, so its change covers seven years and not nine. The water and electricity figures describe whole populations, whereas the account figure describes only the poorest 40% of people aged 15 and over. A rise in the first two therefore says nothing directly about whether the poor in particular were reached, since national averages can be lifted by households that were already better placed. The account series is the only one of the three that isolates the poor, and it has the thinnest country coverage: 138 countries reported in 2024, against 202 for water and 215 for electricity.

Target 1.4 does not fix a single measure of access, which affects how these numbers should be read. The water indicator counts an improved source with a round trip of no more than 30 minutes, so it captures basic service and not water that is safely managed or reliably available. The electricity indicator records whether a population has access, not the quality, affordability or reliability of supply. An account may be held at a bank or with a mobile-money provider, and the data record ownership and use, not whether the account serves a household's economic needs. Sanitation is defined by facilities not shared with other households, a threshold that different readers will treat as more or less demanding. Each figure here is therefore a floor of service and not a statement that the right has been secured.

The arithmetic of the remainder shows why the pace matters. Measured as the gap to 100%, the water shortfall fell by about 3.3 points between 2015 and 2024, the difference between the two published levels, and the electricity shortfall fell by about 5.0 points. People still without these services live mostly in low-income settings and in rural areas, where connection costs per household are highest and providers have the weakest incentive to extend networks. The remaining points are usually the costliest to close.

Accounts show the largest gain, 10.6 points among the poorest 40% in seven years, or about 1.5 points a year. Established explanations include mobile-money services, digital identity schemes and the payment of public transfers into accounts, though the series themselves do not test these causes. The disruption of 2020 did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series, but the data given do not allow its effect on the pace of change to be isolated.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region

Sub-Saharan Africa is the clearest laggard on every measure held on the shelf. In 2024, 67.5% of its people used at least basic drinking water services, against 95.3% in East Asia and Pacific, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia and 99.8% in North America. Access to electricity shows a wider gap: 55.1% of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, while no other region fell below 96.7%. The region began from a low base, with 59.2% for basic water and 39.2% for electricity in 2015. Those gains are real, but they were made from so far behind that the distance to the other regions has narrowed only slowly. Low-income countries, which are mostly in the region, show the same pattern: 60.3% for basic water and 48.8% for electricity in 2024.

Sanitation confirms the regional order. The trend assessment reads Sub-Saharan Africa as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.16 against the pace needed, and low-income countries as stagnating, with a ratio of 0.10. Their expected basic sanitation level for 2030 is 36.2% for low-income countries, so that roughly two in three people in those countries would still lack basic sanitation at the target date. A positive rate is classed as stagnation here because it is far too slow to approach the target by 2030.

South Asia presents the opposite experience. Its electricity access rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, so that a region once level with the global average is now close to universal supply. Such a rise is rarely the result of market expansion alone. It is consistent with sustained public programmes of grid extension and household connection, although the series do not isolate the cause. South Asia also moved from 90.5% to 95.9% on basic drinking water over the same years, and its trend toward the sanitation target is read as on track, with a ratio of 1.11.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan form a more mixed group, and it lags mainly on accounts and sanitation rather than on every measure. On water and electricity the region sits above the global figures of 91.5% and 91.9%, at 92.9% and 96.7% in 2024. Among the poorest 40% of adults, account ownership stood at 46.1% in 2021, up from 39.5% in 2017. Of the regions with values for 2021, only Sub-Saharan Africa, at 43.6%, was lower. The region's sanitation trend is assessed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48, and significant acceleration is required. The grouping joins very different economies, from high-income oil exporters to countries in conflict, so the regional figure hides wide variation among its members.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest gain in account ownership among the poorest 40%. The share rose from 42.9% in 2017 to 67.9% in 2021, an increase of 25.0 points in four years. This interval includes the pandemic, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers into digital accounts. That may have contributed, but the data do not allow the cause to be isolated. Europe and Central Asia rose from 76.4% to 86.3%, and East Asia and Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, over the same four years.

A caution applies to every regional account figure. The regional series end in 2021, except South Asia and the income groups, which carry values for 2024. The regional comparison therefore refers to 2021 and cannot show the three years that followed. For the world, the poorest 40% reached 72.4% in 2024, up from 61.7% in 2017, but this rests on 138 reporting countries and cannot be broken down by region at the same date.

### Rural electricity advanced fastest while sanitation and water lag

Country classes against the 100% target show how uneven the advance has been. For drinking water, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress but needed acceleration. Another 55 countries, with 20.9% of the population, were making only marginal progress. Stagnation applied to 17 countries (1.5% of the population), and 37 countries (9.9%) were regressing. These are the places where service coverage was being lost rather than merely delayed.

Sanitation is the weakest of the three physical services in the class results. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population. Moderate progress, needing acceleration, described 34 countries (17.7%), and marginal progress 54 countries (16.5%). Stagnation affected 37 countries (5.8%) and regression 39 countries (13.4%). The share of population living in regressing countries is larger for sanitation than for water, which may reflect the difficulty of sustaining household facilities and sewerage against population growth and urbanisation, though the indicators do not test this. The world as a whole was classed as making moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed and an expected coverage of 89.2% in 2030, short of universal use. The shelf gives sanitation levels only through these trend results, not as separate level series, and none of the series separates the poor from the rest of the population except account ownership.

The heading refers to rural electricity because that series has the highest share of countries on track. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, with 77.4% of the population concerned. This is a comparison of class shares, not of rates, and the series differ in coverage, so it is a reading rather than a measured ranking. Moderate progress applied to 23 countries (12.8%) and marginal progress to 10 (2.0%). Seven countries (2.3% of the population) were stagnating and 10 (5.4%) were regressing. Grid extension and off-grid solar are well-established routes to rural electrification and reach dispersed households more readily than sewers or piped networks. The countries that are stagnating or regressing are plausibly those where conflict or weak utilities raise the cost of extension, but the indicators do not identify the cause.

Regional trends on sanitation show where the divergence sits. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and upper middle income countries were on track, with ratios of 1.18, 1.11 and 1.08. Lower middle income countries reached a ratio of 0.75, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.16, with an expected 42.0% coverage in 2030, and low income countries at 0.10, with an expected 36.2%. Low income countries are classed as stagnating even though their rate is positive, because that rate is far too slow to close the gap. North America is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -1.03 and an expected 99.4% in 2030. This reflects a marginal fall from a level close to universal and should not be read as a crisis of access.

Convergence in rural drinking water offers some reassurance. Across 167 countries, the 2015 to 2024 regression of growth on initial level gave a beta of -0.0164, with a p-value close to zero and an R2 of 0.27. Countries starting with lower rural coverage gained faster, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Catching up is real but partial: initial level explains little more than a quarter of the variation, so many low-coverage countries did not catch up.

For 2030, universal access is reachable for rural electricity in most countries, but not for sanitation or water at the present pace. The countries furthest from the target are those where the poorest live, so the world average conceals how far the target is missed where it matters most. Changes after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be separated here, since the classes summarise the whole period from 2015 to 2024, and the effect of the pandemic years cannot be isolated from these results.

### Universal access by 2030 is out of reach without acceleration, and proposals follow

Universal access by 2030 is not within reach on present trends, with one exception: rural electricity. For drinking water, only 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress. Together the two groups cover roughly two thirds of the population assessed. The other countries are advancing too slowly, standing still or moving backwards, and 37 of them were in regression.

Sanitation is further behind. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population covered. Another 37 countries were stagnating and 39 were in regression, and the regressing group held 13.4% of the population, against 9.9% for water. The regional trends show why. Low-income countries are classed as stagnating: the rate is positive, at 0.01 a year, but the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.10, and the trend carries them to only 36.2% in 2030. Lower middle income countries are projected to reach 88.9%, with a ratio of 0.75. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 42.0% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.16. By contrast, East Asia and Pacific and South Asia are classed as on track. North America is classed as regressing, with a projection of 99.4% in 2030, a change too small to matter for people but one that shows how a trend class can mislead near the ceiling.

A trend to 100% is a demanding standard, because the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach: they lie among dispersed, displaced or marginalised households. Countries classed as on track may still leave a residual population without services.

Rural electricity is the exception among the classes. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, holding 77.4% of the population covered. Only 10 countries were in regression and 7 in stagnation, though these hold 5.4% and 2.3% of the population respectively. Regression in a share of population often signals that connections have not kept pace with population growth, or that conflict or economic collapse has damaged networks. Falling costs of off-grid solar and national connection programmes are well-established reasons why electricity has moved faster than water and sanitation, although these data do not test that explanation.

For accounts, the world figure for the poorest 40% rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024. At that pace universality by 2030 would not be reached. Low-income countries rose from 22.5% to 37.3%, so more than six in ten of the poorest adults there remained without an account. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021, so the 2030 outlook for accounts is an estimate with wide uncertainty rather than a measured trend.

The weight of the shortfall falls on a small number of places. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 55.1% electricity access in 2024, and low-income countries, with 48.8%, account for most of the people still without power, while South Asia, at 99.8%, has almost closed its gap. Progress at scale within a decade is therefore possible, but global averages will soon be governed by a region where the pace has been slower than the need.

Target 1.4 speaks of the poor and the vulnerable specifically, yet the water, sanitation and electricity series describe whole populations. Only the account series is split to the poorest 40%. The first three could be rising for the average household while the poorest remain unserved, and the shelf cannot show this. The word access is also read in more than one way: basic water means an improved source within a round trip of 30 minutes, which is not safely managed water, and an account that is held is not necessarily one that is used.

w-c02-3-2~tamarind/writer-4~81.text:
### Social protection reaches just over half of the world's population

Social protection and labour programmes reached 56.3% of the world's population in 2021, according to the World Bank's ASPIRE database, which draws on nationally representative household surveys. That is the single reading the bench holds for the world aggregate. The result lists the same value for its first and latest year, so it describes a position and not a change. It cannot show whether coverage rose after 2015 or fell after 2020, and no claim about either period can rest on it.

The indicator counts the share of people participating in social insurance, social safety nets, unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes, and its estimates include indirect beneficiaries, such as family members who live in a household where someone receives a benefit. The measure is therefore generous in one respect: a household with one pensioner counts as covered throughout. It is also broad in what it admits. Contributory pensions, health insurance, paid sick leave, cash transfers, food transfers, training and wage subsidies all count. A figure of 56.3% thus says that just over half of people live in households touched by at least one such programme. It does not say how adequate the benefit is, how regular it is, or whether it replaces a meaningful part of income.

The distinction matters because target 1.3 is about the poor and the vulnerable, not about the population as a whole. Coverage of everyone is a poor proxy for coverage of those in poverty. In wealthier countries, much of the population is covered through social insurance linked to formal employment, and a high national figure can coexist with gaps among informal workers, rural households and people outside the labour market. Conversely, a country with a modest overall figure may target its safety nets tightly on the poorest. The all-population series should therefore be read as an outline of the system's reach, with the coverage of the poorest quintile, taken up in a later part, as the closer test of the target.

The wording of the target also allows more than one reading. It calls for nationally appropriate systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. Neither 'substantial' nor 'vulnerable' carries a numeric threshold. A reader may take substantial to mean a majority, near-universal coverage of the poorest, or simply a clear rise from a starting point. Vulnerability can be defined by a poverty line, by exposure to shocks, or by life-cycle risks such as old age, disability and childhood. With no agreed benchmark, the 56.3% figure cannot be graded as met or missed. It can only be compared across groups of countries and, when repeated readings exist, across time.

The data have further limits. The world value rests on surveys that are carried out in different years in different countries, so a single reference year of 2021 is an alignment of estimates, not a simultaneous census. Only 1 country reports for 2023, the latest year in the series, so the most recent period is almost empty and the bench cannot say what became of coverage as pandemic emergency programmes were wound down. The poorest-quintile safety-net series, for comparison, holds 121 countries reporting in at least one year, which is substantial but not complete, and the countries missing are often those with weaker statistical systems and, plausibly, weaker protection. The world figure should accordingly be taken as indicative.

For 2030, the finding is that just under half of the world's people were outside any recorded programme in 2021, and that the target's own language leaves the finish line undefined. The next parts show where the gaps lie.

### Coverage differs sharply between regions and income groups

Regional coverage in 2021 runs from 50.6% of the population in the grouping of Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan to 72.5% in South Asia. Europe and Central Asia stands at 63.7% and East Asia and Pacific at 61.5%, while Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 54.5%. South Asia, Europe and Central Asia, and East Asia and Pacific lie above the world figure of 56.3%; the other two regions fall below it.

The South Asian figure should be read with care. The indicator counts direct and indirect beneficiaries, so a household is counted as covered when any member takes part in a programme. Large public works schemes, food transfers and subsidised in-kind programmes, which are widespread in the region, can therefore lift the headline share well above what the poorest households receive in cash. Coverage of a population is not adequacy of benefits: the indicator records participation, not the value of transfers, their regularity or whether they lift a household above a poverty line. A high share and a deep floor are different things.

The contrast between income groups is wider than that between regions. Low-income countries reach 18.3% of their people, against 55.1% in lower-middle-income countries, 62.2% in upper-middle-income countries and 77.8% in high-income countries. Coverage therefore rises with income at every step. The largest step lies between the low-income group and the lower-middle-income group; the step from lower-middle to upper-middle income is visibly smaller.

The low-income figure matters most for target 1.3, which asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable. Extreme poverty is concentrated in low-income and fragile countries, and these are the places where fewer than one person in five is reached. Causes are well established as context: narrow tax bases, limited administrative capacity, large informal economies in which contributory insurance does not reach workers, and heavy reliance on short-lived, donor-funded projects instead of permanent national systems. Higher-income countries combine payroll-based insurance with tax-funded pensions and family benefits, which together cover most of the population.

The evidence has limits. Every level quoted is for 2021, and the result lists the same value as first and latest year for each group. No change since 2015 or since 2020 can therefore be stated for any region or income group, and the pandemic's expansion of emergency transfers cannot be separated from lasting coverage. Only 1 country reports for 2023, so the most recent survey year is almost empty. The ordering of regions is firm for 2021; its movement over time is not shown by these data.

### Coverage of the poorest quintile has regressed in many countries with data

The trend classification for the poorest-quintile measure of social safety net coverage is the least encouraging result of the section, but it needs a careful reading. The tool compares each country's compound annual change since 2015, or the first year after, with a target that has no numeric value, and sorts the countries into classes. The classes therefore describe the direction and pace of a series, not a verified fall or rise in what households receive.

Of 55 countries assessed, 19 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 33.4% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 2 countries show moderate progress, needing acceleration, with 12.4% of that population, and 4 show marginal progress, with 2.2%. Another 4 are stagnant, with 3.1%. The series is classed as regressing in 26 countries, which hold 48.9% of the assessed population. Regression is the largest single class by country count and by population. The shares refer to the assessed countries only and not to the world.

Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030 and sets no threshold. The phrase can be read as a majority of the poorest quintile, as near-universal coverage, or simply as a rising share. The trend tool therefore judges direction alone. A country counted as on track has a series moving upward at a pace the tool treats as consistent with improvement, not one shown to reach any agreed level. A country counted as regressing may still cover a large share of its poorest households, having moved down from a higher level.

Several well-established causes can lie behind a downward movement in such a series, stated here as context and not as findings. Coverage can decline when programmes are closed, shrunk or left without indexation while the population grows, and when emergency schemes introduced in a crisis are wound down. Changes in survey design and in the list of programmes captured can also move a figure without any change in what households receive. The data cannot separate these explanations.

The reliability of any trend depends on how often countries are observed, and the record is thin and uneven. Only 2 countries reported in 2000 and 3 in 2002. Reporting rose to 11 in 2005, 36 in 2010 and 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013 before recovering to 35 in 2014. It reached 47 countries in 2018, the best-observed year, and was 36 in 2019. Reporting then dropped to 24 in 2020 and recovered to 30 in 2021. Only 17 countries reported in 2022 and a single country in 2023. In all, 121 countries have reported in at least one year, but no single year approaches that number.

This pattern has two consequences. First, the years after 2020 are poorly observed. Surveys are fielded with a delay and processed into the database later, so the thinning of 2022 and 2023 partly reflects lag and not an end to measurement. The effect of the pandemic and of the withdrawal of emergency support on the poorest households is therefore largely invisible here, and the classes cannot be assigned with confidence to the period after 2015 or to the period after 2020. Second, the countries that enter a trend are those with surveys at both ends of their series, and they may differ systematically from countries never observed twice. Conclusions from the 55 assessed countries should not be extended to the others without that caution.

A separate question is whether the whole-population measure can stand in for the poorest quintile where the latter is missing. The links tool compares the two series across 18 countries between 2015 and 2021. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.93, and that of 2021 levels is 0.91. Countries that gained or lost coverage for the whole population largely did so for the poorest quintile too, and countries with high overall coverage also tend to cover their poorest households well. The association is strong in rank terms and is not a statement of cause.

The sample is small, at 18 countries, and a rank correlation says nothing about the gap between the two measures in any one country. High overall coverage can coexist with weak targeting of the poor, which the correlation does not test. It supports using the whole-population series as a rough guide to direction where the poorest-quintile series is absent, but not as a substitute for it.

For 2030 the implication is cautious. On a direction-only reading, 33.4% of the assessed population lives in countries classed as on track, while 48.9% lives in countries whose series is classed as regressing. Without a numeric target and with sparse recent data, the world cannot say with confidence how far the poorest are covered or how fast that is changing.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence permits a cautious reading of 2030. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable, yet the world figure of 56.3% in 2021 describes the whole population, not the poor. The only measure aimed at the poorest is the safety net coverage of the poorest quintile, and its trend classification is discouraging: of 55 countries assessed, 26 are classed as regression, and they hold 48.9% of the population of the countries assessed, not of the world. Only 19 countries are on track or have met the target. The classes compare each country's rate of change with a target that has no numeric value, so they describe direction and pace and do not prove an observed fall. If these trajectories continue, the poorest are unlikely to be reliably reached by 2030 in a large part of the sample.

The gap between income groups sharpens this reading. Low-income countries reach 18.3% of their population, against 77.8% in high-income countries, a distance that no plausible rate of expansion closes in the years that remain. Extreme poverty is concentrated in the low-income countries, where public budgets and administrative capacity are most constrained. Coverage there often depends on donor-financed programmes, which are exposed to funding cycles, and on household registries that are frequently incomplete. Lower middle income countries stand at 55.1% and upper middle income countries at 62.2%, which shows that expansion is feasible, but it does not transfer automatically to the poorest settings.

The evidence base is itself a constraint. Reporting on poorest-quintile safety net coverage peaked at 47 countries in 2018 and fell to 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022, with a single country in 2023. Surveys were thinned just when the pandemic raised the need for protection, so what changed after 2020 cannot be read with confidence. The recorded regression may reflect real losses, a change in survey design or programme definitions, or the ending of temporary schemes; the data cannot separate these. The count of 121 countries reporting in any year applies to the poorest-quintile series.

The target also lacks a numeric reading. Substantial coverage could mean a majority of the poor, or a threshold such as three in four, and the classification of on track or regressing depends on that choice. Until it is fixed, different readers can judge the same country differently.

The two coverage measures move together. Across 18 countries with data for 2015 to 2021, the rank correlation between changes in poorest-quintile coverage and changes in whole-population coverage is 0.93, and between their 2021 levels it is 0.91. This supports using the broader safety net measure, which is reported by more countries, as a provisional guide where poorest-quintile data are missing. The sample is small, though, and a strong rank correlation does not show that the poorest receive a proportionate share in every country, so the broader figure cannot substitute for the narrower one.

Several proposals follow from these findings, and they are listed below.

proposals: National governments and statistical offices should keep poorest-quintile coverage in every household survey round, so that the series is not thinned as it was after 2020.
The United Nations Statistical Commission and the custodian agencies should fix a numeric reading of substantial coverage under target 1.3, such as a minimum share of the poorest quintile reached.
Donors and development banks should move support for low-income countries from short project cycles to multi-year financing of national safety nets and household registries.
Governments should publish programme definitions and survey changes alongside coverage figures, so that real losses can be told apart from changes in measurement.
