w-c04-1-3~cedar/writer-4~81.text:
### The global ratio fell from 228 to 197 and remains far above 70

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled estimate for the world stood at 228.0 in 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year available. The ratio fell over eight years, but the 2023 value is still nearly three times the target value.

The gap is plain. The trend tool, which extrapolates the compound rate observed since 2015, expects a world ratio of 173.4 in 2030 and classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. On that tool's reading, the world has covered 0.35 of the distance from its 2015 value to the target, with seven years left. Closing the remainder would need a pace far faster than the one observed, so the distance does not shrink by small adjustments; it would require a different trajectory altogether.

The target is worded as a global ratio, not as a national one. A global ratio is a weighted outcome: it is pulled down by countries with low ratios and pulled up by countries with high ratios, in proportion to their live births. The results do not include a births-weighted breakdown or a list of countries, so the text does not say which countries contribute most to the world figure. A reading in which every country must fall below 70 would be stricter still, and the wording of the target does not require it. The later parts of this section take up the country classes drawn from the trend tool; the data used here do not give a count of countries above 70 in 2023.

The quality of the series needs stating plainly. Coverage is not the weakness: the modelled ratio is reported for all 194 countries in every year from 2000 to 2023, so no country drops out of the comparison and no year has gaps. That completeness is however a product of modelling rather than of observation. The estimates are produced by a regression model that, as general context, draws on covariates such as fertility, skilled birth attendance and national income. Where civil registration of deaths with causes is incomplete, as it is in many of the countries with the highest ratios, the estimate leans on those covariates rather than on counted deaths. The figures therefore carry uncertainty that the single published value does not display, and a change of a few points between years should not be read as a firm observation.

This uncertainty does not rescue the target. The fall from 228.0 to 197.0 is small beside the distance from 197.0 to 70, and no plausible revision of the model would close a gap of that size. What the uncertainty does affect is the confidence with which any single country or short period can be judged. For the world as a whole, the finding is robust: the ratio is falling, it is falling slowly, and 2030 will arrive with it well above 70 unless the pace changes sharply.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of forty

The spread between regions is wider than any global average suggests. In 2023 the modelled ratio for Sub-Saharan Africa was 448 deaths per 100,000 live births, against 11 for Europe and Central Asia. The two figures stand roughly forty-one times apart, and they show that Target 3.1 is a global average assembled from very unequal parts. Where a woman gives birth, and in which health system, still decides the risk she faces more than any other single circumstance.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593 in 2015 to 448 in 2023 and carries by far the highest ratio of any region. South Asia fell from 173 to 120, and its proportional fall is the larger of the two. Both remain above 70. The trend tool reads South Asia as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 against a target of 70, so the shortfall there is modest and could be closed with acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is read as making marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 350.5, about five times the target value. Its ratio of progress to the pace required is 0.46, against 0.83 for South Asia. Closing the global gap depends overwhelmingly on the first of these two regions.

Several regions are read by the trend tool as on track or as having met the target. Europe and Central Asia stood at 11 in 2023, down from 14 in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 8.9. North America stood at 16, down from 17, with an expected value of 15.2. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 54 to 47, with an expected 2030 value of 41.6. For the wealthiest regions the ratio is already so low that further gains are small in absolute terms. East Asia and Pacific fell from 70 to 66, so it sits just below the target. Its expected 2030 value of 62.7 leaves little margin, and the classification rests on a gentle slope rather than on a secure lead.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among regions. Its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is the only region classed as in regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. The region was close to the threshold and has moved the wrong way. Well-established explanations include the disruption of health services during the pandemic years, persistent inequality between urban and rural or Indigenous populations, and the weight of unsafe abortion and hypertensive disorders. The data used here cannot apportion the rise among these causes.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 491 in 2015 to 346 in 2023 and are read as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 254.7. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 291 to 235 and are read as making only marginal progress, with an expected value of 194.9 and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61 to 57, with an expected 2030 value of 53.7, and high-income countries from 11 to 10. The two upper groups are already below 70, so the whole of the remaining distance lies in the lower two.

Country classes confirm that the picture is mixed. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of the classified countries. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country is in stagnation and 7 are in regression, together under 1% of the population. The data used here do not give the number of countries above 70 in 2023 under a strict country-by-country reading, nor a births-weighted list of the countries that dominate the global total, so the claim that a few dozen countries will settle the global result cannot be tested here.

### Progress slowed after 2008 and the pandemic years disturbed the series

The series shows that progress was already slowing before the goals were adopted. The breaks analysis identifies a change of regime in 2008. In the segment from 2001 to 2007, the global ratio fell by a mean of 8.4 points a year. In the segment from 2008 to 2019, the mean annual fall was 5.2 points, roughly two-fifths less. The adoption of the goals did not restore the earlier speed, and the fall of the post-2015 years continues the slower trend rather than recovering from it. Well-established explanations include the exhaustion of the easiest gains, such as the expansion of skilled attendance at birth in countries that started from low coverage, and the harder task of reaching the remaining deaths, which are concentrated among women in poor, rural and conflict-affected settings where emergency obstetric care is least available.

The pandemic years then disturbed the series. The annual change was an increase of 4 points in 2020 and an increase of 31 points in 2021. The change reversed to a fall of 39 points in 2022, and the fall in 2023 was 6 points. The pattern is consistent with a shock and a recovery: disrupted maternity services, diversion of health staff and direct deaths from infection in pregnancy are plausible contributors to the rise, and the return of services would explain the fall. The analysis cannot establish this cause. The ratio is a modelled estimate, built by regression from covariates such as fertility, birth attendance and income, and is not a count of registered deaths. A sharp one-year rise followed by a sharp one-year fall may partly reflect the way the model treats pandemic-era inputs and the revision of estimates. The breaks detected from 2020 to 2023 are single-year segments and should be read as flags, not as stable trends. The 2022 fall should be treated as a modelled rebound and not as a durable gain.

The spread among countries has not narrowed in population-weighted terms. The Gini coefficient of the ratio across 194 countries was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 70.9% in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023, so most inequality is still a matter of regional membership, though the within-region component has grown a little.

Convergence is weak. A regression of change on the starting level across the 194 countries gives a coefficient of -0.00372 with a p-value of 0.0024, but an R-squared of only 0.050. Countries with higher ratios in 2015 tended to fall slightly faster, the direction needed for catching up, yet the starting level explains only a small part of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation, which counts countries equally, fell from 1.500 to 1.410, a modest narrowing. The population-weighted measures and the unweighted one point in different directions, and the data given do not show why. For 2030, neither the slowed trend before 2015 nor the weak catching up since offers grounds for expecting the pace to rise.

### At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed, and proposals follow

Extending the recent pace to 2030 gives a global ratio of about 173.4 per 100,000 live births, against a target of 70. The trend tool places the world in the class of marginal progress, with a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.35. The target is therefore not on course. Meeting it would need a pace of decline far above that of 2015 to 2023, and continuing present practice will not deliver it. It would take a change in the scale and the targeting of effort.

The country classification shows where the shortfall lies. In 128 of the 194 countries assessed, the ratio is on track or the target is already met, and these countries hold 74.5% of the classified population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 23 countries, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country stagnates and seven regress, together holding well under 1% of the population. Roughly a quarter of the classified population therefore lives in countries that will miss the target without faster change. A majority of countries being on track does not imply that the global ratio will reach 70. The classification does not give the number of countries above 70 in 2023, so a stricter country-by-country reading of the target cannot be answered from these results.

The regional projections show the same pattern. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 448 in 2023, would reach about 350.5 in 2030 at its present rate, classed as marginal progress with a ratio of 0.46. South Asia, at 120 in 2023, would reach about 87.1, classed as moderate progress with a ratio of 0.83, the closest of the regions needing acceleration. Among income groups, low-income countries would reach about 254.7 and are classed as moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.56. Lower-middle-income countries would reach about 194.9 and are classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries, at 57 in 2023 and projected at about 53.7 in 2030, are classed as on track, as are high-income countries, at 10. East Asia and Pacific, at 66, is also classed as on track, although the margin is narrow, with a projection of about 62.7 in 2030. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the better-placed regions: its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and the trend tool classes it as regression, with a projection of about 79.7 in 2030.

Inequality among countries has not narrowed in the population-weighted measures. The Gini coefficient of country ratios rose from 0.628 in 2015 to 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.739 to 0.793. Differences between regions account for 67.2% of the Theil index in 2023, down from 71.0% in 2015, so the burden remains largely a matter of region, though within-region differences are gaining weight. The convergence test across the 194 countries, unweighted, finds a small negative coefficient of -0.0037, with an R-squared of only 0.05, so catching-up among countries is weak.

The ratios are modelled estimates, and in many high-burden countries they rest on little direct counting. Any projection to 2030 inherits that uncertainty, and the class of a country near a margin should be read with caution.

The proposals follow from these findings.

w-c02-2-2~tamarind/writer-1~82.text:
### National poverty lines give the widest view, with uneven reporting

The national-line headcount ratio is the percentage of a population living below the poverty line or lines that a country sets for itself. It is the measure closest to the wording of target 1.2, which asks for a halving of poverty in all its dimensions according to national definitions. Because each country chooses its own line, and often revises it, the series records how each society judges deprivation rather than a single standard. Estimates come from household surveys. Alongside it, the World Bank publishes multidimensional, societal-line and $3.00-a-day series, which later parts of this section set against the national figures.

The series is wide in reach but irregular in time. Over the whole period 161 countries have reported at least one national-line observation, a broad base for a goal that applies everywhere. In any single year, however, only a fraction report. In 2000 the number of countries with a value was 16, and in 2001 it was 15. It rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, and stood at 40 in 2008 and 50 in 2012. The results do not say why coverage grew; the spread of regular household surveys is a commonly cited context, stated here as background only.

After the adoption of the goals in 2015, reporting was higher than in the years before. In 2015, 55 countries had a value, 57 in 2016 and 53 in 2017. Counts then reached 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. The year 2020, the first of the pandemic, shows 57 countries, a fall from 2019 that is consistent with disrupted fieldwork, although the data alone cannot show the cause. The peak is 72 countries in 2021.

The decline since then is steep. Reporting was 52 countries in 2022, 40 in 2023 and 31 in 2024, and in 2025 it is only 13. The fall does not show that poverty has been abolished or that surveys have stopped. Household survey data take time to be collected, harmonised and released, so the latest years are likely incomplete, and the count for 2025 is best treated as a record of what has been published so far.

The consequence is practical. A comparison of 2025 with 2015 would rest on 13 countries against 55, which are not the same countries and may not represent any region. Any statement about movement toward 2030 has to use the last years of reasonable coverage, up to about 2021 or 2022, and has to separate real change from changes in who reports. The figure on levels in 2025 is shown for completeness, but its thin base calls for caution in every reading drawn from it.

### Dispersion among countries widened as coverage grew

The dispersion of national-line poverty rates among countries rose after 2013. The Gini coefficient across reporting countries stood at 0.28 in 2013 and 0.34 in 2014, then reached 0.39 in 2015, the year the goals took effect. It was 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018 and 0.63 in 2019. The Theil index followed the same course, from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.26 in 2015 and 0.72 in 2019. Read at face value, the spread among countries in the share of people below their own lines widened sharply between 2013 and 2019. The results do not state which countries drove the widening.

This reading needs care, because the set of reporting countries changed at the same time. The number of countries with a national-line estimate was 45 in 2013, 55 in 2015, 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. A rise in the Gini or Theil can reflect poverty rates pulling apart, but it can equally reflect the arrival or loss of countries with very high or very low rates. The series cannot separate these effects, and the figures should not be read as a measured change in inequality between countries over a fixed group. For 2020 the Gini is 0.66 across 57 countries, but no Theil index or regional decomposition is available, so that year cannot be compared in full with its neighbours.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions is high throughout, which indicates that most of the measured dispersion lies between regional groups rather than within them. It was 75.8% in 2013, 88.4% in 2014 and 67.7% in 2015, then 80.7% in 2016, 65.1% in 2017, 86.3% in 2018 and 77.1% in 2019. The swings from year to year are consistent with a changing sample, since adding or dropping a few countries in one region can move the between-region share. National lines are set by each country, so differences in levels also mix real differences in deprivation with differences in how the line is defined.

After 2020 the picture changes. The Gini fell to 0.35 in 2021, when 72 countries reported, the widest coverage of any year in the record. It then stood at 0.40 in 2022 with 52 countries, 0.35 in 2023 with 40 countries and 0.32 in 2024 with 31 countries. The Theil index moved from 0.20 in 2021 to 0.26 in 2022, 0.21 in 2023 and 0.17 in 2024. The between-region share was 82.6% in 2021, 88.5% in 2022, 76.0% in 2023 and 83.5% in 2024. The drop in dispersion from 2019 to 2021 coincides with a large change in the reporting set and cannot be taken as convergence. The shrinking counts after 2021 are consistent with the lag in processing and publishing household surveys, so the latest years describe a thinner and different group of countries.

For 2030 the implication is that national-line data can show whether a given country is halving its own poverty rate, but cannot support a claim about convergence or divergence across the world. Assessment of target 1.2 should proceed country by country, over a fixed set of economies with repeated surveys, and the dispersion statistics should be read as a description of who reports in each year rather than of how poverty is distributed.

### Trend classes show most countries on track but a large regressing group

The classification covers 94 countries, those for which the national-line series holds enough observations to estimate a trend. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 3.8% of the population, and 7 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 4.4%. Five countries are stagnant, with 2.1% of the population. The largest adverse group is regression: 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

The classes are the only evidence in this section on the direction of national rates, since no single rate level or change is reported for a country or group here. They show direction and pace against a reading of the target, not the size of any fall or rise. Regression means that a country's national series is moving away from the target under that reading; it describes the class, and the underlying rate may have risen only slightly. The assessed base is also not tied to the window 2015 to 2021; the trend is measured from the baseline year 2015, or the first year after it, so countries enter with different starting points and spans.

The weight of the favourable class comes from population rather than from numbers alone. The 41 on track countries are fewer than half of the 94 assessed, yet they hold 63.8% of the population. Counts and population shares tell different stories, and a reader should not infer that two thirds of countries are succeeding. The regressing class, 34 countries, is the second largest by count and holds 26.0% of the population.

No numeric target exists for national lines. Target 1.2 asks for a halving of the proportion living in poverty according to national definitions, but it names no common threshold, because each country sets its own line in its own currency and with its own method. The classes therefore rest on a reading of the target. Under the halving reading, a country is on track if its rate is falling fast enough to be halved from its starting level by 2030. Other readings are possible: an absolute reduction in the number of people, a reduction by a set number of points, or a halving from the 2015 level rather than from the earliest available observation. Each would sort some countries differently.

Several cautions follow. A country that revises its line can show a break in the series that looks like progress or regression though living standards did not move in that way. A country with a low rate can be classed as regressing after a small rise, while a country with a very high rate may be classed as on track after a modest fall. The classes do not rank deprivation among countries. Where surveys are infrequent, the trend rests on few points, and the class can change with one new survey.

For 2030, the split carries a clear message. The on track group holds most of the assessed population, so the aggregate picture can look favourable, while 26.0% of the assessed population lives in countries classed as regressing. The data do not show how much the on track group could still contribute, so any conclusion about a world-wide halving would need rate levels that this section does not give.

### National and international lines agree on direction but not fully on size, and the implication for 2030

National and international lines can be set side by side for 36 countries between 2015 and 2021. The comparison pairs the national-line headcount with the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Across these countries the rank correlation of 2021 levels is 0.72 (Spearman), and the Kendall measure of the same levels is 0.58. The rank correlation of changes is lower, at 0.53, with a Kendall value of 0.41. Both are associations, not causes.

The two results say different things. Countries with a high national rate generally also have a high international rate, so the two lines rank societies in a broadly similar order. Agreement on the direction and size of change is weaker. A country can see its national rate fall while the international rate barely moves, or the reverse, because the two lines sit at different points of the income distribution and are adjusted by different rules. As context, not as a finding of these results, national lines are revised for prices and consumption patterns, and a change in survey design or in the basket can move one measure and leave the other untouched. The correlation of changes should therefore be read as a moderate link, not as proof that the two measures can be substituted for one another. Only 36 countries qualify, a small part of the 161 that report a national rate in at least one year, so the finding cannot be extended to all countries without caution.

The movement of national rates is shown here only through the trend classes, since the results give no single rate level or change for the whole group. Of 94 assessed countries, 41 are on track or have met the target, with 63.8% of the assessed population, while 34 are classed as regressing, with 26.0%. The classes rest on a compound annual change from a 2015 baseline, or the first year after, so they are not a direct statement of the rate in any one year. The weaker agreement on change means that a country judged on track at its national line cannot be assumed to be gaining at the international line, and the reverse also holds.

For the 2030 halving in target 1.2, the implications are mixed. The target can be read in more than one way: halving may be measured against a country's own 2015 rate or against a baseline year that varies by country, and a revised national line breaks the series on which either reading depends. The aggregate verdict on 2030 is therefore less secure than the country counts suggest. A large regressing group and uneven reporting make it unlikely that a halving will be shown across the whole population, even if many individual countries meet it.

The evidence has clear limits. Reporting peaked at 72 countries for 2021, then fell to 52 for 2022, 40 for 2023, 31 for 2024 and 13 for 2025. Recent years are thin, so effects after 2020 are seen only in part. The series does not record why a line was changed. The paired comparison rests on 36 countries. Poverty in all its dimensions is only partly captured by a headcount, and the poverty gap and multidimensional measures are not tested here against national lines.

w-c06-1-3~cedar/writer-1~82.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Equal weighting of topics is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The two counts are equal, so every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. This does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot be answered here in magnitude. The remainder of the section therefore sets out what the instrument measures and how its readings should be interpreted, which is a matter of method, and what a measured record of change would have to show. Nothing in it is a measured finding about the direction or size of reform.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice. The coverage result shows 189 economies reporting the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and 189 in any year. The companion series differ in reach, so the three indices will not align perfectly.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the added domains lower the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been verified. If it does not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and no statement about the period after 2015 or after 2020 can rest on it.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed for this section, and the finding available here is limited to coverage: almost every economy is measured, which makes a global comparison feasible once levels are computed.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The bench has computed only the coverage of the Legal Framework Index, so this part sets out what a measured record of change would need to show. It does not report a direction of reform. In 2025, 189 economies reported the index, and 189 economies reported it in at least one year. That coverage is complete enough to support a global reading, but it says nothing about level or movement.

A measured answer would have four elements. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality. The second is the change since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose scores rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and a few large reforms look the same in a mean as many small ones. The third is the distribution, meaning the spread between the highest and lowest scores and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index are likely to differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker most needs to see.

As context only, comparative legal scholarship has often observed that governments amend labour codes more readily than family and personal-status codes, which are bound up with religious authority, customary institutions and national identity. Whether that pattern appears in this index is a question for the topic-level computation, not a finding here.

The period after 2020 poses a separate question. The series could show whether average annual change before and after that year differed, provided its history permits the comparison. Until that is computed, the section cannot say whether legal reform accelerated, slowed or was interrupted. A measure built from statute has one merit: an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any reversal would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. South Asia is the only geographic region among the aggregates listed. A comparison across the other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change, while implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, maternity and paternity benefit schemes, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. It is reasonable to expect, as a hypothesis to be tested, that income relates less strongly to the legal score than to the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking built on it would misdirect attention. The test is simple once the three indices are computed by income group: compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. The tool has reported only that 189 economies reported the index in 2025, so the book cannot yet say whether the economies with the worst outcomes are those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values this section does not hold: the bench has computed only coverage, which shows that 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025.

Each reading calls for its own measure. The strict reading needs the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. The directional reading needs the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Both could be drawn from the series if its history is long enough, and a projection to 2030 at the observed pace would show which groups could reach full formal equality in time.

What can be said without those values is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar and any economy's position should be judged against it. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity, not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the Legal Framework Index is well suited to a global account. In 2025, 189 economies reported it, and 189 economies reported it in at least one year, so a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The bench has so far returned only this coverage. A record of levels, changes since 2015, distributions and topic scores remains to be computed, and the legal score still has to be set beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice becomes visible for every economy.

w-c06-4-2~cedar/writer-3~82.text:
### The global picture: parliaments close to a quarter, management data thinner

Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in single or lower national parliamentary chambers worldwide in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015. The world value rests on near-complete coverage, since 184 countries reported a figure for 2025. Set against a benchmark of 50 per cent, women still hold little more than a quarter of seats.

Target 5.5 does not name a number. Its wording, women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making, can be read as parity, with women and men holding equal shares, or as a threshold of participation sufficient for women to shape decisions, which is often placed lower. The indicator for seats cannot settle the question, because it counts occupants of seats and says nothing about their influence, the committees they chair or the offices they hold. This book uses 50 per cent as the benchmark, since a population that is about half women supplies the plainest reference for equal opportunity, and findings are stated against it while the figure itself is reported in full so that readers may apply a different reading.

The parliamentary measure covers one arena of public life. The economic arena is represented by the female share of employment in senior and middle management, a series built by the International Labour Organization from the occupational classification of managers. It excludes junior management, so it describes positions of real authority rather than all supervisory work. The series has two limits that bear on every statement made from it. First, the World Bank publishes no aggregates for it, so no world or regional share can be quoted, and any comparison must proceed country by country. Second, the number of reporting countries has changed sharply over time. It was 40 in 2000, 72 in 2010 and 77 in 2015, and reached 95 in both 2019 and 2022. It then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and stood at only 48 in 2025. A total of 154 countries have reported in at least one year.

These counts matter as much as the values. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years may reflect a change in who reports rather than a change in women's position, and the drop to 48 in 2025 is most likely a matter of surveys not yet processed, not of a real change in the world. The 2025 observations for management are therefore not a sound basis for a statement of trend, and the later parts of this section rely on the years of fuller coverage when discussing managerial positions. The parliamentary series, by contrast, is reported almost everywhere and is the firmer ground for conclusions about direction and pace.

### Regions and countries differ by more than twenty-five points

Regional averages for 2025 span a wide range. Latin America and the Caribbean leads at 36.6 per cent of parliamentary seats held by women, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 31.7 per cent and North America at 29.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 27.0 per cent, close to the world value of 27.2 per cent. East Asia and Pacific follows at 23.3 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands at 16.9 per cent, and South Asia is lowest at 11.2 per cent. A regional mean can conceal wide differences between countries within a region.

The two lowest regions are also the ones that did not advance. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 17.5 per cent in 2015 to 16.9 per cent in 2025, and its trend is classed as regression. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the only large decline among the regions shown, and its trend at the 2015 rate would reach 8.9 per cent in 2030. The results do not show why. Where a chamber is dissolved or not elected, a reported share can alter sharply, so readers should be cautious about reading such movements as gradual trends.

Income groups show a narrower spread than regions. High-income countries reached 31.2 per cent in 2025, upper middle income 27.0 per cent, low income 24.8 per cent and lower middle income 23.6 per cent. Low-income countries therefore hold a higher share than lower-middle-income ones. The results give income-group means only and offer no explanation of the ordering.

The country distribution of progress towards a target of 50 per cent by 2030 is more sobering than the regional averages. Of 187 countries assessed for parliaments, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold only 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest group is 69 countries with marginal progress that would need significant acceleration, and it covers 44.6 per cent of the population. Another 19 countries are stagnant, with 25.1 per cent of the population, and 39 countries are regressing, with 12.7 per cent. Population weights differ from country counts: regression is the second most common class by number of countries, yet stagnation covers a larger share of people. Stagnation and regression together hold a little under two in five of the assessed population, more than the share living where progress is on track or moderate, while the largest single share sits in marginal progress.

Management shows a similar pattern with a heavier weight at the negative end. Of 121 countries assessed for the female share of senior and middle management, 17 are on track or have met the target, with 8.1 per cent of the population. Moderate progress applies to 27 countries and 17.7 per cent of the population, and marginal progress to 34 countries and 31.3 per cent. Stagnation affects 6 countries with 2.7 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded in 37 countries, which together hold 40.3 per cent of the population, a far larger share than the 12.7 per cent in parliaments. The assessment covers fewer countries than for parliaments, so these shares describe the countries with data rather than the world. The regression finding should be read with caution because survey-based series are revised and can move from one round to the next.

### What changed since 2015, and the limits of the evidence

Since 2015 the largest gain in women's share of parliamentary seats was in Latin America and the Caribbean, where the regional value rose from 27.9 per cent to 36.6 per cent. North America rose from 22.3 per cent to 29.5 per cent. Europe and Central Asia moved from 25.7 per cent to 31.7 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 19.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. These are regional averages and conceal wide differences between countries within each region.

Two regions moved the other way. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region slipped from 17.5 per cent to 16.9 per cent. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the lowest regional value in 2025 and the only large fall. The indicator does not show why. A lower share can arise from an election, from a change in the chamber counted, or from the loss of a quota; these are general possibilities, outside what the series measure.

The country classification against a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 shows how uneven the movement has been. For parliaments, 24 countries are on track or have met the target, 36 show moderate progress needing acceleration, 69 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, 19 are stagnating and 39 are regressing, among 187 countries assessed. The 24 countries on track hold only 4.9 per cent of the population of those assessed. The 69 countries with marginal progress hold 44.6 per cent, the largest population share of any class, and the 19 stagnating countries hold 25.1 per cent. The 39 regressing countries hold 12.7 per cent. The number of countries on track therefore says little about how many women live where parity is approaching.

For senior and middle management, the classification covers fewer countries, 121 in all. There, 17 countries are on track or have met the target, 27 show moderate progress, 34 show marginal progress, 6 stagnate and 37 regress. The 37 regressing countries hold 40.3 per cent of the population assessed, against 8.1 per cent for the 17 on track. Regression is thus more common in management than in parliaments, and it affects a larger share of the people covered. No managerial share is given here for any region or for the world, because the results hold none.

The management evidence is weaker than the parliamentary evidence, and this limits every comparison. Across all years, 154 countries have reported at least one value, but the number reporting in a given year has varied widely: 40 in 2000, 77 in 2015, 90 in 2020 and 95 in 2022. The count then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and only 48 countries had reported for 2025. A fall of that size is most likely a matter of reporting lags, yet it means that comparisons of 2025 with earlier years would rest on different sets of countries and cannot be trusted as a measure of change.

The regional trend summary for management returned no result, so no claim is made about how any region is moving on this indicator. Nor can these indicators say why countries advance or regress. They record outcomes, not the quotas, laws, party practices, employer conduct or social norms that produce them. Whether the period after 2020 slowed or accelerated progress cannot be established for management from this evidence, and for parliaments the series gives levels and class assignments but no separate account of the pandemic years.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the rates observed since 2015, no region reaches parity in parliaments by 2030. The world trend is classed as marginal progress, with an expected value of 29.8 per cent in 2030 against the 50.0 per cent benchmark, a ratio of 0.25. East Asia and Pacific is expected at 25.7 per cent in 2030 (ratio 0.21), and Europe and Central Asia at 35.2 per cent (ratio 0.39); both are classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. The high-income group is expected at 34.7 per cent, so wealth does not by itself close the gap. Latin America and the Caribbean comes closest, at 41.9 per cent, and is the only region classed as moderate progress. Even there, acceleration is needed.

The regions at the bottom of the range are moving in the wrong direction. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected value of 8.9 per cent in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also classed as regression, at 16.7 per cent. Low-income countries are expected at 26.5 per cent and lower-middle-income countries at 25.3 per cent, both marginal. Such projections extend a linear trend and are not forecasts; as general context, a change of electoral rules can shift a national figure within one election cycle, and a suspension of parliament can erase one. The results do not measure such rules or events.

The country classification shows where people live. Of 187 countries assessed for parliamentary seats, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress. Marginal progress covers 69 countries and 44.6 per cent of the population, stagnation covers 19 countries and 25.1 per cent, and regression covers 39 countries and 12.7 per cent. Most of the assessed population therefore lives in countries classed as marginal, stagnating or regressing.

Management is assessed for fewer countries, 121, and the picture is no better. Only 17 countries, with 8.1 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the target, while 37 countries, with 40.3 per cent of the population, are classed as regression. Reporting is also thin at the latest point: 48 countries reported in 2025, against 95 in 2022. The thinning of recent data weakens the case for judging progress in managerial posts, and it is itself a finding about the state of monitoring.

Several proposals follow from these findings, and the gaps are set out below.

w-c08-5-1~juniper/writer-1~82.text:
### Renewable generation has roughly doubled worldwide since 2015

The world share of electricity produced from renewable sources other than hydroelectric power rose from 6.6 % in 2015 to 12.4 % in 2021. The share has therefore come close to doubling in six years. The figure comes from 208 reporting countries in 2021, and the series ends that year, so nothing in it describes the years since. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks of 2022, cannot be read from this indicator.

The indicator needs careful reading. It measures the share of non-hydroelectric renewables (chiefly wind, solar, geothermal and biomass) in total electricity production. It does not measure installed generating capacity, nor the quantity of electricity generated. A rising share is consistent with new capacity being built, and the growth of wind and solar plant is the usual explanation in the wider literature. But the data do not observe that capacity. A share can also rise when other generation falls, or when total output stagnates. Growth in generating capacity is thus inferred here, not observed.

The exclusion of hydroelectric power also shapes the picture. Large hydropower is a long-established source in many developing countries, and it is left out. The indicator therefore captures the newer renewables, whose costs have fallen considerably over the past decade, and it understates the renewable contribution of countries that depend heavily on dams.

The trend tool classes the world as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.1 for the period. Target 7.b carries no numerical value, so this verdict only says the share is moving in the desired direction. It is not a comparison with a quantified goal, and the word target should be read in that sense. The global figure also averages very different experiences, which the next part sets out by region and income group. A world share cannot show whether developing countries, the subject of targets 7.a and 7.b, have shared in the gain.

For 2030 the global direction is encouraging but incompletely observed. A doubling in six years shows that a rapid change in the electricity mix is possible. Whether it has continued, and whether it has reached the countries with the least infrastructure, is a question this series cannot answer from 2021 onward.

### Regions and income groups started from different levels and moved at different speeds

Regional starting points differed widely in 2015, and the gaps in levels have not closed. East Asia & Pacific rose from 4.8% of electricity production in 2015 to 12.0% in 2021, and Latin America & Caribbean rose from 6.9% to 15.1% over the same years. South Asia moved from 4.6% to 8.5%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan began from 0.6% and reached 2.9%, the lowest level among the regions reported. Sub-Saharan Africa started at 2.1% and stood at 4.3% in 2021. All figures here are shares of total electricity production from non-hydroelectric renewable sources.

Income groups show the same pattern more sharply. Upper middle income countries rose from 4.6% to 11.9%, and lower middle income countries from 4.1% to 7.3%. High income countries rose from 8.6% to 14.1%. Low income countries moved the other way, from 0.7% in 2015 to 0.5% in 2021. The poorest countries therefore did not share in the expansion of wind, solar, geothermal and biomass generation that lifted the world figure. Well-established context points to the cost of capital, small and weakly financed grids, and limited public budgets as barriers to new plant in these economies, though the data here do not test those causes.

The trend assessment for the share of renewables in total final energy consumption must be read with care. Low income countries show the highest share, 77.0% in 2015 and 74.6% in 2020, and the trend reads as regression, at a rate of -0.0064. That level does not signal modern clean energy. In these countries the share is dominated by traditional biomass, chiefly wood and charcoal burned for cooking, which is neither clean nor efficient and carries health and forest costs. A falling share there can even accompany a shift to commercial fuels. The indicator also leaves target 7.2 open to more than one reading, since no numeric 2030 value is set for it. The tool classes the World, East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, and upper middle income groups as on track, while Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and lower middle income countries are marked as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The convergence result tempers any reading of catching up. Across 208 countries, the slope of annual change on starting level between 2015 and 2021 was -0.004, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001. No convergence can be distinguished from zero. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021, so spread relative to the mean narrowed. The two results are compatible: the mean rose, which shrinks relative spread, without starting position predicting the pace of change. The data end in 2021, so they say nothing about changes since the pandemic.

### Private investment and concessional finance moved unevenly

Private participation in energy investment moved unevenly across developing regions between 2015 and 2024. In Latin America & Caribbean, investment with private participation fell from US$11.87 billion in 2015 to US$8.40 billion in 2024. South Asia moved the other way, rising from US$2.39 billion to US$3.45 billion. The two regions therefore ended the period on different paths, and the regional total for Latin America & Caribbean is lower than at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals period.

The income groups show a sharper divide. Upper middle income countries rose from US$31.02 billion in 2015 to US$58.39 billion in 2024, so private capital in energy concentrated where borrowing conditions, market size and regulatory frameworks are most developed. Lower middle income countries barely moved, from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion, in current dollars. Because the figures are not adjusted for inflation, the lower middle income total is likely to have lost purchasing power over the period, though the extract gives no deflated series to show it. Low income countries are not shown in the extract, so the position of the poorest economies cannot be read from these results.

Coverage limits what can be concluded. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, and the Private Participation in Infrastructure database records only projects with a contractual private role in low- and middle-income countries. Public investment, which carries much of energy infrastructure in the poorest countries, is outside it. Annual totals can also swing with a few large projects, so the endpoints of 2015 and 2024 do not describe the years between.

Concessional finance is harder to assess. Net official development assistance to the least developed countries was reported by 32 countries in 2023, but the series covers all aid and not aid for energy. The extract therefore gives no clean energy figure for concessional support, and it cannot be said whether international cooperation on clean energy research and technology, the subject of target 7.a, has grown. Targets 7.a and 7.b are worded without a numerical threshold, such as a sum to be mobilised or a capacity to be installed. Progress can therefore be described but not scored as met or missed, and any judgement depends on how expand, enhance and facilitate are read.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to rising renewable shares worldwide, but the gains are uneven and the finance behind them is concentrated. Renewable energy consumption as a share of total final energy consumption is classed as on track or target met for the world, at a trend rate of 0.0255. The same classification applies to East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, high income countries and upper middle income countries. Low income countries show regression, at a rate of -0.0064. Lower middle income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa show marginal progress, and the tool states that significant acceleration is needed. Note that the trend tool was run with no quantified target, so these classifications measure direction and pace and not distance from a defined goal.

Private investment follows the same pattern. Upper middle income countries recorded US$58.39 billion of energy investment with private participation in 2024, against US$31.02 billion in 2015. Lower middle income countries moved from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion over the same years, which is close to flat in current dollars. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, so the totals describe the projects recorded and not all investment. Official assistance cannot be read in the same way: the series for net ODA to the least developed countries shows 32 reporting countries in 2023, and the result gives no regional or income-group levels. Whether concessional finance has offset the weak private flows to poorer countries therefore cannot be shown here.

The spread of non-hydroelectric renewable shares across countries has narrowed, with the coefficient of variation falling from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021 across 208 countries. The slope of change on starting level is -0.0040, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001, so it cannot be distinguished from zero. The narrowing in spread is therefore not evidence that low starters are catching up systematically.

Targets 7.a and 7.b carry no quantified goal, so progress can be read in more than one way. Rising shares, rising private investment in some regions and falling investment in others can each be cited as success or failure, depending on the threshold chosen. Installed capacity in developing countries, the quantity named in the section's question, is not among the series examined, and the data cannot show it directly. For 2030, the pattern implies that the countries furthest behind, low income and lower middle income, are the ones where pace is weakest and private finance is thinnest.

The United Nations Statistical Commission should set a measurable threshold for targets 7.a and 7.b, so that progress is not open to competing readings.
The agencies that compile energy statistics should report the non-biomass renewable share separately, since the headline renewable share in low income countries is dominated by traditional biomass.

w-c03-7-3~juniper/writer-4~82.text:
### Consumer price inflation stands in for food prices

Target 2.c asks for measures that keep food commodity markets and their derivatives working properly and that give timely access to market information, including on food reserves, so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The target names no numerical threshold and no price index. Its indicator in the global framework is a food price anomalies measure, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold among the series available to this book. Volatility is therefore not measured here directly, and every statement in this section about prices is an indirect reading.

The nearest series is headline consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services for the average consumer. Food is one component of that basket, and its weight varies widely: it is large in low-income households and economies, and small in high-income ones. Headline inflation also contains energy, housing, transport and services, so a rise in the headline rate can follow a fuel shock, a currency depreciation or a rent adjustment with food prices barely moving. The series is read here as a signal of pressure on household budgets, not as a record of food price swings. Regional averages of general inflation say nothing about exposure to food price shocks.

The series also has limits as a measure of volatility. The results available to this section give levels at 2015 and 2025 and measures of dispersion among countries in four selected years. They do not give the year-to-year path, which is what volatility requires. What follows describes the price environment and its unevenness, and does not claim to measure instability over time.

Coverage shapes what can be said. In 2015, 189 countries reported consumer price inflation, and the same number reported in 2016. The count then drifted down, to 185 in 2017, 179 in 2020, 176 in 2024 and 169 in 2025. Across all years 193 countries reported at least once, so some economies have gaps in particular years. The data do not show which economies dropped out, and the reasons for interrupted reporting cannot be read from them. The latest year, 2025, is the thinnest and may be revised as late submissions arrive. Comparisons across the period therefore rest on a changing set of countries, and the parts that follow rely mainly on regional and world aggregates, which are less sensitive to the loss of single reporters.

### World inflation doubled between 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025, a little more than double the earlier rate. Both figures are annual percentage changes in the cost of a general basket of goods and services, so they describe the price level that households face and not the price of food alone. Food is a large part of that basket in poorer economies and a smaller part in richer ones.

The two endpoints conceal the path between them. A comparison of 2015 with 2025 does not show how far inflation fell or rose in the years between, and it should not be read as a steady climb. The period contains the weak price environment of the middle 2010s, the disruption of 2020 and the supply shocks that followed, and an endpoint comparison cannot separate these. Volatility concerns movement from year to year, and the result used here reports levels at two dates only. It therefore shows that the world rate ended the period well above where it began, and it does not measure how much the rate moved in between.

Low-income countries show a different pattern from the world as a whole. Their inflation was 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025, so it fell over the decade while the world rate rose. Lower middle income countries also eased, from 4.0% to 3.6%, whereas upper middle income countries rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high income countries from 0.3% to 2.3%. That fall in the poorest group should not be taken as relief. Low-income countries began from the highest rate of any income group in 2015, and they remain above the world rate in 2025. Households there spend the largest share of their budgets on food, so a given rate of general inflation weighs more heavily on them than on households in richer groups. Coverage also changed: 169 countries reported in 2025, against 189 in 2015, so part of the comparison rests on a smaller set of countries at the later date.

The finding matters for Goal 2 because food access depends on what a household can buy with its income, and persistent price growth erodes that. Yet the series cannot show whether food prices moved more or less than prices generally, nor whether any rise came from commodity markets, exchange rates, energy costs or domestic policy. Those causes bear on whether the measures named in target 2.c are working, and the data used here do not distinguish among them.

### Regions began far apart and converged at a higher level

Regional inflation rates stood far apart in 2015. South Asia recorded consumer price inflation of 4.7% and Sub-Saharan Africa 3.5%, while Europe and Central Asia stood at 0.4% and North America at 0.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.8%, was also among the regions with very low rates. Latin America and the Caribbean (1.9%) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (1.7%) sat between the two groups. Income groups showed the same ordering: low-income economies stood at 5.5% and high-income economies at 0.3%.

By 2025 the regional range was narrower, from 2.0% to 3.7%, against 0.4% to 4.7% in 2015, though the order of the regions had changed. South Asia fell to 3.1% and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged at 3.4%, against 3.5% in 2015. Europe and Central Asia rose from 0.4% to 3.7%, the highest rate among the regions in the latest year, narrowly ahead of Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1.7% to 2.0%. Movements in these three were modest, and all three ended 2025 at about 2%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024; its latest observation is for 2024, not 2025, so it is not strictly comparable in date, but its value is below that of Europe and Central Asia, so the ranking holds.

Income groups tell a similar story. Low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower-middle-income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while upper-middle-income economies rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high-income economies from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing therefore reflects falls in South Asia and in low-income economies together with rises elsewhere; the results do not allow it to be apportioned between them. Energy and food price shocks after 2020 are well-established drivers of rises in importing regions, but these series cannot show how far each region's movement was due to them.

The pattern matters for Target 2.c because the region with the lowest inflation in 2015 had the highest in 2025. Regional average inflation rates are closer together in 2025 than in 2015, but this says nothing about food price shocks, and a regional aggregate cannot show differences between countries or how often households met sharp price spikes within single years. For 2030, no region now enjoys the near-zero inflation seen in 2015.

### Dispersion among countries widened after 2022

The spread of annual consumer price inflation among countries, weighted by population, was almost unchanged between 2015 and 2019 on the Gini measure, at 0.538 in 2015 and 0.538 in 2019. It narrowed to 0.511 in 2022, the year in which price pressures were felt in most economies at once, and then rose sharply to 0.660 in 2024. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the upper end of the distribution, gives a similar picture: 0.621 in 2015, 0.751 in 2019, 0.559 in 2022 and 0.982 in 2024. The 2024 values are the highest of the four years examined on both measures.

The composition of the inequality needs careful reading. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015, 32.0% in 2019 and 38.4% in 2022, and then 35.2% in 2024. Because the between-region share is below half in every year, most of the measured inequality lay within regions throughout, and it was in 2015 that the within-region part was largest, at about three quarters of the index. The fall in the between-region share from 2022 to 2024, while the index itself rose, indicates that the rise in dispersion after 2022 came mainly from differences among countries of the same region, not from a return of the regional gaps. Only four years are examined, so the path between them is not shown. Some economies may have brought inflation down as monetary tightening and falling energy costs worked through, while others continued to face currency depreciation, fiscal strain or conflict. The results do not identify which countries fall in which group, so this explanation rests on well-established patterns and not on the series itself. A regional average conceals the divergence, and a policy aimed at a region as a whole could miss the countries where price stress is most acute.

Three cautions apply. First, the number of countries in the calculation differs by year: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 sample is much smaller than the 189 countries that reported inflation that year, so part of the comparison with later years reflects who is included and not only how prices moved. Second, population weighting gives large economies great influence, and a change in one of them can shift the result. Third, the measure is of general consumer prices, so it is an indirect guide to uneven exposure to food price volatility. For 2030, the widening within regions suggests that the risk of extreme price swings may be concentrated in a minority of countries, though the results do not show how many, and monitoring needs to be national in its detail.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.c cannot be scored from these data. It sets no numerical threshold and can be read in two ways: as the proper functioning of commodity markets and the availability of market information, or as the narrower outcome of limited price volatility. The series available touch only the second reading, and only indirectly, through general consumer prices. World inflation of 1.4% in 2015 and 3.0% in 2025 is consistent with greater price pressure on households. It says nothing about whether markets, derivatives or reserve reporting function better or worse than before, and the two endpoint values do not describe the path between them.

The outlook for 2030 is therefore uncertain in direction. Regional rates in 2015 ran from 0.4% in Europe and Central Asia to 4.7% in South Asia. By 2025 the range was from 2.0% in East Asia and Pacific to 3.7% in Europe and Central Asia, so the regional averages were closer together than in 2015. Europe and Central Asia moved from the lowest rate to the highest; North America's latest value, 2.7% in 2024, lies below it, so the ranking holds. Among income groups, low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower middle income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while high-income economies rose from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing reflects falls in South Asia and in low-income economies and rises elsewhere; the data do not apportion it. Closer regional averages say nothing about exposure to food price shocks. Dispersion among countries points the other way: the population-weighted Gini measure stood at 0.660 in 2024, against 0.511 in 2022, so a narrower spread of group averages sits beside a wider spread of country experience. The data do not show which countries make up the upper tail, and the rates cited here are general consumer prices, not food prices.

Coverage bears on any monitoring to 2030. Countries reporting inflation numbered 189 in 2015 and 169 in 2025, and the data do not say whether the fall in 2025 is permanent or reflects later reporting. The proposals below follow from these limits: they aim to replace a proxy with measures that match the wording of the target, and to keep watch on the countries at the upper end of the distribution.

proposals: The United Nations Statistics Division and the World Bank should add the food price anomalies indicator for target 2.c to the catalogue, so that the target is monitored with a series that matches its wording.

National statistical offices should publish monthly food consumer price series with the food share of the basket, and national authorities should report food reserve stocks promptly to market information systems.

Governments and development partners should direct monitoring and reserve support to the countries at the upper end of the inflation distribution, and statistical offices that stopped reporting should resume it.
