w-c05-7-3~cedar/writer-4~85.text:
### The global share of trained primary teachers has risen only slowly

The world share of primary school teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and at 82.2% in 2024, a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030, and the indicator used here reads that as a share of 100%. Against that reading, roughly one primary teacher in five worldwide still lacks the minimum organised training required in the country where they teach. The trend calculation gives a world ratio of 0.15 against the pace needed, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Continuing the 2015 to 2024 slope would bring the world to 83.4% in 2030.

The measure needs careful reading. The indicator counts teachers who have received the minimum organised training, whether before or during service, that a given country requires. That minimum is set nationally and differs widely. A teacher counted as trained in one system might not meet the standard of another, and a share of 100% in one country does not imply equal preparation in the classroom. Nor does the indicator capture the quality of the training, the subject knowledge of teachers, or whether they remain in post. The figure is therefore a floor on qualification, not a measure of teaching quality. Readings of the target also vary: some take 4.c to mean full national qualification, others a substantial rise from a baseline, and the data cannot settle between them.

Coverage adds a second caution. The 2024 world value rests on the latest reporting of each economy, and only 13 countries reported in 2025, so the most recent year says little. Several regional values end in 2022, and the upper middle income group has a single value, for 2022, at 80.7%, which allows no change to be read. Late reporting may be more common where systems are weaker, but the results do not test this.

The section's guiding question also asks whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling. The bench returned no result for that ratio, so the question cannot be answered from the evidence held here. Series on teacher numbers exist for primary and secondary levels, but a count of teachers without matching enrolment does not give a ratio. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is likewise not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings, safety or inclusion. The evidence speaks to the training of teachers, not to class size or the learning environment.

The slow world movement matters for 2030 because training is a precondition for much else in the chapter, from completion and learning to pre-primary provision. A world share that rises by under two points in nine years, spanning the disruption of 2020 and the years after it, leaves the target far out of reach on the present slope. The results do not show why the share has stalled; one possible explanation is that recruitment has outpaced training in some systems, but this remains a conjecture that the series cannot test. The regional parts that follow show where gains and losses lie.

### Regions and income groups differ by more than twenty points

The regional picture in 2024 is one of wide separation. North America stands at 97.9% of primary teachers trained, South Asia at 87.7%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 81.8% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 80.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa, whose latest reading is 2022 rather than 2024, stands at 68.8%. The gap between the best and the weakest of these regions is therefore about twenty-nine percentage points, taking the 2024 reading for North America and the 2022 reading for Sub-Saharan Africa. Readings from different years are not strictly comparable, and the Sub-Saharan figure may understate or overstate the position in 2024.

Income groups show a similar pattern. Low income countries stand at 69.2% in 2022, close to the Sub-Saharan level, which is expected because most low income countries lie in that region. Upper middle income countries have only a 2022 reading, 80.7%, so no change over the period can be given for that group. Training here means the minimum organised preparation required by each country, so the percentages measure compliance with national standards and not a common level of skill. A country with a demanding standard can score lower than one with a modest standard, and comparisons across regions should be read with that in mind.

The spread among countries, weighted by population, is modest in absolute terms. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.094 in 2015, fell to 0.073 in 2020 and rose to 0.097 in 2024, ending slightly above its starting level. The Theil index fell from 0.026 in 2015 to 0.011 in 2020. In that decomposition the share lying between regions was 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020. In those two years about half of the inequality among countries was therefore a difference between regions, and the other half lay among countries within the same region. Policies aimed at a single region would address only part of the gap, though the decomposition is not available for 2024 and may have changed since.

These comparisons carry a caveat about coverage. Countries reporting numbered 85 in 2015 and 93 in 2020, but only 79 in 2024. The Theil index and its regional decomposition are missing for 2024, so the latest year cannot be set against the earlier ones on that measure. A change in the number of reporting countries can alter the Gini by changing who is counted, and the rise to 0.097 may reflect that as much as any real divergence; the series cannot separate the two. Reporting for 2025 is thinner still, with 13 countries. For 2030 the implication is that monitoring of Target 4.c is weakest in the years that matter most for judging it.

### Gains in South Asia contrast with declines in richer regions

South Asia recorded the largest regional gain in the share of trained primary teachers. The share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly fifteen percentage points in nine years. The region moved from below the world average of 80.4% in 2015 to above the world level of 82.2% in 2024. Its trend is the only regional one classed as on track, with an expected 99.3% in 2030 if the rate of change continued. Lower middle income countries, a group that includes several South Asian economies, rose more modestly, from 76.4% in 2015 to 83.3% in 2024, and their expected value for 2030 is 88.2%. The data do not show which measures lay behind the South Asian rise. A change in how a country defines the minimum training required would produce the same movement as a real improvement in preparation, so the gain should be read as a reported change in the share, not as proof of better teaching.

The richer regions moved in the opposite direction. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020, the last year for which the regional reading is given here. High income countries fell from 95.9% in 2015 to 92.1% in 2024, and North America slipped from 99.3% to 97.9% over the same period. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 82.7% to 81.8%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan declined from 83.9% to 80.5%. These falls are small beside the South Asian gain, but they run against the direction of Target 4.c, and the trend tool classes all of these regions as regressing. The results do not explain them. Teacher shortages that lead systems to hire staff before they complete a full programme are one possible cause, and changes in national definitions or reporting are another; neither can be tested with these series.

Across countries, the pattern is one of catching up. A convergence test over 48 countries between 2015 and 2024 gives a coefficient of -0.071 (p below 0.001) with an R2 of 0.342, which means that countries starting from lower shares of trained teachers tended to gain faster than those starting higher. The dispersion of the shares narrowed only slightly: the coefficient of variation moved from 0.165 in 2015 to 0.155 in 2024. Convergence is therefore real but slow, and about a third of the variation in country changes is accounted for by the starting level alone. The test covers only the 48 countries with readings at both ends of the period, so it describes the reporting countries and not the world, and the systems with the sparsest records may be underrepresented.

The size of the teaching workforce does not appear to explain the changes. The rank correlation between changes in the share of trained primary teachers and changes in the number of primary teachers across the same 48 countries is -0.095, and the correlation between 2024 levels is 0.168. Both are weak. Expanding the workforce therefore did not visibly coincide with a higher trained share, and countries that added the most teachers were no more likely to see that share rise. This is a cautionary finding for Target 4.c, which speaks of qualified teachers and not of teachers alone. The correlations are descriptive and say nothing about the mechanism.

The period since 2015 and the years after 2020 cannot be read cleanly from these series. Several regional readings end in 2020 or 2022, and the school closures of 2020 and 2021 disrupted the collection of statistics as well as schooling. A gap in reporting may conceal a change that has not yet been measured. For 2030, the lesson of this part is that large gains are recorded where the share rose fast, as in South Asia, but that they are not general, and that richer regions with falling shares cannot assume the levels of 2015 will return unaided. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings or learning environments.

### Most countries are not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

The country counts show that the 2030 picture is mixed. In primary education, 64 of the 129 countries assessed, holding 65.9% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have already met the target of a fully trained teaching force. This is a large share of people but not of countries, because several populous countries are among those advancing. Against it stand 36 countries with 26.3% of the assessed population whose trained share is falling rather than rising. A further 13 countries, with 2.4% of the population, show marginal progress that would need to speed up considerably, 12 countries, with 4.2% of the population, show moderate progress that still needs acceleration, and 4 countries, with 1.2%, are stagnant. The two largest groups are the on-track countries and the regressing ones, so the pattern is divided at its poles.

Secondary education tells a similar story with less coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 hold 61.5% of the population and are on track or have met the target, while 36 hold 27.6% and are regressing. Fourteen countries with 7.7% of the population show marginal progress, 10 with 2.1% show moderate progress and 7 with 1.0% are stagnant. The share of people living in regressing countries is slightly higher at secondary level than at primary level, and the share living in on-track countries is slightly lower. Fewer countries report secondary data, so the secondary result rests on a thinner base and is the less certain of the two.

The regression count needs careful reading. A falling trained share does not necessarily mean that teaching has worsened. One possible explanation is that systems expanding quickly may recruit teachers faster than they can certify them; another is that a country raising its minimum standard may see teachers once counted as trained fall below the new bar. Both are conjectures drawn from general experience, and the data given here cannot separate them.

The same feature complicates the target itself. Target 4.c speaks of qualified teachers, and the indicator measures minimum organised training, pre-service or in-service, as defined nationally. A share of 100% therefore does not mean equal preparation across countries. The target can be read as a share trained to national standards, a share trained to an international standard, or a growth in the absolute supply of teachers. The assessment here uses the first reading, with 100% as the goal, because it is the one the trained-teacher series can express. The reading of a substantial increase in supply cannot be judged from these results.

Two parts of the section's question remain unanswered. No pupil-teacher ratio series was assessed, so whether ratios are falling cannot be stated; the teacher-count series on the shelf were not combined with enrolment here. Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive school facilities, was not assessed either, because none of the series on the shelf for this section measures it.

For 2030, on the full-training reading the target will be missed at the world level. The projected world share of trained primary teachers is 83.4%, with a trend ratio of 0.15, which falls in the class of marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 72.0% and low income countries at 73.2%, so the groups starting furthest behind are expected to remain furthest behind. South Asia, projected at 99.3%, is the one region on course. The regions that are regressing are mostly those that began from higher levels, such as Europe and Central Asia at a projected 86.9% and high income countries at 89.7%. Their decline lowers the world figure and shows that a high starting point is no guarantee of progress.

Among the 48 countries reporting in both 2015 and 2024, convergence is present but slight: the coefficient of variation of the primary trained share fell from 0.17 to 0.16, with a beta of -0.07. The inequality measures give a final caution. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the trained share was 0.09 in 2015, 0.07 in 2020 and 0.10 in 2024. Differences narrowed up to 2020 and then widened again, though the 2024 reading covers 79 countries against 93 in 2020, so the comparison is imperfect and the cause of the widening cannot be read from these results. The between-region share of inequality, 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020, shows that regional differences account for about half of the spread in those years, so action aimed at one region would leave much of it untouched.

The findings point to the following proposals.

w-c09-7-1~juniper/writer-2~85.text:
### Child labour data thin out as the 2025 target year passes

The indicator available for Target 8.7 is the share of children aged 7 to 14 in employment, defined as involvement in economic activity for at least one hour in the reference week of a household survey. The World Bank's series carries no aggregate for the world or for any region, so the shelf offers no global share of children in employment. Only country values exist, drawn from surveys that countries run at irregular intervals. A global figure would have to be built from those values, and the data do not support that.

The number of countries reporting shows how thin the record is. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2016, 97 countries reported at least once. Coverage in any single year was far smaller. It stood at 24 countries in 2000, fell to 4 in 2002, and rose to a peak of 31 in 2006. It then stayed between 11 and 24 countries in most later years, with 22 in 2011 and 24 in 2012, before dropping to 18 in 2014 and 10 in 2015. In 2016, the latest year, only 2 countries reported. The pattern follows the survey cycle: the household surveys from which the series is built are held every few years, and each country appears only in the years when one was completed and processed.

This matters because Target 8.7 sets a date. It calls for an end to child labour in all its forms by 2025, and that year has now arrived or passed. The latest observations on the shelf are from 2016, so the data cannot say how far the world has moved towards the target since 2015, or what the pandemic after 2020 did to children's work. Closure of schools and loss of household income are widely understood to push children towards work, but nothing in this series measures that effect.

The indicator also covers only part of what the target names. It counts children aged 7 to 14, so older children up to 17, who fall within the usual definition of child labour, are outside it. It counts any economic activity of at least one hour in a week, which is broader than the worst forms of child labour and is not the same as child labour as defined in standards. It says nothing on forced labour, trafficking or the recruitment of child soldiers, which the target also names. Where the target can be read as the elimination of child labour in every form, this series can speak to only a narrow part of it.

### Country values differ widely, and most of the difference lies between regions

Among the countries that reported, the spread of children's employment is wide, and it moves sharply from one year to the next. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of country values was 0.232 in 2006, when 31 countries reported, and 0.625 in 2012, when 24 did. A Gini of 0 would mean every country had the same share; the 2012 figure indicates a distribution in which a few populous countries sit far from the rest. The Theil index tells the same story: 0.135 in 2006 and 0.856 in 2012. The other years shown fall between these two extremes: the Gini was 0.431 in 2000, 0.508 in 2005, 0.532 in 2010 and 0.390 in 2011.

Most of this inequality lies between regions rather than within them. The between-region share of Theil's T was 91.9% in 2000, 92.3% in 2005, 85.4% in 2006, 92.6% in 2010, 77.0% in 2011 and 91.7% in 2012. In five of the six years shown, more than four-fifths of the difference among countries is therefore attributable to differences between regional averages. The lowest share, 77.0% in 2011, still leaves regional position as the largest component. As context rather than a finding of these results, the pattern is consistent with the long-standing concentration of high child employment in poorer, agrarian economies, where household survey evidence has repeatedly shown work in family farming to be the commonest form. The measure does not identify which regions or countries drive the figures, and the results give no basis for naming them.

The swings between years cannot be read as real change in the world. The set of reporting countries changes every year: 24 in 2000, 26 in 2005, 31 in 2006, 21 in 2010, 22 in 2011 and 24 in 2012. A drop in the Gini from 0.508 in 2005 to 0.232 in 2006 coincides with the addition of five countries to the sample, and the rise to 0.625 in 2012 coincides with a different set again. Because each year's calculation covers only the countries that happened to be surveyed, a high or low value may reflect which countries reported as much as any shift in how children's work is distributed. Population weighting sharpens this effect, since one large country entering or leaving the sample can move the whole index.

The spread is also silent on levels. A low Gini could describe uniformly high or uniformly low child employment, so these figures describe inequality among countries and say nothing on whether children's work is rising or falling. No year after 2012 appears in the spread results, and the sparse reporting of later years leaves the 2015 and 2020 periods without a comparable reading. For 2030, the only safe inference is that where child employment persists, it is concentrated by region, and that measuring it will require the same countries to be surveyed repeatedly.

### Change over time cannot be separated from change in coverage

Reading the series as a trend requires first reading the number of countries behind each year. The count of reporting countries was 4 in 2002, rose to 31 in 2006, fell to 12 in 2008, recovered to 24 in 2012 and fell again to 10 in 2015. In 2016 only 2 countries reported. Any comparison of a yearly figure across these years would compare different groups of countries, so a rise or fall in a share could reflect who was surveyed rather than what happened to children. Across the whole period, 97 countries reported at least once, which shows that the series has broad reach over time but little depth in any single year.

The pattern follows from how the data are produced. Children's employment is measured through household surveys, usually run by national statistical offices with international technical support, and these surveys are fielded irregularly, often once every several years and only where funding and priority allow. A country may appear in 2006 and again in 2012 and be absent between. Peaks in reporting, such as the 31 countries of 2006, probably reflect clusters of survey rounds rather than any change in the phenomenon, and the troughs likewise. This is context, not a finding of the data, which do not record why a country did or did not report.

The 2016 observations are the latest on the shelf, and they cannot carry a reading of the period after 2015. The 2 countries reporting in 2016 are too few to indicate a direction, and the shelf holds nothing later, so neither the years after 2015 nor the period after 2020 can be described. The disruptions of 2020 to schooling and household incomes are widely expected to bear on children's work, but the series offers no measurement of it.

The same limit applies to the division between boys and girls. The male and female series each have only 2 countries reporting in 2016, the same 2 as the total. A gap between boys and girls drawn from two countries would describe those countries alone and could not be generalised to any region or to the world. Earlier years hold more countries, but they are not comparable with 2016 for the reasons given above.

For 2030 and for the 2025 date set in Target 8.7, the implication is plain. With 10 countries reporting in 2015 and 2 in 2016, the evidence for judging whether child labour has ended in all its forms is thinner now than in the years when 24 or more countries reported. Progress cannot be confirmed or refuted from this series, and the thinning of the data is itself the main result of the period.

### The 2025 target cannot be verified, and the proposals follow from that

The target year has arrived without a measurable global baseline from this series. Target 8.7 sets 2025 as the date by which child labour in all its forms is to end, yet the latest year in the series is 2016, and in that year only 2 countries reported. Across the whole period 97 countries reported at least once, but never more than a few dozen in any one year. A reading of progress towards 2025, or of the position in 2030, cannot be drawn from figures of this kind.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Its first clause calls for the elimination of the worst forms of child labour, including the recruitment and use of child soldiers; its closing clause calls for an end to child labour in all its forms by 2025. The indicator available here measures neither exactly. It counts children aged 7 to 14 involved in economic activity for at least one hour in the reference week, which includes light work that many national laws permit and excludes children aged 15 to 17 who may be in hazardous work. It also does not capture forced labour, trafficking or armed recruitment. A falling share on this measure would be encouraging but would not show that the worst forms had ended, and a flat share would not show that they persisted.

The sex-specific series, for boys and for girls, also stand at 2 reporting countries in 2016. Differences in employment between the sexes therefore cannot be assessed for the years that matter most for the target, namely those after 2015 and after the disruption of 2020. Causes commonly associated with child labour, such as household poverty, school closures and weak enforcement, may have changed in those years, but the data give no means of testing this.

For these reasons Target 8.7 is best treated as unassessed on the evidence of this series, and the proposals below follow from that finding rather than from any measured trend.

The agencies that compile the series should publish the 7 to 14 series with an agreed age range and a sex split for every country, and should add the 15 to 17 group so that hazardous work can be read.
The World Bank and its partners should publish the number of reporting countries and the survey year beside every estimate, so that readers can see how much each figure rests on.

Reviewers of Target 8.7, including the bodies that report to the United Nations, should record the target as unassessed until the data allow a reading, and should state which reading of the target, all forms or the worst forms, they are applying.

w-c08-2-1~rowan/writer-2~85.text:
### Three-quarters of the world now cooks with clean fuels

Roughly three people in four now cook mainly with clean fuels and technologies. The World Bank's World Development Indicators put the share of the world's population with access at 63.9 per cent in 2015 and at 75.4 per cent in 2024. The series covers 192 countries in 2024. The indicator measures the proportion of the total population primarily using clean cooking fuels and technologies, such as electricity, gas, biogas and the cleanest stoves, as against open fires and stoves burning wood, charcoal, dung, crop residues or kerosene. Primary use is the test: a household that owns a gas ring but cooks mostly on firewood is not counted as having access.

The gain between 2015 and 2024 is real and large, but the figure carries a caveat. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses, which are conducted at intervals of several years and are not available for every country in every year. Values for years between surveys, and the most recent years in particular, are estimates produced by statistical models rather than direct observations. The 2024 world value is therefore best read as a close approximation of the trend, and small year-to-year movements should not be treated as measured events. Nor does the indicator record how much of a household's cooking is done with clean fuels, how affordable the fuel is, or whether supply is reliable, all of which bear on the wording of target 7.1 on affordable and reliable modern energy services.

The remaining share matters because the other side of the figure is large. With 75.4 per cent having access in 2024, about one person in four still depends mainly on polluting fuels and technologies. Smoke from these fuels is a well-established cause of respiratory and cardiovascular illness, and it falls most heavily on women and young children, who spend the most time near the fire. Gathering fuel also consumes time that might otherwise go to schooling or paid work, and the burning of wood and charcoal contributes to local forest loss and to emissions. Clean cooking therefore bears on health, gender equality and climate goals as well as on Goal 7.

The world's average conceals a wide spread between income groups, which later parts of the section take up. High-income countries stood at 98.8 per cent in 2015 and 99.5 per cent in 2024, so almost nothing remained to be gained there. Low-income countries rose only from 13.3 per cent to 15.6 per cent over the same years, while lower-middle-income countries rose from 42.7 per cent to 63.8 per cent and upper-middle-income countries from 76.9 per cent to 90.2 per cent. The global rise is thus driven chiefly by the middle-income groups, and the countries with the lowest access have moved the least. Since the world value is a population-weighted average, it moves mainly with the largest populations, and it can improve even while the poorest countries stand almost still.

For 2030, the reading is straightforward but sobering. Target 7.1 calls for universal access to modern energy services, and the clean cooking series stands well short of that in 2024. The pace of the past nine years, taken alone, would not close a gap of this size within the six years that remain, a point examined in the final part of the section.

### Regions diverge sharply, with Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Regional levels in 2024 span almost the whole range of the scale. North America stands at 100.0 per cent of the population with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking, and Europe and Central Asia at 98.3 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 22.9 per cent, up from 14.7 per cent in 2015. Fewer than one person in four in the region cooks mainly with clean fuels, while the world as a whole stands at 75.4 per cent. The income groups tell the same story: low-income economies stood at 15.6 per cent in 2024, against 99.5 per cent in high-income economies.

The regions between these poles moved at very different speeds after 2015. South Asia made the largest advance in the data, rising from 45.3 per cent to 74.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 70.7 per cent to 87.0 per cent. Both regions are now close to or above the world level. Large national programmes to distribute gas connections and to substitute for solid fuels are well-established contributors to progress of this kind, though the indicator does not show what drove the change in any country. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 86.8 per cent to 90.5 per cent, a smaller gain from a higher base. Europe and Central Asia moved from 96.6 per cent to 98.3 per cent, as the last households switched.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved slowly, from 74.7 per cent to 77.8 per cent. The region began 2015 at a level near that of East Asia and Pacific, which has since moved well ahead. The grouping also mixes economies at very different incomes, so the regional figure conceals wide national differences that this indicator, taken at regional level, cannot display. In Sub-Saharan Africa the gain of 14.7 to 22.9 per cent is real but small against the size of the shortfall, and the region's pace needs to be read against continuing population growth, which the share alone does not capture.

The gap between rural and urban households explains much of the regional picture. Worldwide, rural access rose from 38.2 per cent in 2015 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while urban access rose from 85.1 per cent to 89.4 per cent. Rural households therefore gained more in percentage points, yet remain far behind. Sub-Saharan Africa's rural level is the lowest in the data, at 8.6 per cent in 2024, up from 5.4 per cent in 2015. Urban Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.8 per cent, up from 29.5 per cent. Low-income economies show the same pattern, with rural access at 7.3 per cent and urban access at 31.5 per cent.

Elsewhere the contrast between rural and urban areas has narrowed. South Asia's rural level reached 61.7 per cent against an urban level of 92.0 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific's rural level reached 73.9 per cent against 94.6 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the rural level is 95.2 per cent, and in North America 99.9 per cent. These differences matter for 2030. Where the remaining shortfall is concentrated in dispersed rural households, supply networks for fuel, stoves and finance are costlier to extend, and a regional average rising slowly leaves the poorest households for last. The data show levels and change, not the affordability of fuels, which the target also names and which the indicator does not measure.

### Gains were broad but the pace has not been steady

The global series has not risen at a steady pace. A break analysis of the annual change in the world share with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking finds two breaks, in 2010 and in 2021. In the segment from 2001 to 2009 the mean annual change was 0.9 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2010 to 2020 it was 1.4 points a year. In the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 1.0 point a year. Progress therefore quickened at the start of the 2010s and slowed after 2021, to a pace close to that of the first decade of the century. The 2010 break falls before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, so the faster pace of the 2010s cannot be credited to the goals alone. The 2021 break coincides with the period after the pandemic shock of 2020, but the data show only when the pace changed, not why.

The slowdown matters for 2030. Universal access requires a pace above any of the three segments, and the latest segment is the slowest since the early 2000s. Four years is a short window, and the 2021 break rests on few annual observations, so the estimate of its mean change is less secure than those of the longer segments. The break dates are statistical estimates and could shift with further data.

The second analysis asks whether countries drew together. Across 192 countries from 2015 to 2024, the slope of each country's annual change on its starting level is negative, at -0.0079 (p below 0.001). Countries that began with lower access therefore gained faster on average than countries that began higher, and levels moved closer. The coefficient of variation, which measures spread relative to the mean, fell from 0.57 in 2015 to 0.50 in 2024, which agrees with this reading.

The convergence is real but weak. The R2 of the regression is 0.14, so the starting level explains a small part of the variation in how fast countries gained. Many countries with similar starting points moved at very different speeds, and some low-access countries gained little. Part of the pattern is arithmetical: countries near full access have little room to rise, which pulls the slope below zero without implying that any catch-up mechanism is at work. The coefficient of variation still shows a spread that is wide, since a value near 0.50 means that the typical gap between countries remains about half the world mean.

The data do not show what drove the breaks or the uneven gains. Fuel prices, public programmes, supply chains and household incomes are commonly cited influences on the choice of cooking fuel, but none is measured in these results, and none is asserted here as the cause. The findings describe when and where access changed, and they leave open why.

### Universal access by 2030 will be missed without acceleration, and proposals follow

The trend-to-target reading sets each series against universal access, 100.0 per cent by 2030, and projects the compound annual rate observed since 2015. On that basis the world reaches an expected 84.2 per cent in 2030, from 75.4 per cent in 2024. The ratio of distance covered to distance required is 0.56, which the tool classes as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. Universal access is therefore not on course at the global level.

Regions differ in how near they are. East Asia and Pacific is classed as on track or target met, with an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.99. South Asia is also on track, with a ratio of 1.06, having risen from 45.3 per cent in 2015 to 74.3 per cent in 2024. Its expected value above 100 shows that the extrapolation is mechanical and cannot exceed the ceiling. Europe and Central Asia is classed as needing acceleration, with a ratio of 0.82 and an expected 99.4 per cent, which is a small gap in absolute terms because the region started near the top. Latin America and the Caribbean has a ratio of 0.47 and an expected 93.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan has a ratio of 0.20 and an expected 79.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.19 and an expected 30.9 per cent in 2030. Both of the last two are classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

By income group, upper middle income countries are on track with a ratio of 1.01, and high income countries are on track at 99.5 per cent in 2024. Lower middle income countries need acceleration, with a ratio of 0.71 and an expected 83.4 per cent. Low income countries are classed as stagnant, with a ratio of 0.05: the share moved from 13.3 per cent in 2015 to 15.6 per cent in 2024, and the expected value for 2030 is 17.4 per cent. The ratio reflects the distance still to be covered, so regions starting from a low base are penalised heavily even when their annual rate is high. Sub-Saharan Africa's rate of 0.051 is close to South Asia's 0.057, yet its starting point leaves it far from the target.

Country classes show how widely the gap is spread. Of 190 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 61.5 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 46 countries, with 14.9 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 39 countries, with 13.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Twenty-nine countries, with 8.3 per cent, are stagnant, and 4 countries, with 1.4 per cent, have regressed. The classes are produced by a rule applied to each series, and they say nothing about what drives a country's change.

Two cautions apply to reading these results. Target 7.1 speaks of universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services, and the text does not fix a numerical threshold for cooking. Reading it as exactly 100 per cent is the strictest reading; a reading of near-universal access would count more countries as having met it. The indicator also measures only the primary fuel or technology a household uses. It does not measure whether the fuel is affordable or its supply reliable, and a household with access may still cook partly with solid fuels when prices rise or deliveries fail. The rural series shows the same pattern in sharper form: 8.6 per cent of rural people in Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, against 56.3 per cent of rural people worldwide.

For 2030, the implication is that global progress will be decided largely in the countries classed as stagnant or marginal. Those groups are not large in population in the aggregate, yet they are concentrated in the regions with the lowest levels, where rural households are the hardest to reach.

proposals: National governments and development banks in Sub-Saharan Africa and in the countries classed as stagnant should give priority to rural households in clean cooking programmes, since rural access remains far below the urban and world levels.

Donors and public finance institutions should fund clean-fuel supply chains and the purchase of stoves for stagnant countries, with subsidies designed to keep fuel affordable for low-income households.
National statistical offices and the World Bank should report the indicator every year from household surveys, so that countries off track are identified in time to act before 2030.

w-c08-3-2~dahlia/writer-1~85.text:
### The global share rose by 2.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2020

The world share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption stood at 17.4 per cent in 2015 and 19.7 per cent in 2020. The share therefore rose over the five years, and the direction is clear. Whether the magnitude meets the aim of the target is a separate question, and the data alone do not settle it. Over the period the share grew at a compound rate of 0.0255 a year, which the trend tool classes as on track or target met. That label rests on a trend tool that has no numerical target to measure against, so it should be read as a statement about the pace of change, not as a verdict on sufficiency.

Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix, and it names no threshold. Two readings are available. The first is a rise in the share: renewables supply a larger fraction of all final energy. The second is a rise in absolute use: more renewable energy is consumed, whatever the fraction. The two can diverge. Where total demand grows quickly, absolute renewable use can climb while the share stagnates or falls. The indicator reported here, renewable energy consumption as a percentage of total final energy consumption, measures only the first reading. A rise in the share is the stricter test, because it requires renewables to outpace the growth of demand as a whole.

The word 'substantial' compounds the ambiguity. No agreed numerical benchmark exists in the target text, so any judgement of sufficiency rests on a chosen standard: a doubling, a fixed number of points, or a path consistent with climate goals. Since no such standard is set in the target, this account treats the change from 17.4 to 19.7 per cent as an observed change and states plainly where a reader's own threshold would alter the verdict. By any reading, a gain of this size from a base of 17.4 per cent leaves the large majority of final energy supplied by other sources in 2020.

The composition of the indicator also matters for interpretation. Final energy consumption includes heat and transport as well as electricity, and the renewable share counts traditional biomass such as wood and charcoal burned for cooking and heating. A share can therefore be high in poor countries because of reliance on fuelwood, which is neither modern nor clean, and the aims of Goal 7 treat it differently from wind, solar or hydropower. The headline figure thus mixes two quite different kinds of renewable use, a point taken up in the regional comparisons that follow.

A limit on the evidence must be stated. The series is reported by 212 countries in every year from 2015 to 2021, but only 71 countries report a value for 2022. For most countries, therefore, the record ends in 2020 or 2021 for practical purposes, and the comparison of 2015 with 2020 is the last one that rests on near-complete coverage. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks that followed, cannot be read from this series with confidence. For the 2030 horizon, this means the trajectory is known only for the first five of fifteen years, and the later years remain to be measured.

### Regional levels differ by a factor of ten, and nearly all regions rose

Regional levels of the renewable share span a wide range. In 2020 Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 70.3 per cent of total final energy consumption, South Asia at 36.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 34.2 per cent. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 7.5 per cent. The highest regional value is therefore about nine times the lowest, and the gap is wide in both years.

The ranking does not measure the quality of the energy system. In poorer regions a high share may reflect the burning of wood, charcoal, crop residues and dung for cooking and heating, which counts as renewable in the indicator. These fuels are often gathered unsustainably, carry serious health costs through indoor air pollution, and supply energy of low efficiency. A low share in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan may follow from large oil and gas endowments that have long dominated power generation and final use; this is context from outside the data. The indicator cannot separate traditional biomass from modern capacity such as wind, solar, hydropower or modern bioenergy, so a region can score high with little modern renewable infrastructure and low with a fast-growing one. Other series on the shelf, such as electricity output and output excluding hydropower, give a partial view of modern capacity but cover electricity only.

All regions rose between 2015 and 2020. Latin America and the Caribbean gained from 28.2 to 34.2 per cent, the largest rise of any region. Europe and Central Asia moved from 12.9 to 15.1 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 13.0 to 14.8 per cent, and North America from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent. Possible explanations, which the results do not test, include falling costs of wind and solar and policy support in some of these regions. South Asia rose more slowly, from 34.9 to 36.9 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 68.0 to 70.3 per cent. In both, a rise in the share is ambiguous: it may reflect new modern capacity, or continued reliance on biomass. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 7.1 to 7.5 per cent.

The income groups show the same pattern and one reversal. The low-income group fell from 77.0 to 74.6 per cent between 2015 and 2020, the only group to decline. The fall does not necessarily signal a worsening of the energy system. As incomes rise and electricity and fossil fuels reach more households, the biomass share can fall before modern renewables replace it, so a lower share may accompany a real improvement in access. Equally, it may reflect growth in fossil-fuel use that outpaces renewables. The indicator alone cannot tell which. Lower middle income countries rose from 41.7 to 43.3 per cent, upper middle income countries from 14.9 to 16.8 per cent, and high income countries from 10.6 to 12.8 per cent.

The result for the target is that the rise was broad across regions but small in the regions with the highest shares and in the low-income group, where the share fell. Reading the target as a rise in the share, the world progressed; reading it as growth in modern, sustainable renewables, the aggregate hides much of what matters, because the indicator cannot show modern capacity. Coverage also limits comparison: 71 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot yet confirm whether the post-2015 gains held after the shock of 2020.

### Country trajectories diverge: 73 on track, 85 in regression

The classification of countries separates the world into groups whose experience since 2015 has been very different. Of 202 countries assessed, 73 are classed as on track or target met, and these hold 37.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 11 countries show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed (3.8 per cent of population), and 14 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration (22.2 per cent). Nineteen countries are stagnating (4.8 per cent of population). The largest group by count is the 85 countries in regression, which hold 31.8 per cent of the population.

The label 'on track' needs careful reading. Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the renewable share but gives no numeric value, so no threshold exists against which progress can be measured. The classification therefore rests on an extrapolated rate of change: the observed trend is projected forward to 2030, and a country is called on track when the direction is positive and the pace is adequate by the tool's own scale. 'On track' here means a positive trend only. It does not mean that a country will reach any particular share, and a country that starts from a very low share can be called on track while remaining far from a renewable-based energy system. The reading of 'substantially' is open: a rise of a few points could count under one interpretation and fall short under another.

Count and population tell different stories. The on-track group holds the largest population share of any class, 37.5 per cent, yet it has fewer countries (73) than the regression group (85), whose population share is 31.8 per cent. Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries, and the two classes hold 4.8 and 31.8 per cent of the population respectively. The data therefore show a split world: a large share of people live in countries with a positive trend, and a comparable share live in countries where the share has fallen. The world rate of 0.0255 is positive and classed as on track, but it is an aggregate and does not describe each country.

The regional rates help to explain the pattern. The rates for East Asia and Pacific (0.0267), Europe and Central Asia (0.0325), North America (0.0370) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0390) are all classed as on track, as are the high income (0.0381) and upper middle income (0.0240) groups. The groups under the greatest strain are the low income group, where the rate is negative at -0.0064 and classed as regression, and the lower middle income group, at 0.0079, classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) and South Asia (0.0112) are also marginal, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0129) show moderate progress.

The indicator does not reveal why the share falls in low income settings, and the following is context, not a finding. The renewable share of final consumption in such countries is widely understood to be dominated by traditional biomass used for cooking and heating. If total consumption grows with non-renewable supply, or households shift away from biomass, the share can fall even while other goals advance. A fall is therefore not necessarily a failure of renewable policy. The gains in richer regions are commonly linked to deliberate expansion of modern renewables, but the share alone cannot confirm what was added.

For 2030 the implication is that a positive global rate can coexist with 85 regressing countries. The target will be met in substance only if the lagging groups change course, and the data cannot say whether modern renewables are replacing traditional biomass or merely sitting beside it.

### Convergence is weak and coverage thins after 2020

The convergence test asks whether countries that began with a low renewable share have gained faster than those that began high. Across 71 countries with data for both 2015 and 2022, the estimated coefficient is -0.0101 (p 0.0006, R2 0.190). The negative sign indicates that countries starting higher changed by less each year, so low-share countries gained slightly faster, and the p-value of 0.0006 indicates that the relationship is unlikely to be chance. The magnitude is small, however, and an R2 of 0.190 means that initial level explains under one fifth of the variation in change. The remainder lies elsewhere. National policy, resource endowment, the pace of electrification and the use of traditional biomass are plausible influences, but they are context only, since the results do not measure them.

The coefficient of variation points the same way. It stood at 1.040 in 2015 and at 1.039 in 2022, a change in the third decimal place. Dispersion across these countries is therefore not narrowing. A coefficient near 1.0 means that the standard deviation of national shares is about equal to their mean, which describes a very unequal distribution. Weak catch-up in the slope, combined with unchanged dispersion, means that the spread of national shares in 2022 was about what it had been in 2015.

This result needs careful reading because the renewable share in final consumption mixes two quite different things. In many low-income countries a high share reflects reliance on firewood and charcoal, not modern renewable capacity, and a fall in that share can accompany progress in clean cooking and electrification. In high-income countries a rising share usually reflects wind, solar and hydropower in the electricity system. These are well-established patterns, but the indicator cannot separate them. A convergence test that treats both as one scale cannot distinguish a desirable fall in traditional biomass from a failure to expand modern renewables. The weak convergence found here should not be read as proof that poorer countries are being left behind in modern renewable deployment.

The sample is also a limit. Reporting for this series was broad in the early years: 207 countries in 2000, 210 in 2010 and 212 in every year from 2012 to 2021. In 2022 it fell to 71 countries. The 212 countries of 2021 and the 71 of 2022 are not comparable bases, and the data do not show that the 71 are a random draw from the 212. The convergence estimate describes only those that reported, and it cannot be extended to the world or to any region without that caveat.

The drop matters for 2030 because the years after 2020 are the ones in which the pandemic recovery, the energy price shock and new policies would show. Those years are visible for only a third of countries. The series is fully covered to 2021, so the record to that year is secure, while any statement about 2022 rests on a partial group. This is a reporting lag, not a finding of decline, and it should be read as a gap in evidence.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The share has risen, from 17.4 per cent in 2015 to 19.7 per cent in 2020, but whether that is substantial cannot be settled from the data, because target 7.2 sets no number. Read as any increase, the target is being met at world level. Read as a pace consistent with a transformed energy system, the gain is modest. The countries are also divided. The 85 countries in regression hold 31.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 19 more, with 4.8 per cent, show stagnation. A rising world average therefore conceals a large population living where the share has fallen.

The low-income group shows the problem most clearly. Its share fell from 77.0 per cent in 2015 to 74.6 per cent in 2020, yet the level remains very high. As context outside the data, such levels usually reflect reliance on firewood, charcoal and other traditional biomass, which counts as renewable in this series but is neither modern nor clean. A fall in the share can accompany welcome developments, such as grid expansion, and a high share can accompany poverty and indoor air pollution. The indicator alone cannot separate these cases, and conclusions for the poorest countries must be drawn with that caution.

For 2030, the evidence suggests that the world is unlikely to reach a decisive shift at the pace of 2015 to 2020. The 73 countries on track hold 37.5 per cent of the population, and the 14 countries with marginal progress hold a further 22.2 per cent; acceleration in these large populations would move the global figure most. Convergence is weak and the 2022 data cover only 71 countries, so the picture after 2020 cannot be confirmed for most of the world.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National statistical offices and the World Bank should complete the 2022 and later reporting of the renewable share, since only 71 countries reported for 2022, so that progress after 2020 can be judged.

series.why: Methane from waste (Mt CO2e) is the largest waste-sector greenhouse gas, a proxy for landfill and wastewater pressure under 12.5. It is not a measure of waste generated.

Carbon dioxide from waste (Mt CO2e) reflects incineration and open burning, a partial view of releases under 12.4. Coverage and methods vary by country.
Combustible renewables and waste (% of total energy) shows energy recovery from waste and biomass; it cannot separate waste from fuelwood, so it is a weak recycling proxy.
Safely managed sanitation (% of population) indicates treatment of human waste, a related release pathway for 12.4; it does not cover solid or hazardous waste.

w-c09-4-1~loom/writer-2~86.text:
### Carbon intensity of world output fell between 2015 and 2024

World carbon intensity of GDP, the carbon dioxide emitted per unit of output, stood at 0.3 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar in 2015 (0.2636 before rounding) and had fallen to 0.2 kg (0.2206) by 2024. Expressed to two decimals for comparison, the ratio moved from 0.26 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2024. The series covers 188 countries reporting in 2024, so the world figure rests on near-complete coverage, though the series reaches only to 2024 and later revisions of national inventories may shift it.

The decline did not begin with the Sustainable Development Goals. A break test on the annual change of the world series places a structural break in 2012. In the segment from 2001 to 2011 the mean annual change was -0.00217 kg per dollar, while from 2012 to 2024 it was -0.00531. The fall in intensity was therefore faster in the later period than in the earlier one, and the acceleration predates the adoption of the goals in 2015. The test does not identify what caused the shift. Context from well-established knowledge points to the spread of renewable power, the displacement of coal in several large economies, structural change towards services and efficiency standards, but the result itself shows only the timing and size of the change. It also does not isolate a separate effect of 2020, when output and emissions both fell sharply and then recovered; the annual series passes through that year within the second segment.

What a falling intensity means must be stated carefully. Carbon intensity is a ratio of emissions to output. When it falls, emissions grow more slowly than output, or fall while output rises. That is relative decoupling. It does not show that emissions have fallen in absolute terms: if output grows faster than intensity declines, total emissions still rise. The results held for this part contain no series of absolute emissions for the world, so they cannot settle that question.

Target 8.4 also speaks of resource efficiency in consumption and production, which concerns material use as well as emissions. No material footprint or domestic material consumption series appears among the results, and carbon intensity is only a partial proxy for the use of materials. The target can be read in two ways: as a call for relative decoupling, which the falling ratio would meet, or as a call for absolute decoupling of growth from environmental degradation, which it would not. The wording on developed countries taking the lead adds a further reading, since the pace expected of them differs from that expected elsewhere. The sections that follow treat regional differences and energy efficiency with these limits in mind.

### Regions and countries diverge in the pace of decline

Regional paths differ in both starting point and pace. North America recorded the steepest fall among the regions in the results, from 0.25 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar of GDP in 2015 to 0.19 kg in 2024. East Asia and Pacific began far higher, at 0.38 kg, and reached 0.31 kg in 2024, so it remains the most carbon-intensive of the regions shown despite a large decline. Europe and Central Asia moved from 0.19 kg to 0.15 kg. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 0.15 kg to 0.13 kg, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.16 kg to 0.14 kg. South Asia declined from 0.25 kg to 0.21 kg.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands apart. Its intensity moved only from 0.31 kg in 2015 to 0.28 kg in 2024, and its annual rate of change, a fall of 0.01 kg per year, is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The region's economies rely heavily on hydrocarbons for domestic energy and industry, which is context for a slow decline and not a finding of these results. By income group, upper middle income countries fell from 0.36 kg to 0.31 kg and high income countries from 0.22 kg to 0.17 kg, while low income countries moved from 0.10 kg to 0.08 kg. The low figure for the poorest group reflects small industrial and energy sectors, and a low intensity there is not evidence of efficient production.

The country classification shows a wider spread than any regional average. Of 189 countries assessed, 77 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 24 countries, with 32.7% of that population, show moderate progress, and 13 show marginal progress, with 3.0%. Another 13 are stagnant, with 3.7%. Regression, meaning intensity rose over the period, affects 62 countries and 21.5% of the population. Regional averages therefore conceal a large group of countries moving in the wrong direction, even where the region as a whole improved.

These classes carry a caveat. Target 8.4 sets no numeric value for carbon intensity or any other measure, so the trend tool has no threshold to reach by 2030. The labels rest on an assumed pace of decline, and a different assumption would move countries between classes. The results describe the direction and relative speed of change, and they do not show whether any country meets a legally or politically agreed standard. The target also speaks of decoupling growth from environmental degradation, which a fall in carbon intensity alone does not establish, since total emissions can still rise when output grows faster.

### Energy efficiency gains slowed after 2011 and links to growth are weak

Energy intensity, the primary energy supplied per unit of output, is the companion measure to carbon intensity, and its path for the world shows when efficiency gains were made and when they faded. Break detection on the annual change of the world series finds four breaks, in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.04984 MJ per 2021 PPP dollar. It deepened to -0.11539 in 2005-2008, then stalled at 0.00701 in 2009-2010, the years of the global financial crisis and its aftermath. From 2011 to 2017 the decline resumed at -0.10452 a year, close to the pre-crisis pace. After the break of 2018 the mean annual change shrank to -0.03247 in 2018-2021, less than a third of the preceding segment. The series used for the breaks ends in 2021, so the segment cannot show whether the slowdown continued, and the years after 2020 are only partly covered.

The slowdown matters because lower energy intensity is the most direct route to reducing the energy needed for each unit of growth, and the pace of 2011-2017 is the one that a 2030 trajectory would have to restore. Well-established context points to several possible reasons for the weaker pace: the pandemic shock of 2020, which distorted both energy use and output, a recovery weighted towards energy-heavy activity, and the exhaustion of easy gains from the earlier replacement of old industrial capacity. These are explanations from general knowledge; the break analysis dates the change but does not identify its cause.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the world line. Of 201 countries assessed on the trend to 2030 for energy intensity, 57 are on track or have met the target, holding 52.2% of the population of the countries assessed. Another 29 countries, with 9.9% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 32, with 15.1%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Stagnation applies to 15 countries with 2.1% of the population. Regression, meaning energy intensity is rising, affects 68 countries with 20.7% of the population. Regression is therefore the most common single class by number of countries, although the on-track group covers the larger share of people. No target value is set for this indicator, so the classes rest on a conventional reading of the direction and pace required, and another reading of the target could shift countries between classes.

Growth does not by itself explain these gains. Across 188 countries over 2015-2024, the Spearman correlation between changes in carbon intensity of GDP and GDP per capita growth is 0.151, and between their 2024 levels it is -0.059. Both are close to zero, so faster-growing economies were neither clearly cleaner nor clearly dirtier per unit of output. The result is an association between rankings only and gives no cause: it cannot show that growth did or did not drive the changes, and the link may differ within groups of countries. What it does suggest is that decoupling depends on the energy mix, technology and policy rather than on the rate of growth alone.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Relative decoupling is under way. The world trend for carbon intensity of GDP is classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed, at a rate of -0.0196 (2015 to 2024, kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar per year). Output is therefore being produced with less carbon per unit, and the pace is not yet enough to be read as on track for the world as a whole. High income countries, Europe and Central Asia, East Asia and Pacific, and North America are classed as on track or target met. The rest are not. Target 8.4 carries no numeric value, so the classification rests on the trend method alone, and a different reading of the target would give a different verdict.

The country count shows how uneven the progress is. Of 189 countries assessed on carbon intensity, 77 are on track or have met the target, covering 39.1% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 24 show moderate progress (32.7% of population), 13 marginal progress (3.0%) and 13 stagnation (3.7%). Regression affects 62 countries, home to 21.5% of the assessed population. A fall in the world ratio can coexist with rising intensity in a third of countries, which is why the aggregate cannot stand for the whole. Energy intensity gives a similar picture. Of 201 countries, 57 are on track or have met the target (52.2% of population), while 68 are regressing (20.7% of population).

The evidence supports relative decoupling only. Intensity measures emissions or energy per unit of output, so it can fall while total emissions or total material use rise, if output grows faster. The series examined here do not include material footprint, and they do not show absolute decoupling. Whether growth is separating from environmental degradation, as the target intends, cannot be confirmed from them.

The pace of energy efficiency gains is a further concern. The mean annual change in world energy intensity was -0.10452 MJ per 2021 PPP dollar in 2011-2017, but only -0.03247 in 2018-2021. Around 2018 the gains slowed to roughly a third of the earlier rate. Reaching 2030 on track would require the earlier pace to return. The broad causes are well known: stronger efficiency standards, fuel switching and structural change drove gains in earlier years, while slower policy effort and the disruption of 2020 are plausible contributors to the slowdown, stated here as context rather than as a finding.

Four proposals follow from these findings. Statistical offices and the United Nations bodies that compile the indicators should report material footprint alongside carbon and energy intensity, so that absolute decoupling can be tested. Development banks and bilateral donors should direct technical and financial support to the countries whose carbon or energy intensity is regressing, starting with the largest by population. National governments, especially in regions classed as marginal or moderate, should restore the efficiency policies behind the 2011-2017 gains, namely appliance and building standards, industrial energy audits and removal of fossil fuel subsidies. The parties responsible for the Goals framework should state target 8.4 in numeric form, for example a required annual rate of decline in intensity and a ceiling on footprint per person, so that on-track status can be read in one way only.

w-c06-4-2~tamarind/writer-2~86.text:
### The global picture: parliaments close to a quarter, management data thinner

Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in single or lower national parliamentary chambers worldwide in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015. The world share therefore rose by about 4.4 percentage points in a decade, and 184 countries reported a figure for 2025, so the world value rests on near-complete coverage. Set against a benchmark of 50 per cent, women still hold little more than a quarter of seats. The shortfall from that benchmark in 2025 is 50.0 less 27.2 per cent, a gap that should not be mistaken for the 2015 world share, which happens to be a similar number.

Target 5.5 does not name a number. Its wording, women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making, can be read as parity, with women and men holding equal shares, or as a threshold of participation sufficient for women to shape decisions, which is often placed lower. The indicator for seats cannot settle the question, because it counts occupants of seats and says nothing about their influence, the committees they chair or the offices they hold. This book uses 50 per cent as the benchmark, since a population that is about half women supplies the plainest reference for equal opportunity, and findings are stated against it while the figure itself is reported in full so that readers may apply a different reading.

The parliamentary measure covers one arena of public life. The economic arena is represented by the female share of employment in senior and middle management, a series built by the International Labour Organization from the occupational classification of managers. It excludes junior management, so it describes positions of real authority rather than all supervisory work. The series has two limits that bear on every statement made from it. First, the World Bank publishes no aggregates for it, so no world or regional share can be quoted, and any comparison must proceed country by country. Second, the number of reporting countries has changed sharply over time. It was 40 in 2000, 72 in 2010 and 77 in 2015, and reached 95 in both 2019 and 2022. It then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and stood at only 48 in 2025. A total of 154 countries have reported in at least one year.

These counts matter as much as the values. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years may reflect a change in who reports rather than a change in women's position, and the drop to 48 in 2025 is most likely a matter of surveys not yet processed, not of a real change in the world. The 2025 observations for management are therefore not a sound basis for a statement of trend, and the later parts of this section rely on the years of fuller coverage when discussing managerial positions. The parliamentary series, by contrast, is reported almost everywhere and is the firmer ground for conclusions about direction and pace.

### Regions and countries differ by more than twenty-five points

Regional averages for 2025 span a wide range. Latin America and the Caribbean leads at 36.6 per cent of parliamentary seats held by women, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 31.7 per cent and North America at 29.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 27.0 per cent, close to the world value of 27.2 per cent. East Asia and Pacific follows at 23.3 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands at 16.9 per cent, and South Asia is lowest at 11.2 per cent. A regional average can conceal wide differences between countries within a region, and the results give no country-level figures for this part.

The two lowest regions are also the ones that did not advance. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 17.5 per cent in 2015 to 16.9 per cent in 2025, and the trend tool classes it as regression. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the only large decline among the regions shown, and is also classed as regression. At the observed rate its share would reach 8.9 per cent in 2030. The data do not show why the share fell. Where a chamber is dissolved or not elected, the reported share can alter sharply, so a movement of this size may owe more to political events than to a gradual trend; that is context from general knowledge, not a finding of the results.

Income groups show a narrower spread than regions. High-income countries reached 31.2 per cent in 2025, upper middle income 27.0 per cent, low income 24.8 per cent and lower middle income 23.6 per cent. Low-income countries therefore hold a higher share than lower-middle-income ones, so income alone does not order the outcome. The results contain only group means and offer no explanation for the pattern.

The country distribution of progress towards a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 is more sobering than the regional averages. Of 187 countries assessed for parliaments, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold only 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest group is 69 countries with marginal progress that would need significant acceleration, covering 44.6 per cent of the population. Another 19 countries are stagnant, with 25.1 per cent of the population, and 39 countries are regressing, with 12.7 per cent. Stagnation and regression together hold 37.8 per cent of the assessed population, against 17.6 per cent where progress is on track or moderate. The population weights differ from the country counts: regression is the second most common outcome by number of countries, yet stagnation touches about twice as many people.

Management shows a similar pattern with a heavier weight on the negative end. Of 121 countries assessed for the female share of senior and middle management, 17 are on track or have met the target, with 8.1 per cent of the population. Moderate progress applies to 27 countries and 17.7 per cent of the population, and marginal progress to 34 countries and 31.3 per cent. Stagnation affects 6 countries with 2.7 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded in 37 countries, which hold 40.3 per cent of the population, against 12.7 per cent in parliaments. The assessment covers fewer countries than for parliaments, so these shares describe the countries with data rather than the world, and survey-based series can be revised from one round to the next, so the classification should be read with caution.

### What changed since 2015, and the limits of the evidence

Since 2015 the largest gain in women's share of parliamentary seats was in Latin America and the Caribbean, where the regional value rose from 27.9 per cent to 36.6 per cent. North America rose from 22.3 per cent to 29.5 per cent. Europe and Central Asia moved from 25.7 per cent to 31.7 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 19.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. These are regional averages and conceal wide differences between countries within each region.

Two regions moved the other way. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region slipped from 17.5 per cent to 16.9 per cent. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the lowest regional value in 2025 and the only large fall. The indicator does not separate the causes of these movements. In general, a lower share can arise from an election, from a change in the chamber counted, from a suspended or dissolved legislature or from the loss of a quota, but that is context drawn from general knowledge of how parliaments work, and nothing in these series measures it.

The country classification against a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 shows how uneven the movement has been. For parliaments, 24 countries are on track or have met the target, 36 show moderate progress needing acceleration, 69 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, 19 are stagnating and 39 are regressing, among 187 countries assessed. The 24 countries on track hold only 4.9 per cent of the population of those assessed. The 69 countries with marginal progress hold 44.6 per cent, the largest population share of any class, and the 19 stagnating countries hold a further 25.1 per cent. The 39 regressing countries hold 12.7 per cent. Because the largest population shares sit in the slow classes, the number of countries on track overstates how far most women live in places where parity is approaching.

For senior and middle management, the classification covers fewer countries, 121 in all. There, 17 countries are on track or have met the target, 27 show moderate progress, 34 show marginal progress, 6 stagnate and 37 regress. The population shares are starker: the 37 regressing countries hold 40.3 per cent of the population assessed, against 8.1 per cent for the 17 on track. Regression is thus more common in management than in parliaments, and it affects a larger share of the people covered. As general context, legislative seats can be shifted by quotas and electoral rules, whereas management positions depend on firms, labour markets and care responsibilities; the data do not test this.

The management evidence is weaker than the parliamentary evidence, and this limits every comparison. Across all years, 154 countries have reported at least one value, but the number reporting in a given year has varied widely: 40 in 2000, 77 in 2015, 90 in 2020 and 95 in 2022. The count then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and only 48 countries had reported for 2025. A fall of that size is probably a matter of reporting lags, yet it means that the latest values cover far fewer countries than the year before. Comparisons of 2025 with earlier years would rest on different sets of countries and cannot be trusted as a measure of change.

The regional trend summary for management returned no result, so no claim is made about how any region is moving on this indicator. Nor can these indicators say why countries advance or regress. They record outcomes, not the quotas, laws, party practices, employer conduct or social norms that produce them. Whether the period after 2020 slowed or accelerated progress cannot be established for management from this evidence, and for parliaments the series gives levels and class assignments but no separate account of the pandemic years.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the rates observed since 2015, no region reaches parity in parliaments by 2030. The world trend is classed as marginal progress, with an expected value of 29.8 per cent in 2030 against the 50.0 per cent benchmark, a ratio of 0.25. East Asia and Pacific is expected at 25.7 per cent in 2030 (ratio 0.21), and Europe and Central Asia at 35.2 per cent (ratio 0.39); both are classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. The high-income group is expected at 34.6 per cent, so wealth does not by itself close the gap. Latin America and the Caribbean comes closest, at 41.9 per cent, and is the only region classed as moderate progress. Even there, acceleration is needed.

The regions at the bottom of the range are moving in the wrong direction. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected value of 8.9 per cent in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also classed as regression, at 16.7 per cent. Low-income countries are expected at 26.5 per cent and lower-middle-income countries at 25.3 per cent, both marginal. Such projections extend a linear trend and are not forecasts; the data do not show what would move a national figure, and electoral reform or political disruption, as general context outside these results, can change a country's value within one election cycle.

The country classification shows where most people live. Of 187 countries assessed for parliamentary seats, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress. Marginal progress covers 69 countries and 44.6 per cent of the population, stagnation covers 19 countries and 25.1 per cent, and regression covers 39 countries and 12.7 per cent. Most of the population therefore lives in countries classed as marginal, stagnating or regressing.

Management is assessed for fewer countries, 121, and the picture is no better. Only 17 countries, with 8.1 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the target, while 37 countries, with 40.3 per cent of the population, are classed as regression. Reporting is also thin at the latest point: 48 countries reported in 2025, against 95 in 2022. The thinning of recent data weakens the case for judging progress in managerial posts, and it is itself a finding about the state of monitoring.

Several proposals follow from these findings, and the gaps are set out below.
