w-c06-1-3~cedar/writer-3~86.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on a scale from 0 to 100 on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Equal weighting is a choice of method, not a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. Because national law is read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf, so how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed since 2015 or since 2020 cannot be stated in magnitude here. The sections that follow set out what the instrument measures and what a measured record would need to show, and none of that should be read as a finding.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope is designed to lower the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Legislation against harassment in public spaces and online, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse, and legal provision for childcare services are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the revised scale. Third, the revised series is new, and whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline this book uses throughout, has not been verified. If it does not, a change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and statements about that period would need a different instrument.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. The only result computed so far is coverage: 189 economies report the legal index in 2025, and 189 report it in any year. No level, trend or gap between the indices has yet been computed, so this part makes no claim about how far laws have moved.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The record of 2025 covers 189 economies, and the same number report in at least one year. Coverage is therefore not the obstacle to an answer. What the bench has produced so far is the frame of the record and no values, so this part sets out what a measured account of change would have to contain and why each element bears on target 5.1.

Four elements would be needed. The first is the level of the Legal Framework Index for the world in 2025, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change since 2015, together with the number of economies whose scores rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because a mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and a few large reforms look the same in a mean as many small ones. The third is the distribution. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, so the gap between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed, matters more than the centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, because an average across domains hides the information a policymaker most needs.

Two background points are stated here as context and not as findings. Governments have generally found it easier to amend labour codes, treated as instruments of economic policy, than family and personal-status codes, which are often tied to religious authority and customary institutions. If the topic scores show that pattern, the remaining distance would lie in the rules governing a woman's capacity to act independently. Second, the closure of schools and nurseries in 2020 made childcare visible as an economic matter, and the inclusion of childcare in the revised framework can be read in that light. Whether reform accelerated or slowed after 2020 can be settled only by comparing average annual change before and after that year, which these results do not yet provide.

A measure built from statute has one merit for this purpose: an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores and not as a missing value. Until the level, the change since 2015 and the topic values are computed, the direction of legal change affecting women's economic opportunity remains unmeasured in this section.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates returned. A comparison across the other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change, whereas implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. A reasonable expectation, to be tested rather than asserted, is that income relates less strongly to the legal score than to the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is simple once the three indices are computed by income group: compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. That distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation. The record covers 189 economies in 2025, and the same number report in at least one year, so coverage does not prevent the comparison.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values that the bench has not yet computed. The only result in hand is coverage: 189 economies report the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and 189 report in at least one year.

Under the strict reading, the relevant measures are the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they are the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. A projection to 2030 at the observed pace would then show how long each group needs to reach full formal equality. None of these has been calculated, so no verdict is offered.

What can be said is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy. In federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions on support and enforcement, and with outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the index is well suited to a global account. Its census of 189 economies in 2025, and the same 189 reporting in at least one year, means that a measured answer will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. This section holds only that coverage. It reports no level, no change since 2015 and no change since 2020, so it does not yet say how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed. Those values are the next step: the level of the index, its movement over time, its distribution across income groups, and its topic scores, set beside the support and enforcement measures so that the distance between promise and practice becomes visible for each economy.

w-c02-2-2~juniper/writer-1~86.text:
### National poverty lines give the widest view, with uneven reporting

The national-line headcount ratio is the percentage of a population living below the poverty line or lines that a country sets for itself. It is the measure closest to the wording of target 1.2, which asks for a halving of poverty in all its dimensions according to national definitions. Because each country chooses its own line, and often revises it, the series records how each society judges deprivation rather than a single standard. Estimates come from household surveys. Alongside it, the World Bank publishes multidimensional, societal-line and $3.00-a-day series, which later parts of this section set against the national figures.

The series is wide in reach but irregular in time. Over the whole period 161 countries have reported at least one national-line observation, a broad base for a goal that applies everywhere. In any single year, however, only a fraction report. In 2000 the number of countries with a value was 16, and in 2001 it was 15. It rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, then stood between 40 and 50 from 2006 to 2014, with 40 in 2008 and 50 in 2012. Wider use of regular household surveys is the usual explanation for this expansion, offered here as context rather than as a result of the data.

After the adoption of the goals in 2015, reporting grew rather than shrank. In 2015, 55 countries had a value, and 57 in 2016, followed by 53 in 2017. Counts then reached 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. The year 2020, the first of the pandemic, shows 57 countries, a fall from 2019 that is consistent with disrupted fieldwork, although the data alone cannot show the cause. The peak is 72 countries in 2021.

The decline since then is steep. Reporting was 52 countries in 2022, 40 in 2023 and 31 in 2024, and in 2025 it is only 13. The fall does not mean that poverty has been abolished or that surveys have stopped. Household survey data take a year or more to be collected, harmonised and released, and national-line series are revised as new rounds arrive. The latest years are therefore incomplete, and the count for 2025 is best treated as a record of what has been published so far.

The consequence is practical. A comparison of 2025 with 2015 would rest on 13 countries against 55, which are not the same countries and may not be representative of any region. These results report coverage and not rate levels, so this part does not state how far any national rate has fallen; movement is read from the trend classes in a later part. Any statement about movement toward 2030 has to use the last years of reasonable coverage, up to about 2021 or 2022, and has to separate real change from changes in who reports. The figure on levels for 2025 rests on a thin base and calls for caution in every reading drawn from it.

### Dispersion among countries widened as coverage grew

The dispersion of national-line poverty rates among reporting countries rose after 2013. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.28 in 2013 and 0.34 in 2014, then reached 0.39 in 2015, the year the goals took effect. It was 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018 and 0.63 in 2019. The Theil index followed the same course, from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.26 in 2015 and 0.72 in 2019. Read at face value, the spread among countries in the share of people below their own lines widened markedly over these years. The results list no population weights for the dispersion statistics, so the reading is of the spread across reporting countries as the tool computes it.

This reading needs care, because the set of reporting countries changed at the same time. The number of countries with a national-line estimate was 45 in 2013, 55 in 2015, 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. A rise in the Gini or Theil can reflect poverty rates pulling apart, but it can equally reflect the arrival of countries with very high or very low rates, or the loss of countries in the middle. The series cannot separate these effects, so the figures are not a measured change in inequality between countries over a fixed group. For 2020 the Gini is 0.66 across 57 countries, but no Theil index or regional decomposition is available, so that year cannot be compared in full with its neighbours.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions is high throughout, which indicates that most of the measured dispersion lies between regional groups rather than within them. It was 75.8% in 2013, 88.4% in 2014 and 67.7% in 2015, then 80.7% in 2016, 65.1% in 2017, 86.3% in 2018 and 77.1% in 2019. The swings from year to year are consistent with a changing sample, since adding or dropping a few countries in one region can move the between-region share sharply. Differences in how countries draw their lines also bear on any comparison of levels, as the opening part of this section explains.

After 2020 the picture changes. The Gini fell to 0.35 in 2021, when 72 countries reported, the widest coverage of any year in the record. It then stood at 0.40 in 2022 with 52 countries, 0.35 in 2023 with 40 countries and 0.32 in 2024 with 31 countries. The Theil index moved from 0.20 in 2021 to 0.26 in 2022, 0.21 in 2023 and 0.17 in 2024. The between-region share was 82.6% in 2021, 88.5% in 2022, 76.0% in 2023 and 83.5% in 2024. The fall in dispersion between 2019 and 2021 coincides with a large change in the reporting set and cannot be taken as convergence. Counts fall after 2021, and only 13 countries report for 2025, so the latest years describe a thinner and different group; recent surveys are typically published with a lag.

For 2030 the implication is that national-line data can show whether a given country is reducing its own poverty rate, but cannot support a claim about convergence or divergence across the world. Assessment of target 1.2 should proceed country by country, over a fixed set of economies with repeated surveys, and the dispersion statistics should be read as a description of who reports in each year rather than of how poverty is distributed.

### Trend classes show most countries on track but a large regressing group

The classification covers 94 countries, those for which the national-line series holds enough observations to estimate a trend. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 3.8% of the population, and 7 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 4.4%. Five countries are stagnant, with 2.1% of the population. The largest adverse group is regression, with 34 countries and 26.0% of the population. Regression is therefore not a marginal finding.

The classes are the only evidence in this section on how national rates have moved. The tool reports a class and a share of population for each country group, not a rate level or a change in points, so no national rate is stated here. The classes say which direction and pace each national series has taken against the halving reading; they do not say how far any rate has fallen or risen. In this reading, regression means a series moving away from the target, which is not the same as a stated rise in a particular rate.

The weight of the favourable class comes from population rather than from numbers alone. On track countries are 41 of the 94 assessed, fewer than half by count, yet they hold 63.8% of the assessed population. A reader should not infer that two thirds of countries are succeeding; the count and the population share tell different stories, and both are given here. The tool does not show which countries drive the population share, so nothing is claimed about who holds most of it.

No numeric target exists for national lines. Target 1.2 asks for a halving of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions, but it names no common threshold, because each country sets its own line and method. The classes therefore rest on a reading of the target, not on a fixed value. Under the halving reading, a country is on track if its rate is falling fast enough to be halved by 2030 from its baseline, which is 2015 or the first year after. That is one reading among several. A target could instead be read as an absolute reduction in the number of people, as a reduction by a set number of points, or as a halving from the earliest available observation. Each reading would sort some countries differently, and the date and spacing of observations differ from country to country.

Several cautions follow. A country that revises its line can show a break in the series that looks like progress or regression though living standards did not move in that way. A country with a low rate can be classed as regressing after a small rise, while a country with a very high rate may be classed as on track after a modest fall. The classes do not rank the level of deprivation among countries.

The classification also leaves out countries without a usable trend. Where surveys are infrequent, the trend rests on few points, and the class can change with one new survey. The tool gives no breakdown of the classes by region or by income group, and none by the period before and after 2020, so the effect of the pandemic on the classes cannot be read here.

For 2030, the split carries a clear message. The on track group holds most of the assessed population, so the aggregate picture can look favourable, while 26.0% of the assessed population lives in countries where the national measure is classed as regressing. Meeting the halving reading across the whole group would require the regressing and slower groups to change course.

### National and international lines agree on direction but not fully on size, and the implication for 2030

National and international lines can be set side by side for 36 countries between 2015 and 2021. The comparison pairs the national-line headcount with the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Across these countries the rank correlation of 2021 levels is 0.72 (Spearman), and the Kendall measure of the same levels is 0.58. The rank correlation of changes between 2015 and 2021 is lower, at 0.53, with a Kendall value of 0.41.

The two results say different things. A country with a high national rate generally also has a high international rate, so the two lines rank societies in a broadly similar order. Agreement on direction of change is weaker. A country can see its national rate fall while the international rate barely moves, or the reverse, because the two lines sit at different points of the income distribution and are adjusted by different rules. A rise in living costs, a change in survey design or a revision of the basket can move one measure and leave the other untouched. The correlation of changes should therefore be read as a moderate link, not as proof that the two measures can be substituted for one another. Only 36 countries qualify, a small part of the 161 that report a national rate in at least one year, so the finding cannot be extended to all countries without caution. Both correlations are associations, not causes.

For the 2030 halving in target 1.2, the implications are mixed. The movement of national rates is shown here only through the trend classes, since the results hold no rate level or change for any country or group. Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, with 63.8% of the assessed population. Yet 34 countries are in the regression class, holding 26.0% of that population. The class describes the direction of the series against the target, not the size of any rate. The weaker agreement on change means that a country judged on track at its national line cannot be assumed to be gaining at the international line, and the reverse also holds. The target is also open to more than one reading. Halving may be measured against a country's own 2015 rate or against a baseline year that varies by country, and a revised national line breaks the series on which either reading depends. The aggregate verdict on 2030 is therefore less secure than the country counts suggest. A large regressing group and uneven reporting make it unlikely that the halving will be achieved across the whole population, even if many individual countries meet it.

The evidence has clear limits. Reporting is uneven: 72 countries reported a national rate for 2021, the peak, but 52 did so for 2022, 40 for 2023, 31 for 2024 and 13 for 2025. Recent years are thin, so the effects after 2020 are seen only in part. Country lines differ in definition and in the date of last revision, and the series does not record why a line was changed. The paired comparison rests on 36 countries. Poverty in all its dimensions is only partly captured by a headcount, and the poverty gap and multidimensional measures are not tested here against national lines.

t-ratio-of-two-series-by-country-and-yea.name: ratio-of-two-series-by-country-and-year
t-ratio-of-two-series-by-country-and-yea.code:
def tool(data, params):
    num_code = params['numerator']
    den_code = params['denominator']
    year = params['year']
    scale = params.get('scale', 1.0)
    num = data[num_code]
    den = data[den_code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    def pick(series, c, y):
        d = series.get(c)
        if d is None:
            return None
        v = d.get(y)
        if v is None:
            v = d.get(str(y))
        return v
    ratios = {}
    sums = {}
    missing = 0
    for c in regions:
        n = pick(num, c, year)
        d = pick(den, c, year)
        if n is None or d is None or d == 0:
            missing += 1
            continue
        ratios[c] = n * scale / d
        r = regions[c]
        s = sums.get(r, [0.0, 0.0])
        s[0] += n
        s[1] += d
        sums[r] = s
    facts = {}
    facts['year'] = year
    facts['countries_with_ratio'] = len(ratios)
    facts['countries_missing'] = missing
    if ratios:
        vals = list(ratios.values())
        facts['median_ratio'] = round(statistics.median(vals), 4)
        facts['min_ratio'] = round(min(vals), 4)
        facts['max_ratio'] = round(max(vals), 4)
        hi = max(ratios, key=lambda k: ratios[k])
        lo = min(ratios, key=lambda k: ratios[k])
        facts['highest_country'] = names.get(hi, hi)
        facts['lowest_country'] = names.get(lo, lo)
    for r in sorted(sums):
        s = sums[r]
        if s[1] != 0:
            facts['region_' + str(r)] = round(s[0] * scale / s[1], 4)
    summary = 'Ratio of ' + num_code + ' to ' + den_code + ' in ' + str(year) + ' (scale ' + str(scale) + '): ' + str(len(ratios)) + ' countries have both series; ' + str(missing) + ' lack one or both. Regional values are pooled sums of numerators over pooled denominators for countries with both values.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

w-c09-8-1~cedar/writer-2~87.text:
### Tourism receipts and arrivals as measures of Target 8.9

Target 8.9 commits governments to devise and implement policies for sustainable tourism that creates jobs and promotes local culture and products. The target names three outcomes: sustainability, employment and the promotion of local culture and products. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline, and it leaves open what counts as sustainable. It can be read as a call for policy, as a call for better outcomes, or as both, and the indicators do not settle which.

The World Development Indicators hold tourism series that measure something narrower. International tourism arrivals count overnight visitors who travel to a country other than the one in which they usually live. International tourism receipts record the expenditure of those inbound visitors, including payments to national carriers for international transport. A related series expresses receipts as a share of total exports, and another isolates receipts for passenger transport items. These describe the scale of the sector and its weight in an economy's external earnings.

None of them observes the content of Target 8.9. Arrivals say how many people came, not how long they stayed, what they damaged or what they preserved. Receipts record money entering a country, not how much of it remained with local workers, local producers or cultural institutions, since a large share of spending can leave through imports, foreign ownership and international transport. Neither series counts jobs in tourism, measures pay or conditions, or distinguishes cultural products from other purchases. Domestic tourism, which is large in many countries, falls outside both series.

The bench can therefore read how large and how widely reported international tourism is, and how that changed around 2015 and 2020. It cannot say whether tourism became more sustainable or more locally beneficial. The first result in this section, on the arrivals series, shows how many countries report in each year, which sets the limits of any comparison. In the figures from 2000 to 2020, reporting reached 202 countries in at least one year, and it is on that base that the later parts read the series. Findings on size and recovery are evidence about the economic scale of the sector. They are indirect evidence on the target, and the text says so wherever it matters.

### Coverage of the arrivals series, 2000 to 2020

The arrivals series, International tourism, number of arrivals (ST.INT.ARVL), is reported by 202 countries and territories in at least one year between 2000 and 2020. No single year reaches that figure. In 2000, 175 countries reported. The count then rose with some interruptions: 173 in 2002, 179 in 2005, 186 in 2007 and 190 in 2008. It dipped to 187 in 2009, the year after the global financial crisis, and returned to 190 in 2010. From 2010 to 2014 it stayed between 190 and 191.

The peak came after the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. In 2015 and 2016, 194 countries reported arrivals, the highest counts in the series. The count then eased to 190 in 2017, 186 in 2018 and 179 in 2019. By 2019 the number of reporting countries was back at the level of 2005, and 2020 had not yet begun. Part of this decline may reflect delays in compiling national statistics, as the latest years of many series are filled in later. The data do not show whether that explains it.

The figure for 2020 is the most striking: 132 countries reported, against 179 the year before. Tourism fell sharply in 2020 because of border closures and travel restrictions, and national statistical offices and tourism authorities faced disruption of their own. The data cannot separate the two effects. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded very few arrivals and not reported them, or may have been unable to compile the figure. Either way, the 2020 values come from a smaller and possibly different group of countries than the 2019 values.

This limits what can be said about the recovery. A world total or a regional total for 2020 compared with 2019 mixes a real fall in travel with a change in which countries are counted. Comparisons are sounder when restricted to countries reporting in both years, and even those say little about countries that did not report. The latest year of the series is 2020, so the data held here say nothing on the years after the collapse.

Aggregates are available for the arrivals series: East Asia and Pacific (EAS), Europe and Central Asia (ECS), North America (NAC), Latin America and the Caribbean (LCN), Middle East and North Africa (MEA), South Asia (SAS) and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF), together with the income groups high income (HIC), upper-middle income (UMC), lower-middle income (LMC) and low income (LIC), and the world (WLD). These allow comparison across regions and income groups, but they inherit the reporting gaps described above. How the aggregates treat non-reporting countries is not stated in the results, so aggregate values for 2020 should be read with caution.

### Regional and income-group comparison

The arrivals series is reported not only for individual countries but also for twelve aggregates: East Asia and Pacific (EAS), Europe and Central Asia (ECS), Latin America and the Caribbean (LCN), the Middle East and North Africa (MEA), North America (NAC), South Asia (SAS) and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF), together with the income groups high income (HIC), upper-middle income (UMC), lower-middle income (LMC) and low income (LIC), and the world total (WLD). Seven regions and four income groups therefore allow arrivals to be set side by side, and the world aggregate provides a common reference.

A comparison across these aggregates can show several things once values are in hand. Regional totals would show where visitors concentrate, and whether the concentration lies in the high-income economies or in the developing ones. Income-group totals would show whether tourism is a channel of growth open to low-income countries or one dominated by wealthier destinations. Set against receipts, arrivals would also indicate how much each visitor spends, which bears on Target 8.9 because jobs and local products depend on spending, not on headcounts alone. Differences in size matter as well: a large regional total can reflect many countries, a large population or a small number of heavily visited destinations, and a count of arrivals cannot separate these.

The comparison has limits that should be stated plainly. The coverage result lists which aggregates exist; it gives no arrivals values, no receipts values and no year-on-year changes. No regional ranking is therefore claimed here, and none should be inferred from the order of the codes. Nor can this result say which regions were hit hardest in 2020 or which have recovered. Aggregates also depend on how many member countries report, and reporting fell sharply in 2020, so regional totals for that year may rest on thinner evidence than earlier ones. A ranking will be offered only after the arrivals and receipts values for each aggregate are retrieved and read with their reporting counts.

### The 2020 collapse in reporting and the uncertain recovery

The count of reporting countries fell from 179 in 2019 to 132 in 2020. This is the sharpest single-year change in the whole series. Between 2015 and 2016 the count stood at 194, its highest level, and it then slipped to 190 in 2017 and 186 in 2018 before the fall of 2019 and 2020. The decline began before the pandemic, a pattern the coverage tool records but cannot explain.

The drop of 2020 is a statement about data, not about travel. A country absent from the count in 2020 did not necessarily record fewer visitors; it may have recorded none that were published, or published late, or been unable to collect the survey and border counts on which the series rests. National statistical offices were disrupted during the pandemic, and published figures were often revised afterwards. Reporting by 132 countries also says nothing on which of them reported, so the missing 47 relative to 2019 may be concentrated in some regions or income groups. The coverage result does not show this either way.

The recovery after 2020 cannot be judged from coverage. The arrivals series ends in 2020 on the shelf, and the other tourism series, receipts in current dollars, receipts as a share of exports and receipts for passenger transport, also end in 2020. No value for 2021 or later is available, so neither the depth of the fall nor the pace of any rebound can be measured here. The series for inflation, the GDP deflator, runs to 2025, but it describes economy-wide prices and cannot stand in for tourism volumes.

A reading of the recovery requires, at a minimum, arrivals and receipts for 2021 to 2024 for the same countries that reported in 2019, so that the comparison is made on a fixed group and is not distorted by changing coverage. Receipts would also have to be set against price changes, since a nominal figure in current dollars can rise while the volume of visitors stays below its earlier level. For Target 8.9, whose date is 2030, the consequence is plain: progress after 2020 is at present unmeasured by this shelf.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The coverage record shows that Target 8.9 can be monitored only partly, and that the monitoring has weakened at the point where it matters most. The arrivals series was reported by 194 countries in 2015 and 2016, and by 179 in 2019. By 2020 the count had fallen to 132. The latest year held for the receipts and arrivals series is 2020, so the shelf holds no observation of the recovery. Any statement about how far tourism has returned to its earlier level, or whether it has exceeded it, lies outside the data. Progress towards 2030 cannot be judged from a series that ends in the year of the collapse.

A second implication concerns what the series measure. Arrivals and receipts describe the volume and value of inbound visits. Neither shows whether tourism creates jobs or promotes local culture and products, which are the outcomes the target names. A rise in receipts could coincide with little local employment or with a large share of spending leaving the country. Receipts also include payments to national carriers for international transport, so they are not wholly spending inside the destination. Receipts are quoted in current dollars, and the shelf also holds the GDP deflator, which is a reminder that nominal values drift with prices and must be read with care.

Three proposals follow. National statistical offices, especially those that stopped reporting in 2020, should resume and sustain annual reporting of arrivals, and should publish the years missing from their record. The agencies that compile the indicators should present receipts always alongside arrivals, so that spending per visitor and the weight of transport payments can be read, and neither series should be quoted alone. The custodians of the Sustainable Development Goal indicator framework should add a measure of tourism employment and of local content in tourist spending, since Target 8.9 cannot otherwise be tested against its own wording.

w-c09-2-2~heath/writer-2~87.text:
### World output per worker has risen by a fifth since 2015

Output per worker is the measure the bench uses for target 8.2, which asks for higher levels of economic productivity. GDP per person employed, expressed in constant 2021 purchasing power parity dollars, stood at 42,386 in 2015 and reached 50,672 in 2025. The trend tool puts the compound rate at 1.8 per cent a year over the decade and reads this pace as moderate progress, but with acceleration needed. The world figure has therefore risen by roughly a fifth, a description drawn from the two cited levels rather than from a separate result.

The result matters because productivity is the main route by which employment translates into rising living standards. An economy can raise total output by adding workers, but only gains in output per worker allow wages and public revenue to grow without more labour being drawn in. A global rate of 1.8 per cent a year is positive and sustained, yet it is a pace that would double output per worker only over roughly four decades. The target's call for diversification, technological upgrading and innovation implies a faster and broader movement than this average suggests.

The indicator has no numeric target. Target 8.2 says only that productivity should be higher, so the reading rests on direction and pace rather than a threshold. Any classification of progress, including the one used here, depends on a rule applied by the tool to the observed rate of change, and a different rule would give a different label. The finding that the world has moved in the right direction is firm; the finding that the pace is moderate is a judgement about what pace would suffice.

The period contains breaks. The break tool dates shifts in the annual change of the world series to 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The mean annual change was 967.5 dollars a year across 2010 to 2019, fell to a loss of 369.1 dollars in 2020, rebounded to a gain of 1,566.8 dollars in 2021, and averaged 815.5 dollars a year across 2022 to 2025. Because output per worker is a ratio, a shock can move it in either direction: when low-productivity jobs are lost first, the ratio can rise even as total output falls. The ten-year change reported here therefore compresses a path that was neither smooth nor driven by a single cause, and the endpoints alone do not separate lasting gains from statistical effects of the shock. Weak investment and slow trade expansion in many economies after 2015 are well-known context, though not tested here.

The limits of the series should be stated plainly. Output per worker divides GDP by total employment, so it inherits the weaknesses of both. Employment estimates in many countries rest on modelled values rather than regular labour force surveys, and informal work is imperfectly captured. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, fewer than the 177 of earlier years, so the latest values rest on a smaller set of economies and the world aggregate for 2025 is partly an estimate. Comparisons across years should be read with that in mind.

For 2030, the recent post-2022 pace of change is below the 2010 to 2019 average, so a rate of about 1.8 per cent a year is not assured. Even if it holds, the global average would rest on very uneven foundations. The sections that follow show that the world figure conceals regions where output per worker has risen quickly and others where it has fallen.

### Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker

The regional spread in output per worker is wide. In 2025 a worker in North America produced 152,091 dollars of GDP (constant 2021 PPP), and one in Europe and Central Asia produced 103,033 dollars. South Asia stood at 24,604 dollars, Sub-Saharan Africa at 12,931 dollars and the low-income group at 6,041 dollars. The gap between North America and the low-income group is therefore roughly twenty-five-fold, and between North America and Sub-Saharan Africa roughly twelve-fold. Differences of this size are commonly attributed to capital per worker, the sectoral mix of employment, the quality of institutions and the technology in use. None of these is tested here, since the bench holds no series on them for this section.

Growth since 2015 has not been even. East Asia and Pacific rose from 33,564 dollars to 49,219 dollars, a rate of 3.9 per cent a year, and the trend tool classes it as on track. South Asia rose from 17,922 dollars to 24,604 dollars, at 3.2 per cent a year, also classed on track. Shifts of labour from farming to manufacturing and services, with sustained investment, are the usual route to such gains and match what target 8.2 describes through diversification and technological upgrading, although this section does not test that explanation. East Asia and Pacific now stands close to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, which reached 50,325 dollars in 2025, up from 46,188 dollars in 2015, a pace of 0.9 per cent a year that is classed as marginal progress.

The richer regions advanced at a moderate pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 88,803 dollars to 103,033 dollars, at 1.5 per cent a year. North America rose from 132,207 dollars to 152,091 dollars, at 1.4 per cent a year. Both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Because these gains start from very high levels, a modest rate adds a large absolute amount per worker. Comparing the levels given, North America and Europe and Central Asia each added more dollars per worker than South Asia did, even though South Asia grew faster in proportion. Growth rates may therefore favour poorer regions while absolute gaps persist or widen.

Two regions stand apart for lack of progress. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 42,759 dollars to 43,303 dollars, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 13,373 dollars to 12,931 dollars, a rate of minus 0.3 per cent a year, classed as regression, and the low-income group fell from 6,401 dollars to 6,041 dollars. Possible explanations, offered as context and not tested here, include weak investment, large informal sectors and commodity dependence in Latin America, and rapid growth of a young workforce entering low-productivity work in Sub-Saharan Africa. No employment or sector result in this section confirms them.

For 2030 the implication is that no common global pace can be assumed. Regions already growing at three per cent a year or more can keep climbing, while the two regions with stagnant or falling output per worker fall further behind the others. The target sets no numerical threshold, so classifications such as on track rest on the bench's reading of a rising trend, and a different reading would change them.

### Country outcomes split between rapid gains and decline

Beyond the world average, the bench classifies each of the 177 countries with data by the pace of its output per worker. Because target 8.2 carries no numeric threshold, the classes rest on a model-based reading of each country's trend towards 2030, and the labels should be taken as relative judgements rather than findings against a legal standard.

The result is a split. A total of 48 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 52.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. At the other end, 46 countries are in regression, meaning that output per worker has fallen over the period, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population. Between the two lie 30 countries with moderate progress that needs acceleration, 34 with marginal progress that needs significant acceleration, and 19 in stagnation. Their population shares are 17.0 per cent, 7.4 per cent and 8.1 per cent respectively.

The gap between the count of countries and the share of people is the main interpretive point. Counted by country, 48 of 177 are on track, a little over a quarter. Counted by population, the on-track group holds just over half. The tool does not say which countries drive that share, but it is consistent with populous economies, long associated with labour moving from farming into industry and services, sitting in the on-track class. A reader should therefore not conclude that most countries are advancing: by number, those regressing, 46, nearly match those on track, 48.

Regression is the most troubling class, since it means that workers in these 46 countries produce less than before. Conflict and state fragility, commodity price collapses, macroeconomic crises and, after 2020, lasting pandemic disruption are well-established causes of such declines in general. They are context only: no result here tests which applies to which country. Stagnation, in 19 countries, points to economies where output per worker has barely moved, a pattern often linked to stalled structural change, again untested here.

The classification also depends on choices that could be made differently. Without a numeric target, a different benchmark, such as a rate needed to halve a gap with richer economies, would move countries between classes. Employment estimates, which underlie the denominator, are modelled for many countries, so countries near class boundaries may be misplaced. For 2030, the implication is that the world average conceals a divergence: a group holding 52.9 per cent of the assessed population is advancing, while 46 countries are losing ground and will need a change of course, not just faster growth, to reach higher productivity by the end of the decade.

### Inequality between countries has narrowed, but convergence is weak

The spread of output per worker among countries has narrowed over the decade. Weighting each country by its population, the Gini coefficient of GDP per person employed fell from 0.449 in 2015 to 0.427 in 2020 and 0.412 in 2025. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the top and bottom of the distribution, fell from 0.347 to 0.308 and then to 0.286. Both measures point the same way. The fall was somewhat larger in the first five years than in the second, although the 2025 figures cover 168 countries against 177 earlier, so part of the comparison rests on a changed set of countries.

The narrowing is not matched by catch-up among countries as such. The convergence test regresses each country's annual change in output per worker over 2015 to 2025 on its starting level. If poorer countries were closing the gap, the coefficient would be clearly negative. It is -0.00249, with a p-value of 0.0541, so it falls just short of the conventional 5 per cent threshold, and the R2 is 0.013, meaning that the starting level explains about 1.3 per cent of the variation across the 168 countries. The unweighted coefficient of variation, which treats every country alike, moved only from 0.893 to 0.876 on this common set. The population-weighted measures fell by a larger proportion than the unweighted one. That pattern is consistent with the improvement coming mainly from where large economies stood, not from a general closing of the gap by small and poor ones, although the tools used here do not identify which countries drove it. Fast growth in a few populous economies lowers a population-weighted index even when most countries stay where they were relative to the rest.

The decomposition by region adds to this reading. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions rose from 68.3 per cent in 2015 to 71.9 per cent in 2020 and 75.2 per cent in 2025. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the remaining inequality, and the divide that persists is increasingly one between world regions. This fits the regional levels described earlier in the section, where the lowest-income groups remain a small fraction of the output per worker of the richest.

The period saw two shocks, and they affect how the figures should be read. The pandemic of 2020 cut output in many economies, including some of the richest, and a temporary fall at the top can lower measured inequality without any gain for poorer workers. The lower Gini and Theil values of 2025 show that the earlier narrowing has held rather than reversed. Even so, a weak and statistically marginal convergence coefficient gives little ground to expect that gaps between countries will close by 2030 on present trends. Target 8.2 sets no numeric threshold, and it can be read either as higher productivity everywhere or as faster productivity gains where levels are lowest. On the first reading, the world has made progress. On the second, the evidence is thin, and the narrowing seen in the weighted indices should not be mistaken for it.

### Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals

The pace of productivity growth follows the shocks that struck the world economy more than any steady trend. The break analysis for the world series finds change points in 2004, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. Between 2004 and 2008, output per worker rose by a mean of 1,001 dollars a year (constant 2021 PPP). The global financial crisis interrupted that run in 2009, when the mean annual change was -404.0 dollars. From 2010 to 2019 gains resumed at a mean of 967.5 dollars a year, close to the pre-crisis pace but not above it. The decade before the Goals were adopted therefore ended with no acceleration in the rate of gain.

The pandemic repeated the pattern on a similar scale. In 2020 output per worker fell by 369.1 dollars, and in 2021 it rebounded by 1,567 dollars. Part of the rebound may be a recovery of what was lost, and part may reflect the composition of employment: when low-productivity jobs disappear in a downturn, output per remaining worker can rise even where output is falling. This explanation is context and was not tested here. From 2022 to 2025 the mean annual gain was 815.5 dollars, below the 2010-2019 pace. The recovery has thus not restored the earlier rate of improvement. At the world rate of 1.8 per cent a year, the trend tool reads progress as moderate, with acceleration needed.

The link between productivity and headline growth is weaker than might be assumed. Across 168 countries for 2015-2025, the Spearman correlation between changes in output per worker and GDP growth is -0.048, which is effectively no relation. For 2025 levels the Spearman coefficient is -0.413, a moderate negative association: countries with lower output per worker tend to record higher growth rates. This is consistent with catch-up from a low base, but also with growth that comes from adding workers or hours rather than raising output per worker. Rank correlations say nothing of cause.

The country classification shows why the outlook for 2030 is uneven. Of 177 countries assessed, 46 are in regression, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population assessed, while 19 are stagnating. Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group both show falling output per worker, at annual rates of -0.3 and -0.6 per cent respectively, while South Asia, at 3.2 per cent, is on track. Why employment has outpaced output in the declining regions is not shown by these results and would need employment and sector series. Target 8.2 has no numeric threshold, so these classes are relative readings and not findings against a fixed standard.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. Each concerns the pace of gain, the countries left behind and the quality of the evidence.

w-c04-6-2~farah/writer-1~87.text:
### The global rate barely moved after 2015

The 2020 target to halve road deaths was not met on the evidence available. The World Bank's indicator of mortality caused by road traffic injury, expressed as estimated deaths per 100,000 population, stood at 17.0 for the world in 2015 and at 16.7 in 2019. That is a fall of about 1.5 per cent over four years. A halving would have required a rate near 8.5 by 2020, and the measured rate remained close to double that level.

Two limits on this reading need stating. The series ends in 2019, so the target year itself cannot be observed; the conclusion rests on the last four years before it, and a sudden fall in 2020 of the size required is not plausible given how slowly the rate moved beforehand. The path of 2020 is also disturbed by the pandemic, when restrictions on movement reduced traffic in many places, so any later figure would need careful interpretation before it was read as progress on safety.

The second limit concerns the wording of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of deaths and injuries, and of the number of them, whereas the indicator covers deaths only and is a rate per head of population. A rate can fall while the count of deaths rises if population grows faster, and it can stay flat while the count grows. The target can therefore be read in more than one way: as a halving of the count, or as a halving of the rate. On either reading the evidence points the same way, since the rate has barely changed and no series on non-fatal injuries is held on the shelf. The measure used here is the more lenient of the two, which makes the shortfall harder to dismiss.

Coverage supports the finding. Estimates are available for 183 countries in 2019 and for 190 countries in at least one year, with regional and income aggregates alongside. The series is modelled by the World Health Organization rather than counted directly, since many countries lack complete registration of deaths by cause. A flat global line therefore reflects estimates built from a mix of registered and modelled data, and small movements of the order seen here should not be over-read. What can be said with confidence is the scale of the gap between the target and the outcome, not the precise change of a few tenths of a point.

### Regions diverged, and only Europe and Central Asia moved fast

Regional rates for 2015 and 2019 show that the small global movement conceals very different trajectories. Europe and Central Asia was the only region to record a substantial decline, from 9.2 deaths per 100,000 population in 2015 to 7.4 in 2019. That is the lowest regional rate in the series and the only one that approaches the level a halving would have required. The decline is consistent with long-established road safety policy in much of that region: enforcement of speed limits and seat-belt use, safer vehicle standards, and investment in road design.

East Asia and Pacific moved only slightly, from 17.0 to 16.5. Latin America and Caribbean fell from 18.3 to 17.3, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 17.3 to 17.0. These are declines of a few per cent, far from the pace the 2020 target implied. South Asia was effectively flat, at 15.6 in 2015 and 15.6 in 2019, which means that its rate did not fall while motor vehicle use continued to expand in the region.

Two regions moved in the wrong direction. North America rose from 11.5 to 11.9, an increase from a rate that was already above that of Europe and Central Asia. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.8 to 27.4, and it carries the highest regional rate in either year. The pattern matters for 2030: the places with the most deaths per head are not the places that are improving, and rapid motorisation without matching investment in roads, vehicle standards and emergency care tends to raise road deaths before it lowers them.

These comparisons rest on regional means, and a mean can hide wide spread among the countries inside a region. A region's rate reflects both its safest and its most dangerous countries, and the ranking of regions says little about any single national road network. Coverage is broad but not complete: 183 countries report in 2019, and the indicator is built from modelled estimates, not only from counted deaths, so small year-to-year changes in a regional rate should be read with caution. The country-level spread is taken up in the next part.

### Dispersion widened while few places gained ground

The convergence test asks whether countries with higher road death rates in 2015 changed by less, or by more, than others up to 2019. Across 182 countries the estimated coefficient (beta) is 0.031, with a p-value of 0.0058. The sign is positive. Under the convention of the test, a negative coefficient would indicate that countries with higher starting rates rose less or fell more, so that levels drew together; a positive one indicates that they drew apart. The result is therefore the opposite of convergence, and the slope is distinguished from zero at the conventional 0.05 threshold.

The second measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation, the standard deviation of national rates divided by their mean, rose from 0.54 in 2015 to 0.63 in 2019. Rates across countries were more unequal in relation to their average at the end of the window than at the start. The world rate, 17.0 in 2015 and 16.7 in 2019, scarcely moved while the spread widened. The tests do not identify which countries account for this: no country-level result is reported here, so no count of improving or deteriorating countries can be given.

The limits of the test are considerable. The R-squared is 0.108, so initial rates account for only about one-tenth of the variation in subsequent change. Most of what separates one country's trajectory from another's lies outside this simple relationship. The window is also only four years, from 2015 to 2019, and short intervals magnify the effect of estimation noise. Country figures for road deaths are modelled estimates, since many countries lack complete death registration with cause information, and year-to-year movements in a modelled series may partly reflect revisions of method and inputs rather than real change. The test also stops at 2019 and says nothing of the period after 2020.

The tools measure outcomes, not causes, so any explanation must remain cautious. Well-established experience suggests that road deaths fall where speed management, helmet and seat-belt laws, vehicle safety standards and emergency care are enforced, and that they rise where motorisation grows faster than safe road design and enforcement. Such differences could produce widening dispersion, but this reading is context consistent with the pattern, not a result the data establish.

For 2030 the implication is limited to what the two measures show: a rising spread means that the global rate alone is a poor guide to national progress, and that national trajectories need to be examined individually.

### The 2030 target of 8.5 needs a different pace, and proposals follow

The 2030 horizon asks for a rate of 8.5 deaths per 100,000 population, which is the 2015 world rate of 17.0 halved. Set against that figure, the trend projections show how far the present pace falls short. Each projection extends the average annual movement between 2015 and 2019. The ratio reported with it compares that movement with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio of 1 means the pace is just sufficient and a ratio below 1 means it is too slow. The world rate is expected to reach 16.1 in 2030 if the 2015 to 2019 movement continues, a ratio of 0.11. The classification is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The remaining distance is large: 16.1 stands almost twice as high as 8.5.

Only two groups are on track. Europe and Central Asia is expected to reach 4.1 in 2030, with a ratio of 6.91, meaning its pace is nearly seven times that required for its own path to the target. High-income countries are expected to reach 7.3, a ratio of 2.48, which also lies below 8.5. Both results rest on four years of data. The high-income result is the less secure of the two, since its 2019 rate of 8.7 still stood above 8.5.

East Asia and Pacific shows marginal progress, with an expected rate of 15.2 in 2030 and a ratio of 0.22. Latin America and the Caribbean is similar, at 14.8 and 0.36. Upper middle income countries are expected to reach 15.2, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 16.2. None of these approaches 8.5 on present pace. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnating, at 17.3.

Four groups show regression. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 29.2 and low-income countries at 31.5, both rising. North America is projected at 13.3, and South Asia at 15.7. The groups with the highest rates are therefore moving away from the target on these projections. As context, not as a finding of these results, rapid motorisation combined with weak roads, vehicle standards and emergency care is a well-established source of high road death rates.

The figure of 8.5 is one reading of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of halving the number of deaths and injuries, not the rate. Population growth would make a halving of counts harder than a halving of the rate, and no count series is held here. The 2015 base year is also a convention, since the target text names no baseline. Injuries are not measured by the indicator used here. Readers should treat 8.5 as a benchmark and not as the single correct threshold.

Several proposals follow from these findings.

w-c09-3-2~loom/writer-1~88.text:
### Vulnerable employment is the measured proxy for informality

Informal employment, the condition target 8.3 has in view, is not measured directly by any series on the shelf. The nearest measured proxy is vulnerable employment: the sum of own-account workers and contributing family workers, expressed as a percentage of total employment. The series is a modeled estimate of the International Labour Organization, and it is available for 187 economies, with 182 countries reporting in 2025. The proxy is imperfect. Some own-account workers are registered, taxed and covered by social protection, while some wage jobs are informal, with no contract and no insurance. The share of vulnerable employment therefore indicates the extent of weak job security and thin social protection, and it cannot be read as a count of informal jobs.

A second caution concerns the target itself. Target 8.3 asks for policies that encourage the formalization and growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises, but it names no numeric threshold and no year-specific level. Any statement of progress is thus a reading of direction: whether the share falls, stays flat or rises. The trend tool applies a decreasing direction by 2030 with no fixed goal, and its verdicts should be understood in that light. A different reader might judge the same movement more or less favourably.

At world level, vulnerable employment stood at 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 and at 42.4 per cent in 2025. The fall is about 0.7 percentage points over a decade. Roughly two in five workers worldwide therefore remain in own-account or contributing family work, a share that has barely moved across a period that included the adoption of the goals and the shock of 2020. The trend tool classes the world movement as stagnation, with an annual rate of change of -0.0017 on its scale.

This matters because the world figure conceals very different realities, taken up in the parts that follow. It also matters because vulnerable work is the form of employment least likely to carry a stable wage, a contract or a pension. A global share that has hardly shifted suggests that the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not, on the whole, been converted into a move towards paid employment with protection. The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring in many low-income economies probably weighed on the decade, although the series, being modeled, cannot show the timing of such effects with precision.

### Regions differ by a factor of sixteen

In 2025 the regional range in vulnerable employment is wide. South Asia stands at 69.7 per cent of total employment and Sub-Saharan Africa at 71.0 per cent. North America stands at 4.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 12.9 per cent. The highest regional figure is therefore about sixteen times the lowest (71.0 against 4.5). Two regions, both in the developing world, have roughly seven in ten workers in own-account or contributing family work. In North America the figure is below one in twenty.

The middle group lies between these poles and is more tightly bunched. East Asia and Pacific stands at 35.3 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 36.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 31.5 per cent. In each of these regions roughly one worker in three is in vulnerable employment, although their economic structures, institutions and histories are quite unlike. A region-wide average also conceals differences among countries, and the regional figures are population-weighted aggregates of modeled estimates, not direct counts.

The pattern follows the structure of production, as context rather than a result of this analysis. Where agriculture and small household enterprise employ most people and large firms offering wage contracts are few, own-account work and unpaid family work are the usual forms of employment. Where manufacturing and services are organised in larger firms and wage employment is the norm, the share is small. The income groups show the same ordering: low-income economies stand at 76.1 per cent in 2025 and high-income economies at 8.0 per cent, so income level and the share of vulnerable work move together.

The spread across countries confirms that region is the main divide: 71.9 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2025 lies between regions, and the rest within them. This shows that most of the cross-country inequality in the indicator is a difference between regional means. It does not show how many countries or workers account for the vulnerable total, and it says nothing about variation within any one region.

### Women carry more vulnerability where it is highest

In 2025 the world figure for women stands at 43.1 per cent of female employment, against 41.9 per cent of male employment for men. The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point. It conceals a division by region. Where vulnerable employment is most widespread, women are more exposed than men. Where it is rare, the order reverses.

The gap is widest in South Asia, where 76.2 per cent of employed women are in vulnerable jobs against 67.1 per cent of employed men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the figures are 79.2 per cent for women and 63.9 per cent for men, a difference of more than fifteen points. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the shares are 41.6 per cent and 34.7 per cent. These are the regions in which a large part of women's work is unpaid help in a family farm or business, or own-account activity in small trade and agriculture, with little social protection. Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work, since it can be combined with household duties.

The pattern runs the other way in the richest regions. In Europe and Central Asia the female share is 11.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent for men, and in North America 3.3 per cent against 5.4 per cent. High income economies show 6.9 per cent for women and 9.0 per cent for men. Men are more often self-employed in these economies, in trades, construction and freelance work, while women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts in services, health and education. A lower share of vulnerable employment among women here is not by itself a sign of advantage, since the series does not capture pay, hours or the quality of wage jobs.

By income group the same crossing appears. In low income countries the female share is 82.9 per cent and the male share 70.9 per cent. In lower middle income countries the figures are 74.0 per cent and 61.2 per cent. In upper middle income countries the gap narrows to 35.6 per cent against 34.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is close to parity, at 31.3 per cent for women and 31.6 per cent for men. The gender gap in vulnerability is thus largest in the poorest settings and closes as incomes rise, which bears directly on the inclusive aim of target 8.3.

### Change has been slow, uneven and not convergent

Across the 187 countries assessed, the trend to 2030 is mostly one of slow or absent progress. Only 24 countries, holding 3.7 per cent of the population of the group, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 19 countries, with 6.1 per cent of the population, show moderate progress that would need acceleration. The largest population weight lies in the 48 countries with marginal progress, which hold 51.7 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. Another 59 countries stagnate, with 25.0 per cent of the population, and 37 regress, with 13.5 per cent. Target 8.3 sets no numerical threshold, so the classes measure movement in the desired direction (a decrease) and not distance from an agreed goal; the reading is one of direction only.

The weight of population in the slower classes matters more than the count of countries. Large economies with high shares of own-account and family work move slowly, so the world average is determined by them, while many small and wealthy economies that were already low account for most of the on-track count. Progress that does occur is therefore concentrated where the problem was already smaller.

Between-country inequality in the indicator did not narrow. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.317 in 2015 across 187 countries and 0.320 in 2025 across 182. The Theil index moved from 0.178 to 0.182. The share of that inequality lying between regions, and not within them, stayed near 71 per cent: 70.8 per cent in 2015 and 71.9 per cent in 2025. The geography of vulnerability is thus still mainly a matter of which region a worker lives in. The change in country coverage, from 187 to 182, is small and does not alter the reading.

The convergence test points the same way. The coefficient on initial levels is slightly negative (beta -0.00281, p-value 0.0001), so countries with higher initial shares fell marginally faster, but the fit is weak, with an R-squared of 0.066 across 182 countries. Meanwhile the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.717 to 0.735, meaning that dispersion between countries grew. A weak tendency towards catching up coexists with a widening spread, which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved. Neither the post-2015 nor the post-2020 period can be separated by these summary measures, and the shock of 2020 is not isolated here.

Wage and salaried employment is the mirror of vulnerable employment. The rank correlation of 2025 levels is -0.994, and that of changes since 2015 is -0.920, across 182 countries. Because the two shares are close to complements, with employers forming a small remainder, this is largely definitional and gives no independent evidence that wage growth causes lower vulnerability. It does show that a fall in vulnerable work has meant a rise in paid employment, and not a shift towards other forms of work.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace of 2015 to 2025 the world would not reach a markedly lower share by 2030. The trend tool classes the world as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0017 a year, from 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 to 42.4 per cent in 2025. The calculation extends the recent line and is not a forecast. Target 8.3 sets no number for vulnerable employment, so the reading of 'on track' is the tool's: any decrease counts as movement in the right direction. Measured against the wider aim of decent work, the pace is insufficient.

The populous group of 48 countries with marginal progress holds 51.7 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. South Asia, with a rate of -0.0074, and East Asia and Pacific, with -0.0074, are classed in the marginal group by the regional trend tool. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0007, is classed as stagnating. Low income countries have a rate of 0.0000 (+0.00003), effectively flat, and the tool labels them regression; the sign of the rate alone would not justify that label. Faster movement in the regions with the highest shares would count for more than gains in Europe and Central Asia (-0.0137) or among high income countries (-0.0127), where the share is already low.

The cross-country picture is not one of convergence. The convergence slope is negative (-0.0028), so countries that started higher changed slightly more, falling more or rising less each year. Yet the fit is weak (R-squared 0.07) and the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.73 in 2025, so dispersion in relative terms widened. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini was 0.32 in both 2015 and 2025, and 71.9 per cent of the Theil measure in 2025 lies between regions. Most of the inequality in vulnerable employment is therefore a difference between regions, not within them.

The link between vulnerable employment and wage employment is close: across 182 countries the Spearman correlation of 2025 levels is -0.99, and of changes since 2015 it is -0.92. This is an association, not a cause, but the two series largely mirror one another. It is consistent with a route to lower vulnerability that runs through paid jobs and firms able to employ.

Five proposals follow. The International Labour Organization and national statistical offices should monitor informal employment directly alongside the modeled proxy, using labour force surveys. Governments should set a quantified national reading of target 8.3, stating the share of vulnerable or informal work to be reached by 2030. Ministries of labour and of industry in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where shares stood at 69.7 and 71.0 per cent in 2025, should prioritise wage job creation and the formalisation of micro and small enterprises, with access to finance and simpler registration. National planners should give women's vulnerability its own targets, since women are more exposed where the share is highest. Statistical agencies and the ILO should report data gaps openly, including the modeled status of many national figures.
