w-c06-1-3~tamarind/writer-2~90.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, which gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are combined into one composite on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Giving each topic the same weight is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world. The coverage result also lists regional and income-group aggregates among the reporting entities, so comparisons by income group are possible in principle.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot be answered here in magnitude. This limit governs what follows: the remaining parts describe what the instrument measures and how its readings should be interpreted, and they do not present any measured finding about the direction or pace of reform.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts in each economy judge the law to operate in practice.

The legal index was reported by 189 economies in 2025, and 189 economies have reported in at least one year. Coverage is therefore effectively complete for the legal index. The companion series need not align with it exactly, since their coverage may differ, and no result on the shelf compares them.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope is designed to lower the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse, and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the revised scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether comparable values exist back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been verified. If they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and no finding on direction since 2015 or since 2020 can be stated here.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether the institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. It has not been computed for this section, and for 2030 it is the measure that would show whether formal legal progress is being turned into practice.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

A measured answer to how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed would consist of four elements, none of which the bench has yet produced. Only coverage has been computed: the Legal Framework Index reports for 189 economies in 2025, and the same 189 economies report in at least one year. Coverage of that breadth means the computation is feasible; it does not describe the change itself.

The first element is the world level of the index in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and because a few large reforms and a broad wave of small ones look alike in a mean. The third is the distribution, meaning the spread between the highest and lowest scores and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since an average across topics hides the information a policymaker most needs.

The period after 2020 requires a separate comparison of average annual change before and after that year, if the history of the series permits it. Without it, the record cannot show whether the pandemic prompted reform or diverted legislative attention. Because the index is built from statute rather than from reported statistics, an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data.

Until these computations are made, the section can state coverage and nothing more about direction. What the record implies for 2030 depends entirely on the level and pace still to be measured.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. Values for these aggregates have not been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. South Asia is the only geographic region among the aggregates listed. Comparing the other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison matters because formal law costs little to change, while implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, maternity and paternity benefit schemes, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. If the legal score tracks income less closely than the supportive and enforcement scores do, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. This is context, not a finding. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains this index scores. Without group-level values, the chapter cannot say whether the economies with the worst outcomes are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation. Coverage of 189 economies in 2025 makes the computation feasible.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values the bench has not yet computed. Only coverage has been established: the Legal Framework Index reports for 189 economies in 2025, and the same 189 report in at least one year.

Under the strict reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Both could be computed from the series if its history is long enough, and a projection to 2030 at the observed pace would show how long each income group would need to reach full formal equality.

What can be said now is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar and any economy's position should be judged against it. A perfect legal score is also necessary for equality of economic opportunity but not sufficient. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the legal index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companion series on support and enforcement, and with outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account. Its census of 189 economies in 2025, the same 189 that report in at least one year, means that a measured answer will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The measured record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores has not yet been produced, so this section does not state how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed. What it establishes is that the data to answer the question exist for almost every economy, and that the legal score should be set beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice becomes visible for each one.

w-c05-2-3~cedar/writer-3~90.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

Group values for children of primary school age who are out of school show little sign of a fall since 2015, and they need to be read as group values rather than as a global total. The four income groups held 26.0 million, 52.0 million, 8.1 million and 1.3 million such children in 2015, and 30.1 million, 46.4 million, 9.3 million and 2.1 million in 2025, in the order low, lower middle, upper middle and high income. No total is cited here: the results give no global figure, and a sum of the four would rest on the group values alone. Taken together, they point to a count that has not clearly fallen over a decade that began with the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals.

The composition beneath that picture has changed. Low-income countries counted 30.1 million out-of-school children in 2025, up from 26.0 million in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million over the same period. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. The fall in the lower middle income group offsets rises elsewhere, which suggests a movement of the burden toward the poorest countries. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest count, 46.4 million, because they contain very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate.

The figures must not be taken as a global estimate. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, as the results record, while the count series itself has a much wider coverage across its history, 198 countries. Group values built on so few reporters in the latest year depend on which countries happened to report, and the country sets may differ between 2015 and 2025. The comparison between the two years is therefore indicative of direction only, and no firm conclusion about the decade should be drawn from it. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, so those still in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count. Rises in some groups may partly reflect late entry or pre-primary enrolment rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. Group values that show no clear fall suggest that the first decade of the goals has not closed that gap. The years after 2020 sit in the same data window, and the interruption of schooling during the pandemic, together with conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries, are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up. The available results do not separate these effects, so they cannot be attributed with precision.

For 2030, the implication is that the arithmetic is unfavourable. With the group counts showing no clear decline over ten years, ending exclusion in the five years that remain would require a rate of decline that the period to 2025 has not shown. The rates in the following part show where that difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. A plausible explanation, not tested by these series, is that fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was outrun by the growth in the number of children.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest group value for out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. The group values suggest that this gain offsets increases elsewhere, though the series do not show how far.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion appears to deepen as children grow older. Likely reasons, which the data do not test, are that many enter school but few progress, and that costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push adolescents out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening, although it too rests on 12 reporting countries.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, each group's adolescent exclusion rate changed by less than one and a half percentage points. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which 41.7% of lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, but the direction of the small difference depends on national income. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys, so girls are the larger group there. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys. Both counts rose over the decade, and the girls' count rose slightly more than the boys', so the gap in low-income countries appears to have widened a little in absolute terms, to the girls' disadvantage. This reading rests on sex series from only 8 reporting countries in 2025 and should be treated as indicative.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' counts fell by more than boys' there. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in these three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

Girls are thus the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, barriers that plausibly fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, may remain active, though these results do not test such causes. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. The sex-disaggregated series draw on 8 countries reporting in 2025, whereas the totals by income group draw on 12, so the two sets should not be compared directly. Part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are plausible pressures after the pandemic, though these are explanations the data do not test and cannot separate.

The country classes show that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are the most numerous, and their 34.4% of the population is close to the 34.9% share that is on track or has met the target.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. The group levels rest on 12 reporting countries in 2025, a small base for four income groups. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents are the weakest point. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, while every other group changed by less than 1.5 percentage points over the decade, and upper middle income countries moved from 5.7% to 5.9%. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, and the sex-disaggregated counts rest on 8, so these pictures rest on thin and uneven coverage and should be read as indications. A pattern in which exclusion grows as children pass the end of primary school is consistent with fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and with too few secondary places, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.

w-c06-2-3~juniper/writer-1~90.text:
### Intimate partner violence is measured in few countries and few years

Target 5.2 calls for the elimination of all forms of violence against all women and girls, in public and private life, including trafficking and sexual and other types of exploitation. The indicator that the World Bank's catalogue holds for it is narrower: the proportion of ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49 who were subjected to physical violence, sexual violence or both in the previous 12 months. The series note describes it as drawn from United Nations and World Health Organization sources. It therefore speaks to one form of violence and one age band, and says nothing directly about violence by non-partners, harassment in public, trafficking or exploitation. Women who have never had a partner, girls under 15 and women over 49 fall outside it. A country with a low reading on this series cannot be taken to have met the wider target.

The coverage is thin even for this narrow measure. Across the whole period, 106 countries report in at least one year. Those reports are spread unevenly over time, and in most years very few countries contribute. One country reports for 2000 and 2 for 2005. The counts then run at 4 for 2006, 3 for 2007, 4 for 2008 and 4 for 2009, falling to 2 for 2010 and 3 for 2011. A year with one to four reporting countries cannot support a comparison of regions or a global reading; it records a handful of observations.

The pattern changes sharply in 2012, when 35 countries report. This single peak accounts for a large share of all the country entries on the shelf. The bench results do not say why the count rises in that year, and the reason is not asserted here; whether the values come from direct surveys or from estimation is likewise not recorded in the results. After the peak the counts fall back to 7 for 2013 and rise to 12 for 2014, 8 for 2015, 14 for 2016 and 7 for 2017, the latest year with data. No year after 2017 is held, so the series is silent on the period from 2020, when many observers warned that violence at home had risen. The shelf holds no regional or world aggregates for this indicator, so no summary can be drawn from published totals.

These features shape what the rest of the section can responsibly say. Differences between countries can be described where values exist, but the values rest on different years. A reader should treat the indicator as a partial snapshot of one form of violence, not as a tracked measure of progress towards the target.

### Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap

In 2012 the spread of intimate partner violence among reporting countries can be measured, and it is the only year in which that is possible with confidence. That year 35 countries report, the largest count in the series. The Gini coefficient is 0.29 and the Theil index is 0.17, which indicate a moderate gap between countries: prevalence is neither uniform nor extremely unequal. The coefficient of variation is 0.66. The results do not document the weighting basis, and the population-weighted label is taken from the tool's output.

The decomposition shows where the measured inequality lies. Of the Theil inequality in 2012, 66.2% is between regions rather than within them, and the remaining third lies within regions. This is a descriptive split of a single year among 35 reporting countries. It does not show why regions differ and supports no causal reading. Shared legal traditions, social norms about marriage and household authority, services for survivors and the history of conflict are well-established candidates for explaining regional patterns in violence, but the data hold no variable that could test any of them.

The limits of this result need to be stated plainly. The results do not record which countries are among the 35 or how they were chosen. Surveys on violence are costly and sensitive, and in general they are fielded where governments permit them and funders support them, so absent countries may differ systematically from those present. The between-region share is computed only among reporting countries, so a region represented by two or three countries adds little information on differences within it. The figures describe the spread of a particular sample in a particular year. They are not a global distribution and should not be read as one.

Other years are not compared with 2012 here. Only 7 countries report in 2013 and 8 in 2015, and 14 in 2016, the next largest count after 2012. The tool produced the spread calculation for 2012 alone, and the results state no minimum number of countries for it. Whether the 14 countries of 2016 would support a comparable calculation is therefore left open, as is whether they are the same countries as in 2012. For 2030 the consequence is that the regional pattern visible in 2012 is a snapshot of where evidence was gathered, not a baseline from which progress can be measured.

### Change over time cannot be established, while attitudes are better documented

The trend tool, which classifies each country against the 2030 target of zero, assesses no country for intimate partner violence. All five classes show zero: no country is on track or has met the target, none shows moderate progress, none shows marginal progress, none is stagnating and none is regressing. The count of countries assessed is also zero. This is not a finding of no change. It is a finding that change cannot be measured, because the tool needs repeated observations for the same country and the series does not supply them. Without them, the series cannot show whether prevalence has risen or fallen since 2015, or since 2020, when lockdowns and household stress were widely reported to have raised risks for women at home. That report comes from outside the bench data. Neither progress nor regression can be stated, and any claim about the direction of violence against women over the period rests on sources outside this series.

The attitude indicator, the share of women who believe a husband is justified in beating his wife for at least one of five reasons, is better documented. 72 countries report it in at least one year between 2000 and 2024. Annual coverage is modest and uneven, however. It was 6 countries in 2000 and 4 in 2002, rose to 10 in 2005 and 14 in 2012, and stood at 12 in both 2016 and 2018. After 2018 it fell sharply: 2 countries in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fell around 2019 and 2020. Interrupted fieldwork is a plausible hypothesis, but it needs a source outside these results, and the partial recovery since is likewise unexplained. Even in the best year, 14 countries report, so a global or regional average of attitudes for any single year would describe a shifting group of countries and not a stable panel.

The attitude series therefore offers more scope for comparison over time within countries that survey repeatedly, but it does not allow a global verdict. The results do not record which countries report, or their income level or survey programme, so the composition of the reporting group is not documented here and some groups may be under-represented.

Attitudes are a proxy and not a measure of violence. Acceptance of wife beating can indicate social norms that sustain abuse and discourage women from reporting or seeking help, and falling acceptance is often read as a sign of shifting norms. But a woman may reject violence and still experience it, and a society may hold permissive views with low recorded prevalence, or the reverse. Answers are also shaped by who is asking and who is present during the interview. The indicator should be read as context for the prevalence data, never as a substitute for them, and it cannot show whether target 5.2 is being met for 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals on measurement

A target of zero by 2030 cannot be assessed from these data. The trend tool classifies no country, and the count of countries assessed is 0. Any statement that the world, a region or a country is on track, or off track, for the elimination of intimate partner violence would therefore be unsupported. In all, 106 countries report in at least one year, but the reporting years cluster so tightly that a single survey wave stands in for a trend. The results give yearly counts only, not the number of years each country reports, so how many countries appear once is not established. Reporting peaks at 35 countries in 2012, falls to 7 in 2013 and stands at 7 again in 2017, the latest year. The counts for 2001 to 2004 are not given in the results, so those years are either empty or not held. Nothing is recorded after 2017, so neither the years after 2015 nor the pandemic years after 2020 can be read from the series. Lockdowns and strained services are widely reported to have raised the risk of violence at home, but the catalogue holds no figure that confirms or refutes this.

The measurement gap matters because the target is stated in absolute terms. Zero is reached only by sustained decline, and decline can be shown only by repeated measurement in the same country with the same definition. The attitude series is somewhat better placed, with 72 countries reporting in at least one year, yet it measures what women believe, not what they experience, and it thins sharply after 2018, with 2 countries in 2019 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fall, and the composition of the reporting countries is not recorded in the results, so some groups of countries may be under-represented. Attitudes may change before behaviour does, or behaviour may change without attitudes following, so neither series can stand in for the other. Underreporting is a further limit: women may not disclose violence in a survey, and a rise in measured prevalence can follow improved trust in interviewers as well as a real increase.

The one-year spread for 2012, with 35 countries, is descriptive only. It shows how prevalence was distributed among the countries that happened to report, and supports no causal reading of the regional split. Five proposals follow from these findings; they are set out in the list of proposals. They concern the frequency of surveys, the continued collection of the 12-month indicator with a lifetime series beside it, the range of women and forms of violence covered, the conditions for publishing regional aggregates, and the joint reporting of attitudes and prevalence. Until they are met, the record for Target 5.2 will describe a handful of survey years, not fifteen years of progress.

w-c06-7-3~juniper/writer-3~90.text:
### The global gap in internet use by sex

Target 5.b asks for greater use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The bench's results measure one aspect of that aim: the share of women and of men who have used the internet in the previous three months. They do not measure ownership of a mobile phone by sex. The series on mobile cellular subscriptions is counted per 100 people and is not divided by sex, and one person can hold several subscriptions, so it cannot show who owns a handset. The question of a gap in phone ownership therefore cannot be answered here, and the findings below concern internet use alone.

On that measure, the world's women moved a long way in a short time. Female internet use stood at 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and reached 68.2 per cent in 2024. The rise is 16.4 percentage points in five years, a period that includes the pandemic, when schooling, work, public services and social contact moved online and gave households a strong reason to connect.

Male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and reached 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two world figures do not share an end year: the female series is read at 2024 and the male series at 2025, because the latest world value in each result falls in a different year. Subtracting one from the other gives 8.4 percentage points, but that difference mixes a gap between the sexes with a year of growth in male use. It overstates the gap in any single year and should be read as an upper bound, not as a measurement. The world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. A clean comparison requires both series at the same date, and the regional results, where both are read at 2024, allow it in the parts that follow.

The 2019 figures are on a common footing. They show a gap of 4.2 percentage points, with women at 51.8 per cent and men at 56.0 per cent, so that women used the internet at about 0.93 of the male rate. This is a fact about 2019 only and says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed or widened since. Because use rose for both sexes, a gap in percentage points can grow while the ratio improves, so the two measures can point in different directions and each should be stated with its basis.

The figures also carry a caution about coverage. The results are aggregates over the economies that report, and the count of countries reporting in 2025 is only 7 in each result, against 92 in 2019 and 65 in 2024. The 2025 world and income-group values therefore rest on a thin base of direct observation and on estimates for the rest, and the 2024 regional values are better supported. Internet use as defined here also says nothing about the quality of access, the device used, the cost of data or what women do online, all of which bear on empowerment as much as the bare fact of use. The evidence supports rapid gains by women and a shortfall against men in 2019, while the size of the world gap in 2024 stays undetermined.

### Regional differences in the gap

Among the regions reported here, the point gap between women's and men's internet use in 2024 is largest in two regions at a middle level of use and smaller in the region with the lowest use. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women had used the internet in the previous three months, against 67.6 per cent of men. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 per cent for women and 69.1 per cent for men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the shares were 29.4 per cent and 37.9 per cent. The absolute gap there is smaller than in the two regions above, but the level of use is far lower. Measured by ratio of female to male use, the three regions are close together, with Sub-Saharan Africa only slightly lower than the other two, so a low point gap at a low level should not be read as near equality.

South Asia also shows how the gap can move. In 2019 women's use stood at 24.3 per cent and men's at 34.9 per cent. By 2024 the gap had widened, even though women's use more than doubled. Rapid growth in use among both sexes can thus coexist with a larger point difference.

The gap is small where use is nearly universal. In North America 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia the shares were 90.0 per cent and 91.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean lies between, at 81.3 per cent for women and 82.0 per cent for men. Saturation leaves little room for a difference to persist. Mobile networks, affordable devices and schooling may have contributed in these regions, but that is context from outside the bench's data, not a finding of it.

East Asia and Pacific shows a reversal. In 2019 women's use, at 67.4 per cent, was slightly above men's, at 66.7 per cent. By 2024 women stood at 85.5 per cent and men at 87.6 per cent, so men had moved ahead. The regional aggregate hides large differences among its economies, and the data given here do not show which of them drove the change. The result should be read as a shift in the regional average, not as evidence of decline in women's use, which rose over the period.

Income groups are reported for 2025, when only 7 countries reported these series, so the figures rest on very thin direct observation and probably include estimates; they are indicative only. In low-income countries 18.3 per cent of women used the internet, against 28.6 per cent of men. In lower middle income countries the shares were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent. In high-income countries they were 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The ordering matches the regional one, with the largest point gaps at middle levels, but the evidence is weaker than for the regional figures of 2024.

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, female and male use move closely together: the rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.948 and that of changes is 0.958. Where men gained, women generally gained too, so the gap is tied to a country's overall connectivity and does not behave as a separate trend. This is a statement about association; it does not show why any gap persists.

The regional pattern matters for target 5.b because the gaps that remain are largest in regions where women's use is far from universal. Plausible factors, which lie outside the data and which the bench cannot separate, include the cost of devices and data, differences in schooling and literacy, social norms on women's independent use of phones, and concerns over safety online. They probably operate with different force in each region, which is why a single global figure conceals as much as it reveals.

### What changed since 2019 and what the data can support

South Asia shows the largest change since 2019. Female internet use there rose from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, more than doubling, while male use rose from 34.9 per cent to 69.1 per cent. Women gained a great deal in absolute terms, but the distance to men did not close. Sub-Saharan Africa shows a similar pattern at a lower level: women moved from 20.2 per cent to 29.4 per cent, men from 28.6 per cent to 37.9 per cent.

The comparison across countries points the same way. For the 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male changes is 0.958, and that between 2024 levels is 0.948. Countries where men's use grew quickly are, almost without exception, those where women's use grew quickly. The finding indicates that expansion of access is largely shared, and no group of countries shows women advancing on a separate path. A correlation of this kind does not explain why gaps persist where they do. Differences in income, education, literacy, norms on women's use of devices and the cost of handsets and data are plausible factors, but they lie outside these results, and the series cannot separate them.

Income groups are indicative only, because the 2025 values rest on seven reporting countries. In low-income countries, female use reached 18.3 per cent in 2025 against 28.6 per cent for men. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, and in upper-middle-income countries 87.9 per cent and 89.7 per cent. In high-income countries the gap is small, at 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent. The world figures moved from 51.8 per cent for women and 56.0 per cent for men in 2019 to 68.2 per cent for women in 2024 and 76.6 per cent for men in 2025. Those two world values fall in different years, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be read from them and cannot be measured from these results.

The evidence has limits that bear on every figure above. In 2019, 92 countries reported female internet use; in 2024, 65 did; in 2025, only 7. The fall after 2019 coincides with the pandemic years and later reporting delays, and the reason is not stated in the data. The 2025 values for income groups are likely to be revised as more countries submit data. The 54-country comparison is a subset of the 137 countries that have ever reported, and it may differ from the countries that report least. Poorer countries with weaker statistical systems are the ones most likely to be missing, so measured progress may overstate the global picture. The series also defines use over the previous three months and from any device, so it says nothing about who owns a phone, who controls it, or how it is used.

### Implications for target 5.b by 2030 and proposals

Target 5.b carries no numerical threshold and no date-bound level, so it can be read in more than one way. The reading adopted here is a narrowing of the gap between women's and men's internet use, alongside rising levels for women. On that reading the evidence for 2030 is mixed. Levels have risen sharply, but the regional gaps in 2024 remain wide where female use is lowest or at a middle level, and these results cannot show whether the gaps are closing.

The world figures illustrate the limit of the data. Female use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, while male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The male figure refers to a later year than the female one, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. The regional figures for 2024 are on a common year and are the safer basis. In Sub-Saharan Africa female use was 29.4 per cent in 2024 against 37.9 per cent for men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the figures were 55.0 per cent and 67.6 per cent. In South Asia they were 56.3 per cent and 69.1 per cent. Where use is near universal, as in North America, with 94.1 per cent for women and 94.7 per cent for men, the gap is almost gone.

The income-group figures point the same way, but they should be read as indicative, because only 7 countries reported in 2025. Female use reached 18.3 per cent in low-income countries against 28.6 per cent for men, 56.9 per cent against 68.7 per cent in lower middle income countries, and 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent in high income countries. A gap of this kind closes mainly as a whole population connects, and only the nearly saturated groups have reached that point. The data support only the observed gaps; they contain no projection, so whether any region reaches parity by 2030 cannot be stated. The data do not test the causes of the gaps. Factors commonly proposed outside these results include the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, social norms on who may own a device, and concerns about safety online.

The country evidence suggests that the gap follows general connectivity rather than departing from it. Across 54 countries, changes in female use from 2019 to 2024 and changes in male use correlate at a Spearman coefficient of 0.958, and 2024 levels at 0.948. Women's use therefore rises where men's rises. Specific barriers to women are not isolated by this evidence, and the correlation is silent on whether gaps are closing within countries.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c02-4-4~tamarind/writer-1~91.text:
### Basic services and accounts have spread, but not to everyone

Three of the measures that bear on target 1.4 can be read from the shelf for the world as a whole: drinking water, electricity and account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults. All three rose, and none reached universality. The share of people using at least basic drinking water services went from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024. Access to electricity moved from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same nine years. Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults, measured from 2017, rose from 61.7% to 72.4% in 2024. In each case the direction is right and the pace is real, yet the remaining gap is concentrated in a smaller and harder-to-reach population. Sanitation, treated in the sections that follow, is the fourth measure on the shelf and is read through its trend classes, since the shelf gives no world level for it here.

The three indicators are not strictly comparable. Water and electricity are tracked from 2015, the year the goals took effect, while the account series begins in 2017, the first year with a Findex round in this series, so its change covers seven years and not nine. The water and electricity figures describe whole populations, whereas the account figure describes only the poorest 40% of people aged 15 and over. A rise in the first two therefore says nothing directly about whether the poor in particular were reached, since national averages can be lifted by households that were already better placed. The account series is the only one of the three that isolates the poor, and it has the thinnest country coverage: 138 countries reported in 2024, against 202 for water and 215 for electricity.

Target 1.4 does not fix a single measure of access, which affects how these numbers should be read. The water indicator counts an improved source with a round trip of no more than 30 minutes, so it captures basic service and not water that is safely managed or reliably available. The electricity indicator records whether a population has access, not the quality, affordability or reliability of supply. An account may be held at a bank or with a mobile-money provider, and the data record ownership and use, not whether the account serves a household's economic needs. Sanitation is defined by facilities not shared with other households, a threshold that different readers will treat as more or less demanding. Each figure here is therefore a floor of service and not a statement that the right has been secured.

The arithmetic of the remainder shows why the pace matters. Measured as the gap to 100%, the water shortfall fell by about 3.3 points between 2015 and 2024, the difference between the two published levels, and the electricity shortfall fell by about 5.0 points. People still without these services live mostly in low-income settings and in rural areas, where connection costs per household are highest and providers have the weakest incentive to extend networks. The remaining points are usually the costliest to close.

Accounts show the largest gain, 10.6 points among the poorest 40% in seven years, or about 1.5 points a year. Established explanations include mobile-money services, digital identity schemes and the payment of public transfers into accounts, though the series themselves do not test these causes. The disruption of 2020 did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series, but the data given do not allow its effect on the pace of change to be isolated.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region

Sub-Saharan Africa trails every other region on the measures held on the shelf. In 2024, 67.5% of its people used at least basic drinking water services, against 95.3% in East Asia and Pacific, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia and 99.8% in North America. Access to electricity shows a wider gap: 55.1% of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, while no other region fell below 96.7%. The region began from a low base, with 59.2% for basic water and 39.2% for electricity in 2015. The gains are real, but they were made from so far behind that the distance to the other regions has narrowed only slowly. Low-income countries, which are mostly in the region, show the same pattern: 60.3% for basic water and 48.8% for electricity in 2024.

Sanitation confirms the regional order. The trend assessment reads Sub-Saharan Africa as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.16 against the pace needed, and low-income countries as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.10. Their expected basic sanitation level for 2030 is 36.2% for low-income countries, so that roughly two in three people in those countries would still lack basic sanitation at the target date. A positive rate is classed as stagnation here because it is far too slow to approach the target by 2030.

South Asia presents the opposite experience. Its electricity access rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, so that a region once close to the global average is now near universal supply. Such a rise is consistent with sustained public programmes of grid extension and household connection, although the series do not isolate the cause. South Asia also moved from 90.5% to 95.9% on basic drinking water over the same years, and its trend toward the sanitation target is read as on track, with a ratio of 1.11.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are not a laggard on every measure. On water and electricity the region sits above the global figures of 91.5% and 91.9%, at 92.9% and 96.7% in 2024. Its weaknesses lie in accounts and sanitation. Among the poorest 40% of adults, account ownership stood at 46.1% in 2021, up from 39.5% in 2017, and of the regions with values for 2021 only Sub-Saharan Africa, at 43.6%, was lower. The region's sanitation trend is assessed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48, so significant acceleration is required. The grouping joins very different economies, from high-income oil exporters to countries in conflict, so the regional figure hides wide variation among its members.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest gain in account ownership among the poorest 40% of the regions with 2021 values. The share rose from 42.9% in 2017 to 67.9% in 2021. This interval includes the pandemic, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers into digital accounts. That may have contributed, but the data do not allow the cause to be isolated. Europe and Central Asia rose from 76.4% to 86.3%, and East Asia and Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, over the same four years.

A caution applies to every regional account figure. The regional series end in 2021, except South Asia and the income groups, which carry values for 2024. The regional comparison therefore refers to 2021 and cannot show the three years that followed. For the world, the poorest 40% reached 72.4% in 2024, up from 61.7% in 2017, but this rests on 138 reporting countries and cannot be broken down by region at the same date.

### Rural electricity advanced fastest while sanitation and water lag

Country classes set against the 100% target show how uneven the advance has been. For basic drinking water, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress but needed acceleration, so they are not yet on course for universal coverage. Another 55 countries, with 20.9% of the population, were making only marginal progress. Stagnation applied to 17 countries (1.5% of the population), and 37 countries (9.9%) were regressing. These are the places where service coverage was being lost rather than merely delayed.

Sanitation is the weakest of the physical services in the class results. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population. Moderate progress described 34 countries (17.7%), and marginal progress 54 countries (16.5%). Stagnation affected 37 countries (5.8%) and regression 39 countries (13.4%). The share of population living in regressing countries is larger for sanitation than for water. Difficulty in sustaining household facilities against population growth and urbanisation is a plausible context, though the indicators do not test it. The world as a whole was classed as making moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed and an expected coverage of 89.2% in 2030, short of universal use. The shelf gives sanitation levels only through these trend results, and none of the series separates the poor from the rest of the population except account ownership.

Electricity access for the whole population has the highest share of countries on track. Of 211 countries assessed on the rural electricity series, 161 were on track or had met the target, with 77.4% of the rural population concerned. This compares class shares across series that differ in coverage, so it is a reading rather than a measured ranking. Moderate progress applied to 23 countries (12.8%) and marginal progress to 10 (2.0%). Seven countries (2.3% of the population) were stagnating and 10 (5.4%) were regressing. Grid extension and off-grid solar are well-established routes to electrification and reach dispersed households more readily than sewers or piped networks. Conflict or weak utilities are common reasons why extension stalls, but this is context from outside the series, which do not identify the cause.

Regional trends on sanitation show where the divergence sits. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and upper middle income countries were on track, with ratios of 1.18, 1.11 and 1.08. Lower middle income countries reached a ratio of 0.75, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 0.48, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.16, with an expected 42.0% coverage in 2030, and low income countries at 0.10, with an expected 36.2%. Low income countries are classed as stagnating even though their rate is positive, because that rate is far too slow to close the gap. North America is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -1.03 and an expected 99.4% in 2030. This reflects a marginal fall from a level close to universal and should not be read as a crisis of access.

Convergence in basic drinking water coverage offers some reassurance. Across 167 countries, the 2015 to 2024 regression of annual change on initial level gave a beta of -0.0164, with a p-value close to zero and an R2 of 0.27. Countries starting with lower coverage gained faster, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Catching up is real but partial: initial level explains little more than a quarter of the variation, so many low-coverage countries did not catch up.

For 2030, only 33.9% of the population lives in countries on track for water, and the 33.8% in moderate-progress countries need acceleration. Sanitation will not reach universal use at the present pace. Electricity is closer to the target in most countries, but Sub-Saharan Africa, at 55.1% in 2024, and low income countries, at 48.8%, remain far from it. The world average conceals how far the target is missed where the poorest live. Changes after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be separated here, since the classes summarise the whole period from 2015 to 2024, and the effect of the pandemic years cannot be isolated from these results.

### Universal access by 2030 is out of reach without acceleration, and proposals follow

Universal access by 2030 is not within reach on present trends for basic drinking water, sanitation or accounts, and only rural electricity comes close. For basic drinking water services, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress, but they need acceleration and are not on course for universal coverage. The remaining countries are advancing too slowly, standing still or moving backwards, and 37 of them were in regression, holding 9.9% of the population.

Sanitation is further behind. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population covered. Another 37 countries were stagnating and 39 were in regression, and the regressing group held 13.4% of the population, against 9.9% for water. The regional trends show why. Low-income countries are classed as stagnating: the rate is positive, at 0.01 a year, but the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.10, and the trend carries them to only 36.2% in 2030. Lower middle income countries are projected to reach 88.9%, with a ratio of 0.75. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 42.0% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.16. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are classed as making marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48. East Asia and Pacific and South Asia are classed as on track. North America is classed as regressing, with a projection of 99.4% in 2030, a change too small to matter for people but one that shows how a trend class can mislead near the ceiling.

A trend to 100% is a demanding standard, because the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach: they lie among dispersed, displaced or marginalised households. Countries classed as on track may still leave a residual population without services.

Rural electricity is the exception among the classes. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, holding 77.4% of the population covered. Only 10 countries were in regression and 7 in stagnation, though these hold 5.4% and 2.3% of the population respectively. The class shares are not a ranking of services, since each series is assessed separately. As context not tested by these data, falling costs of off-grid solar and national connection programmes are commonly cited reasons why electricity has moved faster than water and sanitation, and conflict or economic collapse can damage networks where regression occurs.

For accounts held by the poorest 40% of adults, the world figure rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024. Universality by 2030 would not be reached at that pace. Low-income countries rose from 22.5% to 37.3%, so more than six in ten of the poorest adults there remained without an account. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021, so the 2030 outlook for accounts is an estimate with wide uncertainty rather than a measured trend.

The weight of the shortfall falls on a small number of places. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 55.1% electricity access in 2024, and low-income countries, with 48.8%, are far below other groups, while South Asia, at 99.8%, has almost closed its gap. Progress at scale within a decade is therefore possible, but global averages will soon be governed by a region where the pace has been slower than the need.

Target 1.4 speaks of the poor and the vulnerable specifically, yet the water, sanitation and electricity series describe whole populations. Only the account series is split to the poorest 40%. The first three could be rising for the average household while the poorest remain unserved, and the shelf cannot show this. The word access is also read in more than one way: basic water is not safely managed water, and an account that is held is not necessarily one that is used.

proposals: Ministries of water, health and finance in the 37 countries in regression on drinking water and the 39 in regression on sanitation, with development partners, should prioritise rebuilding and maintaining existing systems before extending them, since falling back cancels gains elsewhere.

Governments and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate new electrification and basic water finance there, because these are the groups furthest from universal access, while South Asia and most other regions need only maintenance of near-complete coverage.

National statistical offices and the agencies running household surveys should publish water, sanitation and electricity access by wealth quintile, so that target 1.4 can be judged for the poor and not only for whole populations.

Central banks, regulators and mobile-money providers in low-income countries should pair account opening with measures of use, such as low-cost transfers and wage or benefit payments, so that the poorest 40% hold accounts they actually use.
