w-c08-2-2~willow/writer-1~100.text:
### Three-quarters of the world now cooks with clean fuels

Roughly three people in four now cook mainly with clean fuels and technologies. The World Bank's World Development Indicators put the share of the world's population with access at 63.9 per cent in 2015 and at 75.4 per cent in 2024. The series covers 192 countries in 2024. The indicator measures the proportion of the total population primarily using clean cooking fuels and technologies, such as electricity, gas, biogas and the cleanest stoves, as against open fires and stoves burning wood, charcoal, dung, crop residues or kerosene. Primary use is the test: a household that owns a gas ring but cooks mostly on firewood is not counted as having access.

The gain between 2015 and 2024 is real and large, but the figure carries a caveat. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses, which are conducted at intervals of several years and are not available for every country in every year. Values for years between surveys, and the most recent years in particular, are estimates produced by statistical models rather than direct observations. The 2024 world value is therefore best read as a close approximation of the trend, and small year-to-year movements should not be treated as measured events. Nor does the indicator record how much of a household's cooking is done with clean fuels, how affordable the fuel is, or whether supply is reliable, all of which bear on the wording of target 7.1 on affordable and reliable modern energy services.

The remaining share matters because the other side of the figure is large. With 75.4 per cent having access in 2024, about one person in four still depends mainly on polluting fuels and technologies. As background outside the bench's data, smoke from such fuels is widely recognised as a cause of respiratory and cardiovascular illness, falling most heavily on women and young children, and the time spent gathering fuel and the burning of wood and charcoal are linked to schooling, paid work, forest loss and emissions. None of these links is measured in the results presented here.

The world's average conceals a wide spread between income groups, which later parts of the section take up. High-income countries stood at 98.8 per cent in 2015 and 99.5 per cent in 2024, so almost nothing remained to be gained there. Low-income countries rose only from 13.3 per cent to 15.6 per cent over the same years, while lower-middle-income countries rose from 42.7 per cent to 63.8 per cent and upper-middle-income countries from 76.9 per cent to 90.2 per cent. The global rise accompanies chiefly the middle-income groups, and the countries with the lowest access have moved the least.

For 2030, the reading is sobering. Target 7.1 calls for universal access to modern energy services, and the clean cooking series stands well short of that in 2024. The trend-to-target reading gives a world ratio of 0.56, with an expected value of 84.2 per cent in 2030, so the observed pace would not reach 100 per cent by then. The country classes show where the gap lies: 72 countries holding 61.5 per cent of the assessed population are on track or have met the target, while 46 countries with 14.9 per cent are making moderate progress, 39 with 13.8 per cent marginal progress, 29 with 8.3 per cent stagnation and 4 with 1.4 per cent regression. The point is examined further in the final part of the section.

### Regions diverge sharply, with Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Regional levels in 2024 span almost the whole range of the scale. North America stands at 100.0 per cent of the population with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking, and Europe and Central Asia at 98.3 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 22.9 per cent, up from 14.7 per cent in 2015. Fewer than one person in four in the region cooks mainly with clean fuels, while the world as a whole stands at 75.4 per cent. The income groups tell the same story: low-income economies stood at 15.6 per cent in 2024, against 99.5 per cent in high-income economies.

The regions between these poles moved at very different speeds after 2015. South Asia made the largest advance in the data, rising from 45.3 per cent to 74.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 70.7 per cent to 87.0 per cent. Both regions are now close to or above the world level. Large national programmes to distribute gas connections and to substitute for solid fuels are well-established contributors to progress of this kind, though the indicator does not show what drove the change in any country. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 86.8 per cent to 90.5 per cent, a smaller gain from a higher base. Europe and Central Asia moved from 96.6 per cent to 98.3 per cent, as the last households switched.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved slowly, from 74.7 per cent to 77.8 per cent. The region began 2015 at a level near that of East Asia and Pacific, which has since moved well ahead. The grouping also mixes economies at very different incomes, so the regional figure conceals wide national differences that this indicator, taken at regional level, cannot display. In Sub-Saharan Africa the gain of 14.7 to 22.9 per cent is real but small against the size of the shortfall, and the region's pace needs to be read against continuing population growth, which the share alone does not capture.

The gap between rural and urban households explains much of the regional picture. Worldwide, rural access rose from 38.2 per cent in 2015 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while urban access rose from 85.1 per cent to 89.4 per cent. Rural households therefore gained more in percentage points, yet remain far behind. Sub-Saharan Africa's rural level is the lowest in the data, at 8.6 per cent in 2024, up from 5.4 per cent in 2015. Urban Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.8 per cent, up from 29.5 per cent. Low-income economies show the same pattern, with rural access at 7.3 per cent and urban access at 31.5 per cent.

Elsewhere the contrast between rural and urban areas has narrowed. South Asia's rural level reached 61.7 per cent against an urban level of 92.0 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific's rural level reached 73.9 per cent against 94.6 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the rural level is 95.2 per cent, and in North America 99.9 per cent. These differences matter for 2030. Where the remaining shortfall is concentrated in dispersed rural households, supply networks for fuel, stoves and finance are costlier to extend, and a regional average rising slowly leaves the poorest households for last. The data show levels and change, not the affordability of fuels, which the target also names and which the indicator does not measure.

### Gains were broad but the pace has not been steady

The global series has not risen at a steady pace. A break analysis of the annual change in the world share with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking finds two breaks, in 2010 and in 2021. In the segment from 2001 to 2009 the mean annual change was 0.9 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2010 to 2020 it was 1.4 points a year. In the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 1.0 point a year. Progress therefore quickened at the start of the 2010s and slowed after 2021, to a pace close to that of the first decade of the century. The 2010 break falls before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, so the faster pace of the 2010s cannot be credited to the goals alone. The 2021 break coincides with the period after the pandemic shock of 2020, but the data show only when the pace changed, not why.

The slowdown matters for 2030. Universal access requires a pace above any of the three segments, and the latest segment is the slowest since the early 2000s. Four years is a short window, and the 2021 break rests on few annual observations, so the estimate of its mean change is less secure than those of the longer segments. The break dates are statistical estimates and could shift with further data.

The second analysis asks whether countries drew together. Across 192 countries from 2015 to 2024, the slope of each country's annual change on its starting level is negative, at -0.0079 (p below 0.001). Countries that began with lower access therefore gained faster on average than countries that began higher, and levels moved closer. The coefficient of variation, which measures spread relative to the mean, fell from 0.57 in 2015 to 0.50 in 2024, which agrees with this reading.

The convergence is real but weak. The R2 of the regression is 0.14, so the starting level explains a small part of the variation in how fast countries gained. Many countries with similar starting points moved at very different speeds, and some low-access countries gained little. Part of the pattern is arithmetical: countries near full access have little room to rise, which pulls the slope below zero without implying that any catch-up mechanism is at work. The coefficient of variation still shows a spread that is wide, since a value near 0.50 means that the typical gap between countries remains about half the world mean.

The data do not show what drove the breaks or the uneven gains. Fuel prices, public programmes, supply chains and household incomes are commonly cited influences on the choice of cooking fuel, but none is measured in these results, and none is asserted here as the cause. The findings describe when and where access changed, and they leave open why.

### Universal access by 2030 will be missed without acceleration, and proposals follow

The trend-to-target reading sets each series against universal access, 100.0 per cent by 2030, and projects the compound annual rate observed since 2015. On that basis the world reaches an expected 84.2 per cent in 2030, from 75.4 per cent in 2024. The ratio of distance covered to distance required is 0.56, which the tool classes as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. The observed pace would therefore not reach 100.0 per cent by 2030 at the global level.

Regions differ in how near they are. East Asia and Pacific is classed as on track or target met, with an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.99. South Asia is also on track, with a ratio of 1.06, having risen from 45.3 per cent in 2015 to 74.3 per cent in 2024. Its expected value above 100 shows that the extrapolation is mechanical and cannot exceed the ceiling. Europe and Central Asia is classed as needing acceleration, with a ratio of 0.82 and an expected 99.4 per cent, a small gap in absolute terms because the region started near the top. Latin America and the Caribbean has a ratio of 0.47 and an expected 93.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan has a ratio of 0.20 and an expected 79.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.19 and an expected 30.9 per cent in 2030. Both of the last two are classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

By income group, upper middle income countries are on track with a ratio of 1.01, and high income countries are on track at 99.5 per cent in 2024. Lower middle income countries need acceleration, with a ratio of 0.71 and an expected 83.4 per cent. Low income countries are classed as stagnant, with a ratio of 0.05: the share moved from 13.3 per cent in 2015 to 15.6 per cent in 2024, and the expected value for 2030 is 17.4 per cent. The ratio reflects the distance still to be covered, so regions starting from a low base are penalised heavily even when their annual rate is high. Sub-Saharan Africa's rate of 0.051 is close to South Asia's 0.057, yet its starting point leaves it far from the target.

Country classes show how widely the gap is spread. Of 190 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 61.5 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 46 countries, with 14.9 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 39 countries, with 13.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Twenty-nine countries, with 8.3 per cent, are stagnant, and 4 countries, with 1.4 per cent, have regressed. The classes are produced by a rule applied to each series, and they say nothing about what drives a country's change.

Two cautions apply. Target 7.1 speaks of universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services, and the text does not fix a numerical threshold for cooking. Reading it as exactly 100 per cent is the strictest reading; a reading of near-universal access would count more countries as having met it. The indicator also measures only the primary fuel or technology a household uses. It does not measure affordability or reliability of supply. The rural series shows the same pattern in sharper form: 8.6 per cent of rural people in Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, against 56.3 per cent of rural people worldwide.

For 2030, the country classes show where the shortfall lies by population. The countries classed as marginal, stagnant or regressing hold 13.8, 8.3 and 1.4 per cent of the assessed population, and the 46 moderate-progress countries hold 14.9 per cent, so the unmet gap is spread across several classes and not confined to the weakest. As context outside the bench's data, the lowest levels are usually found where rural households are hardest to reach.

w-c09-2-3~willow/writer-3~100.text:
### World output per worker has risen by a fifth since 2015

Output per worker is the measure the bench uses for target 8.2, which asks for higher levels of economic productivity. GDP per person employed, expressed in constant 2021 purchasing power parity dollars, stood at 42,386 in 2015 and reached 50,672 in 2025. The trend tool puts the compound rate at 1.8 per cent a year over the decade and reads this pace as moderate progress, but with acceleration needed. The world figure has therefore risen by roughly a fifth, a description drawn from the two cited levels rather than from a separate result.

The result matters because productivity is the main route by which employment translates into rising living standards. An economy can raise total output by adding workers, but only gains in output per worker allow wages and public revenue to grow without more labour being drawn in. A global rate of 1.8 per cent a year is positive and sustained, yet it is a pace that would double output per worker only over roughly four decades. The target's call for diversification, technological upgrading and innovation implies a faster and broader movement than this average suggests.

The indicator has no numeric target. Target 8.2 says only that productivity should be higher, so the reading rests on direction and pace rather than a threshold. Any classification of progress, including the one used here, depends on a rule applied by the tool to the observed rate of change, and a different rule would give a different label. The finding that the world has moved in the right direction is firm; the finding that the pace is moderate is a judgement about what pace would suffice.

The period contains breaks. The break tool dates shifts in the annual change of the world series to 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The mean annual change was 967.5 dollars a year across 2010 to 2019, fell to a loss of 369.1 dollars in 2020, rebounded to a gain of 1,566.8 dollars in 2021, and averaged 815.5 dollars a year across 2022 to 2025. Because output per worker is a ratio, a shock can move it in either direction: when low-productivity jobs are lost first, the ratio can rise even as total output falls. The ten-year change reported here therefore compresses a path that was neither smooth nor driven by a single cause, and the endpoints alone do not separate lasting gains from statistical effects of the shock. Weak investment and slow trade expansion in many economies after 2015 are well-known context, though not tested here.

The limits of the series should be stated plainly. Output per worker divides GDP by total employment, so it inherits the weaknesses of both. Employment estimates in many countries rest on modelled values rather than regular labour force surveys, and informal work is imperfectly captured. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, fewer than the 177 of earlier years, so the latest values rest on a smaller set of economies and the world aggregate for 2025 is partly an estimate. Comparisons across years should be read with that in mind.

For 2030, the recent post-2022 pace of change is below the 2010 to 2019 average, so a rate of about 1.8 per cent a year is not assured. Even if it holds, the global average would rest on very uneven foundations. The sections that follow show that the world figure conceals regions where output per worker has risen quickly and others where it has fallen.

### Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker

Regional output per worker in 2025 ranges from 6,041 to 152,091 dollars, and the spread is wide at every level of grouping. In 2025 a worker in North America produced 152,091 dollars of GDP (constant 2021 PPP), and one in Europe and Central Asia produced 103,033 dollars. South Asia stood at 24,604 dollars, Sub-Saharan Africa at 12,931 dollars and the low-income group at 6,041 dollars. Among the regions, North America's level is roughly twelve times that of Sub-Saharan Africa, and against the low-income group, which is an income grouping and not a region, the gap is roughly twenty-five-fold. Differences of this size are commonly attributed to capital per worker, the sectoral mix of employment, the quality of institutions and the technology in use. None of these is tested here, since the bench holds no series on them for this section.

Growth since 2015 has not been even. East Asia and Pacific rose from 33,564 dollars to 49,219 dollars, a rate of 3.9 per cent a year, and the trend tool classes it as on track. South Asia rose from 17,922 dollars to 24,604 dollars, at 3.2 per cent a year, also classed on track. Shifts of labour from farming to manufacturing and services, with sustained investment, are the usual route to such gains and match what target 8.2 describes through diversification and technological upgrading, although this section does not test that explanation. East Asia and Pacific now stands close to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, which reached 50,325 dollars in 2025, up from 46,188 dollars in 2015, a pace of 0.9 per cent a year that is classed as marginal progress.

The richer regions advanced at a moderate pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 88,803 dollars to 103,033 dollars, at 1.5 per cent a year. North America rose from 132,207 dollars to 152,091 dollars, at 1.4 per cent a year. Both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Because these gains start from very high levels, a modest rate adds a large absolute amount per worker. Comparing the levels given, North America and Europe and Central Asia each added more dollars per worker than South Asia did, even though South Asia grew faster in proportion. Growth rates may therefore favour poorer regions while absolute gaps persist or widen.

Two regions stand apart for lack of progress. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 42,759 dollars to 43,303 dollars, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 13,373 dollars to 12,931 dollars, a rate of minus 0.3 per cent a year, classed as regression, and the low-income group fell from 6,401 dollars to 6,041 dollars. Possible explanations, offered as context and not tested here, include weak investment, large informal sectors and commodity dependence in Latin America, and rapid growth of a young workforce entering low-productivity work in Sub-Saharan Africa. No employment or sector result in this section confirms them.

For 2030 the implication is that no common global pace can be assumed. Regions already growing at three per cent a year or more can keep climbing, while the two regions with stagnant or falling output per worker fall further behind the others. The target sets no numerical threshold, so classifications such as on track rest on the bench's reading of a rising trend, and a different reading would change them.

### Country outcomes split between rapid gains and decline

Beyond the world average, the bench classifies each of the 177 countries with data by the pace of its output per worker. Because target 8.2 carries no numeric threshold, the classes rest on a model-based reading of each country's trend towards 2030, and the labels should be taken as relative judgements rather than findings against a legal standard.

The result is a split. A total of 48 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 52.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. At the other end, 46 countries are in regression, meaning that output per worker has fallen over the period, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population. Between the two lie 30 countries with moderate progress that needs acceleration, 34 with marginal progress that needs significant acceleration, and 19 in stagnation. Their population shares are 17.0 per cent, 7.4 per cent and 8.1 per cent respectively.

The gap between the count of countries and the share of people is the main interpretive point. Counted by country, 48 of 177 are on track, a little over a quarter. Counted by population, the on-track group holds just over half. The tool does not say which countries drive that share, but it is consistent with populous economies, long associated with labour moving from farming into industry and services, sitting in the on-track class. A reader should therefore not conclude that most countries are advancing: by number, those regressing, 46, nearly match those on track, 48.

Regression is the most troubling class, since it means that workers in these 46 countries produce less than before. Conflict and state fragility, commodity price collapses, macroeconomic crises and, after 2020, lasting pandemic disruption are well-established causes of such declines in general. They are context only: no result here tests which applies to which country. Stagnation, in 19 countries, points to economies where output per worker has barely moved, a pattern often linked to stalled structural change, again untested here.

The classification also depends on choices that could be made differently. Without a numeric target, a different benchmark, such as a rate needed to halve a gap with richer economies, would move countries between classes. Employment estimates, which underlie the denominator, are modelled for many countries, so countries near class boundaries may be misplaced. For 2030, the implication is that the world average conceals a divergence: a group holding 52.9 per cent of the assessed population is advancing, while 46 countries are losing ground and will need a change of course, not just faster growth, to reach higher productivity by the end of the decade.

### Inequality between countries has narrowed, but convergence is weak

The spread of output per worker among countries has narrowed over the decade. Weighting each country by its population, the Gini coefficient of GDP per person employed fell from 0.449 in 2015 to 0.427 in 2020 and 0.412 in 2025. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the top and bottom of the distribution, fell from 0.347 to 0.308 and then to 0.286. Both measures point the same way. The fall was somewhat larger in the first five years than in the second, although the 2025 figures cover 168 countries against 177 earlier, so part of the comparison rests on a changed set of countries.

The narrowing is not matched by catch-up among countries as such. The convergence test regresses each country's annual change in output per worker over 2015 to 2025 on its starting level. If poorer countries were closing the gap, the coefficient would be clearly negative. It is -0.00249, with a p-value of 0.0541, so it falls just short of the conventional 5 per cent threshold, and the R2 is 0.013, meaning that the starting level explains about 1.3 per cent of the variation across the 168 countries. The unweighted coefficient of variation, which treats every country alike, moved only from 0.893 to 0.876 on this common set. The population-weighted measures fell by a larger proportion than the unweighted one. That pattern is consistent with the improvement coming mainly from where large economies stood, not from a general closing of the gap by small and poor ones, although the tools used here do not identify which countries drove it. Fast growth in a few populous economies lowers a population-weighted index even when most countries stay where they were relative to the rest.

The decomposition by region adds to this reading. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions rose from 68.3 per cent in 2015 to 71.9 per cent in 2020 and 75.2 per cent in 2025. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the remaining inequality, and the divide that persists is increasingly one between world regions. This fits the regional levels described earlier in the section, where the lowest-income groups remain a small fraction of the output per worker of the richest.

The period saw two shocks, and they affect how the figures should be read. The pandemic of 2020 cut output in many economies, including some of the richest, and a temporary fall at the top can lower measured inequality without any gain for poorer workers. The lower Gini and Theil values of 2025 show that the earlier narrowing has held rather than reversed. Even so, a weak and statistically marginal convergence coefficient gives little ground to expect that gaps between countries will close by 2030 on present trends. Target 8.2 sets no numeric threshold, and it can be read either as higher productivity everywhere or as faster productivity gains where levels are lowest. On the first reading, the world has made progress. On the second, the evidence is thin, and the narrowing seen in the weighted indices should not be mistaken for it.

### Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals

The pace of change in output per worker shows breaks around 2009 and 2020. The break analysis of the world series alone, with no regional breaks tested, finds change points in 2004, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The earliest segment shown begins in 2001. Between 2004 and 2008, output per worker rose by a mean of 1,001 dollars a year (constant 2021 PPP). In 2009 the mean annual change was -404.0 dollars, a year that coincides with the global financial crisis. From 2010 to 2019 gains resumed at a mean of 967.5 dollars a year, close to the pre-crisis pace but not above it. The decade before the Goals were adopted therefore ended with no acceleration in the dollar gain per year.

The pandemic year shows a similar pattern on a comparable scale. In 2020 output per worker fell by 369.1 dollars, and in 2021 it rose by 1,567 dollars. Part of the rebound may be a recovery of what was lost, and part may reflect the composition of employment: when low-productivity jobs disappear in a downturn, output per remaining worker can rise even where output is falling. This explanation is context and was not tested here, and the link of the breaks to the crisis and the pandemic is likewise context, since the tool dates changes without attributing them. From 2022 to 2025 the mean annual gain was 815.5 dollars, below the 2010-2019 mean of 967.5 dollars. The recovery has thus not restored the earlier dollar gain. At the world rate of 1.8 per cent a year, the trend tool reads progress as moderate, with acceleration needed.

The link between productivity and headline growth is weak. Across 168 countries for 2015-2025, the Spearman correlation between changes in output per worker and GDP growth is -0.048, effectively no relation. For 2025 levels the coefficient is -0.413, a moderate negative association: countries with lower output per worker tend to record higher growth rates. This is consistent with catch-up from a low base, but also with growth that comes from adding workers or hours rather than raising output per worker. Rank correlations say nothing of cause.

The country classification shows why the outlook for 2030 is uneven. Of 177 countries assessed, 46 are in regression, holding 14.6 per cent of the population assessed, while 19 are stagnating. Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group both show falling output per worker, at annual rates of -0.3 and -0.6 per cent, while South Asia, at 3.2 per cent, is on track. The cause of the decline in these regions is not shown by these results and would need employment and sector series. Target 8.2 has no numeric threshold, so these classes are relative readings and not findings against a fixed standard. The 2025 figures also cover 168 countries, against 177 earlier.

Three proposals follow. Finance ministries and development banks in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries, with their partners, should direct investment towards raising output per worker, since both groups show falling levels while the world average rises. National statistical offices and the World Bank should publish employment by sector and close the reporting gap between 168 and 177 countries, so that the causes of decline can be tested. The United Nations statistical commission should agree a numeric threshold for target 8.2, so that progress can be judged against a fixed standard.

w-c02-1-3~juniper/writer-4~101.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 asks that extreme poverty be eradicated for all people everywhere by 2030, and its wording quotes a line of $1.25 a day. That line belongs to an earlier price base and has been superseded several times as purchasing power parity exchange rates were revised. The measure used here is the current international line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, published by the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform. Poverty rates under this line cannot be compared with those printed in earlier editions of the series, and the figures in this book should not be set beside older statements of the target without that caution.

On this measure, 13.4% of the world's population lived below $3.00 a day in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 the share was 10.1%. The fall is real and of consequence, in a period that included a pandemic and a sharp rise in food and energy prices (context from outside the results, which show the change but not its cause). It also shows how far the world remains from the target. At the 2024 level, roughly one person in ten still lives below the line, and the target date is six years off. Continuing at the compound rate of change observed since 2015, the series would reach 8.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The word eradicate admits more than one reading, and the choice changes the verdict. The strict reading is a headcount of 0%, which no measured aggregate has approached and which survey-based estimation could not confirm even if it were reached, since sampling error and gaps in coverage make an exact zero unobservable. A looser reading treats extreme poverty as ended as a global phenomenon when the share falls below a threshold of 3% of the population. That threshold is the authors' reading, offered as context from outside the results; the results do not test it, and the text of the target does not choose between the readings. Against a 3% threshold the world stands at more than three times the required level in 2024; against zero the distance is the whole of the 10.1%. Both readings lead to the same conclusion for 2030, but they differ in what a successful outcome would mean.

The choice of line matters for a second reason. A line of $3.00 a day is a very low standard, set to reflect the national lines of the poorest countries. Falling below it signals deprivation of food, shelter and basic needs. Rising above it does not signal security, and many households that have crossed it remain close enough to be pushed back by a poor harvest, an illness or a price shock (general context, not a result). This section reports the $3.00 line only; the higher line of $4.20 a day is not analysed here.

The 2024 value must be read with care. The data behind the headcount are household surveys, which are conducted in each country at intervals of several years and are published with a delay. Figures for the most recent years therefore rest partly on estimates that carry forward earlier surveys using national accounts growth and other assumptions. The coverage record shows the effect. In 2015, 87 countries reported a value, and 93 did so in 2018. The number fell to 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted, recovered to 81 in 2021, then fell to 73 in 2022 and 60 in 2023. Only 26 countries reported in 2024, and just 4 in 2025. Coverage is therefore not a steady decline, but the most recent years are thinly observed. The 2024 aggregate of 10.1% is thus a nowcast built on a thin base of direct observation, and later revisions can be expected as surveys arrive.

Two cautions follow for any reader. The fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is a robust direction but not a precise magnitude, and the end point is less firm than the start. The global figure also conceals a very uneven distribution, taken up in the next part, in which the decline has been concentrated in a few regions while others have seen little progress or a reversal.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture beneath the global figure is one of sharp divergence. East Asia & Pacific recorded the largest fall among the regions with a full series: the headcount at $3.00 a day went from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. Europe & Central Asia began from a low base and moved from 1.2% to 0.6%. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 6.0% to 4.3%, a decline that is real but slower in proportion than those of the two regions above. The series shows the change and not its cause; commodity cycles, informal employment and the reach of cash transfers are commonly cited as context for the region, but nothing in the results tests them. North America, at 1.1% in 2015 and 0.9% in 2024, was already close to the floor of what survey-based measurement can distinguish from zero.

South Asia requires a caution. The series for the region begins in 2020, at 9.4%, and reaches 2.6% in 2024. Read at face value, this is the steepest fall of any region in the period. The reading cannot be extended to 2015, because the regional value is not shown for the earlier years, and regional estimates depend on a small number of large countries with infrequent household surveys, so the aggregate may rest on interpolation as much as on fresh observation. The 2020 starting point also falls in the year of the pandemic, so part of the apparent decline may be recovery from a temporary shock rather than a sustained trend. Projected at its 2020 to 2024 rate, the region would stand at 0.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as on track; because the series is short and begins in the pandemic year, that classification is provisional. The figure is best taken as a sign of strong improvement of uncertain size, not as a measured change over the full period since 2015.

The regions where poverty has not fallen are those where the global total is now decided. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan moved in the wrong direction, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024, and the trend tool classes it as regression. The grouping combines economies of very different kinds, so the rise should not be read as a uniform deterioration; armed conflict and displacement in some members are often mentioned as background, but the results do not identify the cause. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, almost no change in nine years. A flat rate in a growing population would imply a rising number of people below the line, but that number is not measured here, and only the rate is reported.

Income groups tell the same story from another side. Low-income countries recorded 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, a rise, so that more than half the population of the poorest group of economies lives below $3.00 a day. Lower middle income countries stood at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024; the series for this group, like that for South Asia, is shown from 2020 only, and the same caution applies. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% to 2.1%, and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. The pattern is that the decline has been concentrated where poverty was already moderate, and that it has bypassed the group where poverty is deepest.

This matters for the target. The global fall from 13.4% to 10.1% coincides with large falls in regions that started with modest rates, while the region and income group with the highest rates did not move or moved backwards. The results do not show who contributes most to the global total, but they do show that the highest rates lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. Data for the most recent years are also thinner, a limit taken up in a later part. Eradication by 2030 would require that the stagnant and regressing groups reverse course abruptly, which no part of the 2015 to 2024 record suggests.

### Country progress and the absence of convergence

Sorting countries by the pace of their progress towards a headcount of zero by 2030 shows how uneven the record is. Of 105 countries assessed on the $3.00 a day line, 18 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 45.5% of the population of the assessed countries. That share is large because it includes some of the most populous economies, but the results do not show which countries drive it or why. The count of countries is far less encouraging than the share of people: 18 of 105 is a small minority of national experiences.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and they hold 23.1% of the assessed population. A further 15 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, holding 11.3%. In neither group is the target reached at the present pace. Moderate progress means the direction is right and the speed is insufficient; marginal progress means that closing the remaining distance would require a change of pace that few countries have managed in a single decade.

The weakest classes matter most for the meaning of the target, which asks for eradication for all people everywhere. 7 countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the assessed population. 24 countries are regressing, with 17.9%. Regression in almost a quarter of the assessed countries is a finding in its own right. The series shows the change but not its cause. As outside context, not a result of this analysis, armed conflict, state fragility, high food and energy prices and the pandemic of 2020 are commonly cited in the wider literature as reasons for setbacks. Because the classification measures movement from each country's own observations, a country can regress from a low level as well as from a high one, and the class does not by itself say how deep the deprivation is.

The convergence test addresses whether poorer countries are catching up. Across 57 countries with data from 2015 to 2022, the regression of change in the headcount on its starting level gives a beta of 0.00658 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029. A negative and significant coefficient would have shown that countries starting with higher headcounts fell faster. The coefficient is instead slightly positive, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 3% of the variation in outcomes. Starting poverty did not predict the later pace of change.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.144 in 2015 to 2.675 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts grew relative to their mean. Two readings are open. It may reflect a true divergence in national fortunes. It may also reflect that the headcount, as it approaches zero in many countries, has a small mean, which can inflate a ratio-based dispersion measure even when absolute differences narrow. The absolute test and the relative one should be read together, and neither shows catching up.

The sample limits both results. The convergence test covers 57 countries, fewer than the 105 classified, because it needs observations close to both 2015 and 2022. Household surveys are generally less frequent in poorer and more fragile countries, which is established context rather than a result here, so the finding of no convergence may understate the divergence. For 2030, the absence of catch-up means the global target cannot be met by the average trend alone.

### A slowing decline and its limits as evidence

The pace of decline in the world headcount at $3.00 a day has not been steady. A break analysis of the annual change in the world series finds two turning points, in 2014 and in 2021. Between 2001 and 2013 the headcount fell by a mean of 1.6 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.9 points, and in the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.3 points. The three segment means all point the same way, towards a smaller annual fall, and the most recent is about a fifth of the first. The two breaks fall close to two events that shaped the period: the end of the commodity-price boom and the slowdown of growth in many low-income economies after 2014, and the pandemic shock of 2020. These are context drawn from general knowledge, not findings of the series. The data show when the pace changed; they do not isolate why. Attribution would need counterfactual modelling that the series alone cannot supply, and the timing of breaks in a short annual series is itself uncertain by a year or more.

A further reason for caution lies outside the results. As context from general experience, and not as a finding, the remaining poor when the headcount is low are often concentrated in places that are poorer, more remote, more often affected by conflict or weak states, and less able to benefit from average growth. A slowing decline may therefore be partly expected even without any change in policy effort, though the series do not test this. Yet that would not make the slowdown benign. The target requires the headcount to reach zero, or a figure close to it, and a falling rate of change moves that outcome further from 2030, not nearer.

The evidence behind the latest segment is thinner than the evidence behind the earlier ones. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly and published with a lag. The number of countries reporting a figure for the headcount was 87 in 2015, 70 in 2020 and 81 in 2021, so coverage has not moved in one direction. It fell to 60 in 2023, to 26 in 2024 and to 4 in 2025. The decline in recent years is partly a matter of surveys not yet processed or not yet conducted, so the world and regional figures for 2023 onward probably lean on estimates that carry forward earlier survey information with growth data and assumptions about distribution. The mean change for 2021-2024 should be read as a provisional estimate, likely to be revised as surveys arrive, and the 2025 figures hardly rest on observed data at all.

The coverage problem may be uneven as well as thin. Countries with infrequent surveys are plausibly those with the highest poverty and the weakest statistical systems, and so the most likely to be absent from a given year; the counts above do not themselves show which countries are missing. The world aggregate could then be least well measured where the number of poor people is largest. Anyone assessing whether 2030 is within reach should weigh the slowdown found here as a signal that is probably real in direction, since the three segment means agree, but uncertain in size.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace observed since 2015, the world will not reach zero extreme poverty by 2030. The world headcount at $3.00 a day stood at 10.1% in 2024, and the trend to the target projects 8.4% in 2030 at the compound rate since 2015, a ratio of 0.38 of the progress needed. The trend classifies the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Target 1.1 can also be read as a threshold of 3%. That is this book's own choice of interpretation, and the results do not test it. On that reading the target is no more attainable, since the world headcount of 10.1% is still more than three times that level. The recent pace is slower than the pace since 2015: the segment from 2021 to 2024 shows a mean annual fall of only 0.325 points.

Even the regions that are advancing need to go faster. East Asia & Pacific, the best performer among the regions with a full series, is expected to stand at 1.0% in 2030 at its present rate, against a target of zero, and its ratio is 0.84. Europe & Central Asia is expected at 0.4%, and upper middle income countries at 1.1%. These are small residual shares, but they are the hardest to remove. As context from outside the results, the people concerned are often in remote, conflict-affected or marginalised groups that growth alone does not reach. South Asia is classed as on track, with an expected 0.4% in 2030, from a start of 9.4% in 2020. That classification is provisional: the series begins in 2020, the pandemic year, so the fall to 2.6% in 2024 covers four years and is measured from a short and unusual base.

The highest rates lie where the trend is flat or reversed. Sub-Saharan Africa is in stagnation, with an expected 44.7% in 2030, and low-income countries are in regression, with 54.2% expected. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also in regression, with 16.7% expected. The series shows these changes but not their causes, and it does not show how much each group contributes to the world total. Among 105 countries assessed, 24 are in regression and hold 17.9% of the assessed population.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. National governments and donors should concentrate poverty-reduction effort and concessional finance on Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. The headcount in Sub-Saharan Africa was 45.0% in 2024, almost unchanged from 45.4% in 2015, and in low-income countries it was 52.5% in 2024, up from 50.1% in 2015. National statistical offices, with the World Bank and bilateral funders, should fund household surveys at a regular and shorter interval. The interval is a proposal, not a finding, and the case for it is that 70 countries reported in 2020 against 26 for 2024 and 4 for 2025, so recent estimates rest on projection. The World Bank and national authorities should name the line and the price base whenever poverty is reported, so that the $1.25 wording of Target 1.1 is not mistaken for the current measure of $3.00 a day. The United Nations statistical system should track regression as a class of its own, since the 24 countries in that class are hidden by averages that mix them with countries that are advancing.

w-c07-4-3~heath/writer-2~101.text:
### Water quality is measured mainly through sanitation and ecosystem proxies

Target 6.3 calls for halving the proportion of untreated wastewater, and Target 6.6 for the protection and restoration of water-related ecosystems, including mountains, forests, wetlands, rivers, aquifers and lakes. Neither can be measured directly with the series on the shelf of the World Bank's World Development Indicators. No series on the share of wastewater treated, on ambient water quality in rivers, lakes and aquifers, or on the condition of wetlands is held. Any reading of these two targets is therefore indirect, and the conclusions drawn from it carry less weight than those for drinking water or sanitation access.

Three kinds of proxy are available. Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using a private facility whose excreta are safely disposed of or treated, is the nearest stand-in for Target 6.3, because untreated human waste is among the main sources of pollution in surface and ground water. Terrestrial protected areas and forest area stand in for Target 6.6, since protected catchments and forested slopes shape the quality and regularity of the water that flows from them. Marine protected areas, water stress and the mortality rate attributed to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene supply context. Each is a proxy in the strict sense. Sanitation safely managed at the household says nothing about industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, which Target 6.3 also names. A land area under protection is a legal designation, not a measure of the health of a river or wetland, and forest area records tree cover without distinguishing natural stands from plantations.

Coverage of the sanitation series is incomplete and has slipped. The number of countries reporting rose from 137 in 2000 to a peak of 146 in 2016, then fell to 141 in 2024. That is a net fall of five between 2016 and 2024, and it does not show which countries stopped reporting, since entries and exits may offset one another. A total of 146 countries reported in at least one year, so some economies are never covered at all. Regional and income-group figures are modelled aggregates, and they rest on fewer observations in the places where sanitation is weakest. The estimates that follow should be read with that limitation in mind.

### Safely managed sanitation rose from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent between 2015 and 2024

Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using improved facilities that are not shared and from which excreta are safely disposed of, stood at 48.4 per cent of the world population in 2015 and at 58.5 per cent in 2024. The gain of about ten percentage points over nine years is substantial, and the series covers 141 countries reporting in 2024, so the global figure rests on a broad base rather than a handful of observations. That base is not complete, however: reporting rose from 137 countries in 2000 to a peak of 146 in 2016 and fell to 141 in 2024, so coverage is incomplete and has slipped in recent years. The fall is a net change, and it does not show which countries stopped reporting.

What this proxy says about Target 6.3 is limited, and the limit matters. The indicator follows excreta through the whole chain of containment, emptying, transport and treatment or disposal, so a rise in it means that more households are served by systems that do not leave waste in streets, fields and watercourses. That is a reasonable stand-in for pressure on water quality from human waste. It does not measure the share of wastewater that is treated, nor industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, and it says nothing about the condition of the rivers, lakes and aquifers that receive the discharge. A country may serve its households well and still pollute its waters from other sources. The rise from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent should therefore be read as evidence of progress on one component of Target 6.3, not as a measure of the target.

A second caution concerns the classification of progress. Target 6.3 carries no numeric threshold in the bench's trend tool: it asks for the proportion of untreated wastewater to be halved, a relative aim that cannot be applied to this proxy without an agreed baseline. The classes returned by the trend method, such as on track or target met, are therefore a judgement about the pace of change, set against the tool's own projection to 2030, and not a comparison with a fixed goal. On that basis the world is classed as on track or target met, with a compound annual rate of change of 0.0213. Because the method rewards steady movement and not attainment of a stated level, a region can be classed as on track while a large share of its people still lack safe sanitation. The trend result classes Sub-Saharan Africa as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.0204, at 25.9 per cent in 2024, up from 21.6 per cent in 2015, and it is still far from universal coverage. The low-income group is likewise classed as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.0248, at 26.9 per cent in 2024, up from 21.6 per cent in 2015. The classes are best read together with the levels, which the following parts set out region by region.

The year of the data also bears on interpretation. The series runs to 2024, so it spans both the period after 2015, when the goals were adopted, and the disruption after 2020. The global series shows no visible break at the aggregate level, though the annual values behind the aggregates are partly modelled from sparse household surveys and censuses, and a short-lived shock could be smoothed away. For 2030, the figures point to continued gains, but no projection of levels is made here, and with the world at 58.5 per cent in 2024 universal safe sanitation remains a distant prospect.

### Regions differ widely, and the gap between them explains most inequality

The contrast between regions is the plainest feature of the series. In 2024 North America stood at 95.4 per cent of its population using safely managed sanitation, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 25.9 per cent. Europe and Central Asia, at 80.2 per cent, and the high-income group, at 84.4 per cent, sit well above the world figure of 58.5 per cent. Between these poles lie East Asia and Pacific at 63.6 per cent, South Asia at 60.1 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 54.4 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 51.2 per cent.

The pace of change differs as much as the level. South Asia rose from 40.8 per cent in 2015 to 60.1 per cent in 2024, the largest gain of any region, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 49.0 per cent to 63.6 per cent. Both are classed as on track in the trend analysis, as are the lower-middle-income group, which moved from 38.3 per cent to 51.9 per cent, and the upper-middle-income group, which moved from 49.1 per cent to 62.4 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean advanced more slowly, from 43.2 per cent to 51.2 per cent, and is judged to need acceleration. At the top, North America moved only from 95.2 per cent to 95.4 per cent, and the high-income group from 80.7 per cent to 84.4 per cent, which the analysis reads as stagnation. Europe and Central Asia, from 76.5 per cent to 80.2 per cent, shows marginal progress. Near-stagnation at a high level may partly reflect a ceiling effect, since the last few points are the costliest to reach; this is a possible explanation and not a finding, and it does not carry the same concern as stagnation at a low level.

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group show a more troubling pattern. The region rose only from 21.6 per cent in 2015 to 25.9 per cent in 2024, and low-income countries from 21.6 per cent to 26.9 per cent. The trend analysis labels both on track (Sub-Saharan Africa at a compound annual rate of 0.0204, low-income countries at 0.0248), but the target is left undefined for this series, so the label reflects how the rate is read and not any prospect of universal coverage. At 25.9 per cent in 2024 the region remains far from universal coverage. Where a target can be read in more than one way, the label should not be taken as a verdict.

Spread among countries narrowed over the period. The population-weighted Gini coefficient fell from 0.261 across 145 countries in 2015 to 0.208 across 141 countries in 2024, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.484 to 0.382 on those same country sets. Differences between regions account for 59.6 per cent of the Theil inequality among countries in 2024, the larger part of the total, with the remainder lying within regions. This is a result for a single year and does not describe change over time. The change in the country set between the two years is a caveat on the comparison. Convergence is assessed on a different set of 140 countries, where the coefficient of variation moved from 0.549 to 0.501; the two pairs rest on different country sets and cannot be compared directly. The beta coefficient is -0.00364 with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R squared of 0.018, so starting level explains very little of later change and the slope is not clearly distinguished from zero.

### Ecosystem indicators show stagnation and regression in many countries

Beyond sanitation, the shelf offers only land-based proxies for the condition of water-related ecosystems, and these show little sign of the protection and restoration that Target 6.6 set for 2020. The classification of country trends for terrestrial protected areas is divided. Of 211 countries assessed, 71 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 34.9 per cent of the assessed population. Against that, 54 countries are classed as regressing, and these hold 33.0 per cent of the population. A further 45 stagnate and 27 show only marginal progress. Protected land is a coarse proxy, since a designated area need not contain a wetland or a river headwater, and the series records designation rather than the quality of management. The regression class also needs careful reading, because the shelf sets no numeric target for the indicator and a decline may reflect boundary revisions or reclassification as well as loss of protection.

The sanitation classes, drawn from the same trend tool, show a similar spread. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target and 42 stagnate, while 25 regress. The regressing countries hold 6.8 per cent of the population assessed, a small share but a signal that gains in the global figure are not universal. These classes matter for water quality because untreated excreta are a plausible route to pollution of rivers, lakes and aquifers, so stagnation in sanitation may also mean stagnation in the protection of freshwater, although no freshwater series on the shelf confirms the link.

Forest area, which regulates flows, filters runoff and shelters headwaters, shows a mixed regional pattern between 2015 and 2023. East Asia and Pacific moved from 27.0 to 27.3 per cent of land area and is classed as stagnating, as are Europe and Central Asia, North America and the high income group. South Asia is also classed as stagnating despite a rising rate. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 47.2 to 46.1 per cent over the same years, and low income countries from 21.0 to 19.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa, the lower middle income group, the upper middle income group and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are also classed as regressing, and the world as a whole is classed as regressing, at an annual rate of -0.0011. The tool does not show what drives these changes. As context only, conversion of forest to farmland and pasture, fuel wood collection and infrastructure expansion are well-established pressures, set against uneven enforcement of protection.

The central limit is that rivers, wetlands, lakes and aquifers have no series on the shelf. Target 6.6 therefore cannot be fully assessed, and the deadline of 2020 has passed without a measured verdict. The results cited here give no regional protected-area figures, so no claim is made about regions combining gains across forest, protected land and sanitation. What the proxies do show is that forest is stagnant or regressing in every region cited, and that the country classes for protected land and sanitation are split, which gives no ground for assuming that unmeasured freshwater ecosystems have improved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Convergence in safely managed sanitation is weak. Across 140 countries between 2015 and 2024 the estimated beta is -0.00364, with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R-squared of 0.018. The negative sign points to a slight tendency for countries that started higher to change by less each year, but the slope is not distinguished from zero at the conventional 0.05 threshold and explains almost none of the variation between countries. On that same set of 140 countries the coefficient of variation fell from 0.549 in 2015 to 0.501 in 2024. This pair rests on a different country set from the pair of 0.484 and 0.382 reported for 145 countries in 2015 and 141 in 2024, and the two cannot be compared directly. The narrowing is too small to say that the gap between regions will close by 2030. At 25.9 per cent in 2024, Sub-Saharan Africa remains far from universal coverage, and no projection of its 2030 level is offered here.

The classification of country trends shows where the burden lies. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target, yet a further 42 are stagnating and 25 are regressing. The 42 countries on track hold 59.6 per cent of the assessed population, a share that shows where most people live but not how concentrated the gains are. This figure is unrelated to the 59.6 per cent between-region share of Theil inequality in 2024. These classes carry no numeric target, since none is set for the indicator, and should be read as direction of travel only. Forest area gives a parallel signal: the world trend is regression, at a rate of -0.0011, and Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.00636) and low-income countries (-0.00682) lose forest at the fastest rates. Catchment forests are generally understood to regulate water quality and flow, so these are settings where water-related ecosystems may be under pressure and are least measured. No freshwater series on the shelf confirms this link.

Four proposals follow. First, national statistical offices, the UN custodian agencies and the World Bank should add the share of wastewater treated and the extent of freshwater ecosystems to the core indicator set, so that Targets 6.3 and 6.6 can be read directly rather than through proxies. Second, governments and development financiers should give priority in sanitation investment to the 42 stagnating and 25 regressing countries, since these are the places where the series shows no progress or decline. Third, forest-rich countries with the steepest losses, supported by climate and conservation funds, should protect forests where losses are recorded. Fourth, reports on the goals should state plainly where data are missing, and not fill the gaps with unsupported estimates.
