w-c05-1-4~cedar/writer-1~102.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The world primary completion rate stood at 87.9% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 88.0% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The change over nine years is too small to register as progress. The period spans the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the school closures of 2020 and the uneven recovery since, and the aggregate shows no surge after 2015 and no visible collapse after 2020. A flat global line can conceal movement in both directions, and the regional and income-group figures show that it does.

The indicator needs careful reading. Primary completion here is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of primary education: new entrants in the last grade, whatever their age, divided by the population at the entrance age for that grade. Because late entrants and early starters are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100, and it is not the share of a birth cohort that finishes primary school. The target can be read in more than one way: as universal completion, meaning every child finishes, or as a rate of 100 or more, which the ratio can reach while some children remain outside school. The trend assessment in this chapter takes the second, arithmetical reading, with 100.0 as the threshold.

The movement beneath the flat world line is large in places. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% to 83.7%, a gain of nearly ten points. East Asia and Pacific rose from 94.1% to 95.4% by 2022, its latest value. Sub-Saharan Africa moved only from 66.3% to 68.9%, and low-income countries from 60.5% in 2015 to 62.9% in 2023, so the poorest groups remain furthest from the target and gained little. Against these gains, South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 98.4% to 96.5%, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% by 2023. Lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% and then 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% by 2023 and high income countries stayed near 98.1% and 97.8%. Gains in one region are therefore offset by losses in others, which is why the world figure does not move.

Under the arithmetical reading, the country classification is sobering. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, holding 19.6% of the assessed population. A further 14 show moderate progress, with 13.0% of the assessed population, and 14 show marginal progress, with 5.7%. Three stagnate, with 0.5%. Regression is the largest class: 92 countries, holding 61.3% of the assessed population. The results do not show how much of this reflects real deterioration. Some of it may arise where ratios above 100 drift back towards 100 as late entry and repetition decline, which the classification counts as movement away from the target. The count alone cannot separate the two.

Reporting is a further limit. Only 11 countries had reported a value for 2025 at the time of access, so the most recent global figure rests on 2024. The finding of near stagnation is firm for the period to 2024 but says little about the last years before the target date.

### Lower secondary completion shows slow, uneven gains

The world lower secondary completion rate stood at 74.8% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 77.9% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The measure is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education, so it counts new entrants in that grade regardless of age. A ratio can therefore exceed 100.0%, and the rate indicates intake to the last grade rather than certified completion. The trend tool gives the world a ratio of 0.21 of the distance from baseline to target, and classes it as marginal progress, which is the tool's own label for that ratio.

Set beside primary completion, which was 88.0% in 2024, the world figure for lower secondary shows that intake falls between the two cycles. Because the indicator is a ratio and not a count of a single cohort, this gap should not be converted into a number of adolescents. Established research on education systems points to rising costs, scarcer and more distant schools, and the demands of household labour after primary school, but the series themselves do not isolate these causes.

The regional series show where the shortfall lies. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 42.3% in 2015 and 44.4% in 2023, and remains far below the world rate; the trend tool classes it as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.07. Low-income countries moved from 37.0% in 2015 to 38.6% in 2023, also classed as stagnation, and are the group furthest from the target. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 57.1% to 66.7% in 2024, a faster pace than most regions, with a trend ratio of 0.39 and a class of marginal progress, yet it remains well below the world rate. South Asia advanced from 83.7% to 86.6%, with a ratio of 0.30 and the same class.

East Asia and Pacific rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, the largest gain among the regional aggregates, with a trend ratio of 1.39 and a class of on track. The results do not show what drives the world rise, but this gain is the largest of any regional series. Europe and Central Asia moved from 90.9% to 91.9%, with a ratio of 0.19, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 81.3% to 81.5%, which the trend tool classes as stagnation. By income group, upper-middle-income countries rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 93.0% in 2023, with a ratio of 0.95 and a class of on track. High-income countries moved from 94.0% to 95.6% in 2024, with a ratio of 0.44, and lower-middle-income countries from 71.0% to 73.7%, with a ratio of 0.16. Both of the latter are classed as marginal progress. Low-income countries have closed little of the distance.

Several series do not cover the full period. The North American series begins in 2016, not 2015, at 104.3%, and ends in 2023 at 100.8%. Both values lie above 100.0% because the ratio counts older entrants, so the decline does not indicate a fall below universal completion. The Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income and upper-middle-income series end in 2023, one year before the world and several other groups, so comparisons across aggregates mix periods of different length. Only 11 countries reported a value for 2025, too few to support any statement about that year.

The aggregates show no break that can be attributed to the school closures of 2020. Projected to 2030 at the observed pace, the world rate reaches about 80.0%, far short of the target. Sub-Saharan Africa reaches about 46.2% and low-income countries about 40.1%, while East Asia and Pacific passes 100.0% on the same method. The country classes for this indicator are set out in the section on divergence and are not repeated here.

### Regions and countries diverge sharply

Regional averages conceal a wide spread in how far children travel through school. In Sub-Saharan Africa the primary completion rate was 68.9% of the relevant age group in 2024, up from 66.3% in 2015. Lower secondary completion in the same region was 44.4% in 2023, up from 42.3% in 2015. Fewer than half of the children in the region reach the last grade of lower secondary, and the small gain leaves the region far from the target of 100.0%. The trend tool classes the region as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected value of 46.2% in 2030. Low-income countries are further from the target than any region: 62.9% at primary in 2023 and 38.6% at lower secondary in 2023, up from 37.0% in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 40.1% at lower secondary, also classed as stagnation.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region shows the largest gain in primary completion, from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024. At lower secondary the region rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. The tool classes it as marginal progress at lower secondary, with a ratio of 0.39 and an expected value of 73.9% in 2030, still well short of 100.0%. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 1.39, is classed as on track. The region's figures combine countries in very different circumstances, and measurement may be uncertain where conflict and displacement are present. The gain should be read as a regional average, not as a uniform improvement.

East Asia and Pacific is the clearest success. Lower secondary completion rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, with an expected 105.4% in 2030. A value above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio, so it does not signal that every child completes on time. Primary completion in the region reached 95.4% in 2022, from 94.1% in 2015. Upper middle income countries are also classed as on track at lower secondary, with a ratio of 0.95, rising from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023. Lower middle income countries moved from 71.0% to 73.7% in 2024, with a ratio of 0.16 and a class of marginal progress. At primary level lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% in 2023.

Several regions went backwards at primary level. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 98.4% in 2015 to 96.5% in 2024. South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4% over the same years, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. These regions began near universal completion, so the declines differ in kind from the shortfalls in Africa. The data do not show why they fell; the 2020 disruption and changes in enrolment and repetition are possible contributors, and because the measure counts new entrants in the last grade, shifts in repetition or age at entry can move it without any change in the number of children finishing. Primary completion in Europe and Central Asia rose from 97.2% to 98.1%. At lower secondary, Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as stagnant, from 81.3% in 2015 to 81.5% in 2024, and South Asia improved from 83.7% to 86.6%. North America is classed as on track at lower secondary although its ratio, 100.8% in 2023, fell from 104.3% in 2016, because the series already sits above the target.

Country classes confirm that the global average hides a divide. Of 173 countries assessed on primary completion, 50 are on track or have met the target, and 92 are in regression, holding 61.3% of the assessed population. The tool does not separate countries that fell from near-universal levels from those that fell from low ones, so the size of the regression class should be read with care. At lower secondary 49 countries are on track and 66 are in regression, holding 21.1% of the assessed population, while the 32 countries in marginal progress hold 38.4%. Many people therefore live in countries advancing too slowly to arrive by 2030.

### Learning lags behind completion, and the data are thin

Completion measures how many children reach the last grade; it does not show what they have learned. The indicator of pupils below the minimum reading proficiency level at the end of primary schooling addresses that gap. Worldwide, 45.9% of assessed pupils at the end of primary were below the minimum level in 2015, and 49.6% in 2019. This is a share of assessed pupils, not of those who completed school, and it refers to years different from the 2024 completion rate of 88.0%, so the two measures are not directly comparable. Read together, they suggest that reaching the last grade does not by itself secure basic reading, which Target 4.1 requires. The series covers reading at the end of primary only. Minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not measured by any series on the shelf, so that part of the question cannot be answered here.

The regional contrasts are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest share below the threshold, at 80.7% in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019. Low income countries stood at 83.5% in 2015 and 87.4% in 2019, and lower middle income countries at 52.9% and 57.4%. South Asia was nearly unchanged, at 55.8% and then 56.0%, and the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 57.7% to 57.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 49.1% to 51.0%. The results do not identify why additional years in school have not translated into basic skills in these regions. Well-established explanations include rapid expansion of enrolment, large classes and limited teacher training, but the data in hand do not test them.

At the other end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.8% to 5.5%, and high income countries from 6.4% to 6.2%. North America was flat, at 3.9% in both years. Low shares in these regions leave little room for movement, so the near absence of change there differs in kind from the stagnation seen in South Asia. Upper middle income countries were close to unchanged, at 28.0% in 2015 and 28.6% in 2019.

The largest movement was in East Asia and Pacific, where the share below the threshold rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019. A rise of that size in a region with strong education systems calls for caution. It may partly reflect a change in which countries and pupils were assessed between the two waves, not only a decline in learning. The data in hand cannot separate the two explanations. The trend calculation for the region extrapolates to 124.3% in 2030, which is impossible as a share and shows only that two points cannot support a projection.

The coverage of the series explains the difficulty. Data come in survey waves, not as annual observations. Countries reporting numbered 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, with an isolated report in 2023 from 1 country. In all, 125 countries reported in at least one year. The aggregates end in 2019, so they do not capture the effect of the school closures of 2020 and after, which is a serious omission for a question about what changed after 2020. The 2021 wave exists at country level but has no regional aggregate in the results here.

For 2030 the evidence supports only a statement of direction. Extrapolating the 2015 to 2019 movement gives 61.3% of pupils below the threshold worldwide, against a target of zero. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 91.0% and low income countries 99.1% on the same arithmetic. Europe and Central Asia would reach 3.0%, from a low base. The extrapolations are mechanical, rest on two points and should be read as the observed direction of change from 2015 to 2019, not as a forecast.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At present rates the world will miss target 4.1. The lower secondary trend to target puts the world on course for an expected completion rate of 80.0% of the relevant age group in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend ratio for the world is 0.21, which the trend tool labels marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Among 173 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target for lower secondary completion, covering 22.1% of the assessed population, while 66 are regressing, covering 21.1% of the assessed population. For primary completion, 50 countries are on track, covering 19.6% of the assessed population, and 92 are regressing, covering 61.3%. Regression is therefore the most common class at primary level. The classes come from a trend to target, so a country that has already reached a high rate and slipped slightly may be recorded as regressing; the reading needs care, and the target can be read as universal completion or as a rate near it.

Completing school is not the same as learning. The learning trend for the world is labelled regression by the trend tool, with an expected share below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary of 61.3% in 2030, against a target of 0.0%. This figure is a projected share of assessed pupils and is distinct from the share of the assessed population in regressing countries at primary completion. In Low income countries the expected share is 99.1% in 2030, and in Sub-Saharan Africa 91.0%. These projections extend a change between 2015 and 2019 mechanically, from two points in time, so they indicate direction rather than forecast. High completion does not guarantee learning: in East Asia & Pacific the share of pupils below the minimum reading level rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019, while lower secondary completion reached 97.3% in 2024, with an expected rate of 105.4% in 2030 and a ratio of 1.39. A rate above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio. Completion gains not matched by learning gains deliver the certificate without the skills. The learning series ends in 2019 for these trends and covers 125 countries, so it cannot show whether recovery after 2020 has changed this. It also addresses reading at the end of primary only; minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not covered, and the learning shares cannot be compared directly with completion rates of other years.

The regional picture shows where acceleration matters most. Low income countries are labelled stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected rate of 40.1% in 2030, the furthest of any group from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is also labelled stagnant, with an expected rate of 46.2% in 2030. The same groups have the worst learning outcomes: 87.4% of assessed pupils in Low income countries and 83.3% in Sub-Saharan Africa were below minimum reading proficiency in 2019, and their learning data are among the thinnest. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region has a ratio of 0.39 and an expected rate of 73.9% in 2030, still short of what the target requires.

Proposals follow from these findings. Governments of low-income and regressing countries, with their development partners, should fund the transition to lower secondary, and should pair every completion gain with learning measurement, since completion alone does not show what pupils have learned. National education ministries and international assessment bodies should run reading assessments at the end of primary at regular intervals in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, so that the post-2020 position is known.

w-c08-1-3~cedar/writer-3~102.text:
### Global access has risen, but not to universality

Access to electricity worldwide stood at 91.9 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 86.9 per cent in 2015. The gain was achieved while the world population grew, but it leaves the world short of the universal access that target 7.1 sets for 2030. The series is reported by 215 countries for 2024, so coverage is nearly complete, though some national figures rest on modelled estimates drawn from industry records and household surveys rather than a fresh count each year.

The divide between rural and urban populations explains much of the shortfall. Rural access rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a larger advance than the urban series, which moved from 96.4 per cent to 97.8 per cent. Urban access was already close to the ceiling at the start of the period, and little room remained for improvement. The remaining deficit is therefore mainly rural: 84.9 per cent rural access leaves 15.1 per cent of rural residents unserved in 2024, against 2.2 per cent of urban residents. This matters for policy, because connecting dispersed households costs more per person than extending an urban grid, and it depends on off-grid and mini-grid solutions as much as on national networks.

A headcount of people without electricity is not published in the series examined here. The scale can only be estimated by applying the 2024 deficit rates to the population series, and the result is the writer's own estimate, not a reported count. Applying 15.1 per cent to the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 gives roughly 523 million rural people; applying 2.2 per cent to the urban population of 4,750,578,960 gives roughly 105 million urban people. Three cautions apply. The access series ends in 2024 while the population series run to 2025, so the years differ. The definition of rural and urban areas is set by each national statistical office and varies between countries. The product of a percentage and a population carries the uncertainty of both inputs. Read with these limits, the estimate suggests a world total of the order of 600 million people, with rural areas holding about five in six of them, even though more people live in cities.

The period also spans two breaks, 2015 and 2020. The first marks the adoption of the goals, the second the pandemic and the economic shocks that followed, which strained public budgets and household incomes and may have slowed some connection programmes. The endpoints given here do not reveal whether progress paused after 2020. The trend projection for the world places access at 95.4 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.65 of the distance to the target covered, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The final stretch of any access target tends to be the hardest, since the unconnected are the most remote and poorest. The sections that follow turn to where that remaining gap lies.

### Sub-Saharan Africa holds most of the remaining gap

Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for most of the remaining gap in access. Access in the region stood at 55.1 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 39.2 per cent in 2015. Every other region reported at least 96.8 per cent in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 96.8 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean at 98.0 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 98.6 per cent. Europe and Central Asia stood at 99.9989 per cent (100.0 to one decimal place), and North America at 100.0 per cent in both years. South Asia rose from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024. Its gain in points was smaller than that of Sub-Saharan Africa, yet it was the region with the largest rural gain, from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent of the rural population, and it now stands close to universality. The contrast shows that universal access is attainable at scale, and that Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception, not one case among several.

The divide between rural and urban areas is sharpest in this region. Rural access in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 35.7 per cent of the rural population in 2024, against 82.9 per cent of the urban population. In 2015 the rural figure was 18.5 per cent and the urban figure 72.7 per cent. Rural access therefore rose faster in proportion than urban access, yet nearly two in three rural residents remained without electricity in 2024. The pattern follows from the economics of supply, stated here as context. Grid extension to dispersed settlements costs more per household and recovers less revenue, so utilities and public programmes have tended to serve towns first. Off-grid solar and mini-grids have widened the options in recent years, although the series reports access without separating the technologies behind it.

Income groups show the same shape. Low-income economies, most of which lie in Sub-Saharan Africa, reached 48.8 per cent access in 2024, up from 32.2 per cent in 2015. Rural access in that group stood at 37.1 per cent and urban access at 77.6 per cent. Lower-middle-income economies reached 91.4 per cent, and upper-middle-income and high-income economies stood at 99.3 per cent and 100.0 per cent respectively.

The results give no reported headcount of people without electricity, so the scale can only be indicated by derivation. Applying the 2024 rural deficit of 35.7 per cent to the 2025 rural population of 731,422,742 in Sub-Saharan Africa suggests that roughly 470 million rural residents lacked access in the region, an approximation. The same method with the urban access rate of 82.9 per cent and an urban population of 590,231,475 suggests a smaller but still large number in towns and cities. These are the writer's own estimates, not figures reported by the series: they mix years, and national definitions of rural and urban areas differ. They indicate that the unserved in the region are concentrated in rural areas. The results do not state what share of the world total lies in the region. Rural population in the region rose from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, and urban population grew from 408,204,795 to 590,231,475. Population growth therefore works against the connection effort: every year of progress in the access rate must also cover new households.

For 2030 the implication is plain. The other regions are within a few points of universality, and their remaining gaps are small, concentrated in particular countries and in rural areas. The target will be met or missed in Sub-Saharan Africa. The trend tool classes the region as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and expects 69.2 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.49 of the distance to the target covered. Closing the gap would require a pace several times faster, concentrated on rural households that are costly to reach.

### Rural areas and South Asia account for the change since 2015

South Asia's gain moved the world average most, but not because its gain in points was the largest. Access in the region rose from 86.5 per cent of the population in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 13 points. Sub-Saharan Africa's overall gain was larger in points, from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, about 16 points. South Asia's rural gain was the largest of any region, from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent. Because South Asia holds a very large rural population, 1,035,602,697 people in 2015 and 1,086,549,811 in 2025, closing its rural gap shifted the world average more than any other change. The region is now close to Europe and Central Asia, where access stood at 99.9989 per cent in 2024 (100.0 to one decimal place), so its contribution to further global gains is nearly exhausted.

The rural gap narrowed worldwide. Rural access in the world rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 8 points, against about 5 points for the population as a whole. Rural areas therefore improved faster than the average, which is what a closing gap requires. Rural gains were also large in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, from 87.6 per cent to 94.0 per cent, and in low-income countries, from 17.2 per cent to 37.1 per cent. In Latin America and the Caribbean the rural rate moved from 89.1 per cent to 91.0 per cent, a smaller change, and it remains well below the region's overall rate of 98.0 per cent in 2024.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows a different pattern. Rural access rose from 18.5 per cent in 2015 to 35.7 per cent in 2024, and urban access from 72.7 per cent to 82.9 per cent. These within-area rises are the reported facts behind the regional gain. Yet the rural population of the region grew from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, so a rising rate is applied to a growing base. Rural access of 35.7 per cent in 2024 means that roughly two in three rural residents of the region remained unconnected. The urban population also rose, from 408,204,795 in 2015 to 590,231,475 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 182,500,508 to 269,862,804. Population shifts between rural and urban areas may also play a part in the regional average, but the series cannot test this and no share of the gain is attributed to it.

The question of how many people lack electricity can be answered only by derivation, since the results give shares and not headcounts. As the writer's own estimate, not a reported count, applying the world rural deficit of 15.1 per cent (100 less 84.9 per cent in 2024) to the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 gives about 523 million rural residents. Applying the urban deficit of 2.2 per cent to the urban population of 4,750,578,960 gives about 105 million. These products mix reference years, 2024 for access and 2025 for population, and rest on national definitions of rural and urban, so they indicate scale only. They also show that the unserved are overwhelmingly rural.

Causes call for restraint. The indicators show where access changed and by how much, not which policies produced it. Well-established experience points to national grid extension programmes, falling costs of solar equipment and off-grid systems, and public financing as usual drivers, but the series cannot attribute the South Asian or African gains to any one of them. Nor do the figures cited show a break after 2020, since the comparison runs between 2015 and 2024 only.

For 2030, the implication is that the world's average is now governed by one region. South Asia has largely finished its part, East Asia and the Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean are above 98 per cent, and the remaining distance lies in rural Sub-Saharan Africa, where population growth works against each point gained.

### Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030, and proposals follow

Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030 on the evidence of the trend classification. Of the 215 countries assessed, 154 are on track or have already met the target, and they hold 74.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 33 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 15.6 per cent of the population. Another 21 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 8.0 per cent of the population. Two countries are stagnant, with 0.4 per cent, and five are regressing, with 1.4 per cent. The count of countries therefore looks reassuring, while the population shares show that about a quarter of the people in the countries assessed live where the present pace will not close the gap.

The aggregate projection agrees. Extending the 2015 to 2024 pace, the world would reach 95.4 per cent access in 2030, and the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.65, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The two groups furthest from the goal are classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 69.2 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.49, and low-income countries would reach 64.4 per cent, with a ratio of 0.48. Latin America and the Caribbean is also classed as marginal, with a ratio of 0.47, but the reason differs: its access was already 98.0 per cent in 2024, so the little that remains moves slowly, and the same pace would bring it to 98.6 per cent in 2030. South Asia, with a ratio of 1.73, and lower middle income countries, with 1.01, are on track, although the lower middle income result rests on a narrow margin.

These readings depend on how target 7.1 is interpreted. The classification treats the target as 100 per cent access by 2030, which is the plainest reading of universal access. A projection above 100, such as South Asia's 109.8 per cent, cannot occur in fact and shows only that a linear extrapolation overshoots a ceiling. The last stretch before universality is also usually harder than the early gains, because the remaining households are the most remote and the poorest, so linear extrapolation may flatter regions near the ceiling. The target further names affordable and reliable energy services. The indicator measures only whether a population has access to electricity. It says nothing about the price paid, the hours of supply or the quality of the connection, so a country classed as on track may still fall short of the full wording of the target.

The implication for 2030 is that the world will not reach universal access on present trends, and that the missing people will be concentrated where the pace is slowest, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries, particularly in rural areas, where access in the region was 35.7 per cent in 2024. Rural access in low-income countries was 37.1 per cent in the same year.

The question of how many people lack electricity can be answered only by a rough derivation, since the results hold no published headcount. Rural access for the world was 84.9 per cent in 2024, leaving a rural deficit of 15.1 per cent, and the rural population was 3,464,845,933 in 2025. Urban access was 97.8 per cent in 2024, leaving a deficit of 2.2 per cent, and the urban population was 4,750,578,960 in 2025. Applying the rates to the populations gives about 523 million rural residents and about 105 million urban residents, or roughly 628 million people in all. This is the writer's own estimate, not a reported count. It mixes years, rounds the rates and relies on national definitions of rural and urban areas, so it indicates scale only. It also shows that the rural deficit is the larger part of the world's shortfall.

w-c09-4-2~cedar/writer-4~102.text:
### Carbon intensity of world output fell between 2015 and 2024

World carbon intensity of GDP, the carbon dioxide emitted per unit of output, stood at 0.26 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar in 2015 and had fallen to 0.22 kg by 2024. The series covers 188 countries reporting in 2024, so the world figure rests on near-complete coverage, though it reaches only to 2024 and later revisions of national inventories may shift it.

The decline did not begin with the Sustainable Development Goals. A break test on the annual change of the world series places a structural break in 2012. In the segment from 2001 to 2011 the mean annual change was -0.00217 kg per dollar, while from 2012 to 2024 it was -0.00531. The fall in intensity was therefore faster in the later period than in the earlier one, and the acceleration predates the adoption of the goals in 2015. The test does not identify what caused the shift. Context from well-established knowledge points to the spread of renewable power, the displacement of coal in several large economies, structural change towards services and efficiency standards, but the result itself shows only the timing and size of the change. It also does not isolate a separate effect of 2020, when output and emissions both fell sharply and then recovered; the annual series passes through that year within the second segment.

What a falling intensity means must be stated carefully. Carbon intensity is a ratio of emissions to output. When it falls, emissions grow more slowly than output, or fall while output rises. That is relative decoupling. It does not show that emissions have fallen in absolute terms: if output grows faster than intensity declines, total emissions still rise. The results held for this part contain no series of absolute emissions for the world, so they cannot settle that question.

Target 8.4 also speaks of resource efficiency in consumption and production, which concerns material use as well as emissions. No material footprint or domestic material consumption series appears among the results, and carbon intensity is only a partial proxy for the use of materials. The target can be read in two ways: as a call for relative decoupling, which the falling ratio would meet, or as a call for absolute decoupling of growth from environmental degradation, which it would not. The wording on developed countries taking the lead adds a further reading, since the pace expected of them differs from that expected elsewhere. The sections that follow treat regional differences and energy efficiency with these limits in mind.

### Regions and countries diverge in the pace of decline

Regional paths differ in both starting point and pace. East Asia and Pacific recorded the largest absolute fall among the regions in the results, from 0.38 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar of GDP in 2015 to 0.31 kg in 2024. It remains the most carbon-intensive region in 2024, with the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 0.28 kg, so the gap between the two is modest. North America fell next most steeply, from 0.25 kg to 0.19 kg. Europe and Central Asia moved from 0.19 kg to 0.15 kg, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.15 kg to 0.13 kg, Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.16 kg to 0.14 kg, and South Asia from 0.25 kg to 0.21 kg.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands apart for pace. Its intensity moved only from 0.31 kg in 2015 to 0.28 kg in 2024, and its trend is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Reliance on hydrocarbons for domestic energy and industry is a commonly cited context for slow decline, and is not a finding of these results. By income group, upper middle income countries fell from 0.36 kg to 0.31 kg and high income countries from 0.22 kg to 0.17 kg, while low income countries moved from 0.10 kg to 0.08 kg. The low level for the poorest group may be associated with small industrial and energy sectors, an explanation offered as context that the results do not test, and a low intensity there is not evidence of efficient production.

The country classification shows a wider spread than any regional average. Of 189 countries assessed, 77 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 24 countries, with 32.7% of that population, show moderate progress, and 13 show marginal progress, with 3.0%. Another 13 are stagnant, with 3.7%. Regression, meaning intensity rose over the period, affects 62 countries and 21.5% of the population. Regional averages therefore conceal a large group of countries moving in the wrong direction, even where the region as a whole improved.

These classes carry a caveat. Target 8.4 sets no numeric value for carbon intensity or any other measure, so the trend tool has no threshold to reach by 2030. The labels rest on an assumed pace of decline, and a different assumption would move countries between classes. The results describe the direction and relative speed of change, and they do not show whether any country meets an agreed standard. The target also speaks of decoupling growth from environmental degradation, which a fall in carbon intensity alone does not establish, since total emissions can still rise when output grows faster.

### Energy efficiency gains slowed after 2011 and links to growth are weak

Energy intensity, the primary energy supplied per unit of output, is the companion measure to carbon intensity, and its path for the world shows when efficiency gains were made and when they faded. Break detection on the annual change of the world series finds four breaks, in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ per 2021 PPP dollar. It deepened to -0.1154 in 2005-2008, then stalled at 0.0070 in 2009-2010, the years of the global financial crisis and its aftermath. From 2011 to 2017 the decline resumed at -0.1045 a year, close to the pre-crisis pace. After the break of 2018 the mean annual change shrank to -0.0325 in 2018-2021, less than a third of the preceding segment. The series used for the breaks ends in 2021, so the segment cannot show whether the slowdown continued, and the years after 2020 are only partly covered.

The slowdown matters because lower energy intensity is the most direct route to reducing the energy needed for each unit of growth, and the pace of 2011-2017 is the one that a 2030 trajectory would have to restore. Well-established context points to several possible reasons for the weaker pace: the pandemic shock of 2020, which distorted both energy use and output, a recovery weighted towards energy-heavy activity, and the exhaustion of easy gains from the earlier replacement of old industrial capacity. These are explanations from general knowledge; the break analysis dates the change but does not identify its cause.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the world line. Of 201 countries assessed on the trend to 2030 for energy intensity, 57 are on track or have met the target, holding 52.2% of the population of the countries assessed. Another 29 countries, with 9.9% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 32, with 15.1%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Stagnation applies to 15 countries with 2.1% of the population. Regression, meaning energy intensity is rising, affects 68 countries with 20.7% of the population. Regression is therefore the most common single class by number of countries, although the on-track group covers the larger share of people. No target value is set for this indicator, so the classes rest on a conventional reading of the direction and pace required, and another reading of the target could shift countries between classes.

Growth does not by itself explain these gains. Across 188 countries over 2015-2024, the Spearman correlation between changes in carbon intensity of GDP and GDP per capita growth is 0.15, and between their 2024 levels it is -0.06. Both are close to zero, so faster-growing economies were neither clearly cleaner nor clearly dirtier per unit of output. The result is an association between rankings only and gives no cause: it cannot show that growth did or did not drive the changes, and the link may differ within groups of countries. What it does suggest is that decoupling depends on the energy mix, technology and policy rather than on the rate of growth alone.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Relative decoupling is under way. The world trend for carbon intensity of GDP is classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed, at a rate of -0.0196 (2015 to 2024, kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar per year). World carbon intensity fell from 0.26 kg in 2015 to 0.22 kg in 2024. Output is therefore being produced with less carbon per unit, and the pace is not yet enough to be read as on track for the world as a whole. Among the regions, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, at a rate of -0.00839. Target 8.4 carries no numeric value, so the classification rests on the trend method alone, and a different reading of the target would give a different verdict.

The country count shows how uneven the progress is. Of 189 countries assessed on carbon intensity, 77 are on track or have met the target, covering 39.1% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 24 show moderate progress (32.7% of population), 13 marginal progress (3.0%) and 13 stagnation (3.7%). Regression affects 62 countries, home to 21.5% of the assessed population. A fall in the world ratio can coexist with rising intensity in about a third of countries, which is why the aggregate cannot stand for the whole. Energy intensity gives a similar picture. Of 201 countries, 57 are on track or have met the target (52.2% of population), while 68 are regressing (20.7% of population).

The evidence supports relative decoupling only. Intensity measures emissions or energy per unit of output, so it can fall while total emissions or total material use rise, if output grows faster. The series examined here do not include material footprint, and they do not show absolute decoupling. Whether growth is separating from environmental degradation, as the target intends, cannot be confirmed from them.

The pace of energy efficiency gains after 2018 is a further concern. The mean annual change in world energy intensity was -0.10452 MJ per 2021 PPP dollar in 2011-2017, but only -0.03247 in 2018-2021. The gains slowed to roughly a third of the earlier rate. Reaching 2030 on track would require the earlier pace to return. The broad causes are well known: stronger efficiency standards, fuel switching and structural change drove gains in earlier years, while slower policy effort and the disruption of 2020 are plausible contributors to the slowdown, stated here as context rather than as a finding.

Four proposals follow from these findings, set out below.

proposals: Statistical offices and the United Nations bodies that compile the indicators should report material footprint alongside carbon and energy intensity, so that absolute decoupling can be tested.
Development banks and bilateral donors should direct technical and financial support to the countries whose carbon or energy intensity is regressing, starting with the largest by population.

National governments, especially where progress is marginal or moderate, should restore the efficiency policies behind the 2011-2017 gains, namely appliance and building standards, industrial energy audits and removal of fossil fuel subsidies.

The parties responsible for the Goals framework should state target 8.4 in numeric form, for example a required annual rate of decline in intensity and a ceiling on footprint per person, so that on-track status can be read in one way only.

w-c04-7-3~heath/writer-1~102.text:
### Adolescent fertility has fallen worldwide since 2015

The world adolescent fertility rate fell from 46.0 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 38.3 in 2024. The decline continues a long movement that predates the Sustainable Development Goals. The figure is a modelled estimate built from registration data, surveys and censuses. The series reports on all 217 countries and territories in 2024, so the global average rests on far fuller coverage than the indicators of contraceptive demand in the same section.

Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold. It calls for universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, including family planning, information and education, and offers no level of adolescent fertility that would count as success. The target can also be read in more than one way. Adolescent births are an outcome of access, schooling, marriage customs and income as much as of health services, so a fall in the rate cannot be credited to health policy alone. Any reading of progress here therefore rests on the trend classes of the bench, which compare each country's own course with the pace needed to keep falling to 2030, and not on a stated goal.

On that reading the picture is favourable in breadth. Of 217 countries assessed, 144 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 26 countries, with 6.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Eight countries, with 0.4% of the population, are stagnant, and five, with 1.0%, are regressing. The population-weighted share on track is far larger than the count of countries alone would suggest, but the results do not show which countries lie in each class by starting rate, so no claim is made here about where the laggards began.

The global decline matters because early childbearing is commonly associated with interrupted schooling, lower lifetime earnings and higher obstetric risk; this is context from established knowledge, not a finding of the bench. The world rate of 38.3 in 2024 remains well above the 8.7 recorded for high-income countries in the same year, so the average conceals a wide gap that the next parts of the section examine. As context from outside the bench, school closures and disrupted clinics after 2020 were widely expected to push adolescent births up. The world series, read at its end points of 2015 and 2024, shows no such lasting reversal, though end points cannot show whether the pace faltered in particular years or places. For 2030, the trend classes indicate that gains are not secure in every country: 13 countries are stagnant or regressing. No projection of the world rate is made here.

### Demand satisfied by modern methods is poorly measured

Demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods cannot be answered at the level the question asks. The bench supplies no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country group, and the answer to how far demand is met is therefore limited to the direction of change in 15 countries and the population shares those countries hold. The indicator is the weakest of the series in this section. It is reported by 73 countries in at least one year between 2000 and 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. In any single year the count is small: 13 countries in 2000, 14 in 2012 among the years shown, and 8 in 2015. After 2015 the count moved unevenly. It was 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021 and 7 in 2022, then 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. There is no steady decline and no steady recovery, and the count in 2024 remains small beside the 217 reporting on adolescent fertility. As context, not a finding of the data, household surveys are fielded at intervals of several years and were disrupted by the pandemic, so a country appears in the series only in the years after a survey has been completed and processed.

The consequence is that the indicator cannot show what happened after 2015 or after 2020 for the world. A year-on-year comparison would compare different sets of countries, and a change in the average would reflect which countries happened to report as much as any change in access to services. The shelf holds aggregates for only three groups: lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The aggregate values were not retrieved by the tools used for this section, so they are not reported here. No world aggregate and no aggregate for other regions can be read from the shelf, so regional comparison of satisfied demand is not possible on this evidence.

The definition adds a second limit. The indicator refers to married women aged 15 to 49 who have a need for family planning, and its denominator is those with demand, not all women. Unmarried women, including sexually active adolescents, fall outside it, as do women in unions not recorded as marriage in some surveys. Target 3.7 speaks of universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, information and education, and the indicator captures only one part of that: the use of modern methods by married women who want to space or limit births. The target also gives no numerical threshold, so no level of satisfied demand can be called the goal, and the trend assessment rests on the direction of change rather than on a fixed value. The target can be read in more than one way, and this section does not choose among the readings.

The trend classification covers only 15 countries, those with enough observations to fit a path to 2030. Of these, 2 are on track or have met the target, holding 1.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Another 5 show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 21.8 per cent. Four show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 70.3 per cent. One is stagnant, with 3.1 per cent, and 3 are regressing, with 3.3 per cent. The results do not show which countries lie in each class, so the large population share of the marginal class cannot be attributed to any particular country. Fifteen countries out of 73 reporting, and out of a world of more than 200, is too few to speak for any region, and the sample is not random. The proportions above describe the sample, not the world, and any global statement drawn from them is tentative.

### Regions differ by a factor of eight in adolescent births

Adolescent births are concentrated to a degree that the world average conceals. In 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 91.9 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19, against 50.4 in Latin America and the Caribbean and 37.8 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. South Asia stood at 21.0, East Asia and Pacific at 14.3, North America at 11.7 and Europe and Central Asia at 11.4. The highest regional rate is therefore about eight times the lowest, and the next region down, Latin America and the Caribbean, is well above the world rate of 38.3.

The pattern follows income. Low-income countries recorded 90.7 births per 1,000 in 2024, lower-middle-income countries 42.5, upper-middle-income countries 23.6 and high-income countries 8.7. The results do not show how far income groups and regions contain the same countries, so the two views should be read as separate cuts of the data. As context rather than a finding of these results, schooling for girls, the age at first marriage, access to contraception and the reach of sexual and reproductive health education are known to differ along similar lines and to act together rather than separately.

Every region and income group named here recorded a fall between 2015 and 2024, but the size of the fall depends on the measure. In absolute terms Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 to 91.9 and Latin America and the Caribbean from 67.3 to 50.4. In proportional terms North America fell from 20.9 to 11.7 and East Asia and Pacific from 21.9 to 14.3, while low-income countries moved only from 103.3 to 90.7. A large absolute fall from a high starting point therefore leaves relative standing little changed: Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest rate in 2015 and remains far above every other region in 2024.

The country classification shows a similar split between breadth and depth of progress. Of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 34 countries, with 7.3 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 26, with 6.3 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. The population-weighted figure of 84.9 per cent should not be read as a statement about each country. The results do not show which regions the lagging classes belong to.

The target gives no numerical threshold for adolescent fertility, so the trend classification measures the pace of decline against a projected path, not against a defined goal. A different reading of what counts as sufficient progress would change the classes. The regional contrasts are nonetheless clear on any reading: the gap between Sub-Saharan Africa and the other regions remains very wide in 2024.

### Progress in family planning is moderate and uneven

Of the 15 countries for which a trend to 2030 could be computed on demand satisfied by modern methods, 2 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 1.5% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 5 countries, with 21.8% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The weight of the picture lies in the slower classes. The 4 countries in marginal progress, which need significant acceleration, hold 70.3% of the assessed population. One country stagnates, with 3.1%, and 3 regress, with 3.3%. The population-weighted result is therefore weaker than the country count alone suggests. The trend tool shows only the share of the assessed population in each class; it does not name the countries or show which of them are the most populous.

The question of how far demand is satisfied cannot be answered at the level asked. The bench supplies no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country, so the answer is limited to the direction of change in 15 countries and the population shares they hold. The 15 countries assessed are a fraction of the 73 that have ever reported the indicator, and the survey-based series leaves most countries without enough observations to draw a trend. Annual reporting is thin and uneven: 8 countries reported in 2015, 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. The count therefore recovered after 2019 but remained far below the 14 reporting in 2012, one of the years shown. The assessment cannot be read as a global verdict. It describes a small group selected by data availability, and how far it represents other countries is not known. The target also carries no numerical threshold in this analysis, so the classes measure the pace of improvement along a path rather than attainment of a fixed level, and a different reading of the goal would sort some countries differently. The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women, including adolescents, are outside it.

The indicators do not identify why countries fall into one class or another, and no cause is asserted here. As general context, not a finding, the pace of change in contraceptive use is commonly understood to depend on the reliability of supply, the range of methods offered, the cost to users and social norms about women's choices; none of these is measured by this series. What the data do show is that regression occurs in 3 of the 15 countries, which means that gains are not automatically retained.

The adolescent fertility trend gives a firmer, though different, reading. Of 217 countries and territories, 144 are on track or have met the target, holding 84.9% of their population, and 34 show moderate progress, with 7.3%. Another 26 are in marginal progress, with 6.3%, 8 stagnate, with 0.4%, and 5 regress, with 1.0%. Progress on adolescent births is thus broad in coverage, while progress on contraceptive demand cannot be shown to be.

For 2030, progress on satisfied demand cannot be assumed to be on course. With few countries on track and most of the assessed population in the slower classes, a result consistent with universal access would require acceleration where the trend is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Adolescent fertility is expected to keep falling to 2030, but this is an expectation and not a finding, and the pace will differ between countries. Of the 217 countries and territories assessed, 144 are on track or have met the direction of travel, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. The remainder is the concern. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of that population, show moderate progress and need acceleration, 26 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. Target 3.7 sets no numerical goal for adolescent fertility, so these classes describe the pace of change in each country and do not measure distance from a value agreed in the Goals. The reading depends on the pace each country is judged against, and it should be taken as indicative.

The regional rates show where the burden lies. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 91.9 in 2024, and low-income countries fell from 103.3 to 90.7. Both remain far above the high-income level of 8.7 in 2024, while the world rate stands at 38.3. The trend classes are computed for countries and are not shown here for regions, and the results do not name the countries that lag, so country-level lag in Sub-Saharan Africa is unknown. As context outside the evidence of this section, schooling for girls, the age at marriage and access to contraception are well-established influences on adolescent births.

The question of how far demand for family planning is satisfied cannot be answered at the level asked. The bench supplies no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country, and only the direction of change in 15 countries is available. Of these, 2 are on track, 5 show moderate progress, 4 show marginal progress, 1 is stagnant and 3 are regressing. The 4 countries in marginal progress hold 70.3% of the population assessed, so a small number of populous countries determines the result. Reporting is also thin: 2 countries reported in 2019 and 7 in 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility. The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women and adolescents lie outside it.

The proposals that follow address both problems: the thinness of measurement and the pace of progress where rates remain highest.

w-c06-1-3~rowan/writer-2~102.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The equal weighting is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. Near-universal coverage is what one would expect of a measure read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, and it contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world. The coverage result also lists aggregates for high-income, low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income and South Asia groupings and for the world, so group comparisons are possible in principle.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change since 2015 or 2020 has been drawn from the shelf for this section, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot be answered here in magnitude. The sections that follow therefore describe what the instrument measures and how its readings should be interpreted, which is a matter of method, and state what a measured record would have to show. They make no claim about the size or direction of change.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. Earlier editions scored a narrower set of legal questions and gave high marks to many economies once the most overt discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope lowers the standing of economies that looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether comparable values exist back to 2015, the baseline this book uses throughout, has not been verified. If they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and any statement about the decade would need a different instrument.

The only computed result for this section is coverage: the legal index reports for 189 economies in 2025, and 189 economies report in at least one year. Coverage is therefore complete for the economies the series addresses. It says nothing about the level of the scores, their direction or their distribution, and no finding about change after 2015 or after 2020 can be drawn from it.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether the institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed here.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The Legal Framework Index has been computed only as to its coverage, so this part does not report a level or a direction of change. What follows sets out what a measured answer would need to show, so that the later computation can be read against a fixed standard. The only figures available are that 189 economies reported in 2025 and that 189 economies reported in any year, which means the full set of economies with data is present in the latest year.

A measured answer would have four elements. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which would show how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and because a few large reforms look the same in a mean as a wave of small ones. The third is the distribution: the spread between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index are likely to differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker needs.

The period after 2020 requires its own comparison. Average annual change before and after that year, if the history of the series permits, would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or was interrupted. Because the index is built from statute rather than from reported statistics, an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data. Until these four elements are computed, the direction of legal change for women's economic opportunity remains unmeasured in this book.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates listed, so a comparison across the other regions would require aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change; implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. The legal index alone could therefore flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it could misdirect attention. The test is to compute the legal, supportive and enforcement indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score. This is stated as a method, not as a finding.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains this index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. That distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation. The only figures established here are that 189 economies reported the index in 2025 and in any year.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values this section does not hold: the bench has computed only the coverage of the Legal Framework Index, which shows 189 economies reporting in 2025 and 189 reporting in any year. That coverage is complete enough to support either reading, but it says nothing about level or direction.

Under the strict reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Neither has been computed, so no verdict on 2030 is offered here.

What can be said without those values is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar and any economy's position should be judged against it. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companion series on supportive frameworks and enforcement perceptions, and with outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the index is well suited to a global account. Its census of 189 economies in 2025, and 189 in any year, means that a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. Coverage is the only result the bench has returned for this section, however, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed remains open. The task left to the bench is to turn that coverage into levels, changes since 2015, income-group comparisons and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the supportive and enforcement measures so that the distance between promise and practice becomes visible.
