w-c09-3-3~dahlia/writer-1~102.text:
### Vulnerable employment is the measured proxy for informality

Informal employment, the condition target 8.3 has in view, is not measured directly by any series on the shelf. The nearest measured proxy is vulnerable employment: the sum of own-account workers and contributing family workers, expressed as a percentage of total employment. The series is a modeled estimate of the International Labour Organization, and it is available for 187 economies, with 182 countries reporting in 2025. The proxy is imperfect. Some own-account workers are registered, taxed and covered by social protection, while some wage jobs are informal, with no contract and no insurance. The share of vulnerable employment therefore indicates the extent of weak job security and thin social protection, and it cannot be read as a count of informal jobs.

A second caution concerns the target itself. Target 8.3 asks for policies that encourage the formalization and growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises, but it names no numeric threshold and no year-specific level. Any statement of progress is thus a reading of direction: whether the share falls, stays flat or rises. The trend tool applies a decreasing direction by 2030 with no fixed goal, and its verdicts should be understood in that light. A different reader might judge the same movement more or less favourably.

At world level, vulnerable employment stood at 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 and at 42.4 per cent in 2025. The fall is about 0.7 percentage points over a decade. Roughly two in five workers worldwide therefore remain in own-account or contributing family work, a share that has barely moved across a period that included the adoption of the goals and the shock of 2020. The trend tool classes the world movement as stagnation, with an annual rate of change of -0.0017 on its scale.

This matters because the world figure conceals very different realities, taken up in the parts that follow. It also matters because vulnerable work is the form of employment least likely to carry a stable wage, a contract or a pension. A global share that has hardly shifted suggests that the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not, on the whole, been converted into a move towards paid employment with protection. The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring in many low-income economies probably weighed on the decade, although the series, being modeled, cannot show the timing of such effects with precision.

### Regions differ by a factor of sixteen

In 2025 the regional range in vulnerable employment is wide. South Asia stands at 69.7 per cent of total employment and Sub-Saharan Africa at 71.0 per cent. North America stands at 4.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 12.9 per cent. The highest regional figure is therefore about sixteen times the lowest (71.0 against 4.5). Two regions, both in the developing world, have roughly seven in ten workers in own-account or contributing family work. In North America the figure is below one in twenty.

The middle group lies between these poles and is more tightly bunched. East Asia and Pacific stands at 35.3 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 36.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 31.5 per cent. In each of these regions roughly one worker in three is in vulnerable employment, although their economic structures, institutions and histories are quite unlike. A region-wide average also conceals differences among countries, and the regional figures are population-weighted aggregates of modeled estimates, not direct counts.

The pattern follows the structure of production, as context rather than a result of this analysis. Where agriculture and small household enterprise employ most people and large firms offering wage contracts are few, own-account work and unpaid family work are the usual forms of employment. Where manufacturing and services are organised in larger firms and wage employment is the norm, the share is small. The income groups show the same ordering: low-income economies stand at 76.1 per cent in 2025 and high-income economies at 8.0 per cent, so income level and the share of vulnerable work move together.

The spread across countries confirms that region is the main divide: 71.9 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2025 lies between regions, and the rest within them. This shows that most of the cross-country inequality in the indicator is a difference between regional means. It does not show how many countries or workers account for the vulnerable total, and it says nothing about variation within any one region.

### Women carry more vulnerability where it is highest

In 2025 the world figure for women stands at 43.1 per cent of female employment, against 41.9 per cent of male employment for men. The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point. It conceals a division by region. Where vulnerable employment is most widespread, women are more exposed than men. Where it is rare, the order reverses.

The gap is widest in South Asia, where 76.2 per cent of employed women are in vulnerable jobs against 67.1 per cent of employed men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the figures are 79.2 per cent for women and 63.9 per cent for men, a difference of more than fifteen points. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the shares are 41.6 per cent and 34.7 per cent. These are the regions in which a large part of women's work is unpaid help in a family farm or business, or own-account activity in small trade and agriculture, with little social protection. Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work, since it can be combined with household duties.

The pattern runs the other way in the richest regions. In Europe and Central Asia the female share is 11.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent for men, and in North America 3.3 per cent against 5.4 per cent. High income economies show 6.9 per cent for women and 9.0 per cent for men. Men are more often self-employed in these economies, in trades, construction and freelance work, while women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts in services, health and education. A lower share of vulnerable employment among women here is not by itself a sign of advantage, since the series does not capture pay, hours or the quality of wage jobs.

By income group the same crossing appears. In low income countries the female share is 82.9 per cent and the male share 70.9 per cent. In lower middle income countries the figures are 74.0 per cent and 61.2 per cent. In upper middle income countries the gap narrows to 35.6 per cent against 34.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is close to parity, at 31.3 per cent for women and 31.6 per cent for men. The gender gap in vulnerability is thus largest in the poorest settings and closes as incomes rise, which bears directly on the inclusive aim of target 8.3.

### Change has been slow, uneven and not convergent

Across the 187 countries assessed, the trend to 2030 is mostly one of slow or absent progress. Only 24 countries, holding 3.7 per cent of the population of the group, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 19 countries, with 6.1 per cent of the population, show moderate progress that would need acceleration. The largest population weight lies in the 48 countries with marginal progress, which hold 51.7 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. Another 59 countries stagnate, with 25.0 per cent of the population, and 37 regress, with 13.5 per cent. Target 8.3 sets no numerical threshold, so the classes measure movement in the desired direction (a decrease) and not distance from an agreed goal; the reading is one of direction only.

The weight of population in the slower classes matters more than the count of countries. Large economies with high shares of own-account and family work move slowly, so the world average is determined by them, while many small and wealthy economies that were already low account for most of the on-track count. Progress that does occur is therefore concentrated where the problem was already smaller.

Between-country inequality in the indicator did not narrow. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.317 in 2015 across 187 countries and 0.320 in 2025 across 182. The Theil index moved from 0.178 to 0.182. The share of that inequality lying between regions, and not within them, stayed near 71 per cent: 70.8 per cent in 2015 and 71.9 per cent in 2025. The geography of vulnerability is thus still mainly a matter of which region a worker lives in. The change in country coverage, from 187 to 182, is small and does not alter the reading.

The convergence test points the same way. The coefficient on initial levels is slightly negative (beta -0.00281, p-value 0.0001), so countries with higher initial shares fell marginally faster, but the fit is weak, with an R-squared of 0.066 across 182 countries. Meanwhile the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.717 to 0.735, meaning that dispersion between countries grew. A weak tendency towards catching up coexists with a widening spread, which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved. Neither the post-2015 nor the post-2020 period can be separated by these summary measures, and the shock of 2020 is not isolated here.

Wage and salaried employment is the mirror of vulnerable employment. The rank correlation of 2025 levels is -0.994, and that of changes since 2015 is -0.920, across 182 countries. Because the two shares are close to complements, with employers forming a small remainder, this is largely definitional and gives no independent evidence that wage growth causes lower vulnerability. It does show that a fall in vulnerable work has meant a rise in paid employment, and not a shift towards other forms of work.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace of 2015 to 2025 the world would not reach a markedly lower share by 2030. The trend tool classes the world as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0017 a year, from 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 to 42.4 per cent in 2025. The calculation extends the recent line and is not a forecast. Target 8.3 sets no number for vulnerable employment, so the reading of 'on track' is the tool's: any decrease counts as movement in the right direction. Measured against the wider aim of decent work, the pace is insufficient.

The populous group of 48 countries with marginal progress holds 51.7 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. The regional trend tool gives South Asia a rate of -0.0074 a year and East Asia and Pacific a rate of -0.0074, and classes both as marginal progress; it gives Sub-Saharan Africa a rate of -0.0007 and classes it as stagnating. Low income countries have a rate of 0.0000 (+0.00003 a year), effectively flat, and the tool labels them regression; the sign of the rate alone would not justify that label. Faster movement in the regions with the highest shares would count for more than gains in Europe and Central Asia (-0.0137) or among high income countries (-0.0127), where the share is already low.

The cross-country picture shows no clear convergence. The convergence slope is negative (-0.0028), so countries that started higher fell slightly faster or rose less each year. Yet the fit is weak (R-squared 0.07) and the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.73 in 2025, so dispersion in relative terms widened. The tests do not show which end of the distribution moved more. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini was 0.32 in both 2015 and 2025, and 71.9 per cent of the Theil measure in 2025 lies between regions. Most of the inequality in vulnerable employment is therefore a difference between regions, not within them.

The link between vulnerable employment and wage employment is close: across 182 countries the Spearman correlation of 2025 levels is -0.99, and of changes since 2015 it is -0.92. This is an association, not a cause, but the two series largely mirror one another. It is consistent with a route to lower vulnerability that runs through paid jobs and firms able to employ.

Five proposals follow. The International Labour Organization and national statistical offices should monitor informal employment directly alongside the modeled proxy, using labour force surveys. Governments should set a quantified national reading of target 8.3, stating the share of vulnerable or informal work to be reached by 2030. Ministries of labour and of industry in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where shares stood at 69.7 and 71.0 per cent in 2025, should prioritise wage job creation and the formalisation of micro and small enterprises, with access to finance and simpler registration. National planners should give women's vulnerability its own targets, since women are more exposed where the share is highest. Statistical agencies and the ILO should report data gaps openly, including the modeled status of many national figures.

w-c02-4-5~loom/writer-1~103.text:
### Basic services and accounts have spread, but not to everyone

Three of the measures that bear on target 1.4 can be read from the shelf for the world as a whole: drinking water, electricity and account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults. All three rose, and none reached universality. The share of people using at least basic drinking water services went from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024. Access to electricity moved from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same nine years. Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults, measured from 2017, rose from 61.7% to 72.4% in 2024. In each case the direction is right and the pace is real, yet the remaining gap is concentrated in a smaller and harder-to-reach population. Sanitation, treated in the sections that follow, is the fourth measure on the shelf and is read through its trend classes, since the shelf gives no world level for it here.

The three indicators are not strictly comparable. Water and electricity are tracked from 2015, the year the goals took effect, while the account series begins in 2017, the first year with a Findex round in this series, so its change covers seven years and not nine. The water and electricity figures describe whole populations, whereas the account figure describes only the poorest 40% of people aged 15 and over. A rise in the first two therefore says nothing directly about whether the poor in particular were reached, since national averages can be lifted by households that were already better placed. The account series is the only one of the three that isolates the poor, and it has the thinnest country coverage: 138 countries reported in 2024, against 202 for water and 215 for electricity.

Target 1.4 does not fix a single measure of access, which affects how these numbers should be read. The water indicator counts an improved source with a round trip of no more than 30 minutes, so it captures basic service and not water that is safely managed or reliably available. The electricity indicator records whether a population has access, not the quality, affordability or reliability of supply. An account may be held at a bank or with a mobile-money provider, and the data record ownership and use, not whether the account serves a household's economic needs. Sanitation is defined by facilities not shared with other households, a threshold that different readers will treat as more or less demanding. Each figure here is therefore a floor of service and not a statement that the right has been secured.

The arithmetic of the remainder shows why the pace matters. Measured as the gap to 100%, the water shortfall fell by about 3.3 points between 2015 and 2024, the difference between the two published levels, and the electricity shortfall fell by about 5.0 points. People still without these services live mostly in low-income settings and in rural areas, where connection costs per household are highest and providers have the weakest incentive to extend networks. The remaining points are usually the costliest to close.

Accounts show the largest gain, 10.6 points among the poorest 40% in seven years, or about 1.5 points a year. Established explanations include mobile-money services, digital identity schemes and the payment of public transfers into accounts, though the series themselves do not test these causes. The disruption of 2020 did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series, but the data given do not allow its effect on the pace of change to be isolated.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region

Sub-Saharan Africa trails every other region on the measures held on the shelf, and low-income countries show the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan lag on accounts and sanitation, but not on water or electricity. In 2024, 67.5% of Sub-Saharan Africa's people used at least basic drinking water services, against 95.3% in East Asia and Pacific, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia and 99.8% in North America. Access to electricity shows a wider gap: 55.1% of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, while no other region fell below 96.7%. The region began from a low base, with 59.2% for basic water and 39.2% for electricity in 2015. The gains are real, but they were made from so far behind that the distance to the other regions has narrowed only slowly. Low-income countries, which are mostly in the region, show the same pattern: 60.3% for basic water and 48.8% for electricity in 2024.

Sanitation confirms the regional order. The trend assessment reads Sub-Saharan Africa as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.16 against the pace needed, and low-income countries as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.10. Their expected basic sanitation level for 2030 is 36.2% for low-income countries, so that roughly two in three people in those countries would still lack basic sanitation at the target date. A positive rate is classed as stagnation here because it is far too slow to approach the target by 2030.

South Asia presents the opposite experience. Its electricity access rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, so that a region once close to the global average is now near universal supply. Such a rise is consistent with sustained public programmes of grid extension and household connection, although the series do not isolate the cause. South Asia also moved from 90.5% to 95.9% on basic drinking water over the same years, and its trend toward the sanitation target is read as on track, with a ratio of 1.11.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan sit above the global figures of 91.5% for water and 91.9% for electricity, at 92.9% and 96.7% in 2024. Its weaknesses lie in accounts and sanitation. Among the poorest 40% of adults, account ownership stood at 46.1% in 2021, up from 39.5% in 2017, and of the regions with values for 2021 only Sub-Saharan Africa, at 43.6%, was lower. The region's sanitation trend is assessed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48, so significant acceleration is required. The grouping joins very different economies, from high-income oil exporters to countries in conflict, so the regional figure hides wide variation among its members.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest gain in account ownership among the poorest 40% of the regions with 2021 values. The share rose from 42.9% in 2017 to 67.9% in 2021. This interval includes the pandemic, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers into digital accounts. That may have contributed, but the data do not allow the cause to be isolated. Europe and Central Asia rose from 76.4% to 86.3%, and East Asia and Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, over the same four years.

A caution applies to every regional account figure. The regional series end in 2021, except South Asia and the income groups, which carry values for 2024. The regional comparison therefore refers to 2021 and cannot show the three years that followed. For the world, the poorest 40% reached 72.4% in 2024, up from 61.7% in 2017, but this rests on 138 reporting countries and cannot be broken down by region at the same date.

### Rural electricity advanced fastest while sanitation and water lag

Country classes set against the 100% target show how uneven the advance has been. For basic drinking water, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress but needed acceleration, so they are not yet on course for universal coverage. Another 55 countries, with 20.9% of the population, were making only marginal progress. Stagnation applied to 17 countries (1.5% of the population), and 37 countries (9.9%) were regressing. These are the places where service coverage was being lost rather than merely delayed.

Sanitation is the weakest of the physical services in the class results. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population. Moderate progress described 34 countries (17.7%), and marginal progress 54 countries (16.5%). Stagnation affected 37 countries (5.8%) and regression 39 countries (13.4%). The share of population living in regressing countries is larger for sanitation than for water. Difficulty in sustaining household facilities against population growth and urbanisation is a plausible context, though the indicators do not test it. The world as a whole was classed as making moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed and an expected coverage of 89.2% in 2030, short of universal use. The shelf gives sanitation levels only through these trend results, and none of the series separates the poor from the rest of the population except account ownership.

Electricity is the service closest to the target in the class results, though the class shares come from different series and are a reading rather than a measured ranking of services. The classes reported here are for rural electricity access: of 211 countries assessed on the rural series, 161 were on track or had met the target, with 77.4% of the rural population concerned. Moderate progress applied to 23 countries (12.8%) and marginal progress to 10 (2.0%). Seven countries (2.3% of the population) were stagnating and 10 (5.4%) were regressing. Grid extension and off-grid solar are well-established routes to electrification and reach dispersed households more readily than sewers or piped networks. Conflict or weak utilities are common reasons why extension stalls, but this is context from outside the series, which do not identify the cause.

Regional trends on sanitation show where the divergence sits. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and upper middle income countries were on track, with ratios of 1.18, 1.11 and 1.08. Lower middle income countries reached a ratio of 0.75, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 0.48, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.16, with an expected 42.0% coverage in 2030, and low income countries at 0.10, with an expected 36.2%. Low income countries are classed as stagnating even though their rate is positive, because that rate is far too slow to close the gap. North America is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -1.03 and an expected 99.4% in 2030. This reflects a marginal fall from a level close to universal and should not be read as a crisis of access.

Convergence in rural drinking water coverage offers some reassurance. Across 167 countries, the 2015 to 2024 regression of annual change on initial level gave a beta of -0.0164, with a p-value close to zero and an R2 of 0.27. Countries starting with lower coverage gained faster, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Catching up is real but partial: initial level explains little more than a quarter of the variation, so many low-coverage countries did not catch up.

For 2030, only 33.9% of the population lives in countries on track for water, and the 33.8% in moderate-progress countries need acceleration. Sanitation will not reach universal use at the present pace. Electricity is closer to the target in most countries, but Sub-Saharan Africa, at 55.1% in 2024, and low income countries, at 48.8%, remain far from it on national access. The world average conceals how far the target is missed where the poorest live. Changes after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be separated here, since the classes summarise the whole period from 2015 to 2024, and the effect of the pandemic years cannot be isolated from these results.

### Universal access by 2030 is out of reach without acceleration, and proposals follow

Universal access by 2030 is not within reach on present trends for basic drinking water or sanitation, and electricity access comes closest. For basic drinking water services, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress, but they need acceleration and are not on course for universal coverage. The remaining countries are advancing too slowly, standing still or moving backwards, and 37 of them were in regression, holding 9.9% of the population.

Sanitation is further behind. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population covered. Another 37 countries were stagnating and 39 were in regression, and the regressing group held 13.4% of the population, against 9.9% for water. The regional trends show why. Low-income countries are classed as stagnating: the rate is positive, at 0.01 a year, but the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.10, and the trend carries them to only 36.2% in 2030. Lower middle income countries are projected to reach 88.9%, with a ratio of 0.75. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 42.0% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.16. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are classed as making marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48. East Asia and Pacific and South Asia are classed as on track. North America is classed as regressing, with a projection of 99.4% in 2030, a change too small to matter for people but one that shows how a trend class can mislead near the ceiling.

A trend to 100% is a demanding standard, because the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach: they lie among dispersed, displaced or marginalised households. Countries classed as on track may still leave a residual population without services.

Electricity access is the closest to the target among the series classed. The classes are national, covering the whole population, and are not a rural result. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, holding 77.4% of the population covered. Only 10 countries were in regression and 7 in stagnation, though these hold 5.4% and 2.3% of the population respectively. The class shares are not a ranking of services, since each series is assessed separately. As context not tested by these data, falling costs of off-grid solar and national connection programmes are commonly cited reasons why electricity has moved faster than water and sanitation, and conflict or economic collapse can damage networks where regression occurs.

For accounts held by the poorest 40% of adults, the world figure rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024. No trend class is available for this series, so no projection to 2030 is a finding; any extension of the recent pace is an illustration only. Low-income countries rose from 22.5% to 37.3%, so more than six in ten of the poorest adults there remained without an account. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021, so the 2030 outlook for accounts is uncertain. The effect of 2020 cannot be isolated from these results, which compare endpoints and not annual values.

The weight of the shortfall falls on a small number of places. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 55.1% electricity access in 2024, and low-income countries, with 48.8%, are far below other groups, while South Asia, at 99.8%, has almost closed its gap. Progress at scale within a decade is therefore possible, but global averages will soon be governed by a region where the pace has been slower than the need.

Target 1.4 speaks of the poor and the vulnerable specifically, yet the water, sanitation and electricity series describe whole populations. Only the account series is split to the poorest 40%. The first three could be rising for the average household while the poorest remain unserved, and the shelf cannot show this. The word access is also read in more than one way: basic water is not safely managed water, and an account that is held is not necessarily one that is used.

w-c04-8-4~loom/writer-4~103.text:
### Service coverage has widened, but the world is far from universal

The UHC service coverage index stood at 68.0 index points for the world in 2015 and at 71.0 in 2023, the latest year, when all 193 countries report. The index is a composite of 14 tracer indicators spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases and service capacity and access. It runs from 0 to 100, and a score of 100 is the natural reading of 'universal' in target 3.8. That reading is one of several. The target also names financial risk protection and access to safe, affordable medicines, which the index does not measure directly, and a country may score high on tracer services while leaving households exposed to heavy costs. The index should therefore be read as a measure of the breadth of essential services, not as a verdict on the whole target.

On that measure, the world rose from 68.0 to 71.0 over eight years and remained well below 100 in 2023. The shortfall is large because the tracer indicators include services that are hard to extend to everyone, such as the control of hypertension and diabetes and the capacity of facilities, alongside those that are easier to scale, such as vaccination and antenatal care. A composite also moves slowly, since a gain in one area can be offset by stagnation in another. These explanations rest on general knowledge of how the index is built, not on the results shown here.

The income groups show the same ordering at both dates. Low-income countries scored 41.2 in 2015 and 43.8 in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6, and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. High-income countries, which started closest to the ceiling, were not saturated and kept improving. The low-income rise was smaller than those of the two middle groups, so the poorest countries did not close the distance to the others in absolute terms. In 2023 they remained below the level the lower-middle-income group had reached in 2015.

The gap between countries narrowed slightly, though not by much. Among the 193 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the index fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index fell from 0.030 to 0.024. Convergence is therefore real, but it takes place at a low overall level. Most of the inequality lies between regions: the between-region share of the Theil index was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, so the region in which a person lives accounts for more of the variation in coverage than differences within a region. Because the weighting is by population, the improvement in South Asia, whose regional score rose from 60.0 to 68.0, plausibly contributes to the narrowing, though the results do not isolate its contribution. The regional pattern is taken up in the next part.

The pace matters for 2030. The assessment was run only against a target of 100, and its sensitivity to other yardsticks was not tested. At the 2015 to 2023 pace, universality by 2030 is not reachable: the world's expected value for 2030 is 73.7, and the trend covers a ratio of 0.18 of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target. Whether the period after 2020 slowed progress cannot be judged, since the endpoints shown do not reveal change in the intervening years.

### Regions differ widely in coverage and in out-of-pocket burden

Coverage differs more between regions than any change in the world average would suggest. In 2023 North America scored 88.0 index points on the UHC service coverage index, Europe and Central Asia 82.0, East Asia and Pacific 80.0 and Latin America and the Caribbean 79.0. South Asia stood at 68.0, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 66.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 50.0.

The direction of travel differs as well. South Asia made the largest regional gain, from 60.0 in 2015 to 68.0 in 2023, and moved from below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 76.0 to 80.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 45.0 to 50.0. Latin America and the Caribbean did not move, at 79.0 in both years. North America, already near the top, rose from 87.0 to 88.0. Among income groups, low-income countries moved from 41.2 to 43.8, lower-middle-income countries from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6 and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. The poorest countries are improving, but from so low a base that the distance to the others has barely closed, and in 2023 the low-income group remained below the level that lower-middle-income countries held in 2015. Only the 2015 and 2023 endpoints are used here, so they do not show whether the pace changed after 2020.

Out-of-pocket spending adds a second view of the same divide. As a share of current health expenditure it was 11.1% in North America in 2023, 16.5% in Europe and Central Asia, 26.0% in East Asia and Pacific, 28.3% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 29.7% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 30.4% in Sub-Saharan Africa and 46.6% in South Asia. The world figure was 17.3%, down from 18.4% in 2015. South Asia fell from 64.3% to 46.6%, the largest fall of any region, yet it remains the highest, so households there still pay nearly half of all health spending directly. Low public funding and a large private provider sector are commonly offered as explanations, but the series do not test them. Latin America and the Caribbean and East Asia and Pacific moved the other way, from 28.2% to 29.7% and from 25.7% to 26.0%.

The share of health spending paid out of pocket and the share of people suffering hardship are related but not the same. Hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on health, affected 26.0% of the world population in 2022, against 28.0% in 2015. By region it ranged from 7.5% in North America and 13.0% in Europe and Central Asia to 20.3% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 26.5% in East Asia and Pacific, 27.5% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 31.7% in South Asia and 35.2% in Sub-Saharan Africa. Sub-Saharan Africa thus has the highest hardship although South Asia has the highest out-of-pocket share. Where incomes are low, even a modest payment can consume much of what remains after basic needs, though this is context and not a result. In Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, hardship rose slightly between 2015 and 2022, and in North America it was nearly flat, from 7.4% to 7.5%. Hardship estimates rest on household surveys fielded irregularly, and only 3 countries report for 2024, so the regional values carry wider uncertainty than the service index.

The spread among countries on the service index narrowed. The Gini coefficient, weighted by population, fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.030 to 0.024. Yet the share of the Theil index lying between regions was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, essentially unchanged. About seven-tenths of the inequality in coverage is therefore associated with which region a country belongs to, and the narrowing has come with a rise across the distribution rather than a dissolving of regional divides. National averages hide this structure, and gains should be judged against the regional floor from which each country starts.

### Coverage gains were modest and financial protection moved unevenly

Financial protection improved only slightly at the global level between 2015 and 2023, and the movement was uneven. The world share of current health expenditure paid directly by households fell from 18.4% in 2015 to 17.3% in 2023. The share of people facing financial hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on out-of-pocket health costs, fell from 28.0% in 2015 to 26.0% in 2022. Both movements are in the right direction, but they are small beside the scale of the problem. More than one person in four is still above the hardship threshold in 2022, the latest year of the world aggregate.

The out-of-pocket share fell most where it began highest. South Asia dropped from 64.3% in 2015 to 46.6% in 2023, and the lower middle income group from 58.3% to 47.0%. Low income countries moved from 53.0% to 44.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa fell to 30.4% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan to 28.3%. These reductions began from very high levels, and in South Asia nearly half of health spending is still paid at the point of care. In East Asia and Pacific the share edged up from 25.7% to 26.0%, and in Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 28.2% to 29.7%. Europe and Central Asia (17.8% to 16.5%), North America (11.9% to 11.1%) and high income countries (14.4% to 13.4%) declined modestly from low bases. Whether the fall in South Asia contributes to the narrowing of coverage differences between countries has not been tested here.

The hardship measure tells a different story from the spending share, and the difference matters. East Asia and Pacific shows a clear fall in hardship, from 30.0% to 26.5%, although its out-of-pocket share did not fall. The two measures are therefore not interchangeable: hardship depends on household budgets, prices and the burden of illness as well as on how the system is financed. Hardship rose in Europe and Central Asia from 12.6% to 13.0%, in Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.5% to 20.3%, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 27.0% to 27.5%. North America was nearly flat, moving from 7.4% to 7.5%, and high income countries moved from 9.5% to 9.7%. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the highest at 35.2% in 2022, down from 38.7%, and South Asia stood at 31.7%, down from 35.7%. Low income countries fell from 38.5% to 34.7% and lower middle income countries from 34.4% to 31.5%, while upper middle income countries moved from 26.5% to 24.9%. The pattern does not follow coverage in a uniform way: hardship fell in East Asia and Pacific, a region of relatively high coverage, and rose in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, a region of lower coverage.

The country-level classification shows the unevenness. Of 72 countries with enough hardship data for a trend assessment, 27 are on track or have met the direction, holding 34.0% of the population of those countries. A further 9 show moderate progress needing acceleration (9.5%) and 4 show marginal progress (22.7%). One country is stagnant, and 31 are regressing, holding 33.7% of the assessed population. The regressing group is thus of similar size and population weight to the on-track group (27 countries, 34.0%). No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures only direction of travel and not distance to a defined goal; target 3.8 can be read as a call for financial risk protection for all, which leaves open what level of hardship would count as acceptable.

Public funding appears to matter. Across 21 countries with data for both series, the share of people in hardship is negatively associated with the share of health spending funded from domestic government sources. The rank correlation is -0.525 for 2022 levels and -0.258 for changes between 2015 and 2022. The level association is moderate and the association for changes is weak. This is association rather than proof of cause: richer countries tend to have both higher public shares and lower hardship, and the weaker link in changes suggests that a higher public share does not by itself reduce hardship, whose course also depends on what is covered, on prices and on who is reached.

The evidence base is uneven. Hardship has thinner coverage than the service index, with 3 countries reporting in 2024 against 22 for the out-of-pocket share, so regional aggregates rest on survey years that differ between countries. Movements of one or two points in a regional hardship figure should be read with caution.

### At the current pace, 2030 will be missed, and proposals follow

The trend assessment leaves little room for optimism about 2030. It was run against a single yardstick, a target of 100 index points, and its sensitivity to any other threshold was not tested. Target 3.8 sets no numerical threshold, and 100 index points is a convention that no health system has reached in practice, so the assessment is severe by construction. On that reading, no country is on track for the UHC service coverage index: 0 of 193 countries assessed are on track or have met the target. Only 2 countries, holding 17.3% of the population, show moderate progress that would still need acceleration. A further 102 countries, holding 64.7% of the population, show marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Another 57 countries, holding 11.0% of the population, stagnate, and 32 countries, holding 7.0% of the population, regress. Most of the world's people therefore live in countries where coverage is rising too slowly to reach the target on the 2015 to 2023 pace. The endpoints alone do not show whether the period after 2020 slowed or quickened progress.

The projections show the scale of the shortfall, and they are conditional on the 2015 to 2023 pace continuing. The world is projected to reach 73.7 index points in 2030, covering a ratio of 0.18 of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 54.8 index points, with a ratio of 0.18, and low-income countries at 46.2, with a ratio of 0.09. Lower middle income countries are projected at 67.6, with a ratio of 0.25. South Asia has the highest ratio of any region, 0.40, and is projected at 75.9 index points in 2030, still short of the target. Latin America and the Caribbean is projected to stay at 79.0, a ratio of 0.00, the same as its 2023 value, so no gain on the 2015 baseline is expected. High-income countries are projected at 86.9 with a ratio of 0.21, and North America at 88.9; both remain below 100. The gap between the poorest and richest groups therefore does not close on current trends.

Financial protection tells a more divided story. The hardship indicator could be assessed for 72 countries, the number with enough data for a trend assessment; this is the sample for that series only, not a comparison with the index. Of these, 27 countries, holding 34.0% of their population, are on track or have met the target. Another 9, holding 9.5%, show moderate progress. Against this, 31 countries, holding 33.7% of their population, are regressing, and 4 more, holding 22.7%, show marginal progress. Only 1 country stagnates. The regressing group is of similar size to the on-track group in both countries and population. Coverage of services is advancing too slowly almost everywhere, while financial protection is improving in some countries and deteriorating in others, so the two cannot be assumed to move together.

Public financing is a plausible lever, though the data do not prove it. Across 21 countries with data for both series from 2015 to 2022, the rank correlation between the level of financial hardship and the domestic government share of current health expenditure was -0.52. Countries that fund more of their health spending from public sources tend to have fewer households in hardship. The rank correlation between the changes in the two series was weaker, at -0.26, so a rise in public financing did not reliably accompany a fall in hardship within the period. The sample is small and the association is not proof of cause. As context outside these results, health-policy experience generally holds that pooled, prepaid funding protects households better than direct payment at the point of care.

The following proposals follow from these findings.

w-c03-2-4~ewan/writer-2~103.text:
### Stunting and wasting set against the 2025 and 2030 targets

The world has moved only slightly towards the internationally agreed nutrition targets since 2015. Stunting, measured as the share of children under five whose height for age is more than two standard deviations below the international reference median, stood at 24.6% in 2015 and 23.2% in 2024 on the modelled estimate. Wasting, the share whose weight for height falls equally far below the reference median, moved from 7.1% to 6.6% over the same period. Neither series is shown here at annual resolution, so no break after 2015 can be identified. The latest year available is 2024, so the effects of the shocks that followed 2020 on food prices, health services and household incomes cannot be separated from the underlying slow decline.

The two indicators describe different conditions and should not be read as one. Stunting reflects chronic deprivation: poor maternal nutrition, repeated infection, inadequate diets in the first two years of life and limited access to water and sanitation. It accumulates over months and years and is difficult to reverse after early childhood, which is why its decline is gradual even where conditions improve. Wasting reflects acute loss of weight, driven by recent illness, famine, conflict or sudden shortfalls in food. It can rise and fall within a season, so a national survey taken at one moment may record a figure that differs from the annual average. A wasting prevalence of 6.6% therefore carries more uncertainty about timing than a stunting prevalence of 23.2%.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. The text of Target 2.2 asks that the internationally agreed targets on stunting and wasting be achieved by 2025, and that all forms of malnutrition end by 2030. The bench's trend tool applies a ceiling of 5.0% by 2030 to both series and projects towards 2030 rather than 2025. That ceiling is a computational convention, not a statement of the agreed stunting benchmark, which is framed as a reduction against a baseline and for which no threshold is held among the facts here; other readings of the benchmark exist and none is quoted as a result. Under the strict reading of the target text, the 2025 deadline falls one year after the latest observation, and with wasting at 6.6% in 2024 and stunting at 23.2%, the 2025 milestone is unlikely to have been met for either indicator under the 5.0% ceiling. Under the trend tool's reading, the question is whether the ceiling is within reach by 2030. The two readings point the same way for 2025 but allow different times, and this book states which is in use wherever a projection is quoted.

For wasting, the world figure of 6.6% in 2024 lies above the 5.0% ceiling. The fall from 7.1% in 2015 is small beside the distance that remains, and the ceiling is unlikely to be reached by continuing at the recent pace. This is a rough inference from the two end-point values, not a projection computed by the tool for the world. For stunting, the trend calculation puts the world at 22.3% in 2030 if the observed rate continues, with a ratio of observed to required pace of 0.12, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. A fall from 24.6% to 23.2% over nine years leaves the world far from a level that could be described as ending the condition.

Why this matters goes beyond the numbers. Children who are stunted face poorer cognitive development, lower school attainment and reduced earnings in adulthood, and severe wasting sharply raises the risk of death in early childhood. A near-flat global line therefore signals a persistent loss of human potential in each new cohort, not merely a missed statistical goal. The links to other Goals are direct: health, education, water and sanitation, and poverty reduction all shape the figures above.

A further caution concerns the global figures themselves. The stunting series is a modelled estimate that combines survey data with statistical methods to fill years without a survey, and the wasting series is built from survey data in which only 6 countries report for 2024. The global picture is therefore a reasonable guide to the direction and approximate scale of change, but small differences between years should not be treated as real movements. The direction is consistent across the readings of the target, although the distance to 2030 cannot be stated precisely: progress since 2015 has been real but slow, and the world does not appear to be on course for either target.

### Regional differences in stunting and wasting

Behind the modest world average lies a wide spread of regional experience. South Asia carries the heaviest burden on both measures. Its stunting prevalence fell from 37.8% in 2015 to 31.5% in 2024, yet nearly one child in three under five remains stunted. Its wasting prevalence stood at 15.7% in 2024, against 16.6% in 2015, a small reduction. Wasting in South Asia is therefore far above the world figure of 6.6% in 2024. Low birth weight, early marriage and adolescent pregnancy, limited dietary diversity and sanitation deficits are commonly cited as causes acting on stunting and wasting together; the series themselves do not test them.

Sub-Saharan Africa presents a different pattern. Stunting declined only from 34.4% in 2015 to 32.3% in 2024. The region, which had a lower rate than South Asia in 2015, ended the period with a slightly higher one (32.3% against 31.5%). Wasting fell more clearly, from 7.0% to 5.9%. The contrast suggests that acute malnutrition, which responds to treatment programmes and seasonal relief, can improve faster than chronic growth failure, which depends on maternal health, diets, sanitation and incomes over many years. Population growth also means that a falling prevalence can coexist with a rising number of affected children, a distinction the prevalence series cannot show.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 27.5% to 24.1% in stunting and from 6.5% to 5.6% in wasting. Conflict, displacement and fiscal stress in parts of this heterogeneous grouping may weigh against the gains, and the regional average conceals very different national circumstances. East Asia and Pacific moved from 14.5% to 13.3% in stunting, a slow decline, and its wasting rate barely changed, from 3.7% to 3.6%.

Europe and Central Asia is the clearest example of steady improvement. Stunting fell from 6.0% to 4.6%, and wasting from 1.5% to 1.0%. For stunting, the trend calculation classes the region as on track for the 5.0% ceiling that the tool applies by 2030, with an expected value of 3.8%, although the level was already close to that mark in 2015. The 5.0% figure is the tool's reference level, not necessarily the agreed stunting benchmark, which can be read in more than one way. Latin America and the Caribbean, by contrast, was flat: stunting stood at 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, which the trend calculation classes as regression. Wasting there eased from 1.5% to 1.3%. Economic disruption after 2020 and the uneven recovery of poorer households' incomes are plausible contributors, offered as context only, since the series do not isolate causes.

North America shows a rise in stunting from 2.8% in 2015 to 4.1% in 2024, while wasting fell from 0.3% to 0.2%. The trend tool labels the region as on track because its level lies below the reference value, but the direction is adverse. The levels are low, the regional average rests on few countries, and modelled estimates for populations with small samples carry wide uncertainty. The rise should be read as a signal worth checking rather than a settled finding. High-income countries as a group moved from 3.9% to 4.0%.

Income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries began at 38.0% stunting in 2015 and ended at 35.8% in 2024, still the highest level of any group listed. Their wasting rate fell from 7.9% to 6.4%. Lower-middle-income countries show the strongest stunting decline, from 33.9% to 28.9%, but their wasting stood at 9.5% in 2024, down from 10.5%. This is the highest among income groups, though South Asia, at 15.7%, is higher among regions; the lower-middle figure may reflect the weight of South Asia within the group. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 11.9% to 10.8% in stunting and from 2.6% to 2.1% in wasting. High-income countries held wasting at 0.4% in 2024, down from 0.6%.

The gradient by income is steep: stunting in 2024 was 35.8% in low-income countries and 4.0% in high-income countries. The lower-middle group shows that faster decline is possible without rich-country incomes, which points to the possible role of health, water, sanitation and social protection policy.

Two cautions apply. The trend summary for some groups is truncated in the output available, so the lower-middle-income and South Asia readings use the levels and expected values. The wasting summary also reports only 6 countries reporting in 2024, against 162 for stunting, so recent regional wasting figures rest on thin and uneven observation.

For 2030, the regional pattern implies that the global figure will be decided largely in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The expected 2030 stunting values from the trend calculation are 27.9% for South Asia and 31.0% for Sub-Saharan Africa, both well above the 5.0% reference level. Only Europe and Central Asia, and the high-income group, sit at or near it.

### Country progress on wasting and the absence of convergence in stunting

Wasting presents a more differentiated national picture than stunting. The trend assessment covered 65 countries against a reference ceiling of 5.0% by 2030. That ceiling is the one the trend tool applies to both indicators; it is one reading of the benchmark, and the agreed benchmarks may be read more strictly. Of the countries assessed, 42, holding 38.6% of their combined population, were on track or had already met the reference level. Four countries, with 7.8% of that population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Three countries showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration, and these three hold 33.7% of the population. No country was classed as stagnating, while 16 countries, with 19.9% of the population, were regressing, that is, wasting was rising rather than falling.

The population shares matter as much as the country counts. A simple count suggests that most assessed countries are doing well, since 42 of 65 is a majority. Weighted by population, the picture is less comfortable. The three countries in the marginal class hold a third of the assessed population. It is a conjecture, not a finding, that the burden is concentrated in a few large countries: the results do not name them and this cannot be confirmed here. The shares of the marginal and regressing classes, 33.7% and 19.9%, add to roughly 53.6%, which is the reader's own approximate sum from rounded shares. It exceeds the 38.6% living where the level is within reach.

Three cautions apply. First, only 65 countries were assessed, although the underlying series cover 162 countries. The assessment depends on enough survey observations to draw a trend, and countries without them are absent from every class. Second, the 5.0% ceiling is not the only way to read the target: other thresholds for 2025 and 2030 have been proposed, and a country counted as on track against 5.0% may still fall short of a stricter one. Third, wasting is volatile. It responds quickly to famine, conflict, floods, disease outbreaks and seasonal food shortages, so a single survey can show a sharp change that does not reflect a lasting one. Regression may reflect a recent crisis, and on-track status may reflect a favourable survey year.

The results do not show why countries regressed, but well-established context points to likely factors. Conflict and displacement disrupt health services and food supply. Price shocks after the pandemic of 2020 and later disturbances to grain and fertiliser markets may have reduced the quality and quantity of children's diets in poorer households. Where treatment for severe acute malnutrition depends on external funding, interruptions in the supply of therapeutic food have direct effects. Countries that moved towards the target have typically combined growth in household incomes with expanded primary health care, immunisation and community-based treatment of acute malnutrition.

Stunting shows a different pattern: the gaps between countries are not closing. The convergence test relates the change in stunting between 2015 and 2024 to the starting level across 162 countries. If countries with high stunting at the start improved faster, the coefficient would be clearly negative. The estimated beta is -0.00244, with a p-value of 0.2275 and an R-squared of 0.0085. The sign points to a slight tendency towards convergence, but the estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 1% of the variation in later change. A country's initial stunting rate says almost nothing about how fast it improved.

The coefficient of variation, which measures dispersion relative to the average, rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Dispersion between countries has therefore widened in relative terms. This is consistent with the lack of convergence: the world average has fallen only slightly while some countries have moved much faster than others. A rising coefficient of variation does not by itself show that high-prevalence countries worsened; it shows that the spread, relative to the mean, grew.

For 2030 the two measures call for different responses. Wasting appears to be a problem of a minority of countries that sit well off course, while many others are already within reach. Stunting is a slow, structural condition tied to maternal health, early-life diet, sanitation and poverty, and the absence of convergence implies that no general catching-up process can be relied on. Without deliberate targeting of the countries with the highest prevalence, the relative gap may go on widening towards 2030; this is conjecture drawn from the 2015 to 2024 pattern, not a finding and not a computed projection.

### Data coverage and the limits of the evidence

Wasting is measured mainly by household surveys, not by continuous registration, and the evidence behind the series is thinner than the regional table suggests. In 2000, 58 countries reported a wasting value. The count fell to 22 in 2001 and varied between 24 and 51 in later years. It stood at 32 in 2015, rose to 48 in 2018 and 46 in 2019, then fell to 26 in 2020. In 2024 only 6 countries reported. Across the whole period 162 countries reported at least once, so the series covers most of the world, but not in any single year.

The counts alone do not show why a given year is thin. A plausible explanation, offered as context and not shown by the series, is the survey cycle: household surveys are fielded every few years in each country, and results are published with a delay. On that reading, the low count for 2024 would reflect results not yet processed, not fewer children measured, and it is no evidence of improvement or decline. The dip to 26 countries in 2020 coincides with the pandemic, when fieldwork was suspended or postponed in many places, but the results give only the count, so the link is likely and not established. Readers comparing 2015 with 2024 should accept that the later point is the less complete one.

The regional and income-group values for 2024 are consequently not simple averages of fresh observations. They are aggregates that, on well-established practice, combine recent surveys with modelled estimates for countries and years without a survey. The figure of 6.6% for the world in 2024, and the regional values around it, probably rest in large part on that modelling. The fall from 7.1% in 2015 is a fall in the estimate, but its size is small relative to the uncertainty that such modelling carries. Changes of that scale between two years should not be treated as established.

The caution applies most strongly where reporting is thinnest. In regions with many countries and uneven survey schedules, notably Sub-Saharan Africa, an aggregate can move because of which countries happened to be surveyed as well as because of nutrition. The fall in that region from 7.0% in 2015 to 5.9% in 2024 is larger than the fall in the world figure, and it would be unwise to attribute it wholly to improved child nutrition without national survey evidence. In South Asia, where the prevalence is highest among regions at 15.7% in 2024, a few large countries may weigh heavily in the aggregate, so that one survey round could shift the regional figure; the results do not show the weights. By contrast, high-income countries and North America, at 0.4% and 0.2% in 2024, have low values whose precision matters little for the argument.

Wasting has a further difficulty that stunting lacks. It is a short-lived condition: a child can be wasted during a hungry season or an illness and recover within weeks. Its prevalence depends on the month in which a survey is fielded, so two surveys in the same country in different seasons can differ for reasons unrelated to policy. Single-year comparisons are therefore weaker for wasting than for stunting, which reflects accumulated deprivation and changes slowly.

For the 2030 assessment these limits matter in two ways. A judgement that a country is on track rests on its own survey history, and countries with long gaps between surveys cannot be assessed with confidence. The 5.0% ceiling used by the trend tool is one reading of the benchmark, not a settled one. The world and regional aggregates should be taken as indications of direction, not as precise measures of distance from that ceiling. Where the series is sparse, the more reliable evidence is the national survey record, and the count of reporting countries should be read alongside every figure quoted in this section.

### What the trajectories imply for 2030, and proposals

At the observed rates, the world will not reach a stunting prevalence of 5.0% by 2030. That figure is the ceiling the trend tool applies to stunting; it is one reading of the agreed benchmarks, which may be read more strictly, and it is not quoted here as the agreed target itself. Global stunting stood at 23.2% in 2024, and the trend projection gives 22.3% in 2030, a ratio of 0.12 against the pace the ceiling requires. The assessment class for the world is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The 2025 milestone in the target text will also be missed on this evidence.

Three groups are classed as on track for stunting. Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.0% in 2015 to 4.6% in 2024, and its projected 2030 value is 3.8%, a ratio of 2.13, the fastest relative pace of any region. High-income countries stood at 3.9% in 2015 and 4.0% in 2024, and North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%. The last two are classed as on track only because their levels already lie below the ceiling of 5.0%. The classification reflects a level, not a gain. The North America rise is small and rests on data of uncertain reliability, so it should be checked before any conclusion is drawn about child growth in wealthy countries.

East Asia and Pacific is classed as marginal. Its prevalence fell from 14.5% to 13.3% and the projection for 2030 is 12.6%, a ratio of 0.20. Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as regression: 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, with 12.4% projected for 2030. A middle-income region with food available in aggregate has therefore made no progress on stunting over the period. Possible causes, stated as context and not shown by these series, include the quality of diets in early childhood, maternal health, sanitation and inequality within countries, which regional averages conceal.

The regions with the highest levels are furthest from the ceiling. South Asia is projected at 27.9% in 2030, a ratio of 0.30, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 31.0%, a ratio of 0.12. Low-income countries are projected at 34.4%, from 38.0% in 2015 and 35.8% in 2024. Lower middle-income countries fell from 33.9% to 28.9%, with 25.9% projected for 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is projected at 22.1%, from 24.1% in 2024. Each would still hold stunting at several times the ceiling in 2030. Population growth is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, so a slow fall in prevalence there could coincide with a rising number of affected children, which the prevalence series cannot show.

Wasting offers a less bleak picture in country counts but a troubling one at the margin. Of 65 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the 5.0% ceiling, while 16 show regression, holding 19.9% of the population assessed. Three countries, holding 33.7% of that population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. The results do not name these countries, so what drives their classes cannot be read from them. Wasting responds quickly to drought, conflict, price surges and disease, so a country can change class within a year or two.

Neither the period since 2015 nor the disruptions after 2020 can be read cleanly from these series. Survey reporting fell to 26 countries in 2020 and to 6 in 2024. A pandemic interruption and a publication lag are plausible explanations, but the counts alone do not establish either. Recent wasting values rest on very few new observations, and modelled stunting estimates for 2024 lean on earlier surveys. A trend between 2015 and 2024 describes the direction of the estimates, not a verified count of children. The direction for 2030 is consistent across the regional and income readings, but the distance cannot be stated precisely, because it depends on the tool ceiling and on thin data. The wasting verdict is a rough inference from country classes and not a computed world projection.

w-c07-2-1~cedar/writer-2~103.text:
### Global access to basic sanitation reached 82.2 per cent in 2024

Basic sanitation, defined as an improved facility not shared with other households, reached 82.2 per cent of the world's population in 2024, up from 72.6 per cent in 2015. The series covers 193 countries in 2024, so the global figure rests on near-complete reporting. Open defecation fell over the same period from 10.6 per cent to 4.3 per cent of the population. Handwashing is measured less fully: the share of people with a handwashing facility with soap and water on the premises was 78.0 per cent in 2024, against 68.8 per cent in 2017, the first year for which a world value exists. Only 91 countries reported handwashing in 2024, so that global figure is a weaker basis for judgement than the other two.

The shares can be turned into rough numbers of people by applying them to the 2025 population of about 8.2 billion (8,215,424,893). The result is an approximation that mixes years, since the shares refer to 2024 and the population to 2025, and the World Bank series do not supply a head count directly. On that basis, the 17.8 per cent without basic sanitation corresponds to roughly 1.5 billion people, the 4.3 per cent still defecating in the open to roughly 360 million, and the 22.0 per cent without basic handwashing facilities to roughly 1.8 billion. These are orders of magnitude, not counts, and should be read as such.

The pace matters for 2030. Open defecation more than halved in nine years, a considerable achievement, yet the target of ending the practice requires the remaining share to reach effectively zero within six years, and the last fraction is usually the hardest to reach because it is concentrated in poor, remote and marginalised households. Population growth also works against progress: the world added about 770 million people between 2015 and 2025, so service has had to expand faster than numbers alone suggest.

The wording of the target requires care. Target 6.2 calls for adequate and equitable sanitation and hygiene for all, and the phrase can be read as basic service, as safely managed service in which excreta are safely disposed of or treated, or as something stricter still. The indicators used in this part measure only the basic level, together with open defecation and handwashing. Reaching basic coverage therefore does not show that the target's higher reading has been met, and the equity and gender dimensions of the wording are not visible in global averages.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries carry the largest deficits

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group stand furthest from the target of adequate sanitation for all. In 2024, 37.1 per cent of people in Sub-Saharan Africa used at least basic sanitation, up from 30.8 per cent in 2015. The low-income group moved from 29.2 per cent to 33.3 per cent over the same years. Both remain far below the world figure of 82.2 per cent, and the change in nine years was small beside the distance still to be covered.

Open defecation shows the same pattern. In Sub-Saharan Africa 15.5 per cent of the population still defecated in the open in 2024, down from 22.0 per cent in 2015. Low-income countries stood at 17.2 per cent in 2024, against 24.6 per cent in 2015. These are the highest rates of any region or income group in the data. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 22.1 per cent to 7.3 per cent, and upper-middle-income countries from 2.4 per cent to 0.4 per cent.

Handwashing is weakest in the same places. Basic handwashing facilities with soap and water reached 25.0 per cent of people in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2024, against 23.0 per cent in 2015, and 24.6 per cent in low-income countries, against 21.8 per cent. The world figure was 78.0 per cent in 2024. Handwashing coverage is thinner than the other series, with 91 countries reporting in 2024. Regional series for Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America are not reported in the handwashing result, so no comparison with them can be drawn here, and the East Asia and Pacific series begins in 2017 rather than 2015.

The contrast with South Asia is instructive. That region rose from 56.8 per cent to 82.0 per cent in basic sanitation and cut open defecation from 27.2 per cent to 5.8 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa began 2015 with a lower access rate and a similar level of open defecation, but moved much more slowly. East Asia and Pacific rose from 83.7 per cent to 94.8 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia from 95.7 per cent to 97.4 per cent. North America stood at 99.5 per cent in 2024, 99.7 per cent in 2015, with no open defecation recorded.

Population growth works against the African gains. The population of Sub-Saharan Africa grew from 1,024,659,421 in 2015 to 1,321,654,217 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 584,512,207 to 767,490,169. A rising share of users can coexist with a large and growing number of people left without service, because new facilities must first serve the added population. The data cited do not separate this effect from others, and the population series ends in 2025 while the sanitation series ends in 2024. Well-established context points to low public investment, rapid urbanisation, and weak sanitation services in informal settlements, but the results do not test these explanations.

For 2030, the gap between these groups and the target is the central concern. At the pace seen since 2015, neither Sub-Saharan Africa nor the low-income group would approach universal access, and ending open defecation by 2030 looks out of reach for them on the evidence given. Target 6.2 can also be read in more than one way: basic sanitation is a lower standard than the adequate sanitation the target text names, so the figures here may flatter the position.

### Progress since 2015 was driven by South Asia, and handwashing lags

The fall in open defecation since 2015 is largely a South Asian change, though the data show only the trajectories, not their causes. South Asia's rate of change in open defecation was -0.1573 a year, which would cover a ratio of 0.92 of the distance from its 2015 level to zero by 2030, and the series is expected to reach 2.1 per cent of the population in 2030. Latin America & Caribbean (rate -0.1638, ratio 0.93) and East Asia & Pacific (rate -0.1416, ratio 0.90) show similar paths from much lower levels, and the upper middle income group is the fastest (rate -0.1751, ratio 0.94). The world as a whole, at a rate of -0.0947 and a ratio of 0.78, is classed as making moderate progress and needing acceleration, with 2.4 per cent of the population still expected to defecate in the open in 2030.

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group follow a different course. Their rates of change are -0.0386 and -0.0387 a year, with ratios of 0.45, and both are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. At these rates open defecation would still affect 12.2 per cent of people in Sub-Saharan Africa and 13.6 per cent in the low-income group in 2030. Because the global figure is weighted by population, a large decline in a populous region can mask slow movement elsewhere, which is the pattern these results show. Large-scale sanitation campaigns, rural latrine programmes and rising incomes are commonly cited as influences on such declines, but the series do not identify what drove any of these changes; these explanations remain hypotheses.

Country classes give a fuller picture. For open defecation, 33 countries are on track or have met the target, holding 38.1 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 50 more show moderate progress (44.3 per cent). Another 36 countries show marginal progress (13.2 per cent), 20 stagnate (3.5 per cent) and 8 regress (0.8 per cent), out of 147 assessed. Shares of population and counts of countries differ, so a class with many countries can hold a small share of people, and the reverse.

Basic sanitation is more uneven. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target (46.6 per cent of their population), but 39 are regressing, and those hold 13.4 per cent of the population. A further 37 stagnate (5.8 per cent). Gains in some places are therefore offset by deterioration in others, which can occur when population growth outpaces the building of facilities, though the data do not show this.

Handwashing lags most. Of 118 countries assessed, only 15 are on track or have met the target (38.2 per cent of their population), while 59 stagnate (20.1 per cent) and 13 regress (4.6 per cent). Another 22 show marginal progress and hold 33.8 per cent of the population. Coverage is also narrower, so these results describe a smaller set of countries than the other series. For 2030, open defecation could come close to ending only with acceleration in the regions that lag, and basic sanitation and handwashing will not reach universal access on current paths.
