w-c05-8-4~juniper/writer-2~103.text:
### Education spending averages 3.6 per cent of GDP and 14 per cent of government budgets

Two measures describe how much of a country's resources goes to schooling. The first expresses general government expenditure on education as a share of gross domestic product, and shows the weight of public education in the whole economy. The second expresses the same expenditure as a share of total government expenditure, and shows the priority given to education within the public budget. The two can diverge: a government may hold education's place in its budget steady while the economy, and the budget with it, changes in size.

On the first measure, the world figure was 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 3.6 per cent in 2023. The period includes the shock of 2020, when output contracted in most economies and public budgets were redirected towards health and income support, which is context and not something these series show. The country classification indicates that the fall was widespread: of 186 countries assessed, 98 regressed on this measure. Coverage matters here: the latest year nominally available is 2025, but only 2 countries reported GDP-share data for that year, so the most recent usable world figure is for 2023.

On the second measure, the picture is different. The world share of government expenditure was 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, essentially unchanged. For this series 60 countries reported in 2025, a much fuller recent record than for the GDP share, though the world aggregate shown here also ends in 2023.

The two results can be set side by side without contradiction, but they cannot be read as a single verdict. No result here shows public spending relative to GDP or the country mix behind the world aggregate, so the reasons for the divergence are not established; possible explanations, such as a change in the size of government budgets relative to the economy, are context only and are not supported by these results. Either way, a steady budget share does not guarantee that schools are better financed in relation to national income. Neither series shows spending per pupil, which depends on the number of children, on prices and on the exchange rate.

Neither target sets a numeric benchmark for these indicators. Target 4.1 concerns completion of free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education, and target 4.c concerns the supply of qualified teachers; spending is an input to both, not a measure of either. Judgements here therefore rest on direction of change alone. Taking an increase in spending as the desired direction, the fall in the GDP share after 2015 is an adverse movement, and the flat budget share is neither progress nor retreat. Reaching either target by 2030 would be harder on a shrinking base of public resources, a point developed in the parts that follow.

### Regions differ by two percentage points of GDP, and country spread is widening

Regional averages of public education spending span roughly two percentage points of GDP. North America spent 4.8 per cent of GDP in 2022, almost unchanged from 4.8 per cent in 2015. Europe and Central Asia stood at 4.6 per cent in 2022, down from 4.8 per cent in 2015. At the other end, South Asia spent 2.9 per cent in 2024, up slightly from 2.7 per cent in 2015, and Sub-Saharan Africa spent 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent in 2015. The regional ranking has changed little since 2015, with North America and Europe and Central Asia at the top and South Asia at the bottom.

The movements after 2015 differ by region. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows the largest rise, from 3.7 per cent in 2015 to 4.4 per cent in 2022, and South Asia rose modestly. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 4.4 per cent to 3.8 per cent in 2023, a period that includes the fiscal strain of the pandemic and its aftermath, offered here as context and not as a finding of the results. East Asia and Pacific stood at 3.5 per cent in 2015 and 3.5 per cent in 2023. The world figure fell from 4.2 per cent in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023, alongside declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, Europe and Central Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and the lower-middle-income group. The results do not analyse the composition of the world aggregate, so they cannot say which regions account for most of the fall.

The ordering changes when spending is measured against the budget rather than the economy. Latin America and the Caribbean devoted 16.6 per cent of government expenditure to education in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa 15.4 per cent in 2024, whereas North America devoted 10.7 per cent in 2022 and Europe and Central Asia 11.7 per cent in 2022. The comparison mixes 2022 and 2024 values, because the latest year reported differs by region. The regions that rank lowest or middling on the share of GDP therefore rank highest on the share of the budget. The results hold no data on revenue or age structure, so they do not show why the two orderings differ.

The spread among countries has widened. The population-weighted Gini coefficient of spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.181 in 2015 to 0.210 in 2020 and 0.230 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.091 and then 0.110 over the same years. The share of this inequality lying between regions was 23.8 per cent in 2015 and 27.0 per cent in 2020, then fell to 10.5 per cent in 2023, on a smaller sample of countries. A lower between-region share means more of the inequality lies within regions, but the fall coincides with the drop in reporting and should be read with care.

A caution applies to the 2023 comparison. The 2023 figures cover 121 countries against 164 in 2015, and the countries that did not report are not known to be a random subset. The rise in inequality may therefore partly reflect who reported rather than what was spent. The direction from 2015 to 2020, when 164 and 170 countries reported, rests on a more stable sample than the level reached in 2023.

### Most countries regressed, and the two measures move together only moderately

Classified against a trajectory towards higher spending, most countries moved the wrong way. Of 186 countries assessed on the share of GDP, 98 regressed, and these hold 62.3 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 40 were on track or had met the direction of travel, covering 11.1 per cent of that population. The remainder were spread across moderate progress (14 countries), marginal progress (20 countries) and stagnation (14 countries). No numerical target exists for either measure, so the classes describe direction and pace, not distance from a goal; the reading depends on the assumption that an increase is the desired movement.

The budget share shows a harsher pattern. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 regressed, holding 78.2 per cent of the population, while 29 were on track, holding 7.1 per cent. Stagnation affected 23 countries with 10.5 per cent of the population. On both measures the population share of regression exceeds the country share, which suggests that populous countries are among those regressing; the results do not identify which countries these are, nor their school-age populations.

Spending levels did not draw together. Across 146 countries, the regression of change in the GDP share on its 2015 level gave a beta of -0.00559 (p 0.64, R2 0.004), which is indistinguishable from no convergence. Low spenders did not catch up, and high spenders did not fall back. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.379 in 2015 to 0.449 in 2022, so dispersion widened in relative terms. This matters for target 4.c and target 4.1, since teacher supply and free schooling depend on a stable funding base.

The two measures are related, but only moderately. Across 131 countries, the Spearman correlation of changes between 2015 and 2022 was 0.415, and that of 2022 levels was 0.468. These are associations, not causes. A fall in the GDP share is therefore only partly accompanied by a lower priority for education within the budget. As context, a country may keep its budget share while the public sector shrinks relative to output, or output may rise faster than outlays during recovery; education may also gain priority within a budget that is itself contracting.

These data cannot identify causes. The periods after 2015 and after 2020 included commodity price falls, pandemic spending on health and income support, rising debt service and, in some cases, rapid growth in GDP that diluted ratios, but which of these shaped each country's result cannot be read from two ratios. The classification also rests on trend fitting for short and gappy series. For 2030, the pattern implies that present trajectories will not lift spending in most countries, and that improving one measure does not guarantee the other.

### Reaching 2030 requires reversing the fall in spending and improving reporting

The implication for 2030 is that targets 4.1 and 4.c are paid for from public budgets. Free primary and secondary schooling and a larger supply of qualified teachers both require sustained financing. The world figure for public education spending stood at 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 and at 3.6 per cent in 2023. Neither target sets a numerical spending level, so the direction of travel is the only yardstick available. Taking an increase in spending as the desired direction, the fall in the share of GDP is adverse, and a fall of that size may leave less room for hiring, training and retaining teachers. The share of government expenditure tells a steadier story: 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023.

The fall is visible in several groups, and the lowest starting points deserve attention. South Asia, at 2.9 per cent of GDP in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent in 2015, remain below the world figure. Low income countries spent 3.0 per cent in 2022, against 3.2 per cent in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 4.1 per cent to 3.4 per cent between 2015 and 2023. Declines also appear in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Europe and Central Asia, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and South Asia, recorded rises. The results hold no population weights for regions, so they cannot show which changes drove the world figure. Regional values for the budget share mix years, some for 2022 and others for 2024, and should be read as approximate. The value for 2025 rests on a small number of reporters and is not used for regions.

Monitoring is also weakening. The number of countries reporting the share of GDP rose to 171 in 2017 and stood at 164 in 2022, but fell to 121 in 2023 and to 40 in 2024, with only 2 in 2025. Part of this is the ordinary lag of reporting, and the latest years will fill in. Even so, any reading of the period after 2020 rests on a thinning sample, and the values for 2023 and 2024 may shift when late reporters arrive. Where data are missing, the position of a country cannot be told from the figures. The series are also short, so any view of 2030 is an extrapolation of the trend since 2015, not a finding.

A further caution concerns interpretation. No single share defines adequate spending, and a country may spend a modest share of income efficiently, or a large share poorly. The share of GDP and the share of the budget answer different questions, and neither says what is spent on each child.

w-c03-3-5~loom/writer-2~104.text:
### Child overweight and anaemia in women stand at 5.5 per cent and 30.7 per cent

Two indicators of malnutrition other than stunting and wasting are measured here: overweight among children under five, and anaemia among women of reproductive age. Target 2.2 names all forms of malnutrition and the nutritional needs of adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, yet its numerical benchmarks cover only stunting and wasting. The two indicators therefore describe parts of the target that carry no quantified goal in the wording given. The overweight series is scored in this section against a reference value of 3.0 per cent by 2030, which is a working benchmark of the bench's trend tool and not a value written into the target. The anaemia series is scored by the same tool without any target value, so its classes describe direction of change and not distance from an agreed goal.

In 2024 the world prevalence of child overweight, defined as weight for height more than two standard deviations above the WHO 2006 median, was 5.5 per cent of children under five, up from 5.2 per cent in 2015. The rise is small, but it runs against the direction the reference value implies. The estimate rests on 163 countries reporting in 2024. It is a modelled estimate, so year-to-year movements are smoothed and partly reflect the model rather than fresh surveys, especially in countries that are surveyed only every few years.

Anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 is far more common. In 2023 the world prevalence was 30.7 per cent, against 28.0 per cent in 2015. The measure combines non-pregnant women with haemoglobin below 12 g/dL and pregnant women below 11 g/dL, and 192 countries are covered. Nearly one woman in three of reproductive age is therefore anaemic, a share that is large but not a majority. The condition matters for maternal health, for birth outcomes and for the nutrition of the next generation of children.

Both world averages were higher at the latest year than in 2015. A rise in child overweight is not necessarily a failure of the same kind as a rise in anaemia, since the two reflect different diets and health conditions. Even so, the direction of both world figures is adverse. Haemoglobin measurement also depends on altitude, smoking and survey method, and country estimates are modelled where surveys are scarce. The levels reported here should be read as well-founded orders of magnitude, not as exact counts. For 2030, the starting point is a world in which both burdens are larger than at the outset of the agenda.

### Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower

Regional levels of the two burdens run in opposite directions. Child overweight is lowest in South Asia, at 3.4 per cent of children under five in 2024, and highest in North America, at 9.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 8.8 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 7.8 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa records 3.8 per cent. Anaemia among women aged 15 to 49 reverses the order: North America has the lowest prevalence, 14.9 per cent in 2023, and South Asia the highest, 51.1 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 36.7 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 35.2 per cent, whereas East Asia and the Pacific, at 18.7 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean, at 20.0 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia, at 21.3 per cent, lie near the lower end.

The pattern by income group repeats the regional one. Overweight is 3.5 per cent in low-income countries and 4.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 8.6 per cent in upper-middle-income and 8.4 per cent in high-income countries. Anaemia is 35.6 per cent in low-income and 46.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 19.8 per cent in upper-middle-income and 17.3 per cent in high-income countries. Child overweight is thus highest in the groups where anaemia is lower, and the reverse holds in the poorest regions. This does not mean that the two conditions exclude one another within a country or a household; regional averages cannot show whether both occur together. Lower overweight in the poorest groups should not be read as a sign of better nutrition, since anaemia there remains heavy.

The spread of anaemia among countries can be stated directly. Among 192 countries, weighted by population, the between-region share of the Theil index was 77.9 per cent in 2023, up from 74.1 per cent in 2015, so most of the measured inequality in anaemia lies between regions rather than within them. The Gini coefficient fell from 0.287 to 0.272 over the same years. Differences among countries have therefore narrowed slightly overall, while the part attributable to regional means has grown. The results do not identify the causes of this pattern.

### Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere

The trend classes show that movement on both indicators has mostly been in the wrong direction since 2015. Child overweight is assessed against a working benchmark of 3.0 per cent by 2030, a figure adopted for this book and not written into Target 2.2. Of the 163 countries assessed, 92, holding 66.6 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing against that working benchmark, meaning that prevalence is rising where the benchmark requires it to fall. Only 33 countries, with 21.3 per cent of the population, are on track or have already met it. A further 10 countries (2.0 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 20 (7.5 per cent) show marginal progress and 8 (2.6 per cent) are stagnant. No test of other benchmark values was run, so how the count of countries on track would change under a stricter or looser line is not established here.

Regionally, regression against the working benchmark is the most common class, with two exceptions. East Asia and Pacific, high-income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are all classed as regressing, as are the low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups. The annual rates of change are small, 0.0153 for East Asia and Pacific and 0.0165 for Latin America and the Caribbean, but they point upward in each case. South Asia shows the highest rate, at 0.0518, from a low base. Europe and Central Asia is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.11, and its expected prevalence of 7.32 per cent in 2030 remains far above 3.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the only region with moderate progress, a ratio of 0.67, and its expected 2030 level of 4.36 per cent would still be above the working benchmark. The regression ratios for low-income and lower-middle-income countries, -6.09 and -2.37, and for high-income countries, -0.36, show the size of the departure from the path the benchmark requires. At the world level the ratio is -0.21, a regression, with 5.67 per cent expected in 2030 if the straight-line trend continued. These expected values are extrapolations, not forecasts of policy effects.

Anaemia among women of reproductive age shows a more uniform picture. The trend tool applies no target value to this indicator, so its classes show only whether prevalence is falling, and there is no benchmark that could be missed. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing. Only 2 countries (1.7 per cent of the population) are classed as on track, 1 shows moderate progress, 9 show marginal progress and 18 are stagnant, so the rise is widespread but not universal. Every region and income group is classed as regressing. The world rate of change is 0.0115. Rates are highest in North America, at 0.0359, and in high-income countries, at 0.0239, and lowest in East Asia and Pacific, at 0.0023. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 0.0036 and South Asia at 0.0070, while Europe and Central Asia, at 0.0202, rises faster than both. South Asia nonetheless has the highest prevalence of any region, at 51.1 per cent in 2023.

The spread across countries narrowed slightly. The Theil index fell from 0.130 in 2015 to 0.116 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index rose from 74.1 per cent to 77.9 per cent, so most of the measured inequality among the 192 countries lies between regions rather than within them. The narrowing does not signal improvement, since prevalence rose in most countries. These data identify no causes. Changing diets, shifts in the measurement of haemoglobin and modelled estimates for countries with sparse surveys could each contribute, and none can be separated here.

### The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course

Change and level tell different stories about the two burdens. Across 162 countries, the Spearman rank correlation between changes in child overweight and changes in women's anaemia over 2015 to 2023 is -0.030, close to zero; no significance test was run, so the result shows no detectable association and nothing more. Countries where overweight rose faster were not visibly more or less likely to see anaemia rise. The Spearman rank correlation of 2023 levels is -0.469, a moderate negative association: countries with higher child overweight tend to have lower anaemia among women. This is a statistical association between levels only. The results do not show why it arises, and they give no sign that one burden displaces the other. Because the two do not move together, a response designed for one cannot be assumed to reach the other.

The outlook for 2030 is a projection and not a forecast. For child overweight, the world is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -0.207 against the book's own working benchmark of 3.0 per cent and an expected 2030 prevalence of 5.7 per cent on the current course. North America is expected to reach 10.8 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 9.7 per cent, while high-income countries are expected to reach 9.1 per cent. South Asia has the lowest level in 2024 but the fastest rate of rise, at 0.052, and is expected to reach 4.6 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 4.3 per cent, below the world figure but still a regression. Two regions depart from this pattern. Europe and Central Asia shows marginal progress, with an expected 7.3 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows moderate progress, with an expected 4.4 per cent; in neither is the working benchmark met on the current course. These projections extend a straight line fitted to 2015 to 2024 and are not forecasts of policy effects. The benchmark choice was not tested against alternatives.

For anaemia, Target 2.2 sets no numerical benchmark, so there is no commitment to be missed, and the trend tool classes countries only by direction of travel from 2015. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing; 18 are stagnant, 9 show marginal progress, 1 shows moderate progress and 2 are on track. Because no agreed benchmark underlies these classes, and no test was run of how they change if the reference is moved, they describe direction in the data and not failure against a commitment. Every region is classed as regressing, with annual rates ranging from 0.002 in East Asia and the Pacific to 0.036 in North America. Both findings rest on modelled estimates, which are revised and which smooth over years in which surveys were absent.

The findings support the proposals below, which are monitoring and targeting measures and not claims about which programmes work, since the results identify no causes.

w-c05-5-4~ewan/writer-1~104.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small and should be read with caution. In the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. The fall is not a loss for girls: it largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, since South Asia moved from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020 and lower middle income countries from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.997 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.997 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.995 in North America and 0.991 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.982. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.970 in 2015 to 0.976 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.956 to 0.958. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.061 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.868 in 2015 and 0.900 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.952 to 0.965. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.018 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.052, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. The data do not show why. One hypothesis, which these series cannot test, is that boys leave school early for paid work in some settings. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.010 to 0.982 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.993.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.122 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 and North America 1.301, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.153, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.128, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.058 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.954 to 1.029. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.794 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.735 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.301 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.992 at primary level in 2020, 0.997 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.038 at tertiary level in 2024, close to parity at the first two levels and above it at the third. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure. The spread is also reported only for 2015, so these data cannot show whether dispersion has narrowed since.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison. The shelf's results give no coverage counts for the male series, so the comparison of girls and boys rests on the female count alone. In 2025 only 11 countries have reported, against 110 in 2024. The 2025 count may reflect the lag with which national statistics reach the international database, but the data cannot show whether collection has stopped. Either way the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading, and the second clause of the target is not measured. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is largely a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for them. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and this pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. The data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that disadvantage girls are concentrated in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa, and they are widest at secondary and tertiary level. Low-income countries were below parity at all three levels: 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.900 in 2020, up from 0.868 in 2015, the largest regional gain at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.952 to 0.965 over the same years and remained below parity, the second largest regional gain. Low-income countries moved from 0.806 to 0.819. The direction is towards parity in each case, but no projection has been run on these series. Whether parity is reached by 2030 is therefore conjecture, and at the pace of 2015 to 2020 the low-income secondary gap would still be wide. At tertiary level the Sub-Saharan African index was 0.794 in 2021, up from 0.735 in 2015. South Asia was below parity at tertiary level in 2015, at 0.954, and stood at 1.029 in 2024.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.103 in 2015 to 1.122 in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.225 to 1.291 and North America from 1.264 to 1.301, so the gap favouring women widened in those two regions; Europe and Central Asia stood at 1.153 in 2024, and East Asia and Pacific eased from 1.136 to 1.128. Target 4.5 can be read in two ways: as the elimination of gaps that disadvantage girls, or as the elimination of any gap in either direction. Under the first reading, the sex index at tertiary level is above parity in most reported regions. The second clause of the target, on equal access for the vulnerable, is not measured by these series, so the target as a whole cannot be declared met.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024. The low 2025 count may reflect the lag in release; the data cannot show whether collection has stopped. Recent completion gaps therefore cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow. Each answers the question of where gaps remain, for a named level and group.

First, national statistical offices and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should complete sex-disaggregated completion and enrolment returns within two years of the reference year, because 11 countries reported primary completion for 2025 and 2 reported secondary enrolment for 2022. This answers where gaps in completion remain unknown. Progress would be monitored by the number of countries reporting each year.

Second, ministries of education and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate on keeping girls in secondary school, because the secondary index was 0.900 and 0.819 in 2020. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps against girls, and would be monitored by the secondary index.

Third, ministries in low-income countries should widen access to tertiary education for women, because the low-income tertiary index was 0.672 in 2021, the lowest of any group reported.

Fourth, education ministries in Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, and Europe and Central Asia should monitor male participation at tertiary level, because the indices were 1.291, 1.301 and 1.153 in 2024. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps in either direction.

w-c06-4-4~tamarind/writer-4~105.text:
### The global picture: parliaments close to a quarter, management data thinner

Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in single or lower national parliamentary chambers worldwide in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015. The world share therefore rose by 4.4 percentage points in a decade, and 184 countries reported a figure for 2025, so the world value rests on near-complete coverage. Set against a benchmark of 50.0 per cent, women still hold little more than a quarter of seats. The shortfall from that benchmark is the distance between 27.2 and 50.0 per cent, which should not be confused with the 2015 world share.

Target 5.5 does not name a number. Its wording, women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making, can be read as parity, with women and men holding equal shares, or as a threshold of participation sufficient for women to shape decisions, which is often placed lower. The indicator for seats cannot settle the question, because it counts occupants of seats and says nothing about their influence, the committees they chair or the offices they hold. This book uses 50.0 per cent as the benchmark, since a population that is about half women supplies the plainest reference for equal opportunity, and findings are stated against it while the figure itself is reported in full so that readers may apply a different reading.

The parliamentary measure covers one arena of public life. The economic arena is represented by the female share of employment in senior and middle management, a series built from the occupational classification of managers. It excludes junior management, so it describes positions of real authority rather than all supervisory work. The question asked here includes the share of managerial positions held by women, and the answer must be stated plainly: the results available to this section give no value of that share for any country, year or group, only counts of reporting countries and classifications of trend. The section therefore cannot say what per cent of senior and middle management positions women hold, and it does not infer one from the parliamentary figure or from the female share of the labour force, which measures something different.

Two features of the series bear on every statement made from it. First, the World Bank publishes no aggregates for it, so no world or regional share can be quoted, and any comparison must proceed country by country. Second, the number of reporting countries has changed sharply over time. It was 40 in 2000, 72 in 2010 and 77 in 2015, and reached 95 in both 2019 and 2022. It then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and stood at only 48 in 2025. A total of 154 countries have reported in at least one year.

These counts matter as much as the values. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years may reflect a change in who reports rather than a change in women's position. The drop to 48 in 2025 may reflect survey lags, as labour force surveys are often processed with delay, but the data show only the count and not its cause. The 2025 observations for management are therefore not a sound basis for a statement of trend, and the later parts of this section rely on the years of fuller coverage when discussing managerial positions. The parliamentary series, by contrast, is reported almost everywhere and is the firmer ground for conclusions about direction and pace.

### Regions and countries differ by more than twenty-five points

Regional averages for 2025 span a wide range. Latin America and the Caribbean leads at 36.6 per cent of parliamentary seats held by women, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 31.7 per cent and North America at 29.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 27.0 per cent, close to the world value of 27.2 per cent. East Asia and Pacific follows at 23.3 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands at 16.9 per cent, and South Asia is lowest at 11.2 per cent. A regional average can conceal wide differences between countries within a region, and the results give no country-level figures for this part.

The two lowest regions are also the ones that did not advance. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 17.5 per cent in 2015 to 16.9 per cent in 2025, and the trend tool classes it as regression. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the only large decline among the regions shown, and is also classed as regression. At the observed rate its share would reach 8.9 per cent in 2030. The data do not show why the share fell. Where a chamber is dissolved or not elected, the reported share can alter sharply, so a movement of this size may owe more to political events than to a gradual trend; that is context from general knowledge, not a finding of the results.

Income groups show a narrower spread than regions. High-income countries reached 31.2 per cent in 2025, upper middle income 27.0 per cent, low income 24.8 per cent and lower middle income 23.6 per cent. Low-income countries therefore hold a higher share than lower-middle-income ones, so income alone does not order the outcome. The results contain only group means and offer no explanation for the pattern.

The country distribution of progress towards a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 is more sobering than the regional averages. Of 187 countries assessed for parliaments, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold only 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest group is 69 countries with marginal progress that would need significant acceleration, covering 44.6 per cent of the population. Another 19 countries are stagnant, with 25.1 per cent of the population, and 39 countries are regressing, with 12.7 per cent. Stagnation and regression together hold 37.8 per cent of the assessed population, against 17.6 per cent where progress is on track or moderate. The population weights differ from the country counts: regression is the second most common outcome by number of countries, yet stagnation touches about twice as many people.

Management shows a similar pattern with a heavier weight on the negative end. Of 121 countries assessed for the female share of senior and middle management, 17 are on track or have met the target, with 8.1 per cent of the population. Moderate progress applies to 27 countries and 17.7 per cent of the population, and marginal progress to 34 countries and 31.3 per cent. Stagnation affects 6 countries with 2.7 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded in 37 countries, which hold 40.3 per cent of the population, against 12.7 per cent in parliaments. The assessment covers fewer countries than for parliaments, so these shares describe the countries with data rather than the world, and survey-based series can be revised from one round to the next, so the classification should be read with caution.

### What changed since 2015, and the limits of the evidence

Since 2015 the largest gain in women's share of parliamentary seats was in Latin America and the Caribbean, where the regional value rose from 27.9 per cent to 36.6 per cent. North America rose from 22.3 per cent to 29.5 per cent. Europe and Central Asia moved from 25.7 per cent to 31.7 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 19.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. These are regional averages and conceal wide differences between countries within each region.

Two regions moved the other way. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region slipped from 17.5 per cent to 16.9 per cent. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the lowest regional value in 2025 and the only large fall. The indicator does not separate the causes of these movements. As general context, a lower share can arise from an election, a change in the chamber counted, a suspended or dissolved legislature or the loss of a quota; nothing in these series measures it.

The classification against a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 shows how uneven the movement has been. For parliaments, 24 countries are on track or have met the target, 36 show moderate progress, 69 show marginal progress, 19 are stagnating and 39 are regressing, among 187 countries assessed. The 24 countries on track hold only 4.9 per cent of the population assessed, whereas the 69 with marginal progress hold 44.6 per cent, the largest share of any class. The number of countries on track therefore overstates how far most women live where parity is approaching.

For senior and middle management, the classification covers 121 countries: 17 are on track or have met the target, 27 show moderate progress, 34 marginal progress, 6 stagnate and 37 regress. The 37 regressing countries hold 40.3 per cent of the population assessed, and the 39 regressing countries in parliaments hold 12.7 per cent of theirs. The two sets of countries and their populations differ, so the two shares are given side by side and are not ranked. As general context, legislative seats can be shifted by quotas and electoral rules, whereas management positions depend on firms, labour markets and care responsibilities; the data do not test this.

The results do not report the female share of senior and middle management itself, whether for a country, a region or the world. They give only classes, counts of countries and population shares, and the coverage tool lists no aggregate for this series. The question of what share of managerial positions women hold therefore cannot be answered with a figure from this evidence, and this section answers it for parliaments alone.

The management evidence is also thin in coverage. Across all years, 154 countries have reported at least one value, but the number reporting in a given year has varied: 40 in 2000, 77 in 2015, 90 in 2020 and 95 in 2022. The count then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and only 48 countries had reported for 2025. Reporting lags in the underlying surveys are one possible explanation, offered as general context and not as a finding. Comparisons of 2025 with earlier years would rest on different sets of countries and cannot be trusted as a measure of change.

The regional trend summary for management returned no result, so no claim is made about how any region is moving on this indicator. Nor can these indicators say why countries advance or regress; they record outcomes, not the quotas, laws, party practices, employer conduct or social norms behind them. Whether the period after 2020 slowed or accelerated progress cannot be established for management, and for parliaments the results give levels and classes but no separate account of the pandemic years.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the rates observed since 2015, no region reaches the 50.0 per cent benchmark for parliaments by 2030. The world trend is classed as marginal progress, with an expected value of 29.8 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.25. East Asia and Pacific is expected at 25.7 per cent (ratio 0.21) and Europe and Central Asia at 35.2 per cent (ratio 0.39), both marginal. The high-income group is expected at 34.6 per cent, so wealth does not by itself close the gap. Latin America and the Caribbean comes closest, at 41.9 per cent, and is the only region classed as moderate progress; even there acceleration is needed.

The regions at the bottom of the range are moving in the wrong direction. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected value of 8.9 per cent in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also classed as regression, at 16.7 per cent. Low-income countries are expected at 26.5 per cent and lower-middle-income countries at 25.3 per cent, both marginal. These projections extend a linear trend and are not forecasts. The data do not show what would move a national figure; electoral reform or political disruption, as general context outside these results, can change a country's value within one election cycle. Target 5.5 can also be read as parity at 50.0 per cent or as a lesser threshold of fair representation, and the classes above follow the first reading.

The country classifications for parliaments and for management, with their counts and population shares, are given earlier in the section and are not restated here. The sets of countries assessed differ, so the two classifications are not ranked against each other.

The results give no female share of senior and middle management for any country, year or group; they give only classes and counts of reporting countries. The managerial half of the question, what share of managerial positions women hold, therefore cannot be answered with a value from these results. Reporting is also thin at the latest point: 48 countries reported in 2025, against 95 in 2022. A lag in survey processing may explain this, as general context and not a finding.

Three proposals follow. National parliaments and electoral bodies in South Asia and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where the regional share has fallen, should review candidate-nomination rules and consider reserved seats or party quotas. National statistical offices should report the female share of senior and middle management every year, so that the 2025 gap in reporting is closed. International statistical agencies should publish regional aggregates for management, which are absent today.

w-c02-3-4~juniper/writer-1~105.text:
### Social protection reaches just over half of the world's population

Social protection and labour programmes reached 56.3% of the world's population in 2021, according to the World Bank's ASPIRE database, which draws on nationally representative household surveys. That is the single reading the bench holds for the world aggregate. The result lists the same value for its first and latest year, so it describes a position and not a change. It cannot show whether coverage rose after 2015 or fell after 2020, and no claim about either period can rest on it.

The indicator counts the share of people participating in social insurance, social safety nets, unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes, and its estimates include indirect beneficiaries, such as family members who live in a household where someone receives a benefit. The measure is therefore generous in one respect: a household with one pensioner counts as covered throughout. It is also broad in what it admits. Contributory pensions, health insurance, paid sick leave, cash transfers, food transfers, training and wage subsidies all count. A figure of 56.3% thus says that just over half of people live in households touched by at least one such programme. It does not say how adequate the benefit is, how regular it is, or whether it replaces a meaningful part of income.

The distinction matters because target 1.3 is about the poor and the vulnerable, not about the population as a whole. Coverage of everyone is a poor proxy for coverage of those in poverty. In wealthier countries, much of the population is covered through social insurance linked to formal employment, and a high national figure can coexist with gaps among informal workers, rural households and people outside the labour market. Conversely, a country with a modest overall figure may target its safety nets tightly on the poorest. The all-population series should therefore be read as an outline of the system's reach, with the coverage of the poorest quintile, taken up in a later part, as the closer test of the target.

The wording of the target also allows more than one reading. It calls for nationally appropriate systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. Neither 'substantial' nor 'vulnerable' carries a numeric threshold. A reader may take substantial to mean a majority, near-universal coverage of the poorest, or simply a clear rise from a starting point. Vulnerability can be defined by a poverty line, by exposure to shocks, or by life-cycle risks such as old age, disability and childhood. With no agreed benchmark, the 56.3% figure cannot be graded as met or missed. It can only be compared across groups of countries and, when repeated readings exist, across time.

The data have further limits. The world value rests on surveys that are carried out in different years in different countries, so a single reference year of 2021 is an alignment of estimates, not a simultaneous census. Only 1 country reports for 2023, the latest year in the series, so the most recent period is almost empty and the bench cannot say what became of coverage as pandemic emergency programmes were wound down. The poorest-quintile safety-net series, for comparison, holds 121 countries reporting in at least one year, which is substantial but not complete, and the countries missing are often those with weaker statistical systems and, plausibly, weaker protection. The world figure should accordingly be taken as indicative.

For 2030, the finding is that just under half of the world's people were outside any recorded programme in 2021, and that the target's own language leaves the finish line undefined. The next parts show where the gaps lie.

### Coverage differs sharply between regions and income groups

Regional coverage in 2021 runs from 50.6% of the population in the grouping of Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan to 72.5% in South Asia. Europe and Central Asia stands at 63.7% and East Asia and Pacific at 61.5%, while Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 54.5%. South Asia, Europe and Central Asia, and East Asia and Pacific lie above the world figure of 56.3%; the other two regions fall below it.

The South Asian figure should be read with care. The indicator counts direct and indirect beneficiaries, so a household is counted as covered when any member takes part in a programme. Large public works schemes, food transfers and subsidised in-kind programmes, which are widespread in the region, can therefore lift the headline share well above what the poorest households receive in cash. Coverage of a population is not adequacy of benefits: the indicator records participation, not the value of transfers, their regularity or whether they lift a household above a poverty line. A high share and a deep floor are different things.

The contrast between income groups is wider than that between regions. Low-income countries reach 18.3% of their people, against 55.1% in lower-middle-income countries, 62.2% in upper-middle-income countries and 77.8% in high-income countries. Coverage therefore rises with income at every step. The largest step lies between the low-income group and the lower-middle-income group; the step from lower-middle to upper-middle income is visibly smaller.

The low-income figure matters most for target 1.3, which asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable. Extreme poverty is concentrated in low-income and fragile countries, and these are the places where fewer than one person in five is reached. Causes are well established as context: narrow tax bases, limited administrative capacity, large informal economies in which contributory insurance does not reach workers, and heavy reliance on short-lived, donor-funded projects instead of permanent national systems. Higher-income countries combine payroll-based insurance with tax-funded pensions and family benefits, which together cover most of the population.

The evidence has limits. Every level quoted is for 2021, and the result lists the same value as first and latest year for each group. No change since 2015 or since 2020 can therefore be stated for any region or income group, and the pandemic's expansion of emergency transfers cannot be separated from lasting coverage. Only 1 country reports for 2023, so the most recent survey year is almost empty. The ordering of regions is firm for 2021; its movement over time is not shown by these data.

### Coverage of the poorest quintile has regressed in many countries with data

The trend classification for the poorest-quintile measure of social safety net coverage places 26 of the 55 countries assessed in regression, more than in any other class, but it needs a careful reading. The tool compares each country's compound annual change since 2015, or the first year after, with a target that has no numeric value, and sorts the countries into classes. The classes therefore describe the direction and pace of a series, not a verified fall or rise in what households receive.

Of 55 countries assessed, 19 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 33.4% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 2 countries show moderate progress, needing acceleration, with 12.4% of that population, and 4 show marginal progress, with 2.2%. Another 4 are stagnant, with 3.1%. The series is classed as regressing in 26 countries, which hold 48.9% of the assessed population. Regression is the largest single class by country count and by population. The shares refer to the assessed countries only and not to the world.

Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030 and sets no threshold. The phrase can be read as a majority of the poorest quintile, as near-universal coverage, or simply as a rising share. The trend tool therefore judges direction alone. A country counted as on track has a series moving upward at a pace the tool treats as consistent with improvement, not one shown to reach any agreed level. A country counted as regressing may still cover a large share of its poorest households, having moved down from a higher level.

Several well-established causes can lie behind a downward movement in such a series, stated here as context and not as findings. Coverage can decline when programmes are closed, shrunk or left without indexation while the population grows, and when emergency schemes introduced in a crisis are wound down. Changes in survey design and in the list of programmes captured can also move a figure without any change in what households receive. The data cannot separate these explanations.

The reliability of any trend depends on how often countries are observed, and the record is thin and uneven. Only 2 countries reported in 2000 and 3 in 2002. Reporting rose to 11 in 2005, 36 in 2010 and 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013 before recovering to 35 in 2014. It reached 47 countries in 2018, the best-observed year, and was 36 in 2019. Reporting then dropped to 24 in 2020 and recovered to 30 in 2021. Only 17 countries reported in 2022 and a single country in 2023. In all, 121 countries have reported in at least one year, but no single year approaches that number.

This pattern has two consequences. First, the years after 2020 are poorly observed. Surveys are fielded with a delay and processed into the database later, so the thinning of 2022 and 2023 partly reflects lag and not an end to measurement. The effect of the pandemic and of the withdrawal of emergency support on the poorest households is therefore largely invisible here, and the classes cannot be assigned with confidence to the period after 2015 or to the period after 2020. Second, the countries that enter a trend are those with surveys at both ends of their series, and they may differ systematically from countries never observed twice. Conclusions from the 55 assessed countries should not be extended to the others without that caution.

A separate question is whether the whole-population measure can stand in for the poorest quintile where the latter is missing. The links tool compares the two series across 18 countries between 2015 and 2021. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.93, and that of 2021 levels is 0.91. Countries that gained or lost coverage for the whole population largely did so for the poorest quintile too, and countries with high overall coverage also tend to cover their poorest households well. The association is strong in rank terms and is not a statement of cause.

The sample is small, at 18 countries, and a rank correlation says nothing about the gap between the two measures in any one country. High overall coverage can coexist with weak targeting of the poor, which the correlation does not test. It supports using the whole-population series as a rough guide to direction where the poorest-quintile series is absent, but not as a substitute for it.

For 2030 the implication is cautious. On a direction-only reading, 33.4% of the assessed population lives in countries classed as on track, while 48.9% lives in countries whose series is classed as regressing. No projection to 2030 was run, and the classes cannot be extrapolated. Without a numeric target and with sparse recent data, the world cannot say with confidence how far the poorest are covered or how fast that is changing.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence permits a limited reading of 2030. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable, yet the world figure of 56.3% in 2021 describes the whole population, not the poor. The only measure aimed at the poorest is safety net coverage of the poorest quintile. Its trend classification places 26 of the 55 countries assessed in regression, and those 26 hold 48.9% of the population of the countries assessed, not of the world. Only 19 countries are classed as on track or target met, with 33.4% of the assessed population. The classes compare each country's rate of change with a target that has no numeric value, so they describe direction and pace and do not prove an observed fall. No projection to 2030 was run, and the classes cannot be extended into one; they show only that, in the countries with data, the direction since 2015 is mixed and, for many, unfavourable.

The gap between income groups is the clearest measured finding. In 2021, low-income countries reached 18.3% of their population, against 77.8% in high-income countries. Lower middle income countries stood at 55.1% and upper middle income countries at 62.2%. The data hold a single year for these groups and no rate of change, so they cannot show how fast the gap is closing or whether it can close by 2030. Donor financing and incomplete household registries are commonly cited as context for low coverage in the poorest countries; these data do not test either explanation.

The evidence base is itself a constraint. Reporting on poorest-quintile safety net coverage reached 47 countries in 2018 and fell to 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022, with a single country in 2023. Surveys thinned just when the pandemic raised the need for protection, so what changed after 2020 cannot be read with confidence. The recorded regression may reflect real losses, a change in survey design or programme definitions, or the ending of temporary schemes; the data cannot separate these. The count of 121 countries reporting in any year applies to the poorest-quintile series.

The target also lacks a numeric reading. Substantial coverage could mean a majority of the poor or a higher threshold, and the classification of on track or regressing depends on that choice. Until it is fixed, different readers can judge the same country differently.

The two coverage measures move together. Across 18 countries with data for 2015 to 2021, the rank correlation between changes in poorest-quintile coverage and changes in whole-population safety net coverage is 0.93, and between their 2021 levels it is 0.91. This supports using the broader measure, which more countries report, as a provisional guide where poorest-quintile data are missing. The sample is small, and a strong rank correlation shows association, not that the poorest receive a proportionate share in every country.

w-c04-6-4~juniper/writer-3~105.text:
### The global rate barely moved after 2015

The 2020 target to halve road deaths was not met on the evidence available. The World Bank's indicator of mortality caused by road traffic injury, expressed as estimated deaths per 100,000 population, stood at 17.0 for the world in 2015 and at 16.7 in 2019. That is a fall of about 1.5 per cent over four years. A halving would have required a rate near 8.5 by 2020, and the measured rate remained close to double that level.

Two limits on this reading need stating. The series ends in 2019, so the target year itself cannot be observed; the conclusion rests on the last four years before it, and a sudden fall in 2020 of the size required is not plausible given how slowly the rate moved beforehand. The path of 2020 is also disturbed by the pandemic, when restrictions on movement reduced traffic in many places, so any later figure would need careful interpretation before it was read as progress on safety.

The second limit concerns the wording of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of deaths and injuries, and of the number of them, whereas the indicator covers deaths only and is a rate per head of population. A rate can fall while the count of deaths rises if population grows faster, and it can stay flat while the count grows. The target can therefore be read in more than one way: as a halving of the count, or as a halving of the rate. On either reading the evidence points the same way, since the rate has barely changed and no series on non-fatal injuries is held on the shelf. The measure used here is the more lenient of the two, which makes the shortfall harder to dismiss.

Coverage supports the finding. Estimates are available for 183 countries in 2019 and for 190 countries in at least one year, with regional and income aggregates alongside. The series is modelled by the World Health Organization rather than counted directly, since many countries lack complete registration of deaths by cause. A flat global line therefore reflects estimates built from a mix of registered and modelled data, and small movements of the order seen here should not be over-read. What can be said with confidence is the scale of the gap between the target and the outcome, not the precise change of a few tenths of a point.

### Regions diverged, and only Europe and Central Asia moved fast

Regional rates for 2015 and 2019 show that the small global movement conceals different trajectories. Europe and Central Asia was the only region to record a substantial decline, from 9.2 deaths per 100,000 population in 2015 to 7.4 in 2019. That is the lowest regional rate in either year, and the only one close to the level a halving would have required. Its projected rate for 2030, on the 2015 to 2019 pace, is 4.1, below the target of 8.5. Long-established road safety policy in much of that region, such as speed enforcement, seat-belt use, vehicle standards and road design, is offered here as context consistent with the pattern; the results do not test it.

East Asia and Pacific moved only slightly, from 17.0 to 16.5. Latin America and Caribbean fell from 18.3 to 17.3, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 17.3 to 17.0. The trend tool classes all three as marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with pace ratios of 0.22, 0.36 and 0.13 respectively. A ratio compares the pace observed with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio below 1 means the pace is too slow. South Asia was effectively flat, at 15.6 in 2015 and 15.6 in 2019, and the tool classes it as regression, with a ratio of -0.01.

Two regions moved in the wrong direction. North America rose from 11.5 to 11.9, and the trend tool classes it as regression with a ratio of -0.63. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.8 to 27.4, the highest regional rate in either year, and is also classed as regression, with a ratio of -0.13 and a projected 2030 rate of 29.2. Rapid growth in motor vehicle use is often cited as a pressure on road deaths in lower-income regions, but no result here measures vehicle use, so that explanation is context and not a finding. The measured pattern matters for 2030: the region with the most deaths per head is not improving.

These comparisons rest on regional means, which can hide wide spread among the countries inside a region, so the ranking of regions says little about any single national road network. Coverage is broad but not complete: 183 countries report in 2019, and the indicator is built from modelled estimates, so small changes in a regional rate should be read with caution. The country-level spread is taken up in the next part.

### Dispersion widened while few places gained ground

The convergence test asks whether countries with higher road death rates in 2015 changed by less, or by more, than others up to 2019. Across 182 countries the estimated coefficient (beta) is 0.031, with a p-value of 0.0058. The sign is positive. Under the convention of the test, a negative coefficient would indicate that countries with higher starting rates rose less or fell more, so that levels drew together; a positive one indicates that they drew apart. The result is therefore the opposite of convergence, and the slope is distinguished from zero at the conventional 0.05 threshold.

The second measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation, the standard deviation of national rates divided by their mean, rose from 0.54 in 2015 to 0.63 in 2019. Rates across countries were more unequal in relation to their average at the end of the window than at the start. The world rate, 17.0 in 2015 and 16.7 in 2019, scarcely moved while the spread widened. The tests do not identify which countries account for this: no country-level result is reported here, so no count of improving or deteriorating countries can be given, and nothing is claimed about how many places gained ground.

The limits of the test are considerable. The R-squared is 0.108, so initial rates account for only about one-tenth of the variation in subsequent change. Most of what separates one country's trajectory from another's lies outside this simple relationship. The window is also only four years, from 2015 to 2019, and short intervals magnify the effect of estimation noise. Country figures for road deaths are modelled estimates, since many countries lack complete death registration with cause information, and year-to-year movements in a modelled series may partly reflect revisions of method and inputs rather than real change. The test also stops at 2019 and says nothing of the period after 2020.

The tools measure outcomes, not causes, so any explanation is context and not a finding of these results. Well-established experience suggests that road deaths fall where speed management, helmet and seat-belt laws, vehicle safety standards and emergency care are enforced, and that they rise where motorisation grows faster than safe road design and enforcement. Such differences could produce widening dispersion, but no result here measures them.

For 2030 the implication is limited to what the two measures show: a rising spread means that the global rate alone is a poor guide to national progress, and that national trajectories need to be examined individually.

### The 2030 target of 8.5 needs a different pace, and proposals follow

The 2030 horizon asks for a rate of 8.5 deaths per 100,000 population, which is the 2015 world rate of 17.0 halved. Each projection below extends the average annual movement between 2015 and 2019, so every figure is an extrapolation of a four-year pace and not a forecast. The ratio reported with it compares that movement with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio of 1 means the pace is just sufficient and a ratio below 1 means it is too slow. The world rate is projected at 16.1 in 2030 if the 2015 to 2019 movement continues, a ratio of 0.11, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. That projection stands almost twice as high as 8.5.

Two groups are projected to pass 8.5 on the 2015 to 2019 pace; this is not the same as being on track, since the window is only four years. Europe and Central Asia is projected at 4.1 in 2030, with a ratio of 6.91. High-income countries are projected at 7.3, a ratio of 2.48, although their 2019 rate of 8.7 still stood above 8.5. The high-income result is therefore the less secure of the two.

East Asia and Pacific shows marginal progress, with a projected rate of 15.2 in 2030 and a ratio of 0.22. Latin America and the Caribbean is similar, at 14.8 and 0.36. Upper middle income countries are projected at 15.2, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 16.2. All of these are falling slightly, yet none approaches 8.5 on present pace. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnating, at 17.3.

Four groups are classed as regression. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 29.2 and low-income countries at 31.5, both rising, and they are the groups with the highest rates, so on these extrapolations they move away from the target. North America is projected at 13.3, and South Asia at 15.7. As context, not a finding of these results, rapid motorisation combined with weak roads, vehicle standards and emergency care is a well-established source of high road death rates.

The figure of 8.5 is one reading of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of halving deaths and injuries, not the rate. The rate and the count may move in different directions, and population growth, which would decide which reading is more demanding, is not examined here. No count series is held, so that question cannot be tested. The 2015 base year is also a convention, since the target text names no baseline, and injuries are not measured by the indicator used. Readers should treat 8.5 as a benchmark and not as the single correct threshold.

The proposals that follow are tied to these findings. Governments of Sub-Saharan African and low-income countries, with development partners, should prioritise speed enforcement, safer road design and emergency care, because their rates are projected to rise rather than fall. National road safety agencies in regions classed as marginal or stagnating should set interim targets for 2025 and report against them annually, because the present pace is far below what 8.5 requires. North American authorities should review why the rate rose from 11.5 in 2015 to 11.9 in 2019. National statistical offices and the World Health Organization should publish annual counts of deaths and injuries, since the target concerns numbers and none is held here. Countries with incomplete cause-of-death registration should strengthen vital registration, since the indicator is modelled where records are lacking.
