t-legal-index-change-by-group~saltmarsh/.name: legal-index-change-by-group
t-legal-index-change-by-group~saltmarsh/.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params.get('year_a', 2015))
    y1 = int(params.get('year_b', 2020))
    y2 = int(params.get('year_c', 2025))
    s = data[code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    facts = {}
    def grp_stats(a, b, label):
        by = {}
        for u in s:
            ser = s[u]
            if u not in regions:
                continue
            va = ser.get(a)
            vb = ser.get(b)
            if va is None or vb is None:
                continue
            g = regions[u]
            by.setdefault(g, []).append(vb - va)
        return by
    lines = []
    for a, b in [(y0, y2), (y1, y2)]:
        by = grp_stats(a, b, '')
        allv = []
        for g in by:
            allv += by[g]
        tag = str(a) + '_' + str(b)
        facts['countries_' + tag] = len(allv)
        facts['rose_' + tag] = len([v for v in allv if v > 0])
        facts['mean_change_' + tag] = round(sum(allv) / len(allv), 2) if allv else 'no data'
        for g in sorted(by):
            v = by[g]
            facts['mean_' + g + '_' + tag] = round(sum(v) / len(v), 2)
            facts['rose_' + g + '_' + tag] = len([x for x in v if x > 0])
        lines.append('Between ' + str(a) + ' and ' + str(b) + ', ' + str(facts['rose_' + tag]) + ' of ' + str(len(allv)) + ' countries with both years recorded raised their score; the mean change was ' + str(facts['mean_change_' + tag]) + ' index points.')
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': ' '.join(lines) + ' Countries missing either year are excluded; groups are those in the regions map.'}

w-c05-5-5~tamarind/writer-2~112.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small and should be read with caution. In the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. The fall is not a loss for girls: it largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, since South Asia moved from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020 and lower middle income countries from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.997 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.997 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.995 in North America and 0.991 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.982. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.970 in 2015 to 0.976 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.956 to 0.958. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.061 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.868 in 2015 and 0.900 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.952 to 0.965. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.018 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.052, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. The data do not show why. One hypothesis, which these series cannot test, is that boys leave school early for paid work in some settings. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.010 to 0.982 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.993.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.122 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 and North America 1.301, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.153, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.128, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.058 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.954 to 1.029. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.794 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.735 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.301 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.992 at primary level in 2020, 0.997 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.038 at tertiary level in 2024, close to parity at the first two levels and above it at the third. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure. The spread is also reported only for 2015, so these data cannot show whether dispersion has narrowed since.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison. The shelf's results give no coverage counts for the male series, so the comparison of girls and boys rests on the female count alone. In 2025 only 11 countries have reported, against 110 in 2024. The 2025 count may reflect the lag with which national statistics reach the international database, but the data cannot show whether collection has stopped. Either way the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading, and the second clause of the target is not measured. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is largely a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for them. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and this pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. The data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that disadvantage girls are largest in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa, and they widen with the level of schooling. Low-income countries were below parity at all three levels: 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Other groups were also below parity in places: South Asia at tertiary level in 2015 (0.954), and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at primary level (0.976 in 2020) and secondary level (0.965 in 2020).

At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.900 in 2020, up from 0.868 in 2015. Among the regions with values for both years, this is the largest gain. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.952 to 0.965 over the same years and remained below parity. Low-income countries moved from 0.806 to 0.819. The direction is towards parity in each case, but no projection has been run on these series. Whether parity is reached by 2030 is therefore conjecture, and at the pace of 2015 to 2020 the low-income secondary gap would still be wide. At tertiary level the Sub-Saharan African index was 0.794 in 2021, up from 0.735 in 2015. South Asia stood at 1.029 in 2024, above parity.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.103 in 2015 to 1.122 in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.225 to 1.291 and North America from 1.264 to 1.301, so the gap favouring women widened in those two regions; Europe and Central Asia stood at 1.153 in 2024, and East Asia and Pacific eased from 1.136 to 1.128. Target 4.5 can be read in two ways: as the elimination of gaps that disadvantage girls, or as the elimination of any gap in either direction. Under the first reading, the tertiary index is above parity in most reported regions. The second clause of the target, on equal access for the vulnerable, is not measured by these series, so the target as a whole cannot be declared met.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024. The low 2025 count may reflect the lag in release; the data cannot show whether collection has stopped. Recent completion gaps therefore cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow, each tied to a finding.

First, national statistical offices and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should complete sex-disaggregated completion and enrolment returns within two years of the reference year, because only 11 countries reported primary completion for 2025 and 2 reported secondary enrolment for 2022. Until they do, current gaps in completion cannot be located. Progress would be monitored by the number of countries reporting each year.

Second, ministries of education and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate on keeping girls in secondary school, because the secondary index was 0.900 and 0.819 in 2020. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps against girls, and would be monitored by the secondary index.

Third, ministries in low-income countries should widen access to tertiary education for women, because the low-income tertiary index was 0.672 in 2021, the lowest of any group reported.

Fourth, education ministries in Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, and Europe and Central Asia should monitor male participation at tertiary level, because the indices were 1.291, 1.301 and 1.153 in 2024. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps in either direction.

w-c08-5-3~willow/writer-1~112.text:
### Renewable generation has roughly doubled worldwide since 2015

The world share of electricity produced from renewable sources other than hydroelectric power rose from 6.6 % in 2015 to 12.4 % in 2021. The share has therefore come close to doubling in six years. The figure comes from 208 reporting countries in 2021, and the series ends that year, so nothing in it describes the years since. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks of 2022, cannot be read from this indicator.

The indicator needs careful reading. It measures the share of non-hydroelectric renewables (chiefly wind, solar, geothermal and biomass) in total electricity production. It does not measure installed generating capacity, nor the quantity of electricity generated. A rising share is consistent with new capacity being built, and the growth of wind and solar plant is the usual explanation in the wider literature. But the data do not observe that capacity. A share can also rise when other generation falls, or when total output stagnates. Growth in generating capacity is thus inferred here, not observed, and the finding concerns a share, not generation. No series on installed capacity, and no series on concessional energy finance by recipient, is among the results used here.

The exclusion of hydroelectric power also shapes the picture. Large hydropower is a long-established source in many developing countries, and it is left out. The indicator therefore captures the newer renewables, whose costs have fallen considerably over the past decade, and it understates the renewable contribution of countries that depend heavily on dams.

The trend tool classes the world as on track or target met for the non-hydroelectric share, with a rate of 0.11 for the period. The separate trend on the renewable share of final energy consumption gives the world a rate of 0.03 and the same verdict; the two series should not be confused. The goal carries no numerical value for these indicators, so the verdicts only say the share is moving in the desired direction. They are not comparisons with a quantified goal, and the word target should be read in that sense. The global figure also averages very different experiences, which the next part sets out by region and income group. A world share cannot show whether developing countries, the subject of targets 7.a and 7.b, have shared in the gain.

For 2030 the global direction is encouraging but incompletely observed. A rise of this size in six years shows that a rapid change in the electricity mix is possible. Whether it has continued, and whether it has reached the countries with the least infrastructure, is a question this series cannot answer from 2021 onward.

### Regions and income groups started from different levels and moved at different speeds

Regional starting points differed widely in 2015, and the gaps in levels have not closed. East Asia & Pacific rose from 4.8% of electricity production in 2015 to 12.0% in 2021, and Latin America & Caribbean rose from 6.9% to 15.1% over the same years. South Asia moved from 4.6% to 8.5%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan began from 0.6% and reached 2.9%, the lowest level among the regions reported. Sub-Saharan Africa started at 2.1% and stood at 4.3% in 2021. All figures here are shares of total electricity production from non-hydroelectric renewable sources.

Income groups show the same pattern more sharply. Upper middle income countries rose from 4.6% to 11.9%, and lower middle income countries from 4.1% to 7.3%. High income countries rose from 8.6% to 14.1%. Low income countries moved the other way, from 0.7% in 2015 to 0.5% in 2021. The poorest countries therefore did not share in the expansion of wind, solar, geothermal and biomass generation that lifted the world figure. Well-established context points to the cost of capital, small and weakly financed grids, and limited public budgets as barriers to new plant in these economies, though the data here do not test those causes.

The trend assessment for the share of renewables in total final energy consumption must be read with care. Low income countries show the highest share, 77.0% in 2015 and 74.6% in 2020, and the trend reads as regression, at a rate of -0.0064. That level does not signal modern clean energy. In these countries the share is dominated by traditional biomass, chiefly wood and charcoal burned for cooking, which is neither clean nor efficient and carries health and forest costs. A falling share there can even accompany a shift to commercial fuels. The indicator also leaves target 7.2 open to more than one reading, since no numeric 2030 value is set for it. The tool classes the World, East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, and upper middle income groups as on track, while Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and lower middle income countries are marked as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The convergence result tempers any reading of catching up. Across 208 countries, the slope of annual change on starting level between 2015 and 2021 was -0.004, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001. No convergence can be distinguished from zero. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021, so spread relative to the mean narrowed. The two results are compatible: the mean rose, which shrinks relative spread, without starting position predicting the pace of change. The data end in 2021, so they say nothing about changes since the pandemic.

### Private investment and concessional finance moved unevenly

Private participation in energy investment moved unevenly across developing regions between 2015 and 2024. In Latin America & Caribbean, investment with private participation fell from US$11.87 billion in 2015 to US$8.40 billion in 2024. South Asia moved the other way, rising from US$2.39 billion to US$3.45 billion. The two regions therefore ended the period on different paths, and the regional total for Latin America & Caribbean is lower than at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals period.

The income groups show a sharper divide. Upper middle income countries rose from US$31.02 billion in 2015 to US$58.39 billion in 2024, so private capital in energy became concentrated in that group. Lower middle income countries barely moved, from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion, in current dollars. The figures are not adjusted for inflation, and the extract gives no deflated series, so changes in real terms cannot be read from it. As context that the data do not test, private capital tends to favour markets with larger domestic demand, deeper credit and more established regulation. Low income countries are not shown in the extract, so the position of the poorest economies cannot be read from these results.

Coverage limits what can be concluded. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, and the Private Participation in Infrastructure database records only projects with a contractual private role in low- and middle-income countries. Public investment, which carries much of energy infrastructure in the poorest countries, is outside it. Annual totals can also swing with a few large projects, so the endpoints of 2015 and 2024 do not describe the years between.

Concessional finance is harder to assess. Net official development assistance to the least developed countries was reported by 32 countries in 2023, but the series covers all aid and not aid for energy. The extract therefore gives no clean energy figure for concessional support, and it cannot be said whether international cooperation on clean energy research and technology, the subject of target 7.a, has grown. Targets 7.a and 7.b are worded without a numerical threshold, such as a sum to be mobilised or a capacity to be installed. Progress can therefore be described but not scored as met or missed, and any judgement depends on how expand, enhance and facilitate are read.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to rising renewable shares worldwide, but the gains are uneven and the finance behind them is concentrated. Two limits apply throughout: the series on electricity production ends in 2021, and neither installed generating capacity nor concessional finance for energy by recipient group appears among the results. Two indicators are read separately here. For the share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption, the trend tool classes the world as on track or target met, at a rate of 0.0255. The same classification applies to East Asia & Pacific (0.0267), Europe & Central Asia (0.0325), Latin America & Caribbean (0.0390), North America (0.0370), high income countries (0.0381) and upper middle income countries (0.0240). Low income countries show regression, at a rate of -0.0064. Lower middle income countries (0.0079), South Asia (0.0112) and Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) show marginal progress, and the tool states that significant acceleration is needed; the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan show moderate progress, at 0.0129, with acceleration needed. For the non-hydroelectric share of electricity production, the world rate is 0.1103, and every group except low income is classed as on track or target met; low income shows regression, at -0.0558. The trend tool was run with no quantified target, so these classifications measure direction and pace and not distance from a defined goal.

Private investment follows a similar pattern. Upper middle income countries recorded US$58.39 billion of energy investment with private participation in 2024, against US$31.02 billion in 2015. Lower middle income countries moved from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion over the same years, which is close to flat in current dollars. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, so the totals describe the projects recorded and not all investment. Official assistance cannot be read in the same way: the series for net ODA to the least developed countries shows 32 reporting countries in 2023, and the result gives no regional or income-group levels. Whether concessional finance has offset the weak private flows to poorer countries therefore cannot be shown here. As context that these data do not test, private capital tends to favour markets with larger demand, deeper finance and more settled regulation.

The spread of non-hydroelectric renewable shares across countries has narrowed, with the coefficient of variation falling from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021 across 208 countries. The slope of change on starting level is -0.0040, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001, so it cannot be distinguished from zero. The narrowing in spread is therefore not evidence that low starters are catching up systematically.

Targets 7.a and 7.b carry no quantified goal, so progress can be read in more than one way. Rising shares, rising private investment in some regions and falling investment in others can each be cited as success or failure, depending on the threshold chosen. Installed capacity in developing countries, the quantity named in the section's question, is not among the series examined. For 2030, the pattern implies that the countries furthest behind, low income and lower middle income, are those where pace is weakest and private finance is thinnest.

w-c04-7-4~willow/writer-2~112.text:
### Adolescent fertility has fallen worldwide since 2015

The world adolescent fertility rate fell from 46.0 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 38.3 in 2024. The figure is a modelled estimate built from registration data, surveys and censuses. The series reports on all 217 countries and territories in 2024, so the global average rests on far fuller coverage than the indicators of contraceptive demand in the same section.

Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold. It calls for universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, including family planning, information and education, and offers no level of adolescent fertility that would count as success. The target can also be read in more than one way. Adolescent births are an outcome of access, schooling, marriage customs and income as much as of health services, so a fall in the rate cannot be credited to health policy alone. Any reading of progress here therefore rests on the trend classes of the bench, which compare each country's own course with the pace needed to keep falling to 2030, and not on a stated goal.

On that reading the picture is favourable in breadth. Of 217 countries assessed, 144 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 26 countries, with 6.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Eight countries, with 0.4% of the population, are stagnant, and five, with 1.0%, are regressing. The population-weighted share on track is far larger than the count of countries alone would suggest, but the results do not show which countries lie in each class by starting rate, so no claim is made here about where the laggards began.

The global decline matters because early childbearing is commonly associated with interrupted schooling, lower lifetime earnings and higher obstetric risk; this is context from established knowledge, not a finding of the bench. The world rate of 38.3 in 2024 remains well above the 8.7 recorded for high-income countries in the same year, so the average conceals a wide gap that the next parts of the section examine. As context from outside the bench, school closures and disrupted clinics after 2020 were widely expected to push adolescent births up. The bench reports only the 2015 and 2024 values of the world series, so it cannot show whether the pace faltered in particular years or places after 2020. For 2030, the trend classes indicate that gains are not secure in every country: 13 countries are stagnant or regressing. No projection of the world rate is made here.

### Demand satisfied by modern methods is poorly measured

Demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods cannot be answered at the level the question asks. The results supply no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country group, and the answer to how far demand is met is therefore limited to the direction of change in 15 countries and the population shares those countries hold. The indicator is the weakest of the series in this section. It is reported by 73 countries in at least one year between 2000 and 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. In any single year the count is small. Counts are available here for 2000, 2012, 2015 and 2019 to 2024 only, and comparison is made only within those years: 13 countries in 2000, 14 in 2012 and 8 in 2015. After 2015 the count moved unevenly. It was 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021 and 7 in 2022, then 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. There is no steady decline and no steady recovery, and the count in 2024 remains small beside the 217 reporting on adolescent fertility. As context, not a finding of the data, household surveys are fielded at intervals of several years and were disrupted by the pandemic, so a country appears in the series only in the years after a survey has been completed and processed.

The consequence is that the indicator cannot show what happened after 2015 or after 2020 for the world. A year-on-year comparison would compare different sets of countries, and a change in the average would reflect which countries happened to report as much as any change in access to services. The shelf holds aggregates for three groups: lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The tools were not run for these groups in this section, so the level of satisfied demand is not reported for any group. Those aggregates would give a partial answer to the level question, and retrieving them is needed before it can be answered even for those three groups. No world aggregate and no aggregate for other regions is held, so regional comparison of satisfied demand is not possible on this evidence.

The definition adds a second limit. The indicator refers to married women aged 15 to 49 who have a need for family planning, and its denominator is those with demand, not all women. Unmarried women, including sexually active adolescents, fall outside it, as do women in unions not recorded as marriage in some surveys. Target 3.7 speaks of universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, information and education, and the indicator captures only one part of that: the use of modern methods by married women who want to space or limit births. The target also gives no numerical threshold, so no level of satisfied demand can be called the goal, and the trend assessment rests on the direction of change rather than on a fixed value. The target can be read in more than one way, and this section does not choose among the readings.

The trend classification covers only 15 countries, those with enough observations to fit a path to 2030. Of these, 2 are on track or have met the target, holding 1.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Another 5 show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 21.8 per cent. Four show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 70.3 per cent. One is stagnant, with 3.1 per cent, and 3 are regressing, with 3.3 per cent. The results do not show which countries lie in each class, so the large population share of the marginal class cannot be attributed to any particular country. Fifteen countries out of 73 reporting, and out of a world of more than 200, is too few to speak for any region, and the sample is not random. The proportions above describe the sample, not the world, and any global statement drawn from them is tentative.

### Regions differ by a factor of eight in adolescent births

Adolescent births are concentrated to a degree that the world average conceals. In 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 91.9 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19, against 50.4 in Latin America and the Caribbean and 37.8 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. South Asia stood at 21.0, East Asia and Pacific at 14.3, North America at 11.7 and Europe and Central Asia at 11.4. The highest regional rate is therefore about eight times the lowest, and the next region down, Latin America and the Caribbean, is well above the world rate of 38.3.

The pattern follows income. Low-income countries recorded 90.7 births per 1,000 in 2024, lower-middle-income countries 42.5, upper-middle-income countries 23.6 and high-income countries 8.7. The results do not show how far income groups and regions contain the same countries, so the two views should be read as separate cuts of the data. As context rather than a finding of these results, schooling for girls, the age at first marriage, access to contraception and the reach of sexual and reproductive health education are known to differ along similar lines and to act together rather than separately.

Every region and income group named here, each with a value for both 2015 and 2024, recorded a fall between those years, but the size of the fall depends on the measure. In absolute terms Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 to 91.9 and Latin America and the Caribbean from 67.3 to 50.4. In proportional terms North America fell from 20.9 to 11.7 and East Asia and Pacific from 21.9 to 14.3, while low-income countries moved only from 103.3 to 90.7. A large absolute fall from a high starting point therefore leaves relative standing little changed: Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest rate in 2015 and remains far above every other region in 2024.

The country classification shows a similar split between breadth and depth of progress. Of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 34 countries, with 7.3 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 26, with 6.3 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. The population-weighted figure of 84.9 per cent should not be read as a statement about each country. The results do not show which regions the lagging classes belong to.

The target gives no numerical threshold for adolescent fertility, so the trend classification measures the pace of decline against a projected path, not against a defined goal. A different reading of what counts as sufficient progress would change the classes. The regional contrasts are nonetheless clear on any reading: the gap between Sub-Saharan Africa and the other regions remains very wide in 2024.

### Progress in family planning is moderate and uneven

Of the 15 countries for which a trend to 2030 could be computed on demand satisfied by modern methods, 2 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 1.5% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 5 countries, with 21.8% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The weight of the picture lies in the slower classes. The 4 countries in marginal progress, which need significant acceleration, hold 70.3% of the assessed population. One country stagnates, with 3.1%, and 3 regress, with 3.3%. The population-weighted result is therefore weaker than the country count alone suggests. The trend tool shows only the share of the assessed population in each class; it does not name the countries or show which of them are the most populous.

The question of how far demand is satisfied cannot be answered at the level asked. No level of satisfied demand was retrieved for the world, for any region or for any country. The shelf holds aggregates for three groups, lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, but the tools were not run for them in this section, so the level of satisfied demand is not reported for any group. Retrieving those aggregates would give a partial answer for those three groups, and it is needed before the question can be answered for them. For now the answer is limited to the direction of change in 15 countries and the population shares they hold. The 15 countries assessed are a fraction of the 73 that have ever reported the indicator, and the survey-based series leaves most countries without enough observations to draw a trend. Annual reporting is thin and uneven: 8 countries reported in 2015, 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. Within the years shown, the count recovered after 2019 but remained below the 14 reporting in 2012. Counts are given only for the years listed, and comparisons are made only among them. The assessment cannot be read as a global verdict. It describes a small group selected by data availability, and how far it represents other countries is not known. The target also carries no numerical threshold in this analysis, so the classes measure the pace of improvement along a path rather than attainment of a fixed level, and a different reading of the goal would sort some countries differently. The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women, including adolescents, are outside it.

The indicators do not identify why countries fall into one class or another, and no cause is asserted here. As general context, not a finding, the pace of change in contraceptive use is commonly understood to depend on the reliability of supply, the range of methods offered, the cost to users and social norms about women's choices; none of these is measured by this series. What the data do show is that regression occurs in 3 of the 15 countries, which means that gains are not automatically retained.

The adolescent fertility trend gives a firmer, though different, reading. Of 217 countries and territories, 144 are on track or have met the target, holding 84.9% of their population, and 34 show moderate progress, with 7.3%. Another 26 are in marginal progress, with 6.3%, 8 stagnate, with 0.4%, and 5 regress, with 1.0%. Progress on adolescent births is thus broad in coverage, while progress on contraceptive demand cannot be shown to be.

For 2030, progress on satisfied demand cannot be assumed to be on course. With few countries on track and most of the assessed population in the slower classes, a result consistent with universal access would require acceleration where the trend is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Adolescent fertility is expected to keep falling to 2030, but this is an expectation and not a finding, and the pace will differ between countries. Of the 217 countries and territories assessed, 144 are on track or have met the direction of travel, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. The remainder is the concern. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of that population, show moderate progress and need acceleration, 26 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. Target 3.7 sets no numerical goal for adolescent fertility, so these classes describe the pace of change in each country and do not measure distance from a value agreed in the Goals. The reading depends on the pace each country is judged against, and it should be taken as indicative.

The regional rates show where the burden lies. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 91.9 in 2024, and low-income countries fell from 103.3 to 90.7. Both remain far above the high-income level of 8.7 in 2024, while the world rate stands at 38.3. The trend classes are computed for countries and are not shown here for regions, and the results do not name the countries that lag, so country-level lag in Sub-Saharan Africa is unknown. As context outside the evidence of this section, schooling for girls, the age at marriage and access to contraception are well-established influences on adolescent births.

The question of how far demand for family planning is satisfied cannot be answered at the level asked. The results of this section supply no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country, and only the direction of change in 15 countries is available. The shelf holds aggregates of the indicator for three groups, lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, but the tools were not run for those groups here, so no level is reported for them either. Retrieving those aggregates would give a partial answer for those groups and is needed before the level question can be addressed for them. Of the 15 countries, 2 are on track, 5 show moderate progress, 4 show marginal progress, 1 is stagnant and 3 are regressing. The 4 countries in marginal progress hold 70.3% of the population assessed. The results do not name those countries, so what drives that share cannot be stated. Reporting is also thin: 2 countries reported in 2019 and 7 in 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility. The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women and adolescents lie outside it.

The proposals that follow address both problems: the thinness of measurement and the pace of progress where rates remain highest.

proposals: National statistical offices and survey programmes in countries with no recent reading should field a household survey on contraceptive demand at least every five years, so that the satisfied-demand indicator can be reported for more than a handful of countries each year.

Ministries of health and education in the countries with the highest adolescent fertility, with the support of development partners, should concentrate funding on keeping girls in school and on contraceptive services that reach adolescents and unmarried women.

The World Bank and the agencies that supply the underlying estimates should publish the satisfied-demand series for all unmarried and married women, and release regional and income-group aggregates for it, so that the level question can be answered.

The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women and adolescents are outside it. Reporting is thin, with 7 countries in 2024. Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold, so trend classes show pace and not distance from a goal. The trend classes for adolescent fertility name no countries, and causes of change are not measured by the data.

w-c08-1-4~heath/writer-1~112.text:
### Global access has risen, but not to universality

Access to electricity worldwide stood at 91.9 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 86.9 per cent in 2015. The gain was achieved while the world population grew, but it leaves the world short of the universal access that target 7.1 sets for 2030. The series is reported by 215 countries for 2024, so coverage is nearly complete, though some national figures rest on modelled estimates drawn from industry records and household surveys rather than a fresh count each year.

The divide between rural and urban populations explains much of the shortfall. Rural access rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a larger advance than the urban series, which moved from 96.4 per cent to 97.8 per cent. Urban access was already close to the ceiling at the start of the period, and little room remained for improvement. The remaining deficit is therefore mainly rural: 84.9 per cent rural access leaves 15.1 per cent of rural residents unserved in 2024, against 2.2 per cent of urban residents. This matters for policy, because connecting dispersed households costs more per person than extending an urban grid, and it depends on off-grid and mini-grid solutions as much as on national networks.

A headcount of people without electricity is not published in the series examined here. The scale can only be estimated by applying the 2024 deficit rates to the population series, and the result is the writer's own estimate, not a reported count. Applying 15.1 per cent to the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 gives roughly 523 million rural people; applying 2.2 per cent to the urban population of 4,750,578,960 gives roughly 105 million urban people. Three cautions apply. The access series ends in 2024 while the population series run to 2025, so the years differ. The definition of rural and urban areas is set by each national statistical office and varies between countries. The product of a percentage and a population carries the uncertainty of both inputs. Read with these limits, the estimate suggests a world total of the order of 600 million people, with rural areas holding about five in six of them, even though more people live in cities.

The period also spans two breaks, 2015 and 2020. The first marks the adoption of the goals, the second the pandemic and the economic shocks that followed, which strained public budgets and household incomes and may have slowed some connection programmes. The endpoints given here do not reveal whether progress paused after 2020. The trend projection for the world places access at 95.4 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.65 of the distance to the target covered, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The final stretch of any access target tends to be the hardest, since the unconnected are the most remote and poorest. The sections that follow turn to where that remaining gap lies.

### Sub-Saharan Africa holds most of the remaining gap

Sub-Saharan Africa is the region furthest from universal access. Access in the region stood at 55.1 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 39.2 per cent in 2015. Every other region reported at least 96.8 per cent in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 96.8 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean at 98.0 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 98.6 per cent. Europe and Central Asia stood at 100.0 per cent, and North America at 100.0 per cent in both years. South Asia rose from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, and its rural access rose from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent of the rural population. The contrast shows that near-universal access is attainable at scale, and that Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception, not one case among several.

The divide between rural and urban areas is sharpest in this region. Rural access in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 35.7 per cent of the rural population in 2024, against 82.9 per cent of the urban population. In 2015 the rural figure was 18.5 per cent and the urban figure 72.7 per cent. Rural access therefore rose faster in proportion than urban access, yet the rural deficit, 100 less 35.7, was still 64.3 per cent in 2024: nearly two in three rural residents remained without electricity. The pattern follows from the economics of supply, stated here as general context outside the results. Grid extension to dispersed settlements costs more per household and recovers less revenue, so utilities and public programmes have tended to serve towns first. Off-grid solar and mini-grids have widened the options in recent years, although the series reports access without separating the technologies behind it.

Income groups show the same shape. Low-income economies reached 48.8 per cent access in 2024, up from 32.2 per cent in 2015. Rural access in that group stood at 37.1 per cent and urban access at 77.6 per cent. The results do not give the regional composition of the group, so no link to Sub-Saharan Africa is asserted here. Lower-middle-income economies reached 91.4 per cent, and upper-middle-income and high-income economies stood at 99.3 per cent and 100.0 per cent respectively.

The results give no reported headcount of people without electricity, so the scale can only be indicated by derivation. Applying the 2024 rural deficit of 64.3 per cent to the 2025 rural population of 731,422,742 in Sub-Saharan Africa suggests roughly 470 million rural residents without access, an approximation. The same method with the urban deficit of 17.1 per cent and an urban population of 590,231,475 suggests a smaller number, about 105 million, in towns and cities. These are the writer's own estimates, not figures reported by the series: they mix years, and national definitions of rural and urban areas differ. They indicate that the unserved in the region are concentrated in rural areas. The results do not state the region's share of the world total, so the heading's claim rests on these derived estimates alone. Rural population in the region rose from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, and urban population grew from 408,204,795 to 590,231,475. Population growth therefore works against the connection effort: every year of progress in the access rate must also cover new households.

For 2030 the implication is plain. The other regions are within a few points of universality, and their remaining gaps are small. The target will be met or missed in Sub-Saharan Africa. The trend tool classes the region as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and expects 69.2 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.49 of the distance to the target covered. That ratio implies the region is covering about half the progress required, so closing the gap would need roughly twice the pace of 2015 to 2024, concentrated on rural households that are costly to reach.

### Rural areas and South Asia account for the change since 2015

South Asia's gain moved the world average most, but not because its gain in points was the largest. Access in the region rose from 86.5 per cent of the population in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 13 points. Sub-Saharan Africa's overall gain was larger in points, from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, about 16 points. South Asia's rural gain was the largest of any region, from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent. Because South Asia holds a very large rural population, 1,035,602,697 people in 2015 and 1,086,549,811 in 2025, closing its rural gap shifted the world average more than any other change. The region is now close to Europe and Central Asia, where access stood at 99.9989 per cent in 2024 (100.0 to one decimal place), so its contribution to further global gains is nearly exhausted.

The rural gap narrowed worldwide. Rural access in the world rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 8 points, against about 5 points for the population as a whole. Rural areas therefore improved faster than the average, which is what a closing gap requires. Rural gains were also large in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, from 87.6 per cent to 94.0 per cent, and in low-income countries, from 17.2 per cent to 37.1 per cent. In Latin America and the Caribbean the rural rate moved from 89.1 per cent to 91.0 per cent, a smaller change, and it remains well below the region's overall rate of 98.0 per cent in 2024.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows a different pattern. Rural access rose from 18.5 per cent in 2015 to 35.7 per cent in 2024, and urban access from 72.7 per cent to 82.9 per cent. These within-area rises are the reported facts behind the regional gain. Yet the rural population of the region grew from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, so a rising rate is applied to a growing base. Rural access of 35.7 per cent in 2024 means that roughly two in three rural residents of the region remained unconnected. The urban population also rose, from 408,204,795 in 2015 to 590,231,475 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 182,500,508 to 269,862,804. Population shifts between rural and urban areas may also play a part in the regional average, but the series cannot test this and no share of the gain is attributed to it.

The question of how many people lack electricity can be answered only by derivation, since the results give shares and not headcounts. As the writer's own estimate, not a reported count, applying the world rural deficit of 15.1 per cent (100 less 84.9 per cent in 2024) to the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 gives about 523 million rural residents. Applying the urban deficit of 2.2 per cent to the urban population of 4,750,578,960 gives about 105 million. These products mix reference years, 2024 for access and 2025 for population, and rest on national definitions of rural and urban, so they indicate scale only. They also show that the unserved are overwhelmingly rural.

Causes call for restraint. The indicators show where access changed and by how much, not which policies produced it. Well-established experience points to national grid extension programmes, falling costs of solar equipment and off-grid systems, and public financing as usual drivers, but the series cannot attribute the South Asian or African gains to any one of them. Nor do the figures cited show a break after 2020, since the comparison runs between 2015 and 2024 only.

For 2030, the implication is that the world's average is now governed by one region. South Asia has largely finished its part, East Asia and the Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean are above 98 per cent, and the remaining distance lies in rural Sub-Saharan Africa, where population growth works against each point gained.

### Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030, and proposals follow

Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030 on the evidence of the trend classification. Of the 215 countries assessed, 154 are on track or have already met the target, and they hold 74.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 33 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 15.6 per cent of the population. Another 21 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 8.0 per cent of the population. Two countries are stagnant, with 0.4 per cent, and five are regressing, with 1.4 per cent. The count of countries therefore looks reassuring, while the population shares show that about a quarter of the people in the countries assessed live where the present pace will not close the gap.

The aggregate projection agrees. Extending the 2015 to 2024 pace, the world would reach 95.4 per cent access in 2030, and the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.65, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Three groups have the lowest ratios, and all are classed as marginal. Latin America and the Caribbean has the lowest, at 0.47, followed by low-income countries at 0.48 and Sub-Saharan Africa at 0.49. The first differs in kind from the other two: its access was already 98.0 per cent in 2024, so the little that remains moves slowly, and the same pace would bring it to 98.6 per cent in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 69.2 per cent in 2030 and low-income countries 64.4 per cent, so these two stay far from the goal. A ratio of 0.49 means the present pace covers under half of the distance to the target, so closing the gap would need roughly twice the pace observed since 2015. South Asia, with a ratio of 1.73, and lower middle income countries, with 1.01, are on track, although the lower middle income result rests on a narrow margin.

These readings depend on how target 7.1 is interpreted. The classification treats the target as 100 per cent access by 2030, which is the plainest reading of universal access. A projection above 100, such as South Asia's 109.8 per cent, cannot occur in fact and shows only that a linear extrapolation overshoots a ceiling. As general context, not a finding of the series, the last stretch before universality is often harder than the early gains, because the remaining households tend to be more remote and poorer, so linear extrapolation may flatter regions near the ceiling. The target further names affordable and reliable energy services. The indicator measures only whether a population has access to electricity. It says nothing about the price paid, the hours of supply or the quality of the connection, so a country classed as on track may still fall short of the full wording of the target.

The implication for 2030 is that the world will not reach universal access on present trends, and that the missing people will be concentrated where the pace is slowest, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries, particularly in rural areas, where access in the region was 35.7 per cent in 2024. Rural access in low-income countries was 37.1 per cent in the same year.

The question of how many people lack electricity can be answered only by a rough derivation, since the results hold no published headcount. Rural access for the world was 84.9 per cent in 2024, leaving a rural deficit of 15.1 per cent, and the rural population was 3,464,845,933 in 2025. Urban access was 97.8 per cent in 2024, leaving a deficit of 2.2 per cent, and the urban population was 4,750,578,960 in 2025. Applying the rates to the populations gives about 523 million rural residents and about 105 million urban residents, or roughly 628 million people in all. This is the writer's own estimate, not a reported count. It mixes years, rounds the rates and relies on national definitions of rural and urban areas, so it indicates scale only. It also shows that the rural deficit is the larger part of the world's shortfall.

w-c09-5-2~rowan/writer-2~112.text:
### Unemployment and the participation gap at the global level

Between 2015 and 2025 the world picture for target 8.5 divides into two movements of very different size. Youth unemployment fell, while female participation in the labour force barely changed. The two series answer different parts of the target, and neither alone shows whether full and productive employment is being reached.

Youth unemployment, measured as the share of the labour force aged 15 to 24 without work but available for and seeking it, stood at 16.0% worldwide in 2015 and at 13.4% in 2025. For young women the rate was 17.0% in 2015 and 14.9% in 2025. Both are modelled ILO estimates. Young women therefore had a higher rate than the youth labour force as a whole at both dates, and the decline for each group was real but left a rate that is still high. A global rate of 13.4% in the latest year, between one in eight and one in seven of the young labour force, shows that the target's wording on young people is far from met, though the target sets no numerical threshold.

Female labour force participation, the labour force as a share of the female population aged 15 and over, was 48.5% in 2015 and 48.9% in 2025. At the global level this is a movement of a few tenths of a percentage point over ten years. Whatever happened to women's access to work in the period, the aggregate shows no broad rise. The figure also conceals movements of opposite sign beneath it, which later parts of this section take up by region and country. These measures draw on 182 reporting countries in 2025.

The figures are modelled estimates, not direct national counts. Modelling allows countries with different survey calendars and definitions to be compared and gives a value for years in which a national survey was not run. The cost is that, where a country has few surveys, the estimate leans on patterns in similar countries and may not reflect that country's own labour market. Year-to-year movements in particular should be read with caution, and the comparison here is deliberately between two end years. The ratio of female to male participation is a national-estimate series, drawn on each country's own definitions, and it is used in the later parts on regions and countries, not for the global comparison made here.

Target 8.5 can be read in more than one way, and the reading changes the verdict. Read as a level of unemployment, it asks that few people who want work lack it, and the falling youth rate counts as progress. Read as parity, it asks that women and men take part in work on equal terms, and the participation rate of women, taken alone, cannot show that: it needs comparison with the male rate, which the ratio series supplies. The target also names equal pay, disabled persons and decent work, none of which these series measure. A fall in unemployment can occur because people leave the labour force or stop searching, so a lower rate is not by itself proof of more or better jobs.

For 2030 the global averages set the frame. At 13.4% youth unemployment is lower than a decade earlier, yet the participation of women at 48.9% has not moved in the way that a path to parity would require. The regional and income-group figures that follow show where the global averages come from and where the gaps are widest.

### Regional differences in youth unemployment and female participation

Regional experience since 2015 departs sharply from the world averages. Youth unemployment, measured as a share of the labour force aged 15 to 24, fell most in Europe and Central Asia, from 19.9 per cent in 2015 to 14.0 per cent in 2025. South Asia shows a similar fall, from 23.2 per cent to 15.4 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 14.7 per cent to 12.2 per cent, and North America from 11.7 per cent to 9.8 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa began lower and ended lower, at 11.3 per cent in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2025. East Asia and Pacific is the exception among the regions: youth unemployment rose from 10.4 per cent to 12.5 per cent over the decade.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands apart for a different reason. Youth unemployment there was 20.1 per cent in 2015 and 18.7 per cent in 2025, a small improvement that leaves it the highest of the regions in the latest year. Young women in that region fare worse still: female youth unemployment was 28.5 per cent in 2015 and 28.3 per cent in 2025, essentially unchanged. By comparison, the same measure for young women in South Asia fell from 22.6 per cent to 16.3 per cent, and in Europe and Central Asia from 20.3 per cent to 14.7 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific it rose from 9.9 per cent to 11.7 per cent, in step with the rise for young people as a whole.

Female participation in the labour force, measured as a share of women aged 15 and over from modelled estimates, shows a different geography. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest rate, 64.6 per cent in 2015 and 65.2 per cent in 2025. East Asia and Pacific follows at 59.7 per cent in 2015 and 58.1 per cent in 2025, a fall. North America is nearly flat, at 56.5 per cent and then 56.8 per cent. Europe and Central Asia rose from 50.2 per cent to 51.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 50.8 per cent to 51.4 per cent. South Asia rose the most, from 27.5 per cent to 33.0 per cent, although the level remains low. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the rate fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent, the lowest of any region in both years. A high participation rate is not in itself a sign of decent work. As context rather than finding, women in low-income settings often work because household incomes leave no alternative, so the rate must be read beside the section on informal and vulnerable employment.

The ratio of female to male participation, a national estimate with 100.0 as the point of parity, puts the gap in relative terms. The trend results give the expected values for 2030 and the class of each path. In Europe and Central Asia the trend is classed as stagnation, with 80.3 expected in 2030. High-income economies are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 83.2 expected in 2030. Latin America and the Caribbean is under the same classification, with 71.9 expected in 2030. North America is expected to reach 86.0 in 2030 on its present path, again with significant acceleration needed. South Asia is expected to reach 60.5 in 2030 and is also classed as marginal progress. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the one region in regression, with an expected ratio of 29.8 in 2030. These are extrapolations of past rates, not forecasts, and say nothing of policy changes that might alter them.

One result calls for caution. The lower-middle-income group is classed as on track or target met, with 99.6 expected in 2030. That path starts in 2018, not 2015, covers a short period, and rests on national estimates, whose coverage and definitions can differ between survey rounds. The classification should be treated with caution and not read as parity within reach.

The regional list in the trend results is also cut short. East Asia and Pacific and Sub-Saharan Africa are not reported there, and the figures for them in this part come only from the participation and unemployment levels. Their ratios of female to male participation are therefore not stated, and no judgement about their path to parity is made.

### How countries are distributed along the path to parity

The classification of 166 countries on the ratio of female to male labour force participation (a national estimate) shows how uneven the path to parity is. The target value is 100.0 per cent by 2030. Each country is placed by the compound annual rate of change from its 2015 baseline, or from the first year after it, and by the share of the distance to the target that this rate would cover by 2030.

Only 13 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 7.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 19 countries, with 2.8 per cent of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest class is the 71 countries making marginal progress and needing significant acceleration. They hold 61.7 per cent of the population, so most people in the countries assessed live where the gap is narrowing too slowly to close by 2030.

The two classes that show no gain are reported separately. In 13 countries, with 10.4 per cent of the population, the ratio is stagnating. In 50 countries, with 17.9 per cent of the population, it is regressing, which means it has moved away from parity. A fall in the ratio can arise in two ways: women's participation may have fallen, or men's may have risen faster. The classification does not distinguish between them and does not show causes. As context only, and not as a finding of these results, the pace of structural change in economies, the availability of care services, legal and social norms on women's work, and the 2020 pandemic's effects on sectors that employ many women are commonly discussed influences.

The regional results show why the population shares look as they do. The lower middle income group is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.103 and an expected ratio of 99.6 in 2030. Its series is short, however: it begins in 2018 and ends in 2024, so it covers a shorter span than the others, rests on fewer observations and is a national estimate. Its trend should be treated with caution. South Asia has a rate of 0.065 and an expected ratio of 60.5 in 2030, covering 0.448 of the distance to the target. This is the largest share among the regions not classed as on track, yet the ratio stays low. Europe and Central Asia is classed as stagnating, with an expected ratio of 80.3 in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan as regressing, with an expected ratio of 29.8.

The rate has limits as a reading. It is a compound annual change measured from a baseline, so it favours countries that start low, where a small absolute gain is a large proportional one, and it penalises those that start near parity. High income economies, at an expected 83.2 in 2030, and North America, at 86.0, are classed as marginal because the remaining distance is covered too slowly, not because they are far from parity. Reaching exactly 100.0 is also only one reading of the target: a ratio above 100.0 would mean women participate more than men, and the target text speaks of equality, not of a particular value. Finally, the classification covers 166 countries, fewer than the 204 with some data on the series, because a trend needs observations at both ends of the period.

### What changed and what may explain it

The movements recorded since 2015 are of two kinds. Youth unemployment is sensitive to the business cycle. Its fall in several regions may be consistent with recovery after the shock of 2020, when hiring stopped and young people, often on temporary contracts, were among the first to lose work; this is context, not a finding of the results. Female participation moves far more slowly, because it reflects household arrangements, schooling, the availability of care, legal restrictions and social norms that change over decades. The two series should therefore be read at different speeds.

The participation rates show divergence beneath a flat world figure. Female participation in South Asia rose from 27.5 per cent of women aged 15 and over in 2015 to 33.0 per cent in 2025. In East Asia and Pacific it fell from 59.7 per cent to 58.1 per cent over the same years. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan it fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent, the lowest level of any region in both years. The world rate, 48.5 per cent in 2015 and 48.9 per cent in 2025, is the result of rises and falls that largely offset each other. Sub-Saharan Africa stayed highest, at 64.6 per cent in 2015 and 65.2 per cent in 2025.

Income groups show a similar split. Female participation rose in lower middle income countries, from 35.5 per cent to 39.2 per cent, and in high income countries, from 52.8 per cent to 54.3 per cent. It fell in low income countries, from 56.6 per cent to 54.7 per cent, and in upper middle income countries, from 55.0 per cent to 53.4 per cent. Youth unemployment among young women moved in a related way: in upper middle income countries it rose from 16.4 per cent to 17.3 per cent, while in high income countries it fell from 16.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

These indicators cannot identify causes. A fall in participation may reflect women withdrawing from work, women staying longer in education, or discouragement that removes them from the count of the unemployed; the series does not distinguish them. A rise may reflect new opportunity or economic necessity. Explanations drawn from the history of regions, such as expanding schooling, changing norms or legal barriers to women's work, remain context and not findings.

The second half of target 8.5, equal pay for work of equal value, is not measured by any of these results. Unemployment and participation describe access to work, not its reward, so progress on pay cannot be judged from this section.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The projections for 2030 show that parity in labour force participation will not be reached on the present paths. The target value for the ratio of female to male participation (a national estimate) is 100.0 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the ratio was stagnant, and the expected value for 2030 is 80.3 per cent. In high-income countries, where progress was marginal and significant acceleration is needed, the expected value is 83.2 per cent. Both fall well short of the target. Latin America and the Caribbean is expected to reach 71.9 per cent, and North America 86.0 per cent. South Asia is expected to reach 60.5 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the series regressed and is expected to stand at 29.8 per cent.

Only one regional group projects to parity. The lower-middle-income group is expected to reach 99.6 per cent, but its series begins in 2018 and rests on a short run of national estimates, so this result should be treated with caution. The target can also be read in more than one way: a ratio of 100.0 per cent means equal participation rates, not equal pay or equal quality of work, and the section's series do not measure pay.

The country classification points the same way. Of 166 countries assessed, 13 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 7.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Thirteen countries stagnate, holding 10.4 per cent of that population, and 50 regressed, holding 17.9 per cent. Most people live in the group of 71 countries with marginal progress, which holds 61.7 per cent. Acceleration, not continuation, is therefore the condition for any gain by 2030.

The proposals below follow from these findings.
