w-c09-7-2~dahlia/writer-1~112.text:
### Child labour data thin out as the 2025 target year passes

The indicator available for Target 8.7 is the share of children aged 7 to 14 in employment, defined as involvement in economic activity for at least one hour in the reference week of a household survey. The World Bank's series carries no aggregate for the world or for any region, so the shelf offers no global share of children in employment. Only country values exist. The bench results used for this part report how many countries have values in each year, not the shares themselves, so no country share is quoted here; the shares and their spread are taken up in the next part.

The number of countries reporting shows how thin the record is. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2016, 97 countries reported at least once. Coverage in any single year was far smaller. It stood at 24 countries in 2000, fell to 4 in 2002, and rose to a peak of 31 in 2006. Later counts were 12 in 2008, 22 in 2011, 24 in 2012, 18 in 2014 and 10 in 2015. In 2016, the latest year, only 2 countries reported. The year of the latest observation is therefore 2016, and it rests on two countries. As context not tested by these results, household surveys are usually held every few years and a country appears only in a year when one was completed and processed.

This matters because Target 8.7 sets a date. It calls for an end to child labour in all its forms by 2025, and that year has now arrived or passed. The latest observations on the shelf are from 2016, so the data cannot say how far the world has moved towards the target since 2015, or what the pandemic after 2020 did to children's work. School closures and loss of household income are widely understood to push children towards work, but nothing in this series measures that effect.

The indicator also covers only part of what the target names. It counts children aged 7 to 14, and the series holds no values for older children up to 17, who fall within the usual definition of child labour. It counts any economic activity of at least one hour in a week, which is broader than the worst forms of child labour and is not the same as child labour as defined in standards. It says nothing on forced labour, trafficking or the recruitment of child soldiers, which the target also names. Where the target can be read as the elimination of child labour in every form, this series can speak to only a narrow part of it.

### Country values differ widely, and most of the difference lies between regions

Among the countries that reported, the spread of children's employment is wide, and it moves sharply from one year to the next. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of country values was 0.232 in 2006, when 31 countries reported, and 0.625 in 2012, when 24 did. A Gini of 0 would mean every country had the same share; the 2012 figure indicates a distribution in which a few populous countries sit far from the rest. The Theil index tells the same story: 0.135 in 2006 and 0.856 in 2012. The other years shown fall between these two extremes: the Gini was 0.431 in 2000, 0.508 in 2005, 0.532 in 2010 and 0.390 in 2011.

Most of this inequality lies between regions rather than within them. The between-region share of Theil's T was 91.9% in 2000, 92.3% in 2005, 85.4% in 2006, 92.6% in 2010, 77.0% in 2011 and 91.7% in 2012. In five of the six years shown, more than four-fifths of the difference among countries is therefore attributable to differences between regional averages. The lowest share, 77.0% in 2011, still leaves regional position as the largest component. As context rather than a finding of these results, the pattern is consistent with the long-standing concentration of high child employment in poorer, agrarian economies, where household survey evidence has repeatedly shown work in family farming to be the commonest form. The measure does not identify which regions or countries drive the figures, and the results give no basis for naming them.

The swings between years cannot be read as real change in the world. The set of reporting countries changes every year: 24 in 2000, 26 in 2005, 31 in 2006, 21 in 2010, 22 in 2011 and 24 in 2012. A drop in the Gini from 0.508 in 2005 to 0.232 in 2006 coincides with the addition of five countries to the sample, and the rise to 0.625 in 2012 coincides with a different set again. Because each year's calculation covers only the countries that happened to be surveyed, a high or low value may reflect which countries reported as much as any shift in how children's work is distributed. Population weighting sharpens this effect, since one large country entering or leaving the sample can move the whole index.

The spread is also silent on levels. A low Gini could describe uniformly high or uniformly low child employment, so these figures describe inequality among countries and say nothing on whether children's work is rising or falling. No year after 2012 appears in the spread results, and the sparse reporting of later years leaves the 2015 and 2020 periods without a comparable reading. For 2030, the only safe inference is that where child employment persists, it is concentrated by region, and that measuring it will require the same countries to be surveyed repeatedly.

### Change over time cannot be separated from change in coverage

Reading the series as a trend requires first reading the number of countries behind each year. The count of reporting countries was 4 in 2002, rose to 31 in 2006, fell to 12 in 2008, recovered to 24 in 2012, and was 10 in 2015. In 2016 only 2 countries reported. A comparison of yearly figures across these years would compare different groups of countries, so a rise or fall in a share could reflect who was surveyed rather than what happened to children. Across the whole period 97 countries reported at least once, so the series reaches widely over time but has little depth in any single year.

The reasons for the pattern are not recorded in the data. As context only, children's employment is measured through household surveys, which are usually fielded irregularly and only where funding and priority allow, and clusters of survey rounds may explain some peaks, such as the 31 countries of 2006. This explanation is not tested by the results.

The 2016 observations are the latest on the shelf, and they cannot carry a reading of the period after 2015. Two countries are too few to indicate a direction, and the shelf holds nothing later, so neither the years after 2015 nor the period after 2020 can be described. The disruptions of 2020 to schooling and household incomes are widely expected to bear on children's work, but the series offers no measurement of it.

The same limit applies to boys and girls. The male and female series each have 2 countries reporting in 2016, the same 2 as the total, so a gap between the sexes drawn from them would describe those countries alone. Earlier years hold more countries but are not comparable with 2016 for the reasons given above.

For 2030 and for the 2025 date set in Target 8.7, the implication is plain. With 10 countries reporting in 2015 and 2 in 2016, the evidence for judging whether child labour has ended is thinner than in 2006, when 31 countries reported. Progress can be neither confirmed nor refuted from this series, and the thinning of the data is itself the main result of the period.

### The 2025 target cannot be verified, and the proposals follow from that

The target year has arrived without a measurable global baseline from this series. Target 8.7 sets 2025 as the date by which child labour in all its forms is to end, yet the latest year in the series is 2016, and in that year only 2 countries reported. Across the whole period 97 countries reported at least once, but the most in any single year was 31, in 2006. The bench results give no share of children in employment for any named country or year, because the summaries report only how many countries reported and how unequal their values were. The question of what share of children are in employment therefore cannot be answered with a figure from these results, and the series carries no aggregate for the world or for any region. A reading of progress towards 2025, or of the position in 2030, cannot be drawn from data of this kind.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Its first clause calls for the elimination of the worst forms of child labour, including the recruitment and use of child soldiers; its closing clause calls for an end to child labour in all its forms by 2025. The indicator available here measures neither exactly. It counts children aged 7 to 14 involved in economic activity for at least one hour in the reference week. That includes light work that many national laws permit. The series holds no values for children aged 15 to 17, who may be in hazardous work. It also does not capture forced labour, trafficking or armed recruitment. A falling share on this measure would be encouraging but would not show that the worst forms had ended, and a flat share would not show that they persisted.

The series for boys and for girls also stand at 2 reporting countries in 2016, so differences between the sexes cannot be assessed for the years that matter most for the target, those after 2015 and after the disruption of 2020. Household poverty, school closures and weak enforcement are commonly associated with child labour and may have changed in those years, but this is outside context and the data give no means of testing it. The spread results cover 2000 to 2012 only and offer no reading for 2030.

For these reasons Target 8.7 is best treated as unassessed on the evidence of this series, and the proposals below follow from that finding rather than from any measured trend.

The World Bank and its partners should publish regional and global aggregates only when enough countries report, and should state the number of reporting countries beside each figure.
The bodies that review Target 8.7 should state which reading of the target they adopt, all forms or the worst forms, so that an indicator can be matched to it.

t-paired-country-comparison~elm/analyst-.code:
def tool(data, params):
    a = params['bottom_code']
    b = params['average_code']
    y0 = params.get('min_year', 0)
    da = data[a]
    db = data[b]
    names = data['names']
    higher = []
    compared = 0
    for unit_a in da:
        break
    for c in da:
        if c not in db:
            continue
        sa = da[c]
        sb = db[c]
        yrs = [y for y in sa if y in sb and int(y) >= y0]
        if not yrs:
            continue
        y = max(yrs, key=lambda k: int(k))
        compared += 1
        if sa[y] > sb[y]:
            higher.append(c)
    share = round(100.0 * len(higher) / compared, 1) if compared else 0
    summary = 'Bottom 40 per cent growth exceeds average growth in ' + str(len(higher)) + ' of ' + str(compared) + ' countries compared (' + str(share) + ' per cent), using each country\'s latest paired survey period from ' + str(y0) + '. Countries without both values are excluded; survey periods differ between countries.'
    return {'facts': {'countries_compared': compared, 'bottom40_exceeds_average': len(higher), 'share_per_cent': share, 'min_year': y0}, 'summary': summary}
t-paired-country-comparison~elm/analyst-.about: Counts countries where the latest growth in income or consumption of the bottom 40 per cent exceeds growth in the survey mean for the same year, and reports the number of countries compared.

params.min_year: Earliest year admitted to the comparison

w-c07-2-2~loom/writer-2~113.text:
### Global access to basic sanitation reached 82.2 per cent in 2024

Basic sanitation, defined as an improved facility not shared with other households, reached 82.2 per cent of the world's population in 2024, up from 72.6 per cent in 2015. In 2024, 193 countries reported this series, so the global figure rests on near-complete reporting. Open defecation fell over the same period from 10.6 per cent to 4.3 per cent of the population, with 184 countries reporting in 2024. Handwashing is measured less fully: the share of people with a handwashing facility with soap and water on the premises was 78.0 per cent in 2024, against 68.8 per cent in 2017, the first year for which a world value exists. Only 91 countries reported handwashing in 2024, so that global figure is a weaker basis for judgement than the other two.

The shares can be turned into rough numbers of people by applying them to the 2025 world population of 8,215,424,893. This is the authors' own calculation, not a published count, and it mixes years, since the shares refer to 2024 and the population to 2025. On that basis, the 17.8 per cent without basic sanitation corresponds to roughly 1.5 billion people, the 4.3 per cent still defecating in the open to roughly 350 million, and the 22.0 per cent without basic handwashing facilities to roughly 1.8 billion. These are orders of magnitude, not counts, and should be read as such.

The pace matters for 2030. Open defecation more than halved in nine years, a considerable achievement, yet the target of ending the practice requires the remaining share to reach effectively zero within six years. At the compound rate observed since 2015, the world share would still stand at 2.4 per cent in 2030, so the trend is classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. The last fraction is usually the hardest to reach because it is concentrated in poor, remote and marginalised households, a point of context that these results do not test. Population growth also works against progress: the world population was 7,441,084,771 in 2015 and 8,215,424,893 in 2025, so service has had to expand faster than the shares alone suggest.

The wording of the target requires care. Target 6.2 calls for adequate and equitable sanitation and hygiene for all, and the phrase can be read as basic service, as safely managed service in which excreta are safely disposed of or treated, or as something stricter still. The indicators used in this part measure only the basic level, together with open defecation and handwashing. Reaching basic coverage therefore does not show that the target's higher reading has been met, and the equity and gender dimensions of the wording are not visible in global averages.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries carry the largest deficits

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group stand furthest from the target of adequate sanitation for all. In 2024, 37.1 per cent of people in Sub-Saharan Africa used at least basic sanitation, up from 30.8 per cent in 2015. The low-income group moved from 29.2 per cent to 33.3 per cent over the same years. Both remain far below the world figure of 82.2 per cent in 2024, and the change in nine years was small beside the distance still to be covered.

Open defecation shows the same pattern. In Sub-Saharan Africa 15.5 per cent of the population still defecated in the open in 2024, down from 22.0 per cent in 2015. Low-income countries stood at 17.2 per cent in 2024, against 24.6 per cent in 2015. These are the highest rates of any region or income group in the data. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 22.1 per cent to 7.3 per cent, and upper-middle-income countries from 2.4 per cent to 0.4 per cent.

Handwashing is weakest in the same places. Basic handwashing facilities with soap and water reached 25.0 per cent of people in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2024, against 23.0 per cent in 2015, and 24.6 per cent in low-income countries, against 21.8 per cent. The world figure was 78.0 per cent in 2024. Handwashing coverage is thinner than the other series, with 91 countries reporting in 2024. Regional series for Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America are not reported in the handwashing result, so no comparison with them can be drawn here, and the East Asia and Pacific series begins in 2017 rather than 2015.

The contrast with South Asia is instructive. That region rose from 56.8 per cent to 82.0 per cent in basic sanitation and cut open defecation from 27.2 per cent to 5.8 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa began 2015 with much lower access, at 30.8 per cent against 56.8 per cent, and with somewhat lower open defecation, at 22.0 per cent against 27.2 per cent, yet moved more slowly on both. East Asia and Pacific rose from 83.7 per cent to 94.8 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia from 95.7 per cent to 97.4 per cent. North America stood at 99.5 per cent in 2024, against 99.7 per cent in 2015.

Population growth works against the African gains. The population of Sub-Saharan Africa grew from 1,024,659,421 in 2015 to 1,321,654,217 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 584,512,207 to 767,490,169. A rising share of users can coexist with a large and growing number of people left without service, because new facilities must first serve the added population. The data cited do not separate this effect from others, and the population series ends in 2025 while the sanitation series ends in 2024. Outside sources suggest, without the results testing it, that low public investment, rapid urbanisation and weak sanitation services in informal settlements contribute.

For 2030, the open defecation projections show the scale of the gap. At the pace seen since 2015, Sub-Saharan Africa would still stand at 12.2 per cent in 2030, and the low-income group at 13.6 per cent, against a target of zero. Both are classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Their ratios, 0.446 and 0.447, give the share of the distance from the 2015 level to the target that the trend would cover, so under half is covered. The results give no 2030 projection for basic sanitation, so no such statement is made here. Target 6.2 can also be read in more than one way: basic sanitation is a lower standard than the adequate sanitation the target text names, so the figures here may flatter the position.

### Progress since 2015 was driven by South Asia, and handwashing lags

Open defecation fell most steeply in South Asia, where the share of the population defecating in the open went from 27.2 per cent in 2015 to 5.8 per cent in 2024. The data show these trajectories, not their causes. The trend tool reads each series by its compound annual rate of change and by a ratio, which is the share of the distance from the 2015 level to the target that the trend would cover by 2030. South Asia's rate was -0.1573 a year, a ratio of 0.92, and the series is expected to reach 2.1 per cent of the population in 2030. Latin America & Caribbean (rate -0.1638, ratio 0.93) and East Asia & Pacific (rate -0.1416, ratio 0.90) show similar paths from much lower levels, and the upper middle income group is the fastest (rate -0.1751, ratio 0.94). The world as a whole, at a rate of -0.0947 and a ratio of 0.78, is classed as making moderate progress and needing acceleration, with 2.4 per cent of the population still expected to defecate in the open in 2030.

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group follow a different course. Their rates are -0.0386 and -0.0387 a year, with ratios of 0.45, and both are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. At these rates open defecation would still affect 12.2 per cent of people in Sub-Saharan Africa and 13.6 per cent in the low-income group in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa began 2015 with much lower access to basic sanitation than South Asia (30.8 against 56.8 per cent) and somewhat lower open defecation (22.0 against 27.2 per cent), yet moved more slowly. Large-scale sanitation campaigns, rural latrine programmes and rising incomes are commonly cited as influences on such declines, but the series do not identify what drove any of these changes; these explanations remain hypotheses.

Country classes give a fuller picture. For open defecation, 33 countries are on track or have met the target, holding 38.1 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 50 more show moderate progress (44.3 per cent). Another 36 countries show marginal progress (13.2 per cent), 20 stagnate (3.5 per cent) and 8 regress (0.8 per cent), out of 147 assessed. Shares of population and counts of countries differ, so a class with many countries can hold a small share of people, and the reverse.

Basic sanitation is more uneven. Of 213 countries assessed across the period, 49 are on track or have met the target (46.6 per cent of their population), but 39 are regressing, and those hold 13.4 per cent of the population. A further 37 stagnate (5.8 per cent). The 213 assessed differ from the 193 that reported in 2024, since the first count spans the period and the second a single year. Gains in some places are therefore offset by deterioration in others, which can occur when population growth outpaces the building of facilities, though the data do not show this.

Handwashing lags most. Of 118 countries assessed, 15 are on track or have met the target (38.2 per cent of their population), 9 show moderate progress (3.2 per cent) and 22 show marginal progress (33.8 per cent). Half of the assessed countries, 59, stagnate (20.1 per cent), and 13 regress (4.6 per cent). Coverage is narrower than for the other series, since 91 countries reported handwashing in 2024, so these results describe a smaller set of countries. Handwashing in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 25.0 per cent in 2024, against 87.4 per cent in South Asia. For 2030, the trend tool projects only open defecation, which could come close to ending only with acceleration in the regions that lag. No 2030 projection is given here for basic sanitation or handwashing, whose country classes show many countries stagnating or regressing.

w-c09-8-3~juniper/writer-1~113.text:
### Tourism receipts and arrivals as measures of Target 8.9

Target 8.9 commits governments to devise and implement policies for sustainable tourism that creates jobs and promotes local culture and products. The target names three outcomes: sustainability, employment and the promotion of local culture and products. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline, and it leaves open what counts as sustainable. It can be read as a call for policy, as a call for better outcomes, or as both, and the indicators do not settle which.

The World Development Indicators hold tourism series that measure something narrower. International tourism arrivals count overnight visitors who travel to a country other than the one in which they usually live. International tourism receipts record the expenditure of those inbound visitors, including payments to national carriers for international transport. A related series expresses receipts as a share of total exports, and another isolates receipts for passenger transport items. These describe the scale of the sector and its weight in an economy's external earnings.

None of them observes the content of Target 8.9. Arrivals say how many people came, not how long they stayed, what they damaged or what they preserved. Receipts record money entering a country, not how much of it remained with local workers, local producers or cultural institutions, since a large share of spending can leave through imports, foreign ownership and international transport. Neither series counts jobs in tourism, measures pay or conditions, or distinguishes cultural products from other purchases. Domestic tourism, which is large in many countries, falls outside both series.

The bench can therefore read how large and how widely reported international tourism is, and how that changed around 2015 and 2020. It cannot say whether tourism became more sustainable or more locally beneficial. The first result in this section, on the arrivals series, shows how many countries report in each year, which sets the limits of any comparison. In the figures from 2000 to 2020, reporting reached 202 countries in at least one year, and it is on that base that the later parts read the series. Findings on size and recovery are evidence about the economic scale of the sector. They are indirect evidence on the target, and the text says so wherever it matters.

### Coverage of the arrivals series, 2000 to 2020

The arrivals series, International tourism, number of arrivals (ST.INT.ARVL), has reports from 202 countries and territories in at least one year of the period covered. No single year reaches that figure. In 2000, 175 countries reported. The count then rose with some interruptions: 173 in 2002, 179 in 2005, 186 in 2007 and 190 in 2008. It dipped to 187 in 2009 and returned to 190 in 2010. Counts of 191 in 2011 and 190 in 2014 show a plateau, although the counts for 2012 and 2013, both 190, are the same as those on either side of them.

The peak came after the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. In 2015 and 2016, 194 countries reported arrivals, the highest counts in the period. The count then eased to 190 in 2017, 186 in 2018 and 179 in 2019. The 2019 count equals that of 2005. Part of the decline after 2016 may reflect delays in compiling national statistics, since the latest years of many series are filled in later. The data do not show whether that explains it.

The figure for 2020 is the most striking: 132 countries reported, against 179 the year before, the largest fall between consecutive years in the period. As general context from outside these results, the pandemic is understood to have sharply reduced international travel, and statistical offices and tourism authorities also faced disruption. The coverage count cannot separate the two effects. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded very few arrivals and not reported them, or may have been unable to compile the figure. The count does not identify which countries are missing. Either way, the 2020 values come from a smaller and possibly different group of countries than the 2019 values.

This section therefore holds no finding on the size of arrivals or receipts, nor on recovery after 2020: only coverage counts were retrieved, and the question of scale is left unanswered here. A total for 2020 compared with 2019 would mix a real fall in travel with a change in which countries are counted. Comparisons are sounder when restricted to countries reporting in both years. The series considered here end in 2020 as listed in the shelf description, so they say nothing on recovery in later years.

The coverage result also lists aggregates for the arrivals series: seven regions, four income groups and the world. They inherit the reporting gaps described above, and the results do not state how non-reporting countries are treated, so aggregate values for 2020 should be read with caution.

### Regional and income-group comparison

The coverage result names the aggregates for which the arrivals series (ST.INT.ARVL) is reported, and it establishes nothing more about them. Seven regions appear: East Asia and Pacific (EAS), Europe and Central Asia (ECS), Latin America and the Caribbean (LCN), the Middle East and North Africa (MEA), North America (NAC), South Asia (SAS) and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF). Four income groups appear: high income (HIC), upper-middle income (UMC), lower-middle income (LMC) and low income (LIC). The world total (WLD) completes the list.

This part therefore holds no finding on size or recovery. The result gives no arrivals value, no receipts value and no year-on-year change for any aggregate. No statement can be made here about how many visitors any region or income group received, how much they spent, or which have recovered since 2020. The order in which the codes are listed carries no meaning and supports no ranking. The question of how large tourism is and how it recovered after 2020 stays unanswered by the results retrieved for this section, and the values needed to answer it are not among the facts available.

Once values are retrieved, a comparison across the aggregates would show where visitors concentrate, and whether tourism is a channel of growth open to low-income countries or one dominated by wealthier destinations. Set against receipts, arrivals would indicate spending per visitor, which bears on Target 8.9 because jobs and local products depend on spending, not on headcounts alone. A large regional total can reflect many countries, a large population or a few heavily visited destinations, and a count of arrivals cannot separate these.

Reporting breadth limits any such comparison. The count of reporting countries was 179 in 2019 and 132 in 2020, as set out in the coverage part. Aggregates depend on how many members report, so totals for 2020 may rest on thinner evidence than those of earlier years. The count does not identify which countries are absent in 2020. Any ranking of regions and income groups, and any reading of recovery, should wait until arrivals and receipts values are retrieved for each aggregate and read alongside their reporting counts.

### The 2020 collapse in reporting and the uncertain recovery

The coverage count for arrivals fell from 179 countries in 2019 to 132 in 2020. This section holds no finding on the size of tourism or on its recovery, only counts of reporting countries, because no arrivals or receipts value was retrieved. The count is the only evidence on 2020 here, and it shows how many countries reported, not how many visitors travelled.

The drop of 2020 mixes two effects that a count cannot separate. The pandemic is generally understood to have curtailed international travel sharply, as context from outside these results, and the same disruption affected national statistical offices, which rely on border counts and accommodation surveys. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded fewer visitors, may have published nothing, or may have published late. The count does not identify which countries are missing, so the gap may be concentrated in some regions or income groups; the coverage result does not show this either way. The earlier slide from 194 countries in 2016 to 179 in 2019 may reflect delays in compiling recent national statistics, which the tool records but cannot explain.

The depth of the 2020 fall in visitors and in dollars is therefore unanswered, and the recovery after 2020 cannot be judged. The series notes list 2020 as the latest year for arrivals, receipts, receipts as a share of exports and passenger transport receipts, but no result retrieved for this section confirms the end year of the three receipts series, and that point is unverified here. If it holds, no later observation exists to measure the pace of a rebound. The GDP deflator describes economy-wide prices and cannot stand in for tourism volumes.

A reading of the recovery would need arrivals and receipts for the same countries that reported in 2019, so that the comparison rests on a fixed group and is not distorted by changing coverage. Receipts in current dollars would also have to be set against price changes, since a figure can rise while visitor numbers stay below earlier levels. For Target 8.9, dated 2030, progress after 2020 is at present unmeasured by this shelf.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

This section holds no finding on the size of tourism receipts or arrivals, and none on the recovery after 2020. The results retrieved contain only counts of reporting countries, so the question of how large the sector is, and how far it recovered, cannot be answered here. What the counts show is that monitoring of Target 8.9 weakened in the year that matters most. The arrivals series was reported by 194 countries in 2016 and by 132 in 2020, and across the whole period 202 countries and territories reported in at least one year.

The series descriptions in the shelf give 2020 as the latest year for arrivals, receipts, the export share and passenger transport receipts, but only the arrivals count is backed by a retrieved result in this section. The end years of the three receipts series are therefore stated as the shelf's own description and have not been checked here. If they are correct, the shelf holds no observation of the recovery at all, and any statement on whether tourism has regained its earlier level lies outside the data. The fall in the count of reporting countries reflects some mixture of a real fall in travel and of changes in reporting, and the count cannot apportion the two. Progress towards 2030 cannot be judged from series that end in the year of the disruption.

A second implication concerns what the series measure. Arrivals and receipts describe the volume and value of inbound visits. Neither shows whether tourism creates jobs or promotes local culture and products, the outcomes the target names. Receipts also include payments to national carriers for international transport, so they are not wholly spending inside the destination. They are defined in current dollars, which drift with prices, and the shelf holds the GDP deflator as a reminder of this.

Three proposals follow. National statistical offices in countries absent from the 2020 count should report arrivals annually and publish the missing years; the count does not identify which countries are absent, so the agencies that compile the series should first publish that list. The same agencies should present receipts always alongside arrivals, so that spending per visitor and the weight of transport payments can be read. The custodians of the Sustainable Development Goal indicator framework should add measures of tourism employment and of local content in tourist spending, since Target 8.9 cannot otherwise be tested against its own wording.

w-c09-4-3~juniper/writer-4~113.text:
### Carbon intensity of world output fell between 2015 and 2024

World carbon intensity of GDP, the carbon dioxide emitted per unit of output, stood at 0.26 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar in 2015 and had fallen to 0.22 kg by 2024. The series covers 188 countries reporting in 2024, so the world figure rests on near-complete coverage, though it reaches only to 2024 and later revisions of national inventories may shift it.

The decline did not begin with the Sustainable Development Goals. A break test on the annual change of the world series places a structural break in 2012. In the segment from 2001 to 2011 the mean annual change was -0.00217 kg per dollar, while from 2012 to 2024 it was -0.00531. The fall in intensity was therefore faster in the later period than in the earlier one, and the acceleration predates the adoption of the goals in 2015. The test does not identify what caused the shift. Context from well-established knowledge points to the spread of renewable power, the displacement of coal in several large economies, structural change towards services and efficiency standards, but the result itself shows only the timing and size of the change. It also does not isolate a separate effect of 2020, when output and emissions both fell sharply and then recovered; the annual series passes through that year within the second segment.

What a falling intensity means must be stated carefully. Carbon intensity is a ratio of emissions to output. When it falls, emissions grow more slowly than output, or fall while output rises. That is relative decoupling. It does not show that emissions have fallen in absolute terms: if output grows faster than intensity declines, total emissions still rise. The results held for this part contain no series of absolute emissions for the world, so they cannot settle that question.

Target 8.4 also speaks of resource efficiency in consumption and production, which concerns material use as well as emissions. No material footprint or domestic material consumption series appears among the results, and carbon intensity is only a partial proxy for the use of materials. The target can be read in two ways: as a call for relative decoupling, which the falling ratio would meet, or as a call for absolute decoupling of growth from environmental degradation, which it would not. The wording on developed countries taking the lead adds a further reading, since the pace expected of them differs from that expected elsewhere. The sections that follow treat regional differences and energy efficiency with these limits in mind.

### Regions and countries diverge in the pace of decline

Regional paths differ in both starting point and pace. East Asia and Pacific recorded the largest absolute fall among the regions in the results, from 0.38 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar of GDP in 2015 to 0.31 kg in 2024. It remains the most carbon-intensive region in 2024, with the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 0.28 kg, so the gap between the two is modest. North America fell next most steeply, from 0.25 kg to 0.19 kg. Europe and Central Asia moved from 0.19 kg to 0.15 kg, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.15 kg to 0.13 kg, Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.16 kg to 0.14 kg, and South Asia from 0.25 kg to 0.21 kg.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands apart for pace. Its intensity moved only from 0.31 kg in 2015 to 0.28 kg in 2024, and its trend is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Reliance on hydrocarbons for domestic energy and industry is a commonly cited context for slow decline, and is not a finding of these results. By income group, upper middle income countries fell from 0.36 kg to 0.31 kg and high income countries from 0.22 kg to 0.17 kg, while low income countries moved from 0.10 kg to 0.08 kg. The low level for the poorest group may be associated with small industrial and energy sectors, an explanation offered as context that the results do not test, and a low intensity there is not evidence of efficient production.

The country classification shows a wider spread than any regional average. Of 189 countries assessed, 77 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 24 countries, with 32.7% of that population, show moderate progress, and 13 show marginal progress, with 3.0%. Another 13 are stagnant, with 3.7%. Regression, meaning intensity rose over the period, affects 62 countries and 21.5% of the population. Regional averages therefore conceal a large group of countries moving in the wrong direction, even where the region as a whole improved.

These classes carry a caveat. Target 8.4 sets no numeric value for carbon intensity or any other measure, so the trend tool has no threshold to reach by 2030. The labels rest on an assumed pace of decline, and a different assumption would move countries between classes. The results describe the direction and relative speed of change, and they do not show whether any country meets an agreed standard. The target also speaks of decoupling growth from environmental degradation, which a fall in carbon intensity alone does not establish, since total emissions can still rise when output grows faster.

### Energy efficiency gains slowed after 2011 and links to growth are weak

Energy intensity, the primary energy supplied per unit of output, is the companion measure to carbon intensity, and its path for the world shows when efficiency gains were made and when they faded. Break detection on the annual change of the world series finds four breaks, in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ per 2021 PPP dollar. It deepened to -0.1154 in 2005-2008, then stalled at 0.0070 in 2009-2010, the years of the global financial crisis and its aftermath. From 2011 to 2017 the decline resumed at -0.1045 a year, close to the pre-crisis pace. After the break of 2018 the mean annual change shrank to -0.0325 in 2018-2021, less than a third of the preceding segment. The series used for the breaks ends in 2021, so the segment cannot show whether the slowdown continued, and the years after 2020 are only partly covered.

The slowdown matters because lower energy intensity is the most direct route to reducing the energy needed for each unit of growth, and the pace of 2011-2017 is the one that a 2030 trajectory would have to restore. Well-established context points to several possible reasons for the weaker pace: the pandemic shock of 2020, which distorted both energy use and output, a recovery weighted towards energy-heavy activity, and the exhaustion of easy gains from the earlier replacement of old industrial capacity. These are explanations from general knowledge; the break analysis dates the change but does not identify its cause.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the world line. Of 201 countries assessed on the trend to 2030 for energy intensity, 57 are on track or have met the target, holding 52.2% of the population of the countries assessed. The energy series covers fewer countries than the carbon series and ends in 2022, so the two are not assessed on the same set of countries or years. Another 29 countries, with 9.9% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 32, with 15.1%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Stagnation applies to 15 countries with 2.1% of the population. Regression, meaning energy intensity is rising, affects 68 countries with 20.7% of the population. Regression is therefore the most common single class by number of countries, although the on-track group covers the larger share of people. No target value is set for this indicator, so the classes rest on a conventional reading of the direction and pace required, and another reading of the target could shift countries between classes.

Growth does not by itself explain these gains. Across 188 countries over 2015-2024, the Spearman correlation between changes in carbon intensity of GDP and GDP per capita growth is 0.15, and between their 2024 levels it is -0.06. Both are close to zero, so faster-growing economies were neither clearly cleaner nor clearly dirtier per unit of output. The result is an association between rankings only and gives no cause: it cannot show that growth did or did not drive the changes, and the link may differ within groups of countries. What it does suggest is that decoupling depends on the energy mix, technology and policy rather than on the rate of growth alone.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Relative decoupling is under way. The world trend for carbon intensity of GDP is classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed, at a rate of -0.0196 (2015 to 2024, kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar per year). World carbon intensity fell from 0.26 kg in 2015 to 0.22 kg in 2024. Output is therefore being produced with less carbon per unit, and the pace is not yet enough to be read as on track for the world as a whole. Among the regions, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, at a rate of -0.00839. Target 8.4 carries no numeric value, so the classification rests on the trend method alone, and a different reading of the target would give a different verdict.

The country count shows how uneven the progress is. Of 189 countries assessed on carbon intensity, 77 are on track or have met the target, covering 39.1% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 24 show moderate progress (32.7% of population), 13 marginal progress (3.0%) and 13 stagnation (3.7%). Regression affects 62 countries, home to 21.5% of the assessed population. A fall in the world ratio can coexist with rising intensity in about a third of countries, which is why the aggregate cannot stand for the whole. Energy intensity gives a similar picture. Of 201 countries, 57 are on track or have met the target (52.2% of population), while 68 are regressing (20.7% of population). The two series differ in country coverage, and the energy series end earlier, in 2022, than the carbon series, which ends in 2024. Emissions embodied in traded goods are not counted in either.

The evidence supports relative decoupling only. Intensity measures emissions or energy per unit of output, so it can fall while total emissions or total material use rise, if output grows faster. The series examined here do not include material footprint, and they do not show absolute decoupling. Whether growth is separating from environmental degradation, as the target intends, cannot be confirmed from them.

The pace of energy efficiency gains after 2018 is a further concern. The mean annual change in world energy intensity was -0.10452 MJ per 2021 PPP dollar in 2011-2017, but only -0.03247 in 2018-2021. The gains slowed to roughly a third of the earlier rate. Reaching 2030 on track would require the earlier pace to return. The broad causes are well known: stronger efficiency standards, fuel switching and structural change drove gains in earlier years, while slower policy effort and the disruption of 2020 are plausible contributors to the slowdown, stated here as context rather than as a finding.

Four proposals follow from these findings, set out below.

w-c02-1-5~tamarind/writer-3~114.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 asks that extreme poverty be eradicated for all people everywhere by 2030, and its wording quotes a line of $1.25 a day. That line belongs to an earlier price base and has been superseded several times as purchasing power parity exchange rates were revised. The measure used here is the current international line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, published by the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform. Poverty rates under this line cannot be compared with those printed in earlier editions of the series, and the figures in this book should not be set beside older statements of the target without that caution.

On this measure, 13.4% of the world's population lived below $3.00 a day in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 the share was 10.1%. The fall is real and of consequence, in a period that included a pandemic and a sharp rise in food and energy prices (context from outside the results, which show the change but not its cause). It also shows how far the world remains from the target. At the 2024 level, roughly one person in ten still lives below the line, and the target date is six years off. Continuing at the compound rate of change observed since 2015, the series would reach 8.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The pace of decline has itself changed. The break analysis of the annual change in the world headcount finds breaks at 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.6 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. The decline has thus slowed from one period to the next, and the latest segment is the shortest and the most thinly observed.

The word eradicate admits more than one reading, and the choice changes the verdict. The strict reading is a headcount of 0%, which no measured aggregate has approached and which survey-based estimation could not confirm even if it were reached, since sampling error and gaps in coverage make an exact zero unobservable. A looser reading treats extreme poverty as ended as a global phenomenon when the share falls below a threshold of 3% of the population. That threshold is the authors' reading, offered as context from outside the results; the results do not test it, and the text of the target does not choose between the readings. Against a 3% threshold the world stands at more than three times the required level in 2024; against zero the distance is the whole of the 10.1%. Both readings lead to the same conclusion for 2030, but they differ in what a successful outcome would mean.

The choice of line matters for a second reason. A line of $3.00 a day is a very low standard, set to reflect the national lines of the poorest countries. Falling below it signals deprivation of food, shelter and basic needs. Rising above it does not signal security, and many households that have crossed it remain close enough to be pushed back by a poor harvest, an illness or a price shock (general context, not a result). This section reports the $3.00 line only; the higher line of $4.20 a day is not analysed here.

The 2024 value must be read with care. The data behind the headcount are household surveys, which are conducted in each country at intervals of several years and are published with a delay. Figures for the most recent years therefore rest partly on estimates that carry forward earlier surveys using national accounts growth and other assumptions. The coverage record shows the effect. In 2015, 87 countries reported a value, and 93 did so in 2018. The number fell to 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted, recovered to 81 in 2021, then fell to 73 in 2022 and 60 in 2023. Only 26 countries reported in 2024, and just 4 in 2025. The most recent years are thus thinly observed. The 2024 aggregate of 10.1% is a nowcast built on a thin base of direct observation, and later revisions can be expected as surveys arrive.

Two cautions follow for any reader. The fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is a robust direction but not a precise magnitude, and the end point is less firm than the start. The global figure also conceals a very uneven distribution, taken up in the next part.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture beneath the global figure is one of sharp divergence. East Asia & Pacific recorded the largest fall among the regions with a full series: the headcount at $3.00 a day went from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. Europe & Central Asia began from a low base and moved from 1.2% to 0.6%. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 6.0% to 4.3%, a decline that is real but slower in proportion than those of the two regions above. The series shows the change and not its cause; commodity cycles, informal employment and the reach of cash transfers are commonly cited as context for the region, but nothing in the results tests them. North America, at 1.1% in 2015 and 0.9% in 2024, was already close to the floor of what survey-based measurement can distinguish from zero.

South Asia requires a caution. The series for the region begins in 2020, at 9.4%, and reaches 2.6% in 2024. Read at face value, this is the largest fall among the regional series, but it covers only four years (2020 to 2024), whereas the falls of the other regions cover the nine years from 2015 to 2024, so the two cannot be ranked against each other. The reading cannot be extended to 2015, because the regional value is not shown for the earlier years, and regional estimates depend on a small number of large countries with infrequent household surveys, so the aggregate may rest on interpolation as much as on fresh observation. The 2020 starting point also falls in the year of the pandemic, so part of the apparent decline may be recovery from a temporary shock rather than a sustained trend. Projected at its 2020 to 2024 rate, the region would stand at 0.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as on track; because the series is short and begins in the pandemic year, that classification is provisional. The figure is best taken as a sign of strong improvement of uncertain size, not as a measured change over the full period since 2015.

Two regions show no fall in the rate. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan moved in the wrong direction, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024, and the trend tool classes it as regression. The grouping combines economies of very different kinds, so the rise should not be read as a uniform deterioration; armed conflict and displacement in some members are often mentioned as background, but the results do not identify the cause. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, almost no change in nine years. A flat rate in a growing population would imply a rising number of people below the line, but that number is not measured here, and only the rate is reported. How much each region contributes to the global total is likewise not measured here.

Income groups tell the same story from another side. Low-income countries recorded 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, a rise, so that more than half the population of the poorest group of economies lives below $3.00 a day. Lower middle income countries stood at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024; the series for this group, like that for South Asia, is shown from 2020 only, and the same caution applies. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% to 2.1%, and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. The pattern is that the decline has been concentrated where poverty was already moderate, and that it has bypassed the group where poverty is deepest.

This matters for the target. The global fall from 13.4% to 10.1% coincides with large falls in regions that started with modest rates, while the region and income group with the highest rates did not move or moved backwards. The results do not show who contributes most to the global total, but they do show that the highest rates lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. Data for the most recent years are also thinner, a limit taken up in a later part. Eradication by 2030 would require that the stagnant and regressing groups reverse course abruptly, which no part of the 2015 to 2024 record suggests.

### Country progress and the absence of convergence

Sorting countries by the pace of their progress towards a headcount of zero by 2030 shows how uneven the record is. Of 105 countries assessed on the $3.00 a day line, 18 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 45.5% of the population of the assessed countries. The results do not show which countries account for that share. The count of countries is far less encouraging than the share of people: 18 of 105 is a small minority of national experiences.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and they hold 23.1% of the assessed population. A further 15 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, holding 11.3%. In neither group is the target reached at the present pace. Moderate progress means the direction is right and the speed is insufficient; marginal progress means that closing the remaining distance would require a change of pace that few countries have managed in a single decade.

The weakest classes matter most for the meaning of the target, which asks for eradication for all people everywhere. 7 countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the assessed population. 24 countries are regressing, with 17.9%. Regression in almost a quarter of the assessed countries is a finding in its own right. The series shows the change but not its cause. As outside context, not a result of this analysis, armed conflict, state fragility, high food and energy prices and the pandemic of 2020 are commonly cited in the wider literature as reasons for setbacks. Because the classification measures movement from each country's own observations, a country can regress from a low level as well as from a high one, and the class does not by itself say how deep the deprivation is.

The convergence test addresses whether poorer countries are catching up. Across 57 countries with data from 2015 to 2022, the regression of change in the headcount on its starting level gives a beta of 0.00658 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029. A negative and significant coefficient would have shown that countries starting with higher headcounts fell faster. The coefficient is instead slightly positive, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 3% of the variation in outcomes. Starting poverty did not predict the later pace of change.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.14 in 2015 to 2.68 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts grew relative to their mean. Two readings are open. It may reflect a true divergence in national fortunes. It may also reflect that the headcount, as it approaches zero in many countries, has a small mean, which can inflate a ratio-based dispersion measure even when absolute differences narrow. The absolute test and the relative one should be read together, and neither shows catching up.

The sample limits both results. The convergence test covers 57 countries, fewer than the 105 classified, because it needs observations close to both 2015 and 2022. Household surveys are generally less frequent in poorer and more fragile countries, which is established context rather than a result here, so the finding of no convergence may understate the divergence. For 2030, the absence of catch-up means the global target cannot be met by the average trend alone.

### A slowing decline and its limits as evidence

The pace of decline in the world headcount at $3.00 a day has not been steady. A break analysis of the annual change in the world series finds two turning points, in 2014 and in 2021. Between 2001 and 2013 the headcount fell by a mean of 1.59 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.88 points, and in the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.325 points. The three segment means all point the same way, towards a smaller annual fall. The two breaks fall close to two events that shaped the period: the end of the commodity-price boom and the slowdown of growth in many low-income economies after 2014, and the pandemic shock of 2020. These are context drawn from general knowledge, not findings of the series. The data show when the pace changed; they do not isolate why. Attribution would need counterfactual modelling that the series alone cannot supply, and the timing of breaks in a short annual series is itself uncertain by a year or more.

A further reason for caution lies outside the results. As context from general experience, and not as a finding, the remaining poor when the headcount is low are often concentrated in places that are poorer, more remote, more often affected by conflict or weak states, and less able to benefit from average growth. A slowing decline may therefore be partly expected even without any change in policy effort, though the series do not test this. Yet that would not make the slowdown benign. The target requires the headcount to reach zero, or a figure close to it, and a falling rate of change moves that outcome further from 2030, not nearer.

The evidence behind the latest segment is thinner than the evidence behind the earlier ones. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly and published with a lag. The number of countries reporting a figure for the headcount was 87 in 2015, 70 in 2020 and 81 in 2021, so coverage has not moved in one direction. It fell to 60 in 2023, to 26 in 2024 and to 4 in 2025. The decline in recent years is partly a matter of surveys not yet processed or not yet conducted, so the world and regional figures for 2023 onward probably lean on estimates that carry forward earlier survey information with growth data and assumptions about distribution. The mean change for 2021-2024 should be read as a provisional estimate, likely to be revised as surveys arrive, and the 2025 figures hardly rest on observed data at all.

The coverage problem may be uneven as well as thin. Countries with infrequent surveys are plausibly those with the highest poverty and the weakest statistical systems, and so the most likely to be absent from a given year; the counts above do not themselves show which countries are missing. The world aggregate could then be least well measured where the number of poor people is largest. Anyone assessing whether 2030 is within reach should weigh the slowdown found here as a signal that is probably real in direction, since the three segment means agree, but uncertain in size.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace observed since 2015, the world will not reach zero extreme poverty by 2030. The world headcount at $3.00 a day stood at 10.1% in 2024, and the trend to the target projects 8.4% in 2030 at the compound rate since 2015, a ratio of 0.38 of the progress needed. The trend classifies the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Target 1.1 can also be read as a threshold of 3%. That is this book's own choice of interpretation, and the results do not test it. On that reading the target is no more attainable, since the world headcount of 10.1% is still more than three times that level. The recent pace is slower than the pace since 2015: the segment from 2021 to 2024 shows a mean annual change of -0.325 points, against -0.88 points for 2014 to 2018 and -1.59 points for 2001 to 2013.

Even the regions that are advancing need to go faster. East Asia & Pacific, the best performer among the regions with a full series, is expected to stand at 1.0% in 2030 at its present rate, against a target of zero, and its ratio is 0.84. Europe & Central Asia is expected at 0.4%, and upper middle income countries at 1.1%. These are small residual shares, but they are the hardest to remove. As context from outside the results, the people concerned are often in remote, conflict-affected or marginalised groups that growth alone does not reach. South Asia is classed as on track, with an expected 0.4% in 2030, from a start of 9.4% in 2020. That classification is provisional: the series begins in 2020, the pandemic year, so the fall to 2.6% in 2024 covers four years and is measured from a short and unusual base. It cannot be ranked against the nine-year falls from 2015 to 2024 in other regions.

The highest rates lie where the trend is flat or reversed. Sub-Saharan Africa is in stagnation, with an expected 44.7% in 2030, and low-income countries are in regression, with 54.2% expected. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also in regression, with 16.7% expected. The series shows these changes but not their causes, and the contribution of each group to the world total is not measured here. Among 105 countries assessed, 24 are in regression and hold 17.9% of the assessed population.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. National governments and donors should concentrate poverty-reduction effort and concessional finance on Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. The headcount in Sub-Saharan Africa was 45.0% in 2024, almost unchanged from 45.4% in 2015, and in low-income countries it was 52.5% in 2024, up from 50.1% in 2015. National statistical offices, with the World Bank and bilateral funders, should fund household surveys at a regular and shorter interval. The interval is a proposal, not a finding, and the case for it is that 70 countries reported in 2020 against 26 for 2024 and 4 for 2025, so recent estimates rest on projection. The World Bank and national authorities should name the line and the price base whenever poverty is reported, so that the $1.25 wording of Target 1.1 is not mistaken for the current measure of $3.00 a day. The United Nations statistical system should track regression as a class of its own, since the 24 countries in that class are hidden by averages that mix them with countries that are advancing.

w-c04-1-6~cedar/writer-1~114.text:
### The global ratio fell from 228 to 197 and remains far above 70

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled estimate for the world stood at 228.0 in 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year available. The ratio fell over eight years, but the 2023 value is still nearly three times the target value.

The gap is plain. The trend tool, which extrapolates the compound rate observed since 2015, expects a world ratio of 173.4 in 2030 and classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The tool's ratio of progress to required pace is 0.35. That figure is not a share of the distance covered: the fall from 228.0 to 197.0 is 31.0 points of the 158.0 needed to reach 70, about 0.20 of the distance, with seven years left. Closing the remainder would need a pace far faster than the one observed, so the distance does not shrink by small adjustments; it would require a different trajectory altogether.

The target is worded as a global ratio, not as a national one. A global ratio is a weighted outcome: it is pulled down by countries with low ratios and pulled up by countries with high ratios, in proportion to their live births. The results do not include a births-weighted breakdown or a list of countries, so the text does not say which countries contribute most to the world figure. A reading in which every country must fall below 70 would be stricter still, and the wording of the target does not require it. The later parts of this section take up the country classes drawn from the trend tool; the data used here do not give a count of countries above 70 in 2023.

The quality of the series needs stating plainly. The modelled ratio is assessed for 194 countries in 2023; the results used here do not state the coverage of earlier years. Whatever the coverage, the estimates are a product of modelling rather than of observation. They are produced by a regression model that, as general context, draws on covariates such as fertility, skilled birth attendance and national income. Where civil registration of deaths with causes is incomplete, as it is in many of the countries with the highest ratios, the estimate leans on those covariates rather than on counted deaths. The figures therefore carry uncertainty that the single published value does not display, and a change of a few points between years should not be read as a firm observation.

This uncertainty does not rescue the target. The fall from 228.0 to 197.0 is small beside the distance from 197.0 to 70, and no plausible revision of the model would close a gap of that size. What the uncertainty does affect is the confidence with which any single country or short period can be judged. For the world as a whole, the finding is robust: the ratio is falling, it is falling slowly, and 2030 will arrive with it well above 70 unless the pace changes sharply.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of forty

The spread between regions is wide, and a global average conceals it. In 2023 the modelled ratio for Sub-Saharan Africa was 448 deaths per 100,000 live births, against 11 for Europe and Central Asia. The two figures stand about forty times apart, a comparison drawn from rounded regional values. Target 3.1 is a global average assembled from very unequal parts. The data used here do not show how far the place of birth outweighs other circumstances.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593 in 2015 to 448 in 2023 and carries the highest ratio of any region. South Asia fell from 173 to 120, and its proportional fall is the larger of the two. Both remain above 70. The trend tool classes South Asia as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 against a target of 70, and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.83. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as making marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 350.5, about five times the target value, and a ratio of 0.46. On the figures shown, Sub-Saharan Africa has the largest gap to 70 in 2023. The results do not weight regions by births, so the contribution of each region to the global figure is not measured here.

For the other regions the results give 2015 and 2023 values and expected 2030 values, set here against the target of 70. Europe and Central Asia stood at 11 in 2023, down from 14 in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 8.9. North America stood at 16, down from 17, with an expected value of 15.2. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 54 to 47, with an expected value of 41.6. East Asia and Pacific fell from 70 to 66, so it sits just below the target. Its expected 2030 value of 62.7 leaves little margin, and any reading of it as on course rests on a gentle slope rather than on a secure lead. As context, where ratios are already low, further absolute gains are necessarily small.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among regions. Its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is the only region classed as in regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. The region was close to the threshold and has moved the wrong way. Well-established explanations include the disruption of health services during the pandemic years, persistent inequality between urban and rural or Indigenous populations, and the weight of unsafe abortion and hypertensive disorders. The data used here cannot apportion the rise among these causes.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 491 in 2015 to 346 in 2023 and are classed as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 254.7. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 291 to 235 and are classed as making marginal progress, with an expected value of 194.9 and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61 to 57, with an expected 2030 value of 53.7, and high-income countries from 11 to 10. The two upper groups are already below 70, so the whole of the remaining distance lies in the lower two.

Country classes confirm that the picture is mixed. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of the classified countries. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country is in stagnation and 7 are in regression, together under 1% of the population. The data used here do not give the number of countries above 70 in 2023 under a strict country-by-country reading, nor a births-weighted list of the countries that dominate the global total.

### Progress slowed after 2008 and the pandemic years disturbed the series

The series shows that progress was already slowing before the goals were adopted. The breaks analysis identifies a change of regime in 2008. In the segment from 2001 to 2007, the global ratio fell by a mean of 8.4 points a year. In the segment from 2008 to 2019, the mean annual fall was 5.2 points, roughly two-fifths less. The adoption of the goals did not restore the earlier speed, and the fall of the post-2015 years continues the slower trend rather than recovering from it. Well-established explanations include the exhaustion of the easiest gains, such as the expansion of skilled attendance at birth in countries that started from low coverage, and the harder task of reaching the remaining deaths, which are concentrated among women in poor, rural and conflict-affected settings where emergency obstetric care is least available.

The pandemic years then disturbed the series. The annual change was an increase of 4 points in 2020 and an increase of 31 points in 2021. The change reversed to a fall of 39 points in 2022, and the fall in 2023 was 6 points. The pattern is consistent with a shock and a recovery: disrupted maternity services, diversion of health staff and direct deaths from infection in pregnancy are plausible contributors to the rise, and the return of services would explain the fall. The analysis cannot establish this cause. The ratio is a modelled estimate, built by regression from covariates such as fertility, birth attendance and income, and is not a count of registered deaths. A sharp one-year rise followed by a sharp one-year fall may partly reflect the way the model treats pandemic-era inputs and the revision of estimates. The breaks detected from 2020 to 2023 are single-year segments and should be read as flags, not as stable trends. The 2022 fall should be treated as a modelled rebound and not as a durable gain.

The spread among countries has not narrowed when measured by the Gini coefficient and the Theil index. Both were computed across the 194 countries, and the results do not state that they are weighted by population or by births. The Gini coefficient of the ratio was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 70.9% in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023, so most inequality is still a matter of regional membership, though the within-region component has grown a little.

Convergence is weak. A regression of change on the starting level across the 194 countries gives a coefficient of -0.00372 with a p-value of 0.0024, but an R-squared of only 0.050. Countries with higher ratios in 2015 tended to fall slightly faster, the direction needed for catching up, yet the starting level explains only a small part of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation fell from 1.500 to 1.410, a modest narrowing, while the Gini and Theil rose. The measures point in different directions, and the data given do not show why. For 2030, neither the slowed trend before 2015 nor the weak catching up since offers grounds for expecting the pace to rise.

### At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed, and proposals follow

Extending the 2015 to 2023 rate to 2030 gives a global ratio of about 173.4 per 100,000 live births, against a target of 70. The trend tool places the world in the class of marginal progress, with a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.35. That ratio is not a share of the distance covered, and the tool does not report that share. The target is therefore not on course. Meeting it would need a pace of decline far above that of 2015 to 2023.

The country classification shows where the shortfall lies. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the classified population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country stagnates and seven regress, and the regression group holds 0.6% of the population. A majority of countries being on track does not imply that the global ratio will reach 70, and the classification does not give the number of countries above 70 in 2023, so a stricter country-by-country reading of the target cannot be answered from these results.

The regional projections follow the same pattern, with classes as the trend tool reports them. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 448 in 2023, would reach about 350.5 in 2030 at its present rate, classed as marginal progress with a ratio of 0.46. South Asia, at 120 in 2023, would reach about 87.1, classed as moderate progress with a ratio of 0.83, the closest of the regions needing acceleration. Low-income countries would reach about 254.7, classed as moderate progress with a ratio of 0.56. Lower-middle-income countries would reach about 194.9, classed as marginal progress with a ratio of 0.44. Upper-middle-income countries, at 57 in 2023, are projected at about 53.7 and classed by the tool as on track, as are high-income countries, at 10. East Asia and Pacific, at 66, is also classed as on track, narrowly, with a projection of about 62.7. Europe and Central Asia, North America, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are likewise classed by the tool as on track or target met. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the better-placed regions: its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is classed as regression, with a projection of about 79.7 in 2030.

The ratios are modelled estimates, and in many high-burden countries they rest on little direct counting. Any projection to 2030 inherits that uncertainty, and the class of a country near a margin should be read with caution. The regional results are not weighted by births, so the contribution of each region to the global figure is not measured here.
