w-c06-7-6~juniper/writer-2~114.text:
### The global gap in internet use by sex

The question asked here has two halves: the gap in mobile phone ownership and the gap in internet use. Only the second can be answered. The bench holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex. The series on mobile cellular subscriptions is counted per 100 people, is not divided by sex, and can count one person several times, so it cannot show who owns a handset. The ownership half therefore remains unanswered, and the findings below concern internet use alone. Answering it would need a survey series on handset ownership by sex, such as a household or demand-side survey, which the bench does not hold.

Target 5.b asks for greater use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The measure available is the share of women and of men who have used the internet in the previous three months.

On that measure, women's use rose sharply. Female internet use stood at 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and reached 68.2 per cent in 2024. The period includes the pandemic years, when schooling, work and public services moved online; the results do not isolate that or any other cause, and it is context only.

Male use stood at 56.0 per cent of the male population in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two world figures do not share an end year: the female series is read at 2024 and the male series at 2025, because the latest world value in each result falls in a different year. Setting one against the other mixes the difference between the sexes with a year of growth in male use. It overstates the gap in any single year and should not be read as a measurement. The world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. A clean comparison requires both series at the same date, and the regional results, where both are read at 2024, allow it in the parts that follow.

The 2019 figures are on a common footing. Women at 51.8 per cent and men at 56.0 per cent give a female-to-male ratio of about 0.93. This is a fact about 2019 only and says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed or widened since. Because use rose for both sexes, a gap in percentage points can grow while the ratio improves, so each measure should be stated with its basis.

The figures also carry a caution about coverage. The count of countries reporting in 2025 is only 7 in each result, against 92 in 2019 and 65 in 2024. The 2025 world and income-group values therefore rest on a thin base of direct observation, and the 2024 regional values are better supported. Internet use as defined here also says nothing about the quality of access, the device used, the cost of data or what women do online. The evidence supports rapid gains by women and a shortfall against men in 2019, while the size of the world gap in 2024 stays undetermined.

### Regional differences in the gap

Among the regions reported here, the point gap between women's and men's internet use in 2024 is largest in two regions at a middle level of use and smaller in the region with the lowest use. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women had used the internet in the previous three months, against 67.6 per cent of men. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 per cent for women and 69.1 per cent for men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the shares were 29.4 per cent and 37.9 per cent. The gap there looks smaller than in the two regions above, but the level of use is far lower, so a small point gap at a low level should not be read as near equality.

South Asia also shows how the gap can move. In 2019 women's use stood at 24.3 per cent and men's at 34.9 per cent. By 2024 women's use had reached 56.3 per cent and men's 69.1 per cent, so the point gap had widened, even though women's use more than doubled. Rapid growth in use among both sexes can thus coexist with a larger point difference.

The gap is small where use is nearly universal. In North America 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia the shares were 90.0 per cent and 91.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean lies between, at 81.3 per cent for women and 82.0 per cent for men. Near-universal use leaves little room for a difference. Mobile networks, affordable devices and schooling may have contributed in these regions, but these are hypotheses from outside the bench's data, which the results do not test.

East Asia and Pacific shows a reversal. In 2019 women's use, at 67.4 per cent, was slightly above men's, at 66.7 per cent. By 2024 women stood at 85.5 per cent and men at 87.6 per cent, so men had moved ahead. The regional aggregate hides large differences among its economies, and the data given here do not show which of them drove the change. The result should be read as a shift in the regional average, not as evidence of decline in women's use, which rose over the period.

Income groups are reported for 2025, when only 7 countries reported these series, so the figures rest on very thin direct observation and probably include estimates; they are indicative only. In low-income countries 18.3 per cent of women used the internet, against 28.6 per cent of men. In lower middle income countries the shares were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent. In high-income countries they were 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The largest point gap again falls at a middle level of use and the smallest where use is highest, but the evidence is weaker than for the regional figures of 2024.

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male use in 2024 is 0.948, and that between their changes is 0.958. Countries with larger gains in one sex therefore generally show larger gains in the other. This is an association only; it does not show why any gap persists or what the gap depends on.

The regional pattern matters for target 5.b because the largest remaining gaps lie in regions where women's use is far from universal. Possible factors, which lie outside the data and which the bench cannot separate, include the cost of devices and data, differences in schooling and literacy, social norms on women's independent use of phones, and concerns over safety online. They may operate with different force in each region, which is why a single global figure conceals as much as it reveals.

### What changed since 2019 and what the data can support

Among the three regions with 2019 figures (East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa), South Asia shows the largest change since 2019. Female internet use there rose from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while male use rose from 34.9 per cent to 69.1 per cent. Women gained a great deal in absolute terms, but they remained behind men in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same ordering at a lower level: women moved from 20.2 per cent to 29.4 per cent, and men from 28.6 per cent to 37.9 per cent. The 2019 and 2024 gaps in points are not among the results given, so they are not restated here; the regional section gives the 2024 comparison. Two years alone also do not show a trend, and the regional gaps should be read as two observations each.

Across the 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male changes is 0.958, and that between 2024 levels is 0.948. The two sexes' changes therefore tend to move together across countries. This is an association only. It does not show why gaps persist where they do, nor that the gap is determined by overall connectivity. Income, education, literacy, norms on women's use of devices and the cost of handsets and data are plausible influences from outside the results, and the series cannot separate them. The period also includes the pandemic years, which the data do not isolate as a cause of any change.

Income groups are indicative only, because the 2025 values rest on 7 reporting countries. In low-income countries, female use was 18.3 per cent in 2025 against 28.6 per cent for men. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, in upper-middle-income countries 87.9 per cent and 89.7 per cent, and in high-income countries 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The world series moved from 51.8 per cent for women and 56.0 per cent for men in 2019 to 68.2 per cent for women in 2024 and 76.6 per cent for men in 2025. Those last two values fall in different years, so a world gap cannot be read from them.

The evidence has limits that bear on every figure above. In 2019, 92 countries reported female internet use; in 2024, 65 did; in 2025, only 7. The data do not state why reporting fell after 2019, and the pandemic and reporting delays are only conjectures from outside them. Which countries are missing is not shown by these results, so whether measured progress overstates or understates the global picture is unknown. The 54-country comparison is a subset of the 137 countries that have ever reported. The series also defines use over the previous three months from any device, so it says nothing about who owns a phone, who controls it, or how it is used.

### Implications for target 5.b by 2030 and proposals

Target 5.b carries no numerical threshold and no date-bound level, so it can be read in more than one way. The reading adopted here is a narrowing of the gap between women's and men's internet use, alongside rising levels for women. The question put to this section has two halves, and only one can be answered: the bench holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex, so the ownership gap is unmeasured here. A survey of handset ownership by sex, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold in this set, would be needed to answer it. For internet use, the evidence for 2030 is mixed. Levels have risen sharply, but the regional gaps in 2024 remain wide, and these results cannot show whether the gaps are closing.

The world figures illustrate the limit of the data. Female use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, while male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The male figure refers to a later year than the female one, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. The regional figures for 2024 are on a common year and are the safer basis. In Sub-Saharan Africa female use was 29.4 per cent against 37.9 per cent for men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the figures were 55.0 per cent and 67.6 per cent. In South Asia they were 56.3 per cent and 69.1 per cent. In North America, with 94.1 per cent for women and 94.7 per cent for men, the gap is almost gone.

The income-group figures point the same way, but they are indicative only, because just 7 countries reported in 2025. Female use reached 18.3 per cent in low income countries against 28.6 per cent for men, 56.9 per cent against 68.7 per cent in lower middle income countries, and 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent in high income countries. The data contain no projection, so whether any region reaches parity by 2030 cannot be stated. They do not test the causes of the gaps either. Factors commonly proposed outside these results include the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, social norms on who may own a device, and concerns about safety online. These are context, not findings.

Across 54 countries, the rank correlation between changes in female and male use from 2019 to 2024 is 0.958, and for 2024 levels it is 0.948. This is an association only: female and male use tend to move together across these countries, and the correlation does not show why, nor whether gaps are closing within countries.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c04-6-5~juniper/writer-3~114.text:
### The global rate barely moved after 2015

The 2020 target to halve road deaths was not met on the evidence available. The World Bank's indicator of mortality caused by road traffic injury, expressed as estimated deaths per 100,000 population, stood at 17.0 for the world in 2015 and at 16.7 in 2019. That is a fall of about 1.5 per cent over four years. A halving would have required a rate near 8.5 by 2020, and the measured rate remained close to double that level.

Two limits on this reading need stating. The series ends in 2019, so the target year itself cannot be observed; the conclusion rests on the last four years before it, and a sudden fall in 2020 of the size required is not plausible given how slowly the rate moved beforehand. The path of 2020 is also disturbed by the pandemic, when restrictions on movement reduced traffic in many places, so any later figure would need careful interpretation before it was read as progress on safety.

The second limit concerns the wording of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of deaths and injuries, and of the number of them, whereas the indicator covers deaths only and is a rate per head of population. A rate can fall while the count of deaths rises if population grows faster, and it can stay flat while the count grows. The target can therefore be read in more than one way: as a halving of the count, or as a halving of the rate. On either reading the evidence points the same way, since the rate has barely changed and no series on non-fatal injuries is held on the shelf. The measure used here is the more lenient of the two, which makes the shortfall harder to dismiss.

Coverage supports the finding. Estimates are available for 183 countries in 2019 and for 190 countries in at least one year, with regional and income aggregates alongside. The series is modelled by the World Health Organization rather than counted directly, since many countries lack complete registration of deaths by cause. A flat global line therefore reflects estimates built from a mix of registered and modelled data, and small movements of the order seen here should not be over-read. What can be said with confidence is the scale of the gap between the target and the outcome, not the precise change of a few tenths of a point.

### Regions diverged, and only Europe and Central Asia moved fast

Regional rates for 2015 and 2019 show that the small global movement conceals different trajectories. Europe and Central Asia was the only region to record a substantial decline, from 9.2 deaths per 100,000 population in 2015 to 7.4 in 2019. That is the lowest regional rate in either year, and the only one close to the level a halving would have required. Its projected rate for 2030, on the 2015 to 2019 pace, is 4.1, below the target of 8.5. Long-established road safety policy in much of that region, such as speed enforcement, seat-belt use, vehicle standards and road design, is offered here as context consistent with the pattern; the results do not test it.

East Asia and Pacific moved only slightly, from 17.0 to 16.5. Latin America and Caribbean fell from 18.3 to 17.3, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 17.3 to 17.0. The trend tool classes all three as marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with pace ratios of 0.22, 0.36 and 0.13 respectively. A ratio compares the pace observed with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio below 1 means the pace is too slow. South Asia was effectively flat, at 15.6 in 2015 and 15.6 in 2019, and the tool classes it as regression, with a ratio of -0.01.

Two regions moved in the wrong direction. North America rose from 11.5 to 11.9, and the trend tool classes it as regression with a ratio of -0.63. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.8 to 27.4, the highest regional rate in either year, and is also classed as regression, with a ratio of -0.13 and a projected 2030 rate of 29.2. Rapid growth in motor vehicle use is often cited as a pressure on road deaths in lower-income regions, but no result here measures vehicle use, so that explanation is context and not a finding. The measured pattern matters for 2030: the region with the most deaths per head is not improving.

These comparisons rest on regional means, which can hide wide spread among the countries inside a region, so the ranking of regions says little about any single national road network. Coverage is broad but not complete: 183 countries report in 2019, and the indicator is built from modelled estimates, so small changes in a regional rate should be read with caution. The country-level spread is taken up in the next part.

### Dispersion widened while few places gained ground

The convergence test asks whether countries with higher road death rates in 2015 changed by less, or by more, than others up to 2019. Across 182 countries the estimated coefficient (beta) is 0.031, with a p-value of 0.0058. The sign is positive. Under the convention of the test, a negative coefficient would indicate that countries with higher starting rates rose less or fell more, so that levels drew together; a positive one indicates that they drew apart. The result is therefore the opposite of convergence, and the slope is distinguished from zero at the conventional 0.05 threshold.

The second measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation, the standard deviation of national rates divided by their mean, rose from 0.54 in 2015 to 0.63 in 2019. Rates across countries were more unequal in relation to their average at the end of the window than at the start. The world rate, 17.0 in 2015 and 16.7 in 2019, scarcely moved while the spread widened. The tests do not identify which countries account for this: no country-level result is reported here, so no count of improving or deteriorating countries can be given, and nothing is claimed about how many places gained ground.

The limits of the test are considerable. The R-squared is 0.108, so initial rates account for only about one-tenth of the variation in subsequent change. Most of what separates one country's trajectory from another's lies outside this simple relationship. The window is also only four years, from 2015 to 2019, and short intervals magnify the effect of estimation noise. Country figures for road deaths are modelled estimates, since many countries lack complete death registration with cause information, and year-to-year movements in a modelled series may partly reflect revisions of method and inputs rather than real change. The test also stops at 2019 and says nothing of the period after 2020.

The tools measure outcomes, not causes, so any explanation is context and not a finding of these results. Well-established experience suggests that road deaths fall where speed management, helmet and seat-belt laws, vehicle safety standards and emergency care are enforced, and that they rise where motorisation grows faster than safe road design and enforcement. Such differences could produce widening dispersion, but no result here measures them.

For 2030 the implication is limited to what the two measures show: a rising spread means that the global rate alone is a poor guide to national progress, and that national trajectories need to be examined individually.

### The 2030 target of 8.5 needs a different pace, and proposals follow

The 2030 horizon asks for a rate of 8.5 deaths per 100,000 population, which is the 2015 world rate of 17.0 halved. Each projection below extends the average annual movement between 2015 and 2019, so every figure is an extrapolation of a four-year pace and not a forecast. The ratio reported with it compares that movement with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio of 1 means the pace is just sufficient and a ratio below 1 means it is too slow. The world rate is projected at 16.1 in 2030 if the 2015 to 2019 movement continues, a ratio of 0.11, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. That projection stands almost twice as high as 8.5.

Two groups are projected to pass 8.5 on the 2015 to 2019 pace; this is not the same as being on track, since the window is only four years. Europe and Central Asia is projected at 4.1 in 2030, with a ratio of 6.91. High-income countries are projected at 7.3, a ratio of 2.48, although their 2019 rate of 8.7 still stood above 8.5. The high-income result is therefore the less secure of the two.

East Asia and Pacific shows marginal progress, with a projected rate of 15.2 in 2030 and a ratio of 0.22. Latin America and the Caribbean is similar, at 14.8 and 0.36. Upper middle income countries are projected at 15.2, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 16.2. All of these are falling slightly, yet none approaches 8.5 on present pace. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnating, at 17.3.

Four groups are classed as regression. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 29.2 and low-income countries at 31.5, both rising, and they are the groups with the highest rates, so on these extrapolations they move away from the target. North America is projected at 13.3, and South Asia at 15.7. As context, not a finding of these results, rapid motorisation combined with weak roads, vehicle standards and emergency care is a well-established source of high road death rates.

The figure of 8.5 is one reading of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of halving deaths and injuries, not the rate. The rate and the count may move differently, and which reading is more demanding depends on population growth and on a count series, neither of which is examined or held here. The 2015 base year is also a convention, since the target text names no baseline, and injuries are not measured by the indicator used. Readers should treat 8.5 as a benchmark and not as the single correct threshold.

The positive convergence slope, with the coefficient of variation rising from 0.54 in 2015 to 0.63 in 2019, suggests that national rates drew apart, which argues for directing effort to the countries with the highest rates and not to averages.

The proposals that follow are tied to these findings. Governments of Sub-Saharan African and low-income countries, with development partners, should prioritise speed enforcement, safer road design and emergency care, because their rates are projected to rise rather than fall. National road safety agencies in regions classed as marginal or stagnating should set interim targets for 2025 and report against them annually, because the present pace is far below what 8.5 requires. North American authorities should review why the rate rose from 11.5 in 2015 to 11.9 in 2019. National statistical offices and the World Health Organization should publish annual counts of deaths and injuries, since the target concerns numbers and none is held here. Countries with incomplete cause-of-death registration should strengthen vital registration, since the indicator is modelled where records are lacking.

w-c03-6-5~heath/writer-2~114.text:
### Agriculture's weight in output and employment is shrinking only slowly

Agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 4.2 per cent of world GDP in 2015 and 4.0 per cent in 2025. The share barely moved over a period that included the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the pandemic of 2020 and the food and energy price shocks that followed. In 2025, 158 countries reported the series, so the global figure rests on a broad but not complete base.

Employment tells a different story from output. Agriculture accounted for 28.5 per cent of total employment worldwide in 2015 and 25.8 per cent in 2025, according to modelled estimates of the International Labour Organization. In 2025 roughly a quarter of the world's workers were in agriculture, while the sector produced 4.0 per cent of measured value added. The gap between the two shares is the central fact for any judgement of public investment, and it points to low output per worker. As context from the wider literature, not a finding of this section and not tested by the bench data, farm productivity is widely held to depend on roads, storage, irrigation, research and advisory services, which are largely public goods.

The pace of change is slow against the horizon of 2030. Between 2015 and 2025 the employment share moved from 28.5 per cent to 25.8 per cent and the output share from 4.2 per cent to 4.0 per cent. A steady continuation of that trend would leave a little over a fifth of the world's workers in agriculture in 2030; this is an illustration of a straight-line trend, not an estimate of the bench. Structural transformation, in which workers move from farms to higher-productivity work, is under way but far from complete, and a falling employment share is not evidence of falling need. As context from the wider literature, and not a result of this section, public spending that raises output per worker is often held to be one means by which the employment share can fall without a loss of rural income.

The benchmark that follows is simple. If public spending on agriculture were to match the sector's weight, it would be proportionate to a share of output of about 4.0 per cent in the world as a whole, and arguably to a higher share where employment is concentrated. The World Development Indicators supply no series for government agricultural expenditure among the results available here, so the match cannot be measured or scored directly. The comparison is made indirectly, through the external flows examined below and through the regional weights. Target 2.a, which calls for greater investment in rural infrastructure, research, extension and gene banks, sets no numerical share to match. Any reading of a shortfall should be made with that limit in view.

### Regions differ most where agriculture matters most

The regional picture is one of extremes. In 2025, agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 17.9 per cent of GDP in Sub-Saharan Africa and 15.6 per cent in South Asia. Both regions also hold the largest shares of employment in the sector: 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa and 41.5 per cent in South Asia, both in 2025. At the other end, Europe and Central Asia drew 2.0 per cent of GDP from agriculture in 2025 and 6.7 per cent of employment, while North America drew 1.0 per cent of GDP in 2021, the latest year reported for that region, and 1.5 per cent of employment in 2025. The years differ between the two measures for North America, and the comparison should be read with that in mind. In North America the sector is a rounding error in the national accounts; in Sub-Saharan Africa it is where about half of all workers earn their living.

The gap between the two measures matters as much as the levels. In Sub-Saharan Africa the employment share (49.3 per cent) stands far above the output share (17.9 per cent), and in South Asia the same holds (41.5 per cent against 15.6 per cent). Where half of workers produce under a fifth of output, average output per agricultural worker is low relative to other sectors, which is the usual reading of such a gap, although these two series do not measure productivity or incomes directly. Public spending proportionate to the sector's share of GDP would therefore still be small relative to the number of people who depend on it. No series on government agricultural spending is held here, so the match between spending and weight cannot be scored.

The direction of change after 2015 differs between regions. In Latin America and the Caribbean the output share rose from 5.5 per cent in 2015 to 6.8 per cent in 2025, while the employment share fell from 14.0 per cent to 12.7 per cent. The series alone does not show whether this reflects prices or output per worker. In Sub-Saharan Africa the output share rose from 16.3 per cent in 2015 to 17.9 per cent in 2025, while the employment share fell from 53.3 per cent to 49.3 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific, by contrast, employment fell from 27.9 per cent to 21.7 per cent and the output share from 6.0 per cent to 5.5 per cent, the pattern of an economy moving labour out of farming. South Asia, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, moved only slightly in output share: South Asia from 15.9 per cent to 15.6 per cent, and the latter region from 6.9 per cent to 6.8 per cent.

By income group, the divide is sharper still. In low-income countries agriculture accounted for 27.2 per cent of GDP in 2025, up from 25.6 per cent in 2015, and for 59.4 per cent of employment in 2025, against 61.5 per cent in 2015. Lower middle income countries stood at 17.8 per cent of GDP and 39.8 per cent of employment in 2025. Upper middle income countries recorded 6.9 per cent of GDP and 19.8 per cent of employment, and high income countries 1.3 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 2.9 per cent of employment in 2025. In the poorest countries the output share has also risen while the employment share eased only slightly; the two movements co-occur and these series do not show that one explains the other. For target 2.a, whose wording singles out developing countries and the least developed among them, this concentration indicates where investment in rural infrastructure, research and extension has the largest population to reach by 2030.

### International flows from UN agencies rose but moved toward one region

Net official flows from UN agencies through IFAD rose over the period, though not evenly. The world total was 399 million US dollars in 2015 and 509 million in 2023. These are current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the apparent rise may reflect higher prices rather than a larger real transfer. The series is also a net measure: repayments of loans are subtracted from disbursements, so a fall in a region's figure can reflect repayment as much as reduced lending. Only IFAD flow values are given here; for the companion FAO series, the section reports counts of reporting countries and no flow values.

The rise was concentrated in one region. Sub-Saharan Africa received 180 million US dollars in 2015 and 405 million in 2023. Every other region with a reported figure moved the other way. East Asia and Pacific fell from 99.9 million to 9.2 million. South Asia fell from 50.3 million to 43.1 million. Europe and Central Asia fell from 20.3 million to 15.5 million, Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.9 million to 9.0 million, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 29.2 million to 24.0 million. North America recorded zero in both years, as expected for a region of donors. The world total therefore rose in a period when one region's figure rose and the others' fell.

The income groups show the same movement. Low-income countries received 109 million US dollars in 2015 and 247 million in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 201 million to 240 million. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 67.2 million to a net negative of 12.6 million, meaning that repayments to IFAD exceeded new disbursements in 2023. The series does not show why; one conjecture, offered as context and not as a finding, is that a lender concentrating concessional resources on the poorest countries sees middle-income borrowers repay. High-income countries show a small figure of 2.8 million in 2023, and the data do not explain it.

The direction is consistent with the regional evidence on agriculture's weight set out earlier, since Sub-Saharan Africa has the largest shares of output and jobs in the sector, although the years differ between the flow series (to 2023) and the output and employment series (to 2025). It matters for 2030 because target 2.a asks for more investment in developing countries, in particular the least developed. A rise confined to a single region and to the lowest income groups is consistent with that wording, yet the sums are small. Half a billion dollars a year, spread across a continent whose farm economy employed 49.3 per cent of workers in 2025, cannot substitute for domestic public spending.

Coverage limits how far the picture can be pressed. IFAD flows were reported by 94 countries in 2023. The companion FAO series was reported by 133 countries in 2013 and 129 in 2023, with a count of 135 in 2019 and 128 in 2022; 139 countries reported in at least one year. Aggregates should therefore be read as sums over reporting countries, and a missing country is not a zero. The comparison before and after 2020 is further limited by the end of the series in 2023, which leaves little room to judge how flows responded to the pandemic and the price shocks that followed.

### Flows follow need, but do not yet change it, and proposals follow

Across the 89 countries for which both series exist, the link between flows and the size of agriculture depends on what is compared. The Spearman correlation of 2023 levels between net official flows from IFAD and agriculture's share of GDP is 0.575, a moderate positive association. Countries where agriculture contributes more to output tend to receive more from the fund. The correlation of changes between 2015 and 2023 is 0.141, which is weak and shows no clear association between how far a country's flows moved and how far its agricultural share of GDP moved. The Kendall coefficients, 0.390 for levels and 0.101 for changes, give the same picture on a stricter rank measure.

The share of GDP is only a proxy for need, and the correlation does not show that allocation follows need. It shows that flows are larger where agriculture's share of output is larger, which is what IFAD's mandate to lend to agricultural economies would produce in any case. The change correlation does not test whether flows alter the sector's share of output or of employment, and employment is not part of it. Context from the wider literature, not a finding of these series, is that rural infrastructure, extension services and research take years to alter productivity, and a falling share of GDP can reflect growth elsewhere as much as any change in farming. Structural change is slow, as the global share of 4.0 per cent in 2025 against 4.2 per cent in 2015 already shows. Ten years is a short window against which to judge a transfer of this kind.

The limits of the evidence are plain. A correlation is not a cause, and the weak link of changes cannot show that flows fail, since the counterfactual is unknown. The series covers one agency's net flows, in current dollars. The companion FAO series is used only through its reporting counts, which narrow what can be compared. The years of latest data also differ across series, with flows ending in 2023 and output and employment shares in 2025, and the pairing of the two series rests on 89 countries. Above all, target 2.a can be read in more than one way: as public spending by governments, as private investment, or as international cooperation. The data on the bench measure only the last, and in part. Whether public spending on agriculture matches the sector's weight, 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2025 and 17.9 per cent of its GDP, cannot be answered from these series, because government agricultural spending is absent.

For 2030 the implication is that the match between investment and need cannot at present be tested, and no expectation about the sector's share can be drawn from the weak change correlation of 0.141. The proposals below follow from that finding and from the measured concentration of agriculture in output and employment, which marks priorities, not shortfalls.

w-c07-5-5~ewan/writer-2~115.text:
### Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015

World net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, measured in constant 2023 dollars. That is a rise of more than half over eight years. In current dollars the series climbs from US$147.1 billion to US$259.5 billion. The two series meet in 2023 because the constant-price base year is 2023, so the gap between them in 2015 reflects the rise in prices since then. The constant-dollar figure is the fairer measure of change, since it removes the effect of rising prices; the current-dollar series shows a larger rise because it includes inflation.

The indicator needs careful reading before it is applied to target 6.a. It records all net official development assistance received by developing countries: grants and concessional loans, net of repayments of principal, across every sector. It does not isolate water and sanitation, nor the activities the target names, such as water harvesting, desalination, wastewater treatment, recycling and reuse. The series is therefore a proxy for the general scale of international support, and a rise in it does not show that more reached water and sanitation programmes. Spending on health, emergency relief, refugee costs or budget support can raise the total without any of it entering the sector.

The target itself adds a second limit. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building support by 2030, but it names no amount, no share of income and no baseline year. It can be read as a call for more money, for more technical assistance, or for better-targeted programmes, and a financial series speaks only to the first of these. Capacity-building, such as training, institutional support and technology transfer, is poorly captured by a measure of net disbursements. A judgement that the target is on track can therefore rest only on the direction of the aggregate, not on a threshold.

Coverage is also partial. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts in this series. The inequality analysis later in this section covers a different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023; the results do not state why the sets differ, and the use of population weights is a likely explanation rather than a finding. North America records zero in both years, which is consistent with a region of donors rather than recipients, and high-income economies receive only small amounts: US$319.3 million in 2015 and US$760.9 million in 2023 in constant dollars. Net receipts measure what arrives, not what is needed, so the series does not say whether the level is adequate against the water-stress and service gaps described elsewhere in this chapter.

With these limits stated, the direction is clear. Assistance received grew substantially after 2015 and, within the years 2015 to 2023 examined here, stood at its highest level in 2023, although the change in 2023 alone was slightly negative, at about -US$0.7 billion. Whether growth is sustained to 2030 is a separate matter, because the donor side of the ledger depends on budget decisions that recipient data cannot anticipate.

### Regions gained unevenly, and Europe and Central Asia gained most

Regional totals of net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, show that the increase since 2015 was not evenly shared. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest gain by a wide margin, rising from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023, about 4.7 times the 2015 level. In 2023 it was the second largest recipient region, behind sub-Saharan Africa (US$64.8 billion) and ahead of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region (US$35.1 billion). The series does not show what drove the rise, and it measures all official assistance, not the share spent on water.

The other regions moved much less. East Asia and Pacific received US$9.9 billion in 2015 and US$10.7 billion in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, almost no change in real terms. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion. These three regions ended the period within a narrow band of one another, near US$10.7 billion each, although their populations and water needs differ greatly. No population or per-person series is used in this section, so the totals say nothing about assistance per person; that comparison would need such a series. North America records zero in both years, as expected of a donor region rather than a recipient.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, a rise well below the world's increase. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the largest recipient, with US$51.8 billion in 2015 and US$64.8 billion in 2023. The largest absolute flows thus stayed in sub-Saharan Africa, while the fastest growth went to Europe and Central Asia.

The distribution by income group, also in constant 2023 dollars, shows a similar movement. Low-income countries received US$35.2 billion in 2015 and US$44.6 billion in 2023, and lower-middle-income countries US$54.9 billion and US$59.2 billion. Upper-middle-income countries rose from US$18.9 billion to US$57.4 billion, the fastest growth of the groups, and by 2023 they received more than the low-income group, whose receipts also rose. Target 6.a names developing countries generally rather than the poorest, so this pattern is not in itself a shortfall against it. Only a sector breakdown, which these series do not provide, could show whether water programmes followed the same path.

### A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase

The path of assistance since 2015 is not a steady climb. A structural break analysis of the annual change in world net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, places breaks in 2022 and 2023. The change in each year is treated as its own segment: from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion; in 2022 alone the change was US$49.8 billion, nearly eight times that long-run average; and in 2023 the change was about -US$0.7 billion, a single-year fall. The rise recorded between 2015 and 2023, when the world total went from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, therefore owes a large part to one year, and the gradual growth of the preceding two decades cannot be extrapolated from it. The 2022 change is large against that rise, but the series does not show a peak level in 2022: the 2023 level fell only slightly below it.

The data do not record why 2022 was exceptional. It is an inference, outside the data, that the jump reflects emergency and humanitarian flows, support to countries affected by conflict and displacement, and pandemic recovery financing. The series covers all purposes of assistance together and cannot separate such flows from spending on water and sanitation. Whether the 2023 fall marks a plateau or the start of a decline cannot be judged from one observation.

The distribution of assistance among recipient countries also changed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received rose from 0.361 in 2015, across 138 countries, to 0.452 in 2023, across 135 countries. The Theil index rose more sharply than the Gini coefficient, from 0.255 to 0.460, and the coefficient of variation rose most of the three, from 0.64 to 1.48. Assistance has thus become more unevenly spread among recipients. The country sets differ between the two years, and the 135 countries in the inequality analysis are not the same set as the 136 countries reporting in 2023 that underlie the world total, so part of the change may reflect which countries are included. The comparison should be read with that caution.

The composition of this inequality shifted too. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023. Differences among countries within the same region now account for a larger part of the disparity than differences between regions. This matters for targeting: regional averages conceal recipients that receive much more or much less than their neighbours, and allocation by region alone would miss them.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise is fragile and its distribution has become less even. Target 6.a calls for expanded cooperation and capacity-building support in water and sanitation. Total assistance, whatever its level, does not show how much reaches that sector, and a total lifted by one exceptional year is a weak guide to the sustained flows that infrastructure and capacity-building require.

### Assistance for 2030 must be tracked by sector and directed by need

The series held by the bench measures total official development assistance received, not assistance to water and sanitation. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building in water-related activities, and total flows cannot show whether that is happening. A rise in the aggregate may reflect humanitarian, budget-support or debt-related disbursements that have little to do with water supply, sewerage or wastewater treatment. For 2030, the first implication is therefore that progress on 6.a cannot be judged from the present evidence, and the headline figure of US$259.5 billion in 2023 should not be read as a measure of support for water.

The second implication concerns durability. The break analysis places breaks in 2022 and 2023. The change in 2022 alone was US$49.8 billion, against a mean annual change of US$6.4 billion over 2001 to 2021, and the change in 2023 alone was -US$0.7 billion, a small fall. A jump of that size, followed by a fall, suggests an exceptional episode, not a new trend; this reading is context, not a finding of the data. Planning that assumes the 2023 level will persist, or keep rising, risks a shortfall by 2030. The target can also be read in more than one way: it names no quantity of assistance, so expansion could mean volume, share of total aid or reach of capacity-building.

The third implication concerns distribution. Among countries, the Gini coefficient of assistance received, population-weighted and in constant 2023 dollars, rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.26 to 0.46. The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 45.3% to 29.6%, so the inequality lies increasingly within regions, among individual countries. The inequality analysis covers 135 countries in 2023, while the world total rests on 136 countries reporting, so the two sets differ slightly. In constant 2023 dollars, low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015, and sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion, yet the data do not show whether flows follow the countries with the weakest water and sanitation coverage. Upper middle income countries received US$57.4 billion in 2023, up from US$18.9 billion in 2015, a faster rise than that of low income countries, which is not a finding about need, since the target names developing countries generally and the data cannot show where water assistance went.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

claims.fact: c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015

proposals: Donors and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report water and sanitation disbursements to the World Bank's catalogue as a regular annual series by recipient country, so that progress on target 6.a can be measured directly instead of inferred from total assistance.

Ministries responsible for aid and national planners in recipient countries should base 2030 financing plans on the pre-2022 trend, not the exceptional 2022 jump, and should not assume the 2023 level will persist.

Donors should publish how water and sanitation allocations relate to service coverage gaps, so that flows can be judged against need, since the data show that assistance is increasingly unequal among countries.

Nor does it hold capacity-building support, technology transfer or the share of commitments actually disbursed. Total assistance coverage differs between the world total and the inequality analysis, and target 6.a sets no quantity, so expansion can be read in more than one way.

w-c06-1-3~dahlia/writer-2~115.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It is a composite on a scale from 0 to 100 that summarises how legal frameworks shape women's economic opportunities across several topics of working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. Because the topic scores are combined into one number, an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The equal treatment of topics is a choice of method, not a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. The result also lists aggregates for the high-income, low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income and South Asia groups and for the world, so group readings are available in principle. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change since 2015 or 2020 has been drawn from the shelf, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot be answered in magnitude here. The sections that follow treat what the instrument measures and what a computed record would need to show, and they carry no measured finding beyond the coverage reported above.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and gave high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope lowers the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the revised scale. Third, the revised series is new, so its history may be short. Whether comparable values exist back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been established. If they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and a different instrument would be needed.

What the bench has established is coverage. The legal index was reported by 189 economies in 2025, and the same number reported in at least one year, so no economy entered the record and later left it. Full coverage in the latest year says nothing yet about levels, direction or the gap between regions and income groups, and no finding on those points is made here.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because its indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether the institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery, and it is the measure through which progress towards 2030 is best judged.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The bench has so far computed only the frame of the legal record: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and 189 reported in at least one year. No level, change since 2015 or change since 2020 has been computed, so direction of reform is not stated here. What follows sets out what a measured answer to the question would consist of.

A measured answer would have four parts. The first is the world level of the index in the latest year, showing how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because a global mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and a gain concentrated in a few large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones. The third is the distribution: the spread between the highest and lowest scores and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index are likely to differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker most needs.

Two comparisons would give the answer its post-2015 and post-2020 reading. Average annual change before and after 2020 would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or paused during the pandemic, if the history of the series permits it. Because the index is built from statute and not from reported statistics, an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data.

As context, not as a finding, comparative law has often observed that labour codes are amended more readily than family and personal-status codes, which are bound up with religious authority and custom. Whether the topic-level scores show this is for the computation to settle.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering is not stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates returned, so a comparison across the other regions would require either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison matters for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change, whereas implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. A reasonable expectation, to be tested rather than asserted, is that income relates less closely to the legal score than to the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. That distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation. The only finding established here is the frame: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and 189 reported in at least one year.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading. The bench has so far computed only coverage: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and the same 189 reported in at least one year. No level, change since 2015 or change since 2020 has been computed, so neither reading can yet be tested.

Under the strict reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Both could be computed from the series if its history extends far enough, and a projection to 2030 at the observed pace would show how long each group would need to reach full formal equality.

What can be said without those numbers is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar, and any economy's position should be judged with that in mind. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the index is well suited to a global account: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and 189 reported in at least one year, so a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The task left to the bench is to turn that coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every economy.

w-c08-4-3~farah/writer-1~115.text:
### World energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured as megajoules of energy supply per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, fell from 4.8556 MJ in 2015 to 4.5449 MJ in 2021. That is a fall of 6.4 per cent, derived directly from the two levels. The direction is the one target 7.3 requires: each dollar of output needed less energy at the end of the period than at the start. The question for the section is whether the pace is the one the target asks for.

The trend tool expresses the world movement as a rate of -0.01096 per year, and classifies it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. That rate is the tool's own measure of change per year, and it is read here only as a direction and a pace relative to the tool's thresholds. The tool was run with no numerical target, so its classification rests on a generic benchmark and not on a figure derived from the wording of target 7.3. The label is a guide to the size of the gap, not a verdict on the target itself.

The target can be read in more than one way. Its wording, to double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, is commonly interpreted as doubling the rate recorded in an earlier period, which requires a baseline period to be chosen. The choice matters, because the earlier rate differs according to the years used. A second reading, used in the monitoring of the goals, sets a fixed annual rate of improvement in energy intensity for the whole period to 2030. The two readings need not give the same answer. The segment comparison in a later part tests only the first, using periods within the series; a rate for the years before 2015 is not held for the world as a whole, and the fixed-rate reading cannot be tested with the bench series.

The data also limit what can be said about the present. The world series ends in 2021, so the latest observation lies well before 2030 and says nothing about the years since. Regional series reach 2022 in some cases, and the number of countries reporting in 2022 was 116, so the final year rests on thinner coverage. Any statement that the world is or is not on course for 2030 is therefore an extrapolation from six years of change, a period that includes the sharp fall and partial rebound in economic activity around 2020. Movements in GDP affect the ratio as much as movements in energy supply, so a change in intensity does not by itself show that efficiency measures were adopted.

Why the measure matters is plain enough. Energy intensity is the broadest indicator available of how much energy an economy needs to produce its output, and a falling value lowers fuel costs, emissions and import dependence for a given level of output. It is, however, a crude proxy for efficiency, because it also reflects the structure of an economy, its climate, and the share of heavy industry in output. The following parts examine how these differences appear across regions and over time.

### Regions diverge from a 2.58 to a 6.14 MJ range by 2021 or 2022

Regional levels of energy intensity, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, span a wide range by the latest year available. Europe and Central Asia is lowest, at 2.5791 MJ in 2022, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest among regions, at 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The latest year differs between regions, 2021 for some and 2022 for others, so the comparison is approximate and the gap between regions is read as indicative rather than exact.

Europe and Central Asia fell from 4.002 MJ in 2015 to 2.5791 MJ in 2022. Its rate of change, -0.0608 per year, is the steepest of any region and the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions. Part of the decline in this region may reflect changes in economic structure and in fuel supply as well as efficiency gains; the data do not separate these.

North America and South Asia also improved substantially. North America moved from 5.0428 MJ in 2015 to 4.364 MJ in 2022, at a rate of -0.0204 per year, and South Asia from 4.5047 MJ to 3.9427 MJ in 2021, at -0.022 per year. Both are classed as on track or target met. South Asia's result is notable because it began from a level close to the world value and has since fallen below it.

The remaining regions made less headway. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5.6997 MJ in 2015 to 5.2313 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0142 per year, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 3.4822 MJ to 3.265 MJ in 2022, at -0.0092 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Its level is low, which may leave less room for further cuts, but the data do not test that.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan barely moved, from 5.3599 MJ in 2015 to 5.332 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0009 per year, classed as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa also stagnated, falling from 6.2412 MJ to 6.1403 MJ in 2021, at -0.0027 per year. Together these two regions combine high or middling levels with almost no improvement.

Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income economies stood at 7.415 MJ in 2015 and 7.1393 MJ in 2021, the highest of any group, with a rate of -0.0063 per year, classed as marginal progress. High-income economies fell from 4.3961 MJ to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, at -0.0334 per year, classed as on track or target met. Lower middle income fell from 4.644 MJ to 4.2707 MJ in 2021, and upper middle income from 5.5767 MJ to 5.2119 MJ. The poorest economies are therefore the most energy-intensive per unit of output and are improving most slowly.

Three cautions apply. First, only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the latest regional values rest on incomplete years, and regions with data only to 2021 are compared with others to 2022. Second, intensity reflects economic structure, climate, fuel mix and the share of traditional biomass in supply, and the purchasing power parity conversion of GDP, not efficiency alone. Third, the world rate of -0.011 per year is classed as marginal progress, so the regional divergence matters for 2030: the regions that are on track are not those with the highest levels, and the highest-intensity regions are those where acceleration is most needed.

### Improvement peaked before 2018 and has since slowed

The structural breaks in the annual change of world energy intensity show that the pace of improvement has not been steady. The series for the world, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, has breaks in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. These divide the record into five segments, each with its own mean annual change. A negative mean change means that intensity fell, so a larger negative figure means faster improvement.

In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ. It steepened to -0.1154 MJ in 2005-2008, the fastest pace of the early period. The break in 2009 marks a pause: in 2009-2010 the mean change was 0.0070 MJ, so intensity rose slightly instead of falling. That coincides with the global financial crisis, and a link between the two is a reasonable reading, though the data do not establish it. One possible mechanism, not tested by the data, is that output fell sharply while much of the energy supply in buildings, transport and industrial plant could not be scaled down as quickly, which tends to raise intensity in a downturn.

The break in 2011 opens the longest segment. In 2011-2017 the mean annual change was -0.1045 MJ, close to the pace of 2005-2008 and about twice that of 2001-2004. This matters for the target. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement, and the baseline year of 2015 sits inside this faster period. Any comparison of later years with the rate at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals is therefore a comparison with a stretch of unusually quick improvement, not with the slower pace of the early 2000s. Reading the target against the rate of -0.0498 MJ would make doubling look nearer than it is when set against the rate that prevailed in 2015.

The final break, in 2018, is the most consequential. In 2018-2021 the mean annual change was -0.0325 MJ, less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017, and a smaller fall than in 2001-2004 (-0.0325 against -0.0498 MJ per year). Improvement therefore peaked before 2018 and has since slowed. The segment is short, four years, and its end includes 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic disturbed both output and energy supply. A short segment with unusual years at its end warrants caution, and the mean should not be taken as a settled new trend.

The data do not identify why the slowdown occurred. Several explanations are plausible and are offered only as interpretations, not findings. The pandemic caused abrupt falls and rebounds in activity that distort a ratio of energy to output. Fuel prices affect the incentive to economise on energy, and the price changes of these years may have weakened it. Structural change in industry, including shifts in the weight of energy-intensive sectors in world output, can move intensity independently of efficiency in any single sector. The series measures energy per unit of GDP, so it blends efficiency with the composition of the economy, and none of these causes can be separated from the others using this result alone.

For 2030 the implication is conditional. If the rate of 2018-2021 persisted, the world would fall well short of doubling the rate of 2011-2017, let alone exceeding it. Meeting the target on the most demanding reading would require a pace far above any segment in the record. The target also admits more than one reading, since the earlier rate may be taken from the period before 2015 or from the baseline decade, and the choice changes the threshold. The segment comparison tests only the reading that uses periods within the series; the pre-2015 reading is not tested here. On the comparison made, the break of 2018 shows that the recent direction is away from the target, not towards it.

### Doubling the earlier rate is not met, and proposals follow

On the segment comparison, doubling the recent rate is not met. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency, but it does not say which earlier rate is to be doubled or which period is to be compared. Three readings are possible: the pace before 2015 set against the pace after it, a fixed earlier rate set against the pace to 2030, and the pace in the years of fastest improvement set against the most recent years. The bench holds no pre-2015 rate, so the first reading cannot be tested here, and the fixed-rate reading also remains untested. The comparison below tests the third reading alone: the 2011-2017 segment of the world series against the 2018-2021 segment. The verdict holds for that comparison only.

From 2011 to 2017 the mean annual change in energy intensity was -0.1045 MJ per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. From 2018 to 2021 it was -0.0325 MJ. Doubling would require a recent pace of about twice the earlier one, and the recent pace is much slower, so intensity is falling more slowly, not twice as fast. The trend tool classes the world rate of -0.01096 as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the results do not state the period of that rate. The segment from 2018 to 2021 includes the pandemic years, when output and energy supply both moved sharply, so part of the slowdown may reflect those disturbances and not a lasting change. Only four years are covered, and the data cannot separate the two explanations.

Regional results show where the world picture is made. Four groups are classed as on track or target met: Europe and Central Asia, with the steepest rate of any region at -0.06083, the high-income group at -0.03337, South Asia at -0.02197 and North America at -0.02044. The label reflects the tool's own benchmark and does not show that those groups are doubling a previous rate. The high-income group fell from 4.3961 MJ in 2015 to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 4.002 MJ to 2.5791 MJ over the same years. Efficiency gains, structural change and fuel switching are familiar possible explanations in richer economies, but the results do not establish which applies.

The regions with the least progress are, in several cases, those with high levels. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a rate of -0.00271, and its intensity moved from 6.2412 MJ in 2015 to 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is also classed as stagnating, at -0.00087, with levels of 5.3599 MJ in 2015 and 5.332 MJ in 2021. East Asia and Pacific shows moderate progress, at -0.01419, but acceleration is needed there: its intensity fell from 5.6997 MJ to 5.2313 MJ. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.00916, and the low-income group, at -0.00629, show marginal progress. The low-income group still has the highest level of any income group, at 7.1393 MJ in 2021. These readings are indicative, since end years and trend periods differ across regions.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Unless the pace rises well above the 2018 to 2021 mean, the doubling is not met on the segment comparison. The latest data point is 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, so later developments are not visible. Only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the most recent figures rest on incomplete reporting.

Intensity is also an imperfect measure of efficiency. It divides energy supply by output, so it moves with the structure of an economy, climate and trade as well as technical efficiency. A fall may come from a shift to services without any gain in equipment efficiency, and a flat series may hide improvements offset by growth in energy-heavy activity. The proposals respond to these limits and to the regional gaps, and none presumes which measures would work.
