w-c09-8-5~heath/writer-2~130.text:
### Tourism receipts and arrivals as measures of Target 8.9

Target 8.9 commits governments to devise and implement policies for sustainable tourism that creates jobs and promotes local culture and products. The target names three outcomes: sustainability, employment and the promotion of local culture and products. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline, and it leaves open what counts as sustainable. It can be read as a call for policy, as a call for better outcomes, or as both, and the indicators do not settle which.

The World Development Indicators hold tourism series that measure something narrower. International tourism arrivals count overnight visitors who travel to a country other than the one in which they usually live. International tourism receipts record the expenditure of those inbound visitors, including payments to national carriers for international transport. A related series expresses receipts as a share of total exports, and another isolates receipts for passenger transport items. These describe the scale of the sector and its weight in an economy's external earnings.

None of them observes the content of Target 8.9. Arrivals say how many people came, not how long they stayed, what they damaged or what they preserved. Receipts record money entering a country, not how much of it remained with local workers, local producers or cultural institutions, since a large share of spending can leave through imports, foreign ownership and international transport. Neither series counts jobs in tourism, measures pay or conditions, or distinguishes cultural products from other purchases. Domestic tourism, which is large in many countries, falls outside both series.

The bench can therefore read how large and how widely reported international tourism is, and how that changed around 2015 and 2020. It cannot say whether tourism became more sustainable or more locally beneficial. The first result in this section, on the arrivals series, shows how many countries report in each year, which sets the limits of any comparison. In the figures from 2000 to 2020, reporting reached 202 countries in at least one year, and it is on that base that the later parts read the series. Findings on size and recovery are evidence about the economic scale of the sector. They are indirect evidence on the target, and the text says so wherever it matters.

### Coverage of the arrivals series, 2000 to 2020

The arrivals series, International tourism, number of arrivals (ST.INT.ARVL), has reports from 202 countries and territories in at least one year of the period covered. No single year reaches that figure. In 2000, 175 countries reported. The count then rose with some interruptions: 173 in 2002, 179 in 2005, 186 in 2007 and 190 in 2008. It dipped to 187 in 2009 and returned to 190 in 2010. Counts of 191 in 2011 and 190 in 2014 show a plateau, although the counts for 2012 and 2013, both 190, are the same as those on either side of them.

The peak came after the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. In 2015 and 2016, 194 countries reported arrivals, the highest counts in the period. The count then eased to 190 in 2017, 186 in 2018 and 179 in 2019. The 2019 count equals that of 2005. Part of the decline after 2016 may reflect delays in compiling national statistics, since the latest years of many series are filled in later. The data do not show whether that explains it.

The figure for 2020 is the most striking: 132 countries reported, against 179 the year before, the largest fall between consecutive years in the period. As general context from outside these results, the pandemic is understood to have sharply reduced international travel, and statistical offices and tourism authorities also faced disruption. The coverage count cannot separate the two effects. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded very few arrivals and not reported them, or may have been unable to compile the figure. The count does not identify which countries are missing. Either way, the 2020 values come from a smaller and possibly different group of countries than the 2019 values.

This section therefore holds no finding on the size of arrivals or receipts, nor on recovery after 2020: only coverage counts were retrieved, and the question of scale is left unanswered here. A total for 2020 compared with 2019 would mix a real fall in travel with a change in which countries are counted. Comparisons are sounder when restricted to countries reporting in both years. The series considered here end in 2020 as listed in the shelf description, so they say nothing on recovery in later years.

The coverage result also lists aggregates for the arrivals series: seven regions, four income groups and the world. They inherit the reporting gaps described above, and the results do not state how non-reporting countries are treated, so aggregate values for 2020 should be read with caution.

### Regional and income-group comparison

The coverage result for the arrivals series (ST.INT.ARVL) names the aggregates for which the series is reported: regional groups, income groups and the world total (WLD). It attaches no value to any of them. It gives no arrivals figure, no receipts figure and no year-on-year change, so the regional and income-group comparison that the question calls for cannot be made from the retrieved results. This part states the limit plainly and does not infer a ranking.

The absence matters for Target 8.9. Without values, nothing can be said about where visitors concentrate, whether tourism is a channel of growth open to low-income countries or one dominated by wealthier destinations, or which groups have regained their position of 2019. How large tourism receipts and arrivals are, and how they recovered after 2020, remains unanswered by the evidence held here. The only retrieved evidence concerns coverage, which measures how many countries report and not how many people travel.

The coverage counts do bear on any later comparison. Reporting stood at 179 countries in 2019 and 132 in 2020. Aggregates depend on how many members report, so a 2020 total may rest on thinner evidence than earlier totals, and the count does not say which countries are absent. A fall in reported arrivals between those years could reflect a fall in travel, changes in reporting, or both, and the counts cannot say which. As context outside the results, the pandemic restrictions of 2020 are well known to have curtailed international travel sharply.

A sound comparison would use a fixed set of countries reporting in both 2019 and 2020, with arrivals set against receipts to indicate spending per visitor. Spending bears on jobs and local products more directly than headcounts do. The unit and end year of the receipts series come from the shelf description and are not confirmed by any retrieved result in this section. Until values are retrieved for each aggregate, any ranking of regions or income groups, and any reading of recovery, should wait.

### The 2020 collapse in reporting and the uncertain recovery

The retrieved results hold no arrivals or receipts value for any year, region or income group, so this section can state nothing on the size of tourism or on its recovery after 2020. The only evidence on 2020 is the count of reporting countries, which stood at 179 in 2019 and 132 in 2020. That count shows how many countries reported arrivals, not how many visitors travelled.

The count cannot say whether the fall reflects a fall in travel, a change in reporting, or both. As context from outside these results, the pandemic is generally understood to have curtailed international travel sharply, and the same disruption affected national statistical offices, which rely on border counts and accommodation surveys. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded fewer visitors, may have published nothing, or may have published late. The count does not identify which countries are missing, so the gap may be concentrated in some regions or income groups; the result does not show this either way. The earlier decline from 194 countries in 2016 to 179 in 2019 may reflect delays in compiling recent national statistics, which the tool records but cannot explain.

The depth of the fall in visitors and in receipts is therefore unanswered, and the recovery cannot be judged. The shelf descriptions list 2020 as the latest year for arrivals, receipts, receipts as a share of exports and passenger transport receipts. No retrieved result checks that end year or the unit of the receipts series, so both remain unverified shelf descriptions. If the end year holds, no later observation exists from which to measure the pace of a rebound. The GDP deflator describes economy-wide prices and cannot stand in for tourism volumes.

A reading of the recovery would need arrivals and receipts for the same countries that reported in 2019, so that the comparison rests on a fixed group and is not distorted by changing coverage. Receipts would also have to be set against price changes, since a nominal figure can rise while visitor numbers stay below earlier levels. For Target 8.9, dated 2030, progress after 2020 is at present unmeasured by this shelf.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The retrieved results hold no arrivals or receipts value for any year, region or income group, so this section cannot say how large tourism receipts and arrivals are, or how far they recovered after 2020. The only retrieved evidence is a count of reporting countries, which is evidence of coverage and not of the economic scale of the sector. That count shows monitoring of Target 8.9 weakening in the year that matters most: the arrivals series was reported by 194 countries in 2016 and by 132 in 2020, and across the whole period 202 countries and territories reported in at least one year.

The shelf describes 2020 as the latest year for arrivals, receipts, the export share and passenger transport receipts, but only the arrivals count is backed by a retrieved result here. The end years of the three receipts series, and their unit of current US dollars, are shelf descriptions that no result in this section confirms. If they are correct, the shelf holds no observation of the recovery at all, and any statement on whether tourism has regained its earlier level lies outside the data. The fall in the count may reflect a fall in travel, changes in reporting, or both. A fall in travel is context from outside the results, and the count cannot say which explanation holds. Progress towards 2030 cannot be judged from series that end in the year of the disruption.

A second implication concerns what the series measure. Arrivals and receipts describe the volume and value of inbound visits. Neither shows whether tourism creates jobs or promotes local culture and products, the outcomes the target names. Receipts also include payments to national carriers for international transport, so they are not wholly spending inside the destination. Values in current dollars drift with prices, and the shelf holds the GDP deflator as a reminder of this.

Three proposals follow. National statistical offices in countries absent from the 2020 count should report arrivals annually and publish the missing years; the count does not identify which countries are absent, so the agencies that compile the series should first publish that list. The same agencies should present receipts always alongside arrivals, so that spending per visitor and the weight of transport payments can be read. The custodians of the Sustainable Development Goal indicator framework should add measures of tourism employment and of local content in tourist spending, since Target 8.9 cannot otherwise be tested against its own wording.

w-c08-4-5~dahlia/writer-1~131.text:
### World energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured as megajoules of energy supply per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, fell from 4.8556 MJ in 2015 to 4.5449 MJ in 2021. That is a fall of 6.4 per cent, derived directly from the two levels. The direction is the one target 7.3 requires: each dollar of output needed less energy at the end of the period than at the start. The question for the section is whether the pace is the one the target asks for.

The trend tool expresses the world movement as a rate of -0.01096 per year, and classifies it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. That rate is the tool's own measure of change per year, and it is read here only as a direction and a pace relative to the tool's thresholds. The tool was run with no numerical target, so its classification rests on a generic benchmark and not on a figure derived from the wording of target 7.3. The label is a guide to the size of the gap, not a verdict on the target itself.

The target can be read in more than one way. Its wording, to double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, is commonly interpreted as doubling the rate recorded in an earlier period, which requires a baseline period to be chosen. The choice matters, because the earlier rate differs according to the years used. A second reading, used in the monitoring of the goals, sets a fixed annual rate of improvement in energy intensity for the whole period to 2030. The two readings need not give the same answer. The segment comparison in a later part tests only the first, using periods within the series; a rate for the years before 2015 is not held for the world as a whole, and the fixed-rate reading cannot be tested with the bench series.

The data also limit what can be said about the present. The world series ends in 2021, so the latest observation lies well before 2030 and says nothing about the years since. Regional series reach 2022 in some cases, and the number of countries reporting in 2022 was 116, so the final year rests on thinner coverage. Any statement that the world is or is not on course for 2030 is therefore an extrapolation from six years of change, a period that includes the sharp fall and partial rebound in economic activity around 2020. Movements in GDP affect the ratio as much as movements in energy supply, so a change in intensity does not by itself show that efficiency measures were adopted.

Why the measure matters is plain enough. Energy intensity is the broadest indicator available of how much energy an economy needs to produce its output, and a falling value lowers fuel costs, emissions and import dependence for a given level of output. It is, however, a crude proxy for efficiency, because it also reflects the structure of an economy, its climate, and the share of heavy industry in output. The following parts examine how these differences appear across regions and over time.

### Regions diverge from a 2.58 to a 6.14 MJ range by 2021 or 2022

Regional levels of energy intensity, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, span a wide range by the latest year available. Europe and Central Asia is lowest, at 2.5791 MJ in 2022, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest among regions, at 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The latest year differs between regions, 2021 for some and 2022 for others, so the comparison is approximate and the gap between regions is read as indicative rather than exact.

Europe and Central Asia fell from 4.002 MJ in 2015 to 2.5791 MJ in 2022. Its rate of change, -0.0608 per year, is the steepest of any region and the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions. Part of the decline in this region may reflect changes in economic structure and in fuel supply as well as efficiency gains; the data do not separate these.

North America and South Asia also improved substantially. North America moved from 5.0428 MJ in 2015 to 4.364 MJ in 2022, at a rate of -0.0204 per year, and South Asia from 4.5047 MJ to 3.9427 MJ in 2021, at -0.022 per year. Both are classed as on track or target met. South Asia's result is notable because it began from a level close to the world value and has since fallen below it.

The remaining regions made less headway. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5.6997 MJ in 2015 to 5.2313 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0142 per year, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 3.4822 MJ to 3.265 MJ in 2022, at -0.0092 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Its level is low, which may leave less room for further cuts, but the data do not test that.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan barely moved, from 5.3599 MJ in 2015 to 5.332 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0009 per year, classed as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa also stagnated, falling from 6.2412 MJ to 6.1403 MJ in 2021, at -0.0027 per year. Together these two regions combine high or middling levels with almost no improvement.

Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income economies stood at 7.415 MJ in 2015 and 7.1393 MJ in 2021, the highest of any group, with a rate of -0.0063 per year, classed as marginal progress. High-income economies fell from 4.3961 MJ to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, at -0.0334 per year, classed as on track or target met. Lower middle income fell from 4.644 MJ to 4.2707 MJ in 2021, and upper middle income from 5.5767 MJ to 5.2119 MJ. The poorest economies are therefore the most energy-intensive per unit of output and are improving most slowly.

Three cautions apply. First, only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the latest regional values rest on incomplete years, and regions with data only to 2021 are compared with others to 2022. Second, intensity reflects economic structure, climate, fuel mix and the share of traditional biomass in supply, and the purchasing power parity conversion of GDP, not efficiency alone. Third, the world rate of -0.011 per year is classed as marginal progress, so the regional divergence matters for 2030: the regions that are on track are not those with the highest levels, and the highest-intensity regions are those where acceleration is most needed.

### Improvement peaked before 2018 and has since slowed

The structural breaks in the annual change of world energy intensity show that the pace of improvement has not been steady. The series for the world, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, has breaks in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. These divide the record into five segments, each with its own mean annual change. A negative mean change means that intensity fell, so a larger negative figure means faster improvement.

In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ. It steepened to -0.1154 MJ in 2005-2008, the fastest pace of the early period. The break in 2009 marks a pause: in 2009-2010 the mean change was 0.0070 MJ, so intensity rose slightly instead of falling. That coincides with the global financial crisis, and a link between the two is a reasonable reading, though the data do not establish it. One possible mechanism, not tested by the data, is that output fell sharply while much of the energy supply in buildings, transport and industrial plant could not be scaled down as quickly, which tends to raise intensity in a downturn.

The break in 2011 opens the longest segment. In 2011-2017 the mean annual change was -0.1045 MJ, close to the pace of 2005-2008 and about twice that of 2001-2004. This matters for the target. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement, and the baseline year of 2015 sits inside this faster period. Any comparison of later years with the rate at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals is therefore a comparison with a stretch of unusually quick improvement, not with the slower pace of the early 2000s. Reading the target against the rate of -0.0498 MJ would make doubling look nearer than it is when set against the rate that prevailed in 2015.

The final break, in 2018, is the most consequential. In 2018-2021 the mean annual change was -0.0325 MJ, less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017, and a smaller fall than in 2001-2004 (-0.0325 against -0.0498 MJ per year). Improvement therefore peaked before 2018 and has since slowed. The segment is short, four years, and its end includes 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic disturbed both output and energy supply. A short segment with unusual years at its end warrants caution, and the mean should not be taken as a settled new trend.

The data do not identify why the slowdown occurred. Several explanations are plausible and are offered only as interpretations, not findings. The pandemic caused abrupt falls and rebounds in activity that distort a ratio of energy to output. Fuel prices affect the incentive to economise on energy, and the price changes of these years may have weakened it. Structural change in industry, including shifts in the weight of energy-intensive sectors in world output, can move intensity independently of efficiency in any single sector. The series measures energy per unit of GDP, so it blends efficiency with the composition of the economy, and none of these causes can be separated from the others using this result alone.

For 2030 the implication is conditional. If the rate of 2018-2021 persisted, the world would fall well short of doubling the rate of 2011-2017, let alone exceeding it. Meeting the target on the most demanding reading would require a pace far above any segment in the record. The target also admits more than one reading, since the earlier rate may be taken from the period before 2015 or from the baseline decade, and the choice changes the threshold. The segment comparison tests only the reading that uses periods within the series; the pre-2015 reading is not tested here. On the comparison made, the break of 2018 shows that the recent direction is away from the target, not towards it.

### Doubling the earlier rate is not met, and proposals follow

On the comparison of the 2011-2017 segment with the 2018-2021 segment, doubling is not met. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency, but it does not say which earlier rate is to be doubled or which period is to be compared. Three readings are possible: the pace before 2015 set against the pace after it, a fixed earlier rate set against the pace to 2030, and the pace in the years of fastest improvement set against the most recent years. The bench holds no pre-2015 rate, so the first reading cannot be tested here, and the fixed-rate reading also remains untested. The comparison below tests only the reading that sets the 2011-2017 segment of the world series against the 2018-2021 segment. The verdict holds for that reading alone.

From 2011 to 2017 the mean annual change in world energy intensity was -0.1045 MJ per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. From 2018 to 2021 it was -0.0325 MJ. Doubling would require a recent pace of about twice the earlier one, and the recent pace is much slower, so intensity is falling more slowly, not twice as fast. The trend tool classes the world rate of -0.0110 as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the results do not state the period of that rate. The segment from 2018 to 2021 includes the pandemic years, when output and energy supply both moved sharply, so part of the slowdown may reflect those disturbances and not a lasting change. Only four years are covered, and the data cannot separate the two explanations.

Regional results show where the world picture is made. Four groups are classed as on track or target met: Europe and Central Asia, with the steepest rate of any region at -0.0608, the high-income group at -0.0334, South Asia at -0.0220 and North America at -0.0204. The label reflects the tool's own benchmark and does not show that those groups are doubling a previous rate. The high-income group fell from 4.3961 MJ in 2015 to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 4.0020 MJ to 2.5791 MJ over the same years. Efficiency gains, structural change and fuel switching are familiar possible explanations in richer economies, but the results do not establish which applies.

Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0027, and its intensity moved from 6.2412 MJ in 2015 to 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is also classed as stagnating, at -0.0009, with levels of 5.3599 MJ in 2015 and 5.3320 MJ in 2021. East Asia and Pacific shows moderate progress, at -0.0142, but acceleration is needed there: its intensity fell from 5.6997 MJ to 5.2313 MJ. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0092, and the low-income group, at -0.0063, show marginal progress. The low-income group still has the highest level of any income group, at 7.1393 MJ in 2021. These readings describe the series only; end years and trend periods differ across regions, and no regional result tests what 2030 requires.

For 2030 the implication is limited. On the segment comparison the doubling is not met, and the latest data point is 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, so later developments are not visible. Only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the most recent figures rest on incomplete reporting.

Intensity is also an imperfect measure of efficiency. It divides energy supply by output, so it moves with the structure of an economy, climate and trade as well as technical efficiency. A fall may come from a shift to services without any gain in equipment efficiency, and a flat series may hide improvements offset by growth in energy-heavy activity. The proposals respond to these limits and to the regional gaps, and none presumes which measures would work.

w-c06-1-3~cedar/writer-1~132.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, which gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on a scale from 0 to 100 according to whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Equal weighting is a choice of method, not a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. Near-universal coverage is what one would expect of a measure read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, and it contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on irregular surveys.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf, so the question this section is set, how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed, cannot be answered in magnitude here. The sections that follow treat what the instrument measures and how its readings should be interpreted, which is a matter of method, and they state what a measured record of change would need to show.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and gave high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. Two companion series accompany the legal index: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. An apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the added domains lower the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether comparable values exist back to 2015, the baseline this book uses, has not been verified. If they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index.

The only result computed so far is coverage. In 2025 the legal index was reported by 189 economies, and 189 economies reported in at least one year, so the frame is complete for the latest year. This says nothing about the level of the index or its direction, which the section does not yet show.

The pairing of the three indices matters for target 5.1 because the target's indicator speaks of enforcement and monitoring as well as laws. The legal score records what the statute book says, the supportive score records whether institutions exist to give the law effect, and the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The gap between the first and the other two is the gap between a promise and its delivery, and it has not been computed here.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The record behind target 5.1 can be read for a change only once a few quantities are in hand, and the bench has so far produced only its coverage: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and the same 189 appear when any year is counted. That is a complete frame, not a measurement of change. What follows sets out what a measured answer would consist of.

The first quantity is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and because a few large reforms look the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones. The third is the distribution. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, not its centre, so the spread between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed, bears directly on the target. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index are likely to differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker needs.

The period after 2020 needs its own comparison. Average annual change before and after that year, if the history of the series permits, would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or was interrupted. A measure built from statute has the merit that an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data.

Until these quantities are computed, the section cannot state a direction of change in laws affecting women's economic opportunity, and it does not do so.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. All 189 economies reported the index in 2025, and the same 189 appear when any year is counted. No values for the aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates listed, so a comparison across the other regions would require either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change; implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. The relation between income and the legal score may therefore be weaker than the relation between income and the supportive and enforcement scores. This is context, not a finding. If it held, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values the bench has not yet computed. Under the strict reading, the relevant measures are the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, the relevant measures are the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. The frame for either is complete: 189 economies reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025.

What can be said without those values is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar, and any economy's position should be judged with that in mind. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companion series and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the index is well suited to a global account. Its census of 189 economies in 2025 means that a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The census is the only finding the bench has produced for this section: no level, change or distribution of the index has been computed, and so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed since 2015 or since 2020 remains open. The task left to the bench is to turn that coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every economy.

w-c09-10-5~cedar/writer-3~134.text:
### Net official assistance reached US$259 billion in 2023, an imperfect proxy for Aid for Trade

The question asks how much official assistance supports trade capacity. The bench cannot answer it directly. Target 8.a calls for more Aid for Trade for developing countries, the least developed above all, including through the Enhanced Integrated Framework, but the shelf holds no Aid for Trade commitments or disbursements. It also holds no least-developed-country breakdown and no Enhanced Integrated Framework record, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The series available is net official development assistance received, which counts concessional loans, net of repayments, and grants for every purpose. It can serve only as an upper bound on the resources from which trade capacity support could be drawn, not as an estimate of that support.

Read at that level, the world total rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US$. Constant prices remove general price changes, so the rise is real. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts, so some recipients lack a figure for the latest year and any total should be read with that gap in mind. The nearest available reading for poorer recipients is by income group: low-income economies received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015. That is not a least-developed-country figure, because the groups do not coincide.

The target sets no numeric threshold and no end level. The trend tool was therefore run on direction alone, with no numeric target: a series is classed as on track when it rises at a meaningful rate, and as stagnating or marginal when it does not. On that reading the world is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.0545. The label is weak evidence. A rising total of general assistance does not show that trade capacity support has grown, that it has gone to the least developed countries, or that it has been effective. Increases may reflect emergency, humanitarian or other spending unrelated to trade.

The point matters for 2030 because the target can be read in more than one way: as a rise in the volume of Aid for Trade, as a rise in its share of assistance, or as improved support to least developed countries specifically. The bench can speak only to the first, and only through a proxy. The parts that follow take the proxy as given, examine how it differs among regions and income groups, and show what changed after 2015 and after 2020, while keeping the limits of the measure in view. In short, the amount supporting trade capacity is not measured here; US$259.5 billion in 2023 is a ceiling on the proxy, not a finding about trade.

### Assistance rose unevenly across regions and concentrated among fewer recipients

Regional totals diverged sharply between 2015 and 2023, measured in constant 2023 US dollars. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest change, from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. The trend tool classes the region as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.213. Established knowledge of the period suggests that the displacement and reconstruction needs created by war in Europe explain part of this, though the series does not show what drove the change. No target level is set in the tool, so the classification reads only the direction of travel.

Other regions moved far less. East Asia and Pacific rose from US$9.9 billion to US$10.7 billion, with a rate of 0.010, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, a rate of 0.002, classed as stagnation. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion and is classed as on track, at a rate of 0.028. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Sub-Saharan Africa remains the largest regional recipient, at US$64.8 billion in 2023, up from US$51.8 billion in 2015. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region without recipients in this series.

The pattern matters for Aid for Trade because a rise in the world total, from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, says little about where trade capacity is being built. Regions with flat inflows in real terms face rising trade-support needs without a matching rise in assistance, while this series cannot show how much of any inflow reaches trade purposes.

The spread among countries widened. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received was 0.361 in 2015, 0.370 in 2019 and 0.452 in 2023. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to large recipients, was 0.255 in 2015 and 0.256 in 2019, then rose to 0.460 in 2023. The jump came after 2019, so the concentration is a feature of the years after 2020 rather than of the first half of the period. The coefficient of variation also rose, from 0.643 in 2015 to 1.477 in 2023.

The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 38.7% in 2019 and 29.6% in 2023. Regional averages therefore explain a shrinking part of the inequality, and differences among countries within the same region now account for most of it. Regional reading alone would hide this, so country-level targeting matters more than regional envelopes.

The country count also shifted: 138 countries in 2015, 134 in 2019 and 135 in 2023. The coverage statement for 2023 elsewhere in the results gives 136 countries reporting. These small differences reflect which countries have data and pass the weighting in each tool, and they mean that part of the change in concentration could arise from changes in who is counted. The change in count is small against the size of the rise in the Gini and Theil measures, but it cannot be excluded as a contributor.

### A single surge in 2022 explains most of the recent rise, and 43 countries regressed

The break analysis of world net official development assistance, in constant 2023 US dollars, detects breaks in 2022 and 2023. In the segment from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. The segment covering 2022 alone has a mean annual change of US$49.8 billion, several times the long-run pace. The segment covering 2023 alone has a mean change of minus US$0.7 billion. The world total stood at US$169.7 billion in 2015 and US$259.5 billion in 2023. The break test shows when the series shifted, not why, and the results do not state what share of the 2015 to 2023 rise the 2022 change represents. This part therefore claims only that the largest movement was placed in 2022 and that the series eased slightly the following year.

Context from outside these data, not tested here, points to war-related emergency and reception flows in Europe in 2022. The series does not attribute the 2022 change to any recipient or purpose. Europe and Central Asia, which rose from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023, is consistent in timing with that context, but the results do not show that it drove the world break. A one-year movement of this kind is also a weak basis for judging whether support for trade capacity has grown, since emergency flows serve humanitarian and budget needs rather than trade facilitation.

The country classes show how little the aggregate says about most recipients. Of 138 countries assessed, 79 are classed as on track or target met, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed group. Another 5 show moderate progress, with 0.4% of the population, 6 show marginal progress, with 3.1%, and 5 are stagnant, with 1.7%. The largest class by population is regression: the trend tool classes 43 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the assessed population. This is a class of the fitted trend rate, not a comparison of 2023 receipts with 2015 levels, and the results do not give those country levels.

This divergence matters for the 2030 horizon. A world total can rise while the trend rate is negative for countries holding more than half of the assessed population. The tool was run with no numeric target, since target 8.a sets none, so the classes describe the direction of the trend rate only and not attainment of a defined threshold. The series ends in 2023 and gives no basis for forecasting the path to 2030 in either direction.

### Reaching 2030 requires better measurement and steadier, better-targeted assistance, with proposals

Reaching 2030 on target 8.a depends first on measurement. The bench cannot give an amount for official assistance that supports trade capacity. Net official development assistance received was US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US dollars, and that figure is an upper bound on what could support trade capacity, not an estimate of it. The series covers every purpose, and the shelf holds no Aid for Trade disbursements. It gives no breakdown for least developed countries and no Enhanced Integrated Framework figure, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The nearest available readings are income-group and regional totals: low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023 and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion. Target 8.a also carries no numeric benchmark. The trend tool was run with no numeric target, so its classes describe the direction of the trend rate only, and the rate is the fitted trend of the series as the tool reports it, not an amount in dollars.

The series gives no basis for forecasting the path to 2030. The mean annual change was US$6.4 billion in 2001-2021. The break test places the largest movement in 2022, with a mean change of US$49.8 billion for that year alone, and 2023 shows a fall of US$0.7 billion. Context from outside these data, not tested here, points to emergency flows linked to the war in Europe; the series does not show what drove the change, nor what share of the rise since 2015 belongs to 2022. A series that ends in 2023 cannot say whether the 2022 level will persist, recede or be exceeded.

The distribution of recipients shows how little the aggregate says. The trend tool classes 43 of 138 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the population assessed. This is a class of the trend rate, meaning the fitted trend of their assistance is negative; it is not a comparison of 2023 with 2015 levels. Inequality among recipients rose: the population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.361 in 2015 and 0.452 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023, so most of the inequality lies within regions. The decomposition locates the inequality but does not show which allocation policy would reduce it.

t-rate-to-count~hana/analyst-1~135.name: rate-to-count
t-rate-to-count~hana/analyst-1~135.code:
def tool(data, params):
    rate_code = params['rate_code']
    pop_code = params['pop_code']
    year = str(params['year'])
    per = params.get('per', 100000)
    rates = data[rate_code]
    pops = data[pop_code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    def pick(series, u, y):
        d = series.get(u)
        if d is None:
            return None
        if y in d:
            return d[y]
        if int(y) in d:
            return d[int(y)]
        return None
    rate_unit = list(rates.keys())
    pop_unit = list(pops.keys())
    total = 0.0
    by_region = {}
    n_used = 0
    n_missing = 0
    for c in regions:
        r = None
        p = None
        if c in rates:
            r = pick(rates, c, year)
        if c in pops:
            p = pick(pops, c, year)
        if r is None or p is None:
            n_missing += 1
            continue
        deaths = r * p / per
        total += deaths
        reg = regions[c]
        by_region[reg] = by_region.get(reg, 0.0) + deaths
        n_used += 1
    facts = {'year': int(year), 'countries_used': n_used, 'countries_missing': n_missing, 'total_deaths': round(total)}
    for reg in sorted(by_region):
        facts['deaths_' + str(reg)] = round(by_region[reg])
    top = sorted(by_region.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
    if top:
        facts['largest_region'] = str(names.get(top[0][0], top[0][0]))
    summary = 'Applying the rate in series ' + rate_code + ' (per ' + str(per) + ' people) to the population in ' + pop_code + ' gives about ' + str(round(total)) + ' deaths across ' + str(n_used) + ' countries in ' + str(year) + '; ' + str(n_missing) + ' countries lacked a rate or a population and are excluded, so the total is a lower bound.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

w-c09-6-5~cedar/writer-4~135.text:
### The world share fell by 1.4 points, from a 2015 base, not by a substantial margin

Target 8.6 asks for a substantial reduction in the proportion of youth not in employment, education or training by 2020. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so any verdict rests on a reading chosen by the analyst. Here the reading is plain: a substantial reduction would be a fall large enough to be visible against the starting level and to change the position of most regions.

The question is about 2020, yet the results do not give the world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be read directly. The verdict is therefore an inference from the available series. The modelled ILO estimate puts the global share at 21.2 per cent of the youth population in 2015 and at 19.8 per cent in 2025. The fall over the decade is 1.4 points, or about 6.8 per cent of the 2015 level. The latest year available is five years after the target date. The series is a modelled estimate, not a count from a single survey: countries with sparse labour force data receive values built from regional patterns and covariates, so small movements in the world figure should be read with caution. The estimate covers 182 countries reporting in 2025.

The pace of change did not follow a steady path. The break analysis of the annual change in the world share finds shifts in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by about 0.2 points a year on average. Between 2013 and 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which means that the share was essentially flat in the years just before the target date. In 2020 the mean annual change was 1.37 points. These windows do not coincide exactly with 2015 to 2020, so they indicate the direction of travel rather than a measured net change. The measured fall belongs to later periods, taken up in a later part, and the results do not show where within the decade most of the decline arose.

The income groups show why the global figure hides unequal movement. In high-income countries the share moved from 12.2 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025, and in upper middle income countries from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent. Lower middle income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The global average is thus pulled down by the middle-income and wealthier groups, while the poorest countries ended the period with a higher share than they began with.

On the reading used here, these results do not support a claim of substantial reduction by 2020. The share was close to flat in the years before the target date, fell by a small amount over ten years, and rose in the poorest countries. A looser reading of 'substantially' could change the verdict, and the target text leaves that question open, but on the stated reading a decline of this size, reached five years after the target date, does not meet the intent of the goal.

### Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden

Regional levels in 2025 range widely. North America holds the lowest share, at 11.8 per cent of youth, down from 12.5 per cent in 2015. East Asia and Pacific stands at 12.8 per cent, down from 14.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 13.0 per cent, down from 15.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is at 19.3 per cent, from 21.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is at 21.4 per cent, slightly above its 2015 level of 20.9 per cent. South Asia shows the largest fall among the regions in this comparison, from 28.4 per cent to 23.4 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is highest at 32.1 per cent, and its share rose from 31.1 per cent. Most regions moved down modestly, while two did not.

Income groups show the same split. Low-income countries rose from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent, while lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent, and high-income countries from 12.2 per cent to 10.9 per cent. The poorest group is thus the one in which the share grew, and by 2025 it stands above the others. Demographic pressure, thin labour demand and limited schooling places are well-established contexts for this pattern in low-income settings, though the series does not show what drives it.

Young women's shares exceed the all-youth share. The world female share was 30.2 per cent in 2015 and 27.1 per cent in 2025, against the all-youth share of 19.8 per cent in 2025. Male shares are not among the results cited, so no comparison with young men is drawn and no claim is made about which sex bears the larger burden. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the female share was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged. South Asia improved from 46.0 per cent to 37.1 per cent, yet remains high. Low-income countries moved against the trend, from 32.6 per cent to 34.4 per cent. Norms on care work and early marriage, and limits on women's mobility and employment, are the usual explanations, stated here as context only.

Among countries, the trend classes are scattered. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the direction of the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 28 show moderate progress and 29 marginal progress, while 21 stagnate and 58 regress. The regressing group holds 18.8 per cent of the population, more than the on-track group. No numeric target exists, and the results do not give the numeric thresholds that separate the classes. The classes are the trend tool's own categories, applied by the same rule to the world, regions and countries, and should be read as direction rather than as a verdict.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, did not narrow. The Gini coefficient was 0.231 in 2015, 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for a little over half of the inequality in both years. Convergence is not shown: the beta of -0.00428 has a p-value of 0.214, not distinguishable from zero. Countries starting higher did not reliably improve faster.

### The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement

The movement of the world share is better read as a sequence of breaks in timing than as a steady trend. The break analysis of the annual change in the modelled ILO series finds breaks in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by a mean of 0.2 points a year. That is the only stretch in which the decline looks like steady progress, and it ended before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.

From 2013 to 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which is near stagnation. This window does not match the 2015 to 2020 span of the target, and the results cited give no world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be derived from them. In 2020 the mean annual change in that single-year segment was 1.37 points. The timing coincides with the closure of schools and workplaces during the pandemic. That link is context drawn from well-established knowledge; the data show when the break occurred and do not test its cause. The evidence bearing on the target year is therefore the 2013 to 2019 mean and the 2020 segment, and both point away from a substantial reduction by 2020. The missing 2020 level is a limit on the verdict, not a finding.

From 2021 to 2023 the share fell by a mean of 1.08 points a year, a separate measured period. The results do not show where the decline recorded by 2025 was produced, nor whether it restored the earlier position or went beyond it. From 2024 to 2025 the share rose again by a mean of 0.15 points a year. The long-run rate of change for the world, at -0.0070 on the trend tool's scale, is read by that tool as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. These classes are the tool's own categories, applied without a numeric target, and their thresholds are not given in the results; regional and country classes rest on the same rule and are not separately tested against a target.

Sub-Saharan Africa followed a different path. Its breaks fall in 2014, 2021, 2023 and 2024. From 2006 to 2013 its mean annual change was -0.04 points. From 2014 to 2020 it rose by 0.45 points a year; that window includes the 2020 break, so the rise cannot be assigned wholly to the period before the pandemic, and no world mean for the same window is cited for comparison. A young population growing faster than jobs and school places is a common explanation, but the data do not test it. After 2020 the region eased, with a mean change of -0.29 points a year in 2021 and 2022 and -1.23 points in 2023, then 0.00 points a year in 2024 and 2025. The trend tool still classes the region as regression to 2030.

The breaks therefore cluster around 2020 and 2021, set against a world share that was nearly flat from 2013 to 2019. The pandemic link is context from outside the data, and the results isolate no cause.

### The 2020 target was missed, and 2030 needs faster progress and a clearer definition

On the reading used here, the 2020 target is unlikely to have been met in a substantial sense, and a looser reading could change that verdict. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so the verdict rests on the analyst's reading. The results give no world level for 2020 and no net change from 2015 to 2020, so the verdict is an inference, not a measurement. It rests on the break analysis already set out: a mean annual change of 0.02 points over 2013 to 2019, then a rise of 1.37 points in 2020. The world share stood at 21.2 per cent of youth in 2015 and 19.8 per cent in 2025.

The trend tool assigns its own classes, and its target is given as none, so the classes describe the direction and pace of change, not distance from a stated goal. The results do not give the numeric thresholds that separate the classes, so the placing of any region or country cannot be checked here. Regional and country classes come from the same rule as the world class, but they are not tested against a target and should not be read as verdicts on target 8.6. The world is classed as marginal progress, with a compound annual rate of -0.7 per cent from the 2015 baseline. Europe and Central Asia, at -1.6 per cent, and South Asia, at -1.9 per cent, reach the moderate class, and both still need acceleration. Low income, at 0.9 per cent a year, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, at 0.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.2 per cent, are classed as regression.

The country count rests on 187 countries assessed by the trend tool, whereas the 2025 levels rest on 182 countries reporting that year. Of the 187, 51 are on track or have met the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the assessed population. Regression affects 58 countries, holding 18.8 per cent of the population.

Countries have not drawn together. The convergence test gives a beta of -0.0043 with a p-value of 0.214, which cannot be told from zero, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.471 in 2015 to 0.532 in 2025. For 2030 the implication is that the present pace leaves the world far from a substantial reduction on the reading used here. The estimates are modelled, so classes for individual countries carry uncertainty.

w-c06-1-3~cedar/writer-1~136.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Equal weighting is a choice of method, not a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. The set of reporting entities in 2025 also includes aggregates for high-income, low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income and South Asian economies and for the world, so regional and income-group readings are available in principle. For a measure of national law, which is read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect, and it contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter.

Coverage is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no group average and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf for this section, so the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot be answered here in magnitude. The sections that follow set out what the instrument measures, how its readings should be interpreted and what a measured record of change would need to show. None of this should be read as a measured finding about the direction or size of reform since 2015 or since 2020.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and gave high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. Scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. An apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. The wider scope also lowers the standing of economies that looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions, since an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Finally, the revised series is recent, so its history may be short. The bench has not verified whether comparable values exist for 2015, the baseline used throughout this book. Where they do not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be read from this index, and the 2020 shock cannot be separated from the trend.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because its indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether the institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. The only result computed for this section is coverage: the legal index reports for 189 economies in 2025, and 189 economies report in at least one year. No score, level or change has been computed, so the section states no finding about direction. What the coverage does show is that the record is close to universal, and that any later comparison across regions or income groups will rest on the full set of economies rather than a sample.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The record of the Legal Framework Index covers 189 economies in 2025, and 189 economies report in at least one year. Coverage is therefore complete on the index's own terms. No level, change or distribution has yet been computed, and the section does not infer them from coverage alone.

A measured answer to the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed would need four elements. The first is the world level of the index in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change since 2015, with the number of economies whose scores rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages: a mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and a few large reforms look the same in a mean as many small ones. The third is the distribution. A target phrased as everywhere concerns the bottom of the distribution, so the gap between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed, is the relevant test. The fourth is the score by topic, because an average across domains hides the information that policymakers need.

Two comparisons would sharpen the reading. Average annual change before and after 2020 would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or paused during the pandemic, if the history of the series permits it. A comparison of reform in labour codes with reform in family and personal-status codes would test a common view in comparative law, stated here only as context: that labour rules are easier to amend than rules bound up with religious authority and custom. Neither is a finding of this section.

Because the index is built from statute rather than from reported statistics, an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report. Any backsliding would therefore appear in scores rather than as a gap in the data, which makes the series well suited to the computations above.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for this index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates returned, so a comparison across the other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change; implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. A reasonable expectation, to be tested rather than asserted, is that the relation between income and the legal score is weaker than the relation between income and the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains this index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values that the bench has not computed: the shelf holds the Legal Framework Index for 189 economies in 2025, but no level or change has been calculated from it.

Under the strict reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. A projection to 2030 at the observed pace would then show how long each income group needs to reach full formal equality. None of these can be stated from coverage alone.

What can be said is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality is a high bar, and any economy's position should be judged against it. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companion series on support and enforcement and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

The legal framework index is well suited to a global account on one count: 189 economies report for 2025, and 189 report in at least one year. A measured answer, once computed, will therefore rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. Coverage is the only result the bench has produced for this index, so the section offers no level, change or direction, and the question of how the laws have changed since 2015 or since 2020 remains open here. What is still needed is the level, the change since the earliest comparable year, the income-group and topic scores, and the legal score set beside the measures of support and enforcement, so that the distance between promise and practice becomes visible for each economy.
