t-wbl-implementation-gap~orchard/analyst.name: wbl-implementation-gap

w-c06-1-3~cedar/writer-1~152.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The equal weighting of topics is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change since 2015 or 2020 has been drawn from the shelf, so the direction and size of change in laws affecting women's economic opportunity cannot be stated here. The sections that follow therefore set out what the instrument measures, how its readings should be interpreted, and what a computed record would have to show. None of the general expectations about legal reform that appear there is a measured finding.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope tends to lower the standing of economies that looked close to parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive protection against harassment, criminalisation of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Third, because the revised series is recent, its history may be short. Whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been verified. If it does not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and no statement about the period after 2015 or after 2020 can rest on it.

The only result computed for this index is its coverage. In 2025 the Legal Framework Index was reported by 189 countries, and the same number reported in at least one year, so the frame is complete for the economies it covers. Regional and income-group aggregates are also held, but no level, trend or comparison has been calculated, and this part draws no conclusion about direction of change.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed here.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The bench has so far computed only the frame of the legal record, and the part that follows sets out what a measured answer would need to show. A measured answer would rest on four elements. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted global mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and an increase concentrated in a few large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones.

The third element is the distribution of scores: the spread between the highest and lowest, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker most needs to see.

The only result available for the Legal Framework Index is its coverage: 189 economies reported in 2025, and 189 economies reported in any year. Full coverage in the latest year means the index can support a comparison of the whole world, but it does not show direction. The shelf holds the series, yet no level, change or topic score has been computed from it. The section therefore does not state whether laws affecting women's economic opportunity have improved since 2015 or since 2020, and any such claim would go beyond the evidence.

One general point from comparative law is recorded as context, not as a finding. Governments have often found it easier to amend labour codes, treated as instruments of economic policy, than family and personal-status codes, which are frequently tied to religious authority and customary institutions. If that pattern holds in this index, the remaining distance would lie in rules governing a woman's capacity to act independently, such as choosing where to live, obtaining identity documents and inheriting on equal terms. Only a topic-level computation can test this.

A measure built from statute has one merit for the years after 2020: an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so backsliding would appear in the scores and not as a gap in the data. A comparison of average annual change before and after 2020 would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or reversed, provided the history of the series permits it.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. South Asia is the only geographic region among the aggregates returned. A comparison across the other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change, whereas implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. A reasonable expectation, to be tested rather than asserted, is that income relates less strongly to the legal score than to the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot yet say whether the economies with the worst outcomes are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first case calls for legislation, the second for implementation. The one result computed so far shows that the index covered 189 countries in 2025, and 189 in any year, so the data for such a comparison exist for nearly every economy.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values that the bench has not yet computed.

The only result available is the coverage of the Legal Framework Index: 189 economies report in 2025, and 189 report in at least one year. Coverage is therefore complete for the economies in the series, and a strict reading could in principle be tested across all of them. Under that reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Neither has been computed, so no verdict on 2030 is offered here.

What can be said is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality on it is a high bar. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions on support and enforcement and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account. The coverage tool shows 189 economies reporting in 2025, and the same number reporting in any year, so a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The coverage result gives no level, change or ranking, and none is claimed here. The task the section leaves to the bench is to turn that coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every economy.

t-wbl-implementation-gap~elm/analyst-1~1.name: wbl-implementation-gap
t-wbl-implementation-gap~elm/analyst-1~1.code:
def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    supp = params['supportive']
    enf = params['enforcement']
    sel = params.get('units')
    names = data['names']
    def ends(d):
        ys = sorted(y for y in d if d[y] is not None)
        if not ys:
            return None
        return ys[0], d[ys[0]], ys[-1], d[ys[-1]]
    facts = {}
    rows = []
    units = sel if sel else sorted(data[legal].keys())
    for u in units:
        l = data[legal].get(u)
        if not l:
            continue
        el = ends(l)
        if el is None:
            continue
        y0, l0, y1, l1 = el
        nm = names.get(u, u)
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = round(l0, 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = y0
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = round(l1, 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = y1
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(l1 - l0, 2)
        parts = []
        for tag, code in (('supportive', supp), ('enforcement', enf)):
            d = data[code].get(u)
            e = ends(d) if d else None
            if e is None:
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_status'] = 'missing'
                continue
            a0, v0, a1, v1 = e
            facts[u + '_' + tag + '_first'] = round(v0, 2)
            facts[u + '_' + tag + '_first_year'] = a0
            facts[u + '_' + tag + '_last'] = round(v1, 2)
            facts[u + '_' + tag + '_last_year'] = a1
            facts[u + '_' + tag + '_change'] = round(v1 - v0, 2)
            if l.get(a1) is not None:
                g = round(l[a1] - v1, 2)
                facts[u + '_gap_legal_minus_' + tag] = g
                parts.append(tag + ' gap ' + str(g) + ' points in ' + str(a1))
        rows.append(nm + ': legal index ' + str(round(l1, 2)) + ' in ' + str(y1) + ' (change ' + str(round(l1 - l0, 2)) + ' since ' + str(y0) + ')' + ('; ' + '; '.join(parts) if parts else '; no implementation series'))
    facts['units_covered'] = len(rows)
    summary = 'Women, Business and the Law scores for ' + str(len(rows)) + ' units. ' + ' | '.join(rows) + '. Gaps are legal score minus the other index in the latest year of the other index; where a series is missing the gap is omitted.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

w-c06-1-4~cedar/writer-1~159.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The equal weighting of topics is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change since 2015 or 2020 has been drawn from the shelf, so the direction and size of change in laws affecting women's economic opportunity cannot be stated here. The sections that follow therefore set out what the instrument measures, how its readings should be interpreted, and what a computed record would have to show. None of the general expectations about legal reform that appear there is a measured finding.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. According to the World Bank's description of the index, the revised framework covers ten topics, among them safety, and it adds domains such as childcare that an earlier, narrower framework largely omitted. Two companion series sit beside it on the shelf. A Supportive Framework Index asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation, and the second and third are expectations drawn from the design of the index, not findings of the bench. First, scores under the revised framework should not be set beside the headline figures of the earlier index. An apparent fall between the two would reflect a change of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope may be expected to lower the standing of economies that looked close to parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive protection against harassment, criminalisation of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy could have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. No computed result yet tests this expectation. Third, because the revised series is recent, its history may be short. Whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been verified. If it does not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and no statement about the period after 2015 or after 2020 can rest on it.

The only result computed for this index is its coverage: 189 countries reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and the same number reported in at least one year. The count is not checked against the total number of economies in the world, so it is read here as the coverage of the series and not as proof that every economy is included. Regional and income-group aggregates are also held, but no level, trend or comparison has been calculated. For that reason the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot yet be answered from the bench's results, and this part draws no conclusion about direction of change.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed here.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The bench has so far computed only the frame of the legal record, and the part that follows sets out what a measured answer would need to show. A measured answer would rest on four elements. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted global mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and an increase concentrated in a few large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones.

The third element is the distribution of scores: the spread between the highest and lowest, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker most needs to see.

The only result available for the Legal Framework Index is its coverage: 189 economies reported in 2025, and 189 economies reported in any year. Full coverage in the latest year means the index can support a comparison of the whole world, but it does not show direction. The shelf holds the series, yet no level, change or topic score has been computed from it. The section therefore does not state whether laws affecting women's economic opportunity have improved since 2015 or since 2020, and any such claim would go beyond the evidence.

One general point from comparative law is recorded as context, not as a finding. Governments have often found it easier to amend labour codes, treated as instruments of economic policy, than family and personal-status codes, which are frequently tied to religious authority and customary institutions. If that pattern holds in this index, the remaining distance would lie in rules governing a woman's capacity to act independently, such as choosing where to live, obtaining identity documents and inheriting on equal terms. Only a topic-level computation can test this.

A measure built from statute has one merit for the years after 2020: an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so backsliding would appear in the scores and not as a gap in the data. A comparison of average annual change before and after 2020 would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or reversed, provided the history of the series permits it.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated, and neither can any change since 2015 or 2020. South Asia is the only geographic region among the aggregates returned. A comparison across other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a stated reason, which is context and not a finding. A common proposition in the study of legal reform is that formal law costs little to change, whereas implementation costs a great deal. No cost data have been computed here, so the proposition remains untested. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. If the proposition holds, income would relate less strongly to the legal score than to the supportive and enforcement scores, and the legal index alone could flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones. That outcome is an expectation, not a result. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot yet say whether the economies with the worst outcomes are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first case calls for legislation, the second for implementation. The one result computed so far shows that the index was reported by 189 countries in 2025, and by 189 in any year. That count is a count of economies in the series; it has not been checked against the total number of economies in the world. It indicates that the data for such a comparison exist for a very large set of economies, though the values themselves have not yet been computed.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values that the bench has not yet computed.

The only result available is the coverage of the Legal Framework Index: 189 economies report in 2025, and 189 report in at least one year. Coverage is therefore complete for the economies in the series, and a strict reading could in principle be tested across all of them. Under that reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Neither has been computed, so no verdict on 2030 is offered here.

What can be said is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality on it is a high bar. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. According to the World Bank's documentation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology, the index scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy. In federal states or plural legal systems it may therefore not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions on support and enforcement and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account. The coverage tool shows 189 economies reporting in 2025, and the same number reporting in any year. This count is the number in the series; it has not been checked against the total number of economies in the world, so it should not be read as a census of every one. A measured answer, once computed, would rest on nearly all the economies the series holds rather than on a sample.

The question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot yet be answered from the results. The coverage result gives no level, change since 2015 or 2020, ranking or topic score, and none is claimed here. Whether the index can be computed back to 2015 has not been established by the bench, and that is the first thing to settle. The task left to the bench is to turn coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice can be seen for each economy. Until then, any statement about direction, or about how the revised scope affects country standings, remains an untested expectation drawn from the design of the index.

t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.name: wbl-implementation-gap
t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.code:
def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    support = params['support']
    enforce = params['enforce']
    sel = params.get('units')
    names = data['names']
    def span(series, u):
        d = data[series].get(u)
        if not d:
            return None
        ys = sorted(y for y in d if d[y] is not None)
        if not ys:
            return None
        return ys[0], d[ys[0]], ys[-1], d[ys[-1]]
    units = set()
    for s in (legal, support, enforce):
        units.update(data[s].keys())
    if sel:
        units = set(u for u in units if u in sel)
    facts = {}
    rows = []
    for u in sorted(units):
        a = span(legal, u)
        b = span(support, u)
        c = span(enforce, u)
        if a is None:
            continue
        nm = names.get(u, u)
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = a[0]
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = round(a[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = a[2]
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = round(a[3], 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(a[3] - a[1], 2)
        txt = nm + ' legal ' + str(round(a[3], 1)) + ' (' + str(a[2]) + ')'
        if b is not None:
            facts[u + '_support_last'] = round(b[3], 2)
            facts[u + '_support_last_year'] = b[2]
            facts[u + '_support_change'] = round(b[3] - b[1], 2)
            facts[u + '_gap_legal_support'] = round(a[3] - b[3], 2)
            txt += ', support gap ' + str(round(a[3] - b[3], 1))
        if c is not None:
            facts[u + '_enforce_last'] = round(c[3], 2)
            facts[u + '_enforce_last_year'] = c[2]
            facts[u + '_enforce_change'] = round(c[3] - c[1], 2)
            facts[u + '_gap_legal_enforce'] = round(a[3] - c[3], 2)
            txt += ', enforcement gap ' + str(round(a[3] - c[3], 1))
        rows.append(txt)
    facts['units_covered'] = len(rows)
    summary = 'Legal framework against implementation indices, latest year per unit: ' + '; '.join(rows[:10]) + '. Units lacking a legal score are omitted; missing indices leave their gaps unreported.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.name: wbl-implementation-gap
t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.code:
def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    supp = params['supportive']
    enf = params['enforcement']
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    def ends(d):
        out = {}
        for u in d:
            ys = sorted(y for y in d[u] if d[u][y] is not None)
            if ys:
                out[u] = (ys[0], d[u][ys[0]], ys[-1], d[u][ys[-1]])
        return out
    L = ends(data[legal])
    S = ends(data[supp])
    E = ends(data[enf])
    facts = {}
    rows = []
    for u in sorted(L):
        y0, v0, y1, v1 = L[u]
        nm = names.get(u, u)
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = round(v0, 1)
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = y0
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = round(v1, 1)
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = y1
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(v1 - v0, 1)
        for tag, X in (('supportive', S), ('enforcement', E)):
            if u in X:
                a0, b0, a1, b1 = X[u]
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_first'] = round(b0, 1)
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_last'] = round(b1, 1)
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_last_year'] = a1
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_change'] = round(b1 - b0, 1)
                if a1 == y1:
                    facts[u + '_gap_legal_minus_' + tag] = round(v1 - b1, 1)
        rows.append((v1 - v0, nm, u))
    n = len(rows)
    facts['units_with_legal_index'] = n
    facts['units_with_supportive_index'] = len(S)
    facts['units_with_enforcement_index'] = len(E)
    gaps = [facts[k] for k in facts if k.endswith('_gap_legal_minus_enforcement')]
    if gaps:
        facts['mean_legal_minus_enforcement_gap'] = round(sum(gaps) / len(gaps), 1)
    rows.sort(reverse=True)
    if rows:
        facts['largest_legal_gain_unit'] = rows[0][1]
        facts['largest_legal_gain'] = round(rows[0][0], 1)
    summary = 'Legal Framework Index, Supportive Framework Index and Enforcement Perceptions Index were compared for ' + str(n) + ' units with legal scores, using each unit\'s earliest and latest available year. '
    if gaps:
        summary += 'Where the latest years coincide, the legal score exceeds the enforcement score by ' + str(facts['mean_legal_minus_enforcement_gap']) + ' index points on average across ' + str(len(gaps)) + ' units. '
    summary += 'Coverage of the supportive and enforcement series is narrower, and gaps are reported only where years match.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}
t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.about: Computes first and latest values and changes of the Legal, Supportive and Enforcement indices for each economy and aggregate, and the gap between law and each of the other two in the latest shared year, to report target 5.1 as both legal reform and implementation distance.

params.legal: Series code of the Legal Framework Index
params.supportive: Series code of the Supportive Framework Index
params.enforcement: Series code of the Enforcement Perceptions Index

cases.expect: Facts per unit with legal first/last values, years and change, plus supportive and enforcement values and gaps where years match; counts of units per series and the mean legal-minus-enforcement gap; summary notes narrower coverage. Series codes are placeholders to be confirmed against the bench catalogue; if a code is absent the run should fail rather than return empty facts.

If it does not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and no statement about the period after 2015 or after 2020 can rest on it.

The only result computed for this index is its coverage: 189 countries reported the Legal Framework Index in 2025, and the same number reported in at least one year. The count is not checked against the total number of economies in the world, so it is read here as the coverage of the series and not as proof that every economy is included. Regional and income-group aggregates are also held, but no level, trend or comparison has been calculated. For that reason the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed cannot yet be answered from the bench's results, and this part draws no conclusion about direction of change.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed here.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The bench has so far computed only the frame of the legal record, and this part sets out what a measured answer would need to show. It would rest on four elements. The first is the level of the Legal Framework Index for the world in the latest year, which shows how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter as much as averages, because an unweighted global mean can rise while a few economies move backwards, and an increase concentrated in a few large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones.

The third element is the distribution of scores: the spread between the highest and lowest, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the domains of the index differ in both level and pace, and an average across them hides what a policymaker most needs to see.

The question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed is therefore unanswered here. The one result available for the Legal Framework Index is its coverage, which gives 189 economies reporting in 2025, the same number as in any year. That is the only figure on which the section rests, and later parts refer back to it without restating it. Full coverage means the index can support a comparison of the whole world, but it shows no direction. No level, change since 2015 or 2020, count of economies or topic score has been computed, so the section does not state whether laws have improved, and any such claim would go beyond the evidence. The computation needed is plain: the world level in the latest year, the change from the earliest comparable year, and the counts of economies rising, falling and unchanged.

One general point from comparative law is recorded as context, not as a finding. Governments have often found it easier to amend labour codes, treated as instruments of economic policy, than family and personal-status codes, which are frequently tied to religious authority and customary institutions. If that pattern holds in this index, the remaining distance would lie in rules governing a woman's capacity to act independently, such as choosing where to live, obtaining identity documents and inheriting on equal terms. Only a topic-level computation can test this.

A measure built from statute may have one merit for the years after 2020. This is an inference from the design of the index, not a property verified in the data: because the scores describe laws in force, an economy might not be able to leave the series by ceasing to report, so backsliding would show in the scores and not as a gap. A comparison of average annual change before and after 2020 would show whether reform accelerated, slowed or reversed, provided the history of the series permits it.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for the Legal Framework Index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated, and neither can any change since 2015 or 2020. South Asia is the only geographic region among the aggregates returned. A comparison across other regions would need either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a stated reason, which is context and not a finding. A common proposition in the study of legal reform is that formal law costs little to change, whereas implementation costs a great deal. No cost data have been computed here, so the proposition remains untested. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. If the proposition holds, income would relate less strongly to the legal score than to the supportive and enforcement scores, and the legal index alone could flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones. That outcome is an expectation, not a result. The test is to compute the three indices by income group and compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also bears on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains the index scores. Without group-level values, the book cannot yet say whether the economies with the worst outcomes are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws already in place. The distinction matters for policy: the first case calls for legislation, the second for implementation. The one result computed so far shows that the index was reported by 189 countries in 2025, and by 189 in any year. That count is a count of economies in the series; it has not been checked against the total number of economies in the world. It indicates that the data for such a comparison exist for a very large set of economies, though the values themselves have not yet been computed.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination against women and girls everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on values that the bench has not yet computed.

The only result available is the coverage of the Legal Framework Index: 189 economies report in 2025, and 189 report in at least one year. Coverage is therefore complete for the economies in the series, and a strict reading could in principle be tested across all of them. Under that reading, the relevant measures would be the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it. Under the directional reading, they would be the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Neither has been computed, so no verdict on 2030 is offered here.

What can be said is a matter of definition. The revised measure demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, so full equality on it is a high bar. A perfect legal score is also a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. According to the World Bank's documentation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology, the index scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy. In federal states or plural legal systems it may therefore not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. The index also measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions on support and enforcement and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account. The coverage tool shows 189 economies reporting in 2025, the same number as in any year, as stated in the opening part of this section. That count is the number in the series; it has not been checked against the total number of economies in the world, so it should not be read as a census of every one. A measured answer, once computed, would rest on nearly all the economies the series holds rather than on a sample.

The question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed is therefore unanswered in this section, and the answer is stated plainly as missing. The coverage result gives no level, change since 2015 or 2020, count of economies rising or falling, income-group value or topic score, and none is claimed here. Whether the index can be computed back to 2015 on a comparable basis has not been established by the bench, and that is the first thing to settle; if the earliest comparable year is later, it must be stated and used in place of 2015. The task left to the bench is to turn coverage into levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice can be seen for each economy. Until then, any statement about direction, or about how the revised scope affects country standings, remains an untested expectation drawn from the design of the index, and no verdict on target 5.1 for 2030 can be given.

t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.code:
def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    supp = params['supportive']
    enf = params['enforcement']
    sel = params.get('units')
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    def ends(series, u):
        d = series.get(u)
        if not d:
            return None
        ys = sorted(y for y in d if d[y] is not None)
        if not ys:
            return None
        return ys[0], d[ys[0]], ys[-1], d[ys[-1]]
    units = sorted(data[legal].keys())
    if sel:
        units = [u for u in units if u in sel]
    facts = {}
    lines = []
    n_gap = 0
    gaps_s = []
    gaps_e = []
    for u in units:
        L = ends(data[legal], u)
        S = ends(data[supp], u)
        E = ends(data[enf], u)
        if L is None:
            continue
        nm = names.get(u, u)
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = round(L[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = L[0]
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = round(L[3], 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = L[2]
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(L[3] - L[1], 2)
        part = nm + ': legal ' + str(round(L[3], 1)) + ' in ' + str(L[2])
        if S:
            facts[u + '_supportive_last'] = round(S[3], 2)
            facts[u + '_supportive_last_year'] = S[2]
            facts[u + '_supportive_change'] = round(S[3] - S[1], 2)
            g = L[3] - S[3]
            facts[u + '_gap_legal_supportive'] = round(g, 2)
            gaps_s.append(g)
            part += ', supportive gap ' + str(round(g, 1))
        if E:
            facts[u + '_enforcement_last'] = round(E[3], 2)
            facts[u + '_enforcement_last_year'] = E[2]
            facts[u + '_enforcement_change'] = round(E[3] - E[1], 2)
            g = L[3] - E[3]
            facts[u + '_gap_legal_enforcement'] = round(g, 2)
            gaps_e.append(g)
            part += ', enforcement gap ' + str(round(g, 1))
        lines.append(part)
        n_gap += 1
    facts['units_covered'] = n_gap
    if gaps_s:
        facts['median_gap_legal_supportive'] = round(statistics.median(gaps_s), 2)
    if gaps_e:
        facts['median_gap_legal_enforcement'] = round(statistics.median(gaps_e), 2)
    summary = 'Legal, supportive and enforcement scores cover ' + str(n_gap) + ' units. ' + '; '.join(lines[:10]) + '. Missing years or series leave the relevant gap unreported.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    support = params['support']
    enforce = params['enforce']
    ser = {'legal': data[legal], 'support': data[support], 'enforce': data[enforce]}
    def ends(d):
        ys = [y for y in d if d[y] is not None]
        if not ys:
            return None
        a = min(ys)
        b = max(ys)
        return (a, d[a], b, d[b])
    facts = {}
    rows = []
    units = set()
    for k in ser:
        for u in ser[k]:
            units.add(u)
    for u in sorted(units):
        r = {}
        ok = True
        for k in ser:
            if u in ser[k]:
                e = ends(ser[k][u])
            else:
                e = None
            if e is None:
                ok = False
                break
            r[k] = e
        if not ok:
            continue
        lg = r['legal']
        sp = r['support']
        en = r['enforce']
        gs = lg[3] - sp[3]
        ge = lg[3] - en[3]
        rows.append((u, lg, sp, en, gs, ge))
    for row in rows:
        u = row[0]
        lg = row[1]
        sp = row[2]
        en = row[3]
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = round(lg[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = lg[0]
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = round(lg[3], 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = lg[2]
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(lg[3] - lg[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_support_last'] = round(sp[3], 2)
        facts[u + '_support_change'] = round(sp[3] - sp[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_enforce_last'] = round(en[3], 2)
        facts[u + '_enforce_change'] = round(en[3] - en[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_gap_legal_support'] = round(row[4], 2)
        facts[u + '_gap_legal_enforce'] = round(row[5], 2)
    facts['economies_covered'] = len(rows)
    if rows:
        facts['mean_gap_legal_support'] = round(statistics.mean([x[4] for x in rows]), 2)
        facts['mean_gap_legal_enforce'] = round(statistics.mean([x[5] for x in rows]), 2)
        w = max(rows, key=lambda x: x[5])
        facts['widest_enforce_gap_economy'] = data['names'].get(w[0], w[0])
    summary = 'Economies with all three indices: ' + str(len(rows)) + '. Gaps are legal score minus the other score in the latest year; missing years are skipped.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.code:
def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    supp = params['supportive']
    enf = params['enforcement']
    sel = params.get('units')
    names = data['names']
    def pick(code):
        d = data[code]
        out = {}
        for u, series in d.items():
            ys = sorted(y for y, v in series.items() if v is not None)
            if ys:
                out[u] = (ys[0], series[ys[0]], ys[-1], series[ys[-1]])
        return out
    L = pick(legal)
    S = pick(supp)
    E = pick(enf)
    units = sorted(u for u in L if (sel is None or u in sel))
    facts = {}
    lines = []
    gaps = []
    for u in units:
        y0, l0, y1, l1 = L[u]
        nm = names.get(u, u)
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = y0
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = round(l0, 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = y1
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = round(l1, 2)
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(l1 - l0, 2)
        txt = nm + ': legal index ' + str(round(l1, 1)) + ' in ' + str(y1) + ' (' + str(round(l1 - l0, 1)) + ' since ' + str(y0) + ')'
        for tag, X in (('supportive', S), ('enforcement', E)):
            if u in X:
                a0, s0, a1, s1 = X[u]
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_first_year'] = a0
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_first'] = round(s0, 2)
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_last_year'] = a1
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_last'] = round(s1, 2)
                facts[u + '_' + tag + '_change'] = round(s1 - s0, 2)
                if a1 == y1:
                    g = l1 - s1
                    facts[u + '_legal_minus_' + tag] = round(g, 2)
                    txt += '; gap to ' + tag + ' ' + str(round(g, 1))
                    if tag == 'enforcement':
                        gaps.append(g)
                else:
                    facts[u + '_legal_minus_' + tag] = 'years differ'
                    txt += '; ' + tag + ' latest year ' + str(a1) + ' differs, gap not computed'
            else:
                txt += '; no ' + tag + ' data'
        lines.append(txt + '.')
    facts['units_covered'] = len(units)

t-wbl-implementation-gap~birchwood/analy.code:
def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    supp = params['supportive']
    enf = params['enforcement']
    sel = params.get('units')
    names = data['names']
    def ends(d):
        ys = sorted(y for y in d if d[y] is not None)
        if not ys:
            return None
        return (ys[0], d[ys[0]], ys[-1], d[ys[-1]])
    L = data[legal]
    S = data[supp]
    E = data[enf]
    units = sorted(L.keys())
    if sel:
        units = [u for u in units if u in sel]
    facts = {}
    rows = []
    for u in units:
        el = ends(L[u])
        if el is None:
            continue
        k = u
        facts[k + '_legal_first_year'] = el[0]
        facts[k + '_legal_first'] = round(el[1], 2)
        facts[k + '_legal_last_year'] = el[2]
        facts[k + '_legal_last'] = round(el[3], 2)
        facts[k + '_legal_change'] = round(el[3] - el[1], 2)
        for tag, src in (('supportive', S), ('enforcement', E)):
            if u not in src:
                facts[k + '_' + tag] = 'missing'
                continue
            e = ends(src[u])
            if e is None:
                facts[k + '_' + tag] = 'missing'
                continue
            facts[k + '_' + tag + '_first_year'] = e[0]
            facts[k + '_' + tag + '_first'] = round(e[1], 2)
            facts[k + '_' + tag + '_last_year'] = e[2]
            facts[k + '_' + tag + '_last'] = round(e[3], 2)
            facts[k + '_' + tag + '_change'] = round(e[3] - e[1], 2)
            lv = L[u].get(e[2])
            if lv is not None:
                g = round(lv - e[3], 2)
                facts[k + '_legal_minus_' + tag + '_gap_' + str(e[2])] = g
                if tag == 'enforcement':
                    rows.append((g, u))
    rows.sort(reverse=True)
    if rows:
        g, u = rows[0]
        facts['widest_enforcement_gap'] = g
        facts['widest_enforcement_gap_unit'] = names.get(u, u)
        summary = 'Units with all three indices: ' + str(len(rows)) + '. Widest legal-minus-enforcement gap: ' + str(g) + ' points, ' + names.get(u, u) + '. Gaps use the legal score for the same year as the other index; missing years are reported as missing.'
    else:
        summary = 'No unit has matching legal and enforcement observations; gaps cannot be stated.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

def tool(data, params):
    legal = params['legal']
    support = params['support']
    enforce = params['enforce']
    ser = {'legal': data[legal], 'support': data[support], 'enforce': data[enforce]}
    names = data['names']
    def span(d):
        ys = sorted(d.keys())
        if len(ys) == 0:
            return None
        return ys[0], d[ys[0]], ys[-1], d[ys[-1]]
    facts = {}
    lines = []
    units = {}
    for k in ser:
        units[k] = sorted(ser[k].keys())
    codes = [u for u in units['legal'] if u in ser['support'] and u in ser['enforce']]
    if 'max_units' in params:
        codes = codes[:params['max_units']]
    n_ok = 0
    gaps_s = []
    gaps_e = []
    for u in codes:
        a = span(ser['legal'][u])
        b = span(ser['support'][u])
        c = span(ser['enforce'][u])
        if a is None or b is None or c is None:
            continue
        n_ok += 1
        nm = names.get(u, u)
        facts[u + '_legal_first'] = a[1]
        facts[u + '_legal_first_year'] = a[0]
        facts[u + '_legal_last'] = a[3]
        facts[u + '_legal_last_year'] = a[2]
        facts[u + '_legal_change'] = round(a[3] - a[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_support_last'] = b[3]
        facts[u + '_support_change'] = round(b[3] - b[1], 2)
        facts[u + '_enforce_last'] = c[3]
        facts[u + '_enforce_change'] = round(c[3] - c[1], 2)
        gs = round(a[3] - b[3], 2)
        ge = round(a[3] - c[3], 2)
        facts[u + '_gap_legal_support'] = gs
        facts[u + '_gap_legal_enforce'] = ge
        gaps_s.append(gs)
        gaps_e.append(ge)
        lines.append(nm + ': legal index ' + str(a[3]) + ' in ' + str(a[2]) + ', ' + str(gs) + ' points above supportive and ' + str(ge) + ' above enforcement perceptions.')
    facts['units_complete'] = n_ok
    if n_ok > 0:
        facts['mean_gap_legal_support'] = round(statistics.mean(gaps_s), 2)
        facts['mean_gap_legal_enforce'] = round(statistics.mean(gaps_e), 2)
    summary = 'Legal framework against implementation, ' + str(n_ok) + ' units with all three indices. ' + ' '.join(lines[:10])
    if n_ok == 0:
        summary = 'No unit carries all three indices; the gap cannot be stated.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

call.task: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.

reasons.charter-1-forum: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps power among the members, since no organisation stands above the communities. A two-thirds rule for the bench stops any single member from blocking a tool while still demanding broad trust in it. A panel with one reviewer from each member lets every community, the forum included, judge first drafts, so that the people the goals concern are heard before the text settles. A two-thirds rule for adopting the book avoids a single veto on about 560 pages, yet
reasons.charter-1-commons: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps every community equal and avoids a standing body above the members, which suits a commons order. A two-thirds rule for admitting tools to the bench protects shared infrastructure from a bare majority while sparing it a single veto. Review by two guild reviewers of other origins mirrors the commons practice of gathering by one and checking by another of a different origin. Adoption of the book by unanimity matches the conference's own rule of every commu
reasons.charter-1-guild: A standing secretariat serves all members equally and keeps the bench and shelf maintained between rounds, without the discontinuity of a rotating chair. A two-thirds rule for admitting tools to the bench guards the shared infrastructure against hasty additions while preventing any single member from blocking it. First review by two peers of other origins matches the guild's principle that no analysis reaches a writer unreplicated by an analyst of another origin. Adopting the book by two thirds
reasons.charter-1-cooperative: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps authority among the members, consistent with a cooperative order that pools its writers rather than delegating to a standing body. Admitting tools to the bench by two thirds protects the shared infrastructure from capture by a bare majority without letting one member block every addition. First review by two guild reviewers of other origins matches the mission: sections drafted from analyses the guild replicated, checked by peers who did not write them.

interventions.text: Round 61: the case's maker, not the society, changed how the cooperative's writers work: asked for a long section in one answer, the writers returned about a third of the words asked, and the keeper had released 57 of 68 versions for length; from this round a writer plans a section's parts and writes each in its own call. To keep within the budget, the six writers on Claude Opus 5.5 (tamarind/writer-1, tamarind/writer-2, tamarind/writer-3, tamarind/writer-4, ewan/writer-1, ewan/writer-2) were moved to Claude Sonnet 5.5, and the keeper's floor set at four fifths of the words asked.

Round 68: the case's maker, not the society, changed the reviewers' form: in 82 reviews no statement of the scorecard had been scored as met, though the comments mostly called the numbers correct; from this round a reviewer lists the faults it finds, each against a statement and of minor or major severity, and the levels and the recommendation follow from the faults by the scorecard's declared rule (no fault, adopted; minor faults only, adopted once corrected; a major fault, revised). Reviewers are shown the facts a version cites. Under the panel the council had chosen, each version is read by four reviewers; to keep within the budget the reviewers lent in the commons, the cooperative and the forum (birch/reviewer, idris/reviewer, juno/reviewer, rowan/reviewer, ewan/reviewer, farah/reviewer, bao/reviewer, chidi/reviewer, dagny/reviewer, amara/reviewer) were moved to Claude Haiku 5.5, the guild's staying on Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Round 72: the case's maker trimmed what each call carries, to keep within the budget: writers are shown shorter notes of the series and summaries of the results, reviewers the facts a version cites and no summaries, and a review lists at most ten faults; envoys reflect on the record every sixteen rounds instead of eight (they still vote on every proposal put to the council).

Round 82: the case's maker added to each tool's summary how its result is read (results already kept were given the same note, their facts unchanged), and told writers never to compute a number the results do not give and to give causes only as context: the guild's reviewers had found first drafts misreading results (a negative beta read backwards, shares read as concentration) and asserting what no result shows.

Round 86: the case's maker, not the society, gave the review a rule of re-review: second versions still drew about two major faults a review, the reviewers finding new faults in each version, so that sections would have been revised until withdrawn. From this round a reviewer of a revision first judges whether each fault found before is mended, and adds a new fault only if it is major and introduced by the revision; a major fault is a false statement of fact or the question left unanswered, an unsupported claim of cause being minor. A revision, like a correction, rewrites only the parts its faults point to. The user raised the budget for the work's models to one hundred dollars at round 82; to keep a margin within it, sections not yet drafted are asked for 850 words a page instead of 950.

Round 93: the user decided to keep the budget for the work's models at one hundred dollars and to shorten the book rather than its review: a section needed about three versions before the panel's four reviewers passed it, about $0.45 to $0.50 a section, and the sections still to finish would have needed some $70 more. From this round the 97 sections not yet drafted are asked for 450 words a page (about 1,300 words a section), half the density first declared; the review is unchanged.

Round 98: the case's maker mended a fault in the case's own code, in the reviewers' calls: their answers were limited to 3,000 tokens, which the reviewers on Claude Haiku 5.5 passed with their reasoning and lists of faults, so that 176 of 243 calls since round 93 were cut off, paid for and asked again, and the panel waited on them. The limit is now 9,000 tokens.

Round 107: the user decided that the book finish what is in hand within the budget of one hundred dollars: reviewers of every model asked for revision about two times in three and the panel needed three of its four votes, so that a section took about three versions, and the sections still to write would have needed some $75 more. The 102 sections not yet drafted are not written, recorded as such; the sections already drafted go on under the review in force, and the overview and the proposals are written as planned.

Round 194: the case's maker mended a second fault of the same kind in the case's own code: the editor's overview, and the envoys' proposals, were limited in tokens below what a model's reasoning, the text and its claims need; nineteen calls for the overview were cut off since round 172 and paid for. The limits are now 20,000 tokens, and with little of the budget left the editors (commons/editor, guild/editor, cooperative/editor, forum/editor) were moved from Claude Opus 5.5 to Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Rounds 216 to 227: the model provider refused every call, the account's credit balance being too low (57 calls refused); the envoys could not vote on the chapter of proposals, put to the council in round 207, nor on the book. The run ended there. The book is set as it stands: its overview and every section adopted, the communities' proposals as they were put to the council and not voted on, and no adoption of the book as a whole.

outline.title: Seventeen Goals, Fifteen Years: A Measured Account of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.question: How far has the world come towards the seventeen goals since 2015, and how much can the World Development Indicators tell?

chapters.title: Goal 1: End poverty in all its forms everywhere
chapters.question: How much has poverty fallen since 2015, and who remains poor?

chapters.title: Goal 2: End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture
chapters.question: Has hunger fallen and has agriculture become more productive and sustainable since 2015?

chapters.title: Goal 3: Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages
chapters.question: How much have mortality and disease fallen since 2015, and how far does health coverage reach?

chapters.title: Goal 4: Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all
chapters.question: Are more children in school, finishing school and learning since 2015?

chapters.title: Goal 5: Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls
chapters.question: How far have laws, outcomes and power become more equal between women and men since 2015?

chapters.title: Goal 6: Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
chapters.question: How close is the world to universal safe water and sanitation, and how stressed are its freshwater resources?

chapters.title: Goal 7: Ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all
chapters.question: Is universal modern energy within reach, and is the energy mix becoming cleaner and more efficient?

chapters.title: Goal 8: Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all
chapters.question: Has growth been sustained and has work become fuller and more decent since 2015?

chapters.title: Goal 9: Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation
chapters.question: Have infrastructure, industry and innovation grown in developing countries since 2015?

chapters.title: Goal 10: Reduce inequality within and among countries
chapters.question: Has inequality narrowed within and among countries since 2015?

am-commons-1.title: Provenance of the series used in this book
am-commons-1.question: Which World Development Indicators series support each section, from which original source, for how many countries and up to which year, and which targets have no series at all?
am-commons-1.why: The commons keeps a shelf of series for every section, each chosen by one gatherer and checked by another of a different origin. A section that records that shelf lets readers trace every number to its series code and year. It also states plainly where data are missing.

am-commons-2.question: How far do the financial soundness indicators in the World Development Indicators cover target 10.5, and what do they show for the years available?
am-commons-2.why: Target 10.5 has thin coverage in the World Development Indicators. The section should state that gap rather than imply a measured trend.

am-commons-3.why: Sustainable tourism (12.b) has no adequate series in the World Development Indicators. Tourism is already treated in c09 section 8, so this section would duplicate it without data.

am-commons-4.why: The added provenance section needs room. The chapter also underpins the honesty about missing data that house style requires throughout the book.

am-cooperative-1.title: Replication of the book's analyses
am-cooperative-1.question: Which of the book's findings were reproduced independently from World Development Indicators series, and where did replications diverge?
am-cooperative-1.why: The cooperative drafts only from analyses the guild replicated; the book should report openly which findings were replicated, with series codes, years and units, and where definitions or data vintages produced different results.

am-cooperative-2.question: How far has each goal moved between 2015 and the latest year with data, measured against a stated reading of its 2030 target, and where do missing data or ambiguous targets prevent a judgement?
am-cooperative-2.why: The overview should state numbers, years and units, and should acknowledge gaps and ambiguous targets, as house style requires.

am-cooperative-3.why: Fixed broadband and internet use split one target thinly across two 2-page sections; internet use alone can carry the connectivity finding, and the pages are better spent on replication.

am-cooperative-4.question: What do World Development Indicators record of North American official assistance, trade access and emissions relative to partnership commitments, 2015 to the latest year?
am-cooperative-4.why: As drafted, the section's title reads as advocacy rather than measurement; restated, its question binds it to series the bench can replicate.

am-guild-1.title: Replication of the book's analyses on the shared bench
am-guild-1.question: How many of the book's findings were reproduced by an analyst of another origin from the same World Development Indicators series, and where did replicated values differ in number, year or unit?
am-guild-1.why: The guild's mission requires every analysis to be run on the shared bench and replicated before use. The book should report that record openly so readers can judge which findings stand on replicated ground.

am-guild-2.question: For each goal, what share of its targets has a World Development Indicators series with a value for 2015 and a recent year, and how far has the world moved on those series?
am-guild-2.why: An overview against 2030 commitments has to state what can be measured before it judges progress. Otherwise it overstates certainty where series are missing or a target admits several readings.

am-guild-3.why: This section is likely to duplicate the manufacturing value added material in section 2, which should cover technology intensity as well. The pages freed would go to replication.

am-guild-4.title: Proposals of the fifth community
am-guild-4.why: The book is written by five communities, but the draft gives proposal sections to only four. Every community should have equal space for its proposals.

am-forum-1.title: Who is left behind: the goals by sex, age, place and income
am-forum-1.why: The forum's mission is to speak for those the goals concern. The draft treats people almost wholly through national and regional averages. A theme chapter can set out what World Development Indicators show by sex, urban or rural residence, age and income quintile, and say plainly where no such breakdown exists. It would draw together disaggregated findings that are now scattered across the goal chapters.

am-forum-2.question: Poverty, nutrition and child survival among the poorest households
am-forum-2.why: The interlinkage between poverty and child survival is starkest within countries rather than between them. The section should state the gaps between quintiles where surveys report them, with their year and unit, so that it shows to whom the averages matter.

am-forum-3.title: Whether the proposals serve those the goals concern
am-forum-3.why: The proposals of four communities need a common test: whom each would help, by how much on the indicator it names, and where the data cannot show this. Without such a section the book proposes without judging whether what is written serves those the goals concern.

am-forum-4.why: Tourism is a weak proxy for decent work and inclusive growth, and Goal 12 already covers sustainable tourism. The two pages are better spent on the distributional evidence the book lacks.

A falling coefficient of variation means the spread narrowed relative to the mean.
