w-c03-4-1.text:
### What the target asks and what the bench can measure

Target 2.3 asks for a doubling, by 2030, of the agricultural productivity and incomes of small-scale food producers, in particular women, indigenous peoples, family farmers, pastoralists and fishers. The wording carries two difficulties. First, the target is defined for a specific population, the small-scale producer, while the World Bank series available to this chapter describe whole economies. Value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing, in constant 2015 US dollars, averages over a large commercial estate and a household plot alike. Second, the target sets no baseline year and does not say whether doubling is to be measured from 2015, from the adoption of the goals, or from some earlier date. This section reads the target from 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and treats a doubling as a rise to twice the 2015 level by 2030.

Two indicators are used. Value added per agricultural worker is the closest available proxy for the official indicator on the volume of production per labour unit. Cereal yield, in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, measures output per unit of land and covers wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains. Cereal production and the land under cereals are the two components of yield. Neither series speaks to incomes, to sex, or to farm size, and neither separates the small-scale producer from the large. They show whether the conditions for a doubling exist; they cannot show that the doubling has happened for the people the target names.

### Value added per worker: a rising world average that conceals a stalled bottom

Global value added per agricultural worker stood at 3,491 US dollars in 2015 and reached 4,264 dollars in 2025, in constant 2015 prices. The annual rate implied by the trend tool is 2.0 per cent. This is an increase, and the trend tool classes the world as on track, but the classification is generous. It compares the rate with a path that the tool sets itself, since the target carries no numerical value in the bench. A doubling over fifteen years requires a compound rate of close to five per cent a year, and a rate of 2.0 per cent is far below it. By 2025, ten of the fifteen years had elapsed, and the world average had not come near twice its 2015 level. Reaching a doubling by 2030 would need a rate in the remaining five years that no region has sustained over the decade.

The world figure is itself a weighted summary of very unequal parts. It is pulled upward by East Asia and Pacific, where value added per worker rose from 4,087 dollars in 2015 to 6,991 dollars in 2025, a rate of 5.5 per cent a year. That is the only regional rate that approaches the pace a doubling demands. The upper-middle-income group, which includes China and several large producers in Latin America and eastern Europe, rose from 4,378 dollars to 7,474 dollars at 5.5 per cent a year. The similarity of the two rates is not an accident: the economies that carry most weight in each group overlap, and the gain in both reflects the movement of labour out of farming as much as the growth of output. When many workers leave the land and output holds or rises, value added per remaining worker rises mechanically. A gain of this kind raises the average without any improvement in the position of the household that stays on a small plot.

The other regions improved at a slower pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 12,217 dollars to 17,325 dollars, at 3.6 per cent a year. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 6,294 dollars to 8,031 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. The group of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4,805 dollars to 6,181 dollars, at 2.6 per cent a year, and South Asia from 1,631 dollars to 2,082 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. All of these are reported as on track by the tool, and none is on a path to doubling by 2030. The finding for the world is therefore that productivity per worker has risen in most regions since 2015, that the rise is real, and that it is too slow for the target as written.

### Where productivity per worker is lowest, it has barely moved

The regions with the lowest starting points show the least progress. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 1,339 dollars per worker in 2015 and 1,496 dollars in 2025, a rate of 1.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries fell from 875 dollars in 2015 to 778 dollars in 2025, a rate of minus 1.2 per cent a year, which the tool classes as regression. In the lowest-income economies, then, value added per agricultural worker is lower in 2025 than it was when the goals were adopted. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 1,915 dollars to 2,336 dollars, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year.

The gap between the top and the bottom is wide enough that the arithmetic of a doubling has a different meaning at each end. North America is shown in the data only at its 2015 value of 67,701 dollars, since the series has no later observation for the region in the extract used here, and the comparison across the decade cannot be made. High-income countries as a group rose from 28,219 dollars to 30,775 dollars, at 0.9 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress. A group already at a high level may not need to double, and the target was written with developing countries in mind. The comparison that matters is the distance between the high-income level and the low-income level in 2025, which is a very large multiple of the low-income figure, and which the decade has not narrowed. A farm worker in a low-income country produces, in value terms, a small fraction of what a worker in a high-income country produces, and the low-income fraction has shrunk.

The reasons are well established. Low-income agriculture is dominated by rain-fed smallholdings with little mechanisation, limited access to improved seed, fertiliser and credit, poor roads to markets, insecure tenure, and exposure to drought, flood and pests. Population growth in these economies has kept the farm labour force growing, so that each worker has less land and capital to work with. In addition, the years since 2015 included conflict in several low-income countries, a series of droughts in the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, the disruption of the pandemic after 2020, and the price shocks that followed the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Each of these weighed most heavily on households with the least reserves. The data do not allow the effect of each shock to be separated, but the combined outcome is visible in the low-income series.

### Cereal yield: a modest rise and a persistent gap

Cereal yield tells a similar story at a smaller scale. The world yield was 3,932 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 4,229 kilograms per hectare in 2023, the latest year for which a world figure is reported. That is a gain well short of a doubling, and indeed far short of the gain in value added per worker. Yield is a slower-moving quantity than value added per worker, because it depends on biology, on the share of land that is irrigated, and on the technology of seed and fertiliser, none of which changes quickly. A doubling of average world cereal yield in fifteen years has no precedent in the record of any large region, and the target should not be read as requiring it of yields. The relevant question is whether yields are rising fast enough in the places where they are low.

They are not. Sub-Saharan Africa had a cereal yield of 1,443 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,453 kilograms per hectare in 2024, a change so small that it amounts to stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 kilograms per hectare to 1,345 kilograms per hectare over the same period. These are less than a third of the yield of North America, which rose from 6,677 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 8,414 kilograms per hectare in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, already at 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015, reached 5,430 kilograms per hectare in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 3,803 to 4,045 kilograms per hectare, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 2,732 to 3,027 kilograms per hectare.

South Asia and Latin America made the larger gains among developing regions. South Asia rose from 3,041 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 3,814 kilograms per hectare in 2024, which reflects the continued spread of irrigation, improved varieties of rice and wheat, and fertiliser use. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 to 4,828 kilograms per hectare, helped by maize and the expansion of no-till practices. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 2,766 to 3,366 kilograms per hectare. By contrast, upper-middle-income countries moved from 4,648 to 4,942 kilograms per hectare, and high-income countries from 4,976 to 5,394 kilograms per hectare, both in 2023. The pattern is that yields have risen where they were already moderate and where irrigation and inputs were spreading, and have stood still where they were lowest.

### Convergence: the poorest are not catching up

A doubling target is in part a target about catching up, and the convergence tool tests directly whether countries that began with low values rose faster than those that began with high values. For cereal yield across 176 countries between 2015 and 2024, the estimated coefficient is minus 0.0016, with a p-value of 0.79 and an R-squared of 0.0013. The coefficient is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in subsequent change. There is no evidence of convergence in the strict sense: low-yield countries did not grow faster than high-yield countries. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.00 in 2015 to 0.91 in 2024, which indicates that dispersion narrowed slightly. The two results are compatible. A narrowing of dispersion without a negative coefficient suggests that some of the highest-variance cases moved towards the middle by chance or by individual shocks, and not that the poorest as a group moved up.

The result for value added per worker is similar. Across 168 countries between 2015 and 2024, the coefficient is 0.0012, with a p-value of 0.49 and an R-squared of 0.0024. The sign is positive, so that the point estimate points to a slight tendency for countries with higher starting values to grow faster, although the estimate is not distinguishable from zero. The coefficient of variation moved from 1.51 to 1.43, a small fall. The reading is that after nearly a decade there is no evidence of a systematic closing of the gap, and the distribution of agricultural labour productivity remains very wide. The implication for 2030 is that a doubling for the lowest-productivity countries cannot be expected from the general forces already at work. If catching up were occurring by itself, the low-income group would show it. It shows the reverse.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020

The series offered by the bench give end points more than yearly paths, and the findings above compare 2015 with the latest year. The conclusions about the pandemic years therefore rest on well-established knowledge more than on the displayed results. The shock of 2020 disrupted labour movement, input supply and transport, and agricultural output in most countries proved more resilient than other sectors, because food production continued as an essential activity. This resilience helps explain why value added per worker in most regions did not fall. The more lasting effect on the poorest came through prices and incomes: higher fertiliser and fuel costs after 2021 and 2022 reduced the use of purchased inputs among smallholders who could not afford them, and this may account for part of the stagnation of yields in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries. A reader should treat this explanation as plausible and not as shown by the series.

A second caution concerns measurement. Value added per worker is the ratio of an output measure to a labour measure, and the labour measure for agriculture depends on household surveys that count part-time, seasonal and unpaid family work unevenly. Women, who make up a large share of the agricultural labour force in many low-income countries and who are named in the target, are often under-counted or recorded as outside the labour force. The series cannot show whether their productivity has changed. Cereal yield, moreover, applies to cereals only. It leaves out roots, tubers, pulses, vegetables, fruit, livestock and fish, which matter for the incomes of many small-scale producers, and in fishing communities it measures nothing at all. Reporting also varies: in some countries the harvested area is reported only as sown or cultivated area, as the series note states.

### Implications for 2030

The evidence supports four conclusions. First, no region, and no income group, is shown to be on course to double value added per agricultural worker by 2030 from its 2015 level; the closest, East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group, advanced at 5.5 per cent a year, and the remainder of the period would have to match or exceed that pace for the doubling to be reached. Because these two groups gained from labour leaving farming, their pace is hard to repeat elsewhere, where the farm labour force is still growing. Second, the world average disguises a split: the economies with the highest productivity gained, the middle gained moderately, and the lowest-income economies lost ground. Third, cereal yields rose modestly and not at all in Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group. Fourth, the lack of convergence in either indicator shows that the market and the existing policy mix are not closing the gaps by themselves.

The reading of the target matters for the verdict. If doubling is read as applying to the world average, the answer is that it will not be met. If it is read as applying to each country, a larger number of countries will fail, and the low-income group has moved backwards. If it is read as applying to small-scale producers specifically, the bench cannot say, because the series do not distinguish them. On any of the three readings, the conclusion that the target will be missed is secure for the regions where the data exist, and the main uncertainty is about the size of the miss for the people the target names.

What would raise productivity where it is lowest is well understood. It includes secure land rights, particularly for women; extension services and farmer organisations; improved and drought-tolerant seed suited to local conditions; affordable fertiliser applied efficiently, with attention to soil health; small-scale irrigation and water harvesting; rural roads, storage and market access that reduce post-harvest losses and raise farm-gate prices; and rural finance and insurance that let households take the risk of investing. Public spending on agricultural research has long delivered high returns, and sustained investment in it for the crops and conditions of low-income countries remains one of the more reliable routes to higher yields. The accounts of land, fertiliser, water and investment appear in other sections of this chapter and are not repeated here.

### Proposals

The findings lead to the following proposals; each names who should act.

proposals: National governments and regional bodies in Sub-Saharan Africa and other low-income regions should concentrate public spending on the inputs that raise yields on smallholdings, namely improved seed, small-scale irrigation, soil fertility programmes and rural roads, and should report each year on the yield and the value added per worker that result.

Ministries of agriculture and national statistical offices, with the FAO and the International Labour Organization, should publish productivity and income figures separately for small-scale producers, and by sex, so that Target 2.3 can be assessed for the people it names.
Land authorities should extend secure and equal tenure rights to women and to family and indigenous farmers, since the target ties productivity gains to secure access to land and resources.

Development banks and donors should direct agricultural research funding to crops and conditions of low-income countries, including drought-tolerant varieties of sorghum, millet and maize, and should protect it from the cuts that follow price shocks.

The United Nations statistical bodies responsible for the goal indicators should state explicitly the baseline year and the unit for judging a doubling, so that countries and regions are measured on the same reading of the target.
w-c03-4-1.gaps: The series describe whole agricultural sectors and cereals only. They do not separate small-scale producers from large ones, women from men, or indigenous peoples and pastoralists from other farmers, and they contain no measure of the incomes of food producers, which the target names. Fishing is mixed with farming and forestry in the value added series, and cereal yield omits roots, pulses, fruit, vegetables and livestock. North America has no 2025 observation in the extract, so the change in the region cannot be shown. Latest years differ between series, and the labour counts behind value added per worker are weak for part-time, seasonal and unpaid family work. The target gives no baseline year and no numerical level, so the verdict depends on the reading adopted, here a doubling from 2015. Annual paths and the separate effects of the pandemic and the price shocks of 2022 are not shown by the results used.

w-c06-1-1.text:
### The legal record now covers almost every economy, but the shelf holds only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that pays her pension at an earlier age and so on a shorter contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. That is why the measurement of laws has become one of the clearest windows on progress towards the target: it records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom.

The instrument used here is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life: safety from violence and harassment, freedom of movement, the right to work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, so a country that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left inheritance and property law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in any year. The two numbers being equal is itself informative. Nearly every member of the United Nations system is scored, and no economy that was once covered has dropped out. For a measure of national law, which can be read from statute books and does not depend on a household survey or an administrative register, such completeness is to be expected, and it contrasts sharply with the patchy coverage of the outcome indicators elsewhere in this chapter.

Coverage, however, is all that the bench has so far computed for this series. No level, regional average or change over time has been drawn from the shelf for this section, and the account that follows therefore does not state any score. That is a real limitation and it is stated plainly here rather than hidden: the question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed can be answered in direction and in structure from the well-documented history of reform, but not yet in magnitude from the numbers this book is bound to use. What the coverage result does establish is that the answer, once computed, will rest on a full census of economies rather than a sample.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index, which the World Bank published for more than a decade and which was widely cited in the first years of the Goals, scored a narrower set of legal questions and gave most economies high marks once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds two domains that the earlier one largely omitted, safety and childcare, and it sits alongside two companion indices also held on the shelf: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts in each country judge the law to work in practice.

This matters for interpretation in three ways. First, scores under the new framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index, and any reader who remembers the older numbers should not set the new ones beside them as though they measured the same thing. Second, the inclusion of safety and childcare lowers the apparent standing of many economies that had been regarded as close to legal parity. Few countries legislate comprehensively against sexual harassment in public spaces and online, criminalise every form of domestic violence including economic and psychological abuse, and require or subsidise childcare services with quality standards. A country can therefore have abolished every explicit restriction on women's work and still be far from the top of the revised scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history is short. The coverage tool's report that the same 189 economies appear in any year and in 2025 is consistent with a series whose run is recent; whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, which this book uses as its baseline, has not been verified by the bench, and where it does not, a change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index at all.

The pairing of the three indices is the most important innovation for target 5.1. The target's own wording speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. A legal framework score records what the statute book says; the supportive framework score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give it effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The gap between the first and the other two is the gap between a promise and its delivery. It is widely understood from the project's own publications that this gap is large almost everywhere, and that the economies with the most complete laws are not always those whose institutions and courts carry them out. Measuring that gap country by country is the natural next computation for this section, and it is the subject of the petition attached to it.

### The direction of reform since 2015 is clear even where its size is not

The history of the past decade, as recorded in successive editions of the World Bank's reports and in national legislation, runs in one direction. Reforms that remove discrimination greatly outnumber those that introduce it. The most common changes have been of a recognisable kind. Many governments repealed rules that barred women from industrial jobs, night work, mining or work deemed arduous or dangerous, provisions that were originally framed as protection and that in practice excluded women from better-paid sectors. Many introduced or strengthened laws against sexual harassment at work, often with civil remedies or criminal penalties. A number mandated equal remuneration for work of equal value, rather than merely for identical work, which is the standard that addresses occupational segregation. Several equalised the ages at which men and women may retire with a full pension, or credited periods of childcare in pension calculations. Paid paternity leave, rare at the start of the period, spread steadily, and some countries introduced shared parental leave designed to reduce the penalty that employers attach to hiring women of childbearing age.

Reform in the domains of marriage and assets has been slower. Provisions that require a wife to obey her husband, that make the husband the legal head of household, that deny a woman the right to choose where to live or to obtain a passport on the same terms as a man, and that give daughters smaller shares of inheritance than sons are rooted in personal-status and family codes that are frequently tied to religious law or customary authority. Governments have proved more willing to change labour codes, which they see as instruments of economic policy, than family codes, which touch questions of identity and legitimacy. The result is a characteristic pattern: an economy may score well on work and pay while scoring poorly on marriage, mobility and assets, and the unweighted average conceals the fact that the remaining restrictions concentrate in the private sphere that governs a woman's ability to act independently in the first place.

The period after 2015 added two forces to this long trend. The Goals themselves gave governments a reference point and a reporting obligation; target 5.1 and its indicator placed legal frameworks on the agenda of every voluntary national review. And the evidence base widened. As economists documented the cost of women's exclusion from paid work to national income, finance ministries and development banks began to treat discriminatory law as a constraint on growth rather than a purely social question, and reform of the legal environment for women became a condition or an objective in a number of lending programmes. Reform waves in parts of the Middle East and North Africa and in sub-Saharan Africa during the late 2010s, including the removal of guardianship requirements for some legal acts and of bans on women's work in certain sectors, were among the most visible results.

### After 2020 the agenda broadened, and implementation became the binding constraint

The pandemic that began in 2020 tested the legal frameworks that had been built. It demonstrated that childcare is economic infrastructure: when schools and nurseries closed, the burden fell disproportionately on women, many of whom left paid work, and the absence of legal entitlements to care services or to flexible working arrangements was felt directly. It also coincided with a widely reported rise in domestic violence during lockdowns, which exposed the distance between laws that exist on paper and the shelters, hotlines, protection orders and police training that make them usable. The decision of the World Bank to add safety and childcare to the legal measure, and to pair it with indices of supportive frameworks and enforcement, can be read as a response to precisely these lessons.

The broad conclusion of the project's recent publications is that legislative reform did continue after 2020, though at a pace that varied sharply across regions and that has been insufficient to close the gap within the Goals' timetable. The more striking finding, and the one that the paired indices were built to reveal, is that the shortfall in implementation exceeds the shortfall in law. Many countries have passed statutes for which no regulations were issued, no budget allocated and no agency charged with enforcement. Equal pay laws without pay-transparency requirements or a labour inspectorate able to investigate complaints change little. Parental leave paid by employers rather than through social insurance gives employers a reason to avoid hiring women. Harassment laws without accessible complaint procedures or protection against retaliation are rarely invoked. The legal framework index is therefore an upper bound on the protection women actually enjoy, and progress measured by it alone will overstate progress towards target 5.1.

There has also been reversal. In a small number of countries, political change since 2020 has removed rights that had been granted, restricting women's movement, education and employment by decree. The coverage of the index includes such cases, and its census character is valuable here: an economy cannot leave the measure by ceasing to report, because the measure is constructed from its laws rather than from its statistics. The fact that 189 economies are scored in 2025, the same number as in any year, means that backsliding is recorded rather than lost.

### How regions and income groups differ, and what the distribution implies for 2030

The coverage tool identifies the aggregates for which the shelf can report the index: the world, the World Bank's high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups, and South Asia. Values for these aggregates have not yet been computed for this section, so their ordering cannot be stated with the book's numbers. The structure of the differences is nevertheless well established in the literature of the project and is worth setting out so that the reader knows what the computation should test.

High-income economies, above all those of the OECD, generally have the most complete legal frameworks, but none has reached full equality under the revised measure, largely because of gaps in childcare provision, in pension treatment of career breaks, and in the comprehensiveness of laws on violence. Upper-middle-income economies are heterogeneous: Latin America and the Caribbean and parts of Europe and Central Asia have undertaken extensive reform, while some resource-rich economies retain restrictive family law. The lowest scores are concentrated in the Middle East and North Africa and in South Asia, where personal-status codes still restrict mobility, marriage and inheritance, and in parts of sub-Saharan Africa where statutory and customary law coexist and the latter governs land and inheritance for much of the rural population. Sub-Saharan Africa has nevertheless been among the most active reforming regions, which is a reminder that the level of a score and its rate of change tell different stories.

The relation between income and law is real but loose. Low-income status does not prevent comprehensive legal reform, and several low-income and lower-middle-income economies have legal frameworks more equal than those of richer neighbours. Where income matters most is in the supportive and enforcement dimensions: courts, inspectorates, social-insurance systems that pay maternity and paternity benefits, and publicly funded childcare all cost money and administrative capacity. A plausible expectation, to be tested when the three indices are compared, is that the gap between law and its implementation is widest in low-income economies, so that the legal index flatters them more than it flatters richer countries.

For 2030 the implications are sober. Target 5.1 says all forms of discrimination, everywhere. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale, which under the revised measure no economy has done, and which at the historical pace of reform would take far longer than the years remaining. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform, which the record does show. The target can thus be read in more than one way, and the book's verdict depends on the reading: on the strict reading the target will be missed by a wide margin; on the directional reading it is being pursued, unevenly. What the distribution implies is that the remaining work is concentrated in particular domains rather than spread evenly. The labour-market provisions that were easiest to reform have largely been reformed in many places; what remains is family law, property and inheritance, comprehensive protection from violence, and the institutions of care. These are harder politically and costlier fiscally, and the pace of the past decade is unlikely to be sustained without deliberate effort. Because the indicators of violence, child marriage, decision-making and ownership treated in other sections of this chapter all depend in part on these remaining legal provisions, slow progress here will constrain progress there.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of this index. First, it scores the formal law of the largest business city in each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that apply to most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law governs marriage and land. Second, a perfect legal score is a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but far from a sufficient one. Social norms, the distribution of unpaid care, discrimination by employers that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much women's work all lie beyond the reach of a statute. The index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them.

With those cautions, the legal framework index remains the most complete instrument available for target 5.1, and its near-universal coverage of 189 economies makes it unusually suitable for a global account. The task for the remaining years is to convert that coverage into a measured record of change, by domain and by region, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every country.

claims.fact: c06-1.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Legislatures in economies that retain husband-headship, obedience, guardianship or unequal inheritance provisions in family and personal-status codes should repeal them before 2030, since these domains now hold most of the remaining legal discrimination.

Finance and labour ministries should attach regulations, budgets and an enforcing agency to every equality statute at the moment of its passage, including pay-transparency duties and an inspectorate empowered to act on equal-pay complaints.

Governments should finance maternity and paternity benefits through social insurance or general revenue rather than employer liability, and legislate for publicly supported childcare with quality standards, so that leave and care rights do not penalise the hiring of women.

The World Bank's Women, Business and the Law team should publish a back-cast of the revised legal framework index to 2015 and the subnational coverage of plural legal systems, so that change since the Goals' adoption can be measured on one consistent scale.

National statistical offices and voluntary national reviews should report the legal, supportive-framework and enforcement scores side by side, treating the gap between them as the headline measure of progress on target 5.1.
w-c06-1-1.gaps: The bench has computed only coverage for the Legal Framework Index (189 economies in 2025 and in any year); no levels, regional or income-group averages, or changes since 2015 or 2020 were drawn, so the section states no scores. It is unverified whether the revised-methodology series on the shelf extends back to 2015; if not, change since the Goals' adoption cannot be measured with it, and the earlier index is not comparable. The companion Supportive Framework and Enforcement Perceptions indices were not analysed. The index scores formal law in the main business city and does not capture customary or religious law in rural areas, subnational variation in federal states, or women's actual use of legal rights; no series on the shelf measures court use, complaints filed or enforcement outcomes.

w-c03-4-2.text:
### What the target asks and what the bench can measure

Target 2.3 asks for a doubling, by 2030, of the agricultural productivity and incomes of small-scale food producers, in particular women, indigenous peoples, family farmers, pastoralists and fishers. The wording carries two difficulties. First, the target is defined for a specific population, the small-scale producer, while the World Bank series available to this chapter describe whole economies. Value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing, in constant 2015 US dollars, averages over a large commercial estate and a household plot alike. Second, the target sets no baseline year and does not say whether doubling is to be measured from 2015, from the adoption of the goals, or from some earlier date. This section reads the target from 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and treats a doubling as a rise to twice the 2015 level by 2030.

Two indicators are used. Value added per agricultural worker is the closest available proxy for the official indicator on the volume of production per labour unit. Cereal yield, in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, measures output per unit of land and covers wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains. Cereal production and the land under cereals are the two components of yield. Neither series speaks to incomes, to sex, or to farm size, and neither separates the small-scale producer from the large. They show whether the conditions for a doubling exist; they cannot show that the doubling has happened for the people the target names.

### Value added per worker: a rising world average that conceals a stalled bottom

Global value added per agricultural worker stood at 3,491 US dollars in 2015 and reached 4,264 dollars in 2025, in constant 2015 prices. The annual rate implied by the trend tool is 2.0 per cent. This is an increase, and the trend tool classes the world as on track, but the classification is generous. It compares the rate with a path that the tool sets itself, since the target carries no numerical value in the bench. A doubling over fifteen years requires a compound rate of a little under five per cent a year, and a rate of 2.0 per cent is well below it. By 2025, ten of the fifteen years had elapsed, and the world average had not come near twice its 2015 level. For the world as a whole, a doubling by 2030 would need a much faster rate in the remaining five years than the one recorded so far.

The world figure is itself a weighted summary of very unequal parts. It is pulled upward by East Asia and Pacific, where value added per worker rose from 4,087 dollars in 2015 to 6,991 dollars in 2025, a rate of 5.5 per cent a year. That is the only regional rate that approaches the pace a doubling demands: sustained over fifteen years it would roughly double the starting level, and the rise over the first ten years was already about seventy per cent. The upper-middle-income group, which includes China and several large producers in Latin America and eastern Europe, rose from 4,378 dollars to 7,474 dollars at 5.5 per cent a year. The similarity of the two rates is not an accident: the economies that carry most weight in each group overlap, and the gain in both reflects the movement of labour out of farming as much as the growth of output. When many workers leave the land and output holds or rises, value added per remaining worker rises mechanically. A gain of this kind raises the average without any improvement in the position of the household that stays on a small plot.

The other regions improved at a slower pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 12,217 dollars to 17,325 dollars, at 3.6 per cent a year. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 6,294 dollars to 8,031 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. The group of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4,805 dollars to 6,181 dollars, at 2.6 per cent a year, and South Asia from 1,631 dollars to 2,082 dollars, at 2.5 per cent a year. All of these are reported as on track by the tool, and none is on a path to doubling by 2030. The finding is therefore that productivity per worker has risen in most regions since 2015, that the rise is real, and that outside East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group it is too slow for the target as written.

### Where productivity per worker is lowest, it has barely moved

The regions with the lowest starting points show the least progress. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 1,339 dollars per worker in 2015 and 1,496 dollars in 2025, a rate of 1.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries fell from 875 dollars in 2015 to 778 dollars in 2025, a rate of -1.2 per cent a year, which the tool classes as regression. In the lowest-income economies, then, value added per agricultural worker is lower in 2025 than it was when the goals were adopted. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 1,915 dollars to 2,336 dollars, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year.

The gap between the top and the bottom is wide. North America is shown in the data only at its 2015 value of 67,701 dollars, since the series has no later observation for the region in the extract used here, and the comparison across the decade cannot be made. High-income countries as a group rose from 28,219 dollars to 30,775 dollars, at 0.9 per cent a year, which the tool classes as marginal progress. A group already at a high level may not need to double, and the target was written with developing countries in mind. The ratio of the high-income group to the low-income group, computed from the figures above, was about 32 times in 2015 and about 40 times in 2025. The gap has widened over the decade, and a farm worker in a low-income country produces, in value terms, a small fraction of what a worker in a high-income country produces, a fraction that has shrunk.

The following is background, not a finding of the series. Low-income agriculture is dominated by rain-fed smallholdings with little mechanisation, limited access to improved seed, fertiliser and credit, poor roads to markets, insecure tenure, and exposure to drought, flood and pests. Population growth in these economies has kept the farm labour force growing, so that each worker has less land and capital to work with. The years since 2015 also included conflict in several low-income countries, droughts in parts of Africa, the disruption of the pandemic after 2020, and the price shocks that followed the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. These are offered as context that may help explain the low-income series; the data do not allow the effect of each to be separated.

### Cereal yield: a modest rise and a persistent gap

Cereal yield tells a similar story at a smaller scale. The world yield was 3,932 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 4,229 kilograms per hectare in 2023, the latest year for which a world figure is reported. That is a gain well short of a doubling, and far short of the gain in value added per worker. Yield is a slower-moving quantity than value added per worker, because it depends on biology, on the share of land that is irrigated, and on the technology of seed and fertiliser, none of which changes quickly. A doubling of average world cereal yield in fifteen years has no precedent in the record of any large region, and the target should not be read as requiring it of yields. The relevant question is whether yields are rising in the places where they are low.

They are not. Sub-Saharan Africa had a cereal yield of 1,443 kilograms per hectare in 2015 and 1,453 kilograms per hectare in 2024, a change so small that it amounts to stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 1,345 kilograms per hectare in 2024. In 2024 the Sub-Saharan African yield was under a fifth of the North American yield, which rose from 6,677 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 8,414 kilograms per hectare in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, already at 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015, reached 5,430 kilograms per hectare in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 3,803 to 4,045 kilograms per hectare by 2023, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 2,732 to 3,027 kilograms per hectare by 2023.

South Asia and Latin America made the larger gains among developing regions. South Asia rose from 3,041 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 3,814 kilograms per hectare in 2024; the spread of irrigation, improved varieties and fertiliser use is the usual explanation, though the series does not test it. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 to 4,828 kilograms per hectare by 2024. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 2,766 to 3,366 kilograms per hectare by 2024. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 4,648 to 4,942 kilograms per hectare, and high-income countries from 4,976 to 5,394 kilograms per hectare, both by 2023. The pattern is that yields have risen where they were already moderate and have stood still where they were lowest.

### Convergence: the poorest are not catching up

A doubling target is in part a target about catching up, and the convergence tool tests directly whether countries that began with low values rose faster than those that began with high values. For cereal yield across 176 countries between 2015 and 2024, the estimated coefficient is -0.0016, with a p-value of 0.79 and an R-squared of 0.0013. The coefficient is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from it, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in subsequent change. There is no evidence of convergence in the strict sense: low-yield countries did not grow faster than high-yield countries. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.00 in 2015 to 0.91 in 2024, which indicates that dispersion narrowed slightly. The two results are compatible: a narrowing of dispersion without a negative coefficient suggests that movements were driven by individual cases and not by the poorest as a group moving up.

The result for value added per worker is similar. Across 168 countries between 2015 and 2024, the coefficient is 0.0012, with a p-value of 0.49 and an R-squared of 0.0024. The sign is positive, so that the point estimate points to a slight tendency for countries with higher starting values to grow faster, although the estimate is not distinguishable from zero. The coefficient of variation moved from 1.51 to 1.43, a small fall. The reading is that there is no evidence of a systematic closing of the gap, and the distribution of agricultural labour productivity remains very wide. The implication for 2030 is that a doubling for the lowest-productivity countries cannot be expected from the forces already at work over this period. If catching up were occurring by itself, the low-income group would show it; it shows the reverse.

### What changed after 2015 and after 2020

The series offered by the bench give end points more than yearly paths, and the findings above compare 2015 with the latest year. The conclusions about the pandemic years therefore rest on general knowledge more than on the displayed results. The shock of 2020 disrupted labour movement, input supply and transport, and agricultural output in most countries proved more resilient than other sectors, because food production continued as an essential activity. This may help explain why value added per worker in most regions did not fall. The more lasting effect on the poorest may have come through prices and incomes: higher fertiliser and fuel costs after 2021 may have reduced the use of purchased inputs among smallholders, which could account for part of the stagnation of yields in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries. A reader should treat this explanation as plausible and not as shown by the series.

A second caution concerns measurement. Value added per worker is the ratio of an output measure to a labour measure, and the labour measure for agriculture depends on household surveys that count part-time, seasonal and unpaid family work unevenly. Women, who make up a large share of the agricultural labour force in many low-income countries and who are named in the target, are often under-counted or recorded as outside the labour force. The series cannot show whether their productivity has changed. Cereal yield, moreover, applies to cereals only. It leaves out roots, tubers, pulses, vegetables, fruit, livestock and fish, which matter for the incomes of many small-scale producers, and in fishing communities it measures nothing at all. Reporting also varies: in some countries the harvested area is reported only as sown or cultivated area, as the series note states.

### Implications for 2030

The evidence supports four conclusions. First, only East Asia and Pacific and the upper-middle-income group, at 5.5 per cent a year, advanced at a pace near that which a doubling from 2015 requires; no other region or income group is shown to be on course. Because these two groups gained in part from labour leaving farming, their pace is hard to repeat where the farm labour force is still growing. Second, the world average disguises a split: the economies with the highest productivity gained, the middle gained moderately, and the lowest-income economies lost ground. Third, cereal yields rose modestly, and barely at all in Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group. Fourth, the absence of convergence in either indicator over 2015 to 2024 shows that the gaps were not closing by themselves in that period.

The reading of the target matters for the verdict. If doubling is read as applying to the world average, the answer is that it will not be met. If it is read as applying to each country, a larger number of countries will fail, and the low-income group has moved backwards. If it is read as applying to small-scale producers specifically, the bench cannot say, because the series do not distinguish them. On the first two readings the conclusion that the target will be missed is secure for the regions where the data exist, and the main uncertainty is about the size of the miss for the people the target names.

What would raise productivity where it is lowest is well understood, though not tested here: secure land rights, particularly for women; extension services and farmer organisations; improved and drought-tolerant seed; affordable fertiliser; small-scale irrigation; rural roads, storage and market access; and rural finance and insurance. The accounts of land, fertiliser, water and investment appear in other sections of this chapter and are not repeated here.

proposals: National agriculture ministries and development partners in low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa should direct productivity programmes to the places where value added per worker fell between 2015 and 2025 and cereal yield stood still, instead of relying on the world average, which masks them.

Statistical offices, the International Labour Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization should report agricultural labour productivity and yield by sex and farm size, so that progress on target 2.3 can be measured for small-scale producers.
The United Nations bodies that maintain the goal framework should fix a baseline year and a numerical reading of the doubling in target 2.3, so that trend classifications rest on a stated path.

Governments and research funders should treat the absence of convergence in yield and value added per worker as a reason to finance crop research and extension suited to low-yield regions, and should review the effect after the next full data year.
w-c03-4-2.gaps: The series describe whole economies and do not separate small-scale producers, women, indigenous peoples, pastoralists or fishers, and none measures incomes. Cereal yield omits other crops, livestock and fish. North America has no observation after 2015 for value added per worker in the extract. Latest years differ by series and region, and the results give end points, not yearly paths, so the effect of the pandemic and of price shocks cannot be isolated. The causes mentioned are background knowledge and not results.

w-c06-6-1.text:
### What the indicators measure

The commitment in target 5.a is wide: equal rights to economic resources, ownership and control of land and other property, financial services, inheritance and natural resources, in accordance with national laws. The World Bank's catalogue measures only part of it. The best-covered strand is financial services, through the Global Findex survey, which asks adults whether they hold an account at a financial institution or have personally used a mobile-money service in the past year. Findex reports the answer separately for women and men, so the gap between the two series is a direct measure of unequal access. No equivalent series on women's ownership of land or housing sits on the shelf, and that absence shapes this section: the account gap can be measured with some precision, while the property gap can only be discussed through proxies and through what is missing.

An account is an entry point, not a measure of economic control. A woman may hold an account that her husband operates, or may have received a mobile-money wallet only to collect a government transfer. The survey definition counts accounts held alone or together with someone else. The indicator therefore shows access to the formal and semi-formal payment system, not who decides how money is used. It is nonetheless one of the few gender-disaggregated economic indicators with near-global coverage, and for that reason it carries much of the evidential weight for the target.

The survey is also periodic rather than annual. Findex rounds have appeared at intervals of roughly three years, and the most recent round reached 139 countries in 2024. Some regional aggregates in the results below end in 2021 rather than 2024, which reflects the vintage of the regional series on the shelf. Comparisons across regions must therefore be made with that difference in end year in mind, and the section states the end year of every figure it quotes.

### The world gap

Globally, the share of women holding an account rose from 65.9% in 2017 to 76.6% in 2024. Over the same period the share of men rose from 72.8% to 80.9%. Both groups gained, and women gained more in percentage points, so the gap narrowed. It has not closed. At the 2024 levels a gap of several points remains at world level, and it is concentrated in a limited set of regions and income groups rather than spread evenly.

The world average conceals the shape of the problem. Where almost everyone holds an account, as in high-income economies, a gender gap cannot be large because there is no room for it. Where account ownership is still being built, as in low-income economies, the gap is determined by who is reached first. The evidence below shows that men are generally reached first, and that the gap is widest in settings where overall ownership is lowest or where social norms restrict women's mobility, employment and independent control of money.

The period 2017 to 2024 straddles two events that bear on this. The first is the global expansion of digital payments, which lowered the cost of opening an account and removed the need to visit a branch. The second is the pandemic after 2020, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers electronically and, in doing so, brought new account holders into the system. Whether these developments favoured women is the question the regional and income data allow the book to answer in part, though the survey cannot separate the effect of each cause.

### Regional differences

In East Asia and the Pacific, women's account ownership rose from 71.2% in 2017 to 81.4% in 2021, against 75.7% and 84.2% for men. In Europe and Central Asia the female share rose from 79.4% to 88.0% while the male share rose from 83.8% to 91.2%. In both regions the gap persisted but was modest, and both sexes gained at a similar pace. These are middle- and upper-middle-income regions where the remaining gap reflects pockets of exclusion, for instance among rural, older and less-educated women, rather than a general barrier.

Latin America and the Caribbean shows the largest absolute gain in the regional table. Women's ownership rose from 52.1% in 2017 to 70.1% in 2021, and men's from 58.7% to 77.0%. Both sexes gained by a very large amount in four years, and the gap stayed visible. The region's expansion owes much to the spread of conditional cash-transfer schemes paid into accounts, which are typically addressed to women as household recipients, together with the growth of digital wallets and low-cost accounts promoted by public banks and financial regulators. A cash-transfer route to an account is real inclusion in the sense of access, but it may be a narrower form of inclusion than an account opened for savings or credit.

South Asia reports through 2024. Women's ownership there rose from 64.0% in 2017 to 75.1% in 2024, while men's rose from 74.7% to 80.1%. The female gain was the larger, and the gap narrowed markedly. This is consistent with national drives to open basic accounts at scale, among them campaigns to give every household a bank account and to route subsidies directly into accounts. Such drives raise ownership quickly, but surveys in several countries have shown that accounts opened in a campaign are often dormant, so ownership may overstate active use. The indicator as defined here counts ownership, not activity.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the region where the gender gap is largest on the shelf. Women's ownership rose from 38.0% in 2017 to 45.6% in 2021, while men's rose from 56.8% to 59.6%. Women gained several points, yet fewer than half of women in the region held an account in 2021, and the male share was far higher. The region combines legal and social restrictions on women's mobility, employment and independent financial decisions with low female labour-force participation, which removes a main reason for an account, namely a wage. The inclusion of Afghanistan in the aggregate matters: since 2021 the restrictions imposed on women there make the regional picture after that year uncertain, and the 2021 end point predates much of that change.

Sub-Saharan Africa has a lower overall level but a gender gap smaller than that of the Middle East and North Africa group. Women's ownership rose from 36.9% in 2017 to 49.0% in 2021, and men's from 48.5% to 61.4%. The region is the global centre of mobile money, and the growth of agent networks allowed millions of people, women among them, to hold a wallet without ever entering a bank branch. Even so, the male share stayed above the female share at both dates, and the gap did not narrow on these figures. Mobile-money inclusion appears to have lifted both sexes in parallel rather than to have closed the difference between them. Women's lower rates of phone ownership, lower literacy and less independent income are the usual explanations, and the chapter's section on mobile technology treats the phone question directly.

North America is the single case in which the pattern reverses. Women's ownership rose from 93.4% in 2017 to 97.1% in 2021, while men's moved from 94.2% to 93.8%. By the later date, women's ownership exceeded men's. The movement is small and the sample for a region with few reporting countries is narrow, so it should not be over-read; still, it illustrates that a gender gap in account ownership is not inevitable once ownership is near universal.

### Income groups and the shape of the gap

The grouping by income level is more revealing than the regional one, because the gap is closely linked to the level of ownership. In low-income countries, women's ownership rose from 26.8% in 2017 to 40.6% in 2024. Men's rose from 37.3% to 52.5%. Even after the rise, well under half of women in these countries held an account in 2024, and the male share was above half. In absolute terms the gap in this group is as wide as in any other group on the shelf, and it did not shrink between the two years.

In lower-middle-income countries, women's ownership rose from 55.6% to 67.6% and men's from 64.4% to 73.2%. The gap here is smaller than among low-income countries and appears to have narrowed slightly. Upper-middle-income countries show a rise from 68.9% to 82.5% for women and from 76.3% to 85.6% for men. The gap narrowed more clearly, because women's gains were larger than men's. High-income countries sit close to the ceiling: women's ownership moved from 92.1% to 94.5%, men's from 93.9% to 95.3%, and the difference is small.

The pattern across the four groups is a familiar one in the diffusion of any financial service. Men adopt first, women follow, and the gap opens in the early and middle stages and narrows when the service approaches universality. The practical implication is that the gender gap in the poorest countries will not close by itself as the average rises; it closes only when the service has largely saturated the male population, and that is far away. For countries in the low-income group, the pace of progress matters more than the world average suggests, because these are also the countries where women have the fewest alternatives to cash.

The result also shows that the world-level improvement is driven in large part by the middle-income groups, where the population is large. This weighting effect should be kept in mind when reading the world figure: the rise from 65.9% to 76.6% reflects mostly the middle-income economies catching up, and it says less about the poorest women, whose ownership remains well below the world level.

### Position against the 2030 target

The trend classification applies a simple benchmark: full account ownership among women, 100%, by 2030. This is an interpretation, since target 5.a itself sets no numerical level, and the reading of the target as universal access to financial services is a choice made by the bench. A different reading, in which the target is met when the gap between women and men closes, would produce a different classification. The reader should treat the benchmark as demanding and as one of several defensible readings.

On that benchmark, of 139 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target. These countries hold 49.9% of the assessed population, a large share because the group includes some very populous economies and many high-income countries already near the ceiling. A further 41 countries, with 18.7% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 29 countries, with 17.8% of the population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries, with 3.2% of the population, show stagnation. Finally, 33 countries, with 10.4% of the population, show regression, meaning that women's ownership fell over the period assessed.

The number of regressing countries deserves attention. That 33 of 139 countries recorded a decline is not a statistical artefact to be dismissed. Declines may reflect survey differences, the closure of dormant accounts opened during campaigns or pandemic payments, a reduction in mobile-money use after a fall in transfers, political upheaval or sanctions, or genuine loss of access. The data cannot distinguish among these. What they do show is that the global rise is not universal; for roughly a quarter of the countries assessed, the direction was the wrong one, though these countries hold a smaller share of the population than those on track.

The weighting also shows the divide between countries and people. Half of the assessed population lives in countries classed as on track, but fewer than half of the countries are in that class on a count of nations. The countries that are not on track are numerous, smaller in population and concentrated in the lower-income groups, which are the ones with the largest gaps. A global target met by population weight can therefore coexist with a majority of countries failing it, and the section's reading is that the aggregate masks the countries where policy attention is most needed.

What changed after 2015 and after 2020 can be stated only in outline. The first Findex round on the shelf for these results is 2017, so the baseline year of the goals is not itself observed here, and the period from 2015 to 2017 is outside the comparison. Between 2017 and 2021 the regional data show large gains in nearly every region, consistent with the effect of digital payments and emergency transfers around 2020. From 2021 to 2024 only the global, income-group and South Asian series are available on the shelf, and they show continued gains for both sexes. The material does not allow the claim that the pandemic itself changed the gender gap, only that ownership rose through it.

### Property, enterprise and the missing evidence

The remaining parts of target 5.a, land, property and inheritance, cannot be measured with the account series. The shelf holds three other series that touch on the target without measuring it. The Women, Business and the Law legal framework index, reported for 189 countries in 2025, scores how laws shape women's economic opportunities, with a topic on assets within it; the chapter's section on legal frameworks treats the index, and here it matters only as context. A legal right to own or inherit property is a precondition, not an outcome. Where statute and custom diverge, as in many systems of customary land tenure, women may hold the right in law and be denied it in practice, and no legal index can show this.

The enterprise survey series on firms with female participation in ownership is the nearest measure of women's ownership of productive assets. It counts firms with at least one female owner, which says nothing about the size of the stake or about control, and it covers formal firms only. It therefore omits the informal farms, household enterprises and market trades in which most women in low-income countries work. The series on women's participation in household decisions, available for 70 countries, measures a different thing again, namely the share of married women with a say in health care, large purchases and family visits. Taken together, the series give pieces of an answer, but none gives the share of women who own land or a dwelling in their own name.

This gap in evidence matters for policy. Land is the main asset of rural households in much of the world, and secure title is associated with greater bargaining power, willingness to invest and access to credit as collateral. Reform of inheritance law, joint titling of land and registration drives are the main policy instruments, and without a global series their effect cannot be tracked against the target. The account data show that women's access to the payment system is improving and that the gap is largest where ownership is lowest; they do not show whether that improvement extends to the assets on which women's economic independence ultimately rests.

On the evidence available, the picture for 2030 is mixed. Account ownership is rising for both sexes and the gap is narrowing in several regions, yet the gap is widest in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan and in low-income countries, which are the places where women have the least access to formal economic life. A target of universal ownership by 2030 will not be met worldwide, given that the world figure stood at 76.6% in 2024 and that so many countries show slow progress or decline. A target of equal ownership is a more realistic aim in middle-income and high-income economies, and a distant one elsewhere.
