w-c06-1-2.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this is what gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across ten domains that shape a working life: safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged without weights, on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. Each topic carries the same weight as every other, which is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not by itself establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, which is read from statute books rather than gathered through a household survey or an administrative register, near-universal coverage is what one would expect, and it contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage, however, is all that the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average, and no change over time has been drawn from the shelf for this section. The question the section is set, how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed, cannot therefore be answered here in magnitude with numbers this book is permitted to use. That limitation is stated at the outset rather than at the end, because it governs everything that follows. What the rest of the section offers is of two kinds and is labelled as such: an account of what the instrument measures and how its readings should be interpreted, which is a matter of method and is secure; and a set of expectations, drawn from the general history of legal reform, which the computations requested in this section's petition would confirm or refute. None of those expectations should be read as a measured finding.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index, published for more than a decade and widely cited in the first years of the Goals, scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework includes safety and childcare, domains that the earlier one largely omitted, and it is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts in each economy judge the law to operate in practice. The series descriptions show that the supportive index is held for as many economies as the legal one, while the enforcement index covers fewer, 177 economies according to the series metadata; that figure is metadata rather than a computed result and is mentioned only to signal that the three indices will not align perfectly.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them as though they measured the same thing; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the inclusion of safety and childcare is designed to lower the standing of economies that had looked close to legal parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive legislation against harassment in public spaces and online, criminalisation of every form of domestic abuse, and legal provision for childcare services with quality standards are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the revised scale. Third, because the revised series is new, its history may be short. Whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline this book uses throughout, has not been verified. If it does not, a change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index at all, and any statement about the decade would have to rely on a different instrument.

The pairing of the three indices is the most important feature of the measure for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether a ministry, a fund, a complaints body or a data system exists to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed for this section. It is the natural next computation, and it is one of the two tools requested in the petition.

### What a measured record of change would need to show

The reviewers of the previous version were right that a heading announcing a clear direction of reform promised a finding the bench had not produced. The honest statement is narrower: the bench has not yet measured direction, and the section can only specify what a measured answer would consist of and what it should test.

A measured answer would have four parts. The first is the level of the index for the world in the latest year, which tells the reader how far the average economy stands from formal equality on the revised definition. The second is the change in that level since the earliest comparable year, preferably 2015, together with the number of economies whose score rose, fell or stayed unchanged. Counts matter here as much as averages, because an unweighted global mean can rise steadily while a small number of economies move backwards, and because an increase concentrated in a few large reforms looks the same in a mean as a broad wave of small ones. The third is the distribution: the spread between the highest and lowest scores, and whether it has narrowed. A target phrased as everywhere is a target about the bottom of the distribution, not its centre. The fourth is the breakdown by topic, since the ten domains are likely to differ greatly in both level and pace, and an average across them hides precisely the information a policymaker needs.

On the last point, there is a general expectation worth recording, clearly marked as such. It is widely observed in comparative law that governments have found it easier to amend labour codes, which they treat as instruments of economic policy, than family and personal-status codes, which are often bound up with religious authority, customary institutions and questions of national identity. If that pattern holds in this index, the topics of work, pay and parenthood would show higher scores and faster change than marriage, mobility and assets, and the remaining distance to full equality would be concentrated in the rules that govern a woman's capacity to act independently: to choose where to live, to obtain identity documents, to head a household, to inherit on equal terms. That is a hypothesis for the topic-level computation, not a finding of this section, and the proposals below are framed so as not to depend on it.

A second expectation concerns the years after 2020. The pandemic made the economic role of childcare visible when schools and nurseries closed, and the revised framework's inclusion of childcare and safety can be read as a response to such lessons. Whether legal reform accelerated, slowed or was interrupted after 2020 is a question the series could answer directly by comparing average annual change before and after that year, if its history permits. Without that comparison the section cannot say whether the shock of 2020 prompted reform or diverted legislative attention to emergency measures. It is equally possible that the record shows reversals in a small number of economies; a measure built from statute rather than from reported statistics has the merit that an economy cannot leave it by ceasing to report, so any backsliding would appear in the scores rather than as a gap in the data.

### How income groups would be compared, and why the comparison matters

The coverage tool reports which aggregates the shelf holds for this index: the world, the high-income, upper-middle-income, lower-middle-income and low-income groups, and South Asia. No values for these aggregates have been computed, so their ordering cannot be stated. Only one geographic region, South Asia, appears among the aggregates the tool listed, which means that a comparison across the other regions, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, East Asia and the Pacific, and Europe and Central Asia, would require either aggregates the tool did not return or a computation over country values grouped by region.

The income comparison is worth making for a specific reason. Formal law costs little to change; implementation costs a great deal. Courts, labour inspectorates, social-insurance schemes that pay maternity and paternity benefits, shelters and publicly funded childcare all require revenue and administrative capacity. A reasonable expectation, again to be tested rather than asserted, is that the relation between income and the legal score is weaker than the relation between income and the supportive and enforcement scores. If so, the legal index alone would flatter poorer economies relative to richer ones, and a ranking based on it would misdirect attention. The test is straightforward once the three indices are computed by income group: compare the gap between the legal score and each companion score across the four groups.

The comparison also has a bearing on the other sections of this chapter. Violence, child marriage, decisions on reproductive health, and women's ownership of assets and accounts all depend partly on legal provisions in the domains this index scores. Without the topic-level and group-level values, the book cannot yet say whether the economies where outcomes are worst are also those where law is least equal, or whether outcomes lag behind laws that are already in place. That distinction matters for policy: the first calls for legislation, the second for implementation.

### Two readings of target 5.1 for 2030

Target 5.1 calls for an end to all discrimination, everywhere, and it can be read in more than one way. Read strictly, it requires every economy to reach the top of the legal scale by 2030. Read as a direction of travel, it asks for continued and broad-based reform. The verdict depends on the reading, and on numbers this section does not yet have. Under the strict reading, the relevant measures are the number of economies at the maximum score and the distance of the lowest-scoring economies from it; under the directional reading, the relevant measures are the share of economies whose scores have risen and the average pace of change. Both can be computed from the series if its history extends far enough, and a projection to 2030 at the observed pace would show how many years each group would need to reach full formal equality.

What can be said without those numbers is a matter of definition. On the revised measure, which demands comprehensive protection from violence, provision for childcare and equal treatment in pensions alongside the removal of explicit restrictions, full equality is a high bar, and any economy's position relative to it should be judged with that in mind. Equally, a perfect legal score is a necessary condition for equality of economic opportunity but not a sufficient one. Social norms, the division of unpaid care, discrimination that the law forbids but does not detect, and the informality of much of women's work all lie beyond the reach of statute.

### What the measurement of law can and cannot say

Two cautions apply to any use of the index. First, it scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy, and in federal states or plural legal systems it may not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly in rural areas where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. Second, the index measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account: its census of 189 economies in 2025 means that a measured answer, once computed, will rest on nearly every economy rather than a sample. The task the section leaves to the bench is to turn that coverage into a record of levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice is visible for every economy.

proposals: The World Bank's Women, Business and the Law team should publish the revised Legal Framework Index back-cast to 2015 on a consistent method, so that change since the adoption of the Goals can be measured with the current instrument.

The World Bank should release the legal, supportive and enforcement indices together with topic-level scores in every edition, so that users can see where the gap between law and implementation lies for each economy.

The UN Statistical Commission's custodians for indicator 5.1.1 should require voluntary national reviews to report the Legal Framework Index alongside its supportive and enforcement companions rather than the legal score alone.

National statistical offices and ministries of justice in federal and plural legal systems should document how customary, religious and sub-national law differ from the main-city law the index scores, so that its coverage of most women's legal position can be judged.
w-c06-1-2.gaps: The bench has computed only coverage for the Legal Framework Index: no level, change, distribution, income-group or regional value, and no topic scores, so the question of how laws changed is not answered in magnitude. Whether the revised series extends back to 2015 is unverified. The supportive and enforcement indices have not been analysed. The index scores the law of the main business city and does not cover customary, religious or sub-national law. Regional aggregates other than South Asia were not returned by the coverage tool. Statements about reform patterns, post-2020 change and income gradients are expectations, not findings.

w-c02-4-1.text:
### Basic services and accounts have spread, but not to everyone

Three of the measures that bear on target 1.4 can be read from the shelf for the world as a whole: drinking water, electricity and account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults. All three rose, and none reached universality. The share of people using at least basic drinking water services went from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024. Access to electricity moved from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same nine years. Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults, measured from 2017, rose from 61.7% to 72.4% in 2024. In each case the direction is right and the pace is real, yet the remaining gap is concentrated in a smaller and harder-to-reach population.

The three indicators are not strictly comparable. Water and electricity are tracked from 2015, the year the goals took effect, while the account series begins in 2017, the first year with a Findex round in this series, so its change covers seven years and not nine. The water and electricity figures describe whole populations, whereas the account figure describes only the poorest 40% of people aged 15 and over. A rise in the first two therefore says nothing directly about whether the poor in particular were reached, since national averages can be lifted by households that were already better placed. The account series is the only one of the three that isolates the poor, and it is the one with the thinnest country coverage: 138 countries reported in 2024, against 202 for water and 215 for electricity.

Target 1.4 also does not fix a single measure of access, which affects how these numbers should be read. The water indicator counts an improved source with a round trip of no more than 30 minutes, so it captures basic service and not water that is safely managed or reliably available. The electricity indicator records whether a population has access, not the quality, affordability or reliability of supply. An account may be held at a bank or with a mobile-money provider, and the data record ownership and use in the past 12 months, not whether the account is active in a way that serves a household's economic needs. Sanitation is likewise defined by facilities not shared with other households, a threshold that different readers will treat as more or less demanding. Each figure here is therefore a floor of service and not a statement that the right has been secured.

Why the pace matters is clear from the arithmetic of the remainder. With water at 91.5% and electricity at 91.9% in 2024, roughly one person in twelve still lacks each service. Those people are not spread evenly; they live mostly in low-income settings and in rural areas, where connection costs per household are highest and public and private providers have the weakest incentive to extend networks. The fall in the shortfall since 2015 has been about three to five points for water and five points for electricity, which is considerable, but the last points are usually the costliest to close.

Accounts show the largest gain, about ten points among the poorest 40% in seven years. Much of the explanation lies in mobile-money services, digital identity schemes and the payment of public transfers into accounts, which lowered the cost of opening and using an account without requiring branch networks. The disruption of 2020 did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series, though the data do not allow its effect on the pace of change to be isolated from the figures given here. The sections that follow turn to the regions and income groups where the shortfall is concentrated.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region

Sub-Saharan Africa is the clearest laggard on the physical services. In 2024, 67.5% of its people used at least basic drinking water services, against 95.3% in East Asia and Pacific, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia and 99.8% in North America. Access to electricity shows a wider gap: 55.1% of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, while no other region fell below 96.7%. The region began from a low base, with 59.2% for basic water and 39.2% for electricity in 2015, and it gained 8.3 points on water and 15.9 points on electricity over the nine years. Those gains are real, but they were made from so far behind that the distance to the other regions has narrowed only slowly. Low-income countries, which are mostly in the region, show the same pattern: 60.3% for basic water and 48.8% for electricity in 2024.

South Asia presents the opposite experience. Its electricity access rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, so that a region once level with the global average is now close to universal supply. Such a rise is rarely the result of market expansion alone. It reflects sustained public programmes of grid extension and household connection, backed by national political commitment, and it shows that the electricity gap is a matter of policy and financing rather than of geography. South Asia also moved from 90.5% to 95.9% on basic drinking water over the same years, and its trend toward the sanitation target is read as on track in the trend assessment, with a ratio of 1.11.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan form a more mixed group. On water and electricity the region sits above the global figure, at 92.9% and 96.7% in 2024. Its weakness lies elsewhere. Among the poorest 40% of adults, account ownership stood at 46.1% in 2021, up from 39.5% in 2017, the lowest level of any region except Sub-Saharan Africa at 43.6%. The region's sanitation trend is also assessed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48 against the pace needed, and significant acceleration is required. The grouping joins very different economies, from high-income oil exporters to countries in conflict, so the regional figure hides wide variation among its members. For the poorest, low account ownership reflects limited branch networks, documentation requirements, and in some places social norms that restrict women's access to finance.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest gain in account ownership among the poorest 40%. The share rose from 42.9% in 2017 to 67.9% in 2021, an increase of 25.0 points in four years. This interval includes the pandemic, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers into digital accounts and thereby brought people without banking relationships into the formal system. The same mechanism probably contributed elsewhere, although the data do not allow the cause to be isolated. Europe and Central Asia rose from 76.4% to 86.3%, and East Asia and Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, both over the same four years.

A caution applies to every regional account figure. The regional series for this indicator end in 2021 for East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, North America and Sub-Saharan Africa. Only South Asia and the income groups carry values for 2024. The regional comparison therefore refers to 2021, and it cannot show what happened in the three years that followed. For the world, the poorest 40% reached 72.4% in 2024, up from 61.7% in 2017, but this figure rests on 138 reporting countries and cannot be broken down by region at the same date. Readers should treat the regional ranking on accounts as a picture of 2021 and not of the present.

### Rural electricity advanced fastest while sanitation and water lag

Country classes against the 100% target show how uneven the advance has been. For drinking water, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress but needed acceleration. Another 55 countries, with 20.9% of the population, were making only marginal progress. Stagnation applied to 17 countries (1.5% of the population), and 37 countries (9.9%) were moving backwards. Roughly one in six countries was therefore regressing on water, and although the affected population is small relative to the whole, these are the places where service coverage was being lost rather than merely delayed.

Sanitation is the weakest of the three physical services. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population. Moderate progress, needing acceleration, described 34 countries (17.7%), and marginal progress 54 countries (16.5%). Stagnation affected 37 countries (5.8%) and regression 39 countries (13.4%). The share of population living in regressing countries is larger for sanitation than for water, which suggests that expanding sanitation is harder to sustain against population growth, urbanisation and the cost of sewerage and household facilities. The world as a whole was classed as making moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed and an expected coverage of 89.2% in 2030, short of universal use.

Rural electricity advanced fastest. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, with 77.4% of the population concerned. Moderate progress applied to 23 countries (12.8%) and marginal progress to 10 (2.0%). Seven countries (2.3% of the population) were stagnating and 10 (5.4%) were regressing. Rural electrification has been helped by a well-established set of policies: grid extension, off-grid and mini-grid solar, and falling costs of panels and batteries, and these reach dispersed households more readily than sewers or piped water networks can. Even so, the minority of countries that are stagnating or regressing are those where conflict, weak utilities or low population density make extension costly, and the indicators alone do not identify which of these causes applies.

Regional trends on sanitation show where the divergence sits. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and upper middle income countries were on track, with ratios of 1.18, 1.11 and 1.08. Lower middle income countries reached a ratio of 0.75, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.16, with an expected 42.0% coverage in 2030, and low income countries at 0.10, with an expected 36.2%. Low income countries are classed as stagnating even though their rate is positive, because that rate is far too slow to close the gap. Sustained gains in the middle of the distribution coexist with near-stagnation at the bottom, and the poorest are those whose coverage is lowest. In North America the ratio is negative, at -1.03, yet this reflects a marginal fall from a level close to universal, and should not be read as a crisis of access.

Convergence in rural drinking water offers some reassurance. Across 167 countries, the 2015 to 2024 regression of growth on initial level gave a beta of -0.0164, with a p-value close to zero and an R2 of 0.27. Countries starting with lower rural coverage gained faster, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Catching up is therefore real, but partial: initial level explains little more than a quarter of the variation in growth, so many low-coverage countries did not catch up, and the dispersion that remains is still considerable. The analysis cannot say why. Governance, financing, conflict, groundwater conditions and donor attention all plausibly matter, and these indicators do not separate them.

For 2030, the implication is that universal access is reachable for rural electricity in most countries, but not for sanitation or water at the present pace. The countries furthest from the target are those where the poorest live, so the world's average will conceal how far the target is missed where it matters most. Changes after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be separated cleanly here, since the classes summarise the whole period from 2015 to 2024, and the effect of the pandemic years on regressing countries cannot be isolated from these results.

### Universal access by 2030 is out of reach without acceleration, and proposals follow

Universal access by 2030 is not within reach on present trends, except in the case of rural electricity. For drinking water, only 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target. Together with the 45 countries making moderate progress, they cover about two thirds of the population assessed, but the remaining countries are advancing too slowly or are moving backwards. Sanitation is further behind: 49 of 213 countries were on track or had met the target, and 37 were in regression or stagnation in addition to 39 in regression. A trend to 100% is a demanding standard, because the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach: they lie among dispersed, displaced or marginalised households. Countries classed as on track may still leave a residual population without services.

Rural electricity is the exception. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, holding 77.4% of the population covered. Only 10 countries were in regression and 7 in stagnation, though these hold 5.4% and 2.3% of the population respectively. Regression in access measured as a share of population is often a sign that connection has not kept pace with population growth, or that conflict or economic collapse has damaged networks. Electricity has benefited from falling costs of off-grid and mini-grid solar and from national programmes with clear connection targets, which water and sanitation have lacked in comparable form.

For accounts, the world figure for the poorest 40% rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024. At that pace of about 1.5 points a year, universality by 2030 would not be reached. Low-income countries rose from 22.5% to 37.3% over the same period, so more than six in ten of the poorest adults there remained without an account. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021, so the 2030 outlook for accounts is an estimate with wide uncertainty rather than a measured trend.

The weight of the shortfall falls on a small number of places. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 55.1% electricity access in 2024, and low-income countries, with 48.8%, account for most of the people still without power, while South Asia, at 99.8%, has almost closed its gap. This shows that progress is possible at scale within a decade, but also that global averages will soon be governed by a region where the pace has been slower than the need. Reaching 100% in Sub-Saharan Africa by 2030 would require a rate of connection well above any seen in the region since 2015.

Target 1.4 also speaks of the poor and the vulnerable specifically, yet three of the four measures here describe whole populations. Only the account series is split to the poorest 40%. Water, sanitation and electricity could be rising for the average household while the poorest remain unserved, and the shelf cannot show this. The word access is likewise read in more than one way: basic water means an improved source within a round trip of 30 minutes, which is not the same as safely managed water, and an account that is held is not necessarily one that is used.

w-c02-5-1.text:
### Disaster displacement is the measure that exists, and it is rising

The only series in the bench that records recent exposure to climate-related disasters is the count of new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre. It stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and at 26,393,278 in 2023. The world total therefore rose over the eight years, by a little more than a third, and it did so in the period that target 1.5 covers, which asks countries to reduce the exposure and vulnerability of the poor and of people in vulnerable situations to climate-related extreme events by 2030.

The unit needs care. The series counts cases of new displacement, not persons. A household that flees a flood in March and a cyclone in September enters the count twice, and a person who returns home and is displaced again is counted again. The figure is also not a count of people affected: those whose crops fail in a drought, whose homes are damaged but who stay, or who lose income without moving do not appear. Displacement measures the part of exposure that is severe enough to force people from their homes and that is visible to the agencies which report it. It is a floor under the scale of exposure, not an estimate of it.

The measure also records hazards beyond those that the target names strictly as climate-related. Storms, floods, wildfires and droughts are included, as are geophysical events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, depending on how events are classified. The series therefore cannot be read as a pure signal of climate change. Part of any rise reflects more people living in harm's way, in coastal cities and river plains, and part reflects better monitoring and reporting. A single large event can move a national figure, and through it a regional one, by millions in one year.

The analysis of breaks in the annual change of the world total finds none. Over 2009 to 2023 the mean annual change is negative, at about 789,790 cases a year, which sits oddly beside the higher 2023 figure than 2015. The reading is that the series is dominated by large swings from year to year, so that the endpoints, and the mean of changes taken from a high early year, tell different stories. Neither 2015 nor 2020 marks a statistical rupture. The rise from 2015 to 2023 should be taken as a movement within a volatile record, not as a trend established against that volatility.

This matters for 2030 because the target has no quantified threshold, and the only indicator that tracks exposure directly has no baseline that fixes what reduction would mean. A target that asks for reduced exposure can be read as fewer displacements in absolute terms or as fewer relative to population at risk; the data support the first reading only, and by that reading the world is, on the endpoints, moving away from the target.

### Coverage has widened, but the wider measure of exposure is a single historical period

The number of countries that report disaster displacement has grown steadily, and this complicates any reading of the rising total. In 2008, 80 countries reported. The count fell to 60 in 2009, recovered to 73 in 2010, dipped again to 62 in 2011 and reached 79 in 2012. It then jumped to 118 in 2013, slipped to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. After 2015 it rose almost every year, reaching 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020. It stood at 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across the whole series, 199 countries and territories have reported in at least one year, so even the latest year leaves some of them without a figure.

This matters for interpretation. A world total built from 112 countries in 2015 and 145 in 2023 is not a sum over the same set of countries. Part of the rise in displacement may reflect better recording, wider monitoring and the entry of countries that were previously silent, rather than a larger number of people forced from their homes. The data as given cannot separate the two effects. A like-for-like comparison over countries reporting in both years would be needed, and the figures here do not provide one. The lower counts of 2009 and 2011 also show that early coverage was uneven, which argues against reading the years before 2013 as a baseline.

The wider measure of exposure is weaker still. The share of the population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures is an annual average for 1990 to 2009, compiled from the EM-DAT disaster database. It is reported for 168 countries in a single year, 2009, with no regional or world aggregates and no later update. It therefore describes the two decades before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. It carries no trend, no value for 2015 and none for 2020, and it cannot show whether exposure has changed since the goals began.

The question of how many people are affected by climate-related disasters therefore cannot be answered from these data. Displacement counts cases of movement, not persons, since one person may be displaced more than once in a year. The historical average gives a share of the population but belongs to a past period. Neither series measures people affected in the sense that target 1.5 implies, and no series on the shelf measures the exposure of the poor in particular.

### Regions differ sharply and the inequality among countries has grown

Regional totals of new disaster displacement diverge widely, and the direction of change differs from one region to the next. East Asia and Pacific remains the largest single contributor. Its count moved from 8,304,660 cases in 2015 to 9,038,561 in 2023, a modest rise that leaves the region with the highest absolute burden in the series. The region is exposed to typhoons, monsoon floods and seismic hazards alike, and it holds very large populations along coasts and river deltas. Only part of that exposure is climate-related, since displacement by earthquakes and volcanic activity is counted in the same series.

South Asia moved in the opposite direction. Its count fell from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 in 2023. A fall of this size should not be read as a lasting gain in resilience. Displacement counts in the region depend heavily on whether a single large cyclone or flood season strikes populated areas in a given year, and early warning and evacuation, which have improved in several countries, can raise recorded displacement as well as save lives, because evacuations are counted as displacement. Two endpoints cannot separate these influences.

The largest proportional rise is in Europe and Central Asia, from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 in 2023. Part of this is likely to reflect wider reporting and a small starting base, and part genuine events, but the data cannot apportion the two. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan roughly doubled, from 1,212,730 to 2,481,660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 to 1,728,025. North America rose from 76,000 to 394,000, a fivefold increase from a low base that is small beside the Asian totals.

The spread among countries has widened. Weighting countries by population, the Gini coefficient of new displacement rose from 0.570 in 2015 to 0.678 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. Both measures say that displacement has become more concentrated in a few countries. The number of countries in the comparison also grew, from 112 to 145, so part of the change may follow from wider coverage rather than from a change in the underlying events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. In 2015 most of the inequality was a matter of which region a country belongs to. By 2023 almost half lay among countries within the same regions. Regional averages therefore describe the pattern less well than they once did, and targeting of resilience support by region alone would miss many of the most exposed countries. For 2030, the implication is that national and subnational monitoring will matter more than regional aggregates, and that a single global total conceals sharply different trajectories.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The trend in the world series should be read with caution. The test for structural breaks in the annual change of world displacement found none. The mean annual change over 2009 to 2023 was -789,790 cases, a negative figure that sits oddly beside the rise already described between 2015 and 2023. The two readings do not contradict each other: the mean is taken over a window that begins in a year when only 60 countries reported, and it reflects a few very large swings rather than a settled direction. Displacement counts follow the occurrence of major storms, floods and earthquakes, so a single severe season can dominate a year. A series of this kind cannot support a statement that exposure is falling or rising steadily, and no break marks 2015 or 2020 as a turning point.

The implication for 2030 is therefore limited. Target 1.5 sets no quantified level. It asks for resilience to be built and for exposure and vulnerability to be reduced, but it names no number of people, no share of population and no date before 2030 at which progress is to be checked. Without a threshold, no trajectory can be judged on or off course. The target can also be read in more than one way: as a fall in the number of people affected, as a fall in the share of the poor among those affected, or as a rise in the capacity to absorb losses. The displacement series speaks to the first reading only, and imperfectly, because it counts movements and not the poor.

The widening of reporting adds a further caution. Coverage rose from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, out of 199 that have reported in any year. Some of the increase in counts may reflect better recording, not greater harm. Inequality among countries also grew over the same years, with the Gini coefficient moving from 0.57 to 0.68, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. Disparity within regions is now a larger part of the picture, which a regional average conceals.

The broader measure of exposure, the share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, ends in 2009 and cannot be set beside recent years. The disaster risk reduction score, from self-assessments for 83 countries ending in 2011, is likewise too old and too subjective to show what has changed since 2015.

The parties to the Sendai Framework should set a quantified level for target 1.5, so that progress to 2030 can be judged against a threshold.

w-c03-1-1.text:
### Global prevalence of undernourishment and food insecurity

The world picture for target 2.1 is set by two indicators from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and they tell different stories. The prevalence of undernourishment stood at 8.0 per cent of the global population in 2015 and at 8.1 per cent in 2024. Over nine years, the first seven of them under the Sustainable Development Goals, the share of people whose habitual food intake cannot supply the dietary energy needed for a normal, active and healthy life did not fall. It was, to the precision the series allows, unchanged. The 2024 figure rests on reports from 165 countries, so the world value is built on near-complete coverage.

The second indicator, the prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity, moved sharply. It rose from 21.4 per cent in 2015 to 28.0 per cent in 2024. This indicator counts people living in households where at least one adult reported, at times during the year, eating poor-quality diets and possibly cutting the quantity of food. It is far broader than undernourishment, and its level is correspondingly higher: in 2024 more than one person in four lived in such a household, against roughly one in twelve classed as undernourished. The 2024 value rests on 135 reporting countries, fewer than for undernourishment, so the world aggregate depends more on modelled estimates for countries without a survey.

The two measures should not be read as duplicates or as rivals. Undernourishment is a modelled estimate. It compares the food available in a country, and how unequally it is distributed, with a minimum energy requirement. It responds to supply, trade and income distribution, and it captures chronic shortfalls in calories. Food insecurity is experience-based. It comes from survey questions about worry, compromised diet quality and reduced portions, so it registers the effect of price shocks, lost income and disrupted markets on households, including those who still reach the energy minimum but eat badly or anxiously. A flat undernourishment line beside a rising food insecurity line is therefore coherent. Calorie shortfall has stayed steady, while access to an adequate and varied diet has worsened for a much larger group. The period contained the disruption of 2020 and the food and energy price rises that followed, shocks of the kind the experience-based measure is designed to detect.

The yardstick for progress needs care. Target 2.1 calls for an end to hunger and for access by all people to safe, nutritious and sufficient food all year round, and it states no number. The convention adopted here reads the end of hunger as undernourishment at or below 2.5 per cent, which is also the lowest value the FAO series reports; the series note says that a value of 2.5 may signify a prevalence below that level. Against that reading, the world in 2024 stands at more than three times the threshold. The target also names no threshold for food insecurity, although its wording on access for all points towards it. Any figure set for that indicator, whether zero or a reduction from a baseline, would be an interpretation by the reader and not a value fixed by the target. The prevalence of undernourishment is therefore treated as the primary measure of the target, and food insecurity as the wider measure of access and sufficiency.

The finding matters for what follows. With undernourishment unchanged and food insecurity higher, the world has not moved towards the end of hunger since 2015, and on the broader measure it has moved away. The sections that follow show where the burden lies and how reliable the figures are.

### Regional and income-group differences

Regional averages conceal a split between a few regions that have moved towards the target and several that have moved away from it. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest prevalence of undernourishment among the regions in both years, rising from 18.4 per cent in 2015 to 22.3 per cent in 2024. The trend tool classes this as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 25.4 per cent against a target of 2.5 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved in the same direction from a lower base, from 9.6 per cent to 12.3 per cent, and the tool projects 14.6 per cent in 2030. Conflict, displacement, currency crises and dependence on imported grain are well-established drivers of such deteriorations, and they cluster in these two regions.

The regions that improved did so from different starting points. South Asia fell from 12.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent, the largest decline among the regions in absolute terms, yet the tool reads this as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, since the expected 2030 value of 7.9 per cent remains well above 2.5 per cent. East Asia and Pacific fell from 4.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent and is the closest of the improving regions to the target, with an expected 2030 value of 2.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean eased only from 5.5 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Europe and Central Asia edged up from 2.8 per cent to 2.9 per cent, and North America remained at 2.5 per cent. Because the published figure is reported as 2.5 where the true prevalence may be lower, North America's flat line signals a floor in the data, not an absence of change.

Income groups show the same gradient more sharply. Low-income countries recorded 24.1 per cent in 2015 and 27.3 per cent in 2024, a regression in the tool's reading. Lower-middle-income countries were almost unchanged, at 12.5 per cent and then 12.1 per cent, which the tool classes as stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries fell from 4.3 per cent to 4.0 per cent, and high-income countries from 2.6 per cent to 2.6 per cent at one decimal place, close to the floor. Hunger is therefore concentrated in the poorest economies, and it is there that the global average is being held up. The world figure of 8.1 per cent in 2024 is the product of improvement in the large populations of South Asia and East Asia offsetting deterioration in Africa and the Middle East, not of broad advance.

The measure of food insecurity, which captures experience of reduced diet quality or quantity and not habitual energy supply, shows a harsher picture. Among low-income countries it reached 65.4 per cent in 2024, up from 55.1 per cent in 2015, so that roughly two in three people lived in moderately or severely food insecure households. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 29.2 per cent to 41.8 per cent, a much steeper deterioration than their flat undernourishment figure suggests. Upper-middle-income countries held at 12.8 per cent and then 12.6 per cent, and high-income countries at 8.2 per cent and then 7.9 per cent. The gap between the two indicators widens as income falls.

South Asia illustrates why both indicators are needed. Undernourishment fell there from 12.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent, while moderate or severe food insecurity rose from 28.0 per cent to 36.7 per cent. The two can diverge because one is modelled from national food supply and distribution, whereas the other is reported by households and responds quickly to price rises, income losses and the strains after 2020, including inflation in staple foods. A region can have enough calories in aggregate and still contain many households that cannot afford a regular, adequate diet. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan show the sharpest case on the household measure, rising from 27.6 per cent to 40.1 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 23.7 per cent to 25.2 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 8.5 per cent to 8.8 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 10.3 per cent to 10.4 per cent, and North America from 10.3 per cent to 10.7 per cent.

For 2030, the implication is that the target will not be met by regional averages moving at their present pace, and that the poorest countries are moving away from it. Only North America is classed as on track, and it is already at the reporting floor.

### Country trajectories and the quality of the data

The country classifications make the global averages easier to read. For undernourishment, the trend tool assessed 168 countries against the target of 2.5 per cent by 2030. Of these, 68 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 41.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 24 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 17 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries are stagnant. Regression affects 53 countries, which hold 20.9 per cent of the population. The classes therefore divide almost evenly in number between countries that are moving towards the target and countries that are not, and the population weights show where the burden lies. The marginal-progress class is small in number but holds 26.5 per cent of the population, so a few very populous countries are improving too slowly to reach the target. Their pace matters more for the 2030 outcome than the count of countries suggests.

The finding that 68 countries are on track or have met the target needs a caveat about the indicator. The FAO reports prevalence values below 2.5 per cent as 2.5, so a country that has already met the target cannot be told apart from one sitting at the threshold. Many of the countries in the on-track class are likely to be middle- and high-income countries that began near the target and have stayed there. Their classification reflects the absence of a problem rather than a gain made since 2015. The class is therefore a weaker sign of progress than its size implies, and it should not be set against the regressing countries as if both groups had moved a similar distance.

Food insecurity gives a harsher picture. The tool assessed 157 countries for moderate or severe food insecurity. Regression is the largest class: 81 countries, holding 60.5 per cent of the population. Only 40 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 28.9 per cent of the population. Three countries show moderate progress, covering 4.5 per cent of the population, and six show marginal progress, covering 2.8 per cent. Stagnation affects 27 countries and 3.3 per cent of the population. The gap between the two indicators is large. Undernourishment, which is estimated from national food balance sheets and a model of how food is distributed, has held roughly steady. Food insecurity, which is measured from what households report about their own experience, has worsened in most of the world's people. Households can report hardship before the national supply of calories changes, and rising food prices, reduced incomes and the shocks of 2020 and after are the kind of pressure that survey-based measures capture first.

The reading of the food insecurity classes rests on a methodological limit. The indicator has no numeric target under the Goals. The trend tool therefore had to judge direction only, with a decrease taken as the aim, and it could not measure distance to a defined value. The classes mean that a country is moving up or down, or is flat. They do not mean that a country is near or far from an agreed end point. A country counted as on track has a falling prevalence, and that may still be a high prevalence. The target can also be read in more than one way: target 2.1 speaks of ending hunger and securing access to sufficient food all year round, which could be read as zero, as a low threshold such as that used for undernourishment, or as a reduction relative to a baseline. The classification is sensitive to that reading, and no single reading has been privileged here.

Coverage is the second limit. The number of countries reporting food insecurity was 99 in 2015 and 100 in 2016. It rose to 115 in 2017, 122 in 2018 and 136 in 2019, then to 144 in 2020, 146 in 2021 and 148 in 2022. It fell back to 135 in 2023 and again in 2024. In all, 157 countries reported in at least one year. The early years rest on about two thirds of the countries that later report, so a comparison between 2015 and a later year may reflect a change in who is counted rather than a change in conditions. The trend tool compares each country with its own record, which reduces this problem, but the regional and global averages are less secure. Countries that joined the survey later may differ systematically from those that reported from the start, since national surveys tend to arrive first where statistical capacity and funding are stronger.

The fall to 135 countries in 2023 and 2024 weakens the latest years in the same way. Some of the decline may reflect reporting delays that later revisions will fill, but that cannot be established from the series as it stands. The most recent estimates are therefore the least settled. For 2030, the lesson is that a monitoring system whose coverage grows and then shrinks cannot give a firm account of how far the world is from the target. The direction of the findings is consistent across the indicators and the classes, but the exact counts should be read as approximate.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The measured rates do not point towards the target. The trend tool classes the world as a whole as regression for undernourishment, with an expected 2030 value of 8.2 per cent against a target of 2.5 per cent. The ratio of progress to the progress required is -0.03, which is to say the global line is flat and slightly inclined the wrong way. Target 2.1 asks for an end to hunger by 2030, and at present rates the world would arrive at the end of the period with roughly the prevalence it had at the start.

The regression is concentrated in a few places. Low-income countries are expected to reach 29.7 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of -0.26. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.4 per cent, with a ratio of -0.44. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region is expected to reach 14.6 per cent, with a ratio of -0.71, the steepest deterioration among the regions in relation to its distance from the target. The causes are well established: armed conflict, displacement, repeated drought and flood, currency weakness that raises import costs, and the price shocks that followed 2020 weigh most on economies that import food and hold few reserves. Europe and Central Asia also shows regression, but from a low base, with an expected 2030 value of 3.1 per cent.

Progress elsewhere is real but insufficient. South Asia is expected to reach 7.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.46, and East Asia and Pacific 2.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.79. High-income countries are expected to reach 2.5 per cent, close to the floor at which the indicator is reported, and North America sits at that floor. Because the FAO note states that a value of 2.5 may signify a prevalence below 2.5 per cent, countries at the floor cannot be distinguished from one another, and a target of 2.5 per cent is in effect a target of reaching the reporting limit. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnant, with an expected 11.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean as marginal, at 4.9 per cent. Even the regions that improve would need to speed up to reach the target.

The country classes confirm the concentration. Of 168 countries, 53 are in regression and hold 20.9 per cent of the assessed population, while 68 are on track or have met the target. The success of many small or already well-fed countries therefore masks the difficulty of the places where hunger is deepest.

Food insecurity adds a harder reading. Among 157 countries assessed for moderate or severe food insecurity, 81 are in regression and hold 60.5 per cent of the assessed population, and 40 are on track, holding 28.9 per cent. Regression covers a far larger share of people than it does for undernourishment, where it covers 20.9 per cent. Food insecurity has therefore worsened in places where undernourishment has eased, which suggests that access, affordability and diet quality have deteriorated even where average energy supply has held. This matters for 2030, because a country can look close to the undernourishment target while a large share of its households still skip meals or eat poor diets. The food insecurity indicator also carries no numeric target, so the classification measures only the direction of change and not the distance to a goal, and the tool cannot say how far any country is from success.

The data base is improving and still uneven. The number of countries reporting food insecurity rose from 99 in 2015 to 148 in 2022, then fell to 135 in 2023 and 2024. Part of the apparent worsening may reflect changes in which countries report, because early coverage was thinner, and the fall in reporting after 2022 weakens the picture for the years that matter most for judging recovery after 2020.

In sum, the aim of ending hunger by 2030 will not be met on present rates, and the shortfall is a matter of where resources and attention are directed. The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c03-3-1.text:
### Child overweight and anaemia in women stand at 5.5 per cent and 30.7 per cent

Two indicators of malnutrition other than stunting and wasting are measured here: overweight among children under five, and anaemia among women of reproductive age. Target 2.2 names all forms of malnutrition and the nutritional needs of adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, yet its numerical benchmarks cover only stunting and wasting. The two indicators therefore describe parts of the target that carry no quantified goal.

In 2024 the world prevalence of child overweight, defined as weight for height more than two standard deviations above the WHO 2006 median, was 5.5 per cent of children under five, up from 5.2 per cent in 2015. The rise is small, at about 0.3 percentage points over nine years, but it runs against the direction the target implies. The estimate rests on 163 countries reporting in 2024. It is a modelled estimate, so year-to-year movements are smoothed and partly reflect the model rather than fresh surveys, especially in countries that are surveyed only every few years.

Anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 is far more common. In 2023 the world prevalence was 30.7 per cent, against 28.0 per cent in 2015, an increase of about 2.7 percentage points. The measure combines non-pregnant women with haemoglobin below 12 g/dL and pregnant women below 11 g/dL, and 192 countries are covered. Nearly one woman in three of reproductive age is therefore anaemic, which matters for maternal health, for birth outcomes and for the nutrition of the next generation of children.

Both series worsened after 2015, and neither has an internationally agreed target value against which progress can be scored. A rise in child overweight is not necessarily a failure of the same kind as a rise in anaemia, since the two reflect different diets and health conditions. Even so, the direction of both indicators is adverse. Anaemia has a history of global commitments to reduce it, but they are not part of the goal framework used here, and the series cannot show whether a trajectory fits any such commitment. Haemoglobin measurement also depends on altitude, smoking and survey method, and country estimates are modelled where surveys are scarce. The levels reported here should be read as well-founded orders of magnitude, not as exact counts. For 2030, the starting point is a world in which both burdens are larger than at the outset of the agenda.

### Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower

Regional levels of the two burdens run in opposite directions. Child overweight is lowest in South Asia, at 3.37 per cent of children under five in 2024, and highest in North America, at 9.85 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 8.77 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 7.84 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa records 3.84 per cent. Anaemia among women aged 15 to 49 reverses the order: North America has the lowest prevalence, 14.89 per cent in 2023, and South Asia the highest, 51.10 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 36.68 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 35.20 per cent, whereas East Asia and the Pacific, at 18.70 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 19.96 per cent, lie close to the lower end.

The pattern by income group repeats the regional one. Overweight is 3.54 per cent in low-income countries and 4.01 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 8.58 per cent in upper-middle-income and 8.41 per cent in high-income countries. Anaemia is 35.60 per cent in low-income and 46.00 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 19.81 per cent in upper-middle-income and 17.25 per cent in high-income countries. Overweight in children is thus highest where the burden of anaemia is lowest, and the reverse holds in the poorest regions. This does not mean that the two conditions exclude one another within a country or a household. Both can coexist, and regional averages cannot show it. What the averages do show is that the places with least food security in the wider sense of the chapter still carry the heavier anaemia burden, while the rise of overweight is concentrated among richer and middle-income economies, which are also those with greater exposure to processed foods and lower physical activity.

Anaemia is also the indicator on which regions differ most in relative terms. The anaemia gap between South Asia and North America is a factor of more than three, while the overweight gap between North America and South Asia is nearer to three. The spread among 192 countries, weighted by population, confirms that geography explains most of the inequality. The between-region share of the Theil index was 77.9 per cent in 2023, up from 74.1 per cent in 2015. Over the same years the Gini coefficient fell from 0.287 to 0.272 and the Theil index from 0.130 to 0.116. Differences among countries have narrowed slightly overall, yet what remains is increasingly a matter of which region a country belongs to, not of differences within regions. Gains and failures are therefore shared by neighbours, which suggests that regional food systems, diets, malaria and parasitic disease, and the reach of iron and folic acid supplementation matter as much as national policy.

### Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere

The trend classes show that movement on both indicators has mostly been in the wrong direction since 2015. Child overweight is assessed against a benchmark of 3.0 per cent by 2030. Of the 163 countries assessed, 92, holding 66.6 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, meaning that prevalence is rising where the benchmark requires it to fall. Only 33 countries, with 21.3 per cent of the population, are on track or have already met the benchmark. A further 10 countries (2.0 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 20 (7.5 per cent) show marginal progress and 8 (2.6 per cent) are stagnant. The benchmark is a reading adopted for this book, not one written into Target 2.2, so a stricter or looser line would change how many countries count as on track. The direction of travel, however, does not depend on the line.

Regionally, the pattern is one of regression almost everywhere. East Asia and Pacific, high-income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are all classed as regressing, as are the low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups. The annual rates of change are small, 0.0153 for East Asia and Pacific and 0.0165 for Latin America and the Caribbean, but they point upward in each case. South Asia shows the fastest rise, at 0.0518, from a low base. The regression ratios for low-income and lower-middle-income countries, at -6.09 and -2.37, are large mainly because those groups began close to the benchmark and have drifted away from it, whereas the ratios for the richer groups, such as -0.36 for high-income countries, reflect a start well above it. Europe and Central Asia is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.11, and expected prevalence in 2030 of 7.32 per cent remains far above 3.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the only region with moderate progress, a ratio of 0.67, and its expected 2030 level of 4.36 per cent would still be above the benchmark. At the world level the ratio is -0.21, a regression, with 5.67 per cent expected in 2030.

Anaemia among women of reproductive age shows a more uniform picture. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are regressing. Only 2 countries (1.7 per cent of the population) are on track, 1 shows moderate progress, 9 show marginal progress and 18 are stagnant. Every region and income group is classed as regressing. The world rate of change is 0.0115. Rates are highest in North America, at 0.0359, and in high-income countries, at 0.0239, and lowest in East Asia and Pacific, at 0.0023. Rises are therefore fastest where anaemia is already least common, while in South Asia, where it is most common, the rate is 0.0070. No target value is set for anaemia in this assessment, so the classes measure only whether prevalence is falling.

The spread across countries narrowed slightly. The Theil index fell from 0.130 in 2015 to 0.116 in 2023, and the Gini coefficient from 0.287 to 0.272. The between-region share of the Theil index rose from 74.1 per cent to 77.9 per cent, so what inequality remains is increasingly a matter of which region a country belongs to. The narrowing does not signal improvement: it is consistent with prevalence rising faster where it was lowest. These data identify no causes. Changing diets, shifts in the measurement of haemoglobin and modelled estimates for countries with sparse surveys could each contribute, and none can be separated here. A rise in prevalence across nearly every country does, however, justify caution about attributing the result to any single national policy.

### The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course

The two burdens are not linked by change. Across 162 countries, the rank correlation between changes in child overweight and changes in women's anaemia over 2015 to 2023 is -0.030, which is indistinguishable from none. Countries where overweight rose faster were no more and no less likely to see anaemia rise. The correlation of 2023 levels is -0.469, a moderate negative association: countries with higher child overweight tend to have lower anaemia among women, and the reverse. This is the pattern expected when both indicators follow national income and the stage of the nutrition transition. It is not evidence that one burden displaces the other. The two occupy different places and move for different reasons, so a response designed for one will not reach the other.

The outlook for 2030 follows from the trend classes. For child overweight, the world is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -0.207 against the 3.0 per cent benchmark and an expected 2030 prevalence of 5.7 per cent. North America is expected to reach 10.8 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 9.7 per cent. High-income countries are expected to reach 9.1 per cent. South Asia, though the lowest in level, has the fastest rise, at a rate of 0.052, and is expected to reach 4.6 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 4.3 per cent, below the world figure but still a regression. Only the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows moderate progress, with an expected 4.4 per cent. Even there the benchmark is not met on the current course.

For anaemia, no numerical target is set, so the classes measure only the direction of travel. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, and only 2 are on track or have met the benchmark applied. Because the benchmark is not an agreed one, these classes should be read as a measure of direction rather than of failure against a commitment. The direction is nonetheless clear and adverse. The finding also depends on modelled estimates, which are revised and which smooth over years in which surveys were absent.

The findings support four proposals, set out below. The first is to give anaemia among women a quantified target, since the lack of one leaves a burden affecting most of the population without a benchmark. The second is to pair overweight prevention with existing nutrition programmes so that action against undernutrition does not feed overweight. The third is to report the gaps in the data. The fourth is to focus effort where each burden is greatest.
