w-c03-5-1.text:
### Farming's footprint on land, fertiliser and water is large and nearly static

Farming occupies a little over a third of the world's land. Agricultural land, which combines arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, stood at 36.8 per cent of land area in 2015 and at 36.9 per cent in 2023. The change is about a tenth of a percentage point over eight years, which is small enough to be read as stability. The series is reported by 208 countries in 2024, so the global figure rests on near-complete coverage. A stable share does not show that pressure on land is unchanged, since the share says nothing about which land is farmed, how degraded it is, or whether forest and wetland were converted while abandoned land reverted elsewhere.

Fertiliser use shows a modest rise. Consumption was 132.9 kilograms per hectare of arable land in 2015 and 136.5 kilograms in 2023, an increase of about three and a half kilograms. The measure counts nitrogenous, potash and phosphate nutrients and excludes manures, so it understates total nutrient application where animal and plant manures are widely used. The world average also conceals a very wide spread between countries, which the next part examines. Here it is enough to note that a flat global mean can coexist with rising use in some places and falling use in others, each with different consequences. Too little fertiliser leaves yields and soils depleted. Too much brings nutrient runoff, water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Water use follows the same pattern. Agriculture accounted for 71.5 per cent of total freshwater withdrawal in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. Roughly seven of every ten units of freshwater taken from rivers, lakes and aquifers go to farming, and that share barely moved across the period. The series is reported by 178 countries in 2022, and the latest year is earlier than for land and fertiliser, so any change after 2022 cannot be observed. A fall of about half a percentage point may reflect growth in industrial and municipal withdrawals as much as any saving in the field. The share also measures the distribution of use between sectors, not the volume withdrawn or whether withdrawals are sustainable.

These three series are measures of intensity and footprint, not of sustainability. Target 2.4 asks for sustainable food production systems and resilient agricultural practices that raise productivity while maintaining ecosystems, and it sets no numerical threshold and no base year. It can be read in more than one way. One reading treats it as a call to produce more on the same land with fewer inputs. Another treats it as a call to restore ecosystems even at some cost to output. A third stresses adaptation to drought and flooding, which none of these series captures. Because the target is open, a figure such as 36.9 per cent of land cannot be judged on or off track. It can only be described and compared over time and across places.

Two points follow from the global picture. First, the period since 2015 shows no sharp break in any of the three measures, and the available years do not reveal a clear shift attributable to the disruption after 2020. Second, a near-static aggregate is the starting point, not the conclusion. The questions of where intensity is high, where it is rising and where it is too low for food security are matters of regional and national difference.

### Regions differ most in fertiliser, and least in the share of land farmed

Regional differences are widest in fertiliser use and narrowest in the share of land that is farmed. In 2015, East Asia and Pacific applied 329.1 kilograms of nutrients per hectare of arable land, the highest of any region. By 2023 the figure had fallen to 304.1. Sub-Saharan Africa sat at the opposite end, with 14.4 kilograms in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023. The gap between the two regions therefore remained above 280 kilograms per hectare, even though the African figure rose by about a third and the Asian figure fell. The fall in East Asia and Pacific is consistent with policies in the largest producers that discourage over-application and promote balanced nutrient use, while the African level reflects the cost of fertiliser, weak distribution and limited credit for smallholders rather than a deliberate choice of low-input farming.

Other regions moved upward. South Asia rose from 175.0 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 206.0 in 2023, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 135.1 to 173.9, the largest relative rise among the larger regions. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 90.0 to 102.0. North America changed little, from 124.3 to 128.8, and Europe and Central Asia drifted down from 78.7 to 76.0. The world average, at 132.9 in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, therefore conceals two opposing movements: a decline in the heaviest-using region and increases in most others. Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income countries rose from 10.0 to 13.9 and lower-middle-income countries from 114.6 to 130.8, while upper-middle-income countries were almost flat at 213.0 and 213.8, and high-income countries eased from 106.3 to 104.3. Low-income countries still use roughly one fifteenth of the amount used in upper-middle-income countries per hectare, which bears directly on the productivity aims of target 2.4.

The share of land in agriculture varies much less between regions, and it hardly moved after 2015. East Asia and Pacific stood at 46.5 per cent in 2015 and 46.8 in 2023, Sub-Saharan Africa at 43.9 and 44.7, and South Asia at 58.6 and 58.3. North America held at about 26.7 per cent in both years. Latin America and the Caribbean slipped from 33.3 to 32.9 per cent. These shares are shaped by climate, terrain and history, so they change slowly, and the small shifts are not evidence of a policy effect. Sub-Saharan Africa is the one region where farmland grew appreciably, which fits a pattern in which output has been raised by expanding cultivated area more than by raising inputs per hectare.

Water use for farming differs by region in a way that follows aridity and the dependence on irrigation. In 2022, agriculture accounted for 90.3 per cent of freshwater withdrawals in South Asia and 87.3 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, which had been 90.1 per cent in 2015. North America stood at 37.5 per cent and Europe and Central Asia at 51.8, where industry and municipal supply take larger shares. The South Asian value is identical in 2015 and 2022, at 90.3 per cent. Withdrawal shares in this series come from national surveys that are updated irregularly, and an unchanged value to four decimals more probably reflects a carried-forward estimate than genuine stability. The figure should be read as a level, not as evidence that the balance of use did not shift. For 2030, the regional spread points to different tasks: restraint and efficiency in the heavily fertilised and water-stressed regions, and access to inputs where use remains very low.

### Yields rose slowly and country outcomes diverged

Cereal yields rose slowly across most of the world after 2015, and the pace differed sharply between regions and countries. The world rate of change is given as 0.9 per cent a year, a figure the tool classes as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 5,430 in 2023, a rate of 0.9 per cent a year. Europe and Central Asia moved from 3,803 to 4,045 over the same years, at 0.8 per cent a year. High-income economies rose from 4,976 to 5,394, at 1.0 per cent a year. All three fall in the marginal class. Upper middle income countries also sit there, at 0.8 per cent a year. These are regions with already high yields, where the room for further gain is narrower and the gains come from breeding, management and precision rather than from added inputs.

The classification needs careful reading. No target value for cereal yield is set in the targets of Goal 2, and target 2.4 speaks of productivity and resilience without a number. The tool therefore judges each series against the rate of a rising trend, not against a fixed goal. A class such as marginal progress is a judgement of pace relative to that trend, and a different reference rate would shift some regions between classes. The labels should be taken as a comparison between places, not as a verdict on whether any region has met an official threshold.

The lower-yield regions show the widest spread of outcomes. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 in 2015 to 4,828 in 2024, at 1.1 per cent a year, still classed as marginal. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached a moderate class at 1.3 per cent a year, with yields going from 2,732 to 3,027 by 2023. South Asia, by contrast, rose from 3,041 to 3,814 by 2024, a rate of 2.6 per cent a year, and North America from 6,677 to 8,414, at 2.6 per cent. Lower middle income countries went from 2,766 to 3,366, at 2.2 per cent. These three groups are the ones classed as on track or target met. South Asia and lower middle income countries gained from wider irrigation, improved seed and expanded input use, while North America gained from an already high base and favourable recent seasons, so the same label stands for different causes.

The weakest results lie where yields are lowest and the need is greatest. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 1,443 to 1,453 kilograms per hectare between 2015 and 2024, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which is stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 to 1,345, a rate of minus 0.2 per cent a year, classed as regression. A yield in these groups is less than a third of that in North America in 2024. Rain-fed farming, thin use of improved seed, limited credit, weak roads and exposure to drought and conflict all weigh on these outcomes, and the period since 2020 added shocks to input costs and supply chains. Because yield is measured per hectare harvested, a rise in cropped area onto poorer land can also hold the average down.

The country tallies confirm that the divergence is wide. Of 180 countries assessed, 39 are on track or have met the trend, and they hold 29.5 per cent of the population covered. Another 19 countries show moderate progress, with 14.0 per cent of the population. A further 27 show marginal progress, with 25.7 per cent, a large share because this class includes populous middle-income economies. Stagnation applies to 25 countries and 15.6 per cent of the population. Regression applies to 70 countries, the largest count of any class, though these hold only 15.2 per cent of the population, which says that the falling yields are mostly in smaller countries.

Two readings follow. By population, most people live where yields are either improving at a fair pace or creeping up, so global averages hide the problem. By country count, however, the commonest outcome is decline, and 95 countries are stagnant or falling in yield. Year-to-year weather can drive a drop between two chosen end years, so some of the 70 may reflect a poor season at the end of the window and not a lasting fall. The trend over 2015 to 2024 is a short window for crops that swing with rainfall, and the result should be treated with that caution. For 2030, the pattern implies that global yield growth will stay modest unless the stagnant and regressing countries change course, and these are the places where food insecurity is concentrated.

### Fertiliser use is converging, but it explains yield levels more than yield change

Fertiliser use has been converging. Across 192 countries, the coefficient of variation of fertiliser consumption per hectare of arable land fell from 2.2 in 2015 to 1.7 in 2022. Countries that began with low application rates tended to increase them faster than countries that began with high rates, and the convergence coefficient of -0.034 is statistically distinguishable from zero (p below 0.001). The model explains 27.5 per cent of the variation in country growth, so the starting level is an important influence but far from the only one. Convergence of this kind reflects two movements at once: a rise from low bases in parts of Africa and South Asia, and a levelling off or decline in some of the most intensive systems, where fertiliser prices, nutrient regulation and efficiency gains have reduced application per hectare.

Convergence in inputs does not mean convergence in outcomes. Across 179 countries, the Spearman rank correlation between fertiliser use and cereal yield in 2022 is 0.72. Countries that apply more nutrients per hectare are, with few exceptions, the countries that harvest more grain per hectare. The relationship between changes is much weaker. The Spearman correlation between the change in fertiliser use and the change in cereal yield from 2015 to 2022 is 0.13, and the Kendall coefficient is 0.10. A country that raised its application rate was only slightly more likely to see yields rise faster than others.

The contrast has a plain reading. High input goes with high yield because intensive systems combine fertiliser with improved seed, irrigation, mechanisation, extension services and reliable markets. Extra input applied alone, in the absence of those complements, does not reliably raise yields. Weather in individual years, soil degradation, pest pressure and the response curve of crops, which flattens at high rates, also weaken the link in changes over a short window of seven years. Where soils are depleted and application is very low, additional nutrients can raise yields substantially, yet the data here do not isolate such cases.

The correlations also do not establish cause. Wealthier countries with better institutions both use more fertiliser and obtain higher yields, and climate and soil quality shape both. The rank measures used here describe association only, and the measure of changes covers a period that includes the disruption to fertiliser prices and supply after 2020, which affected countries unevenly. For 2030, the finding cautions against treating higher fertiliser use as a target in itself. Target 2.4 calls for productive and sustainable systems, and the evidence suggests that gains depend on how nutrients are used, not only on how much is applied.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.4 asks for production systems that raise productivity while maintaining ecosystems, and the evidence in this section shows that the two halves of that wording are moving unevenly. Fertiliser intensity is not falling where it is already high. In East Asia and Pacific it declined from 329.1 kilograms per hectare of arable land in 2015 to 304.1 in 2023, yet remained more than twice the world figure of 136.5 kilograms. In the upper middle income group it was 213.0 in 2015 and 213.8 in 2023, effectively unchanged, and in the high income group it eased only from 106.3 to 104.3. Where use is low it is rising: Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 14.4 to 19.3 kilograms and the low income group from 10.0 to 13.9. These increases begin from so small a base that they leave the continent far from the application levels seen elsewhere.

The yield record offers little reassurance. Of 180 countries assessed on cereal yield, 39 were on track or had met the target, holding 29.5 per cent of the assessed population, while 70 were in regression, holding 15.2 per cent. A further 25 were stagnant and 27 showed only marginal progress. Fertiliser levels track yield levels closely across 179 countries (Spearman 0.72 for 2022 levels), but changes in fertiliser track changes in yield only weakly (0.13 for 2015 to 2022). More nutrients are therefore not a reliable route to faster gains; soils, seed, water control, markets and extension services decide what a kilogram of fertiliser yields.

Water shows the least movement. Agriculture took 71.5 per cent of freshwater withdrawals in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. South Asia stayed at 90.3 per cent in both years, which is consistent with a series that is carried forward rather than newly measured, and the low income group remained near 90.9 per cent. Withdrawal share says nothing about whether extraction is sustainable, so the data cannot show whether the ecosystem clause of the target is being met. For 2030, the likely outcome is intensity that stays high in the leading regions, grows slowly in the low-input regions, and yields that remain short of the pace required.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c04-4-1.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.6% for the world by 2030. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, which is a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The measure is also a ceiling on what can be learned. The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year or two after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 divides into three groups: regions where the probability of premature death from the four main non-communicable diseases fell appreciably, regions where it hardly changed, and one region where it rose. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall among the regions, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, a respectable decline that nonetheless leaves the region with a probability well above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021.

The small movers are the two Americas. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America already began from the lowest regional level, so a modest fall is less surprising there, but the pace is far from the one-third reduction that Target 3.4 describes. Established knowledge points to causes that are familiar: gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking rates have been offset in part by obesity, diabetes and, in some countries, the effects of drug overdose and unequal access to treatment on adult mortality. In Latin America and the Caribbean, rising metabolic risk and fragmented primary care in many health systems plausibly work against faster progress.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, which made it the region with the highest level in 2021, having been marginally below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group in 2015. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates in the 30 to 70 range did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends, which is consistent with high rates of hypertension, diabetes and air-pollution-related respiratory disease, together with late diagnosis and heavy out-of-pocket costs for long-term treatment. The period also includes the pandemic years, when disruption to screening and chronic care, and the effect of infection on people with existing conditions, may have pushed the 2021 figure upward; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves the level close to the South Asian one. The extract supplied for the region is truncated, so the regional series should be read from the full database before any statement about its pace is relied upon. Measurement is also a concern in this region, where death registration is incomplete and the estimates lean heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, which is to say almost no change. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. The two richer groups therefore improved by about one percentage point each, while the lower-middle group, which contains South Asia's large populations, stood still. The gap between the low-income and high-income groups remained roughly ten percentage points in 2021.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability bounded by the experience of all adults, but the direction is towards greater inequality, not less. The share of the Theil index lying between regions, as opposed to within them, grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than it did in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences, and that the regions pulling away from the rest, in both directions, are shaping the global picture.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.2619 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.08728 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. The ratio of the two is 0.33. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted, not towards it.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. Established knowledge points to several plausible contributors that the data here do not separate: the earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from improved treatment of heart disease, and such gains are subject to diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The final years of the window, 2020 and 2021, also coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions and may have raised deaths from these causes among people infected with the virus. The series does not allow those effects to be isolated from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.00156 with a p-value of 0.697 and an R-squared of 0.0011. The coefficient is positive but statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation across the 185 countries rose from 0.360 in 2015 to 0.380 in 2021. Relative spread between countries widened slightly. Because the indicator is a probability expressed as a share, a given absolute fall is a larger proportional fall in a country with a low level, so a widening coefficient of variation is consistent with low-level countries improving proportionally faster, or with high-level countries stagnating or worsening. Either reading means the distribution did not tighten. For a target defined in relative terms, this matters: a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and the data show no sign that such countries are receiving it.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.098, and the Kendall coefficient is 0.0706. Both are weak. Moreover, the positive sign is the wrong direction for a simple expectation: better coverage would be expected to accompany larger falls in mortality, which in this coding would produce a negative correlation of changes. The association is close to nil, and it provides no support for the view that countries with larger coverage gains saw larger mortality gains over this short window.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.247 by the Spearman measure, and -0.1713 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is moderate in size, but it describes a cross-section, in which income, age structure, the health system as a whole and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together. It cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented in them. The mortality series is modelled by the World Health Organization from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths can be read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021 and the trend projection reaches 17.5% in 2030, so the global ratio of progress is 0.22. A ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target; 0.22 means roughly a fifth of that pace. At the observed rate, the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction, and the gap to be closed in the remaining years is larger than the distance covered since 2015.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, is the nearest of the regions to the required pace, with an expected value of 13.4% in 2030. Its path is moderate progress, and the target would still be missed without acceleration. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6% in 2030, which is marginal progress and leaves a wide gap. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030. The same classification should be read with care, since high-income countries began from a lower level, and the target value of 12.57% is itself computed from one baseline.

That last point is an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions at 22% or more would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above follows the first. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected 24.0% in 2030, higher than its 22.9% in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.00 and an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest, and the gap between income groups, already wide in 2021, is on course to persist or widen.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none, and the correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment, chronic respiratory care or the quality of care. A weak link therefore does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the coverage measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality, named in the section's title, cannot be treated here. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. The omission is a gap in this account, not evidence that the matter is minor. Mental health is part of the wording of target 3.4, and the indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover it.

The proposals follow from these findings. Health ministries in countries with weak coverage should give priority to hypertension detection and treatment and to tobacco control, since these are the tracer areas where the sub-index is lowest and where prevention acts most cheaply on cardiovascular death. The World Health Organization and national statistical offices should publish the premature mortality indicator by country each year, so that stagnation, as in lower middle income countries, and regression, as in South Asia, are seen while correction is possible. The same bodies should report suicide mortality alongside it, by sex, so that both parts of target 3.4 are followed together. The United Nations bodies that guide the goals should state the baseline, global or regional, from which the one-third reduction is judged.

w-c04-1-1.text:
### The global ratio fell from 228 to 197 and remains far above 70

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled estimate for the world stood at 228.0 in 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year available. That is a fall of 31 points over eight years, or about 3.9 points a year on average. The ratio in 2023 is still nearly three times the target value.

The arithmetic of the gap is plain. From 197.0 in 2023, a ratio below 70 by 2030 would require a reduction of more than 127 points in seven years, or over 18 points a year. That is nearly five times the average annual fall observed since 2015. The distance does not shrink by small adjustments to the pace; it would require a different trajectory altogether. The comparison is made here on rounded published figures, and the exact required pace depends on the unrounded estimates.

The target is worded as a global ratio, not as a national one. A global ratio is a weighted outcome: it is pulled down by countries with very low ratios and pulled up by countries with very high ratios, weighted by the number of live births. Because births are concentrated in regions where the ratio is highest, the world figure is governed far more by those regions than by the many countries already below 70. Reading the target as global means that a country-by-country reading is a separate question, and the regional sections that follow address it. A reading in which every country must fall below 70 would be stricter still, and the wording of the target does not require it.

The quality of the series needs stating plainly. Coverage is not the weakness: the modelled ratio is reported for all 194 countries in every year from 2000 to 2023, so no country drops out of the comparison and no year has gaps. That completeness is however a product of modelling rather than of observation. The estimates are produced by a regression model that draws on the share of maternal deaths among deaths of women aged 15 to 49, fertility, skilled birth attendance and national income. Where civil registration of deaths with causes is incomplete, as it is in many of the countries with the highest ratios, the estimate leans on those covariates rather than on counted deaths. The figures therefore carry uncertainty that the single published value does not display, and a change of a few points between years should not be read as a firm observation.

This uncertainty does not rescue the target. A fall of 31 points is small beside a shortfall of more than 127, and no plausible revision of the model would close a gap of that size. What the uncertainty does affect is the confidence with which any single country or short period can be judged. For the world as a whole, the finding is robust: the ratio is falling, it is falling slowly, and 2030 will arrive with it well above 70 unless the pace changes sharply.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of forty

The spread between regions is wider than any global average suggests. In 2023 the modelled ratio for Sub-Saharan Africa was 448 deaths per 100,000 live births, against 11 for Europe and Central Asia. The gap between those two regions is a factor of about forty, and it is the clearest sign that Target 3.1 is a global average assembled from very unequal parts. Where a woman gives birth, and in which health system, still decides the risk she faces more than any other single circumstance.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593 in 2015 to 448 in 2023, a fall of 145 points, and carries by far the highest ratio of any region. South Asia fell from 173 to 120, a fall of 53 points, and its fall in proportion is the larger of the two. Both remain well above 70. The trend tool reads South Asia as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 against a target of 70, so the shortfall there is modest in scale and could be closed with acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is read as making marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 350.5, about five times the target. Its ratio of progress to the pace required is 0.46, against 0.83 for South Asia. Closing the global gap depends overwhelmingly on the first of these two regions.

Several regions already lie below the threshold. Europe and Central Asia stood at 11 in 2023, down from 14 in 2015, and North America at 16, down from 17. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 54 to 47, and its expected 2030 value is 41.6. These regions are classed as on track, though for the wealthiest the ratio is already so low that further gains are small in absolute terms. East Asia and Pacific fell from 70 to 66, so it sits just below the target. Its expected 2030 value of 62.7 leaves little margin, and the classification rests on a gentle slope rather than on a secure lead.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among regions. Its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is the only region classed as in regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. A region of middle-income countries, with high rates of facility birth, has moved away from the target. Well-established explanations include the disruption of health services during the pandemic years, persistent inequality between urban and rural or Indigenous populations, and the weight of unsafe abortion and hypertensive disorders. The data used here cannot apportion the rise among these causes. It matters because the region was close to the threshold and has moved the wrong way.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 491 in 2015 to 346 in 2023, and are read as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 254.7. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 291 to 235 and are read as making only marginal progress, with an expected value of 194.9. That is a slower proportional fall than in the poorest group, and it concerns a larger number of births. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61 to 57, and high-income countries from 11 to 10. The two upper groups are already below 70, so the whole of the remaining distance lies in the lower two.

Country classes confirm that the picture is mixed rather than uniformly poor. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of the classified countries. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country is in stagnation and 7 are in regression, together under 1% of the population. The majority of people live in countries that will reach the target, yet the global average is held up by a minority of countries with very high ratios and large numbers of births. For 2030 this means that the global result will be settled by a few dozen countries, mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and not by the many that are already at or near the threshold.

### Progress slowed after 2008 and the pandemic years disturbed the series

The series shows that progress was already slowing before the goals were adopted. The breaks analysis identifies a change of regime in 2008. In the segment from 2001 to 2007, the global ratio fell by a mean of 8.4 points a year. In the segment from 2008 to 2019, the mean annual fall was 5.2 points. The pace of decline therefore dropped by roughly two fifths before 2015, and the adoption of the goals did not restore the earlier speed. The measured fall of the post-2015 years is a continuation of the slower trend, not a recovery from it. Well-established explanations include the exhaustion of the easiest gains, such as the expansion of skilled attendance at birth in countries that started from low coverage, and the harder task of reaching the remaining deaths, which are concentrated among women in poor, rural and conflict-affected settings where emergency obstetric care is least available.

The pandemic years then disturbed the series. The annual change was an increase of 4 points in 2020 and an increase of 31 points in 2021. The change reversed to a fall of 39 points in 2022, and the fall in 2023 was 6 points. The pattern is consistent with a shock and a recovery: disrupted maternity services, diversion of health staff, and direct deaths from infection in pregnancy are all plausible contributors to the rise, and the return of services would explain the fall. The analysis cannot establish this cause, however. The ratio is a modelled estimate, built by regression from covariates such as fertility, birth attendance and income, and not a count of registered deaths. A sharp one-year rise followed by a sharp one-year fall may partly reflect the way the model treats pandemic-era inputs and the revision of estimates, and the breaks detected in 2020 to 2023 are single-year segments that should be read as flags and not as stable trends. The weakness of the evidence is itself a finding, since the source data for most of the countries with the highest ratios are sparse. The coverage series on the completeness of death registration with cause-of-death information reaches only 121 economies, with its latest year at 2017, so the observed record is thin exactly where the burden lies.

The spread among countries has not narrowed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the ratio across 194 countries was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793 over the same period. Both measures point to slightly greater inequality at the end of the period than at the start, even though the global ratio itself fell. The share of the Theil index that lies between regions, instead of within them, was 70.9% in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023. Most of the inequality is therefore still a matter of which region a country belongs to, though the within-region component has grown a little, which suggests that countries in the same region are beginning to diverge.

Convergence is weak. A regression of change on the starting level across the 194 countries gives a coefficient of -0.00372, statistically distinguishable from zero with a p-value of 0.0024, but the R-squared is only 0.050. The sign means that countries with higher ratios in 2015 tended to fall slightly faster, which is the direction needed for catching up, but the starting level explains about 5% of the variation in change. Most of what separates fast improvers from slow ones lies elsewhere, in policy, conflict, financing and the strength of health systems. The unweighted coefficient of variation fell from 1.500 to 1.410 in this analysis, which agrees with a modest narrowing across countries counted equally. The population-weighted measures point the other way, so the two views differ because large countries with high ratios have not improved as quickly as the many small ones. For 2030, the implication is that neither the slowed trend before 2015 nor the weak catching up since offers grounds for expecting the pace to rise. The target depends on a faster fall in the places where the ratio is highest, and the record to 2023 shows no sign that this is under way.

### At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed, and proposals follow

Extending the recent pace to 2030 gives a global ratio of about 173.4 per 100,000 live births, against a target of 70. The trend tool places the world in the class of marginal progress, with a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.35. Reaching the target from the 2023 level of 197.0 would require a fall of about 127 points in seven years, against a fall of 31 points in the eight years since 2015. The required pace is therefore roughly four times the pace of the past eight years in absolute terms (127 points over seven years is about 18 points a year, against about 3.9). The target cannot be met by continuing present practice. It would take a change in the scale and the targeting of effort.

The country classification shows where the shortfall lies. In 128 of the 194 countries assessed, the ratio is on track or the target is already met, and these countries hold 74.5% of the classified population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 23 countries, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country stagnates and seven regress, together holding well under 1% of the population. Roughly a quarter of the classified population therefore lives in countries that will miss the target without faster change. The global average is held up by large countries that are already near or below 70, and a majority of countries being on track does not imply that the global ratio will reach 70, because the shortfall is concentrated in a few places where ratios are very high.

The regional projections confirm this. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 448 in 2023, would reach about 350.5 in 2030 at its present rate, with a ratio of progress of 0.46. South Asia, at 120 in 2023, would reach about 87.1, with a ratio of 0.83, which is the closest of the regions needing acceleration. Among income groups, low-income countries would reach about 254.7 and lower-middle-income countries about 194.9, with ratios of 0.56 and 0.44. Upper-middle-income countries, at 57, and high-income countries, at 10, are already below the threshold. Regions already under 70, among them East Asia and Pacific at 66 and Europe and Central Asia at 11, are classed as on track, although the East Asia and Pacific margin is narrow, with a projection of about 62.7 in 2030. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the better-placed regions: its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and the trend tool classes it as regression, with a projection of about 79.7 in 2030.

Inequality among countries has not narrowed. The Gini coefficient of the population-weighted distribution of country ratios rose from 0.628 in 2015 to 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.739 to 0.793. Differences between regions still account for 67.2% of the Theil index in 2023, down from 71.0% in 2015, so the burden remains largely a matter of which region a woman lives in, though within-region differences are gaining weight. The goal of a low global average is therefore inseparable from a distributional one: the ratio falls fastest where it is already low.

The ratios are modelled estimates, and in many high-burden countries they rest on little direct counting. Any projection to 2030 inherits that uncertainty, and the classification of a single country near the margin should be read with caution.

w-c04-5-1.text:
### Global consumption fell between 2015 and 2020

Global alcohol consumption per adult fell over the first five years of the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization estimate, carried in the World Development Indicators, puts total consumption at 5.9 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 and over in 2015. By 2020 it stood at 4.9 litres. The fall is about 1.0 litre, or roughly one sixth of the 2015 level, in five years. The measure sums recorded sales and an estimate of unrecorded alcohol, such as home production and informal trade, and is adjusted for tourist consumption.

Target 3.5 calls for strengthening the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including the harmful use of alcohol. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline year. The target can therefore be read in more than one way. One reading takes the wording to concern harm, which per capita volume captures only in part, since the same average can conceal heavy episodic drinking in a minority. Another reading treats volume as the best available proxy and counts a sustained decline as progress. This book adopts the second reading, because volume is the only alcohol series the shelf holds, and it states that choice openly. On that reading the world moved in the intended direction after 2015.

The series needs careful handling. The figures are projected estimates, not counts from a survey of drinkers in each year. Statisticians model them from sales, tax records, production data and occasional surveys, and then project forward where observations are thin. A smooth global path is therefore partly a product of the method, and a single year should not be read as a precise count. The final year, 2020, coincides with the first months of the pandemic, when closures of bars and restaurants, lost tourism and shifts in household purchasing altered both drinking and its measurement. Whether the 2020 figure reflects lasting change or a temporary disturbance cannot be settled from this series alone.

Coverage is nearly complete. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2020, 187 countries report in at least one year, and 185 report in 2020. The few countries that drop out in some years do not alter the global picture materially, though the estimates for those places are less secure. The world figure is thus a broad measure, and the sections that follow turn to the regions, income groups and countries that lie behind it.

### Regions differ widely in level and in direction

Regional levels span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia and North America sit at the top, with consumption of 8.9 litres per adult in Europe and Central Asia in 2020, down from 9.5 litres in 2015, and 9.9 litres in North America in 2020, up from 9.5 litres. North America is the only region in which the estimate rose, and the trend tool classes it as regression, with a rate of 0.0075 where the other regions show negative rates. Latin America and the Caribbean lies in the middle band, at 5.8 litres in 2020 against 6.5 litres in 2015. At the bottom, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan record about 0.3 litres in both years, 0.35 litres in 2015 and 0.32 litres in 2020. That figure reflects widespread abstention and legal restriction, and it is also a region in which unrecorded consumption is hardest to measure, so the level should be read with caution.

The largest regional fall is in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020. Its rate of -0.0657 is the steepest of any region and is classed as on track or target met. South Asia fell from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, at a rate of -0.0360, also classed on track. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0216, is placed in the same class. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0138, is classed as moderate progress, but acceleration needed, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0181, receives the same class even though its level is so low. These classes need a caveat: the Goals set no numerical target for alcohol under target 3.5, which asks only for strengthened prevention and treatment of harmful use. The classification therefore measures the direction and speed of change, and does not show whether a region has reached a safe or desired level.

The Sub-Saharan Africa figures in the summary are truncated and have been checked against the fact list before quotation. They show 4.6 litres in 2015 and 4.2 litres in 2020, a rate of -0.0211, classed on track. That is a fall of about half a litre, much smaller than in East Asia and Pacific.

The income groups show a similar divergence. High-income economies fell only from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a rate of -0.0075, classed as marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed. They remain the heaviest-drinking group and moved the least in proportion among the larger groups apart from low-income economies. The pattern matters because the largest reductions came where consumption was already moderate, while the highest levels fell slowly or rose. The period also spans 2020, when closure of bars and restricted travel altered recorded sales, and the projected estimates for that year rest partly on modelling, so part of the fall may not persist.

### Country trajectories split between steep falls and regression

The trend tool classifies 183 countries by their course towards a lower level of consumption. Target 3.5 sets no numerical goal for alcohol, so the classification measures direction and pace against a decrease by 2030, not distance from a stated threshold. That reading is one of several possible, and it should be borne in mind throughout.

The count of countries shows a divided picture. In 75 countries, holding 60.4% of the population of those assessed, consumption is on track or the target is met. A further 21 countries, with 11.0% of their population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 21, with 7.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. In 12 countries, with 3.1%, consumption stagnates. In 54 countries, with 18.2%, it is in regression, meaning that consumption per adult is rising against the desired direction.

The two ways of counting give different weights. Population weighting places most of the weight on a few very populous countries, so the global fall seen earlier depends heavily on the course taken by those countries. By number of countries, 75 of 183 are on track, which is well under half, while 54 are in regression, about three in ten. The population view looks more favourable than the country view because large countries have on balance moved downward, while many smaller ones have not. A reader should not take the 60.4% as a statement that most countries are succeeding.

The reasons for regression are not measured here, but well-established patterns offer a guide. Rising incomes, growing urban populations, expanding commercial marketing and weak taxation or licensing of alcohol have raised consumption in many middle-income settings. Where drinking is already high, fiscal measures, limits on availability and restrictions on advertising have helped to bring it down. Countries that began from very low levels, often for cultural or religious reasons, can show regression from a small base, so the class does not always signal a harmful level.

Coverage is nearly complete. Between 185 and 187 countries report in every year from 2000 to 2020, and 187 report in at least one year. The estimates are projected by the World Health Organization from survey and sales data, not counted directly, so country-level movements, above all for 2020, partly reflect modelling and not observed change. The classification should therefore be read as an indication of direction, not as a precise ranking.

### Change was not convergent and moved alike for men and women

Change between 2015 and 2020 was not convergent. Across 181 countries, a regression of five-year change on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00589, with a p-value of 0.603 and an R-squared of 0.012. The sign is negative, which would mean that countries with higher consumption fell slightly faster, but the coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the starting level explains about 1.2% of the variation in change. High-consumption countries did not systematically close the gap with low-consumption ones.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of consumption across countries rose from 0.722 in 2015 to 0.743 in 2020. The spread of national levels relative to their mean therefore widened slightly. Because the global average fell while dispersion rose, reductions were uneven in proportion: some countries fell sharply, some barely moved, and some rose, so that the distribution became a little more unequal in relative terms. The difference between the two coefficients is small, and a movement of two hundredths in a five-year window should not be read as a settled trend.

The second result concerns the sexes. Across 185 countries, the changes in male and female consumption between 2015 and 2020 are almost perfectly rank-correlated, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.993 and a Kendall coefficient of 0.937. The 2020 levels are nearly as closely aligned, at 0.990 and 0.923. Countries in which men reduced consumption most are, almost without exception, those in which women did so as well. Rank correlation says nothing about the absolute gap between men and women, which is large in nearly every country; it says only that the ordering of countries is shared.

Such a close match suggests that the drivers lie at national level rather than in behaviour specific to either sex. Excise duties and pricing, limits on availability and marketing, enforcement of drink-driving laws, changes in the informal market, and religious or social norms act on whole populations. The method also contributes. The figures are projected estimates, built from national sales, survey and modelling inputs, and the same adjustments to a country's total are likely to carry through to both sex-specific series. Part of the correlation may therefore be an artefact of estimation rather than a finding about behaviour.

No causal claim follows from these results. The window is five years, covers the disruption of 2020, and the lack of convergence is a description of the data rather than a verdict on any policy. What can be said is that national circumstances, not the starting level or the sex of the drinker, organised the change.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to a world that is moving in the right direction on alcohol, but not evenly and not everywhere. The global trend is classed as on track or target met, at a rate of -0.0363, yet that result rests on large falls in East Asia and Pacific and in upper middle income countries, where rates of -0.0657 and -0.0585 pull the aggregate down. Those falls are not matched in the places where consumption was already high. High-income countries show a rate of only -0.0075, classed as marginal progress, and North America moves the wrong way at 0.0075. Because the 2030 horizon is five years closer to the end than the 2020 data, the gap between regions that are on track and regions that are not will widen unless the pace changes.

The country count shows the same division. In 54 countries, holding 18.2% of the assessed population, consumption is regressing, and 12 more are stagnant. A further 21 countries show marginal progress and 21 moderate progress. Only 75 countries are on track, although they hold 60.4% of the population. The aggregate is therefore sensitive to a small number of populous countries, and a global verdict of progress can conceal widespread failure to reduce consumption elsewhere. Target 3.5 sets no numerical threshold, so these readings measure direction and pace, and a country may be classed as on track while still consuming heavily.

The absence of convergence matters for 2030. With a coefficient of -0.00589 and a p-value of 0.603, nothing in the data suggests that high-consumption countries are catching down of their own accord. Falls reflect specific policy, income and demographic circumstances, not a general pull towards a common level. Low-income countries, where consumption is lowest, show only marginal progress, and a rising tendency there as incomes grow remains a risk that the 2020 data cannot rule out. Projected estimates also carry uncertainty, and the 2020 value may reflect pandemic disruption to trade and sales.

w-c04-10-1.text:
### Global prevalence fell from 24.5 to 20.3 per cent of adults

Current tobacco use among adults fell from 24.5 per cent in 2015 to 20.3 per cent in 2024, a decline of about 4.3 percentage points over nine years. The indicator covers people aged 15 years and over who use any tobacco product, smoked or smokeless, on a daily or non-daily basis. Cigarettes, pipes, cigars, waterpipes, bidis, kretek, heated tobacco and oral and nasal products all count; e-cigarettes are excluded. The measure is therefore broader than cigarette smoking alone, and it should not be read as a count of smokers.

The evidence base is complete in form. All 166 countries report in every year listed, from 2000 to 2024, so the series has no gaps in coverage and the 2015 and 2024 values describe the same set of countries. That completeness needs a caution. Few countries survey tobacco use every year, and the annual values are modelled estimates built from periodic surveys, not direct annual counts. A smooth fall across nine years partly reflects the smoothing of the model, and the exact size of the change in any single country carries more uncertainty than the regular series suggests. The global figure is the more secure reading; year-to-year movements, including any change after 2020, are not well resolved.

The decline matters because tobacco is among the largest preventable causes of death from non-communicable disease, and the indicator is the only measure the World Bank holds for target 3.a, which concerns implementation of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. Prevalence is an outcome, not a measure of implementation. Taxation, smoke-free laws, packaging rules and advertising bans are the convention's instruments, and none is recorded in this series. A fall in prevalence is consistent with stronger implementation but does not prove it, since income growth, ageing and shifts in social attitudes also move use.

Target 3.a sets no numeric threshold and no end date. The trend tool's reading, which treats the aim as a decrease with no level to reach by 2030, is an interpretation and not a measured gap. Under that reading the world is moving in the right direction. Under a stricter reading, such as the voluntary global aim of a relative reduction in use set by the World Health Assembly, the same data would give a different verdict. The section that follows therefore describes direction and pace, and does not claim that a target has been met or missed.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than two and inequality has widened

In 2024 the regional averages ranged from 24.9 per cent of adults in Europe and Central Asia to 8.9 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa, a ratio of 2.79 between the highest and the lowest. South Asia stood at 23.6 per cent and East Asia and Pacific at 23.1 per cent, so three regions remained within two percentage points of one another near the top. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 18.9 per cent, North America 15.3 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 13.6 per cent. The low figure for Sub-Saharan Africa reflects, in part, a later and still incomplete spread of the cigarette market, and it should not be read as evidence of effective control. Regional averages also conceal countries that sit far from the mean.

The country-level classification against a 2030 decline shows how uneven the direction of travel is. Of 166 countries assessed, 72 were on track or had met the target, and they held 53.4 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 31 countries, with 12.3 per cent of that population, showed moderate progress that would need to accelerate. Another 26 countries, with 23.5 per cent, showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Eighteen countries, with 6.7 per cent, were stagnating, and 19, with 4.1 per cent, were regressing. The target text of 3.a sets no numerical goal, so the classification rests on a reading of a continuing decline by 2030; another reading, such as a fixed relative reduction, would sort some countries differently. On the reading used here, 94 countries fell short of being on track, and nearly half of the population is in countries that are not yet moving quickly enough.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, widened over the period. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.193 in 2015 to 0.203 in 2024, and the Theil index rose from 0.070 to 0.081. The rise is modest in absolute terms, but its direction is consistent across 2015, 2020 and 2024, and it occurred while the world average fell. Falling averages and widening dispersion together mean that the countries with the lowest prevalence tended to fall further, or the highest stayed high, so the gap between the best and worst performers grew.

The composition of that inequality has also shifted. The share of the Theil index explained by differences between regions fell from 65.8 per cent in 2015 to 57.9 per cent in 2024. Regional membership therefore explains less of the variation than before, and differences between countries within the same region account for a growing part. For policy this matters: regional averages and regional programmes are a weaker guide than they were, and attention to individual countries, particularly the stagnating and regressing ones inside regions that are otherwise improving, is increasingly needed to meet the aims of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control.

### Declines were steepest in South Asia and North America, and countries have not converged

The fastest declines in current tobacco use came in two very different settings. South Asia fell from 32.3 per cent of adults in 2015 to 23.6 per cent in 2024, the largest fall of any region, and its rate of change of -0.0343 a year is classed as on track. North America fell from 21.4 per cent to 15.3 per cent, at -0.0365 a year, the steepest rate of the regions. Latin America and the Caribbean (-0.0221) and the high-income group (-0.0220) sit close together at about -0.022 a year, while Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.0262), low-income countries (-0.0277) and lower-middle-income countries (-0.0322) also fall within the on-track band. The world as a whole, at -0.0210, is classed the same way.

Three groupings lag. East Asia and Pacific fell only from 25.3 per cent to 23.1 per cent, a rate of -0.0098 a year, which the trend tool reads as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region (-0.0119) and the upper-middle-income group (-0.0099) are read the same way, and Europe and Central Asia (-0.0141) is judged moderate progress needing acceleration. Target 3.a sets no numerical goal, so these classifications compare each rate with a generic path to 2030 and are not a verdict against a commitment. The wording of the target, which concerns implementation of the Framework Convention, can also be read as a measure of policy action rather than of prevalence, and the indicator captures only the latter.

Countries have not converged. Across 166 countries, the regression of change on starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00417 (p 0.112, R2 0.0208), so the sign is that of convergence but is not statistically distinguishable from no relationship, and starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.444 in 2015 to 0.507 in 2024, which means that dispersion across countries grew relative to the mean. Countries with low prevalence did not systematically fall further, while the mean itself fell, so the spread widened in relative terms.

Male and female trends move together. The Spearman correlation between country changes in male and female prevalence is 0.567, higher than the 0.416 between their 2024 levels. Countries where men reduced use tended to be those where women did, even though the gap in levels between the sexes is large and differs by country. This points to shared drivers, such as national tax and pricing policy, smoke-free laws, packaging rules and advertising restrictions, which reach both sexes, rather than sex-specific factors. The tools, however, identify no causes. They do not measure taxation, enforcement or the Convention itself, so attribution to any of them is not claimed here, and the correlation describes co-movement only.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The global decline is real, but it is uneven, and what 2030 holds depends on where the slowest movers sit. Target 3.a sets no numeric prevalence goal, so the trend tool reads progress against a decrease with no fixed end point. Under that reading the world's rate of change of -0.0210 a year is classed as on track or target met. The classification measures direction and pace, not arrival at any level of tobacco use that public health would accept, and a different reading of the target would give a different verdict.

The country count shows where attention is most needed. Of 166 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 53.4 per cent of the assessed population. The other 94 are not. Of these, 31 show moderate progress, 26 show marginal progress, 18 are stagnating and 19 are regressing. The 63 countries in the last three groups are the core of the difficulty. The marginal group is the largest by population, at 23.5 per cent, whereas the stagnating and regressing groups hold 6.7 per cent and 4.1 per cent. The problem is therefore both a large-country problem and a problem of many small ones.

Among regions, East Asia and Pacific, at -0.0098 a year, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0119, are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0141, needs acceleration of a lesser kind. The upper middle income group, at -0.0099, is also marginal. At these rates, prevalence in these groups will still be high in 2030, and they will pull the global average away from the faster regions. Convergence is absent: the beta of -0.00417 has a p-value of 0.112, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.444 to 0.507. The countries furthest behind are not catching up.

The following proposals for target 3.a answer these findings.
