w-c03-7-1.text:
### Consumer price inflation stands in for food prices

Target 2.c asks for measures that keep food commodity markets and their derivatives working properly and that give timely access to market information, including on food reserves, so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The target names no numerical threshold and no price index. Its indicator in the global framework is a food price anomalies measure, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold among the series available to this book. Volatility is therefore not measured here directly, and every statement in this section about prices is an indirect reading.

The nearest series is headline consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services for the average consumer. Food is one component of that basket, and its weight varies widely: it is large in low-income households and economies, and small in high-income ones. Headline inflation also contains energy, housing, transport and services. A rise in the headline rate can follow a fuel shock, a currency depreciation or a rent adjustment with food prices barely moving, and the reverse can occur when a harvest fails. The proxy captures the general price environment in which food is bought, and it does not isolate food. Readers should treat movements in it as a signal of pressure on household budgets, not as a record of food price swings.

Coverage shapes what can be said. In 2015, 189 countries reported consumer price inflation, and the same number reported in 2016. The count then drifted down, to 185 in 2017, 179 in 2020, 176 in 2024 and 169 in 2025. Across all years 193 countries reported at least once, so some economies have gaps in particular years. The fall since 2015 is not random in its likely effect: countries affected by conflict or weak statistical capacity are the ones most prone to interrupted reporting, and they are also where food insecurity is often most acute. The latest year, 2025, is the thinnest and may be revised as late submissions arrive. Comparisons across the period therefore rest on a changing set of countries, and the parts that follow rely on regional and world aggregates, which are less sensitive to the loss of single reporters.

### World inflation doubled between 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025, a little more than double the earlier rate. Both figures are annual percentage changes in the cost of a general basket of goods and services, so they describe the price level that households face and not the price of food alone. Food is a large part of that basket in poorer economies and a smaller part in richer ones, which means the world figure weights food unevenly and reads as a loose proxy for the target's concern.

The two endpoints conceal the path between them. A comparison of 2015 with 2025 does not show how far inflation fell or rose in the years between, and it should not be read as a steady climb. The period contains the weak price environment of the middle 2010s, the disruption of 2020 and the supply shocks that followed, and an endpoint comparison cannot separate these. What can be said is that the world rate ended the period well above where it began, and that volatility, which concerns movement from year to year, needs the intervening years to be judged. The present result reports levels only and offers no measure of that movement.

Low-income countries show a different pattern from the world as a whole. Their inflation was 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025, so it fell over the decade while the world rate rose. That fall should not be taken as relief. Low-income countries began from the highest rate of any income group in 2015, and they remain above the world rate in 2025. Households there spend the largest share of their budgets on food, so a given rate of general inflation weighs more heavily on them than on households in richer groups. The fall also reflects the particular economies that report, and coverage is not complete: 169 countries reported in 2025, against 189 in 2015, so part of the comparison rests on a smaller set of countries at the later date.

The finding matters for Goal 2 because food access depends on what a household can buy with its income, and persistent price growth erodes that. Yet the series cannot show whether food prices moved more or less than prices generally, nor whether any rise came from commodity markets, exchange rates, energy costs or domestic policy. Those causes bear on whether the measures named in target 2.c are working, and the data used here do not distinguish among them. The remaining parts of the section take up regional differences and the spread among countries.

### Regions began far apart and converged at a higher level

The regional picture in 2015 was one of wide separation. South Asia recorded consumer price inflation of 4.7% and Sub-Saharan Africa 3.5%, while Europe and Central Asia stood at 0.4% and North America at 0.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.8%, was also among the regions with very low rates. Latin America and the Caribbean (1.9%) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (1.7%) sat between the two groups. That spread reflected the commodity price slump of the middle of the decade, which pushed down prices most where energy and imported goods weigh heavily in the basket, together with structural differences in how far food supply shocks pass into the general price level.

By 2025 the spread had narrowed. South Asia fell to 3.1%, a decline of about 1.6 percentage points, and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged at 3.4%, against 3.5% in 2015. Europe and Central Asia moved furthest in the opposite direction, rising from 0.4% to 3.7%, which made it the region with the highest rate in the latest year. The rise there follows the energy and food price shocks that came with the war in Ukraine and the pandemic recovery, and the region includes both major grain exporters and large importers of energy. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1.7% to 2.0%. Movements in these three were modest, and all three ended 2025 close to one another at about 2%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024; its latest observation is for 2024, not 2025, so it is not strictly comparable in date with the other regions.

The pattern matters for Target 2.c because convergence here did not come from falling prices where they had been rising fastest. It came mostly from regions with low inflation catching up with those that had always been higher. In South Asia, lower inflation may reflect better monetary control and improved food stock management, though these series cannot show causes. Sub-Saharan Africa's flat line hides large differences between countries, and a regional aggregate cannot show how often households there met sharp food price spikes within single years. Readers should also bear in mind that all these figures are for general consumer prices, so they bound food price volatility only loosely. For 2030, the lesson is that exposure to price shocks has become more evenly spread across regions, and that no region now enjoys the near-zero inflation seen in 2015.

### Dispersion among countries widened after 2022

The spread of annual consumer price inflation among countries, weighted by population, was almost unchanged between 2015 and 2019 on the Gini measure, at 0.538 in 2015 and 0.537 in 2019. It narrowed to 0.511 in 2022, the year in which price pressures were felt in most economies at once, and then rose sharply to 0.660 in 2024. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the upper end of the distribution, tells the same story: 0.621 in 2015, 0.559 in 2022 and 0.982 in 2024. The 2024 values are the highest of the four years examined on both measures.

The composition of the inequality matters for interpretation. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015 and 38.4% in 2022, which fits a period in which regional averages moved apart in level before they converged. In 2024 the share fell to 35.2%, so that 64.8% of the Theil index lay within regions. The rise in dispersion after 2022 is therefore mainly a divergence among countries of the same region, not a return of the regional gaps of 2015. Some economies brought inflation down as monetary tightening and falling energy costs worked through, while others continued to face currency depreciation, fiscal strain or conflict, and their price rises stayed high. A regional average conceals this, and a policy aimed at a region as a whole would miss the countries where food price stress is most acute.

Three cautions apply. First, the number of countries in the calculation differs by year: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 sample is much smaller than the 189 countries that reported inflation that year, so part of the comparison with later years reflects who is included and not only how prices moved. Second, population weighting gives large economies great influence, and a change in one of them can shift the result. Third, the series measures general consumer prices, not food prices, so the dispersion shown is an indirect guide to uneven exposure to food price volatility. For 2030, the widening within regions suggests that the risk of extreme price swings will be concentrated in a minority of countries, and that monitoring needs to be national in its detail.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.c cannot be scored from these data. It sets no numerical threshold and can be read in two ways: as the proper functioning of commodity markets and the availability of market information, or as the narrower outcome of price stability. The series available measure the second reading only, and only indirectly, through general consumer prices. A rise in world inflation from 1.4% in 2015 to 3.0% in 2025 is consistent with greater price pressure on households, but it says nothing about whether markets, derivatives or reserve reporting function better or worse than before.

The pattern for 2030 is therefore one of uncertainty about direction. The regional gaps of 2015 have narrowed, and low-income economies, at 4.4% in 2025 against 5.5% in 2015, were the only income group whose inflation fell by much alongside South Asia. High-income economies moved from 0.3% to 2.3%. Yet the dispersion among countries, 0.660 on the Gini measure in 2024, shows that the average conceals a widening tail of economies with very high inflation. Those are the economies in which food price shocks do most harm to the poorest households, and they are also where reporting is weakest. Countries reporting inflation fell from 189 in 2015 to 169 in 2025, and the 2025 figure may be incomplete because of publication lags rather than permanent loss.

The proposals below follow from these limits. They aim to replace a proxy with measures that match the wording of the target, and to keep watch on the countries at the upper end of the distribution.

proposals: The bench's keepers should add a food consumer price index and a food reserve indicator to the shelf, so that Target 2.c can be read on food prices and not on general inflation. The World Bank and the FAO should publish both series by country.

Statistical offices and the IMF should report the dispersion of inflation across countries each year, population-weighted, alongside the world average, so that a widening upper tail is seen even when the mean is stable.

Donors and the IMF should give priority to statistical support for low-income countries whose price data are missing or late, since the falling number of reporting countries weakens the monitoring of price volatility where it matters most.

General consumer prices stand in for food prices, and the share of food in the basket differs between countries. The 2025 figures cover fewer countries than earlier years, and the series do not show volatility within a year.

w-c05-3-1.text:
### Pre-primary enrolment worldwide stood at 60.9 per cent in 2020

The gross pre-primary enrolment ratio for the world stood at 60.9 per cent in 2020, up from 56.0 per cent in 2015. The rise of about five percentage points over five years means that, on this measure, enrolment in organised learning before primary school expanded in the first half of the Sustainable Development Goals period, though it still left a large share of the youngest children without a place.

The measure needs careful reading. A gross enrolment ratio divides all children enrolled in pre-primary programmes, whatever their age, by the population of the age group that officially corresponds to that level. Children who are older or younger than the official age are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator. Late entrants, repeaters and children who start early can therefore push a ratio up without raising the share of children of the right age who take part. The figure is a measure of how much provision is in use relative to the size of the age group, and it is not the share of four- or five-year-olds attending. Where entry ages are loosely enforced, the gap between the two can be considerable. The official age range also differs between countries, which limits the comparability of the ratios.

Target 4.2 asks that all girls and boys have access to quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education so that they are ready for primary education. No threshold is attached to it in this indicator, and the wording can be read in at least three ways: as access to a place, as the quality of what is provided, or as the readiness of children when they reach grade 1. The series examined here measures only the first. It says nothing about whether the programmes are of good quality or whether children arrive at school prepared, so a rising ratio cannot be taken as proof that the target is being met in full.

The latest figures also carry a caution about timing. The ratio is available for 2020, but the reporting of countries fell sharply afterwards, to 71 in 2021 and 4 in 2022, so the world figure for 2020 is the last that rests on broad coverage. Statements about the period after 2020 must therefore be made with restraint.

### Regions differ by more than fifty percentage points

Regional levels in 2020 span a range of more than fifty percentage points. East Asia and Pacific recorded a gross pre-primary enrolment ratio of 83.2 per cent, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 78.3 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean at 75.6 per cent. North America stood at 70.3 per cent, which was barely above its 2015 level of 70.1 per cent. South Asia reached 62.0 per cent, up from 54.2 per cent in 2015, the largest gain among the regions after East Asia and Pacific. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 33.8 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa at 28.1 per cent. The gap between the highest and lowest regions is therefore about 55.1 percentage points.

The income groups tell the same story. Low-income countries reached 20.1 per cent in 2020, up from 17.4 per cent in 2015. That is the lowest level of any group in the data, and roughly one child in five of pre-primary age was enrolled. Because the ratio is gross, it counts all enrolled children regardless of age, so values can overstate participation of children of the official age where late entry is common. Conversely, differences in the official age range between countries mean that the ratios are not strictly comparable across borders.

Among countries, the dispersion narrowed. The population-weighted Gini coefficient of enrolment fell from 0.239 in 2015, across 164 countries, to 0.178 in 2019, across 147 countries. The Theil index fell from 0.117 to 0.065 over the same period. The narrowing is consistent with faster expansion where enrolment was lower, and with the large populous countries of South Asia and East Asia gaining ground. The change in the number of countries reporting means that the two years do not rest on exactly the same sample, so the fall should be read with caution.

The share of inequality lying between regions was 48.1 per cent in 2015 and 48.5 per cent in 2019. Region therefore accounts for close to half of the disparity both before and after the narrowing, and the remainder lies between countries within regions. Overall inequality fell, but its geographical structure did not change. Closing the gap requires attention both to the two lowest regions and to the wide differences within each region, since no regional average describes the position of every country in it.

### Progress was uneven and slowed after 2014

Progress between 2015 and 2020 was uneven, and the pace was slower than in the decade before. South Asia rose from 54.2 per cent in 2015 to 62.0 per cent in 2020, a gain of about eight points, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 74.8 per cent to 83.2 per cent, a gain of about eight and a half points. North America was almost flat, moving from 70.1 per cent to 70.3 per cent. High-income countries as a group gained 2.0 points, from 81.8 per cent to 83.8 per cent. Where enrolment was already high, growth was small; where it was low or middling, gains were larger, though from a lower base.

The long run of the world series shows why the overall picture is less encouraging than the regional gains suggest. A structural-break analysis of the annual change in the world ratio finds breaks in 2005 and 2014. The mean annual change was 0.68 points in 2001-2004, rose to 2.02 points in 2005-2013, and fell to 0.99 points in 2014-2020. The pace of expansion after 2014 was therefore less than half that of the preceding nine years. The analysis cannot say why. Pre-primary provision in many countries expanded quickly once governments added a year of schooling before grade 1, and such one-off expansions tend to slow once the easier gains are made; that is an explanation consistent with the pattern, not one the data demonstrate.

Convergence between countries was weak. Across 137 countries with data for 2015 to 2019, the coefficient linking initial level to subsequent growth was -0.017 (p 0.016), with an R2 of 0.047. The sign is negative, so countries starting lower tended to grow somewhat faster, but the fit is poor and explains under 5 per cent of the variation. The coefficient of variation of the ratio across countries fell only from 0.48 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2019. Gaps between countries are closing slowly, and most of the difference in growth is unrelated to where a country began.

These results must be read with care about coverage. The number of countries reporting fell from 164 in 2015 to 143 in 2020, and then to 71 in 2021 and 4 in 2022. The 2020 figures rest on fewer countries than those of 2015, and later years are too thin to support any regional or world estimate. The period after 2020 cannot be assessed from this series. Whether the pandemic closure of early childhood settings reduced enrolment, or whether reporting simply lagged, cannot be separated with these data. Any account of what happened after 2020 can therefore only be suggested, not shown.

### At current rates most children will not be reached by 2030, and proposals follow

The classification of countries by trend gives a sharper reading of the global average. Of 172 countries assessed, 57 are on track or have met the target direction, and they hold 38.4 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. A further 17 countries, with 7.0 per cent of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 12 countries, with 2.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Sixteen countries, with 11.4 per cent, are classed as stagnant. The largest class is regression, with 70 countries and 40.3 per cent of the population. Target 4.2 sets no numerical threshold for pre-primary enrolment, so the classes measure direction and pace, not distance from a defined goal, and the classification can be read in more than one way.

The regression class needs careful reading. The coverage record shows that 143 countries reported in 2020, 71 in 2021 and only 4 in 2022. Many countries therefore have no recent observation, and the comparison for them rests on earlier years. A fall may reflect school closures during the pandemic, revisions to population estimates, changes in the official age range for pre-primary education, or the loss of a data point, and not a real contraction in places. The count of 70 countries should be treated as an upper bound on true reversals, though it cannot be dismissed, since the closure of early childhood services after 2020 was widespread and these services were often among the last to reopen.

The regional results show where universal access remains distant. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced at a rate of 0.0196 and is classed as needing acceleration, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan advanced at 0.0165 with the same class. Both began from low levels and neither is near universal access. Low-income countries recorded the fastest rate, 0.0298, which is encouraging but starts from a small base, so even sustained pace leaves most young children in those countries outside organised learning in 2030. High-income countries and North America, by contrast, are classed as stagnant, which suggests that the ceiling of the gross ratio is being approached or that policy attention has moved elsewhere. At the global rate of 0.0169 the world will not reach universal participation by 2030.

Three proposals follow. National statistical offices and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should report age-appropriate net participation rates in the year before primary entry, because a gross ratio counts children of any age and can exceed what it is meant to show. Ministries of education and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should restore national reporting after 2020, so that the 2021 and 2022 gaps are closed and regression can be told apart from missing data. Donors and development banks should direct support for early childhood places and trained staff to low-income countries and to Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where access is lowest.

w-c06-3-1.text:
### The global level in 2022

In 2022, 19.5% of women aged 20-24 worldwide had been first married by age 18. The indicator, which the World Bank carries from UNICEF and the Demographic and Health Surveys, counts women in that age band who were married or in union before their eighteenth birthday. The age band is chosen deliberately: women aged 20-24 have all passed the threshold, so the share records a completed experience rather than a risk still running, and it reflects marriages that took place in roughly the preceding decade. Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage, and this share is the measure by which progress towards it is read.

The world figure should be read as a modelled estimate, not as a count. No agency surveys every woman in every country each year. Household surveys are fielded in a given country once every few years, and the aggregate is built from those surveys, carried forward and combined with population weights. The value for 2022 therefore describes the best available picture of that year, and it rests on a much smaller set of direct observations than the single number suggests. The summary also shows the same value, 19.5%, as both its start and its end. This is not a sign of stagnation. Only one year, 2022, is reported for the world aggregate in the summary, so no change over time can be drawn from it, and any claim about movement since 2015 or since 2020 has to be made from other evidence.

The sparseness is visible in the reporting itself. Over the whole series, 145 countries have reported a value in at least one year, yet in any single year only a fraction of them do. The most recent year in the shelf, 2025, holds observations from just 3 countries, which is too few to say anything about the present beyond what the aggregates carry. The latest year with a full set of aggregates is 2022, and it is the reference point for the rest of this section.

The figure matters because early marriage is closely tied to the other outcomes of this chapter. A girl married before 18 is more likely to leave school, to bear children early and to face violence at home, and she has less say over her own health and finances. A level of 19.5% means that about one young woman in five began adult life in that position. The sections that follow set this global value against regional and income differences, the spread among countries, and the pace required to reach 2030.

### Regional and income differences

Regional averages for 2022 show a wide spread behind the world figure of 19.5%. East Asia and Pacific stands lowest, at 5.6% of women aged 20-24 first married by age 18. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan follow at 17.7%, a little below the world level. South Asia reaches 25.6%, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest at 31.1%. Sub-Saharan Africa's share is therefore more than five times that of East Asia and Pacific, a ratio of 5.60.

The regional grouping used here is not the one found in every United Nations or World Bank publication. It joins the Middle East and North Africa with Afghanistan and Pakistan, two countries that other conventions place in South Asia. A comparison with figures published under a different grouping may therefore differ, and the South Asian and Middle Eastern values should be read as belonging to this arrangement only. Regional values are also summaries of countries with very different populations and survey dates, so a single regional share can hide sharp contrasts within it.

Income groups tell a similar story. Lower middle income economies stand at 24.4%, against 8.5% for upper middle income economies, a ratio of 2.89. Child marriage thus falls steeply as income rises, which accords with well-established knowledge: poverty, limited schooling for girls, rural residence and weak enforcement of minimum-age laws sustain early marriage, while longer schooling and wider paid work for women delay it. Income is not the whole account, however, since South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa differ in norms, in the role of dowry and bride price, and in the reach of legal reform.

No figure for high income or low income economies is shown in these results. The absence matters: the lower middle income group lies below the poorest countries, which are likely to record higher levels, and the gradient across the full income range cannot be stated from this evidence. The comparison offered here covers the middle of the distribution, and the gaps at both ends limit what can be concluded about where the practice is most concentrated.

### Inequality among countries and the thin evidence

Inequality among countries in the share of women first married by age 18 appears to have narrowed between 2012 and 2018, though the evidence for the comparison is thin. The population-weighted Gini coefficient across reporting countries stood at 0.282 in 2012, when 21 countries had data, and at 0.273 in 2018, when 20 did. The Theil index fell further, from 0.156 to 0.120. The coefficient of variation, which is more sensitive to the highest values, fell from 0.63 to 0.49. All three measures point the same way: countries with data were closer together in 2018 than in 2012.

The composition of the remaining inequality changed more than its size. The share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 73.0% in 2012 to 89.8% in 2018. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the total, and what separates countries is increasingly the region in which they sit. This is consistent with national declines in countries that began from middling levels, while the regions with the highest prevalence stayed distinct from the rest. For policy, the implication is that regional programmes and regional political commitments carry more weight than they did, and that a global average conceals a divide that is now chiefly geographic.

These readings must be held loosely, because the surveys that feed the indicator are irregular. Household surveys are fielded in each country every few years, so the set of countries reporting changes from one year to the next. Counts range from 5 countries in 2002 and 6 in 2001 to 21 in 2012 and 20 in 2018. Since 2015 the count has run from 11 in 2015 and 2017 to 18 in 2022, with 12 in 2020 and 12 in 2024. In 2025 only 3 countries report, which leaves that year unusable for any comparison. In all, 145 countries have a value in at least one year, but no more than 21 have a value in any single one.

The 2012 and 2018 comparison therefore rests on two different sets of countries, and a fall in the Gini or Theil index may reflect who was surveyed as much as what changed. Neither year allows a clean reading of the effect of the 2015 adoption of the goals or of the disruption after 2020, since the years in between draw on still other country sets. The inequality findings show a plausible direction of travel, not a measured trajectory, and they cannot be extended to countries that were not surveyed.

### Pace against the 2030 target

Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of harmful practices, including child, early and forced marriage, but its text names no numerical threshold. The most direct reading is a rate of zero by 2030. Others are possible: a large fall from a baseline, or convergence on the level of the best-performing regions. The trend assessment adopts the first reading, a target of 0.0% by 2030, and measures each country's recent pace against the pace that reading requires.

Of the 20 countries with enough observations to be classified, none is on track or has met the target. Two show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed there too; they hold 5.8% of the population of the assessed countries. Fourteen show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, and these hold 91.8% of that population. One country is stagnant, and three are regressing. The assessed countries are therefore overwhelmingly ones in which the share is falling too slowly to reach zero, and the few that are moving in the wrong direction are small in population terms.

The classification covers 20 countries out of 145 that have reported at some point. Countries are classed only where repeated surveys allow a trend to be drawn, and survey rounds arrive unevenly: 11 countries reported in 2015, 12 in 2020 and 3 in 2025. The 2025 count reflects data not yet published rather than an absence of marriages. For this reason the pace assessment cannot say how the practice changed after 2015 or after 2020 for most countries. Whether the disruption of schooling, health services and household incomes during the pandemic raised early marriage is a question that the thin post-2020 series cannot settle, though the mechanisms are well established and the risk is widely noted.

What this implies for 2030 is plain. With 91.8% of the assessed population in the marginal class, the world will not reach zero by 2030 on current trends. The regional levels shown earlier, 25.6% in South Asia and 31.1% in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2022, indicate where most of the remaining gap lies. Falls in marriage before 18 have historically followed longer schooling for girls, enforcement of a minimum legal age, and rising household incomes. These change slowly, and acceleration of the scale required would need all three to improve at once.

The proposals that follow from these findings are set out below.

w-c02-2-1.text:
### National poverty lines give the widest view, with uneven reporting

The national-line headcount ratio is the percentage of a population living below the poverty line or lines that a country sets for itself. It is the measure closest to the wording of target 1.2, which asks for a halving of poverty in all its dimensions according to national definitions. Because each country chooses its own line, and often revises it, the series records how each society judges deprivation rather than a single standard. Estimates come from household surveys, and for economies using EU-SILC the reported year is the income reference year, the year before the survey. Alongside it, the World Bank publishes multidimensional, societal-line and $3.00-a-day series, which later parts of this section set against the national figures.

The series is wide in reach but irregular in time. Over the whole period 161 countries have reported at least one national-line observation, which is a broad base for a goal that applies everywhere. In any single year, however, only a fraction report. In 2000 the number of countries with a value was 16, and in 2001 it was 15. It rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, then held between 40 and 50 through 2008 to 2014, with 40 in 2008 and 50 in 2012. The expansion reflects the spread of regular household surveys in low- and middle-income countries during the 2000s, and the inclusion of high-income economies whose poverty lines are drawn from standing statistical programmes.

After the adoption of the goals in 2015, reporting grew rather than shrank. In 2015 55 countries had a value, and 57 in 2016, followed by 53 in 2017. Counts then reached 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. The year 2020, the first of the pandemic, shows 57 countries, a fall from 2019 that is consistent with disrupted fieldwork, although the data alone cannot show the cause. The peak is 72 countries in 2021. That figure should not be read as recovery in survey activity alone: some surveys collected in 2020 are dated to the following income reference year, and the lag in EU-SILC dating is one reason.

The decline since then is steep. Reporting was 52 countries in 2022, 40 in 2023 and 31 in 2024, and in 2025 it is only 13. The fall does not mean that poverty has been abolished or that surveys have stopped. Household survey data take a year or more to be collected, cleaned, harmonised and released, and the national-line series is revised as new rounds arrive. The latest years are therefore incomplete, and the count for 2025 is best treated as a record of what has been published so far.

The consequence is practical. A comparison of 2025 with 2015 would rest on 13 countries against 55, which are not the same countries and may not be representative of any region. Any statement about movement toward 2030 has to use the last years of reasonable coverage, up to about 2021 or 2022, and has to separate real change from changes in who reports. The figure on levels in 2025 is shown for completeness, but its thin base calls for caution in every reading drawn from it.

### Dispersion among countries widened as coverage grew

The dispersion of national-line poverty rates among countries, weighted by population, rose steadily after 2013. The Gini coefficient across reporting countries stood at 0.28 in 2013 and 0.34 in 2014, then passed 0.39 in 2015, the year the goals took effect. It reached 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018 and 0.63 in 2019. The Theil index followed the same course, from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.26 in 2015 and 0.72 in 2019. Read at face value, the spread among countries in the share of people below their own lines more than doubled in six years, with a handful of countries holding very large populations at rates far from the rest.

This reading needs care, because the set of reporting countries changed at the same time. The number of countries with a national-line estimate was 45 in 2013, 55 in 2015, 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. A rise in the Gini or Theil can reflect poverty rates pulling apart, but it can equally reflect the arrival of countries with very high or very low rates, or the loss of countries that sat in the middle. The series cannot separate these effects, and the figures should not be read as a measured change in inequality between countries over a fixed group. The record for 2019 is also truncated, so the 2019 reading is flagged and should be treated as provisional. For 2020 the Gini is given as 0.66 across 57 countries, but no Theil index or regional decomposition is available, so that year cannot be compared in full with its neighbours.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions is high throughout, which indicates that most of the dispersion reflects differences between regional groups rather than differences within them. It was 75.8% in 2013, 88.4% in 2014 and 67.7% in 2015, then 80.7% in 2016, 65.1% in 2017, 86.3% in 2018 and 77.1% in 2019. The swings from year to year are themselves a sign of a changing sample, since adding or dropping a few populous countries in one region moves the between-region share sharply. The persistent finding is that where a country lives, in regional terms, explains most of the gap in national poverty rates, and national lines tend to be set higher in richer regions, which complicates any comparison of levels.

After 2020 the picture changes. The Gini fell to 0.35 in 2021, when 72 countries reported, the widest coverage of any year in the record. It then stood at 0.40 in 2022 with 52 countries, 0.35 in 2023 with 40 countries and 0.32 in 2024 with 31 countries. The Theil index moved from 0.20 in 2021 to 0.26 in 2022, 0.21 in 2023 and 0.17 in 2024. The between-region share was 82.6% in 2021, 88.5% in 2022, 76.0% in 2023 and 83.5% in 2024. The drop in dispersion from 2019 to 2021 coincides with a large change in the reporting set, and cannot be taken as convergence. The shrinking counts after 2021 reflect the lag with which household surveys are processed and published, so the most recent years describe a thinner and different group of countries.

For 2030 the implication is that national-line data can show whether a given country is halving its own poverty rate, but cannot support a claim about convergence or divergence across the world. Any assessment of target 1.2 should be made country by country, over a fixed set of economies with repeated surveys, and should treat the dispersion statistics as a description of who reports in each year rather than of how poverty is distributed.

### Trend classes show most countries on track but a large regressing group

The classification covers 94 countries, those for which the national-line series holds enough observations to estimate a trend. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 3.8% of the population, and 7 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 4.4%. Five countries are stagnant, with 2.1% of the population. The largest adverse group is regression: 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population. Regression is therefore not a marginal finding. Over a third of the assessed countries, holding about a quarter of the assessed population, record national poverty rates that are rising rather than falling.

The weight of the favourable class comes from population rather than from numbers alone. On track countries are 44% of those assessed by count, yet they hold nearly two thirds of the population. This means a few very populous countries with steady declines dominate the population share, while the regressing class is made up of many countries of varied size. A reader should not infer that two thirds of countries are succeeding; the count and the population share tell different stories, and both are given here.

No numeric target exists for national lines. Target 1.2 asks for a halving of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions, but it names no common threshold, because each country sets its own line in its own currency and with its own method. The classes therefore rest on a reading of the target, not on a fixed value. Under the halving reading, a country is on track if its rate is falling fast enough to be halved from its starting level by 2030. That is one reading among several. A target could instead be read as an absolute reduction in the number of people, as a reduction of a set number of points, or as a halving of rates from the 2015 level rather than from the earliest available observation. Each reading would sort some countries differently, and the starting year of each country's series matters, since the observations differ in date and spacing.

Several cautions follow. A country that revises its line, as many do when consumption patterns or price levels change, can show a break in the series that looks like progress or regression though living standards did not move in that way. A country that already has a low rate can be classed as regressing after a small rise, while a country with a very high rate may be classed as on track after a modest fall. The classes describe the direction and pace of each national series against the halving reading; they do not rank the level of deprivation among countries, and a country on track under its own line may still hold more poor people than one in regression under a stricter line.

The classification also covers only the countries with a usable trend, which leaves out many that report rarely. Where surveys are infrequent, the trend rests on few points, and the class can change with one new survey. This is a limit of the evidence, and the later comparison with the international line tests how far these national readings hold when a single common measure is applied.

For 2030, the split carries a clear message. The countries on track account for most of the population, so the aggregate picture can look favourable, while a quarter of the assessed population lives in countries where the national measure has moved the wrong way. Reaching the halving reading for the world as a whole would require the regressing and slow groups to reverse course, since the on track group has little left to add to the total.

### National and international lines agree on direction but not fully on size, and the implication for 2030

National and international lines can be set side by side for 36 countries between 2015 and 2021. The comparison pairs the national-line headcount with the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Across these countries the rank correlation of 2021 levels is 0.72 (Spearman), and the Kendall measure of the same levels is 0.58. The rank correlation of changes between 2015 and 2021 is lower, at 0.53, with a Kendall value of 0.41.

The two results say different things. A country with a high national rate generally also has a high international rate, so the two lines rank societies in a broadly similar order. Agreement on direction of change is weaker. A country can see its national rate fall while the international rate barely moves, or the reverse, because the two lines sit at different points of the income distribution and are adjusted by different rules. National lines are typically revised for prices and consumption patterns, and many are set well above the international line in richer economies and close to it in the poorest. A rise in living costs, a change in survey design or a revision of the basket can move one measure and leave the other untouched. The correlation of changes should therefore be read as a moderate link, not as proof that the two measures can be substituted for one another. Only 36 countries qualify, a small part of the 161 that report a national rate in at least one year, so the finding cannot be extended to all countries without caution.

For the 2030 halving in target 1.2, the implications are mixed. The trend classification shows that 41 of the 94 assessed countries are on track or have met the target, with 63.8% of the assessed population. Yet 34 countries are regressing, holding 26.0% of that population. The weaker agreement on change means that a country judged on track at its national line cannot be assumed to be gaining at the international line, and the reverse also holds. The target is also open to more than one reading. Halving may be measured against a country's own 2015 rate or against a baseline year that varies by country, and a revised national line breaks the series on which either reading depends. The aggregate verdict on 2030 is therefore less secure than the country counts suggest. A large regressing group and uneven reporting make it unlikely that the halving will be achieved across the whole population, even if many individual countries meet it.

The evidence has clear limits. Reporting is uneven: 72 countries reported a national rate for 2021, the peak, but 52 did so for 2022, 40 for 2023, 31 for 2024 and 13 for 2025. Recent years are thin, so the effects after 2020 are seen only in part. Country lines differ in definition and in the date of last revision, and the series does not record why a line was changed. The paired comparison rests on 36 countries. Poverty in all its dimensions is only partly captured by a headcount, and the poverty gap and multidimensional measures are not tested here against national lines.

w-c02-6-1.text:
### Health and education budgets claim stable but modest shares of spending

Government budgets show a stable but modest commitment to the services that bear most directly on poverty. Education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in the world in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, a fall of under a fifth of a percentage point over eight years. The aggregate hides little movement because large regional shifts in opposite directions offset one another, and because the series for the latest years rests on partial reporting. For 2025, only 60 countries had reported, so the most recent observations describe a subset and not the world.

Health is harder to summarise. The health series, domestic general government health expenditure as a share of general government expenditure, is reported by region and income group in this bench, and no world figure is given. Coverage in the latest year is thin: only 7 countries had reported for 2024, so the final year of the series cannot support any statement. The most recent usable readings fall between 2017 and 2023, depending on the group. Comparisons across groups therefore mix end years, and the reader should treat them as indicative of direction and scale, not as a common-year ranking.

Social protection is the third essential service named in the section's question, and no result for its share of public spending is available in this bench. The coverage and benefit-incidence series of the ASPIRE database describe who is reached, not how much governments spend, and they are treated in another section of the chapter. A statement on the budget share for social protection cannot be made here, and the absence should not be read as a low or a high figure.

The targets add a further limit to interpretation. Target 1.a calls for significant mobilisation of resources and for adequate and predictable means, and target 1.b calls for sound policy frameworks that support accelerated investment in poverty eradication. Neither sets a numerical threshold, a base year or a required share of spending. Any classification of progress as on track or off track therefore rests on direction alone: an increase in the share is read as movement towards the target, and a decrease as movement away from it. That reading is open to challenge, since a share of expenditure can fall while the absolute amount rises with growth, and since a share can rise because other spending is cut. The figures that follow are best read with those cautions in mind.

### Regions and income groups differ widely in health priority

Health receives very different priority across regions and income groups. North America devoted 22.1 per cent of general government expenditure to health from domestic sources in 2015 and 22.8 per cent in 2023, the highest share of any region reported. Europe and Central Asia stood at 15.0 per cent in 2015 and 14.5 per cent in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 11.5 per cent to 11.8 per cent over the same years. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2019, the last year in the series. South Asia began far lower, at 3.7 per cent in 2015, and reached 4.8 per cent in 2022. That is the largest proportional gain among the regions shown, yet the region still allocates less than half the share of Europe and Central Asia.

The income groups repeat the pattern. High-income economies assigned 17.9 per cent in 2015 and 18.5 per cent in 2023. Low-income economies assigned 5.4 per cent in 2015 and 5.3 per cent in 2017, and lower-middle-income economies 4.8 per cent in 2015 and 4.7 per cent in 2018. The gap between rich and poor countries is therefore roughly three to one in the share of the budget, before any account is taken of the far smaller budgets that the shares are applied to. A poor country that gives a small share of a small budget to health leaves households to meet the difference from their own pockets, which is a direct route into impoverishment.

These comparisons carry a caveat. The series do not end in the same year: the low-income and lower-middle-income series stop in 2017 and 2018, and the Sub-Saharan African series in 2019, so none of them can show what followed the pandemic of 2020 or the debt pressures that came after. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024 at the time of the data, so the latest year is not yet a basis for comparison. A gap measured in earlier years for the poorest groups may since have narrowed or widened, and the data cannot say which.

Education shares show a different ordering. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 15.4 per cent in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 16.6 per cent in 2024, give education the largest shares of their budgets, while North America gave 10.7 per cent in 2022, down from 12.9 per cent in 2015. Poorer regions thus tend to put more of their budgets into schooling than into health, and richer regions the reverse. The share is a measure of priority, not of adequacy, because a large share of a small budget may still buy little per pupil.

### Education shares fell in most countries while inequality in spending widened

Since 2015 the education share of public budgets has weakened in most countries. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are classed as in regression, and these hold 78.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 29 countries, with 7.1 per cent of that population, are on track or have met the direction of travel. A further 13 countries (1.8 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 12 (2.3 per cent) marginal progress and 23 (10.5 per cent) stagnation. No numerical target exists for these indicators, so the classes measure movement towards an increase and not distance from an agreed level. An increase is itself only one reading of progress, since a falling share can accompany rising total budgets or a growing economy.

The population weighting explains why the picture is so unfavourable. The regressing group contains very populous countries. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent of government expenditure in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in the latest year reported, and South Asia from 13.9 per cent to 11.3 per cent. North America also declined. Competing claims on budgets, such as debt service, pensions, health and the fiscal pressure that followed the pandemic after 2020, are well-established pressures on education shares, although these data do not identify which of them operated in any given country.

Spending relative to national income shows a different problem, that of divergence. Across 164 countries, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of education spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.101, an increase of more than half. The between-region share of that Theil index moved from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent. Regional differences therefore account for under a quarter of the inequality in both years, and the widening came mainly from differences among countries within regions. Regional averages thus conceal the divergence, and policies aimed at whole regions would miss most of it.

Health presents a more favourable record. Of 193 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the direction of travel, holding 40.8 per cent of their population, while 61 are in regression, holding 21.3 per cent. Another 30 countries (22.1 per cent of the population) show marginal progress, 19 (11.5 per cent) stagnation and 11 (4.3 per cent) moderate progress. The experience of the pandemic, which raised the political priority of health budgets, is a plausible contributor, but the series cannot confirm it.

The two shares do not move together. The Spearman correlation between changes in the health share and the education share across 129 countries is 0.16, and between their 2022 levels 0.09. Countries that raised one share were therefore hardly more likely to raise the other, and no common cause, whether fiscal capacity or shared priorities, is shown. Neither is a trade-off between them shown. Governments appear to set the two priorities largely independently, so that a gain in health has not generally been paid for by a loss in education, and the weakening of education shares needs its own explanation in each country.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Spending shares carry no numerical target under targets 1.a and 1.b, so progress can be judged only by direction. The trend classes used here ask whether a share is rising, which is a weak test. A country may be on track while spending too little, and another in regression while spending generously. The classes should be read as signals of priority, not as verdicts on adequacy, and the target wording could be read as concerning domestic budgets, development cooperation, or both. The series examined cover domestic budgets only.

On this reading health is nearer to progress than education. For the domestic health share, 72 of 193 countries assessed are on track or have met the direction of travel, holding 40.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Regression affects 61 countries, with 21.3 per cent of that population, and stagnation 19 countries, with 11.5 per cent. The expansion of public health budgets after 2020 reflects emergency responses to the pandemic, and whether they persist as fiscal pressure from debt service grows is not yet settled by the data. For education the pattern is the reverse: 110 of 187 countries are in regression, with 78.2 per cent of the population, against 29 on track with 7.1 per cent. Because the regression class includes the most populous countries, a few budget decisions shape the outcome for most of the world's children.

The outlook for 2030 is therefore uneven. Health shares may continue to rise in a large group of countries, but a fifth of the population lives where they are falling. Education shares are falling where most people live, while the spread of spending as a share of GDP widened between 2015 and 2022, with the Gini coefficient rising from 0.181 to 0.223 across 164 countries. The between-region share of inequality in that spending eased from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent, which implies that the widening occurred mostly within regions. Regional averages alone would conceal it.

Two limits qualify every reading. Spending data for low-income countries often end years before the latest reporting year, so the most recent shifts there are unseen. Social protection spending is not measured in this section, and the budget lines for it are not comparable across the series examined.

w-c04-11-1.text:
### Immunisation and maternal and child services are largely flat at the global level

The nearest measure the shelf holds for immunisation and related services is the universal health coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health. It combines four tracer indicators: family planning, pregnancy care, child immunisation and child treatment. It is scored from 0 to 100 index points. It is not a direct measure of vaccine coverage, because immunisation is only one of the four components. A movement in the index may therefore reflect changes in family planning or in the treatment of childhood illness rather than in vaccination. The reading offered here is of service coverage in general, with immunisation as one part of it.

Target 3.b can also be read in more than one way. It concerns research and development, access to affordable essential medicines and vaccines, and the terms of the Doha Declaration. Coverage of services is an outcome of access, not a measure of research effort or of the price of medicines. The index speaks to access only in part, and the other elements of the target are not captured by any series held here.

At the global level the index stood at 73 index points in 2015 and 72 in 2023, a regression at a rate of -0.0017 in the trend classification. A world that was expected to advance towards fuller coverage has, on this measure, slipped slightly. The figure is an average across very different countries, and the change is small. Its significance lies in what it fails to show: there is no sign of the steady gain that a fifteen-year agenda implies.

Most regions are flat. East Asia & Pacific stood at 85 in both 2015 and 2023, and Latin America & Caribbean at 78 in both years. High income countries, North America and upper middle income countries are likewise classified as stagnating, with a rate of zero. Europe & Central Asia moved from 80 to 82, a rate of 0.0031, which is still classed as stagnation. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region held at 66. Stagnation at high levels, as in East Asia & Pacific and North America, is less troubling than stagnation at lower levels, since there is less room for gain. It still means that the remaining gaps in these regions are not closing.

The worst movements are in the middle of the income range. The lower middle income group fell from 68 to 66, a rate of -0.0037, and South Asia from 72 to 69, a rate of -0.0053. Both are classed as regression. Disruption to routine services during the pandemic after 2020 is a well-established cause of lost coverage in many countries, and populous countries in these groups weigh heavily in the averages. The data here do not separate the period before 2020 from the period after, so the share of the fall due to the pandemic cannot be stated from these results.

Low income countries stood at 51 in both years, far below every other group, and a rate of zero places them in stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa is the only region with a gain, from 49 to 53, a rate of 0.0099. It is classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. The gain is real but starts from the lowest base, and the region remains well below the 66 of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region.

The country classification confirms the pattern. Of 193 countries assessed, 11 are on track or have met the target, holding 5.0% of the population of the countries assessed. Another 9, with 3.1% of the population, show moderate progress needing acceleration. A further 37 countries, with 14.4%, show marginal progress. Stagnation covers 105 countries and 48.1% of the population, and regression 31 countries and 29.5%. The index carries no fixed 2030 target, so the classes rest on the direction of travel and not on a stated goal. Taken together, nearly four in five people live in countries that are flat or sliding, which makes a general recovery in service coverage by 2030 unlikely without a clear change of course.

### Health spending has risen in dollar terms but barely as a share of output

Domestic general government health expenditure per capita rose from 589.2 current US dollars in 2015 to 803.7 in 2023 for the world as a whole. In dollar terms this is a substantial increase. Current dollars include price changes, however, and the series is not adjusted for inflation or for population structure, so part of the rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger volume of care. The movement also says nothing about how the money was used.

Measured against output, the picture is much flatter. Current health expenditure was 9.7 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2023. Spending has therefore grown roughly in step with the economies that carry it. A rising dollar figure alongside a stable share means that health has held its place in national budgets and household outlays but has not gained priority. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, and a global share that moves by less than half a percentage point over eight years cannot be read as that kind of increase. The share also includes private and external spending, while the per capita series covers only domestic government spending, so the two series measure different things and are not directly comparable.

The global averages conceal a division by income. In high-income countries the share of GDP rose from 12.0 per cent to 12.5 per cent, and in upper middle income countries from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent. In lower middle income countries it fell from 3.9 per cent to 3.7 per cent, and in low income countries from 5.4 per cent to 4.6 per cent. The fall among the poorest is the opposite of what target 3.c requires. A falling share in low income countries may partly reflect faster growth in other parts of the economy, a drop in external funding or the effects of debt and conflict, and the data alone do not separate these causes.

Regional shares tell a similar story. North America stood at 16.0 per cent in 2015 and 16.3 per cent in 2023. South Asia declined from 3.5 per cent to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent in both years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 5.4 per cent to 5.3 per cent. Only East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean moved up, and by small margins.

The period after 2020 matters for interpretation. The pandemic raised health spending in many countries and depressed GDP in the same years, which lifts the share temporarily. The 2023 values are therefore not a clean continuation of the pre-2020 path. Coverage of the latest year is also thin: only 22 countries reported the share for 2024, and only 7 reported domestic government spending per capita, so 2023 is the last year that supports regional comparison.

For 2030, a financing share that has hardly moved offers little ground for expecting a step change. Without a deliberate rise in public priority, the countries with the least spending will remain far from the resources that basic services need.

### Regions and countries differ by orders of magnitude

North America spent 6,959.0 current US dollars per head of domestic government money on health in 2023, against 30.8 dollars in South Asia and 31.7 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa. The ratio between the top and the bottom is therefore above 200 to one. Europe and Central Asia stood at 2,178.0 dollars, East Asia and Pacific at 571.7 dollars, Latin America and the Caribbean at 415.7 dollars, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 190.2 dollars. By income group the gradient is as steep: high-income countries spent 3,847.3 dollars, upper middle income countries 338.9 dollars, lower middle income countries 30.9 dollars and low-income countries 7.3 dollars. These are current dollars at market exchange rates, so they understate what a dollar buys in poorer countries, where wages and many services cost less. Even so, no plausible adjustment closes a gap of this size.

The movement since 2015 widens the distance in absolute terms. North America added roughly 2,372 dollars per head between 2015 and 2023, from 4,587.0 dollars, while Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 29.7 to 31.7 dollars and low-income countries from 7.0 to 7.3 dollars. South Asia is the exception among the poorer regions: its figure roughly doubled, from 14.7 to 30.8 dollars, though from a very small base. The pattern is one of growth proportional to the starting level in the richer groups and near-stillness at the bottom. Rapid population growth in low-income countries also means that any flat per-capita figure conceals a rising national outlay that is merely keeping pace with numbers of people.

The share of output spent on health shows a different and more troubling picture for the poorest. Low-income countries fell from 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 4.6 per cent in 2023, and lower middle income countries from 3.9 to 3.7 per cent. High-income countries rose from 12.0 to 12.5 per cent and upper middle income countries from 5.5 to 6.0 per cent. South Asia slipped from 3.5 to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed. On this measure the poorest groups moved in the opposite direction. The causes are well established: weak tax collection, heavy debt service, and the pressure that the pandemic and the following price rises placed on public budgets. Because the indicator covers all current health spending, including private and external sources, a fall also suggests that donor and household money did not compensate for limited public funds. The latest year is also thinly reported: only 22 countries had a 2024 value for the share of GDP and 7 for domestic government spending per head, so regional figures for 2023 rest on estimates that may be revised.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the regional averages. For domestic government health spending per head, 142 of the 193 countries assessed were on track or had met the direction of travel, holding 80.1 per cent of their combined population. A further 12 countries showed moderate progress needing acceleration, with 4.5 per cent of the population, and 2 showed marginal progress. Three were stagnant and 34 were in regression, those 34 holding 14.0 per cent of the population. No target value is set for this series, so the classes describe the direction and pace of change rather than distance from a numerical goal, and the reading of what counts as on track rests on the tool's own convention. Rising dollar spending in most countries therefore coexists with a sizeable minority of countries, and of people, where it fell.

The service coverage sub-index tells a flatter story. Of the 193 countries, only 11 were on track or had met the target, holding 5.0 per cent of the population, and 9 showed moderate progress, with 3.1 per cent. Marginal progress covered 37 countries and 14.4 per cent of the population. Stagnation covered 105 countries and 48.1 per cent, and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. Nearly four in five people live in a country where coverage of these services stood still or fell. The regression class is large in population because it includes populous countries in South Asia and the lower middle income group, where the regional indices fell. Spending that rises in dollars has plainly not translated into broader coverage in many places, which points to gaps in delivery, workforce and the reach of services rather than money alone.

### Spending has not converged and the workforce cannot be measured well

Spending per head at purchasing power parity shows no sign of countries drawing together. Across 190 countries, the regression of growth in current health expenditure per capita (international dollars) between 2015 and 2023 on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00001, with a p-value of 0.997 and an R-squared of 0.000. Countries that began with low spending did not grow faster than those that began high, and the starting level explains none of the variation in growth. The coefficient of variation, a measure of relative dispersion, moved from 1.24 in 2015 to 1.20 in 2023. That change is small and is not backed by a convergence relationship, so it should be read as little more than stability in the spread.

The result matters for target 3.c, which calls for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed countries and small island developing States. Convergence would be the sign that the gap in resources was narrowing. Its absence means that the large differences in spending described earlier in this section are being carried into the final years of the agenda. Well-established causes help explain this. Health budgets depend on national income, on the capacity of governments to raise revenue, and on debt service burdens, and these did not change in a way that favoured poorer countries during the period. The shocks of 2020 fell on all budgets, but countries with more fiscal room could sustain or expand health spending, while others had to divert funds or rely on external support. The test here is across countries and does not separate these channels, and it covers 2015 to 2023 only, so any later change is not captured.

The health workforce is harder still to assess. The shelf holds one series on community health workers per 1,000 people, and it is thin. Only 64 countries report in any year of the series. The number reporting in a single year ranges from 3 in 2002 and 3 in 2014 to 29 in 2004 and 21 in 2008. After 2010 the count never exceeds 6 or 7 in a year: 6 in 2011, 7 in 2012, 6 in 2013, 3 in 2014, 4 in 2015 and 6 in 2016. The latest year in the series is 2016, so nothing is recorded for the period after 2020.

With so few reporters, and with a different set of countries in each year, a change in the average could not be told from a change in who reports. No trend in workforce density, upward or downward, can be asserted, and no judgement can be made on whether the recruitment and retention called for in target 3.c is occurring. Community health workers are also defined differently from country to country, under titles such as health extension worker or lady health visitor, which weakens comparison even where data exist. The series also says nothing of doctors, nurses or midwives. The honest finding is that spending can be measured and has not converged, whereas the workforce, the input on which services most depend, cannot be measured well enough to be followed towards 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Targets 3.b and 3.c ask for more vaccines and medicines for developing countries, and for substantially more health financing and workforce. On the evidence of the shelf, the financing half of 3.c is being met in dollar terms by most countries, while the access and workforce halves cannot be confirmed. Of 193 countries assessed, 142 are on track or have met the trend test for domestic government health spending per head, and they hold 80.1% of the assessed population. That majority is made of countries that already spend most. A further 34 countries, with 14.0% of the population, show regression, and these are the systems where the target is most at risk.

The reproductive, maternal, newborn and child sub-index gives a different reading for target 3.b. Only 11 countries, with 5.0% of the population, are on track, while 105 countries, with 48.1% of the population, are stagnating and 31, with 29.5%, are regressing. Stagnation in the index is consistent with the disruption to routine services after 2020, but the index is composite and cannot attribute the pattern to vaccines alone. If present trends hold, most of the world's population will reach 2030 with coverage no better than today.

The share of output devoted to health shows why dollar growth is not sufficient. The low-income group fell from 5.4% of GDP in 2015 to 4.6% in 2023, and South Asia from 3.5% to 3.3%. Both are the groups with the least domestic public money per head. High-income countries rose from 12.0% to 12.5%. Spending is therefore growing where it is already high and shrinking in relative terms where need is greatest. Without a deliberate shift, the gap in 2030 will be wider than in 2015, and the finding that spending per head has not converged supports this.

The workforce half of target 3.c cannot be judged. Community health workers were reported by only 64 countries in any year, and by no more than 29 in any single year, with just 6 reporting in 2016, the last year of record. A target to recruit and retain workers cannot be monitored from a series that thin. The reading of 2030 is thus asymmetric: spending is measured and uneven, services are measured and flat, and the workforce is largely unmeasured. Recent estimates for 2024 also come from only 22 reporting countries, so the latest picture is provisional.
