w-c05-1-1.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The world primary completion rate stood at 87.9% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 88.0% in 2024. The gain across nine years is about 0.2 percentage points, set against a target of 100.0% by 2030. At this pace the world does not approach universal completion. The period spans the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the school closures of 2020 and the uneven recovery since, and the aggregate shows little trace of any of them: neither a surge after 2015 nor a visible collapse after 2020. A flat global line can conceal movement in both directions, and the regional figures show that it does.

The indicator needs careful reading. Primary completion here is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of primary education: new entrants in the last grade, whatever their age, divided by the population at the entrance age for that grade. Because late entrants and children who started school early are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100. It is therefore not the share of a birth cohort that finishes primary school. Data limitations also preclude adjusting for pupils who drop out during the final year, so the figure may overstate true completion. The target can be read in more than one way: as universal completion, meaning every child finishes, or as a rate of 100 or more, which the ratio can reach while some children remain outside school and others are counted twice through late entry. The trend assessment in this chapter takes the second, arithmetical reading, with 100.0 as the threshold.

Under that reading, the country classification is sobering. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 19.6% of the assessed population. A further 14 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 13.0% of the population, and 14 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 5.7%. Three countries stagnate, with 0.5%. Regression is the largest class: 92 countries, holding 61.3% of the population. Regression here partly reflects a mechanical feature of the measure. Countries already above 100 that drift back towards it, as late entrants and repeaters decline, are counted as moving away from the target even when nearly all children complete. The class therefore mixes real deterioration with the correction of inflated ratios, and the count alone cannot separate them.

Reporting is a further limit. Only 11 countries had reported a value for 2025 at the time of access, so the latest year is nearly empty and the most recent global figure rests on 2024. Some regional values end earlier still: East Asia and Pacific reaches 2022 and North America 2023. The finding of near stagnation is thus firm for the period to 2024 but says little about the last year before the target date, in which administrative data on enrolment and last-grade entry are published with a lag of one to two years.

### Lower secondary completion shows slow, uneven gains

The world lower secondary completion rate stood at 74.8% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 77.9% in 2024. The gain across nine years is about 3.1 percentage points, set against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The measure is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education, so it counts new entrants in that grade regardless of age. Pupils who enter late are included, and a ratio can therefore exceed 100.0%. The rate is not a count of cohorts that graduate on time, and readers should treat it as an indicator of intake to the last grade rather than of certified completion.

Set beside primary completion, which was 88.0% in 2024, the figure for lower secondary shows how much is lost between the two cycles. The gap is about 10 percentage points, which means that roughly one adolescent in four does not reach the last grade of lower secondary school. The reasons are well established: fees and indirect costs rise after primary school, schools become scarcer and more distant, households weigh the wages that older children can earn, and early marriage and pregnancy remove many girls. Some adolescents are also held back by repeated grades, which delays entry to the last grade even where they stay enrolled.

The regional series show where the shortfall lies. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 42.3% in 2015 and 44.4% in 2023, a rise of about 2.0 percentage points in eight years, so that more than half of adolescents in the region still do not reach the last grade of lower secondary education. Low-income countries as a group moved from 37.0% in 2015 to 38.6% in 2023. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose faster, from 57.1% to 66.7% in 2024, yet it remains well below the world rate. South Asia advanced from 83.7% to 86.6% over the same period.

The regions that were already close to the target have moved little or have already arrived. East Asia and Pacific rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, the largest gain among the regional aggregates and the main reason the world rate has risen at all. Europe and Central Asia moved from 90.9% to 91.9%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 81.3% to 81.5%, which is effectively stagnation. By income group, upper-middle-income countries rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 93.0% in 2023, high-income countries from 94.0% to 95.6% in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries from 71.0% to 73.7%. The world gain is therefore driven by East Asia and the middle-income group, while the poorest countries have scarcely closed any of the distance.

Several series do not cover the full period. The North American series begins in 2016, not 2015, at 104.3%, and ends in 2023 at 100.8%. Both values are above 100.0% because the ratio counts older entrants, so the decline does not indicate a fall below universal completion. The Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income and upper-middle-income series end in 2023, one year before the world and several other groups, so comparisons across aggregates mix periods of eight and nine years. Only 11 countries reported a value for 2025, which is too few to support any statement about that year. Every aggregate for the latest years therefore rests on a changing set of reporting countries, and a rise or fall of a point or two should not be read as firm.

The country trend assessment confirms that the world picture hides divergence. Of 173 countries assessed against a target of 100.0% by 2030, 49 are on track or have met it, and they hold 22.1% of the population covered. A further 21 countries, with 16.1% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 32 countries, with 38.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Five countries, with 2.2%, are stagnating, and 66 countries, with 21.1%, are regressing. More countries are therefore moving away from the target than are on track to meet it. The population-weighted picture is better than the country count suggests, because several populous countries sit in the marginal group, but it still leaves most of the world's adolescents in countries that will not reach universal completion by 2030 without a sharp change of pace.

### Regions and countries diverge sharply

Regional averages conceal a wide spread in how far children travel through school. In Sub-Saharan Africa the primary completion rate was 68.9% of the relevant age group in 2024, up from 66.3% in 2015. Lower secondary completion in the same region was 44.4% in 2023, up from 42.3% in 2015. Fewer than half of the children of lower secondary age complete that stage, and the gain of about two points in eight years leaves the region far from the target of 100.0%. The trend tool classes the region as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected value of 46.2% in 2030. Low-income countries show the same pattern: 62.9% at primary in 2023 and 38.6% at lower secondary, with an expected 2030 value of 40.1% at lower secondary.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region shows the largest gain in primary completion, from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly ten points. At lower secondary the region rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. The pace, at about 0.017 a year in the trend measure, is the fastest of any region except East Asia and Pacific, yet the tool still classes it as marginal progress, with an expected 73.9% in 2030. The region's combined figures also mix countries with very different circumstances, and conflict and displacement make measurement uncertain in some of them. The gain should be read as a regional average, not as a uniform improvement.

East Asia and Pacific is the clearest success. Lower secondary completion rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, and the region is classed as on track, with an expected 105.4% in 2030. A value above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio, which counts late and early entrants alike, so it does not signal that every child completes on time. Primary completion in the region reached 95.4% in 2022, from 94.1% in 2015. Upper middle income countries also reach a classed on-track position at lower secondary, rising from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023. Sustained expansion of lower secondary places, and the removal of fees and distance barriers, are the usual explanations for such gains.

Several regions went backwards at primary level. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 98.4% in 2015 to 96.5% in 2024. South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4% over the same years, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. These regions began near universal completion, so the declines are of a different kind from the shortfalls in Africa, and part of the fall may reflect the disruption of 2020 and changes in enrolment and repetition. Because the measure counts new entrants in the last grade, shifts in repetition and age at entry can move it without any change in the number of children finishing. Primary completion in Europe and Central Asia, by contrast, rose from 97.2% to 98.1%. At lower secondary, Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as stagnant, from 81.3% in 2015 to 81.5% in 2024, and South Asia improved from 83.7% to 86.6%.

Country classes confirm that the global average hides a divide. Of 173 countries assessed on primary completion, 50 are on track or have met the target, holding 19.6% of the population of those classed. A further 14 show moderate progress and 14 marginal progress, while 3 are stagnant. The largest group is the 92 countries in regression, holding 61.3% of the classed population. The regression class is large in part because many countries began close to the ceiling, where small fluctuations register as decline, so it should not be read as 92 failing systems. At lower secondary the picture is less bleak: 49 countries are on track, holding 22.1% of the population, 21 show moderate progress, 32 marginal progress and 5 stagnation, while 66 are in regression, holding 21.1%. The 32 countries in marginal progress hold 38.4% of the classed population, which shows how many people live in countries that are advancing but too slowly to arrive by 2030.

### Learning lags behind completion, and the data are thin

Completion measures how many children reach the last grade; it does not show what they have learned. The indicator of minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary schooling addresses that gap, and it shows a worse picture. Worldwide, 45.9% of pupils at the end of primary were below the minimum reading proficiency level in 2015, and 49.6% were below it in 2019. Set beside a world primary completion rate near nine in ten, the figures mean that a large share of children who finish primary school cannot yet read a simple, short text independently and fluently. Completion without learning does not deliver the quality that Target 4.1 requires.

The regional contrasts are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest share below the threshold, at 80.7% in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019. Among income groups, low-income countries stood at 83.5% in 2015 and 87.4% in 2019, and lower middle income countries at 52.9% and 57.4%. South Asia was nearly unchanged, at 55.8% and then 56.0%, and the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 57.7% to 57.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 49.1% to 51.0%. These are the regions where expansion of enrolment over past decades brought in many first-generation learners, where classes are large and where teachers often lack training and materials. Such conditions explain why additional years in school have not translated into basic skills.

At the other end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.8% to 5.5%, and high income countries from 6.4% to 6.2%. North America was flat, at 3.9% in both years. Low shares in these regions leave little room for movement, so the near absence of change there is not a sign of stagnation of the same kind as in South Asia. Upper middle income countries were close to unchanged, at 28.0% in 2015 and 28.6% in 2019.

The largest movement was in East Asia and Pacific, where the share below the threshold rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019. A rise of that size in a region with strong education systems calls for caution. It may partly reflect a change in which countries and pupils were assessed between the two waves, not only a decline in learning. Where a wave adds countries with weaker results, the regional figure rises with no change in any single country. The data in hand cannot separate the two explanations. The trend calculation for the region, which extrapolates to 124.3% in 2030, is impossible as a share and shows only that two points cannot support a projection.

The coverage of the series explains the difficulty. Data come in survey waves, not as annual observations. Countries reporting numbered 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, with only isolated reports in 2022 and 2023, one country in the latter year. In all, 125 countries reported in at least one year. The aggregates end in 2019, so they do not capture the effect of the school closures of 2020 and after, which is a serious omission for a question about what changed after 2020. The 2021 wave exists at country level but has no regional aggregate in the results here.

For 2030 the implication is plain on the evidence available. Extrapolating the 2015 to 2019 movement gives 61.3% of pupils below the threshold worldwide, against a target of zero, and the trend is classed as regression. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 91.0% and low income countries 99.1% on the same arithmetic. Only Europe and Central Asia shows moderate progress, and it begins from a low base. The extrapolations are mechanical, rest on two points and should be read as direction, not forecast. Still, the direction is away from the target in most regions, and the gap between completion and learning is widening where completion is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At present rates the world will miss target 4.1. The lower secondary trend to target puts the world on course for an expected completion rate of 80.0% of the relevant age group in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend ratio for the world is 0.21, which places it in the class of marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Among 173 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target for lower secondary completion, covering 22.1% of the assessed population, while 66 are regressing, covering 21.1%. For primary completion, 50 countries are on track, covering 19.6% of their population, and 92 are regressing, covering 61.3%. Regression is therefore the most common class at primary level, and it applies to the majority of the population assessed. The classes are drawn from a trend to target, so a country that has already reached a high rate and slipped slightly may be recorded as regressing; the reading needs care, and the target can be read as universal completion or as a rate near it.

Completing school is not the same as learning. The learning indicator shows the world trend classed as regression, with an expected share below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary of 61.3% in 2030, against a target of 0.0%. In Low income countries the expected share is 99.1% in 2030, and in Sub-Saharan Africa 91.0%. Regions where completion is high do not necessarily escape the problem, since East Asia & Pacific is classed as regression on learning while its lower secondary completion is on track, with an expected rate of 105.4% in 2030. A completion rate above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio that counts late entrants and repeaters outside the entrance age. Completion gains that are not matched by learning gains deliver the certificate without the skills, and the learning series, which ends in 2019 for these trends and has coverage of 125 countries, cannot show whether recovery after 2020 has changed this.

The regional picture shows where acceleration matters most. Sub-Saharan Africa has an expected lower secondary completion rate of 46.2% in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region 73.9%, with a ratio of 0.39, still short of what the target requires. Low income countries are classed as stagnant, with an expected rate of 40.1% in 2030. These are the places where the largest numbers of children are left without a completed basic education, and they are also the places where learning data are thinnest.

w-c05-4-1.text:
### Global gross tertiary enrolment rose from 36.6 to 43.6 per cent between 2015 and 2024

Gross tertiary enrolment in the world stood at 36.6 per cent in 2015 and reached 43.6 per cent in 2024. The rise is 7.0 percentage points over nine years, and it places the world in the group the trend tool classes as making moderate progress, with acceleration needed. The annualised rate of change is 0.0196, which the tool reads as short of the pace that a fast improvement would require.

The indicator is a gross enrolment ratio. It divides total enrolment at tertiary level, whatever the age of the students, by the population of the age group that officially corresponds to that level. Because older students, repeaters and returning adults are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100 per cent, and a high value does not mean that every young person of tertiary age is enrolled. The ratio also shifts when a country changes the official age band or the definition of what counts as tertiary, so comparisons across countries and years carry some uncertainty.

The indicator covers only part of target 4.3. The target speaks of equal access for all women and men to affordable and quality technical, vocational and tertiary education. A gross ratio records the number of places taken up. It says nothing about the cost borne by students and families, nothing about the quality of teaching or the value of the qualification, and nothing about who is excluded by income, location, disability or ethnicity. Vocational education below the tertiary level falls outside the series altogether. The sex-disaggregated series, treated in the chapter section on gender parity, add one dimension of equality but not the others.

The target also sets no numeric threshold. The words say "equal access" and give no level of enrolment to be reached by 2030. Progress is therefore judged by direction and pace: whether the ratio rises, and whether it rises fast enough to be called on track by the bench's trend tool. On that reading the world is moving the right way, though more slowly than a full response to the target would imply. The 2024 value is also the latest year with broad reporting, since only 9 countries had reported for 2025 when the data were drawn, and the world figure for that year would not be reliable.

### Regional ratios diverge, from 9.3 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa to 84.9 per cent in Europe and Central Asia

Regional ratios in 2024 span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia stands at 84.9 per cent, and North America at 79.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa sits at 9.3 per cent, and its latest value dates from 2021, not 2024, so the comparison with other regions is not strictly like for like. Gross enrolment is a ratio of all students, whatever their age, to the population of the age group that officially corresponds to tertiary study. It can therefore exceed what a single age cohort would suggest, and it rises where adults return to study or where students repeat years.

The largest gains since 2015 came in East Asia and Pacific, where the ratio rose from 44.3 to 63.3 per cent, and in Europe and Central Asia, where it rose from 67.4 to 84.9 per cent. Both are classed as on track by the trend tool. Behind the East Asian gain lies a long expansion of university systems, funded by public and private providers, as secondary completion became near universal in many economies. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 48.4 to 58.9 per cent, also classed as on track, with a smaller rise than the first two.

South Asia rose from 25.4 to 32.8 per cent and is classed as on track, though from a low base, so the gain of about seven percentage points still leaves it well below the world ratio of 43.6 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 27.3 to 29.7 per cent, and the tool classes progress there as marginal. A grouping that joins several economies with very different systems, and that includes countries where conflict has disrupted universities, hides much variation, and the regional figure should be read with that in mind.

North America is the one region that went backwards, from 86.8 to 79.0 per cent. The fall does not signal a loss of access in the ordinary sense. Likely contributors include demographic change, a strong labour market drawing some young people away from study, the cost of tuition, and the effect of the pandemic years on enrolment at two-year institutions. The data alone cannot apportion these causes.

Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 8.84 to 9.27 per cent, a change of well under one percentage point, and the low-income group shows the same picture, with its ratio at 8.86 per cent in 2015 and 9.28 per cent in 2021. In these settings the binding constraint lies earlier in the system: few young people complete secondary school, and public places are scarce. At this pace the region will remain far from the levels reached elsewhere in 2015, let alone 2030, and the gap with Europe and Central Asia, already large in 2015, has widened in absolute terms.

### Most countries are advancing, yet forty regress and the gaps between countries have not narrowed

Of the 159 countries assessed, 75 are on track or have met the trend benchmark, and they hold 69.8 per cent of the population of the countries classified. A further 22 countries show moderate progress, though acceleration is needed, and 16 show marginal progress that would require significant acceleration. Six are stagnant. Forty countries regress, and they hold 12.3 per cent of that population. The picture is therefore one of broad advance, led by populous countries, alongside a large minority of countries whose enrolment ratios have fallen.

The classes need careful reading. Target 4.3 sets no numerical threshold for tertiary enrolment, so the trend tool has no official target to measure against. The classes describe the direction and pace of each country's own series, not distance from an agreed goal. A country already at a high ratio can be classed as regressing after a small fall, and a country at a low ratio can be classed as on track after a small rise. The count of 40 regressing countries may also reflect causes other than real decline. Revisions to population estimates change the denominator of a gross ratio. Changes in how institutions are counted, or in which programmes are reported as tertiary, can move a series without any change in students. The pandemic years also disturbed enrolment, through deferred entry, falling international study and, in some places, shifts toward work. Whether these effects have faded cannot be settled from the series alone.

The gaps between countries have not narrowed. Across 82 countries with data for both ends of 2015 to 2024, the convergence regression gives a coefficient of -0.00101 (p 0.901), with an R2 of 0.000. Initial levels explain none of the subsequent growth, so there is no sign that low-enrolment countries are catching up, and none that they are falling further behind. The coefficient of variation moved only from 0.591 in 2015 to 0.569 in 2024. Relative dispersion is almost unchanged, even as the world average rose. Growth has been spread across the range of starting points, not concentrated among laggards.

Gender parity and enrolment move largely independently. Across the same 82 countries, the Spearman correlation between changes in the gender parity index and changes in enrolment is -0.083, which is effectively zero. Countries that expanded tertiary enrolment did not systematically improve or worsen the balance between women and men. The correlation between 2024 levels is 0.176, a weak positive link. Higher enrolment goes only loosely with a higher parity index. In many systems women already outnumber men at this level, so a higher parity index does not by itself signal progress toward equal access.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise hides unequal prospects. With no convergence, the countries with the lowest ratios are not on a path to close the distance to the rest. The large regressing group also means that the global average depends on gains in a limited number of populous countries. Until the effects of reporting changes are separated from real losses, the regressing class should be treated as a list of cases to examine, not as a verdict.

### Data gaps limit the reading for 2030, and the proposals follow from them

Reporting thins exactly where the latest comparisons are drawn. In 2015, 147 countries reported gross tertiary enrolment, the highest count of the period since 2000. The number was 136 in 2016 and 133 in 2020, and fell to 125 in 2021. It stood at 94 in 2024 and only 9 in 2025. Every regional and global figure for 2024 therefore rests on fewer countries than the 2015 baseline, and the countries that report late are not a random draw. Where late reporters are poorer or have weaker statistical systems, the 2024 averages may be biased, and the apparent change since 2015 may partly reflect who is counted. The 2025 values are too few to read at all.

With that caution, the picture is of a world that is rising but unevenly. The global ratio has risen at an annualised rate of 0.0196, and East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and the middle-income groups are advancing at rates of 0.0406, 0.0289 and 0.0264 to 0.0368. The poorest regions are not. Low income stands at a rate of 0.0077 and Sub-Saharan Africa at 0.0080, both classed as marginal progress. At those rates, they will not approach the levels of other regions by 2030. The convergence test across 82 countries points the same way: the coefficient is -0.0010 with a p-value of 0.9011, and the coefficient of variation moved only from 0.59 to 0.57. Growth has not been systematically faster in countries that began lower.

The indicator also limits what can be said about target 4.3, which speaks of equal access, affordability and quality. A gross ratio counts all students regardless of age, so it can exceed the share of a cohort that attends, and it says nothing about who enrols, what they study, what they pay or whether they finish. Target 4.3 has no numerical threshold, and it can be read as a universal goal or as a relative improvement. No pace of gross enrolment can settle that question, and the series as it stands cannot show whether growth has reached women, poorer households or technical and vocational routes.

The proposals below follow from these limits.

Target 4.3 carries no numerical threshold, so progress is judged only against trend.

w-c05-7-1.text:
### The global share of trained primary teachers has risen only slowly

The world share of primary school teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and at 82.2% in 2024, a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030, and the indicator used here reads that as a share of 100%. Against that reading, roughly one primary teacher in five worldwide still lacks the minimum organised training required in the country where they teach. The trend calculation gives a world ratio of 0.15 against the pace needed, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Continuing the 2015 to 2024 slope would bring the world to 83.4% in 2030.

The measure needs careful reading. The indicator counts teachers who have received the minimum organised training, whether before or during service, that a given country requires. That minimum is set nationally and differs widely. A teacher counted as trained in one system might not meet the standard of another, and a share of 100% in one country does not imply equal preparation in the classroom. Nor does the indicator capture the quality of the training, the subject knowledge of teachers, or whether they remain in post. The figure is therefore a floor on qualification, not a measure of teaching quality. Readings of the target also vary: some take 4.c to mean full national qualification, others a substantial rise from a baseline, and the data cannot settle between them.

Coverage adds a second caution. The 2024 world value rests on the latest reporting of each economy, and only 13 countries reported in 2025, so the most recent year says little. Several regional values end in 2022, and the upper middle income group has a single value, for 2022, at 80.7%, which allows no change to be read. Slow reporting is itself a finding, since the countries with the weakest systems are often those that report latest.

The section's guiding question also asks whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling. The bench returned no result for that ratio, so the question cannot be answered from the evidence held here. Series on teacher numbers exist for primary and secondary levels, but a count of teachers without matching enrolment does not give a ratio, and nothing in the results allows one to be inferred. The evidence therefore speaks to the training of teachers, not to the size of classes.

The slow world movement matters for 2030 because training is a precondition for much else in the chapter, from completion and learning to pre-primary provision. A world share that rises by under two points in nine years, through the disruption of 2020 and the years after it, suggests that the supply of trained teachers is barely keeping pace with expansion of the teaching force. If new teachers are recruited faster than they are trained, the share stalls even as the number of teachers grows. The regional parts that follow show where gains and losses lie.

### Regions and income groups differ by more than twenty points

The regional picture in 2024 is one of wide separation. North America stands at 97.9% of primary teachers trained, South Asia at 87.7%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 81.8% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 80.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa, whose latest reading is 2022 rather than 2024, stands at 68.8%. The distance between the top and the bottom is therefore well over twenty points, and it is larger than the gap between any two of the other regions named. Readings from different years are not strictly comparable, and the Sub-Saharan figure may understate or overstate the position in 2024 in either direction.

Income groups tell a similar story. Low income countries stand at 69.2% in 2022, close to the Sub-Saharan level, which is unsurprising because most low income countries lie in that region. Training is the minimum organised preparation required by each country, so the percentages measure compliance with national standards and not a common level of skill. A country with a demanding standard can score lower than one with a modest standard, and the comparison across regions should be read with that in mind.

The spread among countries is moderate on the Gini measure, which is population-weighted. It stood at 0.094 in 2015, fell to 0.073 in 2020 and rose again to 0.097 in 2024, ending slightly above its starting level. The improvement of the early period was thus lost by the end. The Theil index, which allows inequality to be split into parts, fell from 0.026 in 2015 to 0.011 in 2020. Within that decomposition, the share lying between regions was 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020. About half of the inequality among countries is therefore a difference between regions, and the other half lies among countries within the same region. Policies aimed at a single region would address only part of the gap.

These comparisons carry a caveat about coverage. Countries reporting numbered 85 in 2015 and 93 in 2020, but only 79 in 2024. The Theil index and its regional decomposition are missing for 2024, so the latest year cannot be set against the earlier ones on that measure. A fall in the number of reporting countries can alter the Gini by changing who is counted, and the rise to 0.097 may reflect that change as much as any real divergence. Reporting for 2025 is thinner still, with 13 countries. For 2030 the implication is that the monitoring of Target 4.c is weakest in the years that matter most for judging it.

### Gains in South Asia contrast with declines in richer regions

South Asia recorded the largest regional gain in the share of trained primary teachers. The share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly fifteen percentage points in nine years. The region moved from well below the world average to above it, and from the second-lowest regional level to the second-highest. Lower middle income countries, a group that includes several South Asian economies, rose more modestly, from 76.4% in 2015 to 83.3% in 2024. Such a large movement in a region with very large teaching workforces is usually the product of policy rather than chance: governments that decide to certify untrained or contract teachers, or to fund in-service courses, can shift a regional average quickly. The data do not show which measures lay behind the rise, and a change in how a country defines the minimum training required would produce the same movement as a real improvement in preparation.

The richer regions moved in the opposite direction. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020, the last year for which the regional reading is given here. High income countries fell from 95.9% in 2015 to 92.1% in 2024, and North America slipped from 99.3% to 97.9% over the same period. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 82.7% to 81.8%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan declined from 83.9% to 80.5%. These falls are small beside the South Asian gain, but they matter because they run against the direction of Target 4.c. Several explanations are consistent with established knowledge: shortages of teachers in rich countries have led many systems to hire people who have not completed the full programme, and expanding enrolment or absorbing refugees and migrants can draw in staff on temporary authorisations. The series cannot separate these causes, and a decline in a share may also reflect changes in national definitions or reporting rather than a change in the classroom.

Across countries, the pattern is one of catching up. A convergence test over 48 countries between 2015 and 2024 gives a coefficient of -0.071 (p below 0.001) with an R2 of 0.342, which means that countries starting from lower shares of trained teachers tended to gain faster than those starting higher. The dispersion of the shares narrowed only slightly: the coefficient of variation moved from 0.165 in 2015 to 0.155 in 2024. Convergence is therefore real but slow, and about a third of the variation in country changes is accounted for by the starting level alone. The remaining two thirds reflect national circumstances that the data do not identify. The test also covers only the 48 countries with readings at both ends of the period, so it describes the reporting countries and not the world, and the poorest systems with the sparsest records may be underrepresented.

The size of the teaching workforce does not appear to explain the changes. The rank correlation between changes in the share of trained primary teachers and changes in the number of primary teachers across the same 48 countries is -0.095, and the correlation between 2024 levels is 0.168. Both are weak. Expanding the workforce therefore did not visibly coincide with improved training, and countries that hired the most teachers were no more likely to see the trained share rise. This is a cautionary finding for Target 4.c. Raising the supply of teachers and raising the supply of qualified teachers are separate undertakings, and a system that grows quickly may dilute its trained share if training places do not keep pace. Equally, a system that trains well but adds few posts may raise the share without enlarging the workforce.

The period since 2015 and the years after 2020 cannot be read cleanly from these series. Several regional readings end in 2020 or 2022, and the school closures of 2020 and 2021 disrupted both teacher training and the collection of statistics. A fall recorded after 2020 may reflect hurried recruitment of replacement staff, while a gap in reporting may conceal a change that has not yet been measured. For 2030, the lesson of this part is that gains are possible and can be large where policy is sustained, as South Asia shows, but that they are not automatic, and that richer regions cannot assume their shares will hold.

### Most countries are not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

The country counts show that the 2030 picture is mixed rather than uniformly bleak. In primary education, 64 of the 129 countries assessed, holding 65.9% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have already met the target of a fully trained teaching force. This is a large share of people but not of countries, because several populous countries are among those advancing. Against it stand 36 countries with 26.3% of the assessed population whose trained share is falling rather than rising. A further 13 countries, with 2.4% of the population, show marginal progress that would need to speed up considerably, 12 show moderate progress that still needs acceleration, and 4 are stagnant. Taken together, the countries that are neither on track nor regressing are few; the pattern is polarised, with many countries close to the goal and many moving away from it.

Secondary education tells a similar story with less coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 hold 61.5% of the population and are on track or have met the target, while 36 hold 27.6% and are regressing. Fourteen countries with 7.7% of the population show marginal progress, 10 show moderate progress and 7 are stagnant. The share of people living in regressing countries is slightly higher at secondary level than at primary level, and the share living in on-track countries is slightly lower. Fewer countries report secondary data, so the secondary result rests on a thinner base and is the less certain of the two.

The regression count deserves care in reading. A falling trained share does not necessarily mean that teaching has worsened. Where systems expand quickly, schools often recruit contract or volunteer teachers faster than training institutions can certify them, and the trained share falls even as the number of teachers rises. Where national training requirements are tightened, teachers once counted as trained may fall below a higher minimum. The indicator records the share meeting each country's own minimum, so a country that raises its standard can appear to regress. Both mechanisms are well known, and the data given here cannot separate them.

The same feature complicates the target itself. Target 4.c speaks of qualified teachers, and the indicator measures minimum organised training, pre-service or in-service, as defined nationally. A trained teacher in one country may hold a degree and a practicum, while in another the minimum may be a short course. A share of 100% therefore does not mean equal preparation across countries, and the target can be read as a share trained to national standards, a share trained to an international standard, or a growth in the absolute supply of teachers. The assessment here uses the first reading, since it is the only one the series allows. Its limits should be kept in view when comparing countries.

For 2030, the world trend implies that the target will be missed. The projected world share of trained primary teachers is 83.4%, with a trend ratio of 0.15, which falls in the class of marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 72.0% and low income countries at 73.2%, so the groups starting furthest behind are expected to remain furthest behind. South Asia, projected at 99.3%, is the one region on course. The regions that are regressing are mostly those that began from higher levels, such as Europe and Central Asia at a projected 86.9% and high income countries at 89.7%. Their decline lowers the world figure and shows that a high starting point is no guarantee of progress.

The inequality measures give a final caution. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the trained share was 0.09 in 2015, 0.07 in 2020 and 0.10 in 2024. Differences narrowed up to 2020 and then widened again, though the 2024 reading covers 79 countries against 93 in 2020, so the comparison is imperfect. The widening is consistent with the pandemic years and their aftermath having halted the convergence that had begun.

The weight of the findings points to the following proposals.

w-c02-1-1.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 asks that extreme poverty be eradicated for all people everywhere by 2030, and its wording quotes a line of $1.25 a day. That line belongs to an earlier price base and has been superseded several times as purchasing power parity exchange rates were revised. The measure used here is the current international line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, published by the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform. Poverty rates under this line cannot be compared with those printed in earlier editions of the series, and the figures in this book should not be set beside older statements of the target without that caution.

On this measure, 13.4% of the world's population lived below $3.00 a day in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 the share was 10.1%. The fall is real and of consequence: a little over three percentage points in nine years, in a period that included a pandemic and a sharp rise in food and energy prices. It also shows how far the world remains from the target. At the 2024 level, roughly one person in ten still lives below the line, and the target date is six years off.

The word eradicate admits more than one reading, and the choice changes the verdict. The strict reading is a headcount of 0%, which no measured aggregate has approached and which survey-based estimation could not confirm even if it were reached, since sampling error and gaps in coverage make an exact zero unobservable. The reading used in World Bank practice is a threshold of 3% of the population, below which extreme poverty is treated as ended as a global phenomenon. Against the 3% threshold the world stands at more than three times the required level in 2024; against zero the distance is the whole of the 10.1%. Both readings lead to the same conclusion for 2030, but they differ in what a successful outcome would mean, and the text of the target does not choose between them.

The choice of line matters for a second reason. A line of $3.00 a day is a very low standard, set to reflect the national lines of the poorest countries. Falling below it signals deprivation of food, shelter and basic needs. Rising above it does not signal security, and many households that have crossed it remain close enough to be pushed back by a poor harvest, an illness or a price shock. Later parts of this section turn to what the higher line of $4.20 a day adds.

The 2024 value must be read with care. The data behind the headcount are household surveys, which are conducted in each country at intervals of several years and are published with a delay. Figures for the most recent years therefore rest partly on estimates that carry forward earlier surveys using national accounts growth and other assumptions. The coverage record shows the effect. In 2015, 87 countries reported a value, and 93 did so in 2018. The number fell to 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted. It stood at 60 in 2023 and only 26 in 2024, and just 4 countries reported in 2025. The 2024 aggregate of 10.1% is thus a nowcast built on a thin base of direct observation, and later revisions can be expected as surveys arrive.

Two cautions follow for any reader. The fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is a robust direction but not a precise magnitude, and the end point is less firm than the start. The global figure also conceals a very uneven distribution, taken up in the next part, in which the decline has been concentrated in a few regions while others have seen little progress or a reversal.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture beneath the global figure is one of sharp divergence. East Asia & Pacific recorded the largest fall among the regions with a full series: the headcount at $3.00 a day went from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. Europe & Central Asia began from a low base and moved from 1.2% to 0.6%. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 6.0% to 4.3%, a decline that is real but slower in proportion than those of the two regions above, and one that reflects a region where progress is sensitive to commodity cycles, informal employment and the reach of cash transfers. North America, at 1.1% in 2015 and 0.9% in 2024, was already close to the floor of what survey-based measurement can distinguish from zero.

South Asia requires a caution. The series for the region begins in 2020, at 9.4%, and reaches 2.6% in 2024. Read at face value, this is the steepest fall of any region in the period. The reading cannot be extended to 2015, because the regional aggregate is not published for the earlier years, and the dependence of regional estimates on a small number of large countries with infrequent household surveys means that the aggregate may rest on interpolation and projection as much as on fresh observation. The 2020 starting point also falls in the year of the pandemic, so part of the apparent decline may be recovery from a temporary shock rather than a sustained trend. The figure is therefore best taken as a sign of strong improvement of uncertain size, not as a measured change over the full period since 2015.

The regions where poverty has not fallen are those where the global total is now decided. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan moved in the wrong direction, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024. The grouping combines economies of very different kinds, and the rise is generally associated with armed conflict, displacement and economic collapse in a limited number of countries, together with the weight of populous members, so it should not be read as a uniform deterioration across the region. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, almost no change in nine years. Because the region's population has grown quickly over the same period, a flat rate means that the number of people living below the line has risen, even though the rate itself is the quantity reported here.

Income groups tell the same story from another side. Low-income countries recorded 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, a rise, so that more than half the population of the poorest group of economies lives below $3.00 a day. Lower middle income countries stood at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024; the series for this group, like that for South Asia, is shown from 2020 only, and the same caution applies. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% to 2.1%, and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. The pattern is that the decline has been concentrated where poverty was already moderate, and that it has bypassed the group where poverty is deepest.

This matters for the target. The global fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is driven chiefly by the regions that started with modest rates and moved quickly, while the regions and income group with the highest rates did not move or moved backwards. As the reservoir of poverty in faster-growing economies is drained, the remaining headcount is increasingly located in fragile, conflict-affected and low-income settings, where growth has been weaker, shocks since 2020 have been more damaging and the capacity to collect household survey data is itself limited. Eradication by 2030 would require that the regions now stagnant reverse course abruptly, which no part of the 2015 to 2024 record suggests.

### Country progress and the absence of convergence

Sorting countries by the pace of their progress towards a headcount of zero by 2030 shows how uneven the record is. Of 105 countries assessed on the $3.00 a day line, 18 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 45.6% of the population of the assessed countries. That share is large because it includes some of the most populous economies, where sustained growth and wide social programmes have taken the headcount low. The count of countries is far less encouraging than the share of people: 18 of 105 is a small minority of national experiences.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and they hold 23.1% of the assessed population. A further 15 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, holding 11.3%. In neither group is the target reached at the present pace. Moderate progress means the direction is right and the speed is insufficient; marginal progress means that closing the remaining distance would take a change of pace that few countries have managed in a single decade.

The weakest classes matter most for the meaning of the target, which asks for eradication for all people everywhere. 7 countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the assessed population. 24 countries are regressing, with 17.9%. Regression in almost a quarter of the assessed countries is a finding in its own right. Established knowledge points to several causes: armed conflict and state fragility, repeated macroeconomic shocks, high food and energy prices, and the loss of income and the setbacks to recovery that followed the pandemic of 2020. Countries that entered the period with a high headcount and weak buffers had the least capacity to absorb these shocks. Because the classification measures movement from each country's own latest observations, a country can regress from a low level as well as from a high one, and the class does not by itself say how deep the deprivation is.

The convergence test addresses whether poorer countries are catching up. Across 57 countries with data from 2015 to 2022, the regression of change in the headcount on its starting level gives a beta of 0.00658 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029. A negative and significant coefficient would have shown that countries starting with higher headcounts fell faster. The coefficient is instead slightly positive, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 3% of the variation in outcomes. Starting poverty did not predict the later pace of change.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.144 in 2015 to 2.675 in 2022. A rising coefficient means that the spread of national headcounts grew relative to their mean. Gains were concentrated in places that already had low rates or favourable conditions, while others stood still or slipped back, and the distribution became more unequal between countries. Two readings of this are open. It may reflect a true divergence in national fortunes. It may also reflect that the headcount, as it approaches zero in many countries, has a small mean, which can inflate a ratio-based dispersion measure even when absolute differences narrow. The absolute test and the relative one should be read together, and neither shows catching up.

The sample limits both results. The convergence test covers 57 countries, fewer than the 105 classified, because it needs observations close to both 2015 and 2022, and household surveys in the poorest and most fragile countries are the least frequent. Countries that go unobserved are disproportionately those where poverty is deepest, so the finding of no convergence may understate the divergence. For 2030, the absence of catch-up has a direct meaning: the global target cannot be met by the average trend alone, because the remaining poverty is concentrated in the countries that are not closing the distance.

### A slowing decline and its limits as evidence

The pace of decline in the world headcount at $3.00 a day has not been steady. A break analysis of the annual change in the world series finds two turning points, in 2014 and in 2021. Between 2001 and 2013 the headcount fell by a mean of 1.6 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.9 points, and in the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.3 points. The pace of decline in the most recent segment is therefore about a fifth of that recorded in the first. The two breaks fall close to two events that shaped the period: the end of the commodity-price boom and the slowdown of growth in many low-income economies after 2014, and the pandemic shock of 2020 followed by uneven recovery, high food and energy prices and rising debt service costs. The data show when the pace changed; they do not isolate why. Attribution would need counterfactual modelling that the series alone cannot supply, and the timing of breaks in a short annual series is itself uncertain by a year or more.

A further reason for caution is mechanical. When the headcount is already low, each point of decline is harder to achieve, because the remaining poor are concentrated in places that are poorer, more remote, more often affected by conflict or weak states, and less able to benefit from average growth. A slowing decline is therefore expected even without any change in policy effort. Yet this does not make the slowdown benign. The target requires the headcount to reach zero, or a figure close to it, and a falling rate of change moves that outcome further from 2030, not nearer.

The evidence behind the latest segment is thinner than the evidence behind the earlier ones. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly and published with a lag. The number of countries reporting a figure for the headcount was 87 in 2015, 70 in 2020 and 81 in 2021. It fell to 60 in 2023, to 26 in 2024 and to 4 in 2025. The decline in recent years is partly a matter of surveys not yet processed or not yet conducted, so the world and regional figures for 2023 onward lean on estimates that carry forward earlier survey information with growth data and assumptions about distribution. The mean change for 2021-2024 should be read as a provisional estimate, likely to be revised as surveys arrive, and the 2025 figures hardly rest on observed data at all.

The coverage problem is uneven as well as thin. Countries with infrequent surveys, often those with the highest poverty and the weakest statistical systems, are the ones most likely to be absent from a given year. The world aggregate can therefore be least well measured where the number of poor people is largest. Anyone assessing whether 2030 is within reach should weigh the slowdown found here as a signal that is probably real in direction, since the breaks are consistent across segments, but uncertain in size.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace observed since 2021, the world will not reach zero extreme poverty by 2030. The world headcount at $3.00 a day stood at 10.1% in 2024, and the trend to the target projects 8.365% in 2030 on the present rate, a ratio of 0.376 of the progress needed. The trend classifies the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. A threshold of 3% is no more attainable at this pace: the gap between 10.1% and 3% is far larger than the few years remaining can close at a mean annual fall of 0.325 points in the segment from 2021 to 2024.

Even the regions that are advancing need to go faster. East Asia & Pacific, the best performer among the regions with a full series, is expected to stand at 0.951% in 2030 on its present rate, against a target of zero, and its ratio is 0.844. Europe & Central Asia is expected at 0.378%, and upper middle income countries at 1.0668%. These are small residual shares, but they are the hardest to remove, because the people concerned are often in remote, conflict-affected or marginalised groups that growth alone does not reach. South Asia is the exception that proves the arithmetic: its rate of fall of 0.27479 a year puts it on track, with an expected 0.3782% in 2030, from a start of 9.4% in 2020. Its record shows what rapid change from a high base can look like, though a series beginning in 2020 is short, and the result should be read with that in mind.

The weight of the problem has moved to places where the trend is flat or reversed. Sub-Saharan Africa is in stagnation, with an expected 44.7353% in 2030, and low-income countries are in regression, with 54.1635% expected. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also in regression, with 16.7305% expected. Because the global headcount is the sum of these parts, the world cannot approach zero while these groups stay where they are. Among 105 countries assessed, 24 are in regression and hold 17.9% of the assessed population.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. National governments and donors should concentrate poverty-reduction effort and concessional finance on Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income countries and conflict-affected states, where the headcount is not falling. National statistical offices, with the World Bank and bilateral funders, should pay for household surveys at least every three years, since only 26 countries reported for 2024 and 4 for 2025, and recent estimates rest on projection. The World Bank and national authorities should report the $3.00 and $4.20 lines side by side, naming the line and the price base used, so that the $1.25 wording of Target 1.1 is not mistaken for the current measure. The United Nations statistical system and the bench's readers should track regression as a class of its own, since the 24 countries in that class are not captured by averages that mix them with countries that are advancing.

w-c04-2-1.text:
### The global picture: most countries are on course, the world is not

Target 3.2 sets two thresholds that every country is asked to reach by 2030: neonatal mortality of at most 12.0 per 1,000 live births, and under-five mortality of at most 25.0 per 1,000 live births. The target is worded as an aspiration for each country, not for the world as a whole. It therefore asks a different question from a global average, and the two readings must be kept apart when the evidence is assessed.

The world averages remain above both thresholds. The global neonatal mortality rate fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024, still above the threshold of 12.0. The global under-five mortality rate fell from 42.9 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024, against a threshold of 25.0. Over nine years the neonatal rate fell by 2.2 points and the under-five rate by 5.5 points. Both series cover all 196 countries reporting in 2024, so the averages are not distorted by missing reporters.

The country classification gives a more favourable picture. Of 196 countries assessed, 130 have reached the neonatal threshold or are on track for it, and 135 have reached the under-five threshold or are on track. In each case that is a clear majority of countries, around two thirds or more. The population shares are close to the country counts: those 130 countries hold 72.4% of the population assessed for neonatal mortality, and the 135 countries hold 74.7% for under-five mortality. A reader may therefore ask how most countries, holding about three quarters of the world's people, can be on course while the world average stays above both lines.

The answer lies in what each figure measures. A count of countries gives every country equal weight, whether it is small or large. A population share weights each country by its number of inhabitants. A world average is weighted differently again: it is dominated by the number of live births, so it reflects where children are born, not where the general population lives. Countries with high birth rates contribute most births, and they are disproportionately those with the highest mortality. A country with a low rate and an ageing population adds little to the world rate, while one with a high rate and many births adds a great deal. The world average is therefore pulled upward by a minority of countries with very high mortality and large numbers of births.

A second distinction concerns the phrase on track. The classification compares each country's recent trend with the path needed to reach the threshold by 2030. A country that is on track has not necessarily reached the threshold; it is projected to do so if its pace holds. A country that has already met the threshold is counted in the same class. The count of 130 and 135 countries thus combines achievement with projection, and the projection can fail if progress slows. Moreover, the threshold itself can be read in more than one way: the target says all countries should aim for at least as low as the stated values, so a country already far below them has no further obligation under the wording, though its rate may still fall.

The remaining countries show why the world average lags. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Four are stagnating and 9 are regressing. Together these 66 countries hold 27.6% of the population assessed, a smaller share than the on-track group but one that includes many births. For under-five mortality the pattern is milder in count but not in character: 39 countries need acceleration, 15 need significant acceleration, 3 are stagnating and 4 are regressing. The stagnating countries hold 4.9% of the population assessed, a far larger share than their count of 3 would suggest, which shows that a few populous countries can matter greatly.

The gap between the two readings matters for policy. A statement that most countries are on course is true and encouraging, but it can mislead if it is taken to mean that the goal is within reach for children worldwide. The children who remain at risk are concentrated in the countries furthest from the thresholds, and the world average is the measure that registers their number. The sections that follow therefore set the counts beside regional and income-group levels, so that the distribution of the shortfall is visible and not hidden by the majority that has succeeded.

### Counting countries: how many have met or are on track for each threshold

The trend classification covers all 196 countries for both indicators, and it gives the plainest count of how many have reached, or are heading for, each threshold. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 target, and they hold 72.4% of the population of the countries assessed. For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met the 25.0 per 1,000 target, with 74.7% of that population. The under-five threshold is therefore the more widely met of the two, by five countries and by 2.3 percentage points of population, although the gap is small.

The class labelled on track or target met joins two different situations. A country that crossed the threshold years ago and a country that is merely on course to cross it by 2030 are counted together. The classification does not separate them, and the data given here cannot say how many of the 130 and the 135 have already arrived. A further count of countries whose latest value lies at or below each threshold would answer the question directly. Until it is made, the figures describe the direction of travel rather than the number of countries that have finished the work. The distinction matters because countries already below the threshold need only hold their position, while those merely on course remain exposed to any slowdown.

Below the leading class, the two indicators diverge in a telling way. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Together these 53 countries hold 19.7% of the population by the shares given, 7.8% and 11.9%. For under-five mortality the order is reversed: 39 countries are in the moderate class, with 16.1% of the population, and only 15 are in the marginal class, with 4.0%. Many countries therefore sit closer to the under-five threshold than to the neonatal one. This agrees with the established pattern that deaths in the first 28 days fall more slowly than deaths later in childhood. Infections, malnutrition and malaria respond to vaccines, nets and treatment, whereas newborn deaths depend on the quality of care around birth, on preterm complications and on skilled attendance, which take longer to build.

The worst classes are small in country count but not in consequence. Four countries stagnate on neonatal mortality, holding 2.1% of the population, and nine regress, holding 5.7%. For under-five mortality, three countries stagnate, holding 4.9%, and four regress, holding only 0.3%. The population weights show that the stagnating three on the under-five indicator are populous, since three countries carry nearly as much population as the 39 moderate countries carry per country on average in neonatal terms. By contrast, the four regressing countries are small. Regression usually accompanies conflict, state collapse or the breakdown of health services, and a small population share does not make it less serious for the children living there.

The population weights also temper the country counts. Neonatal on-track countries are 66.3% of the 196 assessed, yet they hold 72.4% of the population, so the larger countries are slightly more likely to be on course. The same holds for under-five mortality, at 68.9% of countries and 74.7% of population. Even so, about a quarter of the world's people live in countries that are not on course for each threshold. Since the target is written for every country, those countries decide whether the goal is met in the sense the text intends.

The classification carries the usual caution about reading a trend as a forecast. It extrapolates past rates of change to 2030, and the years after 2020 were disturbed by disruption to services and by uncertain estimates in places with weak registration. A country may be assigned a class on a series that is largely modelled rather than counted. The counts should thus be read as a guide to where acceleration is needed, not as a guarantee of where the thresholds will be met.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of seven

The gap between regions is wider than any world average suggests. In 2024 neonatal mortality stood at 3.6 per 1,000 live births in North America and 4.1 in Europe & Central Asia, against 26.6 in Sub-Saharan Africa and 22.7 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan. The ratio between the highest and lowest regional neonatal rates is 7.39, which is the source of the factor of seven in the heading. For under-five mortality the contrast is wider still: 6.4 per 1,000 in North America against 71.2 in Sub-Saharan Africa, a ratio of 11.12. Neonatal deaths make up a larger share of child deaths where overall mortality is low, because the causes that remain there (prematurity, birth complications, congenital conditions) are those that fall last. Where mortality is high, infections, malnutrition and malaria continue to claim children after the first month, and the under-five gap widens accordingly.

Income groups show the same ordering. Low-income countries recorded 24.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024 and 68.8 under-five deaths. High-income countries recorded 2.8 and 5.1. Upper middle income countries, at 6.8 and 13.1, sit well inside both thresholds, and have done so for the whole period since 2015. Lower middle income countries, at 21.6 and 43.8, lie outside both thresholds. The income gradient is steep because the interventions that save newborns and young children are largely a matter of health-system capacity: skilled attendance at birth, emergency obstetric care, neonatal care units, vaccination, and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria. These depend on financing and trained staff that low-income systems have found hard to sustain.

The trend classification separates regions that will reach the thresholds from those that will not. East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, high income and upper middle income groups are all on track or have met both targets. East Asia & Pacific reached 6.7 neonatal and 13.2 under-five in 2024, and Latin America & Caribbean 8.3 and 15.4, so each is already below both thresholds. The expected 2030 values are lower still, at 5.8 neonatal for East Asia & Pacific and 7.3 for Latin America & Caribbean. For these regions the target is no longer a constraint, and the policy question becomes one of equity within countries, which regional averages conceal.

South Asia is the clearest case of rapid change. Its neonatal rate fell from 25.4 in 2015 to 16.6 in 2024, and its under-five rate from 42.6 to 26.8. The pace of decline, -0.0502 a year in the under-five rate, is the fastest of any region, and the trend ratio of 1.30 means that the pace exceeds what the target requires. The expected 2030 values are 12.5 neonatal and 19.7 under-five, so South Asia is on track for the under-five threshold and, with a ratio of 0.96, just short of fully matching the neonatal pace needed. The classification still counts it as on track.

The regions and groups that fall short are those where mortality is highest. Low-income countries cut under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8 per 1,000 between 2015 and 2024, at a rate of -0.0231 a year. At that pace the expected 2030 value is 59.8, far above 25.0, and the trend ratio of 0.42 is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The neonatal record is weaker: 28.1 fell to 24.9, an annual rate of -0.0133, with an expected 2030 value of 23.0 against a threshold of 12.0 and a ratio of 0.32. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same pattern, with an expected 2030 under-five rate of 63.3 and a neonatal rate of 25.0. Neonatal mortality is the harder problem, since it falls more slowly than under-five mortality when health systems are weak, and the share of child deaths occurring in the first month rises as other causes recede.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan group has a mixed profile. Its under-five rate, 36.4 in 2024, is classed as moderate progress needing acceleration, with an expected 2030 value of 31.1. Its neonatal rate, 22.7, is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 20.3. The group combines countries with low mortality and countries in prolonged conflict, so the regional figure conceals wide internal differences, and the figure for the whole group does not describe any single country in it.

The lower middle income group needs a caution. Its under-five rate fell from 55.3 to 43.8 and its neonatal rate from 26.9 to 21.6, which are real gains, and its classifications of moderate progress carry trend ratios of 0.59 and 0.55. The expected 2030 values of 37.5 and 18.7 stay above both thresholds. The figures for this group are truncated in the trend output, and some rows for Sub-Saharan Africa are cut off in the same way, so the full classification text is not reproduced here. Only the numbers and classifications shown above can be relied upon, and conclusions for those groups rest on that partial record.

The implication for 2030 is that regional averages mask a concentrated problem. The thresholds are within reach, or already met, across most of the world, but the regions that remain furthest away are those with the largest number of births and the weakest health systems. A pace that has held steady since 2015 will not close the gap without a marked change in the countries of Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group.

### What changed since 2015, and why the pace differs

Between 2015 and 2024 every region and income group reduced both rates, but the pace varied widely. South Asia fell fastest. Its neonatal mortality went from 25.4 to 16.6 per 1,000 live births, and its under-five mortality from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rates of change, which the trend tool expresses as a proportional rate, were -0.0462 for neonatal and -0.0502 for under-five mortality. That is roughly twice the pace of the world as a whole, at -0.0133 and -0.0151. Sub-Saharan Africa moved slowest on the neonatal measure, from 29.2 to 26.6, a rate of -0.0103. Its under-five rate, from 85.0 to 71.2, fell at -0.0195, which is faster than its neonatal rate but still leaves it far from the threshold.

The pattern across income groups is similar. Low-income countries reduced neonatal mortality from 28.1 to 24.9, a rate of -0.0133, and under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8, a rate of -0.0231. Lower-middle-income countries did better on both, with neonatal mortality falling from 26.9 to 21.6 (-0.0241) and under-five mortality from 55.3 to 43.8 (-0.0256). East Asia & Pacific, already at lower levels, still reduced under-five mortality from 16.6 to 13.2, a rate of -0.0251. High-income countries and North America moved slowly, at -0.0142 and -0.0034 for under-five mortality, but this is expected near a floor, where each further death averted is harder to achieve.

A consistent feature is that neonatal deaths fall more slowly than under-five deaths. For the world, the neonatal rate went from 19.4 to 17.2 while the under-five rate went from 42.9 to 37.4. In Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group the neonatal rate declined at roughly half the pace of the under-five rate. The proportional rates for the world confirm this: -0.0133 against -0.0151. The shares of deaths in the first 28 days therefore rise as overall child mortality falls. A well-established explanation is that deaths after the first month are mostly caused by infections, malnutrition and malaria, which respond to vaccination, sanitation, nutrition programmes and basic treatment. Neonatal deaths come largely from prematurity, birth complications and neonatal infection. These require skilled attendance at birth, functioning referral systems, and specialised newborn care, all of which depend on stronger health systems and take longer to build.

The differences in pace must be treated cautiously. The indicators measure outcomes, not interventions, and nothing in these series shows which policies produced the faster falls in South Asia or the slower ones in Sub-Saharan Africa. Plausible hypotheses include the expansion of facility births and cash transfers linked to institutional delivery in South Asia, and the heavier burden of conflict, fragility and weak health financing in low-income countries. These remain hypotheses, to be tested with the intervention series discussed elsewhere in the chapter. The estimates themselves are modelled from survey and registration data that are sparse in the countries with the highest mortality, so differences of a few tenths in annual change should not be over-read.

The period after 2020 cannot be separated in these series. Both indicators are reported as annual figures to 2024, and the figures give no sign of a reversal at the regional level, but the 2015 to 2024 comparison conceals any pause in particular years. The question of whether the disruption of routine health services in 2020 and 2021 slowed declines, or whether the modelling smooths it out, cannot be answered from the levels used here.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The thresholds will probably be met by most countries by 2030, but not by those that carry the greatest burden. On the trend classification, 130 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 the under-five threshold. The countries still short are concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income settings. The regional projections show how far they are from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2030 against a threshold of 12.0, and 63.3 under-five deaths per 1,000 against 25.0. Low-income countries are expected to reach 23.0 and 59.8 respectively. The world as a whole is expected to reach 15.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000, which is above the threshold, and 34.1 under-five deaths per 1,000, also above it.

Newborn deaths are the harder problem. The under-five rate is falling faster than the neonatal rate in most groupings, so the share of child deaths occurring in the first 28 days is rising. Neonatal deaths depend on skilled care at birth, management of preterm birth and infection, and functioning referral systems, which are costlier to build than the vaccination and treatment campaigns that drove earlier gains. A country can therefore meet the under-five threshold and still miss the neonatal one.

Two cautions apply. First, the classification depends on the trend method and on projecting a past rate of change forward. A different period or method could move countries between classes, particularly those near a boundary. Second, the wording 'at least as low as' can be read as a ceiling for each country in 2030, or as a direction of travel for countries already below it. This section uses the first reading, as the classification does. The wording also says nothing about inequality within countries, where national rates hide wide gaps.

Four proposals follow.

proposals: National governments and statistical offices should report progress on Target 3.2 both by the number of countries and by the number of births affected, so that a count of successful small countries does not mask the burden in the largest ones.

Health ministries and development partners should concentrate support on the 36 countries with marginal neonatal progress and the 13 that are stagnating or regressing, with newborn care at birth, in the first week and in referral facilities as the priority.
Donors and national governments should shift funding from the under-five agenda broadly to neonatal care, where progress lags, including skilled birth attendance and care for small and sick newborns.
