The data do not separate causes of death, and the thresholds can be read in more than one way.

w-c04-3-1.text:
### HIV incidence has fallen by more than a third worldwide

World HIV incidence fell from 0.26 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024. That is a decline of roughly 38 per cent, which supports the heading's claim of more than a third. The estimates come from UNAIDS and rest on modelled data, with 139 countries reporting in 2024. Coverage is therefore broad but not complete, and the world figure should be read as an aggregate of reporting countries rather than a census.

Tuberculosis moved more slowly. Estimated incidence fell from 150.0 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131.0 in 2024, a decline of about 13 per cent. Unlike the HIV series, the tuberculosis series covers 208 countries in 2024, close to universal. The World Health Organization recalculates its estimates for all years as methods improve, so the 2015 value used here may differ from figures published earlier. The comparison is internally consistent, but it should not be set against older reports without caution.

Malaria runs the other way. Incidence among populations at risk rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, because malaria is not a concern everywhere, and the denominator is the population at risk rather than the whole population. A rise in the rate therefore does not mean that malaria spread to new places. It means that, among those exposed, more people fell ill. Disruption to prevention and care during the pandemic years, resistance to drugs and insecticides, conflict, and constrained funding are well-established pressures on malaria control, though the series alone cannot apportion the rise among them.

Target 3.3 calls for ending the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria by 2030, but it sets no numerical threshold. The phrase can be read in more than one way: as zero incidence, as incidence low enough to cease to be a public health threat, or as a given percentage reduction from a baseline. The trend tool therefore applies no target value for HIV, and its classes of on track or target met rest on its own reading of the pace of decline rather than on a official benchmark. On that reading the world's HIV rate of change, a fall of 0.05 per 1,000 each year, is classed as on track. Such a class describes momentum, not arrival at a defined goal.

The contrast between the three diseases matters for 2030. HIV control has benefited from sustained investment in antiretroviral treatment and prevention, which lowers both illness and onward transmission. Tuberculosis has declined, but at a pace that would leave substantial incidence in 2030. Malaria has moved backwards on the measure used here. Reading the three together, the global record is one of clear progress against one disease, modest progress against a second and reversal against a third, and the following parts examine where those differences lie.

### Regions and income groups differ most in where the burden lies

The burden of the three diseases is distributed very unevenly, and the pattern differs by disease. For HIV, Sub-Saharan Africa remains the region with the highest incidence, yet it also recorded the largest fall. Incidence there declined from 1.2036 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.5374 in 2024. Low-income countries show a similar movement, from 0.707 to 0.3534, a halving over the nine years. These gains reflect the wide delivery of antiretroviral treatment and prevention, which has been concentrated where the epidemic was heaviest. Latin America and the Caribbean tells a different story. Its incidence moved only from 0.2438 in 2015 to 0.2154 in 2024. The level is far below that of Sub-Saharan Africa, but the pace of decline is slow, and by 2024 the region's rate is higher than that of low-income countries as a group was at its 2024 level only in the sense of being of the same order of magnitude. Epidemics concentrated among key populations, often with weaker prevention coverage, tend to respond less quickly than generalised epidemics that attract large international funding.

Two entries in the HIV comparison need care. South Asia is reported at 0.0907 in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries at 0.1783 in 2024, but in each case the tool returns the same value for 2015 and 2024. This reflects missing earlier data for the group aggregate, not stability, and no change over time can be read from those rows. Only the 2024 levels are usable: they indicate that South Asia has the lowest HIV incidence of the regions shown, but not whether it has fallen.

Tuberculosis shows a more divided picture than HIV. The world rate fell from 150 new and relapse cases per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131 in 2024, a decline classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. Beneath that average, regions moved in opposite directions. East Asia and Pacific rose from 140 to 144, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 45 to 51; both are classed as regression. Europe and Central Asia fell from 36 to 22, and South Asia from 233 to 189. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 115 to 110, classed as stagnation. North America held at 3.5 in both years, which is stagnation at a very low level and is not a cause for concern in itself.

Income groups show the same gradient. High-income countries fell from 20 to 12, and upper-middle-income countries from 107 to 92. Low-income countries moved from 229 to 199, and lower-middle-income countries from 241 to 208. Both are classed as moderate progress, needing acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 205 in 2024 after 285 in 2015, has the steepest regional decline, and is the only high-burden region classed as on track, together with South Asia. Even so, 205 cases per 100,000 remains among the highest rates of any region, so a fast decline does not mean a small burden. The target in question has no numerical value attached to it in the tool, so the classification relies on a trend rule rather than a stated end point; the target can be read in more than one way, for example as a fixed percentage reduction or as elimination as a public health problem, and the labels should be taken as indicative.

Malaria is the most concentrated of the three. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 232.4935 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 and 229.2614 in 2024, a change too small to count as progress. Low-income countries, which largely overlap with the region, moved from 207.1516 to 206.6892. The world rate rose from 59.0112 to 64.0411, which follows from the weight of Sub-Saharan Africa in the population at risk and from disruption to prevention and care after 2020. The rate in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan more than doubled, from 4.3337 to 9.9708, a signal of resurgence that the available data cannot explain, though conflict, displacement and flooding are well-known drivers. South Asia is the exception, falling from 6.3233 to 1.4562, and upper-middle-income countries fell from 2.0345 to 1.6485. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, since malaria is not endemic everywhere, so the denominators are populations at risk rather than whole populations.

### Country trajectories show progress alongside stagnation and regression

Beneath the regional averages, country trajectories diverge sharply, and the divergence differs by disease. Each country was classed by the direction and pace of its incidence series, and each class is reported both as a count of countries and as a share of the population those countries hold. The two measures answer different questions. A count treats a small island state and a populous country alike, and so shows how widespread a pattern is. A population share shows how many people live under it, and so shows where the weight of the epidemic falls.

For HIV, 49 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 49.7% of the population of the 146 countries assessed. Another 4 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration (0.8% of the population) and 12 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration (3.0%). The largest group by count is stagnation, with 60 countries holding 35.7% of the population, and 21 countries, holding 10.8%, are in regression. Taken together, more than a third of the assessed population lives in countries where HIV incidence has barely moved, and about one in ten lives where it is rising. The world decline already described is therefore carried by roughly half the population, while the remainder has seen little or no benefit. Stagnation is the key finding. It suggests that prevention and treatment programmes have reached a plateau in many places, often where new infections are concentrated in groups that services reach poorly.

Tuberculosis presents a more favourable picture in breadth. Of 203 countries assessed, 123 are on track or have met the target, holding 61.2% of the population. Moderate progress with acceleration needed applies to 18 countries (4.2%), marginal progress to 11 (3.9%), and stagnation to 9 (14.8%). Regression affects 42 countries holding 15.8% of the population. The regressing group is large by count, yet a smaller share of people than the on-track group. Because tuberculosis incidence is estimated from notifications, prevalence surveys and modelling, a rise in some countries can reflect better detection as well as real spread, and the disruption of services during the pandemic years also affected case-finding. The classes cannot separate these causes.

Malaria is assessed in only 85 countries, since the series covers populations at risk and not the whole world. Of these, 36 are on track or have met the target, holding 59.2% of the population. Moderate progress applies to 3 countries (1.4%), marginal progress to 8 (8.0%) and stagnation to 5 (4.0%). Regression covers 33 countries and 27.5% of the population, the highest regressing population share of the three diseases. Malaria control depends on sustained delivery of nets, spraying, diagnostics and treatment, and is vulnerable to funding gaps, conflict, drug and insecticide resistance, and changes in climate. Where such supply is interrupted, incidence can rise quickly. That more than a quarter of the population in assessed countries lives in regression is a warning for the 2030 horizon.

The classification has limits that readers should keep in view. The rule is a trend fitted to a short series, and the period after 2015 is only nine or ten observations. A country with small numbers of cases or a sharp one-off fluctuation can be placed in a class that later years would revise. Modelled estimates are recalculated as methods are refined, so classes may shift between editions. The goal sets no numerical target for these indicators, so the classes judge each country against a decreasing path and not against a fixed threshold. The population weights also depend on which countries have data, which is why the three diseases cover different numbers of countries and cannot be summed. With these cautions, the common finding is that progress is real but concentrated, while stagnation and regression remain widespread.

### Uneven gains leave the 2030 target at risk and call for focused proposals

The evidence for target 3.3 points to three diseases moving at three different speeds. HIV incidence is falling quickly where it is highest. In Sub-Saharan Africa the trend rate is -0.0857 and the series is classed as on track or target met. Low-income countries, at -0.0742, are classed the same way, and so is the world, at -0.0525. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the regions assessed, with a rate of -0.0137, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. If the recent pace holds, the high-burden settings will end 2030 well below their 2015 levels. The target text does not define what ending an epidemic means, so even a continued fall cannot be judged against a fixed threshold.

Tuberculosis shows slower gains. The world trend rate is -0.0149, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. Low-income countries are classed in the same way, at -0.0155, and so are lower middle income countries at -0.0162 and upper middle income countries at -0.0166. These countries carry the largest burden, so slow movement there holds back the global result. High income countries, at -0.0552, and Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0533, are on track, but they start from low incidence and contribute little to the global total. South Asia, at -0.0230, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0359, are classed as on track. Two regions are moving the wrong way: East Asia and the Pacific, at 0.0031, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.0140, are both classed as regression. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0049, and North America, at 0.0000, are classed as stagnation. The period spans the disruption of 2020, when services for finding and treating cases were interrupted in many countries. The series cannot separate that disruption from longer trends, so a rise in recorded incidence may reflect either real transmission or changes in detection and estimation.

Malaria is the weakest result. World incidence rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 232.5 to 229.3, and low-income countries stayed at about 207, from 207.2 to 206.7. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan more than doubled, from 4.3 to 10.0. South Asia is the clear success, falling from 6.3 to 1.5. Of 85 countries assessed, 36 are on track, holding 59.2 per cent of the assessed population. Another 33 countries are in regression, holding 27.5 per cent. A further 8 show marginal progress, 5 show stagnation and 3 show moderate progress. Incidence is measured per population at risk, so changes in the size of that population affect the rate. The 2030 outlook is therefore favourable for HIV, uncertain for tuberculosis and poor for malaria.

The data show what changed and where, not why. Explaining the falls and rises needs other sources, such as programme coverage, funding, drug and insecticide resistance, conflict and climate. These are not held on the shelf and should not be inferred from the incidence series alone.

w-c06-5-1.text:
### The indicator and what it measures

Target 5.6 commits governments to universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The principal measure of progress in this section is the share of women aged 15 to 49 who make their own informed decisions regarding sexual relations, contraceptive use and reproductive health care. It is compiled by the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Statistics Division, mainly from Demographic and Health Surveys, and reported in the World Bank's World Development Indicators as a percentage of women aged 15 to 49.

The indicator is a composite. It applies to women who are married or in a union, and it counts a woman as deciding for herself only if she answers yes to all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner if she does not want it; she decides on the use of contraception; and she decides on her own health care. A woman who answers yes to two of the three is not counted. The measure is therefore strict, and its level is bound to be lower than the level for any single component. It also leaves out women who are not married or in a union, so it describes a particular part of the female population and not all women of reproductive age.

The reading of own decisions is not fixed across surveys. Each component rests on a question put to the respondent, and the wording, the response options and the interpretation of a joint decision with a partner can differ between survey rounds and between countries. A woman who decides jointly with her husband after discussion may be recorded differently from one whose husband decides alone, and cultural norms shape how women describe such arrangements. Answers on refusing sex are also sensitive to the setting of the interview. Differences between countries, or between years in one country, may thus partly reflect measurement and not only a change in women's autonomy.

The indicator is also not the only evidence the shelf holds on target 5.6. Related series cover a wider set of decisions within households, demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods, unmet need for contraception, attitudes towards refusing sex and prenatal care. They measure different things and are cited in the parts that follow only where they help to interpret the composite.

### Thin coverage limits any global picture

Only 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions in 2024, the latest year in the series. No aggregate is published for the indicator in any year, so the World Bank's catalogue gives no regional or world share. A global figure for the share of women who make their own decisions on health care and contraception therefore cannot be stated, and none is offered here.

The 2024 reading rests on the survey calendar rather than on any change in the underlying behaviour. Demographic and Health Surveys are fielded country by country, usually at intervals of several years, and a country appears in a given year only if a survey was completed and processed. A year with few reporting countries is a year in which few surveys were released, not evidence that decision-making has become less common or less measured. The 5 countries of 2024 are an accident of timing, and they are not a sample drawn to represent any region or income group.

For that reason the levels result for 2024 (c06-5.r1) supports only a handful of national readings. Each can describe the country it belongs to. None can be averaged into a regional picture, and none should be read as typical of countries with similar incomes or located in the same region. Averaging five values drawn from whichever surveys happened to conclude would mix countries whose populations, laws and health systems differ widely, and would give a number that describes no real population.

The wider record shows how uneven the coverage is. Across all years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. Yet the number reporting in a single year has ranged from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018. Even in the best year, 15 countries is a small part of those with a measured value at some point, and the set of reporting countries changes from year to year. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years would therefore reflect a change in who reported as much as any change in women's autonomy.

The constraint matters for the 2030 agenda. Target 5.6 is to be judged on whether access and rights are universal, and a measure that most countries report only once in a decade cannot show whether the target is being reached. The indicator is also confined to women who are married or in union, and it counts a woman only if she answers yes to all three components. Women outside unions, and countries without a recent survey, are absent from the evidence. The thin coverage is itself a finding: monitoring of this target depends on a few countries per year.

### Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data

Reporting by year shows why regions and countries cannot be compared on current data. The number of countries reporting the indicator ranged from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018. Between those years, the count moved among 4 in 2009, 7 in 2010, 12 in 2012, 6 in 2013 and 10 in 2016. Each year's reading therefore describes a different group of countries, and a change in a year's picture may reflect who was surveyed rather than any change in women's lives.

The pattern follows the survey cycle. Demographic and Health Surveys visit a country every few years, and the countries reached in one year are seldom those reached in the next. A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2019 and 2020, cannot be set side by side. Regional groupings fare no better, because a region may be represented by one or two countries in one year and by none in another. Without a published aggregate, no regional average exists to correct for this, and constructing one from such uneven entries would imply a precision the data do not hold.

The series has been reported by 81 countries in any year since 2006, yet in 2024 only 5 of them reported. A country's most recent reading may therefore be several years old, and comparing latest values across countries mixes survey years that may be a decade apart. Over that span, access to services, schooling and social norms can shift, so the gap between two countries' values may be partly a gap in dates.

Differences between countries are described only where the same survey design applies, and the same indicator definition holds, since the measure counts a woman only if she answers yes to all three components: refusing sex, deciding on contraception and deciding on her own health care. Where designs differ, or where a survey covers only women married or in union, the comparison is left unclaimed. The 5 countries reporting in 2024 are too few to support any ranking or regional statement, and none is made. What the data allow is a country-by-country reading of each survey on its own terms, with its year stated, and not a league table of regions or of countries.

### Reporting has changed little since 2015

Reporting on women's own informed decisions has not grown steadily since the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. In 2015, 5 countries reported the indicator. The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached a peak of 15 in 2018, then fell to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020. It recovered to 7 in 2021, 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023, before dropping to 5 in 2024. Across all years, 81 countries have reported at least once.

This pattern follows the survey cycle and not women's circumstances. Household surveys are fielded in a country every few years, and each round is processed and compiled some time afterwards. A year with many reporting countries is one in which many survey rounds happened to be completed and published; a year with few is one in which fewer did. The low count in 2024 is likely to reflect publication lag in part, so that later releases may add countries to recent years. The data do not show this, and it should be treated as an expectation and not a finding.

The fall to 4 countries in 2019 and 2020 coincides with the onset of the pandemic, which interrupted fieldwork in many countries from 2020. Interruption cannot explain the 2019 figure, which precedes it, and the series alone cannot separate the effect of disruption from the ordinary variation of survey timing. The recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is consistent with fieldwork resuming, but it too is a count of surveys and not a measure of change.

The consequence is that no before-and-after comparison around 2015 or 2020 can be drawn from this series. Each year's group of reporting countries differs from the last, so a rise or fall in any average would reflect who was surveyed. A trend in women's decision-making since 2015 cannot be stated from these data, and the 2030 horizon cannot be assessed against a baseline that does not exist in comparable form.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 5.6 cannot be judged as on track or off track with the data now held. The indicator on women's own informed decisions has no aggregate in any year, and the number of countries reporting in a given year has swung between 3 and 15. Only 5 countries reported in 2024, the latest year, and 81 countries have reported in at least one year. A trend needs the same countries measured at intervals, and the shelf does not offer that. Whether a country has moved towards 2030 therefore cannot be told from a comparison of one year's reporters with another's.

The reading of the target adds a second difficulty. Target 5.6 speaks of universal access and of reproductive rights, which no single survey question captures. The indicator requires a woman to answer yes to all three components: refusing sex, choosing contraception and deciding on her own health care. It covers women married or in union only, so unmarried women and adolescents fall outside it. A rise or fall in the share could reflect a change in any of the three components, and the series alone does not say which.

The proposals below follow from these findings. They aim to make the next five years of reporting usable for judging the target, since the period to 2030 is short and surveys are slow to field.

claims.fact: c06-5.r2: countries reporting in any year
c06-5.r2: countries reporting in any year
c06-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: National statistical offices and the donors that fund Demographic and Health Surveys should schedule a household survey with the decision-making module in every country at regular intervals, so that each country reports at least once every five years before 2030.

The United Nations Population Fund, the United Nations Statistics Division and the survey programmes should harmonise the wording and the population base of the questions on decisions, and state clearly whether unmarried women are included.
Survey programmes should publish results disaggregated by age, wealth quintile and urban or rural residence, so that governments can see which women are left out of decisions.
The World Bank and the United Nations compilers should add a regional aggregate once enough countries report in a common period, and should state the coverage on which it rests.
w-c06-5-1.gaps: The data give no global or regional share of women who make their own decisions, no trend for any group of countries, and no figures for unmarried women or adolescents. The indicator measures decisions, not access to services or rights as such, so it covers only part of target 5.6. Disaggregation by age, wealth and residence is not held on the shelf.

w-c06-7-1.text:
### The global gap in internet use by sex

Target 5.b asks for greater use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The bench's results measure one aspect of that aim: the share of women and of men who have used the internet in the previous three months. They do not measure ownership of a mobile phone by sex. The series on mobile cellular subscriptions is counted per 100 people and is not divided by sex, and subscriptions can be held by one person in several numbers, so it cannot show who owns a handset. The question of a gap in phone ownership therefore cannot be answered here, and the findings below concern internet use alone.

On that measure, the world's women moved a long way in a short time. Female internet use stood at 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and reached 68.2 per cent in 2024. The rise is 16.4 percentage points in five years, a period that includes the pandemic, when schooling, work, public services and social contact moved online and gave households a strong reason to connect.

Male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and reached 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two world figures do not share an end year. The female series is read at 2024 and the male series at 2025, because the latest world value in each result falls in a different year. Subtracting one from the other gives 8.4 percentage points, but that difference mixes a gap between the sexes with a year of growth in male use. It overstates the gap in any single year, and it should be read as an upper bound rather than a measurement. A clean comparison requires both series at the same date, and the regional results, where both are read at 2024, allow that comparison in the parts that follow.

The 2019 figures are on a common footing and show a gap of 4.2 percentage points, with women at 51.8 per cent and men at 56.0 per cent. On that basis women used the internet at about 0.93 of the male rate. Whatever the true gap in 2024, it is therefore unlikely to have vanished, and the figures give no sign that it has widened beyond what the mismatched endpoints suggest. Because use rose for both sexes, a gap measured in percentage points can grow while the ratio improves, so the two measures can point in different directions and each should be stated with its basis.

The figures also carry a caution about coverage. The results are aggregates over the economies that report, and the count of countries reporting in 2025 is only 7 in each result. The 2025 world and income-group values therefore rest on a thin base of direct observation and on estimates for the rest, and the 2024 regional values are better supported. Internet use as defined here also says nothing about the quality of access, the device used, the cost of data or what women do online, all of which bear on empowerment as much as the bare fact of use. The headline picture is one of rapid gains by women and a persisting, but not precisely dated, shortfall against men.

### Regional differences in the gap

In 2024 the gap between women's and men's internet use is widest where overall connectivity is at a middle level, and narrowest where it is almost universal. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women had used the internet in the previous three months, against 67.6 per cent of men, a difference of 12.6 percentage points. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 per cent for women and 69.1 per cent for men, a difference of 12.8 percentage points. In Sub-Saharan Africa the shares were 29.4 per cent and 37.9 per cent, a difference of 8.5 percentage points. The absolute gap there is smaller than in the two regions above, but the level of use is far lower, so the ratio of female to male use is close to 0.78, against 0.81 in South Asia and 0.81 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Measured by ratio, the three regions are therefore closer together than the point differences suggest.

The gap is small where use is nearly universal. In North America 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024, a difference of 0.6 percentage points. In Europe and Central Asia the shares were 90.0 per cent and 91.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean lies between, at 81.3 per cent for women and 82.0 per cent for men. These are regions where mobile networks, affordable devices and high levels of female schooling have long been in place, and where saturation leaves little room for a difference to persist.

East Asia and Pacific shows a reversal. In 2019 women's use, at 67.4 per cent, was slightly above men's, at 66.7 per cent. By 2024 women stood at 85.5 per cent and men at 87.6 per cent, so men had moved ahead by 2.1 percentage points. The regional aggregate hides large differences among its economies, and the data given here do not show which of them drove the change. The result should be read as a shift in the regional average, not as evidence of decline in women's use, which rose by 18.1 percentage points over the period.

Income groups show the same pattern in sharper form. In low-income countries 18.3 per cent of women used the internet in 2025, against 28.6 per cent of men, a difference of 10.3 percentage points. Fewer than one woman in five was online, and the male share was more than half as large again. Seven countries reported in 2025 for these series, so the income-group figures for that year rest on very thin direct observation and probably include estimates; they should be treated as indicative. Regional figures for 2024 are better supported.

The regional pattern matters for target 5.b because the gap is concentrated in the regions where the most women live without access. Closing the difference in North America or Europe would affect few people, while a similar proportional gain in South Asia or Sub-Saharan Africa would bring tens of millions of women online. Well-established causes of the gap include the cost of devices and data, lower female literacy and schooling, social norms that restrict women's independent use of phones, and concerns over safety and harassment online. These operate with different force in each region, which is why a single global figure conceals as much as it reveals.

### What changed since 2019 and what the data can support

South Asia shows the largest change since 2019. Female internet use there rose from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, more than doubling, while male use rose from 34.9 per cent to 69.1 per cent. The gap in percentage points therefore stayed within a narrow band, at about 10.6 points in 2019 and 12.8 points in 2024. Women gained a great deal in absolute terms, but the distance to men did not close. Sub-Saharan Africa shows a similar pattern at a lower level: women moved from 20.2 per cent to 29.4 per cent, men from 28.6 per cent to 37.9 per cent.

The comparison across countries points the same way. For the 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male changes is 0.958, and that between 2024 levels is 0.948. Countries where men's use grew quickly are, almost without exception, those where women's use grew quickly. The finding indicates that expansion of access is largely shared: networks, devices, prices and public policy lift both sexes together, and no group of countries shows women advancing on a separate path. A correlation of this kind does not explain why gaps persist where they do. Differences in income, education, literacy, norms on women's use of devices and the cost of handsets and data all plausibly contribute, and the series cannot separate them.

Income groups show the same story. In low-income countries, female use reached 18.3 per cent in 2025 against 28.6 per cent for men. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, and in upper-middle-income countries 87.9 per cent and 89.7 per cent. In high-income countries the gap is almost closed, at 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent. The world figures moved from 51.8 per cent for women and 56.0 per cent for men in 2019 to 68.2 per cent for women in 2024 and 76.6 per cent for men in 2025. Those two world values fall in different years, so the world gap cannot be read directly from them.

The evidence has limits that bear on every figure above. In 2019, 92 countries reported female internet use; in 2024, 65 did; in 2025, only 7. The fall after 2019 coincides with the pandemic years and later reporting delays, and the reason is not stated in the data. The 2025 values for income groups therefore rest on very thin reporting, and are likely to be revised as more countries submit data. The 54-country comparison is a subset of the 137 countries that have ever reported, and it may differ from the countries that report least. Poorer countries with weaker statistical systems are the ones most likely to be missing, so measured progress may overstate the global picture. The series also defines use over the previous three months and from any device, so it says nothing about who owns a phone, who controls it, or how it is used.

### Implications for target 5.b by 2030 and proposals

Target 5.b carries no numerical threshold and no date-bound level, so it can be read in more than one way. The reading adopted here is a narrowing of the gap between women's and men's internet use, alongside rising levels for women. On that reading the evidence for 2030 is mixed. Levels have risen sharply, but the gap has not closed where female use is lowest.

The world figure shows the pattern. Female use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, while male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The male figure refers to a later year than the female one, so the two cannot be subtracted without care. The regional figures for 2024 are on a common year and are the safer basis. In Sub-Saharan Africa female use was 29.4 per cent in 2024 against 37.9 per cent for men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the figures were 55.0 per cent and 67.6 per cent. In South Asia they were 56.3 per cent and 69.1 per cent. Where use is near universal, as in North America, with 94.1 per cent for women and 94.7 per cent for men, the gap is almost gone.

By income group the same ordering holds. In low-income countries female use reached 18.3 per cent and male use 28.6 per cent in 2025. In lower middle income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent. In high income countries they were 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. A gap of this kind closes mainly as a whole population connects, and only the groups that are nearly saturated have reached that point. If current trends continue, the regions with the lowest female use are unlikely to reach parity by 2030, even though their levels are rising quickly. Well-established causes include the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, social norms on who may own a device, and concerns about safety online.

The country evidence suggests that the gap follows general connectivity rather than departing from it. Across 54 countries, changes in female use from 2019 to 2024 and changes in male use correlate at a Spearman coefficient of 0.958, and 2024 levels at 0.948. Women's use therefore rises where men's rises. Specific barriers to women are not isolated by this evidence, and the correlation is silent on whether gaps are closing within countries.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

claims.fact: c06-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2024
c06-7.r2: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2024
c06-7.r4: countries reporting in any year
c06-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2024
c06-7.r2: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2024

proposals: National statistical offices and the International Telecommunication Union should report internet use and mobile phone ownership by sex every year, restoring the country coverage that has fallen since 2019.

Governments and regulators in South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan should prioritise affordability and access measures for women, including lower handset and data costs and public access points.
Those who monitor target 5.b should judge progress by the gap in percentage points as well as by levels, so that rising averages do not mask persistent differences between women and men.
w-c06-7-1.gaps: Mobile phone ownership by sex is not held in the series examined, so the section measures internet use only. Country coverage of the sex-disaggregated series fell from 92 countries in 2019 to 65 in 2024, and only 7 reported for 2025. Target 5.b has no numerical threshold. Data on the quality, purpose and affordability of use are absent.

w-c03-6-1.text:
### Agriculture's weight in output and employment is shrinking only slowly

Agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 4.2 per cent of world GDP in 2015 and 4.0 per cent in 2025. The share has fallen by only a fraction of a percentage point in ten years, across a period that included the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the pandemic of 2020 and the food and energy price shocks that followed. In 2025, 158 countries reported the series, so the global figure rests on a broad but not complete base.

Employment tells a different story from output. Agriculture accounted for 28.5 per cent of total employment worldwide in 2015 and 25.8 per cent in 2025, according to modelled estimates of the International Labour Organization. The sector therefore engaged roughly six times its share of output in 2025: a quarter of the world's workers produced about a twenty-fifth of its measured value added. The gap is the central fact for any judgement of public investment. It signals low output per worker, and it shows that a large part of the working population depends on a sector whose productivity is determined by roads, storage, irrigation, research and advisory services, all of which are largely public goods.

The pace of change is slow against the horizon of 2030. The employment share fell by 2.8 percentage points in ten years. At that rate, more than a fifth of the world's workers would still be employed in agriculture at the end of the Goals period. The output share fell by only 0.2 percentage points. Structural transformation, in which workers move from farms to higher-productivity work, is therefore under way but is far from complete, and a falling employment share is not evidence of falling need. Where output per worker is low, public spending that raises it is the means by which the share of employment can fall without a loss of rural income.

The benchmark that follows is simple. If public spending on agriculture were to match the sector's weight, it would be proportionate to a share of output of about 4.0 per cent in the world as a whole, and arguably to a higher share where employment is concentrated. The World Development Indicators supply no series for government agricultural expenditure in the results available here, so the match cannot be measured directly. The comparison must be made indirectly, through the external flows examined in the later parts and through the regional weights that follow. Target 2.a, which calls for greater investment in rural infrastructure, research, extension and gene banks, cannot be scored against a spending figure that the shelf does not hold, and the reading of any shortfall should be made with that limit in view.

### Regions differ most where agriculture matters most

The regional picture is one of extremes. In 2025, agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 17.9 per cent of GDP in Sub-Saharan Africa and 15.6 per cent in South Asia. Both regions also hold the largest shares of employment in the sector: 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa and 41.5 per cent in South Asia. At the other end, Europe and Central Asia drew 2.0 per cent of GDP from agriculture in 2025 and 6.7 per cent of employment, while North America drew 1.0 per cent of GDP in 2021, the latest year reported, and 1.5 per cent of employment in 2025. A farm worker in North America is part of a sector that is a rounding error in the national accounts; in Sub-Saharan Africa, the sector is where about half of all workers earn their living.

The gap between the two measures matters as much as the levels. In Sub-Saharan Africa the employment share is nearly three times the output share (49.3 per cent against 17.9 per cent), and in South Asia it is also close to three times (41.5 per cent against 15.6 per cent). Where half of workers produce under a fifth of output, average agricultural labour productivity is low relative to other sectors, and incomes in farming trail those elsewhere. Public spending that is proportionate to the sector's share of GDP would therefore still be small relative to the number of people who depend on it.

The direction of change after 2015 differs between regions. Latin America and the Caribbean is the one region where the output share rose markedly, from 5.5 per cent in 2015 to 6.8 per cent in 2025, while its employment share fell from 14.0 per cent to 12.7 per cent. A rising share with falling employment is consistent with higher commodity prices or output per worker rising, but the series alone does not settle which. Sub-Saharan Africa also saw its output share rise, from 16.3 per cent to 17.9 per cent, while its employment share fell by a smaller amount, from 53.3 per cent to 49.3 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific, by contrast, employment fell from 27.9 per cent to 21.7 per cent and the output share from 6.0 per cent to 5.5 per cent, the pattern of an economy moving labour out of farming. South Asia, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, moved only slightly in output share.

By income group, the divide is sharper still. In low-income countries agriculture accounted for 27.2 per cent of GDP in 2025, up from 25.6 per cent in 2015, and for 59.4 per cent of employment. Lower middle income countries stood at 17.8 per cent of GDP and 39.8 per cent of employment. Upper middle income countries recorded 6.9 per cent of GDP and 19.8 per cent of employment, and high income countries 1.3 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 2.9 per cent of employment in 2025. The poorest countries are therefore the ones in which the sector has not shrunk, and in which its share of output has risen even as the employment share eased. For target 2.a, whose wording singles out developing countries and the least developed among them, this concentration indicates where investment in rural infrastructure, research and extension has the largest population to reach by 2030.

### International flows from UN agencies rose but moved toward one region

Net official flows from UN agencies to the agricultural sector through IFAD rose across the period, though not evenly. The world total was 399 million US dollars in 2015 and 509 million in 2023. These are current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the apparent rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger real transfer. The series is also a net measure: repayments of loans are subtracted from disbursements, so a fall in a region's figure can reflect repayment as much as reduced lending.

The rise was concentrated in one region. Sub-Saharan Africa received 180 million US dollars in 2015 and 405 million in 2023, more than double. Every other region with a reported figure moved the other way. East Asia and Pacific fell from 99.9 million to 9.2 million. South Asia fell from 50.3 million to 43.1 million. Europe and Central Asia fell from 20.3 million to 15.5 million, Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.9 million to 9.0 million, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 29.2 million to 24.0 million. North America recorded zero in both years, as expected for a region of donors. The world total therefore rose because one region's gain outweighed the combined losses elsewhere.

The income groups show the same movement. Low-income countries received 109 million US dollars in 2015 and 247 million in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 201 million to 240 million. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 67.2 million to a net negative of 12.6 million, meaning that repayments to IFAD exceeded new disbursements in 2023. This is the pattern expected of a lender that shifts concessional resources toward the poorest countries while middle-income borrowers graduate and repay. High-income countries show small figures in both years, a negative of about 74 thousand US dollars in 2015 and 2.8 million in 2023, which reflects the few cases where such countries still appear as recipients or repayers.

The direction matches the regional evidence on need set out earlier, since Sub-Saharan Africa has the largest shares of output and jobs in agriculture. It matters for 2030 because target 2.a asks for more investment in developing countries, in particular the least developed. A rise confined to a single region and to the lowest income groups is consistent with that wording, yet the sums are small. Half a billion dollars a year, spread across a continent whose farm economy employs about half of all workers, cannot substitute for domestic public spending.

Coverage limits how far the picture can be pressed. IFAD flows were reported by 94 countries in 2023. The companion series on flows from FAO was reported by 129 countries in 2023, against 133 in 2013 and 139 in any year, so reporting is broad but not complete, and has drifted slightly downward since 2019, when 135 countries reported. Aggregates should therefore be read as sums over reporting countries, and a missing country is not a zero. The comparison before and after 2020 is further limited by the end of the series in 2023, which leaves little room to judge how flows responded to the pandemic and the price shocks that followed.

### Flows follow need, but do not yet change it, and proposals follow

Across the 89 countries for which both series exist, the link between flows and the size of agriculture depends on what is compared. The Spearman correlation of 2023 levels between net official flows from IFAD and agriculture's share of GDP is 0.575, a moderate positive association. Countries where agriculture contributes more to output tend to receive more from the fund. The correlation of changes between 2015 and 2023 is 0.141, which is weak. Countries that received more over the period did not, in general, see the sector's share move in a different way from those that received less. The Kendall coefficients, 0.390 for levels and 0.101 for changes, tell the same story on a stricter rank measure.

The reading is that flows go where agriculture is large, as a needs-based allocation would predict, but do not yet visibly shift the structure of the economy. That is not surprising. A flow directed at rural infrastructure, extension services or research takes years to alter productivity, and a falling share of GDP can reflect growth elsewhere as much as any change in farming. Structural change is slow, as the sector's global share of 4.0 per cent in 2025 against 4.2 per cent in 2015 already shows. Ten years is a short window against which to judge a transfer of this kind.

The limits of the evidence are plain. A correlation is not a cause: the link of levels may arise because IFAD lends to agricultural economies by mandate, not because the money has any effect. The weak link of changes cannot show that flows fail, since the counterfactual is unknown. The series also covers one agency's net flows, in current dollars, and the coverage of the companion FAO series fell from 135 countries in 2019 to 129 in 2023, which narrows what can be compared. Above all, target 2.a can be read in more than one way: as public spending by governments, as private investment, or as international cooperation. The data on the bench measure only the last, and in part. Whether public spending on agriculture matches the sector's weight, 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2025 and 17.9 per cent of its GDP, cannot be answered from these series, because government agricultural spending is absent.

For 2030 the implication is that the match between investment and need cannot at present be tested, and the weak link of changes gives no ground to expect that current flows will bring the sector's share, or its employment share, into line with the targets. The proposals below follow from that finding.

claims.fact: c03-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c03-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c03-6.r4: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Finance ministries and statistical offices should report government agricultural spending annually, set against the sector's shares of GDP and of employment, so that target 2.a can be tested for public investment.

IFAD, FAO and bilateral donors should direct a larger part of international flows to the regions with the largest gaps, chiefly Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where agriculture's shares of output and jobs are highest.
The World Bank and the OECD should publish country-level coverage and flows for every year to 2030, so that the match between flows and need can be tested country by country.
w-c03-6-1.gaps: The series hold no government agricultural spending, no private investment in agriculture and no measure of results from the flows; only net official flows from two UN agencies are covered, in current dollars, for 129 to 139 countries. Correlations cannot show cause, and target 2.a can be read as public, private or international investment.

w-c05-2-1.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

The headline figure for children of primary school age who are out of school is a sum of group totals, and it needs to be read with that in mind. Adding the four income groups' counts gives about 87.5 million children in 2025, set against about 87.4 million in 2015. The title rounds this to 88 million. The two totals are almost identical, which means a decade that began with the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals has ended with no reduction in the number of children outside school.

The composition beneath that flat total has changed. Low-income countries counted 30.1 million out-of-school children in 2025, up from 26.0 million in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million over the same period. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. The fall in the lower middle income group offset the rises elsewhere, so the global sum conceals a movement of the burden toward the poorest countries. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest share, about 46.4 million of the total, because they contain very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate.

The figures must not be taken as a global estimate. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, as the results record, while the series itself holds a much wider coverage across its history, 198 countries for the count. A sum built on so few reporters in the latest year depends on which countries happened to report, and the group totals may reflect different country sets in 2015 and 2025. The comparison between the two years is therefore indicative of direction only. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, and those in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count as out of school. Rises in some groups may partly reflect late entry or enrolment in pre-primary classes rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. A total that has not fallen since 2015 implies that the first decade of the goals did not close that gap. The years after 2020 sit in the same data window, and the interruption of schooling during the pandemic, together with conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries, are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up. The available results do not separate these effects, so they cannot be attributed with precision.

For 2030, the implication is that the arithmetic is unfavourable. With the global count unchanged over ten years, ending exclusion in the five that remain would require a rate of decline that the period to 2025 has not shown. The rates in the following part show where that difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries. The ratio between the two is about 9.64. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall steadily as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. Fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was therefore outrun by demography.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest number of out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. Much of the global stability in the total, noted earlier, reflects this gain being offset by increases elsewhere.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015. This is a rise of 5.6 percentage points, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion deepens as children grow older: many enter school, few progress, and costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push them out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, adolescent exclusion was broadly flat or slightly lower. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest and where the cohorts are growing fastest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which two in five lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, with a small excess of boys in every income group. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys. The sexes are therefore not far apart, though here girls are the larger group. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys, so the girls' count rose by about 2.17 million over the decade and the boys' by about 1.90 million. The gap in low-income countries widened slightly in absolute terms and remains in the girls' disadvantage.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' exclusion fell faster than boys' there, by about 3.13 million against about 2.44 million. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in all three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

The direction of the sex difference thus changes with national income: girls are the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, the barriers that fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, remain active. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. Only 8 countries are reporting in 2025 in these series, so the group totals rest on thin and uneven reporting, and part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Where the data end at the national level, parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are also well-established pressures after the pandemic. The data do not separate these causes.

The country classes confirm that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are numerous, while the population share on track is nearly as large.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents are the weakest point. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, while every other group held steady or improved slightly. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, so that picture rests on thin and uneven coverage. A pattern in which exclusion grows as children pass the end of primary school is consistent with fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and with too few secondary places, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.

proposals: National statistical offices and UNESCO's Institute for Statistics, with donors financing the work, should fund regular household surveys and administrative reporting so that out-of-school counts are reported for more countries each year and are comparable across them; only 12 countries reported adolescent data in 2025.

Governments of low-income countries and their development partners should direct education financing to access in the poorest systems, covering school places, removal of fees and support for the poorest households, since these countries show stagnation at primary age.

Ministries of education and donors should prioritise lower secondary access in low-income countries, where exclusion rose to 41.7% in 2025, through more places, transport and measures that keep girls and boys enrolled past primary level.

The United Nations statistical system and national governments should monitor the 95 regressing countries individually, and the monitoring should state explicitly whether the target is read as zero exclusion or as a tolerated residual share.
