proposals: National statistical offices, with funding from development partners, should run household surveys that measure social protection on a regular cycle, so that coverage of the poorest quintile can be tracked in every country and not only in those that happen to be surveyed.

The United Nations statistical community and the governments that adopted the goals should agree a numeric reading of substantial coverage under target 1.3, stating the share of the poorest quintile to be reached, so that progress can be judged against a common standard.

Governments of low-income countries and their bilateral and multilateral partners should prioritise extending programmes in low-income countries, with multi-year financing that does not lapse with donor budget cycles.

The World Bank and national agencies should report coverage of the poorest quintile beside the whole-population figure in every release, so that the headline number does not mask the position of the poor.

Analysts and policymakers should use whole-population coverage only as a provisional guide to the position of the poorest, given the strong link between the two measures in a small sample of countries, and should replace it with poorest-quintile data when these become available.
w-c02-3-1.gaps: The data do not show coverage of the poorest quintile in most countries after 2021, nor the adequacy or value of benefits, nor whether the poor are reached by programmes designed for them. Coverage of the world aggregate is held for one year only, so change since 2015 and 2020 cannot be read. Informal and non-state support, and the vulnerable who are not poor, are not measured. Target 1.3 has no numeric threshold for substantial coverage.

w-c03-2-1.text:
### Stunting and wasting set against the 2025 and 2030 targets

The world has moved only slightly towards the internationally agreed nutrition targets since 2015. Stunting, measured as the share of children under five whose height for age is more than two standard deviations below the international reference median, stood at 24.6% in 2015 and 23.2% in 2024 on the modelled estimate. That is a fall of about 1.4 percentage points in nine years, or roughly 0.16 points a year. Wasting, the share whose weight for height falls equally far below the reference median, moved from 7.1% to 6.6% over the same period, a fall of 0.5 points. Neither series shows a break after 2015 that would mark a change of direction, and the latest year available is 2024, so the effects of the shocks that followed 2020 on food prices, health services and household incomes cannot be separated from the underlying slow decline.

The two indicators describe different conditions and should not be read as one. Stunting reflects chronic deprivation: poor maternal nutrition, repeated infection, inadequate diets in the first two years of life and limited access to water and sanitation. It accumulates over months and years and is difficult to reverse after early childhood, which is why its decline is gradual even where conditions improve. Wasting reflects acute loss of weight, driven by recent illness, famine, conflict or sudden shortfalls in food. It can rise and fall within a season, so a national survey taken at one moment may record a figure that differs from the annual average. A prevalence of 6.6% for wasting therefore carries more uncertainty about timing than 23.2% for stunting carries.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. The text of Target 2.2 asks that the internationally agreed targets on stunting and wasting be achieved by 2025, and that all forms of malnutrition end by 2030. The agreed global nutrition benchmarks, as framed for the Goals, set a wasting level of 5.0% by 2030, and the bench's trend tool projects towards 2030 rather than 2025. Two readings follow. Under the strict reading of the target text, the 2025 deadline falls one year after the latest observation, and with wasting at 6.6% in 2024 and stunting at 23.2%, the 2025 milestone cannot plausibly have been met for either indicator. Under the reading used by the trend tool, the question is whether the 2030 benchmark is within reach. The two readings agree on the verdict for 2025 but differ in how much time they allow, and this book states which is in use wherever a projection is quoted.

For wasting, the gap to the 5.0% benchmark is 1.6 percentage points in 2024. At the pace of the past nine years, about 0.06 points a year, six further years would remove well under half of that gap. The benchmark is thus unlikely to be reached by continuing the recent pace, and reaching it would require a rate of improvement several times faster than that recorded since 2015. For stunting, the agreed benchmark is a reduction relative to a baseline rather than a fixed level, and no single threshold is given in the facts held here, so this part does not state one. It can be said, however, that a fall of 1.4 points in nine years leaves the world far from any reduction large enough to be described as ending the condition.

Why this matters goes beyond the numbers. Children who are stunted face poorer cognitive development, lower school attainment and reduced earnings in adulthood, and severe wasting sharply raises the risk of death in early childhood. A near-flat global line therefore signals a persistent loss of human potential in each new cohort, not merely a missed statistical goal. The links to other Goals are direct: health, education, water and sanitation, and poverty reduction all shape the figures above.

A further caution concerns the global figures themselves. The stunting series is a modelled estimate that combines survey data with statistical methods to fill years without a survey, and the wasting series is built from harmonised survey data in which only a few countries report in a given recent year. The global picture is therefore a reasonable guide to the direction and approximate scale of change, but small differences between years should not be treated as real movements. What the evidence does support is a plain conclusion: progress since 2015 has been real but slow, and the world is not on course for either target.

### Regional differences in stunting and wasting

Behind the modest world average lies a wide spread of regional experience. South Asia carries the heaviest burden on both measures. Its stunting prevalence fell from 37.8% in 2015 to 31.5% in 2024, the largest absolute decline among the regions listed, yet one child in three under five remains stunted. Its wasting prevalence stood at 15.7% in 2024, against 16.6% in 2015, a reduction of less than one percentage point. Wasting in South Asia is therefore more than double the world figure of 6.6% in 2024. The region combines high rates of low birth weight, early marriage and adolescent pregnancy, limited dietary diversity and persistent sanitation deficits, and these causes act on stunting and wasting together.

Sub-Saharan Africa presents a different pattern. Stunting declined only from 34.4% in 2015 to 32.3% in 2024, so that the region, which had a lower rate than South Asia in 2015, now has a slightly higher one. Wasting fell more clearly, from 7.0% to 5.9%, a drop of about 1.2 percentage points. The contrast suggests that acute malnutrition, which responds to treatment programmes and seasonal relief, can improve faster than chronic growth failure, which depends on maternal health, diets, sanitation and incomes over many years. Population growth also means that a falling prevalence can coexist with a rising number of affected children, a distinction the prevalence series cannot show.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 27.5% to 24.1% in stunting and from 6.5% to 5.6% in wasting. Conflict, displacement and fiscal stress in parts of this heterogeneous grouping weigh against the gains, and the regional average conceals very different national circumstances. East Asia and Pacific moved from 14.5% to 13.3% in stunting, a slow decline for a region whose income growth has been rapid, and its wasting rate barely changed, from 3.7% to 3.6%.

Europe and Central Asia is the clearest example of steady improvement. Stunting fell from 6.0% to 4.6%, and wasting from 1.5% to 1.0%. The regional trend calculation shows it on track for the 5.0% reference level by 2030, with an expected value of 3.8%, although the level was already close to that mark in 2015. Latin America and the Caribbean, by contrast, was flat: stunting stood at 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, which the trend calculation classes as regression. Wasting there eased from 1.5% to 1.3%. Earlier gains in the region appear to have stalled, and the economic disruption after 2020 and the unequal recovery of incomes among poorer households are plausible contributors, though the series do not isolate causes.

North America shows a rise in stunting from 2.8% in 2015 to 4.1% in 2024, while wasting fell from 0.3% to 0.2%. The trend tool labels the region as on track, because its level lies below the target value, but the direction is adverse. The levels are low, the regional average rests on very few countries, and modelled estimates for populations with small samples carry wide uncertainty. The rise should be read as a signal worth checking rather than as a settled finding. The same applies to high-income countries as a group, where stunting moved from 3.9% to 4.0%.

Income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries began at 37.9% stunting in 2015 and ended at 35.8% in 2024, still the highest level of any group listed. Their wasting rate fell from 7.9% to 6.4%. Lower-middle-income countries show the strongest stunting decline, from 33.9% to 28.9%, a fall of about 5.1 percentage points, but their wasting remained at 9.5% in 2024, down from 10.5%, the highest of any income group, reflecting the weight of South Asia within it. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 11.9% to 10.8% in stunting and from 2.6% to 2.1% in wasting. High-income countries held wasting at 0.4% in 2024, down from 0.6%.

The gradient by income is steep and has not narrowed in relative terms. Low-income countries had a stunting level about nine times that of high-income countries in 2015 and about nine times in 2024 on these rounded figures. Growth in income has helped where it occurred, but the lower-middle group shows that faster decline is possible without rich-country incomes, which points to the role of health, water, sanitation and social protection policy.

Two cautions apply. The trend summary for income groups and for some regions is truncated in the output available, so the South Asia line is read here from the levels and from its computed rate and expected value rather than a complete classification. The wasting summary also reports only six countries reporting in 2024, against 162 for stunting, so recent regional wasting figures rest on thin and uneven observation, and modelled aggregates should be treated with corresponding care.

For 2030, the regional pattern implies that the global figure will be decided largely in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The expected 2030 stunting values from the trend calculation are 27.9% for South Asia and 31.0% for Sub-Saharan Africa, both well above the 5.0% reference level. Only Europe and Central Asia, and the high-income group, sit at or near it.

### Country progress on wasting and the absence of convergence in stunting

Wasting presents a more differentiated national picture than stunting. The trend assessment covered 65 countries against the target of 5.0% by 2030, a ceiling that the Sustainable Development Goals framework sets for wasting. Of these, 42 countries, holding 38.6% of the population of the countries assessed, were on track or had already met the target. Four countries, with 7.8% of that population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Three countries showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration, and these three hold 33.7% of the population. No country was classed as stagnating, while 16 countries, with 19.9% of the population, were regressing, that is, wasting was rising rather than falling.

The population shares matter as much as the country counts. A simple count suggests that most assessed countries are doing well, since 42 of 65 is the majority. Weighted by population, however, the picture is less comfortable. The three countries in the marginal class account for a third of the assessed population, which implies that a small number of very populous countries dominate the global burden and are not close to the target. Together with the 16 regressing countries, the population living in countries that are marginal or going backwards is 53.7% of the total, which is more than the 38.6% living where the target is within reach. The sum is the reader's own arithmetic on the reported shares and should be read as approximate, since the shares are rounded.

Three cautions apply. First, only 65 countries were assessed, although the underlying series cover 162 countries. The assessment depends on there being enough survey observations to draw a trend, and countries without them are absent from every class. Second, the target of 5.0% can be read in more than one way: the 2025 goal agreed by the World Health Assembly was a prevalence below 5%, and the 2030 goal is a prevalence of 3%. The classification here uses 5.0% by 2030, and a country counted as on track against it may still be short of the stricter 3% figure. Third, wasting is volatile. It responds quickly to famine, conflict, floods, disease outbreaks and seasonal food shortages, so a single survey can show a sharp rise or fall that does not reflect a lasting change. Regression in a country may therefore reflect a recent crisis, and on-track status may reflect a favourable survey year.

The causes of regression are well understood in broad terms. Conflict and displacement disrupt health services and food supply. Price shocks following the pandemic in 2020 and later disturbances to grain and fertiliser markets reduced the quality and quantity of children's diets in poorer households. Where treatment for severe acute malnutrition depends on external funding, interruptions in supply of therapeutic food have direct effects. Countries that moved towards the target typically combined growth in household incomes with expanded primary health care, immunisation, and community-based treatment of acute malnutrition.

Stunting shows a different pattern: the gaps between countries are not closing. The convergence test relates the change in stunting between 2015 and 2024 to the starting level across 162 countries. If countries with high stunting at the start improved faster, the coefficient would be clearly negative. The estimated beta is -0.00244, with a p-value of 0.2275 and an R-squared of 0.0085. The sign points to a slight tendency towards convergence, but the estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains less than 1% of the variation in later change. In plain terms, a country's initial stunting rate says almost nothing about how fast it improved.

The coefficient of variation, which measures dispersion relative to the average, rose from 0.7234 in 2015 to 0.7900 in 2024. Dispersion between countries has therefore widened in relative terms. This is consistent with the lack of convergence, and it arises partly because the world average has fallen only slightly while some countries have moved much faster than others, and partly because the countries with low prevalence have reduced it further, so that the remaining high-prevalence countries stand further from the mean in proportion. A rising coefficient of variation does not by itself show that high-prevalence countries worsened; it shows that the spread, relative to the mean, grew.

For 2030 the implication is that the two measures need different responses. Wasting is a problem of a minority of populous and crisis-affected countries that sit well off course, while many smaller countries are already within reach. Stunting is a slow, structural condition tied to maternal health, early-life diet, sanitation and poverty, and the absence of convergence implies that no general catching-up process can be relied on. Without deliberate targeting of the countries with the highest prevalence, the relative gap will probably go on widening towards 2030.

### Data coverage and the limits of the evidence

Wasting is measured by household surveys, not by continuous registration, and the evidence behind the series is thinner than the regional table suggests. In 2000, 58 countries reported a wasting value. The count fell to 22 in 2001 and varied between 24 and 51 in later years. It stood at 32 in 2015, rose to 48 in 2018 and 46 in 2019, then fell to 26 in 2020. In 2024 only 6 countries reported. Across the whole period 162 countries reported at least once, so the series covers most of the world, but not in any single year.

The pattern follows the survey cycle. Large programmes of household surveys are fielded every few years in each country, and the results are published with a delay. A year with few reporting countries is therefore not evidence of fewer children measured, nor of improvement or decline. The low count for 2024 is best read as a lag in publication, since surveys fielded in that year have not yet been processed. The dip in 2020 has a clearer cause: fieldwork was suspended or postponed in many countries during the pandemic, and the count of 26 reflects that interruption. Readers comparing 2015 with 2024 should accept that the later point is the less complete one.

The regional and income-group values for 2024 are consequently not simple averages of fresh observations. They are aggregates produced from the harmonised dataset, which combines recent surveys with modelled estimates for countries and years without a survey. The figure of 6.6% for the world in 2024, and the regional values around it, rest in large part on that modelling. The fall from 7.1% in 2015 is real as a modelled estimate, but its size, about half a percentage point, is small relative to the uncertainty that such modelling carries. Changes of that scale between two years should not be treated as established.

The caution applies most strongly where reporting is thinnest. Regions with many countries and uneven survey schedules, notably Sub-Saharan Africa, have an aggregate that can move because of which countries happened to be surveyed as well as because of nutrition. The fall in that region from 7.0% in 2015 to 5.9% in 2024 is larger than the world change, and it would be unwise to attribute it wholly to improved child nutrition without national survey evidence. In South Asia, where the prevalence is highest at 15.7% in 2024, a few large countries dominate the aggregate, so that one survey round can shift the regional figure materially. By contrast, high-income countries and North America, at 0.4% and 0.2% in 2024, have low values whose precision matters little for the argument.

Wasting has a further difficulty that stunting lacks. It is a short-lived condition: a child can be wasted during a hungry season or an illness and recover within weeks. Its prevalence depends on the month in which a survey is fielded, so two surveys in the same country in different seasons can differ for reasons unrelated to policy. Single-year comparisons are therefore weaker for wasting than for stunting, which reflects accumulated deprivation and changes slowly.

For the 2030 assessment these limits matter in two ways. A judgement that a country is on track rests on its own survey history, and countries with long gaps between surveys cannot be assessed with confidence. And the world and regional aggregates should be taken as indications of direction, not as precise measures of distance from the 5.0% ceiling. Where the series is sparse, the more reliable evidence is the national survey record, and the count of reporting countries should be read alongside every figure quoted in this section.

### What the trajectories imply for 2030, and proposals

At the observed rates, the world will not reach the stunting target of 5.0% by 2030. Global stunting stood at 23.2% in 2024, and the trend projection gives 22.3% in 2030, a ratio of 0.12 against the pace the target requires. The assessment class for the world is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The distance to be covered in the remaining years is many times the distance covered since 2015. The 2025 milestone, which the target text sets ahead of 2030, will also be missed on this evidence.

Only two groups are on track for stunting. Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.0% in 2015 to 4.6% in 2024, and its projected 2030 value is 3.8%, a ratio of 2.13, the fastest relative pace of any region. High-income countries stood at 3.9% in 2015 and 4.0% in 2024, and North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%. Both are classed as on track only because their levels already lie below the ceiling of 5.0%. The classification reflects a level, not a gain, and the slight rise in both groups shows that the target concerns a floor of child health which wealthy countries have not secured against change.

East Asia and Pacific is classed as marginal. Its prevalence fell from 14.5% to 13.3% and the projection for 2030 is 12.6%, a ratio of 0.20. Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as regression: 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, with 12.4% projected for 2030. A region of middle income, with food available in aggregate, has therefore made no progress on stunting for nine years. That points to causes beyond food supply, such as the quality of diets in early childhood, maternal health, sanitation and persistent inequality within countries, which regional averages conceal.

The regions with the highest levels are those furthest from the target. South Asia is projected at 27.9% in 2030, a ratio of 0.30, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 31.0%, a ratio of 0.12. Low-income countries are projected at 34.4%, from 38.0% in 2015 and 35.8% in 2024. Lower middle-income countries fell from 33.9% to 28.9%, with 25.9% projected for 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is projected at 22.1%, from 24.1% in 2024. Each of these would still hold stunting at several times the target in 2030. Because population growth is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, a slow fall in prevalence there can coincide with a rising number of affected children, a point the prevalence series cannot show.

Wasting offers a less bleak picture at the level of country counts but a troubling one at the margin. Of 65 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target, while 16 show regression, holding 19.9% of the population assessed. Three countries, holding 33.7% of that population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Wasting responds quickly to shocks such as drought, conflict, price surges and disease, so a country can move between classes within a year or two, and the regressions deserve attention for that reason.

Neither period since 2015 nor the disruptions after 2020 can be read cleanly from these series. Survey reporting fell to 26 countries in 2020 and to 6 in 2024, so recent wasting values rest on very few new observations, and the modelled stunting estimates for 2024 lean on earlier surveys. A trend computed between 2015 and 2024 describes the direction of the estimates, and not a verified count of children. The conclusion for 2030 is nonetheless robust to this uncertainty, since the gaps are too large to be closed by any plausible revision.

proposals: National governments and development partners in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa should concentrate nutrition financing on maternal health, infant and young child feeding, sanitation and cash support for poor households, since these regions hold the largest gaps to the 5.0% stunting target.

Governments of the 16 countries whose wasting is regressing, with humanitarian agencies and donors, should fund early warning and routine treatment of acute malnutrition so that shocks do not reverse earlier gains.

Statistical offices, UNICEF, WHO and the World Bank should fund regular, comparable household nutrition surveys at least every three years in every country, so that progress to 2030 can be verified and not modelled.
w-c03-2-1.gaps: The series give prevalence and not the number of affected children, so population growth effects are not shown. Wasting rests on sparse survey reporting, with only 6 countries reporting in 2024, and stunting estimates are modelled. Neither series separates children by sex, income group within countries, or place of residence, and the data do not cover the nutritional needs of adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women or older persons named in target 2.2. The 2025 milestone cannot be verified, since data for that year are not yet available. Targets for 2030 can be read as a 5.0% ceiling or as a proportional reduction, and the trend assessment uses the ceiling.

w-c06-2-1.text:
### Intimate partner violence is measured in few countries and few years

Target 5.2 calls for the elimination of all forms of violence against all women and girls, in public and private life, including trafficking and sexual and other types of exploitation. The indicator that the World Bank's catalogue holds for it is narrower: the proportion of ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49 who were subjected to physical violence, sexual violence or both by a current or former intimate partner in the previous 12 months. The series is compiled from United Nations and World Health Organization sources. It therefore speaks to violence within or after a relationship and to one age band, and says nothing directly about violence by non-partners, harassment in public, trafficking or exploitation. Women who have never had a partner, girls under 15 and women over 49 fall outside it. A country with a low reading on this series cannot be taken to have met the wider target.

The coverage is thin even for this narrow measure. Across the whole period, 106 countries report at least once. Those reports are spread unevenly over time, and in most years very few countries contribute. One country reports for 2000 and 2 for 2005. The counts then run at 4 for 2006, 3 for 2007, 4 for 2008 and 4 for 2009, falling to 2 for 2010 and 3 for 2011. A year with one to four reporting countries cannot support a comparison of regions or a global reading; it records a handful of surveys.

The pattern changes sharply in 2012, when 35 countries report. This single peak accounts for a large share of all the country entries on the shelf, and it reflects a coordinated modelled estimation exercise rather than a steady flow of annual surveys. After it the counts fall back to 7 for 2013 and rise to 12 for 2014, 8 for 2015, 14 for 2016 and 7 for 2017, the latest year with data. No year after 2017 is held, so the series is silent on the period of the pandemic from 2020, when many observers warned that violence at home had risen. The shelf holds no regional or world aggregates for this indicator, so no summary can be drawn from published totals.

These features shape what the rest of the section can responsibly say. Differences between countries can be described where values exist, but the values rest on different years and, in many cases, on estimation rather than direct survey. A reader should treat the indicator as a partial snapshot of one form of violence, not as a tracked measure of progress towards the target.

### Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap

The 2012 estimates are the only ones in the series that allow a population-weighted comparison across countries. In that year 35 countries report, far more than in any other year, and the spread among them is measurable. The Gini coefficient is 0.29 and the Theil index is 0.17. Both describe a gap between countries that is real but not extreme: prevalence is neither uniform nor concentrated in a handful of outliers. The coefficient of variation, at 0.66, points the same way, with country values spread widely around the weighted mean.

The more telling figure is the decomposition. Of the Theil inequality in 2012, 66.2% lies between regions rather than within them. Two thirds of the difference in the experience of violence recorded among these countries is therefore associated with where a country sits in the world, and only one third with differences among neighbours. This matters for interpretation. Regional clustering is what would be expected if prevalence were shaped by shared legal traditions, social norms about marriage and household authority, the extent of services for survivors, and the history of armed conflict. It does not show that any of these causes operates, and the data hold no variable that could separate them.

The limits of this result need to be stated plainly. The 35 countries are not a random draw. Surveys on violence are costly and sensitive, and they are fielded where governments permit them and donors fund them. Which countries are absent is therefore itself patterned, and the missing ones may differ systematically from those present. The between-region share is also computed only among the countries that report, so a region represented by two or three countries contributes little to the within-region term. The figures describe the spread of a particular sample in a particular year. They are not a global distribution, and they should not be read as one.

Nor can 2012 be compared with other years. The seven countries reporting in 2013 and the 14 in 2016 are too few for the same calculation, and they are not the same countries. For 2030 the consequence is that the regional pattern visible in 2012 is a snapshot of where evidence was gathered, not a baseline from which progress can be measured.

### Change over time cannot be established, while attitudes are better documented

The trend tool, which classifies each country against the 2030 target of zero, assesses no country for intimate partner violence. All five classes show zero: no country is on track or has met the target, none shows moderate progress, none shows marginal progress, none is stagnating and none is regressing. The count of countries assessed is also zero. This is not a finding of no change. It is a finding that change cannot be measured, because the tool needs repeated observations for the same country and the series does not supply them. Estimates modelled for a single reference period cannot show whether prevalence has risen or fallen since 2015, or since the disruption of 2020, when lockdowns and household stress were widely reported to have raised risks for women at home. Neither progress nor regression can be stated, and any claim about the direction of violence against women over the period rests on sources outside this series.

The attitude indicator, the share of women who believe a husband is justified in beating his wife for at least one of five reasons, is better documented. It is drawn from household surveys, and 72 countries report it in at least one year between 2000 and 2024. Annual coverage is modest and uneven, however. It was 6 countries in 2000 and 4 in 2002, rose to 10 in 2005 and 14 in 2012, and stood at 12 in both 2016 and 2018. After 2018 it fell sharply: 2 countries in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. The drop around 2019 and 2020 coincides with the period in which field surveys were interrupted, and recovery since has been partial. Even in the best years, fewer than 15 countries report, so a global or regional average of attitudes for any single year would describe a shifting group of countries and not a stable panel.

The attitude series therefore allows more comparison over time within countries that survey repeatedly, but it does not allow a global verdict. Surveys are fielded in cycles of several years, and the countries that report are mainly those where the Demographic and Health Surveys programme operates, which are chiefly lower-income countries. Wealthier countries are largely absent, so the series says little about attitudes there.

Attitudes are a proxy and not a measure of violence. Acceptance of wife beating can indicate social norms that sustain abuse and discourage women from reporting or seeking help, and falling acceptance is often read as a sign of shifting norms. But a woman may reject violence and still experience it, and a society may hold permissive views with low recorded prevalence, or the reverse. Answers are also shaped by who is asking and who is present during the interview. The indicator should be read as context for the prevalence data, never as a substitute for them, and it cannot show whether target 5.2 is being met for 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals on measurement

A target of zero by 2030 cannot be assessed from these data. The trend tool classifies no country, and the count of countries assessed is 0. Any statement that the world, a region or a country is on track, or off track, for the elimination of intimate partner violence would therefore be unsupported. The series holds 106 countries in any year, but most appear once, and the reporting years cluster so tightly that a single survey wave stands in for a trend. Reporting peaks at 35 countries in 2012, falls to 7 in 2013 and stands at 7 again in 2017, the latest year. Nothing is recorded after 2017, so neither the years after 2015 nor the pandemic years after 2020 can be read from the series. Lockdowns and strained services are widely reported to have raised the risk of violence at home, but the catalogue holds no figure that confirms or refutes this.

The measurement gap matters because the target is stated in absolute terms. Zero is reached only by sustained decline, and decline can be shown only by repeated measurement in the same country with the same definition. The attitude series is somewhat better placed, with 72 countries reporting in any year, yet it measures what women believe, not what they experience, and it too thins sharply after 2018, with 2 countries in 2019 and 7 in 2024. Attitudes may change before behaviour does, or behaviour may change without attitudes following, so neither series can stand in for the other. Underreporting is a further limit: women may not disclose violence in a survey, and a rise in measured prevalence can follow improved trust in interviewers as well as a real increase.

Five proposals follow from these findings; they are set out in the list of proposals. They concern the frequency of surveys, the consistency of definitions, the range of women and forms of violence covered, the conditions for publishing regional aggregates, and the joint reporting of attitudes and prevalence. Until they are met, the record for Target 5.2 will describe a handful of survey years, not fifteen years of progress.

proposals: National statistics offices, with funders and the UN agencies that support household surveys, should fund repeated national prevalence surveys at least every five years, so that change can be measured within each country.

The UN Statistics Division and the World Health Organization should standardise the 12-month and lifetime definitions of intimate partner violence and publish both consistently, so that countries can be compared and trends joined.
Survey sponsors should extend measurement to women outside the 15 to 49 range and to violence by non-partners, including sexual exploitation, so that data approach the scope of Target 5.2.
Agencies compiling global and regional estimates should publish regional aggregates only when country coverage allows, and should state the coverage beside each aggregate.
Statistical agencies and researchers should report attitude data alongside prevalence, stating the limits of each: attitudes are not experience, and prevalence is subject to underreporting.

Most countries have too few survey years for any trend to be computed, so progress towards zero by 2030 cannot be judged.

w-c02-4-2.text:
### Basic services and accounts have spread, but not to everyone

Three of the measures that bear on target 1.4 can be read from the shelf for the world as a whole: drinking water, electricity and account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults. All three rose, and none reached universality. The share of people using at least basic drinking water services went from 88.1% in 2015 to 91.5% in 2024. Access to electricity moved from 86.9% to 91.9% over the same nine years. Account ownership among the poorest 40% of adults, measured from 2017, rose from 61.7% to 72.4% in 2024. In each case the direction is right and the pace is real, yet the remaining gap is concentrated in a smaller and harder-to-reach population. Sanitation, treated in the sections that follow, is the fourth measure on the shelf and is read through its trend classes, since the shelf gives no world level for it here.

The three indicators are not strictly comparable. Water and electricity are tracked from 2015, the year the goals took effect, while the account series begins in 2017, the first year with a Findex round in this series, so its change covers seven years and not nine. The water and electricity figures describe whole populations, whereas the account figure describes only the poorest 40% of people aged 15 and over. A rise in the first two therefore says nothing directly about whether the poor in particular were reached, since national averages can be lifted by households that were already better placed. The account series is the only one of the three that isolates the poor, and it has the thinnest country coverage: 138 countries reported in 2024, against 202 for water and 215 for electricity.

Target 1.4 does not fix a single measure of access, which affects how these numbers should be read. The water indicator counts an improved source with a round trip of no more than 30 minutes, so it captures basic service and not water that is safely managed or reliably available. The electricity indicator records whether a population has access, not the quality, affordability or reliability of supply. An account may be held at a bank or with a mobile-money provider, and the data record ownership and use in the past 12 months, not whether the account serves a household's economic needs. Sanitation is defined by facilities not shared with other households, a threshold that different readers will treat as more or less demanding. Each figure here is therefore a floor of service and not a statement that the right has been secured.

The arithmetic of the remainder shows why the pace matters. The water shortfall, the gap to 100%, fell from 11.9 points in 2015 to 8.5 points in 2024, a reduction of 3.3 points. The electricity shortfall fell from 13.1 points to 8.1 points, a reduction of 5.0 points. People still without these services live mostly in low-income settings and in rural areas, where connection costs per household are highest and providers have the weakest incentive to extend networks. The remaining points are usually the costliest to close.

Accounts show the largest gain, 10.6 points among the poorest 40% in seven years, or about 1.5 points a year. Established explanations include mobile-money services, digital identity schemes and the payment of public transfers into accounts, though the series themselves do not test these causes. The disruption of 2020 did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series, but the data given do not allow its effect on the pace of change to be isolated.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region

Sub-Saharan Africa is the clearest laggard on the physical services. In 2024, 67.5% of its people used at least basic drinking water services, against 95.3% in East Asia and Pacific, 98.0% in Europe and Central Asia and 99.8% in North America. Access to electricity shows a wider gap: 55.1% of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, while no other region fell below 96.7%. The region began from a low base, with 59.2% for basic water and 39.2% for electricity in 2015. Those gains are real, but they were made from so far behind that the distance to the other regions has narrowed only slowly. Low-income countries, which are mostly in the region, show the same pattern: 60.3% for basic water and 48.8% for electricity in 2024.

Sanitation confirms the regional order. The trend assessment reads Sub-Saharan Africa as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.16 against the pace needed, and low-income countries as stagnating, with a ratio of 0.10. Their basic sanitation levels were 33.3% for low-income countries in 2024, up from 29.2% in 2015, so that roughly two in three people in those countries still lacked basic sanitation. A positive rate is classed as stagnation here because it is far too slow to approach the target by 2030.

South Asia presents the opposite experience. Its electricity access rose from 86.5% in 2015 to 99.8% in 2024, so that a region once level with the global average is now close to universal supply. Such a rise is rarely the result of market expansion alone. It is consistent with sustained public programmes of grid extension and household connection, although the series do not isolate the cause. South Asia also moved from 90.5% to 95.9% on basic drinking water over the same years, and its trend toward the sanitation target is read as on track, with a ratio of 1.11.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan form a more mixed group. On water and electricity the region sits above the global figures of 91.5% and 91.9%, at 92.9% and 96.7% in 2024, so it does not trail every other region on those measures. Its weakness lies elsewhere. Among the poorest 40% of adults, account ownership stood at 46.1% in 2021, up from 39.5% in 2017, the lowest level of any region except Sub-Saharan Africa at 43.6%. The region's sanitation trend is also assessed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.48, and significant acceleration is required. The grouping joins very different economies, from high-income oil exporters to countries in conflict, so the regional figure hides wide variation among its members.

Latin America and the Caribbean made the largest gain in account ownership among the poorest 40%. The share rose from 42.9% in 2017 to 67.9% in 2021, an increase of 25.0 points in four years. This interval includes the pandemic, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers into digital accounts. That may have contributed, but the data do not allow the cause to be isolated. Europe and Central Asia rose from 76.4% to 86.3%, and East Asia and Pacific from 64.1% to 77.4%, over the same four years.

A caution applies to every regional account figure. The regional series end in 2021, except South Asia and the income groups, which carry values for 2024. The regional comparison therefore refers to 2021 and cannot show the three years that followed. For the world, the poorest 40% reached 72.4% in 2024, up from 61.7% in 2017, but this rests on 138 reporting countries and cannot be broken down by region at the same date.

### Rural electricity advanced fastest while sanitation and water lag

Country classes against the 100% target show how uneven the advance has been. For drinking water, 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress but needed acceleration. Another 55 countries, with 20.9% of the population, were making only marginal progress. Stagnation applied to 17 countries (1.5% of the population), and 37 countries (9.9%) were regressing. These are the places where service coverage was being lost rather than merely delayed.

Sanitation is the weakest of the three physical services in the class results. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population. Moderate progress, needing acceleration, described 34 countries (17.7%), and marginal progress 54 countries (16.5%). Stagnation affected 37 countries (5.8%) and regression 39 countries (13.4%). The share of population living in regressing countries is larger for sanitation than for water, which may reflect the difficulty of sustaining household facilities and sewerage against population growth and urbanisation, though the indicators do not test this. The world as a whole was classed as making moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.61 of the pace needed and an expected coverage of 89.2% in 2030, short of universal use. The shelf gives sanitation levels only through these trend results, not as separate level series, and none of the series separates the poor from the rest of the population except account ownership.

The heading refers to rural electricity because that series has the highest share of countries on track. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, with 77.4% of the population concerned. This is a comparison of class shares, not of rates, and the series differ in coverage, so it is a reading rather than a measured ranking. Moderate progress applied to 23 countries (12.8%) and marginal progress to 10 (2.0%). Seven countries (2.3% of the population) were stagnating and 10 (5.4%) were regressing. Grid extension and off-grid solar are well-established routes to rural electrification and reach dispersed households more readily than sewers or piped networks. The countries that are stagnating or regressing are plausibly those where conflict or weak utilities raise the cost of extension, but the indicators do not identify the cause.

Regional trends on sanitation show where the divergence sits. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and upper middle income countries were on track, with ratios of 1.18, 1.11 and 1.08. Lower middle income countries reached a ratio of 0.75, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.16, with an expected 42.0% coverage in 2030, and low income countries at 0.10, with an expected 36.2%. Low income countries are classed as stagnating even though their rate is positive, because that rate is far too slow to close the gap. In North America the ratio is -1.03, yet this reflects a marginal fall from a level close to universal and should not be read as a crisis of access.

Convergence in rural drinking water offers some reassurance. Across 167 countries, the 2015 to 2024 regression of growth on initial level gave a beta of -0.0164, with a p-value close to zero and an R2 of 0.27. Countries starting with lower rural coverage gained faster, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.269 to 0.225. Catching up is real but partial: initial level explains little more than a quarter of the variation, so many low-coverage countries did not catch up.

For 2030, universal access is reachable for rural electricity in most countries, but not for sanitation or water at the present pace. The countries furthest from the target are those where the poorest live, so the world average conceals how far the target is missed where it matters most. Changes after 2015 and after 2020 cannot be separated here, since the classes summarise the whole period from 2015 to 2024, and the effect of the pandemic years cannot be isolated from these results.

### Universal access by 2030 is out of reach without acceleration, and proposals follow

Universal access by 2030 is not within reach on present trends, with one exception: rural electricity. For drinking water, only 60 of 214 countries assessed were on track or had met the target, and they held 33.9% of the population covered. A further 45 countries, with 33.8% of the population, were making moderate progress. Together the two groups cover roughly two thirds of the population assessed. The other countries are advancing too slowly, standing still or moving backwards, and 37 of them were in regression.

Sanitation is further behind. Of 213 countries assessed, 49 were on track or had met the target, holding 46.6% of the population covered. Another 37 countries were stagnating and 39 were in regression, and the regressing group held 13.4% of the population, against 9.9% for water. The regional levels show why. Low-income countries used basic sanitation at 33.3% of the population in 2024, up from 29.2% in 2015, and the trend carries them to only 36.2% in 2030. The ratio of actual to required progress is 0.10, which is why the class is stagnation although the rate is positive. Lower middle income countries rose from 56.0% to 73.9% and are projected to reach 88.9%. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at only 42.0% in the 2030 projection. By contrast, East Asia and Pacific and South Asia are classed as on track. North America is classed as regressing, from 99.7% to 99.5%, a change too small to matter for people but one that shows how a trend class can mislead near the ceiling.

A trend to 100% is a demanding standard, because the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach: they lie among dispersed, displaced or marginalised households. Countries classed as on track may still leave a residual population without services.

Rural electricity is the exception among the classes. Of 211 countries assessed, 161 were on track or had met the target, holding 77.4% of the population covered. Only 10 countries were in regression and 7 in stagnation, though these hold 5.4% and 2.3% of the population respectively. Regression in a share of population often signals that connections have not kept pace with population growth, or that conflict or economic collapse has damaged networks. Falling costs of off-grid solar and national connection programmes are well-established reasons why electricity has moved faster than water and sanitation, although these data do not test that explanation.

For accounts, the world figure for the poorest 40% rose from 61.7% in 2017 to 72.4% in 2024, about 1.5 points a year. At that pace universality by 2030 would not be reached. Low-income countries rose from 22.5% to 37.3%, so more than six in ten of the poorest adults there remained without an account. Only 138 countries reported in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021, so the 2030 outlook for accounts is an estimate with wide uncertainty rather than a measured trend.

The weight of the shortfall falls on a small number of places. Sub-Saharan Africa, with 55.1% electricity access in 2024, and low-income countries, with 48.8%, account for most of the people still without power, while South Asia, at 99.8%, has almost closed its gap. Progress at scale within a decade is therefore possible, but global averages will soon be governed by a region where the pace has been slower than the need.

Target 1.4 speaks of the poor and the vulnerable specifically, yet the water, sanitation and electricity series describe whole populations. Only the account series is split to the poorest 40%. The first three could be rising for the average household while the poorest remain unserved, and the shelf cannot show this. The word access is also read in more than one way: basic water means an improved source within a round trip of 30 minutes, which is not safely managed water, and an account that is held is not necessarily one that is used.

w-c03-3-2.text:
### Child overweight and anaemia in women stand at 5.5 per cent and 30.7 per cent

Two indicators of malnutrition other than stunting and wasting are measured here: overweight among children under five, and anaemia among women of reproductive age. Target 2.2 names all forms of malnutrition and the nutritional needs of adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, yet its numerical benchmarks cover only stunting and wasting. The two indicators therefore describe parts of the target that carry no quantified goal in the wording given. The overweight series is scored in this section against a reference value of 3.0 per cent by 2030, which is a working benchmark of the bench's trend tool and not a value written into the target. The anaemia series has no benchmark at all.

In 2024 the world prevalence of child overweight, defined as weight for height more than two standard deviations above the WHO 2006 median, was 5.5 per cent of children under five, up from 5.2 per cent in 2015. The rise is small, at about 0.3 percentage points over nine years, but it runs against the direction the target implies. The estimate rests on 163 countries reporting in 2024. It is a modelled estimate, so year-to-year movements are smoothed and partly reflect the model rather than fresh surveys, especially in countries that are surveyed only every few years.

Anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 is far more common. In 2023 the world prevalence was 30.7 per cent, against 28.0 per cent in 2015, an increase of about 2.7 percentage points. The measure combines non-pregnant women with haemoglobin below 12 g/dL and pregnant women below 11 g/dL, and 192 countries are covered. Nearly one woman in three of reproductive age is therefore anaemic, a share that is large but not a majority. The condition matters for maternal health, for birth outcomes and for the nutrition of the next generation of children.

Both series worsened after 2015, and neither has an internationally agreed target value within the goal framework used here. A rise in child overweight is not necessarily a failure of the same kind as a rise in anaemia, since the two reflect different diets and health conditions. Even so, the direction of both indicators is adverse. Haemoglobin measurement also depends on altitude, smoking and survey method, and country estimates are modelled where surveys are scarce. The levels reported here should be read as well-founded orders of magnitude, not as exact counts. For 2030, the starting point is a world in which both burdens are larger than at the outset of the agenda.

### Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower

Regional levels of the two burdens run in opposite directions. Child overweight is lowest in South Asia, at 3.4 per cent of children under five in 2024, and highest in North America, at 9.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 8.8 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 7.8 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa records 3.8 per cent. Anaemia among women aged 15 to 49 reverses the order: North America has the lowest prevalence, 14.9 per cent in 2023, and South Asia the highest, 51.1 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 36.7 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 35.2 per cent, whereas East Asia and the Pacific, at 18.7 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 20.0 per cent, lie near the lower end.

The pattern by income group repeats the regional one. Overweight is 3.5 per cent in low-income countries and 4.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 8.6 per cent in upper-middle-income and 8.4 per cent in high-income countries. Anaemia is 35.6 per cent in low-income and 46.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 19.8 per cent in upper-middle-income and 17.3 per cent in high-income countries. Child overweight is thus highest where anaemia is lowest, and the reverse holds in the poorest regions. This does not mean that the two conditions exclude one another within a country or a household; regional averages cannot show whether both occur together. Lower overweight in the poorest groups should not be read as a sign of better nutrition, since anaemia there remains heavy.

In relative terms the regional gap is wider for anaemia than for overweight. The highest regional anaemia prevalence is more than three times the lowest, at a ratio of 3.43, while the highest regional overweight prevalence is 2.92 times the lowest. Among 192 countries, weighted by population, the between-region share of the Theil index was 77.9 per cent in 2023, up from 74.1 per cent in 2015, so geography accounts for most of the inequality in anaemia. The Gini coefficient fell from 0.287 to 0.272 over the same years. Differences among countries have narrowed slightly overall, yet what remains is increasingly a matter of the region to which a country belongs. Neighbouring countries tend to share their fortunes, which points to regional conditions as well as national policy; the results themselves do not identify the causes.

### Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere

The trend classes show that movement on both indicators has mostly been in the wrong direction since 2015. Child overweight is assessed against a benchmark of 3.0 per cent by 2030, a figure adopted for this book and not written into Target 2.2. Of the 163 countries assessed, 92, holding 66.6 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, meaning that prevalence is rising where the benchmark requires it to fall. Only 33 countries, with 21.3 per cent of the population, are on track or have already met the benchmark. A further 10 countries (2.0 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 20 (7.5 per cent) show marginal progress and 8 (2.6 per cent) are stagnant. A stricter or looser line would change how many countries count as on track, but the direction of travel does not depend on the line.

Regionally, regression is the common pattern. East Asia and Pacific, high-income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are all classed as regressing, as are the low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups. The annual rates of change are small, 0.0153 for East Asia and Pacific and 0.0165 for Latin America and the Caribbean, but they point upward in each case. South Asia shows the fastest rise, at 0.0518, from a low base, so the increase is not confined to richer economies. The regression ratios compare the observed rate with the rate the benchmark requires. They are large in magnitude for low-income and lower-middle-income countries, at -6.09 and -2.37, and smaller for high-income countries, at -0.36. Europe and Central Asia is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.11, and its expected prevalence of 7.32 per cent in 2030 remains far above 3.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the only region with moderate progress, a ratio of 0.67, and its expected 2030 level of 4.36 per cent would still be above the benchmark. At the world level the ratio is -0.21, a regression, with 5.67 per cent expected in 2030.

Anaemia among women of reproductive age shows a more uniform picture. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are regressing. Only 2 countries (1.7 per cent of the population) are on track, 1 shows moderate progress, 9 show marginal progress and 18 are stagnant. Every region and income group is classed as regressing. The world rate of change is 0.0115. Rates are highest in North America, at 0.0359, and in high-income countries, at 0.0239, and lowest in East Asia and Pacific, at 0.0023. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.0202, also rises faster than South Asia, at 0.0070, so the fastest rises are not simply those of the highest-prevalence regions; they are concentrated among regions with lower prevalence. No target value is set for anaemia in this assessment, so the classes measure only whether prevalence is falling.

The spread across countries narrowed slightly. The Theil index fell from 0.130 in 2015 to 0.116 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index rose from 74.1 per cent to 77.9 per cent, so what inequality remains is increasingly a matter of which region a country belongs to. The narrowing does not signal improvement, since prevalence rose in nearly every country. These data identify no causes. Changing diets, shifts in the measurement of haemoglobin and modelled estimates for countries with sparse surveys could each contribute, and none can be separated here. A rise across nearly every country justifies caution about attributing the result to any single national policy.

### The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course

Change and level tell different stories about the two burdens. Across 162 countries, the rank correlation between changes in child overweight and changes in women's anaemia over 2015 to 2023 is -0.030, which is indistinguishable from none. Countries where overweight rose faster were no more and no less likely to see anaemia rise. The correlation of 2023 levels is -0.469, a moderate negative association: countries with higher child overweight tend to have lower anaemia among women. This is a statistical association between levels only. The results do not show why it arises, and they give no sign that one burden displaces the other. Because the two do not move together, a response designed for one cannot be assumed to reach the other.

The outlook for 2030 follows from the trend classes. For child overweight, the world is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -0.207 against the benchmark of 3.0 per cent and an expected 2030 prevalence of 5.7 per cent. North America is expected to reach 10.8 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 9.7 per cent, while high-income countries are expected to reach 9.1 per cent. South Asia has the lowest level but the fastest rise, at a rate of 0.052, and is expected to reach 4.6 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 4.3 per cent, below the world figure but still a regression. Only the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows moderate progress, with an expected 4.4 per cent, and even there the benchmark is not met on the current course.

For anaemia, no numerical target is set, so the classes measure only the direction of travel. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, and only 2 are on track against the benchmark applied. Because that benchmark is not an agreed one, these classes describe direction, not failure against a commitment. The direction is nonetheless adverse. Both findings rest on modelled estimates, which are revised and which smooth over years in which surveys were absent.

The findings support four proposals, set out below. They are drawn from the results above, and the data that would test them are noted under the gaps.

Ministries of health in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa should build overweight monitoring into existing child nutrition programmes now, because overweight is rising from low levels in both regions.
Governments in North America and Latin America and the Caribbean, where expected 2030 overweight is highest, should lead prevention policy for children under five.
UNICEF, the World Health Organization and the World Bank should publish survey coverage for each country and year, so that users can distinguish measured values from modelled ones.

w-c04-4-2.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.6% for the world by 2030. The same reading is applied to every region and income group, so the regional verdicts that follow in this section rest on that single convention. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool, a linear extrapolation of the 2015-2021 pace, places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, which is a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 divides into three groups: regions where the probability of premature death from the four main non-communicable diseases fell appreciably, regions where it hardly changed, and one region where it rose. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, a respectable decline that still leaves the region above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021. Extended along its own linear path, the region would stand at 18.5% in 2030, against the target value for the world of 12.57%. The trend tool places it at a ratio of 0.39 of the pace the target requires.

The small movers are the two Americas. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America began from the lowest regional level, so a modest fall is less surprising there, yet its pace reaches a ratio of 0.82 of that required, while Latin America and the Caribbean reaches 0.50. Linear extension gives 13.9% for the latter in 2030. Outside the data, it is widely understood that gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking have been offset in part by obesity and diabetes, and by unequal access to treatment; these causes are not measured by the results used here.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, and its pace ratio is negative, at -0.20, which the trend tool labels regression. Linear extension would place the region at 24.0% in 2030. Among regions it had the highest level in 2021, though low-income countries as an income group stood slightly higher, at 23.0%. In 2015 it was marginally below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates between 30 and 70 did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends. Established knowledge points to hypertension, diabetes, air pollution and the cost of long-term treatment as plausible contributors. The period includes the pandemic years, when disrupted screening and chronic care may have raised the 2021 figure; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves its level close to the South Asian one. Its pace ratio is 0.16, and linear extension gives 20.4% in 2030. Measurement is a concern here, since death registration is incomplete and the estimates rely heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, a ratio of 0.22, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, a ratio of 0.00, which is stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. High-income countries alone are classed as on track, with a ratio of 1.93 and a linear value of 11.4% in 2030, which would lie below the target value. The two richer groups improved by about one percentage point each, while the lower-middle group, which contains South Asia's large populations, stood still. The gap between the low-income and high-income groups remained roughly ten percentage points in 2021.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability that all adults experience, but the direction is towards greater inequality. The share of the Theil index lying between regions grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences. All trend readings here are linear extensions of the 2015 to 2021 change, and the target value is derived from the 2015 world baseline applied as a common benchmark, so regional ratios should be read as indications, not forecasts.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.26 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.09 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. The following explanations rest on general knowledge, not on any result of this section, and the data do not separate them. Earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from better treatment of heart disease, and such gains meet diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The years 2020 and 2021 coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions. The series cannot isolate these effects from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.00156 with a p-value of 0.6965 and an R-squared of 0.0011. The coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measures point the same way, though they are not the same statistic. The convergence test reports a coefficient of variation of 0.3596 in 2015 and 0.3798 in 2021, computed across countries without population weights. The spread tool, which weights countries by population, reports a coefficient of variation of 0.2713 in 2015 and 0.2819 in 2021. The levels differ because of the weighting, but both rise. The population-weighted Gini coefficient moved from 0.1519 to 0.1582, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 27.0% to 33.1%. Relative spread widened slightly, and a growing part of it lies between regions, not within them. For a target defined in relative terms this matters, because a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and no systematic acceleration in such countries appears in the convergence result.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.0981 and the Kendall coefficient is 0.0706. Both are weak. Both changes are taken as end value minus start value, so a rise in coverage and a fall in mortality carry opposite signs. If coverage gains went with larger mortality falls, the correlation would be negative. The weak positive value gives no support for that expectation over this short window, though it is too small to show the opposite either.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.2467 by the Spearman measure and -0.1713 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is modest in size, and it is described here as modest throughout, being larger than the correlation of changes but far from strong. It describes a cross-section in which income, age structure, the wider health system and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together, and it cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented. The mortality series is modelled by the World Health Organization from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths can be read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021 and the trend projection, a linear extrapolation of the 2015 to 2021 pace, reaches 17.5% in 2030, so the global ratio of progress is 0.22. A ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target; 0.22 means roughly a fifth of that pace. At the observed rate the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction, and the gap still to be closed is larger than the distance covered since 2015.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, is the nearest of the regions to the required pace, with an expected value of 13.4% in 2030. North America, at 0.82 in the classification, is expected to reach 12.8%, close to the threshold because it began from a low level. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6%, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.50, 13.9%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 0.39, is expected to reach 18.5%, which is marginal progress. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030. That classification should be read with care, since high-income countries began from a lower level, and the target value of 12.57% is itself computed from one baseline.

That is an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions at 22% or more would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above applies the global reading to every region. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected 24.0% in 2030, higher than its 22.9% in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.00 and an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22 and an expected 21.5%. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest, and the gap between income groups is on course to persist.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none. The correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment, chronic respiratory care or the quality of care. A weak link therefore does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the coverage measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality, named in the section's title, cannot be treated here. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. The omission is a gap in this account, not evidence that the matter is minor. Mental health is part of the wording of target 3.4, and the indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover it.

The proposals follow from these findings. They rest partly on established knowledge about prevention, not on a result of this section.
