w-c07-1-1.text:
### Safely managed drinking water reached 73.7% of the world in 2024

The share of the world's people using safely managed drinking water stood at 73.7% in 2024, up from 67.7% in 2015. The gain of about six percentage points in nine years means that roughly three in four people now have water that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from faecal and priority chemical contamination. The remaining quarter either rely on sources that fail one or more of those three conditions or on sources that are not improved at all.

The indicator is demanding by design. It sits at the top of the ladder used by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, above basic service, which requires only an improved source within a thirty-minute round trip. A household with a piped connection that supplies water only a few hours a day, or a borehole whose water carries contamination, counts as basic at best. For that reason the safely managed share is lower than the basic share, and progress on it is slower and harder to measure, because testing water quality and continuity requires surveys and regulatory records that many countries do not hold in full.

Target 6.1 calls for universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all by 2030. The word universal can be read in more than one way. This book takes the plainest reading, 100% of the population using safely managed services, and measures distance against that line. A looser reading would accept a very high threshold, such as 95%, or would count basic service as sufficient. Affordability and equity, the other elements of the target, have no series on the shelf, so the safely managed share captures only part of what the target asks.

Coverage of reporting is broad but not complete. Some 150 countries reported a value in 2015 and 148 reported one in 2024, with 151 reporting in at least one year. The series reaches back to 2000, when 144 countries reported, so the trend before the goals were adopted can be compared with the trend after. The slight fall in the number of reporting countries after 2016 is small, yet it matters: the missing cases are not drawn at random, and countries with weak statistical systems are often those with the lowest access. The world figure is therefore best read as a firm estimate for the countries that report, and a less certain one for the whole population.

### Regions differ by more than sixty percentage points

The distance between the best and worst served regions in 2024 is larger than sixty percentage points. North America stood at 97.4% and Europe and Central Asia at 92.5%, so that in both regions safely managed water is close to the norm. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 32.4%, which means that roughly two in three people in the region still depend on water that is not on premises, not available when needed or not free from contamination. The gap between the top and bottom regions is 65.0 percentage points, and it has changed little since 2015, when North America stood at 96.3% and Sub-Saharan Africa at 26.4%.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 79.0% in 2024, South Asia 77.6% and East Asia and Pacific 75.2%, all within four percentage points of one another and a little above the world figure of 73.7%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stand apart from them at 65.6%, up only from 64.7% in 2015. That region began the period level with South Asia and East Asia and Pacific, and has since fallen well behind them. Water scarcity, conflict, and weak utilities in several of its countries are well-established reasons why service quality has not improved, though the data do not separate these causes.

The pattern is one of high-income regions near saturation and low-income regions far from it. Europe and Central Asia gained 1.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2024, and North America 1.1 points, because little room remains. The income groups show the same ordering: 95.8% in high-income countries against 33.0% in low-income countries in 2024. The remaining shortfall in wealthy regions is typically a matter of private wells, small rural systems and contamination, rather than absent infrastructure, whereas in poorer regions it reflects missing networks, intermittent supply and unmonitored quality.

The spread among countries tells a consistent story. Across the 148 countries reporting in 2024, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of safely managed water use was 0.222, down from 0.246 across 150 countries in 2015. The fall is real but modest, and it indicates that countries have become somewhat more alike in coverage. The Theil index also fell, from 0.107 to 0.093. Inequality among countries therefore narrowed, though from a high base and not by much.

Regions remain the main source of that inequality. Differences between regions accounted for 59.4% of the Theil index in 2024, down from 61.7% in 2015. A share this large means that knowing the region of a country explains most of the variation in its coverage, and that the remainder lies in differences among countries within regions. The small decline in the between-region share is consistent with the gains in South Asia and East Asia and Pacific, which moved up towards the middle of the distribution and reduced the weight of regional divisions.

These comparisons carry a caution. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, and the 148 countries reporting in 2024 are fewer than all countries, so regional figures rest partly on estimation where data are sparse. Regional aggregates also follow the groupings of the World Bank fiscal year in which the data were released. For 2030 the implication is plain: a regional gap of this size cannot close in the years that remain at the pace observed since 2015, and the burden falls most heavily on Sub-Saharan Africa.

### Gains came from South Asia and East Asia, and convergence is weak

The largest absolute gains came from two regions. South Asia rose from 63.1% in 2015 to 77.6% in 2024, a gain of 14.4 percentage points, and moved from below the world average to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 65.1% to 75.2%, a gain of 10.1 points. Because these regions hold a very large share of the world's population, their progress accounts for most of the rise in the global figure from 67.7% to 73.7%. The world average therefore says more about where population lives than about how widely progress was shared. Established explanations point to sustained public investment in piped supply, borrowing for household connections, and rural programmes for boreholes and treatment, although the data used here do not separate these causes.

Other regions moved far less. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 75.2% to 79.0%, a gain of 3.8 points. Europe and Central Asia moved from 91.2% to 92.5%, and North America from 96.3% to 97.4%, which is the pattern expected where coverage is already high and the remaining gaps are hard to close. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stand apart: the regional share edged from 64.7% to 65.6%, a gain of under one point in nine years. A region with that rate of change is not on course for universal access by 2030. Conflict, displacement, water scarcity and weak utility finance are well-established obstacles in parts of it, and the regional aggregate also combines very different countries, so the figure conceals as much as it shows.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.4% to 32.4%, a gain of about six points. That equals the world's gain in points, but from a base so low that two-thirds of the region's people remain without safely managed water. The income groups tell the same story. Low-income countries rose from 26.4% to 33.0%, and lower-middle-income countries from 60.6% to 69.1%, a gain of 8.5 points. Upper-middle-income countries moved only from 77.4% to 78.1%, and high-income countries from 95.2% to 95.8%. Gains were thus concentrated in the lower-middle-income group, where the largest populations sit, while the upper-middle group has nearly stalled well short of universal coverage. Reaching the last fifth in such countries often means improving the quality and reliability of existing systems, not simply extending pipes.

Whether poorer countries are catching up can be tested directly. Across 147 countries, the relationship between a country's starting level in 2015 and its subsequent change has a coefficient of -0.00491 with a p-value of 0.0004, so lower starting levels are associated with somewhat faster growth, and the pattern is unlikely to be chance. The fit is weak, however: R2 is 0.088, meaning that starting level explains under nine per cent of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation across countries fell from 0.445 in 2015 to 0.416 in 2024. Dispersion has narrowed, but only slightly. Many countries with low coverage improved little, and some with middling coverage improved a great deal, so convergence is a tendency and not a rule. Measurement may add noise, since the Joint Monitoring Programme estimates for countries with few surveys rest on modelled trends, and the safely managed indicator needs water-quality and availability data that many countries collect irregularly.

The link with basic service sheds light on how progress is made. Across 147 countries, the rank correlation between changes in safely managed coverage and changes in at least basic coverage is 0.622, and the rank correlation between their 2024 levels is 0.850. Countries that expanded basic access tended also to expand safely managed access, and the two rankings of countries are very similar. This is consistent with basic coverage acting as a precondition: a household cannot have water on premises, free from contamination, before it has a protected source at all. It is an association, not proof of cause, and the correlation of changes, though substantial, leaves room for countries where safely managed coverage moved separately from basic coverage. Such cases would be those that upgraded existing sources through treatment or piping, or those where quality worsened.

For 2030 the implication is that the pace of the last nine years will not deliver universal access. The regions that gained most did so from middling starting points, and the regions with the largest deficits gained least in relative terms. Convergence is too weak to close the gap unaided, which means that low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries need gains well above the recent trend.

### Current trends fall short of universal access by 2030, and proposals follow

Projecting the post-2015 pace forward shows that universal access to safely managed drinking water will not be reached by 2030. At the rate observed since 2015, the world would stand at 78.0% in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend classification gives the world a ratio of 0.32 of the pace required, which the analysis reads as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Whether the pace of 2015 to 2024 is the right baseline is a matter of reading, since the series is built from household surveys and modelled estimates that move slowly, and a short period can be unrepresentative. On any reading, the gap to be closed is larger than the gap already closed.

The regional projections differ in what they imply. East Asia and Pacific is expected to reach 82.8% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.51, the best among the large regions after South Asia, which is expected at 89.0% with a ratio of 0.70. Europe and Central Asia is expected at 93.4%, and high-income countries at 96.2%. These are high levels, but their ratios are 0.25 and 0.21, because the pace is slow. In rich regions the remaining shortfall is small and concentrated in particular communities, such as private wells, remote settlements and marginalised groups, which regional averages do not reveal. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is classified as stagnating, with an expected 66.2% in 2030, barely above its 2024 level of 65.6%. Upper middle income countries are also classed as stagnating, at an expected 78.6%.

Sub-Saharan Africa is furthest from the target. At 32.4% in 2024, it is expected to reach only 37.2% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.15. Low-income countries show the same picture, with an expected 38.2% and a ratio of 0.16. Their annual gains are not small beside those of other regions; the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.02 a year, is close to that of South Asia. The difference is the starting point, which leaves roughly two in three people without safely managed water even if the present pace holds. Rapid population growth, which means that new connections must outrun the growth in the number of people, makes progress harder still.

Country classifications show how widely the shortfall is spread. Of 151 countries assessed, 20 are on track or have met the target, but they hold only 2.3% of the assessed population. A further 16 countries show moderate progress, and hold 37.0% of the population, largely because South Asia sits in this group. Another 36 countries, with 26.2% of the population, show marginal progress. In 45 countries, with 24.2% of the population, the series is stagnant, and in 34 countries, with 10.2%, it has regressed. Regression is often a matter of services failing to keep pace with growing towns, ageing networks, or conflict, though some of it may reflect revised survey methods. Together, the stagnating and regressing countries number 79, over half of those assessed.

The implication for 2030 is that effort must shift from the countries already improving towards those standing still or sliding back. Raising basic coverage is not enough, because the indicator requires that water be on premises, available when needed and free from contamination, and a source that counts as improved may fail the last two conditions.

proposals: National governments and water utilities in the 79 stagnating and regressing countries should make safely managed service, meaning on premises, available when needed and uncontaminated, the first test of investment, and should fund maintenance and network renewal alongside new connections.

Development banks and donors should direct concessional finance to Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, where the projected level in 2030 remains far below the target, and should tie disbursement to measured service quality.

Water regulators and health ministries should pair expansion of basic services with routine testing for faecal and chemical contamination, so that an improved source is not counted as safe without evidence.

National statistical offices, with the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, should close reporting gaps and publish urban and rural estimates for more countries, so that missing and irregular data do not hide the places furthest behind.
w-c07-1-1.gaps: The series covers 151 countries in all and 148 in 2024, and urban and rural breakdowns cover fewer, so the countries furthest behind may be the least visible. Trend classes extrapolate a linear pace from 2015 and do not model policy change, population growth or conflict. Regional averages hide differences within countries, including those between income groups, settlements and households with private sources. The indicator gives no view of affordability, which target 6.1 also names, nor of equity between groups, and the data do not show whether service is continuous through the year.

w-c02-5-2.text:
### Disaster displacement is the measure that exists, and it is rising

The only series in the bench that records recent exposure to climate-related disasters is the count of new displacement associated with disasters, compiled by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre. It stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and at 26,393,278 in 2023. The world total therefore rose over the eight years, by a little more than a third, and it did so in the period that target 1.5 covers, which asks countries to reduce the exposure and vulnerability of the poor and of people in vulnerable situations to climate-related extreme events by 2030.

The unit needs care. The series counts cases of new displacement, not persons. A household that flees a flood in March and a cyclone in September enters the count twice, and a person who returns home and is displaced again is counted again. The figure is also not a count of people affected: those whose crops fail in a drought, whose homes are damaged but who stay, or who lose income without moving do not appear. Displacement measures the part of exposure that is severe enough to force people from their homes and that is visible to the agencies which report it. It is a floor under the scale of exposure, not an estimate of it.

The measure also records hazards beyond those that the target names strictly as climate-related. Storms, floods, wildfires and droughts are included, as are geophysical events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, depending on how events are classified. The series therefore cannot be read as a pure signal of climate change. Part of any rise reflects more people living in harm's way, in coastal cities and river plains, and part reflects better monitoring and reporting. A single large event can move a national figure, and through it a regional one, by millions in one year.

The analysis of breaks in the annual change of the world total finds none. Over 2009 to 2023 the mean annual change is negative, at about 789,790 cases a year, which sits oddly beside the higher 2023 figure than 2015. The reading is that the series is dominated by large swings from year to year, so that the endpoints, and the mean of changes taken from a high early year, tell different stories. Neither 2015 nor 2020 marks a statistical rupture. The rise from 2015 to 2023 should be taken as a movement within a volatile record, not as a trend established against that volatility.

This matters for 2030 because the target has no quantified threshold, and the only indicator that tracks exposure directly has no baseline that fixes what reduction would mean. A target that asks for reduced exposure can be read as fewer displacements in absolute terms or as fewer relative to population at risk. The data allow only the first reading to be tested. By that reading the endpoints point away from the target, but given the volatility of the record this is an indication, not a settled finding.

### Coverage has widened, but the wider measure of exposure is a single historical period

The number of countries that report disaster displacement has grown over the period, though not without interruption, and this complicates any reading of the rising total. In 2008, 80 countries reported. The count fell to 60 in 2009, recovered to 73 in 2010, dipped again to 62 in 2011 and reached 79 in 2012. It then jumped to 118 in 2013, slipped to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. After 2015 it rose in most years, reaching 133 in 2017 and 141 in 2018, but it fell to 136 in 2019 and to 133 in 2021 after standing at 142 in 2020. It stood at 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across the whole series, 199 countries and territories have reported in at least one year, so even the latest year leaves some of them without a figure.

This matters for interpretation. A world total built from 112 countries in 2015 and 145 in 2023 is not a sum over the same set of countries. Part of the rise in displacement may reflect better recording, wider monitoring and the entry of countries that were previously silent, rather than a larger number of people forced from their homes. The data as given cannot separate the two effects. A like-for-like comparison over countries reporting in both years would be needed, and the figures here do not provide one. The lower counts of 2009 and 2011 also show that early coverage was uneven, which argues against reading the years before 2013 as a baseline.

The wider measure of exposure is weaker still. The share of the population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures is an annual average for 1990 to 2009, compiled from the EM-DAT disaster database. It is reported for 168 countries in a single year, 2009, with no regional or world aggregates and no later update. It therefore describes the two decades before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. It carries no trend, no value for 2015 and none for 2020, and it cannot show whether exposure has changed since the goals began.

The question of how many people are affected by climate-related disasters therefore cannot be answered from these data. Displacement counts cases of movement, not persons, since one person may be displaced more than once in a year. The historical average gives a share of the population but belongs to a past period. Neither series measures people affected in the sense that target 1.5 implies, and no series on the shelf measures the exposure of the poor in particular.

### Regions differ sharply and the inequality among countries has grown

Regional totals of new disaster displacement diverge widely, and the direction of change differs from one region to the next. East Asia and Pacific remains the largest single contributor. Its count moved from 8,304,660 cases in 2015 to 9,038,561 in 2023, a modest rise that leaves the region with the highest absolute burden in the series. The region is exposed to typhoons, monsoon floods and seismic hazards alike, and it holds very large populations along coasts and river deltas. Only part of that exposure is climate-related, since displacement by earthquakes and volcanic activity is counted in the same series.

South Asia moved in the opposite direction. Its count fell from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 in 2023. A fall of this size should not be read as a lasting gain in resilience. Displacement counts in the region depend heavily on whether a single large cyclone or flood season strikes populated areas in a given year, and evacuations are counted as displacement, so improved early warning could raise recorded displacement as well as save lives. Two endpoints cannot separate these influences.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 in 2023, a rise of more than fivefold that is the largest among the regions compared over the same years. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 in 2023, a larger multiple, but from a small base and a later starting year, so the two are not strictly comparable. Part of these rises is likely to reflect wider reporting and part genuine events, but the data cannot apportion the two. Between 2015 and 2023 the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan roughly doubled, from 1,212,730 to 2,481,660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 to 1,728,025. North America rose from 76,000 to 394,000, a fivefold increase from a low base that is small beside the Asian totals.

The spread among countries has widened. Weighting countries by population, the Gini coefficient of new displacement rose from 0.570 in 2015 to 0.678 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. Both measures say that displacement has become more concentrated in a few countries. The number of countries in the comparison also grew, from 112 to 145, so part of the change may follow from wider coverage rather than from a change in the underlying events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. In 2015 most of the inequality was a matter of which region a country belongs to. By 2023 almost half lay among countries within the same regions. Regional averages therefore describe the pattern less well than they once did, and targeting of resilience support by region alone would miss many of the most exposed countries. For 2030, the implication is that national and subnational monitoring will matter more than regional aggregates, and that a single global total conceals sharply different trajectories.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The trend in the world series should be read with caution. The test for structural breaks in the annual change of world displacement found none, and the mean annual change over 2009 to 2023 was -789,790 cases. That negative figure sits oddly beside the rise between 2015 and 2023, and the two readings are not reconciled by the data alone. Displacement counts follow the occurrence of major storms, floods and earthquakes, so a single severe season can dominate a year. A series of this kind cannot support a statement that exposure is rising or falling steadily, and no break marks 2015 or 2020 as a turning point.

The implication for 2030 is therefore limited. Target 1.5 sets no quantified level. It asks for resilience to be built and for exposure and vulnerability to be reduced, but it names no number of people, no share of population and no date before 2030 at which progress is to be checked. Without a threshold, no trajectory can be judged on or off course. The target can also be read in more than one way: as a fall in the number of people affected, as a fall in the share of the poor among those affected, or as a rise in the capacity to absorb losses. The displacement series speaks to the first reading only, and imperfectly, because it counts movements and not the poor. Between 2015 and 2023 the count rose, but the volatility of the series and the change in reporting mean that this rise is an indication and not proof of movement away from the target.

The widening of reporting adds a further caution. Coverage rose from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, out of 199 that have reported in any year, although it dipped in 2019 and 2021. Some of the increase in counts may reflect better recording, not greater harm. Inequality among countries also grew over the same years, with the Gini coefficient moving from 0.57 to 0.68, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%. Disparity within regions is now a larger part of the picture, which a regional average conceals.

The broader measure of exposure, the share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures, ends in 2009 and cannot be set beside recent years. The disaster risk reduction score, from self-assessments for 83 countries ending in 2011, is likewise too old and too subjective to show what has changed since 2015.

w-c03-1-2.text:
### Global prevalence of undernourishment and food insecurity

The world picture for target 2.1 is set by two indicators from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and they tell different stories. The prevalence of undernourishment stood at 8.0 per cent of the global population in 2015 and at 8.1 per cent in 2024. Over nine years, the share of people whose habitual food intake cannot supply the dietary energy needed for a normal, active and healthy life did not fall. It was, to the precision the series allows, unchanged. The 2024 figure rests on reports from 165 countries, so the world value is built on near-complete coverage.

The second indicator, the prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity, moved sharply. It rose from 21.4 per cent in 2015 to 28.0 per cent in 2024. This indicator counts people living in households where at least one adult reported, at times during the year, eating poor-quality diets and possibly cutting the quantity of food. It is far broader than undernourishment, and its level is correspondingly higher: in 2024 more than one person in four lived in such a household, against a much smaller share classed as undernourished. The 2024 value rests on 135 reporting countries, fewer than for undernourishment, so the world aggregate depends more on modelled estimates for countries without a survey.

The two measures should not be read as duplicates or as rivals. Undernourishment is a modelled estimate. It compares the food available in a country, and how unequally it is distributed, with a minimum energy requirement. It responds to supply, trade and income distribution, and it captures chronic shortfalls in calories. Food insecurity is experience-based. It comes from survey questions about worry, compromised diet quality and reduced portions, so it registers the effect of price shocks, lost income and disrupted markets on households, including those who still reach the energy minimum but eat badly or anxiously. A flat undernourishment line beside a rising food insecurity line is therefore coherent. Calorie shortfall has stayed steady, while access to an adequate and varied diet has worsened for a much larger group. The period contained the disruption of 2020 and the food and energy price rises that followed, shocks of the kind the experience-based measure is designed to detect.

The yardstick for progress needs care. Target 2.1 calls for an end to hunger and for access by all people to safe, nutritious and sufficient food all year round, and it states no number. The convention adopted here reads the end of hunger as undernourishment at or below 2.5 per cent, which is also the lowest value the FAO series reports; the series note says that a value of 2.5 may signify a prevalence below that level. Against that reading, the world in 2024 stands at more than three times the threshold, a ratio calculated from the 8.1 per cent reported. The target also names no threshold for food insecurity, although its wording on access for all points towards it. Any figure set for that indicator, whether zero or a reduction from a baseline, would be an interpretation by the reader and not a value fixed by the target. The prevalence of undernourishment is therefore treated as the primary measure of the target, and food insecurity as the wider measure of access and sufficiency.

The finding matters for what follows. With undernourishment unchanged and food insecurity higher, the world has not moved towards the end of hunger since 2015, and on the broader measure it has moved away. The sections that follow show where the burden lies and how reliable the figures are.

### Regional and income-group differences

Regional averages conceal a split between a few regions that have moved towards the target and several that have moved away from it. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest prevalence of undernourishment among the regions in both years, rising from 18.4 per cent in 2015 to 22.3 per cent in 2024. The trend tool classes this as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 25.4 per cent against a target of 2.5 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved in the same direction from a lower base, from 9.6 per cent to 12.3 per cent, and the tool projects 14.6 per cent in 2030. Conflict, displacement, currency crises and dependence on imported grain are well-established drivers of such deteriorations, and they cluster in these two regions.

The regions that improved did so from different starting points. South Asia fell from 12.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent, the largest decline among the regions in absolute terms, yet the tool reads this as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, since the expected 2030 value of 7.9 per cent remains well above 2.5 per cent. East Asia and Pacific fell from 4.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent and is the closest of the improving regions to the target, with an expected 2030 value of 2.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean eased only from 5.5 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Europe and Central Asia edged up from 2.8 per cent to 2.9 per cent, and North America remained at 2.5 per cent. Because the published figure is reported as 2.5 where the true prevalence may be lower, North America's flat line signals a floor in the data, not an absence of change.

Income groups show the same gradient more sharply. Low-income countries recorded 24.1 per cent in 2015 and 27.3 per cent in 2024, a regression in the tool's reading. Lower-middle-income countries were almost unchanged, at 12.5 per cent and then 12.1 per cent, which the tool classes as stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries fell from 4.3 per cent to 4.0 per cent, and high-income countries from 2.6 per cent to 2.6 per cent at one decimal place, close to the floor. Hunger is therefore concentrated in the poorest economies, and it is there that the global average is being held up. The world figure of 8.1 per cent in 2024 is the product of improvement in the large populations of South Asia and East Asia offsetting deterioration in Africa and the Middle East, not of broad advance.

The measure of food insecurity, which captures experience of reduced diet quality or quantity and not habitual energy supply, shows a harsher picture. Among low-income countries it reached 65.4 per cent in 2024, up from 55.1 per cent in 2015, so that roughly two in three people lived in moderately or severely food insecure households. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 29.2 per cent to 41.8 per cent, a much steeper deterioration than their flat undernourishment figure suggests. Upper-middle-income countries held at 12.8 per cent and then 12.6 per cent, and high-income countries at 8.2 per cent and then 7.9 per cent. The gap between the two indicators widens as income falls.

South Asia illustrates why both indicators are needed. Undernourishment fell there from 12.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent, while moderate or severe food insecurity rose from 28.0 per cent to 36.7 per cent. The two can diverge because one is modelled from national food supply and distribution, whereas the other is reported by households and responds quickly to price rises, income losses and the strains after 2020, including inflation in staple foods. A region can have enough calories in aggregate and still contain many households that cannot afford a regular, adequate diet. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan show the sharpest case on the household measure, rising from 27.6 per cent to 40.1 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 23.7 per cent to 25.2 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 8.5 per cent to 8.8 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 10.3 per cent to 10.4 per cent, and North America from 10.3 per cent to 10.7 per cent.

For 2030, the implication is that the target will not be met by regional averages moving at their present pace, and that the poorest countries are moving away from it. Among the regions, only North America is classed as on track, and it is already at the reporting floor. Among income groups, high-income countries are classed as making moderate progress, but they too sit close to the floor.

### Country trajectories and the quality of the data

The country classifications make the global averages easier to read. For undernourishment, the trend tool assessed 168 countries against the target of 2.5 per cent by 2030. Of these, 68 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 41.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 24 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 17 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries are stagnant. Regression affects 53 countries, which hold 20.9 per cent of the population. The classes therefore divide between countries that are moving towards the target and countries that are not, and the population weights show where the burden lies. The marginal-progress class is small in number but holds 26.5 per cent of the population, so a few very populous countries are improving too slowly to reach the target. Their pace matters more for the 2030 outcome than the count of countries suggests.

The finding that 68 countries are on track or have met the target needs a caveat about the indicator. The FAO reports prevalence values below 2.5 per cent as 2.5, so a country that has already met the target cannot be told apart from one sitting at the threshold. Many of the countries in the on-track class are likely to be middle- and high-income countries that began near the target and have stayed there. Their classification reflects the absence of a problem rather than a gain made since 2015. The class is therefore a weaker sign of progress than its size implies, and it should not be set against the regressing countries as if both groups had moved a similar distance.

Food insecurity gives a harsher picture. The tool assessed 157 countries for moderate or severe food insecurity. Regression is the largest class: 81 countries, holding 60.5 per cent of the population. Only 40 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 28.9 per cent of the population. Three countries show moderate progress, covering 4.5 per cent of the population, and six show marginal progress, covering 2.8 per cent. Stagnation affects 27 countries and 3.3 per cent of the population. The gap between the two indicators is large. Undernourishment, which is estimated from national food balance sheets and a model of how food is distributed, has held roughly steady. Food insecurity, which is measured from what households report about their own experience, has worsened for most of the world's people. Households can report hardship before the national supply of calories changes, and rising food prices, reduced incomes and the shocks of 2020 and after are the kind of pressure that survey-based measures capture first.

The reading of the food insecurity classes rests on a methodological limit. The indicator has no numeric target under the Goals. The trend tool therefore had to judge direction only, with a decrease taken as the aim, and it could not measure distance to a defined value. The classes mean that a country is moving up or down, or is flat. They do not mean that a country is near or far from an agreed end point. A country counted as on track has a falling prevalence, and that may still be a high prevalence. The target can also be read in more than one way: target 2.1 speaks of ending hunger and securing access to sufficient food all year round, which could be read as zero, as a low threshold such as that used for undernourishment, or as a reduction relative to a baseline. The classification is sensitive to that reading, and no single reading has been privileged here.

Coverage is the second limit. The number of countries reporting food insecurity was 99 in 2015 and 100 in 2016. It rose to 115 in 2017, 122 in 2018 and 136 in 2019, then to 144 in 2020, 146 in 2021 and 148 in 2022. It fell back to 135 in 2023 and again in 2024. In all, 157 countries reported in at least one year. The early years rest on markedly fewer countries than later ones, so a comparison between 2015 and a later year may reflect a change in who is counted rather than a change in conditions. The trend tool compares each country with its own record, which reduces this problem, but the regional and global averages are less secure. Countries that joined the survey later may differ systematically from those that reported from the start, since national surveys tend to arrive first where statistical capacity and funding are stronger.

The fall to 135 countries in 2023 and 2024 weakens the latest years in the same way. Some of the decline may reflect reporting delays that later revisions will fill, but that cannot be established from the series as it stands. The most recent estimates are therefore the least settled. For 2030, the lesson is that a monitoring system whose coverage grows and then shrinks cannot give a firm account of how far the world is from the target. The direction of the findings is consistent across the indicators and the classes, but the exact counts should be read as approximate.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The measured rates do not point towards the target. The trend tool classes the world as a whole as regression for undernourishment, with an expected 2030 value of 8.2 per cent against a target of 2.5 per cent. The ratio of progress to the progress required is -0.03, which is to say the global line is flat and slightly inclined the wrong way. Target 2.1 asks for an end to hunger by 2030, and at present rates the world would arrive at the end of the period with roughly the prevalence it had at the start.

The regression is most severe in the poorest and most crisis-exposed economies. Low-income countries are expected to reach 29.7 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of -0.26. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.4 per cent, with a ratio of -0.44. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region is expected to reach 14.6 per cent, with a ratio of -0.71, the largest expected level among the regions that regress apart from Sub-Saharan Africa. The causes are well established: armed conflict, displacement, repeated drought and flood, currency weakness that raises import costs, and the price shocks that followed 2020 weigh most on economies that import food and hold few reserves. Europe and Central Asia also shows regression, from a low base, with an expected 2030 value of 3.1 per cent. Because that value lies close to the target, its ratio of -1.16 is the steepest of any region in relation to the distance to be covered, although the absolute rise is small.

Progress elsewhere is real but insufficient. South Asia is expected to reach 7.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.46, and East Asia and Pacific 2.9 per cent, with a ratio of 0.79. High-income countries are expected to reach 2.5 per cent, close to the floor at which the indicator is reported, and North America sits at that floor. Because the FAO note states that a value of 2.5 may signify a prevalence below 2.5 per cent, countries at the floor cannot be distinguished from one another, and a target of 2.5 per cent is in effect a target of reaching the reporting limit. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnant, with an expected 11.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean as marginal, at 4.9 per cent. Even the regions that improve would need to speed up to reach the target.

The country classes confirm that the difficulty lies where hunger is deepest. Of 168 countries, 53 are in regression and hold 20.9 per cent of the assessed population, while 68 are on track or have met the target. The success of many small or already well-fed countries therefore masks the difficulty of the places where hunger is deepest.

Food insecurity adds a harder reading. Among 157 countries assessed for moderate or severe food insecurity, 81 are in regression and hold 60.5 per cent of the assessed population, and 40 are on track, holding 28.9 per cent. Regression covers a far larger share of people than it does for undernourishment, where it covers 20.9 per cent. Food insecurity has therefore worsened across a much wider share of the world's people than undernourishment has. The results do not cross-tabulate the two indicators by country, so they cannot show that insecurity rose where undernourishment fell, but the gap suggests that access, affordability and diet quality have deteriorated even where average energy supply has held. This matters for 2030, because a country can look close to the undernourishment target while a large share of its households still skip meals or eat poor diets. The food insecurity indicator also carries no numeric target, so the classification measures only the direction of change and not the distance to a goal, and the tool cannot say how far any country is from success.

The data base is improving and still uneven. The number of countries reporting food insecurity rose from 99 in 2015 to 148 in 2022, then fell to 135 in 2023 and 2024. Part of the apparent worsening may reflect changes in which countries report, because early coverage was thinner, and the fall in reporting after 2022 weakens the picture for the years that matter most for judging recovery after 2020.

In sum, the aim of ending hunger by 2030 will not be met on present rates, and the shortfall is a matter of where resources and attention are directed. The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National governments and the FAO should fund food insecurity surveys on a regular schedule in the countries that stopped reporting after 2022, so that the recovery after 2020 can be measured.

Donors and development banks should direct hunger financing to low-income countries and to Sub-Saharan Africa, where the trend is regression, and tie it to social protection and food reserves that cushion price shocks.

The 2.5 per cent reporting floor hides differences among the best-performing countries. The food insecurity indicator has no numeric target, and its coverage fell after 2022. The results do not cross-tabulate undernourishment and food insecurity by country.

w-c03-5-2.text:
### Farming's footprint on land, fertiliser and water is large and nearly static

Farming occupies a little over a third of the world's land. Agricultural land, which combines arable land, permanent crops and permanent pasture, stood at 36.8 per cent of land area in 2015 and at 36.9 per cent in 2023. The change is about a tenth of a percentage point over eight years, which is small enough to be read as stability. The series is reported by 208 countries in 2024, so the global figure rests on near-complete coverage. A stable share does not show that pressure on land is unchanged, since the share says nothing about which land is farmed, how degraded it is, or whether forest and wetland were converted while abandoned land reverted elsewhere.

Fertiliser use shows a modest rise. Consumption was 132.9 kilograms per hectare of arable land in 2015 and 136.5 kilograms in 2023, an increase of about three and a half kilograms. The series is reported by 190 countries in 2024. The measure counts nitrogenous, potash and phosphate nutrients and excludes manures, so it understates total nutrient application where animal and plant manures are widely used. The world average also conceals a very wide spread between countries, which the next part examines. Here it is enough to note that a flat global mean can coexist with rising use in some places and falling use in others, each with different consequences. Too little fertiliser leaves yields and soils depleted. Too much brings nutrient runoff, water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Water use follows the same pattern. Agriculture accounted for 71.5 per cent of total freshwater withdrawal in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. Roughly seven of every ten units of freshwater taken from rivers, lakes and aquifers go to farming, and that share barely moved across the period. The series is reported by 178 countries in 2022, and the latest year is earlier than for land and fertiliser, so any change after 2022 cannot be observed. A fall of about half a percentage point may reflect growth in industrial and municipal withdrawals as much as any saving in the field. The share also measures the distribution of use between sectors, not the volume withdrawn or whether withdrawals are sustainable.

These three series are measures of intensity and footprint, not of sustainability. Target 2.4 asks for sustainable food production systems and resilient agricultural practices that raise productivity while maintaining ecosystems, and it sets no numerical threshold and no base year. It can be read in more than one way. One reading treats it as a call to produce more on the same land with fewer inputs. Another treats it as a call to restore ecosystems even at some cost to output. A third stresses adaptation to drought and flooding, which none of these series captures. Because the target is open, a figure such as 36.9 per cent of land cannot be judged on or off track. It can only be described and compared over time and across places.

Two points follow from the global picture. First, the period since 2015 shows no sharp break in any of the three measures, and the available years do not reveal a clear shift attributable to the disruption after 2020. Second, a near-static aggregate is the starting point, not the conclusion. The questions of where intensity is high, where it is rising and where it is too low for food security are matters of regional and national difference.

### Regions differ most in fertiliser, and least in the share of land farmed

Regional differences are widest in fertiliser use and narrowest in the share of land that is farmed. In 2015, East Asia and Pacific applied 329.1 kilograms of nutrients per hectare of arable land, the highest of any region. By 2023 the figure had fallen to 304.1. Sub-Saharan Africa sat at the opposite end, with 14.4 kilograms in 2015 and 19.3 in 2023. The gap between the two regions therefore remained above 280 kilograms per hectare, even though the African figure rose by about a third and the Asian figure fell. The results do not explain either movement. Policies in the largest East Asian producers that discourage over-application, and the cost of fertiliser, weak distribution and limited credit in Africa, are well-known context from outside the data, offered as hypotheses and not as findings.

Other regions moved upward. South Asia rose from 175.0 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 206.0 in 2023, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 135.1 to 173.9, the largest relative rise among the larger regions. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 90.0 to 102.0. North America changed little, from 124.3 to 128.8, and Europe and Central Asia drifted down from 78.7 to 76.0. The world average, at 132.9 in 2015 and 136.5 in 2023, therefore conceals two opposing movements: a decline in the heaviest-using region and increases in most others. Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income countries rose from 10.0 to 13.9 and lower-middle-income countries from 114.6 to 130.8, while upper-middle-income countries were almost flat at 213.0 and 213.8, and high-income countries eased from 106.3 to 104.3. Low-income countries in 2023 used about one sixteenth of the amount used in upper-middle-income countries per hectare, which bears directly on the productivity aims of target 2.4.

The share of land in agriculture varies much less between regions, and it hardly moved after 2015. East Asia and Pacific stood at 46.5 per cent in 2015 and 46.8 in 2023, Sub-Saharan Africa at 43.9 and 44.7, and South Asia at 58.6 and 58.3. North America held at about 26.7 per cent in both years. Latin America and the Caribbean slipped from 33.3 to 32.9 per cent. These shares are shaped by climate, terrain and history, so they change slowly, and the small shifts are not evidence of a policy effect. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the largest regional rise, of 0.8 points, but the change is small, and the results do not show whether output was raised by expanding area or by other means.

Water use for farming differs by region in a way that follows aridity and the dependence on irrigation. In 2022, agriculture accounted for 90.3 per cent of freshwater withdrawals in South Asia and 87.3 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, which had been 90.1 per cent in 2015. North America stood at 37.5 per cent and Europe and Central Asia at 51.8, where industry and municipal supply take larger shares. The South Asian value is identical in 2015 and 2022, at 90.3 per cent. Withdrawal shares in this series come from national surveys that are updated irregularly, and an unchanged value to four decimals more probably reflects a carried-forward estimate than genuine stability. The figure should be read as a level, not as evidence that the balance of use did not shift. For 2030, the regional spread points to different tasks: restraint and efficiency in the heavily fertilised and water-stressed regions, and access to inputs where use remains very low.

### Yields rose slowly and country outcomes diverged

Cereal yields rose slowly across most of the world after 2015, and the pace differed sharply between regions and countries. The world rate of change is 0.9 per cent a year, a figure the tool classes as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5,066 kilograms per hectare in 2015 to 5,430 in 2023, a rate of 0.9 per cent a year. Europe and Central Asia moved from 3,803 to 4,045 over the same years, at 0.8 per cent a year. High-income economies rose from 4,976 to 5,394, at 1.0 per cent a year. All three fall in the marginal class. Upper middle income countries also sit there, at 0.8 per cent a year. These are regions with already high yields, where the room for further gain is narrower. Gains there are commonly attributed to breeding, management and precision rather than to added inputs, though that explanation is context from outside the data.

The classification needs careful reading. No target value for cereal yield is set in the targets of Goal 2, and target 2.4 speaks of productivity and resilience without a number. The tool therefore judges each series against the rate of a rising trend, not against a fixed goal. A class such as marginal progress is a judgement of pace relative to that trend, and a different reference rate would shift some regions between classes. The labels should be taken as a comparison between places, not as a verdict on whether any region has met an official threshold.

The lower-yield regions show the widest spread of outcomes. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 4,385 in 2015 to 4,828 in 2024, at 1.1 per cent a year, still classed as marginal. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached a moderate class at 1.3 per cent a year, with yields going from 2,732 to 3,027 by 2023. South Asia, by contrast, rose from 3,041 to 3,814 by 2024, a rate of 2.6 per cent a year, and North America from 6,677 to 8,414, at 2.6 per cent. Lower middle income countries went from 2,766 to 3,366, at 2.2 per cent. These three groups are the ones classed as on track or target met. The results do not say why. Wider irrigation, improved seed and expanded input use are often cited for South Asia and lower middle income countries, but that is context outside the data and was not tested here. The same label may therefore stand for different causes.

The weakest results lie where yields are lowest and the need is greatest. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 1,443 to 1,453 kilograms per hectare between 2015 and 2024, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which is stagnation. Low-income countries fell from 1,373 to 1,345, a rate of minus 0.2 per cent a year, classed as regression. A yield in these groups is less than a third of that in North America in 2024. Rain-fed farming, thin use of improved seed, limited credit, weak roads and exposure to drought and conflict are commonly named as weights on such outcomes, and the period since 2020 added shocks to input costs and supply chains; none of these is measured in the series examined here. Because yield is measured per hectare harvested, a rise in cropped area onto poorer land could also hold the average down.

The country tallies confirm that the divergence is wide. Of 180 countries assessed, 39 are on track or have met the trend, and they hold 29.5 per cent of the population covered. Another 19 countries show moderate progress, with 14.0 per cent of the population. A further 27 show marginal progress, with 25.7 per cent, a large share because this class includes populous middle-income economies. Stagnation applies to 25 countries and 15.6 per cent of the population. Regression applies to 70 countries, the largest count of any class, though these hold only 15.2 per cent of the population. That contrast suggests the falling yields lie mostly in countries with smaller populations, an inference from the shares and not a separate result.

Two readings follow. By population, most people live where yields are either improving at a fair pace or creeping up, so global averages hide the problem. By country count, however, the commonest outcome is decline, and 95 countries are stagnant or falling in yield. Year-to-year weather can drive a drop between two chosen end years, so some of the 70 may reflect a poor season at the end of the window and not a lasting fall. The trend over 2015 to 2024 is a short window for crops that swing with rainfall, and the result should be treated with that caution. For 2030, the pattern implies that global yield growth will stay modest unless the stagnant and regressing countries change course, and these are the places where food insecurity is concentrated.

### Fertiliser use is converging, but it explains yield levels more than yield change

Fertiliser use has been converging. Across 192 countries, the coefficient of variation of fertiliser consumption per hectare of arable land fell from 2.2 in 2015 to 1.7 in 2022. Countries that began with low application rates tended to increase them faster than countries that began with high rates, and the convergence coefficient of -0.034 is statistically distinguishable from zero (p below 0.001). The model explains 27.5 per cent of the variation in country growth, so the starting level is an important influence but far from the only one. Convergence of this kind reflects two movements at once: a rise from low bases in parts of Africa and South Asia, and a levelling off or decline in some of the most intensive systems. Fertiliser prices, nutrient regulation and efficiency gains are plausible reasons for the latter, but these are context from outside the results, which do not test them.

Convergence in inputs does not mean convergence in outcomes. Across 179 countries, the Spearman rank correlation between fertiliser use and cereal yield in 2022 is 0.72. Countries that apply more nutrients per hectare are, with few exceptions, the countries that harvest more grain per hectare. The relationship between changes is much weaker. The Spearman correlation between the change in fertiliser use and the change in cereal yield from 2015 to 2022 is 0.13, and the Kendall coefficient is 0.10. A country that raised its application rate was only slightly more likely to see yields rise faster than others.

The contrast has a plain reading, offered as a hypothesis that the results do not test. High input may go with high yield because intensive systems combine fertiliser with improved seed, irrigation, mechanisation, extension services and reliable markets, and extra input applied alone, without those complements, may not reliably raise yields. Weather in individual years, soil degradation, pest pressure and the response curve of crops, which flattens at high rates, could also weaken the link in changes over a short window of seven years. Where soils are depleted and application is very low, additional nutrients can raise yields substantially, yet the data here do not isolate such cases.

The correlations also do not establish cause. Wealthier countries with better institutions both use more fertiliser and obtain higher yields, and climate and soil quality shape both. The rank measures used here describe association only, and the measure of changes covers a period that includes the disruption to fertiliser prices and supply after 2020, which affected countries unevenly. For 2030, the finding cautions against treating higher fertiliser use as a target in itself. Target 2.4 calls for productive and sustainable systems, and the evidence suggests that gains depend on how nutrients are used, not only on how much is applied.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.4 asks for production systems that raise productivity while maintaining ecosystems, and the evidence in this section shows that the two halves of that wording are moving unevenly. Fertiliser intensity remains high where it is already high, and eases only modestly. In East Asia and Pacific it declined from 329.1 kilograms per hectare of arable land in 2015 to 304.1 in 2023, yet remained more than twice the world figure of 136.5 kilograms. In the upper middle income group it was 213.0 in 2015 and 213.8 in 2023, effectively unchanged, and in the high income group it eased only from 106.3 to 104.3. Where use is low it is rising: Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 14.4 to 19.3 kilograms and the low income group from 10.0 to 13.9. These increases begin from so small a base that they leave the continent far from the application levels seen elsewhere.

The yield record offers little reassurance. Of 180 countries assessed on cereal yield, 39 were on track or had met the target, holding 29.5 per cent of the assessed population, while 70 were in regression, holding 15.2 per cent. A further 25 were stagnant and 27 showed only marginal progress. Fertiliser levels track yield levels closely across countries (Spearman 0.72 for 2022 levels), but changes in fertiliser track changes in yield only weakly (0.13 for 2015 to 2022). More nutrients are therefore not a reliable route to faster gains; soils, seed, water control, markets and extension services are commonly held to decide what a kilogram of fertiliser yields, though the series examined here do not measure them.

Water shows the least movement. Agriculture took 71.5 per cent of freshwater withdrawals in 2015 and 71.0 per cent in 2022. South Asia stood at 90.3 per cent in both years, which is consistent with a series that is carried forward rather than newly measured, and the low income group stood at 90.9 per cent in 2022. Withdrawal share says nothing about whether extraction is sustainable, so the data cannot show whether the ecosystem clause of the target is being met. For 2030, the likely outcome is intensity that stays high in the leading regions, grows slowly in the low-input regions, and yields that remain short of the pace required.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National agriculture ministries in high-input regions should set and publish fertiliser efficiency targets for arable land, since intensity there has barely eased.

Governments and development partners in Sub-Saharan Africa and low income countries should pair any rise in fertiliser supply with measures on seed, extension and water control, because fertiliser change tracks yield change only weakly.

w-c04-1-2.text:
### The global ratio fell from 228 to 197 and remains far above 70

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled estimate for the world stood at 228.0 in 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year available. That is a fall of 31 points over eight years, or about 3.9 points a year on average. The ratio in 2023 is still nearly three times the target value.

The arithmetic of the gap is plain. From 197.0 in 2023, a ratio below 70 by 2030 would require a reduction of more than 127 points in seven years, or over 18 points a year. That is between four and five times the average annual fall observed since 2015, about 4.6 times on these figures. The distance does not shrink by small adjustments to the pace; it would require a different trajectory altogether. The trend tool, which extrapolates the rate observed since 2015, expects a world ratio of 173.4 in 2030, and classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The comparison of required and observed pace is made on rounded published figures, and the exact required pace depends on the unrounded estimates.

The target is worded as a global ratio, not as a national one. A global ratio is a weighted outcome: it is pulled down by countries with very low ratios and pulled up by countries with very high ratios, weighted by the number of live births. Because births are concentrated in regions where the ratio is highest, the world figure is governed far more by those regions than by the many countries already below 70. Reading the target as global means that a country-by-country reading is a separate question, which the later parts of this section address. A reading in which every country must fall below 70 would be stricter still, and the wording of the target does not require it.

The quality of the series needs stating plainly. Coverage is not the weakness: the modelled ratio is reported for all 194 countries in every year from 2000 to 2023, so no country drops out of the comparison and no year has gaps. That completeness is however a product of modelling rather than of observation. The estimates are produced by a regression model that draws on the share of maternal deaths among deaths of women aged 15 to 49, fertility, skilled birth attendance and national income. Where civil registration of deaths with causes is incomplete, as it is in many of the countries with the highest ratios, the estimate leans on those covariates rather than on counted deaths. The figures therefore carry uncertainty that the single published value does not display, and a change of a few points between years should not be read as a firm observation.

This uncertainty does not rescue the target. A fall of 31 points is small beside a shortfall of more than 127, and no plausible revision of the model would close a gap of that size. What the uncertainty does affect is the confidence with which any single country or short period can be judged. For the world as a whole, the finding is robust: the ratio is falling, it is falling slowly, and 2030 will arrive with it well above 70 unless the pace changes sharply.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of forty

The spread between regions is wider than any global average suggests. In 2023 the modelled ratio for Sub-Saharan Africa was 448 deaths per 100,000 live births, against 11 for Europe and Central Asia. The gap between those two regions is a factor of about forty, and it is the clearest sign that Target 3.1 is a global average assembled from very unequal parts. Where a woman gives birth, and in which health system, still decides the risk she faces more than any other single circumstance.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593 in 2015 to 448 in 2023, a fall of 145 points, and carries by far the highest ratio of any region. South Asia fell from 173 to 120, a fall of 53 points, and its fall in proportion is the larger of the two. Both remain well above 70. The trend tool reads South Asia as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 against a target of 70, so the shortfall there is modest in scale and could be closed with acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is read as making marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 350.5, about five times the target. Its ratio of progress to the pace required is 0.46, against 0.83 for South Asia. Closing the global gap depends overwhelmingly on the first of these two regions.

Several regions already lie below the threshold. Europe and Central Asia stood at 11 in 2023, down from 14 in 2015, and North America at 16, down from 17. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 54 to 47, and its expected 2030 value is 41.6. These regions are classed as on track, though for the wealthiest the ratio is already so low that further gains are small in absolute terms. East Asia and Pacific fell from 70 to 66, so it sits just below the target. Its expected 2030 value of 62.7 leaves little margin, and the classification rests on a gentle slope rather than on a secure lead.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among regions. Its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is the only region classed as in regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. A region of middle-income countries, with high rates of facility birth, has moved away from the target. Well-established explanations include the disruption of health services during the pandemic years, persistent inequality between urban and rural or Indigenous populations, and the weight of unsafe abortion and hypertensive disorders. The data used here cannot apportion the rise among these causes. It matters because the region was close to the threshold and has moved the wrong way.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 491 in 2015 to 346 in 2023, and are read as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 254.7. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 291 to 235 and are read as making only marginal progress, with an expected value of 194.9 and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.43. That is a slower proportional fall than in the poorest group, and it concerns a larger number of births. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61 to 57, with an expected 2030 value of 53.7, and high-income countries from 11 to 10. The two upper groups are already below 70, so the whole of the remaining distance lies in the lower two.

Country classes confirm that the picture is mixed rather than uniformly poor. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of the classified countries. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country is in stagnation and 7 are in regression, together under 1% of the population. The majority of people live in countries that will reach the target, yet the global average is held up by a minority of countries with very high ratios and large numbers of births. For 2030 this means that the global result will be settled by a few dozen countries, mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and not by the many already at or near the threshold.

### Progress slowed after 2008 and the pandemic years disturbed the series

The series shows that progress was already slowing before the goals were adopted. The breaks analysis identifies a change of regime in 2008. In the segment from 2001 to 2007, the global ratio fell by a mean of 8.4 points a year. In the segment from 2008 to 2019, the mean annual fall was 5.2 points. The pace of decline therefore dropped by about 38% before 2015, and the adoption of the goals did not restore the earlier speed. The measured fall of the post-2015 years continues the slower trend and is not a recovery from it. Well-established explanations include the exhaustion of the easiest gains, such as the expansion of skilled attendance at birth in countries that started from low coverage, and the harder task of reaching the remaining deaths, which are concentrated among women in poor, rural and conflict-affected settings where emergency obstetric care is least available.

The pandemic years then disturbed the series. The annual change was an increase of 4 points in 2020 and an increase of 31 points in 2021. The change reversed to a fall of 39 points in 2022, and the fall in 2023 was 6 points. The pattern is consistent with a shock and a recovery: disrupted maternity services, diversion of health staff and direct deaths from infection in pregnancy are all plausible contributors to the rise, and the return of services would explain the fall. The analysis cannot establish this cause. The ratio is a modelled estimate, built by regression from covariates such as fertility, birth attendance and income, and is not a count of registered deaths. A sharp one-year rise followed by a sharp one-year fall may partly reflect the way the model treats pandemic-era inputs and the revision of estimates. The breaks detected in 2020 to 2023 are single-year segments and should be read as flags, not as stable trends. The 2022 fall should therefore be treated as a modelled rebound and not as a durable gain.

The spread among countries has not narrowed in population-weighted terms. The Gini coefficient of the ratio across 194 countries was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 70.9% in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023, so most inequality is still a matter of regional membership, though the within-region component has grown a little.

Convergence is weak. A regression of change on the starting level across the 194 countries gives a coefficient of -0.00372 with a p-value of 0.0024, but an R-squared of only 0.050. Countries with higher ratios in 2015 tended to fall slightly faster, the direction needed for catching up, yet the starting level explains about 5% of the variation in change. Most of what separates fast improvers from slow ones lies in policy, conflict, financing and the strength of health systems. The convergence analysis, which counts countries equally, gives a coefficient of variation falling from 1.500 to 1.410, a modest narrowing. The population-weighted spread measures rose, and the two views differ because large countries with high ratios have not improved as quickly as the many small ones. For 2030, neither the slowed trend before 2015 nor the weak catching up since offers grounds for expecting the pace to rise. The target depends on a faster fall where the ratio is highest, and the record to 2023 shows no sign that this is under way.

### At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed, and proposals follow

Extending the recent pace to 2030 gives a global ratio of about 173.4 per 100,000 live births, against a target of 70. The trend tool places the world in the class of marginal progress, with a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.35. Reaching the target from the 2023 level of 197.0 would require a fall of about 127 points in seven years, or about 18 points a year, against an average fall of about 3.9 points a year since 2015. The required pace is therefore between four and five times the pace of the past eight years. The target cannot be met by continuing present practice. It would take a change in the scale and the targeting of effort.

The country classification shows where the shortfall lies. In 128 of the 194 countries assessed, the ratio is on track or the target is already met, and these countries hold 74.5% of the classified population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 23 countries, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country stagnates and seven regress, together holding well under 1% of the population. Roughly a quarter of the classified population therefore lives in countries that will miss the target without faster change. A majority of countries being on track does not imply that the global ratio will reach 70, because the global figure is governed by the few places where ratios are very high and births are numerous.

The regional projections confirm this. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 448 in 2023, would reach about 350.5 in 2030 at its present rate, with a ratio of progress of 0.46. South Asia, at 120 in 2023, would reach about 87.1, with a ratio of 0.83, the closest of the regions needing acceleration. Among income groups, low-income countries would reach about 254.7 and lower-middle-income countries about 194.9, with ratios of 0.56 and 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries, at 57 in 2023 and projected at about 53.7 in 2030, and high-income countries, at 10, are on track. East Asia and Pacific, at 66, is also classed as on track, although the margin is narrow, with a projection of about 62.7 in 2030. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the better-placed regions: its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and the trend tool classes it as regression, with a projection of about 79.7 in 2030.

Inequality among countries has not narrowed in the population-weighted measures. The Gini coefficient of country ratios rose from 0.628 in 2015 to 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.739 to 0.793. Differences between regions still account for 67.2% of the Theil index in 2023, down from 71.0% in 2015 (0.7095 before rounding), so the burden remains largely a matter of which region a woman lives in, though within-region differences are gaining weight. The convergence test across the 194 countries, unweighted, finds a small negative coefficient of -0.0037, with an R-squared of only 0.05, so catching-up among countries is weak.

The ratios are modelled estimates, and in many high-burden countries they rest on little direct counting. Any projection to 2030 inherits that uncertainty, and the classification of a single country near the margin should be read with caution.
