w-c04-9-1.text:
### The global picture rests on rates, not counts

The question posed for this section asks for a number of deaths. The evidence retrieved cannot supply one. The only result available is a rate: deaths attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene per 100,000 population, for 2019, across 183 countries. A rate is a count divided by population, so it cannot be turned back into a count without population figures that this result does not carry. No absolute total of deaths from unsafe water appears in the retrieved material, and none is offered here.

The position for air pollution is weaker still. The shelf holds a series on the mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, age-standardised, as well as a series on mean annual exposure to fine particulate matter. Neither was retrieved as a result for this section. Nothing is therefore stated about how many people die from air pollution, how fast the rate is falling, or which regions carry most of it. Any statement on those points would rest on no evidence in hand, and the section declines to make one.

This limit bears on how Target 3.9 is read. The target calls for a substantial reduction in the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and from air, water and soil pollution. The wording can be read as a count, in which case population growth works against progress even when conditions improve, or as a rate, in which case a falling risk counts as success even if the number of deaths stays high. The wording does not settle the matter. The indicator series the World Bank reports measures a rate, and it is the rate that the evidence here can describe. A reader should take any later statement about progress in this section as a statement about risk per head of population, not about the total toll.

The one result that exists does show how unevenly that risk is spread. Across the 183 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the unsafe-water mortality rate in 2019 is 0.53, and the coefficient of variation is 1.03. A coefficient of variation above one means that the spread of national rates is wider than their average, which is the signature of a distribution with a long tail of countries where the risk is far above the norm. The next part examines where that tail lies and how much of the inequality is a matter of region.

### Regions explain most of the inequality between countries

The spread of the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate across the 183 countries covered in 2019 is wide. The Gini coefficient is 0.535 and the Theil index is 0.502. Both measures are computed with countries weighted by population, so the result describes how the rate is distributed among people rather than among states. A populous country with a high rate therefore pulls the figures upward more than a small one would. The coefficient of variation is 1.03, which means the standard deviation of the rate is slightly larger than its mean. That pattern is typical of a distribution in which a minority of countries carry rates far above the rest.

The most informative figure is the between-region share of the Theil index, 75.2%. Three quarters of the measured inequality is therefore accounted for by differences between regions, and only about a quarter by differences among countries inside the same region. Where a country lies is a stronger predictor of its mortality from unsafe water and sanitation than anything that distinguishes it from its neighbours. This is consistent with well-established knowledge of the causes. Deaths from diarrhoeal disease, intestinal worm infections and malnutrition linked to poor hygiene depend on piped water, sewerage, treatment services, nutrition and primary care, and these are shared in broad terms by countries at similar stages of development and in similar climates. Regional patterns of income, public investment and health-system reach are therefore reflected closely in the rate.

The finding matters for how action is organised. If most of the gap lies between regions, then closing it depends on raising the level of whole regions, through regional financing, shared infrastructure programmes and commitments that cover many countries at once, rather than on correcting a few outliers within each region. The remaining quarter is not trivial, though. It signals that some countries do markedly better or worse than their regional setting would predict, and those cases are worth examining for policies that can be copied.

The limits of the result should be stated plainly. The decomposition reports a share, not a ranking, so it does not name the regions or countries with the highest rates, nor does it show which regions contribute most to the between-region component. It covers a single year, 2019, and so says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed since 2015 or been affected by events after 2020. The inequality measures also rest on modelled estimates rather than complete death registration, which in many low-income countries is partial. Readers should treat the figures as a robust indication of structure rather than a precise count of deaths.

### Change since 2015 cannot be measured from one year

The single observation for 2019 describes a position, not a movement. Target 3.9 calls for a substantial reduction in deaths from pollution and contamination by 2030, and a reduction can only be shown by comparing at least two points in time. The result retrieved for this section holds one year, 2019, for 183 countries. No statement is therefore made here on whether mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene fell after 2015, nor on how the years after 2020 compare with those before. The bench's tools return no earlier or later reading for this indicator, and an inference from a single cross-section would be a guess presented as a finding.

Three kinds of evidence would be needed to turn the position into a trend. The first is a series of annual rates from 2015 onward, ideally from 2000, so that a pre-2015 trajectory exists against which the post-2015 period can be judged. The shelf lists the indicator with 2019 as its latest year, which means that the period of the pandemic and its disruption to health services, to water programmes and to household incomes is not observed at all. The second is a count of deaths. A rate can fall while the number of deaths stays level or rises if populations grow, and the reverse is also possible, so the two answer different questions. The third is an air pollution indicator read alongside the water measure. The shelf holds a rate of deaths attributed to household and ambient air pollution and a measure of mean exposure to fine particles, but neither was returned as a result for this section, so the two halves of the question on pollution and unsafe water cannot be set side by side here.

Caution is also due on causes. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2%, and the Gini coefficient is 0.535. These figures show that the rate is unequally distributed and that regional grouping accounts for most of that inequality. They do not show why. It is well established that water and sanitation infrastructure, income, the quality of primary health care and the treatment of diarrhoeal disease all bear on such deaths, but the spread of one year's rates cannot separate these influences from one another or from the age structure of populations, from climate, or from conflict. Attributing the pattern to water infrastructure or to national income on this evidence alone would go beyond what was measured. The coefficient of variation, 1.03, confirms the dispersion without explaining it.

For 2030 the consequence is that progress on this part of target 3.9 cannot at present be judged from the evidence in hand. The target also does not define what "substantially" means, and it can be read against a baseline of 2015, of 2000 or of the latest available year. Until a series spanning those years is assembled, any statement on whether the goal is on course would be unsupported.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 3.9 asks for a substantial reduction by 2030, and the 2019 evidence shows where that reduction has to happen. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2% across 183 countries. Three quarters of the inequality in mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene therefore lies between regions rather than within them. Progress on the target depends on the regions where rates are highest. Because the Gini coefficient of 0.54 and a coefficient of variation of 1.03 describe a distribution with a long upper tail, a global average would be pulled down by regions with low rates and would conceal the places where most of the avoidable deaths occur.

This has a practical consequence for how 2030 is judged. A global rate can fall while the highest-rate regions barely move, if the improvement is concentrated where rates were already low. Such a result would satisfy a global reading of the target and fail the people the target is meant to reach. The target text does not say whether reduction is to be assessed in numbers of deaths or in rates, and it sets no baseline or percentage. Both readings are defensible, and they can diverge where populations are growing quickly, which is often where rates are highest. Where the rate falls but the population grows, the count may fall little or rise.

The data held for this section limit what can be concluded. Only one year, 2019, was analysed, so no trend since 2015 or 2020 is claimed here. The air pollution mortality series and the unintentional poisoning series are on the shelf but were not analysed for this section, although Target 3.9 covers air, water and soil pollution and hazardous chemicals together. The conclusions above concern one of those components only.
proposals: The World Health Organization and national statistical offices should report the mortality rate and the count of deaths together, so that population growth does not hide or exaggerate progress on Target 3.9.

The custodians of the Sustainable Development Goal indicator framework should add the air pollution mortality series to the assessment of Target 3.9, so that water, sanitation and air are read together.
The World Health Organization should publish regional breakdowns of attributed mortality alongside national figures, since 75.2% of the 2019 inequality lies between regions.

The United Nations regional commissions and national governments should set regional milestones for 2030, each tied to the 2019 inequality figures (a Gini of 0.54 and a between-region Theil share of 75.2%), so that the highest-rate regions are held to account.
w-c04-9-1.gaps: Only 2019 was analysed for the water, sanitation and hygiene rate, so no change since 2015 or 2020 can be stated. Counts of deaths were not retrieved. The air pollution and poisoning series were not analysed here, and soil contamination has no series on the shelf. The target sets no numerical baseline, so 'substantially reduce' can be read in more than one way.

w-c04-10-2.text:
### Global prevalence fell from 24.5 to 20.3 per cent of adults

Current tobacco use among adults fell from 24.5 per cent in 2015 to 20.3 per cent in 2024, a decline of about 4.3 percentage points over nine years. The indicator covers people aged 15 years and over who use any tobacco product, smoked or smokeless, on a daily or non-daily basis. Cigarettes, pipes, cigars, waterpipes, bidis, kretek, heated tobacco and oral and nasal products all count; e-cigarettes are excluded. The measure is therefore broader than cigarette smoking alone, and it should not be read as a count of smokers.

The evidence base is complete in form. All 166 countries report in every year listed, from 2000 to 2024, so the series has no gaps in coverage and the 2015 and 2024 values describe the same set of countries. That completeness needs a caution. Few countries survey tobacco use every year, and the annual values are modelled estimates built from periodic surveys, not direct annual counts. A smooth fall across nine years partly reflects the smoothing of the model, and the exact size of the change in any single country carries more uncertainty than the regular series suggests. The global figure is the more secure reading; year-to-year movements, including any change after 2020, are not well resolved.

The decline matters because tobacco is among the largest preventable causes of death from non-communicable disease, and the indicator is the only measure the World Bank holds for target 3.a, which concerns implementation of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. Prevalence is an outcome, not a measure of implementation. Taxation, smoke-free laws, packaging rules and advertising bans are the convention's instruments, and none is recorded in this series. A fall in prevalence is consistent with stronger implementation but does not prove it, since income growth, ageing and shifts in social attitudes also move use.

Target 3.a sets no numeric threshold and no end date. The trend tool's reading, which treats the aim as a decrease with no level to reach by 2030, is an interpretation and not a measured gap. Under that reading the world is moving in the right direction. Under a stricter reading, such as the voluntary global aim of a relative reduction in use set by the World Health Assembly, the same data would give a different verdict. The section that follows therefore describes direction and pace, and does not claim that a target has been met or missed.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than two and inequality has widened

In 2024 the regional averages ranged from 24.9 per cent of adults in Europe and Central Asia to 8.9 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa, a ratio of 2.79 between the highest and the lowest. South Asia stood at 23.6 per cent and East Asia and Pacific at 23.1 per cent, so three regions remained within two percentage points of one another near the top. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 18.9 per cent, North America 15.3 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 13.6 per cent. The low figure for Sub-Saharan Africa reflects, in part, a later and still incomplete spread of the cigarette market, and it should not be read as evidence of effective control. Regional averages also conceal countries that sit far from the mean.

The country-level classification against a 2030 decline shows how uneven the direction of travel is. Of 166 countries assessed, 72 were on track or had met the target, and they held 53.4 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 31 countries, with 12.3 per cent of that population, showed moderate progress that would need to accelerate. Another 26 countries, with 23.5 per cent, showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Eighteen countries, with 6.7 per cent, were stagnating, and 19, with 4.1 per cent, were regressing. The target text of 3.a sets no numerical goal, so the classification rests on a reading of a continuing decline by 2030; another reading, such as a fixed relative reduction, would sort some countries differently. On the reading used here, 94 countries fell short of being on track, and nearly half of the population is in countries that are not yet moving quickly enough.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, widened modestly over the period. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.193 in 2015 to 0.203 in 2024, and the Theil index rose from 0.070 to 0.081. The rise is small in absolute terms, but its direction is consistent across 2015, 2020 and 2024, and it occurred while the world average fell. Falling averages and widening dispersion together mean that the gap between the best and worst performers grew.

The composition of that inequality has also shifted. The share of the Theil index explained by differences between regions fell from 65.8 per cent in 2015 to 57.9 per cent in 2024. Regional membership therefore explains less of the variation than before, and differences between countries within the same region account for a growing part. For policy this matters: regional averages and regional programmes are a weaker guide than they were, and attention to individual countries, particularly the stagnating and regressing ones inside regions that are otherwise improving, is increasingly needed to meet the aims of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control.

### Declines were steepest in South Asia and North America, and countries have not converged

The fastest declines in current tobacco use came in two very different settings. South Asia fell from 32.3 per cent of adults in 2015 to 23.6 per cent in 2024, the largest fall of any region, and its rate of change of -0.0343 a year is classed as on track. North America fell from 21.4 per cent to 15.3 per cent, at -0.0365 a year, the steepest rate of the regions. Latin America and the Caribbean (-0.0221) and the high-income group (-0.0220) sit close together at about -0.022 a year, while Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.0262), low-income countries (-0.0277) and lower-middle-income countries (-0.0322) also fall within the on-track band. The world as a whole, at -0.0210, is classed the same way.

Three groupings lag. East Asia and Pacific fell only from 25.3 per cent to 23.1 per cent, a rate of -0.0098 a year, which the trend tool reads as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region (-0.0119) and the upper-middle-income group (-0.0099) are read the same way, and Europe and Central Asia (-0.0141) is judged moderate progress needing acceleration. Target 3.a sets no numerical goal, so these classifications compare each rate with a generic path to 2030 and are not a verdict against a commitment. The wording of the target, which concerns implementation of the Framework Convention, can also be read as a measure of policy action rather than of prevalence, and the indicator captures only the latter.

Countries have not converged. Across 166 countries, the regression of change on starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00417 (p 0.112, R2 0.0208), so the sign is that of convergence but is not statistically distinguishable from no relationship, and starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation in this regression sample rose from 0.444 in 2015 to 0.507 in 2024, which means that dispersion across countries grew relative to the mean. The spread analysis reports a different coefficient of variation for the same years, 0.352 in 2015 and 0.377 in 2024, because it weights countries by population whereas the regression treats each country equally. Both measures rise. Countries with low prevalence did not systematically fall further, while the mean itself fell, so the spread widened in relative terms.

Male and female trends move together. The Spearman correlation between country changes in male and female prevalence is 0.567, higher than the 0.416 between their 2024 levels. Countries where men reduced use tended to be those where women did, even though the gap in levels between the sexes is large and differs by country. This points to shared drivers, such as national tax and pricing policy, smoke-free laws, packaging rules and advertising restrictions, which reach both sexes, rather than sex-specific factors. The tools, however, identify no causes. They do not measure taxation, enforcement or the Convention itself, so attribution to any of them is not claimed here, and the correlation describes co-movement only.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The global decline is real, but it is uneven, and what 2030 holds depends on where the slowest movers sit. Target 3.a sets no numeric prevalence goal, so the trend tool reads progress against a decrease with no fixed end point. Under that reading the world's rate of change of -0.0210 a year is classed as on track or target met. The classification measures direction and pace, not arrival at any level of tobacco use that public health would accept, and a different reading of the target would give a different verdict.

The country count shows where attention is most needed. Of 166 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 53.4 per cent of the assessed population. The other 94 are not. Of these, 31 show moderate progress, 26 show marginal progress, 18 are stagnating and 19 are regressing. The 63 countries in the last three groups are the core of the difficulty. The marginal group is the largest by population among them, at 23.5 per cent, whereas the stagnating and regressing groups hold 6.7 per cent and 4.1 per cent. The shortfall is therefore concentrated in population terms in the marginal group, while stagnation and regression are found in many countries that each hold a small share. The population shares do not show the size of individual countries.

Among regions, East Asia and Pacific, at -0.0098 a year, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0119, are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0141, needs acceleration of a lesser kind. The upper middle income group, at -0.0099, is also marginal. At these rates, prevalence in these groups will still be high in 2030, and they will pull the global average away from the faster regions. Convergence is absent: the beta of -0.00417 has a p-value of 0.112, and the coefficient of variation across the 166 countries, each counted equally, rose from 0.444 to 0.507. The population-weighted spread gives a different coefficient of variation, 0.352 in 2015 and 0.377 in 2024, because large countries count for more; both measures rise. The countries furthest behind are not catching up.

The following proposals for target 3.a answer these findings.

The World Health Organization and regional health bodies should give technical support first to East Asia and Pacific and to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, the regions whose pace is marginal, and report the pace of each yearly.

The series covers tobacco use at ages 15 and over and excludes e-cigarettes, so it does not capture their spread. It does not show intensity of use, age at starting, or the split between smoked and smokeless products. The population shares are shares of the assessed countries, and no results here give individual country populations or the effect of any single policy.

w-c03-7-2.text:
### Consumer price inflation stands in for food prices

Target 2.c asks for measures that keep food commodity markets and their derivatives working properly and that give timely access to market information, including on food reserves, so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The target names no numerical threshold and no price index. Its indicator in the global framework is a food price anomalies measure, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold among the series available to this book. Volatility is therefore not measured here directly, and every statement in this section about prices is an indirect reading.

The nearest series is headline consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services for the average consumer. Food is one component of that basket, and its weight varies widely: it is large in low-income households and economies, and small in high-income ones. Headline inflation also contains energy, housing, transport and services, so a rise in the headline rate can follow a fuel shock, a currency depreciation or a rent adjustment with food prices barely moving. The series is read here as a signal of pressure on household budgets, not as a record of food price swings.

The series also has limits as a measure of volatility. The results available to this section give levels at 2015 and 2025 and measures of dispersion among countries in four selected years. They do not give the year-to-year path, which is what volatility requires. What follows describes the price environment and its unevenness, and does not claim to measure instability over time.

Coverage shapes what can be said. In 2015, 189 countries reported consumer price inflation, and the same number reported in 2016. The count then drifted down, to 185 in 2017, 179 in 2020, 176 in 2024 and 169 in 2025. Across all years 193 countries reported at least once, so some economies have gaps in particular years. The data do not show which economies dropped out, and the reasons for interrupted reporting cannot be read from them. The latest year, 2025, is the thinnest and may be revised as late submissions arrive. Comparisons across the period therefore rest on a changing set of countries, and the parts that follow rely mainly on regional and world aggregates, which are less sensitive to the loss of single reporters.

### World inflation doubled between 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025, a little more than double the earlier rate. Both figures are annual percentage changes in the cost of a general basket of goods and services, so they describe the price level that households face and not the price of food alone. Food is a large part of that basket in poorer economies and a smaller part in richer ones.

The two endpoints conceal the path between them. A comparison of 2015 with 2025 does not show how far inflation fell or rose in the years between, and it should not be read as a steady climb. The period contains the weak price environment of the middle 2010s, the disruption of 2020 and the supply shocks that followed, and an endpoint comparison cannot separate these. Volatility concerns movement from year to year, and the result used here reports levels at two dates only. It therefore shows that the world rate ended the period well above where it began, and it does not measure how much the rate moved in between.

Low-income countries show a different pattern from the world as a whole. Their inflation was 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025, so it fell over the decade while the world rate rose. Lower middle income countries also eased, from 4.0% to 3.6%, whereas upper middle income countries rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high income countries from 0.3% to 2.3%. That fall in the poorest group should not be taken as relief. Low-income countries began from the highest rate of any income group in 2015, and they remain above the world rate in 2025. Households there spend the largest share of their budgets on food, so a given rate of general inflation weighs more heavily on them than on households in richer groups. Coverage also changed: 169 countries reported in 2025, against 189 in 2015, so part of the comparison rests on a smaller set of countries at the later date.

The finding matters for Goal 2 because food access depends on what a household can buy with its income, and persistent price growth erodes that. Yet the series cannot show whether food prices moved more or less than prices generally, nor whether any rise came from commodity markets, exchange rates, energy costs or domestic policy. Those causes bear on whether the measures named in target 2.c are working, and the data used here do not distinguish among them.

### Regions began far apart and converged at a higher level

The regional picture in 2015 was one of wide separation. South Asia recorded consumer price inflation of 4.7% and Sub-Saharan Africa 3.5%, while Europe and Central Asia stood at 0.4% and North America at 0.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.8%, was also among the regions with very low rates. Latin America and the Caribbean (1.9%) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (1.7%) sat between the two groups. Income groups showed the same ordering: low-income economies stood at 5.5% and high-income economies at 0.3%.

By 2025 the gap between the highest and lowest regional rates had narrowed, though the order of the regions had changed. South Asia fell to 3.1%, a decline of about 1.6 percentage points, and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged at 3.4%, against 3.5% in 2015. Europe and Central Asia moved furthest in the opposite direction, rising from 0.4% to 3.7%, which made it the region with the highest rate in the latest year, narrowly ahead of Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1.7% to 2.0%. Movements in these three were modest, and all three ended 2025 at about 2%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024; its latest observation is for 2024, not 2025, so it is not strictly comparable in date with the other regions.

Income groups tell a similar story. Low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower-middle-income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while upper-middle-income economies rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high-income economies from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing therefore came partly from falls at the top and mostly from rises at the bottom of the 2015 distribution. Energy and food price shocks after 2020 are well-established drivers of the rises in importing regions, but these series cannot show how far each region's movement was due to them.

The pattern matters for Target 2.c because the regional spread now conceals a change of rank: the region with the lowest inflation in 2015 had the highest in 2025. Sub-Saharan Africa's flat line may hide large differences between countries, and a regional aggregate cannot show how often households met sharp price spikes within single years. For 2030, exposure to price shocks has become more evenly spread across regions, and no region now enjoys the near-zero inflation seen in 2015.

### Dispersion among countries widened after 2022

The spread of annual consumer price inflation among countries, weighted by population, was almost unchanged between 2015 and 2019 on the Gini measure, at 0.538 in 2015 and 0.538 in 2019. It narrowed to 0.511 in 2022, the year in which price pressures were felt in most economies at once, and then rose sharply to 0.660 in 2024. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the upper end of the distribution, gives a similar picture: 0.621 in 2015, 0.751 in 2019, 0.559 in 2022 and 0.982 in 2024. The 2024 values are the highest of the four years examined on both measures.

The composition of the inequality matters for interpretation. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015, 32.0% in 2019 and 38.4% in 2022, which fits a period in which regional averages moved apart before the 2024 observation. In 2024 the between-region share fell to 35.2%, so that most of the Theil index lay within regions. The rise in dispersion after 2022 is therefore mainly a divergence among countries of the same region, not a return of the regional gaps of 2015. Some economies may have brought inflation down as monetary tightening and falling energy costs worked through, while others continued to face currency depreciation, fiscal strain or conflict. The results do not identify which countries fall in which group, so this explanation rests on well-established patterns and not on the series itself. A regional average conceals the divergence, and a policy aimed at a region as a whole could miss the countries where food price stress is most acute.

Three cautions apply. First, the number of countries in the calculation differs by year: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 sample is much smaller than the 189 countries that reported inflation that year, so part of the comparison with later years reflects who is included and not only how prices moved. Second, population weighting gives large economies great influence, and a change in one of them can shift the result. Third, the measure is of general consumer prices, so it is an indirect guide to uneven exposure to food price volatility. For 2030, the widening within regions suggests that the risk of extreme price swings will be concentrated in a minority of countries, and that monitoring needs to be national in its detail.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.c cannot be scored from these data. It sets no numerical threshold and can be read in two ways: as the proper functioning of commodity markets and the availability of market information, or as the narrower outcome of limited price volatility. The series available touch only the second reading, and only indirectly, through general consumer prices. World inflation of 1.4% in 2015 and 3.0% in 2025 is consistent with greater price pressure on households. It says nothing about whether markets, derivatives or reserve reporting function better or worse than before, and the two endpoint values do not describe the path between them.

The outlook for 2030 is therefore uncertain in direction. Regional rates in 2015 ran from 0.4% in Europe and Central Asia to 4.7% in South Asia. By 2025 the range was narrower, from 2.0% in East Asia and Pacific to 3.7% in Europe and Central Asia, which moved from the lowest rate to the highest. Among income groups, low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower middle income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while high-income economies rose from 0.3% to 2.3%. The ranking of regions was thus reshuffled as well as compressed. Dispersion among countries points the other way: the population-weighted Gini measure stood at 0.660 in 2024, against 0.511 in 2022, so a narrower spread of group averages sits beside a wider spread of country experience. The data do not show which countries make up the upper tail, and the rates cited here are general consumer prices, not food prices.

Coverage bears on any monitoring to 2030. Countries reporting inflation numbered 189 in 2015 and 169 in 2025, and the data do not say whether the fall in 2025 is permanent or reflects later reporting. The proposals below follow from these limits: they aim to replace a proxy with measures that match the wording of the target, and to keep watch on the countries at the upper end of the distribution.

The FAO and the agencies responsible for the framework indicator on food price anomalies should release it in the World Bank catalogue, with country values, so that the target can be scored.

w-c05-3-2.text:
### Pre-primary enrolment worldwide stood at 60.9 per cent in 2020

The gross pre-primary enrolment ratio for the world stood at 60.9 per cent in 2020, up from 56.0 per cent in 2015. The rise of about five percentage points over five years means that, on this measure, enrolment in organised learning before primary school expanded in the first half of the Sustainable Development Goals period, though it still left a large share of the youngest children without a place.

The measure needs careful reading. A gross enrolment ratio divides all children enrolled in pre-primary programmes, whatever their age, by the population of the age group that officially corresponds to that level. Children who are older or younger than the official age are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator. Late entrants, repeaters and children who start early can therefore push a ratio up without raising the share of children of the right age who take part. The figure is a measure of how much provision is in use relative to the size of the age group, and it is not the share of four- or five-year-olds attending. Where entry ages are loosely enforced, the gap between the two can be considerable. The official age range also differs between countries, which limits the comparability of the ratios.

Target 4.2 asks that all girls and boys have access to quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education so that they are ready for primary education. No threshold is attached to it in this indicator, and the wording can be read in at least three ways: as access to a place, as the quality of what is provided, or as the readiness of children when they reach grade 1. The series examined here measures only the first. It says nothing about whether the programmes are of good quality or whether children arrive at school prepared, so a rising ratio cannot be taken as proof that the target is being met in full.

The latest figures also carry a caution about timing. The ratio is available for 2020, but the number of countries reporting fell sharply afterwards, to 71 in 2021 and 4 in 2022, so the world figure for 2020 is the last that rests on broad coverage. Statements about the period after 2020 must therefore be made with restraint.

### Regions differ by more than fifty percentage points

Regional levels in 2020 span a range of more than fifty percentage points. East Asia and Pacific recorded a gross pre-primary enrolment ratio of 83.2 per cent, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 78.3 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean at 75.6 per cent. North America stood at 70.3 per cent, which was barely above its 2015 level of 70.1 per cent. South Asia reached 62.0 per cent, up from 54.2 per cent in 2015, the largest gain among the regions after East Asia and Pacific. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 33.8 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa at 28.1 per cent. The gap between the highest and lowest regions is therefore about 55.1 percentage points.

The income groups tell the same story. Low-income countries reached 20.1 per cent in 2020, up from 17.4 per cent in 2015. That is the lowest level of any group in the data, and roughly one child in five of pre-primary age was enrolled. Because the ratio is gross, it counts all enrolled children regardless of age, and differences in official age ranges mean that the ratios are not strictly comparable across borders.

Among countries, the dispersion narrowed. The Gini coefficient of enrolment, calculated across countries and weighted by population, fell from 0.239 in 2015, across 164 countries, to 0.178 in 2019, across 147 countries. The Theil index fell from 0.117 to 0.065 over the same period. The narrowing is consistent with faster expansion where enrolment was lower, and with the large populous countries of South Asia and East Asia gaining ground. The change in the number of countries reporting means that the two years do not rest on exactly the same sample, so the fall should be read with caution. A separate convergence analysis, restricted to the 137 countries reporting in both years, gives an unweighted coefficient of variation of 0.48 in 2015 and 0.45 in 2019, a smaller fall than the 0.44 and 0.33 obtained for the full, population-weighted samples of 164 and 147 countries. The two sets differ because the samples and weighting differ.

The share of inequality lying between regions was 48.1 per cent in 2015 and 48.5 per cent in 2019. Region therefore accounts for close to half of the disparity both before and after the narrowing, and the remainder lies between countries within regions. Overall inequality fell, but its geographical structure did not change. Closing the gap requires attention both to the two lowest regions and to the wide differences within each region, since no regional average describes the position of every country in it.

### Progress was uneven and slowed after 2014

Progress between 2015 and 2020 was uneven, and the pace was slower than in the decade before. South Asia rose from 54.2 per cent in 2015 to 62.0 per cent in 2020, a gain of about eight points, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 74.8 per cent to 83.2 per cent, a gain of about eight and a half points. The trend classification rates both as on track or target met, as it does low-income countries, lower middle income countries and upper middle income countries. North America was almost flat, moving from 70.1 per cent to 70.3 per cent, and is classed as stagnant, as are high-income countries as a group, which gained 2.0 points, from 81.8 per cent to 83.8 per cent. Where enrolment was already high, growth was small; where it was low or middling, gains were larger, though from a lower base. Whether high-income enrolment is nearing a ceiling cannot be shown with these data.

The long run of the world series shows why the overall picture is less encouraging than the regional gains suggest. A structural-break analysis of the annual change in the world ratio finds breaks in 2005 and 2014. The mean annual change was 0.68 points in 2001-2004, rose to 2.02 points in 2005-2013, and fell to 0.99 points in 2014-2020. The pace of expansion after 2014 was therefore less than half that of the preceding nine years. The analysis cannot say why. Pre-primary provision in many countries expanded quickly once governments added a year of schooling before grade 1, and such one-off expansions tend to slow once the easier gains are made; that is an explanation consistent with the pattern, not one the data demonstrate.

Convergence between countries was weak. Across 137 countries with data for 2015 to 2019, the coefficient linking initial level to subsequent growth was -0.017 (p 0.016), with an R2 of 0.047. The sign is negative, so countries starting lower tended to grow somewhat faster, but the fit is poor and explains under 5 per cent of the variation. In this sample of 137 countries the coefficient of variation of the ratio fell only from 0.48 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2019. A separate population-weighted spread analysis, which covers 164 countries in 2015 and 147 in 2019, gives different coefficients of variation, and the two samples should not be mixed. Gaps between countries are closing slowly, and most of the difference in growth is unrelated to where a country began.

These results must be read with care about coverage. The number of countries reporting fell from 164 in 2015 to 143 in 2020, and then to 71 in 2021 and 4 in 2022. The 2020 figures rest on fewer countries than those of 2015, and later years are too thin to support any regional or world estimate. The period after 2020 cannot be assessed from this series. Whether the pandemic closure of early childhood settings reduced enrolment, or whether reporting simply lagged, cannot be separated with these data. Any account of what happened after 2020 can therefore only be suggested, not shown.

### At current rates most children will not be reached by 2030, and proposals follow

The classification of countries by trend gives a sharper reading of the global average. Of 172 countries assessed, 57 are on track or have met the target direction, and they hold 38.4 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. A further 17 countries, with 7.0 per cent of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 12 countries, with 2.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Sixteen countries, with 11.4 per cent, are classed as stagnant. The largest class is regression, with 70 countries and 40.3 per cent of the population. Target 4.2 sets no numerical threshold for pre-primary enrolment, so the classes measure direction and pace, not distance from a defined goal, and the classification can be read in more than one way.

The regression class needs careful reading. The coverage record shows that 143 countries reported in 2020, 71 in 2021 and only 4 in 2022. Many countries therefore have no recent observation, and the comparison for them rests on earlier years. A fall may reflect school closures during the pandemic, revisions to population estimates, changes in the official age range for pre-primary education, or the loss of a data point, and not a real contraction. The count of 70 countries may therefore include data artefacts as well as real reversals, and the data do not allow the two to be separated. Closures of early childhood services after 2020 were widespread, and these services were often among the last to reopen.

The regional results show where participation remains low. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced at an annual growth rate of 0.0196 and is classed as needing acceleration, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan advanced at 0.0165 with the same class. Both began from low levels and neither is near universal access. Low-income countries recorded the fastest rate, 0.0298, and are classed as on track or target met, as are South Asia at 0.0275, lower-middle-income countries at 0.0211 and upper-middle-income countries at 0.0205. Yet the low-income group started from a small base, so even a sustained pace would leave many young children in those countries outside organised learning in 2030. High-income countries and North America are classed as stagnant. This may mean that their ratios are already high, but the results do not show why. The world as a whole is classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration, at an annual growth rate of 0.0169. No projection to 2030 was computed and the target has no threshold, so the data do not show whether universal participation will be reached.

The spread of enrolment among countries narrowed over the period. The coefficient of variation across 137 countries with data in both years fell from 0.48 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2019, and this sample is the one used here. A separate population-weighted calculation over all countries reporting in each year gives a different value, because its sample differs.

Three proposals follow. National statistical offices and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should report age-appropriate net participation rates in the year before primary entry, because a gross ratio counts children of any age and can exceed what it is meant to show. Ministries of education and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should restore national reporting after 2020, so that the 2021 and 2022 gaps are closed and regression can be told apart from missing data. Donors and development banks should direct support for early childhood places and trained staff to low-income countries and to Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where access is lowest.

w-c06-4-1.text:
### The global picture: parliaments close to a quarter, management data thinner

Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in single or lower national parliamentary chambers worldwide in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015. The gain is about 4.4 percentage points in a decade, and 184 countries reported a figure for 2025, so the world value rests on near-complete coverage. Set against a benchmark of 50 per cent, women still hold little more than a quarter of seats, and the distance to parity in 2025 is roughly 22.8 points.

Target 5.5 does not name a number. Its wording, women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making, can be read as parity, with women and men holding equal shares, or as a threshold of participation sufficient for women to shape decisions, which is often placed lower. The indicator for seats cannot settle the question, because it counts occupants of seats and says nothing about their influence, the committees they chair or the offices they hold. This book uses 50 per cent as the benchmark, since a population that is about half women supplies the plainest reference for equal opportunity, and findings are stated against it while the figure itself is reported in full so that readers may apply a different reading.

The parliamentary measure covers one arena of public life. The economic arena is represented by the female share of employment in senior and middle management, a series built by the International Labour Organization from the occupational classification of managers. It excludes junior management, so it describes positions of real authority rather than all supervisory work. The series has two limits that bear on every statement made from it. First, the World Bank publishes no aggregates for it, so no world or regional share can be quoted, and any comparison must proceed country by country. Second, the number of reporting countries has changed sharply over time. It was 40 in 2000, 72 in 2010 and 77 in 2015, and reached 95 in both 2019 and 2022. It then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and stood at only 48 in 2025. A total of 154 countries have reported in at least one year.

These counts matter as much as the values. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years may reflect a change in who reports rather than a change in women's position, and the drop to 48 in 2025 is most likely a matter of surveys not yet processed, not of a real change in the world. The 2025 observations for management are therefore not a sound basis for a statement of trend, and the later parts of this section rely on the years of fuller coverage when discussing managerial positions. The parliamentary series, by contrast, is reported almost everywhere and is the firmer ground for conclusions about direction and pace.

### Regions and countries differ by more than twenty-five points

Regional averages for 2025 span more than twenty-five points. Latin America and the Caribbean leads at 36.6 per cent of parliamentary seats held by women, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 31.7 per cent and North America at 29.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 27.0 per cent, close to the world value of 27.2 per cent. East Asia and Pacific follows at 23.3 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands at 16.9 per cent, and South Asia is lowest at 11.2 per cent. The gap between the highest and lowest regions is therefore about 25.4 points. Regional means are unweighted or population-weighted according to the aggregation used, and a mean can conceal wide differences between countries within a region.

The two lowest regions are also the ones that did not advance. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 17.5 per cent in 2015 to 16.9 per cent in 2025, which is stagnation in effect. South Asia fell by 6.7 points, from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the only large decline among the regions shown. Part of that fall reflects the loss or suspension of elected national assemblies in some countries, and the changes in how seats are filled, rather than a steady erosion of women's representation in functioning parliaments. Where a chamber is dissolved or not elected, the reported share can alter sharply, and readers should treat such movements as political events more than gradual trends. Reserved seats and candidate quotas explain much of the progress elsewhere, and the regions that rose most are those where such rules are widespread.

Income groups show a narrower spread than regions. High-income countries reached 31.2 per cent in 2025, upper middle income 27.0 per cent, low income 24.8 per cent and lower middle income 23.6 per cent. Income alone does not decide the outcome: low-income countries hold a higher share than lower-middle-income ones, which suggests that electoral rules and party practice matter more than national wealth.

The country distribution of progress towards a target of 50 per cent by 2030 is more sobering than the regional averages. Of 187 countries assessed for parliaments, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold only 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest group is 69 countries with marginal progress that would need significant acceleration, and it covers 44.6 per cent of the population. Another 19 countries are stagnant, with 25.1 per cent of the population, and 39 countries are regressing, with 12.7 per cent. The population weights matter because they differ sharply from the country counts: a count of countries suggests that regression is the second most common outcome, while the population view shows that stagnation touches twice as many people. Together, stagnation and regression affect about two in five people in the assessed countries, a share that exceeds the population living where progress is moderate or better.

Management shows a similar pattern with a heavier weight on the negative end. Of 121 countries assessed for the female share of senior and middle management, 17 are on track or have met the target, with 8.1 per cent of the population. Moderate progress applies to 27 countries and 17.7 per cent of the population, and marginal progress to 34 countries and 31.3 per cent. Stagnation affects 6 countries with 2.7 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded in 37 countries, which together hold 40.3 per cent of the population, a far larger share than the 12.7 per cent in parliaments. The assessment covers fewer countries than for parliaments, so these shares describe the countries with data rather than the world. The finding that regression in management involves the largest populations, including very populous economies, should be read with caution because survey-based series are revised and can move from one round to the next.

### What changed since 2015, and the limits of the evidence

Since 2015 the largest gain in women's share of parliamentary seats was in Latin America and the Caribbean, where the regional value rose from 27.9 per cent to 36.6 per cent, a rise of 8.7 percentage points. North America rose from 22.3 per cent to 29.5 per cent, a gain of 7.3 points. Europe and Central Asia moved from 25.7 per cent to 31.7 per cent, a gain of 6.0 points, and East Asia and Pacific from 19.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent, a gain of 4.1 points. These are regional averages and conceal wide differences between countries within each region.

Two regions moved the other way. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region slipped from 17.5 per cent to 16.9 per cent. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the lowest regional value in 2025 and the only large fall. Part of the South Asian and Middle Eastern movement may reflect changes in the composition of reporting bodies, suspended or dissolved legislatures and political upheaval, but the indicator itself does not separate these causes. A lower share can arise from an election, from a change in the chamber counted, or from the loss of a quota. Such explanations rest on general knowledge of how parliaments work, not on anything these series measure.

The country classification against a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 shows how uneven the movement has been. For parliaments, 24 countries are on track or have met the target, 36 show moderate progress needing acceleration, 69 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, 19 are stagnating and 39 are regressing, among 187 countries assessed. The 24 countries on track hold only 4.9 per cent of the population of those assessed. The 69 countries with marginal progress hold 44.6 per cent, the largest population share of any class, and the 19 stagnating countries hold a further 25.1 per cent. Because the most populous countries sit in the slow classes, the number of countries on track overstates how far most women live in places where parity is approaching. The 39 regressing countries hold 12.7 per cent of the population.

For senior and middle management, the classification covers fewer countries, 121 in all. There, 17 countries are on track or have met the target, 27 show moderate progress, 34 show marginal progress, 6 stagnate and 37 regress. The population shares tell a harder story: the 37 regressing countries hold 40.3 per cent of the population assessed, against 8.1 per cent for the 17 on track. Regression is thus more common in management than in parliaments, and it affects a larger share of the people covered. Where legislative seats can be raised by quotas and electoral rules, management positions depend on firms, labour markets and care responsibilities, which no policy lever moves as quickly.

The management evidence is weaker than the parliamentary evidence, and this limits every comparison. Across all years, 154 countries have reported at least one value, but the number reporting in a given year has varied widely: 40 in 2000, 77 in 2015, 90 in 2020 and 95 in 2022. The count then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and only 48 countries had reported by 2025. A fall of that size is most likely a matter of reporting lags, not of any change in practice, yet it means that the latest values cover roughly half the countries that were present a year earlier. Comparisons of 2025 with earlier years would rest on different sets of countries and cannot be trusted as a measure of change.

The regional trend summary for management returned no result, so no claim is made about how any region is moving on this indicator. Nor can these indicators say why countries advance or regress. They record outcomes, not the quotas, laws, party practices, employer conduct or social norms that produce them. Whether the period after 2020 slowed or accelerated progress cannot be established for management from this evidence, and for parliaments the series gives levels and class assignments but no separate account of the pandemic years.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the rates observed since 2015, no region reaches parity in parliaments by 2030. The world trend is classed as marginal progress, with an expected value of 29.8 per cent in 2030 against the 50.0 per cent benchmark, a ratio of 0.25. East Asia and Pacific is expected at 25.7 per cent in 2030 (ratio 0.21), and Europe and Central Asia at 35.2 per cent (ratio 0.39); both are classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. The high-income group is expected at 34.7 per cent, so wealth does not by itself close the gap. Latin America and the Caribbean comes closest, at 41.9 per cent, and is the only region classed as moderate progress. Even there, acceleration is needed.

The regions at the bottom of the range are moving in the wrong direction. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected value of 8.9 per cent in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also classed as regression, at 16.7 per cent. Low-income countries are expected at 26.5 per cent and lower-middle-income countries at 25.3 per cent, both marginal. Such projections extend a linear trend and are not forecasts; a change of electoral rules, such as the adoption of candidate quotas, can shift a national figure within one election cycle, and a suspension of parliament or a coup can erase one.

The country classification shows where most people live. Of 187 countries assessed for parliamentary seats, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress. Marginal progress covers 69 countries and 44.6 per cent of the population, stagnation covers 19 countries and 25.1 per cent, and regression covers 39 countries and 12.7 per cent. Most of the population therefore lives in countries classed as marginal, stagnating or regressing.

Management is assessed for fewer countries, 121, and the picture is no better. Only 17 countries, with 8.1 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the target, while 37 countries, with 40.3 per cent of the population, are classed as regression. Reporting is also thin at the latest point: 48 countries reported in 2025, against 95 in 2022. The thinning of recent data weakens the case for judging progress in managerial posts, and it is itself a finding about the state of monitoring.

Several proposals follow from these findings, and the gaps are set out below.

w-c02-6-2.text:
### Health and education budgets claim stable but modest shares of spending

Government budgets show a stable but modest commitment to the services that bear most directly on poverty. Education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in the world in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, a fall of about 0.1 of a percentage point over eight years. The world figure is nearly flat, but regional movements beneath it differ. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, while Latin America and the Caribbean held at 16.4 per cent in 2015 and 16.6 per cent in 2024. Low-income countries moved against the general direction, from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022. Reporting for 2025 is partial, with 60 countries, so the latest observations describe a subset and not the world.

Health is harder to summarise. The series, domestic general government health expenditure as a share of general government expenditure, is reported here by region and income group, and no world figure is given. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024, so the final year supports no statement. The most recent usable readings fall between 2017 and 2023, depending on the group, and comparisons across groups therefore mix end years. They indicate direction and scale and are not a common-year ranking.

Social protection is the third service named in the section's question, and no result for its share of public spending is available in this bench. The coverage and benefit-incidence series describe who is reached, not how much governments spend, and they are treated in another section of the chapter. The absence should not be read as a low or a high figure.

The targets add a further limit. Target 1.a calls for significant mobilisation of resources and for adequate and predictable means, and target 1.b calls for sound policy frameworks that support accelerated investment in poverty eradication. Neither sets a threshold, a base year or a required share of spending, and the series held here measure domestic budgets, not development cooperation, so target 1.a is only partly addressed. Any classification of progress therefore rests on direction alone: a rising share is read as movement towards the target. That reading is open to challenge, since a share can fall while the absolute amount rises with growth, and can rise because other spending is cut.

### Regions and income groups differ widely in health priority

Health receives very different priority across regions and income groups. North America devoted 22.1 per cent of general government expenditure to health from domestic sources in 2015 and 22.8 per cent in 2023, the highest share of any region reported. Europe and Central Asia stood at 15.0 per cent in 2015 and 14.5 per cent in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 11.5 per cent to 11.8 per cent over the same years. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2019, the last year in its series. South Asia began far lower, at 3.7 per cent in 2015, and reached 4.8 per cent in 2022. That is the largest proportional gain among the regions shown, yet the region still allocates less than a third of the share of Europe and Central Asia in 2023.

The income groups repeat the pattern. High-income economies assigned 17.9 per cent in 2015 and 18.5 per cent in 2023. Low-income economies assigned 5.4 per cent in 2015 and 5.3 per cent in 2017, and lower-middle-income economies 4.8 per cent in 2015 and 4.7 per cent in 2018. Comparing 2015 alone, the high-income share is about 3.3 times the low-income share and about 3.7 times the lower-middle-income share. These ratios apply to shares only, before account is taken of the far smaller budgets to which they are applied. A poor country that gives a small share of a small budget to health leaves households to meet the difference from their own pockets, which is a recognised route into impoverishment.

These comparisons carry a caveat. The series do not end in the same year: the low-income and lower-middle-income series stop in 2017 and 2018, and the Sub-Saharan African series in 2019, so none of them can show what followed the pandemic of 2020 or the debt pressures that came after. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024 at the time of the data, so the latest year is not yet a basis for comparison. A gap measured in earlier years for the poorest groups may since have narrowed or widened, and the data cannot say which.

Education shares show a different ordering, though not a clean one. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 15.4 per cent in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 16.6 per cent in 2024, give education the largest shares of their budgets among the regions listed, while North America gave 10.7 per cent in 2022, down from 12.9 per cent in 2015. Low-income economies raised their education share from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, a period in which their health share did not move. Poorer groups thus tend to put more of their budgets into schooling than into health, and richer groups the reverse. The share is a measure of priority, not of adequacy, because a large share of a small budget may still buy little per pupil.

### Education shares fell in most countries while inequality in spending widened

Since 2015 the education share of public budgets has weakened in most countries. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are classed as in regression, and these hold 78.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 29 countries, with 7.1 per cent of that population, are on track or have met the direction of travel. A further 13 countries (1.8 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 12 (2.3 per cent) marginal progress and 23 (10.5 per cent) stagnation. No numerical target exists for these indicators, so the classes measure movement towards an increase and not distance from an agreed level. An increase is itself only one reading of progress, since a falling share can accompany rising total budgets or a growing economy.

The population weighting explains why the picture is so unfavourable, for the regressing group includes populous regions. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent of government expenditure in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, and South Asia from 13.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2025. North America also declined, from 12.9 per cent in 2015 to 10.7 per cent in 2022. The movement was not universal. Low-income countries rose from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, and Latin America and the Caribbean edged up from 16.4 per cent to 16.6 per cent in 2024. Competing claims on budgets, such as debt service, pensions and health, and the fiscal pressure that followed the pandemic after 2020, are commonly cited pressures on education shares, although these data do not identify which of them operated in any given country.

Spending relative to national income shows a different problem, that of divergence. Across 164 countries, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of education spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.101, an increase of more than half. The between-region share of that Theil index moved from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent. Regional differences therefore account for under a quarter of the inequality in both years, and the widening came mainly from differences among countries within regions. Regional averages thus conceal the divergence, and policies aimed at whole regions would miss most of it.

Health presents a more favourable record. Of 193 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the direction of travel, holding 40.8 per cent of their population, while 61 are in regression, holding 21.3 per cent. Another 30 countries (22.1 per cent of the population) show marginal progress, 19 (11.5 per cent) stagnation and 11 (4.3 per cent) moderate progress. The series cannot show whether the pandemic raised the priority of health budgets, though that is a plausible contributor.

The two shares do not move together. The Spearman correlation between changes in the health share and the education share across 129 countries over 2015 to 2022 is 0.16, and between their levels in the later year of that span 0.09. Countries that raised one share were therefore hardly more likely to raise the other, and no common cause is shown. Neither is a trade-off. Governments appear to set the two priorities largely independently, so the weakening of education shares needs its own explanation in each country.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Spending shares carry no numerical target under targets 1.a and 1.b, so progress can be judged only by direction. The trend classes ask whether a share is rising, which is a weak test: a country may be on track while spending too little, and another in regression while spending generously. The classes are signals of priority, not verdicts on adequacy. The target wording can also be read as concerning domestic budgets, development cooperation, or both. The series examined cover domestic budgets only, so nothing here speaks to external resources under target 1.a.

On this reading health is nearer to progress than education. For the domestic health share, 72 of 193 countries assessed are on track, holding 40.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, while regression affects 61 countries with 21.3 per cent. Whether any rise after 2020 reflects emergency responses to the pandemic cannot be shown by these results, and whether health budgets persist under fiscal pressure is not settled by the data. For education the pattern is the reverse: 110 of 187 countries are in regression, with 78.2 per cent of the population, against 29 on track with 7.1 per cent. Because the regression class holds most of the population, the direction of education budgets matters for most of the world's children, though the results do not identify which countries drive it.

The outlook for 2030 is uneven. Health shares may keep rising in a large group of countries, but 21.3 per cent of the population lives where they are falling. Education shares are falling where most people live, and the pattern is not uniform: the low-income group rose from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, so falling shares are not confined to poorer countries. Spending as a share of GDP became more unequal, as the Theil index rose from 0.065 in 2015 to 0.101 in 2022. The between-region share eased from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent, which implies that the widening occurred mostly within regions.

Two limits qualify every reading. Spending data for low-income countries often end years before the latest reporting year, so recent shifts there are unseen. Social protection spending is not covered by the spending series examined, and its coverage and targeting are treated in other sections of this chapter.
