w-c04-5-2.text:
### Global consumption fell between 2015 and 2020

Global alcohol consumption per adult fell over the first five years of the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization estimate, carried in the World Development Indicators, puts total consumption at 5.9 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 and over in 2015. By 2020 it stood at 4.9 litres. The fall is about 1.0 litre, or roughly one sixth of the 2015 level, in five years. The measure sums recorded sales and an estimate of unrecorded alcohol, such as home production and informal trade, and is adjusted for tourist consumption.

Target 3.5 calls for strengthening the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including the harmful use of alcohol. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline year. The target can therefore be read in more than one way. One reading takes the wording to concern harm, which per capita volume captures only in part, since the same average can conceal heavy episodic drinking in a minority. Another reading treats volume as the best available proxy and counts a sustained decline as progress. This book adopts the second reading, because volume is the only alcohol series the shelf holds, and it states that choice openly. On that reading the world moved in the intended direction after 2015.

The series needs careful handling. The figures are projected estimates, not counts from a survey of drinkers in each year. Statisticians model them from sales, tax records, production data and occasional surveys, and then project forward where observations are thin. A smooth global path is therefore partly a product of the method, and a single year should not be read as a precise count. The final year, 2020, coincides with the first months of the pandemic, when closures of bars and restaurants, lost tourism and shifts in household purchasing altered both drinking and its measurement. Whether the 2020 figure reflects lasting change or a temporary disturbance cannot be settled from this series alone.

Coverage is nearly complete. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2020, 187 countries report in at least one year, and 185 report in 2020. The few countries that drop out in some years do not alter the global picture materially, though the estimates for those places are less secure. The world figure is thus a broad measure, and the sections that follow turn to the regions, income groups and countries that lie behind it.

### Regions differ widely in level and in direction

Regional levels span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia and North America sit at the top. Consumption in Europe and Central Asia was 8.9 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2020, down from 9.5 litres in 2015. North America stood at 9.9 litres in 2020, up from 9.5 litres. Among the regions reported, North America is the only one in which the estimate rose. Its rate of 0.0075 is classed as regression, while every other region shows a negative rate. Latin America and the Caribbean lies in the middle band, at 5.8 litres in 2020 against 6.5 litres in 2015. At the bottom, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan record about 0.3 litres in both years, 0.4 litres in 2015 and 0.3 litres in 2020. That level reflects widespread abstention and legal restriction. It is also a region in which unrecorded consumption is hardest to measure, so the level should be read with caution.

The largest regional fall is in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020. Its rate of -0.0657 is the steepest of any region and is classed as on track or target met. South Asia fell from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, at a rate of -0.0360, also classed on track. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0216, is placed in the same class. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0138, is classed as moderate progress, but acceleration needed. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0181, receives the same class even though its level is so low. These classes need a caveat. The Goals set no numerical target for alcohol under target 3.5, which asks only for strengthened prevention and treatment of harmful use. The classification therefore measures the direction and speed of change, and does not show whether a region has reached a safe or desired level.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 4.6 litres in 2015 to 4.2 litres in 2020, at a rate of -0.0211, classed on track. That is a fall of about half a litre, much smaller than in East Asia and Pacific, where consumption fell by almost two litres.

The income groups show a similar divergence. High-income economies fell only from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, at a rate of -0.0075, classed as marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed. They remain the heaviest-drinking group. Low-income economies, at 2.9 litres in 2015 and 2.8 litres in 2020, moved even less, at -0.0054, and are classed in the same way. Upper-middle-income economies fell from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres, at -0.0585, and lower-middle-income economies from 3.9 litres to 3.3 litres, at -0.0340; both are classed on track. The largest reductions therefore came in the middle-income groups, while the highest-consuming group fell slowly and the lowest-consuming group barely moved. The period also spans 2020, when closure of bars and restricted travel altered recorded sales, and the projected estimates for that year rest partly on modelling, so part of the fall may not persist.

### Country trajectories split between steep falls and regression

The trend classification covers 183 countries and rates each by its course towards a lower level of consumption. Target 3.5 sets no numerical goal for alcohol, so the classes measure direction and pace against a decrease by 2030, not distance from a stated threshold. That is one of several possible readings and applies throughout.

The country picture is divided. In 75 countries, holding 60.4% of the population of those assessed, consumption is on track or the target is met. A further 21 countries, with 11.0% of their population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 21, with 7.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. In 12 countries, with 3.1%, consumption stagnates. In 54 countries, with 18.2%, it is in regression, meaning that consumption per adult is rising.

The two ways of counting give different weights. By number of countries, 75 of 183 are on track, well under half, while 54 are in regression, about three in ten. By population, the on-track class holds 60.4% and the regression class 18.2%. The gap between the two views shows that the on-track group includes populous countries, and that the regressing group is made up largely of smaller ones. The country-level data are not tabulated here, so which countries these are is not stated. The 60.4% is therefore a statement about people, not a sign that most countries are succeeding.

The reasons for regression are not measured in these results. Well-established experience suggests that rising incomes, urbanisation, commercial marketing and weak taxation or licensing of alcohol have raised consumption in many middle-income settings, while taxes, limits on availability and restrictions on advertising have helped to lower it where drinking is high. Countries that begin from very low levels, often for cultural or religious reasons, can register regression from a small base, so the class does not always signal a harmful level.

Coverage is nearly complete. Between 185 and 187 countries report in every year from 2000 to 2020, and 187 report in at least one year. The estimates are projected by the World Health Organization from survey and sales data, not counted directly, so country-level movements, above all for 2020, partly reflect modelling and not observed change. The classification should be read as an indication of direction, not as a precise ranking.

### Change was not convergent and moved alike for men and women

Change between 2015 and 2020 was not convergent. Across 181 countries, a regression of five-year change on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00589, with a p-value of 0.603 and an R-squared of 0.012. The sign is negative, which would mean that countries with higher consumption fell slightly faster, but the coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the starting level explains about 1.2% of the variation in change. High-consumption countries did not systematically close the gap with low-consumption ones.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of consumption across countries rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.74 in 2020. The spread of national levels relative to their mean therefore widened slightly. Because the global average fell while dispersion rose, reductions were uneven in proportion: some countries fell sharply, some barely moved, and some rose. The difference between the two coefficients is small, and a movement of two hundredths in a five-year window should not be read as a settled trend.

The second result concerns the sexes. Across 185 countries, the changes in male and female consumption between 2015 and 2020 are almost perfectly rank-correlated, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.99 and a Kendall coefficient of 0.94. The 2020 levels are nearly as closely aligned, at 0.99 and 0.92. Countries in which men reduced consumption most are, almost without exception, those in which women did so as well. Rank correlation says nothing about the absolute gap between men and women, which is large in nearly every country; it says only that the ordering of countries is shared.

Such a close match is consistent with drivers operating at national level rather than in behaviour specific to either sex. Taxation and pricing, limits on availability and marketing, and social norms act on whole populations, although the results do not test any of these. The method also contributes. The figures are projected estimates, built from national sales, survey and modelling inputs, and the same adjustments to a country's total are likely to carry through to both sex-specific series. Part of the correlation may therefore be an artefact of estimation rather than a finding about behaviour.

No causal claim follows from these results. The window is five years and covers the disruption of 2020, and the lack of convergence describes the data rather than judging any policy. What can be said is that the starting level did not organise the change, and that the sex of the drinker did not alter a country's place in the ordering.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to a world moving in the right direction on alcohol, though not evenly. The world rate of -0.0363 is classed as on track or target met, yet it leans on large falls in East Asia and Pacific, where consumption went from 6.4 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020, and in upper middle income countries, where it went from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres. In high-income countries the fall was from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a rate of -0.0075 classed as marginal progress, and North America moved the other way, from 9.5 litres to 9.9 litres. Target 3.5 sets no numerical threshold, so every class here describes direction and pace against a decrease. Whether the gap between regions narrows or widens by 2030 cannot be read from two observation points, and the 2030 horizon lies ten years after the last observation in 2020.

The country picture shows the same division, and it should be read together with the population shares. Consumption is regressing in 54 countries holding 18.2% of the assessed population, and 12 more are stagnant. Population weighting is why the 75 countries on track account for 60.4% of that population: they are fewer than half of the 183 assessed, but they include populous ones. The global verdict therefore depends on a limited set of large countries, and the results alone do not name them. A global verdict of progress can coexist with widespread failure elsewhere.

The absence of convergence matters for 2030. With a coefficient of -0.00589 and a p-value of 0.603, nothing in the data suggests that high-consumption countries are catching down unaided. Falls are more likely to follow national policy choices, such as taxation, availability controls and marketing rules, than a general pull towards a common level, though the results do not test these causes. Low-income countries, where consumption is lowest at 2.8 litres in 2020, show only marginal progress, and the data cannot say whether rising incomes will push consumption upward there. Projected estimates carry uncertainty, and the 2020 value may reflect pandemic disruption to trade and sales.

w-c04-11-2.text:
### Immunisation and maternal and child services are largely flat at the global level

The nearest measure the shelf holds for immunisation and related services is the universal health coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health. It combines four tracer indicators: family planning, pregnancy care, child immunisation and child treatment, and it is scored from 0 to 100 index points. It is not a direct measure of vaccine coverage, because immunisation is only one of the four components. A movement in the index may therefore reflect changes in family planning or in the treatment of childhood illness rather than in vaccination. The reading offered here is of service coverage in general, with immunisation as one part of it.

Target 3.b can be read in more than one way. It concerns research and development, access to affordable essential medicines and vaccines, and the terms of the Doha Declaration. Coverage of services is an outcome of access, not a measure of research effort or of the price of medicines. The index speaks to access only in part, and the other elements of the target are not captured by any series held here.

At the global level the trend classification is regression, at a rate of -0.0017. The index values behind the regional classes are not carried among the facts of this section, so levels are not quoted here; only the classes and rates are. The change is small. Its significance lies in what it fails to show: there is no sign of the steady gain that a fifteen-year agenda implies, and a world expected to advance towards fuller coverage has, on this measure, slipped slightly.

Most regions are flat. East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, high income countries, North America, upper middle income countries and low income countries are all classified as stagnating, each with a rate of zero. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also stagnant. Europe & Central Asia shows a small positive rate of 0.0031, which is still classed as stagnation. Stagnation at high levels is less troubling than stagnation at low ones, since there is less room for gain, yet it means that remaining gaps are not closing. Low income countries remain far below every other group on the index, and a rate of zero offers no sign that this distance is narrowing.

The worst movements are in the middle of the income range. The lower middle income group has a rate of -0.0037 and South Asia a rate of -0.0053, and both are classed as regression. Disruption to routine services during the pandemic after 2020 is a recognised cause of lost coverage in many countries, and populous countries weigh heavily in group averages. The results do not separate the period before 2020 from the period after, so the share of the fall due to the pandemic cannot be stated. Sub-Saharan Africa is the only region with a clear gain, at a rate of 0.0099, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. The gain is real but begins from a low base.

The country classification confirms the pattern. Of 193 countries assessed, 11 are on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population. Another 9, with 3.1 per cent, show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 37, with 14.4 per cent, show marginal progress. Stagnation covers 105 countries and 48.1 per cent of the population, and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. The index carries no fixed 2030 target, so these classes rest on the direction of travel, not on a stated goal; 'on track' here means a rising trend, not a target met. Taken together, stagnation and regression cover 77.6 per cent of the population, which makes a general recovery in service coverage by 2030 unlikely without a clear change of course.

### Health spending has risen in dollar terms but barely as a share of output

Domestic general government health expenditure per capita rose from 589.2 current US dollars in 2015 to 803.7 in 2023 for the world as a whole. The series is in current dollars and is not adjusted for inflation or for population structure, so part of the rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger volume of care. The movement also says nothing about how the money was used.

Measured against output, the picture is much flatter. Current health expenditure was 9.7 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2023. Spending has therefore grown roughly in step with the economies that carry it. A rising dollar figure alongside a stable share means that health has held its place in national budgets and household outlays but has not gained priority. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, and a global share that moves by less than half a percentage point over eight years cannot be read as that kind of increase. The share also includes private and external spending, while the per capita series covers only domestic government spending, so the two measure different things and are not directly comparable.

The global average conceals a division by income. In high income countries the share of GDP rose from 12.0 per cent to 12.5 per cent, and in upper middle income countries from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent. In lower middle income countries it fell from 3.9 per cent to 3.7 per cent, and in low income countries from 5.4 per cent to 4.6 per cent. The fall among the poorest runs against the direction target 3.c requires. The data do not show why it fell. Faster growth elsewhere in the economy, reduced external funding, debt pressure and conflict are all plausible contributors, but none can be separated here.

Regional shares tell a similar story. North America stood at 16.0 per cent in 2015 and 16.3 per cent in 2023. South Asia declined from 3.5 per cent to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent in both years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 5.4 per cent to 5.3 per cent. Only East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean moved up, and by small margins.

The period after 2020 matters for interpretation. The pandemic raised health spending in many countries and depressed GDP in the same years, which lifts the share temporarily. The 2023 values are therefore not a clean continuation of the pre-2020 path. Coverage of the latest year is also thin: only 22 countries reported the share for 2024, and only 7 reported domestic government spending per capita, so 2023 is the last year that supports regional comparison.

For 2030, a financing share that has hardly moved offers little ground for expecting a step change. Without a deliberate rise in public priority, the countries with the least spending will remain far from the resources that basic services need.

### Regions and countries differ by orders of magnitude

North America spent 6,959.0 current US dollars per head of domestic government money on health in 2023, against 30.8 dollars in South Asia and 31.7 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa. The ratio between the top and the bottom is therefore above 200 to one. Europe and Central Asia stood at 2,178.0 dollars, East Asia and Pacific at 571.7 dollars, Latin America and the Caribbean at 415.7 dollars, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 190.2 dollars. By income group the gradient is as steep: high-income countries spent 3,847.3 dollars, upper middle income countries 338.9 dollars, lower middle income countries 30.9 dollars and low-income countries 7.3 dollars. These are current dollars at market exchange rates, so they understate what a dollar buys in poorer countries, where wages and many services cost less. Even so, no plausible adjustment closes a gap of this size.

The movement since 2015 widens the distance in absolute terms. North America started from 4,587.0 dollars and gained roughly 2,372 dollars per head by 2023, while Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 29.7 to 31.7 dollars and low-income countries from 7.0 to 7.3 dollars. South Asia is the exception among the poorer regions: its figure roughly doubled, from 14.7 to 30.8 dollars, though from a very small base. The pattern is one of growth proportional to the starting level in the richer groups and near-stillness at the bottom. Rapid population growth in low-income countries also means that a flat per-capita figure can conceal a rising national outlay that merely keeps pace with numbers of people.

The share of output spent on health gives a less favourable picture for the poorest. Low-income countries fell from 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 4.6 per cent in 2023, and lower middle income countries from 3.9 to 3.7 per cent. High-income countries rose from 12.0 to 12.5 per cent and upper middle income countries from 5.5 to 6.0 per cent. South Asia slipped from 3.5 to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed. On this measure the poorest groups moved the other way. The results do not identify the reasons. Weak tax bases, debt service and the strain of the pandemic and later price rises on public budgets are commonly cited, but none is tested here. Because the indicator covers all current health spending, a fall also means that private and external money did not offset the shortfall in the poorest groups. The latest year is thinly reported: only 7 countries had a 2024 value for domestic government spending per head and 22 for the share of GDP, so the regional figures for 2023 rest on estimates that may be revised.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the regional averages. For domestic government health spending per head, 142 of the 193 countries assessed were classed as on track, holding 80.1 per cent of their combined population. No target value is set for this series, so the classes describe direction and pace of change in current dollars, not distance from a goal, and they do not show that the financing aim of target 3.c has been met. A further 12 countries showed moderate progress, and 34 were in regression, holding 14.0 per cent of the population. Rising dollar spending in most countries therefore coexists with a sizeable minority of countries, and of people, where it fell.

The service coverage sub-index is flatter. Only 11 of the 193 countries were on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population, while stagnation covered 105 countries and 48.1 per cent and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. Nearly four in five people live in a country where coverage of these services stood still or fell. The regression class is large in population because it includes South Asia and the lower middle income group, where the regional indices fell. The two series are not linked in these results, so they cannot show why rising spending in many countries sits beside flat coverage; delivery, workforce and reach of services are plausible candidates, but the data do not test them.

### Spending has not converged and the workforce cannot be measured well

Spending per head at purchasing power parity shows no sign of countries drawing together. Across 190 countries, the regression of growth in current health expenditure per capita (international dollars) between 2015 and 2023 on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00001, with a p-value of 0.997 and an R-squared of 0.0. Countries that began with low spending did not grow faster than those that began high, and the starting level explains none of the variation in growth. The coefficient of variation, a measure of relative dispersion, moved from 1.24 in 2015 to 1.20 in 2023. That change is small and is not backed by a convergence relationship, so it should be read as little more than stability in the spread.

The result matters for target 3.c, which calls for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed countries and small island developing States. Convergence would be the sign that the gap in resources was narrowing. Its absence means that the large differences in spending described earlier in this section are being carried into the final years of the agenda. Health budgets depend on national income, on the capacity of governments to raise revenue and on debt service burdens, and these did not obviously change in a way that favoured poorer countries during the period; this is background knowledge and not a result of the test. The shocks of 2020 fell on all budgets, but countries with more fiscal room could more easily sustain health spending. The test here is across countries and does not separate these channels, and it covers 2015 to 2023 only, so any later change is not captured.

The health workforce is harder still to assess. The shelf holds one series on community health workers per 1,000 people, and it is thin. Only 64 countries report in any year of the series. The number reporting in a single year ranges from 3 in 2002 and 3 in 2014 to 29 in 2004 and 21 in 2008. After 2010 the count never exceeds 13: 6 in 2011, 7 in 2012, 6 in 2013, 3 in 2014, 4 in 2015 and 6 in 2016. The latest year in the series is 2016, so nothing is recorded for the period after 2015 beyond those few reporters, and nothing after 2020.

With so few reporters, and with a different set of countries in each year, a change in the average could not be told from a change in who reports. No trend in workforce density, upward or downward, can be asserted, and no judgement can be made on whether the recruitment and retention called for in target 3.c is occurring. Community health workers are also defined differently from country to country, under varied national titles, which weakens comparison even where data exist. The series also says nothing of doctors, nurses or midwives. The honest finding is that spending can be measured and has not converged, whereas the workforce, the input on which services most depend, cannot be measured well enough to be followed towards 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Targets 3.b and 3.c ask for more vaccines and medicines for developing countries, and for substantially more health financing and workforce. The shelf supports only a partial reading. The financing evidence is a direction-of-travel test on current dollars, with no target attached, so it cannot show that the financing half of 3.c has been met. It shows that 142 of 193 countries, holding 80.1% of the assessed population, are rising in domestic government health spending per head. That majority is dominated by countries that already spend most. A further 34 countries, with 14.0% of the population, show regression, and these are the systems where the target is most at risk.

For 3.b the shelf holds only the composite reproductive, maternal, newborn and child index, which is not a measure of vaccine coverage or of access to medicines. Read as a proxy, it is discouraging. Only 11 countries, with 5.0% of the population, are on track, while 105, with 48.1%, are stagnating and 31, with 29.5%, are regressing. Together, stagnation and regression cover 77.6% of the assessed population. The index is consistent with disrupted routine services after 2020, but it cannot attribute the pattern to vaccines, and it cannot be linked to spending with the series held. If present trends hold, most of the world's population will reach 2030 with coverage no better than today.

The share of output devoted to health shows that dollar growth alone is not sufficient. Low-income countries fell from 5.4% of GDP in 2015 to 4.6% in 2023, while high-income countries rose from 12.0% to 12.5%. South Asia's share slipped from 3.5% to 3.3%, even though its per-head public spending rose from a very low base. Spending therefore grew in absolute terms nearly everywhere, but did not keep pace with output where need is greatest. Why is a matter for national studies: tax capacity, debt service, competing pressures after 2020 and the pattern of external aid are the usual explanations, and none can be tested with these series. Without a deliberate shift, the gap in 2030 is likely to be wider than in 2015.

The workforce half of 3.c cannot be judged. Community health workers were reported by only 64 countries in any year, by no more than 29 in any single year, and by just 6 countries in 2016, the last year of record. A target to recruit and retain workers cannot be monitored from a series that thin. Estimates for 2024 also rest on 7 reporting countries for domestic government spending and 22 for spending as a share of GDP, so the latest picture is provisional.

w-c06-3-2.text:
### The global level in 2022

In 2022, 19.5% of women aged 20-24 worldwide had been first married by age 18. The indicator, which the World Bank carries from UNICEF and the Demographic and Health Surveys, counts women in that age band who were married or in union before their eighteenth birthday. The age band is chosen deliberately: women aged 20-24 have all passed the threshold, so the share records a completed experience rather than a risk still running, and it reflects marriages that took place in roughly the preceding decade, a general property of the age band and not a result drawn from the data here. Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of child, early and forced marriage, and this share is the measure by which progress towards it is read.

The world figure should be read as a modelled estimate, not as a count. No agency surveys every woman in every country each year. Household surveys are fielded in a given country once every few years, and the aggregate is built from those surveys, carried forward and combined with population weights. The value for 2022 therefore describes the best available picture of that year, and it rests on a much smaller set of direct observations than the single number suggests. The world aggregate is reported for 2022 only, so no change over time can be drawn from it, and any claim about movement since 2015 or since 2020 has to be made from other evidence. The absence of a second year is a limit of the data and does not indicate stagnation.

The sparseness is visible in the reporting itself. Over the whole series, 145 countries have reported a value in at least one year, yet in any single year only a fraction of them do. The most recent year, 2025, holds observations from just 3 countries, which is too few to say anything about the present beyond what the aggregates carry. The latest year with a full set of aggregates is 2022, and it is the reference point for the rest of this section.

The figure matters because early marriage is closely tied to the other outcomes of this chapter. Well-established research links marriage before 18 to earlier school leaving, earlier childbearing and greater exposure to violence at home, and to less say over a woman's own health and finances; these links come from outside knowledge, not from the results reported here. A level of 19.5% means that about one young woman in five began adult life in that position. The sections that follow set this global value against regional and income differences, the spread among countries, and the pace required to reach 2030.

### Regional and income differences

Regional averages for 2022 show a wide spread behind the world figure of 19.5%. East Asia and Pacific stands lowest, at 5.6% of women aged 20-24 first married by age 18. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan follow at 17.7%, a little below the world level. South Asia reaches 25.6%, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest at 31.1%. Sub-Saharan Africa's share is therefore more than five times that of East Asia and Pacific, a ratio of 5.60 derived from the two regional values.

The regional grouping used here is not the one found in every United Nations or World Bank publication. It joins the Middle East and North Africa with Afghanistan and Pakistan, two countries that other conventions place in South Asia. A comparison with figures published under a different grouping may therefore differ, and the South Asian and Middle Eastern values should be read as belonging to this arrangement only. Regional values are also summaries of countries with very different populations and survey dates, so a single regional share can hide sharp contrasts within it.

Income groups tell a similar story. Lower middle income economies stand at 24.4%, against 8.5% for upper middle income economies, a ratio of 2.89 derived from those two values. Child marriage is thus markedly less common in the upper middle income group. The results do not explain the gradient. Outside the data, it is widely held that poverty, limited schooling for girls, rural residence and weak enforcement of minimum-age laws sustain early marriage, while longer schooling and wider paid work for women delay it; this is background knowledge, not a finding of these results. Income is not the whole account, since South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa may differ in norms, in the role of dowry and bride price, and in the reach of legal reform.

No figure for high income or low income economies is shown in these results. The absence matters: the gradient across the full income range cannot be stated from this evidence, and nothing here shows where the practice is most concentrated among the poorest countries. The comparison offered covers the middle of the income distribution only.

### Inequality among countries and the thin evidence

Inequality among countries in the share of women first married by age 18 appears to have narrowed between 2012 and 2018, though the evidence for the comparison is thin. The population-weighted Gini coefficient across reporting countries stood at 0.282 in 2012, when 21 countries had data, and at 0.273 in 2018, when 20 did. The Theil index fell further, from 0.156 to 0.120. The coefficient of variation, which is more sensitive to the highest values, fell from 0.63 to 0.49. All three measures point the same way: countries with data were closer together in 2018 than in 2012.

The composition of the remaining inequality changed more than its size. The share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 73.0% in 2012 to 89.8% in 2018. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the total, and what separates the countries with data is increasingly the region in which they sit. The pattern could arise in several ways, and these results do not show which applies. If it holds beyond the countries surveyed, regional programmes and regional political commitments would matter more, but two different country sets cannot establish that, and a global average may conceal a divide that is largely geographic.

These readings must be held loosely, because the surveys that feed the indicator are irregular. Household surveys are fielded in each country every few years, so the set of countries reporting changes from one year to the next. Counts range from 5 countries in 2002 and 6 in 2001 to 21 in 2012 and 20 in 2018. Since 2015 the count has run from 11 in 2015 and 2017 to 18 in 2022, with 12 in 2020 and 12 in 2024. In 2025 only 3 countries report, which leaves that year unusable for any comparison. In all, 145 countries have a value in at least one year, but no more than 21 have a value in any single one.

The 2012 and 2018 comparison therefore rests on two different sets of countries, and a fall in the Gini or Theil index may reflect who was surveyed as much as what changed. Neither year allows a clean reading of the effect of the 2015 adoption of the goals or of the disruption after 2020, since the years in between draw on still other country sets. The inequality findings show a plausible direction of travel, not a measured trajectory, and they cannot be extended to countries that were not surveyed.

### Pace against the 2030 target

Target 5.3 calls for the elimination of harmful practices, including child, early and forced marriage, but its text names no numerical threshold. The most direct reading is a rate of zero by 2030. Others are possible: a large fall from a baseline, or convergence on the level of the best-performing regions. The trend assessment adopts the first reading, a target of 0.0% by 2030, and measures each country's recent pace against the pace that reading requires.

Of the 20 countries with enough observations to be classified, none is on track or has met the target. Two show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed there too; they hold 5.8% of the population of the assessed countries. Fourteen show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, and these hold 91.8% of that population. One country is stagnant, and three are regressing. The assessed countries are therefore overwhelmingly ones in which the share is falling too slowly to reach zero, and the few that are moving in the wrong direction are small in population terms.

The classification covers 20 countries out of 145 that have reported at some point. Countries are classed only where repeated surveys allow a trend to be drawn, and survey rounds arrive unevenly: 11 countries reported in 2015, 12 in 2020 and 3 in 2025. The 2025 count is very low, and the data do not show why; it may reflect surveys not yet published, but that cannot be confirmed from these results. For this reason the pace assessment cannot say how the practice changed after 2015 or after 2020 for most countries. Whether the disruption of schooling, health services and household incomes during the pandemic raised early marriage cannot be settled by the thin post-2020 series, though the mechanisms are widely noted in outside literature.

What this implies for 2030 is plain. With 91.8% of the assessed population in the marginal class, the world will not reach zero by 2030 on current trends. The regional levels shown earlier, 25.6% in South Asia and 31.1% in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2022, indicate where most of the remaining gap lies. Outside the results, experience in many countries links falls in marriage before 18 to longer schooling for girls, enforcement of a minimum legal age, and rising household incomes. These change slowly, and acceleration of the scale required would need all three to improve at once.

The proposals that follow from these findings are set out below.

w-c05-4-2.text:
### Global gross tertiary enrolment rose from 36.6 to 43.6 per cent between 2015 and 2024

Gross tertiary enrolment in the world stood at 36.6 per cent in 2015 and reached 43.6 per cent in 2024. The rise is 7.0 percentage points over nine years, and it places the world in the group the trend tool classes as making moderate progress, with acceleration needed. The annualised rate of change is 0.0196, a unitless proportional rate per year, which the tool reads as short of the pace that a fast improvement would require.

The indicator is a gross enrolment ratio. It divides total enrolment at tertiary level, whatever the age of the students, by the population of the age group that officially corresponds to that level. Because older students, repeaters and returning adults are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100 per cent, and a high value does not mean that every young person of tertiary age is enrolled. The ratio also shifts when a country changes the official age band or the definition of what counts as tertiary, so comparisons across countries and years carry some uncertainty.

The indicator covers only part of target 4.3. The target speaks of equal access for all women and men to affordable and quality technical, vocational and tertiary education. A gross ratio records the number of places taken up. It says nothing about the cost borne by students and families, nothing about the quality of teaching or the value of the qualification, and nothing about who is excluded by income, location, disability or ethnicity. Vocational education below the tertiary level falls outside the series altogether. The sex-disaggregated series, treated in the chapter section on gender parity, add one dimension of equality but not the others.

The target also sets no numeric threshold. The words say "equal access" and give no level of enrolment to be reached by 2030. Progress is therefore judged by direction and pace: whether the ratio rises, and whether it rises fast enough to be called on track by the bench's trend tool. On that reading the world is moving the right way, though more slowly than a full response to the target would imply. The 2024 value is also the latest year with broad reporting, since only 9 countries had reported for 2025 when the data were drawn, and the world figure for that year would not be reliable.

### Regional ratios diverge, from 9.3 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa to 84.9 per cent in Europe and Central Asia

Regional ratios in 2024 span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia stands at 84.9 per cent, and North America at 79.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa sits at 9.3 per cent, but its latest value dates from 2021, not 2024, so the comparison with other regions is not strictly like for like. Gross enrolment is a ratio of all students, whatever their age, to the population of the age group that officially corresponds to tertiary study. It can therefore exceed what a single age cohort would suggest, and it rises where adults return to study or where students repeat years.

The largest gains among the regions since 2015 came in East Asia and Pacific, where the ratio rose from 44.3 to 63.3 per cent, and in Europe and Central Asia, where it rose from 67.4 to 84.9 per cent. Both are classed as on track by the trend tool. The East Asian gain is consistent with the expansion of university systems and with rising secondary completion, though the results do not test this explanation and it is offered as conjecture. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 48.4 to 58.9 per cent, also classed as on track, with a smaller rise than the first two.

South Asia rose from 25.4 to 32.8 per cent and is classed as on track, though from a low base, so the gain of about seven percentage points still leaves it well below the world ratio of 43.6 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 27.3 to 29.7 per cent, and the tool classes progress there as marginal. A grouping that joins several economies with very different systems hides much variation, and the regional figure should be read with that in mind.

The high-income group rose from 76.2 to 82.0 per cent. Its annualised rate of 0.0083 is a unitless proportional rate per year, and the tool classes it as marginal progress, which reflects a high starting level and the fall in North America rather than a lack of access.

North America is the one region that went backwards, from 86.8 to 79.0 per cent. The results do not explain the fall. Demographic change, labour-market conditions, the cost of tuition and the pandemic years are plausible contributors, but these are conjecture, and the data alone cannot apportion causes.

Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 8.84 to 9.27 per cent, a change of well under one percentage point, and the low-income group shows the same picture, with its ratio at 8.86 per cent in 2015 and 9.28 per cent in 2021. Both are classed as marginal progress. The gap with Europe and Central Asia, already large in 2015, has widened in absolute terms, although the comparison sets 2021 values against 2024 values and should be read with that caveat. Progress in the poorest settings is therefore slow, not absent.

### Most countries are advancing, yet forty regress and the gaps between countries have not narrowed

Of the 159 countries assessed, 75 are on track or have met the trend benchmark, and they hold 69.8 per cent of the population of the countries classified. A further 22 countries show moderate progress, though acceleration is needed, and 16 show marginal progress that would require significant acceleration. Six are stagnant. Forty countries regress, and they hold 12.3 per cent of that population. The picture is therefore one of broad advance, with a large minority of countries whose enrolment ratios have fallen.

The classes need careful reading. Target 4.3 sets no numerical threshold for tertiary enrolment, so the trend tool has no official target to measure against. The classes describe the direction and pace of each country's own series, not distance from an agreed goal. A country already at a high ratio can be classed as regressing after a small fall, and a country at a low ratio can be classed as on track after a small rise. The count of 40 regressing countries may also reflect causes other than real decline. Revisions to population estimates change the denominator of a gross ratio. Changes in how institutions are counted, or in which programmes are reported as tertiary, can move a series without any change in students. The pandemic years also disturbed enrolment, through deferred entry, falling international study and, in some places, shifts toward work. Whether these effects have faded cannot be settled from the series alone.

The gaps between countries have not narrowed. Across 82 countries with data for both ends of 2015 to 2024, the convergence regression gives a coefficient of -0.00101 (p 0.901), with an R2 of 0.000. Initial levels explain none of the subsequent growth, so there is no sign that low-enrolment countries are catching up, and none that they are falling further behind. The coefficient of variation moved only from 0.591 in 2015 to 0.569 in 2024. Relative dispersion is almost unchanged, even as the world average rose.

Gender parity and enrolment move largely independently. Across the same 82 countries, the Spearman correlation between changes in the gender parity index and changes in enrolment is -0.083, which is effectively zero. Countries that expanded tertiary enrolment did not systematically improve or worsen the balance between women and men. The correlation between 2024 levels is 0.176, a weak positive link. Higher enrolment goes only loosely with a higher parity index. A parity index above one would mean more women than men enrolled, so a higher index does not by itself signal progress toward equal access.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise hides unequal prospects. With no convergence, the countries with the lowest ratios are not on a path to close the distance to the rest. The large regressing group means that the global average rests on gains in the countries that are advancing, which the results do not identify individually. Until the effects of reporting changes are separated from real losses, the regressing class should be treated as a list of cases to examine, not as a verdict.

### Data gaps limit the reading for 2030, and the proposals follow from them

Reporting thins exactly where the latest comparisons are drawn. In 2015, 147 countries reported gross tertiary enrolment, the highest count of the period since 2000. The number was 136 in 2016 and 133 in 2020, and fell to 125 in 2021. It stood at 94 in 2024 and only 9 in 2025. Every regional and global figure for 2024 therefore rests on fewer countries than the 2015 baseline, and the countries that report late are not a random draw. Where late reporters are poorer or have weaker statistical systems, the 2024 averages may be biased, and the apparent change since 2015 may partly reflect who is counted. The 2025 values are too few to read at all.

With that caution, the picture is of a world that is rising but unevenly. The global ratio has risen at an annualised rate of 0.0196. The rate is a proportional change per year and has no unit. East Asia and Pacific, South Asia and the middle-income groups are advancing at rates of 0.0406, 0.0289 and 0.0264 to 0.0368. Low income and Sub-Saharan Africa are advancing slowly, at 0.0077 and 0.0080, both classed as marginal progress. High income is classed in the same way, at 0.0083, but from a far higher base. The poorest regions start lowest and gain least, so their ratios remain far below those of other regions. The convergence test across 82 countries points the same way: the coefficient is -0.0010 with a p-value of 0.9011, and the coefficient of variation moved only from 0.59 to 0.57. No tendency for countries that began lower to grow faster can be detected.

The indicator also limits what can be said about target 4.3, which speaks of equal access, affordability and quality. A gross ratio counts all students regardless of age, so it can exceed the share of a cohort that attends, and it says nothing about who enrols, what they study, what they pay or whether they finish. Target 4.3 has no numerical threshold, and it can be read as a universal goal or as a relative improvement. No pace of gross enrolment can settle that question, and the series as it stands cannot show whether growth has reached women, poorer households or technical and vocational routes.

These limits shape the proposals that follow.

w-c06-6-2.text:
### What the indicators measure

The commitment in target 5.a is wide: equal rights to economic resources, ownership and control of land and other property, financial services, inheritance and natural resources, in accordance with national laws. The World Bank's catalogue measures only part of it. The best-covered strand is financial services, through the Global Findex survey, which asks adults whether they hold an account at a financial institution or have personally used a mobile-money service in the past year. Findex reports the answer separately for women and men, so the gap between the two series is a direct measure of unequal access. No equivalent series on women's ownership of land or housing sits on the shelf, and that absence shapes this section: the account gap can be measured with some precision, while the property gap can only be discussed through proxies and through what is missing.

An account is an entry point, not a measure of economic control. A woman may hold an account that her husband operates, or may have received a mobile-money wallet only to collect a government transfer. The survey definition counts accounts held alone or together with someone else. The indicator therefore shows access to the formal and semi-formal payment system, not who decides how money is used. It is nonetheless one of the few gender-disaggregated economic indicators with near-global coverage, and for that reason it carries much of the evidential weight for the target.

The survey is also periodic rather than annual. Findex rounds have appeared at intervals of roughly three years, and the most recent round reached 139 countries in 2024. Some regional aggregates in the results below end in 2021 rather than 2024, which reflects the vintage of the regional series on the shelf. Comparisons across regions must therefore be made with that difference in end year in mind, and the section states the end year of every figure it quotes.

### The world gap

Globally, the share of women holding an account rose from 65.9% in 2017 to 76.6% in 2024. Over the same period the share of men rose from 72.8% to 80.9%. Both groups gained, and women gained more in percentage points, so the gap narrowed. It has not closed. Measured from the results, the gap between men and women stood at 6.9 points in 2017 and at 4.3 points in 2024, so a gap of several points remains at world level. It is concentrated in a limited set of regions and income groups rather than spread evenly.

The world average conceals the shape of the problem. Where almost everyone holds an account, as in high-income economies, a gender gap cannot be large because there is no room for it. Where account ownership is still being built, as in low-income economies, the gap is determined by who is reached first. The evidence below shows that men are generally reached first, and that the gap is widest in settings where overall ownership is lowest or where social norms restrict women's mobility, employment and independent control of money.

The period 2017 to 2024 straddles two events that bear on this. The first is the global expansion of digital payments, which lowered the cost of opening an account and removed the need to visit a branch. The second is the pandemic after 2020, when governments in many countries paid emergency transfers electronically and, as background knowledge suggests, brought new account holders into the system. Whether these developments favoured women is a question the regional and income data allow the book to answer only in part, since the survey cannot separate the effect of each cause.

### Regional differences

In East Asia and the Pacific, women's account ownership rose from 71.2% in 2017 to 81.4% in 2021, against 75.7% and 84.2% for men. In Europe and Central Asia the female share rose from 79.4% to 88.0% while the male share rose from 83.8% to 91.2%. In both regions the gap persisted but was modest, and both sexes gained at a similar pace. These are middle- and upper-middle-income regions where the remaining gap plausibly reflects pockets of exclusion, for instance among rural, older and less-educated women, rather than a general barrier. The results do not test this explanation.

Latin America and the Caribbean shows the largest absolute gain in the regional table. Women's ownership rose from 52.1% in 2017 to 70.1% in 2021, and men's from 58.7% to 77.0%. Both sexes gained by a very large amount in four years, and the gap stayed visible. As background, not as a finding of the results, the region's expansion is often linked to conditional cash-transfer schemes paid into accounts and addressed to women as household recipients, and to the growth of digital wallets and low-cost accounts. If that link holds, a cash-transfer route to an account is real inclusion in the sense of access, but may be a narrower form of inclusion than an account opened for savings or credit.

South Asia reports through 2024. Women's ownership there rose from 64.0% in 2017 to 75.1% in 2024, while men's rose from 74.7% to 80.1%. The female gain was the larger, and the gap narrowed markedly. National drives to open basic accounts at scale and to route subsidies into accounts are a plausible contributor, though the results do not identify the cause. Surveys in several countries have suggested that accounts opened in a campaign can be dormant, so ownership may overstate active use. The indicator as defined here counts ownership, not activity.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the region where the gender gap is largest on the shelf. Women's ownership rose from 38.0% in 2017 to 45.6% in 2021, while men's rose from 56.8% to 59.6%. Women gained several points, yet fewer than half of women in the region held an account in 2021, and the male share was far higher. Legal and social restrictions on women's mobility, employment and independent financial decisions, together with low female labour-force participation, are the usual explanations, since a wage is a main reason for holding an account. The inclusion of Afghanistan in the aggregate matters: since 2021 the restrictions imposed on women there make the regional picture after that year uncertain, and the 2021 end point predates much of that change.

Sub-Saharan Africa has a higher level than the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, and a smaller gender gap. Women's ownership rose from 36.9% in 2017 to 49.0% in 2021, and men's from 48.5% to 61.4%. The male gain exceeded the female gain, so the gap widened slightly between the two dates rather than narrowing. The region is the global centre of mobile money, and the growth of agent networks has allowed many people to hold a wallet without entering a bank branch. Mobile-money inclusion appears to have lifted both sexes, with men gaining a little more. Women's lower rates of phone ownership, lower literacy and less independent income are commonly offered as explanations, though the results do not test them; the chapter's section on mobile technology treats the phone question directly.

North America is the single case in which the pattern reverses. Women's ownership rose from 93.4% in 2017 to 97.1% in 2021, while men's moved from 94.2% to 93.8%. By the later date, women's ownership exceeded men's. The movement is small and the sample for a region with few reporting countries is narrow, so it should not be over-read; still, it illustrates that a gender gap in account ownership is not inevitable once ownership is near universal.

### Income groups and the shape of the gap

The grouping by income level is more revealing than the regional one, because the gap is closely linked to the level of ownership. In low-income countries, women's ownership rose from 26.8% in 2017 to 40.6% in 2024. Men's rose from 37.3% to 52.5%. Even after the rise, well under half of women in these countries held an account in 2024, and the male share was above half. The gap in this group widened, from 10.5 points in 2017 to 11.9 points in 2024. It is among the widest on the shelf, though not the widest: in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the gap was larger, at 14.0 points in 2021.

In lower-middle-income countries, women's ownership rose from 55.6% to 67.6% and men's from 64.4% to 73.2%. The gap here is smaller than among low-income countries and narrowed clearly, from 8.8 points in 2017 to 5.6 points in 2024. Upper-middle-income countries show a rise from 68.9% to 82.5% for women and from 76.3% to 85.6% for men. The gap narrowed as well, from 7.4 points to 3.2 points, because women's gains were larger than men's. High-income countries sit close to the ceiling: women's ownership moved from 92.1% to 94.5%, men's from 93.9% to 95.3%, and the difference is small, at 0.8 points in 2024.

The pattern across the four groups is a familiar one in the diffusion of any financial service. Men adopt first, women follow, and the gap opens in the early and middle stages and narrows when the service approaches universality. This is a general pattern of diffusion, not a result established by the series held here. The practical implication is that the gender gap in the poorest countries is unlikely to close by itself as the average rises; it would close only when the service has largely saturated the male population, and that is far away. For countries in the low-income group, the pace of progress matters more than the world average suggests, because these are also the countries where women have the fewest alternatives to cash.

The result also shows that the world-level improvement is driven in large part by the middle-income groups, where the population is large. This weighting effect should be kept in mind when reading the world figure: the rise from 65.9% to 76.6% reflects mostly the middle-income economies catching up, and it says less about the poorest women, whose ownership remains well below the world level.

### Position against the 2030 target

The trend classification applies a simple benchmark: full account ownership among women, 100%, by 2030. This is an interpretation, since target 5.a itself sets no numerical level, and the reading of the target as universal access to financial services is a choice made by the bench. A different reading, in which the target is met when the gap between women and men closes, would produce a different classification. The reader should treat the benchmark as demanding and as one of several defensible readings.

On that benchmark, of 139 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target. These countries hold 49.9% of the assessed population, a large share because the group includes some very populous economies and many high-income countries already near the ceiling. A further 41 countries, with 18.7% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 29 countries, with 17.8% of the population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Six countries, with 3.2% of the population, show stagnation. Finally, 33 countries, with 10.4% of the population, show regression, meaning that women's ownership fell over the period assessed.

The number of regressing countries deserves attention. That 33 of 139 countries recorded a decline is not a statistical artefact to be dismissed. Possible explanations, offered as background and not as findings of the results, include survey differences, the closure of dormant accounts, a reduction in mobile-money use, political upheaval or sanctions, or genuine loss of access. The data cannot distinguish among these. What they do show is that the global rise is not universal; for roughly a quarter of the countries assessed, the direction was the wrong one, though these countries hold a smaller share of the population than those on track.

The weighting also shows the divide between countries and people. Half of the assessed population lives in countries classed as on track, but fewer than half of the countries are in that class on a count of nations. The countries that are not on track are numerous and smaller in population. The results do not classify them by income group, so their concentration in lower-income groups is a presumption and not a finding, although those groups do show the largest gaps. A global target met by population weight can therefore coexist with a majority of countries failing it, and the section's reading is that the aggregate masks the countries where policy attention is most needed.

What changed after 2015 and after 2020 can be stated only in outline. The first Findex round on the shelf for these results is 2017, so the baseline year of the goals is not itself observed here, and the period from 2015 to 2017 is outside the comparison. Between 2017 and 2021 the regional data show large gains in nearly every region, a period that includes the years of digital payments and emergency transfers around 2020. From 2021 to 2024 only the global, income-group and South Asian series are available on the shelf, and they show continued gains for both sexes. The material does not allow the claim that the pandemic itself changed the gender gap, only that ownership rose through it.

### Property, enterprise and the missing evidence

The remaining parts of target 5.a, land, property and inheritance, cannot be measured with the account series. The shelf holds three other series that touch on the target without measuring it. The Women, Business and the Law legal framework index, reported for 189 countries in 2025, scores how laws shape women's economic opportunities, with a topic on assets within it; the chapter's section on legal frameworks treats the index, and here it matters only as context. A legal right to own or inherit property is a precondition, not an outcome. Where statute and custom diverge, as in many systems of customary land tenure, women may hold the right in law and be denied it in practice, and no legal index can show this.

The enterprise survey series on firms with female participation in ownership is the nearest measure of women's ownership of productive assets. It counts firms with at least one female owner, which says nothing about the size of the stake or about control, and it covers formal firms only. It therefore omits the informal farms, household enterprises and market trades in which most women in low-income countries work. The series on women's participation in household decisions measures a different thing again, namely the share of married women with a say in health care, large purchases and family visits; it is available for only 70 countries, a coverage the bench's results do not otherwise cite. Taken together, the series give pieces of an answer, but none gives the share of women who own land or a dwelling in their own name.

This gap in evidence matters for policy. Land is the main asset of rural households in much of the world, and secure title is associated with greater bargaining power, willingness to invest and access to credit as collateral. Reform of inheritance law, joint titling of land and registration drives are the main policy instruments, and without a global series their effect cannot be tracked against the target. The account data show that women's access to the payment system is improving; they do not show whether that improvement extends to the assets on which women's economic independence ultimately rests.

On the evidence available, the picture for 2030 is mixed. Account ownership is rising for both sexes and the world gap is narrowing, yet the gap is widest in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and it widened in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa between 2017 and the latest year, which are the places where women have the least access to formal economic life. A target of universal ownership by 2030 will not be met worldwide, given that the world figure stood at 76.6% in 2024 and that so many countries show slow progress or decline. A target of equal ownership is a more realistic aim in middle-income and high-income economies, and a distant one elsewhere.

w-c05-7-2.text:
### The global share of trained primary teachers has risen only slowly

The world share of primary school teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and at 82.2% in 2024, a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030, and the indicator used here reads that as a share of 100%. Against that reading, roughly one primary teacher in five worldwide still lacks the minimum organised training required in the country where they teach. The trend calculation gives a world ratio of 0.15 against the pace needed, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Continuing the 2015 to 2024 slope would bring the world to 83.4% in 2030.

The measure needs careful reading. The indicator counts teachers who have received the minimum organised training, whether before or during service, that a given country requires. That minimum is set nationally and differs widely. A teacher counted as trained in one system might not meet the standard of another, and a share of 100% in one country does not imply equal preparation in the classroom. Nor does the indicator capture the quality of the training, the subject knowledge of teachers, or whether they remain in post. The figure is therefore a floor on qualification, not a measure of teaching quality. Readings of the target also vary: some take 4.c to mean full national qualification, others a substantial rise from a baseline, and the data cannot settle between them.

Coverage adds a second caution. The 2024 world value rests on the latest reporting of each economy, and only 13 countries reported in 2025, so the most recent year says little. Several regional values end in 2022, and the upper middle income group has a single value, for 2022, at 80.7%, which allows no change to be read. Late reporting may be more common where systems are weaker, but the results do not test this.

The section's guiding question also asks whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling. The bench returned no result for that ratio, so the question cannot be answered from the evidence held here. Series on teacher numbers exist for primary and secondary levels, but a count of teachers without matching enrolment does not give a ratio. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is likewise not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings, safety or inclusion. The evidence speaks to the training of teachers, not to class size or the learning environment.

The slow world movement matters for 2030 because training is a precondition for much else in the chapter, from completion and learning to pre-primary provision. A world share that rises by under two points in nine years, spanning the disruption of 2020 and the years after it, leaves the target far out of reach on the present slope. The results do not show why the share has stalled; one possible explanation is that recruitment has outpaced training in some systems, but this remains a conjecture that the series cannot test. The regional parts that follow show where gains and losses lie.

### Regions and income groups differ by more than twenty points

The regional picture in 2024 is one of wide separation. North America stands at 97.9% of primary teachers trained, South Asia at 87.7%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 81.8% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 80.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa, whose latest reading is 2022 rather than 2024, stands at 68.8%. The gap between the best and the weakest of these regions is therefore close to thirty percentage points. Readings from different years are not strictly comparable, and the Sub-Saharan figure may understate or overstate the position in 2024.

Income groups show a similar pattern. Low income countries stand at 69.2% in 2022, close to the Sub-Saharan level, which is expected because most low income countries lie in that region. Upper middle income countries have only a 2022 reading, 80.7%, so no change over the period can be given for that group. Training here means the minimum organised preparation required by each country, so the percentages measure compliance with national standards and not a common level of skill. A country with a demanding standard can score lower than one with a modest standard, and comparisons across regions should be read with that in mind.

The spread among countries, weighted by population, is modest in absolute terms. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.094 in 2015, fell to 0.073 in 2020 and rose to 0.097 in 2024, ending slightly above its starting level. The Theil index fell from 0.026 in 2015 to 0.011 in 2020. In that decomposition the share lying between regions was 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020. About half of the inequality among countries is therefore a difference between regions, and the other half lies among countries within the same region. Policies aimed at a single region would address only part of the gap.

These comparisons carry a caveat about coverage. Countries reporting numbered 85 in 2015 and 93 in 2020, but only 79 in 2024. The Theil index and its regional decomposition are missing for 2024, so the latest year cannot be set against the earlier ones on that measure. A change in the number of reporting countries can alter the Gini by changing who is counted, and the rise to 0.097 may reflect that as much as any real divergence; the series cannot separate the two. Reporting for 2025 is thinner still, with 13 countries. For 2030 the implication is that monitoring of Target 4.c is weakest in the years that matter most for judging it.

### Gains in South Asia contrast with declines in richer regions

South Asia recorded the largest regional gain in the share of trained primary teachers. The share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly fifteen percentage points in nine years. The region moved from below the world average of 80.4% in 2015 to above the world level of 82.2% in 2024. Its trend is the only regional one classed as on track, with an expected 99.3% in 2030 if the rate of change continued. Lower middle income countries, a group that includes several South Asian economies, rose more modestly, from 76.4% in 2015 to 83.3% in 2024, and their expected value for 2030 is 88.2%. The data do not show which measures lay behind the South Asian rise. A change in how a country defines the minimum training required would produce the same movement as a real improvement in preparation, so the gain should be read as a reported change in the share, not as proof of better teaching.

The richer regions moved in the opposite direction. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020, the last year for which the regional reading is given here. High income countries fell from 95.9% in 2015 to 92.1% in 2024, and North America slipped from 99.3% to 97.9% over the same period. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 82.7% to 81.8%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan declined from 83.9% to 80.5%. These falls are small beside the South Asian gain, but they run against the direction of Target 4.c, and the trend tool classes all of these regions as regressing. The results do not explain them. Teacher shortages that lead systems to hire staff before they complete a full programme are one possible cause, and changes in national definitions or reporting are another; neither can be tested with these series.

Across countries, the pattern is one of catching up. A convergence test over 48 countries between 2015 and 2024 gives a coefficient of -0.071 (p below 0.001) with an R2 of 0.342, which means that countries starting from lower shares of trained teachers tended to gain faster than those starting higher. The dispersion of the shares narrowed only slightly: the coefficient of variation moved from 0.165 in 2015 to 0.155 in 2024. Convergence is therefore real but slow, and about a third of the variation in country changes is accounted for by the starting level alone. The test covers only the 48 countries with readings at both ends of the period, so it describes the reporting countries and not the world, and the systems with the sparsest records may be underrepresented.

The size of the teaching workforce does not appear to explain the changes. The rank correlation between changes in the share of trained primary teachers and changes in the number of primary teachers across the same 48 countries is -0.095, and the correlation between 2024 levels is 0.168. Both are weak. Expanding the workforce therefore did not visibly coincide with a higher trained share, and countries that added the most teachers were no more likely to see that share rise. This is a cautionary finding for Target 4.c, which speaks of qualified teachers and not of teachers alone. The correlations are descriptive and say nothing about the mechanism.

The period since 2015 and the years after 2020 cannot be read cleanly from these series. Several regional readings end in 2020 or 2022, and the school closures of 2020 and 2021 disrupted the collection of statistics as well as schooling. A gap in reporting may conceal a change that has not yet been measured. For 2030, the lesson of this part is that large gains are recorded where the share rose fast, as in South Asia, but that they are not general, and that richer regions with falling shares cannot assume the levels of 2015 will return unaided. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings or learning environments.

### Most countries are not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

The country counts show that the 2030 picture is mixed. In primary education, 64 of the 129 countries assessed, holding 65.9% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have already met the target of a fully trained teaching force. This is a large share of people but not of countries, because several populous countries are among those advancing. Against it stand 36 countries with 26.3% of the assessed population whose trained share is falling rather than rising. A further 13 countries, with 2.4% of the population, show marginal progress that would need to speed up considerably, 12 show moderate progress that still needs acceleration, and 4 are stagnant. Together the 29 countries that are neither on track nor regressing amount to about a fifth of those assessed, but the largest two groups are the on-track countries and the regressing ones, so the pattern is divided at its poles.

Secondary education tells a similar story with less coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 hold 61.5% of the population and are on track or have met the target, while 36 hold 27.6% and are regressing. Fourteen countries with 7.7% of the population show marginal progress, 10 show moderate progress and 7 are stagnant. The share of people living in regressing countries is slightly higher at secondary level than at primary level, and the share living in on-track countries is slightly lower. Fewer countries report secondary data, so the secondary result rests on a thinner base and is the less certain of the two.

The regression count needs careful reading. A falling trained share does not necessarily mean that teaching has worsened. One possible explanation is that systems expanding quickly may recruit teachers faster than they can certify them; another is that a country raising its minimum standard may see teachers once counted as trained fall below the new bar. Both are conjectures drawn from general experience, and the data given here cannot separate them.

The same feature complicates the target itself. Target 4.c speaks of qualified teachers, and the indicator measures minimum organised training, pre-service or in-service, as defined nationally. A share of 100% therefore does not mean equal preparation across countries, and the target can be read as a share trained to national standards, a share trained to an international standard, or a growth in the absolute supply of teachers. The assessment here uses the first reading, since it is the only one the series allows.

Two parts of the section's question remain unanswered by the data examined. No pupil-teacher ratio series was assessed, so whether ratios are falling cannot be stated. Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive school facilities, was not assessed either, because none of the series on the shelf for this section measures it.

For 2030, the world trend implies that the target will be missed. The projected world share of trained primary teachers is 83.4%, with a trend ratio of 0.15, which falls in the class of marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 72.0% and low income countries at 73.2%, so the groups starting furthest behind are expected to remain furthest behind. South Asia, projected at 99.3%, is the one region on course. The regions that are regressing are mostly those that began from higher levels, such as Europe and Central Asia at a projected 86.9% and high income countries at 89.7%. Their decline lowers the world figure and shows that a high starting point is no guarantee of progress.

The inequality measures give a final caution. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the trained share was 0.09 in 2015, 0.07 in 2020 and 0.10 in 2024. Differences narrowed up to 2020 and then widened again, though the 2024 reading covers 79 countries against 93 in 2020, so the comparison is imperfect and the cause of the widening cannot be read from these results.

The findings point to the following proposals.
