w-c04-2-2.text:
### The global picture: most countries are on course, the world is not

Target 3.2 sets two thresholds that every country is asked to reach by 2030: neonatal mortality of at most 12.0 per 1,000 live births, and under-five mortality of at most 25.0 per 1,000 live births. The target is worded as an aspiration for each country, not for the world as a whole. It therefore asks a different question from a global average, and the two readings must be kept apart when the evidence is assessed.

The direct answer to how many countries have reached the thresholds is that the data cannot give a single count. The classification used here merges countries that have met a threshold with countries projected to meet it, so it states how many are on track or have met the target, not how many have already arrived. On that combined reading, 130 of 196 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 of 196 are on track or have met the under-five threshold.

The world averages remain above both thresholds. The global neonatal mortality rate fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024, still above the threshold of 12.0. The global under-five mortality rate fell from 42.9 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024, against a threshold of 25.0. Over nine years the neonatal rate fell by 2.2 points and the under-five rate by 5.5 points. Both series cover all 196 countries reporting in 2024, so the averages are not distorted by missing reporters.

The country classification gives a more favourable picture. In each case the on-track class is a clear majority of countries, around two thirds or more. The population shares are close to the country counts: the 130 countries hold 72.4% of the population assessed for neonatal mortality, and the 135 countries hold 74.7% for under-five mortality. A reader may therefore ask how most countries, holding about three quarters of the world's people, can be on course while the world average stays above both lines.

The answer lies in what each figure measures. A count of countries gives every country equal weight, whether it is small or large. A population share weights each country by its number of inhabitants. A world average is weighted differently again: it is dominated by the number of live births, so it reflects where children are born, not where the general population lives. Countries with high birth rates contribute most births, and they are disproportionately those with the highest mortality. The world average is therefore pulled upward by a minority of countries with very high mortality and large numbers of births.

A second distinction concerns the phrase on track. The classification compares each country's recent trend with the path needed to reach the threshold by 2030. A country that is on track has not necessarily reached the threshold; it is projected to do so if its pace holds, and the projection can fail if progress slows. The threshold itself can also be read in more than one way: the target says all countries should aim for at least as low as the stated values, so a country already far below them has no further obligation under the wording, though its rate may still fall.

The remaining countries show why the world average lags. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Four are stagnating and 9 are regressing. These 66 countries hold about 27.5% of the population assessed, a smaller share than the on-track group but one that includes many births. For under-five mortality, 39 countries need acceleration, 15 need significant acceleration, 3 are stagnating and 4 are regressing. The 3 stagnating countries hold 4.9% of the population assessed, far more than their count suggests, which shows that a few populous countries can matter greatly.

The gap between the two readings matters for policy. A statement that most countries are on course is true and encouraging, but it can mislead if it is taken to mean that the goal is within reach for children worldwide. The children who remain at risk are concentrated in the countries furthest from the thresholds, and the world average registers their number. The sections that follow therefore set the counts beside regional and income-group levels, so that the distribution of the shortfall is visible.

### Counting countries: how many have met or are on track for each threshold

The trend classification covers all 196 countries for both indicators, and it gives the plainest count of how many have reached, or are heading for, each threshold. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 target, and they hold 72.4% of the population of the countries assessed. For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met the 25.0 per 1,000 target, with 74.7% of that population. The under-five threshold is therefore the more widely met of the two, by five countries and by 2.3 percentage points of population, although the gap is small.

The class labelled on track or target met joins two different situations. A country that crossed the threshold years ago and a country that is merely on course to cross it by 2030 are counted together. The classification does not separate them, and the data given here cannot say how many of the 130 and the 135 have already arrived. A further count of countries whose latest value lies at or below each threshold would answer the question directly. Until it is made, the figures describe the direction of travel rather than the number of countries that have finished the work. The distinction matters because countries already below the threshold need only hold their position, while those merely on course remain exposed to any slowdown.

Below the leading class, the two indicators diverge in a telling way. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Together these 53 countries hold 19.7% of the population, from shares of 7.8% and 11.9%. For under-five mortality the order is reversed: 39 countries are in the moderate class, with 16.1% of the population, and only 15 are in the marginal class, with 4.0%. Many countries therefore sit closer to the under-five threshold than to the neonatal one. This agrees with the established pattern that deaths in the first 28 days fall more slowly than deaths later in childhood. Infections, malnutrition and malaria respond to vaccines, nets and treatment, whereas newborn deaths depend on the quality of care around birth, on preterm complications and on skilled attendance, which take longer to build.

The worst classes are small in country count but not in consequence. Four countries stagnate on neonatal mortality, holding 2.1% of the population, and nine regress, holding 5.7%. Together, the countries outside the on-track and moderate classes for neonatal mortality hold 27.5% of the population if the stagnating and regressing groups are added to the marginal one. For under-five mortality, three countries stagnate, holding 4.9%, and four regress, holding only 0.3%. The three stagnating countries on the under-five indicator are populous: they hold 4.9% of the population between them, about 1.6% each, whereas the 39 moderate countries hold 16.1% between them, about 0.4% each. By contrast, the four regressing countries are small. Regression usually accompanies conflict, state collapse or the breakdown of health services, and a small population share does not make it less serious for the children living there.

The population weights also temper the country counts. Neonatal on-track countries are 66.3% of the 196 assessed, yet they hold 72.4% of the population, so the larger countries are slightly more likely to be on course. The same holds for under-five mortality, at 68.9% of countries and 74.7% of population. Even so, about a quarter of the world's people live in countries that are not on course for each threshold. Since the target is written for every country, those countries decide whether the goal is met in the sense the text intends.

The classification carries the usual caution about reading a trend as a forecast. It extrapolates past rates of change to 2030, and the years after 2020 were disturbed by disruption to services and by uncertain estimates in places with weak registration. A country may be assigned a class on a series that is largely modelled rather than counted. The counts should thus be read as a guide to where acceleration is needed, not as a guarantee of where the thresholds will be met.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of seven

Regional neonatal mortality in 2024 ranged from 3.6 per 1,000 live births in North America and 4.1 in Europe & Central Asia to 22.7 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan and 26.6 in Sub-Saharan Africa. The ratio between the highest and lowest regional neonatal rates is 7.39. Under-five mortality shows a wider spread, from 6.4 in North America to 71.2 in Sub-Saharan Africa, a ratio of 11.12. The heading's factor of seven therefore describes the neonatal gap; the under-five gap is closer to eleven. Neonatal deaths make up a larger share of child deaths where overall mortality is low, because the causes that remain there (prematurity, birth complications, congenital conditions) fall last. Where mortality is high, infections, malnutrition and malaria continue to claim children after the first month, and the under-five gap widens accordingly.

Income groups show the same ordering. Low-income countries recorded 24.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024 and 68.8 under-five deaths. High-income countries recorded 2.8 and 5.1. Upper middle income countries, at 6.8 and 13.1, sit well inside both thresholds. Lower middle income countries, at 21.6 and 43.8, lie outside both. The income gradient is steep because the interventions that save newborns and young children depend on health-system capacity: skilled attendance at birth, emergency obstetric care, neonatal care units, vaccination, and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria. These need financing and trained staff that low-income systems have found hard to sustain.

The trend classification separates regions that will reach the thresholds from those that will not. East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, and the high income and upper middle income groups are on track or have met both targets. East Asia & Pacific reached 6.7 neonatal and 13.2 under-five in 2024, and Latin America & Caribbean 8.3 and 15.4, so each is already below both thresholds. The expected 2030 neonatal values are lower still, at 5.8 for East Asia & Pacific and 7.3 for Latin America & Caribbean. For these regions the target is no longer a constraint, and the policy question becomes one of equity within countries, which regional averages conceal.

South Asia is the clearest case of rapid change. Its neonatal rate fell from 25.4 in 2015 to 16.6 in 2024, and its under-five rate from 42.6 to 26.8. The pace of decline in the under-five rate, -0.0502 a year, is the fastest of any region, and the trend ratio of 1.30 means the pace exceeds what the target requires. The expected 2030 values are 12.5 neonatal and 19.7 under-five. The neonatal ratio of 0.96 is just short of the pace needed, and the expected value sits marginally above 12.0, yet the classification still counts South Asia as on track.

The regions and groups that fall short are those where mortality is highest. Low-income countries cut under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8 per 1,000 between 2015 and 2024, at a rate of -0.0231 a year. At that pace the expected 2030 value is 59.8, far above 25.0, and the trend ratio of 0.42 is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The neonatal record is weaker: 28.1 fell to 24.9, an annual rate of -0.0133, with an expected 2030 value of 23.0 against a threshold of 12.0 and a ratio of 0.32. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same pattern, with an expected 2030 under-five rate of 63.3 and a neonatal rate of 25.0. Neonatal mortality is the harder problem, since it falls more slowly than under-five mortality when health systems are weak, and the share of child deaths occurring in the first month rises as other causes recede.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan group has a mixed profile. Its under-five rate, 36.4 in 2024, is classed as moderate progress needing acceleration, with an expected 2030 value of 31.1. Its neonatal rate, 22.7, is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 20.3. The group combines countries with low mortality and countries in prolonged conflict, so the regional figure conceals wide internal differences and describes no single country in it.

The lower middle income group needs a caution. Its under-five rate fell from 55.3 to 43.8 and its neonatal rate from 26.9 to 21.6, which are real gains, and both are classed as moderate progress, with trend ratios of 0.59 and 0.55. The expected 2030 values of 37.5 and 18.7 stay above both thresholds. The trend output for this group, and for some Sub-Saharan Africa rows, was truncated, so only the numbers and classifications shown above can be relied upon.

The implication for 2030 is that regional averages mask a concentrated problem. The thresholds are met or within reach across most of the world, but the regions furthest away are those with the largest numbers of births and the weakest health systems. The pace held since 2015 will not close the gap without a marked change in Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group.

### What changed since 2015, and why the pace differs

Between 2015 and 2024 every region and income group reduced both rates, but the pace varied widely. South Asia fell fastest. Its neonatal mortality went from 25.4 to 16.6 per 1,000 live births, and its under-five mortality from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rates of change, which the trend tool expresses as a proportional rate, were -0.0462 for neonatal and -0.0502 for under-five mortality. That is more than three times the pace of the world as a whole, at -0.0133 and -0.0151. Sub-Saharan Africa moved slowest on the neonatal measure, from 29.2 to 26.6, a rate of -0.0103. Its under-five rate, from 85.0 to 71.2, fell at -0.0195, which is faster than its neonatal rate but still leaves it far from the threshold.

The pattern across income groups is similar. Low-income countries reduced neonatal mortality from 28.1 to 24.9, a rate of -0.0133, and under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8, a rate of -0.0231. Lower-middle-income countries did better on both, with neonatal mortality falling from 26.9 to 21.6 (-0.0241) and under-five mortality from 55.3 to 43.8 (-0.0256). East Asia & Pacific, already at lower levels, still reduced under-five mortality from 16.6 to 13.2, a rate of -0.0251. High-income countries and North America moved slowly, at -0.0142 and -0.0034 for under-five mortality, but this is expected near a floor, where each further death averted is harder to achieve.

A consistent feature is that neonatal deaths fall more slowly than under-five deaths. For the world, the neonatal rate went from 19.4 to 17.2 while the under-five rate went from 42.9 to 37.4. In Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group the neonatal rate declined at roughly half to three-fifths of the pace of the under-five rate. The proportional rates for the world confirm this: -0.0133 against -0.0151. The share of deaths in the first 28 days therefore rises as overall child mortality falls. A well-established explanation is that deaths after the first month are mostly caused by infections, malnutrition and malaria, which respond to vaccination, sanitation, nutrition programmes and basic treatment. Neonatal deaths come largely from prematurity, birth complications and neonatal infection. These require skilled attendance at birth, functioning referral systems and specialised newborn care, all of which depend on stronger health systems and take longer to build.

The differences in pace must be treated cautiously. The indicators measure outcomes, not interventions, and nothing in these series shows which policies produced the faster falls in South Asia or the slower ones in Sub-Saharan Africa. Plausible hypotheses include the expansion of facility births and cash transfers linked to institutional delivery in South Asia, and the heavier burden of conflict, fragility and weak health financing in low-income countries. These remain hypotheses, to be tested with the intervention series discussed elsewhere in the chapter. The estimates themselves are modelled from survey and registration data that are sparse in the countries with the highest mortality, so differences of a few thousandths in the annual rate should not be over-read.

The period after 2020 cannot be separated in these series. Both indicators are reported as annual figures to 2024, and the comparison of 2015 with 2024 used here gives no sign of a reversal at the regional level, but it conceals any pause in particular years. Whether the disruption of routine health services in 2020 and 2021 slowed declines, or whether the modelling smooths it out, cannot be answered from the levels used here.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The thresholds will probably be met by most countries by 2030, but not by those that carry the greatest burden. On the trend classification, 130 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 the under-five threshold, out of 196 assessed for each. The countries still short are concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income settings. The regional projections show how far they are from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.0 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2030 against a threshold of 12.0, and 63.3 under-five deaths per 1,000 against 25.0. Low-income countries are expected to reach 23.0 and 59.8 respectively. The world as a whole is expected to reach 15.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000, which is above the threshold, and 34.1 under-five deaths per 1,000, also above it.

Newborn deaths are the harder problem. The under-five rate is falling faster than the neonatal rate in most groupings, so the share of child deaths occurring in the first 28 days is rising. Neonatal deaths depend on skilled care at birth, management of preterm birth and infection, and functioning referral systems, which are costlier to build than the vaccination and treatment campaigns that drove earlier gains. A country can therefore meet the under-five threshold and still miss the neonatal one. Of the countries assessed, 13 stagnate or regress on neonatal mortality (4 stagnating and 9 regressing), and 7 do so on under-five mortality (3 and 4).

Two cautions apply. First, the classification depends on the trend method and on projecting a past rate of change forward. A different period or method could move countries between classes, particularly those near a boundary. Second, the wording 'at least as low as' can be read as a ceiling for each country in 2030, or as a direction of travel for countries already below it. This section uses the first reading, as the classification does. The wording also says nothing about inequality within countries, where national rates hide wide gaps.

Four proposals follow.

proposals: National health ministries and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate resources on skilled birth attendance, newborn care units and referral systems, since these settings are projected far above both thresholds in 2030.

Health ministries and development partners should give first attention to the 13 countries that stagnate or regress on neonatal mortality, with country-specific reviews of service coverage and data quality.

Estimates for countries with weak vital registration rest on models and surveys, and the wording of the target admits more than one reading.

w-c04-3-2.text:
### HIV incidence has fallen by more than a third worldwide

World HIV incidence fell from 0.26 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024. That is a decline of about 38 per cent, which supports the heading's claim of more than a third. The estimates rest on modelled data, with 139 countries reporting in 2024. Coverage is therefore broad but not complete, and the world figure should be read as an aggregate of reporting countries rather than a census.

Tuberculosis moved more slowly. Estimated incidence fell from 150.0 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131.0 in 2024, a decline of about 13 per cent. Unlike the HIV series, the tuberculosis series covers 208 countries in 2024, close to universal. Estimates are recalculated for all years as methods improve, so the 2015 value used here may differ from figures published earlier. The comparison is internally consistent, but it should not be set against older reports without caution.

Malaria runs the other way. Incidence among populations at risk rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, because malaria is not a concern everywhere, and the denominator is the population at risk rather than the whole population. A rise in the rate therefore does not mean that malaria spread to new places. It means that, among those exposed, more people fell ill. Disruption to prevention and care during the pandemic years, resistance to drugs and insecticides, conflict and constrained funding are recognised pressures on malaria control, but the series cannot apportion the rise among them.

Target 3.3 calls for ending the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria by 2030, but it sets no numerical threshold. The phrase can be read as zero incidence, as incidence low enough to cease to be a public health threat, or as a given percentage reduction from a baseline. The trend tool therefore applies no target value for HIV, and its class of on track or target met rests on its own reading of the pace of decline rather than on an official benchmark. On that reading the world's HIV rate of change, a fall of 0.05 per 1,000 a year, is classed as on track. Such a class describes momentum, not arrival at a defined goal.

The contrast between the three diseases matters for 2030. The HIV decline is consistent with sustained investment in treatment and prevention, though the series itself does not show the cause. Tuberculosis has declined at a pace that would leave substantial incidence in 2030. Malaria has moved backwards on the measure used here. Taken together, the global record is one of clear progress against one disease, modest progress against a second and reversal against a third, and the following parts examine where those differences lie.

### Regions and income groups differ most in where the burden lies

The burden of the three diseases is distributed very unevenly, and the pattern differs by disease. For HIV, Sub-Saharan Africa remains the region with the highest incidence, yet it also recorded the largest fall. Incidence there declined from 1.2036 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.5374 in 2024. Low-income countries show a similar movement, from 0.707 to 0.3534, a halving over the nine years. The scale-up of antiretroviral treatment and prevention in the most affected settings is the usual explanation for such falls, though the series themselves do not isolate causes. Latin America and the Caribbean tells a different story. Its incidence moved only from 0.2438 in 2015 to 0.2154 in 2024. By 2024 the region's rate of 0.2154 remains below that of low-income countries (0.3534), though the gap has narrowed because the low-income rate fell much faster. Epidemics concentrated among key populations, often with weaker prevention coverage, tend to respond less quickly than generalised epidemics that attract large international funding.

Two entries in the HIV comparison need care. South Asia is reported at 0.0907 in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries at 0.1783 in 2024, but in each case the tool returns the same value for 2015 and 2024. This reflects missing earlier data for the group aggregate, not stability, and no change over time can be read from those rows. Only the 2024 levels are usable: they indicate that South Asia has the lowest HIV incidence of the regions shown, but not whether it has fallen.

Tuberculosis shows a more divided picture than HIV. The world rate fell from 150 new and relapse cases per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131 in 2024, a decline classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. Beneath that average, regions moved in opposite directions. East Asia and Pacific rose from 140 to 144, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 45 to 51; both are classed as regression. Europe and Central Asia fell from 36 to 22, and South Asia from 233 to 189. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 115 to 110, classed as stagnation. North America held at 3.5 in both years, which is stagnation at a very low level and is not a cause for concern in itself.

Income groups show the same gradient. High-income countries fell from 20 to 12, and upper-middle-income countries from 107 to 92. Low-income countries moved from 229 to 199, and lower-middle-income countries from 241 to 208. Low-income and lower-middle-income groups are classed as moderate progress, needing acceleration. Among the regions with the highest burden, Sub-Saharan Africa, at 205 in 2024 after 285 in 2015 (rate -0.036), and South Asia (rate -0.023) are both classed as on track. Even so, 205 cases per 100,000 remains among the highest rates of any region, so a fast decline does not mean a small burden. The target has no numerical value attached to it in the tool, so the classification relies on a trend rule rather than a stated end point; the target can be read in more than one way, for example as a fixed percentage reduction or as elimination as a public health problem, and the labels should be taken as indicative.

Malaria is the most concentrated of the three. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 232.4935 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 and 229.2614 in 2024, a change too small to count as progress. Low-income countries, which largely overlap with the region, moved from 207.1516 to 206.6892. The world rate rose from 59.0112 to 64.0411, which is consistent with the weight of Sub-Saharan Africa in the population at risk; the series do not show whether disruption to prevention and care after 2020 contributed. The rate in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4.3337 to 9.9708, a signal of resurgence that the available data cannot explain, though conflict, displacement and flooding are well-known drivers elsewhere. South Asia is the exception, falling from 6.3233 to 1.4562, and upper-middle-income countries fell from 2.0345 to 1.6485. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, since malaria is not endemic everywhere, so the denominators are populations at risk rather than whole populations.

### Country trajectories show progress alongside stagnation and regression

Beneath the regional averages, country trajectories diverge sharply, and the divergence differs by disease. Each country was classed by the direction and pace of its incidence series, and each class is reported both as a count of countries and as a share of the population those countries hold. The two measures answer different questions. A count treats a small island state and a populous country alike, and so shows how widespread a pattern is. A population share shows how many people live under it, and so shows where the weight of the epidemic falls.

For HIV, 49 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 49.7% of the population of the 146 countries assessed. Another 4 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration (0.8% of the population) and 12 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration (3.0%). The largest group by count is stagnation, with 60 countries holding 35.7% of the population, and 21 countries, holding 10.8%, are in regression. More than a third of the assessed population lives in countries where HIV incidence has barely moved, and about one in ten lives where it is rising. The world decline already described is therefore carried by roughly half the population, while the remainder has seen little or no benefit. Stagnation is the key finding. It is consistent with a plateau in prevention and treatment in many places, but the classes record only the direction of the series and cannot show why.

Tuberculosis presents a more favourable picture in breadth. Of 203 countries assessed, 123 are on track or have met the target, holding 61.2% of the population. Moderate progress with acceleration needed applies to 18 countries (4.2%), marginal progress to 11 (3.9%), and stagnation to 9 (14.8%). Regression affects 42 countries holding 15.8% of the population. The regressing group is large by count, yet a smaller share of people than the on-track group. Because tuberculosis incidence is estimated from notifications, prevalence surveys and modelling, a rise in some countries can reflect better detection as well as real spread, and the disruption of services during the pandemic years also affected case-finding. The classes cannot separate these causes.

Malaria is assessed in only 85 countries, since the series covers populations at risk and not the whole world. Of these, 36 are on track or have met the target, holding 59.2% of the population. Moderate progress applies to 3 countries (1.4%), marginal progress to 8 (8.0%) and stagnation to 5 (4.0%). Regression covers 33 countries and 27.5% of the population, the highest regressing population share of the three diseases. Malaria control depends on sustained delivery of nets, spraying, diagnostics and treatment, and is vulnerable to funding gaps, conflict, resistance and changes in climate. Where such supply is interrupted, incidence can rise quickly. That more than a quarter of the population in assessed countries lives in regression is a warning for the 2030 horizon, though the data do not identify which of these pressures applies in any one country.

The classification has limits that readers should keep in view. The rule is a trend fitted to a short series, and the period after 2015 is only nine or ten observations. A country with small numbers of cases or a sharp one-off fluctuation can be placed in a class that later years would revise. Modelled estimates are recalculated as methods are refined, so classes may shift between editions. Target 3.3 sets no numerical threshold for these indicators, so the classes judge each country against a decreasing path and not against a fixed value. The population weights also depend on which countries have data, which is why the three diseases cover different numbers of countries and cannot be summed. With these cautions, the common finding is that progress is real but concentrated, while stagnation and regression remain widespread.

### Uneven gains leave the 2030 target at risk and call for focused proposals

The evidence for target 3.3 points to three diseases moving at three different speeds. HIV incidence is falling quickly where it is highest. In Sub-Saharan Africa the trend rate is -0.0857 and the series is classed as on track or target met. Low-income countries, at -0.0742, are classed the same way, and so is the world, at -0.0525. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the regions assessed, with a rate of -0.0137, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. By 2024 the region's incidence of 0.2154 remains below that of low-income countries (0.3534), though the gap has narrowed. If the recent pace holds, the high-burden settings will end 2030 well below their 2015 levels. The target text does not define what ending an epidemic means, so even a continued fall cannot be judged against a fixed threshold.

Tuberculosis shows slower gains. The world trend rate is -0.0149, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. Low-income countries are classed in the same way, at -0.0155, and so are lower middle income countries at -0.0162 and upper middle income countries at -0.0166. These countries carry the largest burden, so slow movement there holds back the global result. High income countries, at -0.0552, and Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0532, are on track, but they start from low incidence and contribute little to the global total. South Asia, at -0.0230, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0359, are the high-burden regions classed as on track. Two regions are moving the wrong way: East Asia and the Pacific, at 0.0031, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.0140, are both classed as regression. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0049, and North America, at 0.0000, are classed as stagnation. The period spans the disruption of 2020, when services for finding and treating cases were interrupted in many countries. The series cannot separate that disruption from longer trends, so a rise in recorded incidence may reflect either real transmission or changes in detection and estimation.

Malaria is the weakest result. World incidence rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 232.5 to 229.3, and low-income countries stayed at about 207, from 207.2 to 206.7. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4.3 to 10.0. South Asia is the clear success, falling from 6.3 to 1.5. Of 85 countries assessed, 36 are on track, holding 59.2 per cent of the assessed population. Another 33 countries are in regression, holding 27.5 per cent. A further 8 show marginal progress, 5 show stagnation and 3 show moderate progress. Incidence is measured per population at risk, so changes in the size of that population affect the rate. The 2030 outlook is therefore favourable for HIV, uncertain for tuberculosis and poor for malaria.

The data show what changed and where, not why. Explaining the falls and rises needs other sources, such as programme coverage, funding, drug and insecticide resistance, conflict and climate. These are not held on the shelf and should not be inferred from the incidence series alone.

w-c06-7-2.text:
### The global gap in internet use by sex

Target 5.b asks for greater use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The bench's results measure one aspect of that aim: the share of women and of men who have used the internet in the previous three months. They do not measure ownership of a mobile phone by sex. The series on mobile cellular subscriptions is counted per 100 people and is not divided by sex, and one person can hold several subscriptions, so it cannot show who owns a handset. The question of a gap in phone ownership therefore cannot be answered here, and the findings below concern internet use alone.

On that measure, the world's women moved a long way in a short time. Female internet use stood at 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and reached 68.2 per cent in 2024. The rise is 16.4 percentage points in five years, a period that includes the pandemic, when schooling, work, public services and social contact moved online and gave households a strong reason to connect.

Male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and reached 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two world figures do not share an end year: the female series is read at 2024 and the male series at 2025, because the latest world value in each result falls in a different year. Subtracting one from the other gives 8.4 percentage points, but that difference mixes a gap between the sexes with a year of growth in male use. It overstates the gap in any single year and should be read as an upper bound, not as a measurement. The world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. A clean comparison requires both series at the same date, and the regional results, where both are read at 2024, allow it in the parts that follow.

The 2019 figures are on a common footing. They show a gap of 4.2 percentage points, with women at 51.8 per cent and men at 56.0 per cent, so that women used the internet at about 0.93 of the male rate. This is a fact about 2019 only and says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed or widened since. Because use rose for both sexes, a gap in percentage points can grow while the ratio improves, so the two measures can point in different directions and each should be stated with its basis.

The figures also carry a caution about coverage. The results are aggregates over the economies that report, and the count of countries reporting in 2025 is only 7 in each result, against 92 in 2019 and 65 in 2024. The 2025 world and income-group values therefore rest on a thin base of direct observation and on estimates for the rest, and the 2024 regional values are better supported. Internet use as defined here also says nothing about the quality of access, the device used, the cost of data or what women do online, all of which bear on empowerment as much as the bare fact of use. The evidence supports rapid gains by women and a shortfall against men in 2019, while the size of the world gap in 2024 stays undetermined.

### Regional differences in the gap

In 2024 the point gap between women's and men's internet use is largest in two regions at a middle level of use and smaller in the region with the lowest use. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women had used the internet in the previous three months, against 67.6 per cent of men, a difference of 12.6 percentage points. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 per cent for women and 69.1 per cent for men, a difference of 12.8 percentage points. In Sub-Saharan Africa the shares were 29.4 per cent and 37.9 per cent, a difference of 8.5 percentage points. The absolute gap there is smaller than in the two regions above, but the level of use is far lower, so the ratio of female to male use is 0.78, against 0.81 in South Asia and 0.81 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Measured by ratio, the three regions are therefore closer together than the point differences suggest, and a low point gap at a low level should not be read as near equality.

South Asia also shows how the gap can move. In 2019 women's use stood at 24.3 per cent and men's at 34.9 per cent, a difference of 10.6 percentage points. By 2024 the gap had widened to 12.8 percentage points, even though women's use more than doubled. Rapid growth in use among both sexes can thus coexist with a larger point difference.

The gap is small where use is nearly universal. In North America 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024, a difference of 0.6 percentage points. In Europe and Central Asia the shares were 90.0 per cent and 91.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean lies between, at 81.3 per cent for women and 82.0 per cent for men. These are regions where mobile networks, affordable devices and high levels of female schooling have long been in place, and where saturation leaves little room for a difference to persist.

East Asia and Pacific shows a reversal. In 2019 women's use, at 67.4 per cent, was slightly above men's, at 66.7 per cent. By 2024 women stood at 85.5 per cent and men at 87.6 per cent, so men had moved ahead by 2.1 percentage points. The regional aggregate hides large differences among its economies, and the data given here do not show which of them drove the change. The result should be read as a shift in the regional average, not as evidence of decline in women's use, which rose by 18.1 percentage points over the period.

Income groups are reported for 2025, when only 7 countries reported these series, so the figures rest on very thin direct observation and probably include estimates; they are indicative only. In low-income countries 18.3 per cent of women used the internet, against 28.6 per cent of men, a difference of 10.3 percentage points. In lower middle income countries the shares were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, a difference of 11.8 percentage points. In high-income countries they were 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The ordering matches the regional one, with the largest point gaps at middle levels, but the evidence is weaker than for the regional figures of 2024.

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, female and male use move closely together: the rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.95 and that of changes is 0.96. Where men gained, women generally gained too, so the gap is tied to a country's overall connectivity and does not behave as a separate trend. This is a statement about association; it does not show why any gap persists.

The regional pattern matters for target 5.b because the gaps that remain are largest in regions where women's use is far from universal. Well-established causes include the cost of devices and data, lower female literacy and schooling, social norms that restrict women's independent use of phones, and concerns over safety and harassment online. These operate with different force in each region, which is why a single global figure conceals as much as it reveals.

### What changed since 2019 and what the data can support

South Asia shows the largest change since 2019. Female internet use there rose from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, more than doubling, while male use rose from 34.9 per cent to 69.1 per cent. The gap in percentage points widened from 10.6 points in 2019 to 12.8 points in 2024. Women gained a great deal in absolute terms, but the distance to men did not close. Sub-Saharan Africa shows a similar pattern at a lower level: women moved from 20.2 per cent to 29.4 per cent, men from 28.6 per cent to 37.9 per cent, so the gap there was 8.4 points in 2019 and 8.5 points in 2024.

The comparison across countries points the same way. For the 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male changes is 0.958, and that between 2024 levels is 0.948. Countries where men's use grew quickly are, almost without exception, those where women's use grew quickly. The finding indicates that expansion of access is largely shared: networks, devices, prices and public policy lift both sexes together, and no group of countries shows women advancing on a separate path. A correlation of this kind does not explain why gaps persist where they do. Differences in income, education, literacy, norms on women's use of devices and the cost of handsets and data all plausibly contribute, and the series cannot separate them.

Income groups are indicative only, because the 2025 values rest on seven reporting countries. In low-income countries, female use reached 18.3 per cent in 2025 against 28.6 per cent for men. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, and in upper-middle-income countries 87.9 per cent and 89.7 per cent. In high-income countries the gap is small, at 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent. The world figures moved from 51.8 per cent for women and 56.0 per cent for men in 2019 to 68.2 per cent for women in 2024 and 76.6 per cent for men in 2025. Those two world values fall in different years, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be read from them and cannot be measured from these results.

The evidence has limits that bear on every figure above. In 2019, 92 countries reported female internet use; in 2024, 65 did; in 2025, only 7. The fall after 2019 coincides with the pandemic years and later reporting delays, and the reason is not stated in the data. The 2025 values for income groups are likely to be revised as more countries submit data. The 54-country comparison is a subset of the 137 countries that have ever reported, and it may differ from the countries that report least. Poorer countries with weaker statistical systems are the ones most likely to be missing, so measured progress may overstate the global picture. The series also defines use over the previous three months and from any device, so it says nothing about who owns a phone, who controls it, or how it is used.

### Implications for target 5.b by 2030 and proposals

Target 5.b carries no numerical threshold and no date-bound level, so it can be read in more than one way. The reading adopted here is a narrowing of the gap between women's and men's internet use, alongside rising levels for women. On that reading the evidence for 2030 is mixed. Levels have risen sharply, but the regional gaps in 2024 remain wide where female use is lowest or at a middle level, and these results cannot show whether the gaps are closing.

The world figures illustrate the limit of the data. Female use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, while male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The male figure refers to a later year than the female one, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. The 2019 pair is on a common year and gives a gap of 4.2 points. The regional figures for 2024 are also on a common year and are the safer basis. In Sub-Saharan Africa female use was 29.4 per cent in 2024 against 37.9 per cent for men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the figures were 55.0 per cent and 67.6 per cent. In South Asia they were 56.3 per cent and 69.1 per cent. Where use is near universal, as in North America, with 94.1 per cent for women and 94.7 per cent for men, the gap is almost gone.

The income-group figures point the same way, but they should be read as indicative, because only 7 countries reported in 2025. Female use reached 18.3 per cent in low-income countries against 28.6 per cent for men, 56.9 per cent against 68.7 per cent in lower middle income countries, and 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent in high income countries. A gap of this kind closes mainly as a whole population connects, and only the nearly saturated groups have reached that point. The data support only the observed gaps; they contain no projection, so whether any region reaches parity by 2030 cannot be stated. Well-established causes of the gaps include the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, social norms on who may own a device, and concerns about safety online.

The country evidence suggests that the gap follows general connectivity rather than departing from it. Across 54 countries, changes in female use from 2019 to 2024 and changes in male use correlate at a Spearman coefficient of 0.958, and 2024 levels at 0.948. Women's use therefore rises where men's rises. Specific barriers to women are not isolated by this evidence, and the correlation is silent on whether gaps are closing within countries.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National statistical offices and the International Telecommunication Union should report internet use by sex for every country on a common reference year, so that world and regional gaps can be measured without mismatched end years.

Ministries responsible for communications, with mobile operators, should target affordability of handsets and data in the regions where female use is lowest, and should report progress by both the point gap and the ratio of female to male use.
The World Bank and national statistical offices should publish sex-disaggregated data on mobile phone ownership, which the present series do not hold, so that target 5.b can be assessed directly.

Female and male internet use end in different years at world and income-group level, only 7 countries reported in 2025, and no projection or population count is available. The data do not show whether gaps are closing within countries or which barriers affect women specifically.

w-c07-4-1.text:
### Water quality is measured mainly through sanitation and ecosystem proxies

Target 6.3 calls for halving the proportion of untreated wastewater, and Target 6.6 for the protection and restoration of water-related ecosystems, including mountains, forests, wetlands, rivers, aquifers and lakes. Neither can be measured directly with the series on the shelf of the World Bank's World Development Indicators. No series on the share of wastewater treated, on ambient water quality in rivers, lakes and aquifers, or on the condition of wetlands is held. Any reading of these two targets is therefore indirect, and the conclusions drawn from it carry less weight than those for drinking water or sanitation access.

Three kinds of proxy are available. Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using a private facility whose excreta are safely disposed of or treated, is the nearest stand-in for Target 6.3, because untreated human waste is among the main sources of pollution in surface and ground water. Terrestrial protected areas and forest area stand in for Target 6.6, since protected catchments and forested slopes shape the quality and regularity of the water that flows from them. Marine protected areas, water stress and the mortality rate attributed to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene supply context. Each is a proxy in the strict sense. Sanitation safely managed at the household says nothing about industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, which Target 6.3 also names. A land area under protection is a legal designation, not a measure of the health of a river or wetland, and forest area records tree cover without distinguishing natural stands from plantations.

The sanitation series is also the thinnest of its kind among the household indicators, though its coverage is stable. Countries reporting numbered 137 in 2000, 146 in 2016, the highest count in the series, and 141 in 2024. The count therefore fell by five countries between 2016 and 2024, a drift that began after 2019 and deepened after 2020, when disruption to household surveys and to national statistical offices was widespread. A total of 146 countries reported in at least one year, so some economies are never covered at all. Regional and income-group figures are modelled aggregates, and they rest on fewer observations in the places where sanitation is weakest. The estimates that follow should be read with that limitation in mind.

### Safely managed sanitation rose from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent between 2015 and 2024

Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using improved facilities that are not shared and from which excreta are safely disposed of, stood at 48.4 per cent of the world population in 2015 and at 58.5 per cent in 2024. The gain of about ten percentage points over nine years is substantial, and the series covers 141 countries reporting in 2024, so the global figure rests on a broad base rather than a handful of observations.

What this proxy says about Target 6.3 is limited, and the limit matters. The indicator follows excreta through the whole chain of containment, emptying, transport and treatment or disposal, so a rise in it means that more households are served by systems that do not leave waste in streets, fields and watercourses. That is a reasonable stand-in for pressure on water quality from human waste. It does not measure the share of wastewater that is treated, nor industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, and it says nothing about the condition of the rivers, lakes and aquifers that receive the discharge. A country may serve its households well and still pollute its waters from other sources. The rise from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent should therefore be read as evidence of progress on one component of Target 6.3, not as a measure of the target.

A second caution concerns the classification of progress. Target 6.3 carries no numeric threshold in the bench's trend tool: it asks for the proportion of untreated wastewater to be halved, a relative aim that cannot be applied to this proxy without an agreed baseline. The classes returned by the trend method, such as on track or target met, are therefore a judgement about the pace of change, set against the tool's own projection to 2030, and not a comparison with a fixed goal. On that basis the world is classed as on track or target met, with an annual rate of change of 0.0213 in the tool's units. Because the method rewards steady movement and not attainment of a stated level, a region can be classed as on track while a large share of its people still lack safe sanitation. The classes are best read together with the levels, which the following parts set out region by region.

The year of the data also bears on interpretation. The series runs to 2024, so it spans both the period after 2015, when the goals were adopted, and the disruption after 2020. The global rate shows no sign of a break in that disruption at the aggregate level, though the annual values behind the aggregates are partly modelled from sparse household surveys and censuses, and a short-lived shock could be smoothed away. For 2030, the figures imply continued gains, yet not universal coverage: at the pace recorded, the world would remain well short of full safe sanitation.

### Regions differ widely, and the gap between them explains most inequality

The contrast between regions is the plainest feature of the series. In 2024 North America stood at 95.4 per cent of its population using safely managed sanitation, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 25.9 per cent. Europe and Central Asia, at 80.2 per cent, and the high-income group, at 84.4 per cent, sit well above the world figure of 58.5 per cent. Between these poles lie East Asia and Pacific at 63.6 per cent, South Asia at 60.1 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 54.4 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 51.2 per cent. A person born in the best-served region is almost four times as likely to use a safely managed service as one born in the worst-served.

The pace of change differs as much as the level. South Asia rose from 40.8 per cent in 2015 to 60.1 per cent in 2024, the largest gain of any region, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 49.0 per cent to 63.6 per cent. Both are classed as on track in the trend analysis, as are the lower-middle-income group, which moved from 38.3 per cent to 51.9 per cent, and the upper-middle-income group, which moved from 49.1 per cent to 62.4 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean advanced more slowly, from 43.2 per cent to 51.2 per cent, and is judged to need acceleration. At the top, North America moved only from 95.2 per cent to 95.4 per cent, and the high-income group from 80.7 per cent to 84.4 per cent, which the analysis reads as stagnation. Europe and Central Asia, at a high level, shows marginal progress. Near-stagnation at a high level is partly a ceiling effect, since the last few points are the costliest to reach, and it does not carry the same concern as stagnation at a low level.

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group show a more troubling pattern. The region rose only from 21.6 per cent to 25.9 per cent, and low-income countries from 21.6 per cent to 26.9 per cent. The trend tool labels both on track, but this reflects the way the rate is read against a target that the tool leaves undefined, not any prospect of universal coverage. At these rates, three quarters of the region's population would still lack safely managed sanitation in 2030. Where a target can be read in more than one way, the label should not be taken as a verdict.

Spread among countries narrowed over the period. The population-weighted Gini coefficient fell from 0.261 across 145 countries in 2015 to 0.208 across 141 countries in 2024, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.484 to 0.382. Differences between regions account for 59.6 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2024, so most of the remaining disparity lies in where a country is located and not in variation within regions. The change in the country set between the two years is a caveat on the comparison. Convergence across 140 countries is weak: the beta coefficient is -0.00364 with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R squared of 0.018, so initial level explains very little of later gains. The narrowing owes more to the large populous gainers in Asia than to a systematic catching up by the poorest.

### Ecosystem indicators show stagnation and regression in many countries

Beyond sanitation, the shelf offers only land-based proxies for the condition of water-related ecosystems, and these show little sign of the protection and restoration that Target 6.6 set for 2020. The classification of country trends for terrestrial protected areas is divided. Of 211 countries assessed, 71 are on track or have met the target, covering 34.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Against that, 54 countries are classed as regressing, and these hold 33.0 per cent of the population. A further 45 stagnate and 27 show only marginal progress. Protected land is a coarse proxy, since a designated area need not contain a wetland or a river headwater, and the series records designation rather than the quality of management. The regression class also needs careful reading, because the shelf sets no numeric target for the indicator and a decline may reflect boundary revisions or reclassification as well as loss of protection.

The sanitation classes, drawn from the same trend tool, show a similar spread. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target and 42 stagnate, while 25 regress. The regressing countries hold 6.8 per cent of the population assessed, a small share but a signal that gains in the global figure are not universal. These classes matter for water quality because untreated excreta remain a leading source of pollution in rivers, lakes and aquifers, so stagnation in sanitation is also stagnation in the protection of freshwater.

Forest area, which regulates flows, filters runoff and shelters headwaters, is stagnant in most regions. East Asia and Pacific moved from 26.98 to 27.26 per cent of land area between 2015 and 2023, and South Asia is classed as stagnating despite a rising rate. The losses are concentrated where pressure on land is greatest. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 47.18 to 46.11 per cent over the same years, and low income countries from 20.98 to 19.86 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa and the lower middle income group are also classed as regressing, and the world as a whole is classed as regressing, at a rate of -0.0011. The drivers are well established: conversion of forest to farmland and pasture, fuel wood collection and infrastructure expansion, set against uneven enforcement of protection.

The central limit is that rivers, wetlands, lakes and aquifers have no series on the shelf. Target 6.6 therefore cannot be fully assessed, and the deadline of 2020 has passed without a measured verdict. What the proxies do show is that no region combines gains in forest, protected land and sanitation, which gives no ground for assuming that unmeasured freshwater ecosystems have improved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Convergence in safely managed sanitation is weak. Across 140 countries between 2015 and 2024 the estimated beta is -0.00364, with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R-squared of 0.018. The negative sign points to a slight tendency for countries with lower starting levels to gain faster, but the relationship is at best marginal by conventional thresholds and explains almost none of the variation between countries. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.549 in 2015 to 0.501 in 2024, a narrowing too small to close the gap between regions before 2030. Current trends therefore leave Sub-Saharan Africa far behind, while the countries already on track continue to advance.

The classification of country trends shows where the burden lies. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target, yet a further 42 are stagnating and 25 are regressing. Countries on track hold 59.6 per cent of the population of those assessed, so the global average is carried largely by a few populous countries. Forest area tells a similar story: the world trend is regression, at a rate of -0.0011, and Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.00636) and low-income countries (-0.00682) lose forest fastest. These are the settings where water-related ecosystems and sanitation are least protected and least measured.

Three proposals follow. First, national statistical offices, the UN custodian agencies and the World Bank should add the share of wastewater treated and the extent of freshwater ecosystems to the core indicator set, so that Targets 6.3 and 6.6 can be read directly rather than through proxies. Second, governments and development financiers should direct sanitation investment to the 42 stagnating and 25 regressing countries, rather than to those already on track. Third, forest-rich countries with the steepest losses, with the support of climate and conservation funds, should protect forests where losses concentrate, since catchment forests regulate water quality and flow. Finally, reports on the goals should state plainly where data are missing, and not fill the gaps with unsupported estimates.

w-c05-2-2.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

The headline figure for children of primary school age who are out of school is a sum of group totals, and it needs to be read with that in mind. Adding the four income groups' counts gives about 87.8 million children in 2025, set against about 87.4 million in 2015. The title rounds this to 88 million. The two totals are almost identical, which means a decade that began with the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals has ended with no reduction in the number of children outside school.

The composition beneath that flat total has changed. Low-income countries counted 30.1 million out-of-school children in 2025, up from 26.0 million in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million over the same period. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. The fall in the lower middle income group offset the rises elsewhere, so the global sum conceals a movement of the burden toward the poorest countries. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest share, about 46.4 million of the total, because they contain very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate.

The figures must not be taken as a global estimate. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, as the results record, while the series itself holds a much wider coverage across its history, 198 countries for the count. A sum built on so few reporters in the latest year depends on which countries happened to report, and the group totals may reflect different country sets in 2015 and 2025. The comparison between the two years is therefore indicative of direction only. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, and those in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count as out of school. Rises in some groups may partly reflect late entry or enrolment in pre-primary classes rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. A total that has not fallen since 2015 implies that the first decade of the goals did not close that gap. The years after 2020 sit in the same data window, and the interruption of schooling during the pandemic, together with conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries, are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up. The available results do not separate these effects, so they cannot be attributed with precision.

For 2030, the implication is that the arithmetic is unfavourable. With the global count unchanged over ten years, ending exclusion in the five years that remain would require a rate of decline that the period to 2025 has not shown. The rates in the following part show where that difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries, roughly ten times the rate. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall steadily as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. A plausible explanation, not tested by these series, is that fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was outrun by the growth in the number of children.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest number of out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. Much of the global stability in the total, noted earlier, reflects this gain being offset by increases elsewhere.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015. This is a rise of 5.6 percentage points, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion deepens as children grow older. Likely reasons, which the data do not test, are that many enter school but few progress, and that costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push adolescents out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, adolescent exclusion was broadly flat or slightly lower. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which 41.7% of lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, but the direction of the small difference depends on national income. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys, so girls are the larger group there. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys. The girls' count therefore rose by about 2.17 million over the decade and the boys' by about 1.90 million, and the gap in low-income countries widened slightly in absolute terms, to the girls' disadvantage.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' exclusion fell faster than boys' there, by about 3.13 million against about 2.44 million. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in these three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

Girls are thus the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, barriers that plausibly fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, may remain active, though these results do not test such causes. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. The sex-disaggregated series draw on 8 countries reporting in 2025, whereas the totals by income group draw on 12, so the two sets should not be compared directly. Part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are plausible pressures after the pandemic, though these are explanations the data do not test and cannot separate.

The country classes show that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are the most numerous, and their 34.4% of the population is close to the 34.9% share that is on track or has met the target.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. The group levels rest on 12 reporting countries in 2025, a small base for four income groups. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents are the weakest point. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, while every other group held steady or improved slightly. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, so that picture rests on thin and uneven coverage. A pattern in which exclusion grows as children pass the end of primary school is consistent with fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and with too few secondary places, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.
