The data do not test causes of exclusion, and do not identify children with disabilities, those in conflict zones or those in the poorest households within countries.

w-c05-5-2.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small and should be read with caution. In the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. The fall is not a loss for girls: it largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, since South Asia moved from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020 and lower middle income countries from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.997 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.997 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.995 in North America and 0.991 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.982. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.970 in 2015 to 0.976 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.956 to 0.958. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.061 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.868 in 2015 and 0.900 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.952 to 0.965. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.018 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.052, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. The data do not show why. One hypothesis, which these series cannot test, is that boys leave school early for paid work in some settings. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.010 to 0.982 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.993.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.122 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 and North America 1.301, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.153, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.128, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.058 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.954 to 1.029. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.794 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.735 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.301 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.992 at primary level in 2020, 0.997 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.038 at tertiary level in 2024, close to parity at the first two levels and above it at the third. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure. The spread is also reported only for 2015, so these data cannot show whether dispersion has narrowed since.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison, and the male series has the same coverage in the shelf's description. In 2025, however, only 11 countries have reported. The count was 110 in 2024, and reporting for the latest year is always incomplete because national statistics reach the international database after a lag. The 2025 figure is therefore a feature of data release, not evidence that countries stopped collecting, but the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is largely a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for them. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and this pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. The data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that remain to the disadvantage of girls are concentrated at the secondary and tertiary levels and in two regions. At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.900 in 2020, up from 0.868 in 2015, and low-income countries stood at 0.819, up from 0.806. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.952 to 0.965 over the same years. Both regions are closing the gap, but at these rates parity by 2030 is uncertain. For Sub-Saharan Africa the tertiary index of 0.794 in 2021 shows that the gap widens at higher levels, and the low-income figure of 0.672 in 2021 is lower still. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.103 in 2015 to 1.122 in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 in 2024 and North America 1.301, while Europe and Central Asia reached 1.153 and high-income countries 1.209. Target 4.5 asks for the elimination of disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, so an index well above 1.00 is a disparity of a different kind. In South Asia the tertiary index crossed parity, from 0.954 to 1.029, and the lower-middle-income group did likewise, from 0.959 to 1.038. The fall in the world primary index, from 0.999 in 2015 to 0.983 in 2020, largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for girls.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024, so recent completion gaps cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, which is too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow, each tied to a finding above. They concern reporting, survey coverage, retention of girls in the lagging regions, and monitoring of boys at tertiary level.

w-c06-5-2.text:
### The indicator and what it measures

Target 5.6 commits governments to universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The principal measure of progress in this section is the share of married or partnered women aged 15 to 49 who make their own informed decisions regarding sexual relations, contraceptive use and reproductive health care. It is compiled by the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Statistics Division, mainly from Demographic and Health Surveys, and reported in the World Bank's World Development Indicators as a percentage of those women.

The indicator is a composite, and its base is women who are married or in a union, not all women of that age. A woman counts as deciding for herself only if she answers yes to all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner if she does not want it; she decides on the use of contraception; and she decides on her own health care. A woman who answers yes to two of the three is not counted. The measure is therefore strict, and its level is bound to be lower than the level for any single component. Unmarried women are left out, so the series describes one part of the female population.

The reading of own decisions is not fixed across surveys. Each component rests on a question put to the respondent, and the wording, the response options and the interpretation of a joint decision with a partner can differ between survey rounds and between countries. A woman who decides jointly with her husband after discussion may be recorded differently from one whose husband decides alone, and cultural norms shape how women describe such arrangements. Answers on refusing sex are also sensitive to the setting of the interview. Differences between countries, or between years in one country, may thus partly reflect measurement and not only a change in women's autonomy.

The retrieved results for this section report how many countries supply the indicator, not the share values themselves. In 2024 the count was 5 countries, and across 2006 to 2024 a total of 81 countries have reported at least once. The share of women who decide for themselves is therefore not stated here for any country or year, and the question this section asks cannot be answered with a figure from these results. The indicator is also not the only evidence the shelf holds on target 5.6. Related series cover a wider set of household decisions, demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods, unmet need for contraception, attitudes towards refusing sex and prenatal care. They measure different things and are cited in the parts that follow only where they help to interpret the composite.

### Thin coverage limits any global picture

Only 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions in 2024, the latest year in the series. The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries but no share values for those five, so the share of women who make their own decisions on health care and contraception cannot be stated for any country or year in this section. No aggregate is published for the indicator in any year, so the World Bank's catalogue gives no regional or world share either. The question is therefore answered only in part: no global figure exists, and the national readings are not in the material available to this part.

The 2024 count rests on the survey calendar rather than on any change in the underlying behaviour. Demographic and Health Surveys are fielded country by country, usually at intervals of several years, and a country appears in a given year only if a survey was completed and processed. A year with few reporting countries is a year in which few surveys were released, not evidence that decision-making has become less common or less measured. The 5 countries of 2024 are an accident of timing, and they are not a sample drawn to represent any region or income group.

For that reason the 2024 levels result supports only a handful of national readings. Each can describe the country it belongs to. None can be averaged into a regional picture, and none should be read as typical of countries with similar incomes or located in the same region. Averaging five values drawn from whichever surveys happened to conclude would mix countries whose populations, laws and health systems differ widely, and would give a number that describes no real population.

The wider record shows how uneven the coverage is. Across all years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. Yet the number reporting in a single year has ranged from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018. Even in the best year, 15 countries is a small part of the 81 that have a measured value at some point, and the set of reporting countries changes from year to year. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years would therefore reflect a change in who reported as much as any change in women's autonomy.

The constraint matters for the 2030 agenda. Target 5.6 is to be judged on whether access and rights are universal, and a measure reported by only 3 to 15 countries in any year cannot show whether the target is being reached. The indicator is also confined to women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in union, and it counts a woman only if she answers yes to all three components: refusing sex, using contraception and seeking health care. Women outside unions, and countries without a recent survey, are absent from the evidence, and the composite cannot separate decisions on health care from decisions on contraception. The thin coverage is itself a finding: monitoring of this target depends on a few countries per year.

### Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data

Reporting by year shows why regions and countries cannot be compared on current data. The number of countries reporting the indicator ranged from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018. Between those years, the count moved among 4 in 2009, 7 in 2010, 12 in 2012, 6 in 2013 and 10 in 2016. Each year's reading therefore describes a different group of countries, and a change in a year's picture may reflect who was surveyed rather than any change in women's lives.

The pattern follows the survey cycle. Demographic and Health Surveys visit a country every few years, and the countries reached in one year are seldom those reached in the next. A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2018 and 2019, cannot be set side by side. Regional groupings fare no better, because a region may be represented by one or two countries in one year and by none in another. Without a published aggregate, no regional average exists to correct for this, and constructing one from such uneven entries would imply a precision the data do not hold.

Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once, yet in 2024 only 5 reported. A country's most recent reading may therefore be several years old, and comparing latest values across countries mixes survey years that may be a decade apart. Over that span, access to services, schooling and social norms can shift, so the gap between two countries' values may be partly a gap in dates.

The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries and no share values, so no country's reading for 2024 is stated here, and the question of the share of women who decide for themselves is unanswered for that year. Differences between countries could be described only where the same survey design and indicator definition apply, since the measure counts a woman only if she decides on all three areas: refusing sex, using contraception and her own health care. The base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so women outside unions are not covered. The 5 countries reporting in 2024 are too few to support any ranking or regional statement, and none is made.

### Reporting has changed little since 2015

Reporting on women's own informed decisions has swung widely since the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, without a trend. In 2015, 5 countries reported the indicator. The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached a peak of 15 in 2018, then fell to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020. It recovered to 7 in 2021, 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023, before dropping to 5 in 2024. Across the years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once.

This pattern follows the survey cycle and not women's circumstances. Household surveys are fielded in a country every few years, and each round is processed and compiled some time afterwards. A year with many reporting countries is one in which many survey rounds happened to be completed and published; a year with few is one in which fewer did. The low count in 2024 is likely to reflect publication lag in part, so that later releases may add countries to recent years. The data do not show this, and it should be treated as an expectation and not a finding.

The count of 4 countries in 2020 coincides with the onset of the pandemic, which interrupted fieldwork in many countries from that year. The count of 4 in 2019 precedes the pandemic, and the series alone cannot separate the effect of disruption from the ordinary variation of survey timing. The recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is consistent with fieldwork resuming, but it too is a count of surveys and not a measure of change.

The consequence is that no before-and-after comparison around 2015 or 2020 can be drawn from this series. Each year's group of reporting countries differs from the last, so a rise or fall in any average would reflect who was surveyed. The retrieved results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, so a trend in women's decision-making since 2015 cannot be stated from these data, and the 2030 horizon cannot be assessed against a baseline that does not exist in comparable form.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 5.6 cannot be judged as on track or off track with the data now held. The indicator on women's own informed decisions has no aggregate in any year, and the number of countries reporting in a given year has swung between 3 in 2008 and 15 in 2018. Only 5 countries reported in 2024, the latest year. Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. The retrieved results give the count of reporting countries and no share values, so the question of what share of women make their own decisions has no figure to answer it here. A trend needs the same countries measured at intervals, and the shelf does not offer that. Whether a country has moved towards 2030 therefore cannot be told from a comparison of one year's reporters with another's.

The reading of the target adds a second difficulty. Target 5.6 speaks of universal access and of reproductive rights, which no single survey question captures. The indicator requires a woman to answer yes to all three components: refusing sex, choosing contraception and deciding on her own health care. Its base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so unmarried women and adolescents fall outside it. A rise or fall in the share could reflect a change in any of the three components, and the series alone does not say which.

The proposals below follow from these findings. They aim to make the next five years of reporting usable for judging the target, since the period to 2030 is short and surveys are slow to field.

proposals: National statistical offices and the agencies that compile the indicator should publish the five 2024 country values with survey years, so that the share of women deciding for themselves can be stated at least for those countries.

Survey sponsors should schedule repeat surveys in countries that have already reported, so that the same countries are measured at intervals before 2030 and change can be separated from changes in who reports.
Compilers should publish the three components (refusing sex, choosing contraception, deciding on health care) separately, so that a movement in the composite can be traced to its source.
Statistical offices and funders should extend measurement to unmarried women and adolescents, who fall outside the present base.

w-c05-1-2.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The world primary completion rate stood at 87.9% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 88.0% in 2024. The gain across nine years is about 0.2 percentage points, set against a target of 100.0% by 2030. At this pace the world does not approach universal completion. The period spans the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the school closures of 2020 and the uneven recovery since, and the aggregate shows little trace of any of them: neither a surge after 2015 nor a visible collapse after 2020. A flat global line can conceal movement in both directions, and the regional and income-group figures show that it does.

The indicator needs careful reading. Primary completion here is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of primary education: new entrants in the last grade, whatever their age, divided by the population at the entrance age for that grade. Because late entrants and early starters are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100, and it is not the share of a birth cohort that finishes primary school. The target can be read in more than one way: as universal completion, meaning every child finishes, or as a rate of 100 or more, which the ratio can reach while some children remain outside school. The trend assessment in this chapter takes the second, arithmetical reading, with 100.0 as the threshold.

The movement beneath the flat world line is large in places. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% to 83.7%, a gain of nearly ten points. East Asia and Pacific rose from 94.1% to 95.4% by 2022, its latest value. Sub-Saharan Africa moved only from 66.3% to 68.9%, and low-income countries from 60.5% in 2015 to 62.9% in 2023, so the poorest groups remain furthest from the target and gained little. Against these gains, South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 98.4% to 96.5%, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% by 2023. Lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% and then 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% by 2023 and high income countries stayed near 98.1% and 97.8%. Gains in one region are therefore offset by losses in others, which is why the world figure does not move.

Under the arithmetical reading, the country classification is sobering. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, holding 19.6% of the assessed population. A further 14 show moderate progress, with 13.0% of the population, and 14 show marginal progress, with 5.7%. Three stagnate, with 0.5%. Regression is the largest class: 92 countries, holding 61.3% of the population. The results do not show how much of this reflects real deterioration. Some of it may arise where ratios above 100 drift back towards 100 as late entry and repetition decline, which the classification counts as movement away from the target. The count alone cannot separate the two.

Reporting is a further limit. Only 11 countries had reported a value for 2025 at the time of access, so the most recent global figure rests on 2024. The finding of near stagnation is firm for the period to 2024 but says little about the last years before the target date.

### Lower secondary completion shows slow, uneven gains

The world lower secondary completion rate stood at 74.8% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 77.9% in 2024. The gain across nine years is about 3.1 percentage points, set against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The measure is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education, so it counts new entrants in that grade regardless of age. A ratio can therefore exceed 100.0%, and the rate indicates intake to the last grade rather than certified completion.

Set beside primary completion, which was 88.0% in 2024, the figure for lower secondary shows how much is lost between the two cycles. The gap is about 10 percentage points. Because the indicator is a ratio and not a count of a single cohort, this gap should not be converted into a number of adolescents. Established research on education systems points to rising costs, scarcer and more distant schools, and the demands of household labour after primary school, but the series themselves do not isolate these causes.

The regional series show where the shortfall lies. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 42.3% in 2015 and 44.4% in 2023, a rise of about 2.0 percentage points in eight years, so the region remains far below the world rate. Low-income countries as a group moved from 37.0% in 2015 to 38.6% in 2023, and are the group furthest from the target. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 57.1% to 66.7% in 2024, a faster pace than most regions, with a trend ratio of 0.39 and a class of marginal progress, yet it remains well below the world rate. South Asia advanced from 83.7% to 86.6%.

The regions already close to the target have moved little or have arrived. East Asia and Pacific rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, the largest gain among the regional aggregates, with a trend ratio of 1.39 and the class on track. It is the main reason the world rate has risen. Europe and Central Asia moved from 90.9% to 91.9%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 81.3% to 81.5%, which the trend tool classes as stagnation. By income group, upper-middle-income countries rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 93.0% in 2023, high-income countries from 94.0% to 95.6% in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries from 71.0% to 73.7%. The world gain is therefore driven by East Asia and the upper-middle-income group, while low-income countries have closed little of the distance.

Several series do not cover the full period. The North American series begins in 2016, not 2015, at 104.3%, and ends in 2023 at 100.8%. Both values lie above 100.0% because the ratio counts older entrants, so the decline does not indicate a fall below universal completion. The Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income and upper-middle-income series end in 2023, one year before the world and several other groups, so comparisons across aggregates mix periods of eight and nine years. Only 11 countries reported a value for 2025, too few to support any statement about that year. Aggregates for the latest years rest on a changing set of reporting countries, and a change of a point or two should not be read as firm.

The World Bank series cannot say how much of the post-2015 pattern reflects the school closures of 2020, since the aggregates show no break that can be attributed to them. Projected to 2030 at the observed pace, the world rate reaches about 80.0%, which is far short of the target. Sub-Saharan Africa reaches about 46.2% and low-income countries about 40.1%, while East Asia and Pacific passes 100.0% on the same method. The country classes for this indicator are set out in the section on divergence, and are not repeated here.

### Regions and countries diverge sharply

Regional averages conceal a wide spread in how far children travel through school. In Sub-Saharan Africa the primary completion rate was 68.9% of the relevant age group in 2024, up from 66.3% in 2015. Lower secondary completion in the same region was 44.4% in 2023, up from 42.3% in 2015. Fewer than half of the children in the region complete the lower secondary stage, and a gain of about two points in eight years leaves the region far from the target of 100.0%. The trend tool classes the region as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected value of 46.2% in 2030. Low-income countries are further from the target than any region: 62.9% at primary in 2023 and 38.6% at lower secondary in 2023, up from 37.0% in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 40.1% at lower secondary.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region shows the largest gain in primary completion, from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly ten points. At lower secondary the region rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. The tool nonetheless classes it as marginal progress at lower secondary, with an expected 66.7% rising to 73.9% in 2030, still well short of 100.0%. Only East Asia and Pacific has a higher lower secondary ratio to target among the regions classed on track, and the Middle East region's own ratio is 0.39. The region's figures combine countries in very different circumstances, and measurement may be uncertain where conflict and displacement are present. The gain should be read as a regional average, not as a uniform improvement.

East Asia and Pacific is the clearest success. Lower secondary completion rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, and the region is classed as on track, with an expected 105.4% in 2030. A value above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio, so it does not signal that every child completes on time. Primary completion in the region reached 95.4% in 2022, from 94.1% in 2015. Upper middle income countries are also classed as on track at lower secondary, rising from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023, while lower middle income countries moved from 71.0% to 73.7% in 2024 and are classed as marginal progress. At primary level lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% in 2023.

Several regions went backwards at primary level. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 98.4% in 2015 to 96.5% in 2024. South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4% over the same years, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. These regions began near universal completion, so the declines differ in kind from the shortfalls in Africa. The data do not show why they fell; the 2020 disruption and changes in enrolment and repetition are possible contributors, and because the measure counts new entrants in the last grade, shifts in repetition or age at entry can move it without any change in the number of children finishing. Primary completion in Europe and Central Asia rose from 97.2% to 98.1%. At lower secondary, Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as stagnant, from 81.3% in 2015 to 81.5% in 2024, and South Asia improved from 83.7% to 86.6%. North America is classed as on track at lower secondary although its ratio, 100.8% in 2023, fell from 104.3% in 2016, because the series already sits above the target.

Country classes confirm that the global average hides a divide. Of 173 countries assessed on primary completion, 50 are on track or have met the target, and 92 are in regression, holding 61.3% of the classed population. The size of the regression class should be read with care: the tool does not separate countries that fell from near-universal levels from those that fell from low ones. At lower secondary 49 countries are on track and 66 are in regression, holding 21.1% of the classed population, while the 32 countries in marginal progress hold 38.4%. Many people therefore live in countries advancing too slowly to arrive by 2030.

### Learning lags behind completion, and the data are thin

Completion measures how many children reach the last grade; it does not show what they have learned. The indicator of pupils below the minimum reading proficiency level at the end of primary schooling addresses that gap, and it shows a worse picture. Worldwide, 45.9% of pupils at the end of primary were below the minimum level in 2015, and 49.6% in 2019. Set beside a world primary completion rate of 88.0% in 2024, the figures mean that a large share of children who finish primary school cannot yet read a simple text with fluency. Completion without learning does not deliver the quality that Target 4.1 requires. The series covers reading at the end of primary only. Minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not measured by any series on the shelf, so that part of the question cannot be answered here.

The regional contrasts are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest share below the threshold, at 80.7% in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019. Low income countries stood at 83.5% in 2015 and 87.4% in 2019, and lower middle income countries at 52.9% and 57.4%. South Asia was nearly unchanged, at 55.8% and then 56.0%, and the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 57.7% to 57.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 49.1% to 51.0%. The results do not identify why additional years in school have not translated into basic skills in these regions. Well-established explanations include rapid expansion of enrolment, large classes and limited teacher training, but the data in hand do not test them.

At the other end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.8% to 5.5%, and high income countries from 6.4% to 6.2%. North America was flat, at 3.9% in both years. Low shares in these regions leave little room for movement, so the near absence of change there differs in kind from the stagnation seen in South Asia. Upper middle income countries were close to unchanged, at 28.0% in 2015 and 28.6% in 2019.

The largest movement was in East Asia and Pacific, where the share below the threshold rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019. A rise of that size in a region with strong education systems calls for caution. It may partly reflect a change in which countries and pupils were assessed between the two waves, not only a decline in learning. The data in hand cannot separate the two explanations. The trend calculation for the region extrapolates to 124.3% in 2030, which is impossible as a share and shows only that two points cannot support a projection.

The coverage of the series explains the difficulty. Data come in survey waves, not as annual observations. Countries reporting numbered 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, with an isolated report in 2023 from 1 country. In all, 125 countries reported in at least one year. The aggregates end in 2019, so they do not capture the effect of the school closures of 2020 and after, which is a serious omission for a question about what changed after 2020. The 2021 wave exists at country level but has no regional aggregate in the results here.

For 2030 the implication is plain on the evidence available. Extrapolating the 2015 to 2019 movement gives 61.3% of pupils below the threshold worldwide, against a target of zero, and the trend is classed as regression. This projection is a different quantity from the 61.3% figure of population shares in countries with regressing primary completion, and the two should not be confused. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 91.0% and low income countries 99.1% on the same arithmetic. Only Europe and Central Asia shows moderate progress, and it begins from a low base. The extrapolations are mechanical, rest on two points and should be read as direction, not forecast. The direction is away from the target in most regions, and the gap between completion and learning is widest where completion is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At present rates the world will miss target 4.1. The lower secondary trend to target puts the world on course for an expected completion rate of 80.0% of the relevant age group in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend ratio for the world is 0.21, which places it in the class of marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Among 173 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target for lower secondary completion, covering 22.1% of the assessed population, while 66 are regressing, covering 21.1%. For primary completion, 50 countries are on track, covering 19.6% of their population, and 92 are regressing, covering 61.3%. Regression is therefore the most common class at primary level. The classes come from a trend to target, so a country that has already reached a high rate and slipped slightly may be recorded as regressing; the reading needs care, and the target can be read as universal completion or as a rate near it.

Completing school is not the same as learning. The learning trend for the world is classed as regression, with an expected share below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary of 61.3% in 2030, against a target of 0.0%. This figure is a projected share of pupils and is distinct from the share of the assessed population in regressing countries. In Low income countries the expected share is 99.1% in 2030, and in Sub-Saharan Africa 91.0%. High completion does not guarantee learning: East Asia & Pacific is classed as regression on learning while its lower secondary completion is on track, with an expected rate of 105.4% in 2030. A rate above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio. Completion gains not matched by learning gains deliver the certificate without the skills. The learning series ends in 2019 for these trends and covers 125 countries, so it cannot show whether recovery after 2020 has changed this. It also addresses reading at the end of primary only; minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not covered.

The regional picture shows where acceleration matters most. Low income countries are classed as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected rate of 40.1% in 2030, the furthest of any group from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa has an expected rate of 46.2% in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region 73.9%, with a ratio of 0.39, still short of what the target requires. These are the places where the largest shares of children are left without a completed basic education, and they are also where learning data are thinnest.

w-c03-2-2.text:
### Stunting and wasting set against the 2025 and 2030 targets

The world has moved only slightly towards the internationally agreed nutrition targets since 2015. Stunting, measured as the share of children under five whose height for age is more than two standard deviations below the international reference median, stood at 24.6% in 2015 and 23.2% in 2024 on the modelled estimate. That is a fall of about 1.4 percentage points in nine years, or roughly 0.16 points a year. Wasting, the share whose weight for height falls equally far below the reference median, moved from 7.1% to 6.6% over the same period, a fall of 0.5 points. Neither series shows a break after 2015 that would mark a change of direction, and the latest year available is 2024, so the effects of the shocks that followed 2020 on food prices, health services and household incomes cannot be separated from the underlying slow decline.

The two indicators describe different conditions and should not be read as one. Stunting reflects chronic deprivation: poor maternal nutrition, repeated infection, inadequate diets in the first two years of life and limited access to water and sanitation. It accumulates over months and years and is difficult to reverse after early childhood, which is why its decline is gradual even where conditions improve. Wasting reflects acute loss of weight, driven by recent illness, famine, conflict or sudden shortfalls in food. It can rise and fall within a season, so a national survey taken at one moment may record a figure that differs from the annual average. A wasting prevalence of 6.6% therefore carries more uncertainty about timing than a stunting prevalence of 23.2%.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. The text of Target 2.2 asks that the internationally agreed targets on stunting and wasting be achieved by 2025, and that all forms of malnutrition end by 2030. The bench's trend tool applies a ceiling of 5.0% by 2030 to both series, and projects towards 2030 rather than 2025. That ceiling is a computational convention, not a statement of the agreed stunting benchmark, which is framed as a reduction against a baseline and for which no threshold is held among the facts here; other readings of the benchmark exist and none is quoted as a result. Under the strict reading of the target text, the 2025 deadline falls one year after the latest observation, and with wasting at 6.6% in 2024 and stunting at 23.2%, the 2025 milestone cannot plausibly have been met for either indicator. Under the trend tool's reading, the question is whether the 5.0% ceiling is within reach by 2030. The two readings agree on the verdict for 2025 but differ in the time they allow, and this book states which is in use wherever a projection is quoted.

For wasting, the gap to the 5.0% ceiling is 1.6 percentage points in 2024. At the pace of the past nine years, about 0.06 points a year, six further years would remove well under half of that gap. The ceiling is thus unlikely to be reached by continuing the recent pace, and reaching it would require improvement several times faster than that recorded since 2015. For stunting, the same trend calculation puts the world at 22.3% in 2030 if the observed rate continues, with a ratio of observed to required pace of 0.12, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. A fall of 1.4 points in nine years leaves the world far from any reduction large enough to be described as ending the condition.

Why this matters goes beyond the numbers. Children who are stunted face poorer cognitive development, lower school attainment and reduced earnings in adulthood, and severe wasting sharply raises the risk of death in early childhood. A near-flat global line therefore signals a persistent loss of human potential in each new cohort, not merely a missed statistical goal. The links to other Goals are direct: health, education, water and sanitation, and poverty reduction all shape the figures above.

A further caution concerns the global figures themselves. The stunting series is a modelled estimate that combines survey data with statistical methods to fill years without a survey, and the wasting series is built from harmonised survey data in which only 6 countries report for 2024. The global picture is therefore a reasonable guide to the direction and approximate scale of change, but small differences between years should not be treated as real movements. What the evidence does support is a plain conclusion: progress since 2015 has been real but slow, and the world is not on course for either target.

### Regional differences in stunting and wasting

Behind the modest world average lies a wide spread of regional experience. South Asia carries the heaviest burden on both measures. Its stunting prevalence fell from 37.8% in 2015 to 31.5% in 2024, the largest absolute decline among the regions listed, yet nearly one child in three under five remains stunted. Its wasting prevalence stood at 15.7% in 2024, against 16.6% in 2015, a reduction of less than one percentage point. Wasting in South Asia is therefore more than double the world figure of 6.6% in 2024. The region combines high rates of low birth weight, early marriage and adolescent pregnancy, limited dietary diversity and persistent sanitation deficits, and these causes act on stunting and wasting together.

Sub-Saharan Africa presents a different pattern. Stunting declined only from 34.4% in 2015 to 32.3% in 2024, so that the region, which had a lower rate than South Asia in 2015, now has a slightly higher one. Wasting fell more clearly, from 7.0% to 5.9%, a drop of about 1.2 percentage points. The contrast suggests that acute malnutrition, which responds to treatment programmes and seasonal relief, can improve faster than chronic growth failure, which depends on maternal health, diets, sanitation and incomes over many years. Population growth also means that a falling prevalence can coexist with a rising number of affected children, a distinction the prevalence series cannot show.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 27.5% to 24.1% in stunting and from 6.5% to 5.6% in wasting. Conflict, displacement and fiscal stress in parts of this heterogeneous grouping weigh against the gains, and the regional average conceals very different national circumstances. East Asia and Pacific moved from 14.5% to 13.3% in stunting, a slow decline for a region whose income growth has been rapid, and its wasting rate barely changed, from 3.7% to 3.6%.

Europe and Central Asia is the clearest example of steady improvement. Stunting fell from 6.0% to 4.6%, and wasting from 1.5% to 1.0%. For stunting, the trend calculation shows the region on track for the 5.0% ceiling that the tool applies by 2030, with an expected value of 3.8%, although the level was already close to that mark in 2015. The 5.0% figure is the tool's reference level, not necessarily the agreed stunting benchmark, which can be read in more than one way. Latin America and the Caribbean, by contrast, was flat: stunting stood at 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, which the trend calculation classes as regression. Wasting there eased from 1.5% to 1.3%. Earlier gains in the region appear to have stalled, and the economic disruption after 2020 and the unequal recovery of incomes among poorer households are plausible contributors, though the series do not isolate causes.

North America shows a rise in stunting from 2.8% in 2015 to 4.1% in 2024, while wasting fell from 0.3% to 0.2%. The trend tool labels the region as on track, because its level lies below the reference value, but the direction is adverse. The levels are low, the regional average rests on very few countries, and modelled estimates for populations with small samples carry wide uncertainty. The rise should be read as a signal worth checking rather than as a settled finding. The same applies to high-income countries as a group, where stunting moved from 3.9% to 4.0%.

Income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries began at 38.0% stunting in 2015 and ended at 35.8% in 2024, still the highest level of any group listed. Their wasting rate fell from 7.9% to 6.4%. Lower-middle-income countries show the strongest stunting decline, from 33.9% to 28.9%, a fall of about 5.1 percentage points, but their wasting remained at 9.5% in 2024, down from 10.5%, the highest of any income group, reflecting the weight of South Asia within it. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 11.9% to 10.8% in stunting and from 2.6% to 2.1% in wasting. High-income countries held wasting at 0.4% in 2024, down from 0.6%.

The gradient by income is steep and has narrowed only slightly in relative terms. Low-income countries had a stunting level about 9.73 times that of high-income countries in 2015 and about 8.86 times in 2024. Growth in income has helped where it occurred, but the lower-middle group shows that faster decline is possible without rich-country incomes, which points to the role of health, water, sanitation and social protection policy.

Two cautions apply. The trend summary for some groups is truncated in the output available, so the South Asia line is read here from the levels and from its computed expected value rather than a complete classification. The wasting summary also reports only 6 countries reporting in 2024, against 162 for stunting, so recent regional wasting figures rest on thin and uneven observation, and modelled aggregates should be treated with corresponding care.

For 2030, the regional pattern implies that the global figure will be decided largely in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The expected 2030 stunting values from the trend calculation are 27.9% for South Asia and 31.0% for Sub-Saharan Africa, both well above the 5.0% reference level. Only Europe and Central Asia, and the high-income group, sit at or near it.

### Country progress on wasting and the absence of convergence in stunting

Wasting presents a more differentiated national picture than stunting. The trend assessment covered 65 countries against a reference ceiling of 5.0% by 2030. That ceiling is the one the trend tool applies to both indicators; it is one reading of the benchmark, and the agreed benchmarks may be read more strictly. Of the countries assessed, 42, holding 38.6% of the population of the countries assessed, were on track or had already met the reference level. Four countries, with 7.8% of that population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Three countries showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration, and these three hold 33.7% of the population. No country was classed as stagnating, while 16 countries, with 19.9% of the population, were regressing, that is, wasting was rising rather than falling.

The population shares matter as much as the country counts. A simple count suggests that most assessed countries are doing well, since 42 of 65 is a majority. Weighted by population, the picture is less comfortable. The three countries in the marginal class account for a third of the assessed population, which implies that a small number of very populous countries dominate the burden and are not close to the reference level. Together with the 16 regressing countries, the population living where progress is marginal or reversed is 53.7%, more than the 38.6% living where the level is within reach. That sum is the reader's own arithmetic on rounded shares and should be read as approximate.

Three cautions apply. First, only 65 countries were assessed, although the underlying series cover 162 countries. The assessment depends on enough survey observations to draw a trend, and countries without them are absent from every class. Second, the 5.0% ceiling is not the only way to read the target: other thresholds for 2025 and 2030 have been proposed, and a country counted as on track against 5.0% may still fall short of a stricter one. Third, wasting is volatile. It responds quickly to famine, conflict, floods, disease outbreaks and seasonal food shortages, so a single survey can show a sharp change that does not reflect a lasting one. Regression may reflect a recent crisis, and on-track status may reflect a favourable survey year.

The causes of regression are well understood in broad terms. Conflict and displacement disrupt health services and food supply. Price shocks following the pandemic of 2020 and later disturbances to grain and fertiliser markets reduced the quality and quantity of children's diets in poorer households. Where treatment for severe acute malnutrition depends on external funding, interruptions in the supply of therapeutic food have direct effects. Countries that moved towards the target typically combined growth in household incomes with expanded primary health care, immunisation and community-based treatment of acute malnutrition.

Stunting shows a different pattern: the gaps between countries are not closing. The convergence test relates the change in stunting between 2015 and 2024 to the starting level across 162 countries. If countries with high stunting at the start improved faster, the coefficient would be clearly negative. The estimated beta is -0.00244, with a p-value of 0.2275 and an R-squared of 0.0085. The sign points to a slight tendency towards convergence, but the estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 1% of the variation in later change. A country's initial stunting rate says almost nothing about how fast it improved.

The coefficient of variation, which measures dispersion relative to the average, rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Dispersion between countries has therefore widened in relative terms. This is consistent with the lack of convergence: the world average has fallen only slightly while some countries have moved much faster than others, so the remaining high-prevalence countries stand further from the mean in proportion. A rising coefficient of variation does not by itself show that high-prevalence countries worsened; it shows that the spread, relative to the mean, grew.

For 2030 the two measures need different responses. Wasting is a problem of a minority of populous and crisis-affected countries that sit well off course, while many smaller countries are already within reach. Stunting is a slow, structural condition tied to maternal health, early-life diet, sanitation and poverty, and the absence of convergence implies that no general catching-up process can be relied on. Without deliberate targeting of the countries with the highest prevalence, the relative gap will probably go on widening towards 2030.

### Data coverage and the limits of the evidence

Wasting is measured by household surveys, not by continuous registration, and the evidence behind the series is thinner than the regional table suggests. In 2000, 58 countries reported a wasting value. The count fell to 22 in 2001 and varied between 24 and 51 in later years. It stood at 32 in 2015, rose to 48 in 2018 and 46 in 2019, then fell to 26 in 2020. In 2024 only 6 countries reported. Across the whole period 162 countries reported at least once, so the series covers most of the world, but not in any single year.

The pattern follows the survey cycle. Large programmes of household surveys are fielded every few years in each country, and the results are published with a delay. A year with few reporting countries is therefore not evidence of fewer children measured, nor of improvement or decline. The low count for 2024 is best read as a lag in publication, since surveys fielded in that year have not yet been processed. The dip in 2020 has a clearer cause: fieldwork was suspended or postponed in many countries during the pandemic, and the count of 26 reflects that interruption. Readers comparing 2015 with 2024 should accept that the later point is the less complete one.

The regional and income-group values for 2024 are consequently not simple averages of fresh observations. They are aggregates produced from the harmonised dataset, which combines recent surveys with modelled estimates for countries and years without a survey. The figure of 6.6% for the world in 2024, and the regional values around it, rest in large part on that modelling. The fall from 7.1% in 2015 is real as a modelled estimate, but its size, about half a percentage point, is small relative to the uncertainty that such modelling carries. Changes of that scale between two years should not be treated as established.

The caution applies most strongly where reporting is thinnest. Regions with many countries and uneven survey schedules, notably Sub-Saharan Africa, have an aggregate that can move because of which countries happened to be surveyed as well as because of nutrition. The fall in that region from 7.0% in 2015 to 5.9% in 2024 is larger than the world change, and it would be unwise to attribute it wholly to improved child nutrition without national survey evidence. In South Asia, where the prevalence is highest at 15.7% in 2024, a few large countries dominate the aggregate, so that one survey round can shift the regional figure materially. By contrast, high-income countries and North America, at 0.4% and 0.2% in 2024, have low values whose precision matters little for the argument.

Wasting has a further difficulty that stunting lacks. It is a short-lived condition: a child can be wasted during a hungry season or an illness and recover within weeks. Its prevalence depends on the month in which a survey is fielded, so two surveys in the same country in different seasons can differ for reasons unrelated to policy. Single-year comparisons are therefore weaker for wasting than for stunting, which reflects accumulated deprivation and changes slowly.

For the 2030 assessment these limits matter in two ways. A judgement that a country is on track rests on its own survey history, and countries with long gaps between surveys cannot be assessed with confidence. The 5.0% ceiling used by the trend tool is one reading of the benchmark, not a settled one. And the world and regional aggregates should be taken as indications of direction, not as precise measures of distance from that ceiling. Where the series is sparse, the more reliable evidence is the national survey record, and the count of reporting countries should be read alongside every figure quoted in this section.

### What the trajectories imply for 2030, and proposals

At the observed rates, the world will not reach a stunting prevalence of 5.0% by 2030. That figure is the ceiling the trend tool applies to stunting; it is one reading of the agreed benchmarks, which may be read more strictly, and it is not quoted here as the agreed target itself. Global stunting stood at 23.2% in 2024, and the trend projection gives 22.3% in 2030, a ratio of 0.12 against the pace the ceiling requires. The assessment class for the world is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The distance still to be covered is many times the distance covered since 2015. The 2025 milestone in the target text will also be missed on this evidence.

Three groups are classed as on track for stunting. Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.0% in 2015 to 4.6% in 2024, and its projected 2030 value is 3.8%, a ratio of 2.13, the fastest relative pace of any region. High-income countries stood at 3.9% in 2015 and 4.0% in 2024, and North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%. The last two are classed as on track only because their levels already lie below the ceiling of 5.0%. The classification reflects a level, not a gain, and the slight rise in both groups shows that wealthy countries have not secured child growth against change.

East Asia and Pacific is classed as marginal. Its prevalence fell from 14.5% to 13.3% and the projection for 2030 is 12.6%, a ratio of 0.20. Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as regression: 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, with 12.4% projected for 2030. A middle-income region with food available in aggregate has therefore made no progress on stunting for nine years. That points to causes beyond food supply, such as the quality of diets in early childhood, maternal health, sanitation and inequality within countries, which regional averages conceal.

The regions with the highest levels are furthest from the ceiling. South Asia is projected at 27.9% in 2030, a ratio of 0.30, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 31.0%, a ratio of 0.12. Low-income countries are projected at 34.4%, from 38.0% in 2015 and 35.8% in 2024. Lower middle-income countries fell from 33.9% to 28.9%, with 25.9% projected for 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is projected at 22.1%, from 24.1% in 2024. Each would still hold stunting at several times the ceiling in 2030. Because population growth is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, a slow fall in prevalence there can coincide with a rising number of affected children, which the prevalence series cannot show.

Wasting offers a less bleak picture in country counts but a troubling one at the margin. Of 65 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the 5.0% ceiling, while 16 show regression, holding 19.9% of the population assessed. Three countries, holding 33.7% of that population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Wasting responds quickly to drought, conflict, price surges and disease, so a country can change class within a year or two.

Neither the period since 2015 nor the disruptions after 2020 can be read cleanly from these series. Survey reporting fell to 26 countries in 2020 and to 6 in 2024, so recent wasting values rest on very few new observations, and modelled stunting estimates for 2024 lean on earlier surveys. A trend between 2015 and 2024 describes the direction of the estimates, not a verified count of children. The conclusion for 2030 is nonetheless robust, since the gaps are too large to be closed by any plausible revision.

proposals: National governments in Latin America and the Caribbean and in the high-income countries where stunting has risen should publish stunting data disaggregated by income, region and ethnicity, and target the poorest groups, since averages conceal where progress has stalled.

Ministries of health in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, with their development partners, should concentrate funding on the package of maternal nutrition, complementary feeding, sanitation and early-childhood care that acts on stunting, and report annually against a stated benchmark.

National statistical offices and survey sponsors should restore annual survey coverage for wasting, so that fewer than 10 countries do not report in a given year, and should state which reading of the 2025 and 2030 benchmarks they apply.
