w-c03-6-2.text:
### Agriculture's weight in output and employment is shrinking only slowly

Agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 4.2 per cent of world GDP in 2015 and 4.0 per cent in 2025. The share has fallen by only a fraction of a percentage point in ten years, across a period that included the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the pandemic of 2020 and the food and energy price shocks that followed. In 2025, 158 countries reported the series, so the global figure rests on a broad but not complete base.

Employment tells a different story from output. Agriculture accounted for 28.5 per cent of total employment worldwide in 2015 and 25.8 per cent in 2025, according to modelled estimates of the International Labour Organization. The sector therefore engaged roughly six times its share of output in 2025: a quarter of the world's workers produced about a twenty-fifth of its measured value added. The gap is the central fact for any judgement of public investment. It signals low output per worker, and it shows that a large part of the working population depends on a sector whose productivity is determined by roads, storage, irrigation, research and advisory services, all of which are largely public goods.

The pace of change is slow against the horizon of 2030. The employment share fell by 2.8 percentage points in ten years. At that rate, more than a fifth of the world's workers would still be employed in agriculture at the end of the Goals period. The output share fell by only 0.2 percentage points. Structural transformation, in which workers move from farms to higher-productivity work, is therefore under way but is far from complete, and a falling employment share is not evidence of falling need. Where output per worker is low, public spending that raises it is the means by which the share of employment can fall without a loss of rural income.

The benchmark that follows is simple. If public spending on agriculture were to match the sector's weight, it would be proportionate to a share of output of about 4.0 per cent in the world as a whole, and arguably to a higher share where employment is concentrated. The World Development Indicators supply no series for government agricultural expenditure in the results available here, so the match cannot be measured directly. The comparison must be made indirectly, through the external flows examined in the later parts and through the regional weights that follow. Target 2.a, which calls for greater investment in rural infrastructure, research, extension and gene banks, sets no numerical share to match, and cannot be scored against a spending figure that the shelf does not hold. The reading of any shortfall should be made with that limit in view.

### Regions differ most where agriculture matters most

The regional picture is one of extremes. In 2025, agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 17.9 per cent of GDP in Sub-Saharan Africa and 15.6 per cent in South Asia. Both regions also hold the largest shares of employment in the sector: 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa and 41.5 per cent in South Asia. At the other end, Europe and Central Asia drew 2.0 per cent of GDP from agriculture in 2025 and 6.7 per cent of employment, while North America drew 1.0 per cent of GDP in 2021, the latest year reported, and 1.5 per cent of employment in 2025. A farm worker in North America is part of a sector that is a rounding error in the national accounts; in Sub-Saharan Africa, the sector is where about half of all workers earn their living.

The gap between the two measures matters as much as the levels. In Sub-Saharan Africa the employment share is nearly three times the output share (49.3 per cent against 17.9 per cent), and in South Asia it is also close to three times (41.5 per cent against 15.6 per cent). Where half of workers produce under a fifth of output, average agricultural labour productivity is low relative to other sectors, and incomes in farming trail those elsewhere. Public spending that is proportionate to the sector's share of GDP would therefore still be small relative to the number of people who depend on it.

The direction of change after 2015 differs between regions. In Latin America and the Caribbean the output share rose from 5.5 per cent in 2015 to 6.8 per cent in 2025, while the employment share fell from 14.0 per cent to 12.7 per cent. The series alone does not show whether this reflects prices or output per worker. In Sub-Saharan Africa the output share rose by 1.6 points, from 16.3 per cent to 17.9 per cent, while the employment share fell by 4.0 points, from 53.3 per cent to 49.3 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific, by contrast, employment fell from 27.9 per cent to 21.7 per cent and the output share from 6.0 per cent to 5.5 per cent, the pattern of an economy moving labour out of farming. South Asia, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, moved only slightly in output share.

By income group, the divide is sharper still. In low-income countries agriculture accounted for 27.2 per cent of GDP in 2025, up from 25.6 per cent in 2015, and for 59.4 per cent of employment. Lower middle income countries stood at 17.8 per cent of GDP and 39.8 per cent of employment. Upper middle income countries recorded 6.9 per cent of GDP and 19.8 per cent of employment, and high income countries 1.3 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 2.9 per cent of employment in 2025. The poorest countries are therefore the ones in which the sector has not shrunk, and in which its share of output has risen even as the employment share eased. For target 2.a, whose wording singles out developing countries and the least developed among them, this concentration indicates where investment in rural infrastructure, research and extension has the largest population to reach by 2030.

### International flows from UN agencies rose but moved toward one region

Net official flows from UN agencies to the agricultural sector through IFAD rose across the period, though not evenly. The world total was 399 million US dollars in 2015 and 509 million in 2023. These are current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the apparent rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger real transfer. The series is also a net measure: repayments of loans are subtracted from disbursements, so a fall in a region's figure can reflect repayment as much as reduced lending.

The rise was concentrated in one region. Sub-Saharan Africa received 180 million US dollars in 2015 and 405 million in 2023, more than double. Every other region with a reported figure moved the other way. East Asia and Pacific fell from 99.9 million to 9.2 million. South Asia fell from 50.3 million to 43.1 million. Europe and Central Asia fell from 20.3 million to 15.5 million, Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.9 million to 9.0 million, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 29.2 million to 24.0 million. North America recorded zero in both years, as expected for a region of donors. The world total therefore rose because one region's gain outweighed the combined losses elsewhere.

The income groups show the same movement. Low-income countries received 109 million US dollars in 2015 and 247 million in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 201 million to 240 million. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 67.2 million to a net negative of 12.6 million, meaning that repayments to IFAD exceeded new disbursements in 2023. This is the pattern expected of a lender that shifts concessional resources toward the poorest countries while middle-income borrowers graduate and repay. High-income countries show a small figure of 2.8 million in 2023, which reflects the few cases where such countries still appear as recipients or repayers.

The direction matches the regional evidence on need set out earlier, since Sub-Saharan Africa has the largest shares of output and jobs in agriculture. It matters for 2030 because target 2.a asks for more investment in developing countries, in particular the least developed. A rise confined to a single region and to the lowest income groups is consistent with that wording, yet the sums are small. Half a billion dollars a year, spread across a continent whose farm economy employs about half of all workers, cannot substitute for domestic public spending.

Coverage limits how far the picture can be pressed. IFAD flows were reported by 94 countries in 2023. The companion series on flows from FAO was reported by 129 countries in 2023, against 133 in 2013, and 139 countries reported in at least one year. The count fell from 135 in 2019 to 129 in 2023, with a low of 128 in 2022. Aggregates should therefore be read as sums over reporting countries, and a missing country is not a zero. The comparison before and after 2020 is further limited by the end of the series in 2023, which leaves little room to judge how flows responded to the pandemic and the price shocks that followed.

### Flows follow need, but do not yet change it, and proposals follow

Across the 89 countries for which both series exist, the link between flows and the size of agriculture depends on what is compared. The Spearman correlation of 2023 levels between net official flows from IFAD and agriculture's share of GDP is 0.575, a moderate positive association. Countries where agriculture contributes more to output tend to receive more from the fund. The correlation of changes between 2015 and 2023 is 0.141, which is weak and shows no clear association between how far a country's flows moved and how far its agricultural share of GDP moved. The Kendall coefficients, 0.390 for levels and 0.101 for changes, give the same picture on a stricter rank measure.

The reading is that flows go where agriculture is large, as a needs-based allocation would predict. The change correlation does not test whether flows alter the sector's share of output or of employment, and employment is not part of it. A flow directed at rural infrastructure, extension services or research takes years to alter productivity, and a falling share of GDP can reflect growth elsewhere as much as any change in farming. Structural change is slow, as the global share of 4.0 per cent in 2025 against 4.2 per cent in 2015 already shows. Ten years is a short window against which to judge a transfer of this kind.

The limits of the evidence are plain. A correlation is not a cause: the link of levels may arise because IFAD lends to agricultural economies by mandate, not because the money has any effect. The weak link of changes cannot show that flows fail, since the counterfactual is unknown. The series also covers one agency's net flows, in current dollars. The companion FAO series was reported by 139 countries in at least one year, but the annual count fell from 135 in 2019 to 129 in 2023, with a low of 128 in 2022, which narrows what can be compared. Above all, target 2.a can be read in more than one way: as public spending by governments, as private investment, or as international cooperation. The data on the bench measure only the last, and in part. Whether public spending on agriculture matches the sector's weight, 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2025 and 17.9 per cent of its GDP, cannot be answered from these series, because government agricultural spending is absent.

For 2030 the implication is that the match between investment and need cannot at present be tested, and no expectation about the sector's share can be drawn from the weak change correlation of 0.141. The proposals below follow from that finding.

Donors and evaluators should assess rural infrastructure, extension and research flows over horizons longer than a decade, with output and employment outcomes measured, before judging whether they change the sector's structure.

The IFAD and FAO flows are in current dollars, net of repayments and cover one agency each; the IFAD series reaches 94 countries in 2023. Flows are not linked to employment shares, and causal effects cannot be identified from the correlations.

w-c04-7-1.text:
### Adolescent fertility has fallen worldwide since 2015

The world adolescent fertility rate fell from 46.0 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 38.3 in 2024. That is a decline of about 17 per cent over nine years, and it continues a long movement that predates the Sustainable Development Goals. The figure is a modelled estimate built from registration data, surveys and censuses, and the series reports on all 217 countries and territories in 2024, so the global average rests on far fuller coverage than the indicators of contraceptive demand in the same section.

Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold. It calls for universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, including family planning, information and education, and offers no level of adolescent fertility that would count as success. The target can also be read in more than one way: adolescent births are an outcome of access, schooling, marriage customs and income as much as of health services, so a fall in the rate cannot be credited to health policy alone. Any reading of progress here therefore rests on the trend classes of the bench, which compare each country's own course with the pace needed to keep falling to 2030, and not on a stated goal.

On that reading the picture is favourable in breadth. Of 217 countries assessed, 144 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 26 countries, with 6.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Eight countries, with 0.4% of the population, are stagnant, and five, with 1.0%, are regressing. The population-weighted result is better than the count of countries suggests, because several of the most populous countries have recorded steep falls. The countries that lag are fewer, but they tend to be those where the rate started highest.

The global decline matters because early childbearing is closely tied to interrupted schooling, lower lifetime earnings and higher obstetric risk for mother and child. A fall of this size over nine years is also not uniform in its meaning. The world rate of 38.3 in 2024 remains well above the 8.7 recorded for high-income countries in the same year, so the average conceals a wide gap that the next parts of the section examine. The period since 2015 also includes the pandemic after 2020, when school closures and disrupted clinics were widely expected to push adolescent births up. The world series, read at its end points, shows no lasting reversal, though end points cannot show whether the pace faltered in particular years or places. For 2030, continued decline at the pace of 2015 to 2024 would lower the world rate further, but the trend classes show that the gains are not secure in every country.

### Demand satisfied by modern methods is poorly measured

The indicator on demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods is the weakest of the series in this section. It is reported by 73 countries in at least one year between 2000 and 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility. In any single year the count is small. It ranged from 2 to 14 countries a year across the period: 13 in 2000, a peak of 14 in 2012, and 8 in 2015. Since 2019 the count has fallen further, to 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. The thinning follows the pattern of household surveys, which are fielded at intervals of several years and were disrupted by the pandemic, so a country appears in the series only in the years after a survey is completed and processed.

The consequence is that the indicator cannot show what happened after 2015 or after 2020 for the world. A year-on-year comparison would compare different sets of countries, and a change in the average would reflect which countries happened to report as much as any change in access to services. The shelf holds aggregates for only three groups: lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. No world aggregate and no aggregate for other regions can be read from it, so regional comparison of satisfied demand is not possible on this evidence.

The definition adds a second limit. The indicator refers to married women aged 15 to 49 who have a need for family planning, and its denominator is those with demand, not all women. Unmarried women, including sexually active adolescents, fall outside it, as do women in unions not recorded as marriage in some surveys. Target 3.7 speaks of universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, information and education, and the indicator captures only one part of that: the use of modern methods by those married women who want to space or limit births. Where adolescent births are concentrated among unmarried girls, the indicator says little about them. The target also gives no numerical threshold, so that no level of satisfied demand can be called the goal, and the trend assessment therefore rests on the direction of change rather than on a fixed value.

The trend classification covers only 15 countries, those with enough observations to fit a path to 2030. Of these, 2 are on track or have met the target, holding 1.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Another 5 show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 21.8 per cent. Four show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 70.3 per cent. One is stagnant, with 3.1 per cent, and 3 are regressing, with 3.3 per cent. The population shares are dominated by the 4 countries in the marginal class, probably because one or two very large countries sit there, which is why more than two thirds of the assessed population falls in one class. Fifteen countries out of 73 reporting, and out of a world of more than 200, is too few to speak for any region, and the sample is not random: countries with repeated surveys are often those with donor-supported programmes. Any global statement drawn from these results is therefore tentative, and the proportions above describe the sample, not the world.

### Regions differ by a factor of eight in adolescent births

Adolescent births are concentrated to a degree that the world average conceals. In 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 91.9 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19, against 50.4 in Latin America and the Caribbean and 37.8 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. South Asia stood at 21.0, East Asia and Pacific at 14.3, North America at 11.7 and Europe and Central Asia at 11.4. The highest regional rate is therefore about eight times the lowest, and the next region down, Latin America and the Caribbean, is well above the world rate of 38.3.

The pattern follows income. Low-income countries recorded 90.7 births per 1,000 in 2024, lower-middle-income countries 42.5, upper-middle-income countries 23.6 and high-income countries 8.7. Income groups and regions overlap heavily, so the two views largely describe the same countries. Schooling for girls, the age at first marriage, access to contraception and the reach of sexual and reproductive health education all differ along the same lines, and they act together rather than separately.

Since 2015 every region has recorded a fall, but the size of the fall depends on the measure. In absolute terms Sub-Saharan Africa fell furthest, from 109.4 to 91.9, a drop of about 17 births per 1,000. Latin America and the Caribbean fell by a similar amount, from 67.3 to 50.4. Proportionally the ranking is different. North America fell from 20.9 to 11.7, about 44 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 21.9 to 14.3, about 35 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa fell about 16 per cent, and low-income countries about 12 per cent, from 103.3 to 90.7. Large absolute gains from a high starting point therefore mean little change in relative standing: the region with the highest rate in 2015 remains far above the rest in 2024.

The country classification shows a similar split between breadth and depth of progress. Of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 34 countries, with 7.3 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 26, with 6.3 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. Together the last three classes number 39 countries. They are few in population terms, but they are the places where girls face the highest risks, and the population-weighted figure of 84.9 per cent should not be read as a statement about each country.

The target gives no numerical threshold for adolescent fertility, so the trend classification measures the pace of decline against a projected path, not against a defined goal. A different reading of what counts as sufficient progress would change the classes. The regional contrasts are nonetheless clear on any reading: the countries that began with the highest rates are falling too slowly to close the gap by 2030.

### Progress in family planning is moderate and uneven

Of the 15 countries for which a trend to 2030 could be computed on demand satisfied by modern methods, only 2 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 1.5% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 5 countries, with 21.8% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The weight of the picture lies in the slower classes. The 4 countries in marginal progress, which need significant acceleration, hold 70.3% of the assessed population. One country stagnates, with 3.1%, and 3 regress, with 3.3%. The population-weighted result is therefore weaker than the country count alone suggests, because the most populous countries with a computable trend are those moving slowest.

This finding must be read with its limits in view. The 15 countries assessed are a fraction of the 73 that have ever reported the indicator, and the survey-based series leaves most countries without enough observations to draw a trend. The assessment cannot be read as a global verdict. It describes a small, self-selected group, probably weighted towards countries where household surveys are repeated, which are often those with a large unmet need and a strong donor presence. Nor does the target carry a numerical threshold in this analysis, so the classes measure the pace of improvement against a path rather than against a fixed level of satisfied demand, and a different reading of the goal would sort some countries differently.

The indicators do not identify why countries fall into one class or another, and no cause is asserted here. Well-established experience suggests that the pace of change in contraceptive use depends on the reliability of supply, the range of methods offered, the cost to users, and social norms about women's choices, but none of these is measured by this series. What the data do show is that regression occurs in 3 of the 15 countries, which means that gains are not automatically retained, and that stagnation in a country of any size would hold back the aggregate for its region.

For 2030, the implication is that progress on this measure cannot be assumed to be on course. With so few countries on track and most of the assessed population in the slower classes, a global result consistent with universal access would require acceleration in precisely those countries where the trend is already weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Adolescent fertility is likely to keep falling to 2030, but not evenly. Of the 217 countries and territories assessed, 144 are on track or have met the direction of travel, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. The remainder is the concern. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of that population, show moderate progress and need acceleration, 26 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. Target 3.7 sets no numerical goal for adolescent fertility, so these classes describe the pace of change in each country and do not measure distance from a value agreed in the Goals. The reading depends on the pace each country is judged against, and it should be taken as indicative.

The regional picture sharpens the concern. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 91.9 in 2024, and low-income countries fell from 103.3 to 90.7. Both remain several times above the high-income level of 8.7 in 2024. A continued decline at the pace of the past nine years would leave these groups far above where other regions already stand in 2030. The gap is therefore likely to persist, even as the world rate falls from 38.3 in 2024. Where schooling for girls, child marriage, and access to contraception improve together, rates have fallen fastest. Where they do not, population growth can raise the number of births even as the rate declines.

Family planning cannot be judged with confidence on current data. Only 15 countries could be assessed for demand satisfied by modern methods. Of these, 2 are on track, 5 show moderate progress, 4 show marginal progress, 1 is stagnant and 3 are regressing. The 4 countries in marginal progress hold 70.3% of the population assessed, so a small number of populous countries determines the result. Reporting is also thin: only 7 countries reported in 2024 and 2 in 2019. A finding on 2030 for this indicator rests on few countries and on sparse, irregular survey rounds.

The proposals that follow address both problems: the thinness of measurement and the pace of progress where it is slowest.

w-c04-8-2.text:
### Service coverage has widened, but the world is far from universal

The UHC service coverage index stood at 68.0 index points for the world in 2015 and at 71.0 in 2023, the latest year for which all 193 countries report. The index is a composite of 14 tracer indicators spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases and service capacity and access. It runs from 0 to 100, and a score of 100 is the natural reading of 'universal' in target 3.8. That reading is one of several. The target also names financial risk protection and access to safe, affordable medicines, which the index does not measure directly, and a country may score high on tracer services while leaving households exposed to heavy costs. The index should therefore be read as a measure of the breadth of essential services, not as a verdict on the whole target.

On that measure, the gain over eight years was 3.0 points, and the world remained 29.0 points short of 100 in 2023. The shortfall is large because the tracer indicators include services that are hard to extend to everyone, such as the control of hypertension and diabetes and the capacity of facilities, alongside those that are easier to scale, such as vaccination and antenatal care. A composite also moves slowly, since a gain in one area can be offset by stagnation in another. These explanations rest on general knowledge of how the index is built, not on the results shown here.

The income groups show the same ordering at both dates. Low-income countries scored 41.2 in 2015 and 43.8 in 2023, a rise of 2.6 points. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 56.8 to 62.4, a gain of 5.5 points, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6, a gain of 4.0 points, and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2, a gain of 1.9 points. High-income countries, which started closest to the ceiling, were not saturated and kept improving. The low-income gain was therefore larger than that of the high-income group but smaller than those of the two middle groups, so the poorest countries did not close the distance to the others in absolute terms. They remained in 2023 below the level the lower-middle-income group had reached in 2015.

The gap between countries narrowed slightly, though not by much. Among the 193 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the index fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index fell from 0.030 to 0.024. Convergence is therefore real, but it takes place at a low overall level. Most of the inequality lies between regions: the between-region share of the Theil index was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, so where a person lives, more than differences within a region, accounts for the variation in service coverage. Because the weighting is by population, the improvement in South Asia, whose regional score rose from 60.0 to 68.0, plausibly accounts for much of the narrowing, though the results do not isolate its contribution. The regional pattern is taken up in the next part.

The pace matters for 2030. A rise of 3.0 points in eight years, set against a distance of 29.0 points, shows that universality by 2030 was not within reach on the present trajectory. Whether the period after 2020 slowed progress cannot be judged from these figures alone, since the results offer only the endpoints reported here and the latest year is 2023.

### Regions differ widely in coverage and in out-of-pocket burden

Coverage differs more between regions than any year-on-year change in the world average would suggest. In 2023 North America scored 88.0 index points on the UHC service coverage index, Europe and Central Asia 82.0, East Asia and Pacific 80.0 and Latin America and the Caribbean 79.0. South Asia stood at 68.0, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 66.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 50.0. The gap between North America and Sub-Saharan Africa was therefore 38.0 points.

The direction of travel differs as well. South Asia made the largest regional gain, from 60.0 in 2015 to 68.0 in 2023, and moved from below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 76.0 to 80.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 45.0 to 50.0. Latin America and the Caribbean did not move at all, at 79.0 in both years. North America, already near the top, added 1.0 point. Among income groups, low-income countries moved from 41.2 to 43.8, lower-middle-income countries from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6 and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. The low-income gain of 2.6 points was smaller than those of the lower-middle and upper-middle groups (5.5 and 4.0 points) but larger than that of high-income countries (1.9 points). The poorest countries are improving, but from so low a base that the distance to the others has barely closed, and in 2023 they remained below the 2015 level of lower-middle-income countries.

Out-of-pocket spending adds a second view of the same divide. As a share of current health expenditure it was 11.1% in North America in 2023, 16.5% in Europe and Central Asia, 26.0% in East Asia and Pacific, 28.3% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 29.7% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 30.4% in Sub-Saharan Africa and 46.6% in South Asia. The world figure was 17.3%, down from 18.4% in 2015. South Asia is the striking case: its share fell from 64.3% to 46.6%, the largest fall of any region, yet it remains the highest. Households there still pay nearly half of all health spending directly. Low public funding and a large private provider sector are plausible explanations, but these are hypotheses that the series do not test. Latin America and the Caribbean and East Asia and Pacific moved the other way, from 28.2% to 29.7% and from 25.7% to 26.0%, so reliance on household payments grew slightly even where coverage was already high.

The share of health spending paid out of pocket and the share of people suffering hardship are related but not the same. Hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on health, affected 26.0% of the world population in 2022, against 28.0% in 2015. By region it ranged from 7.5% in North America and 13.0% in Europe and Central Asia to 20.3% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 26.5% in East Asia and Pacific, 27.5% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 31.7% in South Asia and 35.2% in Sub-Saharan Africa. Sub-Saharan Africa thus has the highest hardship even though South Asia has the highest out-of-pocket share. One possible reason is that where incomes are low, even a modest absolute payment can consume most of what remains after basic needs. In three regions, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, hardship rose slightly between 2015 and 2022, and in North America it was nearly flat, from 7.4% to 7.5%. High-income countries as a group moved from 9.5% to 9.7%. Hardship estimates rest on household surveys that are fielded irregularly, and only three countries report for 2024, so these regional values are modelled and carry wider uncertainty than the service index.

The spread among countries on the service index narrowed. The Gini coefficient, weighted by population, fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.030 to 0.024. This is convergence, and it is the right direction. Yet the share of the Theil index lying between regions was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, essentially unchanged. About seven-tenths of the inequality in coverage is therefore explained by which region a country belongs to, and the narrowing has come about by lifting the whole distribution rather than by dissolving regional divides. For 2030 this means that national averages hide a structure, and that policies raising coverage should be judged against the regional floor from which each country starts.

### Coverage gains were modest and financial protection moved unevenly

Financial protection improved only slightly at the global level between 2015 and 2023, and the improvement was concentrated in a few regions. The world share of current health expenditure paid directly by households fell from 18.4% in 2015 to 17.3% in 2023. The share of people facing financial hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on out-of-pocket health costs, fell from 28.0% in 2015 to 26.0% in 2022. Both movements are in the right direction, but they are small beside the scale of the problem. More than one person in four still sits above the hardship threshold in the latest year with broad data.

The global averages conceal opposite movements. South Asia accounts for much of the fall in the out-of-pocket share, which dropped from 64.3% in 2015 to 46.6% in 2023, and the lower middle income group fell from 58.3% to 47.0% over the same years. Low income countries moved from 53.0% to 44.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan also fell, to 30.4% and 28.3% respectively. These are large reductions, yet they began from very high levels, and in South Asia nearly half of health spending is still paid at the point of care. In East Asia and Pacific the out-of-pocket share edged up from 25.7% to 26.0%, and in Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 28.2% to 29.7%. Europe and Central Asia (17.8% to 16.5%), North America (11.9% to 11.1%) and high income countries (14.4% to 13.4%) declined modestly from low bases.

The hardship measure tells a different story from the spending share, and the difference matters. East Asia and Pacific shows a clear fall in hardship, from 30.0% to 26.5%, although its out-of-pocket share did not fall. This shows that the two measures are not interchangeable: hardship depends on household budgets, prices and the burden of illness as well as on how the system is financed. In Europe and Central Asia hardship rose from 12.6% to 13.0%, in Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.5% to 20.3%, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 27.0% to 27.5%. North America moved from 7.4% to 7.5% and high income countries from 9.5% to 9.7%. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the highest at 35.2% in 2022, down from 38.7%, and South Asia stood at 31.7%, down from 35.7%. Low income countries fell from 38.5% to 34.7% and lower middle income countries from 34.4% to 31.5%, while upper middle income countries moved from 26.5% to 24.9%. Hardship is therefore not confined to the poorest countries: in several middle and high income regions it is stagnant or slightly worse. One hypothesis, which these data do not test, is that the cost of care for chronic conditions, medicines and long-term services is partly covered by public schemes.

The country-level classification confirms the unevenness. Of 72 countries assessed against the direction of the target, 27 are on track or have met it, holding 34.0% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 9 show moderate progress needing acceleration (9.5%), and 4 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration (22.7%). One country is stagnant, and 31 are regressing, holding 33.7% of the assessed population. Regression is thus as common as success, and the two groups are of similar demographic weight. No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures only direction of travel and not distance to a defined goal; the reading of target 3.8 as a call for financial risk protection for all leaves open what level of hardship would count as acceptable.

Public funding appears to matter. Across 21 countries with data for both series, the share of people in hardship is negatively associated with the share of health spending funded from domestic government sources. The rank correlation is -0.525 for 2022 levels and -0.258 for changes between 2015 and 2022. The level association is moderate, and the association for changes is weak. This is association rather than proof of cause: richer countries tend to have both higher public shares and lower hardship, and the weaker link in changes suggests that raising the public share does not by itself reduce hardship, whose course also depends on what is covered, on prices and on who is reached.

The evidence base itself is uneven. Hardship has thinner coverage than the service index, with 3 countries reporting in 2024 against 22 for the out-of-pocket share, so regional aggregates rest on survey years that differ between countries. Movements of one or two points in a regional hardship figure should be read with caution. The broad picture is nevertheless consistent: protection improved where out-of-pocket reliance was highest, and it stalled or reversed in regions that had already moved furthest on coverage.

### At the current pace, 2030 will be missed, and proposals follow

The trend assessment leaves little room for optimism about 2030. Measured against a target of 100 index points, no country is on track for the UHC service coverage index: 0 of 193 countries assessed are on track or have met the target. Only 2 countries, holding 17.3% of the population, show moderate progress that would still need acceleration. A further 102 countries, holding 64.7% of the population, show marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Another 57 countries, holding 11.0% of the population, stagnate, and 32 countries, holding 7.0% of the population, regress. Most of the world's people therefore live in countries where coverage is rising too slowly to matter for the target. The reading depends on the target. Target 3.8 sets no numerical threshold, and 100 index points is a convention that no health system has reached in practice. Judged against it, the assessment is severe by construction, but the direction of the finding holds under a gentler yardstick, because the projected 2030 values sit well below any plausible aspiration.

The projections show the scale of the shortfall. The world is expected to reach 73.7 index points in 2030, a ratio of 0.18 of the pace needed. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 54.8 index points, with a ratio of 0.18, and low-income countries at 46.2, a ratio of 0.09 that the assessment classes as stagnation. Lower middle income countries are projected at 67.6, with a ratio of 0.25. South Asia has the highest ratio of any region, 0.40, and is projected at 75.9 index points in 2030, still short of what the target requires. Latin America and the Caribbean is projected to stay at 79.0, with a ratio of 0.00, which the assessment classes as stagnation. Even high-income countries, projected at 86.9 with a ratio of 0.21, and North America, projected at 88.9, fall short of the target. The gap between the poorest and richest groups therefore does not close. The groups with the most to gain advance slowly, and the groups with the highest coverage have reached a plateau at which further gains are hard to win.

Financial protection tells a more divided story. Among the 72 countries with enough data to assess the hardship indicator, 27 countries, holding 34.0% of their population, are on track or have met the target. Another 9, holding 9.5%, show moderate progress. Against this, 31 countries, holding 33.7% of their population, are regressing, and 4 more, holding 22.7%, show marginal progress. Only 1 country stagnates. Progress is real in some places, but the regressing group is nearly as large in population as the group that is succeeding, and the assessment covers only 72 of the countries that report the coverage index. Reading the two assessments together, coverage of services is advancing too slowly almost everywhere, while financial protection is improving in some countries and deteriorating in others, so that the two cannot be assumed to move together.

Public financing is the most plausible lever, though the data do not prove it. Across 21 countries with data for both series from 2015 to 2022, the rank correlation between the level of financial hardship and the domestic government share of current health expenditure was -0.52. Countries that fund more of their health spending from public sources tend to have fewer households in hardship. The rank correlation between the changes in the two series was weaker, at -0.26, so a rise in public financing did not reliably produce a fall in hardship within the period. The sample is small and the association is not proof of cause, but it agrees with the long-established finding that pooled, prepaid funding protects households better than direct payment at the point of care.

The following proposals follow from these findings.

w-c06-2-2.text:
### Intimate partner violence is measured in few countries and few years

Target 5.2 calls for the elimination of all forms of violence against all women and girls, in public and private life, including trafficking and sexual and other types of exploitation. The indicator that the World Bank's catalogue holds for it is narrower: the proportion of ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49 who were subjected to physical violence, sexual violence or both in the previous 12 months. The series note describes it as drawn from United Nations and World Health Organization sources. It therefore speaks to one form of violence and one age band, and says nothing directly about violence by non-partners, harassment in public, trafficking or exploitation. Women who have never had a partner, girls under 15 and women over 49 fall outside it. A country with a low reading on this series cannot be taken to have met the wider target.

The coverage is thin even for this narrow measure. Across the whole period, 106 countries report in at least one year. Those reports are spread unevenly over time, and in most years very few countries contribute. One country reports for 2000 and 2 for 2005. The counts then run at 4 for 2006, 3 for 2007, 4 for 2008 and 4 for 2009, falling to 2 for 2010 and 3 for 2011. A year with one to four reporting countries cannot support a comparison of regions or a global reading; it records a handful of observations.

The pattern changes sharply in 2012, when 35 countries report. This single peak accounts for a large share of all the country entries on the shelf. The bench results do not say why the count rises in that year, and the reason is not asserted here; whether the values come from direct surveys or from estimation is likewise not recorded in the results. After the peak the counts fall back to 7 for 2013 and rise to 12 for 2014, 8 for 2015, 14 for 2016 and 7 for 2017, the latest year with data. No year after 2017 is held, so the series is silent on the period from 2020, when many observers warned that violence at home had risen. The shelf holds no regional or world aggregates for this indicator, so no summary can be drawn from published totals.

These features shape what the rest of the section can responsibly say. Differences between countries can be described where values exist, but the values rest on different years. A reader should treat the indicator as a partial snapshot of one form of violence, not as a tracked measure of progress towards the target.

### Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap

The 2012 estimates are the only ones in the series for which a comparison of spread among countries is possible. In that year 35 countries report, far more than in any other year. The Gini coefficient is 0.29 and the Theil index is 0.17. The Gini coefficient indicates a moderate gap between countries: prevalence is neither uniform nor extremely unequal. The coefficient of variation is 0.66. The weighting basis for these measures is not documented in the results, and the population-weighted label is taken from the tool's output.

The decomposition shows where the measured inequality lies. Of the Theil inequality in 2012, 66.2% is between regions rather than within them, and the remaining third is within regions. This is a descriptive split of a single year among 35 reporting countries. It does not show why regions differ, and it supports no causal reading. Shared legal traditions, social norms about marriage and household authority, services for survivors and the history of conflict are well-established candidates for explaining regional patterns in violence, but the data hold no variable that could test any of them.

The limits of this result need to be stated plainly. The results do not record which countries are in the 35 or how they were chosen. Surveys on violence are costly and sensitive, and in general they are fielded where governments permit them and funders support them, so the absent countries may differ systematically from those present. The between-region share is also computed only among reporting countries, so a region represented by two or three countries adds little information on differences within it. The figures describe the spread of a particular sample in a particular year. They are not a global distribution and should not be read as one.

Nor can 2012 be compared with other years. The 7 countries reporting in 2013 and the 14 in 2016 are too few for the same calculation, and the results do not show whether they are the same countries as in 2012. For 2030 the consequence is that the regional pattern visible in 2012 is a snapshot of where evidence was gathered, not a baseline from which progress can be measured.

### Change over time cannot be established, while attitudes are better documented

The trend tool, which classifies each country against the 2030 target of zero, assesses no country for intimate partner violence. All five classes show zero: no country is on track or has met the target, none shows moderate progress, none shows marginal progress, none is stagnating and none is regressing. The count of countries assessed is also zero. This is not a finding of no change. It is a finding that change cannot be measured, because the tool needs repeated observations for the same country and the series does not supply them. Without them, the series cannot show whether prevalence has risen or fallen since 2015, or since 2020, when lockdowns and household stress were widely reported to have raised risks for women at home. That report comes from outside the bench data. Neither progress nor regression can be stated, and any claim about the direction of violence against women over the period rests on sources outside this series.

The attitude indicator, the share of women who believe a husband is justified in beating his wife for at least one of five reasons, is better documented. 72 countries report it in at least one year between 2000 and 2024. Annual coverage is modest and uneven, however. It was 6 countries in 2000 and 4 in 2002, rose to 10 in 2005 and 14 in 2012, and stood at 12 in both 2016 and 2018. After 2018 it fell sharply: 2 countries in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fell around 2019 and 2020. Interrupted fieldwork is a plausible hypothesis, but it needs a source outside these results, and the partial recovery since is likewise unexplained. Even in the best year, 14 countries report, so a global or regional average of attitudes for any single year would describe a shifting group of countries and not a stable panel.

The attitude series therefore offers more scope for comparison over time within countries that survey repeatedly, but it does not allow a global verdict. The results do not record which countries report, or their income level or survey programme, so the composition of the reporting group is not documented here and some groups may be under-represented.

Attitudes are a proxy and not a measure of violence. Acceptance of wife beating can indicate social norms that sustain abuse and discourage women from reporting or seeking help, and falling acceptance is often read as a sign of shifting norms. But a woman may reject violence and still experience it, and a society may hold permissive views with low recorded prevalence, or the reverse. Answers are also shaped by who is asking and who is present during the interview. The indicator should be read as context for the prevalence data, never as a substitute for them, and it cannot show whether target 5.2 is being met for 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals on measurement

A target of zero by 2030 cannot be assessed from these data. The trend tool classifies no country, and the count of countries assessed is 0. Any statement that the world, a region or a country is on track, or off track, for the elimination of intimate partner violence would therefore be unsupported. In all, 106 countries report in at least one year, but most appear once, and the reporting years cluster so tightly that a single survey wave stands in for a trend. Reporting peaks at 35 countries in 2012, falls to 7 in 2013 and stands at 7 again in 2017, the latest year. Nothing is recorded after 2017, so neither the years after 2015 nor the pandemic years after 2020 can be read from the series. Lockdowns and strained services are widely reported to have raised the risk of violence at home, but the catalogue holds no figure that confirms or refutes this.

The measurement gap matters because the target is stated in absolute terms. Zero is reached only by sustained decline, and decline can be shown only by repeated measurement in the same country with the same definition. The attitude series is somewhat better placed, with 72 countries reporting in at least one year, yet it measures what women believe, not what they experience, and it thins sharply after 2018, with 2 countries in 2019 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fall, and the composition of the reporting countries is not recorded in the results, so some groups of countries may be under-represented. Attitudes may change before behaviour does, or behaviour may change without attitudes following, so neither series can stand in for the other. Underreporting is a further limit: women may not disclose violence in a survey, and a rise in measured prevalence can follow improved trust in interviewers as well as a real increase.

Five proposals follow from these findings; they are set out in the list of proposals. They concern the frequency of surveys, the continued collection of the 12-month indicator with a lifetime series beside it, the range of women and forms of violence covered, the conditions for publishing regional aggregates, and the joint reporting of attitudes and prevalence. Until they are met, the record for Target 5.2 will describe a handful of survey years, not fifteen years of progress.

proposals: National statistical offices, with survey programmes and their funders, should repeat the intimate partner violence survey at fixed intervals of no more than five years, so that change within a country can be measured against the 2030 target.

The agencies that compile the indicator should publish a lifetime prevalence series beside the 12-month series, because the catalogue holds only the 12-month measure, and should keep definitions unchanged across waves.

Survey designers and national statistical offices should extend coverage beyond ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49 and beyond partner violence, towards the all women, all girls and all forms named in Target 5.2.
The World Bank and its partners should publish regional aggregates only where a stated minimum share of countries report in the same period, and should state that threshold.
Statistical agencies should field the attitude questions and the prevalence questions in the same surveys and report them together, so that belief and experience can be compared within a country.
w-c06-2-2.gaps: The catalogue holds no intimate partner violence prevalence after 2017, no lifetime prevalence, no series on violence by non-partners, on trafficking or on sexual exploitation, and no figures on girls under 15 or women over 49. The results record no country list or income grouping for reporting countries, no weighting basis for the 2012 spread measures, and no cause for the falls in reporting counts. Underreporting cannot be measured.

w-c08-1-1.text:
### Global access has risen, but not to universality

Access to electricity worldwide stood at 91.9 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 86.9 per cent in 2015. The gain of five percentage points over nine years is real and was achieved while the world population grew, but it leaves roughly one person in twelve without a connection. Target 7.1 calls for universal access by 2030, and a world at 91.9 per cent has not reached that threshold. The series is reported by 215 countries for 2024, so coverage is nearly complete, though some national figures rest on modelled estimates drawn from industry records and household surveys rather than a fresh count each year.

The divide between rural and urban populations explains much of the shortfall. Rural access rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a faster advance than the urban series, which moved from 96.4 per cent to 97.8 per cent. Urban access was therefore already close to the ceiling at the start of the period, and little room remained for improvement. The remaining deficit is overwhelmingly rural, which matters for policy: connecting dispersed households costs more per person than extending an urban grid, and it depends on off-grid and mini-grid solutions as much as on national networks. The gap between the two series fell from 19.8 points to 12.9 points, a narrowing, but a gap of this size still marks a sharp difference in daily life between town and countryside.

A headcount of people without electricity is not published in the series examined here. It can only be derived by applying the access percentages to population series, and the derivation carries three cautions. First, the access series ends in 2024, while the rural and urban population series run to 2025, so the two do not refer to the same year; the population figures would have to be matched to 2024 or the access rates assumed unchanged for a year. Second, the definition of rural and urban areas is set by each national statistical office and differs between countries, so a rural share is not strictly comparable across borders. Third, the product of a percentage and a population is an estimate, with the uncertainty of both inputs, and should not be read as a reported count. With these limits, the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 and the urban population of 4,750,578,960 give the scale: a rural deficit of about fifteen per cent applies to a population of roughly 3.5 billion, while a urban deficit of about two per cent applies to roughly 4.8 billion. Rural areas therefore hold the larger share of people without electricity, even though a larger number of people live in cities.

The period also spans two breaks, 2015 and 2020. The first marks the adoption of the goals, the second the pandemic and the economic shocks that followed, which strained public budgets and household incomes and slowed some connection programmes. The annual series shown for the world does not by itself separate those effects, and the endpoints given here do not reveal whether progress paused after 2020. What the endpoints do show is that the average pace of about 0.6 percentage points a year since 2015 would not close a gap of 8.1 points by 2030 without acceleration, and that the final stretch of any access target tends to be the hardest, since the unconnected are the most remote and poorest. The sections that follow turn to where that remaining gap lies.

### Sub-Saharan Africa holds most of the remaining gap

Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for most of the remaining gap. Access in the region stood at 55.1 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 39.2 per cent in 2015. Every other region reported at least 96.8 per cent in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 96.8 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean at 98.0 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 98.6 per cent. Europe and Central Asia reached 100.0 per cent when rounded to one decimal place, and North America stood at 100.0 per cent in both years. South Asia made the largest advance of any region, from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, so the region that once held a large share of the unserved now stands close to universality. The contrast shows that universal access is attainable at scale. It also shows that Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception, not one case among several.

The divide between rural and urban areas is sharpest in this region. Rural access in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 35.7 per cent of the rural population in 2024, against 82.9 per cent of the urban population. In 2015 the rural figure was 18.5 per cent and the urban figure 72.7 per cent. Rural access therefore roughly doubled, a faster proportional gain than urban access, yet nearly two in three rural residents remained without electricity in 2024. The pattern follows from the economics of supply. Grid extension to dispersed settlements costs more per household and recovers less revenue, so utilities and public programmes have tended to serve towns first. Off-grid solar and mini-grids have widened the options in recent years, although the series reports access without separating the technologies behind it.

Income groups show the same shape. Low-income economies, most of which lie in Sub-Saharan Africa, reached 48.8 per cent access in 2024, up from 32.2 per cent in 2015. Rural access in that group stood at 37.1 per cent and urban access at 77.6 per cent. Lower-middle-income economies reached 91.4 per cent, and upper-middle-income and high-income economies stood at 99.3 per cent and 99.97 per cent respectively. The extract of the low-income figures supplied to the bench is truncated in places, so the reading here rests on the values shown and not on a full country list. The gap between the low-income group and the rest is large enough that the truncation does not alter the conclusion.

Combining access rates with population counts indicates the scale of the unserved population. Sub-Saharan Africa had 731422742 rural residents in 2025 and 590231475 urban residents. Rural access of 35.7 per cent and urban access of 82.9 per cent in 2024 imply that roughly 470 million rural residents and roughly 100 million urban residents lacked electricity, a total near 570 million. This is an approximation, because the access rates refer to 2024 and the population counts to 2025, and because national definitions of rural and urban areas differ. Even so, it places the great majority of the world's unserved population in this one region. Rural population there rose from 616454626 in 2015 to 731422742 in 2025, and urban population grew from 408204795 to 590231475. Population growth therefore works against the connection effort: every year of progress in the access rate must also cover new households.

For 2030 the implication is plain. The other regions are within a few points of universality, and their remaining gaps are small, concentrated in particular countries and in rural areas. The target will be met or missed in Sub-Saharan Africa. At the pace of 2015 to 2024, the regional rate rose by about 16 percentage points in nine years, which would leave it well short of 100 per cent in 2030. Closing the gap would require a pace several times faster, concentrated on rural households that are costly to reach.

### Rural areas and South Asia account for the change since 2015

The global gain between 2015 and 2024 was not spread evenly. South Asia supplied the largest single movement. Access in the region rose from 86.5 per cent of the population in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 13 points, and in rural areas from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent. Because South Asia holds a very large rural population, 1,035,602,697 people in 2015 and 1,086,549,811 in 2025, closing its rural gap moved the world average more than any other change. The region is now close to the level of Europe and Central Asia, where access stood at 99.9989 per cent of the population in 2024, so its contribution to further global gains is nearly exhausted.

The rural gap narrowed worldwide. Rural access in the world rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 8 points, against a gain of 5 points for the population as a whole. Rural areas therefore improved faster than the average, which is what a closing gap requires. Rural gains were also large in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, from 87.6 per cent to 94.0 per cent, and in low-income countries, from 17.2 per cent to 37.1 per cent. In Latin America and the Caribbean the rural rate moved from 89.1 per cent to 91.0 per cent, a smaller change, and the region's rural rate remains well below its overall rate of 98.0 per cent in 2024.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows a different pattern. Its overall access rose by about 16 points, from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, and its rural access rose from 18.5 per cent to 35.7 per cent. These are large percentage gains, comparable in size to South Asia's. Yet the rural population of the region grew from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, so a rising rate is applied to a growing base. Rural access of 35.7 per cent in 2024 means that roughly two in three rural residents of the region remained unconnected, and the number of people without access depends on how fast connections grow relative to population. The indicators here are shares, and the section cannot assert from them alone that the absolute number of unconnected rural residents fell in the region.

Urban growth matters as well. The urban population of Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 408,204,795 in 2015 to 590,231,475 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 182,500,508 to 269,862,804. Part of the regional gain in access comes from people moving to towns and cities, where connection is cheaper per household, rather than from connection of people who stayed in rural areas. The data given do not separate the two effects.

Causes call for restraint. The indicators show where access changed and by how much, not which policies produced it. Well-established experience points to national grid extension programmes, falling costs of solar equipment and off-grid systems, and public financing as the usual drivers, but the series cannot attribute the South Asian or African gains to any one of them. Nor do they show a break after 2020 in the figures cited here, since the comparison runs between 2015 and 2024 only.

For 2030, the implication is that the world's average is now governed by one region. South Asia has largely finished its part, East Asia and the Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean are above 98 per cent, and the remaining distance lies in rural Sub-Saharan Africa, where population growth works against each point gained.

### Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030, and proposals follow

Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030 on the evidence of the trend classification. Of the 215 countries assessed, 154 are on track or have already met the target, and they hold 74.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 33 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 15.6 per cent of the population. Another 21 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 8.0 per cent of the population. Two countries are stagnant, with 0.4 per cent, and five are regressing, with 1.4 per cent. The count of countries therefore looks reassuring, while the population shares show that a quarter of the people in the countries assessed live where the present pace will not close the gap.

The aggregate projection agrees. Extending the 2015 to 2024 pace, the world would reach 95.4 per cent access in 2030, and the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.65, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The two groups furthest from the goal are classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 69.2 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.49, and low-income countries would reach 64.4 per cent, with a ratio of 0.48. Latin America and the Caribbean is also classed as marginal, with a ratio of 0.47, but the reason differs: its access was already 98.0 per cent in 2024, so the little that remains moves slowly, and the same pace would bring it to 98.6 per cent in 2030. South Asia, with a ratio of 1.73, and lower middle income countries, with 1.01, are on track, although the lower middle income result rests on a narrow margin.

These readings depend on how target 7.1 is interpreted. The classification treats the target as 100 per cent access by 2030, which is the plainest reading of universal access. A projection above 100, such as South Asia's 109.8 per cent, cannot occur in fact and shows only that a linear extrapolation overshoots a ceiling. The last stretch before universality is also usually harder than the early gains, because the remaining households are the most remote and the poorest, so linear extrapolation may flatter regions near the ceiling. The target further names affordable and reliable energy services. The indicator measures only whether a population has access to electricity. It says nothing about the price paid, the hours of supply or the quality of the connection, so a country classed as on track may still fall short of the full wording of the target.

The implication for 2030 is that the world will not reach universal access on present trends, and that the missing people will be concentrated where the pace is slowest, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries, particularly in rural areas, where access was 35.7 per cent in 2024 for the region. Proposals follow from these findings.

The agencies responsible for the energy goal should add indicators of affordability and reliability, such as the cost of a basic household supply and hours of outage, so that target 7.1 can be assessed in full.
