The target can be read as a global average or as a standard for every country, and the results address the first reading.

w-c03-7-3.text:
### Consumer price inflation stands in for food prices

Target 2.c asks for measures that keep food commodity markets and their derivatives working properly and that give timely access to market information, including on food reserves, so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The target names no numerical threshold and no price index. Its indicator in the global framework is a food price anomalies measure, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold among the series available to this book. Volatility is therefore not measured here directly, and every statement in this section about prices is an indirect reading.

The nearest series is headline consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services for the average consumer. Food is one component of that basket, and its weight varies widely: it is large in low-income households and economies, and small in high-income ones. Headline inflation also contains energy, housing, transport and services, so a rise in the headline rate can follow a fuel shock, a currency depreciation or a rent adjustment with food prices barely moving. The series is read here as a signal of pressure on household budgets, not as a record of food price swings. Regional averages of general inflation say nothing about exposure to food price shocks.

The series also has limits as a measure of volatility. The results available to this section give levels at 2015 and 2025 and measures of dispersion among countries in four selected years. They do not give the year-to-year path, which is what volatility requires. What follows describes the price environment and its unevenness, and does not claim to measure instability over time.

Coverage shapes what can be said. In 2015, 189 countries reported consumer price inflation, and the same number reported in 2016. The count then drifted down, to 185 in 2017, 179 in 2020, 176 in 2024 and 169 in 2025. Across all years 193 countries reported at least once, so some economies have gaps in particular years. The data do not show which economies dropped out, and the reasons for interrupted reporting cannot be read from them. The latest year, 2025, is the thinnest and may be revised as late submissions arrive. Comparisons across the period therefore rest on a changing set of countries, and the parts that follow rely mainly on regional and world aggregates, which are less sensitive to the loss of single reporters.

### World inflation doubled between 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025, a little more than double the earlier rate. Both figures are annual percentage changes in the cost of a general basket of goods and services, so they describe the price level that households face and not the price of food alone. Food is a large part of that basket in poorer economies and a smaller part in richer ones.

The two endpoints conceal the path between them. A comparison of 2015 with 2025 does not show how far inflation fell or rose in the years between, and it should not be read as a steady climb. The period contains the weak price environment of the middle 2010s, the disruption of 2020 and the supply shocks that followed, and an endpoint comparison cannot separate these. Volatility concerns movement from year to year, and the result used here reports levels at two dates only. It therefore shows that the world rate ended the period well above where it began, and it does not measure how much the rate moved in between.

Low-income countries show a different pattern from the world as a whole. Their inflation was 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025, so it fell over the decade while the world rate rose. Lower middle income countries also eased, from 4.0% to 3.6%, whereas upper middle income countries rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high income countries from 0.3% to 2.3%. That fall in the poorest group should not be taken as relief. Low-income countries began from the highest rate of any income group in 2015, and they remain above the world rate in 2025. Households there spend the largest share of their budgets on food, so a given rate of general inflation weighs more heavily on them than on households in richer groups. Coverage also changed: 169 countries reported in 2025, against 189 in 2015, so part of the comparison rests on a smaller set of countries at the later date.

The finding matters for Goal 2 because food access depends on what a household can buy with its income, and persistent price growth erodes that. Yet the series cannot show whether food prices moved more or less than prices generally, nor whether any rise came from commodity markets, exchange rates, energy costs or domestic policy. Those causes bear on whether the measures named in target 2.c are working, and the data used here do not distinguish among them.

### Regions began far apart and converged at a higher level

Regional inflation rates stood far apart in 2015. South Asia recorded consumer price inflation of 4.7% and Sub-Saharan Africa 3.5%, while Europe and Central Asia stood at 0.4% and North America at 0.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.8%, was also among the regions with very low rates. Latin America and the Caribbean (1.9%) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (1.7%) sat between the two groups. Income groups showed the same ordering: low-income economies stood at 5.5% and high-income economies at 0.3%.

By 2025 the regional range was narrower, from 2.0% to 3.7%, against 0.4% to 4.7% in 2015, though the order of the regions had changed. South Asia fell to 3.1% and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged at 3.4%, against 3.5% in 2015. Europe and Central Asia rose from 0.4% to 3.7%, the highest rate among the regions in the latest year, narrowly ahead of Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1.7% to 2.0%. Movements in these three were modest, and all three ended 2025 at about 2%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024; its latest observation is for 2024, not 2025, so it is not strictly comparable in date, but its value is below that of Europe and Central Asia, so the ranking holds.

Income groups tell a similar story. Low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower-middle-income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while upper-middle-income economies rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high-income economies from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing therefore reflects falls in South Asia and in low-income economies together with rises elsewhere; the results do not allow it to be apportioned between them. Energy and food price shocks after 2020 are well-established drivers of rises in importing regions, but these series cannot show how far each region's movement was due to them.

The pattern matters for Target 2.c because the region with the lowest inflation in 2015 had the highest in 2025. Regional average inflation rates are closer together in 2025 than in 2015, but this says nothing about food price shocks, and a regional aggregate cannot show differences between countries or how often households met sharp price spikes within single years. For 2030, no region now enjoys the near-zero inflation seen in 2015.

### Dispersion among countries widened after 2022

The spread of annual consumer price inflation among countries, weighted by population, was almost unchanged between 2015 and 2019 on the Gini measure, at 0.538 in 2015 and 0.538 in 2019. It narrowed to 0.511 in 2022, the year in which price pressures were felt in most economies at once, and then rose sharply to 0.660 in 2024. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the upper end of the distribution, gives a similar picture: 0.621 in 2015, 0.751 in 2019, 0.559 in 2022 and 0.982 in 2024. The 2024 values are the highest of the four years examined on both measures.

The composition of the inequality needs careful reading. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015, 32.0% in 2019 and 38.4% in 2022, and then 35.2% in 2024. Because the between-region share is below half in every year, most of the measured inequality lay within regions throughout, and it was in 2015 that the within-region part was largest, at about three quarters of the index. The fall in the between-region share from 2022 to 2024, while the index itself rose, indicates that the rise in dispersion after 2022 came mainly from differences among countries of the same region, not from a return of the regional gaps. Only four years are examined, so the path between them is not shown. Some economies may have brought inflation down as monetary tightening and falling energy costs worked through, while others continued to face currency depreciation, fiscal strain or conflict. The results do not identify which countries fall in which group, so this explanation rests on well-established patterns and not on the series itself. A regional average conceals the divergence, and a policy aimed at a region as a whole could miss the countries where price stress is most acute.

Three cautions apply. First, the number of countries in the calculation differs by year: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 sample is much smaller than the 189 countries that reported inflation that year, so part of the comparison with later years reflects who is included and not only how prices moved. Second, population weighting gives large economies great influence, and a change in one of them can shift the result. Third, the measure is of general consumer prices, so it is an indirect guide to uneven exposure to food price volatility. For 2030, the widening within regions suggests that the risk of extreme price swings may be concentrated in a minority of countries, though the results do not show how many, and monitoring needs to be national in its detail.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.c cannot be scored from these data. It sets no numerical threshold and can be read in two ways: as the proper functioning of commodity markets and the availability of market information, or as the narrower outcome of limited price volatility. The series available touch only the second reading, and only indirectly, through general consumer prices. World inflation of 1.4% in 2015 and 3.0% in 2025 is consistent with greater price pressure on households. It says nothing about whether markets, derivatives or reserve reporting function better or worse than before, and the two endpoint values do not describe the path between them.

The outlook for 2030 is therefore uncertain in direction. Regional rates in 2015 ran from 0.4% in Europe and Central Asia to 4.7% in South Asia. By 2025 the range was from 2.0% in East Asia and Pacific to 3.7% in Europe and Central Asia, so the regional averages were closer together than in 2015. Europe and Central Asia moved from the lowest rate to the highest; North America's latest value, 2.7% in 2024, lies below it, so the ranking holds. Among income groups, low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower middle income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while high-income economies rose from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing reflects falls in South Asia and in low-income economies and rises elsewhere; the data do not apportion it. Closer regional averages say nothing about exposure to food price shocks. Dispersion among countries points the other way: the population-weighted Gini measure stood at 0.660 in 2024, against 0.511 in 2022, so a narrower spread of group averages sits beside a wider spread of country experience. The data do not show which countries make up the upper tail, and the rates cited here are general consumer prices, not food prices.

Coverage bears on any monitoring to 2030. Countries reporting inflation numbered 189 in 2015 and 169 in 2025, and the data do not say whether the fall in 2025 is permanent or reflects later reporting. The proposals below follow from these limits: they aim to replace a proxy with measures that match the wording of the target, and to keep watch on the countries at the upper end of the distribution.

claims.fact: c03-7.r3: countries reporting in any year
c03-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c03-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2025

proposals: The United Nations Statistics Division and the World Bank should add the food price anomalies indicator for target 2.c to the catalogue, so that the target is monitored with a series that matches its wording.

National statistical offices should publish monthly food consumer price series with the food share of the basket, and national authorities should report food reserve stocks promptly to market information systems.

Governments and development partners should direct monitoring and reserve support to the countries at the upper end of the inflation distribution, and statistical offices that stopped reporting should resume it.
w-c03-7-3.gaps: The data hold no food price series and no measure of commodity market functioning, derivatives or reserve reporting. General consumer inflation stands in for food prices, the countries in the upper tail are not identified, and reporting fell to 169 countries in 2025.

w-c04-4-3.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.57% for the world by 2030. The same reading is applied to every region and income group, so the regional verdicts that follow in this section rest on that single convention. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool, a linear extrapolation of the 2015-2021 pace, places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 divides into three groups: regions where the probability of premature death from the four main non-communicable diseases fell appreciably, regions where it hardly changed, and one region where it rose. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, a respectable decline that still leaves the region above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021. Extended along its own linear path, the region would stand at 18.5% in 2030, against the target value of 12.57% derived from the world baseline. The trend tool places it at a ratio of 0.39 of the pace the target requires.

The two Americas moved least in absolute terms. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America began from the lowest regional level. Its ratio of 0.82 should not be read as near-target progress: it rests on a very small absolute fall from a low base, and the trend tool's ratio is sensitive to such starting points. Latin America and the Caribbean reaches a ratio of 0.50, and linear extension gives 13.9% for it in 2030. Outside the data, it is widely understood that gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking have been offset in part by obesity and diabetes, and by unequal access to treatment; these causes are not measured by the results used here.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, and its pace ratio is negative, at -0.20, which the trend tool labels regression. Linear extension would place the region at 24.0% in 2030. Among regions it had the highest level in 2021, though low-income countries as an income group stood slightly higher, at 23.0%. In 2015 it was marginally below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates between 30 and 70 did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends. Established knowledge points to hypertension, diabetes, air pollution and the cost of long-term treatment as plausible contributors. The period includes the pandemic years, when disrupted screening and chronic care may have raised the 2021 figure; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves its level close to the South Asian one. Its pace ratio is 0.16, and linear extension gives 20.4% in 2030. Measurement is a concern here, since death registration is incomplete and the estimates rely heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, a ratio of 0.22, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, a ratio of 0.00, which is stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. High-income countries alone are classed as on track, with a ratio of 1.93 and a linear value of 11.4% in 2030, which would lie below the target value. The two richer groups improved by about one percentage point each, while the lower-middle group, which contains South Asia's large populations, stood still.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability that all adults experience, but the direction is towards greater inequality. The share of the Theil index lying between regions grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences. All trend readings here are linear extensions of the 2015 to 2021 change, so regional ratios should be read as indications, not forecasts.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.26 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.09 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted. The world value stood at 18.3% in 2021, against a target value of 12.57% for 2030. The trend tool expects 17.5% in 2030 at the post-2015 rate.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. The following explanations rest on general knowledge, not on any result of this section, and the data do not separate them. Earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from better treatment of heart disease, and such gains meet diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The years 2020 and 2021 coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions. The series cannot isolate these effects from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.0016 with a p-value of 0.70 and an R-squared of 0.001. The coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measures point the same way, though they are not the same statistic. The convergence test reports a coefficient of variation of 0.36 in 2015 and 0.38 in 2021, computed across countries without population weights. The spread tool, which weights countries by population, reports a coefficient of variation of 0.27 in 2015 and 0.28 in 2021. The levels differ because of the weighting, but both rise. The population-weighted Gini coefficient moved from 0.15 to 0.16, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 27.0% to 33.1%. Relative spread widened slightly, and a growing part of it lies between regions, not within them. For a target defined in relative terms this matters, because a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and no systematic acceleration in such countries appears in the convergence result.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.10 and the Kendall coefficient is 0.07. Both are weak. Both changes are taken as end value minus start value, so a rise in coverage and a fall in mortality carry opposite signs. If coverage gains went with larger mortality falls, the correlation would be negative. The weak positive value gives no support for that expectation over this short window, though it is too small to show the opposite either.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.25 by the Spearman measure and -0.17 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is modest in size, larger than the correlation of changes but far from strong. It describes a cross-section in which income, age structure, the wider health system and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together, and it cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented. The mortality series is modelled by the World Health Organization from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths are read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021, and the trend projection, a linear extrapolation of the 2015 to 2021 pace, reaches 17.5% in 2030. The global ratio of progress is 0.22, where a ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target. At the observed rate the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction, and the distance still to be closed exceeds the distance covered since 2015.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is, and they need careful reading because a ratio depends on the starting level as well as on the pace. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, records the largest fall of any region, from 17.5% to 15.7%, and is expected to reach 13.4% in 2030. North America also has a ratio of 0.82, but it rests on a very small absolute movement, from 13.6% in 2015 to 13.3% in 2021, from a low base already near the threshold. Its expected 12.8% in 2030 should not be read as near-target progress. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6%, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.50, 13.9%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 0.39, is expected to reach 18.5%, which is marginal progress. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030, but they began from 13.8%, already close to the threshold, so the class reflects the starting point as much as the pace.

That points to an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions above 22% would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above applies the global reading to every region. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, rising from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, with an expected 24.0% in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnation, with an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22 and an expected 21.5%. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest, and the gap between income groups is on course to persist.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none. The correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment, chronic respiratory care or the quality of care. A weak link does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the coverage measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality, named in the section's title, cannot be treated here. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. The omission is a gap in this account, not evidence that the matter is minor. Mental health is part of the wording of target 3.4, and the indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover it.

The proposals follow from these findings. The first two rest on the section's results; the third rests on established knowledge about prevention, not on a result of this section.

claims.fact: c04-4.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c04-4.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2021
c04-4.r5: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan expected 2030
c04-4.r5: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan ratio
c04-4.r5: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan ratio
c04-4.r5: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan expected 2030

proposals: National health ministries in the regions classed as stagnation or regression, notably South Asia and lower middle income countries, should set explicit national targets for premature non-communicable disease mortality and report progress annually against them.

The United Nations statistical bodies and the World Health Organization should state in the indicator framework whether the one-third reduction is measured from a global or a regional baseline, and from which year, so that classifications are comparable.

Ministries of health, with donors, should expand prevention and treatment of hypertension, diabetes and tobacco dependence, and extend coverage measures to cancer and chronic respiratory care; the case rests on established knowledge about prevention, not on a result of this section.
w-c04-4-3.gaps: The results hold no analysis of suicide mortality, so its level, its difference between men and women and its change since 2015 are not covered, and mental health is not captured by the premature mortality indicator. The indicator is modelled, its latest year is 2021 so the full effect of the pandemic and later years is unseen, and the coverage sub-index omits cancer and chronic respiratory care. The target's baseline is not specified, so the classification of regions depends on the reading chosen.

w-c08-5-1.text:
### Renewable generation has roughly doubled worldwide since 2015

The world share of electricity produced from renewable sources other than hydroelectric power rose from 6.6 % in 2015 to 12.4 % in 2021. The share has therefore come close to doubling in six years. The figure comes from 208 reporting countries in 2021, and the series ends that year, so nothing in it describes the years since. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks of 2022, cannot be read from this indicator.

The indicator needs careful reading. It measures the share of non-hydroelectric renewables (chiefly wind, solar, geothermal and biomass) in total electricity production. It does not measure installed generating capacity, nor the quantity of electricity generated. A rising share is consistent with new capacity being built, and the growth of wind and solar plant is the usual explanation in the wider literature. But the data do not observe that capacity. A share can also rise when other generation falls, or when total output stagnates. Growth in generating capacity is thus inferred here, not observed.

The exclusion of hydroelectric power also shapes the picture. Large hydropower is a long-established source in many developing countries, and it is left out. The indicator therefore captures the newer renewables, whose costs have fallen considerably over the past decade, and it understates the renewable contribution of countries that depend heavily on dams.

The trend tool classes the world as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.1 for the period. Target 7.b carries no numerical value, so this verdict only says the share is moving in the desired direction. It is not a comparison with a quantified goal, and the word target should be read in that sense. The global figure also averages very different experiences, which the next part sets out by region and income group. A world share cannot show whether developing countries, the subject of targets 7.a and 7.b, have shared in the gain.

For 2030 the global direction is encouraging but incompletely observed. A doubling in six years shows that a rapid change in the electricity mix is possible. Whether it has continued, and whether it has reached the countries with the least infrastructure, is a question this series cannot answer from 2021 onward.

### Regions and income groups started from different levels and moved at different speeds

Regional starting points differed widely in 2015, and the gaps in levels have not closed. East Asia & Pacific rose from 4.8% of electricity production in 2015 to 12.0% in 2021, and Latin America & Caribbean rose from 6.9% to 15.1% over the same years. South Asia moved from 4.6% to 8.5%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan began from 0.6% and reached 2.9%, the lowest level among the regions reported. Sub-Saharan Africa started at 2.1% and stood at 4.3% in 2021. All figures here are shares of total electricity production from non-hydroelectric renewable sources.

Income groups show the same pattern more sharply. Upper middle income countries rose from 4.6% to 11.9%, and lower middle income countries from 4.1% to 7.3%. High income countries rose from 8.6% to 14.1%. Low income countries moved the other way, from 0.7% in 2015 to 0.5% in 2021. The poorest countries therefore did not share in the expansion of wind, solar, geothermal and biomass generation that lifted the world figure. Well-established context points to the cost of capital, small and weakly financed grids, and limited public budgets as barriers to new plant in these economies, though the data here do not test those causes.

The trend assessment for the share of renewables in total final energy consumption must be read with care. Low income countries show the highest share, 77.0% in 2015 and 74.6% in 2020, and the trend reads as regression, at a rate of -0.0064. That level does not signal modern clean energy. In these countries the share is dominated by traditional biomass, chiefly wood and charcoal burned for cooking, which is neither clean nor efficient and carries health and forest costs. A falling share there can even accompany a shift to commercial fuels. The indicator also leaves target 7.2 open to more than one reading, since no numeric 2030 value is set for it. The tool classes the World, East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, and upper middle income groups as on track, while Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and lower middle income countries are marked as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The convergence result tempers any reading of catching up. Across 208 countries, the slope of annual change on starting level between 2015 and 2021 was -0.004, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001. No convergence can be distinguished from zero. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021, so spread relative to the mean narrowed. The two results are compatible: the mean rose, which shrinks relative spread, without starting position predicting the pace of change. The data end in 2021, so they say nothing about changes since the pandemic.

### Private investment and concessional finance moved unevenly

Private participation in energy investment moved unevenly across developing regions between 2015 and 2024. In Latin America & Caribbean, investment with private participation fell from US$11.87 billion in 2015 to US$8.40 billion in 2024. South Asia moved the other way, rising from US$2.39 billion to US$3.45 billion. The two regions therefore ended the period on different paths, and the regional total for Latin America & Caribbean is lower than at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals period.

The income groups show a sharper divide. Upper middle income countries rose from US$31.02 billion in 2015 to US$58.39 billion in 2024, so private capital in energy concentrated where borrowing conditions, market size and regulatory frameworks are most developed. Lower middle income countries barely moved, from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion, in current dollars. Because the figures are not adjusted for inflation, the lower middle income total is likely to have lost purchasing power over the period, though the extract gives no deflated series to show it. Low income countries are not shown in the extract, so the position of the poorest economies cannot be read from these results.

Coverage limits what can be concluded. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, and the Private Participation in Infrastructure database records only projects with a contractual private role in low- and middle-income countries. Public investment, which carries much of energy infrastructure in the poorest countries, is outside it. Annual totals can also swing with a few large projects, so the endpoints of 2015 and 2024 do not describe the years between.

Concessional finance is harder to assess. Net official development assistance to the least developed countries was reported by 32 countries in 2023, but the series covers all aid and not aid for energy. The extract therefore gives no clean energy figure for concessional support, and it cannot be said whether international cooperation on clean energy research and technology, the subject of target 7.a, has grown. Targets 7.a and 7.b are worded without a numerical threshold, such as a sum to be mobilised or a capacity to be installed. Progress can therefore be described but not scored as met or missed, and any judgement depends on how expand, enhance and facilitate are read.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to rising renewable shares worldwide, but the gains are uneven and the finance behind them is concentrated. Renewable energy consumption as a share of total final energy consumption is classed as on track or target met for the world, at a trend rate of 0.0255. The same classification applies to East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, high income countries and upper middle income countries. Low income countries show regression, at a rate of -0.0064. Lower middle income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa show marginal progress, and the tool states that significant acceleration is needed. Note that the trend tool was run with no quantified target, so these classifications measure direction and pace and not distance from a defined goal.

Private investment follows the same pattern. Upper middle income countries recorded US$58.39 billion of energy investment with private participation in 2024, against US$31.02 billion in 2015. Lower middle income countries moved from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion over the same years, which is close to flat in current dollars. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, so the totals describe the projects recorded and not all investment. Official assistance cannot be read in the same way: the series for net ODA to the least developed countries shows 32 reporting countries in 2023, and the result gives no regional or income-group levels. Whether concessional finance has offset the weak private flows to poorer countries therefore cannot be shown here.

The spread of non-hydroelectric renewable shares across countries has narrowed, with the coefficient of variation falling from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021 across 208 countries. The slope of change on starting level is -0.0040, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001, so it cannot be distinguished from zero. The narrowing in spread is therefore not evidence that low starters are catching up systematically.

Targets 7.a and 7.b carry no quantified goal, so progress can be read in more than one way. Rising shares, rising private investment in some regions and falling investment in others can each be cited as success or failure, depending on the threshold chosen. Installed capacity in developing countries, the quantity named in the section's question, is not among the series examined, and the data cannot show it directly. For 2030, the pattern implies that the countries furthest behind, low income and lower middle income, are the ones where pace is weakest and private finance is thinnest.

claims.fact: c08-5.r2: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c08-5.r2: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2021

proposals: The World Bank, the International Energy Agency and the OECD should report installed generating capacity and clean energy finance flows to least developed countries on a consistent annual basis, so that targets 7.a and 7.b can be tracked directly.

Bilateral donors and multilateral development banks should direct concessional finance, and the guarantees that draw in private capital, towards lower middle income and low income countries, where private investment has been flat and renewable progress weakest.
The United Nations Statistical Commission should set a measurable threshold for targets 7.a and 7.b, so that progress is not open to competing readings.
The agencies that compile energy statistics should report the non-biomass renewable share separately, since the headline renewable share in low income countries is dominated by traditional biomass.
w-c08-5-1.gaps: The shelf holds no series for installed generating capacity in developing countries, and none for clean energy finance flows by recipient country or by technology. The private investment series covers only countries reporting to the PPI database, and net ODA to the least developed countries has no regional or income-group breakdown in the results. Non-hydroelectric renewable shares end in 2021 and renewable consumption shares in 2022, so recent years are not described. Targets 7.a and 7.b have no quantified goal, so no trajectory to 2030 can be measured against them.

w-c04-9-2.text:
### The global picture rests on rates, not counts

The question posed for this section asks for a number of deaths. The evidence retrieved cannot supply one. The only result available is a rate: deaths attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene per 100,000 population, for 2019, across 183 countries. A rate is a count divided by population, so it cannot be turned back into a count without population figures that this result does not carry. No absolute total of deaths from unsafe water appears in the retrieved material, and none is offered here. The level of the rate, whether global or national, is likewise not among the retrieved results; only the inequality of the rate between countries is.

The question is therefore only partly answerable from what was retrieved, and the air pollution half is not answered at all. The shelf holds a series on the mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, age-standardised, as well as a series on mean annual exposure to fine particulate matter. Neither was retrieved as a result for this section. Nothing is therefore stated about how many people die from air pollution, how fast the rate is falling, or which regions carry most of it. Any statement on those points would rest on no evidence in hand, and the section declines to make one. Target 3.9 also covers hazardous chemicals and soil pollution, for which no result was retrieved either.

This limit bears on how Target 3.9 is read. The target calls for a substantial reduction in the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and from air, water and soil pollution. The wording can be read as a count, in which case population growth works against progress even when conditions improve, or as a rate, in which case a falling risk counts as success even if the number of deaths stays high. The wording does not settle the matter. The indicator series the World Bank reports measures a rate, and it is the rate that the evidence here can describe. A reader should take any later statement about progress in this section as a statement about risk per head of population, not about the total toll.

The one result that exists shows how unevenly that risk is spread. Across the 183 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the unsafe-water mortality rate in 2019 is 0.535, and the coefficient of variation is 1.03. A coefficient of variation above one means that the spread of national rates is wider than their average. Because the measures are weighted by population, they describe how unequal the rate is among people living in different countries; they do not by themselves establish how many countries hold high rates. The next part examines how much of this inequality is a matter of region.

### Regions explain most of the inequality between countries

Most of the measured inequality in the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate lies between regions. In 2019, across 183 countries, the Theil index of the rate was 0.502 and the Gini coefficient was 0.535. Both measures weight countries by population, so they describe how the rate is distributed among people rather than among states. A populous country with a high rate raises both figures more than a small one would. The coefficient of variation was 1.03, so the standard deviation of the rate was slightly larger than its mean, which indicates a wide spread of values.

The between-region share of the Theil index was 75.2% in 2019. Regional grouping therefore accounts for about three quarters of the measured inequality, and differences among countries within the same region account for the remaining quarter. This is a descriptive split. It does not test why regions differ, and it contains no measure of income, infrastructure or health services. Established knowledge suggests plausible causes: diarrhoeal disease and related infections depend on piped water, sewerage, nutrition and primary care, and these tend to be shared among neighbouring countries at similar stages of development. That is context offered as a hypothesis, not a finding of this result.

The split matters for how reporting and action are organised. Where most inequality lies between regions, regional figures are needed to see where the gap is, and the global average alone can hide regions with high rates. This result does not identify those regions, give their rates or show how many deaths occur in them. The remaining quarter, lying within regions, shows that countries in the same region still differ, and the countries that do better than their neighbours merit study for policies that can be copied.

The limits of the result are plain. A decomposition reports a share, not a ranking, so it names no region or country. It covers one year, 2019, and so says nothing about change since 2015 or about the effects of events after 2020. The retrieved results do not document how the underlying estimates were produced; from general knowledge of the source, such estimates are modelled in places where death registration is incomplete, and the figures are best read as an indication of structure rather than a count of deaths.

### Change since 2015 cannot be measured from one year

The single observation for 2019 describes a position, not a movement. Target 3.9 calls for a substantial reduction in deaths from pollution and contamination by 2030, and a reduction can only be shown by comparing at least two points in time. The result retrieved for this section holds one year, 2019, for 183 countries. No statement is therefore made here on whether mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene fell after 2015, nor on how the years after 2020 compare with those before. The result gives no earlier or later reading for this indicator, and an inference from a single cross-section would be a guess presented as a finding.

Three kinds of evidence would be needed to turn the position into a trend. The first is a series of annual rates from 2015 onward, ideally with earlier years too, so that a pre-2015 trajectory exists against which the post-2015 period can be judged. The shelf lists the indicator with 2019 as its latest year, which means that the period of the pandemic and its disruption to health services, to water programmes and to household incomes is not observed at all. The second is a count of deaths. A rate can fall while the number of deaths stays level or rises if populations grow, and the reverse is also possible, so the two answer different questions. The third is an air pollution indicator read alongside the water measure. The shelf holds a rate of deaths attributed to household and ambient air pollution and a measure of mean exposure to fine particles, but neither was returned as a result for this section. The question on air pollution is therefore not answered here, and the two halves of the question cannot be set side by side.

Caution is also due on causes. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2%, and the Gini coefficient is 0.535. These figures show that the rate is unequally distributed among people in 2019 and that regional grouping accounts for most of that measured inequality. They do not show why. Water and sanitation infrastructure, income, the quality of primary health care and the treatment of diarrhoeal disease are well established as bearing on such deaths, but these are plausible influences that the decomposition does not test, and one year's spread cannot separate them from the age structure of populations, from climate or from conflict. The coefficient of variation, 1.03, confirms the dispersion without explaining it.

For 2030 the consequence is that progress on this part of target 3.9 cannot at present be judged from the evidence in hand. The target also does not define what "substantially" means, and it can be read against a baseline of 2015, of an earlier year or of the latest available year. Until a series spanning those years is assembled, any statement on whether the goal is on course would be unsupported.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 3.9 asks for a substantial reduction by 2030, and the only evidence analysed for this section is one year of one rate. In 2019, across 183 countries, the between-region share of the Theil index for mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene was 75.2%. Most of the measured inequality in that rate therefore lies between regions rather than within them. The result does not name the regions, give their rates or show why they differ. Differences in income, infrastructure and health services are plausible explanations, but this decomposition does not test them.

The Gini coefficient was 0.535 and the coefficient of variation was 1.03. Both are population-weighted measures of how unequal the rate is among countries, and they show that the rate is unevenly spread. They do not show where the highest rates lie or how many deaths occur in any region. Where rates are unequal, a global average can hide regions with higher rates per 100,000 population. This result does not identify those regions, so it cannot say where avoidable deaths are concentrated.

This bears on how 2030 is judged. The target text does not say whether the reduction is to be assessed in numbers of deaths or in rates, and it sets no baseline or percentage. Both readings are defensible and they can diverge when populations grow. A fall in the rate with a growing population may leave the count little changed. The 2019 evidence offers no trend since 2015 or 2020, so whether the target is on course cannot be stated from it.

The question also asks about air pollution. The air pollution mortality series, the PM2.5 exposure series and the unintentional poisoning series are held on the shelf but were not analysed here. The conclusions above concern the water, sanitation and hygiene component only, and no count of deaths is given for any component.
proposals: National statistical offices and the World Health Organization should publish mortality from unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene, and from air pollution, as annual series with regional breakdowns and death counts, since the 2019 decomposition shows most inequality lies between regions and regional figures are needed to see where the gap is.

The United Nations bodies that monitor Target 3.9 should state whether the reduction is to be judged in rates or in numbers of deaths, and fix a baseline year, so that progress to 2030 can be assessed unambiguously.
Regional commissions and donors should set regional milestones in rates and counts once regional data are published, and not in inequality measures such as the Gini coefficient or the Theil share.
w-c04-9-2.gaps: The analysis holds one year, 2019, for one rate, so there is no trend since 2015 or 2020 and no regional rates. No count of deaths is given for any cause. The air pollution mortality, PM2.5 exposure and unintentional poisoning series were not analysed, and soil pollution and hazardous chemicals beyond poisoning are not covered. The retrieved results do not document how the estimates were produced.

w-c04-11-3.text:
### Immunisation and maternal and child services are largely flat at the global level

The nearest measure the shelf holds for immunisation and related services is the universal health coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health. It combines four tracer indicators: family planning, pregnancy care, child immunisation and child treatment, and it is scored from 0 to 100 index points. It is not a direct measure of vaccine coverage, because immunisation is only one of the four components. A movement in the index may therefore reflect changes in family planning or in the treatment of childhood illness rather than in vaccination. The reading offered here is of service coverage in general, with immunisation as one part of it.

Target 3.b can be read in more than one way. It concerns research and development, access to affordable essential medicines and vaccines, and the terms of the Doha Declaration. Coverage of services is an outcome of access, not a measure of research effort or of the price of medicines. The index speaks to access only in part, and the other elements of the target are not captured by any series held here.

At the global level the trend classification is regression, at a rate of -0.0017. The index values behind the regional classes are not carried among the facts of this section, so levels are not quoted here, and no comparison of levels between groups is made; only the classes and rates are given. The change is small. Its significance lies in what it fails to show: there is no sign of the steady gain that a fifteen-year agenda implies, and the world, on this measure, has slipped slightly.

Most regions are flat. East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, high income countries, North America, upper middle income countries and low income countries are all classified as stagnating, each with a rate of zero. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also stagnant. Europe & Central Asia shows a small positive rate of 0.0031, which is still classed as stagnation. A rate of zero means that whatever gaps exist between groups were not closing over the period measured.

The worst movements are in lower middle income countries and South Asia. The lower middle income group has a rate of -0.0037 and South Asia a rate of -0.0053, and both are classed as regression. Disruption to routine services during the pandemic after 2020 is a recognised cause of lost coverage in many countries, and populous countries weigh heavily in group averages. The results do not separate the period before 2020 from the period after, so the share of the fall due to the pandemic cannot be stated. Sub-Saharan Africa is the only region with a clear gain, at a rate of 0.0099, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed.

The country classification confirms the pattern. Of 193 countries assessed, 11 are on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population. Another 9, with 3.1 per cent, show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 37, with 14.4 per cent, show marginal progress. Stagnation covers 105 countries and 48.1 per cent of the population, and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. The index carries no fixed 2030 target, so these classes rest on the direction of travel to date, not on a stated goal; 'on track' here means a rising trend, not a target met. Stagnation and regression together cover more than three in four people, 77.6 per cent of the population. The classes describe past direction only; no projection to 2030 is made here.

### Health spending has risen in dollar terms but barely as a share of output

Domestic general government health expenditure per capita rose from 589.2 current US dollars in 2015 to 803.7 in 2023 for the world as a whole. The series is in current dollars and is not adjusted for inflation or for population structure, so part of the rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger volume of care. The movement also says nothing about how the money was used.

Measured against output, the picture is much flatter. Current health expenditure was 9.7 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2023. Spending has therefore grown roughly in step with the economies that carry it. A rising dollar figure alongside a stable share means that health has held its place in national budgets and household outlays but has not gained priority. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, and a global share that moves by less than half a percentage point over eight years cannot be read as that kind of increase. The share also includes private and external spending, while the per capita series covers only domestic government spending, so the two measure different things and are not directly comparable.

The global average conceals a division by income. In high income countries the share of GDP rose from 12.0 per cent to 12.5 per cent, and in upper middle income countries from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent. In lower middle income countries it fell from 3.9 per cent to 3.7 per cent, and in low income countries from 5.4 per cent to 4.6 per cent. The fall among the poorest runs against the direction target 3.c requires. The data do not show why it fell, nor which source of spending changed, because the share covers all current spending. Faster growth elsewhere in the economy, reduced external funding, debt pressure and conflict are plausible contributors as context, but none can be separated here.

Regional shares tell a similar story. North America stood at 16.0 per cent in 2015 and 16.3 per cent in 2023. South Asia declined from 3.5 per cent to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent in both years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 5.4 per cent to 5.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 6.4 per cent to 6.8 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 9.3 per cent to 9.6 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 7.8 per cent to 7.9 per cent, all by small margins.

The period after 2020 matters for interpretation. The pandemic raised health spending in many countries and depressed GDP in the same years, which lifts the share temporarily. The 2023 values are therefore not a clean continuation of the pre-2020 path. Coverage of the latest year is also thin: only 22 countries reported the share for 2024, and only 7 reported domestic government spending per capita, so 2023 is the last year that supports regional comparison.

The results describe movement to 2023 and make no projection to 2030. A financing share that has hardly moved gives little ground for expecting a step change without a deliberate rise in public priority.

### Regions and countries differ by orders of magnitude

North America spent 6,959.0 current US dollars per head of domestic government money on health in 2023, against 30.8 dollars in South Asia and 31.7 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa. The top and bottom figures therefore differ by a factor of more than two hundred. Europe and Central Asia stood at 2,178.0 dollars, East Asia and Pacific at 571.7 dollars, Latin America and the Caribbean at 415.7 dollars, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 190.2 dollars. By income group the gradient is as steep: high-income countries spent 3,847.3 dollars, upper middle income countries 338.9 dollars, lower middle income countries 30.9 dollars and low-income countries 7.3 dollars. These are current dollars at market exchange rates, so they understate what a dollar buys in poorer countries, where wages and many services cost less. Even so, a gap of this size is unlikely to be closed by any such adjustment.

The movement since 2015 widens the distance in absolute terms. North America started from 4,587.0 dollars and reached 6,959.0 dollars by 2023, while Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 29.7 to 31.7 dollars and low-income countries from 7.0 to 7.3 dollars. South Asia is the exception among the poorer regions: its figure rose from 14.7 to 30.8 dollars, though from a very small base. The pattern is one of large gains in the richer groups and near-stillness at the bottom. Rapid population growth in low-income countries may also mean that a flat per-capita figure conceals a rising national outlay, though the results do not test this.

The share of output spent on health gives a less favourable picture for the poorest. Low-income countries fell from 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 4.6 per cent in 2023, and lower middle income countries from 3.9 to 3.7 per cent. High-income countries rose from 12.0 to 12.5 per cent and upper middle income countries from 5.5 to 6.0 per cent. South Asia slipped from 3.5 to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed. On this measure the poorest groups moved the other way. The results do not identify the reasons. Weak tax bases, debt service and the strain of the pandemic and later price rises on public budgets are commonly cited as context, but none is tested here. The results do not separate public, private and external spending, so they do not show how each source changed. Coverage of the latest year is thin: only 7 countries had a 2024 value for domestic government spending per head and 22 for the share of GDP.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the regional averages. For domestic government health spending per head, 142 of the 193 countries assessed were classed as on track, holding 80.1 per cent of their combined population. No target value is set for this series, so the classes describe direction and pace of change in current dollars, not distance from a goal, and they do not show that the financing aim of target 3.c has been met. A further 12 countries showed moderate progress, and 34 were in regression, holding 14.0 per cent of the population. Rising dollar spending in most countries therefore coexists with a sizeable minority of countries, and of people, where it fell.

The service coverage sub-index is flatter. Only 11 of the 193 countries were on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population, while stagnation covered 105 countries and 48.1 per cent of the population and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. The stagnation and regression classes together hold more than three in four people. The regression class is large in population because it includes South Asia and the lower middle income group, where the regional indices fell. The two series are not linked in these results, so they cannot show why rising spending in many countries sits beside flat coverage; delivery, workforce and reach of services are plausible candidates, but the data do not test them.

### Spending has not converged and the workforce cannot be measured well

Spending per head at purchasing power parity shows no sign of countries drawing together. Across 190 countries, the regression of growth in current health expenditure per capita (international dollars) between 2015 and 2023 on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00001, with a p-value of 0.997 and an R-squared of 0.0. Countries that began with low spending did not grow faster than those that began high, and the starting level explains none of the variation in growth. The coefficient of variation, a measure of relative dispersion, moved from 1.24 in 2015 to 1.20 in 2023. That change is small and is not backed by a convergence relationship, so it should be read as little more than stability in the spread.

The result matters for target 3.c, which calls for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed countries and small island developing States. Convergence would be the sign that the gap in resources was narrowing. Its absence means that the large differences in spending described earlier in this section persist through 2023, the last year tested. Health budgets depend on national income, on the capacity of governments to raise revenue and on debt service burdens; this is background knowledge and not a result of the test. The shocks of 2020 fell on all budgets, but countries with more fiscal room could more easily sustain health spending. The test here is across countries and does not separate these channels, and it covers 2015 to 2023 only, so any later change is not captured. It shows direction to date and makes no projection to 2030.

The health workforce is harder still to assess. The shelf holds one series on community health workers per 1,000 people, and it is thin. Only 64 countries report in any year of the series. The number reporting in a single year ranges from 3 in 2002 and 3 in 2014 to 29 in 2004 and 21 in 2008. After 2010 the count never exceeds 13: 6 in 2011, 7 in 2012, 6 in 2013, 3 in 2014, 4 in 2015 and 6 in 2016. The latest year in the series is 2016, so nothing is recorded for the period after 2015 beyond those few reporters, and nothing after 2020.

With so few reporters, and with a different set of countries in each year, a change in the average could not be told from a change in who reports. No trend in workforce density, upward or downward, can be asserted, and no judgement can be made on whether the recruitment and retention called for in target 3.c is occurring. Community health workers are also defined differently from country to country, under varied national titles, which weakens comparison even where data exist. The series also says nothing of doctors, nurses or midwives. The finding is that spending can be measured and has not converged, whereas the workforce, the input on which services most depend, cannot be measured well enough to be followed towards 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Targets 3.b and 3.c ask for more vaccines and medicines for developing countries, and for substantially more health financing and workforce. The shelf supports only a partial reading. The financing evidence is a direction-of-travel test on current dollars, with no target attached, so it cannot show that the financing half of 3.c has been met. It shows that 142 of 193 countries, holding 80.1% of the assessed population, are rising in domestic government health spending per head. That majority is dominated by countries that already spend most. A further 34 countries, with 14.0% of the population, show regression, and these are the systems where the target is most at risk.

For 3.b the shelf holds only the composite reproductive, maternal, newborn and child index, which is not a measure of vaccine coverage or of access to medicines. Read as a proxy, it is discouraging. Only 11 countries, with 5.0% of the population, are on track, while 105, with 48.1%, are stagnating and 31, with 29.5%, are regressing. The trend classes show direction of travel from 2015 to 2023 and no projection to 2030 is made here. They do show that, to date, most of the assessed population has seen no gain in these services, and that acceleration would be needed for any improvement by 2030. The index is consistent with disrupted routine services after 2020, but it cannot attribute the pattern to vaccines, and it cannot be linked to spending with the series held.

The share of output devoted to health shows that dollar growth alone is not sufficient. Low-income countries fell from 5.4% of GDP in 2015 to 4.6% in 2023, while high-income countries rose from 12.0% to 12.5%. South Asia's share slipped from 3.5% to 3.3%, even though its per-head public spending rose from a very low base. The share covers all current health spending and does not separate public, private and external sources, so it cannot show which source moved. Why the share lagged is a matter for national studies: tax capacity, debt service and competing pressures after 2020 are the usual explanations, and none can be tested with these series.

The workforce half of 3.c cannot be judged. Community health workers were reported by only 64 countries in any year, by no more than 29 in any single year, and by just 6 countries in 2016, the last year of record. A target to recruit and retain workers cannot be monitored from a series that thin. Coverage for 2024 is also thin, resting on 7 reporting countries for domestic government spending and 22 for spending as a share of GDP, so the latest picture is provisional.
