w-c07-1-2.text:
### Safely managed drinking water reached 73.7% of the world in 2024

The share of the world's people using safely managed drinking water stood at 73.7% in 2024, up from 67.7% in 2015. Roughly three in four people now have water that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from faecal and priority chemical contamination. The remaining quarter rely on sources that fail one or more of those three conditions, or on sources that are not improved at all.

The indicator is demanding by design. It sits at the top of the ladder used by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, above basic service, which requires only an improved source within a thirty-minute round trip. A household with a piped connection that supplies water only a few hours a day, or a borehole whose water carries contamination, counts as basic at best. For that reason the safely managed share is lower than the basic share, and progress on it is slower and harder to measure, because testing water quality and continuity requires surveys and regulatory records that many countries do not hold in full.

Target 6.1 calls for universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all by 2030. The word universal can be read in more than one way. This book takes the plainest reading, 100% of the population using safely managed services, and measures distance against that line. A looser reading would accept a very high threshold, such as 95%, or would count basic service as sufficient. Affordability and equity, the other elements of the target, have no series on the shelf, so the safely managed share captures only part of what the target asks.

Coverage of reporting is broad but not complete. In 2015, 150 countries reported a value and in 2024, 148 did, with 151 reporting in at least one year. The series reaches back to 2000, when 144 countries reported, so the years before the goals were adopted can be set beside the years after. The slight fall in the number of reporting countries after 2016 is small, yet it matters: the missing cases are not drawn at random, and countries with weak statistical systems are often those with the lowest access. The world figure is therefore best read as a firm estimate for the countries that report, and a less certain one for the whole population.

### Regions differ by more than sixty percentage points

The distance between the best and worst served regions in 2024 is larger than sixty percentage points. North America stood at 97.4% and Europe and Central Asia at 92.5%, so that in both regions safely managed water is close to the norm. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 32.4%, which means that roughly two in three people in the region still depend on water that is not on premises, not available when needed or not free from contamination. In 2015 North America stood at 96.3% and Sub-Saharan Africa at 26.4%. The gap between the top and bottom regions therefore narrowed between 2015 and 2024, from 69.9 to 65.0 percentage points, but it remains very large.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 79.0% in 2024, South Asia 77.6% and East Asia and Pacific 75.2%, all within four percentage points of one another and a little above the world figure of 73.7%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stand apart from them at 65.6%, up only from 64.7% in 2015. That region began the period at a level close to South Asia (63.1%) and East Asia and Pacific (65.1%), and has since fallen well behind them. Water scarcity, conflict and weak utilities in some of its countries are possible contributing factors, offered as context only; the data do not separate these causes or show that any of them explains the pattern.

The pattern is one of high-income regions near saturation and low-income regions far from it. Europe and Central Asia gained 1.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2024, and North America 1.1 points, because little room remains. The income groups show the same ordering: 95.8% in high-income countries against 33.0% in low-income countries in 2024. The remaining shortfall in wealthy regions is typically a matter of private wells, small rural systems and contamination, rather than absent infrastructure, whereas in poorer regions it reflects missing networks, intermittent supply and unmonitored quality.

The spread among countries tells a consistent story. Across the 148 countries reporting in 2024, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of safely managed water use was 0.222, down from 0.246 across 150 countries in 2015. The fall is real but modest, and it indicates that countries have become somewhat more alike in coverage. The Theil index also fell, from 0.107 to 0.093. Inequality among countries therefore narrowed, though from a high base and not by much.

Regions remain the main source of that inequality. Differences between regions accounted for 59.4% of the Theil index in 2024, down from 61.7% in 2015. A share this large means that knowing the region of a country explains most of the variation in its coverage, and that the remainder lies in differences among countries within regions. The small decline in the between-region share is consistent with the gains in South Asia and East Asia and Pacific, though the measure does not itself show what produced it.

These comparisons carry a caution. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, and the 148 countries reporting in 2024 are fewer than all countries, so regional figures rest partly on estimation where data are sparse. For 2030 the implication is plain: a regional gap of this size cannot close in the years that remain at the pace observed since 2015, and the burden falls most heavily on Sub-Saharan Africa.

### Gains came from South Asia and East Asia, and convergence is weak

The largest absolute gains came from two regions. South Asia rose from 63.1% in 2015 to 77.6% in 2024, a gain of 14.4 percentage points, and moved from below the world average to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 65.1% to 75.2%, a gain of 10.1 points. Because these regions hold a very large share of the world's population, their progress is consistent with most of the rise in the global figure from 67.7% to 73.7%, though the tools used here do not decompose that rise. The world average therefore says more about where population lives than about how widely progress was shared. Established explanations point to sustained public investment in piped supply, household connections and rural programmes for boreholes and treatment; these are context only, since the data used here do not separate such causes.

Other regions moved far less. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 75.2% to 79.0%, a gain of 3.8 points. Europe and Central Asia moved from 91.2% to 92.5%, and North America from 96.3% to 97.4%, the pattern expected where coverage is already high and the remaining gaps are hard to close. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stand apart: the regional share edged from 64.7% to 65.6%, a gain of under one point in nine years, from a start close to that of South Asia and East Asia and Pacific. The trend tool classes the region as stagnating, with a ratio of 0.043 of the distance to the target covered. Conflict, displacement, water scarcity and weak utility finance are commonly cited obstacles in parts of it, but the regional aggregate combines very different countries and the data here cannot attribute the stagnation to any of them.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.4% to 32.4%, a gain of about six points, against 14.4 for South Asia, so its pace was less than half as fast in points. From so low a base, two-thirds of the region's people remain without safely managed water. The income groups tell the same story. Low-income countries rose from 26.4% to 33.0%, and lower-middle-income countries from 60.6% to 69.1%, a gain of 8.5 points. Upper-middle-income countries moved only from 77.4% to 78.1%, and high-income countries from 95.2% to 95.8%. Gains were thus concentrated in the lower-middle-income group, while the upper-middle group is classed as stagnating, with a ratio of 0.057, well short of universal coverage. Reaching the last fifth in such countries often means improving the quality and reliability of existing systems, not simply extending pipes.

Whether poorer countries are catching up can be tested directly. Across 147 countries, the slope of annual change on the 2015 level is -0.00491 with a p-value of 0.0004, so lower starting levels are associated with somewhat faster gains, and the pattern is unlikely to be chance. The fit is weak, however: R2 is 0.088, meaning that starting level explains under nine per cent of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation across countries fell from 0.445 in 2015 to 0.416 in 2024. Dispersion has narrowed, but only slightly. Many countries with low coverage improved little, and some with middling coverage improved a great deal, so convergence is a tendency and not a rule. Measurement may add noise, since estimates for countries with few surveys rest on modelled trends, and the safely managed indicator needs water-quality and availability data that many countries collect irregularly.

The link with basic service sheds light on how progress is made. Across 147 countries, the rank correlation between changes in safely managed coverage and changes in at least basic coverage is 0.622, and the rank correlation between their 2024 levels is 0.850. Countries that expanded basic access tended also to expand safely managed access, and the two rankings of countries are very similar. This is consistent with basic coverage acting as a precondition: a household cannot have water on premises, free from contamination, before it has a protected source at all. It is an association, not proof of cause, and the correlation of changes leaves room for countries where safely managed coverage moved separately from basic coverage.

For 2030 the implication is that the pace of the last nine years will not deliver universal access. The regions that gained most did so from middling starting points, and the regions with the largest deficits gained fewer points than South Asia and East Asia and Pacific. Convergence is too weak to close the gap unaided, which means that low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries need gains well above the recent trend.

### Current trends fall short of universal access by 2030, and proposals follow

Projecting the post-2015 pace forward shows that universal access to safely managed drinking water will not be reached by 2030. At the rate observed since 2015, the world would stand at 78.0% in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend classification gives the world a ratio of 0.32 of the pace required, which the analysis reads as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Whether the pace of 2015 to 2024 is the right baseline is a matter of reading, since the series is built from household surveys and modelled estimates that move slowly, and a short period can be unrepresentative. Universal access can also be read strictly, as 100.0% of people, or loosely, as near-universal coverage; on the strict reading every projection below falls short.

The regional projections differ in what they imply. East Asia and Pacific is expected to reach 82.8% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.51, the best among the large regions after South Asia, which is expected at 89.0% with a ratio of 0.70. Europe and Central Asia is expected at 93.4%, and high-income countries at 96.2%. These are high levels, but their ratios are 0.25 and 0.21, because the pace is slow. In rich regions the remaining shortfall is small and concentrated in particular communities, such as private wells, remote settlements and marginalised groups, which regional averages do not reveal. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is classified as stagnating, with an expected 66.2% in 2030, barely above its 2024 level of 65.6%. Upper middle income countries are also classed as stagnating, at an expected 78.6%.

Sub-Saharan Africa is furthest from the target. At 32.4% in 2024, it is expected to reach only 37.2% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.15. Low-income countries show the same picture, with an expected 38.2% and a ratio of 0.16. South Asia, by contrast, rose from 63.1% in 2015 to 77.6% in 2024, a much larger gain in points than Sub-Saharan Africa's rise from 26.4% to 32.4%. Even if the present pace holds, roughly two in three people in Sub-Saharan Africa would remain without safely managed water. Rapid population growth, a well-established context for the region, means that new connections must outrun the growth in the number of people, though these results do not measure its effect.

Country classifications show how widely the shortfall is spread. Of 151 countries assessed, 20 are on track or have met the target, but they hold only 2.3% of the assessed population. A further 16 countries show moderate progress, and hold 37.0% of the population, largely because South Asia sits in this group. Another 36 countries, with 26.2% of the population, show marginal progress. In 45 countries, with 24.2% of the population, the series is stagnant, and in 34 countries, with 10.2%, it has regressed. Regression can arise from services failing to keep pace with growing towns, ageing networks, conflict or revised survey methods; the data do not separate these causes.

The implication for 2030 is that effort must shift from the countries already improving towards those standing still or sliding back. Raising basic coverage is not enough, although the two measures are linked: across 147 countries the rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.85 and of changes 0.62. The indicator requires that water be on premises, available when needed and free from contamination, and a source that counts as improved may fail the last two conditions.

Proposals follow from these findings. National governments and utilities in countries classed as stagnating or regressing should be the first priority for investment and monitoring, since these countries hold a large share of the assessed population. Donors and development banks should direct concessional finance towards low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa, where the projected level in 2030 remains far from the target. Statistical offices in rich regions should report on marginalised and off-network communities, so that averages near 96.2% do not hide those left behind.

w-c02-6-3.text:
### Health and education budgets claim stable but modest shares of spending

Government budgets show a stable but modest commitment to the services that bear most directly on poverty. Education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in the world in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, a nearly flat movement over eight years. Regional movements beneath the world figure differ. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, while Latin America and the Caribbean held at 16.4 per cent in 2015 and 16.6 per cent in 2024. Low-income countries moved against the general direction, from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022. Reporting for 2025 is partial, with 60 countries, so the latest observations, including the South Asia reading for that year, describe a subset and not the world.

Health is harder to summarise. The series, domestic general government health expenditure as a share of general government expenditure, is reported here by region and income group, and no world figure is given. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024, so the final year supports no statement. The most recent usable readings fall between 2017 and 2023, depending on the group, and comparisons across groups therefore mix end years. They indicate direction and scale and are not a common-year ranking.

Social protection is the third service named in the section's question, and no result for its share of public spending is available in this bench. The coverage and benefit-incidence series describe who is reached, not how much governments spend, and they are treated in another section of the chapter. The absence should not be read as a low or a high figure.

The targets add a further limit. Target 1.a calls for significant mobilisation of resources and for adequate and predictable means, and target 1.b calls for sound policy frameworks that support accelerated investment in poverty eradication. Neither sets a threshold, a base year or a required share of spending, and the series held here measure domestic budgets, not development cooperation, so target 1.a is only partly addressed. Any classification of progress therefore rests on direction alone: a rising share is read as movement towards the target. That reading is open to challenge, since a share can fall while the absolute amount rises with growth, and can rise because other spending is cut.

### Regions and income groups differ widely in health priority

Health receives very different priority across regions and income groups. North America devoted 22.1 per cent of general government expenditure to health from domestic sources in 2015 and 22.8 per cent in 2023, the highest share of any region reported. Europe and Central Asia stood at 15.0 per cent in 2015 and 14.5 per cent in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 11.5 per cent to 11.8 per cent over the same years. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2019, the last year in its series. South Asia began far lower, at 3.7 per cent in 2015, and reached 4.8 per cent in 2022. Its share in 2022 remained well below that of Europe and Central Asia in 2023, even after the rise.

The income groups repeat the pattern. High-income economies assigned 17.9 per cent in 2015 and 18.5 per cent in 2023. Low-income economies assigned 5.4 per cent in 2015 and 5.3 per cent in 2017, and lower-middle-income economies 4.8 per cent in 2015 and 4.7 per cent in 2018. These are shares only, and they are applied to budgets of very different size. As context rather than a finding of these series, a small share of a small budget commonly leaves households to meet the difference from their own pockets, which is a recognised route into impoverishment.

These comparisons carry a caveat. The series do not end in the same year: the low-income and lower-middle-income series stop in 2017 and 2018, and the Sub-Saharan African series in 2019, so none of them can show what followed 2020. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024 at the time of the data, so the latest year is not yet a basis for comparison. A gap measured in earlier years for the poorest groups may since have narrowed or widened, and the data cannot say which.

Education shares show a different ordering, though not a clean one. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 15.4 per cent in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 16.6 per cent in 2024, give education the largest shares of their budgets among the regions listed, while North America gave 10.7 per cent in 2022, down from 12.9 per cent in 2015. Low-income economies raised their education share from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, a period in which their health share, in the series available to 2017, barely moved. Poorer groups thus tend to put more of their budgets into schooling than into health, and richer groups the reverse. The share is a measure of priority, not of adequacy, because a large share of a small budget may still buy little per pupil.

### Education shares fell in most countries while inequality in spending widened

Since 2015 the education share of public budgets has weakened in most countries. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are classed as in regression, and these hold 78.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 29 countries, with 7.1 per cent of that population, are on track or have met the direction of travel. A further 13 countries (1.8 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 12 (2.3 per cent) marginal progress and 23 (10.5 per cent) stagnation. No numerical target exists for these indicators, so the classes measure movement towards an increase and not distance from an agreed level. An increase is itself only one reading of progress, since a falling share can accompany rising total budgets or a growing economy.

The population weighting explains why the picture is so unfavourable, for the regressing group includes populous regions. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent of government expenditure in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, and South Asia from 13.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2025, an endpoint that rests on partial reporting, since only 60 countries reported in 2025. North America also declined, from 12.9 per cent in 2015 to 10.7 per cent in 2022. The movement was not universal. Low-income countries rose from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, and Latin America and the Caribbean edged up from 16.4 per cent to 16.6 per cent in 2024. Competing claims on budgets, such as debt service, pensions and health, are commonly cited pressures on education shares, although these data do not identify which of them operated in any given country.

Spending relative to national income is a different measure, education expenditure as a share of GDP and not as a share of government expenditure, and it shows a different problem, that of divergence. Across 164 countries, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of that measure rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.101. The between-region share of that Theil index moved from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent. Regional differences therefore account for under a quarter of the inequality in both years, and the rest lies within regions. Because the between-region share barely moved, the data point to differences among countries within regions as the larger part of the inequality, without showing what widened it. Regional averages thus conceal much of the divergence.

Health, on the same direction-of-travel test, shows a different distribution of classes. Of 193 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the direction of travel, holding 40.8 per cent of their population, while 61 are in regression, holding 21.3 per cent. Another 30 countries (22.1 per cent of the population) show marginal progress, 19 (11.5 per cent) stagnation and 11 (4.3 per cent) moderate progress. This is a comparison of direction only, a weak test that says nothing of the level of spending or its adequacy.

The two shares do not move together. The Spearman correlation between changes in the health share and the education share across 129 countries over 2015 to 2022 is 0.16, and between their levels in the later year of that span 0.09. Countries that raised one share were therefore hardly more likely to raise the other, and no common cause is shown. Neither is a trade-off. Governments appear to set the two priorities largely independently, so the weakening of education shares needs its own explanation in each country.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Spending shares carry no numerical target under targets 1.a and 1.b, so progress can be judged only by direction. The trend classes ask whether a share is rising, which is a weak test: a country may be rising while spending too little, and another may be falling while spending generously. The classes are signals of priority, not verdicts on adequacy. The target wording can also be read as concerning domestic budgets, development cooperation, or both. The series examined cover domestic budgets only, so nothing here speaks to external resources under target 1.a.

On direction alone, and with that caution, the health share looks less discouraging than the education share. For the domestic health share, 72 of 193 countries assessed are on track, holding 40.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, while regression affects 61 countries with 21.3 per cent. For education the pattern is the reverse: 110 of 187 countries are in regression, with 78.2 per cent of the population, against 29 on track with 7.1 per cent. Because the regression class holds most of the population, the direction of education budgets matters for most of the world's children, though the results do not identify which countries drive it. The results do not show why health shares moved as they did, and they cannot say whether the pattern will persist.

The outlook for 2030 is uneven, and the results support no projection of either share. In health, 21.3 per cent of the population lives where the share is falling. In education, falls are visible in East Asia and Pacific, from 15.1 per cent in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, in South Asia, from 13.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2025, and in North America, from 12.9 per cent in 2015 to 10.7 per cent in 2022. The low-income group moved the other way, from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, so the pattern is not uniform. The South Asia endpoint of 2025 rests on partial reporting, since only 60 countries reported in that year. A separate measure, education spending as a share of GDP, became more unequal among countries, with the population-weighted Theil index rising from 0.065 in 2015 to 0.101 in 2022. The between-region share of that index moved only from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent, so the data point to differences within regions as the larger part, without showing their cause.

Two limits qualify every reading. Spending data for low-income countries often end years before the latest reporting year, so recent shifts there are unseen. Social protection spending is not covered by the spending series examined, and its coverage and targeting are treated in other sections of this chapter.

w-c04-5-3.text:
### Global consumption fell between 2015 and 2020

Global alcohol consumption per adult fell over the first five years of the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization estimate, carried in the World Development Indicators, puts total consumption at 5.9 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 and over in 2015. By 2020 it stood at 4.9 litres. The fall is about 1.0 litre, or roughly one sixth of the 2015 level, in five years. The measure sums recorded sales and an estimate of unrecorded alcohol, such as home production and informal trade, and is adjusted for tourist consumption.

Target 3.5 calls for strengthening the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including the harmful use of alcohol. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline year. The target can therefore be read in more than one way. One reading takes the wording to concern harm, which per capita volume captures only in part, since the same average can conceal heavy episodic drinking in a minority. Another reading treats volume as the best available proxy and counts a sustained decline as progress. This book adopts the second reading, because volume is the only alcohol series the shelf holds, and it states that choice openly. On that reading the world moved in the intended direction after 2015.

The series needs careful handling. The figures are projected estimates, not counts from a survey of drinkers in each year. Statisticians model them from sales, tax records, production data and occasional surveys, and then project forward where observations are thin. A smooth global path is therefore partly a product of the method, and a single year should not be read as a precise count. The final year, 2020, coincides with the first months of the pandemic, when closures of bars and restaurants, lost tourism and shifts in household purchasing altered both drinking and its measurement. Whether the 2020 figure reflects lasting change or a temporary disturbance cannot be settled from this series alone.

Coverage is nearly complete. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2020, 187 countries report in at least one year, and 185 report in 2020. The few countries that drop out in some years do not alter the global picture materially, though the estimates for those places are less secure. The world figure is thus a broad measure, and the sections that follow turn to the regions, income groups and countries that lie behind it.

### Regions differ widely in level and in direction

Regional levels span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia and North America sit at the top. Consumption in Europe and Central Asia was 8.9 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2020, down from 9.5 litres in 2015. North America stood at 9.9 litres in 2020, up from 9.5 litres in 2015. Of the seven regions reported, North America is the only one in which the estimate rose. Its rate of 0.0075 is classed as regression, while every other region shows a negative rate. Latin America and the Caribbean lies in the middle band, at 5.8 litres in 2020 against 6.5 litres in 2015. At the bottom, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan record 0.4 litres in 2015 and 0.3 litres in 2020. That level is consistent with widespread abstention and legal restriction. It is also a region in which unrecorded consumption is hardest to measure, so the level should be read with caution.

The largest regional fall is in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020. Its rate of -0.0657 is the steepest of any region and is classed as on track or target met. South Asia fell from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, at a rate of -0.0360, also classed on track. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0216, is placed in the same class. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0138, is classed as moderate progress, but acceleration needed. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0181, receives the same class even though its level is so low. These classes need a caveat. The Goals set no numerical target for alcohol under target 3.5, which asks only for strengthened prevention and treatment of harmful use. The classification therefore measures the direction and speed of change, and does not show whether a region has reached a safe or desired level.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 4.6 litres in 2015 to 4.2 litres in 2020, at a rate of -0.0211, classed on track. The fall in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres to 4.5 litres, was much larger in litres.

The income groups show a similar divergence. High-income economies fell only from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, at a rate of -0.0075, classed as marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed. They remain the heaviest-drinking group. Low-income economies, at 2.9 litres in 2015 and 2.8 litres in 2020, moved even less, at -0.0054, and are classed in the same way. Upper-middle-income economies fell from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres, at -0.0585, and lower-middle-income economies from 3.9 litres to 3.3 litres, at -0.0340; both are classed on track. The largest reductions therefore came in the middle-income groups, while the highest-consuming group fell slowly and the lowest-consuming group barely moved. The period also spans 2020, when closure of bars and restricted travel altered recorded sales, and the projected estimates for that year rest partly on modelling, so part of the fall may not persist. The results do not identify what drove any of these regional differences.

### Country trajectories split between steep falls and regression

The trend classification covers 183 countries and rates each by its course towards a lower level of consumption. Target 3.5 sets no numerical goal for alcohol, so the classes measure direction and pace against a decrease by 2030, not distance from a stated threshold. That is one of several possible readings and applies throughout.

The country picture is divided. In 75 countries, holding 60.4% of the population of those assessed, consumption is on track or the target is met. A further 21 countries, with 11.0% of their population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 21, with 7.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. In 12 countries, with 3.1%, consumption stagnates. In 54 countries, with 18.2%, it is in regression, meaning that consumption per adult is rising.

The two ways of counting give different weights. By number of countries, 75 of 183 are on track, well under half, while 54 are in regression. By population, the on-track class holds 60.4% and the regression class 18.2%. The regressing group therefore holds a smaller share of people than of countries, while the on-track group holds a larger one. The country-level data are not tabulated here, so which countries these are is not stated, and nothing is shown about their size beyond these shares. The 60.4% is a statement about people, not a sign that most countries are succeeding.

The results do not identify why consumption rose in the regressing countries or fell in the others. Causes can be offered only as context. Income growth, changes in marketing and changes in taxation or licensing are among the factors commonly discussed in the public-health literature, but none is measured here. Countries that begin from very low levels can also register regression from a small base, so the class does not always signal a harmful level of drinking.

Coverage is nearly complete: 185 countries report in 2020, and 187 report in at least one year. The estimates are projected by the World Health Organization from survey and sales data, not counted directly, so country-level movements, above all for 2020, partly reflect modelling and not observed change. The classification should be read as an indication of direction, not as a precise ranking.

### Change was not convergent and moved alike for men and women

Change between 2015 and 2020 was not convergent. Across 181 countries, a regression of annual change on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00589, with a p-value of 0.603 and an R-squared of 0.012. The sign is negative, which would mean that countries with higher consumption fell slightly faster, but the coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the starting level explains about 1.2% of the variation in change. High-consumption countries did not systematically close the gap with low-consumption ones.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of consumption across countries rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.74 in 2020. The spread of national levels relative to their mean therefore widened slightly. Because the global average fell while dispersion rose, reductions were uneven in proportion: some countries fell sharply, some barely moved, and some rose. The difference between the two coefficients is small, and a movement of two hundredths in a five-year window should not be read as a settled trend.

The second result concerns the sexes. Across 185 countries, the changes in male and female consumption between 2015 and 2020 are almost perfectly rank-correlated, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.99 and a Kendall coefficient of 0.94. The 2020 levels are nearly as closely aligned, at 0.99 and 0.92. Countries in which men reduced consumption most are, almost without exception, those in which women did so as well. Rank correlation says nothing about the absolute gap between men and women; it says only that the ordering of countries is shared.

The results do not identify why the ordering is shared. One possible reading is that influences operating on whole populations, such as pricing, availability and social norms, affect both sexes together; the data do not test this. The method may also contribute. The figures are projected estimates, built from national sales, survey and modelling inputs, and the same adjustments to a country's total are likely to carry through to both sex-specific series. Part of the correlation may therefore be an artefact of estimation rather than a finding about behaviour.

No causal claim follows from these results. The window is five years and covers the disruption of 2020, and the lack of convergence describes the data rather than judging any policy. What can be said is that the starting level did not organise the change, and that the sex of the drinker did not alter a country's place in the ordering.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to a world moving in the right direction on alcohol, though not evenly. The world rate of -0.0363 is classed as on track or target met, yet it leans on large falls in East Asia and Pacific, where consumption went from 6.4 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020, and in upper middle income countries, where it went from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres. In high-income countries the fall was from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a rate of -0.0075 classed as marginal progress, and North America moved the other way, from 9.5 litres to 9.9 litres. Target 3.5 sets no numerical threshold, so every class here describes direction and pace against a decrease, which is one of several possible readings. Whether the gap between regions narrows or widens by 2030 cannot be read from two observation points, and the 2030 horizon lies ten years after the last observation in 2020.

The country picture shows the same division, and it should be read together with the population shares. Consumption is regressing in 54 countries holding 18.2% of the assessed population, and 12 more are stagnant, holding 3.1%. The 75 countries on track hold 60.4% of that population, although they are fewer than half of the 183 assessed. The regressing group therefore holds a smaller share of population than of countries, but the results name no countries, so its composition cannot be described. The global verdict depends on a limited set of populous countries that the results do not identify, and a global verdict of progress can coexist with widespread failure elsewhere.

The absence of convergence matters for 2030. With a coefficient of -0.00589 and a p-value of 0.603, the data show no tendency for high-consumption countries to catch down, nor for the gap to widen in any measurable way. The results do not identify what drove the falls or the rises, and the pace seen in 2015 to 2020 cannot be assumed to continue to 2030. Low-income countries, where consumption is lowest at 2.8 litres in 2020, show only marginal progress. Projected estimates carry uncertainty, and the 2020 value may reflect pandemic disruption to trade and sales, so the five-year change may not represent the underlying course.

The proposals follow from these findings and are framed as monitoring and analysis, since the results establish direction and not cause. First, the World Health Organization and national statistical offices should publish observed, not only projected, estimates for the 54 countries classed as regressing, so that the rise can be told apart from modelling artefact and from growth off a small base. Second, health ministries in those countries and in North America, where consumption rose to 9.9 litres in 2020, should commission analyses of what lies behind the rise before choosing among policy responses. Third, the bodies that set indicators under Goal 3 should state whether target 3.5 carries a quantitative reduction for alcohol, so that progress can be measured against a threshold and not only a direction.

w-c09-1-1.text:
### World income per person has grown at under 2 per cent a year

World GDP per capita grew by 1.9 per cent in 2015 and by 2.0 per cent in 2025, according to the World Bank's World Development Indicators. A decade that opened and closed at almost the same rate, a little under 2 per cent a year, is the first finding of this section. Growth of that size doubles average income only over several decades, and it sits far below the pace that the second reading of target 8.1 asks of the least developed countries.

Target 8.1 can be read in two ways. Its first clause asks for per capita economic growth 'in accordance with national circumstances', which sets no number. Its second asks for at least 7 per cent GDP growth a year in the least developed countries, a figure for total output, not for income per person. The two measure different things: GDP growth includes the effect of a rising population, and in countries with fast population growth the gap between the two can be wide. This section uses GDP per capita growth as its main indicator, because it describes the change in output available to each resident, and turns to total GDP growth when the 7 per cent threshold is considered. Gross national income per capita is a third measure, which adds income earned abroad and subtracts income paid out; it is reported for fewer countries and is not the basis of the comparisons here.

The path of world growth over the longer run reads as a sequence of shocks rather than as a steady rise. The break analysis of the annual change in the world rate finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The mean annual change was -2.8 percentage points across 2008 and 2009, the years of the global financial crisis, and then +5.8 in 2010 as output recovered. The pattern repeated with greater force around the pandemic: the mean change was -5.4 in 2020 and +9.4 in 2021, followed by -3.1 in 2022. Between 2011 and 2019 the mean annual change was -0.2, a gentle drift downward and not a collapse, and from 2023 to 2025 it was again -0.2. These are changes in the growth rate from one year to the next, not growth rates themselves, and they should be read as the size of each swing.

The reading matters for 2030. A world economy that returns each time to roughly 2 per cent growth, after shocks that arrive about once in a decade, offers no sign of the acceleration that sustained income gains would need. The figure for 2025 rests on 186 countries reporting, against 211 in 2015, so the latest year is less complete than earlier ones and may be revised as late reports arrive.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than six

Regional growth rates in the World Bank's World Development Indicators spread widely at both ends of the decade. In 2015 GDP per capita in South Asia grew by 6.5 per cent, against 0.2 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa and 0.8 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Latin America and the Caribbean contracted, at -0.7 per cent. The heading's factor of more than six describes this spread between the fastest region and the slowest positive ones, and it should be read as a description of a single year, not of a settled order.

South Asia remained the fastest region throughout, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, a little below its 2015 rate. East Asia and Pacific held close to the same position, at 4.0 per cent in 2015 and 3.9 per cent in 2025. Both are regions in which sustained investment and expanding manufacturing and services have long pushed incomes upwards, and neither fell far from its starting pace. South Asia's trend over the decade is classed as on track or target met, with an annual rate of 0.0465 on income per person in constant 2015 US dollars. East Asia and Pacific shows the same classification, at 0.0357. Since no numerical target is set for income per person in this series, the classification reflects only the direction and pace of the trend.

The wealthier regions moved the other way. Europe and Central Asia slowed from 1.6 per cent in 2015 to 1.3 per cent in 2025, and North America from 1.9 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Their trend rates over the decade, 0.0150 and 0.0167, are classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. High-income countries as a group went from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent. Slower growth at high levels of income is the common pattern, since economies near the technological frontier cannot gain by catching up, and ageing populations restrain the supply of labour.

The two regions that recovered most from their 2015 positions are Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from -0.7 per cent to 1.6 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.2 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Both ended the period close to the world rate of 2.0 per cent, yet the decade-long trend tells a less comfortable story. Latin America and the Caribbean has a trend rate of 0.0054, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and Sub-Saharan Africa a rate of -0.0020, classed as regression. A single good year at the end does not offset a decade in which the level of income per person barely rose or fell. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew by 0.8 per cent in 2015 and 0.9 per cent in 2025, with a trend rate of 0.0076, also classed as marginal progress.

Levels matter as much as rates. In constant 2015 US dollars, East Asia and Pacific rose from 9,731 in 2015 to 13,810 in 2025, while Latin America and the Caribbean moved only from 8,547 to 9,017. The two regions began the decade within a modest distance of each other and ended it well apart. Europe and Central Asia rose from 22,740 to 26,380, and high-income countries from 36,730 to 42,650, so that the absolute distance between rich and middle-income groups did not close even where middle-income growth was faster.

By income group the pattern is sharper still. Low-income countries grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after -2.9 per cent in 2015, yet their income per person was 714.8 dollars in 2015 and 719.7 in 2025, a trend rate of 0.0007 that is classed as stagnation. Lower-middle-income countries grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025, up from 4.0 per cent in 2015, and their income rose from 1,781 to 2,374 dollars, a trend rate of 0.0292. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0371. The poorest countries therefore gain least in the level of income, which is the reason the gap between regions persists. For 2030, a rate close to 2.5 per cent in the poorest group, if sustained, would be needed for several years before it altered that picture.

### Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015

The structural breaks in the annual change of world GDP per capita growth show how much of the decade's movement came from single years. The break analysis of the World Development Indicators series finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The segments between them are short, and several consist of one year. Read with care, the breaks describe changes in the rate of growth, not its level: a mean change of -2.8 points in 2008-2009 means that growth fell by that amount each year on average across those two years.

The global financial crisis is the first large shock in the series. The 2008-2009 segment has a mean annual change of -2.8 points, and 2010 follows with a rebound of 5.8 points. The long segment from 2011 to 2019 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points. That is a slow drift downward in the growth rate across nine years, not a collapse, and it shows that the decade before 2015 was one of gradual loss of momentum after the rebound.

The period after 2015 is dominated by the pandemic. In 2020 the annual change in world growth was -5.4 points, the largest fall in the series. The 2021 segment records a recovery of 9.4 points, the largest rise. The 2022 segment then shows a reversal of -3.1 points, as the rebound faded. Finally, the segment from 2023 to 2025 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, so growth was drifting down again, much as in 2011-2019. These shocks are the reason the world rate in 2025, at 2.0 per cent, can resemble the rate in 2015, at 1.9 per cent, while the path between them was violent. Well-established context explains the pattern: the 2020 fall followed lockdowns and the collapse of travel and trade, and the 2021 gain was largely a base effect of recovering from a depressed year.

Across income groups, the endpoints tell a story that needs the same caution. Low-income countries recorded GDP per capita growth of -2.9 per cent in 2015 and 2.5 per cent in 2025. That is a swing from contraction to modest expansion, but it is a comparison of two single years. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 4.0 per cent to 4.6 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, and high-income countries from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent. The low-income figure for 2015 reflects a year of weak outcomes for the group, and a rate of 2.5 per cent in 2025 is still well below the 7 per cent that target 8.1 sets for the least developed countries, although that group is not the same as the low-income group and the two should not be equated.

A ten-year endpoint comparison therefore hides the volatility that the breaks reveal. Two years that happen to be close in value say nothing about the swings between them, and a large gain between two endpoints may only be recovery from a poor starting year. The comparison also depends on the coverage of the latest year. The number of countries reporting GDP growth was 211 in 2015, 210 in 2019 and 210 in 2021, but only 186 in 2025. The fall from 2022, when 209 countries reported, to 204 in 2023 and 200 in 2024 suggests that data arrive late, so the 2025 values rest on fewer countries and may be revised as more report. For 2030 this implies that the latest readings are provisional, and that any judgment on target 8.1 should wait for the revised series.

### Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence

Beyond regional averages, the trend classification sorts countries by how fast GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) has moved since 2015. No numerical 2030 target exists for this measure, so the classes are relative: each country is judged by the compound annual rate it has sustained since the baseline, and by the share of the distance to a notional target that this rate would cover by 2030. The classes are a reading of momentum, not a verdict against a legal threshold, and a different reading of target 8.1 would shift some countries between them.

Of 209 countries assessed, 74 are on track or have met the notional target, and they hold 56.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 36 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 16.4 per cent of the population. Another 44 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 11.8 per cent. Fifteen countries stagnate, with 5.0 per cent of the population, and 40 are in regression, with 10.3 per cent. The heading's quarter is therefore a rough description of the countries that stagnate or regress, together with some of the marginal group; it should not be read as an exact share.

The regional trends agree with this picture. South Asia has a compound rate of 0.0465, East Asia and the Pacific 0.0357, the upper middle income group 0.0371 and the lower middle income group 0.0292, and all four are classed as on track or target met. Europe and Central Asia (0.0150), high income countries (0.0151) and North America (0.0167) show moderate progress, as does the world as a whole at 0.0176. Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0054) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0076) show marginal progress. The low income group, at 0.0007, is classed as stagnating. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0020, is classed as regression: its income per person in 2025 sits slightly below its level of 2015, even though its annual growth rate recovered from 0.2 per cent in 2015 to 1.6 per cent in 2025.

The question of the 7 per cent target needs a careful answer. Target 8.1 sets that rate for GDP, not per capita GDP, in the least developed countries. The results hold no group figure for the least developed countries, so no direct test is possible. The nearest evidence is the low income group, whose GDP per capita grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after a contraction of -2.9 per cent in 2015. That rate is well below 7 per cent, and per capita growth is by construction lower than GDP growth where population is rising. Only South Asia, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, comes near the threshold, and it is not a least developed group. On present evidence the target is out of reach for the low income group, though the missing group figure means the claim rests on a proxy.

The post-2020 recovery matters for the reading. The low income rebound from -2.9 per cent to 2.5 per cent is a sizeable swing, yet the level of income per person in that group has barely moved, from 714.8 in 2015 to 719.7 in 2025 in constant 2015 US dollars. Growth after a shock restores lost ground before it adds new income, so a good year does not by itself change the long-run class. Coverage also thins at the end of the series: 186 countries reported growth in 2025, against 211 in 2015, so the latest figures are less complete than earlier ones.

For 2030 the implication is plain. If present rates hold, most of the world's people live in countries whose incomes are rising at a pace that meets the notional test, while the countries in regression and stagnation, which are concentrated among the poorest, fall further behind. The 7 per cent goal is a different measure and is not met by any group in the results.

w-c05-7-3.text:
### The global share of trained primary teachers has risen only slowly

The world share of primary school teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and at 82.2% in 2024, a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030, and the indicator used here reads that as a share of 100%. Against that reading, roughly one primary teacher in five worldwide still lacks the minimum organised training required in the country where they teach. The trend calculation gives a world ratio of 0.15 against the pace needed, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Continuing the 2015 to 2024 slope would bring the world to 83.4% in 2030.

The measure needs careful reading. The indicator counts teachers who have received the minimum organised training, whether before or during service, that a given country requires. That minimum is set nationally and differs widely. A teacher counted as trained in one system might not meet the standard of another, and a share of 100% in one country does not imply equal preparation in the classroom. Nor does the indicator capture the quality of the training, the subject knowledge of teachers, or whether they remain in post. The figure is therefore a floor on qualification, not a measure of teaching quality. Readings of the target also vary: some take 4.c to mean full national qualification, others a substantial rise from a baseline, and the data cannot settle between them.

Coverage adds a second caution. The 2024 world value rests on the latest reporting of each economy, and only 13 countries reported in 2025, so the most recent year says little. Several regional values end in 2022, and the upper middle income group has a single value, for 2022, at 80.7%, which allows no change to be read. Late reporting may be more common where systems are weaker, but the results do not test this.

The section's guiding question also asks whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling. The bench returned no result for that ratio, so the question cannot be answered from the evidence held here. Series on teacher numbers exist for primary and secondary levels, but a count of teachers without matching enrolment does not give a ratio. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is likewise not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings, safety or inclusion. The evidence speaks to the training of teachers, not to class size or the learning environment.

The slow world movement matters for 2030 because training is a precondition for much else in the chapter, from completion and learning to pre-primary provision. A world share that rises by under two points in nine years, spanning the disruption of 2020 and the years after it, leaves the target far out of reach on the present slope. The results do not show why the share has stalled; one possible explanation is that recruitment has outpaced training in some systems, but this remains a conjecture that the series cannot test. The regional parts that follow show where gains and losses lie.

### Regions and income groups differ by more than twenty points

The regional picture in 2024 is one of wide separation. North America stands at 97.9% of primary teachers trained, South Asia at 87.7%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 81.8% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 80.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa, whose latest reading is 2022 rather than 2024, stands at 68.8%. The gap between the best and the weakest of these regions is therefore about twenty-nine percentage points, taking the 2024 reading for North America and the 2022 reading for Sub-Saharan Africa. Readings from different years are not strictly comparable, and the Sub-Saharan figure may understate or overstate the position in 2024.

Income groups show a similar pattern. Low income countries stand at 69.2% in 2022, close to the Sub-Saharan level, which is expected because most low income countries lie in that region. Upper middle income countries have only a 2022 reading, 80.7%, so no change over the period can be given for that group. Training here means the minimum organised preparation required by each country, so the percentages measure compliance with national standards and not a common level of skill. A country with a demanding standard can score lower than one with a modest standard, and comparisons across regions should be read with that in mind.

The spread among countries, weighted by population, is modest in absolute terms. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.094 in 2015, fell to 0.073 in 2020 and rose to 0.097 in 2024, ending slightly above its starting level. The Theil index fell from 0.026 in 2015 to 0.011 in 2020. In that decomposition the share lying between regions was 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020. In those two years about half of the inequality among countries was therefore a difference between regions, and the other half lay among countries within the same region. Policies aimed at a single region would address only part of the gap, though the decomposition is not available for 2024 and may have changed since.

These comparisons carry a caveat about coverage. Countries reporting numbered 85 in 2015 and 93 in 2020, but only 79 in 2024. The Theil index and its regional decomposition are missing for 2024, so the latest year cannot be set against the earlier ones on that measure. A change in the number of reporting countries can alter the Gini by changing who is counted, and the rise to 0.097 may reflect that as much as any real divergence; the series cannot separate the two. Reporting for 2025 is thinner still, with 13 countries. For 2030 the implication is that monitoring of Target 4.c is weakest in the years that matter most for judging it.

### Gains in South Asia contrast with declines in richer regions

South Asia recorded the largest regional gain in the share of trained primary teachers. The share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly fifteen percentage points in nine years. The region moved from below the world average of 80.4% in 2015 to above the world level of 82.2% in 2024. Its trend is the only regional one classed as on track, with an expected 99.3% in 2030 if the rate of change continued. Lower middle income countries, a group that includes several South Asian economies, rose more modestly, from 76.4% in 2015 to 83.3% in 2024, and their expected value for 2030 is 88.2%. The data do not show which measures lay behind the South Asian rise. A change in how a country defines the minimum training required would produce the same movement as a real improvement in preparation, so the gain should be read as a reported change in the share, not as proof of better teaching.

The richer regions moved in the opposite direction. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020, the last year for which the regional reading is given here. High income countries fell from 95.9% in 2015 to 92.1% in 2024, and North America slipped from 99.3% to 97.9% over the same period. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 82.7% to 81.8%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan declined from 83.9% to 80.5%. These falls are small beside the South Asian gain, but they run against the direction of Target 4.c, and the trend tool classes all of these regions as regressing. The results do not explain them. Teacher shortages that lead systems to hire staff before they complete a full programme are one possible cause, and changes in national definitions or reporting are another; neither can be tested with these series.

Across countries, the pattern is one of catching up. A convergence test over 48 countries between 2015 and 2024 gives a coefficient of -0.071 (p below 0.001) with an R2 of 0.342, which means that countries starting from lower shares of trained teachers tended to gain faster than those starting higher. The dispersion of the shares narrowed only slightly: the coefficient of variation moved from 0.165 in 2015 to 0.155 in 2024. Convergence is therefore real but slow, and about a third of the variation in country changes is accounted for by the starting level alone. The test covers only the 48 countries with readings at both ends of the period, so it describes the reporting countries and not the world, and the systems with the sparsest records may be underrepresented.

The size of the teaching workforce does not appear to explain the changes. The rank correlation between changes in the share of trained primary teachers and changes in the number of primary teachers across the same 48 countries is -0.095, and the correlation between 2024 levels is 0.168. Both are weak. Expanding the workforce therefore did not visibly coincide with a higher trained share, and countries that added the most teachers were no more likely to see that share rise. This is a cautionary finding for Target 4.c, which speaks of qualified teachers and not of teachers alone. The correlations are descriptive and say nothing about the mechanism.

The period since 2015 and the years after 2020 cannot be read cleanly from these series. Several regional readings end in 2020 or 2022, and the school closures of 2020 and 2021 disrupted the collection of statistics as well as schooling. A gap in reporting may conceal a change that has not yet been measured. For 2030, the lesson of this part is that large gains are recorded where the share rose fast, as in South Asia, but that they are not general, and that richer regions with falling shares cannot assume the levels of 2015 will return unaided. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings or learning environments.

### Most countries are not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

The country counts show that the 2030 picture is mixed. In primary education, 64 of the 129 countries assessed, holding 65.9% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have already met the target of a fully trained teaching force. This is a large share of people but not of countries, because several populous countries are among those advancing. Against it stand 36 countries with 26.3% of the assessed population whose trained share is falling rather than rising. A further 13 countries, with 2.4% of the population, show marginal progress that would need to speed up considerably, 12 countries, with 4.2% of the population, show moderate progress that still needs acceleration, and 4 countries, with 1.2%, are stagnant. The two largest groups are the on-track countries and the regressing ones, so the pattern is divided at its poles.

Secondary education tells a similar story with less coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 hold 61.5% of the population and are on track or have met the target, while 36 hold 27.6% and are regressing. Fourteen countries with 7.7% of the population show marginal progress, 10 with 2.1% show moderate progress and 7 with 1.0% are stagnant. The share of people living in regressing countries is slightly higher at secondary level than at primary level, and the share living in on-track countries is slightly lower. Fewer countries report secondary data, so the secondary result rests on a thinner base and is the less certain of the two.

The regression count needs careful reading. A falling trained share does not necessarily mean that teaching has worsened. One possible explanation is that systems expanding quickly may recruit teachers faster than they can certify them; another is that a country raising its minimum standard may see teachers once counted as trained fall below the new bar. Both are conjectures drawn from general experience, and the data given here cannot separate them.

The same feature complicates the target itself. Target 4.c speaks of qualified teachers, and the indicator measures minimum organised training, pre-service or in-service, as defined nationally. A share of 100% therefore does not mean equal preparation across countries. The target can be read as a share trained to national standards, a share trained to an international standard, or a growth in the absolute supply of teachers. The assessment here uses the first reading, with 100% as the goal, because it is the one the trained-teacher series can express. The reading of a substantial increase in supply cannot be judged from these results.

Two parts of the section's question remain unanswered. No pupil-teacher ratio series was assessed, so whether ratios are falling cannot be stated; the teacher-count series on the shelf were not combined with enrolment here. Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive school facilities, was not assessed either, because none of the series on the shelf for this section measures it.

For 2030, on the full-training reading the target will be missed at the world level. The projected world share of trained primary teachers is 83.4%, with a trend ratio of 0.15, which falls in the class of marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 72.0% and low income countries at 73.2%, so the groups starting furthest behind are expected to remain furthest behind. South Asia, projected at 99.3%, is the one region on course. The regions that are regressing are mostly those that began from higher levels, such as Europe and Central Asia at a projected 86.9% and high income countries at 89.7%. Their decline lowers the world figure and shows that a high starting point is no guarantee of progress.

Among the 48 countries reporting in both 2015 and 2024, convergence is present but slight: the coefficient of variation of the primary trained share fell from 0.17 to 0.16, with a beta of -0.07. The inequality measures give a final caution. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the trained share was 0.09 in 2015, 0.07 in 2020 and 0.10 in 2024. Differences narrowed up to 2020 and then widened again, though the 2024 reading covers 79 countries against 93 in 2020, so the comparison is imperfect and the cause of the widening cannot be read from these results. The between-region share of inequality, 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020, shows that regional differences account for about half of the spread in those years, so action aimed at one region would leave much of it untouched.

The findings point to the following proposals.
