w-c08-2-1.text:
### Three-quarters of the world now cooks with clean fuels

Roughly three people in four now cook mainly with clean fuels and technologies. The World Bank's World Development Indicators put the share of the world's population with access at 63.9 per cent in 2015 and at 75.4 per cent in 2024. The series covers 192 countries in 2024. The indicator measures the proportion of the total population primarily using clean cooking fuels and technologies, such as electricity, gas, biogas and the cleanest stoves, as against open fires and stoves burning wood, charcoal, dung, crop residues or kerosene. Primary use is the test: a household that owns a gas ring but cooks mostly on firewood is not counted as having access.

The gain between 2015 and 2024 is real and large, but the figure carries a caveat. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses, which are conducted at intervals of several years and are not available for every country in every year. Values for years between surveys, and the most recent years in particular, are estimates produced by statistical models rather than direct observations. The 2024 world value is therefore best read as a close approximation of the trend, and small year-to-year movements should not be treated as measured events. Nor does the indicator record how much of a household's cooking is done with clean fuels, how affordable the fuel is, or whether supply is reliable, all of which bear on the wording of target 7.1 on affordable and reliable modern energy services.

The remaining share matters because the other side of the figure is large. With 75.4 per cent having access in 2024, about one person in four still depends mainly on polluting fuels and technologies. Smoke from these fuels is a well-established cause of respiratory and cardiovascular illness, and it falls most heavily on women and young children, who spend the most time near the fire. Gathering fuel also consumes time that might otherwise go to schooling or paid work, and the burning of wood and charcoal contributes to local forest loss and to emissions. Clean cooking therefore bears on health, gender equality and climate goals as well as on Goal 7.

The world's average conceals a wide spread between income groups, which later parts of the section take up. High-income countries stood at 98.8 per cent in 2015 and 99.5 per cent in 2024, so almost nothing remained to be gained there. Low-income countries rose only from 13.3 per cent to 15.6 per cent over the same years, while lower-middle-income countries rose from 42.7 per cent to 63.8 per cent and upper-middle-income countries from 76.9 per cent to 90.2 per cent. The global rise is thus driven chiefly by the middle-income groups, and the countries with the lowest access have moved the least. Since the world value is a population-weighted average, it moves mainly with the largest populations, and it can improve even while the poorest countries stand almost still.

For 2030, the reading is straightforward but sobering. Target 7.1 calls for universal access to modern energy services, and the clean cooking series stands well short of that in 2024. The pace of the past nine years, taken alone, would not close a gap of this size within the six years that remain, a point examined in the final part of the section.

### Regions diverge sharply, with Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Regional levels in 2024 span almost the whole range of the scale. North America stands at 100.0 per cent of the population with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking, and Europe and Central Asia at 98.3 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 22.9 per cent, up from 14.7 per cent in 2015. Fewer than one person in four in the region cooks mainly with clean fuels, while the world as a whole stands at 75.4 per cent. The income groups tell the same story: low-income economies stood at 15.6 per cent in 2024, against 99.5 per cent in high-income economies.

The regions between these poles moved at very different speeds after 2015. South Asia made the largest advance in the data, rising from 45.3 per cent to 74.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 70.7 per cent to 87.0 per cent. Both regions are now close to or above the world level. Large national programmes to distribute gas connections and to substitute for solid fuels are well-established contributors to progress of this kind, though the indicator does not show what drove the change in any country. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 86.8 per cent to 90.5 per cent, a smaller gain from a higher base. Europe and Central Asia moved from 96.6 per cent to 98.3 per cent, as the last households switched.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved slowly, from 74.7 per cent to 77.8 per cent. The region began 2015 at a level near that of East Asia and Pacific, which has since moved well ahead. The grouping also mixes economies at very different incomes, so the regional figure conceals wide national differences that this indicator, taken at regional level, cannot display. In Sub-Saharan Africa the gain of 14.7 to 22.9 per cent is real but small against the size of the shortfall, and the region's pace needs to be read against continuing population growth, which the share alone does not capture.

The gap between rural and urban households explains much of the regional picture. Worldwide, rural access rose from 38.2 per cent in 2015 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while urban access rose from 85.1 per cent to 89.4 per cent. Rural households therefore gained more in percentage points, yet remain far behind. Sub-Saharan Africa's rural level is the lowest in the data, at 8.6 per cent in 2024, up from 5.4 per cent in 2015. Urban Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.8 per cent, up from 29.5 per cent. Low-income economies show the same pattern, with rural access at 7.3 per cent and urban access at 31.5 per cent.

Elsewhere the contrast between rural and urban areas has narrowed. South Asia's rural level reached 61.7 per cent against an urban level of 92.0 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific's rural level reached 73.9 per cent against 94.6 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the rural level is 95.2 per cent, and in North America 99.9 per cent. These differences matter for 2030. Where the remaining shortfall is concentrated in dispersed rural households, supply networks for fuel, stoves and finance are costlier to extend, and a regional average rising slowly leaves the poorest households for last. The data show levels and change, not the affordability of fuels, which the target also names and which the indicator does not measure.

### Gains were broad but the pace has not been steady

The global series has not risen at a steady pace. A break analysis of the annual change in the world share with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking finds two breaks, in 2010 and in 2021. In the segment from 2001 to 2009 the mean annual change was 0.9 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2010 to 2020 it was 1.4 points a year. In the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 1.0 point a year. Progress therefore quickened at the start of the 2010s and slowed after 2021, to a pace close to that of the first decade of the century. The 2010 break falls before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, so the faster pace of the 2010s cannot be credited to the goals alone. The 2021 break coincides with the period after the pandemic shock of 2020, but the data show only when the pace changed, not why.

The slowdown matters for 2030. Universal access requires a pace above any of the three segments, and the latest segment is the slowest since the early 2000s. Four years is a short window, and the 2021 break rests on few annual observations, so the estimate of its mean change is less secure than those of the longer segments. The break dates are statistical estimates and could shift with further data.

The second analysis asks whether countries drew together. Across 192 countries from 2015 to 2024, the slope of each country's annual change on its starting level is negative, at -0.0079 (p below 0.001). Countries that began with lower access therefore gained faster on average than countries that began higher, and levels moved closer. The coefficient of variation, which measures spread relative to the mean, fell from 0.57 in 2015 to 0.50 in 2024, which agrees with this reading.

The convergence is real but weak. The R2 of the regression is 0.14, so the starting level explains a small part of the variation in how fast countries gained. Many countries with similar starting points moved at very different speeds, and some low-access countries gained little. Part of the pattern is arithmetical: countries near full access have little room to rise, which pulls the slope below zero without implying that any catch-up mechanism is at work. The coefficient of variation still shows a spread that is wide, since a value near 0.50 means that the typical gap between countries remains about half the world mean.

The data do not show what drove the breaks or the uneven gains. Fuel prices, public programmes, supply chains and household incomes are commonly cited influences on the choice of cooking fuel, but none is measured in these results, and none is asserted here as the cause. The findings describe when and where access changed, and they leave open why.

### Universal access by 2030 will be missed without acceleration, and proposals follow

The trend-to-target reading sets each series against universal access, 100.0 per cent by 2030, and projects the compound annual rate observed since 2015. On that basis the world reaches an expected 84.2 per cent in 2030, from 75.4 per cent in 2024. The ratio of distance covered to distance required is 0.56, which the tool classes as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. Universal access is therefore not on course at the global level.

Regions differ in how near they are. East Asia and Pacific is classed as on track or target met, with an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.99. South Asia is also on track, with a ratio of 1.06, having risen from 45.3 per cent in 2015 to 74.3 per cent in 2024. Its expected value above 100 shows that the extrapolation is mechanical and cannot exceed the ceiling. Europe and Central Asia is classed as needing acceleration, with a ratio of 0.82 and an expected 99.4 per cent, which is a small gap in absolute terms because the region started near the top. Latin America and the Caribbean has a ratio of 0.47 and an expected 93.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan has a ratio of 0.20 and an expected 79.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.19 and an expected 30.9 per cent in 2030. Both of the last two are classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

By income group, upper middle income countries are on track with a ratio of 1.01, and high income countries are on track at 99.5 per cent in 2024. Lower middle income countries need acceleration, with a ratio of 0.71 and an expected 83.4 per cent. Low income countries are classed as stagnant, with a ratio of 0.05: the share moved from 13.3 per cent in 2015 to 15.6 per cent in 2024, and the expected value for 2030 is 17.4 per cent. The ratio reflects the distance still to be covered, so regions starting from a low base are penalised heavily even when their annual rate is high. Sub-Saharan Africa's rate of 0.051 is close to South Asia's 0.057, yet its starting point leaves it far from the target.

Country classes show how widely the gap is spread. Of 190 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 61.5 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 46 countries, with 14.9 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 39 countries, with 13.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Twenty-nine countries, with 8.3 per cent, are stagnant, and 4 countries, with 1.4 per cent, have regressed. The classes are produced by a rule applied to each series, and they say nothing about what drives a country's change.

Two cautions apply to reading these results. Target 7.1 speaks of universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services, and the text does not fix a numerical threshold for cooking. Reading it as exactly 100 per cent is the strictest reading; a reading of near-universal access would count more countries as having met it. The indicator also measures only the primary fuel or technology a household uses. It does not measure whether the fuel is affordable or its supply reliable, and a household with access may still cook partly with solid fuels when prices rise or deliveries fail. The rural series shows the same pattern in sharper form: 8.6 per cent of rural people in Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, against 56.3 per cent of rural people worldwide.

For 2030, the implication is that global progress will be decided largely in the countries classed as stagnant or marginal. Those groups are not large in population in the aggregate, yet they are concentrated in the regions with the lowest levels, where rural households are the hardest to reach.

proposals: National governments and development banks in Sub-Saharan Africa and in the countries classed as stagnant should give priority to rural households in clean cooking programmes, since rural access remains far below the urban and world levels.

Donors and public finance institutions should fund clean-fuel supply chains and the purchase of stoves for stagnant countries, with subsidies designed to keep fuel affordable for low-income households.
National statistical offices and the World Bank should report the indicator every year from household surveys, so that countries off track are identified in time to act before 2030.
The custodians of target 7.1 should state whether universal access for cooking means 100 per cent or a near-universal threshold, so that countries are judged by one reading.
w-c08-2-1.gaps: The indicator records the primary cooking fuel only. It does not measure affordability, reliability of supply, or continued use of solid fuels alongside clean ones. Values rest on modelled estimates from household surveys that are not available every year in every country. The trend classes extrapolate a 2015 to 2024 rate and do not forecast policy change, and the target text allows more than one reading.

w-c08-3-2.text:
### The global share rose by 2.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2020

The world share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption stood at 17.4 per cent in 2015 and 19.7 per cent in 2020. The share therefore rose over the five years, and the direction is clear. Whether the magnitude meets the aim of the target is a separate question, and the data alone do not settle it. Over the period the share grew at a compound rate of 0.0255 a year, which the trend tool classes as on track or target met. That label rests on a trend tool that has no numerical target to measure against, so it should be read as a statement about the pace of change, not as a verdict on sufficiency.

Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix, and it names no threshold. Two readings are available. The first is a rise in the share: renewables supply a larger fraction of all final energy. The second is a rise in absolute use: more renewable energy is consumed, whatever the fraction. The two can diverge. Where total demand grows quickly, absolute renewable use can climb while the share stagnates or falls. The indicator reported here, renewable energy consumption as a percentage of total final energy consumption, measures only the first reading. A rise in the share is the stricter test, because it requires renewables to outpace the growth of demand as a whole.

The word 'substantial' compounds the ambiguity. No agreed numerical benchmark exists in the target text, so any judgement of sufficiency rests on a chosen standard: a doubling, a fixed number of points, or a path consistent with climate goals. Since no such standard is set in the target, this account treats the change from 17.4 to 19.7 per cent as an observed change and states plainly where a reader's own threshold would alter the verdict. By any reading, a gain of this size from a base of 17.4 per cent leaves the large majority of final energy supplied by other sources in 2020.

The composition of the indicator also matters for interpretation. Final energy consumption includes heat and transport as well as electricity, and the renewable share counts traditional biomass such as wood and charcoal burned for cooking and heating. A share can therefore be high in poor countries because of reliance on fuelwood, which is neither modern nor clean, and the aims of Goal 7 treat it differently from wind, solar or hydropower. The headline figure thus mixes two quite different kinds of renewable use, a point taken up in the regional comparisons that follow.

A limit on the evidence must be stated. The series is reported by 212 countries in every year from 2015 to 2021, but only 71 countries report a value for 2022. For most countries, therefore, the record ends in 2020 or 2021 for practical purposes, and the comparison of 2015 with 2020 is the last one that rests on near-complete coverage. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks that followed, cannot be read from this series with confidence. For the 2030 horizon, this means the trajectory is known only for the first five of fifteen years, and the later years remain to be measured.

### Regional levels differ by a factor of ten, and nearly all regions rose

Regional levels of the renewable share span a wide range. In 2020 Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 70.3 per cent of total final energy consumption, South Asia at 36.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 34.2 per cent. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 7.5 per cent. The highest regional value is therefore about nine times the lowest, and the gap is wide in both years.

The ranking does not measure the quality of the energy system. In poorer regions a high share may reflect the burning of wood, charcoal, crop residues and dung for cooking and heating, which counts as renewable in the indicator. These fuels are often gathered unsustainably, carry serious health costs through indoor air pollution, and supply energy of low efficiency. A low share in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan may follow from large oil and gas endowments that have long dominated power generation and final use; this is context from outside the data. The indicator cannot separate traditional biomass from modern capacity such as wind, solar, hydropower or modern bioenergy, so a region can score high with little modern renewable infrastructure and low with a fast-growing one. Other series on the shelf, such as electricity output and output excluding hydropower, give a partial view of modern capacity but cover electricity only.

All regions rose between 2015 and 2020. Latin America and the Caribbean gained from 28.2 to 34.2 per cent, the largest rise of any region. Europe and Central Asia moved from 12.9 to 15.1 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 13.0 to 14.8 per cent, and North America from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent. Possible explanations, which the results do not test, include falling costs of wind and solar and policy support in some of these regions. South Asia rose more slowly, from 34.9 to 36.9 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 68.0 to 70.3 per cent. In both, a rise in the share is ambiguous: it may reflect new modern capacity, or continued reliance on biomass. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 7.1 to 7.5 per cent.

The income groups show the same pattern and one reversal. The low-income group fell from 77.0 to 74.6 per cent between 2015 and 2020, the only group to decline. The fall does not necessarily signal a worsening of the energy system. As incomes rise and electricity and fossil fuels reach more households, the biomass share can fall before modern renewables replace it, so a lower share may accompany a real improvement in access. Equally, it may reflect growth in fossil-fuel use that outpaces renewables. The indicator alone cannot tell which. Lower middle income countries rose from 41.7 to 43.3 per cent, upper middle income countries from 14.9 to 16.8 per cent, and high income countries from 10.6 to 12.8 per cent.

The result for the target is that the rise was broad across regions but small in the regions with the highest shares and in the low-income group, where the share fell. Reading the target as a rise in the share, the world progressed; reading it as growth in modern, sustainable renewables, the aggregate hides much of what matters, because the indicator cannot show modern capacity. Coverage also limits comparison: 71 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot yet confirm whether the post-2015 gains held after the shock of 2020.

### Country trajectories diverge: 73 on track, 85 in regression

The classification of countries separates the world into groups whose experience since 2015 has been very different. Of 202 countries assessed, 73 are classed as on track or target met, and these hold 37.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 11 countries show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed (3.8 per cent of population), and 14 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration (22.2 per cent). Nineteen countries are stagnating (4.8 per cent of population). The largest group by count is the 85 countries in regression, which hold 31.8 per cent of the population.

The label 'on track' needs careful reading. Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the renewable share but gives no numeric value, so no threshold exists against which progress can be measured. The classification therefore rests on an extrapolated rate of change: the observed trend is projected forward to 2030, and a country is called on track when the direction is positive and the pace is adequate by the tool's own scale. 'On track' here means a positive trend only. It does not mean that a country will reach any particular share, and a country that starts from a very low share can be called on track while remaining far from a renewable-based energy system. The reading of 'substantially' is open: a rise of a few points could count under one interpretation and fall short under another.

Count and population tell different stories. The on-track group holds the largest population share of any class, 37.5 per cent, yet it has fewer countries (73) than the regression group (85), whose population share is 31.8 per cent. Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries, and the two classes hold 4.8 and 31.8 per cent of the population respectively. The data therefore show a split world: a large share of people live in countries with a positive trend, and a comparable share live in countries where the share has fallen. The world rate of 0.0255 is positive and classed as on track, but it is an aggregate and does not describe each country.

The regional rates help to explain the pattern. The rates for East Asia and Pacific (0.0267), Europe and Central Asia (0.0325), North America (0.0370) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0390) are all classed as on track, as are the high income (0.0381) and upper middle income (0.0240) groups. The groups under the greatest strain are the low income group, where the rate is negative at -0.0064 and classed as regression, and the lower middle income group, at 0.0079, classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) and South Asia (0.0112) are also marginal, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0129) show moderate progress.

The indicator does not reveal why the share falls in low income settings, and the following is context, not a finding. The renewable share of final consumption in such countries is widely understood to be dominated by traditional biomass used for cooking and heating. If total consumption grows with non-renewable supply, or households shift away from biomass, the share can fall even while other goals advance. A fall is therefore not necessarily a failure of renewable policy. The gains in richer regions are commonly linked to deliberate expansion of modern renewables, but the share alone cannot confirm what was added.

For 2030 the implication is that a positive global rate can coexist with 85 regressing countries. The target will be met in substance only if the lagging groups change course, and the data cannot say whether modern renewables are replacing traditional biomass or merely sitting beside it.

### Convergence is weak and coverage thins after 2020

The convergence test asks whether countries that began with a low renewable share have gained faster than those that began high. Across 71 countries with data for both 2015 and 2022, the estimated coefficient is -0.0101 (p 0.0006, R2 0.190). The negative sign indicates that countries starting higher changed by less each year, so low-share countries gained slightly faster, and the p-value of 0.0006 indicates that the relationship is unlikely to be chance. The magnitude is small, however, and an R2 of 0.190 means that initial level explains under one fifth of the variation in change. The remainder lies elsewhere. National policy, resource endowment, the pace of electrification and the use of traditional biomass are plausible influences, but they are context only, since the results do not measure them.

The coefficient of variation points the same way. It stood at 1.040 in 2015 and at 1.039 in 2022, a change in the third decimal place. Dispersion across these countries is therefore not narrowing. A coefficient near 1.0 means that the standard deviation of national shares is about equal to their mean, which describes a very unequal distribution. Weak catch-up in the slope, combined with unchanged dispersion, means that the spread of national shares in 2022 was about what it had been in 2015.

This result needs careful reading because the renewable share in final consumption mixes two quite different things. In many low-income countries a high share reflects reliance on firewood and charcoal, not modern renewable capacity, and a fall in that share can accompany progress in clean cooking and electrification. In high-income countries a rising share usually reflects wind, solar and hydropower in the electricity system. These are well-established patterns, but the indicator cannot separate them. A convergence test that treats both as one scale cannot distinguish a desirable fall in traditional biomass from a failure to expand modern renewables. The weak convergence found here should not be read as proof that poorer countries are being left behind in modern renewable deployment.

The sample is also a limit. Reporting for this series was broad in the early years: 207 countries in 2000, 210 in 2010 and 212 in every year from 2012 to 2021. In 2022 it fell to 71 countries. The 212 countries of 2021 and the 71 of 2022 are not comparable bases, and the data do not show that the 71 are a random draw from the 212. The convergence estimate describes only those that reported, and it cannot be extended to the world or to any region without that caveat.

The drop matters for 2030 because the years after 2020 are the ones in which the pandemic recovery, the energy price shock and new policies would show. Those years are visible for only a third of countries. The series is fully covered to 2021, so the record to that year is secure, while any statement about 2022 rests on a partial group. This is a reporting lag, not a finding of decline, and it should be read as a gap in evidence.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The share has risen, from 17.4 per cent in 2015 to 19.7 per cent in 2020, but whether that is substantial cannot be settled from the data, because target 7.2 sets no number. Read as any increase, the target is being met at world level. Read as a pace consistent with a transformed energy system, the gain is modest. The countries are also divided. The 85 countries in regression hold 31.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 19 more, with 4.8 per cent, show stagnation. A rising world average therefore conceals a large population living where the share has fallen.

The low-income group shows the problem most clearly. Its share fell from 77.0 per cent in 2015 to 74.6 per cent in 2020, yet the level remains very high. As context outside the data, such levels usually reflect reliance on firewood, charcoal and other traditional biomass, which counts as renewable in this series but is neither modern nor clean. A fall in the share can accompany welcome developments, such as grid expansion, and a high share can accompany poverty and indoor air pollution. The indicator alone cannot separate these cases, and conclusions for the poorest countries must be drawn with that caution.

For 2030, the evidence suggests that the world is unlikely to reach a decisive shift at the pace of 2015 to 2020. The 73 countries on track hold 37.5 per cent of the population, and the 14 countries with marginal progress hold a further 22.2 per cent; acceleration in these large populations would move the global figure most. Convergence is weak and the 2022 data cover only 71 countries, so the picture after 2020 cannot be confirmed for most of the world.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c09-5-1.text:
### Unemployment and the participation gap at the global level

Between 2015 and 2025 the world picture for target 8.5 divides into two movements of very different size. Youth unemployment fell, while female participation in the labour force barely changed. The two series answer different parts of the target, and neither alone shows whether full and productive employment is being reached.

Youth unemployment, measured as the share of the labour force aged 15 to 24 without work but available for and seeking it, stood at 15.9582% worldwide in 2015 and at 13.4088% in 2025. For young women the rate was 16.9964% in 2015 and 14.9214% in 2025. Young women therefore remained more exposed to unemployment than young people as a whole at both dates, and the decline for each group was real but left a rate that is still high. A global rate above one in eight of the young labour force, in the latest year, shows that the target's wording on young people is far from met, though the target sets no numerical threshold.

Female labour force participation, the labour force as a share of the female population aged 15 and over, was 48.5461% in 2015 and 48.9389% in 2025. At the global level this is a movement of a few tenths of a percentage point over ten years. Whatever happened to women's access to work in the period, the aggregate shows no broad rise. The figure also conceals movements of opposite sign beneath it, which later parts of this section take up by region and country. Both measures draw on 182 reporting countries in 2025.

The figures are modelled ILO estimates, not direct national counts. Modelling allows countries with different survey calendars and definitions to be compared and gives a value for years in which a national survey was not run. The cost is that, where a country has few surveys, the estimate leans on patterns in similar countries and may not reflect that country's own labour market. Year-to-year movements in particular should be read with caution, and the comparison here is deliberately between two end years. A national-estimate series also exists for unemployment and for the ratio of female to male participation, but those draw on each country's own definitions and are not used for the global comparison.

Target 8.5 can be read in more than one way, and the reading changes the verdict. Read as a level of unemployment, it asks that few people who want work lack it, and the falling youth rate counts as progress. Read as parity, it asks that women and men take part in work on equal terms, and the participation rate of women, taken alone, cannot show that: it needs comparison with the male rate, which the ratio series supplies. The target also names equal pay, disabled persons and decent work, none of which these three series measure. A fall in unemployment can occur because people leave the labour force or stop searching, so a lower rate is not by itself proof of more or better jobs.

For 2030 the global averages set the frame. At 13.4088% youth unemployment is lower than a decade earlier, yet the participation of women at 48.9389% has not moved in the way that a path to parity would require. The regional and income-group figures that follow show where the global averages come from and where the gaps are widest.

### Regional differences in youth unemployment and female participation

Regional experience since 2015 departs sharply from the world averages. Youth unemployment, measured as a share of the labour force aged 15 to 24, fell most in Europe and Central Asia, where it went from 19.9 per cent in 2015 to 14.0 per cent in 2025. South Asia shows a similar fall, from 23.2 per cent to 15.4 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 14.7 per cent to 12.2 per cent, and North America from 11.7 per cent to 9.8 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa began lower and ended lower, at 11.3 per cent in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2025. East Asia and Pacific is the exception among the regions: youth unemployment rose from 10.4 per cent to 12.5 per cent over the decade.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands apart for a different reason. Youth unemployment there was 20.1 per cent in 2015 and 18.7 per cent in 2025, a small improvement that leaves it the highest of the regions in the latest year. The young women in that region fare worse still: female youth unemployment was 28.5 per cent in 2015 and 28.3 per cent in 2025, essentially unchanged. By comparison, the same measure for young women in South Asia fell from 22.6 per cent to 16.3 per cent, and in Europe and Central Asia from 20.3 per cent to 14.7 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific it rose from 9.9 per cent to 11.7 per cent, in step with the rise for young people as a whole.

Female participation in the labour force, measured as a share of women aged 15 and over, shows a different geography. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest rate, 64.6 per cent in 2015 and 65.2 per cent in 2025. East Asia and Pacific follows at 59.7 per cent in 2015 and 58.1 per cent in 2025, a fall. North America is nearly flat, at 56.5 per cent and then 56.8 per cent. Europe and Central Asia rose from 50.2 per cent to 51.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 50.8 per cent to 51.4 per cent. South Asia rose the most, from 27.5 per cent to 33.0 per cent, although the level remains low. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the rate fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent, the lowest of any region in both years. A high participation rate is not in itself a sign of decent work: in low-income settings, women often work because household incomes leave no alternative, so the rate must be read beside the other sections on informal and vulnerable employment.

The ratio of female to male participation, taken from national estimates, puts the gap in relative terms, with 100.0 as the point of parity. The trend results give regions whose paths differ widely. In Europe and Central Asia the ratio was 79.1 in 2015 and 79.9 in 2025, a trend classed as stagnation, with 80.3 expected in 2030. High-income economies moved from 78.6 to 81.6, with 83.2 expected in 2030, which the tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 66.3 to 70.0, with 71.9 expected in 2030, under the same classification. North America is expected to reach 86.0 in 2030 on its present path, again with significant acceleration needed. South Asia is expected to reach 60.5 in 2030 and is also classed as marginal progress. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the one region in regression, with an expected ratio of 29.8 in 2030. These are extrapolations of past rates, not forecasts, and say nothing of the policy changes that might alter them.

One result stands out and calls for caution. The lower-middle-income group is classed as on track or target met, with the ratio rising from 30.5 in 2018 to 55.2 in 2024 and 99.6 expected in 2030. That path starts in 2018, not 2015, covers a short period, and reflects a steep rise over six years in a series built from national estimates, whose coverage and definitions can change between survey rounds. A jump of that size is more likely to reflect changes in the countries reporting, or in how work is counted, than a real change in women's employment. It does not agree with the modelled participation rate for the same income group, which moved from 35.5 per cent in 2015 to 39.2 per cent in 2025. It should not be read as parity within reach.

The regional list in the trend results is also cut short. Only some regions appear in the summary: East Asia and Pacific and Sub-Saharan Africa are not reported there, and the figures for them in this part come only from the participation and unemployment levels. Their ratios of female to male participation are therefore not stated, and no judgement about their path to parity is made.

### How countries are distributed along the path to parity

The classification of 166 countries on the ratio of female to male labour force participation (national estimate) shows how uneven the path to parity is. The target value is 100.0 per cent by 2030, and each country is placed by the compound annual rate of change from its 2015 baseline, or from the first year after it, and by the share of the distance to the target that this rate would cover by 2030.

Only 13 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 7.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 19 countries, with 2.8 per cent of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest class is the 71 countries making marginal progress and needing significant acceleration. They hold 61.7 per cent of the population, so most of the world's people live in countries where the gap is narrowing too slowly to close by 2030. Another 13 countries, with 10.4 per cent of the population, are stagnating.

Regression is widespread. In 50 countries, with 17.9 per cent of the population, the ratio has moved away from parity. Taken together with the stagnating group, 63 countries are no closer to parity than in 2015, although fewer people live in them than in the marginal class. Regression in the ratio can arise in two ways: women's participation may have fallen, or men's may have risen faster. The classification does not distinguish between them, and it does not show causes. Among well-established influences are the pace of structural change in economies, the availability of care services, legal and social norms on women's work, and the effects of the 2020 pandemic on sectors that employ many women.

The regional results show why the population shares look as they do. The lower middle income group is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.103 and an expected ratio of 99.6 in 2030, but the series for this group begins in 2018 and ends in 2024, so it covers a shorter span than the others and rests on fewer observations. The regional aggregate also moves with the countries that report, and its rise from 30.5 in 2018 to 55.2 in 2024 should be read with that in mind. South Asia has a rate of 0.065 and an expected ratio of 60.5 in 2030, covering 0.448 of the distance to the target; this is the largest share among the regions not classed as on track, yet the ratio stays low. Europe and Central Asia is classed as stagnating, with an expected ratio of 80.3 in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan as regressing, with an expected ratio of 29.8.

The rate has limits as a reading. It is a compound annual change measured from a baseline, so it favours countries that start low, where a small absolute gain is a large proportional one, and it penalises those that start near parity. Countries with high ratios, such as high income economies at an expected 83.2 in 2030 and North America at 86.0, are classed as marginal because the remaining distance is covered too slowly, not because they are far from parity. Reaching exactly 100.0 is also one reading of the target; a ratio above 100.0 would mean women participate more than men, and the target text speaks of equality, not of a particular value. Finally, the classification covers 166 countries, fewer than the 204 with some data on the series, because a trend needs observations at both ends of the period.

### What changed and what may explain it

The movements recorded since 2015 are of two kinds. Youth unemployment is sensitive to the business cycle, and its fall in several regions is consistent with recovery from the shock of 2020, when hiring stopped and young people, often on temporary contracts, were among the first to lose work. Female participation moves far more slowly, because it reflects household arrangements, schooling, the availability of care, legal restrictions and social norms that change over decades. The two series should therefore be read at different speeds.

The participation rates show divergence beneath a flat world figure. Female participation in South Asia rose from 27.5 per cent of women aged 15 and over in 2015 to 33.0 per cent in 2025. In East Asia and Pacific it fell from 59.7 per cent to 58.1 per cent over the same years. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan it fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent, the lowest level of any region in both years. The world rate, 48.5 per cent in 2015 and 48.9 per cent in 2025, is the result of rises and falls that largely offset each other. Sub-Saharan Africa stayed highest, at 64.6 per cent in 2015 and 65.2 per cent in 2025.

Income groups show a similar split. Female participation rose in lower middle income countries, from 35.5 per cent to 39.2 per cent, and in high income countries, from 52.8 per cent to 54.3 per cent. It fell in low income countries, from 56.6 per cent to 54.7 per cent, and in upper middle income countries, from 55.0 per cent to 53.4 per cent. Youth unemployment among young women moved in a related way: in upper middle income countries it rose from 16.4 per cent to 17.3 per cent, while in high income countries it fell from 16.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

These indicators cannot identify causes. A fall in participation may reflect women withdrawing from work, women staying longer in education, or discouragement that removes them from the count of the unemployed; the series does not distinguish them. A rise may reflect new opportunity or economic necessity. Explanations drawn from the history of regions, such as expanding schooling, changing norms or legal barriers to women's work, remain context and not findings.

The second half of target 8.5, equal pay for work of equal value, is not measured by any of these results. Unemployment and participation describe access to work, not its reward, so progress on pay cannot be judged from this section.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The projections for 2030 show that parity in labour force participation will not be reached on the present paths. The target value for the ratio of female to male participation (national estimate) is 100.0 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the ratio was stagnant, and the expected value for 2030 is 80.3 per cent. In high-income countries, where progress was marginal and significant acceleration is needed, the expected value is 83.2 per cent. Both fall well short of the target, and the pace of change in both is slow. Latin America and the Caribbean is expected to reach 71.9 per cent, and North America 86.0 per cent. South Asia is expected to reach 60.5 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the series regressed and is expected to stand at 29.8 per cent.

Only one regional group projects to parity. The lower-middle-income group is expected to reach 99.6 per cent, but its series begins in 2018 and rests on a short run of national estimates, so this result should be read with caution. It may reflect changes in which countries report as much as changes in behaviour. The target can also be read in more than one way: a ratio of 100.0 per cent means equal participation rates, not equal pay or equal quality of work, and the section's series do not measure pay.

The country classification points the same way. Of 166 countries assessed, 13 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 7.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 50 countries regressed, holding 17.9 per cent of that population. Most people live in the group of 71 countries with marginal progress, which holds 61.7 per cent. Acceleration, not continuation, is therefore the condition for any gain by 2030.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c09-7-1.text:
### Child labour data thin out as the 2025 target year passes

The indicator available for Target 8.7 is the share of children aged 7 to 14 in employment, defined as involvement in economic activity for at least one hour in the reference week of a household survey. The World Bank's series carries no aggregate for the world or for any region, so the shelf offers no global share of children in employment. Only country values exist, drawn from surveys that countries run at irregular intervals. A global figure would have to be built from those values, and the data do not support that.

The number of countries reporting shows how thin the record is. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2016, 97 countries reported at least once. Coverage in any single year was far smaller. It stood at 24 countries in 2000, fell to 4 in 2002, and rose to a peak of 31 in 2006. It then stayed between 11 and 24 countries in most later years, with 22 in 2011 and 24 in 2012, before dropping to 18 in 2014 and 10 in 2015. In 2016, the latest year, only 2 countries reported. The pattern follows the survey cycle: the household surveys from which the series is built are held every few years, and each country appears only in the years when one was completed and processed.

This matters because Target 8.7 sets a date. It calls for an end to child labour in all its forms by 2025, and that year has now arrived or passed. The latest observations on the shelf are from 2016, so the data cannot say how far the world has moved towards the target since 2015, or what the pandemic after 2020 did to children's work. Closure of schools and loss of household income are widely understood to push children towards work, but nothing in this series measures that effect.

The indicator also covers only part of what the target names. It counts children aged 7 to 14, so older children up to 17, who fall within the usual definition of child labour, are outside it. It counts any economic activity of at least one hour in a week, which is broader than the worst forms of child labour and is not the same as child labour as defined in standards. It says nothing on forced labour, trafficking or the recruitment of child soldiers, which the target also names. Where the target can be read as the elimination of child labour in every form, this series can speak to only a narrow part of it.

### Country values differ widely, and most of the difference lies between regions

Among the countries that reported, the spread of children's employment is wide, and it moves sharply from one year to the next. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of country values was 0.232 in 2006, when 31 countries reported, and 0.625 in 2012, when 24 did. A Gini of 0 would mean every country had the same share; the 2012 figure indicates a distribution in which a few populous countries sit far from the rest. The Theil index tells the same story: 0.135 in 2006 and 0.856 in 2012. The other years shown fall between these two extremes: the Gini was 0.431 in 2000, 0.508 in 2005, 0.532 in 2010 and 0.390 in 2011.

Most of this inequality lies between regions rather than within them. The between-region share of Theil's T was 91.9% in 2000, 92.3% in 2005, 85.4% in 2006, 92.6% in 2010, 77.0% in 2011 and 91.7% in 2012. In five of the six years shown, more than four-fifths of the difference among countries is therefore attributable to differences between regional averages. The lowest share, 77.0% in 2011, still leaves regional position as the largest component. As context rather than a finding of these results, the pattern is consistent with the long-standing concentration of high child employment in poorer, agrarian economies, where household survey evidence has repeatedly shown work in family farming to be the commonest form. The measure does not identify which regions or countries drive the figures, and the results give no basis for naming them.

The swings between years cannot be read as real change in the world. The set of reporting countries changes every year: 24 in 2000, 26 in 2005, 31 in 2006, 21 in 2010, 22 in 2011 and 24 in 2012. A drop in the Gini from 0.508 in 2005 to 0.232 in 2006 coincides with the addition of five countries to the sample, and the rise to 0.625 in 2012 coincides with a different set again. Because each year's calculation covers only the countries that happened to be surveyed, a high or low value may reflect which countries reported as much as any shift in how children's work is distributed. Population weighting sharpens this effect, since one large country entering or leaving the sample can move the whole index.

The spread is also silent on levels. A low Gini could describe uniformly high or uniformly low child employment, so these figures describe inequality among countries and say nothing on whether children's work is rising or falling. No year after 2012 appears in the spread results, and the sparse reporting of later years leaves the 2015 and 2020 periods without a comparable reading. For 2030, the only safe inference is that where child employment persists, it is concentrated by region, and that measuring it will require the same countries to be surveyed repeatedly.

### Change over time cannot be separated from change in coverage

Reading the series as a trend requires first reading the number of countries behind each year. The count of reporting countries was 4 in 2002, rose to 31 in 2006, fell to 12 in 2008, recovered to 24 in 2012 and fell again to 10 in 2015. In 2016 only 2 countries reported. Any comparison of a yearly figure across these years would compare different groups of countries, so a rise or fall in a share could reflect who was surveyed rather than what happened to children. Across the whole period, 97 countries reported at least once, which shows that the series has broad reach over time but little depth in any single year.

The pattern follows from how the data are produced. Children's employment is measured through household surveys, usually run by national statistical offices with international technical support, and these surveys are fielded irregularly, often once every several years and only where funding and priority allow. A country may appear in 2006 and again in 2012 and be absent between. Peaks in reporting, such as the 31 countries of 2006, probably reflect clusters of survey rounds rather than any change in the phenomenon, and the troughs likewise. This is context, not a finding of the data, which do not record why a country did or did not report.

The 2016 observations are the latest on the shelf, and they cannot carry a reading of the period after 2015. The 2 countries reporting in 2016 are too few to indicate a direction, and the shelf holds nothing later, so neither the years after 2015 nor the period after 2020 can be described. The disruptions of 2020 to schooling and household incomes are widely expected to bear on children's work, but the series offers no measurement of it.

The same limit applies to the division between boys and girls. The male and female series each have only 2 countries reporting in 2016, the same 2 as the total. A gap between boys and girls drawn from two countries would describe those countries alone and could not be generalised to any region or to the world. Earlier years hold more countries, but they are not comparable with 2016 for the reasons given above.

For 2030 and for the 2025 date set in Target 8.7, the implication is plain. With 10 countries reporting in 2015 and 2 in 2016, the evidence for judging whether child labour has ended in all its forms is thinner now than in the years when 24 or more countries reported. Progress cannot be confirmed or refuted from this series, and the thinning of the data is itself the main result of the period.

### The 2025 target cannot be verified, and the proposals follow from that

The target year has arrived without a measurable global baseline from this series. Target 8.7 sets 2025 as the date by which child labour in all its forms is to end, yet the latest year in the series is 2016, and in that year only 2 countries reported. Across the whole period 97 countries reported at least once, but never more than a few dozen in any one year. A reading of progress towards 2025, or of the position in 2030, cannot be drawn from figures of this kind.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Its first clause calls for the elimination of the worst forms of child labour, including the recruitment and use of child soldiers; its closing clause calls for an end to child labour in all its forms by 2025. The indicator available here measures neither exactly. It counts children aged 7 to 14 involved in economic activity for at least one hour in the reference week, which includes light work that many national laws permit and excludes children aged 15 to 17 who may be in hazardous work. It also does not capture forced labour, trafficking or armed recruitment. A falling share on this measure would be encouraging but would not show that the worst forms had ended, and a flat share would not show that they persisted.

The sex-specific series, for boys and for girls, also stand at 2 reporting countries in 2016. Differences in employment between the sexes therefore cannot be assessed for the years that matter most for the target, namely those after 2015 and after the disruption of 2020. Causes commonly associated with child labour, such as household poverty, school closures and weak enforcement, may have changed in those years, but the data give no means of testing this.

For these reasons Target 8.7 is best treated as unassessed on the evidence of this series, and the proposals below follow from that finding rather than from any measured trend.

proposals: National statistical offices, supported by international donors and the agencies that run household survey programmes, should fund child labour modules as a regular part of household surveys, on a fixed cycle, so that most countries report in the same years.

The agencies that compile the series should publish the 7 to 14 series with an agreed age range and a sex split for every country, and should add the 15 to 17 group so that hazardous work can be read.
The World Bank and its partners should publish the number of reporting countries and the survey year beside every estimate, so that readers can see how much each figure rests on.

Reviewers of Target 8.7, including the bodies that report to the United Nations, should record the target as unassessed until the data allow a reading, and should state which reading of the target, all forms or the worst forms, they are applying.

w-c02-2-2.text:
### National poverty lines give the widest view, with uneven reporting

The national-line headcount ratio is the percentage of a population living below the poverty line or lines that a country sets for itself. It is the measure closest to the wording of target 1.2, which asks for a halving of poverty in all its dimensions according to national definitions. Because each country chooses its own line, and often revises it, the series records how each society judges deprivation rather than a single standard. Estimates come from household surveys. Alongside it, the World Bank publishes multidimensional, societal-line and $3.00-a-day series, which later parts of this section set against the national figures.

The series is wide in reach but irregular in time. Over the whole period 161 countries have reported at least one national-line observation, a broad base for a goal that applies everywhere. In any single year, however, only a fraction report. In 2000 the number of countries with a value was 16, and in 2001 it was 15. It rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, then stood between 40 and 50 from 2006 to 2014, with 40 in 2008 and 50 in 2012. Wider use of regular household surveys is the usual explanation for this expansion, offered here as context rather than as a result of the data.

After the adoption of the goals in 2015, reporting grew rather than shrank. In 2015, 55 countries had a value, and 57 in 2016, followed by 53 in 2017. Counts then reached 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. The year 2020, the first of the pandemic, shows 57 countries, a fall from 2019 that is consistent with disrupted fieldwork, although the data alone cannot show the cause. The peak is 72 countries in 2021.

The decline since then is steep. Reporting was 52 countries in 2022, 40 in 2023 and 31 in 2024, and in 2025 it is only 13. The fall does not mean that poverty has been abolished or that surveys have stopped. Household survey data take a year or more to be collected, harmonised and released, and national-line series are revised as new rounds arrive. The latest years are therefore incomplete, and the count for 2025 is best treated as a record of what has been published so far.

The consequence is practical. A comparison of 2025 with 2015 would rest on 13 countries against 55, which are not the same countries and may not be representative of any region. These results report coverage and not rate levels, so this part does not state how far any national rate has fallen; movement is read from the trend classes in a later part. Any statement about movement toward 2030 has to use the last years of reasonable coverage, up to about 2021 or 2022, and has to separate real change from changes in who reports. The figure on levels for 2025 rests on a thin base and calls for caution in every reading drawn from it.

### Dispersion among countries widened as coverage grew

The dispersion of national-line poverty rates among reporting countries rose after 2013. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.28 in 2013 and 0.34 in 2014, then reached 0.39 in 2015, the year the goals took effect. It was 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018 and 0.63 in 2019. The Theil index followed the same course, from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.26 in 2015 and 0.72 in 2019. Read at face value, the spread among countries in the share of people below their own lines widened markedly over these years. The results list no population weights for the dispersion statistics, so the reading is of the spread across reporting countries as the tool computes it.

This reading needs care, because the set of reporting countries changed at the same time. The number of countries with a national-line estimate was 45 in 2013, 55 in 2015, 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. A rise in the Gini or Theil can reflect poverty rates pulling apart, but it can equally reflect the arrival of countries with very high or very low rates, or the loss of countries in the middle. The series cannot separate these effects, so the figures are not a measured change in inequality between countries over a fixed group. For 2020 the Gini is 0.66 across 57 countries, but no Theil index or regional decomposition is available, so that year cannot be compared in full with its neighbours.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions is high throughout, which indicates that most of the measured dispersion lies between regional groups rather than within them. It was 75.8% in 2013, 88.4% in 2014 and 67.7% in 2015, then 80.7% in 2016, 65.1% in 2017, 86.3% in 2018 and 77.1% in 2019. The swings from year to year are consistent with a changing sample, since adding or dropping a few countries in one region can move the between-region share sharply. Differences in how countries draw their lines also bear on any comparison of levels, as the opening part of this section explains.

After 2020 the picture changes. The Gini fell to 0.35 in 2021, when 72 countries reported, the widest coverage of any year in the record. It then stood at 0.40 in 2022 with 52 countries, 0.35 in 2023 with 40 countries and 0.32 in 2024 with 31 countries. The Theil index moved from 0.20 in 2021 to 0.26 in 2022, 0.21 in 2023 and 0.17 in 2024. The between-region share was 82.6% in 2021, 88.5% in 2022, 76.0% in 2023 and 83.5% in 2024. The fall in dispersion between 2019 and 2021 coincides with a large change in the reporting set and cannot be taken as convergence. Counts fall after 2021, and only 13 countries report for 2025, so the latest years describe a thinner and different group; recent surveys are typically published with a lag.

For 2030 the implication is that national-line data can show whether a given country is reducing its own poverty rate, but cannot support a claim about convergence or divergence across the world. Assessment of target 1.2 should proceed country by country, over a fixed set of economies with repeated surveys, and the dispersion statistics should be read as a description of who reports in each year rather than of how poverty is distributed.

### Trend classes show most countries on track but a large regressing group

The classification covers 94 countries, those for which the national-line series holds enough observations to estimate a trend. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 3.8% of the population, and 7 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 4.4%. Five countries are stagnant, with 2.1% of the population. The largest adverse group is regression, with 34 countries and 26.0% of the population. Regression is therefore not a marginal finding.

The classes are the only evidence in this section on how national rates have moved. The tool reports a class and a share of population for each country group, not a rate level or a change in points, so no national rate is stated here. The classes say which direction and pace each national series has taken against the halving reading; they do not say how far any rate has fallen or risen. In this reading, regression means a series moving away from the target, which is not the same as a stated rise in a particular rate.

The weight of the favourable class comes from population rather than from numbers alone. On track countries are 41 of the 94 assessed, fewer than half by count, yet they hold 63.8% of the assessed population. A reader should not infer that two thirds of countries are succeeding; the count and the population share tell different stories, and both are given here. The tool does not show which countries drive the population share, so nothing is claimed about who holds most of it.

No numeric target exists for national lines. Target 1.2 asks for a halving of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions, but it names no common threshold, because each country sets its own line and method. The classes therefore rest on a reading of the target, not on a fixed value. Under the halving reading, a country is on track if its rate is falling fast enough to be halved by 2030 from its baseline, which is 2015 or the first year after. That is one reading among several. A target could instead be read as an absolute reduction in the number of people, as a reduction by a set number of points, or as a halving from the earliest available observation. Each reading would sort some countries differently, and the date and spacing of observations differ from country to country.

Several cautions follow. A country that revises its line can show a break in the series that looks like progress or regression though living standards did not move in that way. A country with a low rate can be classed as regressing after a small rise, while a country with a very high rate may be classed as on track after a modest fall. The classes do not rank the level of deprivation among countries.

The classification also leaves out countries without a usable trend. Where surveys are infrequent, the trend rests on few points, and the class can change with one new survey. The tool gives no breakdown of the classes by region or by income group, and none by the period before and after 2020, so the effect of the pandemic on the classes cannot be read here.

For 2030, the split carries a clear message. The on track group holds most of the assessed population, so the aggregate picture can look favourable, while 26.0% of the assessed population lives in countries where the national measure is classed as regressing. Meeting the halving reading across the whole group would require the regressing and slower groups to change course.

### National and international lines agree on direction but not fully on size, and the implication for 2030

National and international lines can be set side by side for 36 countries between 2015 and 2021. The comparison pairs the national-line headcount with the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Across these countries the rank correlation of 2021 levels is 0.72 (Spearman), and the Kendall measure of the same levels is 0.58. The rank correlation of changes between 2015 and 2021 is lower, at 0.53, with a Kendall value of 0.41.

The two results say different things. A country with a high national rate generally also has a high international rate, so the two lines rank societies in a broadly similar order. Agreement on direction of change is weaker. A country can see its national rate fall while the international rate barely moves, or the reverse, because the two lines sit at different points of the income distribution and are adjusted by different rules. A rise in living costs, a change in survey design or a revision of the basket can move one measure and leave the other untouched. The correlation of changes should therefore be read as a moderate link, not as proof that the two measures can be substituted for one another. Only 36 countries qualify, a small part of the 161 that report a national rate in at least one year, so the finding cannot be extended to all countries without caution. Both correlations are associations, not causes.

For the 2030 halving in target 1.2, the implications are mixed. The movement of national rates is shown here only through the trend classes, since the results hold no rate level or change for any country or group. Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, with 63.8% of the assessed population. Yet 34 countries are in the regression class, holding 26.0% of that population. The class describes the direction of the series against the target, not the size of any rate. The weaker agreement on change means that a country judged on track at its national line cannot be assumed to be gaining at the international line, and the reverse also holds. The target is also open to more than one reading. Halving may be measured against a country's own 2015 rate or against a baseline year that varies by country, and a revised national line breaks the series on which either reading depends. The aggregate verdict on 2030 is therefore less secure than the country counts suggest. A large regressing group and uneven reporting make it unlikely that the halving will be achieved across the whole population, even if many individual countries meet it.

The evidence has clear limits. Reporting is uneven: 72 countries reported a national rate for 2021, the peak, but 52 did so for 2022, 40 for 2023, 31 for 2024 and 13 for 2025. Recent years are thin, so the effects after 2020 are seen only in part. Country lines differ in definition and in the date of last revision, and the series does not record why a line was changed. The paired comparison rests on 36 countries. Poverty in all its dimensions is only partly captured by a headcount, and the poverty gap and multidimensional measures are not tested here against national lines.
