No series covers tourism employment, local content, cultural promotion or sustainability, and Target 8.9 sets no numerical threshold. The coverage result shows only which countries reported, not the size of arrivals or receipts.

w-c04-2-3.text:
### The global picture: most countries are on course, the world is not

Target 3.2 sets two thresholds that every country is asked to reach by 2030: neonatal mortality of at most 12.0 per 1,000 live births, and under-five mortality of at most 25.0 per 1,000 live births. The target is worded as an aspiration for each country, not for the world as a whole. It therefore asks a different question from a global average, and the two readings must be kept apart when the evidence is assessed.

The direct answer to how many countries have reached the thresholds is that the data cannot give a single count. The classification used here merges countries that have met a threshold with countries projected to meet it, so it states how many are on track or have met the target, not how many have already arrived. On that combined reading, 130 of 196 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 of 196 are on track or have met the under-five threshold.

The world averages remain above both thresholds. The global neonatal mortality rate fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024, still above the threshold of 12.0. The global under-five mortality rate fell from 42.9 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024, against a threshold of 25.0. Both series cover all 196 countries reporting in 2024, so the averages are not distorted by missing reporters.

The country classification gives a more favourable picture. In each case the on-track class is a clear majority of countries, around two thirds or more. The population shares are close to the country counts: the 130 countries hold 72.4% of the population assessed for neonatal mortality, and the 135 countries hold 74.7% for under-five mortality. A reader may therefore ask how most countries, holding about three quarters of the world's people, can be on course while the world average stays above both lines.

The answer lies in what each figure measures. A count of countries gives every country equal weight. A population share weights each country by its inhabitants. A world average is a rate per live birth, so it reflects where children are born rather than where the general population lives. As a hypothesis that the results here do not test, countries with many births and high mortality would pull the average upward; the data given do not show birth numbers by country.

A second distinction concerns the phrase on track. The classification compares each country's recent trend with the path needed to reach the threshold by 2030. A country that is on track has not necessarily reached the threshold; it is projected to do so if its pace holds, and the projection can fail if progress slows. The threshold can also be read in more than one way: the target says all countries should aim for at least as low as the stated values, so a country already far below them has no further obligation under the wording, though its rate may still fall.

The remaining countries show where the shortfall lies. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Four are stagnating and 9 are regressing. These 66 countries hold 27.5% of the population assessed, a smaller share than the on-track group. For under-five mortality, 39 countries need acceleration, 15 need significant acceleration, 3 are stagnating and 4 are regressing. The 3 stagnating countries hold 4.9% of the population assessed, a larger share than their count alone would suggest.

The gap between the two readings matters for policy. A statement that most countries are on course is true and encouraging, but it can mislead if it is taken to mean that the goal is within reach for children everywhere. The sections that follow therefore set the counts beside regional and income-group levels, so that the distribution of the shortfall is visible.

### Counting countries: how many have met or are on track for each threshold

The trend classification covers all 196 countries for both indicators, and it gives the plainest count of how many have reached, or are heading for, each threshold. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 target, and they hold 72.4% of the population of the countries assessed. For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met the 25.0 per 1,000 target, with 74.7% of that population. The under-five threshold is therefore the more widely met of the two, although the gap is small.

The class labelled on track or target met joins two different situations. A country that crossed the threshold years ago and a country that is merely on course to cross it by 2030 are counted together. The classification does not separate them, and the data given here cannot say how many of the 130 and the 135 have already arrived. A further count of countries whose latest value lies at or below each threshold would answer the question directly. Until it is made, the figures describe the direction of travel rather than the number of countries that have finished the work. The distinction matters because countries already below the threshold need only hold their position, while those merely on course remain exposed to any slowdown.

Below the leading class, the two indicators diverge. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 7.8% of the population, and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 11.9%. For under-five mortality the order is reversed: 39 countries are in the moderate class, with 16.1% of the population, and only 15 are in the marginal class, with 4.0%. Many countries therefore sit closer to the under-five threshold than to the neonatal one. This agrees with the established pattern that deaths in the first 28 days fall more slowly than deaths later in childhood. Infections, malnutrition and malaria respond to vaccines, nets and treatment, whereas newborn deaths depend on the quality of care around birth, on preterm complications and on skilled attendance, which take longer to build.

The worst classes are small in country count but not in consequence. Four countries stagnate on neonatal mortality, holding 2.1% of the population, and nine regress, holding 5.7%. For under-five mortality, three countries stagnate, holding 4.9% of the population, and four regress, holding 0.3%. The stagnating group on the under-five indicator thus carries a notable population share for so few countries, whereas the regressing group is small. Regression usually accompanies conflict, state collapse or the breakdown of health services, and a small population share does not make it less serious for the children living there.

The population shares also show that the country counts and the people counts do not coincide. Neonatal on-track countries are 130 of the 196 assessed, yet hold 72.4% of the population; under-five on-track countries are 135 of 196, with 74.7%. Even so, a substantial minority of the world's people live in countries that are not on course for each threshold. Since the target is written for every country, those countries decide whether the goal is met in the sense the text intends.

The classification carries the usual caution about reading a trend as a forecast. It extrapolates past rates of change to 2030, and the years after 2020 were disturbed by disruption to services and by uncertain estimates in places with weak registration. A country may be assigned a class on a series that is largely modelled rather than counted. The counts should thus be read as a guide to where acceleration is needed, not as a guarantee of where the thresholds will be met.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of seven

Regional neonatal mortality in 2024 ranged from 3.6 per 1,000 live births in North America and 4.1 in Europe & Central Asia to 22.7 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan and 26.6 in Sub-Saharan Africa. Under-five mortality shows a similarly wide spread, from 6.4 in North America to 71.2 in Sub-Saharan Africa. The tools give no ratio between regions, so the gap is stated here by the pair of values: the highest regional rate is several times the lowest for neonatal mortality and more than ten times the lowest for under-five mortality, as the figures above show. Neonatal deaths make up a larger share of child deaths where overall mortality is low, because the causes that remain there (prematurity, birth complications, congenital conditions) fall last. Where mortality is high, infections, malnutrition and malaria continue to claim children after the first month, and the under-five gap widens accordingly. This is context drawn from established knowledge, not a result of the data.

Income groups show the same ordering. Low-income countries recorded 24.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024 and 68.8 under-five deaths. High-income countries recorded 2.8 and 5.1. Upper middle income countries, at 6.8 and 13.1, sit well inside both thresholds. Lower middle income countries, at 21.6 and 43.8, lie outside both. The income gradient is steep because the interventions that save newborns and young children depend on health-system capacity: skilled attendance at birth, emergency obstetric care, neonatal care units, vaccination, and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria. These need financing and trained staff that low-income systems have found hard to sustain.

The trend classification separates regions that will reach the thresholds from those that will not. East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, and the high income and upper middle income groups are on track or have met both targets. East Asia & Pacific reached 6.7 neonatal and 13.2 under-five in 2024, and Latin America & Caribbean 8.3 and 15.4, so each is already below both thresholds. The expected 2030 neonatal values are lower still, at 5.8 for East Asia & Pacific and 7.3 for Latin America & Caribbean. For these regions the target is no longer a constraint, and the policy question becomes one of equity within countries, which regional averages conceal.

South Asia is the clearest case of rapid change. Its neonatal rate fell from 25.4 in 2015 to 16.6 in 2024, and its under-five rate from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rate of decline in the under-five rate, -0.0502, is the fastest of any region, and the trend ratio of 1.30 means the pace exceeds what the target requires. The expected 2030 under-five value is 19.7. For neonatal mortality the classification also reads on track, with a ratio of 0.96 and an expected 2030 value of 12.5, marginally above 12.0. The class and the expected value therefore sit uneasily together, and the neonatal result is better read as close to the threshold than as secured.

The regions and groups that fall short are those where mortality is highest. Low-income countries cut under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8 per 1,000 between 2015 and 2024, at a rate of -0.0231 a year. At that pace the expected 2030 value is 59.8, far above 25.0, and the trend ratio of 0.42 is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The neonatal record is weaker: 28.1 fell to 24.9, an annual rate of -0.0133, with an expected 2030 value of 23.0 against a threshold of 12.0 and a ratio of 0.32. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same pattern, with an expected 2030 under-five rate of 63.3 and a neonatal rate of 25.0. Neonatal mortality tends to fall more slowly than under-five mortality when health systems are weak, as a matter of general experience.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan group has a mixed profile. Its under-five rate, 36.4 in 2024, is classed as moderate progress needing acceleration, with an expected 2030 value of 31.1. Its neonatal rate, 22.7, is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 20.3. The group combines countries with low mortality and countries in prolonged conflict, so the regional figure conceals wide internal differences.

The lower middle income group needs a caution. Its under-five rate fell from 55.3 to 43.8 and its neonatal rate from 26.9 to 21.6, which are real gains, and both are classed as moderate progress, with trend ratios of 0.59 and 0.55. The expected 2030 values of 37.5 and 18.7 stay above both thresholds. The trend output for this group was partly truncated, so only the numbers and classifications shown can be relied upon.

### What changed since 2015, and why the pace differs

Between 2015 and 2024 every region and income group reduced both rates, but the pace varied widely. South Asia fell fastest. Its neonatal mortality went from 25.4 to 16.6 per 1,000 live births, and its under-five mortality from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rates of change, which the trend tool expresses as a proportional rate, were -0.0462 for neonatal and -0.0502 for under-five mortality, against -0.0133 and -0.0151 for the world as a whole. The region is classed as on track for both indicators, although its neonatal trend would leave it at an expected 12.5 in 2030, with a ratio of 0.96 of the distance to the target covered, so the neonatal result is close to the threshold and not clear of it. Sub-Saharan Africa moved slowest on the neonatal measure, from 29.2 to 26.6, a rate of -0.0103. Its under-five rate, from 85.0 to 71.2, fell at -0.0195, which is faster than its neonatal rate but still leaves it far from the threshold, with an expected 63.3 in 2030 against a target of 25.0.

The pattern across income groups is similar. Low-income countries reduced neonatal mortality from 28.1 to 24.9, a rate of -0.0133, and under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8, a rate of -0.0231. Both are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Lower-middle-income countries did better on both, with neonatal mortality falling from 26.9 to 21.6 (-0.0241) and under-five mortality from 55.3 to 43.8 (-0.0256); both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. East Asia & Pacific, already at lower levels, still reduced under-five mortality from 16.6 to 13.2, a rate of -0.0251. High-income countries and North America moved slowly, at -0.0142 and -0.0034 for under-five mortality, but this is expected near a floor, where each further gain is harder to achieve.

A consistent feature is that neonatal mortality falls more slowly than under-five mortality. For the world, the neonatal rate went from 19.4 to 17.2 while the under-five rate went from 42.9 to 37.4, and the proportional rates confirm it: -0.0133 against -0.0151. In Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group the neonatal rate declined at a visibly slower pace than the under-five rate. A well-established explanation, given as context and not shown by these series, is that deaths after the first month are mostly caused by infections, malnutrition and malaria, which respond to vaccination, sanitation, nutrition programmes and basic treatment. Neonatal deaths come largely from prematurity, birth complications and neonatal infection, which require skilled attendance at birth, functioning referral systems and specialised newborn care. These depend on stronger health systems and take longer to build.

The differences in pace must be treated cautiously. The indicators measure outcomes, not interventions, and nothing in these series shows which policies produced the faster falls in South Asia or the slower ones in Sub-Saharan Africa. Plausible hypotheses include the expansion of facility births in South Asia, and the heavier burden of conflict, fragility and weak health financing in low-income countries. These remain hypotheses. The estimates are modelled from survey and registration data that are sparse where mortality is highest, so differences of a few thousandths in the annual rate should not be over-read.

The period after 2020 cannot be separated in these series. Both indicators are reported as annual figures to 2024, and the comparison of 2015 with 2024 shows no reversal at the regional level, but it conceals any pause in particular years. Whether the disruption of routine health services in 2020 and 2021 slowed declines cannot be answered from the levels used here.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The thresholds will probably be met by most countries by 2030, but not by those that carry the greatest burden. On the trend classification, 130 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 the under-five threshold, out of 196 assessed for each. The countries still short are concentrated, on the regional and income-group projections, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income settings. Those projections show how far they are from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.0 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2030 against a threshold of 12.0, and 63.3 under-five deaths per 1,000 against 25.0. Low-income countries are expected to reach 23.0 and 59.8 respectively. The world as a whole is expected to reach 15.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000, above the threshold, and 34.1 under-five deaths per 1,000, also above it. South Asia is the exception among the poorer regions: its neonatal rate is projected at 12.5, close to but just above 12.0, though the classification counts it as on track, and its under-five rate is projected at 19.7, below 25.0.

Newborn deaths are the harder problem. Neonatal deaths depend on skilled care at birth, management of preterm birth and infection, and functioning referral systems, which are costlier to build than the vaccination and treatment campaigns that drove earlier gains. A country can therefore meet the under-five threshold and still miss the neonatal one. Of the countries assessed, 13 stagnate or regress on neonatal mortality (4 stagnating and 9 regressing), and 7 do so on under-five mortality (3 and 4). Those that regress on neonatal mortality hold 5.7% of the population assessed.

Two cautions apply. First, the classification depends on the trend method and on projecting a past rate of change forward. A different period or method could move countries between classes, particularly those near a boundary. Second, the wording 'at least as low as' can be read as a ceiling for each country in 2030, or as a direction of travel for countries already below it. This section uses the first reading, as the classification does. The wording also says nothing about inequality within countries, where national rates hide wide gaps.

Four proposals follow.

proposals: National health ministries in the countries classed as stagnating or regressing should publish costed plans for care at birth and for small and sick newborns, and should report neonatal mortality each year.
Donors and development banks should direct a larger share of child-health financing to Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, and fund newborn care and referral systems alongside immunisation.

Statistical offices and the agencies that estimate mortality should publish rates by region within countries, by wealth and by sex, so that national averages no longer hide the groups furthest from the thresholds.
The bodies that monitor Target 3.2 should report both the country count and the world rate, and state which reading of 'at least as low as' they apply.

w-c04-3-3.text:
### HIV incidence has fallen by more than a third worldwide

World HIV incidence fell from 0.26 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024, a decline of roughly 38 per cent, which supports the heading's claim of more than a third. The estimates are modelled, and 139 countries reported in 2024. Coverage is broad but not complete, so the world figure is an aggregate of reporting countries rather than a census.

Tuberculosis moved more slowly. Estimated incidence fell from 150.0 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131.0 in 2024. The series covers 208 countries in 2024, close to universal. Estimates are recalculated for all years as methods improve, so the 2015 value used here may differ from figures published earlier. The comparison is internally consistent, but it should not be set against older reports without caution.

Malaria runs the other way. Incidence among populations at risk rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, because malaria is not a concern everywhere, and the denominator is the population at risk rather than the whole population. The rise in the rate therefore does not show that malaria spread to new places. Disruption to prevention and care in the pandemic years, resistance to drugs and insecticides, conflict and constrained funding are recognised pressures on malaria control, but the series cannot apportion the rise among them.

Target 3.3 calls for ending the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria by 2030, but sets no numerical threshold. The phrase can be read as zero incidence, as incidence low enough to cease to be a public health threat, or as a given percentage reduction from a baseline. The trend tool therefore applies no target value for HIV, and its class of on track or target met rests on its own reading of the pace of decline rather than on an official benchmark. On that reading the world's HIV rate of change, -0.0525 a year, is classed as on track. Such a class describes momentum, not arrival at a defined goal.

The contrast between the three diseases matters for 2030. The HIV decline is consistent with sustained investment in treatment and prevention, which is context only, since the series does not show the cause. Tuberculosis has declined at a pace that would leave substantial incidence in 2030. Malaria has moved backwards on the measure used here. The global record is therefore one of clear progress against one disease, modest progress against a second and a rise against a third, and the following parts examine where those differences lie.

### Regions and income groups differ most in where the burden lies

The burden of the three diseases is distributed very unevenly, and the pattern differs by disease. For HIV, Sub-Saharan Africa remains the region with the highest incidence, yet it also recorded the largest fall. Incidence there declined from 1.2036 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.5374 in 2024. Low-income countries show a similar movement, from 0.707 to 0.3534, a halving over the nine years. The scale-up of antiretroviral treatment and prevention in the most affected settings is the usual explanation for such falls, though the series themselves do not isolate causes. Latin America and the Caribbean tells a different story, one of slow movement rather than of a large burden. Its incidence moved only from 0.2438 in 2015 to 0.2154 in 2024. The region started below low-income countries (0.707 in 2015) and still sits below them (0.3534 in 2024); the gap has closed only because the low-income rate halved, not because the region's own rate fell quickly. Epidemics concentrated among key populations, often with weaker prevention coverage, tend to respond less quickly than generalised epidemics that attract large international funding.

Two entries in the HIV comparison need care. South Asia is reported at 0.0907 in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries at 0.1783 in 2024, but in each case the tool returns the same value for 2015 and 2024. This reflects missing earlier data for the group aggregate, not stability, and no change over time can be read from those rows. Only the 2024 levels are usable: they indicate that South Asia has the lowest HIV incidence of the regions shown, but not whether it has fallen.

Tuberculosis shows a more divided picture than HIV. The world rate fell from 150 new and relapse cases per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131 in 2024, a decline classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. Beneath that average, regions moved in opposite directions. East Asia and Pacific rose from 140 to 144, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 45 to 51; both are classed as regression. Europe and Central Asia fell from 36 to 22, and South Asia from 233 to 189. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 115 to 110, classed as stagnation. North America held at 3.5 in both years, which is stagnation at a very low level and is not a cause for concern in itself.

Income groups show the same gradient. High-income countries fell from 20 to 12, and upper-middle-income countries from 107 to 92. Low-income countries moved from 229 to 199, and lower-middle-income countries from 241 to 208. Low-income and lower-middle-income groups are classed as moderate progress, needing acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 205 in 2024 after 285 in 2015 (rate -0.036), and South Asia (rate -0.023) are both classed as on track. Even so, 205 cases per 100,000 remains a high rate, so a fast decline does not mean a small burden. These are incidence rates; the series give no case counts, so they do not show which groups hold most of the world's cases. The target has no numerical value attached to it in the tool, so the classification relies on a trend rule rather than a stated end point; the target can be read in more than one way, for example as a fixed percentage reduction or as elimination as a public health problem, and the labels should be taken as indicative.

Malaria is the most concentrated of the three. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 232.4935 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 and 229.2614 in 2024, a change too small to count as progress. Low-income countries moved from 207.1516 to 206.6892. The world rate rose from 59.0112 to 64.0411, yet the rate in Sub-Saharan Africa fell slightly and that in low-income countries was flat, so these groups do not explain the rise; the series do not show which groups drive it, nor whether disruption to prevention and care after 2020 contributed. The rate in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4.3337 to 9.9708, a signal of resurgence that the available data cannot explain, though conflict, displacement and flooding are well-known drivers elsewhere. South Asia is the exception, falling from 6.3233 to 1.4562, and upper-middle-income countries fell from 2.0345 to 1.6485. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, since malaria is not endemic everywhere, so the denominators are populations at risk rather than whole populations.

### Country trajectories show progress alongside stagnation and regression

Beneath the regional averages, country trajectories diverge sharply, and the divergence differs by disease. Each country was classed by the direction and pace of its incidence series, and each class is reported both as a count of countries and as a share of the population those countries hold. The two measures answer different questions. A count treats a small island state and a populous country alike, and so shows how widespread a pattern is. A population share shows how many people live under it, and so shows where the weight of the epidemic falls.

For HIV, 49 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 49.7% of the population of the 146 countries assessed. Another 4 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration (0.8% of the population) and 12 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration (3.0%). The largest group by count is stagnation, with 60 countries holding 35.7% of the population, and 21 countries, holding 10.8%, are in regression. More than a third of the assessed population lives in countries where HIV incidence has barely moved, and about one in ten lives where it is rising. The world decline already described is therefore carried by roughly half the population, while the remainder has seen little or no benefit. Stagnation is the key finding. It is consistent with a plateau in prevention and treatment in many places, but the classes record only the direction of the series and cannot show why.

Tuberculosis presents a more favourable picture in breadth. Of 203 countries assessed, 123 are on track or have met the target, holding 61.2% of the population. Moderate progress with acceleration needed applies to 18 countries (4.2%), marginal progress to 11 (3.9%), and stagnation to 9 (14.8%). Regression affects 42 countries holding 15.8% of the population. The regressing group is large by count, yet a smaller share of people than the on-track group. Because tuberculosis incidence is estimated from notifications, prevalence surveys and modelling, a rise in some countries can reflect better detection as well as real spread, and the disruption of services during the pandemic years also affected case-finding. The classes cannot separate these causes.

Malaria is assessed in only 85 countries, since the series covers populations at risk and not the whole world. Of these, 36 are on track or have met the target, holding 59.2% of the population. Moderate progress applies to 3 countries (1.4%), marginal progress to 8 (8.0%) and stagnation to 5 (4.0%). Regression covers 33 countries and 27.5% of the population, the highest regressing population share of the three diseases. Malaria control depends on sustained delivery of nets, spraying, diagnostics and treatment, and is vulnerable to funding gaps, conflict, resistance and changes in climate. Where such supply is interrupted, incidence can rise quickly. That more than a quarter of the population in assessed countries lives in regression is a warning for the 2030 horizon, though the data do not identify which of these pressures applies in any one country.

The classification has limits that readers should keep in view. The rule is a trend fitted to a short series, and the period after 2015 is only nine or ten observations. A country with small numbers of cases or a sharp one-off fluctuation can be placed in a class that later years would revise. Modelled estimates are recalculated as methods are refined, so classes may shift between editions. Target 3.3 sets no numerical threshold for these indicators, so the classes judge each country against a decreasing path and not against a fixed value. The population weights also depend on which countries have data, which is why the three diseases cover different numbers of countries and cannot be summed. With these cautions, the common finding is that progress is real but concentrated, while stagnation and regression remain widespread.

### Uneven gains leave the 2030 target at risk and call for focused proposals

The evidence for target 3.3 points to three diseases moving at three different speeds. HIV incidence is falling quickly where it is highest. In Sub-Saharan Africa the trend rate is -0.0857 and the series is classed as on track or target met. Low-income countries, at -0.0742, are classed the same way, and so is the world, at -0.0525. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the regions assessed, with a rate of -0.0137, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. The region started below low-income countries in 2015 (0.2438 against 0.707) and is still below them in 2024 (0.2154 against 0.3534). The gap has closed only because the low-income rate halved, not because the region's own rate fell quickly. The target text does not define what ending an epidemic means, so even a continued fall cannot be judged against a fixed threshold.

Tuberculosis shows slower gains. The world trend rate is -0.0149, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. Low-income countries are classed in the same way, at -0.0155, and so are lower middle income countries at -0.0162 and upper middle income countries at -0.0166. Incidence rates are highest in these groups, but the series carry no case counts, so their share of the global total cannot be read from them. High income countries, at -0.0552, and Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0532, are on track from low incidence. South Asia, at -0.0230, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0359, are the high-rate regions classed as on track. Two regions are moving the wrong way: East Asia and the Pacific, at 0.0031, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.0140, are both classed as regression. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0049, and North America, at 0.0000, are classed as stagnation. The period spans the disruption of 2020, when services for finding and treating cases were interrupted in many countries. The series cannot separate that disruption from longer trends, so a rise in recorded incidence may reflect either real transmission or changes in detection and estimation.

Malaria is the weakest result. World incidence rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 232.5 to 229.3, and low-income countries stayed at about 207, from 207.2 to 206.7. The series do not show which groups drive the rise in the world rate. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4.3 to 10.0, a rise from a low base that still merits attention. South Asia is the clear success, falling from 6.3 to 1.5. Of 85 countries assessed, 36 are on track, holding 59.2 per cent of the assessed population. Another 33 countries are in regression, holding 27.5 per cent. Incidence is measured per population at risk, so changes in the size of that population affect the rate. The 2030 outlook is therefore favourable for HIV, uncertain for tuberculosis and poor for malaria.

Proposals follow from these findings. Governments and funders in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate malaria resources there, since incidence in these groups stayed near 229.3 and 206.7 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2024. Health ministries in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan should investigate the rise from 4.3 to 10.0 and report whether it reflects transmission or detection. National tuberculosis programmes in East Asia and the Pacific and in Latin America and the Caribbean should review why incidence rose, to 144 and 51 per 100,000 in 2024. Donors should keep HIV financing in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the rate is still 0.5374 per 1,000 uninfected population.

The data show what changed and where, not why. Explaining the falls and rises needs other sources, such as programme coverage, funding, drug and insecticide resistance, conflict and climate. These are not held on the shelf and should not be inferred from the incidence series alone.

w-c06-5-3.text:
### The indicator and what it measures

Target 5.6 commits governments to universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The principal measure of progress in this section is the share of married or partnered women aged 15 to 49 who make their own informed decisions regarding sexual relations, contraceptive use and reproductive health care. It is compiled by the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Statistics Division, mainly from Demographic and Health Surveys, and reported in the World Bank's World Development Indicators as a percentage of those women.

The question this section asks concerns health care and contraception. The indicator answers a broader question, because it also counts the ability to refuse sex. Its reading of the question is therefore wider than the one posed, and the part of the question about health care and contraception alone cannot be separated out from it.

The indicator is a composite, and its base is women who are married or in a union, not all women of that age. A woman counts as deciding for herself only if she answers yes to all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner if she does not want it; she decides on the use of contraception; and she decides on her own health care. A woman who answers yes to two of the three is not counted. The measure is therefore strict, and its level cannot exceed the level for any single component. Unmarried women are left out, so the series describes one part of the female population.

The reading of own decisions is not fixed across surveys. Each component rests on a question put to the respondent, and the wording, the response options and the interpretation of a joint decision with a partner can differ between survey rounds and between countries. A woman who decides jointly with her husband after discussion may be recorded differently from one whose husband decides alone, and cultural norms shape how women describe such arrangements. Answers on refusing sex are also sensitive to the setting of the interview. Differences between countries, or between years in one country, may thus partly reflect measurement and not only a change in women's autonomy.

The retrieved results for this section report how many countries supply the indicator, not the share values themselves. In 2024 the count was 5 countries, and across 2006 to 2024 a total of 81 countries have reported at least once. The share of women who decide for themselves is therefore not stated here for any country or year, and the question cannot be answered with a figure from these results. The shelf also lists related series on wider household decisions, demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods, unmet need for contraception, attitudes towards refusing sex and prenatal care. No result for them was retrieved for this section, so they are not read here, and they measure different things from the composite.

### Thin coverage limits any global picture

Only 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions in 2024, the latest year in the series. The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries but no share values for those five, so the share of women who make their own decisions cannot be stated for any country or year in this section. No aggregate appears in the coverage result for any year, so no regional or world share is available from these results. The question is therefore answered only in part: no global figure exists in the material, and the national readings are absent from it.

The question asks about decisions on health care and contraception, while the indicator also counts a woman's ability to refuse sexual intercourse. It counts a woman only if she makes her own decision on all three areas. The measure therefore answers a broader question than the one posed, and its share cannot exceed the share for any single component. The results do not separate the components, so the share deciding on health care and contraception alone cannot be read from this series.

The count of 5 in 2024 says nothing about why so few countries appear. The results give counts only, and they do not show whether the figure reflects survey timing, processing delays or other causes. As context, such data come mainly from household surveys that are fielded country by country at intervals of several years, so a country enters a year's count only when a survey has been completed and released. A low count should not be read as evidence that decision-making has become less common. Nor are the reporting countries a sample drawn to represent any region or income group.

For that reason the five reporting countries could support national readings only, if their values were available. Each reading could describe its own country. None could be averaged into a regional picture, because countries whose populations, laws and health systems differ widely would be combined into a number describing no real population. In the present material there are five country counts and no values to average.

The wider record shows how uneven coverage is. Across 2006 to 2024, 81 countries reported at least once. Among the years whose counts the results give, the number reporting in a single year runs from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018, and 12 countries reported in 2022 and 14 in 2023. Even in the best of these years, 15 countries is a small part of the 81 with a value at some point, and the set of reporting countries changes from year to year. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years would therefore reflect a change in who reported as much as any change in women's autonomy.

The constraint matters for the 2030 agenda. Target 5.6 concerns universal access and rights, and a measure reported by so few countries in a year cannot show whether the target is being reached. Women outside unions, and countries without a recent survey, are absent from the evidence. The thin coverage is itself a finding: monitoring of this target rests on a handful of countries in each year.

### Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data

Reporting by year shows why regions and countries cannot be compared on current data. The results give the number of countries reporting the indicator for every year from 2006 to 2024. The lowest count is 3 countries in 2008 and the highest is 15 in 2018. Counts for the intervening years are cited only where they serve the argument: 4 in 2009, 7 in 2010, 12 in 2012, 6 in 2013 and 10 in 2016. Each year's reading therefore describes a different group of countries, and a change between years may reflect who was surveyed rather than any change in women's lives.

The pattern is consistent with a survey cycle. Household surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys visit a country every few years, and the countries reached in one year are seldom those reached in the next; this is context, not something the counts themselves show. A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2018 and 2019, cannot be set side by side. Regional groupings fare no better, because a region may be represented by one or two countries in one year and by none in another. The coverage result lists no aggregates, so no regional average exists to correct for this, and constructing one from such uneven entries would imply a precision the data do not hold.

Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once, yet in 2024 only 5 reported. A country's most recent reading may therefore be older than 2024, but the results do not give the survey years of individual countries, so the date gap between latest values cannot be measured. Comparing latest values across countries would mix survey years of unknown spread, and the gap between two countries' values could be partly a gap in dates.

The results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, so no country's reading for 2024 is stated here, and the share of women who decide for themselves is unanswered for that year. The question asks about health care and contraception, whereas the indicator also counts the ability to refuse sex, so it answers a broader question than the one posed. A woman is counted only if she decides on all three areas, and the base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so women outside unions are not covered. The 5 countries reporting in 2024 are too few to support any ranking or regional statement, and none is made.

### Reporting has changed little since 2015

Reporting on women's own informed decisions has swung widely since the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, without a trend. In 2015, 5 countries reported the indicator. The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached a peak of 15 in 2018, then fell to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020. It recovered to 7 in 2021, 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023, before dropping to 5 in 2024. Across the years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. Counts for 2006 to 2014 are held in the results as well, but only the years from 2015 onward bear on the period after the adoption of the Goals.

The results give counts of reporting countries and nothing about why those counts differ from year to year. Household surveys are fielded in a country every few years and compiled some time afterwards, so a year with many reporting countries is one in which many survey rounds were completed and published. That is context from general knowledge of how such surveys work, and the series does not show it. The cause of the low count of 5 in 2024 is not known from these data. Later releases may or may not add countries to recent years, and nothing in the results indicates which.

The counts of 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020 are equal, and the series alone cannot explain either. The pandemic began in 2020 and disrupted many household surveys in general, but this lies outside the retrieved results and is offered only as a hypothesis that the series does not test, particularly as the count was already 4 in 2019. The recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is a rise in the number of countries reporting and is not a measure of change in women's decisions.

The consequence is that no before-and-after comparison around 2015 or 2020 can be drawn from this series. Each year's group of reporting countries differs from the last, so a rise or fall in any average would reflect who was surveyed. The retrieved results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, so a trend in women's decision-making since 2015 cannot be stated from these data. The 2030 horizon cannot be assessed against a baseline that does not exist in comparable form.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 5.6 cannot be judged as on track or off track with the data now held. The indicator on women's own informed decisions has no aggregate in any year, and the results hold no share values for any country. Only 5 countries reported in 2024, the latest year. Across 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once. Counts are given in the results for most years, though not for all of them, and the lowest and highest counts cited here, 3 in 2008 and 15 in 2018, are the extremes only of the years for which the results give a count. The question of what share of women make their own decisions has therefore no figure to answer it here.

A trend needs the same countries measured at intervals, and the shelf does not offer that. Whether a country has moved towards 2030 cannot be told from a comparison of one year's reporters with another's. The counts show how many countries reported in a year. They do not show why a count was high or low, and the series cannot link the 4 countries of 2020 to the pandemic, since 2019 also had 4. Any such link would be a hypothesis from outside the results. The cause of the low count of 5 in 2024 is likewise not known from the data.

The reading of the target adds a second difficulty. Target 5.6 speaks of universal access and of reproductive rights, which no single survey question captures. The question posed asks about health care and contraception, while the indicator also counts the ability to refuse sex, so it answers a broader question than the one asked. It requires a woman to answer yes to all three components, so its level cannot exceed that of any single component. Its base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so unmarried women and adolescents fall outside it. A rise or fall in the share could reflect a change in any of the three components, and the series alone does not say which.

The proposals below follow from these findings. They aim to make the next five years of reporting usable for judging the target, since the period to 2030 is short and surveys are slow to field.

Survey designers should release the three components of the indicator (refusing sex, using contraception, deciding on health care) separately as well as combined, so that a change in the composite can be traced and the question on health care and contraception answered directly.

w-c07-4-2.text:
### Water quality is measured mainly through sanitation and ecosystem proxies

Target 6.3 calls for halving the proportion of untreated wastewater, and Target 6.6 for the protection and restoration of water-related ecosystems, including mountains, forests, wetlands, rivers, aquifers and lakes. Neither can be measured directly with the series on the shelf of the World Bank's World Development Indicators. No series on the share of wastewater treated, on ambient water quality in rivers, lakes and aquifers, or on the condition of wetlands is held. Any reading of these two targets is therefore indirect, and the conclusions drawn from it carry less weight than those for drinking water or sanitation access.

Three kinds of proxy are available. Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using a private facility whose excreta are safely disposed of or treated, is the nearest stand-in for Target 6.3, because untreated human waste is among the main sources of pollution in surface and ground water. Terrestrial protected areas and forest area stand in for Target 6.6, since protected catchments and forested slopes shape the quality and regularity of the water that flows from them. Marine protected areas, water stress and the mortality rate attributed to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene supply context. Each is a proxy in the strict sense. Sanitation safely managed at the household says nothing about industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, which Target 6.3 also names. A land area under protection is a legal designation, not a measure of the health of a river or wetland, and forest area records tree cover without distinguishing natural stands from plantations.

Coverage of the sanitation series is incomplete and has slipped. The number of countries reporting rose from 137 in 2000 to a peak of 146 in 2016, then fell to 141 in 2024. Five countries that reported at the peak therefore no longer report in the latest year. A total of 146 countries reported in at least one year, so some economies are never covered at all. Regional and income-group figures are modelled aggregates, and they rest on fewer observations in the places where sanitation is weakest. The estimates that follow should be read with that limitation in mind.

### Safely managed sanitation rose from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent between 2015 and 2024

Safely managed sanitation, the share of people using improved facilities that are not shared and from which excreta are safely disposed of, stood at 48.4 per cent of the world population in 2015 and at 58.5 per cent in 2024. The gain of about ten percentage points over nine years is substantial, and the series covers 141 countries reporting in 2024, so the global figure rests on a broad base rather than a handful of observations. That base is not complete, however: reporting rose from 137 countries in 2000 to a peak of 146 in 2016 and fell to 141 in 2024, so coverage is incomplete and has slipped in recent years.

What this proxy says about Target 6.3 is limited, and the limit matters. The indicator follows excreta through the whole chain of containment, emptying, transport and treatment or disposal, so a rise in it means that more households are served by systems that do not leave waste in streets, fields and watercourses. That is a reasonable stand-in for pressure on water quality from human waste. It does not measure the share of wastewater that is treated, nor industrial effluent, agricultural runoff or hazardous chemicals, and it says nothing about the condition of the rivers, lakes and aquifers that receive the discharge. A country may serve its households well and still pollute its waters from other sources. The rise from 48.4 to 58.5 per cent should therefore be read as evidence of progress on one component of Target 6.3, not as a measure of the target.

A second caution concerns the classification of progress. Target 6.3 carries no numeric threshold in the bench's trend tool: it asks for the proportion of untreated wastewater to be halved, a relative aim that cannot be applied to this proxy without an agreed baseline. The classes returned by the trend method, such as on track or target met, are therefore a judgement about the pace of change, set against the tool's own projection to 2030, and not a comparison with a fixed goal. On that basis the world is classed as on track or target met, with a compound annual rate of change of 0.0213. Because the method rewards steady movement and not attainment of a stated level, a region can be classed as on track while a large share of its people still lack safe sanitation. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as on track at 25.9 per cent in 2024, up from 21.6 per cent in 2015, and is still far from universal coverage. The classes are best read together with the levels, which the following parts set out region by region.

The year of the data also bears on interpretation. The series runs to 2024, so it spans both the period after 2015, when the goals were adopted, and the disruption after 2020. The global series shows no visible break at the aggregate level, though the annual values behind the aggregates are partly modelled from sparse household surveys and censuses, and a short-lived shock could be smoothed away. For 2030, the figures point to continued gains, but no projection of levels is made here, and with the world at 58.5 per cent in 2024 universal safe sanitation remains a distant prospect.

### Regions differ widely, and the gap between them explains most inequality

The contrast between regions is the plainest feature of the series. In 2024 North America stood at 95.4 per cent of its population using safely managed sanitation, while Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 25.9 per cent. Europe and Central Asia, at 80.2 per cent, and the high-income group, at 84.4 per cent, sit well above the world figure of 58.5 per cent. Between these poles lie East Asia and Pacific at 63.6 per cent, South Asia at 60.1 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 54.4 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 51.2 per cent.

The pace of change differs as much as the level. South Asia rose from 40.8 per cent in 2015 to 60.1 per cent in 2024, the largest gain of any region, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 49.0 per cent to 63.6 per cent. Both are classed as on track in the trend analysis, as are the lower-middle-income group, which moved from 38.3 per cent to 51.9 per cent, and the upper-middle-income group, which moved from 49.1 per cent to 62.4 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean advanced more slowly, from 43.2 per cent to 51.2 per cent, and is judged to need acceleration. At the top, North America moved only from 95.2 per cent to 95.4 per cent, and the high-income group from 80.7 per cent to 84.4 per cent, which the analysis reads as stagnation. Europe and Central Asia, from 76.5 per cent to 80.2 per cent, shows marginal progress. Near-stagnation at a high level is partly a ceiling effect, since the last few points are the costliest to reach, and it does not carry the same concern as stagnation at a low level.

Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group show a more troubling pattern. The region rose only from 21.6 per cent in 2015 to 25.9 per cent in 2024, and low-income countries from 21.6 per cent to 26.9 per cent. The trend tool labels both on track, but the target is left undefined for this series, so the label reflects how the rate is read and not any prospect of universal coverage. At 25.9 per cent in 2024 the region remains far from universal coverage. Where a target can be read in more than one way, the label should not be taken as a verdict.

Spread among countries narrowed over the period. The population-weighted Gini coefficient fell from 0.261 across 145 countries in 2015 to 0.208 across 141 countries in 2024, and the coefficient of variation fell from 0.484 to 0.382. Differences between regions account for 59.6 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2024, the larger part of the total, with the remainder lying within regions. This is a result for a single year and does not describe change over time. The change in the country set between the two years is a caveat on the comparison. Convergence across 140 countries is weak: the beta coefficient is -0.00364 with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R squared of 0.018, so starting level explains very little of later change and the slope is not clearly distinguished from zero.

### Ecosystem indicators show stagnation and regression in many countries

Beyond sanitation, the shelf offers only land-based proxies for the condition of water-related ecosystems, and these show little sign of the protection and restoration that Target 6.6 set for 2020. The classification of country trends for terrestrial protected areas is divided. Of 211 countries assessed, 71 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 34.9 per cent of the assessed population. Against that, 54 countries are classed as regressing, and these hold 33.0 per cent of the population. A further 45 stagnate and 27 show only marginal progress. Protected land is a coarse proxy, since a designated area need not contain a wetland or a river headwater, and the series records designation rather than the quality of management. The regression class also needs careful reading, because the shelf sets no numeric target for the indicator and a decline may reflect boundary revisions or reclassification as well as loss of protection.

The sanitation classes, drawn from the same trend tool, show a similar spread. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target and 42 stagnate, while 25 regress. The regressing countries hold 6.8 per cent of the population assessed, a small share but a signal that gains in the global figure are not universal. These classes matter for water quality because untreated excreta remain a leading source of pollution in rivers, lakes and aquifers, so stagnation in sanitation is also stagnation in the protection of freshwater.

Forest area, which regulates flows, filters runoff and shelters headwaters, is stagnant in most regions. East Asia and Pacific moved from 27.0 to 27.3 per cent of land area between 2015 and 2023, and South Asia is classed as stagnating despite a rising rate. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 47.2 to 46.1 per cent over the same years, and low income countries from 21.0 to 19.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa and the lower middle income group are also classed as regressing, and the world as a whole is classed as regressing, at an annual rate of -0.0011. The tool does not show what drives these changes. As context only, conversion of forest to farmland and pasture, fuel wood collection and infrastructure expansion are well-established pressures, set against uneven enforcement of protection.

The central limit is that rivers, wetlands, lakes and aquifers have no series on the shelf. Target 6.6 therefore cannot be fully assessed, and the deadline of 2020 has passed without a measured verdict. What the proxies do show is that no region combines gains in forest, protected land and sanitation, which gives no ground for assuming that unmeasured freshwater ecosystems have improved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Convergence in safely managed sanitation is weak. Across 140 countries between 2015 and 2024 the estimated beta is -0.00364, with a p-value of 0.0545 and an R-squared of 0.018. The negative sign points to a slight tendency for countries that started higher to change by less each year, but the slope is not distinguished from zero at the conventional 0.05 threshold and explains almost none of the variation between countries. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.549 in 2015 to 0.501 in 2024, a narrowing too small to say that the gap between regions will close by 2030. At 25.9 per cent in 2024, Sub-Saharan Africa remains far from universal coverage, and no projection of its 2030 level is offered here.

The classification of country trends shows where the burden lies. Of 145 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the target, yet a further 42 are stagnating and 25 are regressing. The 42 countries on track hold 59.6 per cent of the assessed population, a share that shows where most people live but not how concentrated the gains are. These classes carry no numeric target, since none is set for the indicator, and should be read as direction of travel only. Forest area gives a parallel signal: the world trend is regression, at a rate of -0.0011, and Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.00636) and low-income countries (-0.00682) lose forest at the fastest rates. Catchment forests are generally understood to regulate water quality and flow, so these are settings where water-related ecosystems are under pressure and least measured.

Three proposals follow. First, national statistical offices, the UN custodian agencies and the World Bank should add the share of wastewater treated and the extent of freshwater ecosystems to the core indicator set, so that Targets 6.3 and 6.6 can be read directly rather than through proxies. Second, governments and development financiers should give priority in sanitation investment to the 42 stagnating and 25 regressing countries, since these are the places where the series shows no progress or decline. Third, forest-rich countries with the steepest losses, supported by climate and conservation funds, should protect forests where losses are recorded. Finally, reports on the goals should state plainly where data are missing, and not fill the gaps with unsupported estimates.

w-c07-5-2.text:
### Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015

World net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, measured in constant 2023 dollars. That is an increase of about half over eight years. In current dollars the series climbs from US$147.1 billion to US$259.5 billion. The two series meet in 2023 because the constant-price base year is 2023, so the gap between them in 2015 reflects the accumulated rise in prices since then. The constant-dollar figure is the fairer measure of change, since it removes the effect of rising prices; the current-dollar figure overstates the rise.

The indicator needs careful reading before it is applied to target 6.a. It records all net official development assistance received by developing countries: grants and concessional loans, net of repayments of principal, across every sector. It does not isolate water and sanitation, nor the activities the target names, such as water harvesting, desalination, wastewater treatment, recycling and reuse. The series is therefore a proxy for the general scale of international support, and a rise in it does not show that more reached water and sanitation programmes. Spending on health, emergency relief, refugee costs or budget support can raise the total without any of it entering the sector.

The target itself adds a second limit. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building support by 2030, but it names no amount, no share of income and no baseline year. It can be read as a call for more money, for more technical assistance, or for better-targeted programmes, and a financial series speaks only to the first of these. Capacity-building, such as training, institutional support and technology transfer, is poorly captured by a measure of net disbursements. A judgement that the target is on track can therefore rest only on the direction of the aggregate, not on a threshold.

Coverage is also partial. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts in this series, and the world figure is the sum of those recipients; the inequality analysis later in this section uses a slightly different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023, because it requires population weights. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region whose countries are donors rather than recipients, and high-income economies receive only small amounts: US$319.3 million in 2015 and US$760.9 million in 2023 in constant dollars. Net receipts measure what arrives, not what is needed, so the series does not say whether the level is adequate against the water-stress and service gaps described elsewhere in this chapter.

With these limits stated, the direction is clear. Assistance received grew substantially after 2015 and stood at its highest level in the series in the latest year available, 2023. Whether that growth is sustained to 2030 is a separate matter, because the donor side of the ledger depends on budget decisions that recipient data cannot anticipate.

### Regions gained unevenly, and Europe and Central Asia gained most

Regional totals of net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, show that the increase since 2015 was not evenly shared. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest gain by a wide margin, rising from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. That is close to a fivefold increase, and it lifted the region from one of the smaller recipients to the second largest, behind only sub-Saharan Africa and ahead of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region. The series does not show what drove the rise. As context only, emergency and budget support directed to the region in the early 2020s is a plausible contributor, and the series measures all official assistance, not the share spent on water.

The other regions moved much less. East Asia and Pacific received US$9.9 billion in 2015 and US$10.7 billion in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, almost no change in real terms. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion. These three regions ended the period within a narrow band of one another, near US$10.7 billion each, although their populations and water needs differ greatly. The data given here do not include population, but South Asia is known to be far more populous than the other two, so its assistance per person is likely to be much lower.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, a rise well below the world's increase. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the largest recipient, with US$51.8 billion in 2015 and US$64.8 billion in 2023. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region of donors rather than recipients. The largest absolute flows thus stayed in sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, while the fastest growth went to Europe and Central Asia.

The distribution by income group, also in constant 2023 dollars, shows a similar movement. Low-income countries received US$35.2 billion in 2015 and US$44.6 billion in 2023, and lower-middle-income countries US$54.9 billion and US$59.2 billion. Upper-middle-income countries rose from US$18.9 billion to US$57.4 billion, overtaking the low-income group. Assistance is therefore moving up the income scale rather than toward the poorest, a pattern that sits uneasily with target 6.a, which stresses support to developing countries in water and sanitation activities. Only a sector breakdown, which these series do not provide, could show whether water programmes followed the same path.

### A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase

The aggregate path of assistance since 2015 is not a steady climb. A structural break analysis of the annual change in world net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, places breaks in 2022 and 2023. Between 2001 and 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. In 2022 alone the change was US$49.8 billion, nearly eight times that long-run average. In 2023 the series turned and fell by US$0.7 billion. A single year therefore accounts for a large part of the rise recorded between 2015 and 2023, when the world total went from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, and the preceding two decades of gradual growth cannot be extrapolated from it.

The data do not record why 2022 was exceptional. It is an inference, not a finding, that the jump reflects emergency and humanitarian flows, support to countries affected by conflict and displacement, and pandemic recovery financing. That reading fits the earlier observation that Europe and Central Asia gained most, but the series covers all purposes of assistance together and cannot separate such flows from spending on water and sanitation. The small fall in 2023 shows that the 2022 level was not matched by a further rise. Whether it marks a plateau or the start of a decline cannot be judged from one observation.

The distribution of assistance among recipient countries also changed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received rose from 0.361 in 2015, across 138 countries, to 0.452 in 2023, across 135 countries. The Theil index rose more sharply, from 0.255 to 0.460, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.64 to 1.48. Assistance has thus become more unevenly spread among recipients. The country count differs slightly between the two years, so part of the change may reflect which countries report, and the comparison should be read with that caution.

The composition of this inequality shifted too. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023. Differences among countries within the same region now account for a larger part of the disparity than differences between regions. This matters for targeting: regional averages conceal recipients that receive much more or much less than their neighbours, and allocation by region alone would miss them.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise is fragile and its distribution has become less even. Target 6.a calls for expanded cooperation and capacity-building support in water and sanitation. Total assistance, whatever its level, does not show how much reaches that sector, and a total inflated by one exceptional year is a weak guide to the sustained flows that infrastructure and capacity-building require.

### Assistance for 2030 must be tracked by sector and directed by need

The series held by the bench measures total official development assistance received, not assistance to water and sanitation. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building in water-related activities, and total flows cannot show whether that is happening. A rise in the aggregate may reflect humanitarian, budget-support or debt-related disbursements that have little to do with water supply, sewerage or wastewater treatment. For 2030, the first implication is therefore that progress on 6.a cannot be judged from the present evidence, and the headline figure of US$259.5 billion in 2023 should not be read as a measure of support for water.

The second implication concerns durability. The break analysis found a mean annual change of US$49.8 billion in 2022, against US$6.4 billion over 2001 to 2021, followed by a mean change of US$-0.7 billion in 2023. A jump of that size, followed by a fall, suggests an exceptional episode, not a new trend. Planning that assumes the 2023 level will persist, or keep rising, risks a shortfall by 2030. The target can also be read in more than one way: it names no quantity of assistance, so expansion could mean volume, share of total aid or reach of capacity-building.

The third implication concerns distribution. Among countries, the Gini coefficient of assistance received, population-weighted and in constant 2023 dollars, rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.26 to 0.46. The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 45.3 per cent to 29.6 per cent, so the growing concentration lies increasingly within regions, among individual countries. In constant 2023 dollars, low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023 and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion, yet the data do not show whether flows follow the countries with the weakest water and sanitation coverage. Upper middle income countries received US$57.4 billion in 2023, up from US$18.9 billion in 2015, which suggests allocation is shaped by factors beyond service need; this is an inference, not a finding of the data.

The proposals below follow from these findings.
