c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023

proposals: Donor governments and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report assistance for water supply, sanitation and wastewater by recipient country each year, so that progress on target 6.a can be tracked directly.
Donors and recipient governments should plan 2030 water financing on the pre-2022 trend, not the 2023 level, and treat the 2022 surge as exceptional until later years show otherwise.
Bilateral and multilateral donors should direct water and sanitation assistance toward countries with the lowest service coverage, and publish the allocation criteria they use.
w-c07-5-2.gaps: The World Development Indicators hold no series for assistance to water and sanitation specifically, nor for capacity-building, so target 6.a cannot be measured directly. Total assistance cannot be split by purpose, and the data do not show what drove the 2022 jump or whether flows reach the countries with the weakest services.

w-c09-3-2.text:
### Vulnerable employment is the measured proxy for informality

Informal employment, the condition target 8.3 has in view, is not measured directly by any series on the shelf. The nearest measured proxy is vulnerable employment: the sum of own-account workers and contributing family workers, expressed as a percentage of total employment. The series is a modeled estimate of the International Labour Organization, and it is available for 187 economies, with 182 countries reporting in 2025. The proxy is imperfect. Some own-account workers are registered, taxed and covered by social protection, while some wage jobs are informal, with no contract and no insurance. The share of vulnerable employment therefore indicates the extent of weak job security and thin social protection, and it cannot be read as a count of informal jobs.

A second caution concerns the target itself. Target 8.3 asks for policies that encourage the formalization and growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises, but it names no numeric threshold and no year-specific level. Any statement of progress is thus a reading of direction: whether the share falls, stays flat or rises. The trend tool applies a decreasing direction by 2030 with no fixed goal, and its verdicts should be understood in that light. A different reader might judge the same movement more or less favourably.

At world level, vulnerable employment stood at 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 and at 42.4 per cent in 2025. The fall is about 0.7 percentage points over a decade. Roughly two in five workers worldwide therefore remain in own-account or contributing family work, a share that has barely moved across a period that included the adoption of the goals and the shock of 2020. The trend tool classes the world movement as stagnation, with an annual rate of change of -0.0017 on its scale.

This matters because the world figure conceals very different realities, taken up in the parts that follow. It also matters because vulnerable work is the form of employment least likely to carry a stable wage, a contract or a pension. A global share that has hardly shifted suggests that the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not, on the whole, been converted into a move towards paid employment with protection. The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring in many low-income economies probably weighed on the decade, although the series, being modeled, cannot show the timing of such effects with precision.

### Regions differ by a factor of sixteen

In 2025 the regional range in vulnerable employment is wide. South Asia stands at 69.7 per cent of total employment and Sub-Saharan Africa at 71.0 per cent. North America stands at 4.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 12.9 per cent. The highest regional figure is therefore about sixteen times the lowest (71.0 against 4.5). Two regions, both in the developing world, have roughly seven in ten workers in own-account or contributing family work. In North America the figure is below one in twenty.

The middle group lies between these poles and is more tightly bunched. East Asia and Pacific stands at 35.3 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 36.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 31.5 per cent. In each of these regions roughly one worker in three is in vulnerable employment, although their economic structures, institutions and histories are quite unlike. A region-wide average also conceals differences among countries, and the regional figures are population-weighted aggregates of modeled estimates, not direct counts.

The pattern follows the structure of production, as context rather than a result of this analysis. Where agriculture and small household enterprise employ most people and large firms offering wage contracts are few, own-account work and unpaid family work are the usual forms of employment. Where manufacturing and services are organised in larger firms and wage employment is the norm, the share is small. The income groups show the same ordering: low-income economies stand at 76.1 per cent in 2025 and high-income economies at 8.0 per cent, so income level and the share of vulnerable work move together.

The spread across countries confirms that region is the main divide: 71.9 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2025 lies between regions, and the rest within them. This shows that most of the cross-country inequality in the indicator is a difference between regional means. It does not show how many countries or workers account for the vulnerable total, and it says nothing about variation within any one region.

### Women carry more vulnerability where it is highest

In 2025 the world figure for women stands at 43.1 per cent of female employment, against 41.9 per cent of male employment for men. The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point. It conceals a division by region. Where vulnerable employment is most widespread, women are more exposed than men. Where it is rare, the order reverses.

The gap is widest in South Asia, where 76.2 per cent of employed women are in vulnerable jobs against 67.1 per cent of employed men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the figures are 79.2 per cent for women and 63.9 per cent for men, a difference of more than fifteen points. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the shares are 41.6 per cent and 34.7 per cent. These are the regions in which a large part of women's work is unpaid help in a family farm or business, or own-account activity in small trade and agriculture, with little social protection. Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work, since it can be combined with household duties.

The pattern runs the other way in the richest regions. In Europe and Central Asia the female share is 11.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent for men, and in North America 3.3 per cent against 5.4 per cent. High income economies show 6.9 per cent for women and 9.0 per cent for men. Men are more often self-employed in these economies, in trades, construction and freelance work, while women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts in services, health and education. A lower share of vulnerable employment among women here is not by itself a sign of advantage, since the series does not capture pay, hours or the quality of wage jobs.

By income group the same crossing appears. In low income countries the female share is 82.9 per cent and the male share 70.9 per cent. In lower middle income countries the figures are 74.0 per cent and 61.2 per cent. In upper middle income countries the gap narrows to 35.6 per cent against 34.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is close to parity, at 31.3 per cent for women and 31.6 per cent for men. The gender gap in vulnerability is thus largest in the poorest settings and closes as incomes rise, which bears directly on the inclusive aim of target 8.3.

### Change has been slow, uneven and not convergent

Across the 187 countries assessed, the trend to 2030 is mostly one of slow or absent progress. Only 24 countries, holding 3.7 per cent of the population of the group, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 19 countries, with 6.1 per cent of the population, show moderate progress that would need acceleration. The largest population weight lies in the 48 countries with marginal progress, which hold 51.7 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. Another 59 countries stagnate, with 25.0 per cent of the population, and 37 regress, with 13.5 per cent. Target 8.3 sets no numerical threshold, so the classes measure movement in the desired direction (a decrease) and not distance from an agreed goal; the reading is one of direction only.

The weight of population in the slower classes matters more than the count of countries. Large economies with high shares of own-account and family work move slowly, so the world average is determined by them, while many small and wealthy economies that were already low account for most of the on-track count. Progress that does occur is therefore concentrated where the problem was already smaller.

Between-country inequality in the indicator did not narrow. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.317 in 2015 across 187 countries and 0.320 in 2025 across 182. The Theil index moved from 0.178 to 0.182. The share of that inequality lying between regions, and not within them, stayed near 71 per cent: 70.8 per cent in 2015 and 71.9 per cent in 2025. The geography of vulnerability is thus still mainly a matter of which region a worker lives in. The change in country coverage, from 187 to 182, is small and does not alter the reading.

The convergence test points the same way. The coefficient on initial levels is slightly negative (beta -0.00281, p-value 0.0001), so countries with higher initial shares fell marginally faster, but the fit is weak, with an R-squared of 0.066 across 182 countries. Meanwhile the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.717 to 0.735, meaning that dispersion between countries grew. A weak tendency towards catching up coexists with a widening spread, which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved. Neither the post-2015 nor the post-2020 period can be separated by these summary measures, and the shock of 2020 is not isolated here.

Wage and salaried employment is the mirror of vulnerable employment. The rank correlation of 2025 levels is -0.994, and that of changes since 2015 is -0.920, across 182 countries. Because the two shares are close to complements, with employers forming a small remainder, this is largely definitional and gives no independent evidence that wage growth causes lower vulnerability. It does show that a fall in vulnerable work has meant a rise in paid employment, and not a shift towards other forms of work.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace of 2015 to 2025 the world would not reach a markedly lower share by 2030. The trend tool classes the world as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0017 a year, from 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 to 42.4 per cent in 2025. The calculation extends the recent line and is not a forecast. Target 8.3 sets no number for vulnerable employment, so the reading of 'on track' is the tool's: any decrease counts as movement in the right direction. Measured against the wider aim of decent work, the pace is insufficient.

The populous group of 48 countries with marginal progress holds 51.7 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. South Asia, with a rate of -0.0074, and East Asia and Pacific, with -0.0074, are classed in the marginal group by the regional trend tool. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0007, is classed as stagnating. Low income countries have a rate of 0.0000 (+0.00003), effectively flat, and the tool labels them regression; the sign of the rate alone would not justify that label. Faster movement in the regions with the highest shares would count for more than gains in Europe and Central Asia (-0.0137) or among high income countries (-0.0127), where the share is already low.

The cross-country picture is not one of convergence. The convergence slope is negative (-0.0028), so countries that started higher changed slightly more, falling more or rising less each year. Yet the fit is weak (R-squared 0.07) and the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.73 in 2025, so dispersion in relative terms widened. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini was 0.32 in both 2015 and 2025, and 71.9 per cent of the Theil measure in 2025 lies between regions. Most of the inequality in vulnerable employment is therefore a difference between regions, not within them.

The link between vulnerable employment and wage employment is close: across 182 countries the Spearman correlation of 2025 levels is -0.99, and of changes since 2015 it is -0.92. This is an association, not a cause, but the two series largely mirror one another. It is consistent with a route to lower vulnerability that runs through paid jobs and firms able to employ.

Five proposals follow. The International Labour Organization and national statistical offices should monitor informal employment directly alongside the modeled proxy, using labour force surveys. Governments should set a quantified national reading of target 8.3, stating the share of vulnerable or informal work to be reached by 2030. Ministries of labour and of industry in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where shares stood at 69.7 and 71.0 per cent in 2025, should prioritise wage job creation and the formalisation of micro and small enterprises, with access to finance and simpler registration. National planners should give women's vulnerability its own targets, since women are more exposed where the share is highest. Statistical agencies and the ILO should report data gaps openly, including the modeled status of many national figures.

w-c02-1-2.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 asks that extreme poverty be eradicated for all people everywhere by 2030, and its wording quotes a line of $1.25 a day. That line belongs to an earlier price base and has been superseded several times as purchasing power parity exchange rates were revised. The measure used here is the current international line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, published by the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform. Poverty rates under this line cannot be compared with those printed in earlier editions of the series, and the figures in this book should not be set beside older statements of the target without that caution.

On this measure, 13.4% of the world's population lived below $3.00 a day in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 the share was 10.1%. The fall is real and of consequence, in a period that included a pandemic and a sharp rise in food and energy prices (context from outside the results, which show the change but not its cause). It also shows how far the world remains from the target. At the 2024 level, roughly one person in ten still lives below the line, and the target date is six years off. Continuing at the compound rate of change observed since 2015, the series would reach 8.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The word eradicate admits more than one reading, and the choice changes the verdict. The strict reading is a headcount of 0%, which no measured aggregate has approached and which survey-based estimation could not confirm even if it were reached, since sampling error and gaps in coverage make an exact zero unobservable. The reading used in World Bank practice is a threshold of 3% of the population, below which extreme poverty is treated as ended as a global phenomenon. Against the 3% threshold the world stands at more than three times the required level in 2024; against zero the distance is the whole of the 10.1%. Both readings lead to the same conclusion for 2030, but they differ in what a successful outcome would mean, and the text of the target does not choose between them.

The choice of line matters for a second reason. A line of $3.00 a day is a very low standard, set to reflect the national lines of the poorest countries. Falling below it signals deprivation of food, shelter and basic needs. Rising above it does not signal security, and many households that have crossed it remain close enough to be pushed back by a poor harvest, an illness or a price shock. Later parts of this section turn to what the higher line of $4.20 a day adds.

The 2024 value must be read with care. The data behind the headcount are household surveys, which are conducted in each country at intervals of several years and are published with a delay. Figures for the most recent years therefore rest partly on estimates that carry forward earlier surveys using national accounts growth and other assumptions. The coverage record shows the effect. In 2015, 87 countries reported a value, and 93 did so in 2018. The number fell to 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted. It stood at 60 in 2023 and only 26 in 2024, and just 4 countries reported in 2025. The 2024 aggregate of 10.1% is thus a nowcast built on a thin base of direct observation, and later revisions can be expected as surveys arrive.

Two cautions follow for any reader. The fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is a robust direction but not a precise magnitude, and the end point is less firm than the start. The global figure also conceals a very uneven distribution, taken up in the next part, in which the decline has been concentrated in a few regions while others have seen little progress or a reversal.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture beneath the global figure is one of sharp divergence. East Asia & Pacific recorded the largest fall among the regions with a full series: the headcount at $3.00 a day went from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. Europe & Central Asia began from a low base and moved from 1.2% to 0.6%. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 6.0% to 4.3%, a decline that is real but slower in proportion than those of the two regions above. The series shows the change and not its cause; commodity cycles, informal employment and the reach of cash transfers are commonly cited as context for the region, but nothing in the results tests them. North America, at 1.1% in 2015 and 0.9% in 2024, was already close to the floor of what survey-based measurement can distinguish from zero.

South Asia requires a caution. The series for the region begins in 2020, at 9.4%, and reaches 2.6% in 2024. Read at face value, this is the steepest fall of any region in the period. The reading cannot be extended to 2015, because the regional value is not shown for the earlier years, and regional estimates depend on a small number of large countries with infrequent household surveys, so the aggregate may rest on interpolation as much as on fresh observation. The 2020 starting point also falls in the year of the pandemic, so part of the apparent decline may be recovery from a temporary shock rather than a sustained trend. Projected at its 2020 to 2024 rate, the region would stand at 0.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as on track; because the series is short and begins in the pandemic year, that classification is provisional. The figure is best taken as a sign of strong improvement of uncertain size, not as a measured change over the full period since 2015.

The regions where poverty has not fallen are those where the global total is now decided. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan moved in the wrong direction, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024, and the trend tool classes it as regression. The grouping combines economies of very different kinds, so the rise should not be read as a uniform deterioration; armed conflict and displacement in some members are often mentioned as background, but the results do not identify the cause. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, almost no change in nine years. A flat rate in a growing population would imply a rising number of people below the line, but that number is not measured here, and only the rate is reported.

Income groups tell the same story from another side. Low-income countries recorded 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, a rise, so that more than half the population of the poorest group of economies lives below $3.00 a day. Lower middle income countries stood at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024; the series for this group, like that for South Asia, is shown from 2020 only, and the same caution applies. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% to 2.1%, and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. The pattern is that the decline has been concentrated where poverty was already moderate, and that it has bypassed the group where poverty is deepest.

This matters for the target. The global fall from 13.4% to 10.1% coincides with large falls in regions that started with modest rates, while the region and income group with the highest rates did not move or moved backwards. The results do not show who contributes most to the global total, but they do show that the highest rates lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. Data for the most recent years are also thinner, a limit taken up in a later part. Eradication by 2030 would require that the stagnant and regressing groups reverse course abruptly, which no part of the 2015 to 2024 record suggests.

### Country progress and the absence of convergence

Sorting countries by the pace of their progress towards a headcount of zero by 2030 shows how uneven the record is. Of 105 countries assessed on the $3.00 a day line, 18 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 45.5% of the population of the assessed countries. That share is large because it includes some of the most populous economies, but the results do not show which countries drive it or why. The count of countries is far less encouraging than the share of people: 18 of 105 is a small minority of national experiences.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and they hold 23.1% of the assessed population. A further 15 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, holding 11.3%. In neither group is the target reached at the present pace. Moderate progress means the direction is right and the speed is insufficient; marginal progress means that closing the remaining distance would require a change of pace that few countries have managed in a single decade.

The weakest classes matter most for the meaning of the target, which asks for eradication for all people everywhere. 7 countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the assessed population. 24 countries are regressing, with 17.9%. Regression in almost a quarter of the assessed countries is a finding in its own right. The series shows the change but not its cause. As outside context, not a result of this analysis, armed conflict, state fragility, high food and energy prices and the pandemic of 2020 are commonly cited in the wider literature as reasons for setbacks. Because the classification measures movement from each country's own observations, a country can regress from a low level as well as from a high one, and the class does not by itself say how deep the deprivation is.

The convergence test addresses whether poorer countries are catching up. Across 57 countries with data from 2015 to 2022, the regression of change in the headcount on its starting level gives a beta of 0.00658 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029. A negative and significant coefficient would have shown that countries starting with higher headcounts fell faster. The coefficient is instead slightly positive, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 3% of the variation in outcomes. Starting poverty did not predict the later pace of change.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.144 in 2015 to 2.675 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts grew relative to their mean. Two readings are open. It may reflect a true divergence in national fortunes. It may also reflect that the headcount, as it approaches zero in many countries, has a small mean, which can inflate a ratio-based dispersion measure even when absolute differences narrow. The absolute test and the relative one should be read together, and neither shows catching up.

The sample limits both results. The convergence test covers 57 countries, fewer than the 105 classified, because it needs observations close to both 2015 and 2022. Household surveys are generally less frequent in poorer and more fragile countries, which is established context rather than a result here, so the finding of no convergence may understate the divergence. For 2030, the absence of catch-up means the global target cannot be met by the average trend alone.

### A slowing decline and its limits as evidence

The pace of decline in the world headcount at $3.00 a day has not been steady. A break analysis of the annual change in the world series finds two turning points, in 2014 and in 2021. Between 2001 and 2013 the headcount fell by a mean of 1.6 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.9 points, and in the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.3 points. The pace of decline in the most recent segment is therefore about a fifth of that recorded in the first. The two breaks fall close to two events that shaped the period: the end of the commodity-price boom and the slowdown of growth in many low-income economies after 2014, and the pandemic shock of 2020. These are context drawn from general knowledge, not findings of the series. The data show when the pace changed; they do not isolate why. Attribution would need counterfactual modelling that the series alone cannot supply, and the timing of breaks in a short annual series is itself uncertain by a year or more.

A further reason for caution is mechanical. When the headcount is already low, each point of decline is harder to achieve, because the remaining poor are, as a matter of general experience, concentrated in places that are poorer, more remote, more often affected by conflict or weak states, and less able to benefit from average growth. A slowing decline is therefore expected even without any change in policy effort. Yet this does not make the slowdown benign. The target requires the headcount to reach zero, or a figure close to it, and a falling rate of change moves that outcome further from 2030, not nearer.

The evidence behind the latest segment is thinner than the evidence behind the earlier ones. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly and published with a lag. The number of countries reporting a figure for the headcount was 87 in 2015, 70 in 2020 and 81 in 2021. It fell to 60 in 2023, to 26 in 2024 and to 4 in 2025. The decline in recent years is partly a matter of surveys not yet processed or not yet conducted, so the world and regional figures for 2023 onward probably lean on estimates that carry forward earlier survey information with growth data and assumptions about distribution. The mean change for 2021-2024 should be read as a provisional estimate, likely to be revised as surveys arrive, and the 2025 figures hardly rest on observed data at all.

The coverage problem may be uneven as well as thin. Countries with infrequent surveys are plausibly those with the highest poverty and the weakest statistical systems, and so the most likely to be absent from a given year; the counts above do not themselves show which countries are missing. The world aggregate could then be least well measured where the number of poor people is largest. Anyone assessing whether 2030 is within reach should weigh the slowdown found here as a signal that is probably real in direction, since the breaks are consistent across segments, but uncertain in size.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace observed since 2021, the world will not reach zero extreme poverty by 2030. The world headcount at $3.00 a day stood at 10.1% in 2024, and the trend to the target projects 8.4% in 2030 at the rate since 2015, a ratio of 0.38 of the progress needed. The trend classifies the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Target 1.1 can also be read as a threshold of 3%, as is often done in practice. That reading is no more attainable at this pace, since the world headcount of 10.1% is still more than three times that level, and the segment from 2021 to 2024 shows a mean annual fall of only 0.325 points.

Even the regions that are advancing need to go faster. East Asia & Pacific, the best performer among the regions with a full series, is expected to stand at 1.0% in 2030 at its present rate, against a target of zero, and its ratio is 0.84. Europe & Central Asia is expected at 0.4%, and upper middle income countries at 1.1%. These are small residual shares, but they are the hardest to remove. As context from outside the results, the people concerned are often in remote, conflict-affected or marginalised groups that growth alone does not reach. South Asia is classed as on track, with an expected 0.4% in 2030, from a start of 9.4% in 2020. That classification is provisional: the series begins in 2020, the pandemic year, so the fall to 2.6% in 2024 is measured from a short and unusual base.

The weight of the problem lies where the trend is flat or reversed. Sub-Saharan Africa is in stagnation, with an expected 44.7% in 2030, and low-income countries are in regression, with 54.2% expected. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also in regression, with 16.7% expected. The series shows these changes but not their causes. Because the world headcount is built from these parts, it cannot approach zero while they stay where they are. Among 105 countries assessed, 24 are in regression and hold 17.9% of the assessed population.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. National governments and donors should concentrate poverty-reduction effort and concessional finance on Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, where the headcount of 45.0% and 52.5% respectively in 2024 is not falling. National statistical offices, with the World Bank and bilateral funders, should fund household surveys at a regular and shorter interval; the interval is a proposal, not a finding, and the case for it is that 70 countries reported in 2020 against 26 for 2024 and 4 for 2025, so recent estimates rest on projection. The World Bank and national authorities should report the $3.00 and $4.20 lines side by side, naming the line and the price base, so that the $1.25 wording of Target 1.1 is not mistaken for the current measure. The United Nations statistical system should track regression as a class of its own, since the 24 countries in that class are hidden by averages that mix them with countries that are advancing.

w-c05-5-3.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small and should be read with caution. In the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. The fall is not a loss for girls: it largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, since South Asia moved from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020 and lower middle income countries from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.997 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.997 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.995 in North America and 0.991 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.982. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.970 in 2015 to 0.976 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.956 to 0.958. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.061 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.868 in 2015 and 0.900 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.952 to 0.965. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.018 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.052, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. The data do not show why. One hypothesis, which these series cannot test, is that boys leave school early for paid work in some settings. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.010 to 0.982 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.993.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.122 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 and North America 1.301, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.153, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.128, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.058 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.954 to 1.029. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.794 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.735 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.301 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.992 at primary level in 2020, 0.997 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.038 at tertiary level in 2024, close to parity at the first two levels and above it at the third. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure. The spread is also reported only for 2015, so these data cannot show whether dispersion has narrowed since.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison, and the male series has the same coverage in the shelf's description. In 2025, however, only 11 countries have reported. The count was 110 in 2024, and reporting for the latest year is always incomplete because national statistics reach the international database after a lag. The 2025 figure is therefore a feature of data release, not evidence that countries stopped collecting, but the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is largely a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for them. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and this pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. The data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that disadvantage girls are concentrated at the secondary and tertiary levels, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries. At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.900 in 2020, up from 0.868 in 2015, and low-income countries stood at 0.819, up from 0.806. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.952 to 0.965 over the same years and remained below parity. The direction is towards parity in each case, but no projection has been run on these series. Whether parity is reached by 2030 is therefore conjecture, and at the pace of 2015 to 2020 the low-income gap would still be wide. At tertiary level the Sub-Saharan African index was 0.794 in 2021 and the low-income index 0.672. Low-income countries were below parity at all three levels.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.103 in 2015 to 1.122 in 2024, with Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.291 and North America at 1.301 in 2024. Target 4.5 can be read in two ways: as the elimination of gaps that disadvantage girls, or as the elimination of any gap in either direction. Under the first reading much of the world has met the target at tertiary level. Under the second it has not, and the gap favouring women is widening in several regions.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024, so recent completion gaps cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow, each tied to a finding above.

First, national statistical offices and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should complete sex-disaggregated completion and enrolment returns within two years of the reference year, because 11 countries reported primary completion for 2025 and 2 reported secondary enrolment for 2022. Progress would be monitored by the number of countries reporting each year.

Second, ministries of education and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate on keeping girls in lower and upper secondary school, because the secondary index was 0.900 and 0.819 in 2020. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps against girls, and would be monitored by the secondary index.

Third, ministries in low-income countries should widen access to tertiary education for women, because the low-income tertiary index was 0.672 in 2021, the lowest of any group reported.

Fourth, education ministries in Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, and Europe and Central Asia should monitor male participation at tertiary level, because the indices were 1.291, 1.301 and 1.153 in 2024. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps in either direction.

w-c05-1-3.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The world primary completion rate stood at 87.9% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 88.0% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The change over nine years is too small to register as progress. The period spans the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the school closures of 2020 and the uneven recovery since, and the aggregate shows no surge after 2015 and no visible collapse after 2020. A flat global line can conceal movement in both directions, and the regional and income-group figures show that it does.

The indicator needs careful reading. Primary completion here is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of primary education: new entrants in the last grade, whatever their age, divided by the population at the entrance age for that grade. Because late entrants and early starters are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100, and it is not the share of a birth cohort that finishes primary school. The target can be read in more than one way: as universal completion, meaning every child finishes, or as a rate of 100 or more, which the ratio can reach while some children remain outside school. The trend assessment in this chapter takes the second, arithmetical reading, with 100.0 as the threshold.

The movement beneath the flat world line is large in places. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% to 83.7%, a gain of nearly ten points. East Asia and Pacific rose from 94.1% to 95.4% by 2022, its latest value. Sub-Saharan Africa moved only from 66.3% to 68.9%, and low-income countries from 60.5% in 2015 to 62.9% in 2023, so the poorest groups remain furthest from the target and gained little. Against these gains, South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 98.4% to 96.5%, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% by 2023. Lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% and then 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% by 2023 and high income countries stayed near 98.1% and 97.8%. Gains in one region are therefore offset by losses in others, which is why the world figure does not move.

Under the arithmetical reading, the country classification is sobering. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, holding 19.6% of the assessed population. A further 14 show moderate progress, with 13.0% of the population, and 14 show marginal progress, with 5.7%. Three stagnate, with 0.5%. Regression is the largest class: 92 countries, holding 61.3% of the population. The results do not show how much of this reflects real deterioration. Some of it may arise where ratios above 100 drift back towards 100 as late entry and repetition decline, which the classification counts as movement away from the target. The count alone cannot separate the two.

Reporting is a further limit. Only 11 countries had reported a value for 2025 at the time of access, so the most recent global figure rests on 2024. The finding of near stagnation is firm for the period to 2024 but says little about the last years before the target date.

### Lower secondary completion shows slow, uneven gains

The world lower secondary completion rate stood at 74.8% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 77.9% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The measure is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education, so it counts new entrants in that grade regardless of age. A ratio can therefore exceed 100.0%, and the rate indicates intake to the last grade rather than certified completion. The trend tool classes the world as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.21 of the distance from baseline to target.

Set beside primary completion, which was 88.0% in 2024, the world figure for lower secondary shows that intake falls between the two cycles. Because the indicator is a ratio and not a count of a single cohort, this gap should not be converted into a number of adolescents. Established research on education systems points to rising costs, scarcer and more distant schools, and the demands of household labour after primary school, but the series themselves do not isolate these causes.

The regional series show where the shortfall lies. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 42.3% in 2015 and 44.4% in 2023, and remains far below the world rate; the trend tool classes it as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.07. Low-income countries moved from 37.0% in 2015 to 38.6% in 2023, also classed as stagnation, and are the group furthest from the target. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 57.1% to 66.7% in 2024, a faster pace than most regions, with a trend ratio of 0.39 and a class of marginal progress, yet it remains well below the world rate. South Asia advanced from 83.7% to 86.6%, also classed as marginal progress.

East Asia and Pacific rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, the largest gain among the regional aggregates, with a trend ratio of 1.39. It is the only region classed on track, and it is the main visible reason the world rate has risen. Europe and Central Asia moved from 90.9% to 91.9%, classed as marginal progress, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 81.3% to 81.5%, which the trend tool classes as stagnation. By income group, upper-middle-income countries rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 93.0% in 2023 and are classed on track, high-income countries moved from 94.0% to 95.6% in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries from 71.0% to 73.7%. Both of the latter are classed as marginal progress. Low-income countries have closed little of the distance.

Several series do not cover the full period. The North American series begins in 2016, not 2015, at 104.3%, and ends in 2023 at 100.8%. Both values lie above 100.0% because the ratio counts older entrants, so the decline does not indicate a fall below universal completion. The Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income and upper-middle-income series end in 2023, one year before the world and several other groups, so comparisons across aggregates mix periods of different length. Only 11 countries reported a value for 2025, too few to support any statement about that year.

The aggregates show no break that can be attributed to the school closures of 2020. Projected to 2030 at the observed pace, the world rate reaches about 80.0%, far short of the target. Sub-Saharan Africa reaches about 46.2% and low-income countries about 40.1%, while East Asia and Pacific passes 100.0% on the same method. The country classes for this indicator are set out in the section on divergence and are not repeated here.

### Regions and countries diverge sharply

Regional averages conceal a wide spread in how far children travel through school. In Sub-Saharan Africa the primary completion rate was 68.9% of the relevant age group in 2024, up from 66.3% in 2015. Lower secondary completion in the same region was 44.4% in 2023, up from 42.3% in 2015. Fewer than half of the children in the region reach the last grade of lower secondary, and the small gain over eight years leaves the region far from the target of 100.0%. The trend tool classes the region as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected value of 46.2% in 2030. Low-income countries are further from the target than any region: 62.9% at primary in 2023 and 38.6% at lower secondary in 2023, up from 37.0% in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 40.1% at lower secondary.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region shows the largest gain in primary completion, from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly ten points. At lower secondary the region rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. The tool classes it as marginal progress at lower secondary, with a ratio of 0.39 and an expected value of 73.9% in 2030, still well short of 100.0%. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 1.39, is the only region classed as on track at this stage among the regions assessed. The region's figures combine countries in very different circumstances, and measurement may be uncertain where conflict and displacement are present. The gain should be read as a regional average, not as a uniform improvement.

East Asia and Pacific is the clearest success. Lower secondary completion rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, and the region is classed as on track, with an expected 105.4% in 2030. A value above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio, so it does not signal that every child completes on time. Primary completion in the region reached 95.4% in 2022, from 94.1% in 2015. Upper middle income countries are also classed as on track at lower secondary, rising from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023, while lower middle income countries moved from 71.0% to 73.7% in 2024 and are classed as marginal progress. At primary level lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% in 2023.

Several regions went backwards at primary level. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 98.4% in 2015 to 96.5% in 2024. South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4% over the same years, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. These regions began near universal completion, so the declines differ in kind from the shortfalls in Africa. The data do not show why they fell; the 2020 disruption and changes in enrolment and repetition are possible contributors, and because the measure counts new entrants in the last grade, shifts in repetition or age at entry can move it without any change in the number of children finishing. Primary completion in Europe and Central Asia rose from 97.2% to 98.1%. At lower secondary, Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as stagnant, from 81.3% in 2015 to 81.5% in 2024, and South Asia improved from 83.7% to 86.6%. North America is classed as on track at lower secondary although its ratio, 100.8% in 2023, fell from 104.3% in 2016, because the series already sits above the target.

Country classes confirm that the global average hides a divide. Of 173 countries assessed on primary completion, 50 are on track or have met the target, and 92 are in regression, holding 61.3% of the classed population. The size of the regression class should be read with care: the tool does not separate countries that fell from near-universal levels from those that fell from low ones. At lower secondary 49 countries are on track and 66 are in regression, holding 21.1% of the classed population, while the 32 countries in marginal progress hold 38.4%. Many people therefore live in countries advancing too slowly to arrive by 2030.

### Learning lags behind completion, and the data are thin

Completion measures how many children reach the last grade; it does not show what they have learned. The indicator of pupils below the minimum reading proficiency level at the end of primary schooling addresses that gap. Worldwide, 45.9% of assessed pupils at the end of primary were below the minimum level in 2015, and 49.6% in 2019. This is a share of assessed pupils, not of those who completed school, and it refers to years different from the 2024 completion rate of 88.0%, so the two measures are not directly comparable. Read together, they suggest that reaching the last grade does not by itself secure basic reading, which Target 4.1 requires. The series covers reading at the end of primary only. Minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not measured by any series on the shelf, so that part of the question cannot be answered here.

The regional contrasts are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest share below the threshold, at 80.7% in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019. Low income countries stood at 83.5% in 2015 and 87.4% in 2019, and lower middle income countries at 52.9% and 57.4%. South Asia was nearly unchanged, at 55.8% and then 56.0%, and the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 57.7% to 57.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 49.1% to 51.0%. The results do not identify why additional years in school have not translated into basic skills in these regions. Well-established explanations include rapid expansion of enrolment, large classes and limited teacher training, but the data in hand do not test them.

At the other end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.8% to 5.5%, and high income countries from 6.4% to 6.2%. North America was flat, at 3.9% in both years. Low shares in these regions leave little room for movement, so the near absence of change there differs in kind from the stagnation seen in South Asia. Upper middle income countries were close to unchanged, at 28.0% in 2015 and 28.6% in 2019.

The largest movement was in East Asia and Pacific, where the share below the threshold rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019. A rise of that size in a region with strong education systems calls for caution. It may partly reflect a change in which countries and pupils were assessed between the two waves, not only a decline in learning. The data in hand cannot separate the two explanations. The trend calculation for the region extrapolates to 124.3% in 2030, which is impossible as a share and shows only that two points cannot support a projection.

The coverage of the series explains the difficulty. Data come in survey waves, not as annual observations. Countries reporting numbered 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, with an isolated report in 2023 from 1 country. In all, 125 countries reported in at least one year. The aggregates end in 2019, so they do not capture the effect of the school closures of 2020 and after, which is a serious omission for a question about what changed after 2020. The 2021 wave exists at country level but has no regional aggregate in the results here.

For 2030 the evidence supports only a statement of direction. Extrapolating the 2015 to 2019 movement gives 61.3% of pupils below the threshold worldwide, against a target of zero, and the trend is classed as regression. This projection is a different quantity from the population share in countries with regressing primary completion, and the two should not be confused. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 91.0% and low income countries 99.1% on the same arithmetic. Europe and Central Asia is classed as moderate progress in the trend result for this indicator, and it begins from a low base. The extrapolations are mechanical, rest on two points and should be read as the observed direction of change from 2015 to 2019, not as a forecast.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At present rates the world will miss target 4.1. The lower secondary trend to target puts the world on course for an expected completion rate of 80.0% of the relevant age group in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend ratio for the world is 0.21, which places it in the class of marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Among 173 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target for lower secondary completion, covering 22.1% of the assessed population, while 66 are regressing, covering 21.1%. For primary completion, 50 countries are on track, covering 19.6% of their population, and 92 are regressing, covering 61.3%. Regression is therefore the most common class at primary level. The classes come from a trend to target, so a country that has already reached a high rate and slipped slightly may be recorded as regressing; the reading needs care, and the target can be read as universal completion or as a rate near it.

Completing school is not the same as learning. The learning trend for the world is classed as regression, with an expected share below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary of 61.3% in 2030, against a target of 0.0%. This figure is a projected share of assessed pupils and is distinct from the share of the assessed population in regressing countries at primary completion. In Low income countries the expected share is 99.1% in 2030, and in Sub-Saharan Africa 91.0%. These projections extend a two-point change between 2015 and 2019 mechanically, so they indicate direction rather than forecast. High completion does not guarantee learning: East Asia & Pacific is classed as regression on learning, while its lower secondary completion is classed on track, with an expected rate of 105.4% in 2030. A rate above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio. Completion gains not matched by learning gains deliver the certificate without the skills. The learning series ends in 2019 for these trends and covers 125 countries, so it cannot show whether recovery after 2020 has changed this. It also addresses reading at the end of primary only; minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not covered, and the learning shares cannot be compared directly with completion rates of other years.

The regional picture shows where acceleration matters most. Low income countries are classed as stagnant on lower secondary completion, with an expected rate of 40.1% in 2030, the furthest of any group from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is also classed as stagnant, with an expected rate of 46.2% in 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.39 and an expected rate of 73.9% in 2030, still short of what the target requires. East Asia & Pacific, with a ratio of 1.39, is the one region of these classed on track. These are the places where the largest shares of children are likely to be left without a completed basic education, and they are also where learning data are thinnest.
