The account series for the poorest 40% reports only 138 countries in 2024, and several regions have no figure later than 2021. Basic water and sanitation are not safely managed services, and an account held is not an account used. A trend to 100% by 2030 is one reading of target 1.4, which sets no numerical level.

w-c04-7-2.text:
### Adolescent fertility has fallen worldwide since 2015

The world adolescent fertility rate fell from 46.0 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 38.3 in 2024. The decline continues a long movement that predates the Sustainable Development Goals. The figure is a modelled estimate built from registration data, surveys and censuses. The series reports on all 217 countries and territories in 2024, so the global average rests on far fuller coverage than the indicators of contraceptive demand in the same section.

Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold. It calls for universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, including family planning, information and education, and offers no level of adolescent fertility that would count as success. The target can also be read in more than one way. Adolescent births are an outcome of access, schooling, marriage customs and income as much as of health services, so a fall in the rate cannot be credited to health policy alone. Any reading of progress here therefore rests on the trend classes of the bench, which compare each country's own course with the pace needed to keep falling to 2030, and not on a stated goal.

On that reading the picture is favourable in breadth. Of 217 countries assessed, 144 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 26 countries, with 6.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Eight countries, with 0.4% of the population, are stagnant, and five, with 1.0%, are regressing. The population-weighted share on track is far larger than the count of countries alone would suggest, but the results do not show which countries lie in each class by starting rate, so no claim is made here about where the laggards began.

The global decline matters because early childbearing is commonly associated with interrupted schooling, lower lifetime earnings and higher obstetric risk; this is context from established knowledge, not a finding of the bench. The world rate of 38.3 in 2024 remains well above the 8.7 recorded for high-income countries in the same year, so the average conceals a wide gap that the next parts of the section examine. The period since 2015 also includes the pandemic after 2020, when school closures and disrupted clinics were widely expected to push adolescent births up. The world series, read at its end points of 2015 and 2024, shows no lasting reversal, though end points cannot show whether the pace faltered in particular years or places. For 2030, continued decline at the pace of 2015 to 2024 would lower the world rate further, but the trend classes show that the gains are not secure in every country.

### Demand satisfied by modern methods is poorly measured

The indicator on demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods is the weakest of the series in this section. It is reported by 73 countries in at least one year between 2000 and 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. In any single year the count is small: 13 countries in 2000, a peak of 14 in 2012, and 8 in 2015. Since 2019 the count has fallen further, to 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. As context, not a finding of the data, household surveys are fielded at intervals of several years and were disrupted by the pandemic, so a country appears in the series only in the years after a survey has been completed and processed.

The consequence is that the indicator cannot show what happened after 2015 or after 2020 for the world. A year-on-year comparison would compare different sets of countries, and a change in the average would reflect which countries happened to report as much as any change in access to services. The shelf holds aggregates for only three groups: lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. No world aggregate and no aggregate for other regions can be read from it, so regional comparison of satisfied demand is not possible on this evidence, and no level of satisfied demand for the world is available to report.

The definition adds a second limit. The indicator refers to married women aged 15 to 49 who have a need for family planning, and its denominator is those with demand, not all women. Unmarried women, including sexually active adolescents, fall outside it, as do women in unions not recorded as marriage in some surveys. Target 3.7 speaks of universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, information and education, and the indicator captures only one part of that: the use of modern methods by married women who want to space or limit births. The target also gives no numerical threshold, so no level of satisfied demand can be called the goal, and the trend assessment rests on the direction of change rather than on a fixed value. The target can be read in more than one way, and this section does not choose among the readings.

The trend classification covers only 15 countries, those with enough observations to fit a path to 2030. Of these, 2 are on track or have met the target, holding 1.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Another 5 show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 21.8 per cent. Four show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 70.3 per cent. One is stagnant, with 3.1 per cent, and 3 are regressing, with 3.3 per cent. The results do not show which countries lie in each class, so the large population share of the marginal class cannot be attributed to any particular country. Fifteen countries out of 73 reporting, and out of a world of more than 200, is too few to speak for any region, and the sample is not random. The proportions above describe the sample, not the world, and any global statement drawn from them is tentative.

### Regions differ by a factor of eight in adolescent births

Adolescent births are concentrated to a degree that the world average conceals. In 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 91.9 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19, against 50.4 in Latin America and the Caribbean and 37.8 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. South Asia stood at 21.0, East Asia and Pacific at 14.3, North America at 11.7 and Europe and Central Asia at 11.4. The highest regional rate is therefore about eight times the lowest, and the next region down, Latin America and the Caribbean, is well above the world rate of 38.3.

The pattern follows income. Low-income countries recorded 90.7 births per 1,000 in 2024, lower-middle-income countries 42.5, upper-middle-income countries 23.6 and high-income countries 8.7. Income groups and regions overlap heavily, so the two views largely describe the same countries. As context rather than a finding of these results, schooling for girls, the age at first marriage, access to contraception and the reach of sexual and reproductive health education are known to differ along similar lines and to act together rather than separately.

Since 2015 every region has recorded a fall, but the size of the fall depends on the measure. In absolute terms Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 to 91.9 and Latin America and the Caribbean from 67.3 to 50.4. In proportional terms North America fell from 20.9 to 11.7 and East Asia and Pacific from 21.9 to 14.3, while low-income countries moved only from 103.3 to 90.7. A large absolute fall from a high starting point therefore leaves relative standing little changed: Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest rate in 2015 and remains far above every other region in 2024.

The country classification shows a similar split between breadth and depth of progress. Of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 34 countries, with 7.3 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 26, with 6.3 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. The population-weighted figure of 84.9 per cent should not be read as a statement about each country. The results do not show which regions the lagging classes belong to.

The target gives no numerical threshold for adolescent fertility, so the trend classification measures the pace of decline against a projected path, not against a defined goal. A different reading of what counts as sufficient progress would change the classes. The regional contrasts are nonetheless clear on any reading: the gap between Sub-Saharan Africa and the other regions remains very wide in 2024.

### Progress in family planning is moderate and uneven

Of the 15 countries for which a trend to 2030 could be computed on demand satisfied by modern methods, only 2 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 1.5% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 5 countries, with 21.8% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The weight of the picture lies in the slower classes. The 4 countries in marginal progress, which need significant acceleration, hold 70.3% of the assessed population. One country stagnates, with 3.1%, and 3 regress, with 3.3%. The population-weighted result is therefore weaker than the country count alone suggests. The trend tool shows only the share of the assessed population in each class; it does not name the countries or show which of them are the most populous.

This finding must be read with its limits in view. The 15 countries assessed are a fraction of the 73 that have ever reported the indicator, and the survey-based series leaves most countries without enough observations to draw a trend. The assessment cannot be read as a global verdict. It describes a small group selected by data availability, and how far it represents other countries is not known. The target also carries no numerical threshold in this analysis, and no level of satisfied demand is available against which to judge progress. The classes measure the pace of improvement along a path rather than the attainment of a fixed level, and a different reading of the goal would sort some countries differently. The indicator also covers married women only, so unmarried women, including adolescents, are outside it.

The indicators do not identify why countries fall into one class or another, and no cause is asserted here. As general context, not a finding, the pace of change in contraceptive use is commonly understood to depend on the reliability of supply, the range of methods offered, the cost to users and social norms about women's choices; none of these is measured by this series. What the data do show is that regression occurs in 3 of the 15 countries, which means that gains are not automatically retained.

The adolescent fertility trend gives a firmer, though different, reading. Of 217 countries and territories, 144 are on track or have met the target, holding 84.9% of their population, and 34 show moderate progress, with 7.3%. Another 26 are in marginal progress, with 6.3%, 8 stagnate, with 0.4%, and 5 regress, with 1.0%. Progress on adolescent births is thus broad in coverage, while progress on contraceptive demand cannot be shown to be.

For 2030, progress on satisfied demand cannot be assumed to be on course. With few countries on track and most of the assessed population in the slower classes, a result consistent with universal access would require acceleration where the trend is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Adolescent fertility is likely to keep falling to 2030, but not evenly. Of the 217 countries and territories assessed, 144 are on track or have met the direction of travel, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. The remainder is the concern. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of that population, show moderate progress and need acceleration, 26 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. Target 3.7 sets no numerical goal for adolescent fertility, so these classes describe the pace of change in each country and do not measure distance from a value agreed in the Goals. The reading depends on the pace each country is judged against, and it should be taken as indicative.

The regional picture sharpens the concern. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 91.9 in 2024, and low-income countries fell from 103.3 to 90.7. Both remain far above the high-income level of 8.7 in 2024. The results do not show which countries lag, and no claim is made here about where the slowest-moving countries lie. The regional rates alone show that Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries start 2030's approach far above every other group, while the world rate stands at 38.3 in 2024. As context outside the evidence of this section, schooling for girls, the age at marriage and access to contraception are well-established influences on adolescent births.

Family planning cannot be judged with confidence on current data. No level of satisfied demand is reported here, and target 3.7 sets no threshold for it, so the indicator can be read only as a direction of change. Only 15 countries could be assessed. Of these, 2 are on track, 5 show moderate progress, 4 show marginal progress, 1 is stagnant and 3 are regressing. The 4 countries in marginal progress hold 70.3% of the population assessed, so a small number of populous countries determines the result. Reporting is also thin: only 7 countries reported in 2024 and 2 in 2019. A finding on 2030 for this indicator rests on few countries and on sparse, irregular survey rounds. The indicator also covers married women only, so unmarried women and adolescents lie outside it.

The proposals that follow address both problems: the thinness of measurement and the pace of progress where rates remain highest.

proposals: National governments in Sub-Saharan Africa and other high-rate settings should set their own targets for adolescent fertility and report progress against them, since target 3.7 gives no numerical value.
National statistical offices and survey programmes should run demand-for-family-planning surveys on a regular schedule, so that more than a handful of countries report in any year.
The World Bank and partner agencies should publish indicators of satisfied demand that cover unmarried women and adolescents, not only married women.
w-c04-7-2.gaps: No level of satisfied demand or threshold is set for target 3.7. Demand satisfied by modern methods is reported by only 73 countries in any year, and by 7 in 2024. The indicators cover married women, so unmarried women are missing. The data do not show which countries drive the regional falls or lags, and they do not show the causes of change.

w-c04-8-3.text:
### Service coverage has widened, but the world is far from universal

The UHC service coverage index stood at 68.0 index points for the world in 2015 and at 71.0 in 2023, the latest year, when all 193 countries report. The index is a composite of 14 tracer indicators spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases and service capacity and access. It runs from 0 to 100, and a score of 100 is the natural reading of 'universal' in target 3.8. That reading is one of several. The target also names financial risk protection and access to safe, affordable medicines, which the index does not measure directly, and a country may score high on tracer services while leaving households exposed to heavy costs. The index should therefore be read as a measure of the breadth of essential services, not as a verdict on the whole target.

On that measure, the world rose from 68.0 to 71.0 over eight years and remained well below 100 in 2023. The shortfall is large because the tracer indicators include services that are hard to extend to everyone, such as the control of hypertension and diabetes and the capacity of facilities, alongside those that are easier to scale, such as vaccination and antenatal care. A composite also moves slowly, since a gain in one area can be offset by stagnation in another. These explanations rest on general knowledge of how the index is built, not on the results shown here.

The income groups show the same ordering at both dates. Low-income countries scored 41.2 in 2015 and 43.8 in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6, and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. High-income countries, which started closest to the ceiling, were not saturated and kept improving. The low-income rise was smaller than those of the two middle groups, so the poorest countries did not close the distance to the others in absolute terms. In 2023 they remained below the level the lower-middle-income group had reached in 2015.

The gap between countries narrowed slightly, though not by much. Among the 193 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the index fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index fell from 0.030 to 0.024. Convergence is therefore real, but it takes place at a low overall level. Most of the inequality lies between regions: the between-region share of the Theil index was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, so the region in which a person lives accounts for more of the variation in coverage than differences within a region. Because the weighting is by population, the improvement in South Asia, whose regional score rose from 60.0 to 68.0, plausibly contributes to the narrowing, though the results do not isolate its contribution. The regional pattern is taken up in the next part.

The pace matters for 2030. The assessment was run only against a target of 100, and its sensitivity to other yardsticks was not tested. At the 2015 to 2023 pace, universality by 2030 is not reachable: the world's expected value for 2030 is 73.7, and the trend covers a ratio of 0.18 of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target. Whether the period after 2020 slowed progress cannot be judged, since the endpoints shown do not reveal change in the intervening years.

### Regions differ widely in coverage and in out-of-pocket burden

Coverage differs more between regions than any change in the world average would suggest. In 2023 North America scored 88.0 index points on the UHC service coverage index, Europe and Central Asia 82.0, East Asia and Pacific 80.0 and Latin America and the Caribbean 79.0. South Asia stood at 68.0, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 66.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 50.0.

The direction of travel differs as well. South Asia made the largest regional gain, from 60.0 in 2015 to 68.0 in 2023, and moved from below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 76.0 to 80.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 45.0 to 50.0. Latin America and the Caribbean did not move, at 79.0 in both years. North America, already near the top, rose from 87.0 to 88.0. Among income groups, low-income countries moved from 41.2 to 43.8, lower-middle-income countries from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6 and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. The poorest countries are improving, but from so low a base that the distance to the others has barely closed, and in 2023 the low-income group remained below the level that lower-middle-income countries held in 2015. Only the 2015 and 2023 endpoints are used here, so they do not show whether the pace changed after 2020.

Out-of-pocket spending adds a second view of the same divide. As a share of current health expenditure it was 11.1% in North America in 2023, 16.5% in Europe and Central Asia, 26.0% in East Asia and Pacific, 28.3% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 29.7% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 30.4% in Sub-Saharan Africa and 46.6% in South Asia. The world figure was 17.3%, down from 18.4% in 2015. South Asia fell from 64.3% to 46.6%, the largest fall of any region, yet it remains the highest, so households there still pay nearly half of all health spending directly. Low public funding and a large private provider sector are commonly offered as explanations, but the series do not test them. Latin America and the Caribbean and East Asia and Pacific moved the other way, from 28.2% to 29.7% and from 25.7% to 26.0%.

The share of health spending paid out of pocket and the share of people suffering hardship are related but not the same. Hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on health, affected 26.0% of the world population in 2022, against 28.0% in 2015. By region it ranged from 7.5% in North America and 13.0% in Europe and Central Asia to 20.3% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 26.5% in East Asia and Pacific, 27.5% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 31.7% in South Asia and 35.2% in Sub-Saharan Africa. Sub-Saharan Africa thus has the highest hardship although South Asia has the highest out-of-pocket share. Where incomes are low, even a modest payment can consume much of what remains after basic needs, though this is context and not a result. In Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, hardship rose slightly between 2015 and 2022, and in North America it was nearly flat, from 7.4% to 7.5%. Hardship estimates rest on household surveys fielded irregularly, and only 3 countries report for 2024, so the regional values carry wider uncertainty than the service index.

The spread among countries on the service index narrowed. The Gini coefficient, weighted by population, fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.030 to 0.024. Yet the share of the Theil index lying between regions was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, essentially unchanged. About seven-tenths of the inequality in coverage is therefore associated with which region a country belongs to, and the narrowing has come with a rise across the distribution rather than a dissolving of regional divides. National averages hide this structure, and gains should be judged against the regional floor from which each country starts.

### Coverage gains were modest and financial protection moved unevenly

Financial protection improved only slightly at the global level between 2015 and 2023, and the improvement was concentrated in a few regions. The world share of current health expenditure paid directly by households fell from 18.4% in 2015 to 17.3% in 2023. The share of people facing financial hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on out-of-pocket health costs, fell from 28.0% in 2015 to 26.0% in 2022. Both movements are in the right direction, but they are small beside the scale of the problem. More than one person in four still sits above the hardship threshold in 2022, the latest year for the world aggregate.

The global averages conceal opposite movements. South Asia accounts for much of the fall in the out-of-pocket share, which dropped from 64.3% in 2015 to 46.6% in 2023, and the lower middle income group fell from 58.3% to 47.0% over the same years. Low income countries moved from 53.0% to 44.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan also fell, to 30.4% and 28.3% respectively. These are large reductions, yet they began from very high levels, and in South Asia nearly half of health spending is still paid at the point of care. In East Asia and Pacific the out-of-pocket share edged up from 25.7% to 26.0%, and in Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 28.2% to 29.7%. Europe and Central Asia (17.8% to 16.5%), North America (11.9% to 11.1%) and high income countries (14.4% to 13.4%) declined modestly from low bases.

The hardship measure tells a different story from the spending share, and the difference matters. East Asia and Pacific shows a clear fall in hardship, from 30.0% to 26.5%, although its out-of-pocket share did not fall. The two measures are therefore not interchangeable: hardship depends on household budgets, prices and the burden of illness as well as on how the system is financed. In Europe and Central Asia hardship rose from 12.6% to 13.0%, in Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.5% to 20.3%, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 27.0% to 27.5%. North America moved from 7.4% to 7.5% and high income countries from 9.5% to 9.7%. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the highest at 35.2% in 2022, down from 38.7%, and South Asia stood at 31.7%, down from 35.7%. Low income countries fell from 38.5% to 34.7% and lower middle income countries from 34.4% to 31.5%, while upper middle income countries moved from 26.5% to 24.9%. Hardship is therefore not confined to the poorest countries: in several middle and high income regions it is stagnant or slightly worse.

The country-level classification shows the unevenness. Of 72 countries assessed on direction of travel, 27 are on track or have met the direction, holding 34.0% of the population of the assessed countries. A further 9 show moderate progress needing acceleration (9.5%), and 4 show marginal progress (22.7%). One country is stagnant, and 31 are regressing, holding 33.7% of the assessed population. Regression is thus as common as success, and the two groups are of similar demographic weight. No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures only direction of travel and not distance to a defined goal; target 3.8 can be read as a call for financial risk protection for all, which leaves open what level of hardship would count as acceptable.

Public funding appears to matter. Across 21 countries with data for both series, the share of people in hardship is negatively associated with the share of health spending funded from domestic government sources. The rank correlation is -0.525 for 2022 levels and -0.258 for changes between 2015 and 2022. The level association is moderate and the association for changes is weak. This is association rather than proof of cause: richer countries tend to have both higher public shares and lower hardship, and the weaker link in changes suggests that a higher public share does not by itself reduce hardship, whose course also depends on what is covered, on prices and on who is reached.

The evidence base itself is uneven. Hardship has thinner coverage than the service index, with 3 countries reporting in 2024 against 22 for the out-of-pocket share, so regional aggregates rest on survey years that differ between countries. Movements of one or two points in a regional hardship figure should be read with caution. The broad picture is nevertheless consistent: the out-of-pocket share fell most where it was highest, while hardship stalled or edged up in several regions that had already moved furthest on coverage.

### At the current pace, 2030 will be missed, and proposals follow

The trend assessment leaves little room for optimism about 2030. It was run against a single yardstick, a target of 100 index points, and its sensitivity to any other threshold was not tested. Target 3.8 sets no numerical threshold, and 100 index points is a convention that no health system has reached in practice, so the assessment is severe by construction. On that reading, no country is on track for the UHC service coverage index: 0 of 193 countries assessed are on track or have met the target. Only 2 countries, holding 17.3% of the population, show moderate progress that would still need acceleration. A further 102 countries, holding 64.7% of the population, show marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Another 57 countries, holding 11.0% of the population, stagnate, and 32 countries, holding 7.0% of the population, regress. Most of the world's people therefore live in countries where coverage is rising too slowly to reach the target on the 2015 to 2023 pace. The endpoints alone do not show whether the period after 2020 slowed or quickened progress.

The projections show the scale of the shortfall. The world is expected to reach 73.7 index points in 2030, covering a ratio of 0.18 of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 54.8 index points, with a ratio of 0.18, and low-income countries at 46.2, with a ratio of 0.09. Lower middle income countries are projected at 67.6, with a ratio of 0.25. South Asia has the highest ratio of any region, 0.40, and is projected at 75.9 index points in 2030, still short of the target. Latin America and the Caribbean is projected to stay at 79.0, with a ratio of 0.00, and the assessment classes that region as stagnating. Even high-income countries, projected at 86.9 with a ratio of 0.21, and North America, projected at 88.9, fall short of 100. The gap between the poorest and richest groups therefore does not close on current trends. The groups with the most to gain advance slowly, and the groups with the highest coverage approach a plateau at which further gains are hard to win.

Financial protection tells a more divided story. Among the 72 countries with enough data to assess the hardship indicator, 27 countries, holding 34.0% of their population, are on track or have met the target. Another 9, holding 9.5%, show moderate progress. Against this, 31 countries, holding 33.7% of their population, are regressing, and 4 more, holding 22.7%, show marginal progress. Only 1 country stagnates. Progress is real in some places, but the regressing group is nearly as large in population as the group that is succeeding, and the assessment covers only 72 of the countries that report the coverage index. Coverage of services is advancing too slowly almost everywhere, while financial protection is improving in some countries and deteriorating in others, so the two cannot be assumed to move together.

Public financing is the most plausible lever, though the data do not prove it. Across 21 countries with data for both series from 2015 to 2022, the rank correlation between the level of financial hardship and the domestic government share of current health expenditure was -0.52. Countries that fund more of their health spending from public sources tend to have fewer households in hardship. The rank correlation between the changes in the two series was weaker, at -0.26, so a rise in public financing did not reliably accompany a fall in hardship within the period. The sample is small and the association is not proof of cause, but it agrees with the long-established finding that pooled, prepaid funding protects households better than direct payment at the point of care.

The following proposals follow from these findings.

w-c04-9-3.text:
### The global picture rests on rates, not counts

The question posed for this section asks for a number of deaths. The evidence retrieved cannot supply one. The only result in hand is a rate: deaths attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene per 100,000 population, for 2019, across 183 countries. A rate is a count divided by population, and it cannot be turned back into a count without population figures that this result does not carry. No absolute total of deaths from unsafe water appears in the retrieved material, and none is offered here. The level of the rate, whether global, regional or national, is likewise not among the results; only the inequality of the rate between countries is.

The question is therefore answered in neither of its halves. For unsafe water, the book can report how unequal the rate is but not how many deaths it represents. For air pollution, the shelf holds a series on the age-standardised mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, with 183 countries and a latest year of 2019, and a series on mean annual exposure to fine particulate matter, but neither was analysed as a result for this section. Nothing is stated here about how many people die from air pollution, how fast the rate is falling or which regions carry most of it. A statement on those points would rest on no evidence in hand. Target 3.9 also covers hazardous chemicals and soil pollution, and no result was analysed for those either. The gap is a limit of the analysis performed, not a finding about the world.

This limit bears on how Target 3.9 is read. The target calls for a substantial reduction in the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and from air, water and soil pollution. The wording can be read as a count, in which case population growth works against progress even when conditions improve, or as a rate, in which case a falling risk counts as success even if the number of deaths stays high. The wording does not settle the matter. The indicator series the World Bank reports measures a rate, and it is the rate that the evidence here can describe. Any later statement about progress in this section should be taken as a statement about risk per head of population, not about the total toll.

The one result that exists shows how unevenly that risk is spread. Across the 183 countries in 2019, the Gini coefficient of the unsafe-water mortality rate is 0.535 and the coefficient of variation is 1.03. A coefficient of variation above one means that the spread of national rates is wider than their average. The bench reports these measures as population-weighted, so they describe inequality among people living in different countries; the source's own weighting method was not retrieved, and the measures do not establish how many countries hold high rates. The next part examines how much of this inequality is a matter of region.

### Regions explain most of the inequality between countries

Regional grouping accounts for most of the measured inequality in the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate. The result, for 2019 across 183 countries, is a rate per 100,000 population, not a count of deaths. The Theil index of the rate was 0.502 and the Gini coefficient was 0.535. The bench's summary states that both measures are weighted by population, so they describe how the rate is distributed among people living in different countries, not among states as units. A populous country with a high rate raises both figures more than a small one would. The coefficient of variation was 1.03, so the standard deviation of the rate was slightly larger than its mean, which indicates a wide spread of values.

The between-region share of the Theil index was 75.2% in 2019. Differences between the regions' mean rates therefore account for about three quarters of the measured inequality, and differences among countries within the same region account for the remaining quarter. This is a descriptive split of a statistic. It does not test why regions differ, and it contains no measure of income, infrastructure or health services. Well-established knowledge suggests plausible causes, offered as context and not as a finding: diarrhoeal disease and related infections depend on piped water, sewerage, nutrition and primary care, and these conditions tend to be shared among neighbouring countries at similar stages of development.

The split matters for how reporting and action are organised. Where most inequality lies between regions, regional figures are needed to see where the gap is, and a global average alone can hide regions with high rates. This result does not identify those regions, give their rates or show how many deaths occur in them, so the levels by region remain to be read from the underlying series. The remaining quarter, lying within regions, shows that countries in the same region still differ, and those that do better than their neighbours merit study for policies that could be copied.

The limits of the result are plain. A decomposition reports a share, not a ranking, so it names no region or country. It covers one year, 2019, and so says nothing about change since 2015 or about the effects of events after 2020. It concerns unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene only; no result in this part covers air pollution mortality or PM2.5 exposure, so the air half of Target 3.9 is not addressed here. The retrieved results do not document how the underlying estimates were produced; from general knowledge of the source, such estimates are modelled where death registration is incomplete, and the figures are best read as an indication of structure rather than a count of deaths.

### Change since 2015 cannot be measured from one year

The single observation for 2019 describes a position, not a movement. Target 3.9 calls for a substantial reduction in deaths from pollution and contamination by 2030, and a reduction can only be shown by comparing at least two points in time. The result retrieved for this section holds one year, 2019, for 183 countries. No statement is therefore made here on whether mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene fell after 2015, nor on how the years after 2020 compare with those before. The result gives no earlier or later reading for this indicator, and an inference from a single cross-section would be a guess presented as a finding.

Three kinds of evidence would be needed to turn the position into a trend. The first is a series of annual rates from 2015 onward, ideally with earlier years too, so that a pre-2015 trajectory exists against which the post-2015 period can be judged. The shelf lists the indicator with 2019 as its latest year, which means that the period of the pandemic and its disruption to health services, to water programmes and to household incomes is not observed at all. The second is a count of deaths. A rate can fall while the number of deaths stays level or rises if populations grow, and the reverse is also possible, so the two answer different questions. The third is an air pollution indicator read alongside the water measure. The shelf holds a rate of deaths attributed to household and ambient air pollution and a measure of mean exposure to fine particles, but neither was returned as a result for this section. The question on air pollution is therefore not answered here, and the two halves of the question cannot be set side by side.

Caution is also due on causes. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2%, and the Gini coefficient is 0.535. These figures show that the rate is unequally distributed among people in 2019 and that regional grouping accounts for most of that measured inequality. They do not show why. Water and sanitation infrastructure, income, the quality of primary health care and the treatment of diarrhoeal disease are well established as bearing on such deaths, but these are plausible influences that the decomposition does not test, and one year's spread cannot separate them from the age structure of populations, from climate or from conflict. The coefficient of variation, 1.03, confirms the dispersion without explaining it.

For 2030 the consequence is that progress on this part of target 3.9 cannot at present be judged from the evidence in hand. The target also does not define what "substantially" means, and it can be read against a baseline of 2015, of an earlier year or of the latest available year. Until a series spanning those years is assembled, any statement on whether the goal is on course would be unsupported.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 3.9 asks for a substantial reduction by 2030, and the only evidence analysed for this section is one year of one rate. In 2019, across 183 countries, the between-region share of the Theil index for mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene was 75.2%. Most of the measured inequality in that rate therefore lies between regions rather than within them. The result does not name the regions, give their rates or show why they differ. Differences in income, infrastructure and health services are plausible explanations, but this decomposition does not test them.

The Gini coefficient was 0.535 and the coefficient of variation was 1.03. The bench's summary describes both as measures of inequality among countries weighted by population, so they describe how the rate is spread among people living in different countries. They show that the rate is unevenly spread, but not where the highest rates lie or how many deaths occur in any region. A global average can hide regions with higher rates per 100,000 population, and this result cannot say where avoidable deaths are concentrated.

This bears on how 2030 is judged. The target text does not say whether the reduction is to be assessed in numbers of deaths or in rates, and it sets no baseline or percentage. Both readings are defensible and they can diverge when populations grow. A fall in the rate with a growing population may leave the count little changed. The 2019 evidence offers no trend since 2015 or 2020, so whether the target is on course cannot be stated from it.

The question asks for numbers of deaths from air pollution and from unsafe water and sanitation. It remains unanswered here: no count is given for either cause, and no result for air pollution was analysed. The air pollution mortality series, the PM2.5 exposure series and the unintentional poisoning series are held on the shelf, but their values are not reported in this section. The conclusions above concern the water, sanitation and hygiene rate only.
proposals: The Council of the cooperative should have the air pollution mortality and PM2.5 exposure series analysed for several years, so that the air half of Target 3.9 is answered with rates, years and units.

National statistical offices and the bodies that estimate cause-specific mortality should publish death counts alongside rates, and the UN statistical community should state whether Target 3.9 is to be judged on counts or on rates.
Health and water ministries in the regions with the highest rates should be examined first once regional values are retrieved, since most measured inequality lies between regions.
w-c04-9-3.gaps: The evidence holds a single year, 2019, of the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate. It gives no death counts, no regional values, no trend since 2015 or 2020, and no analysed result for air pollution or poisoning. The target sets no baseline, and its reading as counts or rates is open.

w-c08-1-2.text:
### Global access has risen, but not to universality

Access to electricity worldwide stood at 91.9 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 86.9 per cent in 2015. The gain was achieved while the world population grew, but it leaves a world short of the universal access that target 7.1 sets for 2030. The series is reported by 215 countries for 2024, so coverage is nearly complete, though some national figures rest on modelled estimates drawn from industry records and household surveys rather than a fresh count each year.

The divide between rural and urban populations explains much of the shortfall. Rural access rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a larger advance than the urban series, which moved from 96.4 per cent to 97.8 per cent. Urban access was already close to the ceiling at the start of the period, and little room remained for improvement. The remaining deficit is therefore mainly rural: rural access leaves 15.1 per cent of rural residents unserved in 2024, against 2.2 per cent of urban residents. This matters for policy, because connecting dispersed households costs more per person than extending an urban grid, and it depends on off-grid and mini-grid solutions as much as on national networks. A gap of this size still marks a sharp difference in daily life between town and countryside.

A headcount of people without electricity is not published in the series examined here. It could only be derived by applying the access percentages to population series, and any such derivation would be the writer's own estimate, not a reported count, with three cautions. First, the access series ends in 2024, while the rural and urban population series run to 2025, so the two do not refer to the same year. Second, the definition of rural and urban areas is set by each national statistical office and differs between countries, so the rural share is not strictly comparable across borders. Third, the product of a percentage and a population carries the uncertainty of both inputs. With these limits, the scale can still be read: a rural deficit of 15.1 per cent applies to a rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025, while an urban deficit of 2.2 per cent applies to an urban population of 4,750,578,960. The rural deficit applies to a smaller population but at a far higher rate, so rural areas appear to hold the larger share of people without electricity, even though more people live in cities.

The period also spans two breaks, 2015 and 2020. The first marks the adoption of the goals, the second the pandemic and the economic shocks that followed, which strained public budgets and household incomes and may have slowed some connection programmes. The endpoints given here do not reveal whether progress paused after 2020. The trend projection for the world places access at 95.4 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.65 of the distance to the target covered, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The final stretch of any access target tends to be the hardest, since the unconnected are the most remote and poorest. The sections that follow turn to where that remaining gap lies.

### Sub-Saharan Africa holds most of the remaining gap

Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for most of the remaining gap. Access in the region stood at 55.1 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 39.2 per cent in 2015. Every other region reported at least 96.8 per cent in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 96.8 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean at 98.0 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 98.6 per cent. Europe and Central Asia reached 100.0 per cent when rounded to one decimal place, and North America stood at 100.0 per cent in both years. South Asia made the largest advance of any region, from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, so the region that once held a large share of the unserved now stands close to universality. The contrast shows that universal access is attainable at scale. It also shows that Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception, not one case among several.

The divide between rural and urban areas is sharpest in this region. Rural access in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 35.7 per cent of the rural population in 2024, against 82.9 per cent of the urban population. In 2015 the rural figure was 18.5 per cent and the urban figure 72.7 per cent. Rural access therefore rose faster in proportion than urban access, yet nearly two in three rural residents remained without electricity in 2024. The pattern follows from the economics of supply, stated here as context. Grid extension to dispersed settlements costs more per household and recovers less revenue, so utilities and public programmes have tended to serve towns first. Off-grid solar and mini-grids have widened the options in recent years, although the series reports access without separating the technologies behind it.

Income groups show the same shape. Low-income economies, most of which lie in Sub-Saharan Africa, reached 48.8 per cent access in 2024, up from 32.2 per cent in 2015. Rural access in that group stood at 37.1 per cent and urban access at 77.6 per cent. Lower-middle-income economies reached 91.4 per cent, and upper-middle-income and high-income economies stood at 99.3 per cent and 100.0 per cent respectively.

The scale of the unserved population can be indicated by applying the 2024 access rates to the 2025 population counts. Sub-Saharan Africa had 731422742 rural residents in 2025 and 590231475 urban residents. This is the writer's own approximation, not a figure reported by the series: it mixes years, and national definitions of rural and urban areas differ. It suggests that the unserved there are concentrated in rural areas, with a smaller but still large number in towns and cities. No world headcount of the unserved is given by the results, so this part does not state what share of it lies in the region. Rural population in the region rose from 616454626 in 2015 to 731422742 in 2025, and urban population grew from 408204795 to 590231475. Population growth therefore works against the connection effort: every year of progress in the access rate must also cover new households.

For 2030 the implication is plain. The other regions are within a few points of universality, and their remaining gaps are small, concentrated in particular countries and in rural areas. The target will be met or missed in Sub-Saharan Africa. The trend tool classes the region as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and expects 69.2 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.49 of the distance to the target covered. Closing the gap would require a pace several times faster, concentrated on rural households that are costly to reach.

### Rural areas and South Asia account for the change since 2015

The global gain between 2015 and 2024 was not spread evenly. South Asia supplied the largest single movement. Access in the region rose from 86.5 per cent of the population in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 13 points, and in rural areas from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent. Because South Asia holds a very large rural population, 1,035,602,697 people in 2015 and 1,086,549,811 in 2025, closing its rural gap moved the world average more than any other change. The region is now close to the level of Europe and Central Asia, where access stood at 99.9989 per cent of the population in 2024, so its contribution to further global gains is nearly exhausted.

The rural gap narrowed worldwide. Rural access in the world rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 8 points, against a gain of 5 points for the population as a whole. Rural areas therefore improved faster than the average, which is what a closing gap requires. Rural gains were also large in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, from 87.6 per cent to 94.0 per cent, and in low-income countries, from 17.2 per cent to 37.1 per cent. In Latin America and the Caribbean the rural rate moved from 89.1 per cent to 91.0 per cent, a smaller change, and the region's rural rate remains well below its overall rate of 98.0 per cent in 2024.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows a different pattern. Its overall access rose by about 16 points, from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, and its rural access rose from 18.5 per cent to 35.7 per cent. These are large percentage gains, comparable in size to South Asia's. Yet the rural population of the region grew from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, so a rising rate is applied to a growing base. Rural access of 35.7 per cent in 2024 means that roughly two in three rural residents of the region remained unconnected, and the number of people without access depends on how fast connections grow relative to population. The indicators here are shares, and the section cannot assert from them alone that the absolute number of unconnected rural residents fell in the region.

Urban growth matters as well. The urban population of Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 408,204,795 in 2015 to 590,231,475 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 182,500,508 to 269,862,804. Part of the regional gain in access comes from people moving to towns and cities, where connection is cheaper per household, rather than from connection of people who stayed in rural areas. The data given do not separate the two effects.

Causes call for restraint. The indicators show where access changed and by how much, not which policies produced it. Well-established experience points to national grid extension programmes, falling costs of solar equipment and off-grid systems, and public financing as the usual drivers, but the series cannot attribute the South Asian or African gains to any one of them. Nor do they show a break after 2020 in the figures cited here, since the comparison runs between 2015 and 2024 only.

For 2030, the implication is that the world's average is now governed by one region. South Asia has largely finished its part, East Asia and the Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean are above 98 per cent, and the remaining distance lies in rural Sub-Saharan Africa, where population growth works against each point gained.

### Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030, and proposals follow

Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030 on the evidence of the trend classification. Of the 215 countries assessed, 154 are on track or have already met the target, and they hold 74.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 33 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 15.6 per cent of the population. Another 21 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 8.0 per cent of the population. Two countries are stagnant, with 0.4 per cent, and five are regressing, with 1.4 per cent. The count of countries therefore looks reassuring, while the population shares show that about a quarter of the people in the countries assessed live where the present pace will not close the gap.

The aggregate projection agrees. Extending the 2015 to 2024 pace, the world would reach 95.4 per cent access in 2030, and the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.65, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The two groups furthest from the goal are classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 69.2 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.49, and low-income countries would reach 64.4 per cent, with a ratio of 0.48. Latin America and the Caribbean is also classed as marginal, with a ratio of 0.47, but the reason differs: its access was already 98.0 per cent in 2024, so the little that remains moves slowly, and the same pace would bring it to 98.6 per cent in 2030. South Asia, with a ratio of 1.73, and lower middle income countries, with 1.01, are on track, although the lower middle income result rests on a narrow margin.

These readings depend on how target 7.1 is interpreted. The classification treats the target as 100 per cent access by 2030, which is the plainest reading of universal access. A projection above 100, such as South Asia's 109.8 per cent, cannot occur in fact and shows only that a linear extrapolation overshoots a ceiling. The last stretch before universality is also usually harder than the early gains, because the remaining households are the most remote and the poorest, so linear extrapolation may flatter regions near the ceiling. The target further names affordable and reliable energy services. The indicator measures only whether a population has access to electricity. It says nothing about the price paid, the hours of supply or the quality of the connection, so a country classed as on track may still fall short of the full wording of the target.

The implication for 2030 is that the world will not reach universal access on present trends, and that the missing people will be concentrated where the pace is slowest, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries, particularly in rural areas, where access in the region was 35.7 per cent in 2024. Rural access in low-income countries was 37.1 per cent in the same year.

w-c03-2-3.text:
### Stunting and wasting set against the 2025 and 2030 targets

The world has moved only slightly towards the internationally agreed nutrition targets since 2015. Stunting, measured as the share of children under five whose height for age is more than two standard deviations below the international reference median, stood at 24.6% in 2015 and 23.2% in 2024 on the modelled estimate. Wasting, the share whose weight for height falls equally far below the reference median, moved from 7.1% to 6.6% over the same period. Neither series is shown here at annual resolution, so no break after 2015 can be identified. The latest year available is 2024, so the effects of the shocks that followed 2020 on food prices, health services and household incomes cannot be separated from the underlying slow decline.

The two indicators describe different conditions and should not be read as one. Stunting reflects chronic deprivation: poor maternal nutrition, repeated infection, inadequate diets in the first two years of life and limited access to water and sanitation. It accumulates over months and years and is difficult to reverse after early childhood, which is why its decline is gradual even where conditions improve. Wasting reflects acute loss of weight, driven by recent illness, famine, conflict or sudden shortfalls in food. It can rise and fall within a season, so a national survey taken at one moment may record a figure that differs from the annual average. A wasting prevalence of 6.6% therefore carries more uncertainty about timing than a stunting prevalence of 23.2%.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. The text of Target 2.2 asks that the internationally agreed targets on stunting and wasting be achieved by 2025, and that all forms of malnutrition end by 2030. The bench's trend tool applies a ceiling of 5.0% by 2030 to both series and projects towards 2030 rather than 2025. That ceiling is a computational convention, not a statement of the agreed stunting benchmark, which is framed as a reduction against a baseline and for which no threshold is held among the facts here; other readings of the benchmark exist and none is quoted as a result. Under the strict reading of the target text, the 2025 deadline falls one year after the latest observation, and with wasting at 6.6% in 2024 and stunting at 23.2%, the 2025 milestone is unlikely to have been met for either indicator under the 5.0% ceiling. Under the trend tool's reading, the question is whether the ceiling is within reach by 2030. The two readings point the same way for 2025 but allow different times, and this book states which is in use wherever a projection is quoted.

For wasting, the world figure of 6.6% in 2024 lies above the 5.0% ceiling. The fall from 7.1% in 2015 is small beside the distance that remains, and the ceiling is unlikely to be reached by continuing at the recent pace. This is a rough inference from the two end-point values, not a projection computed by the tool for the world. For stunting, the trend calculation puts the world at 22.3% in 2030 if the observed rate continues, with a ratio of observed to required pace of 0.12, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. A fall from 24.6% to 23.2% over nine years leaves the world far from a level that could be described as ending the condition.

Why this matters goes beyond the numbers. Children who are stunted face poorer cognitive development, lower school attainment and reduced earnings in adulthood, and severe wasting sharply raises the risk of death in early childhood. A near-flat global line therefore signals a persistent loss of human potential in each new cohort, not merely a missed statistical goal. The links to other Goals are direct: health, education, water and sanitation, and poverty reduction all shape the figures above.

A further caution concerns the global figures themselves. The stunting series is a modelled estimate that combines survey data with statistical methods to fill years without a survey, and the wasting series is built from survey data in which only 6 countries report for 2024. The global picture is therefore a reasonable guide to the direction and approximate scale of change, but small differences between years should not be treated as real movements. The direction is consistent across the readings of the target, although the distance to 2030 cannot be stated precisely: progress since 2015 has been real but slow, and the world does not appear to be on course for either target.

### Regional differences in stunting and wasting

Behind the modest world average lies a wide spread of regional experience. South Asia carries the heaviest burden on both measures. Its stunting prevalence fell from 37.8% in 2015 to 31.5% in 2024, yet nearly one child in three under five remains stunted. Its wasting prevalence stood at 15.7% in 2024, against 16.6% in 2015, a small reduction. Wasting in South Asia is therefore far above the world figure of 6.6% in 2024. Low birth weight, early marriage and adolescent pregnancy, limited dietary diversity and sanitation deficits are commonly cited as causes acting on stunting and wasting together; the series themselves do not test them.

Sub-Saharan Africa presents a different pattern. Stunting declined only from 34.4% in 2015 to 32.3% in 2024. The region, which had a lower rate than South Asia in 2015, ended the period with a slightly higher one (32.3% against 31.5%). Wasting fell more clearly, from 7.0% to 5.9%. The contrast suggests that acute malnutrition, which responds to treatment programmes and seasonal relief, can improve faster than chronic growth failure, which depends on maternal health, diets, sanitation and incomes over many years. Population growth also means that a falling prevalence can coexist with a rising number of affected children, a distinction the prevalence series cannot show.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping fell from 27.5% to 24.1% in stunting and from 6.5% to 5.6% in wasting. Conflict, displacement and fiscal stress in parts of this heterogeneous grouping may weigh against the gains, and the regional average conceals very different national circumstances. East Asia and Pacific moved from 14.5% to 13.3% in stunting, a slow decline for a region whose income growth has been rapid, and its wasting rate barely changed, from 3.7% to 3.6%.

Europe and Central Asia is the clearest example of steady improvement. Stunting fell from 6.0% to 4.6%, and wasting from 1.5% to 1.0%. For stunting, the trend calculation classes the region as on track for the 5.0% ceiling that the tool applies by 2030, with an expected value of 3.8%, although the level was already close to that mark in 2015. The 5.0% figure is the tool's reference level, not necessarily the agreed stunting benchmark, which can be read in more than one way. Latin America and the Caribbean, by contrast, was flat: stunting stood at 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, which the trend calculation classes as regression. Wasting there eased from 1.5% to 1.3%. Economic disruption after 2020 and the uneven recovery of poorer households' incomes are plausible contributors, offered as context only, since the series do not isolate causes.

North America shows a rise in stunting from 2.8% in 2015 to 4.1% in 2024, while wasting fell from 0.3% to 0.2%. The trend tool labels the region as on track because its level lies below the reference value, but the direction is adverse. The levels are low, the regional average rests on few countries, and modelled estimates for populations with small samples carry wide uncertainty. The rise should be read as a signal worth checking rather than a settled finding. High-income countries as a group moved from 3.9% to 4.0%.

Income groups sharpen the picture. Low-income countries began at 38.0% stunting in 2015 and ended at 35.8% in 2024, still the highest level of any group listed. Their wasting rate fell from 7.9% to 6.4%. Lower-middle-income countries show the strongest stunting decline, from 33.9% to 28.9%, but their wasting stood at 9.5% in 2024, down from 10.5%, the highest of any income group, which may reflect the weight of South Asia within the group. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 11.9% to 10.8% in stunting and from 2.6% to 2.1% in wasting. High-income countries held wasting at 0.4% in 2024, down from 0.6%.

The gradient by income is steep: stunting in 2024 was 35.8% in low-income countries and 4.0% in high-income countries. The lower-middle group shows that faster decline is possible without rich-country incomes, which points to the possible role of health, water, sanitation and social protection policy.

Two cautions apply. The trend summary for some groups is truncated in the output available, so the lower-middle-income and South Asia readings use the levels and expected values. The wasting summary also reports only 6 countries reporting in 2024, against 162 for stunting, so recent regional wasting figures rest on thin and uneven observation.

For 2030, the regional pattern implies that the global figure will be decided largely in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The expected 2030 stunting values from the trend calculation are 27.9% for South Asia and 31.0% for Sub-Saharan Africa, both well above the 5.0% reference level. Only Europe and Central Asia, and the high-income group, sit at or near it.

### Country progress on wasting and the absence of convergence in stunting

Wasting presents a more differentiated national picture than stunting. The trend assessment covered 65 countries against a reference ceiling of 5.0% by 2030. That ceiling is the one the trend tool applies to both indicators; it is one reading of the benchmark, and the agreed benchmarks may be read more strictly. Of the countries assessed, 42, holding 38.6% of their combined population, were on track or had already met the reference level. Four countries, with 7.8% of that population, showed moderate progress but needed acceleration. Three countries showed marginal progress and would need significant acceleration, and these three hold 33.7% of the population. No country was classed as stagnating, while 16 countries, with 19.9% of the population, were regressing, that is, wasting was rising rather than falling.

The population shares matter as much as the country counts. A simple count suggests that most assessed countries are doing well, since 42 of 65 is a majority. Weighted by population, the picture is less comfortable. The three countries in the marginal class hold a third of the assessed population, so the burden may be concentrated in a few large countries, although the results do not name them and this cannot be confirmed here. The shares of the marginal and regressing classes, 33.7% and 19.9%, add to roughly 53.6%, which is the reader's own approximate sum from rounded shares. It exceeds the 38.6% living where the level is within reach.

Three cautions apply. First, only 65 countries were assessed, although the underlying series cover 162 countries. The assessment depends on enough survey observations to draw a trend, and countries without them are absent from every class. Second, the 5.0% ceiling is not the only way to read the target: other thresholds for 2025 and 2030 have been proposed, and a country counted as on track against 5.0% may still fall short of a stricter one. Third, wasting is volatile. It responds quickly to famine, conflict, floods, disease outbreaks and seasonal food shortages, so a single survey can show a sharp change that does not reflect a lasting one. Regression may reflect a recent crisis, and on-track status may reflect a favourable survey year.

The results do not show why countries regressed, but well-established context points to likely factors. Conflict and displacement disrupt health services and food supply. Price shocks after the pandemic of 2020 and later disturbances to grain and fertiliser markets may have reduced the quality and quantity of children's diets in poorer households. Where treatment for severe acute malnutrition depends on external funding, interruptions in the supply of therapeutic food have direct effects. Countries that moved towards the target have typically combined growth in household incomes with expanded primary health care, immunisation and community-based treatment of acute malnutrition.

Stunting shows a different pattern: the gaps between countries are not closing. The convergence test relates the change in stunting between 2015 and 2024 to the starting level across 162 countries. If countries with high stunting at the start improved faster, the coefficient would be clearly negative. The estimated beta is -0.00244, with a p-value of 0.2275 and an R-squared of 0.0085. The sign points to a slight tendency towards convergence, but the estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 1% of the variation in later change. A country's initial stunting rate says almost nothing about how fast it improved.

The coefficient of variation, which measures dispersion relative to the average, rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2024. Dispersion between countries has therefore widened in relative terms. This is consistent with the lack of convergence: the world average has fallen only slightly while some countries have moved much faster than others. A rising coefficient of variation does not by itself show that high-prevalence countries worsened; it shows that the spread, relative to the mean, grew.

For 2030 the two measures call for different responses. Wasting appears to be a problem of a minority of countries that sit well off course, while many others are already within reach. Stunting is a slow, structural condition tied to maternal health, early-life diet, sanitation and poverty, and the absence of convergence implies that no general catching-up process can be relied on. Without deliberate targeting of the countries with the highest prevalence, the relative gap will probably go on widening towards 2030, though this is an inference from the 2015 to 2024 pattern and not a computed projection.

### Data coverage and the limits of the evidence

Wasting is measured mainly by household surveys, not by continuous registration, and the evidence behind the series is thinner than the regional table suggests. In 2000, 58 countries reported a wasting value. The count fell to 22 in 2001 and varied between 24 and 51 in later years. It stood at 32 in 2015, rose to 48 in 2018 and 46 in 2019, then fell to 26 in 2020. In 2024 only 6 countries reported. Across the whole period 162 countries reported at least once, so the series covers most of the world, but not in any single year.

The counts alone do not show why a given year is thin. A plausible explanation, offered as context and not shown by the series, is the survey cycle: household surveys are fielded every few years in each country, and results are published with a delay. On that reading, the low count for 2024 would reflect results not yet processed, not fewer children measured, and it is no evidence of improvement or decline. The dip to 26 countries in 2020 coincides with the pandemic, when fieldwork was suspended or postponed in many places, but the results give only the count, so the link is likely and not established. Readers comparing 2015 with 2024 should accept that the later point is the less complete one.

The regional and income-group values for 2024 are consequently not simple averages of fresh observations. They are aggregates that, on well-established practice, combine recent surveys with modelled estimates for countries and years without a survey. The figure of 6.6% for the world in 2024, and the regional values around it, probably rest in large part on that modelling. The fall from 7.1% in 2015 is a fall in the estimate, but its size is small relative to the uncertainty that such modelling carries. Changes of that scale between two years should not be treated as established.

The caution applies most strongly where reporting is thinnest. In regions with many countries and uneven survey schedules, notably Sub-Saharan Africa, an aggregate can move because of which countries happened to be surveyed as well as because of nutrition. The fall in that region from 7.0% in 2015 to 5.9% in 2024 is larger than the fall in the world figure, and it would be unwise to attribute it wholly to improved child nutrition without national survey evidence. In South Asia, where the prevalence is highest at 15.7% in 2024, a few large countries may weigh heavily in the aggregate, so that one survey round could shift the regional figure; the results do not show the weights. By contrast, high-income countries and North America, at 0.4% and 0.2% in 2024, have low values whose precision matters little for the argument.

Wasting has a further difficulty that stunting lacks. It is a short-lived condition: a child can be wasted during a hungry season or an illness and recover within weeks. Its prevalence depends on the month in which a survey is fielded, so two surveys in the same country in different seasons can differ for reasons unrelated to policy. Single-year comparisons are therefore weaker for wasting than for stunting, which reflects accumulated deprivation and changes slowly.

For the 2030 assessment these limits matter in two ways. A judgement that a country is on track rests on its own survey history, and countries with long gaps between surveys cannot be assessed with confidence. The 5.0% ceiling used by the trend tool is one reading of the benchmark, not a settled one. The world and regional aggregates should be taken as indications of direction, not as precise measures of distance from that ceiling. Where the series is sparse, the more reliable evidence is the national survey record, and the count of reporting countries should be read alongside every figure quoted in this section.

### What the trajectories imply for 2030, and proposals

At the observed rates, the world will not reach a stunting prevalence of 5.0% by 2030. That figure is the ceiling the trend tool applies to stunting; it is one reading of the agreed benchmarks, which may be read more strictly, and it is not quoted here as the agreed target itself. Global stunting stood at 23.2% in 2024, and the trend projection gives 22.3% in 2030, a ratio of 0.12 against the pace the ceiling requires. The assessment class for the world is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The 2025 milestone in the target text will also be missed on this evidence.

Three groups are classed as on track for stunting. Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.0% in 2015 to 4.6% in 2024, and its projected 2030 value is 3.8%, a ratio of 2.13, the fastest relative pace of any region. High-income countries stood at 3.9% in 2015 and 4.0% in 2024, and North America rose from 2.8% to 4.1%. The last two are classed as on track only because their levels already lie below the ceiling of 5.0%. The classification reflects a level, not a gain, and the slight rise in both groups shows that wealthy countries have not secured child growth against change.

East Asia and Pacific is classed as marginal. Its prevalence fell from 14.5% to 13.3% and the projection for 2030 is 12.6%, a ratio of 0.20. Latin America and the Caribbean is classed as regression: 12.3% in 2015 and 12.4% in 2024, with 12.4% projected for 2030. A middle-income region with food available in aggregate has therefore made no progress on stunting over the period. Possible causes, stated as context and not shown by these series, include the quality of diets in early childhood, maternal health, sanitation and inequality within countries, which regional averages conceal.

The regions with the highest levels are furthest from the ceiling. South Asia is projected at 27.9% in 2030, a ratio of 0.30, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 31.0%, a ratio of 0.12. Low-income countries are projected at 34.4%, from 38.0% in 2015 and 35.8% in 2024. Lower middle-income countries fell from 33.9% to 28.9%, with 25.9% projected for 2030. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is projected at 22.1%, from 24.1% in 2024. Each would still hold stunting at several times the ceiling in 2030. Population growth is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, so a slow fall in prevalence there could coincide with a rising number of affected children, which the prevalence series cannot show.

Wasting offers a less bleak picture in country counts but a troubling one at the margin. Of 65 countries assessed, 42 are on track or have met the 5.0% ceiling, while 16 show regression, holding 19.9% of the population assessed. Three countries, holding 33.7% of that population, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. The results do not name these countries, so what drives their classes cannot be read from them. Wasting responds quickly to drought, conflict, price surges and disease, so a country can change class within a year or two.

Neither the period since 2015 nor the disruptions after 2020 can be read cleanly from these series. Survey reporting fell to 26 countries in 2020 and to 6 in 2024. A pandemic interruption and a publication lag are plausible explanations, but the counts alone do not establish either. Recent wasting values rest on very few new observations, and modelled stunting estimates for 2024 lean on earlier surveys. A trend between 2015 and 2024 describes the direction of the estimates, not a verified count of children. The direction for 2030 is consistent across the regional and income readings, but the distance cannot be stated precisely, because it depends on the tool ceiling and on thin data. The wasting verdict is a rough inference from country classes and not a computed world projection.
