w-c03-6-3.text:
### Agriculture's weight in output and employment is shrinking only slowly

Agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 4.2 per cent of world GDP in 2015 and 4.0 per cent in 2025. The share barely moved over a period that included the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the pandemic of 2020 and the food and energy price shocks that followed. In 2025, 158 countries reported the series, so the global figure rests on a broad but not complete base.

Employment tells a different story from output. Agriculture accounted for 28.5 per cent of total employment worldwide in 2015 and 25.8 per cent in 2025, according to modelled estimates of the International Labour Organization. In 2025 the employment share (25.8 per cent) was about six and a half times the output share (4.0 per cent): roughly a quarter of the world's workers produced about four per cent of measured value added. This ratio is read from the two cited levels and is not itself a series of the bench. The gap is the central fact for any judgement of public investment. It points to low output per worker. As context from the wider literature, not a finding of this section and not tested by the bench data, farm productivity is widely held to depend on roads, storage, irrigation, research and advisory services, which are largely public goods.

The pace of change is slow against the horizon of 2030. Between 2015 and 2025 the employment share moved from 28.5 per cent to 25.8 per cent and the output share from 4.2 per cent to 4.0 per cent. If movement continued at a similar pace, more than a fifth of the world's workers would still be employed in agriculture in 2030, a projection that assumes a steady trend and is not an estimate of the bench. Structural transformation, in which workers move from farms to higher-productivity work, is under way but far from complete, and a falling employment share is not evidence of falling need. Where output per worker is low, public spending that raises it is one means by which the employment share can fall without a loss of rural income.

The benchmark that follows is simple. If public spending on agriculture were to match the sector's weight, it would be proportionate to a share of output of about 4.0 per cent in the world as a whole, and arguably to a higher share where employment is concentrated. The World Development Indicators supply no series for government agricultural expenditure among the results available here, so the match cannot be measured or scored directly. The comparison is made indirectly, through the external flows examined below and through the regional weights. Target 2.a, which calls for greater investment in rural infrastructure, research, extension and gene banks, sets no numerical share to match. Any reading of a shortfall should be made with that limit in view.

### Regions differ most where agriculture matters most

The regional picture is one of extremes. In 2025, agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 17.9 per cent of GDP in Sub-Saharan Africa and 15.6 per cent in South Asia. Both regions also hold the largest shares of employment in the sector: 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa and 41.5 per cent in South Asia, both in 2025. At the other end, Europe and Central Asia drew 2.0 per cent of GDP from agriculture in 2025 and 6.7 per cent of employment, while North America drew 1.0 per cent of GDP in 2021, the latest year reported for that region, and 1.5 per cent of employment in 2025. The years differ between the two measures for North America, and the comparison should be read with that in mind. In North America the sector is a rounding error in the national accounts; in Sub-Saharan Africa it is where about half of all workers earn their living.

The gap between the two measures matters as much as the levels. In Sub-Saharan Africa the employment share (49.3 per cent) stands far above the output share (17.9 per cent), and in South Asia the same holds (41.5 per cent against 15.6 per cent). Where half of workers produce under a fifth of output, average output per agricultural worker is low relative to other sectors, which is the usual reading of such a gap, although these two series do not measure productivity or incomes directly. Public spending proportionate to the sector's share of GDP would therefore still be small relative to the number of people who depend on it. No series on government agricultural spending is held here, so the match between spending and weight cannot be scored.

The direction of change after 2015 differs between regions. In Latin America and the Caribbean the output share rose from 5.5 per cent in 2015 to 6.8 per cent in 2025, while the employment share fell from 14.0 per cent to 12.7 per cent. The series alone does not show whether this reflects prices or output per worker. In Sub-Saharan Africa the output share rose from 16.3 per cent in 2015 to 17.9 per cent in 2025, while the employment share fell from 53.3 per cent to 49.3 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific, by contrast, employment fell from 27.9 per cent to 21.7 per cent and the output share from 6.0 per cent to 5.5 per cent, the pattern of an economy moving labour out of farming. South Asia, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, moved only slightly in output share: South Asia from 15.9 per cent to 15.6 per cent, and the latter region from 6.9 per cent to 6.8 per cent.

By income group, the divide is sharper still. In low-income countries agriculture accounted for 27.2 per cent of GDP in 2025, up from 25.6 per cent in 2015, and for 59.4 per cent of employment in 2025, against 61.5 per cent in 2015. Lower middle income countries stood at 17.8 per cent of GDP and 39.8 per cent of employment in 2025. Upper middle income countries recorded 6.9 per cent of GDP and 19.8 per cent of employment, and high income countries 1.3 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 2.9 per cent of employment in 2025. In the poorest countries the output share has therefore risen even as the employment share eased only slightly. For target 2.a, whose wording singles out developing countries and the least developed among them, this concentration indicates where investment in rural infrastructure, research and extension has the largest population to reach by 2030.

### International flows from UN agencies rose but moved toward one region

Net official flows from UN agencies through IFAD rose over the period, though not evenly. The world total was 399 million US dollars in 2015 and 509 million in 2023. These are current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the apparent rise may reflect higher prices rather than a larger real transfer. The series is also a net measure: repayments of loans are subtracted from disbursements, so a fall in a region's figure can reflect repayment as much as reduced lending. Only IFAD flow values are given here; for the companion FAO series, the section reports counts of reporting countries and no flow values.

The rise was concentrated in one region. Sub-Saharan Africa received 180 million US dollars in 2015 and 405 million in 2023. Every other region with a reported figure moved the other way. East Asia and Pacific fell from 99.9 million to 9.2 million. South Asia fell from 50.3 million to 43.1 million. Europe and Central Asia fell from 20.3 million to 15.5 million, Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.9 million to 9.0 million, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 29.2 million to 24.0 million. North America recorded zero in both years, as expected for a region of donors. The world total therefore rose in a period when one region's figure rose and the others' fell.

The income groups show the same movement. Low-income countries received 109 million US dollars in 2015 and 247 million in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 201 million to 240 million. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 67.2 million to a net negative of 12.6 million, meaning that repayments to IFAD exceeded new disbursements in 2023. The series does not show why; one conjecture, offered as context and not as a finding, is that a lender concentrating concessional resources on the poorest countries sees middle-income borrowers repay. High-income countries show a small figure of 2.8 million in 2023, and the data do not explain it.

The direction is consistent with the regional evidence on agriculture's weight set out earlier, since Sub-Saharan Africa has the largest shares of output and jobs in the sector, although the years differ between the flow series (to 2023) and the output and employment series (to 2025). It matters for 2030 because target 2.a asks for more investment in developing countries, in particular the least developed. A rise confined to a single region and to the lowest income groups is consistent with that wording, yet the sums are small. Half a billion dollars a year, spread across a continent whose farm economy employed 49.3 per cent of workers in 2025, cannot substitute for domestic public spending.

Coverage limits how far the picture can be pressed. IFAD flows were reported by 94 countries in 2023. The companion FAO series was reported by 129 countries in 2023, against 133 in 2013, and 139 countries reported in at least one year. The count was 135 in 2019 and 128 in 2022. Aggregates should therefore be read as sums over reporting countries, and a missing country is not a zero. The comparison before and after 2020 is further limited by the end of the series in 2023, which leaves little room to judge how flows responded to the pandemic and the price shocks that followed.

### Flows follow need, but do not yet change it, and proposals follow

Across the 89 countries for which both series exist, the link between flows and the size of agriculture depends on what is compared. The Spearman correlation of 2023 levels between net official flows from IFAD and agriculture's share of GDP is 0.575, a moderate positive association. Countries where agriculture contributes more to output tend to receive more from the fund. The correlation of changes between 2015 and 2023 is 0.141, which is weak and shows no clear association between how far a country's flows moved and how far its agricultural share of GDP moved. The Kendall coefficients, 0.390 for levels and 0.101 for changes, give the same picture on a stricter rank measure.

The share of GDP is only a proxy for need, and the correlation does not show that allocation follows need. It shows that flows are larger where agriculture's share of output is larger, which is what IFAD's mandate to lend to agricultural economies would produce in any case. The change correlation does not test whether flows alter the sector's share of output or of employment, and employment is not part of it. Context from the wider literature, not a finding of these series, is that rural infrastructure, extension services and research take years to alter productivity, and a falling share of GDP can reflect growth elsewhere as much as any change in farming. Structural change is slow, as the global share of 4.0 per cent in 2025 against 4.2 per cent in 2015 already shows. Ten years is a short window against which to judge a transfer of this kind.

The limits of the evidence are plain. A correlation is not a cause, and the weak link of changes cannot show that flows fail, since the counterfactual is unknown. The series covers one agency's net flows, in current dollars. The companion FAO series is not quantified here: only the counts of reporting countries are used. It was reported by 139 countries in at least one year, but the annual count fell from 135 in 2019 to 129 in 2023, with a low of 128 in 2022, which narrows what can be compared. The years of latest data also differ across series, with flows ending in 2023 and output and employment shares in 2025, and the pairing of the two series rests on 89 countries. Above all, target 2.a can be read in more than one way: as public spending by governments, as private investment, or as international cooperation. The data on the bench measure only the last, and in part. Whether public spending on agriculture matches the sector's weight, 49.3 per cent of jobs in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2025 and 17.9 per cent of its GDP, cannot be answered from these series, because government agricultural spending is absent.

For 2030 the implication is that the match between investment and need cannot at present be tested, and no expectation about the sector's share can be drawn from the weak change correlation of 0.141. The proposals below follow from that finding.

c03-6.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2025
c03-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c03-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c03-6.r4: countries reporting in any year
c03-6.r4: countries reporting in any year

proposals: National governments and the African Union and South Asian regional bodies should publish annual government expenditure on agriculture in a common classification, so that spending can be set against the sector's share of output and jobs.

The World Bank and the FAO should report public agricultural spending in the World Development Indicators catalogue for all countries, including those where agriculture employs the largest share of workers.
IFAD and the FAO should publish flows in constant dollars and by purpose, such as rural infrastructure, research and extension, so that later reviews can test whether flows change productivity.
w-c03-6-3.gaps: Government spending on agriculture, private investment in the sector and flows by purpose are absent from the bench. The IFAD and FAO flows are net, in current dollars, and cover few countries in some years. The data do not show why flows shifted between regions, and the correlations cannot show cause or effect.

w-c08-4-1.text:
### World energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured as megajoules of energy supply per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, fell from 4.8556 MJ in 2015 to 4.5449 MJ in 2021. The title of this part gives the fall as 6.4 per cent, a figure that the results do not state directly and that is therefore not relied on here; the two levels are the evidence. The direction is the one target 7.3 requires: each dollar of output needed less energy at the end of the period than at the start. The question for the section is whether the pace is the one the target asks for.

The trend tool expresses the world movement as a rate of -0.01096 for the indicator, and classifies it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. That rate is the tool's own measure of change per year, and it is read here only as a direction and a pace relative to the tool's thresholds. The tool was run with no numerical target, so its classification rests on a generic benchmark and not on a figure derived from the text of target 7.3. The label should be taken as a guide to the size of the gap, not as a verdict on the target itself.

The target can be read in more than one way. Its wording, to double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, is commonly interpreted as doubling the rate recorded in an earlier period, which requires a baseline period to be chosen. The choice matters, because the earlier rate differs according to the years used, and the series available through the bench begins its comparison in 2015. A second reading, used in the monitoring of the goals, sets a fixed annual rate of improvement in energy intensity for the whole period to 2030. The two readings need not give the same answer, and neither can be tested fully here, since the bench does not hold a rate for the period before 2015 for the world as a whole.

The data also limit what can be said about the present. The world series ends in 2021, not in 2022 or later, so the latest observation lies well before 2030 and says nothing about the years since. Regional series reach 2022 in some cases, but the world aggregate depends on coverage that thins in the final year. Any statement that the world is or is not on course for 2030 is therefore an extrapolation from six years of change, a period that includes the sharp fall and partial rebound in economic activity around 2020. Movements in GDP in that period affect the ratio as much as movements in energy supply, so a change in intensity does not by itself show that efficiency measures were adopted.

Why the measure matters is plain enough. Energy intensity is the broadest indicator available of how much energy an economy needs to produce its output, and a falling value lowers fuel costs, emissions and import dependence for a given level of output. It is, however, a crude proxy for efficiency, because it also reflects the structure of an economy, its climate, and the share of heavy industry in output. The following parts examine how these differences appear across regions and over time.

### Regions diverge from a 2.58 to a 6.14 MJ range by 2021 or 2022

Regional levels of energy intensity, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, span a wide range by the latest year available. Europe and Central Asia is lowest, at 2.5791 MJ in 2022, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest among regions, at 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The latest year differs between regions, 2021 for some and 2022 for others, so the comparison is approximate and the gap between regions is read as indicative rather than exact.

Europe and Central Asia fell from 4.002 MJ in 2015 to 2.5791 MJ in 2022. Its rate of change, -0.0608 per year, is the steepest of any region and the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions. Part of the decline in this region may reflect changes in economic structure and in fuel supply as well as efficiency gains; the data do not separate these.

North America and South Asia also improved substantially. North America moved from 5.0428 MJ in 2015 to 4.364 MJ in 2022, at a rate of -0.0204 per year, and South Asia from 4.5047 MJ to 3.9427 MJ in 2021, at -0.022 per year. Both are classed as on track or target met. South Asia's result is notable because it began from a level close to the world value and has since fallen below it.

The remaining regions made less headway. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5.6997 MJ in 2015 to 5.2313 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0142 per year, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 3.4822 MJ to 3.265 MJ in 2022, at -0.0092 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Its level is low, which may leave less room for further cuts, but the data do not test that.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan barely moved, from 5.3599 MJ in 2015 to 5.332 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0009 per year, classed as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa also stagnated, falling from 6.2412 MJ to 6.1403 MJ in 2021, at -0.0027 per year. Together these two regions combine high or middling levels with almost no improvement.

Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income economies stood at 7.415 MJ in 2015 and 7.1393 MJ in 2021, the highest of any group, with a rate of -0.0063 per year, classed as marginal progress. High-income economies fell from 4.3961 MJ to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, at -0.0334 per year, classed as on track or target met. Lower middle income fell from 4.644 MJ to 4.2707 MJ in 2021, and upper middle income from 5.5767 MJ to 5.2119 MJ. The poorest economies are therefore the most energy-intensive per unit of output and are improving most slowly.

Three cautions apply. First, only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the latest regional values rest on incomplete years, and regions with data only to 2021 are compared with others to 2022. Second, intensity reflects economic structure, climate, fuel mix and the share of traditional biomass in supply, and the purchasing power parity conversion of GDP, not efficiency alone. Third, the world rate of -0.011 per year is classed as marginal progress, so the regional divergence matters for 2030: the regions that are on track are not those with the highest levels, and the highest-intensity regions are those where acceleration is most needed.

### Improvement peaked before 2018 and has since slowed

The structural breaks in the annual change of world energy intensity show that the pace of improvement has not been steady. The series for the world, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, has breaks in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. These divide the record into five segments, each with its own mean annual change. A negative mean change means that intensity fell, so a larger negative figure means faster improvement.

In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ. It steepened to -0.1154 MJ in 2005-2008, the fastest pace of the early period. The break in 2009 marks a pause: in 2009-2010 the mean change was +0.0070 MJ, so intensity rose slightly instead of falling. That coincides with the global financial crisis, and a link between the two is a reasonable reading, though the data do not by themselves establish it. Output fell sharply while much of the energy supply, in buildings, transport and industrial plant, could not be scaled down as quickly, which tends to raise intensity in a downturn.

The break in 2011 opens the longest segment. In 2011-2017 the mean annual change was -0.1045 MJ, close to the pace of 2005-2008 and about twice that of 2001-2004. This matters for the target. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement, and the baseline year of 2015 sits inside this faster period. Any comparison of later years with the rate at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals is therefore a comparison with a stretch of unusually quick improvement, not with the slower pace of the early 2000s. Reading the target against the earlier rate of -0.0498 MJ would make doubling look nearer than it is when set against the rate that prevailed in 2015.

The final break, in 2018, is the most consequential. In 2018-2021 the mean annual change was -0.0325 MJ, less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017 and below even the 2001-2004 rate. Improvement therefore peaked before 2018 and has since slowed. The segment is short, four years, and its end includes 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic disturbed both output and energy supply. A short segment with unusual years at its end warrants caution, and the mean should not be taken as a settled new trend.

The data do not identify why the slowdown occurred. Several explanations are plausible and are offered here only as interpretations, not findings. The pandemic caused abrupt falls and rebounds in activity that distort a ratio of energy to output. Fuel prices affect the incentive to economise on energy, and the price changes of these years may have weakened it. Structural change in industry, including shifts in the weight of energy-intensive sectors in world output, can move intensity independently of efficiency in any single sector. The series measures energy per unit of GDP, so it blends efficiency with the composition of the economy, and none of these causes can be separated from the others using this result alone.

For 2030 the implication is plain, though conditional. If the rate of 2018-2021 persisted, the world would fall well short of doubling the rate of 2011-2017, let alone exceeding it. Meeting the target on the most demanding reading would require a pace far above any segment in the record. The target also admits more than one reading, since the earlier rate may be taken from the period before 2015 or from the baseline decade, and the choice changes the threshold. Under either reading, the break of 2018 shows that the recent direction is away from the target, not towards it.

### Doubling the earlier rate is not met, and proposals follow

Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency, and the series held by the bench allow a reading of that target only in outline. The target does not say which earlier rate is to be doubled, nor which period is to be compared. Two readings are therefore possible: the pace before 2015 set against the pace after it, or the pace in the years of fastest improvement set against the most recent years. Under either reading the world series gives no sign of doubling.

The clearest comparison is between the two latest segments of the world series. From 2011 to 2017 the mean annual change in energy intensity was -0.1045 MJ per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. From 2018 to 2021 it was -0.03247 MJ. The recent pace is therefore roughly a third of the earlier one, so intensity is falling more slowly, not twice as fast. The trend tool reaches a similar verdict from a longer baseline: the world rate of -0.01096 is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The segment from 2018 to 2021 includes the pandemic years, when output and energy supply both moved sharply, so part of the slowdown may reflect those disturbances and not a lasting change. Only four years are covered, and the data cannot separate the two explanations.

Regional results show where the world picture is made. Only Europe and Central Asia, at a rate of -0.06083, and the high-income group, at -0.03337, are classed as on track or target met. North America, at -0.02044, and South Asia, at -0.02197, also carry that label in the trend result. The label reflects the tool's own benchmark and does not show that those regions are doubling a previous rate. The high-income group fell from 4.3961 MJ in 2015 to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 4.002 MJ to 2.5791 MJ over the same years. These falls come from groups that already had comparatively low intensity, which is consistent with the familiar pattern of efficiency gains, structural change in economies and fuel switching in richer countries.

The regions where improvement is most needed are moving least. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a rate of -0.00271, and its intensity moved from 6.2412 MJ in 2015 to 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is also classed as stagnating, at -0.00087, with levels of 5.3599 MJ in 2015 and 5.332 MJ in 2021. East Asia and Pacific shows moderate progress, at -0.01419, but acceleration is needed there: its intensity fell from 5.6997 MJ to 5.2313 MJ. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.00916, and the low-income group, at -0.00629, show marginal progress. The low-income group still has the highest level of any income group, at 7.1393 MJ in 2021.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Unless the pace of recent years rises well above the 2018 to 2021 mean, the world will not reach a doubled rate, and the regions with the highest or slowest-falling intensity are those where the gap is widest. Two cautions apply. The latest data point is 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, so developments after those years are not visible. The number of countries reporting in 2022 is 116, against coverage of 201 economies for the series as a whole, so the most recent regional figures rest on incomplete reporting.

Intensity is also an imperfect measure of efficiency. It divides energy supply by output, so it moves with the structure of an economy, the mix of industry and services, climate, and the exchange of goods across borders, as well as with technical efficiency. A fall may come from shifting to services without any gain in the efficiency of equipment. A flat series may hide improvements offset by growth in energy-heavy activity. The proposals below respond to these limits as well as to the regional gaps.

claims.value: marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed

c08-4.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2021
c08-4.r2: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rate
c08-4.r2: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rate
c08-4.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c08-4.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2021

proposals: Governments and regional development banks in East Asia and Pacific, the Middle East and North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa should target efficiency programmes (building codes, appliance standards, industrial retrofits) at these regions, where intensity is high and falling slowly or not at all.
The United Nations statistical and energy custodian agencies should agree and publish a fixed baseline and a definition of the earlier rate for Target 7.3, so that doubling can be read in one way.
The World Bank and the custodian agencies should publish the intensity series to a later year and raise the number of countries reporting, so that post-2021 progress can be judged.

National statistical offices and the custodian agencies should publish absolute energy-use data alongside intensity, so that efficiency gains can be told apart from changes in economic structure and in total demand.
w-c08-4-1.gaps: The series end in 2021 or 2022 for most aggregates, so recent change is not visible, and only 116 countries reported in 2022. The target names no baseline rate, so doubling has no single reading. Intensity mixes efficiency with economic structure, and the results do not separate them. The pandemic years fall inside the latest segment and cannot be isolated with four years of data.

w-c03-3-4.text:
### Child overweight and anaemia in women stand at 5.5 per cent and 30.7 per cent

Two indicators of malnutrition other than stunting and wasting are measured here: overweight among children under five, and anaemia among women of reproductive age. Target 2.2 names all forms of malnutrition and the nutritional needs of adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, yet its numerical benchmarks cover only stunting and wasting. The two indicators therefore describe parts of the target that carry no quantified goal in the wording given. The overweight series is scored in this section against a reference value of 3.0 per cent by 2030, which is a working benchmark of the bench's trend tool and not a value written into the target. The anaemia series is scored by the same tool without any target value, so its classes describe direction of change and not distance from an agreed goal.

In 2024 the world prevalence of child overweight, defined as weight for height more than two standard deviations above the WHO 2006 median, was 5.5 per cent of children under five, up from 5.2 per cent in 2015. The rise is small, but it runs against the direction the reference value implies. The estimate rests on 163 countries reporting in 2024. It is a modelled estimate, so year-to-year movements are smoothed and partly reflect the model rather than fresh surveys, especially in countries that are surveyed only every few years.

Anaemia in women aged 15 to 49 is far more common. In 2023 the world prevalence was 30.7 per cent, against 28.0 per cent in 2015. The measure combines non-pregnant women with haemoglobin below 12 g/dL and pregnant women below 11 g/dL, and 192 countries are covered. Nearly one woman in three of reproductive age is therefore anaemic, a share that is large but not a majority. The condition matters for maternal health, for birth outcomes and for the nutrition of the next generation of children.

Both world averages were higher at the latest year than in 2015. A rise in child overweight is not necessarily a failure of the same kind as a rise in anaemia, since the two reflect different diets and health conditions. Even so, the direction of both world figures is adverse. Haemoglobin measurement also depends on altitude, smoking and survey method, and country estimates are modelled where surveys are scarce. The levels reported here should be read as well-founded orders of magnitude, not as exact counts. For 2030, the starting point is a world in which both burdens are larger than at the outset of the agenda.

### Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower

Regional levels of the two burdens run in opposite directions. Child overweight is lowest in South Asia, at 3.4 per cent of children under five in 2024, and highest in North America, at 9.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 8.8 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 7.8 per cent, while Sub-Saharan Africa records 3.8 per cent. Anaemia among women aged 15 to 49 reverses the order: North America has the lowest prevalence, 14.9 per cent in 2023, and South Asia the highest, 51.1 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 36.7 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 35.2 per cent, whereas East Asia and the Pacific, at 18.7 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean, at 20.0 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia, at 21.3 per cent, lie near the lower end.

The pattern by income group repeats the regional one. Overweight is 3.5 per cent in low-income countries and 4.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 8.6 per cent in upper-middle-income and 8.4 per cent in high-income countries. Anaemia is 35.6 per cent in low-income and 46.0 per cent in lower-middle-income countries, against 19.8 per cent in upper-middle-income and 17.3 per cent in high-income countries. Child overweight is thus highest where anaemia is lower, and the reverse holds in the poorest regions. This does not mean that the two conditions exclude one another within a country or a household; regional averages cannot show whether both occur together. Lower overweight in the poorest groups should not be read as a sign of better nutrition, since anaemia there remains heavy.

The spread of anaemia among countries can be stated directly. Among 192 countries, weighted by population, the between-region share of the Theil index was 77.9 per cent in 2023, up from 74.1 per cent in 2015, so most of the measured inequality in anaemia lies between regions rather than within them. The Gini coefficient fell from 0.287 to 0.272 over the same years. Differences among countries have therefore narrowed slightly overall, while the part attributable to regional means has grown. The results do not identify the causes of this pattern.

### Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere

The trend classes show that movement on both indicators has mostly been in the wrong direction since 2015. Child overweight is assessed against a working benchmark of 3.0 per cent by 2030, a figure adopted for this book and not written into Target 2.2. Of the 163 countries assessed, 92, holding 66.6 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing, meaning that prevalence is rising where the benchmark requires it to fall. Only 33 countries, with 21.3 per cent of the population, are on track or have already met the benchmark. A further 10 countries (2.0 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 20 (7.5 per cent) show marginal progress and 8 (2.6 per cent) are stagnant. No test of other benchmark values was run, so how the count of countries on track would change under a stricter or looser line is not established here.

Regionally, regression is the most common class, with two exceptions. East Asia and Pacific, high-income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are all classed as regressing, as are the low-income, lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income groups. The annual rates of change are small, 0.0153 for East Asia and Pacific and 0.0165 for Latin America and the Caribbean, but they point upward in each case. South Asia shows the highest rate, at 0.0518, from a low base. Europe and Central Asia is classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.11, and its expected prevalence of 7.32 per cent in 2030 remains far above 3.0. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the only region with moderate progress, a ratio of 0.67, and its expected 2030 level of 4.36 per cent would still be above the benchmark. The regression ratios for low-income and lower-middle-income countries, -6.09 and -2.37, and for high-income countries, -0.36, show the size of the departure from the path the benchmark requires. At the world level the ratio is -0.21, a regression, with 5.67 per cent expected in 2030.

Anaemia among women of reproductive age shows a more uniform picture. The trend tool applies no target value to this indicator, so its classes show only whether prevalence is falling. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing. Only 2 countries (1.7 per cent of the population) are classed as on track, 1 shows moderate progress, 9 show marginal progress and 18 are stagnant, so the rise is widespread but not universal. Every region and income group is classed as regressing. The world rate of change is 0.0115. Rates are highest in North America, at 0.0359, and in high-income countries, at 0.0239, and lowest in East Asia and Pacific, at 0.0023. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 0.0036 and South Asia at 0.0070, while Europe and Central Asia, at 0.0202, rises faster than both. South Asia nonetheless has the highest prevalence of any region, at 51.1 per cent in 2023.

The spread across countries narrowed slightly. The Theil index fell from 0.130 in 2015 to 0.116 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index rose from 74.1 per cent to 77.9 per cent, so most of the measured inequality among the 192 countries lies between regions rather than within them. The narrowing does not signal improvement, since prevalence rose in most countries. These data identify no causes. Changing diets, shifts in the measurement of haemoglobin and modelled estimates for countries with sparse surveys could each contribute, and none can be separated here.

### The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course

Change and level tell different stories about the two burdens. Across 162 countries, the rank correlation between changes in child overweight and changes in women's anaemia over 2015 to 2023 is -0.030, which is indistinguishable from none. Countries where overweight rose faster were no more and no less likely to see anaemia rise. The correlation of 2023 levels is -0.469, a moderate negative association: countries with higher child overweight tend to have lower anaemia among women. This is a statistical association between levels only. The results do not show why it arises, and they give no sign that one burden displaces the other. Because the two do not move together, a response designed for one cannot be assumed to reach the other.

The outlook for 2030 follows from the trend classes. For child overweight, the world is classed as regressing, with a ratio of -0.207 against the book's own working benchmark of 3.0 per cent and an expected 2030 prevalence of 5.7 per cent. North America is expected to reach 10.8 per cent and Latin America and the Caribbean 9.7 per cent, while high-income countries are expected to reach 9.1 per cent. South Asia has the lowest level in 2024 but the fastest rate of rise, at 0.052, and is expected to reach 4.6 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 4.3 per cent, below the world figure but still a regression. Two regions depart from this pattern. Europe and Central Asia shows marginal progress, with an expected 7.3 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows moderate progress, with an expected 4.4 per cent; in neither is the benchmark met on the current course. These projections extend a straight line fitted to 2015 to 2024 and are not forecasts of policy effects.

For anaemia, the Target sets no numerical benchmark, and the trend tool classes countries only by direction of travel from 2015. Of 192 countries, 162, holding 83.8 per cent of the assessed population, are classed as regressing; 18 are stagnant, 9 show marginal progress, 1 shows moderate progress and 2 are on track. Because no agreed benchmark underlies these classes, and no test was run of how they change if the reference is moved, they describe direction in the data and not failure against a commitment. Every region is classed as regressing, with annual rates ranging from 0.002 in East Asia and the Pacific to 0.036 in North America. Both findings rest on modelled estimates, which are revised and which smooth over years in which surveys were absent.

The findings support the proposals below, which are monitoring and targeting measures and not claims about which programmes work, since the results identify no causes.

w-c04-1-4.text:
### The global ratio fell from 228 to 197 and remains far above 70

Target 3.1 asks for a global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. The modelled estimate for the world stood at 228.0 in 2015, the year the goals were adopted, and at 197.0 in 2023, the latest year available. The ratio fell over eight years, but the 2023 value is still nearly three times the target value.

The gap is plain. The trend tool, which extrapolates the compound rate observed since 2015, expects a world ratio of 173.4 in 2030 and classes the world as making marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. On that tool's reading, the world has covered 0.35 of the distance from its 2015 value to the target, with seven years left. Closing the remainder would need a pace far faster than the one observed, so the distance does not shrink by small adjustments; it would require a different trajectory altogether.

The target is worded as a global ratio, not as a national one. A global ratio is a weighted outcome: it is pulled down by countries with low ratios and pulled up by countries with high ratios, in proportion to their live births. The results do not include a births-weighted breakdown or a list of countries, so the text does not say which countries contribute most to the world figure. A reading in which every country must fall below 70 would be stricter still, and the wording of the target does not require it. The later parts of this section take up the country classes drawn from the trend tool; the data used here do not give a count of countries above 70 in 2023.

The quality of the series needs stating plainly. Coverage is not the weakness: the modelled ratio is reported for all 194 countries in every year from 2000 to 2023, so no country drops out of the comparison and no year has gaps. That completeness is however a product of modelling rather than of observation. The estimates are produced by a regression model that, as general context, draws on covariates such as fertility, skilled birth attendance and national income. Where civil registration of deaths with causes is incomplete, as it is in many of the countries with the highest ratios, the estimate leans on those covariates rather than on counted deaths. The figures therefore carry uncertainty that the single published value does not display, and a change of a few points between years should not be read as a firm observation.

This uncertainty does not rescue the target. The fall from 228.0 to 197.0 is small beside the distance from 197.0 to 70, and no plausible revision of the model would close a gap of that size. What the uncertainty does affect is the confidence with which any single country or short period can be judged. For the world as a whole, the finding is robust: the ratio is falling, it is falling slowly, and 2030 will arrive with it well above 70 unless the pace changes sharply.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of forty

The spread between regions is wide, and a global average conceals it. In 2023 the modelled ratio for Sub-Saharan Africa was 448 deaths per 100,000 live births, against 11 for Europe and Central Asia. The two figures stand about forty times apart, a comparison drawn from rounded regional values. Target 3.1 is a global average assembled from very unequal parts, and the regional figures show that ratios differ widely between regions. The data used here do not show how far the place of birth outweighs other circumstances.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 593 in 2015 to 448 in 2023 and carries the highest ratio of any region. South Asia fell from 173 to 120, and its proportional fall is the larger of the two. Both remain above 70. The trend tool classes South Asia as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 87.1 against a target of 70, and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.83. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as making marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 350.5, about five times the target value, and a ratio of 0.46. On the figures shown, Sub-Saharan Africa has the largest gap to 70 in 2023. The results do not weight regions by births, so the contribution of each region to the global figure is not measured here.

The trend tool classes several regions as on track or as having met the target: Europe and Central Asia, North America, East Asia and Pacific, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Europe and Central Asia stood at 11 in 2023, down from 14 in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 8.9. North America stood at 16, down from 17, with an expected value of 15.2. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 54 to 47, with an expected value of 41.6. For the wealthiest regions the ratio is already so low that further gains are small in absolute terms. East Asia and Pacific fell from 70 to 66, so it sits just below the target. Its expected 2030 value of 62.7 leaves little margin, and the classification rests on a gentle slope rather than on a secure lead.

Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among regions. Its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and it is the only region classed as in regression, with an expected 2030 value of 79.7. The region was close to the threshold and has moved the wrong way. Well-established explanations include the disruption of health services during the pandemic years, persistent inequality between urban and rural or Indigenous populations, and the weight of unsafe abortion and hypertensive disorders. The data used here cannot apportion the rise among these causes.

Income groups show the same gradient. Low-income countries fell from 491 in 2015 to 346 in 2023 and are classed as making moderate progress, with an expected 2030 value of 254.7. Lower-middle-income countries fell from 291 to 235 and are classed as making marginal progress, with an expected value of 194.9 and a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 61 to 57, with an expected 2030 value of 53.7, and high-income countries from 11 to 10. The two upper groups are already below 70, so the whole of the remaining distance lies in the lower two.

Country classes confirm that the picture is mixed. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the population of the classified countries. Another 35 countries, with 16.5% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 23, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country is in stagnation and 7 are in regression, together under 1% of the population. The data used here do not give the number of countries above 70 in 2023 under a strict country-by-country reading, nor a births-weighted list of the countries that dominate the global total.

### Progress slowed after 2008 and the pandemic years disturbed the series

The series shows that progress was already slowing before the goals were adopted. The breaks analysis identifies a change of regime in 2008. In the segment from 2001 to 2007, the global ratio fell by a mean of 8.4 points a year. In the segment from 2008 to 2019, the mean annual fall was 5.2 points, roughly two-fifths less. The adoption of the goals did not restore the earlier speed, and the fall of the post-2015 years continues the slower trend rather than recovering from it. Well-established explanations include the exhaustion of the easiest gains, such as the expansion of skilled attendance at birth in countries that started from low coverage, and the harder task of reaching the remaining deaths, which are concentrated among women in poor, rural and conflict-affected settings where emergency obstetric care is least available.

The pandemic years then disturbed the series. The annual change was an increase of 4 points in 2020 and an increase of 31 points in 2021. The change reversed to a fall of 39 points in 2022, and the fall in 2023 was 6 points. The pattern is consistent with a shock and a recovery: disrupted maternity services, diversion of health staff and direct deaths from infection in pregnancy are plausible contributors to the rise, and the return of services would explain the fall. The analysis cannot establish this cause. The ratio is a modelled estimate, built by regression from covariates such as fertility, birth attendance and income, and is not a count of registered deaths. A sharp one-year rise followed by a sharp one-year fall may partly reflect the way the model treats pandemic-era inputs and the revision of estimates. The breaks detected from 2020 to 2023 are single-year segments and should be read as flags, not as stable trends. The 2022 fall should be treated as a modelled rebound and not as a durable gain.

The spread among countries has not narrowed in population-weighted terms. The Gini coefficient of the ratio across 194 countries was 0.628 in 2015 and 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.739 to 0.793. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 70.9% in 2015 and 67.2% in 2023, so most inequality is still a matter of regional membership, though the within-region component has grown a little.

Convergence is weak. A regression of change on the starting level across the 194 countries gives a coefficient of -0.00372 with a p-value of 0.0024, but an R-squared of only 0.050. Countries with higher ratios in 2015 tended to fall slightly faster, the direction needed for catching up, yet the starting level explains only a small part of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation, which counts countries equally, fell from 1.500 to 1.410, a modest narrowing. The population-weighted measures and the unweighted one point in different directions, and the data given do not show why. For 2030, neither the slowed trend before 2015 nor the weak catching up since offers grounds for expecting the pace to rise.

### At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed, and proposals follow

Extending the 2015 to 2023 rate to 2030 gives a global ratio of about 173.4 per 100,000 live births, against a target of 70. The trend tool places the world in the class of marginal progress. Its ratio of progress to the required pace is 0.35. This is not a share of the distance covered, and the tool does not report that share. The target is therefore not on course. Meeting it would need a pace of decline far above that of 2015 to 2023, and continuing present practice will not deliver it.

The country classification shows where the shortfall lies. Of the 194 countries assessed, 128 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 74.5% of the classified population. A further 35 countries, with 16.5% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 23 countries, with 8.4%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. One country stagnates and seven regress, and they hold 0.6% of the population between the regression group and a negligible share for stagnation. A majority of countries being on track does not imply that the global ratio will reach 70. The classification does not give the number of countries above 70 in 2023, so a stricter country-by-country reading of the target cannot be answered from these results.

The regional projections follow the same pattern, with classes as reported by the trend tool. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 448 in 2023, would reach about 350.5 in 2030 at its present rate, classed as marginal progress with a ratio of 0.46. South Asia, at 120 in 2023, would reach about 87.1, classed as moderate progress with a ratio of 0.83, the closest of the regions needing acceleration. Among income groups, low-income countries would reach about 254.7 and are classed as moderate progress, with a ratio of 0.56. Lower-middle-income countries would reach about 194.9 and are classed as marginal progress, with a ratio of 0.43. Upper-middle-income countries, at 57 in 2023 and projected at about 53.7, are classed as on track, as are high-income countries, at 10. East Asia and Pacific, at 66, is also on track, though narrowly, with a projection of about 62.7. Europe and Central Asia, North America, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are likewise classed as on track or target met. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the better-placed regions: its ratio rose from 74 in 2015 to 77 in 2023, and the trend tool classes it as regression, with a projection of about 79.7 in 2030.

Inequality among countries has not narrowed in the Gini and Theil measures. The Gini coefficient of country ratios rose from 0.628 in 2015 to 0.640 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.739 to 0.793. Differences between regions account for 67.2% of the Theil index in 2023, down from 71.0% in 2015. The unweighted convergence test across the 194 countries finds a small negative coefficient of -0.0037, with an R-squared of only 0.05, so catching-up among countries is weak.

The ratios are modelled estimates, and in many high-burden countries they rest on little direct counting. Any projection to 2030 inherits that uncertainty, and the class of a country near a margin should be read with caution. The regional results are not weighted by births, so the contribution of each region to the global figure is not measured here.

The proposals follow from these findings.

w-c09-10-1.text:
### Net official assistance reached US$259 billion in 2023, an imperfect proxy for Aid for Trade

Target 8.a calls for more Aid for Trade support for developing countries, the least developed above all, including through the Enhanced Integrated Framework. The measure that the bench holds does not match that wording. The series available is net official development assistance received, which counts concessional loans, net of repayments, and grants across every purpose. Aid for Trade commitments and disbursements, which would identify the share that builds ports, customs systems, trade policy capacity and productive sectors, are not among the series on the shelf. Net official development assistance is therefore an imperfect proxy: it bounds the resources from which trade capacity support could be drawn, but it does not show how much reached that purpose.

Read at that level, the world total rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US$. The use of constant prices matters, because it removes general price changes and shows a real increase in the resources received. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts. The coverage of the series is 150 countries, so some recipients lack a figure for the latest year, and any total should be read with that gap in mind.

The target also sets no numeric threshold and no end level. The trend tool therefore judges progress by direction alone: a series is 'on track or target met' when it is rising at a meaningful rate, and it counts as stagnating or marginal when it is not. On that reading the world is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.0545. The label is weak evidence. A rising total of general assistance does not show that trade capacity support has grown, nor that it has gone to the least developed countries that the target names, nor that it is effective. Increases may reflect emergency, humanitarian or other spending whose purpose is unrelated to trade.

The point matters for 2030 because the target can be read in more than one way: as a rise in the volume of Aid for Trade, as a rise in its share of assistance, or as improved support to least developed countries specifically. The bench can speak only to the first, and only through a proxy. The parts that follow take the proxy as given, examine how it differs among regions and income groups, and show what changed after 2015 and after 2020, while keeping the limits of the measure in view.

### Assistance rose unevenly across regions and concentrated among fewer recipients

Regional totals diverged sharply between 2015 and 2023, measured in constant 2023 US dollars. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest change, from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. The trend tool classes the region as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.213. Established knowledge of the period suggests that the displacement and reconstruction needs created by war in Europe explain part of this, though the series does not show what drove the change. No target level is set in the tool, so the classification reads only the direction of travel.

Other regions moved far less. East Asia and Pacific rose from US$9.9 billion to US$10.7 billion, with a rate of 0.010, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, a rate of 0.002, classed as stagnation. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion and is classed as on track, at a rate of 0.028. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Sub-Saharan Africa remains the largest regional recipient, at US$64.8 billion in 2023, up from US$51.8 billion in 2015. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region without recipients in this series.

The pattern matters for Aid for Trade because a rise in the world total, from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, says little about where trade capacity is being built. Regions with flat inflows in real terms face rising trade-support needs without a matching rise in assistance, while this series cannot show how much of any inflow reaches trade purposes.

The spread among countries widened. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received was 0.361 in 2015, 0.370 in 2019 and 0.452 in 2023. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to large recipients, was 0.255 in 2015 and 0.256 in 2019, then rose to 0.460 in 2023. The jump came after 2019, so the concentration is a feature of the years after 2020 rather than of the first half of the period. The coefficient of variation also rose, from 0.643 in 2015 to 1.477 in 2023.

The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 38.7% in 2019 and 29.6% in 2023. Regional averages therefore explain a shrinking part of the inequality, and differences among countries within the same region now account for most of it. Regional reading alone would hide this, so country-level targeting matters more than regional envelopes.

The country count also shifted: 138 countries in 2015, 134 in 2019 and 135 in 2023. The coverage statement for 2023 elsewhere in the results gives 136 countries reporting. These small differences reflect which countries have data and pass the weighting in each tool, and they mean that part of the change in concentration could arise from changes in who is counted. The change in count is small against the size of the rise in the Gini and Theil measures, but it cannot be excluded as a contributor.

### A single surge in 2022 explains most of the recent rise, and 43 countries regressed

The break analysis of world net official development assistance, in constant 2023 US dollars, locates the recent movement in a single year. Two breaks are detected, in 2022 and 2023. In the segment from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. In 2022 alone the change averaged US$49.8 billion, several times the long-run pace. In 2023 the change turned negative, at a mean of minus US$0.7 billion. The rise in the aggregate therefore comes mainly from one year, not from a steady build-up across the period, and the following year gave back a small part of it.

The regional pattern is consistent with this reading. Europe and Central Asia shows the largest rise in the preceding part, and the timing of the 2022 break coincides with the onset of war in Europe, which prompted large emergency and reception flows. That explanation is context drawn from the history of the period. The data held here do not attribute the 2022 change to any recipient or purpose, and the break test shows only when the world series shifted, not why. A one-year surge of this kind is also a weak basis for judging whether support for trade capacity has grown, since emergency flows serve humanitarian and budget needs rather than trade facilitation.

The country classes show how little the aggregate says about most recipients. Of 138 countries assessed, 79 are on track or have met the target of an increase, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed group. Another 5 show moderate progress, with 0.4% of the population, 6 show marginal progress, with 3.1%, and 5 are stagnant, with 1.7%. The largest class by population is regression: 43 countries, holding 55.7% of the assessed population, received less assistance in real terms in 2023 than at the start of the period. The number of countries on track is larger, but the number of people living in countries with falling assistance is greater.

This divergence matters for the 2030 horizon. A world total lifted by a few exceptional recipients and a single year can rise while most of the population of recipient countries sees less support. Because the surge of 2022 was followed by a decline in 2023, there is no evidence in these results that the higher level will persist. The trend classes also carry a caveat of reading: the tool assumes a target of increase, since target 8.a sets no numeric goal, so classes such as on track describe direction of change and not the attainment of a defined threshold.

### Reaching 2030 requires better measurement and steadier, better-targeted assistance, with proposals

Reaching 2030 on target 8.a depends first on measurement. The rise in net official development assistance is not evidence of more support for trade capacity, because the series covers every purpose and the bench holds no Aid for Trade disbursements. A recipient whose assistance grew may have received it for humanitarian relief or budget support, and one whose assistance fell may still have gained trade-related help. Target 8.a also carries no numeric benchmark, so even a precise series would have nothing to be measured against. The trend tool was run with no target value, and its classes show only the direction of movement of the series.

The record of the period gives little reason to expect the 2022 surge to persist. Mean annual change was US$6.4 billion in 2001-2021, rose to US$49.8 billion in 2022, and turned to a fall of US$0.7 billion in 2023. Established knowledge of the period suggests that the 2022 rise reflected emergency responses to war in Europe and to its wider consequences, which are exceptional rather than structural. If so, a falling or flat path is the plausible reading for the years ahead, though the data cannot confirm it.

The distribution of recipients sharpens the concern. Of 138 countries assessed, 79 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 39.1% of the recipient population. Another 5 countries show moderate progress, 6 show marginal progress and 5 show stagnation. Regression affects 43 countries, which hold 55.7% of the population assessed. A majority of recipient people therefore live in countries where assistance has declined in real terms, while a global total that is rising conceals this. Concentration has also increased: the Gini coefficient across countries, weighted by population, was 0.36 in 2015, 0.37 in 2019 and 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index rose from 0.26 in 2015 to 0.46 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023, so inequality has increasingly arisen among countries within regions.

Four proposals follow from these findings, and each names its actor.

Donors should ring-fence trade-related support from reallocation to emergency responses, so that crisis spending does not displace it.
w-c09-10-1.gaps: The bench holds no series of Aid for Trade commitments or disbursements, no breakdown of assistance by purpose, and no separate record of Enhanced Integrated Framework support. Least developed countries cannot be isolated from the series used, and target 8.a has no numeric benchmark. The series ends in 2023, so the persistence of the 2022 surge cannot be observed.

w-c03-7-4.text:
### Consumer price inflation stands in for food prices

Target 2.c asks for measures that keep food commodity markets and their derivatives working properly and that give timely access to market information, including on food reserves, so that extreme food price volatility is limited. The target names no numerical threshold and no price index. Its indicator in the global framework is a food price anomalies measure, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold among the series available to this book. Volatility is therefore not measured here directly, and every statement in this section about prices is an indirect reading.

The nearest series is headline consumer price inflation, the annual percentage change in the cost of a basket of goods and services for the average consumer. Food is one component of that basket, and its weight varies widely: it is large in low-income households and economies, and small in high-income ones. Headline inflation also contains energy, housing, transport and services, so a rise in the headline rate can follow a fuel shock, a currency depreciation or a rent adjustment with food prices barely moving. The series is read here as a signal of pressure on household budgets, not as a record of food price swings. Regional averages of general inflation say nothing about exposure to food price shocks.

The series also has limits as a measure of volatility. The results available to this section give levels at 2015 and 2025 and measures of dispersion among countries in four selected years. They do not give the year-to-year path, which is what volatility requires. What follows describes the price environment and its unevenness, and does not claim to measure instability over time.

Coverage shapes what can be said. In 2015, 189 countries reported consumer price inflation, and the same number reported in 2016. The count then drifted down, to 185 in 2017, 179 in 2020, 176 in 2024 and 169 in 2025. Across all years 193 countries reported at least once, so some economies have gaps in particular years. The data do not show which economies dropped out, and the reasons for interrupted reporting cannot be read from them. The latest year, 2025, is the thinnest and may be revised as late submissions arrive. Comparisons across the period therefore rest on a changing set of countries, and the parts that follow rely mainly on regional and world aggregates, which are less sensitive to the loss of single reporters.

### World inflation doubled between 2015 and 2025

World consumer price inflation stood at 1.4% in 2015 and at 3.0% in 2025, a little more than double the earlier rate. Both figures are annual percentage changes in the cost of a general basket of goods and services, so they describe the price level that households face and not the price of food alone. Food is a large part of that basket in poorer economies and a smaller part in richer ones.

The two endpoints conceal the path between them. A comparison of 2015 with 2025 does not show how far inflation fell or rose in the years between, and it should not be read as a steady climb. The period contains the weak price environment of the middle 2010s, the disruption of 2020 and the supply shocks that followed, and an endpoint comparison cannot separate these. Volatility concerns movement from year to year, and the result used here reports levels at two dates only. It therefore shows that the world rate ended the period well above where it began, and it does not measure how much the rate moved in between.

Low-income countries show a different pattern from the world as a whole. Their inflation was 5.5% in 2015 and 4.4% in 2025, so it fell over the decade while the world rate rose. Lower middle income countries also eased, from 4.0% to 3.6%, whereas upper middle income countries rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high income countries from 0.3% to 2.3%. That fall in the poorest group should not be taken as relief. Low-income countries began from the highest rate of any income group in 2015, and they remain above the world rate in 2025. Outside these series, it is generally observed that households in poorer economies spend the largest share of their budgets on food, so a given rate of general inflation weighs more heavily on them than on households in richer groups. Coverage also changed: 169 countries reported in 2025, against 189 in 2015, so part of the comparison rests on a smaller set of countries at the later date.

The finding matters for Goal 2 because food access depends on what a household can buy with its income, and persistent price growth erodes that. Yet the series cannot show whether food prices moved more or less than prices generally, nor whether any rise came from commodity markets, exchange rates, energy costs or domestic policy. Those causes bear on whether the measures named in target 2.c are working, and the data used here do not distinguish among them.

### Regions began far apart and converged at a higher level

Regional inflation rates stood far apart in 2015. South Asia recorded consumer price inflation of 4.7% and Sub-Saharan Africa 3.5%, while Europe and Central Asia stood at 0.4% and North America at 0.6%. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.8%, was also among the regions with very low rates. Latin America and the Caribbean (1.9%) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (1.7%) sat between the two groups. Income groups showed the same ordering: low-income economies stood at 5.5% and high-income economies at 0.3%.

By 2025 the regional range was narrower, from 2.0% to 3.7%, against 0.4% to 4.7% in 2015, though the order of the regions had changed. South Asia fell to 3.1% and Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged at 3.4%, against 3.5% in 2015. Europe and Central Asia rose from 0.4% to 3.7%, the highest rate among the regions in the latest year, narrowly ahead of Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.8% to 2.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 1.9% to 2.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 1.7% to 2.0%. Movements in these three were modest, and all three ended 2025 at about 2%. North America rose from 0.6% in 2015 to 2.7% in 2024; its latest observation is for 2024, not 2025, so it is not strictly comparable in date, but its value is below that of Europe and Central Asia, so the ranking holds.

Income groups tell a similar story. Low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower-middle-income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while upper-middle-income economies rose from 1.8% to 3.3% and high-income economies from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing therefore reflects falls in South Asia and in low-income economies together with rises elsewhere; the results do not allow it to be apportioned between them. Energy and food price shocks after 2020 are well-established drivers of rises in importing regions, but these series cannot show how far each region's movement was due to them.

The pattern matters for Target 2.c because the region with the lowest inflation in 2015 had the highest in 2025. Regional average inflation rates are closer together in 2025 than in 2015, but this says nothing about food price shocks, and a regional aggregate cannot show differences between countries or how often households met sharp price spikes within single years. For 2030, no region now enjoys the near-zero inflation seen in 2015.

### Dispersion among countries widened after 2022

The spread of annual consumer price inflation among countries, weighted by population, was almost unchanged between 2015 and 2019 on the Gini measure, at 0.538 in 2015 and 0.538 in 2019. It narrowed to 0.511 in 2022, the year in which price pressures were felt in most economies at once, and then rose sharply to 0.660 in 2024. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the upper end of the distribution, gives a similar picture: 0.621 in 2015, 0.751 in 2019, 0.559 in 2022 and 0.982 in 2024. The 2024 values are the highest of the four years examined on both measures.

The composition of the inequality needs careful reading. The share of the Theil index lying between regions was 27.1% in 2015, 32.0% in 2019 and 38.4% in 2022, and then 35.2% in 2024. Because the between-region share is below half in every year, most of the measured inequality lay within regions throughout, and it was in 2015 that the within-region part was largest, at about three quarters of the index. The fall in the between-region share from 2022 to 2024, while the index itself rose, indicates that the rise in dispersion after 2022 came mainly from differences among countries of the same region, not from a return of the regional gaps. Only four years are examined, so the path between them is not shown. Some economies may have brought inflation down as monetary tightening and falling energy costs worked through, while others continued to face currency depreciation, fiscal strain or conflict. The results do not identify which countries fall in which group, so this explanation rests on well-established patterns and not on the series itself. A regional average conceals the divergence, and a policy aimed at a region as a whole could miss the countries where price stress is most acute.

Three cautions apply. First, the number of countries in the calculation differs by year: 144 in 2015, 170 in 2019, 178 in 2022 and 171 in 2024. The 2015 sample is much smaller than the 189 countries that reported inflation that year, so part of the comparison with later years reflects who is included and not only how prices moved. Second, population weighting gives large economies great influence, and a change in one of them can shift the result. Third, the measure is of general consumer prices, so it is an indirect guide to uneven exposure to food price volatility. For 2030, the widening within regions suggests that the risk of extreme price swings may be concentrated in a minority of countries, though the results do not show how many, and monitoring needs to be national in its detail.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 2.c cannot be scored from these data. It sets no numerical threshold and can be read in two ways: as the proper functioning of commodity markets and the availability of market information, or as the narrower outcome of limited price volatility. The series available touch only the second reading, and only indirectly, through general consumer prices. World inflation of 1.4% in 2015 and 3.0% in 2025 is consistent with greater price pressure on households. It says nothing about whether markets, derivatives or reserve reporting function better or worse than before, and the two endpoint values do not describe the path between them.

The outlook for 2030 is therefore uncertain in direction. Regional rates in 2015 ran from 0.4% in Europe and Central Asia to 4.7% in South Asia. By 2025 the range was from 2.0% in East Asia and Pacific to 3.7% in Europe and Central Asia, so the regional averages were closer together than in 2015. Europe and Central Asia moved from the lowest rate to the highest; North America's latest value, 2.7% in 2024, lies below it, so the ranking holds. Among income groups, low-income economies fell from 5.5% to 4.4% and lower middle income economies from 4.0% to 3.6%, while high-income economies rose from 0.3% to 2.3%. The narrowing coincides with falls in South Asia and in low-income economies and rises elsewhere; the data do not apportion it or identify its causes. Closer regional averages say nothing about exposure to food price shocks. Dispersion among countries points the other way: the population-weighted Gini measure stood at 0.660 in 2024, against 0.511 in 2022, so a narrower spread of group averages sits beside a wider spread of country experience. The data do not show which countries make up the upper tail, and the rates cited here are general consumer prices, not food prices.

Coverage bears on any monitoring to 2030. Countries reporting inflation numbered 189 in 2015 and 169 in 2025, and the data do not say whether the fall in 2025 is permanent or reflects later reporting. The proposals below follow from these limits: they aim to replace a proxy with measures that match the wording of the target, and to keep watch on the countries at the upper end of the distribution.
