c03-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c03-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2025
c03-7.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2025

proposals: National statistical offices and the World Bank should publish a food-specific consumer price series alongside general inflation for every reporting country, so that progress on target 2.c can be read from food prices and not from a general proxy.
The agencies that maintain the global indicator framework should make food price anomalies available in the World Bank's catalogue, and countries should report them annually.

Governments of countries with the highest inflation rates should publish information on food reserves and market conditions promptly, as the wording of target 2.c asks, and international lenders should support that reporting.
Statistical offices that stopped reporting inflation after 2015 should resume annual submissions, and the World Bank should state each year which countries are missing and why.
w-c03-7-4.gaps: The World Bank's catalogue holds no food price anomalies series, no food-specific consumer price index across countries and no measure of market functioning, derivatives or reserve transparency, so target 2.c cannot be scored directly. Annual inflation is a general consumer price measure and does not isolate food. The data do not identify which countries make up the upper tail of dispersion, nor the causes of regional movements. Reporting fell from 189 countries in 2015 to 169 in 2025, and the figures for 2025 may be incomplete.

w-c04-11-4.text:
### Immunisation and maternal and child services are largely flat at the global level

The nearest measure the shelf holds for immunisation and related services is the universal health coverage sub-index on reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health. It combines four tracer indicators: family planning, pregnancy care, child immunisation and child treatment, and it is scored from 0 to 100 index points. It is not a direct measure of vaccine coverage, because immunisation is only one of the four components. A movement in the index may therefore reflect changes in family planning or in the treatment of childhood illness rather than in vaccination. The reading offered here is of service coverage in general, with immunisation as one part of it.

Target 3.b can be read in more than one way. It concerns research and development, access to affordable essential medicines and vaccines, and the terms of the Doha Declaration. Coverage of services is an outcome of access, not a measure of research effort or of the price of medicines. The index speaks to access only in part, and the other elements of the target are not captured by any series held here.

At the global level the trend classification is regression, at a rate of -0.0017. The index values behind the regional classes are not carried among the facts of this section, so levels are not quoted here, and no comparison of levels between groups is made; only the classes and rates are given. The change is small. Its significance lies in what it fails to show: there is no sign of the steady gain that a fifteen-year agenda implies, and the world, on this measure, has slipped slightly.

Most groups are classed as stagnating: East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, high income countries, North America, upper middle income countries, low income countries, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region. Each of these has a rate of zero. Europe & Central Asia shows a small positive rate of 0.0031, which is still classed as stagnation. A rate of zero means that whatever gaps exist between groups were not closing over the period measured.

The worst movements are in lower middle income countries and South Asia. The lower middle income group has a rate of -0.0037 and South Asia a rate of -0.0053, and both are classed as regression. Disruption to routine services during the pandemic after 2020 is a plausible contributor, and populous countries weigh heavily in group averages, but the results do not test this. They do not separate the period before 2020 from the period after, so the share of the fall due to the pandemic cannot be stated. Sub-Saharan Africa is the only region with a clear gain, at a rate of 0.0099, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed.

The country classification confirms the pattern. Of 193 countries assessed, 11 are on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population. Another 9, with 3.1 per cent, show moderate progress needing acceleration, and 37, with 14.4 per cent, show marginal progress. Stagnation covers 105 countries and 48.1 per cent of the population, and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. The index carries no fixed 2030 target, so these classes rest on the direction of travel to date, not on a stated goal; 'on track' here means a rising trend, not a target met. Stagnation and regression together cover more than three in four people, 77.6 per cent of the population. The classes describe past direction only; no projection to 2030 is made here.

### Health spending has risen in dollar terms but barely as a share of output

Domestic general government health expenditure per capita rose from 589.2 current US dollars in 2015 to 803.7 in 2023 for the world as a whole. The series is in current dollars and is not adjusted for inflation or for population structure, so part of the rise reflects higher prices rather than a larger volume of care. The movement also says nothing about how the money was used.

Measured against output, the picture is much flatter. Current health expenditure was 9.7 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2023. Spending has therefore grown roughly in step with the economies that carry it. A rising dollar figure alongside a stable share means that health has held its place in national budgets and household outlays but has not gained priority. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, and a global share that moves by less than half a percentage point over eight years cannot be read as that kind of increase. The share also includes private and external spending, while the per capita series covers only domestic government spending, so the two measure different things and are not directly comparable.

The global average conceals a division by income. In high income countries the share of GDP rose from 12.0 per cent to 12.5 per cent, and in upper middle income countries from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent. In lower middle income countries it fell from 3.9 per cent to 3.7 per cent, and in low income countries from 5.4 per cent to 4.6 per cent. The fall among the poorest runs against the direction target 3.c requires. The data do not show why it fell, nor which source of spending changed, because the share covers all current spending. Faster growth elsewhere in the economy, reduced external funding, debt pressure and conflict are plausible contributors as context, but none can be separated here.

Regional shares tell a similar story. North America stood at 16.0 per cent in 2015 and 16.3 per cent in 2023. South Asia declined from 3.5 per cent to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent in both years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 5.4 per cent to 5.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 6.4 per cent to 6.8 per cent, Europe and Central Asia from 9.3 per cent to 9.6 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 7.8 per cent to 7.9 per cent, all by small margins.

The period after 2020 matters for interpretation. The pandemic raised health spending in many countries and depressed GDP in the same years, which lifts the share temporarily. The 2023 values are therefore not a clean continuation of the pre-2020 path. Coverage of the latest year is also thin: only 22 countries reported the share for 2024, and only 7 reported domestic government spending per capita, so 2023 is the last year that supports regional comparison.

The results describe movement to 2023 and make no projection to 2030. A financing share that has hardly moved gives little ground for expecting a step change without a deliberate rise in public priority.

### Regions and countries differ by orders of magnitude

North America spent 6,959.0 current US dollars per head of domestic government money on health in 2023, against 30.8 dollars in South Asia and 31.7 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa. The top and bottom figures therefore differ by a factor of more than two hundred. Europe and Central Asia stood at 2,178.0 dollars, East Asia and Pacific at 571.7 dollars, Latin America and the Caribbean at 415.7 dollars, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 190.2 dollars. By income group the gradient is as steep: high-income countries spent 3,847.3 dollars, upper middle income countries 338.9 dollars, lower middle income countries 30.9 dollars and low-income countries 7.3 dollars. These are current dollars at market exchange rates, so they understate what a dollar buys in poorer countries, where wages and many services cost less. Even so, a gap of this size is unlikely to be closed by any such adjustment.

The movement since 2015 widens the distance in absolute terms. North America started from 4,587.0 dollars and reached 6,959.0 dollars by 2023, while Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 29.7 to 31.7 dollars and low-income countries from 7.0 to 7.3 dollars. South Asia is the exception among the poorer regions: its figure rose from 14.7 to 30.8 dollars, though from a very small base. The pattern is one of large gains in the richer groups and near-stillness at the bottom. Rapid population growth in low-income countries may also mean that a flat per-capita figure conceals a rising national outlay, though the results do not test this.

The share of output spent on health gives a less favourable picture for the poorest. Low-income countries fell from 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 4.6 per cent in 2023, and lower middle income countries from 3.9 to 3.7 per cent. High-income countries rose from 12.0 to 12.5 per cent and upper middle income countries from 5.5 to 6.0 per cent. South Asia slipped from 3.5 to 3.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa was unchanged at 4.9 per cent. Target 3.c asks for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed. On this measure the poorest groups moved the other way. The results do not identify the reasons. Weak tax bases, debt service and the strain of the pandemic and later price rises on public budgets are commonly cited as context, but none is tested here. The results do not separate public, private and external spending, so they do not show how each source changed. Coverage of the latest year is thin: only 7 countries had a 2024 value for domestic government spending per head and 22 for the share of GDP.

Country classes show how uneven the picture is beneath the regional averages. For domestic government health spending per head, 142 of the 193 countries assessed were classed as on track, holding 80.1 per cent of their combined population. No target value is set for this series, so the classes describe direction and pace of change in current dollars, not distance from a goal, and they do not show that the financing aim of target 3.c has been met. A further 12 countries showed moderate progress, and 34 were in regression, holding 14.0 per cent of the population. Rising dollar spending in most countries therefore coexists with a sizeable minority of countries, and of people, where it fell.

The service coverage sub-index is flatter. Only 11 of the 193 countries were on track, holding 5.0 per cent of the population, while stagnation covered 105 countries and 48.1 per cent of the population and regression 31 countries and 29.5 per cent. The stagnation and regression classes together hold more than three in four people. South Asia and the lower middle income group are themselves classed as regression, and the country classes may overlap with them, but the results do not show that these groups account for the population share in the regression class. The two series are not linked in these results, so they cannot show why rising spending in many countries sits beside flat coverage; delivery, workforce and reach of services are plausible candidates, but the data do not test them.

### Spending has not converged and the workforce cannot be measured well

Spending per head at purchasing power parity shows no sign of countries drawing together. Across 190 countries, the regression of growth in current health expenditure per capita (international dollars) between 2015 and 2023 on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00001, with a p-value of 0.997 and an R-squared of 0.0. Countries that began with low spending did not grow faster than those that began high, and the starting level explains none of the variation in growth. The coefficient of variation, a measure of relative dispersion, moved from 1.24 in 2015 to 1.20 in 2023. That change is small and is not backed by a convergence relationship, so it should be read as little more than stability in the spread.

The result matters for target 3.c, which calls for a substantial increase in health financing in developing countries, especially the least developed countries and small island developing States. Convergence would be the sign that the gap in resources was narrowing. Its absence means that total health spending per head, measured in international dollars, did not draw together between 2015 and 2023, the last year tested. The test uses total current health expenditure per capita at purchasing power parity, a different series from the domestic government spending per head in current dollars used for the regional and income gaps described earlier in this section. It therefore does not directly confirm that those government spending gaps persist; that claim is limited to the series actually tested. Health budgets depend on national income, on the capacity of governments to raise revenue and on debt service burdens; this is background knowledge and not a result of the test. The shocks of 2020 fell on all budgets, but countries with more fiscal room could more easily sustain health spending. The test is across countries and does not separate these channels, and it covers 2015 to 2023 only, so any later change is not captured. It shows direction to date and makes no projection to 2030.

The health workforce is harder still to assess. The shelf holds one series on community health workers per 1,000 people, and it is thin. Only 64 countries report in any year of the series. The number reporting in a single year ranges from 3 in 2002 and 3 in 2014 to 29 in 2004 and 21 in 2008. After 2010 the count never exceeds 13: 6 in 2011, 7 in 2012, 6 in 2013, 3 in 2014, 4 in 2015 and 6 in 2016. The latest year in the series is 2016, so nothing is recorded for the period after 2015 beyond those few reporters, and nothing after 2020.

With so few reporters, and with a different set of countries in each year, a change in the average could not be told from a change in who reports. No trend in workforce density, upward or downward, can be asserted, and no judgement can be made on whether the recruitment and retention called for in target 3.c is occurring. Community health workers are also defined differently from country to country, under varied national titles, which weakens comparison even where data exist. The series also says nothing of doctors, nurses or midwives. The finding is that spending can be measured and has not converged, whereas the workforce, the input on which services most depend, cannot be measured well enough to be followed towards 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Targets 3.b and 3.c ask for more vaccines and medicines for developing countries, and for substantially more health financing and workforce. The shelf supports only a partial reading. The financing evidence is a direction-of-travel test on current dollars, with no target attached, so it cannot show that the financing half of 3.c has been met. It shows that 142 of 193 countries, holding 80.1% of the assessed population, are rising in domestic government health spending per head. The classes give counts and population shares only and do not show spending levels by group, so whether the rising majority is made up mainly of countries that already spend most is a hypothesis the series do not test. A further 34 countries, with 14.0% of the population, show falling domestic government spending per head in current dollars. The classes do not measure risk to the target, and the data do not show how far each of these countries is from it.

For 3.b the shelf holds only the composite reproductive, maternal, newborn and child index, which is not a measure of vaccine coverage or of access to medicines. Read as a proxy, it is discouraging. Only 11 countries, with 5.0% of the population, are on track, while 105, with 48.1%, are stagnating and 31, with 29.5%, are regressing. The trend classes show direction of travel from 2015 to 2023 and no projection to 2030 is made here. They do show that, to date, most of the assessed population has seen no gain in these services, and that acceleration would be needed for any improvement by 2030. Disruption to routine services after 2020 is a plausible contributor, but the results do not test it. The index cannot attribute the pattern to vaccines, and it cannot be linked to spending with the series held.

The share of output devoted to health shows that dollar growth alone is not sufficient. Low-income countries fell from 5.4% of GDP in 2015 to 4.6% in 2023, while high-income countries rose from 12.0% to 12.5%. South Asia's share slipped from 3.5% to 3.3%, even though its per-head public spending rose from a very low base. The share covers all current health spending and does not separate public, private and external sources, so it cannot show which source moved. Why the share lagged is a matter for national studies: tax capacity, debt service and competing pressures after 2020 are the usual explanations, and none can be tested with these series.

The convergence test rests on total current health expenditure per head in international dollars, a different series from the domestic government spending in current dollars used for the regional gaps. It therefore does not confirm that those government spending gaps persist.

The workforce half of 3.c cannot be judged. Community health workers were reported by only 64 countries in any year, by no more than 29 in any single year, and by just 6 countries in 2016, the last year of record. A target to recruit and retain workers cannot be monitored from a series that thin. Coverage for 2024 is also thin, resting on 7 reporting countries for domestic government spending and 22 for spending as a share of GDP, so the latest picture is provisional.

w-c05-8-3.text:
### Education spending averages 3.6 per cent of GDP and 14 per cent of government budgets

Two measures describe how much of a country's resources goes to schooling. The first expresses general government expenditure on education as a share of gross domestic product, and shows the weight of public education in the whole economy. The second expresses the same expenditure as a share of total government expenditure, and shows the priority given to education within the public budget. The two can diverge: a government may hold education's place in its budget steady while the economy, and the budget with it, changes in size.

On the first measure, the world figure was 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 and 3.6 per cent in 2023. The period includes the shock of 2020, when output contracted in most economies and public budgets were redirected towards health and income support, which is context and not something these series show. The country classification indicates that the fall was widespread: of 186 countries assessed, 98 regressed on this measure. Coverage matters here: the latest year nominally available is 2025, but only 2 countries reported GDP-share data for that year, so the most recent usable world figure is for 2023.

On the second measure, the picture is different. The world share of government expenditure was 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, essentially unchanged. For this series 60 countries reported in 2025, a much fuller recent record than for the GDP share, though the world aggregate shown here also ends in 2023.

The two results can be set side by side without contradiction, but they cannot be read as a single verdict. A steady budget share alongside a falling GDP share is consistent with government spending itself falling relative to GDP, or with a shift in the country mix behind the world aggregate; the results do not say which. Either way, a steady budget share does not guarantee that schools are better financed in relation to national income. Neither series shows spending per pupil, which depends on the number of children, on prices and on the exchange rate.

Neither target sets a numeric benchmark for these indicators. Target 4.1 concerns completion of free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education, and target 4.c concerns the supply of qualified teachers; spending is an input to both, not a measure of either. Judgements here therefore rest on direction of change alone. On that reading, the fall in the GDP share after 2015 is an adverse movement, and the flat budget share is neither progress nor retreat. Reaching either target by 2030 would be harder on a shrinking base of public resources, a point developed in the parts that follow.

### Regions differ by two percentage points of GDP, and country spread is widening

Regional averages of public education spending span roughly two percentage points of GDP. North America spent 4.8 per cent of GDP in 2022, almost unchanged from 4.8 per cent in 2015. Europe and Central Asia stood at 4.6 per cent in 2022, down from 4.8 per cent in 2015. At the other end, South Asia spent 2.9 per cent in 2024, up slightly from 2.7 per cent in 2015, and Sub-Saharan Africa spent 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent in 2015. The regional ranking has changed little since 2015, with North America and Europe and Central Asia at the top and South Asia at the bottom.

The movements after 2015 differ by region. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan shows the largest rise, from 3.7 per cent in 2015 to 4.4 per cent in 2022, and South Asia rose modestly. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 4.4 per cent to 3.8 per cent in 2023, a period that includes the fiscal strain of the pandemic and its aftermath, offered here as context and not as a finding of the results. East Asia and Pacific stood at 3.5 per cent in 2015 and 3.5 per cent in 2023. The world figure fell from 4.2 per cent in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023, alongside declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, Europe and Central Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and the lower-middle-income group. The results do not analyse the composition of the world aggregate, so they cannot say which regions account for most of the fall.

The ordering changes when spending is measured against the budget rather than the economy. Latin America and the Caribbean devoted 16.6 per cent of government expenditure to education in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa 15.4 per cent in 2024, whereas North America devoted 10.7 per cent in 2022 and Europe and Central Asia 11.7 per cent in 2022. The comparison mixes 2022 and 2024 values, because the latest year reported differs by region. The regions that rank lowest or middling on the share of GDP therefore rank highest on the share of the budget. The results hold no data on revenue or age structure, so they do not show why the two orderings differ.

The spread among countries has widened. The population-weighted Gini coefficient of spending as a share of GDP rose from 0.181 in 2015 to 0.210 in 2020 and 0.230 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.091 and then 0.110 over the same years. The share of this inequality lying between regions was 23.8 per cent in 2015 and 27.0 per cent in 2020, then fell to 10.5 per cent in 2023, on a smaller sample of countries. A lower between-region share means more of the inequality lies within regions, but the fall coincides with the drop in reporting and should be read with care.

A caution applies to the 2023 comparison. The 2023 figures cover 121 countries against 164 in 2015, and the countries that did not report are not known to be a random subset. The rise in inequality may therefore partly reflect who reported rather than what was spent. The direction from 2015 to 2020, when 164 and 170 countries reported, rests on a more stable sample than the level reached in 2023.

### Most countries regressed, and the two measures move together only moderately

Classified against a trajectory towards higher spending, most countries moved the wrong way. Of 186 countries assessed on the share of GDP, 98 regressed, and these hold 62.3 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 40 were on track or had met the direction of travel, covering 11.1 per cent of that population. The remainder were spread across moderate progress (14 countries), marginal progress (20 countries) and stagnation (14 countries). No numerical target exists for either measure, so the classes describe direction and pace, not distance from a goal; the reading depends on the assumption that an increase is the desired movement.

The budget share shows a harsher pattern. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 regressed, holding 78.2 per cent of the population, while 29 were on track, holding 7.1 per cent. Stagnation affected 23 countries with 10.5 per cent of the population. On both measures the population share of regression exceeds the country share, which suggests that populous countries are among those regressing; the results do not identify which countries these are, nor their school-age populations.

Spending levels did not draw together. Across 146 countries, the regression of change in the GDP share on its 2015 level gave a beta of -0.00559 (p 0.64, R2 0.004), which is indistinguishable from no convergence. Low spenders did not catch up, and high spenders did not fall back. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.379 in 2015 to 0.449 in 2022, so dispersion widened in relative terms. This matters for target 4.c and target 4.1, since teacher supply and free schooling depend on a stable funding base.

The two measures are related, but only moderately. Across 131 countries, the Spearman correlation of changes between 2015 and 2022 was 0.415, and that of 2022 levels was 0.468. These are associations, not causes. A fall in the GDP share is therefore only partly accompanied by a lower priority for education within the budget. As context, a country may keep its budget share while the public sector shrinks relative to output, or output may rise faster than outlays during recovery; education may also gain priority within a budget that is itself contracting.

These data cannot identify causes. The periods after 2015 and after 2020 included commodity price falls, pandemic spending on health and income support, rising debt service and, in some cases, rapid growth in GDP that diluted ratios, but which of these shaped each country's result cannot be read from two ratios. The classification also rests on trend fitting for short and gappy series. For 2030, the pattern implies that present trajectories will not lift spending in most countries, and that improving one measure does not guarantee the other.

### Reaching 2030 requires reversing the fall in spending and improving reporting

The implication for 2030 is that targets 4.1 and 4.c are paid for from public budgets. Free primary and secondary schooling and a larger supply of qualified teachers both require sustained financing. The world figure for public education spending stood at 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 and at 3.6 per cent in 2023. A fall of that size leaves less room for hiring, training and retaining teachers. Neither target sets a numerical spending level, so the direction of travel is the only yardstick available, and on the share of GDP it points the wrong way. The share of government expenditure tells a steadier story: 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023.

The fall is visible in several groups, and the lowest starting points deserve attention. South Asia, at 2.9 per cent of GDP in 2024, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 3.3 per cent in 2023, down from 3.6 per cent in 2015, remain below the world figure. Low income countries spent 3.0 per cent in 2022, against 3.2 per cent in 2015. Lower middle income countries fell from 4.1 per cent to 3.4 per cent between 2015 and 2023. Declines also appear in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Europe and Central Asia, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and South Asia, recorded rises. The results hold no population weights for regions, so they cannot show which changes drove the world figure. Regional values for the budget share mix years, some for 2022 and others for 2024 or 2025, and should be read as approximate.

Monitoring is also weakening. The number of countries reporting the share of GDP rose to 171 in 2017 and stood at 164 in 2022, but fell to 121 in 2023 and to 40 in 2024, with only 2 in 2025. Part of this is the ordinary lag of reporting, and the latest years will fill in. Even so, any reading of the period after 2020 rests on a thinning sample, and the values for 2023 and 2024 may shift when late reporters arrive. Where data are missing, the position of a country cannot be told from the figures.

A further caution concerns interpretation. No single share defines adequate spending, and a country may spend a modest share of income efficiently, or a large share poorly. The share of GDP and the share of the budget answer different questions, and neither says what is spent on each child.

w-c09-9-1.text:
### Account ownership reached 78.7 per cent of adults worldwide by 2024

Account ownership among adults aged 15 and over stood at 78.7 per cent worldwide in 2024, up from 69.3 per cent in 2017. The indicator counts respondents who report having an account, alone or with someone else, at a bank or another type of financial institution, or with a mobile-money-service provider. It therefore measures a person's formal link to the financial system, not the use made of the account, its cost or its quality. An account that is opened for a single transfer and then lies dormant counts in the same way as one used daily.

Target 8.10 asks countries to strengthen the capacity of domestic financial institutions to encourage and expand access to banking, insurance and financial services for all. The target carries no numeric threshold. This book therefore reads full access as 100 per cent of adults aged 15 and over holding an account. That reading is strict, and it is only one of several possible; a lower benchmark, or a measure that includes insurance or credit, would give a different distance to travel. On the strict reading, the world in 2024 was still short of the mark by a wide margin, though it had moved in the right direction.

The survey years of the data need care. Account ownership is collected in periodic household surveys, not annually. For most regions the series offers two readings, 2017 and 2021, while the World aggregate and South Asia carry a 2024 reading. The regional figures are therefore not all measured at the same end date, and the rise in the World figure to 2024 cannot be split neatly into regional contributions from the 2021 values alone. The regional pictures are taken up in the next part. Here the point is that the global rise is real in the data, and that it spans the years before and after 2020, although the gap in survey years prevents any exact reading of what the pandemic changed.

The physical infrastructure of banking moved differently. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.16 in 2015 to 11.12 in 2024, while automated teller machines per 100,000 adults rose from 36.09 to 41.91 over the same years. Accounts spread while branches thinned, so the growth in account holding cannot be attributed to a larger branch network. As context, not as a finding of these series, the period saw banks consolidate branches and customers move towards phones and digital channels, and the data on branches and ATMs do not show why either count changed. Branches and machines are also a count of outlets relative to adults, not of the distance any person must travel to reach one.

These three series together suggest that access to a financial account has become less dependent on a branch. That matters for 2030, since the target's aim of access for all can be pursued through channels other than buildings. It also leaves open who has been reached and who has not, which the parts that follow examine by region, income group, sex and poverty.

### Regions and countries differ widely in ownership and in physical access

Regional levels of account ownership span a wide range. In 2021, North America stood at 95.5 per cent of adults aged 15 and over, Europe and Central Asia at 89.6 per cent and East Asia and Pacific at 82.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 73.6 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa 55.1 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping recorded 52.8 per cent. South Asia, whose latest reading falls in 2024, stood at 77.6 per cent. The survey years differ between South Asia and the other regions, so the South Asian figure is not strictly comparable with the 2021 readings.

The starting points in 2017 show where the movement has been fastest. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 55.2 per cent to 73.6 per cent by 2021, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 42.6 per cent to 55.1 per cent. North America moved from 93.8 per cent to 95.5 per cent, a region close to saturation. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping advanced from 47.5 per cent to 52.8 per cent, the slowest gain among the developing regions listed. Convergence is therefore under way, yet the gap between the top and bottom regions remains large.

Physical access tells a different story, and it does not line up with ownership. Commercial bank branches numbered 21.9 per 100,000 adults in North America in 2024 and 19.0 in Europe and Central Asia, against 4.0 in Sub-Saharan Africa. North America and Europe and Central Asia nonetheless have fewer branches than in 2015, when the figures were 27.7 and 26.8. Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged from 3.9 in 2015. South Asia moved the other way, from 11.3 to 16.0. Branch networks have contracted where digital banking is established and have barely grown where they were thin. Well-established explanations include branch closures after consolidation in mature banking systems and the use of mobile channels in place of new buildings elsewhere.

Automated teller machines show the same unevenness. North America had 173.8 machines per 100,000 adults in 2024, down from 222.1 in 2015, while Sub-Saharan Africa had 6.9 and South Asia 24.5. South Asia's figure was 13.2 in 2015, so the region has added machines while adding accounts. Sub-Saharan Africa began at 5.3. The densest region still has many times the provision of the sparsest, which matters for people who must withdraw cash, especially where cash remains the main means of payment.

The income groups confirm the pattern. In 2024 account ownership was 46.4 per cent in low-income economies, 70.4 per cent in lower-middle-income, 84.0 per cent in upper-middle-income and 94.9 per cent in high-income economies. Low-income economies had 2.8 branches per 100,000 adults in 2023, fewer than 3.0 in 2015, but their ATM density rose from 3.1 to 4.0. Lower-middle-income economies roughly doubled ATM density, from 10.6 to 21.7 in 2024.

Country classes set against the target of universal ownership by 2030 show how uneven progress is. Of 141 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, holding 16.4 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 36 show moderate progress needing acceleration, covering 51.8 per cent of that population. A further 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, at 20.3 per cent. Three countries stagnate, at 0.7 per cent, and 36 regress, at 10.8 per cent. Because the survey is conducted in a few rounds, these classes rest on very few observations per country, and a single weak survey can place a country in regression. The classes are best read as a guide to where the pace is insufficient, not as a firm forecast. Under any reading, fewer than one-fifth of the population of assessed countries lives in a country on course for the 2030 aim.

### Mobile money and account growth outpaced branches, and the poorest and women gained

Gains in account ownership were largest where ownership started low. In Latin America and the Caribbean the share of adults with an account rose from 55.2 per cent in 2017 to 73.6 per cent in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 42.6 per cent to 55.1 per cent over the same four years. In North America, where ownership was already high, the share moved from 93.8 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Income groups show the same pattern between 2017 and 2024: low-income economies rose from 32.0 per cent to 46.4 per cent, while high-income economies moved from 93.0 per cent to 94.9 per cent. Ownership has therefore converged from below, though low-income economies remain far from the level already reached elsewhere.

The poorest 40 per cent of adults gained substantially. Worldwide their ownership rose from 61.7 per cent in 2017 to 72.4 per cent in 2024. In Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 42.9 per cent to 67.9 per cent between 2017 and 2021, a faster advance than for all adults in that region. In low-income economies the poorest 40 per cent reached 37.3 per cent in 2024, from 22.5 per cent in 2017. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.6 per cent in 2021 for this group, up from 32.0 per cent. The poorest group still trails the full adult population in every region reported.

Women's ownership also rose, from 65.9 per cent worldwide in 2017 to 76.6 per cent in 2024, against 78.7 per cent for all adults in 2024. South Asia shows a notable pattern: women stood at 75.1 per cent in 2024, from 64.0 per cent in 2017, against 77.6 per cent for all adults. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping remains the clearest case of difficulty. Women's ownership was 45.6 per cent in 2021, up from 38.0 per cent in 2017, against 52.8 per cent for all adults that year. The regional level there rose by less than in Latin America or Sub-Saharan Africa.

Physical access moved differently. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.2 in 2015 to 11.1 in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 26.8 to 19.0, and North America from 27.7 to 21.9. High-income economies fell from 22.3 to 15.5. South Asia rose from 11.3 to 16.0, and East Asia and Pacific from 9.7 to 11.2. Sub-Saharan Africa was close to unchanged, at 3.9 in 2015 and 4.0 in 2024, and low-income economies stood at 3.0 in 2015 and 2.8 in 2023. ATMs per 100,000 adults rose worldwide from 36.1 to 41.9, and in lower middle income economies from 10.6 to 21.7. In East Asia and Pacific they fell from 52.5 to 46.5, and in North America from 222.1 to 173.8.

The contrast is that account ownership rose across the world while branches in many regions did not. Accounts therefore spread in large part without a matching spread of branches. Mobile-money services, digital payments and the channelling of public transfers into accounts are well-established ways in which ownership can grow without bank premises, and branch networks in richer economies have also been shaped by consolidation and a shift to online banking. These are context, not findings: the data do not identify what drove the gains, and attributing them to mobile money is an inference, not a measured result. The indicator also counts an account as owned whether or not it is used, so dormant accounts cannot be separated from active ones.

For 2030 the pattern implies that the post-2017 gains were broad, but that those who start lowest, including the poorest, women in some regions and residents of low-income economies, still have the furthest to go. Regional figures for 2021 and global figures for 2024 come from different survey rounds, so the years are not strictly comparable.

### Projected trends leave universal access short of 2030 outside a few regions, and proposals follow

Extrapolating the 2017 to latest-year trend towards universal access, defined here as 100 per cent of adults holding an account, shows a split picture. East Asia and Pacific and Europe and Central Asia read as on track or target met, with expected values in 2030 of 108.8 and 110.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reads the same way, with an expected 140.1 per cent. Values above 100 show that the extrapolation is mechanical: a share of adults cannot exceed 100 per cent, and the figures are not forecasts. Sub-Saharan Africa also reads as on track, with a ratio of 0.965 and an expected 98.0 per cent in 2030, which is close to the line and sensitive to the years chosen.

Other groups fall short. The world as a whole is in the class of moderate progress, but acceleration needed, with an expected 87.8 per cent in 2030. High income rises by only 0.0030 a year, from 92.96 per cent in 2017 to 94.91 per cent in 2024, and projects to 96.62 per cent. The shortfall there is small in level but slow in pace, since the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach. Low income reads as marginal progress, with an expected 63.9 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping, also marginal, reaches 67.1 per cent. Lower middle income projects to 80.7 per cent and South Asia to 85.3 per cent.

Country counts confirm that the global average hides wide differences. Of 141 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, holding 16.4 per cent of the assessed population. Another 36 show moderate progress, and these hold 51.8 per cent of the population. A further 36 show marginal progress, with 20.3 per cent. Three are stagnant, and 36 are regressing, with 10.8 per cent of the population. Regression in 36 countries is notable in a period of rapid expansion. Survey-based measures carry sampling error and rounds differ between countries, so some of these readings may reflect noise and the choice of end year, not a real fall.

Physical access does not offer a route to universal access. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.2 in 2015 to 11.1 in 2024, and in high income countries from 22.3 to 15.5. Sub-Saharan Africa stayed near 4.0, and low income countries stood at 2.8 in 2023. Expansion of accounts has therefore come mainly through other channels, such as mobile money, and 2030 outcomes depend on those channels more than on new branches.

Target 8.10 sets no number, so the reading of 100 per cent is a choice, and a different reading would change the classes above. The poorest 40 per cent stood at 72.4 per cent worldwide in 2024, and women at 76.6 per cent, so aggregate progress does not show who remains outside.

w-c02-3-3.text:
### Social protection reaches just over half of the world's population

Social protection and labour programmes reached 56.3% of the world's population in 2021, according to the World Bank's ASPIRE database, which draws on nationally representative household surveys. That is the single reading the bench holds for the world aggregate. The result lists the same value for its first and latest year, so it describes a position and not a change. It cannot show whether coverage rose after 2015 or fell after 2020, and no claim about either period can rest on it.

The indicator counts the share of people participating in social insurance, social safety nets, unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes, and its estimates include indirect beneficiaries, such as family members who live in a household where someone receives a benefit. The measure is therefore generous in one respect: a household with one pensioner counts as covered throughout. It is also broad in what it admits. Contributory pensions, health insurance, paid sick leave, cash transfers, food transfers, training and wage subsidies all count. A figure of 56.3% thus says that just over half of people live in households touched by at least one such programme. It does not say how adequate the benefit is, how regular it is, or whether it replaces a meaningful part of income.

The distinction matters because target 1.3 is about the poor and the vulnerable, not about the population as a whole. Coverage of everyone is a poor proxy for coverage of those in poverty. In wealthier countries, much of the population is covered through social insurance linked to formal employment, and a high national figure can coexist with gaps among informal workers, rural households and people outside the labour market. Conversely, a country with a modest overall figure may target its safety nets tightly on the poorest. The all-population series should therefore be read as an outline of the system's reach, with the coverage of the poorest quintile, taken up in a later part, as the closer test of the target.

The wording of the target also allows more than one reading. It calls for nationally appropriate systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. Neither 'substantial' nor 'vulnerable' carries a numeric threshold. A reader may take substantial to mean a majority, near-universal coverage of the poorest, or simply a clear rise from a starting point. Vulnerability can be defined by a poverty line, by exposure to shocks, or by life-cycle risks such as old age, disability and childhood. With no agreed benchmark, the 56.3% figure cannot be graded as met or missed. It can only be compared across groups of countries and, when repeated readings exist, across time.

The data have further limits. The world value rests on surveys that are carried out in different years in different countries, so a single reference year of 2021 is an alignment of estimates, not a simultaneous census. Only 1 country reports for 2023, the latest year in the series, so the most recent period is almost empty and the bench cannot say what became of coverage as pandemic emergency programmes were wound down. The poorest-quintile safety-net series, for comparison, holds 121 countries reporting in at least one year, which is substantial but not complete, and the countries missing are often those with weaker statistical systems and, plausibly, weaker protection. The world figure should accordingly be taken as indicative.

For 2030, the finding is that just under half of the world's people were outside any recorded programme in 2021, and that the target's own language leaves the finish line undefined. The next parts show where the gaps lie.

### Coverage differs sharply between regions and income groups

Regional coverage in 2021 runs from 50.6% of the population in the grouping of Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan to 72.5% in South Asia. Europe and Central Asia stands at 63.7% and East Asia and Pacific at 61.5%, while Latin America and the Caribbean stands at 54.5%. South Asia, Europe and Central Asia, and East Asia and Pacific lie above the world figure of 56.3%; the other two regions fall below it.

The South Asian figure should be read with care. The indicator counts direct and indirect beneficiaries, so a household is counted as covered when any member takes part in a programme. Large public works schemes, food transfers and subsidised in-kind programmes, which are widespread in the region, can therefore lift the headline share well above what the poorest households receive in cash. Coverage of a population is not adequacy of benefits: the indicator records participation, not the value of transfers, their regularity or whether they lift a household above a poverty line. A high share and a deep floor are different things.

The contrast between income groups is wider than that between regions. Low-income countries reach 18.3% of their people, against 55.1% in lower-middle-income countries, 62.2% in upper-middle-income countries and 77.8% in high-income countries. Coverage therefore rises with income at every step. The largest step lies between the low-income group and the lower-middle-income group; the step from lower-middle to upper-middle income is visibly smaller.

The low-income figure matters most for target 1.3, which asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable. Extreme poverty is concentrated in low-income and fragile countries, and these are the places where fewer than one person in five is reached. Causes are well established as context: narrow tax bases, limited administrative capacity, large informal economies in which contributory insurance does not reach workers, and heavy reliance on short-lived, donor-funded projects instead of permanent national systems. Higher-income countries combine payroll-based insurance with tax-funded pensions and family benefits, which together cover most of the population.

The evidence has limits. Every level quoted is for 2021, and the result lists the same value as first and latest year for each group. No change since 2015 or since 2020 can therefore be stated for any region or income group, and the pandemic's expansion of emergency transfers cannot be separated from lasting coverage. Only 1 country reports for 2023, so the most recent survey year is almost empty. The ordering of regions is firm for 2021; its movement over time is not shown by these data.

### Coverage of the poorest quintile has regressed in many countries with data

The trend classification for the poorest-quintile measure of social safety net coverage places more countries in regression than in any other class, but it needs a careful reading. The tool compares each country's compound annual change since 2015, or the first year after, with a target that has no numeric value, and sorts the countries into classes. The classes therefore describe the direction and pace of a series, not a verified fall or rise in what households receive.

Of 55 countries assessed, 19 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 33.4% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 2 countries show moderate progress, needing acceleration, with 12.4% of that population, and 4 show marginal progress, with 2.2%. Another 4 are stagnant, with 3.1%. The series is classed as regressing in 26 countries, which hold 48.9% of the assessed population. Regression is the largest single class by country count and by population. The shares refer to the assessed countries only and not to the world.

Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030 and sets no threshold. The phrase can be read as a majority of the poorest quintile, as near-universal coverage, or simply as a rising share. The trend tool therefore judges direction alone. A country counted as on track has a series moving upward at a pace the tool treats as consistent with improvement, not one shown to reach any agreed level. A country counted as regressing may still cover a large share of its poorest households, having moved down from a higher level.

Several well-established causes can lie behind a downward movement in such a series, stated here as context and not as findings. Coverage can decline when programmes are closed, shrunk or left without indexation while the population grows, and when emergency schemes introduced in a crisis are wound down. Changes in survey design and in the list of programmes captured can also move a figure without any change in what households receive. The data cannot separate these explanations.

The reliability of any trend depends on how often countries are observed, and the record is thin and uneven. Only 2 countries reported in 2000 and 3 in 2002. Reporting rose to 11 in 2005, 36 in 2010 and 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013 before recovering to 35 in 2014. It reached 47 countries in 2018, the best-observed year, and was 36 in 2019. Reporting then dropped to 24 in 2020 and recovered to 30 in 2021. Only 17 countries reported in 2022 and a single country in 2023. In all, 121 countries have reported in at least one year, but no single year approaches that number.

This pattern has two consequences. First, the years after 2020 are poorly observed. Surveys are fielded with a delay and processed into the database later, so the thinning of 2022 and 2023 partly reflects lag and not an end to measurement. The effect of the pandemic and of the withdrawal of emergency support on the poorest households is therefore largely invisible here, and the classes cannot be assigned with confidence to the period after 2015 or to the period after 2020. Second, the countries that enter a trend are those with surveys at both ends of their series, and they may differ systematically from countries never observed twice. Conclusions from the 55 assessed countries should not be extended to the others without that caution.

A separate question is whether the whole-population measure can stand in for the poorest quintile where the latter is missing. The links tool compares the two series across 18 countries between 2015 and 2021. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.93, and that of 2021 levels is 0.91. Countries that gained or lost coverage for the whole population largely did so for the poorest quintile too, and countries with high overall coverage also tend to cover their poorest households well. The association is strong in rank terms and is not a statement of cause.

The sample is small, at 18 countries, and a rank correlation says nothing about the gap between the two measures in any one country. High overall coverage can coexist with weak targeting of the poor, which the correlation does not test. It supports using the whole-population series as a rough guide to direction where the poorest-quintile series is absent, but not as a substitute for it.

For 2030 the implication is cautious. On a direction-only reading, 33.4% of the assessed population lives in countries classed as on track, while 48.9% lives in countries whose series is classed as regressing. No projection to 2030 was run, and the classes cannot be extrapolated. Without a numeric target and with sparse recent data, the world cannot say with confidence how far the poorest are covered or how fast that is changing.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence permits a limited reading of 2030. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable, yet the world figure of 56.3% in 2021 describes the whole population, not the poor. The only measure aimed at the poorest is safety net coverage of the poorest quintile. Its trend classification places 26 of the 55 countries assessed in regression, and those 26 hold 48.9% of the population of the countries assessed, not of the world. Only 19 countries are classed as on track or target met, with 33.4% of the assessed population. The classes compare each country's rate of change with a target that has no numeric value, so they describe direction and pace and do not prove an observed fall. No projection to 2030 was run, and the classes cannot be extended into one; they show only that, in the countries with data, the direction since 2015 is mixed and, for many, unfavourable.

The gap between income groups is the clearest measured finding. In 2021, low-income countries reached 18.3% of their population, against 77.8% in high-income countries. Lower middle income countries stood at 55.1% and upper middle income countries at 62.2%. The data hold a single year for these groups and no rate of change, so they cannot show how fast the gap is closing or whether it can close by 2030. Donor financing and incomplete household registries are commonly cited as context for low coverage in the poorest countries; these data do not test either explanation.

The evidence base is itself a constraint. Reporting on poorest-quintile safety net coverage reached 47 countries in 2018 and fell to 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022, with a single country in 2023. Surveys thinned just when the pandemic raised the need for protection, so what changed after 2020 cannot be read with confidence. The recorded regression may reflect real losses, a change in survey design or programme definitions, or the ending of temporary schemes; the data cannot separate these. The count of 121 countries reporting in any year applies to the poorest-quintile series.

The target also lacks a numeric reading. Substantial coverage could mean a majority of the poor or a higher threshold, and the classification of on track or regressing depends on that choice. Until it is fixed, different readers can judge the same country differently.

The two coverage measures move together. Across 18 countries with data for 2015 to 2021, the rank correlation between changes in poorest-quintile coverage and changes in whole-population safety net coverage is 0.93, and between their 2021 levels it is 0.91. This supports using the broader measure, which more countries report, as a provisional guide where poorest-quintile data are missing. The sample is small, and a strong rank correlation shows association, not that the poorest receive a proportionate share in every country.

The bodies that maintain the Sustainable Development Goals indicator framework should give target 1.3 a numeric reading of substantial coverage, so that the trend classes judge each country against the same threshold.

Target 1.3 has no numeric threshold. The indicators measure participation and not the adequacy of benefits, and they do not cover the vulnerable as a separate group.

w-c02-6-4.text:
### Health and education budgets claim stable but modest shares of spending

Government budgets show a stable commitment to the services that bear most directly on poverty, though the results contain no benchmark of adequacy. A share of expenditure measures priority, not sufficiency. Education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in the world in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023, a nearly flat movement over eight years. Regional movements beneath the world figure differ. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, while Latin America and the Caribbean held at 16.4 per cent in 2015 and 16.6 per cent in 2024. Low-income countries moved against the general direction, from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022. Reporting of the education share for 2025 is partial, with 60 countries, so the latest observations, including the South Asia reading for that year, describe a subset and not the world.

Health is harder to summarise. The series, domestic general government health expenditure as a share of general government expenditure, is reported here by region and income group, and no world figure is given. Only 7 countries had reported this health series for 2024, so the final year supports no statement. The most recent usable readings fall between 2017 and 2023, depending on the group, and comparisons across groups therefore mix end years. They indicate direction and scale and are not a common-year ranking.

Social protection is the third service named in the section's question, and no result for its share of public spending is available in this bench. The coverage and benefit-incidence series describe who is reached, not how much governments spend, and they are treated in another section of the chapter. The absence should not be read as a low or a high figure.

The targets add a further limit. Target 1.a calls for significant mobilisation of resources and for adequate and predictable means, and target 1.b calls for sound policy frameworks that support accelerated investment in poverty eradication. Neither sets a threshold, a base year or a required share of spending, and the series held here measure domestic budgets, not development cooperation, so target 1.a is only partly addressed. Any classification of progress therefore rests on direction alone: a rising share is read as movement towards the target. That reading is open to challenge, since a share can fall while the absolute amount rises with growth, and can rise because other spending is cut.

### Regions and income groups differ widely in health priority

Health receives very different priority across regions and income groups. North America devoted 22.1 per cent of general government expenditure to health from domestic sources in 2015 and 22.8 per cent in 2023, the highest share of any region reported. Europe and Central Asia stood at 15.0 per cent in 2015 and 14.5 per cent in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 11.5 per cent to 11.8 per cent over the same years. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2019, the last year in its series. South Asia began far lower, at 3.7 per cent in 2015, and reached 4.8 per cent in 2022. Its share in 2022 remained well below that of Europe and Central Asia in 2023, even after the rise.

The income groups repeat the pattern. High-income economies assigned 17.9 per cent in 2015 and 18.5 per cent in 2023. Low-income economies assigned 5.4 per cent in 2015 and 5.3 per cent in 2017, and lower-middle-income economies 4.8 per cent in 2015 and 4.7 per cent in 2018. These are shares only, and they are applied to budgets of very different size. As context rather than a finding of these series, a small share of a small budget commonly leaves households to meet the difference from their own pockets, which is a recognised route into impoverishment.

These comparisons carry a caveat. The series do not end in the same year: the low-income and lower-middle-income series stop in 2017 and 2018, and the Sub-Saharan African series in 2019, so none of them can show what followed 2020. Only 7 countries had reported for 2024 at the time of the data, so the latest year is not yet a basis for comparison. A gap measured in earlier years for the poorest groups may since have narrowed or widened, and the data cannot say which.

Education shares show a different ordering, though not a clean one. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 15.4 per cent in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 16.6 per cent in 2024, give education the largest shares of their budgets among the regions listed, while North America gave 10.7 per cent in 2022, down from 12.9 per cent in 2015. Low-income economies raised their education share from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, a period in which their health share, in the series available to 2017, barely moved. Poorer groups thus tend to put more of their budgets into schooling than into health, and richer groups the reverse. The share is a measure of priority, not of adequacy, because a large share of a small budget may still buy little per pupil.

### Education shares fell in most countries while inequality in spending widened

Since 2015 the education share of public budgets has weakened in most countries. Of 187 countries assessed, 110 are classed as in regression, and these hold 78.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Only 29 countries, with 7.1 per cent of that population, are on track or have met the direction of travel. A further 13 countries (1.8 per cent of the population) show moderate progress, 12 (2.3 per cent) marginal progress and 23 (10.5 per cent) stagnation. No numerical target exists for these indicators, so the classes measure movement towards an increase and not distance from an agreed level. An increase is itself only one reading of progress, since a falling share can accompany rising total budgets or a growing economy.

The population weighting explains why the picture is so unfavourable, for the regressing group includes populous regions. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 per cent of government expenditure in 2015 to 13.0 per cent in 2023, and South Asia from 13.9 per cent in 2015 to 11.3 per cent in 2025, an endpoint that rests on partial reporting, since only 60 countries reported education expenditure in 2025. North America also declined, from 12.9 per cent in 2015 to 10.7 per cent in 2022. The movement was not universal. Low-income countries rose from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, and Latin America and the Caribbean edged up from 16.4 per cent to 16.6 per cent in 2024. Competing claims on budgets, such as debt service, pensions and health, are commonly cited pressures on education shares, although these data do not identify which of them operated in any given country.

Spending relative to national income is a different measure from the share of government expenditure used above. It is education expenditure as a share of GDP, and it describes a separate matter, the spread of spending among countries, which should not be read as a continuation of the finding on budget shares. Across 164 countries, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of that measure rose from 0.18 in 2015 to 0.22 in 2022. The Theil index rose from 0.065 to 0.101. The between-region share of that Theil index moved from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent. Regional differences therefore account for under a quarter of the inequality in both years, and the remainder, by arithmetic, lies within regions. The data do not show what widened the spread. Regional averages thus conceal much of the divergence.

Health can be set against education on the same direction-of-travel test, but the class counts differ in coverage, 193 countries for health against 187 for education, and they are not a ranking of the two services. Of the 193 countries assessed for the health share of government expenditure, 72 are on track or have met the direction of travel, holding 40.8 per cent of their population, while 61 are in regression, holding 21.3 per cent. Another 30 countries (22.1 per cent of the population) show marginal progress, 19 (11.5 per cent) stagnation and 11 (4.3 per cent) moderate progress. This is a statement about direction of travel only, a weak test that says nothing of the level of spending or its adequacy.

The two shares do not move together. The Spearman correlation between changes in the health share and the education share across 129 countries over 2015 to 2022 is 0.16, and between their levels in the later year of that span 0.09. Countries that raised one share were therefore hardly more likely to raise the other, and no common cause is shown. Neither is a trade-off. Governments appear to set the two priorities largely independently, so the weakening of education shares needs its own explanation in each country.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Spending shares carry no numerical target under targets 1.a and 1.b, so progress can be judged only by direction. The trend classes ask whether a share is rising, which is a weak test: a country may be rising while spending too little, and another may be falling while spending generously. The classes are signals of priority, not verdicts on adequacy. The target wording can also be read as concerning domestic budgets, development cooperation, or both. The series examined cover domestic budgets only, so nothing here speaks to external resources under target 1.a.

The class counts for the two shares are statements about direction of travel only, and they are not a ranking of the two services, since the sets of countries differ in coverage. For the domestic health share, 72 of 193 countries assessed are on track, holding 40.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, while regression affects 61 countries with 21.3 per cent. For the education share of government expenditure, 110 of 187 countries are in regression, with 78.2 per cent of the population, against 29 on track with 7.1 per cent. Because the regression class holds most of the population, the direction of education budgets matters for most of the world's children, though the results do not identify which countries drive it. The results do not show why health shares moved as they did, and they cannot say whether the pattern will persist.

The outlook for 2030 is uneven, and the results support no projection of either share. In health, 21.3 per cent of the population lives where the share is falling. In education, the regional falls set out earlier in this section sit beside a rise in the low-income group, from 14.9 per cent in 2015 to 16.7 per cent in 2022, so the pattern is not uniform. The South Asia endpoint of 2025 for the education share rests on partial reporting, since only 60 countries reported on that series in that year. A separate measure, education spending as a share of GDP, diverged among countries, with the population-weighted Theil index rising from 0.065 in 2015 to 0.101 in 2022. This is a different measure from the share of government expenditure, and the two should not be read as one finding. The between-region share of that index moved only from 23.8 per cent to 22.3 per cent, so the remainder of the index, the larger part, lies within regions; the data do not show its cause.

Two limits qualify every reading. Spending data for low-income countries often end years before the latest reporting year, so recent shifts there are unseen. Social protection spending is not covered by the spending series examined, and its coverage and targeting are treated in other sections of this chapter.
