w-c04-4-4.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.57% for the world by 2030. The same reading is applied to every region and income group, so the regional verdicts that follow in this section rest on that single convention. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool, a linear extrapolation of the 2015-2021 pace, places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 can be sorted by one rule: the direction and size of the change in the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease. Under that rule, most regions fell, by margins that differ widely, and one region rose.

Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, which still leaves the region above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021. Its pace ratio is 0.39, meaning the decline ran at well under half the pace the target requires, and extending its own linear path gives 18.5% in 2030, against the target value of 12.57% derived from the world baseline.

The two Americas moved least in absolute terms. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America began from the lowest regional level. Its ratio of 0.82 should not be read as near-target progress: it rests on a very small absolute fall from a low base, and the trend tool's ratio is sensitive to such starting points. Latin America and the Caribbean reaches a ratio of 0.50, and linear extension gives 13.9% for it in 2030. Outside the data, it is widely understood that gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking have been offset in part by obesity and diabetes, and by unequal access to treatment; these causes are not measured by the results used here.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, and its pace ratio is negative, at -0.20, which the trend tool labels regression. Linear extension would place the region at 24.0% in 2030. Among regions it had the highest level in 2021, though low-income countries as an income group stood slightly higher, at 23.0%. In 2015 it was marginally below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates between 30 and 70 did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends. Established knowledge points to hypertension, diabetes, air pollution and the cost of long-term treatment as plausible contributors. The period includes the pandemic years, when disrupted screening and chronic care may have raised the 2021 figure; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves its level close to the South Asian one. Its pace ratio is 0.16, and linear extension gives 20.4% in 2030. Measurement is a concern here, since death registration is incomplete and the estimates rely heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, a ratio of 0.22, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, a ratio of 0.00, which is stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. High-income countries alone are classed as on track, with a ratio of 1.93 and a linear value of 11.4% in 2030, which would lie below the target value. The two richer groups improved by about one percentage point each, while the lower-middle group, which contains South Asia's large populations, stood still.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability that all adults experience, but the direction is towards greater inequality. The share of the Theil index lying between regions grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences. All trend readings here are linear extensions of the 2015 to 2021 change, so regional ratios should be read as indications, not forecasts.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.26 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.09 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted. The world value stood at 18.3% in 2021, against a target value of 12.57% for 2030. The trend tool expects 17.5% in 2030 at the post-2015 rate.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. The following explanations rest on general knowledge, not on any result of this section, and the data do not separate them. Earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from better treatment of heart disease, and such gains meet diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The years 2020 and 2021 coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions. The series cannot isolate these effects from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.0016 with a p-value of 0.70 and an R-squared of 0.001. The coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measures point the same way, though they are not the same statistic. The convergence test reports a coefficient of variation of 0.36 in 2015 and 0.38 in 2021, computed across countries without population weights. The spread tool, which weights countries by population, reports a coefficient of variation of 0.27 in 2015 and 0.28 in 2021. The levels differ because of the weighting, but both rise. The population-weighted Gini coefficient moved from 0.152 to 0.158, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 27.0% to 33.1%. Relative spread widened slightly, and a growing part of it lies between regions, not within them. For a target defined in relative terms this matters, because a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and no systematic acceleration in such countries appears in the convergence result.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.10 and the Kendall coefficient is 0.07. Both are weak. If coverage gains went with larger mortality falls, the correlation would be negative. The weak positive value gives no support for that expectation over this short window, though it is too small to show the opposite either.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.25 by the Spearman measure and -0.17 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is modest in size, larger than the correlation of changes but far from strong. It describes a cross-section in which income, age structure, the wider health system and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together, and it cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented. The mortality series is modelled from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths are read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021, and the trend projection, a linear extrapolation of the 2015 to 2021 pace, reaches 17.5% in 2030. The global ratio of progress is 0.22, where a ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target. At the observed rate the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is, and they need careful reading because a ratio depends on the starting level as well as on the pace. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, records the largest fall of any region, from 17.5% to 15.7%, and is expected to reach 13.4% in 2030. North America also has a ratio of 0.82, but it rests on a very small absolute movement, from 13.6% in 2015 to 13.3% in 2021, from a low base already near the threshold. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6%, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.50, 13.9%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 0.39, is expected to reach 18.5% in 2030, well above the 12.57% threshold, and is classed as marginal progress. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030, but they began from 13.8%, already close to the threshold, so the class reflects the starting point as much as the pace.

That points to an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions above 22% would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above applies the global reading to every region. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, rising from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, with an expected 24.0% in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnation, with an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22 and an expected 21.5%. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none. The correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment or chronic respiratory care. A weak link does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality, named in the section's title, is outside this account. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. Mental health is part of the wording of target 3.4, and the indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover it. The section should be read as an account of non-communicable disease mortality only.

The proposals follow from the findings above and are set out in the list. The first rests on the regression in South Asia and the stagnation of lower middle income countries. The second rests on the baseline ambiguity of the target. The third rests on the weak link between coverage and outcome, and is a measurement proposal, not a claim about what works.

w-c04-5-4.text:
### Global consumption fell between 2015 and 2020

Global alcohol consumption per adult fell over the first five years of the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization estimate, carried in the World Development Indicators, puts total consumption at 5.9 litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15 and over in 2015. By 2020 it stood at 4.9 litres. The fall is about 1.0 litre, or roughly one sixth of the 2015 level, in five years. The measure sums recorded sales and an estimate of unrecorded alcohol, such as home production and informal trade, and is adjusted for tourist consumption.

Target 3.5 calls for strengthening the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including the harmful use of alcohol. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline year. The target can therefore be read in more than one way. One reading takes the wording to concern harm, which per capita volume captures only in part, since the same average can conceal heavy episodic drinking in a minority. Another reading treats volume as the best available proxy and counts a sustained decline as progress. This book adopts the second reading, because volume is the only alcohol series the shelf holds, and it states that choice openly. On that reading the world moved in the intended direction after 2015.

The series needs careful handling. The figures are projected estimates, not counts from a survey of drinkers in each year. Statisticians model them from sales, tax records, production data and occasional surveys, and then project forward where observations are thin. A smooth global path is therefore partly a product of the method, and a single year should not be read as a precise count. The final year, 2020, coincides with the first months of the pandemic, when closures of bars and restaurants, lost tourism and shifts in household purchasing altered both drinking and its measurement. Whether the 2020 figure reflects lasting change or a temporary disturbance cannot be settled from this series alone.

Coverage is nearly complete. Across the whole period from 2000 to 2020, 187 countries report in at least one year, and 185 report in 2020. The few countries that drop out in some years do not alter the global picture materially, though the estimates for those places are less secure. The world figure is thus a broad measure, and the sections that follow turn to the regions, income groups and countries that lie behind it.

### Regions differ widely in level and in direction

Regional levels span a wide range. Europe and Central Asia and North America sit at the top. Consumption in Europe and Central Asia was 8.9 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2020, down from 9.5 litres in 2015. North America stood at 9.9 litres in 2020, up from 9.5 litres in 2015. Of the seven regions reported, North America is the only one in which the estimate rose. Its rate of 0.0075 is classed as regression, while every other region shows a negative rate. Latin America and the Caribbean lies in the middle band, at 5.8 litres in 2020 against 6.5 litres in 2015. At the bottom, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan record 0.4 litres in 2015 and 0.3 litres in 2020. That level is consistent with widespread abstention and legal restriction. It is also a region in which unrecorded consumption is hardest to measure, so the level should be read with caution.

The largest regional fall is in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020. Its rate of -0.0657 is the steepest of any region and is classed as on track or target met. South Asia fell from 4.4 litres to 3.6 litres, at a rate of -0.0360, also classed on track. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0216, is placed in the same class. Europe and Central Asia, at -0.0138, is classed as moderate progress, but acceleration needed. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at -0.0181, receives the same class even though its level is so low. These classes need a caveat. The Goals set no numerical target for alcohol under target 3.5, which asks only for strengthened prevention and treatment of harmful use. The classification therefore measures the direction and speed of change, and does not show whether a region has reached a safe or desired level.

Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 4.6 litres in 2015 to 4.2 litres in 2020, at a rate of -0.0211, classed on track. The fall in East Asia and Pacific, from 6.4 litres to 4.5 litres, was much larger in litres.

The income groups show a similar divergence. High-income economies fell only from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, at a rate of -0.0075, classed as marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed. They remain the heaviest-drinking group. Low-income economies, at 2.9 litres in 2015 and 2.8 litres in 2020, moved even less, at -0.0054, and are classed in the same way. Upper-middle-income economies fell from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres, at -0.0585, and lower-middle-income economies from 3.9 litres to 3.3 litres, at -0.0340; both are classed on track. The largest reductions therefore came in the middle-income groups, while the highest-consuming group fell slowly and the lowest-consuming group barely moved. The period also spans 2020, when closure of bars and restricted travel altered recorded sales, and the projected estimates for that year rest partly on modelling, so part of the fall may not persist. The results do not identify what drove any of these regional differences.

### Country trajectories split between steep falls and regression

The trend classification covers 183 countries and rates each by its course towards a lower level of consumption. Target 3.5 sets no numerical goal for alcohol, so the classes measure direction and pace against a decrease by 2030, not distance from a stated threshold. That is one of several possible readings and applies throughout.

The country picture is divided. In 75 countries, holding 60.4% of the population of those assessed, consumption is on track or the target is met. A further 21 countries, with 11.0% of their population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 21, with 7.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. In 12 countries, with 3.1%, consumption stagnates. In 54 countries, with 18.2%, it is in regression, meaning that consumption per adult is rising.

The two ways of counting give different weights. By number of countries, 75 of 183 are on track, well under half, while 54 are in regression. By population, the on-track class holds 60.4% and the regression class 18.2%. The regressing group therefore holds a smaller share of people than of countries, while the on-track group holds a larger one. The country-level data are not tabulated here, so which countries these are is not stated, and nothing is shown about their size beyond these shares. The 60.4% is a statement about people, not a sign that most countries are succeeding.

The results do not identify why consumption rose in the regressing countries or fell in the others. Causes can be offered only as context. Income growth, changes in marketing and changes in taxation or licensing are among the factors commonly discussed in the public-health literature, but none is measured here. Countries that begin from very low levels can also register regression from a small base, so the class does not always signal a harmful level of drinking.

Coverage is nearly complete: 185 countries report in 2020, and 187 report in at least one year. The estimates are projected by the World Health Organization from survey and sales data, not counted directly, so country-level movements, above all for 2020, partly reflect modelling and not observed change. The classification should be read as an indication of direction, not as a precise ranking.

### Change was not convergent and moved alike for men and women

Change between 2015 and 2020 was not convergent. Across 181 countries, a regression of annual change on the starting level gives a coefficient of -0.00589, with a p-value of 0.603 and an R-squared of 0.012. The sign is negative, which would mean that countries with higher consumption fell slightly faster, but the coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the starting level explains about 1.2% of the variation in change. High-consumption countries did not systematically close the gap with low-consumption ones.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of consumption across countries rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.74 in 2020. The spread of national levels relative to their mean therefore widened slightly. Because the global average fell while dispersion rose, reductions were uneven in proportion: some countries fell sharply, some barely moved, and some rose. The difference between the two coefficients is small, and a movement of two hundredths in a five-year window should not be read as a settled trend.

The second result concerns the sexes. Across 185 countries, the changes in male and female consumption between 2015 and 2020 are almost perfectly rank-correlated, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.99 and a Kendall coefficient of 0.94. The 2020 levels are nearly as closely aligned, at 0.99 and 0.92. Countries in which men reduced consumption most are, almost without exception, those in which women did so as well. Rank correlation says nothing about the absolute gap between men and women; it says only that the ordering of countries is shared.

The results do not identify why the ordering is shared. One possible reading is that influences operating on whole populations, such as pricing, availability and social norms, affect both sexes together; the data do not test this. The method may also contribute. The figures are projected estimates, built from national sales, survey and modelling inputs, and the same adjustments to a country's total are likely to carry through to both sex-specific series. Part of the correlation may therefore be an artefact of estimation rather than a finding about behaviour.

No causal claim follows from these results. The window is five years and covers the disruption of 2020, and the lack of convergence describes the data rather than judging any policy. What can be said is that the starting level did not organise the change, and that the sex of the drinker did not alter a country's place in the ordering.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to a world moving in the right direction on alcohol, though not evenly. The world rate of -0.0363 is classed as on track or target met, yet it leans on large falls in East Asia and Pacific, where consumption went from 6.4 litres of pure alcohol per adult in 2015 to 4.5 litres in 2020, and in upper middle income countries, where it went from 6.1 litres to 4.5 litres. In high-income countries the fall was from 9.5 litres to 9.2 litres, a rate of -0.0075 classed as marginal progress, and North America moved the other way, from 9.5 litres to 9.9 litres. Target 3.5 sets no numerical threshold, so every class here describes direction and pace against a decrease, which is one of several possible readings. Whether the gap between regions narrows or widens by 2030 cannot be read from two observation points, and the 2030 horizon lies ten years after the last observation in 2020.

The country picture shows the same division, and it should be read together with the population shares. Consumption is regressing in 54 countries holding 18.2% of the assessed population, and 12 more are stagnant, holding 3.1%. The 75 countries on track hold 60.4% of that population, although they are fewer than half of the 183 assessed. The results name no countries, so the composition of each group is not shown. A global verdict of progress can coexist with regression in 54 countries holding 18.2% of the assessed population.

The absence of convergence matters for 2030. With a coefficient of -0.00589 and a p-value of 0.603, the data show no tendency for high-consumption countries to catch down, nor for the gap to widen in any measurable way. The results do not identify what drove the falls or the rises, and the pace seen in 2015 to 2020 cannot be assumed to continue to 2030. Low-income countries, where consumption is lowest at 2.8 litres in 2020, show only marginal progress. Projected estimates carry uncertainty, and the 2020 value may reflect pandemic disruption to trade and sales, so the five-year change may not represent the underlying course.

The proposals follow from these findings and are framed as monitoring and analysis, since the results establish direction and not cause. First, the World Health Organization and national statistical offices should publish observed, not only projected, estimates for the 54 countries classed as regressing, so that the rise can be told apart from modelling artefact and from growth off a small base. Second, health ministries in those countries and in North America, where consumption rose to 9.9 litres in 2020, should commission analyses of what lies behind the rise before choosing among policy responses. Third, the bodies that set indicators under Goal 3 should state whether target 3.5 carries a quantitative reduction for alcohol, so that progress can be measured against a threshold and not only a direction.

w-c04-6-3.text:
### The global rate barely moved after 2015

The 2020 target to halve road deaths was not met on the evidence available. The World Bank's indicator of mortality caused by road traffic injury, expressed as estimated deaths per 100,000 population, stood at 17.0 for the world in 2015 and at 16.7 in 2019. That is a fall of about 1.5 per cent over four years. A halving would have required a rate near 8.5 by 2020, and the measured rate remained close to double that level.

Two limits on this reading need stating. The series ends in 2019, so the target year itself cannot be observed; the conclusion rests on the last four years before it, and a sudden fall in 2020 of the size required is not plausible given how slowly the rate moved beforehand. The path of 2020 is also disturbed by the pandemic, when restrictions on movement reduced traffic in many places, so any later figure would need careful interpretation before it was read as progress on safety.

The second limit concerns the wording of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of deaths and injuries, and of the number of them, whereas the indicator covers deaths only and is a rate per head of population. A rate can fall while the count of deaths rises if population grows faster, and it can stay flat while the count grows. The target can therefore be read in more than one way: as a halving of the count, or as a halving of the rate. On either reading the evidence points the same way, since the rate has barely changed and no series on non-fatal injuries is held on the shelf. The measure used here is the more lenient of the two, which makes the shortfall harder to dismiss.

Coverage supports the finding. Estimates are available for 183 countries in 2019 and for 190 countries in at least one year, with regional and income aggregates alongside. The series is modelled by the World Health Organization rather than counted directly, since many countries lack complete registration of deaths by cause. A flat global line therefore reflects estimates built from a mix of registered and modelled data, and small movements of the order seen here should not be over-read. What can be said with confidence is the scale of the gap between the target and the outcome, not the precise change of a few tenths of a point.

### Regions diverged, and only Europe and Central Asia moved fast

Regional rates for 2015 and 2019 show that the small global movement conceals different trajectories. Europe and Central Asia was the only region to record a substantial decline, from 9.2 deaths per 100,000 population in 2015 to 7.4 in 2019. That is the lowest regional rate in either year, and the only one close to the level a halving would have required. Its projected rate for 2030, on the 2015 to 2019 pace, is 4.1, below the target of 8.5. Long-established road safety policy in much of that region, such as speed enforcement, seat-belt use, vehicle standards and road design, is offered here as context consistent with the pattern; the results do not test it.

East Asia and Pacific moved only slightly, from 17.0 to 16.5. Latin America and Caribbean fell from 18.3 to 17.3, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group from 17.3 to 17.0. The trend tool classes all three as marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with pace ratios of 0.22, 0.36 and 0.13 respectively. A ratio compares the pace observed with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio below 1 means the pace is too slow. South Asia was effectively flat, at 15.6 in 2015 and 15.6 in 2019, and the tool classes it as regression, with a ratio of -0.01.

Two regions moved in the wrong direction. North America rose from 11.5 to 11.9, and the trend tool classes it as regression with a ratio of -0.63. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.8 to 27.4, the highest regional rate in either year, and is also classed as regression, with a ratio of -0.13 and a projected 2030 rate of 29.2. Rapid growth in motor vehicle use is often cited as a pressure on road deaths in lower-income regions, but no result here measures vehicle use, so that explanation is context and not a finding. The measured pattern matters for 2030: the region with the most deaths per head is not improving.

These comparisons rest on regional means, which can hide wide spread among the countries inside a region, so the ranking of regions says little about any single national road network. Coverage is broad but not complete: 183 countries report in 2019, and the indicator is built from modelled estimates, so small changes in a regional rate should be read with caution. The country-level spread is taken up in the next part.

### Dispersion widened while few places gained ground

The convergence test asks whether countries with higher road death rates in 2015 changed by less, or by more, than others up to 2019. Across 182 countries the estimated coefficient (beta) is 0.031, with a p-value of 0.0058. The sign is positive. Under the convention of the test, a negative coefficient would indicate that countries with higher starting rates rose less or fell more, so that levels drew together; a positive one indicates that they drew apart. The result is therefore the opposite of convergence, and the slope is distinguished from zero at the conventional 0.05 threshold.

The second measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation, the standard deviation of national rates divided by their mean, rose from 0.54 in 2015 to 0.63 in 2019. Rates across countries were more unequal in relation to their average at the end of the window than at the start. The world rate, 17.0 in 2015 and 16.7 in 2019, scarcely moved while the spread widened. The tests do not identify which countries account for this: no country-level result is reported here, so no count of improving or deteriorating countries can be given, and nothing is claimed about how many places gained ground.

The limits of the test are considerable. The R-squared is 0.108, so initial rates account for only about one-tenth of the variation in subsequent change. Most of what separates one country's trajectory from another's lies outside this simple relationship. The window is also only four years, from 2015 to 2019, and short intervals magnify the effect of estimation noise. Country figures for road deaths are modelled estimates, since many countries lack complete death registration with cause information, and year-to-year movements in a modelled series may partly reflect revisions of method and inputs rather than real change. The test also stops at 2019 and says nothing of the period after 2020.

The tools measure outcomes, not causes, so any explanation is context and not a finding of these results. Well-established experience suggests that road deaths fall where speed management, helmet and seat-belt laws, vehicle safety standards and emergency care are enforced, and that they rise where motorisation grows faster than safe road design and enforcement. Such differences could produce widening dispersion, but no result here measures them.

For 2030 the implication is limited to what the two measures show: a rising spread means that the global rate alone is a poor guide to national progress, and that national trajectories need to be examined individually.

### The 2030 target of 8.5 needs a different pace, and proposals follow

The 2030 horizon asks for a rate of 8.5 deaths per 100,000 population, which is the 2015 world rate of 17.0 halved. Each projection below extends the average annual movement between 2015 and 2019. The ratio reported with it compares that movement with the pace needed to reach 8.5 by 2030, so a ratio of 1 means the pace is just sufficient and a ratio below 1 means it is too slow. The world rate is projected at 16.1 in 2030 if the 2015 to 2019 movement continues, a ratio of 0.11, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. That projection stands almost twice as high as 8.5.

Two groups are projected to pass 8.5 on the 2015 to 2019 pace; this is not the same as being on track, since the window is only four years. Europe and Central Asia is projected at 4.1 in 2030, with a ratio of 6.91. High-income countries are projected at 7.3, a ratio of 2.48, although their 2019 rate of 8.7 still stood above 8.5. The high-income result is therefore the less secure of the two.

East Asia and Pacific shows marginal progress, with a projected rate of 15.2 in 2030 and a ratio of 0.22. Latin America and the Caribbean is similar, at 14.8 and 0.36. Upper middle income countries are projected at 15.2, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 16.2. None of these approaches 8.5 on present pace. Lower middle income countries are classed as stagnating, at 17.3.

Four groups are classed as regression. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 29.2 and low-income countries at 31.5, both rising. North America is projected at 13.3, and South Asia at 15.7. The groups with the highest rates are therefore moving away from the target on these projections. As context, not a finding of these results, rapid motorisation combined with weak roads, vehicle standards and emergency care is a well-established source of high road death rates.

The figure of 8.5 is one reading of the target. Target 3.6 speaks of halving deaths and injuries, not the rate. The rate and the count can move in opposite directions, and no count series is held here to test which reading is more demanding. The 2015 base year is also a convention, since the target text names no baseline, and injuries are not measured by the indicator used. Readers should treat 8.5 as a benchmark and not as the single correct threshold.

The proposals that follow are tied to these findings. Governments of Sub-Saharan African and low-income countries, with development partners, should prioritise speed enforcement, safer road design and emergency care, because their rates are projected to rise rather than fall. National road safety agencies in regions classed as marginal or stagnating should set interim targets for 2025 and report against them annually, because the present pace is far below what 8.5 requires. North American authorities should review why the rate rose from 11.5 in 2015 to 11.9 in 2019. National statistical offices and the World Health Organization should publish annual counts of deaths and injuries, since the target concerns numbers and none is held here. Countries with incomplete cause-of-death registration should strengthen vital registration, since the indicator is modelled where records are lacking.

w-c06-7-4.text:
### The global gap in internet use by sex

Target 5.b asks for greater use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The bench's results measure one aspect of that aim: the share of women and of men who have used the internet in the previous three months. They do not measure ownership of a mobile phone by sex. The series on mobile cellular subscriptions is counted per 100 people and is not divided by sex, and one person can hold several subscriptions, so it cannot show who owns a handset. The question of a gap in phone ownership therefore cannot be answered here, and the findings below concern internet use alone.

On that measure, the world's women moved a long way in a short time. Female internet use stood at 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and reached 68.2 per cent in 2024. This is a period that includes the pandemic, when schooling, work, public services and social contact moved online and gave households a strong reason to connect.

Male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and reached 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two world figures do not share an end year: the female series is read at 2024 and the male series at 2025, because the latest world value in each result falls in a different year. Setting one against the other mixes a gap between the sexes with a year of growth in male use. It overstates the gap in any single year and should not be read as a measurement. The world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. A clean comparison requires both series at the same date, and the regional results, where both are read at 2024, allow it in the parts that follow.

The 2019 figures are on a common footing. They show women at 51.8 per cent and men at 56.0 per cent, so that women used the internet at about 0.93 of the male rate. This is a fact about 2019 only and says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed or widened since. Because use rose for both sexes, a gap in percentage points can grow while the ratio improves, so the two measures can point in different directions and each should be stated with its basis.

The figures also carry a caution about coverage. The results are aggregates over the economies that report, and the count of countries reporting in 2025 is only 7 in each result, against 92 in 2019 and 65 in 2024. The 2025 world and income-group values therefore rest on a thin base of direct observation and on estimates for the rest, and the 2024 regional values are better supported. Internet use as defined here also says nothing about the quality of access, the device used, the cost of data or what women do online, all of which bear on empowerment as much as the bare fact of use. The evidence supports rapid gains by women and a shortfall against men in 2019, while the size of the world gap in 2024 stays undetermined.

### Regional differences in the gap

Among the regions reported here, the point gap between women's and men's internet use in 2024 is largest in two regions at a middle level of use and smaller in the region with the lowest use. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women had used the internet in the previous three months, against 67.6 per cent of men. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 per cent for women and 69.1 per cent for men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the shares were 29.4 per cent and 37.9 per cent. The absolute gap there is smaller than in the two regions above, but the level of use is far lower, so a low point gap at a low level should not be read as near equality.

South Asia also shows how the gap can move. In 2019 women's use stood at 24.3 per cent and men's at 34.9 per cent. By 2024 women's use had reached 56.3 per cent and men's 69.1 per cent, so the point gap had widened, even though women's use more than doubled. Rapid growth in use among both sexes can thus coexist with a larger point difference.

The gap is small where use is nearly universal. In North America 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia the shares were 90.0 per cent and 91.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean lies between, at 81.3 per cent for women and 82.0 per cent for men. Saturation leaves little room for a difference to persist. Mobile networks, affordable devices and schooling may have contributed in these regions, but that is context from outside the bench's data, not a finding of it.

East Asia and Pacific shows a reversal. In 2019 women's use, at 67.4 per cent, was slightly above men's, at 66.7 per cent. By 2024 women stood at 85.5 per cent and men at 87.6 per cent, so men had moved ahead. The regional aggregate hides large differences among its economies, and the data given here do not show which of them drove the change. The result should be read as a shift in the regional average, not as evidence of decline in women's use, which rose over the period.

Income groups are reported for 2025, when only 7 countries reported these series, so the figures rest on very thin direct observation and probably include estimates; they are indicative only. In low-income countries 18.3 per cent of women used the internet, against 28.6 per cent of men. In lower middle income countries the shares were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent. In high-income countries they were 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The ordering matches the regional one, with the largest point gaps at middle levels, but the evidence is weaker than for the regional figures of 2024.

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, female and male use move closely together: the rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.948 and that of changes is 0.958. Where men gained, women generally gained too, so the gap is tied to a country's overall connectivity and does not behave as a separate trend. This is a statement about association; it does not show why any gap persists.

The regional pattern matters for target 5.b because the gaps that remain are largest in regions where women's use is far from universal. Plausible factors, which lie outside the data and which the bench cannot separate, include the cost of devices and data, differences in schooling and literacy, social norms on women's independent use of phones, and concerns over safety online. They probably operate with different force in each region, which is why a single global figure conceals as much as it reveals.

### What changed since 2019 and what the data can support

South Asia shows the largest change since 2019. Female internet use there rose from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while male use rose from 34.9 per cent to 69.1 per cent. Women gained a great deal in absolute terms, but the distance to men did not close. Sub-Saharan Africa shows a similar pattern at a lower level: women moved from 20.2 per cent to 29.4 per cent, men from 28.6 per cent to 37.9 per cent.

The comparison across countries points the same way. For the 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male changes is 0.958, and that between 2024 levels is 0.948. Countries where men's use grew quickly are, almost without exception, those where women's use grew quickly. The finding indicates that expansion of access is largely shared, and no group of countries shows women advancing on a separate path. A correlation of this kind does not explain why gaps persist where they do. Differences in income, education, literacy, norms on women's use of devices and the cost of handsets and data are plausible factors, but they lie outside these results, and the series cannot separate them.

Income groups are indicative only, because the 2025 values rest on 7 reporting countries. In low-income countries, female use reached 18.3 per cent in 2025 against 28.6 per cent for men. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, and in upper-middle-income countries 87.9 per cent and 89.7 per cent. In high-income countries the gap is small, at 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent. The world figures moved from 51.8 per cent for women and 56.0 per cent for men in 2019 to 68.2 per cent for women in 2024 and 76.6 per cent for men in 2025. Those two world values fall in different years, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be read from them and cannot be measured from these results.

The evidence has limits that bear on every figure above. In 2019, 92 countries reported female internet use; in 2024, 65 did; in 2025, only 7. The fall after 2019 coincides with the pandemic years and later reporting delays, and the reason is not stated in the data. The 2025 values for income groups are likely to be revised as more countries submit data. The 54-country comparison is a subset of the 137 countries that have ever reported, and it may differ from the countries that report least. Poorer countries with weaker statistical systems are the ones most likely to be missing, so measured progress may overstate the global picture. The series also defines use over the previous three months and from any device, so it says nothing about who owns a phone, who controls it, or how it is used.

### Implications for target 5.b by 2030 and proposals

Target 5.b carries no numerical threshold and no date-bound level, so it can be read in more than one way. The reading adopted here is a narrowing of the gap between women's and men's internet use, alongside rising levels for women. On that reading the evidence for 2030 is mixed. Levels have risen sharply, but the regional gaps in 2024 remain wide where female use is lowest or at a middle level, and these results cannot show whether the gaps are closing.

The world figures illustrate the limit of the data. Female use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, while male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The male figure refers to a later year than the female one, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. The regional figures for 2024 are on a common year and are the safer basis. In Sub-Saharan Africa female use was 29.4 per cent in 2024 against 37.9 per cent for men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the figures were 55.0 per cent and 67.6 per cent. In South Asia they were 56.3 per cent and 69.1 per cent. Where use is near universal, as in North America, with 94.1 per cent for women and 94.7 per cent for men, the gap is almost gone.

The income-group figures point the same way, but they should be read as indicative, because only 7 countries reported in 2025. Female use reached 18.3 per cent in low-income countries against 28.6 per cent for men, 56.9 per cent against 68.7 per cent in lower middle income countries, and 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent in high income countries. A gap of this kind closes mainly as a whole population connects, and only the nearly saturated groups have reached that point. The data support only the observed gaps; they contain no projection, so whether any region reaches parity by 2030 cannot be stated. The data do not test the causes of the gaps. Factors commonly proposed outside these results include the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, social norms on who may own a device, and concerns about safety online.

The country evidence suggests that the gap follows general connectivity rather than departing from it. Across 54 countries, changes in female use from 2019 to 2024 and changes in male use correlate at a Spearman coefficient of 0.958, and 2024 levels at 0.948. Women's use therefore rises where men's rises. Specific barriers to women are not isolated by this evidence, and the correlation is silent on whether gaps are closing within countries.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National statistical offices and telecom regulators should publish internet use and mobile phone ownership by sex every year in the same reference year, so that gaps can be measured on a common basis.

Ministries of communications and operators in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa should target affordable handsets and data at women, and report progress by sex against the gap.
International statistical bodies and donors should fund sex-disaggregated household surveys in low-income countries, where few countries report recent data.

Internet use by sex covers 137 countries, and only 7 reported for 2025, so the latest income-group figures are thin. The results contain no projection to 2030, no within-country trend in the gap, and no evidence on causes.

w-c08-5-2.text:
### Renewable generation has roughly doubled worldwide since 2015

The world share of electricity produced from renewable sources other than hydroelectric power rose from 6.6 % in 2015 to 12.4 % in 2021. The share has therefore come close to doubling in six years. The figure comes from 208 reporting countries in 2021, and the series ends that year, so nothing in it describes the years since. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks of 2022, cannot be read from this indicator.

The indicator needs careful reading. It measures the share of non-hydroelectric renewables (chiefly wind, solar, geothermal and biomass) in total electricity production. It does not measure installed generating capacity, nor the quantity of electricity generated. A rising share is consistent with new capacity being built, and the growth of wind and solar plant is the usual explanation in the wider literature. But the data do not observe that capacity. A share can also rise when other generation falls, or when total output stagnates. Growth in generating capacity is thus inferred here, not observed, and the part's heading speaks of a doubling of the share, not of generation.

The exclusion of hydroelectric power also shapes the picture. Large hydropower is a long-established source in many developing countries, and it is left out. The indicator therefore captures the newer renewables, whose costs have fallen considerably over the past decade, and it understates the renewable contribution of countries that depend heavily on dams.

The trend tool classes the world as on track or target met for the non-hydroelectric share, with a rate of 0.11 for the period. The separate trend on the renewable share of final energy consumption gives the world a rate of 0.03 and the same verdict; the two series should not be confused. Target 7.b carries no numerical value, so these verdicts only say the share is moving in the desired direction. They are not comparisons with a quantified goal, and the word target should be read in that sense. The global figure also averages very different experiences, which the next part sets out by region and income group. A world share cannot show whether developing countries, the subject of targets 7.a and 7.b, have shared in the gain.

For 2030 the global direction is encouraging but incompletely observed. A doubling in six years shows that a rapid change in the electricity mix is possible. Whether it has continued, and whether it has reached the countries with the least infrastructure, is a question this series cannot answer from 2021 onward.

### Regions and income groups started from different levels and moved at different speeds

Regional starting points differed widely in 2015, and the gaps in levels have not closed. East Asia & Pacific rose from 4.8% of electricity production in 2015 to 12.0% in 2021, and Latin America & Caribbean rose from 6.9% to 15.1% over the same years. South Asia moved from 4.6% to 8.5%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan began from 0.6% and reached 2.9%, the lowest level among the regions reported. Sub-Saharan Africa started at 2.1% and stood at 4.3% in 2021. All figures here are shares of total electricity production from non-hydroelectric renewable sources.

Income groups show the same pattern more sharply. Upper middle income countries rose from 4.6% to 11.9%, and lower middle income countries from 4.1% to 7.3%. High income countries rose from 8.6% to 14.1%. Low income countries moved the other way, from 0.7% in 2015 to 0.5% in 2021. The poorest countries therefore did not share in the expansion of wind, solar, geothermal and biomass generation that lifted the world figure. Well-established context points to the cost of capital, small and weakly financed grids, and limited public budgets as barriers to new plant in these economies, though the data here do not test those causes.

The trend assessment for the share of renewables in total final energy consumption must be read with care. Low income countries show the highest share, 77.0% in 2015 and 74.6% in 2020, and the trend reads as regression, at a rate of -0.0064. That level does not signal modern clean energy. In these countries the share is dominated by traditional biomass, chiefly wood and charcoal burned for cooking, which is neither clean nor efficient and carries health and forest costs. A falling share there can even accompany a shift to commercial fuels. The indicator also leaves target 7.2 open to more than one reading, since no numeric 2030 value is set for it. The tool classes the World, East Asia & Pacific, Latin America & Caribbean, and upper middle income groups as on track, while Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and lower middle income countries are marked as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The convergence result tempers any reading of catching up. Across 208 countries, the slope of annual change on starting level between 2015 and 2021 was -0.004, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001. No convergence can be distinguished from zero. The coefficient of variation did fall, from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021, so spread relative to the mean narrowed. The two results are compatible: the mean rose, which shrinks relative spread, without starting position predicting the pace of change. The data end in 2021, so they say nothing about changes since the pandemic.

### Private investment and concessional finance moved unevenly

Private participation in energy investment moved unevenly across developing regions between 2015 and 2024. In Latin America & Caribbean, investment with private participation fell from US$11.87 billion in 2015 to US$8.40 billion in 2024. South Asia moved the other way, rising from US$2.39 billion to US$3.45 billion. The two regions therefore ended the period on different paths, and the regional total for Latin America & Caribbean is lower than at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals period.

The income groups show a sharper divide. Upper middle income countries rose from US$31.02 billion in 2015 to US$58.39 billion in 2024, so private capital in energy concentrated where borrowing conditions, market size and regulatory frameworks are most developed. Lower middle income countries barely moved, from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion, in current dollars. Because the figures are not adjusted for inflation, the lower middle income total is likely to have lost purchasing power over the period, though the extract gives no deflated series to show it. Low income countries are not shown in the extract, so the position of the poorest economies cannot be read from these results.

Coverage limits what can be concluded. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, and the Private Participation in Infrastructure database records only projects with a contractual private role in low- and middle-income countries. Public investment, which carries much of energy infrastructure in the poorest countries, is outside it. Annual totals can also swing with a few large projects, so the endpoints of 2015 and 2024 do not describe the years between.

Concessional finance is harder to assess. Net official development assistance to the least developed countries was reported by 32 countries in 2023, but the series covers all aid and not aid for energy. The extract therefore gives no clean energy figure for concessional support, and it cannot be said whether international cooperation on clean energy research and technology, the subject of target 7.a, has grown. Targets 7.a and 7.b are worded without a numerical threshold, such as a sum to be mobilised or a capacity to be installed. Progress can therefore be described but not scored as met or missed, and any judgement depends on how expand, enhance and facilitate are read.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The evidence points to rising renewable shares worldwide, but the gains are uneven and the finance behind them is concentrated. Two indicators are read separately here. For the share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption, the trend tool classes the world as on track or target met, at a rate of 0.0255. The same classification applies to East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, high income countries and upper middle income countries. Low income countries show regression, at a rate of -0.0064. Lower middle income countries (0.0079), South Asia (0.0112) and Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) show marginal progress, and the tool states that significant acceleration is needed; the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan show moderate progress, at 0.0129, with acceleration needed. For the non-hydroelectric share of electricity production, the world rate is 0.11, and every group except low income is classed as on track or target met; low income shows regression, at -0.0558. The trend tool was run with no quantified target, so these classifications measure direction and pace and not distance from a defined goal.

Private investment follows a similar pattern. Upper middle income countries recorded US$58.39 billion of energy investment with private participation in 2024, against US$31.02 billion in 2015. Lower middle income countries moved from US$7.42 billion to US$7.89 billion over the same years, which is close to flat in current dollars. Only 46 countries reported in 2024, so the totals describe the projects recorded and not all investment. Official assistance cannot be read in the same way: the series for net ODA to the least developed countries shows 32 reporting countries in 2023, and the result gives no regional or income-group levels. Whether concessional finance has offset the weak private flows to poorer countries therefore cannot be shown here. As context that these data do not test, private capital tends to favour markets with larger demand, deeper finance and more settled regulation.

The spread of non-hydroelectric renewable shares across countries has narrowed, with the coefficient of variation falling from 1.712 in 2015 to 1.358 in 2021 across 208 countries. The slope of change on starting level is -0.0040, with a p-value of 0.882 and an R-squared of 0.001, so it cannot be distinguished from zero. The narrowing in spread is therefore not evidence that low starters are catching up systematically.

Targets 7.a and 7.b carry no quantified goal, so progress can be read in more than one way. Rising shares, rising private investment in some regions and falling investment in others can each be cited as success or failure, depending on the threshold chosen. Installed capacity in developing countries, the quantity named in the section's question, is not among the series examined. For 2030, the pattern implies that the countries furthest behind, low income and lower middle income, are those where pace is weakest and private finance is thinnest.

Three proposals follow. Development finance institutions and bilateral donors should direct concessional funds and risk guarantees towards low income and lower middle income countries, where private flows are thinnest. National governments in those countries should publish procurement and permitting rules for renewable projects, so that private participation is not confined to upper middle income markets. The statistical offices of the OECD and the World Bank should report net ODA for energy by recipient group, so that the support the targets name can be followed.

w-c09-1-2.text:
### World income per person has grown at under 2 per cent a year

World GDP per capita grew by 1.9 per cent in 2015 and by 2.0 per cent in 2025, according to the World Bank's World Development Indicators. A decade that opened and closed at almost the same rate, a little under 2 per cent a year, is the first finding of this section. Growth of that size doubles average income only over several decades, and it sits far below the pace that the second reading of target 8.1 asks of the least developed countries.

Target 8.1 can be read in two ways. Its first clause asks for per capita economic growth 'in accordance with national circumstances', which sets no number. Its second asks for at least 7 per cent GDP growth a year in the least developed countries, a figure for total output, not for income per person. The two measure different things: GDP growth includes the effect of a rising population, and in countries with fast population growth the gap between the two can be wide. This section uses GDP per capita growth as its main indicator, because it describes the change in output available to each resident, and turns to total GDP growth when the 7 per cent threshold is considered. Gross national income per capita is a third measure, which adds income earned abroad and subtracts income paid out; it is reported for fewer countries and is not the basis of the comparisons here.

The path of world growth over the longer run reads as a sequence of shocks rather than as a steady rise. The break analysis of the annual change in the world rate finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The mean annual change was -2.8 percentage points across 2008 and 2009, the years of the global financial crisis, and then +5.8 in 2010 as output recovered. The pattern repeated with greater force around the pandemic: the mean change was -5.4 in 2020 and +9.4 in 2021, followed by -3.1 in 2022. Between 2011 and 2019 the mean annual change was -0.2, a gentle drift downward and not a collapse, and from 2023 to 2025 it was again -0.2. These are changes in the growth rate from one year to the next, not growth rates themselves, and they should be read as the size of each swing.

The reading matters for 2030. A world economy that returns each time to roughly 2 per cent growth, after shocks that arrive about once in a decade, offers no sign of the acceleration that sustained income gains would need. The figure for 2025 rests on 186 countries reporting, against 211 in 2015, so the latest year is less complete than earlier ones and may be revised as late reports arrive.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than six

Regional growth rates in the World Bank's World Development Indicators spread widely at both ends of the decade. In 2015 GDP per capita in South Asia grew by 6.5 per cent, against 0.2 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa and 0.8 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Latin America and the Caribbean contracted, at -0.7 per cent. The spread is a description of a single year, not of a settled order, and no ratio between regions is claimed here.

South Asia remained the fastest region throughout, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, a little below its 2015 rate. East Asia and Pacific held close to the same position, at 4.0 per cent in 2015 and 3.9 per cent in 2025. As context, both are regions in which investment and expanding manufacturing and services have long pushed incomes upwards. South Asia's trend over the decade is classed as on track or target met, with an annual rate of 0.0465 on income per person in constant 2015 US dollars. East Asia and Pacific shows the same classification, at 0.0357. Since no numerical target is set for income per person in this series, the classification reflects only the direction and pace of the trend.

The wealthier regions moved the other way. Europe and Central Asia slowed from 1.6 per cent in 2015 to 1.3 per cent in 2025, and North America from 1.9 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Their trend rates over the decade, 0.0150 and 0.0167, are classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. High-income countries as a group went from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0151, in the same class. Slower growth at high levels of income is a common pattern, usually explained as context by the limited scope for catching up and by ageing populations, though the results do not test this.

The two regions that recovered most from their 2015 positions are Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from -0.7 per cent to 1.6 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.2 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Both ended the period close to the world rate of 2.0 per cent, yet the decade-long trend tells a less comfortable story. Latin America and the Caribbean has a trend rate of 0.0054, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and Sub-Saharan Africa a rate of -0.0020, classed as regression. A single good year at the end does not offset a decade in which income per person barely rose or fell. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew by 0.8 per cent in 2015 and 0.9 per cent in 2025, with a trend rate of 0.0076, also classed as marginal progress.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after -2.9 per cent in 2015, yet their trend rate in income per person over the decade is 0.0007, classed as stagnation. Lower-middle-income countries grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025, up from 4.0 per cent in 2015, with a trend rate of 0.0292. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0371. The poorest countries therefore gain least in the level of income, which helps explain why gaps between groups persist. For 2030, a growth rate near 2.5 per cent in the poorest group would have to be sustained for many years before it altered that picture.

### Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015

The breaks in the annual change of world GDP per capita growth locate the large movements in the series. The break analysis of the World Development Indicators finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The segments between them are short, and several consist of one year. The breaks describe changes in the rate of growth, not its level: a mean change of -2.8 points in 2008-2009 means that the growth rate fell by that amount each year on average across those two years. The analysis does not measure what share of the movement each shock explains, so the section claims only where the breaks fall and how large they are.

The global financial crisis is the first large shock in the series, and it lies before 2015. The 2008-2009 segment has a mean annual change of -2.8 points, and 2010 follows with a rebound of 5.8 points. The long segment from 2011 to 2019 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, and it straddles the 2015 baseline. That is a slow drift downward in the growth rate across nine years, not a collapse.

The period after 2015 is dominated by the pandemic. In 2020 the annual change in world growth was -5.4 points, the largest fall in the series. The 2021 segment records a rise of 9.4 points, the largest rise. The 2022 segment then shows a change of -3.1 points. The segment from 2023 to 2025 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, so growth was drifting down again, much as in 2011-2019. These shocks are why the world rate in 2025, at 2.0 per cent, can resemble the rate in 2015, at 1.9 per cent, while the path between them was violent. As context, not a result of the analysis, the 2020 fall is usually attributed to lockdowns and the collapse of travel and trade, and the 2021 gain largely to recovery from a depressed base.

Across income groups, the endpoints need the same caution. Low-income countries recorded GDP per capita growth of -2.9 per cent in 2015 and 2.5 per cent in 2025. That is a swing from contraction to modest expansion, but it compares two single years. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 4.0 per cent to 4.6 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, and high-income countries from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent. The low-income rate of 2.5 per cent in 2025 is well below the 7 per cent that target 8.1 sets for the least developed countries, although that group is not the same as the low-income group and the two should not be equated.

A ten-year endpoint comparison therefore hides the volatility that the breaks reveal. Two years close in value say nothing about the swings between them, and a large gain between endpoints may only be recovery from a poor starting year. The comparison also depends on coverage. The number of countries reporting GDP growth was 211 in 2015, 210 in 2019 and 210 in 2021, but only 186 in 2025. The fall from 209 countries in 2022 to 204 in 2023 and 200 in 2024 suggests that data arrive late, so the 2025 values rest on fewer countries and may be revised. For 2030 this implies that the latest readings are provisional, and that any judgment on target 8.1 should wait for the revised series.

### Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence

Beyond regional averages, the trend classification sorts countries by how fast GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) has moved since 2015. No numerical 2030 target exists for this measure, so the classes are relative: each country is judged by the compound annual rate it has sustained since the baseline, and by the share of the distance to a notional target that this rate would cover by 2030. The classes are a reading of momentum, not a verdict against a legal threshold, and a different reading of target 8.1 would shift some countries between them.

Of 209 countries assessed, 74 are on track or have met the notional target, and they hold 56.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 36 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 16.4 per cent of the population. Another 44 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 11.8 per cent. Fifteen countries stagnate, with 5.0 per cent of the population, and 40 are in regression, with 10.3 per cent. Stagnation and regression together therefore cover 55 countries but a much smaller share of people, and the marginal group is a further part of those that lag. The results give no country-level income figures, so they do not show whether the lagging countries are the poorest.

The regional trends agree with this picture. South Asia has a compound rate of 0.0465, East Asia and the Pacific 0.0357, the upper middle income group 0.0371 and the lower middle income group 0.0292, and all four are classed as on track or target met. Europe and Central Asia (0.0150), high income countries (0.0151) and North America (0.0167) show moderate progress, as does the world as a whole at 0.0176. Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0054) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0076) show marginal progress. The low income group, at 0.0007, is classed as stagnating. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0020, is classed as regression, even though its annual growth rate recovered from 0.2 per cent in 2015 to 1.6 per cent in 2025.

The question of the 7 per cent target needs a careful answer. Target 8.1 sets that rate for GDP, not per capita GDP, in the least developed countries. The results hold no group figure for the least developed countries, so no direct test is possible. The nearest evidence is the low income group, whose GDP per capita grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after a contraction of -2.9 per cent in 2015. That rate is well below 7 per cent, and per capita growth is lower than GDP growth where population is rising. Only South Asia, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, comes near the threshold, and it is not a least developed group. On present evidence the target looks out of reach for the low income group, though the claim rests on a proxy.

The post-2020 recovery matters for the reading. The low income rebound from -2.9 per cent to 2.5 per cent is a sizeable swing, yet the trend classification still reads that group as stagnating, at a rate of 0.0007. Growth after a shock restores lost ground before it adds new income, so a good year does not by itself change the long-run class. Coverage also thins at the end of the series: 186 countries reported growth in 2025, against 211 in 2015, so the latest figures are less complete than earlier ones.

For 2030 the implication is plain. If present rates hold, most of the people in the countries assessed live where incomes rise at a pace that meets the notional test, while 40 countries are in regression and 15 stagnate. The 7 per cent goal is a different measure, and none of the groups in the results reaches it.
