w-c09-6-1.text:
### The world share fell by 1.4 points, from a 2015 base, not by a substantial margin

Target 8.6 asks for a substantial reduction in the proportion of youth not in employment, education or training by 2020. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so any verdict rests on a reading chosen by the analyst. Here the reading is plain: a substantial reduction would be a fall large enough to be visible against the starting level and to change the position of most regions.

On that reading, the world record is modest. The modelled ILO estimate puts the global share at 21.2 per cent of the youth population in 2015 and at 19.8 per cent in 2025. The share therefore declined over the decade, but by a margin of well under a tenth of the 2015 level in relative terms, and the latest year available is five years after the target date. The series is a modelled estimate, not a count from a single survey. Countries with sparse labour force data receive values built from regional patterns and covariates, so small movements in the world figure should be read with caution. The estimate covers 182 countries reporting in 2025.

The pace of change did not follow a steady path. The break analysis of the annual change in the world share finds shifts in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by about 0.2 points a year on average. Between 2013 and 2019 the mean annual change was close to zero, at 0.02 points, which means that the share was essentially flat in the years just before the target date. The first five years after 2015 therefore delivered almost no reduction, and the decline recorded by 2025 was produced mainly after the pandemic year, a pattern taken up in a later part.

The income groups show why the global figure hides unequal movement. In high-income countries the share moved from 12.2 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025, and in upper middle income countries from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent. Lower middle income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The global average is thus pulled down by the middle-income and wealthier groups, while the poorest countries ended the period with a higher share than they began with.

Taken together, these results do not support a claim of substantial reduction by 2020. The 2015 base fell by a small amount over ten years, was flat before 2020, and rose in the poorest countries. Whether a stricter or looser reading of 'substantially' would change the verdict is a question the target text leaves open, but no plausible reading treats a decline of this size, reached five years late, as meeting the intent of the goal.

### Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden

Regional levels in 2025 range widely. North America holds the lowest share, at 11.8 per cent of youth, down from 12.5 per cent in 2015. East Asia and Pacific stands at 12.8 per cent, down from 14.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 13.0 per cent, down from 15.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is at 19.3 per cent, from 21.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is at 21.4 per cent, slightly above its 2015 level of 20.9 per cent. South Asia shows the largest fall among the regions, from 28.4 per cent to 23.4 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is highest at 32.1 per cent, and its share rose from 31.1 per cent. The regional picture therefore runs in two directions: most regions moved down modestly, while two did not.

Income groups show the same split. Low-income countries rose from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent, while lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent, and high-income countries from 12.2 per cent to 10.9 per cent. The poorest group is thus the one in which the share grew, and by 2025 it stands well above the others. Demographic pressure, thin labour demand and limited schooling places are well-established contexts for this pattern in low-income settings, though the series itself does not show what drives it.

Women carry the largest burden. The world female share was 30.2 per cent in 2015 and 27.1 per cent in 2025, far above the total of 19.8 per cent. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the female share was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged, so nearly half of young women are outside work and study. South Asia improved from 46.0 per cent to 37.1 per cent, yet remains high. Low-income countries moved against the trend, from 32.6 per cent to 34.4 per cent. Norms on care work and early marriage, and limits on women's mobility and employment, are the usual explanations, stated here as context only.

Among countries, the classes of the trend assessment are scattered. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the direction of the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 28 show moderate progress and 29 marginal progress, while 21 stagnate and 58 regress. The regressing group holds 18.8 per cent of the population, more than the on-track group. No numeric target exists, so the classes rest on the analyst's reading of the trend, and they should be read as direction rather than as a verdict.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, did not narrow. The Gini coefficient was 0.231 in 2015, 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for a little over half of the inequality in both years. Convergence is not shown: the beta of -0.00428 has a p-value of 0.214, not distinguishable from zero. Countries starting higher did not reliably improve faster.

### The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement

The movement of the world share is better read as a sequence of shocks than as a steady trend. The break analysis of the annual change in the modelled ILO series finds breaks in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by a mean of 0.22 points a year. That is the only stretch in which the decline looks like steady progress, and it ended before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.

From 2013 to 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which is near stagnation. The share did not fall during the years in which the target's clock was running towards 2020. In 2020 the annual change jumped by 1.37 points, the largest movement in the series. The timing coincides with the closure of schools and workplaces during the pandemic. That explanation is context drawn from well-established knowledge; the data show the timing of the break and cannot isolate its cause.

The recovery was nearly as sharp. From 2021 to 2023 the share fell by a mean of 1.08 points a year, which took back much of the 2020 rise. From 2024 to 2025 the mean annual change was 0.15 points, so the recovery has stopped. The long-run rate of change to 2030 for the world, at -0.0070 on the trend tool's scale, is read by that tool as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. A series that rises and falls with the cycle of 2020 gives a weak basis for expecting steady gains.

Sub-Saharan Africa followed a different path. Its breaks fall in 2014, 2021, 2023 and 2024. From 2006 to 2013 its mean annual change was -0.04 points. From 2014 to 2020 it rose by 0.45 points a year, well before the pandemic and faster than the world as a whole in the same years. The rise is consistent with a young population growing faster than jobs and school places, but that is an inference the data do not test. After 2020 the region eased, with a change of -0.29 points a year in 2021 and 2022 and -1.23 points in 2023, then a flat 0.00 points a year in 2024 and 2025. The trend tool still classes the region as regression to 2030.

The pandemic therefore explains the large swings, but not the stagnation that preceded it. Because the world share was already flat in 2013 to 2019, the recovery of 2021 to 2023 restored a position rather than advancing it.

### The 2020 target was missed, and 2030 needs faster progress and a clearer definition

The target was not met in a substantial sense by 2020, and the trend to 2030 does not close the gap. The trend assessment classes the world as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a compound annual rate of -0.7 per cent from the 2015 baseline. The regional rates show the same pattern. East Asia and Pacific stands at -1.2 per cent a year and High income at -1.2 per cent, both marginal. Latin America and the Caribbean is at -0.9 per cent, and North America at -0.6 per cent. Only Europe and Central Asia, at -1.6 per cent, and South Asia, at -1.9 per cent, reach the moderate class, and both still need acceleration.

Three groups are classed as regression: Low income, with a rate of 0.9 per cent a year, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, at 0.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.2 per cent. The country count is as stark. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the assessed population. A further 28 show moderate progress, 29 marginal progress and 21 stagnation. Regression affects 58 countries, holding 18.8 per cent of the population. The largest single population share, 32.1 per cent, sits in the marginal class.

The gender gap sharpens the picture. Among young women the world share fell from 30.2 per cent in 2015 to 27.1 per cent in 2025. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan it was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged. South Asia fell from 46.0 to 37.1 per cent, a real gain from a very high base. Low income rose from 32.6 to 34.4 per cent.

Countries have not drawn together. Population-weighted Gini across countries rose from 0.231 in 2015 to 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025, and Theil's T from 0.088 to 0.096 and then 0.100. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015, 60.3 per cent in 2020 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for more than half of the inequality throughout. The convergence test gives a beta of -0.0043 with a p-value of 0.214, which cannot be told from zero, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.471 to 0.532 across 182 countries.

For 2030 the implication is that the present pace leaves the world far from any reading of substantial reduction. The estimates are modelled, and survey coverage behind them is thin in several low-income countries, so classes for individual countries carry uncertainty.

w-c09-8-2.text:
### Tourism receipts and arrivals as measures of Target 8.9

Target 8.9 commits governments to devise and implement policies for sustainable tourism that creates jobs and promotes local culture and products. The target names three outcomes: sustainability, employment and the promotion of local culture and products. It sets no numerical threshold and no baseline, and it leaves open what counts as sustainable. It can be read as a call for policy, as a call for better outcomes, or as both, and the indicators do not settle which.

The World Development Indicators hold tourism series that measure something narrower. International tourism arrivals count overnight visitors who travel to a country other than the one in which they usually live. International tourism receipts record the expenditure of those inbound visitors, including payments to national carriers for international transport. A related series expresses receipts as a share of total exports, and another isolates receipts for passenger transport items. These describe the scale of the sector and its weight in an economy's external earnings.

None of them observes the content of Target 8.9. Arrivals say how many people came, not how long they stayed, what they damaged or what they preserved. Receipts record money entering a country, not how much of it remained with local workers, local producers or cultural institutions, since a large share of spending can leave through imports, foreign ownership and international transport. Neither series counts jobs in tourism, measures pay or conditions, or distinguishes cultural products from other purchases. Domestic tourism, which is large in many countries, falls outside both series.

The bench can therefore read how large and how widely reported international tourism is, and how that changed around 2015 and 2020. It cannot say whether tourism became more sustainable or more locally beneficial. The first result in this section, on the arrivals series, shows how many countries report in each year, which sets the limits of any comparison. In the figures from 2000 to 2020, reporting reached 202 countries in at least one year, and it is on that base that the later parts read the series. Findings on size and recovery are evidence about the economic scale of the sector. They are indirect evidence on the target, and the text says so wherever it matters.

### Coverage of the arrivals series, 2000 to 2020

The arrivals series, International tourism, number of arrivals (ST.INT.ARVL), has reports from 202 countries and territories in at least one year of the period covered. No single year reaches that figure. In 2000, 175 countries reported. The count then rose with some interruptions: 173 in 2002, 179 in 2005, 186 in 2007 and 190 in 2008. It dipped to 187 in 2009 and returned to 190 in 2010. Counts of 191 in 2011 and 190 in 2014 show a plateau, although the counts for 2012 and 2013 are not cited here.

The peak came after the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted. In 2015 and 2016, 194 countries reported arrivals, the highest counts among the years cited. The count then eased to 190 in 2017, 186 in 2018 and 179 in 2019. The 2019 count equals that of 2005. Part of the decline after 2016 may reflect delays in compiling national statistics, since the latest years of many series are filled in later. The data do not show whether that explains it.

The figure for 2020 is the most striking: 132 countries reported, against 179 the year before, the largest fall between consecutive years among those cited. As general context from outside these results, the pandemic is understood to have sharply reduced international travel, and statistical offices and tourism authorities also faced disruption. The coverage count cannot separate the two effects. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded very few arrivals and not reported them, or may have been unable to compile the figure. Either way, the 2020 values come from a smaller and possibly different group of countries than the 2019 values.

This limits what can be said about size and recovery. This part reports coverage only and gives no values for arrivals or receipts. A total for 2020 compared with 2019 would mix a real fall in travel with a change in which countries are counted. Comparisons are sounder when restricted to countries reporting in both years, and even those say little about countries that did not report. The data cited here do not extend beyond 2020, so they say nothing on recovery in later years.

The coverage result also lists aggregates for the arrivals series: seven regions, four income groups and the world. They inherit the reporting gaps described above, and the results do not state how non-reporting countries are treated, so aggregate values for 2020 should be read with caution.

### Regional and income-group comparison

The coverage result names the aggregates for which the arrivals series (ST.INT.ARVL) is reported: seven regions, four income groups and the world total. The regions are East Asia and Pacific (EAS), Europe and Central Asia (ECS), Latin America and the Caribbean (LCN), the Middle East and North Africa (MEA), North America (NAC), South Asia (SAS) and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF). The income groups are high income (HIC), upper-middle income (UMC), lower-middle income (LMC) and low income (LIC). The world aggregate (WLD) supplies a common reference. Their existence is the only thing the result establishes about them.

The question of size is therefore left open in this part. The result gives no arrivals value, no receipts value and no year-on-year change for any aggregate, so no statement can be made here about how many visitors any region or income group received, or how much they spent. The size of tourism, the main matter the section was asked to answer, cannot be read from the coverage result alone, and it would be wrong to infer a ranking from the order in which the codes are listed.

Once values are retrieved, a comparison across the aggregates would show where visitors concentrate, and whether tourism is a channel of growth open to low-income countries or one dominated by wealthier destinations. Set against receipts, arrivals would indicate spending per visitor, which bears on Target 8.9 because jobs and local products depend on spending, not on headcounts alone. A large regional total can reflect many countries, a large population or a few heavily visited destinations, and a count of arrivals cannot separate these.

The reporting record also constrains any later comparison. In 2019, 179 countries reported arrivals; in 2020 the number was 132. Aggregates depend on how many members report, so totals for 2020 may rest on thinner evidence than those of earlier years. The pandemic is generally understood to have sharply reduced international travel, but the coverage count cannot show how much of the 2020 change reflects fewer journeys and how much reflects changes in reporting. A ranking of regions and income groups, and any reading of which have recovered, should wait until arrivals and receipts values are retrieved for each aggregate and read alongside their reporting counts.

### The 2020 collapse in reporting and the uncertain recovery

The count of countries reporting arrivals fell from 179 in 2019 to 132 in 2020. Among the years cited, this is the largest single-year change. The count stood at 194 in 2015 and again in 2016, its highest level among the years cited, then slipped to 190 in 2017, 186 in 2018 and 179 in 2019. That earlier decline may reflect delays in compiling national statistics for recent years; the coverage tool records it but cannot explain it.

The drop of 2020 mixes two effects that the coverage count cannot separate. The pandemic is generally understood to have reduced international travel sharply, as context from outside these results, and the same disruption affected national statistical offices, which rely on border counts and accommodation surveys. A country absent from the 2020 count may have recorded fewer visitors, may have published nothing, or may have published late. The difference between the 179 countries of 2019 and the 132 of 2020 is a difference between two counts. It does not show which countries are missing, so the gap may be concentrated in some regions or income groups. The coverage result does not show this either way.

No arrivals or receipts value was retrieved for this section. The size of tourism, in visitors and in dollars, and the depth of the 2020 fall are therefore left unanswered here, and the recovery after 2020 cannot be judged. The shelf lists 2020 as the latest year for arrivals, for receipts in current US dollars, for receipts as a share of exports and for passenger transport receipts. No value for 2021 or later is available, so the pace of any rebound cannot be measured. The GDP deflator series describes economy-wide prices and cannot stand in for tourism volumes.

A reading of the recovery requires arrivals and receipts for 2021 onward for the same countries that reported in 2019, so that the comparison is made on a fixed group and is not distorted by changing coverage. Receipts would also have to be set against price changes, since a figure in current dollars can rise while visitor numbers stay below earlier levels. For Target 8.9, whose date is 2030, progress after 2020 is at present unmeasured by this shelf.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The coverage record shows that Target 8.9 can be monitored only in part, and that monitoring weakened in the year that matters most. The arrivals series was reported by 194 countries in 2015 and in 2016, and by 179 in 2019. In 2020 the count was 132. Across the whole period 202 countries and territories reported in at least one year, so no single year gives full coverage.

The question of how large tourism receipts and arrivals are, and how far they recovered after 2020, cannot be answered from the results retrieved for this section. They contain counts of reporting countries only, and no value of arrivals or receipts for any year, region or income group. The series descriptions show that the arrivals, receipts, export-share and passenger-transport series all have 2020 as their latest year, so the shelf holds no observation of the recovery. Any statement about whether tourism has returned to its earlier level lies outside the data. The fall from 179 countries in 2019 to 132 in 2020 reflects some mixture of a real fall in travel and changes in reporting, and the coverage count alone cannot apportion the two. Progress towards 2030 cannot be judged from series that end in the year of the disruption.

A second implication concerns what the series measure. Arrivals and receipts describe the volume and value of inbound visits. Neither shows whether tourism creates jobs or promotes local culture and products, the outcomes the target names. Receipts also include payments to national carriers for international transport, so they are not wholly spending inside the destination. They are quoted in current dollars, and the shelf also holds the GDP deflator, a reminder that nominal values drift with prices.

Three proposals follow. National statistical offices, especially those that stopped reporting in 2020, should resume annual reporting of arrivals and publish the missing years. The agencies that compile the indicators should present receipts always alongside arrivals, so that spending per visitor and the weight of transport payments can be read. The custodians of the Sustainable Development Goal indicator framework should add measures of tourism employment and of local content in tourist spending, since Target 8.9 cannot otherwise be tested against its own wording.

w-c06-4-3.text:
### The global picture: parliaments close to a quarter, management data thinner

Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in single or lower national parliamentary chambers worldwide in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015. The world share therefore rose by about four percentage points in a decade, and 184 countries reported a figure for 2025, so the world value rests on near-complete coverage. Set against a benchmark of 50.0 per cent, women still hold little more than a quarter of seats. The shortfall from that benchmark is the distance between 27.2 and 50.0 per cent, which should not be confused with the 2015 world share.

Target 5.5 does not name a number. Its wording, women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making, can be read as parity, with women and men holding equal shares, or as a threshold of participation sufficient for women to shape decisions, which is often placed lower. The indicator for seats cannot settle the question, because it counts occupants of seats and says nothing about their influence, the committees they chair or the offices they hold. This book uses 50.0 per cent as the benchmark, since a population that is about half women supplies the plainest reference for equal opportunity, and findings are stated against it while the figure itself is reported in full so that readers may apply a different reading.

The parliamentary measure covers one arena of public life. The economic arena is represented by the female share of employment in senior and middle management, a series built from the occupational classification of managers. It excludes junior management, so it describes positions of real authority rather than all supervisory work. The question asked here includes the share of managerial positions held by women, and the answer must be stated plainly: the results available to this section give no value of that share for any country, year or group, only counts of reporting countries and classifications of trend. The section therefore cannot say what per cent of senior and middle management positions women hold, and it does not infer one from the parliamentary figure or from the female share of the labour force, which measures something different.

Two features of the series bear on every statement made from it. First, the World Bank publishes no aggregates for it, so no world or regional share can be quoted, and any comparison must proceed country by country. Second, the number of reporting countries has changed sharply over time. It was 40 in 2000, 72 in 2010 and 77 in 2015, and reached 95 in both 2019 and 2022. It then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and stood at only 48 in 2025. A total of 154 countries have reported in at least one year.

These counts matter as much as the values. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years may reflect a change in who reports rather than a change in women's position. The drop to 48 in 2025 may reflect survey lags, as labour force surveys are often processed with delay, but the data show only the count and not its cause. The 2025 observations for management are therefore not a sound basis for a statement of trend, and the later parts of this section rely on the years of fuller coverage when discussing managerial positions. The parliamentary series, by contrast, is reported almost everywhere and is the firmer ground for conclusions about direction and pace.

### Regions and countries differ by more than twenty-five points

Regional averages for 2025 span a wide range. Latin America and the Caribbean leads at 36.6 per cent of parliamentary seats held by women, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 31.7 per cent and North America at 29.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 27.0 per cent, close to the world value of 27.2 per cent. East Asia and Pacific follows at 23.3 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands at 16.9 per cent, and South Asia is lowest at 11.2 per cent. A regional average can conceal wide differences between countries within a region, and the results give no country-level figures for this part.

The two lowest regions are also the ones that did not advance. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 17.5 per cent in 2015 to 16.9 per cent in 2025, and the trend tool classes it as regression. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the only large decline among the regions shown, and is also classed as regression. At the observed rate its share would reach 8.9 per cent in 2030. The data do not show why the share fell. Where a chamber is dissolved or not elected, the reported share can alter sharply, so a movement of this size may owe more to political events than to a gradual trend; that is context from general knowledge, not a finding of the results.

Income groups show a narrower spread than regions. High-income countries reached 31.2 per cent in 2025, upper middle income 27.0 per cent, low income 24.8 per cent and lower middle income 23.6 per cent. Low-income countries therefore hold a higher share than lower-middle-income ones, so income alone does not order the outcome. The results contain only group means and offer no explanation for the pattern.

The country distribution of progress towards a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 is more sobering than the regional averages. Of 187 countries assessed for parliaments, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold only 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest group is 69 countries with marginal progress that would need significant acceleration, covering 44.6 per cent of the population. Another 19 countries are stagnant, with 25.1 per cent of the population, and 39 countries are regressing, with 12.7 per cent. Stagnation and regression together hold 37.8 per cent of the assessed population, against 17.6 per cent where progress is on track or moderate. The population weights differ from the country counts: regression is the second most common outcome by number of countries, yet stagnation touches about twice as many people.

Management shows a similar pattern with a heavier weight on the negative end. Of 121 countries assessed for the female share of senior and middle management, 17 are on track or have met the target, with 8.1 per cent of the population. Moderate progress applies to 27 countries and 17.7 per cent of the population, and marginal progress to 34 countries and 31.3 per cent. Stagnation affects 6 countries with 2.7 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded in 37 countries, which hold 40.3 per cent of the population, against 12.7 per cent in parliaments. The assessment covers fewer countries than for parliaments, so these shares describe the countries with data rather than the world, and survey-based series can be revised from one round to the next, so the classification should be read with caution.

### What changed since 2015, and the limits of the evidence

Since 2015 the largest gain in women's share of parliamentary seats was in Latin America and the Caribbean, where the regional value rose from 27.9 per cent to 36.6 per cent. North America rose from 22.3 per cent to 29.5 per cent. Europe and Central Asia moved from 25.7 per cent to 31.7 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 19.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. These are regional averages and conceal wide differences between countries within each region.

Two regions moved the other way. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region slipped from 17.5 per cent to 16.9 per cent. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the lowest regional value in 2025 and the only large fall. The indicator does not separate the causes of these movements. As general context, a lower share can arise from an election, a change in the chamber counted, a suspended or dissolved legislature or the loss of a quota; nothing in these series measures it.

The classification against a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 shows how uneven the movement has been. For parliaments, 24 countries are on track or have met the target, 36 show moderate progress, 69 show marginal progress, 19 are stagnating and 39 are regressing, among 187 countries assessed. The 24 countries on track hold only 4.9 per cent of the population assessed, whereas the 69 with marginal progress hold 44.6 per cent, the largest share of any class. The number of countries on track therefore overstates how far most women live where parity is approaching.

For senior and middle management, the classification covers 121 countries: 17 are on track or have met the target, 27 show moderate progress, 34 marginal progress, 6 stagnate and 37 regress. The 37 regressing countries hold 40.3 per cent of the population assessed, against 12.7 per cent for the 39 regressing countries in parliaments. The two sets of countries differ, so the comparison is indicative only, but regression appears to touch a larger share of people in management. As general context, legislative seats can be shifted by quotas and electoral rules, whereas management positions depend on firms, labour markets and care responsibilities; the data do not test this.

The results do not report the female share of senior and middle management itself, whether for a country, a region or the world. They give only classes, counts of countries and population shares, and the coverage tool lists no aggregate for this series. The question of what share of managerial positions women hold therefore cannot be answered with a figure from this evidence, and this section answers it for parliaments alone.

The management evidence is also thin in coverage. Across all years, 154 countries have reported at least one value, but the number reporting in a given year has varied: 40 in 2000, 77 in 2015, 90 in 2020 and 95 in 2022. The count then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and only 48 countries had reported for 2025. Reporting lags in the underlying surveys are one possible explanation, offered as general context and not as a finding. Comparisons of 2025 with earlier years would rest on different sets of countries and cannot be trusted as a measure of change.

The regional trend summary for management returned no result, so no claim is made about how any region is moving on this indicator. Nor can these indicators say why countries advance or regress; they record outcomes, not the quotas, laws, party practices, employer conduct or social norms behind them. Whether the period after 2020 slowed or accelerated progress cannot be established for management, and for parliaments the results give levels and classes but no separate account of the pandemic years.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the rates observed since 2015, no region reaches the 50.0 per cent benchmark for parliaments by 2030. The world trend is classed as marginal progress, with an expected value of 29.8 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.25. East Asia and Pacific is expected at 25.7 per cent (ratio 0.21) and Europe and Central Asia at 35.2 per cent (ratio 0.39), both marginal. The high-income group is expected at 34.6 per cent, so wealth does not by itself close the gap. Latin America and the Caribbean comes closest, at 41.9 per cent, and is the only region classed as moderate progress; even there acceleration is needed.

The regions at the bottom of the range are moving in the wrong direction. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected value of 8.9 per cent in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also classed as regression, at 16.7 per cent. Low-income countries are expected at 26.5 per cent and lower-middle-income countries at 25.3 per cent, both marginal. These projections extend a linear trend and are not forecasts. The data do not show what would move a national figure; electoral reform or political disruption, as general context outside these results, can change a country's value within one election cycle. Target 5.5 can also be read as parity at 50.0 per cent or as a lesser threshold of fair representation, and the classes above follow the first reading.

The country classification for parliaments, given in full earlier in the section, places 24 of 187 countries on track and 39 in regression. For management, 121 countries are assessed, 17 are on track and 37 are in regression, which hold 40.3 per cent of the assessed population against 12.7 per cent for parliaments. The sets of countries differ, so the comparison is indicative only.

The results give no female share of senior and middle management for any country, year or group; they give only classes and counts of reporting countries. The managerial half of the question, what share of managerial positions women hold, therefore cannot be answered with a value from these results. Reporting is also thin at the latest point: 48 countries reported in 2025, against 95 in 2022. A lag in survey processing may explain this, as general context and not a finding.

Three proposals follow. National parliaments and electoral bodies in South Asia and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where the regional share has fallen, should review candidate-nomination rules and consider reserved seats or party quotas. National statistical offices should report the female share of senior and middle management every year, so that the 2025 gap in reporting is closed. International statistical agencies should publish regional aggregates for management, which are absent today.

w-c08-3-3.text:
### The global share rose by 2.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2020

The world share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption stood at 17.4 per cent in 2015 and 19.7 per cent in 2020. The share therefore rose over the five years, and the direction is clear. Whether the magnitude meets the aim of the target is a separate question, and the data alone do not settle it. Over the period the share grew at a compound rate of 0.0255 a year, which the trend tool classes as on track or target met. That label rests on a trend tool that has no numerical target to measure against, so it should be read as a statement about the pace of change, not as a verdict on sufficiency.

Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix, and it names no threshold. Two readings are available. The first is a rise in the share: renewables supply a larger fraction of all final energy. The second is a rise in absolute use: more renewable energy is consumed, whatever the fraction. The two can diverge. Where total demand grows quickly, absolute renewable use can climb while the share stagnates or falls. The indicator reported here, renewable energy consumption as a percentage of total final energy consumption, measures only the first reading. A rise in the share is the stricter test, because it requires renewables to outpace the growth of demand as a whole.

The word 'substantial' compounds the ambiguity. No agreed numerical benchmark exists in the target text, so any judgement of sufficiency rests on a chosen standard: a doubling, a fixed number of points, or a path consistent with climate goals. Since no such standard is set in the target, this account treats the change from 17.4 to 19.7 per cent as an observed change and states plainly where a reader's own threshold would alter the verdict. By any reading, a gain of this size from a base of 17.4 per cent leaves the large majority of final energy supplied by other sources in 2020.

The composition of the indicator also matters for interpretation. Final energy consumption includes heat and transport as well as electricity, and the renewable share counts traditional biomass such as wood and charcoal burned for cooking and heating. A share can therefore be high in poor countries because of reliance on fuelwood, which is neither modern nor clean, and the aims of Goal 7 treat it differently from wind, solar or hydropower. The headline figure thus mixes two quite different kinds of renewable use, a point taken up in the regional comparisons that follow.

A limit on the evidence must be stated. The series is reported by 212 countries in every year from 2015 to 2021, but only 71 countries report a value for 2022. For most countries, therefore, the record ends in 2020 or 2021 for practical purposes, and the comparison of 2015 with 2020 is the last one that rests on near-complete coverage. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks that followed, cannot be read from this series with confidence. For the 2030 horizon, this means the trajectory is known only for the first five of fifteen years, and the later years remain to be measured.

### Regional levels differ by a factor of ten, and nearly all regions rose

Regional levels of the renewable share span a wide range. In 2020 Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 70.3 per cent of total final energy consumption, South Asia at 36.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 34.2 per cent. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 7.5 per cent. The highest regional value is therefore about nine times the lowest, and the gap is wide in both years.

The ranking does not measure the quality of the energy system. In poorer regions a high share may reflect the burning of wood, charcoal, crop residues and dung for cooking and heating, which counts as renewable in the indicator. These fuels are often gathered unsustainably, carry serious health costs through indoor air pollution, and supply energy of low efficiency. A low share in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan may follow from large oil and gas endowments that have long dominated power generation and final use; this is context from outside the data. The indicator cannot separate traditional biomass from modern capacity such as wind, solar, hydropower or modern bioenergy, so a region can score high with little modern renewable infrastructure and low with a fast-growing one. Other series on the shelf, such as electricity output and output excluding hydropower, give a partial view of modern capacity but cover electricity only.

All six regions rose between 2015 and 2020. Latin America and the Caribbean gained from 28.2 to 34.2 per cent, the largest rise of any region. Europe and Central Asia moved from 12.9 to 15.1 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 13.0 to 14.8 per cent, and North America from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent. The results do not test why these regions rose; falling costs of wind and solar and policy support are commonly cited in the wider literature, and are context outside the data. South Asia rose more slowly, from 34.9 to 36.9 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 68.0 to 70.3 per cent. In both, a rise in the share is ambiguous: it may reflect new modern capacity, or continued reliance on biomass. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 7.1 to 7.5 per cent.

The income groups show the same pattern and one reversal. The low-income group fell from 77.0 to 74.6 per cent between 2015 and 2020, the only group to decline. The fall does not necessarily signal a worsening of the energy system. As incomes rise and electricity and fossil fuels reach more households, the biomass share can fall before modern renewables replace it, so a lower share may accompany a real improvement in access. Equally, it may reflect growth in fossil-fuel use that outpaces renewables. The indicator alone cannot tell which. Lower middle income countries rose from 41.7 to 43.3 per cent, upper middle income countries from 14.9 to 16.8 per cent, and high income countries from 10.6 to 12.8 per cent.

The rise was broad across regions but small in the regions with the highest shares and absent in the low-income group, where the share fell. Reading target 7.2 as a rise in the share, the world rose; reading it as growth in modern, sustainable renewables, the aggregate hides much of what matters, because the indicator cannot show modern capacity. Coverage also limits comparison: 71 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot yet confirm whether the gains held after the shock of 2020. The results do not project values for 2030.

### Country trajectories diverge: 73 on track, 85 in regression

The classification of countries separates the world into groups whose experience since 2015 has been very different. Of 202 countries assessed, 73 are classed as on track or target met, and these hold 37.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 11 countries show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed (3.8 per cent of population), and 14 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration (22.2 per cent). Nineteen countries are stagnating (4.8 per cent of population). The largest group by count is the 85 countries in regression, which hold 31.8 per cent of the population.

The label 'on track' needs careful reading. Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the renewable share but gives no numeric value, so no threshold exists against which progress can be measured. The classification therefore rests on an extrapolated rate of change: the observed trend is projected forward to 2030, and a country is called on track when the direction is positive and the pace is adequate by the tool's own scale. 'On track' here means a positive trend only. It does not mean that a country will reach any particular share, and a country that starts from a very low share can be called on track while remaining far from a renewable-based energy system. The reading of 'substantially' is open: a rise of a few points could count under one interpretation and fall short under another.

Count and population tell different stories. The on-track group holds the largest population share of any class, 37.5 per cent, yet it has fewer countries (73) than the regression group (85), whose population share is 31.8 per cent. Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries, and the two classes hold 4.8 and 31.8 per cent of the population respectively. The data therefore show a split world: a large share of people live in countries with a positive trend, and a comparable share live in countries where the share has fallen. The world rate of 0.0255 is positive and classed as on track, but it is an aggregate and does not describe each country.

The regional rates help to explain the pattern. The rates for East Asia and Pacific (0.0267), Europe and Central Asia (0.0325), North America (0.0370) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0390) are all classed as on track, as are the high income (0.0381) and upper middle income (0.0240) groups. The groups under the greatest strain are the low income group, where the rate is negative at -0.0064 and classed as regression, and the lower middle income group, at 0.0079, classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) and South Asia (0.0112) are also marginal, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0129) show moderate progress.

The indicator does not reveal why the share falls in low income settings, and the following is context, not a finding. The renewable share of final consumption in such countries is widely understood to be dominated by traditional biomass used for cooking and heating. If total consumption grows with non-renewable supply, or households shift away from biomass, the share can fall even while other goals advance. A fall is therefore not necessarily a failure of renewable policy. The gains in richer regions are commonly linked to deliberate expansion of modern renewables, but the share alone cannot confirm what was added.

For 2030 the implication is that a positive global rate can coexist with 85 regressing countries. The target will be met in substance only if the lagging groups change course, and the data cannot say whether modern renewables are replacing traditional biomass or merely sitting beside it.

### Convergence is weak and coverage thins after 2020

The convergence test asks whether countries that began with a low renewable share have gained faster than those that began high. Across 71 countries with data for both 2015 and 2022, the estimated coefficient is -0.0101 (p 0.0006, R2 0.190). The negative sign indicates that countries starting higher changed by less each year, so low-share countries gained slightly faster, and the p-value of 0.0006 indicates that the relationship is unlikely to be chance. The magnitude is small, however, and an R2 of 0.190 means that initial level explains under one fifth of the variation in change. The remainder lies elsewhere. National policy, resource endowment, the pace of electrification and the use of traditional biomass are plausible influences, but they are context only, since the results do not measure them.

The coefficient of variation points the same way. It stood at 1.040 in 2015 and at 1.039 in 2022, a change in the third decimal place. Dispersion across these countries is therefore not narrowing. A coefficient near 1.0 means that the standard deviation of national shares is about equal to their mean, which describes a very unequal distribution. Weak catch-up in the slope, combined with unchanged dispersion, means that the spread of national shares in 2022 was about what it had been in 2015.

This result needs careful reading because the renewable share in final consumption mixes two quite different things. In many low-income countries a high share reflects reliance on firewood and charcoal, not modern renewable capacity, and a fall in that share can accompany progress in clean cooking and electrification. In high-income countries a rising share usually reflects wind, solar and hydropower in the electricity system. These are well-established patterns, but the indicator cannot separate them. A convergence test that treats both as one scale cannot distinguish a desirable fall in traditional biomass from a failure to expand modern renewables. The weak convergence found here should not be read as proof that poorer countries are being left behind in modern renewable deployment.

The sample is also a limit. Reporting for this series was broad in the early years: 207 countries in 2000, 210 in 2010 and 212 in every year from 2012 to 2021. In 2022 it fell to 71 countries. The 212 countries of 2021 and the 71 of 2022 are not comparable bases, and the data do not show that the 71 are a random draw from the 212. The convergence estimate describes only those that reported, and it cannot be extended to the world or to any region without that caveat.

The drop matters for 2030 because the years after 2020 are the ones in which the pandemic recovery, the energy price shock and new policies would show. Those years are visible for only a third of countries. The series is fully covered to 2021, so the record to that year is secure, while any statement about 2022 rests on a partial group. This is a reporting lag, not a finding of decline, and it should be read as a gap in evidence.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The share has risen, from 17.4 per cent in 2015 to 19.7 per cent in 2020. Whether that is substantial cannot be settled from the data, because target 7.2 sets no number. Read as any increase, the world figure moved in the right direction. The world rate of 0.0255 a year is a pace of change only, and it is not a verdict on whether that pace suffices. The results do not project 2030, so no forecast of the 2030 share is offered here.

The countries are divided. The 85 countries in regression hold 31.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 19 more, with 4.8 per cent, show stagnation. A rising world average therefore conceals a large population living where the share has fallen or stood still.

The low-income group shows the problem most clearly. Its share fell from 77.0 per cent in 2015 to 74.6 per cent in 2020, yet the level remains very high. As context outside the data, such levels usually reflect reliance on firewood, charcoal and other traditional biomass, which counts as renewable in this series but is neither modern nor clean. A fall in the share can accompany welcome developments, such as grid expansion, and a high share can accompany poverty and indoor air pollution. The indicator alone cannot separate these cases, and conclusions for the poorest countries must be drawn with that caution.

For 2030, the results show where acceleration would count. The 73 countries on track hold 37.5 per cent of the population, and the 14 countries with marginal progress hold a further 22.2 per cent; faster gains in the latter large populations would move the global figure most, although the tools do not measure each group's contribution. Convergence is weak, and the 2022 data cover only 71 countries, so the picture after 2020 cannot be confirmed for most of the world.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c04-2-4.text:
### The global picture: most countries are on course, the world is not

Target 3.2 sets two thresholds that every country is asked to reach by 2030: neonatal mortality of at most 12.0 per 1,000 live births, and under-five mortality of at most 25.0 per 1,000 live births. The target is worded as an aspiration for each country, not for the world as a whole. It therefore asks a different question from a global average, and the two readings must be kept apart when the evidence is assessed.

The direct answer to how many countries have reached the thresholds is that the data cannot give a single count. The classification used here merges countries that have met a threshold with countries projected to meet it, so it states how many are on track or have met the target, not how many have already arrived. On that combined reading, 130 of 196 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 of 196 are on track or have met the under-five threshold.

The world averages remain above both thresholds. The global neonatal mortality rate fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024, still above the threshold of 12.0. The global under-five mortality rate fell from 42.9 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024, against a threshold of 25.0. Both series cover all 196 countries reporting in 2024, so the averages are not distorted by missing reporters.

The country classification gives a more favourable picture. In each case the on-track class is a clear majority of countries, around two thirds or more. The population shares are close to the country counts: the 130 countries hold 72.4% of the population assessed for neonatal mortality, and the 135 countries hold 74.7% for under-five mortality. A reader may therefore ask how most countries, holding about three quarters of the world's people, can be on course while the world average stays above both lines.

The answer lies in what each figure measures. A count of countries gives every country equal weight. A population share weights each country by its inhabitants. A world average is a rate per live birth, so it reflects where children are born rather than where the general population lives. As a hypothesis that the results here do not test, countries with many births and high mortality would pull the average upward; the data given do not show birth numbers by country.

A second distinction concerns the phrase on track. The classification compares each country's recent trend with the path needed to reach the threshold by 2030. A country that is on track has not necessarily reached the threshold; it is projected to do so if its pace holds, and the projection can fail if progress slows. The threshold can also be read in more than one way: the target says all countries should aim for at least as low as the stated values, so a country already far below them has no further obligation under the wording, though its rate may still fall.

The remaining countries show where the shortfall lies. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Four are stagnating and 9 are regressing. These 66 countries hold 27.5% of the population assessed, a smaller share than the on-track group. For under-five mortality, 39 countries need acceleration, 15 need significant acceleration, 3 are stagnating and 4 are regressing. The 3 stagnating countries hold 4.9% of the population assessed, a larger share than their count alone would suggest.

The gap between the two readings matters for policy. A statement that most countries are on course is true and encouraging, but it can mislead if it is taken to mean that the goal is within reach for children everywhere. The sections that follow therefore set the counts beside regional and income-group levels, so that the distribution of the shortfall is visible.

### Counting countries: how many have met or are on track for each threshold

The trend classification covers all 196 countries for both indicators, and it gives the plainest count of how many have reached, or are heading for, each threshold. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 target, and they hold 72.4% of the population of the countries assessed. For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met the 25.0 per 1,000 target, with 74.7% of that population. The under-five threshold is therefore the more widely met of the two, although the gap is small.

The class labelled on track or target met joins two different situations. A country that crossed the threshold years ago and a country that is merely on course to cross it by 2030 are counted together. The classification does not separate them, and the data given here cannot say how many of the 130 and the 135 have already arrived. A further count of countries whose latest value lies at or below each threshold would answer the question directly. Until it is made, the figures describe the direction of travel rather than the number of countries that have finished the work. The distinction matters because countries already below the threshold need only hold their position, while those merely on course remain exposed to any slowdown.

Below the leading class, the two indicators diverge. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 7.8% of the population, and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 11.9%. For under-five mortality the order is reversed: 39 countries are in the moderate class, with 16.1% of the population, and only 15 are in the marginal class, with 4.0%. Many countries therefore sit closer to the under-five threshold than to the neonatal one. This agrees with the established pattern that deaths in the first 28 days fall more slowly than deaths later in childhood. Infections, malnutrition and malaria respond to vaccines, nets and treatment, whereas newborn deaths depend on the quality of care around birth, on preterm complications and on skilled attendance, which take longer to build.

The worst classes are small in country count but not in consequence. Four countries stagnate on neonatal mortality, holding 2.1% of the population, and nine regress, holding 5.7%. For under-five mortality, three countries stagnate, holding 4.9% of the population, and four regress, holding 0.3%. The stagnating group on the under-five indicator thus carries a notable population share for so few countries, whereas the regressing group is small. Regression usually accompanies conflict, state collapse or the breakdown of health services, and a small population share does not make it less serious for the children living there.

The population shares also show that the country counts and the people counts do not coincide. Neonatal on-track countries are 130 of the 196 assessed, yet hold 72.4% of the population; under-five on-track countries are 135 of 196, with 74.7%. Even so, a substantial minority of the world's people live in countries that are not on course for each threshold. Since the target is written for every country, those countries decide whether the goal is met in the sense the text intends.

The classification carries the usual caution about reading a trend as a forecast. It extrapolates past rates of change to 2030, and the years after 2020 were disturbed by disruption to services and by uncertain estimates in places with weak registration. A country may be assigned a class on a series that is largely modelled rather than counted. The counts should thus be read as a guide to where acceleration is needed, not as a guarantee of where the thresholds will be met.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of seven

Regional neonatal mortality in 2024 ranged from 3.6 per 1,000 live births in North America and 4.1 in Europe & Central Asia to 22.7 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan and 26.6 in Sub-Saharan Africa. Under-five mortality spans a wider range, from 6.4 in North America to 71.2 in Sub-Saharan Africa. The tools give no ratio between regions, so the gap is stated here only by the pairs of values, as the figures show. Neonatal deaths make up a larger share of child deaths where overall mortality is low, because the causes that remain there (prematurity, birth complications, congenital conditions) fall last. Where mortality is high, infections, malnutrition and malaria continue to claim children after the first month, and the under-five gap widens accordingly. This is context drawn from established knowledge, not a result of the data.

Income groups show the same ordering. Low-income countries recorded 24.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024 and 68.8 under-five deaths. High-income countries recorded 2.8 and 5.1. Upper middle income countries, at 6.8 and 13.1, sit well inside both thresholds. Lower middle income countries, at 21.6 and 43.8, lie outside both. The income gradient is steep because the interventions that save newborns and young children depend on health-system capacity: skilled attendance at birth, emergency obstetric care, neonatal care units, vaccination, and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria. These need financing and trained staff that low-income systems have found hard to sustain.

The trend classification separates regions that will reach the thresholds from those that will not. East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, and the high income and upper middle income groups are classed as on track or target met for both indicators. East Asia & Pacific reached 6.7 neonatal and 13.2 under-five in 2024, and Latin America & Caribbean 8.3 and 15.4, so each is already below both thresholds. The expected 2030 neonatal values are lower still, at 5.8 for East Asia & Pacific and 7.3 for Latin America & Caribbean. For these regions the target is no longer a constraint, and the policy question becomes one of equity within countries, which regional averages conceal.

South Asia is the clearest case of rapid change. Its neonatal rate fell from 25.4 in 2015 to 16.6 in 2024, and its under-five rate from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rate of decline in the under-five rate, -0.0502, is the fastest of any region, and the trend ratio of 1.30 means the pace exceeds what the target requires. The expected 2030 under-five value is 19.7. For neonatal mortality the tool also gives the class on track or target met, with a ratio of 0.96 and a rate of -0.0462 a year. The expected 2030 value of 12.5 nonetheless lies above the 12.0 threshold. The class is reported as the tool gives it, but the neonatal result is better read as close to the threshold than as secured.

The regions and groups that fall short are those where mortality is highest. Low-income countries cut under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8 per 1,000 between 2015 and 2024, at a rate of -0.0231 a year. At that pace the expected 2030 value is 59.8, far above 25.0, and the trend ratio of 0.42 is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The neonatal record is weaker: 28.1 fell to 24.9, an annual rate of -0.0133, with an expected 2030 value of 23.0 against a threshold of 12.0 and a ratio of 0.32. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same pattern, with an expected 2030 under-five rate of 63.3 and a neonatal rate of 25.0. Neonatal mortality tends to fall more slowly than under-five mortality when health systems are weak, as a matter of general experience.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan group has a mixed profile. Its under-five rate, 36.4 in 2024, is classed as moderate progress needing acceleration, with an expected 2030 value of 31.1. Its neonatal rate, 22.7, is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 20.3. The group combines countries with low mortality and countries in prolonged conflict, so the regional figure conceals wide internal differences.

The lower middle income group needs a caution. Its under-five rate fell from 55.3 to 43.8 and its neonatal rate from 26.9 to 21.6, which are real gains, and both are classed as moderate progress, with trend ratios of 0.59 and 0.55. The expected 2030 values of 37.5 and 18.7 stay above both thresholds. The trend output for this group was partly truncated, so only the numbers and classifications shown can be relied upon.

### What changed since 2015, and why the pace differs

Between 2015 and 2024 every region and income group reduced both rates, but the pace varied widely. South Asia fell fastest. Its neonatal mortality went from 25.4 to 16.6 per 1,000 live births, and its under-five mortality from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rates of change, which the trend tool expresses as a proportional rate, were -0.0462 for neonatal and -0.0502 for under-five mortality, against -0.0133 and -0.0151 for the world as a whole. The region is classed as on track for both indicators, although its neonatal trend would leave it at an expected 12.5 in 2030, with a ratio of 0.96 of the distance to the target covered, so the neonatal result is close to the threshold and not clear of it. Sub-Saharan Africa moved slowest on the neonatal measure, from 29.2 to 26.6, a rate of -0.0103. Its under-five rate, from 85.0 to 71.2, fell at -0.0195, which is faster than its neonatal rate but still leaves it far from the threshold, with an expected 63.3 in 2030 against a target of 25.0.

The pattern across income groups is similar. Low-income countries reduced neonatal mortality from 28.1 to 24.9, a rate of -0.0133, and under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8, a rate of -0.0231. Both are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Lower-middle-income countries did better on both, with neonatal mortality falling from 26.9 to 21.6 (-0.0241) and under-five mortality from 55.3 to 43.8 (-0.0256); both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. East Asia & Pacific, already at lower levels, still reduced under-five mortality from 16.6 to 13.2, a rate of -0.0251. High-income countries and North America moved slowly, at -0.0142 and -0.0034 for under-five mortality, but this is expected near a floor, where each further gain is harder to achieve.

A consistent feature is that neonatal mortality falls more slowly than under-five mortality. For the world, the neonatal rate went from 19.4 to 17.2 while the under-five rate went from 42.9 to 37.4, and the proportional rates confirm it: -0.0133 against -0.0151. In Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group the neonatal rate declined at a visibly slower pace than the under-five rate. A well-established explanation, given as context and not shown by these series, is that deaths after the first month are mostly caused by infections, malnutrition and malaria, which respond to vaccination, sanitation, nutrition programmes and basic treatment. Neonatal deaths come largely from prematurity, birth complications and neonatal infection, which require skilled attendance at birth, functioning referral systems and specialised newborn care. These depend on stronger health systems and take longer to build.

The differences in pace must be treated cautiously. The indicators measure outcomes, not interventions, and nothing in these series shows which policies produced the faster falls in South Asia or the slower ones in Sub-Saharan Africa. Plausible hypotheses include the expansion of facility births in South Asia, and the heavier burden of conflict, fragility and weak health financing in low-income countries. These remain hypotheses. The estimates are modelled from survey and registration data that are sparse where mortality is highest, so differences of a few thousandths in the annual rate should not be over-read.

The period after 2020 cannot be separated in these series. Both indicators are reported as annual figures to 2024, and the comparison of 2015 with 2024 shows no reversal at the regional level, but it conceals any pause in particular years. Whether the disruption of routine health services in 2020 and 2021 slowed declines cannot be answered from the levels used here.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The trend classification projects most countries to be on track for both thresholds in 2030, but this is a projection and not an observed count. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries of the 196 assessed are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 threshold, and 135 are on track or have met the under-five threshold of 25.0. Each count mixes countries already at or below the threshold with countries only projected to reach it, and no tool separates the two. The number of countries that have already arrived is therefore unknown, and the forecast depends on past rates of change continuing.

The countries still short are concentrated, on the regional and income-group projections, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income settings. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.0 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2030 against a threshold of 12.0, and 63.3 under-five deaths per 1,000 against 25.0. Low-income countries are expected to reach 23.0 and 59.8 respectively. The world as a whole is expected to reach 15.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 and 34.1 under-five deaths per 1,000, above both thresholds. South Asia needs a precise reading. For neonatal mortality its projected 2030 value is 12.5, above 12.0, and the tool classes it as on track, so the class and the projected value sit in tension and the region should be treated as close to the threshold, not clearly past it. For under-five mortality its projected value is 19.7, below 25.0.

Newborn deaths are the harder problem. As context, neonatal deaths depend on skilled care at birth, management of preterm birth and infection, and functioning referral systems, which are costlier to build than the campaigns that drove earlier gains. A country can therefore meet the under-five threshold and still miss the neonatal one. On neonatal mortality, 4 countries stagnate and 9 regress; on under-five mortality, 3 stagnate and 4 regress. The countries that regress on neonatal mortality hold 5.7% of the population assessed.

Two cautions apply. The classification projects a past rate of change forward, and a different period or method could move countries near a class boundary. The wording 'at least as low as' can be read as a ceiling for every country in 2030 or as a direction of travel for those already below it; this section uses the first reading. National rates also hide inequality within countries.

Four proposals follow.

proposals: Ministries of health in countries classed as stagnating or regressing should prioritise skilled birth attendance, newborn care units and referral systems, since neonatal mortality is the threshold furthest from reach.
