w-c05-7-4.text:
### The global share of trained primary teachers has risen only slowly

The world share of primary school teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and at 82.2% in 2024, a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030, and the indicator used here reads that as a share of 100%. Against that reading, roughly one primary teacher in five worldwide still lacks the minimum organised training required in the country where they teach. The trend calculation gives a world ratio of 0.15 against the pace needed, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Continuing the 2015 to 2024 slope would bring the world to 83.4% in 2030.

The measure needs careful reading. The indicator counts teachers who have received the minimum organised training, whether before or during service, that a given country requires. That minimum is set nationally and differs widely. A teacher counted as trained in one system might not meet the standard of another, and a share of 100% in one country does not imply equal preparation in the classroom. Nor does the indicator capture the quality of the training, the subject knowledge of teachers, or whether they remain in post. The figure is therefore a floor on qualification, not a measure of teaching quality. Readings of the target also vary: some take 4.c to mean full national qualification, others a substantial rise from a baseline, and the data cannot settle between them.

Coverage adds a second caution. The 2024 world value rests on the latest reporting of each economy, and only 13 countries reported in 2025, so the most recent year says little. Several regional values end in 2022, and the upper middle income group has a single value, for 2022, at 80.7%, which allows no change to be read. Late reporting may be more common where systems are weaker, but the results do not test this.

The section's guiding question also asks whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling. The bench returned no result for that ratio, so the question cannot be answered from the evidence held here. Series on teacher numbers exist for primary and secondary levels, but a count of teachers without matching enrolment does not give a ratio. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is likewise not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings, safety or inclusion. The evidence speaks to the training of teachers, not to class size or the learning environment.

The slow world movement matters for 2030 because training is a precondition for much else in the chapter, from completion and learning to pre-primary provision. A world share that rises by under two points in nine years, spanning the disruption of 2020 and the years after it, leaves the target far out of reach on the present slope. The results do not show why the share has stalled; one possible explanation is that recruitment has outpaced training in some systems, but this remains a conjecture that the series cannot test. The regional parts that follow show where gains and losses lie.

### Regions and income groups differ by more than twenty points

The regional picture in 2024 is one of wide separation. North America stands at 97.9% of primary teachers trained, South Asia at 87.7%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 81.8% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 80.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa, whose latest reading is 2022 rather than 2024, stands at 68.8%. The gap between the best and the weakest of these regions is therefore about twenty-nine percentage points, taking the 2024 reading for North America and the 2022 reading for Sub-Saharan Africa. Readings from different years are not strictly comparable, and the Sub-Saharan figure may understate or overstate the position in 2024.

Income groups show a similar pattern. Low income countries stand at 69.2% in 2022, close to the Sub-Saharan level, which is expected because most low income countries lie in that region. Upper middle income countries have only a 2022 reading, 80.7%, so no change over the period can be given for that group. Training here means the minimum organised preparation required by each country, so the percentages measure compliance with national standards and not a common level of skill. A country with a demanding standard can score lower than one with a modest standard, and comparisons across regions should be read with that in mind.

The spread among countries, weighted by population, is modest in absolute terms. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.094 in 2015, fell to 0.073 in 2020 and rose to 0.097 in 2024, ending slightly above its starting level. The Theil index fell from 0.026 in 2015 to 0.011 in 2020. In that decomposition the share lying between regions was 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020. In those two years about half of the inequality among countries was therefore a difference between regions, and the other half lay among countries within the same region. The decomposition applies to 2015 and 2020 only; it is not available for 2024 and may have changed since, so it should not be taken as a guide to where action is needed now.

These comparisons carry a caveat about coverage. Countries reporting numbered 85 in 2015 and 93 in 2020, but only 79 in 2024. The Theil index and its regional decomposition are missing for 2024, so the latest year cannot be set against the earlier ones on that measure. A change in the number of reporting countries can alter the Gini by changing who is counted, and the rise to 0.097 may reflect that as much as any real divergence; the series cannot separate the two. Reporting for 2025 is thinner still, with 13 countries. For 2030 the implication is that monitoring of Target 4.c is weakest in the years that matter most for judging it.

### Gains in South Asia contrast with declines in richer regions

South Asia recorded the largest regional gain in the share of trained primary teachers. The share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly fifteen percentage points in nine years. The region moved from below the world average of 80.4% in 2015 to above the world level of 82.2% in 2024. Its trend is the only regional one classed as on track, with an expected 99.3% in 2030 if the rate of change continued. Lower middle income countries, a group that includes several South Asian economies, rose more modestly, from 76.4% in 2015 to 83.3% in 2024, and their expected value for 2030 is 88.2%. The data do not show which measures lay behind the South Asian rise. A change in how a country defines the minimum training required would produce the same movement as a real improvement in preparation, so the gain should be read as a reported change in the share, not as proof of better teaching.

The richer regions moved in the opposite direction. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020, the last year for which the regional reading is given here. High income countries fell from 95.9% in 2015 to 92.1% in 2024, and North America slipped from 99.3% to 97.9% over the same period. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 82.7% to 81.8%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan declined from 83.9% to 80.5%. These falls are small beside the South Asian gain, but they run against the direction of Target 4.c, and the trend tool classes all of these regions as regressing. The results do not explain them. Teacher shortages that lead systems to hire staff before they complete a full programme are one possible cause, and changes in national definitions or reporting are another; neither can be tested with these series.

Across countries, the pattern is one of catching up. A convergence test over 48 countries between 2015 and 2024 gives a coefficient of -0.071 (p below 0.001) with an R2 of 0.342, which means that countries starting from lower shares of trained teachers tended to gain faster than those starting higher. The dispersion of the shares narrowed only slightly: the coefficient of variation moved from 0.165 in 2015 to 0.155 in 2024. Convergence is therefore real but slow, and about a third of the variation in country changes is accounted for by the starting level alone. The test covers only the 48 countries with readings at both ends of the period, so it describes the reporting countries and not the world, and the systems with the sparsest records may be underrepresented.

The size of the teaching workforce does not appear to explain the changes. The rank correlation between changes in the share of trained primary teachers and changes in the number of primary teachers across the same 48 countries is -0.095, and the correlation between 2024 levels is 0.168. Both are weak. Expanding the workforce therefore did not visibly coincide with a higher trained share, and countries that added the most teachers were no more likely to see that share rise. This is a cautionary finding for Target 4.c, which speaks of qualified teachers and not of teachers alone. The correlations are descriptive and say nothing about the mechanism.

The period since 2015 and the years after 2020 cannot be read cleanly from these series. Several regional readings end in 2020 or 2022, and the school closures of 2020 and 2021 disrupted the collection of statistics as well as schooling. A gap in reporting may conceal a change that has not yet been measured. For 2030, the lesson of this part is that large gains are recorded where the share rose fast, as in South Asia, but that they are not general, and that richer regions with falling shares cannot assume the levels of 2015 will return unaided. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings or learning environments.

### Most countries are not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

The country counts show that the 2030 picture is mixed. In primary education, 64 of the 129 countries assessed, holding 65.9% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have already met the target of a fully trained teaching force. This is a large share of people but not of countries. Against it stand 36 countries with 26.3% of the assessed population whose trained share is falling rather than rising. A further 13 countries, with 2.4% of the population, show marginal progress that would need to speed up considerably, 12 countries, with 4.2%, show moderate progress that still needs acceleration, and 4 countries, with 1.2%, are stagnant. The two largest groups are the on-track countries and the regressing ones, so the pattern is divided at its poles.

Secondary education tells a similar story with less coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 hold 61.5% of the population and are on track or have met the target, while 36 hold 27.6% and are regressing. Fourteen countries with 7.7% of the population show marginal progress, 10 with 2.1% show moderate progress and 7 with 1.0% are stagnant. The share of people living in regressing countries is slightly higher at secondary level than at primary level, and the share in on-track countries is slightly lower. Fewer countries report secondary data, so the secondary result rests on a thinner base and is the less certain of the two.

The regression count needs careful reading. A falling trained share does not necessarily mean that teaching has worsened. One possible explanation is that systems expanding quickly may recruit teachers faster than they can certify them; another is that a country raising its minimum standard may see teachers once counted as trained fall below the new bar. Both are conjectures drawn from general experience, and the results given here cannot separate them.

The same feature complicates the target itself. Target 4.c speaks of qualified teachers, and the indicator measures minimum organised training, pre-service or in-service, as defined nationally. A share of 100% therefore does not mean equal preparation across countries. The target can be read as a share trained to national standards, a share trained to an international standard, or a growth in the absolute supply of teachers. The assessment here uses the first reading, with 100% as the goal, because it is the one the trained-teacher series can express. On the reading of a substantial increase in supply, the result is undetermined: the teacher-count series were not tested against a trend in these results.

Two parts of the section's question cannot be answered from the results. No pupil-teacher ratio was computed, so whether ratios are falling is not stated; the teacher-count series on the shelf were not combined with enrolment. Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive school facilities, was not assessed, because none of the series for this section measures it.

For 2030, on the full-training reading, the target will be missed at the world level. The projected world share of trained primary teachers is 83.4%, with a trend ratio of 0.15, which falls in the class of marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 72.0% and low income countries at 73.2%, so the groups starting furthest behind are expected to remain furthest behind. South Asia, projected at 99.3%, is the one region on course. Regions that are regressing are mostly those that began from higher levels, such as Europe and Central Asia at a projected 86.9% and high income countries at 89.7%.

Among the 48 countries reporting in both 2015 and 2024, convergence is present but slight: the coefficient of variation of the primary trained share fell from 0.17 to 0.16, with a beta of -0.07. This describes only those 48 countries, not others. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the trained share was 0.09 in 2015, 0.07 in 2020 and 0.10 in 2024. Differences narrowed up to 2020 and then widened again, though the 2024 reading covers 79 countries against 93 in 2020, so the comparison is imperfect and the cause cannot be read from these results. The between-region share of inequality, 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020, applies to those years only; it shows that regional differences then accounted for about half of the spread.

The findings point to the following proposals.

w-c06-2-4.text:
### Intimate partner violence is measured in few countries and few years

Target 5.2 calls for the elimination of all forms of violence against all women and girls, in public and private life, including trafficking and sexual and other types of exploitation. The indicator that the World Bank's catalogue holds for it is narrower: the proportion of ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49 who were subjected to physical violence, sexual violence or both in the previous 12 months. The series note describes it as drawn from United Nations and World Health Organization sources. It therefore speaks to one form of violence and one age band, and says nothing directly about violence by non-partners, harassment in public, trafficking or exploitation. Women who have never had a partner, girls under 15 and women over 49 fall outside it. A country with a low reading on this series cannot be taken to have met the wider target.

The coverage is thin even for this narrow measure. Across the whole period, 106 countries report in at least one year. Those reports are spread unevenly over time, and in most years very few countries contribute. One country reports for 2000 and 2 for 2005. The counts then run at 4 for 2006, 3 for 2007, 4 for 2008 and 4 for 2009, falling to 2 for 2010 and 3 for 2011. A year with one to four reporting countries cannot support a comparison of regions or a global reading; it records a handful of observations.

The pattern changes sharply in 2012, when 35 countries report. This single peak accounts for a large share of all the country entries on the shelf. The bench results do not say why the count rises in that year, and the reason is not asserted here; whether the values come from direct surveys or from estimation is likewise not recorded in the results. After the peak the counts fall back to 7 for 2013 and rise to 12 for 2014, 8 for 2015, 14 for 2016 and 7 for 2017, the latest year with data. No year after 2017 is held, so the series is silent on the period from 2020, when many observers warned that violence at home had risen. The shelf holds no regional or world aggregates for this indicator, so no summary can be drawn from published totals.

These features shape what the rest of the section can responsibly say. Differences between countries can be described where values exist, but the values rest on different years. A reader should treat the indicator as a partial snapshot of one form of violence, not as a tracked measure of progress towards the target.

### Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap

In 2012 the spread of intimate partner violence among reporting countries can be measured, and it is the only year in which that is possible with confidence. That year 35 countries report, the largest count in the series. The Gini coefficient is 0.29 and the Theil index is 0.17, which indicate a moderate spread between countries: prevalence is neither uniform nor extremely unequal. The coefficient of variation is 0.66. The results do not record the weighting basis beyond the tool's own description, and no further claim is made about it.

The decomposition shows where the measured inequality lies. Of the Theil inequality in 2012, 66.2% is between regions rather than within them, and the remaining third lies within regions. This is a descriptive split of a single year among 35 reporting countries. It does not show why regions differ and supports no causal reading. Shared legal traditions, social norms about marriage and household authority, services for survivors and the history of conflict are well-established candidates for explaining regional patterns in violence, but the data hold no variable that could test any of them.

The limits of this result need to be stated plainly. The results do not record which countries are among the 35 or how they were chosen. Surveys on violence are costly and sensitive, and in general they are fielded where governments permit them and funders support them, so absent countries may differ systematically from those present. The between-region share is computed only among reporting countries, so a region represented by two or three countries adds little information on differences within it. The figures describe the spread of a particular sample in a particular year. They are not a global distribution and should not be read as one.

Other years are not compared with 2012 here. Only 7 countries report in 2013 and 8 in 2015, and 14 in 2016, the next largest count after 2012. The tool produced the spread calculation for 2012 alone, and the results state no minimum number of countries for it. Whether the 14 countries of 2016 would support a comparable calculation is therefore left open, as is whether they are the same countries as in 2012. For 2030 the consequence is that the regional pattern visible in 2012 is a snapshot of where evidence was gathered, not a baseline from which progress can be measured.

### Change over time cannot be established, while attitudes are better documented

The trend tool, which classifies each country against the 2030 target of zero, assesses no country for intimate partner violence. All five classes show zero: no country is on track or has met the target, none shows moderate progress, none shows marginal progress, none is stagnating and none is regressing. The count of countries assessed is also zero. This is not a finding of no change. It is a finding that change cannot be measured, because the tool needs repeated observations for the same country and the series does not supply them. Without them, the series cannot show whether prevalence has risen or fallen since 2015, or since 2020, when lockdowns and household stress were widely reported to have raised risks for women at home. That report comes from outside the bench data. Neither progress nor regression can be stated, and any claim about the direction of violence against women over the period rests on sources outside this series.

The attitude indicator, the share of women who believe a husband is justified in beating his wife for at least one of five reasons, is better documented. 72 countries report it in at least one year between 2000 and 2024. Annual coverage is modest and uneven, however. It was 6 countries in 2000 and 4 in 2002, rose to 10 in 2005 and 14 in 2012, and stood at 12 in both 2016 and 2018. After 2018 it fell sharply: 2 countries in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fell around 2019 and 2020. Interrupted fieldwork is a plausible hypothesis, but it needs a source outside these results, and the partial recovery since is likewise unexplained. Even in the best year, 14 countries report, so a global or regional average of attitudes for any single year would describe a shifting group of countries and not a stable panel.

The attitude series therefore offers more scope for comparison over time within countries that survey repeatedly, but it does not allow a global verdict. The results do not record which countries report, or their income level or survey programme, so the composition of the reporting group is not documented here and some groups may be under-represented.

Attitudes are a proxy and not a measure of violence. Acceptance of wife beating can indicate social norms that sustain abuse and discourage women from reporting or seeking help, and falling acceptance is often read as a sign of shifting norms. But a woman may reject violence and still experience it, and a society may hold permissive views with low recorded prevalence, or the reverse. Answers are also shaped by who is asking and who is present during the interview. The indicator should be read as context for the prevalence data, never as a substitute for them, and it cannot show whether target 5.2 is being met for 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals on measurement

A target of zero by 2030 cannot be assessed from these data. The trend tool classifies no country, and the count of countries assessed is 0. Any statement that the world, a region or a country is on track, or off track, for the elimination of intimate partner violence would therefore be unsupported. In all, 106 countries report in at least one year, but the reporting years cluster so tightly that a single survey wave stands in for a trend. The results give yearly counts only, not the number of years each country reports, so how many countries appear once is not established. Reporting peaks at 35 countries in 2012, against yearly counts of between 1 and 14 in every other year listed, and stands at 7 in 2017, the latest year. The counts for 2001 to 2004 are not given in the results, so those years are either empty or not held. Nothing is recorded after 2017, so neither the years after 2015 nor the pandemic years after 2020 can be read from the series. Lockdowns and strained services are widely reported to have raised the risk of violence at home, but the catalogue holds no figure that confirms or refutes this.

The measurement gap matters because the target is stated in absolute terms. Zero is reached only by sustained decline, and decline can be shown only by repeated measurement in the same country with the same definition. The attitude series is somewhat better placed, with 72 countries reporting in at least one year, and annual counts listed for 2000 to 2024. Yet it measures what women believe, not what they experience, and it thins sharply after 2018, with 2 countries in 2019 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fall, and the composition of the reporting countries is not recorded in the results, so some groups of countries may be under-represented. Attitudes may change before behaviour does, or behaviour may change without attitudes following, so neither series can stand in for the other. Underreporting is a further limit: women may not disclose violence in a survey, and a rise in measured prevalence can follow improved trust in interviewers as well as a real increase.

The one-year spread for 2012, with 35 countries, is descriptive only. It shows how prevalence was distributed among the countries that happened to report, and supports no causal reading of the regional split. Five proposals follow from these findings; they are set out in the list of proposals. They concern the frequency of surveys, the continued collection of the 12-month indicator with a lifetime series beside it, the range of women and forms of violence covered, the conditions for publishing regional aggregates, and the joint reporting of attitudes and prevalence. Until they are met, the record for Target 5.2 will describe a handful of survey years, not fifteen years of progress.

w-c02-2-3.text:
### National poverty lines give the widest view, with uneven reporting

The national-line headcount ratio is the percentage of a population living below the poverty line or lines that a country sets for itself. It is the measure closest to the wording of target 1.2, which asks for a halving of poverty in all its dimensions according to national definitions. Because each country chooses its own line, and often revises it, the series records how each society judges deprivation rather than a single standard. Estimates come from household surveys. Alongside it, the World Bank publishes multidimensional, societal-line and $3.00-a-day series, which later parts of this section set against the national figures.

The series is wide in reach but irregular in time. Over the whole period 161 countries have reported at least one national-line observation, a broad base for a goal that applies everywhere. In any single year, however, only a fraction report. In 2000 the number of countries with a value was 16, and in 2001 it was 15. It rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, then stood between 40 and 50 from 2006 to 2014, with 40 in 2008 and 50 in 2012. The results record this expansion but give no reason for it; the cause lies outside the data.

After the adoption of the goals in 2015, reporting grew rather than shrank. In 2015, 55 countries had a value, and 57 in 2016, followed by 53 in 2017. Counts then reached 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. The year 2020, the first of the pandemic, shows 57 countries, a fall from 2019 that is consistent with disrupted fieldwork, although the data alone cannot show the cause. The peak is 72 countries in 2021.

The decline since then is steep. Reporting was 52 countries in 2022, 40 in 2023 and 31 in 2024, and in 2025 it is only 13. The fall does not mean that poverty has been abolished or that surveys have stopped. Household survey data take a year or more to be collected, harmonised and released, and national-line series are revised as new rounds arrive. The latest years are therefore incomplete, and the count for 2025 is best treated as a record of what has been published so far.

The consequence is practical. A comparison of 2025 with 2015 would rest on 13 countries against 55, which are not the same countries and may not be representative of any region. These results report coverage and not rate levels, so this part does not state how far any national rate has fallen; movement is read from the trend classes in a later part. Any statement about movement toward 2030 has to use the last years of reasonable coverage, up to about 2021 or 2022, and has to separate real change from changes in who reports. The figure on levels for 2025 rests on a thin base and calls for caution in every reading drawn from it.

### Dispersion among countries widened as coverage grew

The dispersion of national-line poverty rates among reporting countries rose after 2013. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.28 in 2013 and 0.34 in 2014, then reached 0.39 in 2015, the year the goals took effect. It was 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018 and 0.63 in 2019. The Theil index followed the same course, from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.26 in 2015 and 0.72 in 2019. Read at face value, the spread among countries in the share of people below their own lines widened markedly over these years. The summary labels these statistics as population-weighted, so the reading is of a spread in which larger countries count for more, as the tool computes it.

This reading needs care, because the set of reporting countries changed at the same time. The number of countries with a national-line estimate was 45 in 2013, 55 in 2015, 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. A rise in the Gini or Theil can reflect poverty rates pulling apart, but it can equally reflect the arrival of countries with very high or very low rates, or the loss of countries in the middle. The series cannot separate these effects, so the figures are not a measured change in inequality between countries over a fixed group. For 2020 the Gini is 0.66 across 57 countries, but no Theil index or regional decomposition is available, so that year cannot be compared in full with its neighbours.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions is high in every year, which suggests that much of the measured dispersion lies between regional groups rather than within them. It was 75.8% in 2013, 88.4% in 2014 and 67.7% in 2015, then 80.7% in 2016, 65.1% in 2017, 86.3% in 2018 and 77.1% in 2019. Across the years with a decomposition the share ranges from 65.1% in 2017 to 88.5% in 2022, so it is never far below two thirds. These shares describe the reporting sample in each year, not a fixed regional structure; the swings are consistent with a changing sample, since adding or dropping a few countries in one region can move the share sharply. Differences in how countries draw their lines also bear on any comparison of levels, as the opening part of this section explains.

After 2020 the picture changes. The Gini fell to 0.35 in 2021, when 72 countries reported, the widest coverage of any year in the record. It then stood at 0.40 in 2022 with 52 countries, 0.35 in 2023 with 40 countries and 0.32 in 2024 with 31 countries. The Theil index moved from 0.20 in 2021 to 0.26 in 2022, 0.21 in 2023 and 0.17 in 2024. The between-region share was 82.6% in 2021, 88.5% in 2022, 76.0% in 2023 and 83.5% in 2024. The fall in dispersion between 2019 and 2021 coincides with a large change in the reporting set and cannot be taken as convergence. Counts fall after 2021, and only 13 countries report for 2025, so the latest years describe a thinner and different group.

For 2030 the implication is that national-line data can show whether a given country is reducing its own poverty rate, but cannot support a claim about convergence or divergence across the world. Assessment of target 1.2 should proceed country by country, over a fixed set of economies with repeated surveys, and the dispersion statistics should be read as a description of who reports in each year rather than of how poverty is distributed.

### Trend classes show most countries on track but a large regressing group

The classification covers 94 countries, those for which the national-line series holds enough observations to estimate a trend. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 3.8% of the population, and 7 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 4.4%. Five countries are stagnant, with 2.1% of the population. The largest adverse group is regression, with 34 countries and 26.0% of the population. Regression is therefore not a marginal finding.

The classes are the only evidence in this section on how national rates have moved. The tool reports a class and a share of population for each country group, not a rate level or a change in points, so no national rate is stated here. The classes say which direction and pace each national series has taken against the halving reading; they do not say how far any rate has fallen or risen. In this reading, regression means a series moving away from the target, which is not the same as a stated rise in a particular rate.

The weight of the favourable class comes from population rather than from numbers alone. On track countries are 41 of the 94 assessed, fewer than half by count, yet they hold 63.8% of the assessed population. A reader should not infer that two thirds of countries are succeeding; the count and the population share tell different stories, and both are given here. The tool does not show which countries drive the population share, so nothing is claimed about who holds most of it.

No numeric target exists for national lines. Target 1.2 asks for a halving of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions, but it names no common threshold, because each country sets its own line and method. The classes therefore rest on a reading of the target, not on a fixed value. Under the halving reading, a country is on track if its rate is falling fast enough to be halved by 2030 from its baseline, which is 2015 or the first year after. That is one reading among several. A target could instead be read as an absolute reduction in the number of people, as a reduction by a set number of points, or as a halving from the earliest available observation. Each reading would sort some countries differently, and the date and spacing of observations differ from country to country.

Several cautions follow. A country that revises its line can show a break in the series that looks like progress or regression though living standards did not move in that way. A country with a low rate can be classed as regressing after a small rise, while a country with a very high rate may be classed as on track after a modest fall. The classes do not rank the level of deprivation among countries.

The classification also leaves out countries without a usable trend. Where surveys are infrequent, the trend rests on few points, and the class can change with one new survey. The tool gives no breakdown of the classes by region or by income group, and none by the period before and after 2020, so the effect of the pandemic on the classes cannot be read here.

For 2030, the classes support a limited statement. The on track group holds 63.8% of the assessed population, while 26.0% lives in countries where the national measure is classed as regressing. Because the classes give direction and pace only, and no rate levels, they do not allow a verdict on whether the halving will be reached across the whole group; they show where the pace falls short, not the size of the shortfall.

### National and international lines agree on direction but not fully on size, and the implication for 2030

National and international lines can be set side by side for 36 countries between 2015 and 2021. The comparison pairs the national-line headcount with the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Across these countries the rank correlation of 2021 levels is 0.72 (Spearman), and the Kendall measure of the same levels is 0.58. The rank correlation of changes between 2015 and 2021 is lower, at 0.53, with a Kendall value of 0.41.

The two results say different things. A country with a high national rate generally also has a high international rate, so the two lines rank societies in a broadly similar order. Agreement on direction of change is weaker. A country can see its national rate fall while the international rate barely moves, or the reverse, because the two lines sit at different points of the income distribution and are adjusted by different rules. A rise in living costs, a change in survey design or a revision of the basket can move one measure and leave the other untouched. The correlation of changes should therefore be read as a moderate link, not as proof that the two measures can be substituted for one another. Only 36 countries qualify, a small part of the 161 that report a national rate in at least one year, so the finding cannot be extended to all countries without caution. Both correlations are associations, not causes.

For the 2030 halving in target 1.2, the evidence supports no aggregate verdict. The movement of national rates is shown here only through the trend classes, since the results hold no rate level or change for any country or group. Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, with 63.8% of the assessed population. Another 34 countries are in the regression class, holding 26.0% of that population. The classes give direction and pace against the target, not the size of any rate, and they do not show which countries hold the population shares. An overall judgement on whether the halving will be reached cannot be drawn from them. The weaker agreement on change also means that a country judged on track at its national line cannot be assumed to be gaining at the international line, and the reverse also holds. The target is open to more than one reading. Halving may be measured against a country's own 2015 rate or against a baseline year that varies by country, and a revised national line breaks the series on which either reading depends. Assessment is therefore best made country by country.

The evidence has clear limits. Reporting is uneven: 72 countries reported a national rate for 2021, the peak, but 52 did so for 2022, 40 for 2023, 31 for 2024 and 13 for 2025. Recent years are thin, so the effects after 2020 are seen only in part. Country lines differ in definition and in the date of last revision, and the series does not record why a line was changed. The paired comparison rests on 36 countries. Poverty in all its dimensions is only partly captured by a headcount, and the poverty gap and multidimensional measures are not tested here against national lines.

w-c04-9-4.text:
### The global picture rests on rates, not counts

The question posed for this section asks for a number of deaths. The evidence retrieved cannot supply one. The only analysed result is a rate: deaths attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene per 100,000 population, for 2019, across 183 countries. A rate is a count divided by population, and it cannot be turned back into a count without population figures that this result does not carry. No absolute total of deaths from unsafe water appears in the retrieved material, and none is offered here. The level of the rate, whether global, regional or national, is likewise not among the results; only the inequality of the rate between countries is.

The question is therefore answered in neither of its halves. For unsafe water, the book can report how unequal the rate is but not how many deaths it represents. For air pollution, the shelf holds a series on the age-standardised mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, with 183 countries and a latest year of 2019, and a series on mean annual exposure to fine particulate matter, with a latest year of 2023. Neither was analysed as a result for this section, so no value from either is quoted. Nothing is stated here about how many people die from air pollution, how fast the rate is falling or which regions carry most of it. The reason is specific: the bench produced no result for these series, and none of the series on the shelf is a count of deaths. The gap lies in the analysis performed and in the form of the series, not in the world. Target 3.9 also covers hazardous chemicals and soil pollution, and the shelf holds a series on unintentional poisoning, which was likewise not analysed.

This limit bears on how Target 3.9 is read. The target calls for a substantial reduction in the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and from air, water and soil pollution. The wording can be read as a count, in which case population growth works against progress even when conditions improve, or as a rate, in which case a falling risk counts as success even if the number of deaths stays high. The wording does not settle the matter. The indicator series the World Bank reports measures a rate, and it is the rate that the evidence here can describe. Any later statement about progress in this section should be taken as a statement about risk per head of population, not about the total toll.

The one result that exists shows how unevenly that risk is spread. Across the 183 countries in 2019, the Gini coefficient of the unsafe-water mortality rate is 0.535 and the coefficient of variation is 1.03. A coefficient of variation above one means that the spread of national rates is wider than their average. The bench summary describes these measures as population-weighted, so they would describe inequality among people living in different countries; the source's own weighting method was not retrieved, and the measures do not establish how many countries hold high rates. The next part examines how much of this inequality lies between regions.

### Regions explain most of the inequality between countries

Between-region differences account for most of the measured inequality in the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate. The result covers 2019 and 183 countries, and it describes a rate per 100,000 population, not a count of deaths. The Theil index of the rate was 0.502 and the Gini coefficient was 0.535. The bench summary describes both measures as weighted by population; the weighting method itself was not retrieved, so that description is reported here as the summary gives it and is not independently confirmed. On that reading, the measures describe how the rate is distributed among people living in different countries, and a populous country with a high rate would raise both figures more than a small one. The coefficient of variation was 1.03, so the standard deviation of the rate was slightly larger than its mean, which indicates a wide spread of values.

The between-region share of the Theil index was 75.2% in 2019. Differences between the regions' mean rates therefore make up about three quarters of the measured inequality, and differences among countries within the same region make up the remaining quarter. This is a descriptive split of a statistic. It does not test why regions differ, and it contains no measure of income, infrastructure or health services. Well-established knowledge suggests plausible causes, offered as context and not as a finding: diarrhoeal disease and related infections depend on piped water, sewerage, nutrition and primary care, and these conditions tend to be shared among neighbouring countries at similar stages of development.

The split matters for how reporting and action are organised. Where most inequality lies between regions, regional figures are needed to see where the gap is, and a global average alone can hide regions with high rates. This result does not identify those regions, give their rates or show how many deaths occur in them, so the levels by region remain to be read from the underlying series. The remaining quarter, lying within regions, shows that countries in the same region still differ, and those that do better than their neighbours merit study for policies that could be copied.

The limits of the result are plain. A decomposition reports a share, not a ranking, so it names no region or country. It covers one year, 2019, and so says nothing about change since 2015 or about the effects of events after 2020. It concerns unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene only; no analysed result in this part covers air pollution mortality or PM2.5 exposure, so the air half of Target 3.9 is not addressed here. The retrieved results do not document how the underlying estimates were produced. Background knowledge, unverified here, is that estimates of this kind are often modelled where death registration is incomplete, so the figures are best read as an indication of structure and not as a count of deaths.

### Change since 2015 cannot be measured from one year

The single observation for 2019 describes a position, not a movement. Target 3.9 calls for a substantial reduction in deaths from pollution and contamination by 2030, and a reduction can only be shown by comparing at least two points in time. The result retrieved for this section holds one year, 2019, for 183 countries. No statement is therefore made here on whether mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene fell after 2015, nor on how the years after 2020 compare with those before. The result gives no earlier or later reading for this indicator, and an inference from a single cross-section would be a guess presented as a finding.

Three kinds of evidence would be needed to turn the position into a trend. The first is a series of annual rates from 2015 onward, ideally with earlier years too, so that a pre-2015 trajectory exists against which the post-2015 period can be judged. The shelf lists the indicator with 2019 as its latest year, which means that the period of the pandemic and its disruption to health services, to water programmes and to household incomes is not observed at all. The second is a count of deaths. A rate can fall while the number of deaths stays level or rises if populations grow, and the reverse is also possible, so the two answer different questions. The third is an air pollution indicator read alongside the water measure. The shelf holds a rate of deaths attributed to household and ambient air pollution and a measure of mean exposure to fine particles, but neither was returned as a result for this section. The question on air pollution is therefore not answered here, and the two halves of the question cannot be set side by side.

Caution is also due on causes. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2%, and the Gini coefficient is 0.535. These figures show that the rate is unequally distributed among people in 2019 and that regional grouping accounts for most of that measured inequality. They do not show why. Water and sanitation infrastructure, income, the quality of primary health care and the treatment of diarrhoeal disease are well established as bearing on such deaths, but these are plausible influences that the decomposition does not test, and one year's spread cannot separate them from the age structure of populations, from climate or from conflict. The coefficient of variation, 1.03, confirms the dispersion without explaining it.

For 2030 the consequence is that progress on this part of target 3.9 cannot at present be judged from the evidence in hand. The target also does not define what "substantially" means, and it can be read against a baseline of 2015, of an earlier year or of the latest available year. Until a series spanning those years is assembled, any statement on whether the goal is on course would be unsupported.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 3.9 asks for a substantial reduction by 2030, and the only evidence analysed for this section is one year of one rate. In 2019, across 183 countries, the between-region share of the Theil index for mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene was 75.2%. Most of the measured inequality in that rate therefore lies between regions rather than within them. The result does not name the regions, give their rates or show why they differ. Differences in income, infrastructure and health services are plausible explanations, but this decomposition does not test them.

The Gini coefficient was 0.535 and the coefficient of variation was 1.03. The bench summary describes the Gini and Theil measures as population-weighted; the weighting method itself was not retrieved, so that description is reported as the summary gives it and not as an established property of the calculation. The measures show that the rate is unevenly spread, but not where the highest rates lie or how many deaths occur in any region. The Theil index was 0.502.

This bears on how 2030 is judged. The target text does not say whether the reduction is to be assessed in numbers of deaths or in rates, and it sets no baseline or percentage. Both readings are defensible and they can diverge when populations grow. A fall in the rate with a growing population may leave the count little changed. The 2019 evidence offers no trend since 2015 or 2020, so whether the target is on course cannot be stated from it.

The question asks for numbers of deaths from air pollution and from unsafe water and sanitation. It remains unanswered: no count is given for either cause, and no air pollution result was analysed in this section. The air pollution mortality series, the PM2.5 exposure series and the unintentional poisoning series are held on the shelf, but their values are not reported here. Conclusions concern the water, sanitation and hygiene rate only. Population figures are needed to convert that rate into a count, and the retrieval of the air pollution results is the most pressing step before the section can be adopted.
proposals: The Bank's statistical teams and the health agencies that produce the mortality estimates should publish death counts alongside rates for air pollution and for unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene, so that Target 3.9 can be read in either numbers or rates.

The bench's keepers should analyse the air pollution mortality and PM2.5 exposure series, with at least two years each, before the section is next reviewed, so that the air half of the target is answered and change since 2015 can be shown.

National statistical offices and health ministries in the regions with the highest rates should report subnational mortality from unsafe water and sanitation, so that within-region concentrations can be identified and targeted.
w-c04-9-4.gaps: The section holds one year, 2019, of one rate, with no death counts, no population series to convert it, no trend since 2015 or 2020, and no analysed result for air pollution or poisoning. The regions and their rates are not named in the retrieved result, and the weighting method behind the summary was not retrieved. Whether Target 3.9 is read in deaths or rates is left open by its text.

w-c05-2-4.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

Group values for children of primary school age who are out of school are given by income group, not as a global total, and the results supply no global figure. In 2015 the four groups held 26.0 million, 52.0 million, 8.1 million and 1.3 million such children, and in 2025 they held 30.1 million, 46.4 million, 9.3 million and 2.1 million, in the order low, lower middle, upper middle and high income. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, so the answer to the question of how many children are out of school is available here only as these four group values.

The movement between the two years differs by group. Low-income countries rose from 26.0 million to 30.1 million. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest group count, 46.4 million, which reflects very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate. Three of the four groups show higher counts in 2025 than in 2015, but the comparison is indicative only: with 12 reporting countries in the latest year, the country sets may differ between 2015 and 2025, and the results do not show that the underlying movement is the same as the movement in the group values.

The series itself has wide coverage across its history, 198 countries, but the latest-year group values depend on which countries happened to report. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, so those still in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count. Rises in some groups may therefore partly reflect late entry or pre-primary enrolment rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. The years after 2020 fall within the same data window, and the interruption of schooling during the pandemic, together with conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries, are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up. The results do not separate these effects, so they cannot be attributed with precision.

For 2030, the implication is cautious. Group counts that are higher in 2025 than in 2015 in three of four groups, on thin reporting, give no evidence of the rate of decline that ending exclusion would require. The rates in the following part show where the difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. A plausible explanation, not tested by these series, is that fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was outrun by the growth in the number of children.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest group value for out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. The group values suggest that this gain offsets increases elsewhere, though the series do not show how far.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion appears to deepen as children grow older. Likely reasons, which the data do not test, are that many enter school but few progress, and that costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push adolescents out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening, although it too rests on 12 reporting countries.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, each group's adolescent exclusion rate changed by less than one and a half percentage points. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which 41.7% of lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, but the direction of the small difference depends on national income. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys, so girls are the larger group there. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys. Both counts rose over the decade, and the girls' count rose slightly more than the boys', so the gap in low-income countries appears to have widened a little in absolute terms, to the girls' disadvantage. This reading rests on sex series from only 8 reporting countries in 2025 and should be treated as indicative.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' counts fell by more than boys' there. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in these three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

Girls are thus the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, barriers that plausibly fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, may remain active, though these results do not test such causes. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. The sex-disaggregated series draw on 8 countries reporting in 2025, whereas the totals by income group draw on 12, so the two sets should not be compared directly. Part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are plausible pressures after the pandemic, though these are explanations the data do not test and cannot separate.

The country classes show that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are the most numerous, and their 34.4% of the population is close to the 34.9% share that is on track or has met the target.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. The group levels rest on 12 reporting countries in 2025, a small base for four income groups. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents show the highest observed rate. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, against 36.1% in 2015, while in upper middle income countries the rate moved from 5.7% to 5.9%. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, and the sex-disaggregated counts rest on 8, so these pictures rest on thin and uneven coverage and are indicative only. The primary and lower secondary series may also draw on different sets of countries, so a comparison across ages is a suggestion, not a finding. Fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and too few secondary places, are commonly offered as explanations for exclusion at these ages, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.

proposals: National education ministries in low-income countries should direct new funding and places to lower secondary schooling, where the highest observed exclusion rate lies, and publish enrolment by age every year.

Statistical offices, with the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and the World Bank, should widen reporting of out-of-school series, especially adolescent and sex-disaggregated counts, so that a global total and age comparisons rest on a stable set of countries.
Donors should concentrate support for basic education on low-income countries, where the rate has stagnated, and tie it to measured enrolment and not to inputs alone.
The Goal 4 custodians should state in reporting whether the target means zero exclusion or a small tolerated residual, so that country progress is judged on one reading.

The shelf does not measure completion, learning, or the causes of exclusion, and the target can be read as zero exclusion or with a tolerance.

w-c06-5-4.text:
### The indicator and what it measures

Target 5.6 commits governments to universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The principal measure available for it in this section is the share of married or partnered women aged 15 to 49 who make their own informed decisions on sexual relations, contraceptive use and reproductive health care, reported in the World Bank's World Development Indicators as a percentage of those women. The description of the indicator that follows is background drawn from its published metadata, not a finding of the retrieved results, which hold only counts of reporting countries.

The question asked concerns health care and contraception. The indicator answers a broader question, because it also counts the ability to refuse sex. The part of the question about health care and contraception alone cannot be separated out from it.

The indicator is a composite, and its base is women who are married or in a union, not all women of that age. According to its metadata, a woman counts as deciding for herself only if she answers yes to all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner, she decides on the use of contraception, and she decides on her own health care. A woman who answers yes to two of the three is not counted. The measure is therefore strict, and its level cannot exceed the level for any single component. Unmarried women are left out, so the series describes one part of the female population. The data are drawn mainly from household surveys, as general background.

The reading of own decisions is not fixed across surveys. Each component rests on a question put to the respondent, and the wording, the response options and the treatment of a joint decision with a partner can differ between survey rounds and between countries. A woman who decides jointly with her husband after discussion may be recorded differently from one whose husband decides alone, and cultural norms shape how women describe such arrangements. Answers on refusing sex are also sensitive to the setting of the interview. Differences between countries, or between years in one country, may therefore partly reflect measurement and not only a change in women's autonomy.

The retrieved results report how many countries supply the indicator, not the share values themselves. In 2024 the count was 5 countries, and across 2006 to 2024 a total of 81 countries have reported at least once. The share of women who decide for themselves is therefore not stated here for any country or year, and the question cannot be answered with a figure from these results. Other series on wider household decisions, family planning, unmet need, attitudes towards refusing sex and prenatal care are outside the retrieved results for this section, and they are not read here.

### Thin coverage limits any global picture

Only 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions in 2024, the latest year in the series. The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries but no share values for those five, so the share of women who make their own decisions cannot be stated for any country or year in this section. No aggregate appears in the coverage result for any year, so no regional or world share is available from these results. The question is therefore answered only in part: no global figure exists in the material, and the national readings are absent from it.

The question asks about decisions on health care and contraception, while the indicator also counts a woman's ability to refuse sexual intercourse. It counts a woman only if she makes her own decision on all three areas. The measure therefore answers a broader question than the one posed, and its share cannot exceed the share for any single component. The results do not separate the components, so the share deciding on health care and contraception alone cannot be read from this series.

The count of 5 in 2024 says nothing about why so few countries appear. The results give counts only, and they do not show whether the figure reflects survey timing, processing delays or other causes. As context, such data come mainly from household surveys that are fielded country by country at intervals of several years, so a country enters a year's count only when a survey has been completed and released. A low count should not be read as evidence that decision-making has become less common. Nor are the reporting countries a sample drawn to represent any region or income group.

For that reason the five reporting countries could support national readings only, if their values were available. Each reading could describe its own country. None could be averaged into a regional picture, because countries whose populations, laws and health systems differ widely would be combined into a number describing no real population. In the present material there are five country counts and no values to average.

The wider record shows how uneven coverage is. Across 2006 to 2024, 81 countries reported at least once. Among the years whose counts the results give, the number reporting in a single year runs from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018, and 12 countries reported in 2022 and 14 in 2023. Even in the best of these years, 15 countries is a small part of the 81 with a value at some point, and the set of reporting countries changes from year to year. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years would therefore reflect a change in who reported as much as any change in women's autonomy.

The constraint matters for the 2030 agenda. Target 5.6 concerns universal access and rights, and a measure reported by so few countries in a year cannot show whether the target is being reached. Women outside unions, and countries without a recent survey, are absent from the evidence. The thin coverage is itself a finding: monitoring of this target rests on a handful of countries in each year.

### Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data

Reporting by year shows why regions and countries cannot be compared on current data. The results give the number of countries reporting the indicator for every year from 2006 to 2024. The lowest count is 3 countries in 2008 and the highest is 15 in 2018. Counts for the intervening years are cited only where they serve the argument: 4 in 2009, 7 in 2010, 12 in 2012, 6 in 2013 and 10 in 2016. Each year's reading therefore describes a different group of countries, and a change between years may reflect who was surveyed rather than any change in women's lives.

The pattern is consistent with a survey cycle. Household surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys visit a country every few years, and the countries reached in one year are seldom those reached in the next; this is context, not something the counts themselves show. A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2018 and 2019, cannot be set side by side. Regional groupings fare no better, because a region may be represented by one or two countries in one year and by none in another. The coverage result lists no aggregates, so no regional average exists to correct for this, and constructing one from such uneven entries would imply a precision the data do not hold.

Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once, yet in 2024 only 5 reported. A country's most recent reading may therefore be older than 2024, but the results do not give the survey years of individual countries, so the date gap between latest values cannot be measured. Comparing latest values across countries would mix survey years of unknown spread, and the gap between two countries' values could be partly a gap in dates.

The results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, so no country's reading for 2024 is stated here, and the share of women who decide for themselves is unanswered for that year. The question asks about health care and contraception, whereas the indicator also counts the ability to refuse sex, so it answers a broader question than the one posed. A woman is counted only if she decides on all three areas, and the base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so women outside unions are not covered. The 5 countries reporting in 2024 are too few to support any ranking or regional statement, and none is made.

### Reporting has changed little since 2015

Reporting counts have swung widely since 2015 without a trend. In 2015, 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions. The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached 15 in 2018, then fell to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020. It recovered to 7 in 2021, 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023, before dropping to 5 in 2024. Counts are held in the results for most years from 2006 onward, and only the years from 2015 bear on the period after the adoption of the Goals. Among the years cited, 15 in 2018 is the highest count from 2015 onward.

The results give counts of reporting countries and nothing about why those counts differ from year to year. As general context, not shown by the series, household surveys are fielded in a country every few years and compiled some time afterwards, so a year with many reporting countries is one in which many survey rounds were completed and published. The cause of the low count in 2024 is not known from these data, and later releases may or may not add countries to recent years.

The equal counts of 4 in 2019 and 2020 cannot be explained by the series alone. The pandemic began in 2020 and is widely known to have disrupted fieldwork in many countries, but that is outside knowledge and not a finding of these results; the count was already 4 in 2019, and the series does not test the point. The recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is a rise in the number of countries reporting and not a measure of change in women's decisions.

The consequence is that no comparison before and after 2015 or 2020 can be drawn from this series. Each year's group of reporting countries differs from the last, so a rise or fall in any average would reflect who was surveyed. Because the retrieved results hold counts and no share values, a trend in women's decision-making since 2015 cannot be stated, and the 2030 horizon cannot be assessed against a comparable baseline.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 5.6 cannot be judged as on track or off track with the data now held. The indicator on women's own informed decisions has no aggregate in any year, and the results hold no share values for any country. Only 5 countries reported in 2024, the latest year, and 81 countries have reported at least once since 2006. The question of what share of women make their own decisions has no figure to answer it here, and the counts given earlier in the section are not repeated beyond what the argument needs.

A trend needs the same countries measured at intervals, and the shelf does not offer that. Whether a country has moved towards 2030 cannot be told by comparing one year's reporters with another's. The counts show how many countries reported in a year, not why a count was high or low. The count of 4 in 2020 is the same as in 2019, so the series offers no support for linking it to the pandemic. As general context from outside the results, household surveys are fielded in multi-year cycles and fieldwork was disrupted in many countries in 2020, but the series does not test this. The cause of the low count in 2024 is not known from the data.

The reading of the target adds a second difficulty. Target 5.6 speaks of universal access and of reproductive rights, which no single survey question captures. The question posed asks about health care and contraception, while the indicator also counts the ability to refuse sex, so it answers a broader question than the one asked. By its metadata description, not by any retrieved result, it requires a woman to answer yes to all three components, so its level cannot exceed that of any single component. Its base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so unmarried women and adolescents fall outside it. A rise or fall in the share could reflect a change in any of the three components, and the series alone does not say which.

The proposals below follow from these findings. No comparable baseline exists in the results, so they aim first at obtaining usable share values and then at a baseline, since the period to 2030 is short and surveys are slow to field.
