w-c07-1-3.text:
### Safely managed drinking water reached 73.7% of the world in 2024

The share of the world's people using safely managed drinking water stood at 73.7% in 2024, up from 67.7% in 2015. Roughly three in four people now have water that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from faecal and priority chemical contamination. The remaining quarter rely on sources that fail one or more of those three conditions, or on sources that are not improved at all.

The indicator is demanding by design. It sits at the top of the ladder used by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, above basic service, which requires only an improved source within a thirty-minute round trip. A household with a piped connection that supplies water only a few hours a day, or a borehole whose water carries contamination, counts as basic at best. For that reason the safely managed share is lower than the basic share, and progress on it is slower and harder to measure, because testing water quality and continuity requires surveys and regulatory records that many countries do not hold in full.

Target 6.1 calls for universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all by 2030. The word universal can be read in more than one way. This book takes the plainest reading, 100% of the population using safely managed services, and measures distance against that line. A looser reading would accept a very high threshold, such as 95%, or would count basic service as sufficient. Affordability and equity, the other elements of the target, have no series on the shelf, so the safely managed share captures only part of what the target asks.

Coverage of reporting is broad but not complete. In 2015, 150 countries reported a value and in 2024, 148 did, with 151 reporting in at least one year. The series reaches back to 2000, when 144 countries reported, so the years before the goals were adopted can be set beside the years after. The slight fall in the number of reporting countries after 2016 is small, yet it matters: the missing cases are not drawn at random, and countries with weak statistical systems are often those with the lowest access. The world figure is therefore best read as a firm estimate for the countries that report, and a less certain one for the whole population.

### Regions differ by more than sixty percentage points

The distance between the best and worst served regions in 2024 is larger than sixty percentage points. North America stood at 97.4% and Europe and Central Asia at 92.5%, so that in both regions safely managed water is close to the norm. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 32.4%, which means that roughly two in three people in the region still depend on water that is not on premises, not available when needed or not free from contamination. In 2015 North America stood at 96.3% and Sub-Saharan Africa at 26.4%. The gap between the top and bottom regions therefore narrowed between 2015 and 2024, from 69.9 to 65.0 percentage points, but it remains very large.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 79.0% in 2024, South Asia 77.6% and East Asia and Pacific 75.2%, all within four percentage points of one another and a little above the world figure of 73.7%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stand apart from them at 65.6%, up only from 64.7% in 2015. That region began the period at a level close to South Asia (63.1%) and East Asia and Pacific (65.1%), and has since fallen well behind them. Water scarcity, conflict and weak utilities in some of its countries are possible contributing factors, offered as context only; the data do not separate these causes or show that any of them explains the pattern.

The pattern is one of high-income regions near saturation and low-income regions far from it. Europe and Central Asia gained 1.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2024, and North America 1.1 points, because little room remains. The income groups show the same ordering: 95.8% in high-income countries against 33.0% in low-income countries in 2024. As context outside the data, which do not separate the causes of shortfalls, the remaining gap in wealthy regions is often associated with private wells, small rural systems and contamination, whereas in poorer regions missing networks, intermittent supply and unmonitored quality are commonly cited.

The spread among countries tells a consistent story. Across the 148 countries reporting in 2024, the population-weighted Gini coefficient of safely managed water use was 0.222, down from 0.246 across 150 countries in 2015. The fall is real but modest, and it indicates that countries have become somewhat more alike in coverage. The Theil index also fell, from 0.107 to 0.093. Inequality among countries therefore narrowed, though from a high base and not by much.

Regions remain the main source of that inequality. Differences between regions accounted for 59.4% of the Theil index in 2024, down from 61.7% in 2015. A share this large means that knowing the region of a country explains most of the variation in its coverage, and that the remainder lies in differences among countries within regions. The decomposition does not show which regions produced the small decline in the between-region share.

These comparisons carry a caution. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, and the 148 countries reporting in 2024 are fewer than all countries, so regional figures rest partly on estimation where data are sparse. For 2030 the implication is plain: a regional gap of this size cannot close in the years that remain at the pace observed since 2015, and the burden falls most heavily on Sub-Saharan Africa.

### Gains came from South Asia and East Asia, and convergence is weak

The largest absolute gains came from two regions. South Asia rose from 63.1% in 2015 to 77.6% in 2024, a gain of 14.4 percentage points, and moved from below the world average to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 65.1% to 75.2%, a gain of 10.1 points. Both regions' gains are large, and both regions are populous, but the world rise from 67.7% to 73.7% cannot be apportioned between regions with the tools used here. The world average therefore says more about where population lives than about how widely progress was shared. Established explanations point to sustained public investment in piped supply, household connections and rural programmes for boreholes and treatment; these are context only, since the data used here do not separate such causes.

Other regions moved far less. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 75.2% to 79.0%, a gain of 3.8 points. Europe and Central Asia moved from 91.2% to 92.5%, and North America from 96.3% to 97.4%, the pattern expected where coverage is already high and the remaining gaps are hard to close. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stand apart: the regional share edged from 64.7% to 65.6%, a gain of under one point in nine years, from a start close to that of South Asia and East Asia and Pacific. The trend tool classes the region as stagnating, with a ratio of 0.043 of the distance to the target covered. Conflict, displacement, water scarcity and weak utility finance are commonly cited obstacles in parts of it, but the regional aggregate combines very different countries and the data here cannot attribute the stagnation to any of them.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 26.4% to 32.4%, a gain of about six points, against 14.4 for South Asia, so its pace was less than half as fast in points. From so low a base, two-thirds of the region's people remain without safely managed water. The income groups tell the same story. Low-income countries rose from 26.4% to 33.0%, and lower-middle-income countries from 60.6% to 69.1%, a gain of 8.5 points. Upper-middle-income countries moved only from 77.4% to 78.1%, and high-income countries from 95.2% to 95.8%. Gains were thus concentrated in the lower-middle-income group, while the upper-middle group is classed as stagnating, with a ratio of 0.057, well short of universal coverage. Reaching the last fifth in such countries often means improving the quality and reliability of existing systems, not simply extending pipes.

Whether poorer countries are catching up can be tested directly. Across 147 countries, the slope of annual change on the 2015 level is -0.00491 with a p-value of 0.0004, so lower starting levels are associated with somewhat faster gains, and the pattern is unlikely to be chance. The fit is weak, however: R2 is 0.088, meaning that starting level explains under nine per cent of the variation in change. The coefficient of variation across countries fell from 0.445 in 2015 to 0.416 in 2024. Dispersion has narrowed, but only slightly. Many countries with low coverage improved little, and some with middling coverage improved a great deal, so convergence is a tendency and not a rule. Measurement may add noise, since estimates for countries with few surveys rest on modelled trends, and the safely managed indicator needs water-quality and availability data that many countries collect irregularly.

The link with basic service sheds light on how progress is made. Across 147 countries, the rank correlation between changes in safely managed coverage and changes in at least basic coverage is 0.622, and the rank correlation between their 2024 levels is 0.850. Countries that expanded basic access tended also to expand safely managed access, and the two rankings of countries are very similar. This is consistent with basic coverage acting as a precondition: a household cannot have water on premises, free from contamination, before it has a protected source at all. It is an association, not proof of cause, and the correlation of changes leaves room for countries where safely managed coverage moved separately from basic coverage.

For 2030 the implication is that the pace of the last nine years will not deliver universal access. The regions that gained most did so from middling starting points, and the regions with the largest deficits gained fewer points than South Asia and East Asia and Pacific. Convergence is too weak to close the gap unaided, which means that low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries need gains well above the recent trend.

### Current trends fall short of universal access by 2030, and proposals follow

Projecting the post-2015 pace forward shows that universal access to safely managed drinking water will not be reached by 2030. At the rate observed since 2015, the world would stand at 78.0% in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend classification gives the world a ratio of 0.32 of the pace required, which the analysis reads as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Whether the pace of 2015 to 2024 is the right baseline is a matter of reading, since the series is built from household surveys and modelled estimates that move slowly, and a short period can be unrepresentative. Universal access can also be read strictly, as 100.0% of people, or loosely, as near-universal coverage; on the strict reading every projection below falls short.

The regional projections differ in what they imply. East Asia and Pacific is expected to reach 82.8% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.51, against 0.70 for South Asia, which is expected at 89.0%. Europe and Central Asia is expected at 93.4%, and high-income countries at 96.2%. These are high levels, but their ratios are 0.25 and 0.21, because the pace is slow. In rich regions the remaining shortfall is small, and regional averages do not reveal where it lies. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is classified as stagnating, with an expected 66.2% in 2030, barely above its 2024 level of 65.6%. Upper middle income countries are also classed as stagnating, at an expected 78.6%.

Sub-Saharan Africa is furthest from the target. At 32.4% in 2024, it is expected to reach only 37.2% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.15. Low-income countries show the same picture, with an expected 38.2% and a ratio of 0.16. South Asia, by contrast, rose from 63.1% in 2015 to 77.6% in 2024, a much larger gain in points than Sub-Saharan Africa's rise from 26.4% to 32.4%. Even if the present pace holds, roughly two in three people in Sub-Saharan Africa would remain without safely managed water.

Country classifications show how widely the shortfall is spread. Of 151 countries assessed, 20 are on track or have met the target, but they hold only 2.3% of the assessed population. A further 16 countries show moderate progress, and hold 37.0% of the population; the tools do not show which countries or regions fall in this group. Another 36 countries, with 26.2% of the population, show marginal progress. In 45 countries, with 24.2% of the population, the series is stagnant, and in 34 countries, with 10.2%, it has regressed. Regression can arise from services failing to keep pace with growing towns, ageing networks, conflict or revised survey methods; this is context only, and the data do not separate these causes.

The implication for 2030 is that effort must shift from the countries already improving towards those standing still or sliding back. Raising basic coverage is not enough, although the two measures are linked: across 147 countries the rank correlation of 2024 levels is 0.85 and of changes 0.62. The indicator requires that water be on premises, available when needed and free from contamination, and a source that counts as improved may fail the last two conditions.

Proposals follow from these findings. National governments and utilities in countries classed as stagnating or regressing should be the first priority for investment and monitoring, since these 79 countries hold 34.4% of the assessed population, about a third. Donors and development banks should direct concessional finance towards low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa, where the projected level in 2030 remains far from the target. Statistical offices in rich regions should report on marginalised and off-network communities, so that averages near 96.2% do not hide those left behind.

w-c04-3-4.text:
### HIV incidence has fallen by more than a third worldwide

World HIV incidence fell from 0.26 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.16 in 2024, a decline of roughly 38 per cent, which supports the heading's claim of more than a third. The estimates are modelled, and 139 countries reported in 2024. Coverage is broad but not complete, so the world figure is an aggregate of reporting countries rather than a census.

Tuberculosis moved more slowly. Estimated incidence fell from 150.0 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131.0 in 2024. The series covers 208 countries in 2024, close to universal. Estimates are recalculated for all years as methods improve, so the 2015 value used here may differ from figures published earlier. The comparison is internally consistent, but it should not be set against older reports without caution.

Malaria runs the other way. Incidence among populations at risk rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, because malaria is not a concern everywhere, and the denominator is the population at risk rather than the whole population. The rise in the rate therefore does not show that malaria spread to new places. Disruption to prevention and care in the pandemic years, resistance to drugs and insecticides, conflict and constrained funding are recognised pressures on malaria control, but the series cannot apportion the rise among them.

Target 3.3 calls for ending the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria by 2030, but sets no numerical threshold. The phrase can be read as zero incidence, as incidence low enough to cease to be a public health threat, or as a given percentage reduction from a baseline. The trend tool therefore applies no target value for HIV, and its class of on track or target met rests on its own reading of the pace of decline rather than on an official benchmark. On that reading the world's HIV rate of change, -0.0525 a year, is classed as on track. Such a class describes momentum, not arrival at a defined goal.

The contrast between the three diseases matters for 2030. The HIV decline is consistent with sustained investment in treatment and prevention, which is context only, since the series does not show the cause. Tuberculosis has declined at a pace that would leave substantial incidence in 2030. Malaria has moved backwards on the measure used here. The global record is therefore one of clear progress against one disease, modest progress against a second and a rise against a third, and the following parts examine where those differences lie.

### Regions and income groups differ most in where the burden lies

The burden of the three diseases is distributed very unevenly, and the pattern differs by disease. For HIV, Sub-Saharan Africa remains the region with the highest incidence, yet it also recorded the largest fall. Incidence there declined from 1.2036 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population in 2015 to 0.5374 in 2024. Low-income countries show a similar movement, from 0.707 to 0.3534, a halving over the nine years. The scale-up of antiretroviral treatment and prevention in the most affected settings is the usual explanation for such falls, though the series themselves do not isolate causes. Latin America and the Caribbean tells a different story, one of slow movement rather than of a large burden. Its incidence moved only from 0.2438 in 2015 to 0.2154 in 2024. The region started below low-income countries (0.707 in 2015) and still sits below them (0.3534 in 2024); the gap has closed only because the low-income rate halved, not because the region's own rate fell quickly. Epidemics concentrated among key populations, often with weaker prevention coverage, tend to respond less quickly than generalised epidemics that attract large international funding.

Two entries in the HIV comparison need care. South Asia is reported at 0.0907 in 2024, and lower-middle-income countries at 0.1783 in 2024, but in each case the tool returns the same value for 2015 and 2024. This reflects missing earlier data for the group aggregate, not stability, and no change over time can be read from those rows. Only the 2024 levels are usable: they indicate that South Asia has the lowest HIV incidence of the regions shown, but not whether it has fallen.

Tuberculosis shows a more divided picture than HIV. The world rate fell from 150 new and relapse cases per 100,000 people in 2015 to 131 in 2024, a decline classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. Beneath that average, regions moved in opposite directions. East Asia and Pacific rose from 140 to 144, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 45 to 51; both are classed as regression. Europe and Central Asia fell from 36 to 22, and South Asia from 233 to 189. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 115 to 110, classed as stagnation. North America held at 3.5 in both years, which is stagnation at a very low level and is not a cause for concern in itself.

Income groups show the same gradient. High-income countries fell from 20 to 12, and upper-middle-income countries from 107 to 92. Low-income countries moved from 229 to 199, and lower-middle-income countries from 241 to 208. Low-income and lower-middle-income groups are classed as moderate progress, needing acceleration. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 205 in 2024 after 285 in 2015 (rate -0.036), and South Asia (rate -0.023) are both classed as on track. Even so, 205 cases per 100,000 remains a high rate, so a fast decline does not mean a small burden. These are incidence rates; the series give no case counts, so they do not show which groups hold most of the world's cases. The target has no numerical value attached to it in the tool, so the classification relies on a trend rule rather than a stated end point; the target can be read in more than one way, for example as a fixed percentage reduction or as elimination as a public health problem, and the labels should be taken as indicative.

Malaria is the most concentrated of the three. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 232.4935 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 and 229.2614 in 2024, a change too small to count as progress. Low-income countries moved from 207.1516 to 206.6892. The world rate rose from 59.0112 to 64.0411, yet the rate in Sub-Saharan Africa fell slightly and that in low-income countries was flat, so these groups do not explain the rise; the series do not show which groups drive it, nor whether disruption to prevention and care after 2020 contributed. The rate in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 4.3337 to 9.9708, a signal of resurgence that the available data cannot explain, though conflict, displacement and flooding are well-known drivers elsewhere. South Asia is the exception, falling from 6.3233 to 1.4562, and upper-middle-income countries fell from 2.0345 to 1.6485. Only 105 countries reported in 2024, since malaria is not endemic everywhere, so the denominators are populations at risk rather than whole populations.

### Country trajectories show progress alongside stagnation and regression

Beneath the regional averages, country trajectories diverge sharply, and the divergence differs by disease. Each country was classed by the direction and pace of its incidence series, and each class is reported both as a count of countries and as a share of the population those countries hold. The two measures answer different questions. A count treats a small island state and a populous country alike, and so shows how widespread a pattern is. A population share shows how many people live under it, and so shows where the weight of the epidemic falls.

For HIV, 49 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 49.7% of the population of the 146 countries assessed. Another 4 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration (0.8% of the population) and 12 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration (3.0%). The largest group by count is stagnation, with 60 countries holding 35.7% of the population, and 21 countries, holding 10.8%, are in regression. More than a third of the assessed population lives in countries where HIV incidence has barely moved, and about one in ten lives where it is rising. The world decline already described is therefore carried by roughly half the population, while the remainder has seen little or no benefit. Stagnation is the key finding. It is consistent with a plateau in prevention and treatment in many places, but the classes record only the direction of the series and cannot show why.

Tuberculosis presents a more favourable picture in breadth. Of 203 countries assessed, 123 are on track or have met the target, holding 61.2% of the population. Moderate progress with acceleration needed applies to 18 countries (4.2%), marginal progress to 11 (3.9%), and stagnation to 9 (14.8%). Regression affects 42 countries holding 15.8% of the population. The regressing group is large by count, yet a smaller share of people than the on-track group. Because tuberculosis incidence is estimated from notifications, prevalence surveys and modelling, a rise in some countries can reflect better detection as well as real spread, and the disruption of services during the pandemic years also affected case-finding. The classes cannot separate these causes.

Malaria is assessed in only 85 countries, since the series covers populations at risk and not the whole world. Of these, 36 are on track or have met the target, holding 59.2% of the population. Moderate progress applies to 3 countries (1.4%), marginal progress to 8 (8.0%) and stagnation to 5 (4.0%). Regression covers 33 countries and 27.5% of the population, the highest regressing population share of the three diseases. Malaria control depends on sustained delivery of nets, spraying, diagnostics and treatment, and is vulnerable to funding gaps, conflict, resistance and changes in climate. Where such supply is interrupted, incidence can rise quickly. That more than a quarter of the population in assessed countries lives in regression is a warning for the 2030 horizon, though the data do not identify which of these pressures applies in any one country.

The classification has limits that readers should keep in view. The rule is a trend fitted to a short series, and the period after 2015 is only nine or ten observations. A country with small numbers of cases or a sharp one-off fluctuation can be placed in a class that later years would revise. Modelled estimates are recalculated as methods are refined, so classes may shift between editions. Target 3.3 sets no numerical threshold for these indicators, so the classes judge each country against a decreasing path and not against a fixed value. The population weights also depend on which countries have data, which is why the three diseases cover different numbers of countries and cannot be summed. With these cautions, the common finding is that progress is real but concentrated, while stagnation and regression remain widespread.

### Uneven gains leave the 2030 target at risk and call for focused proposals

The evidence for target 3.3 points to three diseases moving at three different speeds. HIV incidence is falling quickly where it is highest. In Sub-Saharan Africa the trend rate is -0.0857 and the series is classed as on track or target met. Low-income countries, at -0.0742, and the world, at -0.0525, are classed the same way. Latin America and the Caribbean is the exception among the regions assessed, with a rate of -0.0137, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration. The target text does not define what ending an epidemic means, so even a continued fall cannot be judged against a fixed threshold.

Tuberculosis shows slower gains. The world trend rate is -0.0149, classed as moderate progress but needing acceleration, as are low-income, lower middle income and upper middle income countries. High income countries and Europe and Central Asia are on track from low incidence, and South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa are the high-rate regions classed as on track. Two regions are moving the wrong way: East Asia and the Pacific, at 0.0031, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.0140, are both classed as regression. The series carry no case counts, so the share of the global total held by any group cannot be read from them. The period spans the disruption of 2020, when services for finding and treating cases were interrupted in many countries. The series cannot separate that disruption from longer trends, so a rise in recorded incidence may reflect either real transmission or changes in detection and estimation.

Malaria is the weakest result. World incidence rose from 59.0 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2015 to 64.0 in 2024. The series do not show which groups drive that rise. South Asia is the clear success, falling from 6.3 to 1.5. Of 85 countries assessed, 33 are in regression, holding 27.5 per cent of the assessed population, while 36 are on track. Incidence is measured per population at risk, so changes in the size of that population affect the rate. The 2030 outlook is therefore favourable for HIV, uncertain for tuberculosis and poor for malaria.

Proposals follow from these findings. Governments and funders should give priority to malaria control in the countries in regression, which hold 27.5 per cent of the assessed population. Within that, Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries carry the highest burden, at 229.3 and 206.7 cases per 1,000 population at risk in 2024, and their incidence has barely fallen since 2015. Health ministries in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan should investigate the rise from 4.3 to 10.0 and report whether it reflects transmission or detection. National tuberculosis programmes in East Asia and the Pacific and in Latin America and the Caribbean should review why incidence rose, to 144 and 51 per 100,000 in 2024. Donors should keep HIV financing in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the rate is still 0.5374 per 1,000 uninfected population.

The data show what changed and where, not why. Explaining the falls and rises needs other sources, such as programme coverage, funding, drug and insecticide resistance, conflict and climate. These are not held on the shelf and should not be inferred from the incidence series alone. The target's neglected tropical diseases, hepatitis and water-borne diseases are also outside these four series.

w-c05-6-2.text:
### Global literacy stands at 87.7 per cent among adults and 93.1 per cent among youth

Literacy, as the World Bank series defines it, is the share of people who can both read and write, with understanding, a short simple statement about their everyday life. Adults are those aged 15 and above; youth are those aged 15 to 24. The measure is a threshold of basic ability. It says nothing about fluency, about comprehension of complex texts, or about the skills needed to function in a digital economy.

On this measure the world is largely literate. The adult rate stood at 85.96 per cent in 2015 and reached 87.74 per cent in 2024. The youth rate rose from 91.4 per cent in 2015 to 93.11 per cent in 2024. Youth rates exceed adult rates in every year shown. As context rather than a finding, this is consistent with younger cohorts having had more schooling than older adults, which would also lift the adult rate as cohorts replace one another; the results hold no schooling or cohort data to test that explanation.

Target 4.6 asks for more than the indicator can show. It commits countries to ensure that all youth and a substantial proportion of adults, men and women alike, achieve literacy and numeracy. The series held on the bench measures literacy only; it gives no figure for numeracy, so half of the target's wording cannot be assessed here. The phrase 'a substantial proportion of adults' also has no fixed threshold. It can be read as a majority, as most adults, or as a rate close to universal, and the reading chosen decides whether the world is already on course or far from it. For youth the wording is stricter: 'all' implies 100 per cent, and the 2024 figure of 93.11 per cent falls short of it.

The figures are global averages and conceal wide differences between regions and income groups, which the later parts of this section take up. They also rest on a limited number of surveys and censuses: only 29 countries reported an adult or youth value in 2024, so most of the figures for that year are not fresh national measurements. The next part examines how far the headline values can be trusted given that coverage.

### Data coverage is thin and uneven, so the latest values are partly modelled or dated

Literacy data are reported by far fewer countries in any single year than the headline coverage suggests. Across all years, 155 countries have at least one adult literacy value and 160 have at least one youth value. Yet in any one year only a fraction report. Adult reporting ranged from 13 countries in 2003 to 56 in 2019, and youth reporting from 23 countries in 2003 to 62 in 2019. The latest year, 2024, holds only 29 countries in each series.

As general context, outside the results, literacy rates usually come from population censuses and household surveys, which arrive at intervals of several years rather than annually. A country then appears in the record in the year of an exercise and is absent in the years between. The counts are consistent with such a calendar: adult reporting climbed from 32 countries in 2008 to 48 in 2010 and 53 in 2011, then fell to 33 in 2013. Swings of this kind are better read as differences in which countries reported than as changes in literacy itself.

The period after 2015 shows the same unevenness. Adult reporting stood at 47 countries in 2015, reached 56 in 2019, then fell to 42 in 2020, the year the pandemic disrupted fieldwork in many places, as general context. Youth reporting went from 62 countries in 2019 to 43 in 2020. A partial recovery appeared in 2022, with 45 countries for adults and 58 for youth, before the counts dropped to 33 and 35 in 2023 and to 29 in both series in 2024. Surveys held late in the period are commonly processed and published after a delay, so recent years may be filled in later; the results do not show this directly.

Three cautions follow. First, regional and world values for recent years rest on few direct observations. The aggregates are published for the world and for regional and income groups, but the results do not show whether a given value is observed, carried forward from an earlier survey or modelled, so the latest values may be dated or partly modelled. Second, a country's latest value may be several years old even when labelled with a recent year. Third, year-on-year comparison is unreliable, because a change between two years may reflect a different set of countries or method rather than real movement. Comparisons are safer over longer spans, and the findings that follow are read with this limit in mind.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia hold the largest gaps, and women trail men

The widest gaps lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. In 2024 adult literacy in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 68.7 per cent and in South Asia at 78.2 per cent, against 96.6 per cent in East Asia and Pacific. Europe and Central Asia, at 98.8 per cent in 2023, and North America, at 98.8 per cent in 2022, sit close to the ceiling. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached 75.6 per cent in 2024. The adult figure covers everyone aged 15 and above, so it moves slowly. As outside context rather than a finding of these results, regions in which many older people never attended school carry that history in their totals.

The youth series shows a different and more encouraging pattern. South Asia's youth literacy rose from 89.6 per cent in 2015 to 96.9 per cent in 2024, the largest regional gain in the results. Whether schooling expansion explains the rise is not tested here; it is the usual context offered for such changes, and the results contain no schooling data. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 75.2 to 79.0 per cent over the same period, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 85.0 to 86.9 per cent. Youth literacy in East Asia and Pacific, at 99.1 per cent in 2024, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, at 98.7 per cent, has little room left to grow. By income group, low-income countries reached 75.4 per cent among youth in 2024 and 63.6 per cent among adults, while upper middle income countries stood at 99.3 and 96.2 per cent. Lower middle income countries recorded 92.0 per cent for youth and 78.3 per cent for adults.

Women trail men, and the shortfall is largest where overall literacy is lowest. Worldwide, adult female literacy was 84.6 per cent in 2024, below the adult total of 87.7 per cent. In Sub-Saharan Africa it was 62.7 per cent, in South Asia 71.6 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 67.4 per cent. In low-income countries it was 56.4 per cent. Female literacy rose in every region between 2015 and 2024, with South Asia moving from 63.5 to 71.6 per cent, but starting levels were low.

The youth gender parity index, the ratio of female to male literacy, shows younger women closing the gap. It stood at 0.98 worldwide in 2024, up from 0.97 in 2015. South Asia rose from 0.96 to 0.99. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 0.90 to 0.94, and low-income countries from 0.87 to 0.93. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached only 0.92, up from 0.90, the lowest regional value in 2024. Parity of 1.00 had already been reached in East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Only 29 countries reported in 2024, so the latest regional values rest on a small and shifting set of observations, and part of any change may reflect which countries report. Shifts after 2020 cannot be separated from this reporting pattern in these results.

### Progress is real but too slow to reach universal youth literacy by 2030, and the proposals follow

The trend-to-target results for youth literacy show progress that is real but, in every region on the current pace, too slow to reach the 2030 target. The target value is 100.0 per cent, and the tool compares the observed pace since 2015 with the pace needed to reach it. The world as a whole is rated as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a ratio of 0.33 and an expected youth literacy rate of 94.3 per cent in 2030.

Even regions close to the ceiling are not rated as on track. East Asia and Pacific rose from 98.9 per cent in 2015 to 99.1 per cent in 2024 and is expected to reach 99.2 per cent in 2030, a ratio of 0.28 and a marginal rating. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 98.3 per cent to 98.7 per cent, with an expected 98.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.39. Europe and Central Asia is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.68 and an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030. High income is also moderate, with a ratio of 0.53 and an expected 99.6 per cent. North America is rated as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.07. Regions near the ceiling have little distance left to close, which is context rather than a finding, and the results give no measurement-error figure against which these small movements could be judged.

The larger shortfalls lie in regions where the starting level was lower. Low income is rated marginal and is expected to reach 77.9 per cent in 2030 on its current pace, with a ratio of 0.22. Sub-Saharan Africa is rated marginal, with an expected 81.6 per cent and a ratio of 0.26. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is rated marginal, with an expected 88.2 per cent and a ratio of 0.21. Lower middle income is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.63 and an expected 95.3 per cent. South Asia is the single region rated on track, with a ratio of 1.20. Its expected 2030 value is 102.1 per cent, which exceeds the 100 per cent ceiling and so cannot be a literal rate. The rating therefore rests on a projection that overshoots the ceiling, and on a regional value drawn from few reporting countries. South Asia's adult rate was 78.2 per cent in 2024, so the rating does not show that adult literacy is near universal.

These readings carry a caution. In 2024 only 29 countries reported adult literacy, and the results do not show which regional values rest on older surveys or modelled estimates. Target 4.6 can also be read in more than one way: it asks for all youth but only a substantial proportion of adults, and it names numeracy, for which the series held here offers no measure. A projection to 100 per cent therefore addresses only part of the target. On present evidence, universal youth literacy by 2030 is unlikely in any region on its current pace, including those already near the ceiling, and no trend-to-target result is held for adults, whose goal is further off.

w-c07-5-3.text:
### Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015

World net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, measured in constant 2023 dollars. That is an increase of about half over eight years. In current dollars the series climbs from US$147.1 billion to US$259.5 billion. The two series meet in 2023 because the constant-price base year is 2023, so the gap between them in 2015 reflects the rise in prices since then. The constant-dollar figure is the fairer measure of change, since it removes the effect of rising prices; the current-dollar series shows a larger rise because it includes inflation.

The indicator needs careful reading before it is applied to target 6.a. It records all net official development assistance received by developing countries: grants and concessional loans, net of repayments of principal, across every sector. It does not isolate water and sanitation, nor the activities the target names, such as water harvesting, desalination, wastewater treatment, recycling and reuse. The series is therefore a proxy for the general scale of international support, and a rise in it does not show that more reached water and sanitation programmes. Spending on health, emergency relief, refugee costs or budget support can raise the total without any of it entering the sector.

The target itself adds a second limit. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building support by 2030, but it names no amount, no share of income and no baseline year. It can be read as a call for more money, for more technical assistance, or for better-targeted programmes, and a financial series speaks only to the first of these. Capacity-building, such as training, institutional support and technology transfer, is poorly captured by a measure of net disbursements. A judgement that the target is on track can therefore rest only on the direction of the aggregate, not on a threshold.

Coverage is also partial. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts in this series, and the world figure is the sum of those recipients. The inequality analysis later in this section covers a different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023, because it requires population weights, so the two counts are not the same set. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region whose countries are donors rather than recipients, and high-income economies receive only small amounts: US$319.3 million in 2015 and US$760.9 million in 2023 in constant dollars. Net receipts measure what arrives, not what is needed, so the series does not say whether the level is adequate against the water-stress and service gaps described elsewhere in this chapter.

With these limits stated, the direction is clear. Assistance received grew substantially after 2015 and stood at its highest level in the series in the latest year available, 2023. Whether that growth is sustained to 2030 is a separate matter, because the donor side of the ledger depends on budget decisions that recipient data cannot anticipate.

### Regions gained unevenly, and Europe and Central Asia gained most

Regional totals of net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, show that the increase since 2015 was not evenly shared. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest gain by a wide margin, rising from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. That is close to a fivefold increase, and it lifted the region from one of the smaller recipients to the second largest, behind only sub-Saharan Africa and ahead of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region. The series does not show what drove the rise. As context only, emergency and budget support directed to the region in the early 2020s is a plausible contributor, and the series measures all official assistance, not the share spent on water.

The other regions moved much less. East Asia and Pacific received US$9.9 billion in 2015 and US$10.7 billion in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, almost no change in real terms. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion. These three regions ended the period within a narrow band of one another, near US$10.7 billion each, although their populations and water needs differ greatly. No population or per-person series is used in this section, so the totals say nothing about assistance per person; that comparison would need such a series.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, a rise well below the world's increase. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the largest recipient, with US$51.8 billion in 2015 and US$64.8 billion in 2023. The largest absolute flows thus stayed in sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, while the fastest growth went to Europe and Central Asia.

The distribution by income group, also in constant 2023 dollars, shows a similar movement. Low-income countries received US$35.2 billion in 2015 and US$44.6 billion in 2023, and lower-middle-income countries US$54.9 billion and US$59.2 billion. Upper-middle-income countries rose from US$18.9 billion to US$57.4 billion, the fastest growth of the groups, and by 2023 they received more than the low-income group, whose receipts also rose. Assistance in total is therefore not concentrating on the poorest, a pattern that sits uneasily with target 6.a, which stresses support to developing countries in water and sanitation activities. Only a sector breakdown, which these series do not provide, could show whether water programmes followed the same path.

### A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase

The aggregate path of assistance since 2015 is not a steady climb. A structural break analysis of the annual change in world net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, places breaks in 2022 and 2023. Between 2001 and 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. In 2022 alone the change was US$49.8 billion, nearly eight times that long-run average. In 2023 the series fell by US$0.7 billion. A single year therefore accounts for a large part of the rise recorded between 2015 and 2023, when the world total went from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, and the preceding two decades of gradual growth cannot be extrapolated from it.

The data do not record why 2022 was exceptional. It is an inference, not a finding, that the jump reflects emergency and humanitarian flows, support to countries affected by conflict and displacement, and pandemic recovery financing. That reading fits the earlier observation that Europe and Central Asia gained most, but the series covers all purposes of assistance together and cannot separate such flows from spending on water and sanitation. The 2023 fall shows that the 2022 level was not matched by a further rise. Whether it marks a plateau or the start of a decline cannot be judged from one observation.

The distribution of assistance among recipient countries also changed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received rose from 0.361 in 2015, across 138 countries, to 0.452 in 2023, across 135 countries. The Theil index rose more sharply, from 0.255 to 0.460, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.64 to 1.48. Assistance has thus become more unevenly spread among recipients. The country count differs between the two years, and the 135 countries in the inequality analysis are not the same set as the 136 countries reporting in 2023 that underlie the world total, so part of the change may reflect which countries are included, and the comparison should be read with that caution.

The composition of this inequality shifted too. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023. Differences among countries within the same region now account for a larger part of the disparity than differences between regions. This matters for targeting: regional averages conceal recipients that receive much more or much less than their neighbours, and allocation by region alone would miss them.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise is fragile and its distribution has become less even. Target 6.a calls for expanded cooperation and capacity-building support in water and sanitation. Total assistance, whatever its level, does not show how much reaches that sector, and a total inflated by one exceptional year is a weak guide to the sustained flows that infrastructure and capacity-building require.

### Assistance for 2030 must be tracked by sector and directed by need

The series held by the bench measures total official development assistance received, not assistance to water and sanitation. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building in water-related activities, and total flows cannot show whether that is happening. A rise in the aggregate may reflect humanitarian, budget-support or debt-related disbursements that have little to do with water supply, sewerage or wastewater treatment. For 2030, the first implication is therefore that progress on 6.a cannot be judged from the present evidence, and the headline figure of US$259.5 billion in 2023 should not be read as a measure of support for water.

The second implication concerns durability. The break analysis found a mean annual change of US$49.8 billion in 2022, against US$6.4 billion over 2001 to 2021, followed by a fall of US$0.7 billion in 2023. A jump of that size, followed by a fall, suggests an exceptional episode, not a new trend. Planning that assumes the 2023 level will persist, or keep rising, risks a shortfall by 2030. The target can also be read in more than one way: it names no quantity of assistance, so expansion could mean volume, share of total aid or reach of capacity-building.

The third implication concerns distribution. Among countries, the Gini coefficient of assistance received, population-weighted and in constant 2023 dollars, rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.26 to 0.46. The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 45.3 per cent to 29.6 per cent, so the growing concentration lies increasingly within regions, among individual countries. The inequality analysis covers 135 countries in 2023, while the world total rests on 136 countries reporting, so the two sets differ slightly. In constant 2023 dollars, low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015, and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion, yet the data do not show whether flows follow the countries with the weakest water and sanitation coverage. Upper middle income countries received US$57.4 billion in 2023, up from US$18.9 billion in 2015, the faster growth of the two groups, which suggests allocation is shaped by factors beyond service need; this is an inference, not a finding of the data.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: Donors and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report water and sanitation assistance as a sector series that the World Bank can publish alongside total flows, so that progress on target 6.a can be measured.

National planning ministries and development partners should avoid assuming that the 2023 level of total assistance will persist or keep rising when financing water and sanitation to 2030, given the exceptional 2022 jump and the fall in 2023.
Donors should publish how allocations relate to service coverage, so that flows can be directed to the countries with the weakest water and sanitation access.

It holds no series of capacity-building support and no per-person assistance series, and the target names no quantity, so expansion can be read as volume, share or reach. The 2022 jump is not explained by the data, and the country sets behind the world total and the inequality analysis differ slightly.

w-c08-2-2.text:
### Three-quarters of the world now cooks with clean fuels

Roughly three people in four now cook mainly with clean fuels and technologies. The World Bank's World Development Indicators put the share of the world's population with access at 63.9 per cent in 2015 and at 75.4 per cent in 2024. The series covers 192 countries in 2024. The indicator measures the proportion of the total population primarily using clean cooking fuels and technologies, such as electricity, gas, biogas and the cleanest stoves, as against open fires and stoves burning wood, charcoal, dung, crop residues or kerosene. Primary use is the test: a household that owns a gas ring but cooks mostly on firewood is not counted as having access.

The gain between 2015 and 2024 is real and large, but the figure carries a caveat. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses, which are conducted at intervals of several years and are not available for every country in every year. Values for years between surveys, and the most recent years in particular, are estimates produced by statistical models rather than direct observations. The 2024 world value is therefore best read as a close approximation of the trend, and small year-to-year movements should not be treated as measured events. Nor does the indicator record how much of a household's cooking is done with clean fuels, how affordable the fuel is, or whether supply is reliable, all of which bear on the wording of target 7.1 on affordable and reliable modern energy services.

The remaining share matters because the other side of the figure is large. With 75.4 per cent having access in 2024, about one person in four still depends mainly on polluting fuels and technologies. As background outside the bench's data, smoke from such fuels is widely recognised as a cause of respiratory and cardiovascular illness, falling most heavily on women and young children, and the time spent gathering fuel and the burning of wood and charcoal are linked to schooling, paid work, forest loss and emissions. None of these links is measured in the results presented here.

The world's average conceals a wide spread between income groups, which later parts of the section take up. High-income countries stood at 98.8 per cent in 2015 and 99.5 per cent in 2024, so almost nothing remained to be gained there. Low-income countries rose only from 13.3 per cent to 15.6 per cent over the same years, while lower-middle-income countries rose from 42.7 per cent to 63.8 per cent and upper-middle-income countries from 76.9 per cent to 90.2 per cent. The global rise accompanies chiefly the middle-income groups, and the countries with the lowest access have moved the least.

For 2030, the reading is sobering. Target 7.1 calls for universal access to modern energy services, and the clean cooking series stands well short of that in 2024. The trend-to-target reading gives a world ratio of 0.56, with an expected value of 84.2 per cent in 2030, so the observed pace would not reach 100 per cent by then. The country classes show where the gap lies: 72 countries holding 61.5 per cent of the assessed population are on track or have met the target, while 46 countries with 14.9 per cent are making moderate progress, 39 with 13.8 per cent marginal progress, 29 with 8.3 per cent stagnation and 4 with 1.4 per cent regression. The point is examined further in the final part of the section.

### Regions diverge sharply, with Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Regional levels in 2024 span almost the whole range of the scale. North America stands at 100.0 per cent of the population with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking, and Europe and Central Asia at 98.3 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 22.9 per cent, up from 14.7 per cent in 2015. Fewer than one person in four in the region cooks mainly with clean fuels, while the world as a whole stands at 75.4 per cent. The income groups tell the same story: low-income economies stood at 15.6 per cent in 2024, against 99.5 per cent in high-income economies.

The regions between these poles moved at very different speeds after 2015. South Asia made the largest advance in the data, rising from 45.3 per cent to 74.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 70.7 per cent to 87.0 per cent. Both regions are now close to or above the world level. Large national programmes to distribute gas connections and to substitute for solid fuels are well-established contributors to progress of this kind, though the indicator does not show what drove the change in any country. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 86.8 per cent to 90.5 per cent, a smaller gain from a higher base. Europe and Central Asia moved from 96.6 per cent to 98.3 per cent, as the last households switched.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved slowly, from 74.7 per cent to 77.8 per cent. The region began 2015 at a level near that of East Asia and Pacific, which has since moved well ahead. The grouping also mixes economies at very different incomes, so the regional figure conceals wide national differences that this indicator, taken at regional level, cannot display. In Sub-Saharan Africa the gain of 14.7 to 22.9 per cent is real but small against the size of the shortfall, and the region's pace needs to be read against continuing population growth, which the share alone does not capture.

The gap between rural and urban households explains much of the regional picture. Worldwide, rural access rose from 38.2 per cent in 2015 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while urban access rose from 85.1 per cent to 89.4 per cent. Rural households therefore gained more in percentage points, yet remain far behind. Sub-Saharan Africa's rural level is the lowest in the data, at 8.6 per cent in 2024, up from 5.4 per cent in 2015. Urban Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.8 per cent, up from 29.5 per cent. Low-income economies show the same pattern, with rural access at 7.3 per cent and urban access at 31.5 per cent.

Elsewhere the contrast between rural and urban areas has narrowed. South Asia's rural level reached 61.7 per cent against an urban level of 92.0 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific's rural level reached 73.9 per cent against 94.6 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the rural level is 95.2 per cent, and in North America 99.9 per cent. These differences matter for 2030. Where the remaining shortfall is concentrated in dispersed rural households, supply networks for fuel, stoves and finance are costlier to extend, and a regional average rising slowly leaves the poorest households for last. The data show levels and change, not the affordability of fuels, which the target also names and which the indicator does not measure.

### Gains were broad but the pace has not been steady

The global series has not risen at a steady pace. A break analysis of the annual change in the world share with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking finds two breaks, in 2010 and in 2021. In the segment from 2001 to 2009 the mean annual change was 0.9 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2010 to 2020 it was 1.4 points a year. In the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 1.0 point a year. Progress therefore quickened at the start of the 2010s and slowed after 2021, to a pace close to that of the first decade of the century. The 2010 break falls before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, so the faster pace of the 2010s cannot be credited to the goals alone. The 2021 break coincides with the period after the pandemic shock of 2020, but the data show only when the pace changed, not why.

The slowdown matters for 2030. Universal access requires a pace above any of the three segments, and the latest segment is the slowest since the early 2000s. Four years is a short window, and the 2021 break rests on few annual observations, so the estimate of its mean change is less secure than those of the longer segments. The break dates are statistical estimates and could shift with further data.

The second analysis asks whether countries drew together. Across 192 countries from 2015 to 2024, the slope of each country's annual change on its starting level is negative, at -0.0079 (p below 0.001). Countries that began with lower access therefore gained faster on average than countries that began higher, and levels moved closer. The coefficient of variation, which measures spread relative to the mean, fell from 0.57 in 2015 to 0.50 in 2024, which agrees with this reading.

The convergence is real but weak. The R2 of the regression is 0.14, so the starting level explains a small part of the variation in how fast countries gained. Many countries with similar starting points moved at very different speeds, and some low-access countries gained little. Part of the pattern is arithmetical: countries near full access have little room to rise, which pulls the slope below zero without implying that any catch-up mechanism is at work. The coefficient of variation still shows a spread that is wide, since a value near 0.50 means that the typical gap between countries remains about half the world mean.

The data do not show what drove the breaks or the uneven gains. Fuel prices, public programmes, supply chains and household incomes are commonly cited influences on the choice of cooking fuel, but none is measured in these results, and none is asserted here as the cause. The findings describe when and where access changed, and they leave open why.

### Universal access by 2030 will be missed without acceleration, and proposals follow

The trend-to-target reading sets each series against universal access, 100.0 per cent by 2030, and projects the compound annual rate observed since 2015. On that basis the world reaches an expected 84.2 per cent in 2030, from 75.4 per cent in 2024. The ratio of distance covered to distance required is 0.56, which the tool classes as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. The observed pace would therefore not reach 100.0 per cent by 2030 at the global level.

Regions differ in how near they are. East Asia and Pacific is classed as on track or target met, with an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.99. South Asia is also on track, with a ratio of 1.06, having risen from 45.3 per cent in 2015 to 74.3 per cent in 2024. Its expected value above 100 shows that the extrapolation is mechanical and cannot exceed the ceiling. Europe and Central Asia is classed as needing acceleration, with a ratio of 0.82 and an expected 99.4 per cent, a small gap in absolute terms because the region started near the top. Latin America and the Caribbean has a ratio of 0.47 and an expected 93.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan has a ratio of 0.20 and an expected 79.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.19 and an expected 30.9 per cent in 2030. Both of the last two are classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

By income group, upper middle income countries are on track with a ratio of 1.01, and high income countries are on track at 99.5 per cent in 2024. Lower middle income countries need acceleration, with a ratio of 0.71 and an expected 83.4 per cent. Low income countries are classed as stagnant, with a ratio of 0.05: the share moved from 13.3 per cent in 2015 to 15.6 per cent in 2024, and the expected value for 2030 is 17.4 per cent. The ratio reflects the distance still to be covered, so regions starting from a low base are penalised heavily even when their annual rate is high. Sub-Saharan Africa's rate of 0.051 is close to South Asia's 0.057, yet its starting point leaves it far from the target.

Country classes show how widely the gap is spread. Of 190 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 61.5 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 46 countries, with 14.9 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 39 countries, with 13.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Twenty-nine countries, with 8.3 per cent, are stagnant, and 4 countries, with 1.4 per cent, have regressed. The classes are produced by a rule applied to each series, and they say nothing about what drives a country's change.

Two cautions apply. Target 7.1 speaks of universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services, and the text does not fix a numerical threshold for cooking. Reading it as exactly 100 per cent is the strictest reading; a reading of near-universal access would count more countries as having met it. The indicator also measures only the primary fuel or technology a household uses. It does not measure affordability or reliability of supply. The rural series shows the same pattern in sharper form: 8.6 per cent of rural people in Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, against 56.3 per cent of rural people worldwide.

For 2030, the country classes show where the shortfall lies by population. The countries classed as marginal, stagnant or regressing hold 13.8, 8.3 and 1.4 per cent of the assessed population, and the 46 moderate-progress countries hold 14.9 per cent, so the unmet gap is spread across several classes and not confined to the weakest. As context outside the bench's data, the lowest levels are usually found where rural households are hardest to reach.
