w-c06-4-4.text:
### The global picture: parliaments close to a quarter, management data thinner

Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in single or lower national parliamentary chambers worldwide in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015. The world share therefore rose by 4.4 percentage points in a decade, and 184 countries reported a figure for 2025, so the world value rests on near-complete coverage. Set against a benchmark of 50.0 per cent, women still hold little more than a quarter of seats. The shortfall from that benchmark is the distance between 27.2 and 50.0 per cent, which should not be confused with the 2015 world share.

Target 5.5 does not name a number. Its wording, women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making, can be read as parity, with women and men holding equal shares, or as a threshold of participation sufficient for women to shape decisions, which is often placed lower. The indicator for seats cannot settle the question, because it counts occupants of seats and says nothing about their influence, the committees they chair or the offices they hold. This book uses 50.0 per cent as the benchmark, since a population that is about half women supplies the plainest reference for equal opportunity, and findings are stated against it while the figure itself is reported in full so that readers may apply a different reading.

The parliamentary measure covers one arena of public life. The economic arena is represented by the female share of employment in senior and middle management, a series built from the occupational classification of managers. It excludes junior management, so it describes positions of real authority rather than all supervisory work. The question asked here includes the share of managerial positions held by women, and the answer must be stated plainly: the results available to this section give no value of that share for any country, year or group, only counts of reporting countries and classifications of trend. The section therefore cannot say what per cent of senior and middle management positions women hold, and it does not infer one from the parliamentary figure or from the female share of the labour force, which measures something different.

Two features of the series bear on every statement made from it. First, the World Bank publishes no aggregates for it, so no world or regional share can be quoted, and any comparison must proceed country by country. Second, the number of reporting countries has changed sharply over time. It was 40 in 2000, 72 in 2010 and 77 in 2015, and reached 95 in both 2019 and 2022. It then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and stood at only 48 in 2025. A total of 154 countries have reported in at least one year.

These counts matter as much as the values. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years may reflect a change in who reports rather than a change in women's position. The drop to 48 in 2025 may reflect survey lags, as labour force surveys are often processed with delay, but the data show only the count and not its cause. The 2025 observations for management are therefore not a sound basis for a statement of trend, and the later parts of this section rely on the years of fuller coverage when discussing managerial positions. The parliamentary series, by contrast, is reported almost everywhere and is the firmer ground for conclusions about direction and pace.

### Regions and countries differ by more than twenty-five points

Regional averages for 2025 span a wide range. Latin America and the Caribbean leads at 36.6 per cent of parliamentary seats held by women, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 31.7 per cent and North America at 29.5 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 27.0 per cent, close to the world value of 27.2 per cent. East Asia and Pacific follows at 23.3 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands at 16.9 per cent, and South Asia is lowest at 11.2 per cent. A regional average can conceal wide differences between countries within a region, and the results give no country-level figures for this part.

The two lowest regions are also the ones that did not advance. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan edged down from 17.5 per cent in 2015 to 16.9 per cent in 2025, and the trend tool classes it as regression. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the only large decline among the regions shown, and is also classed as regression. At the observed rate its share would reach 8.9 per cent in 2030. The data do not show why the share fell. Where a chamber is dissolved or not elected, the reported share can alter sharply, so a movement of this size may owe more to political events than to a gradual trend; that is context from general knowledge, not a finding of the results.

Income groups show a narrower spread than regions. High-income countries reached 31.2 per cent in 2025, upper middle income 27.0 per cent, low income 24.8 per cent and lower middle income 23.6 per cent. Low-income countries therefore hold a higher share than lower-middle-income ones, so income alone does not order the outcome. The results contain only group means and offer no explanation for the pattern.

The country distribution of progress towards a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 is more sobering than the regional averages. Of 187 countries assessed for parliaments, 24 are on track or have met the target, and they hold only 4.9 per cent of the assessed population. A further 36 countries, with 12.7 per cent of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest group is 69 countries with marginal progress that would need significant acceleration, covering 44.6 per cent of the population. Another 19 countries are stagnant, with 25.1 per cent of the population, and 39 countries are regressing, with 12.7 per cent. Stagnation and regression together hold 37.8 per cent of the assessed population, against 17.6 per cent where progress is on track or moderate. The population weights differ from the country counts: regression is the second most common outcome by number of countries, yet stagnation touches about twice as many people.

Management shows a similar pattern with a heavier weight on the negative end. Of 121 countries assessed for the female share of senior and middle management, 17 are on track or have met the target, with 8.1 per cent of the population. Moderate progress applies to 27 countries and 17.7 per cent of the population, and marginal progress to 34 countries and 31.3 per cent. Stagnation affects 6 countries with 2.7 per cent of the population. Regression is recorded in 37 countries, which hold 40.3 per cent of the population, against 12.7 per cent in parliaments. The assessment covers fewer countries than for parliaments, so these shares describe the countries with data rather than the world, and survey-based series can be revised from one round to the next, so the classification should be read with caution.

### What changed since 2015, and the limits of the evidence

Since 2015 the largest gain in women's share of parliamentary seats was in Latin America and the Caribbean, where the regional value rose from 27.9 per cent to 36.6 per cent. North America rose from 22.3 per cent to 29.5 per cent. Europe and Central Asia moved from 25.7 per cent to 31.7 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific from 19.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. These are regional averages and conceal wide differences between countries within each region.

Two regions moved the other way. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region slipped from 17.5 per cent to 16.9 per cent. South Asia fell from 18.0 per cent to 11.2 per cent, the lowest regional value in 2025 and the only large fall. The indicator does not separate the causes of these movements. As general context, a lower share can arise from an election, a change in the chamber counted, a suspended or dissolved legislature or the loss of a quota; nothing in these series measures it.

The classification against a target of 50.0 per cent by 2030 shows how uneven the movement has been. For parliaments, 24 countries are on track or have met the target, 36 show moderate progress, 69 show marginal progress, 19 are stagnating and 39 are regressing, among 187 countries assessed. The 24 countries on track hold only 4.9 per cent of the population assessed, whereas the 69 with marginal progress hold 44.6 per cent, the largest share of any class. The number of countries on track therefore overstates how far most women live where parity is approaching.

For senior and middle management, the classification covers 121 countries: 17 are on track or have met the target, 27 show moderate progress, 34 marginal progress, 6 stagnate and 37 regress. The 37 regressing countries hold 40.3 per cent of the population assessed, and the 39 regressing countries in parliaments hold 12.7 per cent of theirs. The two sets of countries and their populations differ, so the two shares are given side by side and are not ranked. As general context, legislative seats can be shifted by quotas and electoral rules, whereas management positions depend on firms, labour markets and care responsibilities; the data do not test this.

The results do not report the female share of senior and middle management itself, whether for a country, a region or the world. They give only classes, counts of countries and population shares, and the coverage tool lists no aggregate for this series. The question of what share of managerial positions women hold therefore cannot be answered with a figure from this evidence, and this section answers it for parliaments alone.

The management evidence is also thin in coverage. Across all years, 154 countries have reported at least one value, but the number reporting in a given year has varied: 40 in 2000, 77 in 2015, 90 in 2020 and 95 in 2022. The count then fell to 93 in 2023 and 89 in 2024, and only 48 countries had reported for 2025. Reporting lags in the underlying surveys are one possible explanation, offered as general context and not as a finding. Comparisons of 2025 with earlier years would rest on different sets of countries and cannot be trusted as a measure of change.

The regional trend summary for management returned no result, so no claim is made about how any region is moving on this indicator. Nor can these indicators say why countries advance or regress; they record outcomes, not the quotas, laws, party practices, employer conduct or social norms behind them. Whether the period after 2020 slowed or accelerated progress cannot be established for management, and for parliaments the results give levels and classes but no separate account of the pandemic years.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the rates observed since 2015, no region reaches the 50.0 per cent benchmark for parliaments by 2030. The world trend is classed as marginal progress, with an expected value of 29.8 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.25. East Asia and Pacific is expected at 25.7 per cent (ratio 0.21) and Europe and Central Asia at 35.2 per cent (ratio 0.39), both marginal. The high-income group is expected at 34.6 per cent, so wealth does not by itself close the gap. Latin America and the Caribbean comes closest, at 41.9 per cent, and is the only region classed as moderate progress; even there acceleration is needed.

The regions at the bottom of the range are moving in the wrong direction. South Asia is classed as regression, with an expected value of 8.9 per cent in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also classed as regression, at 16.7 per cent. Low-income countries are expected at 26.5 per cent and lower-middle-income countries at 25.3 per cent, both marginal. These projections extend a linear trend and are not forecasts. The data do not show what would move a national figure; electoral reform or political disruption, as general context outside these results, can change a country's value within one election cycle. Target 5.5 can also be read as parity at 50.0 per cent or as a lesser threshold of fair representation, and the classes above follow the first reading.

The country classifications for parliaments and for management, with their counts and population shares, are given earlier in the section and are not restated here. The sets of countries assessed differ, so the two classifications are not ranked against each other.

The results give no female share of senior and middle management for any country, year or group; they give only classes and counts of reporting countries. The managerial half of the question, what share of managerial positions women hold, therefore cannot be answered with a value from these results. Reporting is also thin at the latest point: 48 countries reported in 2025, against 95 in 2022. A lag in survey processing may explain this, as general context and not a finding.

Three proposals follow. National parliaments and electoral bodies in South Asia and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where the regional share has fallen, should review candidate-nomination rules and consider reserved seats or party quotas. National statistical offices should report the female share of senior and middle management every year, so that the 2025 gap in reporting is closed. International statistical agencies should publish regional aggregates for management, which are absent today.

w-c06-7-5.text:
### The global gap in internet use by sex

The question asked here has two halves: the gap in mobile phone ownership and the gap in internet use. Only the second can be answered. The bench holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex. The series on mobile cellular subscriptions is counted per 100 people, is not divided by sex, and can count one person several times, so it cannot show who owns a handset. The ownership half therefore remains unanswered, and the findings below concern internet use alone. Answering it would need a survey series on handset ownership by sex, such as a household or demand-side survey, which the bench does not hold.

Target 5.b asks for greater use of enabling technology, in particular information and communications technology, to promote the empowerment of women. The measure available is the share of women and of men who have used the internet in the previous three months.

On that measure, women's use rose sharply. Female internet use stood at 51.8 per cent of the female population in 2019 and reached 68.2 per cent in 2024. The period includes the pandemic years, when schooling, work and public services moved online; the results do not isolate that or any other cause, and it is context only.

Male use stood at 56.0 per cent of the male population in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The two world figures do not share an end year: the female series is read at 2024 and the male series at 2025, because the latest world value in each result falls in a different year. Setting one against the other mixes the difference between the sexes with a year of growth in male use. It overstates the gap in any single year and should not be read as a measurement. The world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. A clean comparison requires both series at the same date, and the regional results, where both are read at 2024, allow it in the parts that follow.

The 2019 figures are on a common footing. Women at 51.8 per cent and men at 56.0 per cent give a female-to-male ratio of about 0.93. This is a fact about 2019 only and says nothing about whether the gap has narrowed or widened since. Because use rose for both sexes, a gap in percentage points can grow while the ratio improves, so each measure should be stated with its basis.

The figures also carry a caution about coverage. The count of countries reporting in 2025 is only 7 in each result, against 92 in 2019 and 65 in 2024. The 2025 world and income-group values therefore rest on a thin base of direct observation, and the 2024 regional values are better supported. Internet use as defined here also says nothing about the quality of access, the device used, the cost of data or what women do online. The evidence supports rapid gains by women and a shortfall against men in 2019, while the size of the world gap in 2024 stays undetermined.

### Regional differences in the gap

Among the regions reported here, the point gap between women's and men's internet use in 2024 is largest in two regions at a middle level of use and smaller in the region with the lowest use. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 55.0 per cent of women had used the internet in the previous three months, against 67.6 per cent of men. In South Asia the figures were 56.3 per cent for women and 69.1 per cent for men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the shares were 29.4 per cent and 37.9 per cent. The gap there looks smaller than in the two regions above, but the level of use is far lower, so a small point gap at a low level should not be read as near equality.

South Asia also shows how the gap can move. In 2019 women's use stood at 24.3 per cent and men's at 34.9 per cent. By 2024 women's use had reached 56.3 per cent and men's 69.1 per cent, so the point gap had widened, even though women's use more than doubled. Rapid growth in use among both sexes can thus coexist with a larger point difference.

The gap is small where use is nearly universal. In North America 94.1 per cent of women and 94.7 per cent of men used the internet in 2024. In Europe and Central Asia the shares were 90.0 per cent and 91.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean lies between, at 81.3 per cent for women and 82.0 per cent for men. Near-universal use leaves little room for a difference. Mobile networks, affordable devices and schooling may have contributed in these regions, but these are hypotheses from outside the bench's data, which the results do not test.

East Asia and Pacific shows a reversal. In 2019 women's use, at 67.4 per cent, was slightly above men's, at 66.7 per cent. By 2024 women stood at 85.5 per cent and men at 87.6 per cent, so men had moved ahead. The regional aggregate hides large differences among its economies, and the data given here do not show which of them drove the change. The result should be read as a shift in the regional average, not as evidence of decline in women's use, which rose over the period.

Income groups are reported for 2025, when only 7 countries reported these series, so the figures rest on very thin direct observation and probably include estimates; they are indicative only. In low-income countries 18.3 per cent of women used the internet, against 28.6 per cent of men. In lower middle income countries the shares were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent. In high-income countries they were 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The largest point gap again falls at a middle level of use and the smallest where use is highest, but the evidence is weaker than for the regional figures of 2024.

Across 54 countries with data in both 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male use in 2024 is 0.948, and that between their changes is 0.958. Countries with larger gains in one sex therefore generally show larger gains in the other. This is an association only; it does not show why any gap persists or what the gap depends on.

The regional pattern matters for target 5.b because the largest remaining gaps lie in regions where women's use is far from universal. Possible factors, which lie outside the data and which the bench cannot separate, include the cost of devices and data, differences in schooling and literacy, social norms on women's independent use of phones, and concerns over safety online. They may operate with different force in each region, which is why a single global figure conceals as much as it reveals.

### What changed since 2019 and what the data can support

South Asia shows the largest change since 2019 among the regions reported here. Female internet use there rose from 24.3 per cent in 2019 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while male use rose from 34.9 per cent to 69.1 per cent. Women gained a great deal in absolute terms, but they remained behind men in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same ordering at a lower level: women moved from 20.2 per cent to 29.4 per cent, and men from 28.6 per cent to 37.9 per cent. Whether the gap in points widened or narrowed in either region is a difference that these results do not give, and it is not asserted here.

Across the 54 countries with data for both sexes in 2019 and 2024, the rank correlation between female and male changes is 0.958, and that between 2024 levels is 0.948. The two sexes' changes therefore tend to move together across countries. This is an association only. It does not show why gaps persist where they do, nor that the gap is determined by overall connectivity. Income, education, literacy, norms on women's use of devices and the cost of handsets and data are plausible influences from outside the results, and the series cannot separate them. The period also includes the pandemic years, which the data do not isolate as a cause of any change.

Income groups are indicative only, because the 2025 values rest on 7 reporting countries. In low-income countries, female use was 18.3 per cent in 2025 against 28.6 per cent for men. In lower-middle-income countries the figures were 56.9 per cent and 68.7 per cent, in upper-middle-income countries 87.9 per cent and 89.7 per cent, and in high-income countries 93.6 per cent and 94.9 per cent. The world series moved from 51.8 per cent for women and 56.0 per cent for men in 2019 to 68.2 per cent for women in 2024 and 76.6 per cent for men in 2025. Those last two values fall in different years, so a world gap cannot be read from them.

The evidence has limits that bear on every figure above. In 2019, 92 countries reported female internet use; in 2024, 65 did; in 2025, only 7. The data do not state why reporting fell after 2019, and the pandemic and reporting delays are only conjectures from outside them. Which countries are missing is not shown by these results, so whether measured progress overstates or understates the global picture is unknown. The 54-country comparison is a subset of the 137 countries that have ever reported. The series also defines use over the previous three months from any device, so it says nothing about who owns a phone, who controls it, or how it is used.

### Implications for target 5.b by 2030 and proposals

Target 5.b carries no numerical threshold and no date-bound level, so it can be read in more than one way. The reading adopted here is a narrowing of the gap between women's and men's internet use, alongside rising levels for women. The question put to this section has two halves, and only one can be answered: the bench holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex, so the ownership gap is unmeasured here. A survey of handset ownership by sex, which the World Bank's catalogue does not hold in this set, would be needed to answer it. For internet use, the evidence for 2030 is mixed. Levels have risen sharply, but the regional gaps in 2024 remain wide, and these results cannot show whether the gaps are closing.

The world figures illustrate the limit of the data. Female use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, while male use stood at 56.0 per cent in 2019 and 76.6 per cent in 2025. The male figure refers to a later year than the female one, so the world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results. The regional figures for 2024 are on a common year and are the safer basis. In Sub-Saharan Africa female use was 29.4 per cent against 37.9 per cent for men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the figures were 55.0 per cent and 67.6 per cent. In South Asia they were 56.3 per cent and 69.1 per cent. In North America, with 94.1 per cent for women and 94.7 per cent for men, the gap is almost gone.

The income-group figures point the same way, but they are indicative only, because just 7 countries reported in 2025. Female use reached 18.3 per cent in low income countries against 28.6 per cent for men, 56.9 per cent against 68.7 per cent in lower middle income countries, and 93.6 per cent against 94.9 per cent in high income countries. The data contain no projection, so whether any region reaches parity by 2030 cannot be stated. They do not test the causes of the gaps either. Factors commonly proposed outside these results include the cost of handsets and data, lower female literacy and income, social norms on who may own a device, and concerns about safety online. These are context, not findings.

Across 54 countries, the rank correlation between changes in female and male use from 2019 to 2024 is 0.958, and for 2024 levels it is 0.948. This is an association only: female and male use tend to move together across these countries, and the correlation does not show why, nor whether gaps are closing within countries.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

Ministries responsible for communications and gender in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan should set sex-specific targets for internet use, since the 2024 gaps there remain wide; cost of devices and data is a plausible but untested barrier, and programmes should evaluate it.

The World Bank and the International Telecommunication Union should raise the number of countries reporting sex-disaggregated internet use each year, as only 7 reported in 2025, so that gaps can be tracked on a common year.

w-c07-5-4.text:
### Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015

World net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, measured in constant 2023 dollars. That is an increase of about half over eight years. In current dollars the series climbs from US$147.1 billion to US$259.5 billion. The two series meet in 2023 because the constant-price base year is 2023, so the gap between them in 2015 reflects the rise in prices since then. The constant-dollar figure is the fairer measure of change, since it removes the effect of rising prices; the current-dollar series shows a larger rise because it includes inflation.

The indicator needs careful reading before it is applied to target 6.a. It records all net official development assistance received by developing countries: grants and concessional loans, net of repayments of principal, across every sector. It does not isolate water and sanitation, nor the activities the target names, such as water harvesting, desalination, wastewater treatment, recycling and reuse. The series is therefore a proxy for the general scale of international support, and a rise in it does not show that more reached water and sanitation programmes. Spending on health, emergency relief, refugee costs or budget support can raise the total without any of it entering the sector.

The target itself adds a second limit. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building support by 2030, but it names no amount, no share of income and no baseline year. It can be read as a call for more money, for more technical assistance, or for better-targeted programmes, and a financial series speaks only to the first of these. Capacity-building, such as training, institutional support and technology transfer, is poorly captured by a measure of net disbursements. A judgement that the target is on track can therefore rest only on the direction of the aggregate, not on a threshold.

Coverage is also partial. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts in this series, and the world figure is the sum of those recipients. The inequality analysis later in this section covers a different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023, because it requires population weights, so the two counts are not the same set. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region whose countries are donors rather than recipients, and high-income economies receive only small amounts: US$319.3 million in 2015 and US$760.9 million in 2023 in constant dollars. Net receipts measure what arrives, not what is needed, so the series does not say whether the level is adequate against the water-stress and service gaps described elsewhere in this chapter.

With these limits stated, the direction is clear. Assistance received grew substantially after 2015 and stood at its highest level in the series in the latest year available, 2023, although the annual change in 2023 was slightly negative, at a mean of about -US$0.7 billion. Whether growth is sustained to 2030 is a separate matter, because the donor side of the ledger depends on budget decisions that recipient data cannot anticipate.

### Regions gained unevenly, and Europe and Central Asia gained most

Regional totals of net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, show that the increase since 2015 was not evenly shared. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest gain by a wide margin, rising from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. That is close to a fivefold increase, and it lifted the region from one of the smaller recipients to the third largest, behind sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, and ahead of every other region. The series does not show what drove the rise. As context only, emergency and budget support directed to the region in the early 2020s is a plausible contributor, and the series measures all official assistance, not the share spent on water.

The other regions moved much less. East Asia and Pacific received US$9.9 billion in 2015 and US$10.7 billion in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, almost no change in real terms. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion. These three regions ended the period within a narrow band of one another, near US$10.7 billion each, although their populations and water needs differ greatly. No population or per-person series is used in this section, so the totals say nothing about assistance per person; that comparison would need such a series.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, a rise well below the world's increase. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the largest recipient, with US$51.8 billion in 2015 and US$64.8 billion in 2023. The largest absolute flows thus stayed in sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, while the fastest growth went to Europe and Central Asia.

The distribution by income group, also in constant 2023 dollars, shows a similar movement. Low-income countries received US$35.2 billion in 2015 and US$44.6 billion in 2023, and lower-middle-income countries US$54.9 billion and US$59.2 billion. Upper-middle-income countries rose from US$18.9 billion to US$57.4 billion, the fastest growth of the groups, and by 2023 they received more than the low-income group, whose receipts also rose. Assistance in total is therefore not concentrating on the poorest, a pattern that sits uneasily with target 6.a, which stresses support to developing countries in water and sanitation activities. Only a sector breakdown, which these series do not provide, could show whether water programmes followed the same path.

### A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase

The aggregate path of assistance since 2015 is not a steady climb. A structural break analysis of the annual change in world net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, places breaks in 2022 and 2023. Between 2001 and 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. In 2022 alone the change was US$49.8 billion, nearly eight times that long-run average. In 2023 the series fell by US$0.7 billion. A single year therefore accounts for a large part of the rise recorded between 2015 and 2023, when the world total went from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, and the preceding two decades of gradual growth cannot be extrapolated from it.

The data do not record why 2022 was exceptional. It is an inference, not a finding, that the jump reflects emergency and humanitarian flows, support to countries affected by conflict and displacement, and pandemic recovery financing. That reading fits the earlier observation that Europe and Central Asia gained most, but the series covers all purposes of assistance together and cannot separate such flows from spending on water and sanitation. The 2023 fall shows that the 2022 level was not matched by a further rise. Whether it marks a plateau or the start of a decline cannot be judged from one observation.

The distribution of assistance among recipient countries also changed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received rose from 0.361 in 2015, across 138 countries, to 0.452 in 2023, across 135 countries. The Theil index rose more sharply, from 0.255 to 0.460, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.64 to 1.48. Assistance has thus become more unevenly spread among recipients. The country count differs between the two years, and the 135 countries in the inequality analysis are not the same set as the 136 countries reporting in 2023 that underlie the world total, so part of the change may reflect which countries are included, and the comparison should be read with that caution.

The composition of this inequality shifted too. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023. Differences among countries within the same region now account for a larger part of the disparity than differences between regions. This matters for targeting: regional averages conceal recipients that receive much more or much less than their neighbours, and allocation by region alone would miss them.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise is fragile and its distribution has become less even. Target 6.a calls for expanded cooperation and capacity-building support in water and sanitation. Total assistance, whatever its level, does not show how much reaches that sector, and a total inflated by one exceptional year is a weak guide to the sustained flows that infrastructure and capacity-building require.

### Assistance for 2030 must be tracked by sector and directed by need

The series held by the bench measures total official development assistance received, not assistance to water and sanitation. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building in water-related activities, and total flows cannot show whether that is happening. A rise in the aggregate may reflect humanitarian, budget-support or debt-related disbursements that have little to do with water supply, sewerage or wastewater treatment. For 2030, the first implication is therefore that progress on 6.a cannot be judged from the present evidence, and the headline figure of US$259.5 billion in 2023 should not be read as a measure of support for water.

The second implication concerns durability. The break analysis found a mean annual change of US$49.8 billion in 2022, against US$6.4 billion over 2001 to 2021, followed by a mean annual change of -US$0.7 billion in 2023, a small fall. A jump of that size, followed by a fall, suggests an exceptional episode, not a new trend. Planning that assumes the 2023 level will persist, or keep rising, risks a shortfall by 2030. The target can also be read in more than one way: it names no quantity of assistance, so expansion could mean volume, share of total aid or reach of capacity-building.

The third implication concerns distribution. Among countries, the Gini coefficient of assistance received, population-weighted and in constant 2023 dollars, rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.26 to 0.46. The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 45.3 per cent to 29.6 per cent, so the growing concentration lies increasingly within regions, among individual countries. The inequality analysis covers 135 countries in 2023, while the world total rests on 136 countries reporting, so the two sets differ slightly. In constant 2023 dollars, low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015, and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion, yet the data do not show whether flows follow the countries with the weakest water and sanitation coverage. Upper middle income countries received US$57.4 billion in 2023, up from US$18.9 billion in 2015, the faster growth of the two groups, which suggests allocation is shaped by factors beyond service need; this is an inference, not a finding of the data.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

claims.fact: c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023

proposals: Donors and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report water and sanitation disbursements, including capacity-building, as a series open to the World Bank's catalogue, so that Target 6.a can be tracked directly.
Donor governments should plan water and sanitation support on a baseline below the 2022 peak, and commit multi-year funds so that the one-off rise is not mistaken for a lasting level.

Donors and recipient governments should direct water assistance by measured service gaps, using coverage of safely managed water and sanitation to target the countries furthest behind, including within regions.
The United Nations bodies responsible for Goal 6 should state what expansion under Target 6.a means, whether volume, share of aid or reach of capacity-building.
w-c07-5-4.gaps: No series on assistance to water and sanitation, or on capacity-building, is held; the data show only total assistance received. Disbursements by purpose, donor commitments, and recipient-level need are not covered, and the 2023 data cover 136 countries.

w-c08-4-2.text:
### World energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured as megajoules of energy supply per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, fell from 4.8556 MJ in 2015 to 4.5449 MJ in 2021. The direction is the one target 7.3 requires: each dollar of output needed less energy at the end of the period than at the start. The size of the fall is read directly from the two levels, and no further percentage is relied on here. The question for the section is whether the pace is the one the target asks for.

The trend tool expresses the world movement as a rate of -0.011 per year for the indicator, and classifies it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. That rate is the tool's own measure of change per year, and it is read here only as a direction and a pace relative to the tool's thresholds. The tool was run with no numerical target, so its classification rests on a generic benchmark and not on a figure derived from the wording of target 7.3. The label is a guide to the size of the gap, not a verdict on the target itself.

The target can be read in more than one way. Its wording, to double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, is commonly interpreted as doubling the rate recorded in an earlier period, which requires a baseline period to be chosen. The choice matters, because the earlier rate differs according to the years used. A second reading, used in the monitoring of the goals, sets a fixed annual rate of improvement in energy intensity for the whole period to 2030. The two readings need not give the same answer. The segment comparison in a later part tests only the first, using periods within the series; a rate for the years before 2015 is not held for the world as a whole, and the fixed-rate reading cannot be tested with the bench series.

The data also limit what can be said about the present. The world series ends in 2021, not in 2022 or later, so the latest observation lies well before 2030 and says nothing about the years since. Regional series reach 2022 in some cases, and the number of countries reporting in 2022 was 116, so the final year rests on thinner coverage. Any statement that the world is or is not on course for 2030 is therefore an extrapolation from six years of change, a period that includes the sharp fall and partial rebound in economic activity around 2020. Movements in GDP affect the ratio as much as movements in energy supply, so a change in intensity does not by itself show that efficiency measures were adopted.

Why the measure matters is plain enough. Energy intensity is the broadest indicator available of how much energy an economy needs to produce its output, and a falling value lowers fuel costs, emissions and import dependence for a given level of output. It is, however, a crude proxy for efficiency, because it also reflects the structure of an economy, its climate, and the share of heavy industry in output. The following parts examine how these differences appear across regions and over time.

### Regions diverge from a 2.58 to a 6.14 MJ range by 2021 or 2022

Regional levels of energy intensity, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, span a wide range by the latest year available. Europe and Central Asia is lowest, at 2.5791 MJ in 2022, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest among regions, at 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The latest year differs between regions, 2021 for some and 2022 for others, so the comparison is approximate and the gap between regions is read as indicative rather than exact.

Europe and Central Asia fell from 4.002 MJ in 2015 to 2.5791 MJ in 2022. Its rate of change, -0.0608 per year, is the steepest of any region and the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions. Part of the decline in this region may reflect changes in economic structure and in fuel supply as well as efficiency gains; the data do not separate these.

North America and South Asia also improved substantially. North America moved from 5.0428 MJ in 2015 to 4.364 MJ in 2022, at a rate of -0.0204 per year, and South Asia from 4.5047 MJ to 3.9427 MJ in 2021, at -0.022 per year. Both are classed as on track or target met. South Asia's result is notable because it began from a level close to the world value and has since fallen below it.

The remaining regions made less headway. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5.6997 MJ in 2015 to 5.2313 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0142 per year, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 3.4822 MJ to 3.265 MJ in 2022, at -0.0092 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Its level is low, which may leave less room for further cuts, but the data do not test that.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan barely moved, from 5.3599 MJ in 2015 to 5.332 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0009 per year, classed as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa also stagnated, falling from 6.2412 MJ to 6.1403 MJ in 2021, at -0.0027 per year. Together these two regions combine high or middling levels with almost no improvement.

Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income economies stood at 7.415 MJ in 2015 and 7.1393 MJ in 2021, the highest of any group, with a rate of -0.0063 per year, classed as marginal progress. High-income economies fell from 4.3961 MJ to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, at -0.0334 per year, classed as on track or target met. Lower middle income fell from 4.644 MJ to 4.2707 MJ in 2021, and upper middle income from 5.5767 MJ to 5.2119 MJ. The poorest economies are therefore the most energy-intensive per unit of output and are improving most slowly.

Three cautions apply. First, only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the latest regional values rest on incomplete years, and regions with data only to 2021 are compared with others to 2022. Second, intensity reflects economic structure, climate, fuel mix and the share of traditional biomass in supply, and the purchasing power parity conversion of GDP, not efficiency alone. Third, the world rate of -0.011 per year is classed as marginal progress, so the regional divergence matters for 2030: the regions that are on track are not those with the highest levels, and the highest-intensity regions are those where acceleration is most needed.

### Improvement peaked before 2018 and has since slowed

The structural breaks in the annual change of world energy intensity show that the pace of improvement has not been steady. The series for the world, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, has breaks in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. These divide the record into five segments, each with its own mean annual change. A negative mean change means that intensity fell, so a larger negative figure means faster improvement.

In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ. It steepened to -0.1154 MJ in 2005-2008, the fastest pace of the early period. The break in 2009 marks a pause: in 2009-2010 the mean change was +0.0070 MJ, so intensity rose slightly instead of falling. That coincides with the global financial crisis, and a link between the two is a reasonable reading, though the data do not by themselves establish it. Output fell sharply while much of the energy supply, in buildings, transport and industrial plant, could not be scaled down as quickly, which tends to raise intensity in a downturn.

The break in 2011 opens the longest segment. In 2011-2017 the mean annual change was -0.1045 MJ, close to the pace of 2005-2008 and about twice that of 2001-2004. This matters for the target. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement, and the baseline year of 2015 sits inside this faster period. Any comparison of later years with the rate at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals is therefore a comparison with a stretch of unusually quick improvement, not with the slower pace of the early 2000s. Reading the target against the earlier rate of -0.0498 MJ would make doubling look nearer than it is when set against the rate that prevailed in 2015.

The final break, in 2018, is the most consequential. In 2018-2021 the mean annual change was -0.0325 MJ, less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017 and below even the 2001-2004 rate. Improvement therefore peaked before 2018 and has since slowed. The segment is short, four years, and its end includes 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic disturbed both output and energy supply. A short segment with unusual years at its end warrants caution, and the mean should not be taken as a settled new trend.

The data do not identify why the slowdown occurred. Several explanations are plausible and are offered here only as interpretations, not findings. The pandemic caused abrupt falls and rebounds in activity that distort a ratio of energy to output. Fuel prices affect the incentive to economise on energy, and the price changes of these years may have weakened it. Structural change in industry, including shifts in the weight of energy-intensive sectors in world output, can move intensity independently of efficiency in any single sector. The series measures energy per unit of GDP, so it blends efficiency with the composition of the economy, and none of these causes can be separated from the others using this result alone.

For 2030 the implication is plain, though conditional. If the rate of 2018-2021 persisted, the world would fall well short of doubling the rate of 2011-2017, let alone exceeding it. Meeting the target on the most demanding reading would require a pace far above any segment in the record. The target also admits more than one reading, since the earlier rate may be taken from the period before 2015 or from the baseline decade, and the choice changes the threshold. Under either reading, the break of 2018 shows that the recent direction is away from the target, not towards it.

### Doubling the earlier rate is not met, and proposals follow

Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency, and the series held by the bench allow a reading of that target only in outline. The target does not say which earlier rate is to be doubled, nor which period is to be compared. Two readings are therefore possible: the pace before 2015 set against the pace after it, or the pace in the years of fastest improvement set against the most recent years. The bench holds no pre-2015 rate, so the first reading cannot be tested here. The verdict below holds for the segment comparison alone.

The test is a comparison of the two latest segments of the world series. From 2011 to 2017 the mean annual change in energy intensity was -0.1045 MJ per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. From 2018 to 2021 it was -0.0325 MJ. Doubling would require a recent pace of about twice the earlier one, and the recent pace is far slower, so intensity is falling more slowly, not twice as fast. The trend tool classes the world rate of -0.01096 as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the results do not state the period of that rate. The segment from 2018 to 2021 includes the pandemic years, when output and energy supply both moved sharply, so part of the slowdown may reflect those disturbances and not a lasting change. Only four years are covered, and the data cannot separate the two explanations.

Regional results show where the world picture is made. Four groups are classed as on track or target met: Europe and Central Asia, at a rate of -0.06083, the high-income group, at -0.03337, South Asia, at -0.02197, and North America, at -0.02044. The label reflects the tool's own benchmark and does not show that those groups are doubling a previous rate. The high-income group fell from 4.3961 MJ in 2015 to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 4.002 MJ to 2.5791 MJ over the same years. Efficiency gains, structural change and fuel switching are familiar possible explanations in richer economies, but the results do not establish which applies.

The regions where improvement is most needed are moving least. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a rate of -0.00271, and its intensity moved from 6.2412 MJ in 2015 to 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is also classed as stagnating, at -0.00087, with levels of 5.3599 MJ in 2015 and 5.332 MJ in 2021. East Asia and Pacific shows moderate progress, at -0.01419, but acceleration is needed there: its intensity fell from 5.6997 MJ to 5.2313 MJ. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.00916, and the low-income group, at -0.00629, show marginal progress. The low-income group still has the highest level of any income group, at 7.1393 MJ in 2021.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Unless the pace rises well above the 2018 to 2021 mean, the doubling is not met on the segment comparison, and the regions with the highest or slowest-falling intensity are those where the gap is widest. The latest data point is 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, so later developments are not visible. Only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the most recent figures rest on incomplete reporting.

Intensity is also an imperfect measure of efficiency. It divides energy supply by output, so it moves with the structure of an economy, climate and trade as well as technical efficiency. A fall may come from a shift to services without any gain in equipment efficiency, and a flat series may hide improvements offset by growth in energy-heavy activity. The proposals respond to these limits and to the regional gaps.

w-c08-4-2.gaps: The bench holds no pre-2015 rate of improvement, so the reading of target 7.3 that compares the period before and after 2015 cannot be tested. The 2018 to 2021 segment is short and includes the pandemic. Data stop at 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, and only 116 countries reported in 2022. Intensity mixes technical efficiency with economic structure, climate and trade, and the series cannot separate them.

w-c04-4-5.text:
### Premature mortality from non-communicable diseases has barely moved since 2015

Target 3.4 asks for a one-third reduction in premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by 2030. The indicator is the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, assuming current age-specific mortality rates persist and no other cause of death intervenes. It is a modelled probability, not a count of deaths, and it is not affected by population growth or ageing in the way a crude death rate would be. A fall in the indicator therefore reflects lower risk at each age, not a change in the number of people who die.

The world level was 18.9% in 2015 and 18.3% in 2021, on figures from 185 reporting countries in the latest year. The decline over six years is therefore about half a percentage point. The target can be read in more than one way: as a one-third cut in the percentage itself, or as a one-third cut in the number of premature deaths. The bench uses the first reading, applied to the 2015 baseline, which sets a threshold of 12.57% for the world by 2030. The same reading is applied to every region and income group, so the regional verdicts that follow in this section rest on that single convention. The probability measure also does not show whether a fall comes from prevention, such as lower tobacco use and better blood pressure control, or from treatment, such as earlier cancer care.

Against that threshold the world is far behind. The trend tool, a linear extrapolation of the 2015-2021 pace, places the world on a path to 17.5% in 2030, with a ratio of 0.22 of the progress needed. The ratio compares the annual rate of decline observed with the rate that would reach the target, so a value of 1 would mean on track. A value near one fifth means that the pace would need to roughly quintuple over the remaining years. The classification given is marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

The series ends in 2021, so it captures only the first year after the pandemic shock of 2020, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and chronic care and may have raised deaths from cardiovascular disease and diabetes in some countries. Whether the small fall since 2015 would have been larger without that disruption cannot be separated using this series alone. Many low-income countries also rely on modelled estimates, because vital registration of causes of death is incomplete, so the global figure carries uncertainty that is not shown in the point values. The finding that holds despite these cautions is that a decline of half a percentage point in six years is far short of the one-third cut the target requires.

### Regions differ in level and in direction

Regional experience since 2015 can be sorted by one rule: the direction and size of the change in the probability that a 30-year-old would die before the 70th birthday from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease. Under that rule, most regions fell, by margins that differ widely, and one region rose.

Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest fall, from 17.5% in 2015 to 15.7% in 2021. East Asia and Pacific moved from 17.8% to 16.9% over the same years. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 22.3% to 20.7%, which still leaves the region above the world figure of 18.3% in 2021. Its pace ratio is 0.39, meaning the decline ran at well under half the pace the target requires, and extending its own linear path gives 18.5% in 2030, against the target value of 12.57% derived from the world baseline.

The two Americas moved least in absolute terms. North America went from 13.6% to 13.3%, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 15.3% to 14.7%. North America began from the lowest regional level. Its ratio of 0.82 should not be read as near-target progress: it rests on a very small absolute fall from a low base, and the trend tool's ratio is sensitive to such starting points. Latin America and the Caribbean reaches a ratio of 0.50, and linear extension gives 13.9% for it in 2030. Outside the data, it is widely understood that gains in cardiovascular care and falling smoking have been offset in part by obesity and diabetes, and by unequal access to treatment; these causes are not measured by the results used here.

South Asia is the exception. The probability there rose from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, and its pace ratio is negative, at -0.20, which the trend tool labels regression. Linear extension would place the region at 24.0% in 2030. In 2015 South Asia, at 22.1%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, at 22.3%, were effectively level; by 2021 South Asia, at 22.9%, stood above that group's 20.7% and had the highest level among regions, though low-income countries as an income group stood slightly higher, at 23.0%. A rise in a modelled lifetime-risk indicator means that age-specific death rates between 30 and 70 did not fall fast enough to offset adverse trends. Established knowledge points to hypertension, diabetes, air pollution and the cost of long-term treatment as plausible contributors. The period includes the pandemic years, when disrupted screening and chronic care may have raised the 2021 figure; the data cannot separate these influences from the underlying trend.

Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 21.9% in 2015 and 21.3% in 2021, a small fall that leaves its level close to the South Asian one. Its pace ratio is 0.16, and linear extension gives 20.4% in 2030. Measurement is a concern here, since death registration is incomplete and the estimates rely heavily on modelling rather than on recorded causes of death.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries fell from 24.0% to 23.0%, a ratio of 0.22, and lower-middle-income countries from 22.8% to 22.8%, a ratio of 0.00, which is stagnation. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.1% to 17.1%, and high-income countries from 13.8% to 12.8%. High-income countries alone are classed as on track, with a ratio of 1.93 and a linear value of 11.4% in 2030, which would lie below the target value. Regional and income groupings overlap but are not the same, and the results do not say how far South Asia's rise and the lower-middle-income stagnation share the same countries.

The spread among the 185 reporting countries, weighted by population, widened slightly. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.152 in 2015 to 0.158 in 2021, and the Theil index from 0.038 to 0.041. Both are low in absolute terms, since the indicator is a probability that all adults experience, but the direction is towards greater inequality. The share of the Theil index lying between regions grew from 27.0% to 33.1%. Regional location therefore explains a larger part of the disparity than in 2015, and the remainder lies among countries inside the same region. For Target 3.4 this implies that regional averages hide wide national differences. All trend readings here are linear extensions of the 2015 to 2021 change, so regional ratios should be read as indications, not forecasts.

### The pace of decline slowed after 2015 and countries did not converge

The annual change in the world probability of premature death from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease shows a structural break at 2015. In the segment from 2001 to 2014 the mean annual change was -0.26 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2015 to 2021 it was -0.09 percentage points a year. The pace of decline over the first six years of the Sustainable Development Goals was therefore roughly a third of the pace of the preceding fourteen years. A target framed as a one-third reduction by 2030 depends on that pace, and the break indicates that the trajectory moved away from it at the moment the target was adopted. The world value stood at 18.3% in 2021, against a target value of 12.57% for 2030. The trend tool expects 17.5% in 2030 at the post-2015 rate.

The break is a statistical finding about the world series, and its timing should be read with care. A break detected at 2015 means that the average change differs on either side of that year; it does not show that anything in the Goals themselves caused the slowdown. The following explanations rest on general knowledge, not on any result of this section, and the data do not separate them. Earlier gains in many countries came from falling blood pressure and smoking in high-income settings and from better treatment of heart disease, and such gains meet diminishing returns. Rising obesity, diabetes and air pollution exposure work in the opposite direction. The years 2020 and 2021 coincide with the pandemic, which disrupted screening, diagnosis and routine care for chronic conditions. The series cannot isolate these effects from the underlying trend.

A slower world pace could still be consistent with narrowing gaps, if countries with high probabilities were falling faster than the rest. The convergence test shows that this did not happen. Across 185 countries, regressing the change from 2015 to 2021 on the starting level gives a coefficient of 0.0016 with a p-value of 0.70 and an R-squared of 0.001. The coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains almost none of the variation in change. Countries with the worst starting positions were not catching up, and those with the best were not pulling away in any systematic fashion.

The dispersion measures point the same way, though they are not the same statistic. The convergence test reports a coefficient of variation of 0.36 in 2015 and 0.38 in 2021, computed across countries without population weights. The spread tool, which weights countries by population, reports a coefficient of variation of 0.27 in 2015 and 0.28 in 2021. The levels differ because of the weighting, but both rise. The population-weighted Gini coefficient moved from 0.152 to 0.158, and the share of the Theil index lying between regions rose from 27.0% to 33.1%. Relative spread widened slightly, and a growing part of it lies between regions, not within them. For a target defined in relative terms this matters, because a country starting from a high probability needs a larger absolute fall to deliver one third, and no systematic acceleration in such countries appears in the convergence result.

The section also asks whether service coverage accompanies better outcomes. The bench links the change in the probability with the change in the UHC service coverage sub-index on non-communicable diseases, which is built from tracer indicators for hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, across 184 countries from 2015 to 2021. The Spearman correlation between the two changes is 0.10 and the Kendall coefficient is 0.07. Both are weak. If coverage gains went with larger mortality falls, the correlation would be negative. The weak positive value gives no support for that expectation over this short window, though it is too small to show the opposite either.

The correlation of 2021 levels is -0.25 by the Spearman measure and -0.17 by the Kendall measure. Countries with higher service coverage tend to have a lower probability of premature death from these diseases. This is the expected direction and is modest in size, larger than the correlation of changes but far from strong. It describes a cross-section in which income, age structure, the wider health system and the prevalence of risk factors all differ together, and it cannot be read as a measure of what coverage achieves.

These are associations, not causes. The tracer indicators cover only three of many interventions that bear on the four disease groups; cancer care, cardiac surgery and chronic respiratory treatment are not represented. The mortality series is modelled from partial vital registration, and in many low-income countries it rests on estimates, so differences in change between countries partly reflect modelling and not observation. A window of six years is short for a slow-moving outcome, and the pandemic years sit inside it. Taken together, the evidence shows a decline that slowed, no convergence, and only weak links between recent changes in coverage and in mortality.

### Reaching 2030 requires acceleration and proposals follow

The target value of 12.57% by 2030 sets the standard against which the regional paths are read. The world stood at 18.3% in 2021, and the trend projection, a linear extrapolation of the 2015 to 2021 pace, reaches 17.5% in 2030. The global ratio of progress is 0.22, where a ratio of 1 would mean the pace needed to meet the target. At the observed rate the world would end the period far from a one-third reduction.

The regional ratios show how uneven that shortfall is, and they need careful reading because a ratio depends on the starting level as well as on the pace. Europe and Central Asia, at 0.82, records the largest fall of any region, from 17.5% to 15.7%, and is expected to reach 13.4% in 2030. North America also has a ratio of 0.82, but it rests on a very small absolute movement, from 13.6% in 2015 to 13.3% in 2021, from a low base already near the threshold. East Asia and Pacific, at 0.42, is expected to reach 15.6%, and Latin America and the Caribbean, at 0.50, 13.9%. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, at 0.39, is expected to reach 18.5% in 2030, well above the 12.57% threshold, and is classed as marginal progress. High-income countries, at 1.93, are classed as on track or target met, with an expected 11.4% in 2030, but they began from 13.8%, already close to the threshold, so the class reflects the starting point as much as the pace.

That points to an ambiguity of the target. Target 3.4 speaks of a one-third reduction but does not say from which baseline, whether a global figure or each region's own starting value. A global baseline yields a single threshold of 12.57%, which regions already near it meet easily and regions above 22% would need to cross by a very large margin. A regional baseline would ask each region for the same proportional fall, and a different list of regions would then be on track. Both readings are defensible, and the classification above applies the global reading to every region. The 2015 reference year is also a choice, and a different base year would alter the required pace. No result here tests national baselines, so any national reading is a limit of this account, not a finding.

The regions furthest from the target are those with the highest levels. South Asia is classed as regression, rising from 22.1% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2021, with an expected 24.0% in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.16, is expected to reach 20.4%. Lower middle income countries, an income grouping distinct from the regions, are classed as stagnation, with an expected 22.8%. Low income countries have a ratio of 0.22 and an expected 21.5%. The burden of premature death from these diseases is therefore not falling where it is heaviest.

The link with service coverage offers little guidance. Across 184 countries the rank correlation between changes in premature mortality and changes in the coverage sub-index for non-communicable diseases is 0.098, close to none. The correlation between 2021 levels is -0.247, a weak association in which higher coverage goes with lower mortality. The sub-index rests on three tracer indicators, hypertension, diabetes and tobacco, and does not capture cancer treatment or chronic respiratory care. A weak link does not show that services are unimportant; it shows that the measure is too narrow to explain the movement of the outcome.

Suicide mortality and mental health, named in target 3.4 and in the section's title, are outside this account. The results prepared for this section hold no analysis of the suicide series, so no finding on its level, its difference between men and women, or its change since 2015 is offered. The indicator for premature mortality from the four diseases does not cover mental health. The section answers the question of non-communicable disease mortality only, and its title overstates its scope.

Three proposals follow. First, health ministries and development partners in South Asia and in lower middle income countries should concentrate prevention and treatment of cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic respiratory disease where the indicator rose or stagnated, since South Asia is classed as regression and lower middle income countries as stagnation. Second, the United Nations statistical and health bodies should state whether target 3.4 is read against a global baseline or each region's own, because the classification of regions changes with the reading. National targets would be a recommendation untested by these results. Third, the World Health Organization and national statistical offices should widen the coverage sub-index beyond hypertension, diabetes and tobacco to cancer and respiratory care, because the weak link between coverage and outcome may reflect a narrow measure; this is a measurement proposal, not a claim about what works.
