w-c05-7-5.text:
### The global share of trained primary teachers has risen only slowly

The world share of primary school teachers who are trained stood at 80.4% in 2015 and at 82.2% in 2024, a gain of under two percentage points in nine years. Target 4.c asks for a substantial increase in the supply of qualified teachers by 2030, and the indicator used here reads that as a share of 100%. On that full-training reading, roughly one primary teacher in five worldwide still lacks the minimum organised training required in the country where they teach. The trend calculation gives a world ratio of 0.15 against the pace needed, which it classes as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Continuing the 2015 to 2024 slope would bring the world to 83.4% in 2030. This is an extrapolation of a slope, not a forecast. On the full-training reading the target is projected to be missed at the world level; the alternative reading, a substantial rise from the baseline, was not tested, and the data cannot settle between them.

The measure needs careful reading. The indicator counts teachers who have received the minimum organised training, whether before or during service, that a given country requires. That minimum is set nationally and differs widely. A teacher counted as trained in one system might not meet the standard of another, and a share of 100% in one country does not imply equal preparation in the classroom. Nor does the indicator capture the quality of the training, the subject knowledge of teachers, or whether they remain in post. The figure is therefore a floor on qualification, not a measure of teaching quality.

Coverage adds a second caution. Only 13 countries reported in 2025, so the most recent year says little. Several regional values end in 2022, and the upper middle income group has a single value, for 2022, at 80.7%, which allows no change to be read. The results give no count of countries whose latest value predates 2024, so how far the world value mixes reporting years cannot be stated. Late reporting may be more common where systems are weaker, but the results do not test this.

The scope of this section should be stated at the outset. The guiding question also asks whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling, and Target 4.a concerns school facilities. The bench returned no pupil-teacher ratio result, and none of the series examined measures enrolment against teachers, buildings, safety or inclusion. The series on teacher numbers for primary and secondary levels cannot yield a ratio without matching enrolment. The evidence here therefore speaks to the training of teachers, not to class size or the learning environment, and the final part returns to this gap.

The slow world movement matters for 2030 because training is a precondition for much else in the chapter, from completion and learning to pre-primary provision. A world share that rises by under two points in nine years, spanning the disruption of 2020 and the years after it, leaves the full-training reading far out of reach on the present slope. The results do not show why the share has stalled; one possible explanation is that recruitment has outpaced training in some systems, but this remains a conjecture that the series cannot test. The regional parts that follow show where gains and losses lie.

### Regions and income groups differ by more than twenty points

The regional picture in 2024 is one of wide separation. North America stands at 97.9% of primary teachers trained, South Asia at 87.7%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 81.8% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 80.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa, whose latest reading is 2022 rather than 2024, stands at 68.8%. The best and the weakest of these regions therefore lie more than twenty points apart, taking the 2024 reading for North America and the 2022 reading for Sub-Saharan Africa. Readings from different years are not strictly comparable, and the Sub-Saharan figure may understate or overstate the position in 2024.

Income groups show a similar pattern. Low income countries stand at 69.2% in 2022, close to the Sub-Saharan level, which is expected because most low income countries lie in that region. Upper middle income countries have only a 2022 reading, 80.7%, so no change over the period can be given for that group. Training here means the minimum organised preparation required by each country, so the percentages measure compliance with national standards and not a common level of skill. A country with a demanding standard can score lower than one with a modest standard, and comparisons across regions should be read with that in mind.

The spread among countries, with each country weighted by its population, is modest in absolute terms. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.094 in 2015, fell to 0.073 in 2020 and rose to 0.097 in 2024, ending slightly above its starting level. The Theil index fell from 0.026 in 2015 to 0.011 in 2020. In that decomposition the share lying between regions was 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020. In those two years about half of the inequality among countries was therefore a difference between regions, and the other half lay among countries within the same region. The decomposition is not available for 2024 and may have changed since, so it should not be taken as a guide to where action is needed now.

These comparisons carry a caveat about coverage. Countries reporting numbered 85 in 2015 and 93 in 2020, but only 79 in 2024. The Theil index and its regional decomposition are missing for 2024, so the latest year cannot be set against the earlier ones on that measure. A change in the number of reporting countries can alter the Gini by changing who is counted, and the rise to 0.097 may reflect that as much as any real divergence; the series cannot separate the two. Reporting for 2025 is thinner still, with 13 countries. For 2030 the implication is that monitoring of Target 4.c is weakest in the years that matter most for judging it.

### Gains in South Asia contrast with declines in richer regions

South Asia recorded the largest regional gain in the share of trained primary teachers. The share rose from 72.9% in 2015 to 87.7% in 2024, a rise of nearly fifteen percentage points in nine years. The region moved from below the world average of 80.4% in 2015 to above the world level of 82.2% in 2024. Its trend is the only regional one classed as on track, with an expected 99.3% in 2030 if the rate of change continued. Lower middle income countries, a group that includes several South Asian economies, rose more modestly, from 76.4% in 2015 to 83.3% in 2024, and their expected value for 2030 is 88.2%. The data do not show which measures lay behind the South Asian rise. A change in how a country defines the minimum training required would produce the same movement as a real improvement in preparation, so the gain should be read as a reported change in the share, not as proof of better teaching.

The richer regions moved in the opposite direction. Europe and Central Asia fell from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020, the last year for which the regional reading is given here. High income countries fell from 95.9% in 2015 to 92.1% in 2024, and North America slipped from 99.3% to 97.9% over the same period. Latin America and the Caribbean moved little, from 82.7% to 81.8%, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan declined from 83.9% to 80.5%. These falls are small beside the South Asian gain, but they run against the direction of Target 4.c, and the trend tool classes all of these regions as regressing. The results do not explain them. Teacher shortages that lead systems to hire staff before they complete a full programme are one possible cause, and changes in national definitions or reporting are another; neither can be tested with these series.

Across countries, the pattern is one of catching up. A convergence test over 48 countries between 2015 and 2024 gives a coefficient of -0.071 (p below 0.001) with an R2 of 0.342, which means that countries starting from lower shares of trained teachers tended to gain faster than those starting higher. The dispersion of the shares narrowed only slightly: the coefficient of variation moved from 0.165 in 2015 to 0.155 in 2024. Convergence is therefore real but slow, and about a third of the variation in country changes is accounted for by the starting level alone. The test covers only the 48 countries with readings at both ends of the period, so it describes the reporting countries and not the world, and the systems with the sparsest records may be underrepresented.

The size of the teaching workforce does not appear to explain the changes. The rank correlation between changes in the share of trained primary teachers and changes in the number of primary teachers across the same 48 countries is -0.095, and the correlation between 2024 levels is 0.168. Both are weak. Expanding the workforce therefore did not visibly coincide with a higher trained share, and countries that added the most teachers were no more likely to see that share rise. This is a cautionary finding for Target 4.c, which speaks of qualified teachers and not of teachers alone. The correlations are descriptive and say nothing about the mechanism.

The period since 2015 and the years after 2020 cannot be read cleanly from these series. Several regional readings end in 2020 or 2022, and the school closures of 2020 and 2021 disrupted the collection of statistics as well as schooling. A gap in reporting may conceal a change that has not yet been measured. For 2030, the lesson of this part is that large gains are recorded where the share rose fast, as in South Asia, but that they are not general, and that richer regions with falling shares cannot assume the levels of 2015 will return unaided. Target 4.a, on school facilities, is not assessed in this section, because none of the series examined measures buildings or learning environments.

### Most countries are not on course for 2030, and proposals follow

The country counts show that the 2030 picture is mixed. In primary education, 64 of the 129 countries assessed, holding 65.9% of the population of those assessed, are on track or have already met the target of a fully trained teaching force. This is a large share of people but not of countries. Against it stand 36 countries with 26.3% of the assessed population whose trained share is falling rather than rising. A further 13 countries, with 2.4% of the population, show marginal progress that would need to speed up considerably, 12 countries, with 4.2%, show moderate progress that still needs acceleration, and 4 countries, with 1.2%, are stagnant. The two largest groups are the on-track countries and the regressing ones, so the pattern is divided at its poles.

Secondary education tells a similar story with less coverage. Of 108 countries assessed, 41 hold 61.5% of the population and are on track or have met the target, while 36 hold 27.6% and are regressing. Fourteen countries with 7.7% of the population show marginal progress, 10 with 2.1% show moderate progress and 7 with 1.0% are stagnant. The share of people living in regressing countries is slightly higher at secondary level than at primary level, and the share in on-track countries is slightly lower. Fewer countries report secondary data, so the secondary result rests on a thinner base and is the less certain of the two.

The regression count needs careful reading. A falling trained share does not necessarily mean that teaching has worsened. One possible explanation is that systems expanding quickly may recruit teachers faster than they can certify them; another is that a country raising its minimum standard may see teachers once counted as trained fall below the new bar. Both are conjectures drawn from general experience, and the results given here cannot separate them.

The same feature complicates the target itself. Target 4.c speaks of qualified teachers, and the indicator measures minimum organised training, pre-service or in-service, as defined nationally. A share of 100% therefore does not mean equal preparation across countries. The target can be read as a share trained to national standards, a share trained to an international standard, or a growth in the absolute supply of teachers. The assessment here uses the first reading, with 100% as the goal, because it is the one the trained-teacher series can express. On the reading of a substantial increase in supply, the result is undetermined: the teacher-count series were not tested against a trend in these results.

The section's question therefore receives an answer on training only. Whether pupil-teacher ratios are falling is not established: no ratio was computed, because the teacher-count series on the shelf were not combined with enrolment in these results, and no figure for ratios is stated. Target 4.a, on safe and inclusive school facilities, was not assessed, because none of the series for this section measures it. The section's findings concern the trained share of teachers alone.

For 2030, on the full-training reading, the target is projected to be missed at the world level. The projected world share of trained primary teachers is 83.4%, with a trend ratio of 0.15, which falls in the class of marginal progress needing significant acceleration. These 2030 values are slope projections extrapolated from readings between 2015 and the latest year, 2022 for Sub-Saharan Africa and low income countries, and are context, not forecasts. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 72.0% and low income countries at 73.2%, so on this extrapolation the groups starting furthest behind remain furthest behind. South Asia, projected at 99.3%, is the one region on course. Regions that are regressing are mostly those that began from higher levels, such as Europe and Central Asia at a projected 86.9% and high income countries at 89.7%.

Among the 48 countries reporting in both 2015 and 2024, convergence is present and slight: the coefficient of variation of the primary trained share fell from 0.17 to 0.16, with a beta of -0.07. This describes only those 48 countries, not the world or countries without readings at both ends. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the trained share was 0.09 in 2015, 0.07 in 2020 and 0.10 in 2024. Differences narrowed up to 2020 and then widened again, though the 2024 reading covers 79 countries against 93 in 2020, so the comparison is imperfect and the cause cannot be read from these results. The between-region share of inequality, 49.3% in 2015 and 53.3% in 2020, applies to those years only; it shows that regional differences then accounted for about half of the spread.

The findings point to the following proposals.

w-c02-2-4.text:
### National poverty lines give the widest view, with uneven reporting

The national-line headcount ratio is the percentage of a population living below the poverty line or lines that a country sets for itself. It is the measure closest to the wording of target 1.2, which asks for a halving of poverty in all its dimensions according to national definitions. Because each country chooses its own line, and often revises it, the series records how each society judges deprivation rather than a single standard. Estimates come from household surveys. Alongside it, the World Bank publishes multidimensional, societal-line and $3.00-a-day series, which later parts of this section set against the national figures.

The series is wide in reach but irregular in time. Over the whole period 161 countries have reported at least one national-line observation, a broad base for a goal that applies everywhere. In any single year, however, only a fraction report. In 2000 the number of countries with a value was 16, and in 2001 it was 15. It rose to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005, and then stood at 40 in 2008, 50 in 2012 and 45 in 2013. The results record this expansion but give no reason for it; the cause lies outside the data.

After the adoption of the goals in 2015, reporting grew rather than shrank. In 2015, 55 countries had a value, and 57 in 2016, followed by 53 in 2017. Counts then reached 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. The year 2020, the first of the pandemic, shows 57 countries, a fall from 2019 that is consistent with disrupted fieldwork, although the data alone cannot show the cause. The peak is 72 countries in 2021.

The decline since then is steep. Reporting was 52 countries in 2022, 40 in 2023 and 31 in 2024, and in 2025 it is only 13. The fall does not mean that poverty has been abolished or that surveys have stopped. Household survey data take a year or more to be collected, harmonised and released, and national-line series are revised as new rounds arrive. The latest years are therefore incomplete, and the count for 2025 is best treated as a record of what has been published so far.

The consequence is practical. A comparison of 2025 with 2015 would rest on 13 countries against 55, which are not the same countries and may not be representative of any region. These results report coverage and not rate levels, so this part does not state how far any national rate has fallen; movement is read from the trend classes in a later part. Any statement about movement toward 2030 has to use the last years of reasonable coverage, up to about 2021 or 2022, and has to separate real change from changes in who reports. The count of 13 reporting countries for 2025 rests on a thin base and calls for caution in every reading drawn from it.

### Dispersion among countries widened as coverage grew

The dispersion of national-line poverty rates among reporting countries rose after 2013. The Gini coefficient stood at 0.28 in 2013 and 0.34 in 2014, then reached 0.39 in 2015, the year the goals took effect. It was 0.47 in 2016, 0.52 in 2018 and 0.63 in 2019. The Theil index followed the same course, from 0.14 in 2013 to 0.26 in 2015 and 0.72 in 2019. Read at face value, the spread among countries in the share of people below their own lines widened markedly over these years. The summary labels these statistics as population-weighted, so the reading is of a spread in which larger countries count for more, as the tool computes it.

This reading needs care, because the set of reporting countries changed at the same time. The number of countries with a national-line estimate was 45 in 2013, 55 in 2015, 67 in 2018 and 62 in 2019. A rise in the Gini or Theil can reflect poverty rates pulling apart, but it can equally reflect the arrival of countries with very high or very low rates, or the loss of countries in the middle. The series cannot separate these effects, so the figures are not a measured change in inequality between countries over a fixed group. For 2020 the Gini is 0.66 across 57 countries, but no Theil index or regional decomposition is available, so that year cannot be compared in full with its neighbours.

The between-region share of the Theil index is high in the reporting sample in every year. It was 75.8% in 2013, 88.4% in 2014 and 67.7% in 2015, then 80.7% in 2016, 65.1% in 2017, 86.3% in 2018 and 77.1% in 2019. Across the years with a decomposition the share ranges from 65.1% in 2017 to 88.5% in 2022. These shares describe the reporting sample in each year and cannot be read as the share of dispersion lying in fixed regions; the swings are consistent with a changing sample, since adding or dropping a few countries in one region can move the share sharply. Differences in how countries draw their lines also bear on any comparison of levels, as the opening part of this section explains.

After 2020 the picture changes. The Gini fell to 0.35 in 2021, when 72 countries reported, the highest count among the years cited here. It then stood at 0.40 in 2022 with 52 countries, 0.35 in 2023 with 40 countries and 0.32 in 2024 with 31 countries. The Theil index moved from 0.20 in 2021 to 0.26 in 2022, 0.21 in 2023 and 0.17 in 2024. The between-region share was 82.6% in 2021, 88.5% in 2022, 76.0% in 2023 and 83.5% in 2024. The fall in dispersion between 2019 and 2021 coincides with a large change in the reporting set and cannot be taken as convergence. Counts fall after 2021, and only 13 countries report for 2025, so the latest years describe a thinner and different group.

For 2030 the implication is that national-line data can show whether a given country is reducing its own poverty rate, but cannot support a claim about convergence or divergence across the world. Assessment of target 1.2 should proceed country by country, over a fixed set of economies with repeated surveys, and the dispersion statistics should be read as a description of who reports in each year rather than of how poverty is distributed.

### Trend classes show most countries on track but a large regressing group

The classification covers 94 countries, those for which the national-line series holds enough observations to estimate a trend. Of these, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 3.8% of the population, and 7 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 4.4%. Five countries are stagnant, with 2.1% of the population. The largest adverse group is regression, with 34 countries and 26.0% of the population. Regression is therefore not a marginal finding.

The classes are the only evidence in this section on how national rates have moved. The tool reports a class and a share of population for each country group, not a rate level or a change in points, so no national rate is stated here. The classes say which direction and pace each national series has taken against the halving reading; they do not say how far any rate has fallen or risen. In this reading, regression means a series moving away from the target, which is not the same as a stated rise in a particular rate.

The weight of the favourable class comes from population rather than from numbers alone. On track countries are 41 of the 94 assessed, fewer than half by count, yet they hold 63.8% of the assessed population. A reader should not infer that two thirds of countries are succeeding; the count and the population share tell different stories, and both are given here. The tool does not show which countries drive the population share, so nothing is claimed about who holds most of it.

No numeric target exists for national lines. Target 1.2 asks for a halving of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions, but it names no common threshold, because each country sets its own line and method. The classes therefore rest on a reading of the target, not on a fixed value. Under the halving reading, a country is on track if its rate is falling fast enough to be halved by 2030 from its baseline, which is 2015 or the first year after. That is one reading among several. A target could instead be read as an absolute reduction in the number of people, as a reduction by a set number of points, or as a halving from the earliest available observation. Each reading would sort some countries differently, and the date and spacing of observations differ from country to country.

Several cautions follow. A country that revises its line can show a break in the series that looks like progress or regression though living standards did not move in that way. A country with a low rate can be classed as regressing after a small rise, while a country with a very high rate may be classed as on track after a modest fall. The classes do not rank the level of deprivation among countries.

The classification also leaves out countries without a usable trend. Where surveys are infrequent, the trend rests on few points, and the class can change with one new survey. The tool gives no breakdown of the classes by region or by income group, and none by the period before and after 2020, so the effect of the pandemic on the classes cannot be read here.

For 2030, the classes support a limited statement. The on track group holds 63.8% of the assessed population, while 26.0% lives in countries where the national measure is classed as regressing. Because the classes give direction and pace only, and no rate levels, they do not allow a verdict on whether the halving will be reached across the whole group; they show where the pace falls short, not the size of the shortfall.

### National and international lines agree on direction but not fully on size, and the implication for 2030

National and international lines can be set side by side for 36 countries between 2015 and 2021. The comparison pairs the national-line headcount with the share of the population living on less than $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Across these countries the rank correlation of 2021 levels is 0.72 (Spearman), and the Kendall measure of the same levels is 0.58. The rank correlation of changes between 2015 and 2021 is lower, at 0.53, with a Kendall value of 0.41.

The two results say different things. A country with a high national rate generally also has a high international rate, so the two lines rank societies in a broadly similar order. Agreement on direction of change is weaker. A country can see its national rate fall while the international rate barely moves, or the reverse, because the two lines sit at different points of the income distribution and are adjusted by different rules. A rise in living costs, a change in survey design or a revision of the basket can move one measure and leave the other untouched. The correlation of changes should therefore be read as a moderate link, not as proof that the two measures can be substituted for one another. Only 36 countries qualify, a small part of the 161 that report a national rate in at least one year, so the finding cannot be extended to all countries without caution. Both correlations are associations, not causes.

For the 2030 halving in target 1.2, the evidence supports no aggregate verdict. The movement of national rates is shown here only through the trend classes, since the results hold no rate level or change for any country or group. Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, with 63.8% of the assessed population. Another 34 countries are in the regression class, holding 26.0% of that population. The classes give direction and pace against the target, not the size of any rate, and they do not show which countries hold the population shares. An overall judgement on whether the halving will be reached cannot be drawn from them. The weaker agreement on change also means that a country judged on track at its national line cannot be assumed to be gaining at the international line, and the reverse also holds. The target is open to more than one reading. Halving may be measured against a country's own 2015 rate or against a baseline year that varies by country, and a revised national line breaks the series on which either reading depends. Assessment is therefore best made country by country.

The evidence has clear limits. Reporting is uneven: 72 countries reported a national rate for 2021, the highest count of any year since 2000, but 52 did so for 2022, 40 for 2023, 31 for 2024 and 13 for 2025. Recent years are thin, so the effects after 2020 are seen only in part. Country lines differ in definition and in the date of last revision, and the series does not record why a line was changed. The paired comparison rests on 36 countries. Poverty in all its dimensions is only partly captured by a headcount, and the poverty gap and multidimensional measures are not tested here against national lines.

w-c04-9-5.text:
### The global picture rests on rates, not counts

The question posed for this section asks for a number of deaths. The evidence retrieved cannot supply one. The only analysed result is a rate: deaths attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene per 100,000 population, for 2019, across 183 countries. A rate is a count divided by population, and it cannot be turned back into a count without population figures that this result does not carry. No absolute total of deaths from unsafe water appears in the retrieved material, and none is offered here. The level of the rate, whether global, regional or national, is likewise not among the results; only the inequality of the rate between countries is.

The question is therefore answered in neither of its halves, and the reason is stated exactly. For unsafe water, the book can report how unequal the rate is but not how many deaths it represents. For air pollution, the shelf holds a series on the age-standardised mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, with 183 countries and a latest year of 2019, and a series on mean annual exposure to fine particulate matter, with a latest year of 2023. Neither was analysed as a result for this section, so no value from either is quoted. Nothing is stated here about how many people die from air pollution, how fast the rate is falling or which regions carry most of it. None of the series on the shelf is a count of deaths, and the missing item is a series of absolute deaths by cause, which the shelf does not hold. The gap lies in the form of the series and in the analysis performed, not in the world. Target 3.9 also covers hazardous chemicals and soil pollution, and the shelf holds a series on unintentional poisoning, which was likewise not analysed.

This limit bears on how Target 3.9 is read. The target calls for a substantial reduction in the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and from air, water and soil pollution. The wording can be read as a count, in which case population growth works against progress even when conditions improve, or as a rate, in which case a falling risk counts as success even if the number of deaths stays high. The wording does not settle the matter. The indicator series the World Bank reports measures a rate, and it is the rate that the evidence here can describe. Any later statement about progress in this section should be taken as a statement about risk per head of population, not about the total toll.

The one result that exists shows how unevenly that risk is spread. Across the 183 countries in 2019, the Gini coefficient of the unsafe-water mortality rate is 0.535 and the coefficient of variation is 1.03. A coefficient of variation above one means that the spread of national rates is wider than their average. The bench summary describes these measures as population-weighted, so they would describe inequality among people living in different countries; the source's own weighting method was not retrieved, and the measures do not establish how many countries hold high rates. The next part examines how much of this inequality lies between regions.

### Regions explain most of the inequality between countries

Between-region differences account for most of the measured inequality in the water, sanitation and hygiene mortality rate. The result covers 2019 and 183 countries, and it describes a rate per 100,000 population, not a count of deaths. The Theil index of the rate was 0.502 and the Gini coefficient was 0.535. The bench summary describes both measures as weighted by population, so they describe how the rate is distributed among people living in different countries, and a populous country with a high rate raises both figures more than a small one. The coefficient of variation was 1.03, so the standard deviation of the rate was slightly larger than its mean, which indicates a wide spread of values.

The between-region share of the Theil index was 75.2% in 2019. Differences between the regions' mean rates therefore make up about three quarters of the measured inequality, and differences among countries within the same region make up the remaining quarter. This is a descriptive split of a statistic. It does not test why regions differ, and it contains no measure of income, infrastructure or health services. Well-established knowledge suggests plausible causes, offered as context and not as a finding: diarrhoeal disease and related infections depend on piped water, sewerage, nutrition and primary care, and these conditions tend to be shared among neighbouring countries at similar stages of development.

The split matters for how reporting and action are organised. Where most inequality lies between regions, regional figures are needed to see where the gap is, and a global average alone can hide regions with high rates. This result does not identify those regions, give their rates or show how many deaths occur in them. The remaining quarter, lying within regions, shows that countries in the same region still differ, and those that do better than their neighbours merit study for policies that could be copied.

The limits of the result are plain. A decomposition reports a share, not a ranking, so it names no region or country. It covers one year, 2019, and so says nothing about change since 2015 or about the effects of events after 2020. It concerns unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene only; no analysed result in this part covers air pollution mortality or PM2.5 exposure, so the air half of Target 3.9 is not addressed here. The retrieved results do not document how the underlying estimates were produced, and they give no death count for either cause.

### Change since 2015 cannot be measured from one year

The single observation for 2019 describes a position, not a movement. Target 3.9 calls for a substantial reduction in deaths from pollution and contamination by 2030, and a reduction can only be shown by comparing at least two points in time. The result retrieved for this section holds one year, 2019, for 183 countries. No statement is therefore made here on whether mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene fell after 2015, nor on how the years after 2020 compare with those before. The result gives no earlier or later reading for this indicator, and an inference from a single cross-section would be a guess presented as a finding.

Three kinds of evidence would be needed to turn the position into a trend. The first is a series of annual rates from 2015 onward, ideally with earlier years too, so that a pre-2015 trajectory exists against which the post-2015 period can be judged. The shelf lists the indicator with 2019 as its latest year, which means that the period of the pandemic and its disruption to health services, to water programmes and to household incomes is not observed at all. The second is a count of deaths. A rate can fall while the number of deaths stays level or rises if populations grow, and the reverse is also possible, so the two answer different questions. The third is an air pollution indicator read alongside the water measure. The shelf holds a rate of deaths attributed to household and ambient air pollution and a measure of mean exposure to fine particles, but neither was returned as a result for this section. The question on air pollution is therefore not answered here, and the two halves of the question cannot be set side by side.

Caution is also due on causes. The between-region share of the Theil index is 75.2%, and the Gini coefficient is 0.535. These figures show that the rate is unequally distributed among people in 2019 and that regional grouping accounts for most of that measured inequality. They do not show why. Water and sanitation infrastructure, income, the quality of primary health care and the treatment of diarrhoeal disease are well established as bearing on such deaths, but these are plausible influences that the decomposition does not test, and one year's spread cannot separate them from the age structure of populations, from climate or from conflict. The coefficient of variation, 1.03, confirms the dispersion without explaining it.

For 2030 the consequence is that progress on this part of target 3.9 cannot at present be judged from the evidence in hand. The target also does not define what "substantially" means, and it can be read against a baseline of 2015, of an earlier year or of the latest available year. Until a series spanning those years is assembled, any statement on whether the goal is on course would be unsupported.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 3.9 asks for a substantial reduction by 2030, and the only evidence analysed for this section is one year of one rate. In 2019, across 183 countries, the between-region share of the Theil index for mortality from unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene was 75.2%. Most of the measured inequality in that rate therefore lies between regions rather than within them. The result does not name the regions, give their rates or show why they differ. Differences in income, infrastructure and health services are plausible explanations, but this decomposition does not test them.

The Gini coefficient was 0.535 and the coefficient of variation was 1.03. The bench summary describes the Gini and Theil measures as population-weighted, and that description is reported as the summary gives it. The measures show that the rate is unevenly spread, but not where the highest rates lie or how many deaths occur in any region. The Theil index was 0.502.

This bears on how 2030 is judged. The target text does not say whether the reduction is to be assessed in numbers of deaths or in rates, and it sets no baseline or percentage. Both readings are defensible and they can diverge when populations grow. A fall in the rate with a growing population may leave the count little changed. The 2019 evidence offers no trend since 2015 or 2020, so whether the target is on course cannot be stated from it.

The question asks for numbers of deaths from air pollution and from unsafe water and sanitation. This section cannot supply them: no count is given for either cause, and no air pollution result was analysed. The air pollution mortality series, the PM2.5 exposure series and the unintentional poisoning series are held on the shelf, but their values are not reported here. Conclusions concern the water, sanitation and hygiene rate only, and the air pollution half of Target 3.9 remains unassessed.

The proposals below follow from these limits. They ask that the missing analyses be made before the section is relied on for 2030.
proposals: The bench's analysts should run the air pollution mortality series and the PM2.5 exposure series for at least two years, including 2015 and the latest year, so that change since 2015 can be reported for both pollution causes.

National statistical offices and the bodies that publish the estimates should release population-based counts of deaths from unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene beside the rates, so that Target 3.9 can be read in either numbers or rates.
Governments in the regions with the highest rates should report subnational figures, because the between-region share of 75.2% in 2019 says nothing about inequality within a region.
w-c04-9-5.gaps: No death counts for air pollution or for unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene were retrieved. No air pollution result was analysed. The water, sanitation and hygiene rate is a single year, 2019, so no trend since 2015 or 2020 can be shown. The regional rates and the method behind the estimates were not retrieved. The Target 3.9 text sets no baseline or percentage for a substantial reduction.

w-c06-2-5.text:
### Intimate partner violence is measured in few countries and few years

Target 5.2 calls for the elimination of all forms of violence against all women and girls, in public and private life, including trafficking and sexual and other types of exploitation. The indicator that the World Bank's catalogue holds for it is narrower: the proportion of ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49 who were subjected to physical violence, sexual violence or both in the previous 12 months. The series note describes it as drawn from United Nations and World Health Organization sources. It therefore speaks to one form of violence and one age band, and says nothing directly about violence by non-partners, harassment in public, trafficking or exploitation. Women who have never had a partner, girls under 15 and women over 49 fall outside it. A country with a low reading on this series cannot be taken to have met the wider target.

The coverage is thin even for this narrow measure. Across the whole period, 106 countries report in at least one year. Those reports are spread unevenly over time, and in most years very few countries contribute. One country reports for 2000 and 2 for 2005. The counts then run at 4 for 2006, 3 for 2007, 4 for 2008 and 4 for 2009, falling to 2 for 2010 and 3 for 2011. A year with one to four reporting countries cannot support a comparison of regions or a global reading; it records a handful of observations.

The pattern changes sharply in 2012, when 35 countries report. This single peak accounts for a large share of all the country entries on the shelf. The bench results do not say why the count rises in that year, and the reason is not asserted here; whether the values come from direct surveys or from estimation is likewise not recorded in the results. After the peak the counts fall back to 7 for 2013 and rise to 12 for 2014, 8 for 2015, 14 for 2016 and 7 for 2017, the latest year with data. No year after 2017 is held, so the series is silent on the period from 2020, when many observers warned that violence at home had risen. The shelf holds no regional or world aggregates for this indicator, so no summary can be drawn from published totals.

These features shape what the rest of the section can responsibly say. Differences between countries can be described where values exist, but the values rest on different years. A reader should treat the indicator as a partial snapshot of one form of violence, not as a tracked measure of progress towards the target.

### Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap

In 2012 the spread of intimate partner violence among reporting countries can be measured, and it is the only year in which that is possible. That year 35 countries report, the largest count of any year in the series, against 1 to 14 countries in every other year listed. The Gini coefficient is 0.29 and the Theil index is 0.17, which indicate a moderate spread between countries: prevalence is neither uniform nor extremely unequal. The coefficient of variation is 0.66. The results state that the tool weights countries by population, and no further claim is made about the weighting.

The decomposition shows where the measured inequality lies. Of the Theil inequality in 2012, 66.2% is between regions rather than within them, and the remaining third lies within regions. This is a descriptive split of a single year among 35 reporting countries. It does not show why regions differ and supports no causal reading. Shared legal traditions, social norms about marriage and household authority, services for survivors and the history of conflict are well-established candidates for explaining regional patterns in violence, but the data hold no variable that could test any of them.

The limits of this result need to be stated plainly. The results do not record which countries are among the 35 or how they were chosen. Surveys on violence are costly and sensitive, and in general they are fielded where governments permit them and funders support them, so absent countries may differ systematically from those present. The between-region share is computed only among reporting countries, so a region represented by two or three countries adds little information on differences within it. The figures describe the spread of a particular sample in a particular year. They are not a global distribution and should not be read as one.

Other years are not compared with 2012 here. Only 7 countries report in 2013 and 8 in 2015, and 14 in 2016, the next largest count after 2012. The tool produced the spread calculation for 2012 alone, and the results state no minimum number of countries for it. Whether the 14 countries of 2016 would support a comparable calculation is therefore left open, as is whether they are the same countries as in 2012. For 2030 the consequence is that the regional pattern visible in 2012 is a snapshot of where evidence was gathered, not a baseline from which progress can be measured.

### Change over time cannot be established, while attitudes are better documented

The trend tool, which classifies each country against the 2030 target of zero, assesses no country for intimate partner violence. All five classes show zero: no country is on track or has met the target, none shows moderate progress, none shows marginal progress, none is stagnating and none is regressing. The count of countries assessed is also zero. This is not a finding of no change. It is a finding that change cannot be measured, because the tool needs repeated observations for the same country and the series does not supply them. Without them, the series cannot show whether prevalence has risen or fallen since 2015, or since 2020, when lockdowns and household stress were widely reported to have raised risks for women at home. That report comes from outside the bench data. Neither progress nor regression can be stated, and any claim about the direction of violence against women over the period rests on sources outside this series.

The attitude indicator, the share of women who believe a husband is justified in beating his wife for at least one of five reasons, is better documented. 72 countries report it in at least one year between 2000 and 2024. Annual coverage is modest and uneven, however. It was 6 countries in 2000 and 4 in 2002, rose to 10 in 2005 and 14 in 2012, and stood at 12 in both 2016 and 2018. After 2018 it fell sharply: 2 countries in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fell around 2019 and 2020. Interrupted fieldwork is a plausible hypothesis, but it needs a source outside these results, and the partial recovery since is likewise unexplained. Even in the best year, 14 countries report, so a global or regional average of attitudes for any single year would describe a shifting group of countries and not a stable panel.

The attitude series therefore offers more scope for comparison over time within countries that survey repeatedly, but it does not allow a global verdict. The results do not record which countries report, or their income level or survey programme, so the composition of the reporting group is not documented here and some groups may be under-represented.

Attitudes are a proxy and not a measure of violence. Acceptance of wife beating can indicate social norms that sustain abuse and discourage women from reporting or seeking help, and falling acceptance is often read as a sign of shifting norms. But a woman may reject violence and still experience it, and a society may hold permissive views with low recorded prevalence, or the reverse. Answers are also shaped by who is asking and who is present during the interview. The indicator should be read as context for the prevalence data, never as a substitute for them, and it cannot show whether target 5.2 is being met for 2030.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals on measurement

A target of zero by 2030 cannot be assessed from these data. The trend tool classifies no country, and the count of countries assessed is 0. Any statement that the world, a region or a country is on track, or off track, for the elimination of intimate partner violence would therefore be unsupported. In all, 106 countries report in at least one year, but the reporting years cluster so tightly that a single survey wave stands in for a trend. The results give yearly counts only, not the number of years each country reports, so how many countries appear once is not established. Reporting peaks at 35 countries in 2012, against yearly counts of between 1 and 14 in every other year listed, and stands at 7 in 2017, the latest year. The counts for 2001 to 2004 are not given in the results, so those years are either empty or not held. Nothing is recorded after 2017, so neither the years after 2015 nor the pandemic years after 2020 can be read from the series. Lockdowns and strained services are widely reported to have raised the risk of violence at home, but the catalogue holds no figure that confirms or refutes this.

The measurement gap matters because the target is stated in absolute terms. Zero is reached only by sustained decline, and decline can be shown only by repeated measurement in the same country with the same definition. The attitude series is somewhat better placed, with 72 countries reporting in at least one year, and annual counts listed from 2000 to 2024. Yet it measures what women believe, not what they experience, and it thins sharply after 2018, with 2 countries in 2019 and 7 in 2024. The series does not establish why the counts fall, and the composition of the reporting countries is not recorded in the results, so some groups of countries may be under-represented. Attitudes may change before behaviour does, or behaviour may change without attitudes following, so neither series can stand in for the other. Underreporting is a further limit: women may not disclose violence in a survey, and a rise in measured prevalence can follow improved trust in interviewers as well as a real increase.

The one-year spread for 2012, with 35 countries, is descriptive only. The Gini coefficient of 0.29 is moderate, and the between-region share of Theil inequality, 66.2%, is a split of that one year among the countries that happened to report. It supports no causal reading of the regional pattern. Five proposals follow from these findings; they are set out in the list of proposals. They concern the frequency of surveys, the continued collection of the 12-month indicator with a lifetime series beside it, the range of women and forms of violence covered, the conditions for publishing regional aggregates, and the joint reporting of attitudes and prevalence. Until they are met, the record for Target 5.2 will describe a handful of survey years, not fifteen years of progress.

w-c04-2-5.text:
### The global picture: most countries are on course, the world is not

Target 3.2 sets two thresholds that every country is asked to reach by 2030: neonatal mortality of at most 12.0 per 1,000 live births, and under-five mortality of at most 25.0 per 1,000 live births. The target is worded as an aspiration for each country, not for the world as a whole. It therefore asks a different question from a global average, and the two readings must be kept apart when the evidence is assessed.

The direct answer to how many countries have reached the thresholds is that the data cannot give a single count. The classification used here merges countries that have met a threshold with countries projected to meet it, so it states how many are on track or have met the target, not how many have already arrived. On that combined reading, 130 of 196 countries are on track or have met the neonatal threshold, and 135 of 196 are on track or have met the under-five threshold.

The world averages remain above both thresholds. The global neonatal mortality rate fell from 19.4 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 17.2 in 2024, still above the threshold of 12.0. The global under-five mortality rate fell from 42.9 per 1,000 live births in 2015 to 37.4 in 2024, against a threshold of 25.0. Both series cover all 196 countries reporting in 2024, so the averages are not distorted by missing reporters.

The country classification gives a more favourable picture. In each case the on-track class is a clear majority of countries, around two thirds or more. The population shares are close to the country counts: the 130 countries hold 72.4% of the population assessed for neonatal mortality, and the 135 countries hold 74.7% for under-five mortality. A reader may therefore ask how most countries, holding about three quarters of the world's people, can be on course while the world average stays above both lines.

The answer lies in what each figure measures. A count of countries gives every country equal weight. A population share weights each country by its inhabitants. A world average is a rate per live birth, so it reflects where children are born rather than where the general population lives. As a hypothesis that the results here do not test, countries with many births and high mortality would pull the average upward; the data given do not show birth numbers by country.

A second distinction concerns the phrase on track. The classification compares each country's recent trend with the path needed to reach the threshold by 2030. A country that is on track has not necessarily reached the threshold; it is projected to do so if its pace holds, and the projection can fail if progress slows. The threshold can also be read in more than one way: the target says all countries should aim for at least as low as the stated values, so a country already far below them has no further obligation under the wording, though its rate may still fall.

The remaining countries show where the shortfall lies. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Four are stagnating and 9 are regressing. These 66 countries hold 27.5% of the population assessed, a smaller share than the on-track group. For under-five mortality, 39 countries need acceleration, 15 need significant acceleration, 3 are stagnating and 4 are regressing. The 3 stagnating countries hold 4.9% of the population assessed, a larger share than their count alone would suggest.

The gap between the two readings matters for policy. A statement that most countries are on course is true and encouraging, but it can mislead if it is taken to mean that the goal is within reach for children everywhere. The sections that follow therefore set the counts beside regional and income-group levels, so that the distribution of the shortfall is visible.

### Counting countries: how many have met or are on track for each threshold

The trend classification covers all 196 countries for both indicators, and it gives the plainest count of how many have reached, or are heading for, each threshold. For neonatal mortality, 130 countries are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 target, and they hold 72.4% of the population of the countries assessed. For under-five mortality, 135 countries are on track or have met the 25.0 per 1,000 target, with 74.7% of that population. The under-five threshold is therefore the more widely met of the two, although the gap is small.

The class labelled on track or target met joins two different situations. A country that crossed the threshold years ago and a country that is merely on course to cross it by 2030 are counted together. The classification does not separate them, and the data given here cannot say how many of the 130 and the 135 have already arrived. A further count of countries whose latest value lies at or below each threshold would answer the question directly. Until it is made, the figures describe the direction of travel rather than the number of countries that have finished the work. The distinction matters because countries already below the threshold need only hold their position, while those merely on course remain exposed to any slowdown.

Below the leading class, the two indicators diverge. For neonatal mortality, 17 countries show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 7.8% of the population, and 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 11.9%. For under-five mortality the order is reversed: 39 countries are in the moderate class, with 16.1% of the population, and only 15 are in the marginal class, with 4.0%. Many countries therefore sit closer to the under-five threshold than to the neonatal one. This agrees with the established pattern that deaths in the first 28 days fall more slowly than deaths later in childhood. Infections, malnutrition and malaria respond to vaccines, nets and treatment, whereas newborn deaths depend on the quality of care around birth, on preterm complications and on skilled attendance, which take longer to build.

The worst classes are small in country count but not in consequence. Four countries stagnate on neonatal mortality, holding 2.1% of the population, and nine regress, holding 5.7%. For under-five mortality, three countries stagnate, holding 4.9% of the population, and four regress, holding 0.3%. The stagnating group on the under-five indicator thus carries a notable population share for so few countries, whereas the regressing group is small. Regression usually accompanies conflict, state collapse or the breakdown of health services, and a small population share does not make it less serious for the children living there.

The population shares also show that the country counts and the people counts do not coincide. Neonatal on-track countries are 130 of the 196 assessed, yet hold 72.4% of the population; under-five on-track countries are 135 of 196, with 74.7%. Even so, a substantial minority of the world's people live in countries that are not on course for each threshold. Since the target is written for every country, those countries decide whether the goal is met in the sense the text intends.

The classification carries the usual caution about reading a trend as a forecast. It extrapolates past rates of change to 2030, and the years after 2020 were disturbed by disruption to services and by uncertain estimates in places with weak registration. A country may be assigned a class on a series that is largely modelled rather than counted. The counts should thus be read as a guide to where acceleration is needed, not as a guarantee of where the thresholds will be met.

### Regions and income groups differ by a factor of seven

Regional neonatal mortality in 2024 ranged from 3.6 per 1,000 live births in North America and 4.1 in Europe & Central Asia to 22.7 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan and 26.6 in Sub-Saharan Africa. Under-five mortality spans a wider range, from 6.4 in North America to 71.2 in Sub-Saharan Africa. The tools give no ratio between regions, so each gap is stated only by its pair of values, as the figures show. Neonatal deaths make up a larger share of child deaths where overall mortality is low, because the causes that remain there (prematurity, birth complications, congenital conditions) fall last. Where mortality is high, infections, malnutrition and malaria continue to claim children after the first month, and the under-five gap widens accordingly. This is context drawn from established knowledge, not a result of the data.

Income groups show the same ordering. Low-income countries recorded 24.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024 and 68.8 under-five deaths. High-income countries recorded 2.8 and 5.1. Upper middle income countries, at 6.8 and 13.1, sit well inside both thresholds. Lower middle income countries, at 21.6 and 43.8, lie outside both. The income gradient is steep because the interventions that save newborns and young children depend on health-system capacity: skilled attendance at birth, emergency obstetric care, neonatal care units, vaccination, and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria. These need financing and trained staff that low-income systems have found hard to sustain.

The trend classification separates regions that will reach the thresholds from those that will not. East Asia & Pacific, Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, and the high income and upper middle income groups are classed as on track or target met for both indicators. East Asia & Pacific reached 6.7 neonatal and 13.2 under-five in 2024, and Latin America & Caribbean 8.3 and 15.4, so each is already below both thresholds. The expected 2030 neonatal values are lower still, at 5.8 for East Asia & Pacific and 7.3 for Latin America & Caribbean. For these regions the target is no longer a constraint, and the policy question becomes one of equity within countries, which regional averages conceal.

South Asia is the clearest case of rapid change, but its two results differ. Its neonatal rate fell from 25.4 in 2015 to 16.6 in 2024, and its under-five rate from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rate of decline in the under-five rate, -0.0502, is the fastest of any region, and the trend ratio of 1.30 means the pace exceeds what the target requires. The expected 2030 under-five value is 19.7, below 25.0, so the under-five threshold is projected to be met.

For neonatal mortality the tool returns the class on track or target met, with a ratio of 0.96 and a rate of -0.0462 a year. Yet the expected 2030 value of 12.5 lies above the 12.0 threshold. The class and the projection therefore disagree, and the region is not secured on either reading. South Asia is best described as close to the neonatal threshold but not clear of it, and it should not be counted as having been shown to meet it.

The regions and groups that fall short are those where mortality is highest. Low-income countries cut under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8 per 1,000 between 2015 and 2024, at a rate of -0.0231 a year. At that pace the expected 2030 value is 59.8, far above 25.0, and the trend ratio of 0.42 is classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. The neonatal record is weaker: 28.1 fell to 24.9, an annual rate of -0.0133, with an expected 2030 value of 23.0 against a threshold of 12.0 and a ratio of 0.32. Sub-Saharan Africa shows the same pattern, with an expected 2030 under-five rate of 63.3 and a neonatal rate of 25.0. Neonatal mortality tends to fall more slowly than under-five mortality when health systems are weak, as a matter of general experience.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan group has a mixed profile. Its under-five rate, 36.4 in 2024, is classed as moderate progress needing acceleration, with an expected 2030 value of 31.1. Its neonatal rate, 22.7, is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 20.3. The group combines countries with low mortality and countries in prolonged conflict, so the regional figure conceals wide internal differences.

The lower middle income group needs a caution. Its under-five rate fell from 55.3 to 43.8 and its neonatal rate from 26.9 to 21.6, which are real gains, and both are classed as moderate progress, with trend ratios of 0.59 and 0.55. The expected 2030 values of 37.5 and 18.7 stay above both thresholds. The trend output for this group was partly truncated, so only the numbers and classifications shown can be relied upon.

### What changed since 2015, and why the pace differs

Between 2015 and 2024 every region and income group reduced both rates, but the pace varied widely. South Asia fell fastest. Its neonatal mortality went from 25.4 to 16.6 per 1,000 live births, and its under-five mortality from 42.6 to 26.8. The annual rates of change, which the trend tool expresses as a proportional rate, were -0.0462 for neonatal and -0.0502 for under-five mortality, against -0.0133 and -0.0151 for the world as a whole. The region is classed as on track for both indicators, although its neonatal trend would leave it at an expected 12.5 in 2030, with a ratio of 0.96 of the distance to the target covered, so the neonatal result is close to the threshold and not clear of it. Sub-Saharan Africa moved slowest on the neonatal measure, from 29.2 to 26.6, a rate of -0.0103. Its under-five rate, from 85.0 to 71.2, fell at -0.0195, which is faster than its neonatal rate but still leaves it far from the threshold, with an expected 63.3 in 2030 against a target of 25.0.

The pattern across income groups is similar. Low-income countries reduced neonatal mortality from 28.1 to 24.9, a rate of -0.0133, and under-five mortality from 84.9 to 68.8, a rate of -0.0231. Both are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration. Lower-middle-income countries did better on both, with neonatal mortality falling from 26.9 to 21.6 (-0.0241) and under-five mortality from 55.3 to 43.8 (-0.0256); both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. East Asia & Pacific, already at lower levels, still reduced under-five mortality from 16.6 to 13.2, a rate of -0.0251. High-income countries and North America moved slowly, at -0.0142 and -0.0034 for under-five mortality, but this is expected near a floor, where each further gain is harder to achieve.

A consistent feature is that neonatal mortality falls more slowly than under-five mortality. For the world, the neonatal rate went from 19.4 to 17.2 while the under-five rate went from 42.9 to 37.4, and the proportional rates confirm it: -0.0133 against -0.0151. In Sub-Saharan Africa and the low-income group the neonatal rate declined at a visibly slower pace than the under-five rate. A well-established explanation, given as context and not shown by these series, is that deaths after the first month are mostly caused by infections, malnutrition and malaria, which respond to vaccination, sanitation, nutrition programmes and basic treatment. Neonatal deaths come largely from prematurity, birth complications and neonatal infection, which require skilled attendance at birth, functioning referral systems and specialised newborn care. These depend on stronger health systems and take longer to build.

The differences in pace must be treated cautiously. The indicators measure outcomes, not interventions, and nothing in these series shows which policies produced the faster falls in South Asia or the slower ones in Sub-Saharan Africa. Plausible hypotheses include the expansion of facility births in South Asia, and the heavier burden of conflict, fragility and weak health financing in low-income countries. These remain hypotheses. The estimates are modelled from survey and registration data that are sparse where mortality is highest, so differences of a few thousandths in the annual rate should not be over-read.

The period after 2020 cannot be separated in these series. Both indicators are reported as annual figures to 2024, and the comparison of 2015 with 2024 shows no reversal at the regional level, but it conceals any pause in particular years. Whether the disruption of routine health services in 2020 and 2021 slowed declines cannot be answered from the levels used here.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The trend classification projects most countries to be on track for both thresholds in 2030, but this is a projection and not an observed count. For neonatal mortality, 130 of the 196 countries assessed are on track or have met the 12.0 per 1,000 threshold, and 135 are on track or have met the under-five threshold of 25.0. Each count mixes countries already at or below the threshold with countries only projected to reach it, and no tool separates the two. The number of countries that have already arrived is therefore unknown, and the forecast depends on past rates of change continuing.

The countries still short are concentrated, on the regional and income-group projections, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income settings. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to reach 25.0 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births in 2030 against a threshold of 12.0, and 63.3 under-five deaths per 1,000 against 25.0. Low-income countries are expected to reach 23.0 and 59.8 respectively. The world as a whole is expected to reach 15.9 neonatal deaths per 1,000 and 34.1 under-five deaths per 1,000, above both thresholds.

South Asia needs a precise reading. For neonatal mortality the tool returns the class on track or target met, with a ratio of 0.96, yet its projected 2030 value of 12.5 per 1,000 is above 12.0. The class and the projection disagree, so the region is close to the neonatal threshold but not clear of it, and it should not be counted as secured on either reading. For under-five mortality its projected value of 19.7 is below 25.0.

Newborn deaths are the harder problem. As context, neonatal deaths depend on skilled care at birth, management of preterm birth and infection, and functioning referral systems, which are costlier to build than the campaigns that drove earlier gains. A country can therefore meet the under-five threshold and still miss the neonatal one. On neonatal mortality, 4 countries stagnate and 9 regress; on under-five mortality, 3 stagnate and 4 regress. The countries that regress on neonatal mortality hold 5.7% of the population assessed.

Two cautions apply. The classification projects a past rate of change forward, and a different period or method could move countries near a class boundary. The wording 'at least as low as' can be read as a ceiling for every country in 2030 or as a direction of travel for those already below it; this section uses the first reading. National rates also hide inequality within countries.

Four proposals follow.

proposals: National governments of the countries that stagnate or regress on neonatal mortality, with their development partners, should fund skilled birth attendance, care for preterm and sick newborns, and referral systems as a priority within health budgets.

Donors and multilateral health funders should direct a larger share of child-survival finance to low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa, where projected 2030 rates stay far above both thresholds.
National statistical offices and the agencies that estimate mortality should publish, for each country, whether it is already at or below each threshold, so that arrival can be told from projection.
Governments should report neonatal and under-five mortality by region, wealth and residence within countries, so that national rates do not hide those left furthest behind.
