The classification rests on a past rate of change, and the target wording can be read in more than one way. Within-country inequality is not covered by national rates, and the projections carry no uncertainty bounds.

w-c06-5-5.text:
### The indicator and what it measures

Target 5.6 commits governments to universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The principal measure available for it in this section is the share of married or partnered women aged 15 to 49 who make their own informed decisions on sexual relations, contraceptive use and reproductive health care, reported in the World Bank's World Development Indicators as a percentage of those women. The description of the indicator that follows is background drawn from its published metadata, not a finding of the retrieved results, which hold only counts of reporting countries.

The question asked concerns health care and contraception. The indicator answers a broader question, because it also counts the ability to refuse sex. The part of the question about health care and contraception alone cannot be separated out from it.

The indicator is a composite, and its base is women who are married or in a union, not all women of that age. According to its metadata, a woman counts as deciding for herself only if she answers yes to all three components: she can refuse sexual intercourse with her husband or partner, she decides on the use of contraception, and she decides on her own health care. A woman who answers yes to two of the three is not counted. The measure is therefore strict, and its level cannot exceed the level for any single component. Unmarried women are left out, so the series describes one part of the female population. The data are drawn mainly from household surveys, as general background.

The reading of own decisions is not fixed across surveys. Each component rests on a question put to the respondent, and the wording, the response options and the treatment of a joint decision with a partner can differ between survey rounds and between countries. A woman who decides jointly with her husband after discussion may be recorded differently from one whose husband decides alone, and cultural norms shape how women describe such arrangements. Answers on refusing sex are also sensitive to the setting of the interview. Differences between countries, or between years in one country, may therefore partly reflect measurement and not only a change in women's autonomy.

The retrieved results report how many countries supply the indicator, not the share values themselves. In 2024 the count was 5 countries, and across 2006 to 2024 a total of 81 countries have reported at least once. The share of women who decide for themselves is therefore not stated here for any country or year, and the question cannot be answered with a figure from these results. Other series on wider household decisions, family planning, unmet need, attitudes towards refusing sex and prenatal care are outside the retrieved results for this section, and they are not read here.

### Thin coverage limits any global picture

Only 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions in 2024, the latest year in the series. The retrieved results hold the number of reporting countries but no share values for those five, so the share of women who make their own decisions cannot be stated for any country or year in this section. No aggregate appears in the coverage result for any year, so no regional or world share is available from these results. The question is therefore answered only in part: no global figure exists in the material, and the national readings are absent from it.

The question asks about decisions on health care and contraception, while the indicator also counts a woman's ability to refuse sexual intercourse. It counts a woman only if she makes her own decision on all three areas. The measure therefore answers a broader question than the one posed, and its share cannot exceed the share for any single component. The results do not separate the components, so the share deciding on health care and contraception alone cannot be read from this series.

The count of 5 in 2024 says nothing about why so few countries appear. The results give counts only, and they do not show whether the figure reflects survey timing, processing delays or other causes. As context, such data come mainly from household surveys that are fielded country by country at intervals of several years, so a country enters a year's count only when a survey has been completed and released. A low count should not be read as evidence that decision-making has become less common. Nor are the reporting countries a sample drawn to represent any region or income group.

For that reason the five reporting countries could support national readings only, if their values were available. Each reading could describe its own country. None could be averaged into a regional picture, because countries whose populations, laws and health systems differ widely would be combined into a number describing no real population. In the present material there are five country counts and no values to average.

The wider record shows how uneven coverage is. Across 2006 to 2024, 81 countries reported at least once. Among the years whose counts the results give, the number reporting in a single year runs from 3 in 2008 to 15 in 2018, and 12 countries reported in 2022 and 14 in 2023. Even in the best of these years, 15 countries is a small part of the 81 with a value at some point, and the set of reporting countries changes from year to year. A change in the average of reporting countries between two years would therefore reflect a change in who reported as much as any change in women's autonomy.

The constraint matters for the 2030 agenda. Target 5.6 concerns universal access and rights, and a measure reported by so few countries in a year cannot show whether the target is being reached. Women outside unions, and countries without a recent survey, are absent from the evidence. The thin coverage is itself a finding: monitoring of this target rests on a handful of countries in each year.

### Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data

Reporting by year shows why regions and countries cannot be compared on current data. The results give the number of countries reporting the indicator for each year from 2006 to 2024, and the facts available here include a count for every one of those years. Among them, the lowest count is 3 countries in 2008 and the highest is 15 in 2018. Counts for some intervening years serve the argument: 4 in 2009, 7 in 2010, 12 in 2012, 6 in 2013 and 10 in 2016. Each year's reading therefore describes a different group of countries, and a change between years may reflect who was surveyed rather than any change in women's lives.

The pattern is consistent with a survey cycle. Household surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys visit a country every few years, and the countries reached in one year are seldom those reached in the next; this is context, not something the counts themselves show. A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2018 and 2019, cannot be set side by side. Regional groupings fare no better, because a region may be represented by one or two countries in one year and by none in another. The coverage result lists no aggregates, so no regional average exists to correct for this, and constructing one from such uneven entries would imply a precision the data do not hold.

Across the years 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once, yet in 2024 only 5 reported. A country's most recent reading may therefore be older than 2024, but the results do not give the survey years of individual countries, so the date gap between latest values cannot be measured. Comparing latest values across countries would mix survey years of unknown spread, and the gap between two countries' values could be partly a gap in dates.

The results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, so no country's reading for 2024 is stated here. The question asks about health care and contraception, whereas the indicator also counts the ability to refuse sex, so it answers a broader question than the one posed. A woman is counted only if she decides on all three areas, and the base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so women outside unions are not covered. The 5 countries reporting in 2024 are too few to support any ranking or regional statement, and none is made.

### Reporting has changed little since 2015

Reporting counts have swung widely since 2015 without a trend. In 2015, 5 countries reported the indicator on women's own informed decisions. The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached 15 in 2018, then fell to 4 in 2019 and 4 in 2020. It recovered to 7 in 2021, 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023, before dropping to 5 in 2024. Counts are cited here for 2015, 2016, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024; the year 2017, with a count of 6, is the only year from 2015 onward not mentioned above. Among the years from 2015 onward, 15 in 2018 is the highest count.

The results give counts of reporting countries and nothing about why those counts differ from year to year. As general context, not shown by the series, household surveys are fielded in a country every few years and compiled some time afterwards, so a year with many reporting countries is one in which many survey rounds were completed and published. The cause of the low count in 2024 is not known from these data, and later releases may or may not add countries to recent years.

The equal counts of 4 in 2019 and 2020 cannot be explained by the series alone, and the series does not test any cause. The recovery to 12 in 2022 and 14 in 2023 is a rise in the number of countries reporting and not a measure of change in women's decisions.

The consequence is that no comparison before and after 2015 or 2020 can be drawn from this series. Each year's group of reporting countries differs from the last, so a rise or fall in any average would reflect who was surveyed. Because the retrieved results hold counts and no share values, a trend in women's decision-making since 2015 cannot be stated, and the 2030 horizon cannot be assessed against a comparable baseline.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Target 5.6 cannot be judged as on track or off track with the data now held. The indicator on women's own informed decisions has no aggregate in any year, and the results hold no share values for any country. Only 5 countries reported in 2024, the latest year, and 81 countries have reported at least once since 2006. The question of what share of women make their own decisions therefore has no figure to answer it here.

A trend needs the same countries measured at intervals, and the shelf does not offer that. Whether a country has moved towards 2030 cannot be told by comparing one year's reporters with another's. The counts show how many countries reported in a year, not why a count was high or low. The count of 4 in 2020 equals that of 2019, so the series offers no support for linking it to the pandemic. As context not tested by the series, household surveys are fielded in multi-year cycles, and the timing of those cycles shapes which countries appear in a given year. The cause of the low count in 2024 is not known from the data.

The reading of the target adds a second difficulty. Target 5.6 speaks of universal access and of reproductive rights, which no single survey question captures. The question posed asks about health care and contraception, while the indicator also counts the ability to refuse sex, so it answers a broader question than the one asked. By its metadata description, not by any retrieved result, it requires a woman to answer yes to all three components, so its level cannot exceed that of any single component. Its base is women aged 15 to 49 who are married or in a union, so unmarried women and adolescents fall outside it. A rise or fall in the share could reflect a change in any of the three components, and the series alone does not say which.

The proposals below follow from these findings. No comparable baseline exists in the results, so they aim first at obtaining usable share values and then at a baseline, since the period to 2030 is short and surveys are slow to field.

proposals: National statistical offices and the agencies that field household surveys should publish the share of women making their own informed decisions for every survey round, so that values, and not only counts, reach the World Bank's series.

The agencies that coordinate demographic and health surveys should keep the three components of the indicator, and the ability to refuse sex in particular, in a fixed questionnaire module, so that the same countries can be compared across rounds before 2030.
Statistical offices in countries with no reading should field the module in the next survey cycle and report it, to set a baseline for the target.

The World Bank and its partners should publish each component of the indicator separately, together with the age and marital status of the women covered, so that readers can see which component moves and who is left outside the base.
w-c06-5-5.gaps: The results hold counts of reporting countries but no share values for any country or year, and no aggregate for any region or the world. Women who are unmarried, and adolescents, fall outside the indicator's base. The three components cannot be read separately, and the series does not cover reproductive rights or universal access as the target words them. No result tests the causes of changes in reporting.

w-c08-3-4.text:
### The global share rose by 2.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2020

The world share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption stood at 17.4 per cent in 2015 and 19.7 per cent in 2020. The share therefore rose over the five years, and the direction is clear. Whether the magnitude meets the aim of the target is a separate question, and the data alone do not settle it. Over the period the share grew at a compound rate of 0.0255 a year, which the trend tool classes as on track or target met. That label rests on a trend tool that has no numerical target to measure against, so it should be read as a statement about the pace of change, not as a verdict on sufficiency.

Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix, and it names no threshold. Two readings are available. The first is a rise in the share: renewables supply a larger fraction of all final energy. The second is a rise in absolute use: more renewable energy is consumed, whatever the fraction. The two can diverge. Where total demand grows quickly, absolute renewable use can climb while the share stagnates or falls. The indicator reported here, renewable energy consumption as a percentage of total final energy consumption, measures only the first reading. A rise in the share is the stricter test, because it requires renewables to outpace the growth of demand as a whole.

The word 'substantial' compounds the ambiguity. No agreed numerical benchmark exists in the target text, so any judgement of sufficiency rests on a chosen standard: a doubling, a fixed number of points, or a path consistent with climate goals. Since no such standard is set in the target, this account treats the change from 17.4 to 19.7 per cent as an observed change and states plainly where a reader's own threshold would alter the verdict. By any reading, a gain of this size from a base of 17.4 per cent leaves the large majority of final energy supplied by other sources in 2020.

The composition of the indicator also matters for interpretation. Final energy consumption includes heat and transport as well as electricity, and the renewable share counts traditional biomass such as wood and charcoal burned for cooking and heating. A share can therefore be high in poor countries because of reliance on fuelwood, which is neither modern nor clean, and the aims of Goal 7 treat it differently from wind, solar or hydropower. The headline figure thus mixes two quite different kinds of renewable use, a point taken up in the regional comparisons that follow.

A limit on the evidence must be stated. The series is reported by 212 countries in every year from 2015 to 2021, but only 71 countries report a value for 2022. For most countries, therefore, the record ends in 2020 or 2021 for practical purposes, and the comparison of 2015 with 2020 is the last one that rests on near-complete coverage. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks that followed, cannot be read from this series with confidence. For the 2030 horizon, this means the trajectory is known only for the first five of fifteen years, and the later years remain to be measured.

### Regional levels differ by a factor of ten, and nearly all regions rose

Regional levels of the renewable share span a wide range. In 2020 Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 70.3 per cent of total final energy consumption, South Asia at 36.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 34.2 per cent. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 7.5 per cent. The highest regional value is therefore several times the lowest, a gap of roughly a factor of nine, and it is wide in both years.

The ranking does not measure the quality of the energy system. In poorer regions a high share may reflect the burning of wood, charcoal, crop residues and dung for cooking and heating, which counts as renewable in the indicator. These fuels are often gathered unsustainably, carry serious health costs through indoor air pollution, and supply energy of low efficiency. A low share in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan may follow from large oil and gas endowments that have long dominated power generation and final use; this is context from outside the data. The indicator cannot separate traditional biomass from modern capacity such as wind, solar, hydropower or modern bioenergy, so a region can score high with little modern renewable infrastructure and low with a fast-growing one. Other series on the shelf, such as electricity output and output excluding hydropower, give a partial view of modern capacity but cover electricity only.

All six regions rose between 2015 and 2020. Latin America and the Caribbean gained from 28.2 to 34.2 per cent, the largest rise of any region. Europe and Central Asia moved from 12.9 to 15.1 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 13.0 to 14.8 per cent, and North America from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent. The results do not test why these regions rose; falling costs of wind and solar and policy support are commonly cited in the wider literature, and are context outside the data. South Asia rose more slowly, from 34.9 to 36.9 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 68.0 to 70.3 per cent. In both, a rise in the share is ambiguous: it may reflect new modern capacity, or continued reliance on biomass. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 7.1 to 7.5 per cent.

The income groups show the same pattern and one reversal. The low-income group fell from 77.0 to 74.6 per cent between 2015 and 2020, the only group to decline. The fall does not necessarily signal a worsening of the energy system. As incomes rise and electricity and fossil fuels reach more households, the biomass share can fall before modern renewables replace it, so a lower share may accompany a real improvement in access. Equally, it may reflect growth in fossil-fuel use that outpaces renewables. The indicator alone cannot tell which. Lower middle income countries rose from 41.7 to 43.3 per cent, upper middle income countries from 14.9 to 16.8 per cent, and high income countries from 10.6 to 12.8 per cent.

The rise was broad across regions but small in the regions with the highest shares and absent in the low-income group, where the share fell. Reading target 7.2 as a rise in the share, the world rose; reading it as growth in modern, sustainable renewables, the aggregate hides much of what matters, because the indicator cannot show modern capacity. Coverage also limits comparison: 71 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot yet confirm whether the gains held after the shock of 2020. The results do not project values for 2030.

### Country trajectories diverge: 73 on track, 85 in regression

The classification of countries separates the world into groups whose experience since 2015 has been very different. Of 202 countries assessed, 73 are classed as on track or target met, and these hold 37.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 11 countries show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed (3.8 per cent of population), and 14 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration (22.2 per cent). Nineteen countries are stagnating (4.8 per cent of population). The largest group by count is the 85 countries in regression, which hold 31.8 per cent of the population.

The label 'on track' needs careful reading. Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the renewable share but gives no numeric value, so no threshold exists against which progress can be measured. The classification therefore rests on an extrapolated rate of change: the observed trend is projected forward to 2030, and a country is called on track when the direction is positive and the pace is adequate by the tool's own scale. 'On track' here means a positive trend only. It does not mean that a country will reach any particular share, and a country that starts from a very low share can be called on track while remaining far from a renewable-based energy system. The reading of 'substantially' is open: a rise of a few points could count under one interpretation and fall short under another.

Count and population tell different stories. The on-track group holds the largest population share of any class, 37.5 per cent, yet it has fewer countries (73) than the regression group (85), whose population share is 31.8 per cent. Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries, and the two classes hold 4.8 and 31.8 per cent of the population respectively. The data therefore show a split world: a large share of people live in countries with a positive trend, and a comparable share live in countries where the share has fallen. The world rate of 0.0255 is positive and classed as on track, but it is an aggregate and does not describe each country.

The regional rates help to explain the pattern. The rates for East Asia and Pacific (0.0267), Europe and Central Asia (0.0325), North America (0.0370) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0390) are all classed as on track, as are the high income (0.0381) and upper middle income (0.0240) groups. The groups under the greatest strain are the low income group, where the rate is negative at -0.0064 and classed as regression, and the lower middle income group, at 0.0079, classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) and South Asia (0.0112) are also marginal, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0129) show moderate progress.

The indicator does not reveal why the share falls in low income settings, and the following is context, not a finding. The renewable share of final consumption in such countries is widely understood to be dominated by traditional biomass used for cooking and heating. If total consumption grows with non-renewable supply, or households shift away from biomass, the share can fall even while other goals advance. A fall is therefore not necessarily a failure of renewable policy. The gains in richer regions are commonly linked to deliberate expansion of modern renewables, but the share alone cannot confirm what was added.

For 2030 the implication is that a positive global rate can coexist with 85 regressing countries. The target will be met in substance only if the lagging groups change course, and the data cannot say whether modern renewables are replacing traditional biomass or merely sitting beside it.

### Convergence is weak and coverage thins after 2020

The convergence test asks whether countries that began with a low renewable share have gained faster than those that began high. Across 71 countries with data for both 2015 and 2022, the estimated coefficient is -0.0101 (p 0.0006, R2 0.190). The negative sign indicates that countries starting higher changed by less each year, so low-share countries gained slightly faster, and the p-value of 0.0006 indicates that the relationship is unlikely to be chance. The magnitude is small, however, and an R2 of 0.190 means that initial level explains under one fifth of the variation in change. The remainder lies elsewhere. National policy, resource endowment, the pace of electrification and the use of traditional biomass are plausible influences, but they are context only, since the results do not measure them.

The coefficient of variation points the same way. It stood at 1.040 in 2015 and at 1.039 in 2022, a change in the third decimal place. Dispersion across these countries is therefore not narrowing. A coefficient near 1.0 means that the standard deviation of national shares is about equal to their mean, which describes a very unequal distribution. Weak catch-up in the slope, combined with unchanged dispersion, means that the spread of national shares in 2022 was about what it had been in 2015.

This result needs careful reading because the renewable share in final consumption mixes two quite different things. In many low-income countries a high share reflects reliance on firewood and charcoal, not modern renewable capacity, and a fall in that share can accompany progress in clean cooking and electrification. In high-income countries a rising share usually reflects wind, solar and hydropower in the electricity system. These are well-established patterns, but the indicator cannot separate them. A convergence test that treats both as one scale cannot distinguish a desirable fall in traditional biomass from a failure to expand modern renewables. The weak convergence found here should not be read as proof that poorer countries are being left behind in modern renewable deployment.

The sample is also a limit. Reporting for this series was broad in the early years: 207 countries in 2000, 210 in 2010 and 212 in every year from 2012 to 2021. In 2022 it fell to 71 countries. The 212 countries of 2021 and the 71 of 2022 are not comparable bases, and the data do not show that the 71 are a random draw from the 212. The convergence estimate describes only those that reported, and it cannot be extended to the world or to any region without that caveat.

The drop matters for 2030 because the years after 2020 are the ones in which the pandemic recovery, the energy price shock and new policies would show. Those years are visible for only a third of countries. The series is fully covered to 2021, so the record to that year is secure, while any statement about 2022 rests on a partial group. This is a reporting lag, not a finding of decline, and it should be read as a gap in evidence.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The share has risen, from 17.4 per cent in 2015 to 19.7 per cent in 2020. Whether that is substantial cannot be settled from the data, because target 7.2 sets no number. Read as any increase, the world figure moved in the right direction. The world rate of 0.0255 a year is a pace of change only, and it is not a verdict on whether that pace suffices. The results do not project 2030, so no forecast of the 2030 share is offered here.

The countries are divided. Of the 202 countries assessed, 85 are in regression, holding 31.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 19 more show stagnation, holding 4.8 per cent. A rising world average therefore conceals a large population living where the share has fallen or stood still. Set against the 37.5 per cent of the population in the 73 on-track countries, the 31.8 per cent in regression is of a similar order.

The low-income group shows the problem most clearly. Its share fell from 77.0 per cent in 2015 to 74.6 per cent in 2020, yet the level remains very high. As context outside the data, such levels usually reflect reliance on firewood, charcoal and other traditional biomass, which counts as renewable in this series but is neither modern nor clean. A fall in the share can accompany welcome developments, such as grid expansion, and a high share can accompany poverty and indoor air pollution. The indicator alone cannot separate these cases, and conclusions for the poorest countries must be drawn with that caution.

For 2030, the results show where acceleration is needed. The 14 countries with marginal progress hold 22.2 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. The tools do not measure how much each group contributes to the global figure, so no claim is made about which group would move it most. Convergence is weak, and the 2022 data cover only 71 countries, so the picture after 2020 cannot be confirmed for most of the world.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

proposals: National energy ministries in the 85 regression countries should publish the split of their renewable share between modern sources and traditional biomass, so that falls and rises can be read correctly.
The bodies that set the Goals framework should define a numerical threshold for 'substantially' in target 7.2, so that progress can be judged against a stated standard.

w-c02-1-4.text:
### The global headcount at $3.00 a day

Target 1.1 asks that extreme poverty be eradicated for all people everywhere by 2030, and its wording quotes a line of $1.25 a day. That line belongs to an earlier price base and has been superseded several times as purchasing power parity exchange rates were revised. The measure used here is the current international line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, published by the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform. Poverty rates under this line cannot be compared with those printed in earlier editions of the series, and the figures in this book should not be set beside older statements of the target without that caution.

On this measure, 13.4% of the world's population lived below $3.00 a day in 2015, the year the goals were adopted. By 2024 the share was 10.1%. The fall is real and of consequence, in a period that included a pandemic and a sharp rise in food and energy prices (context from outside the results, which show the change but not its cause). It also shows how far the world remains from the target. At the 2024 level, roughly one person in ten still lives below the line, and the target date is six years off. Continuing at the compound rate of change observed since 2015, the series would reach 8.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as marginal progress needing significant acceleration.

The word eradicate admits more than one reading, and the choice changes the verdict. The strict reading is a headcount of 0%, which no measured aggregate has approached and which survey-based estimation could not confirm even if it were reached, since sampling error and gaps in coverage make an exact zero unobservable. A looser reading treats extreme poverty as ended as a global phenomenon when the share falls below a threshold of 3% of the population. That threshold is the authors' reading, offered as context from outside the results; the results do not test it, and the text of the target does not choose between the readings. Against a 3% threshold the world stands at more than three times the required level in 2024; against zero the distance is the whole of the 10.1%. Both readings lead to the same conclusion for 2030, but they differ in what a successful outcome would mean.

The choice of line matters for a second reason. A line of $3.00 a day is a very low standard, set to reflect the national lines of the poorest countries. Falling below it signals deprivation of food, shelter and basic needs. Rising above it does not signal security, and many households that have crossed it remain close enough to be pushed back by a poor harvest, an illness or a price shock (general context, not a result). This section reports the $3.00 line only; the higher line of $4.20 a day is not analysed here.

The 2024 value must be read with care. The data behind the headcount are household surveys, which are conducted in each country at intervals of several years and are published with a delay. Figures for the most recent years therefore rest partly on estimates that carry forward earlier surveys using national accounts growth and other assumptions. The coverage record shows the effect. In 2015, 87 countries reported a value, and 93 did so in 2018. The number fell to 70 in 2020, the year of the pandemic, when fieldwork was disrupted, recovered to 81 in 2021, then fell to 73 in 2022 and 60 in 2023. Only 26 countries reported in 2024, and just 4 in 2025. Coverage is therefore not a steady decline, but the most recent years are thinly observed. The 2024 aggregate of 10.1% is thus a nowcast built on a thin base of direct observation, and later revisions can be expected as surveys arrive.

Two cautions follow for any reader. The fall from 13.4% to 10.1% is a robust direction but not a precise magnitude, and the end point is less firm than the start. The global figure also conceals a very uneven distribution, taken up in the next part, in which the decline has been concentrated in a few regions while others have seen little progress or a reversal.

### Regions and income groups diverge

The regional picture beneath the global figure is one of sharp divergence. East Asia & Pacific recorded the largest fall among the regions with a full series: the headcount at $3.00 a day went from 6.1% in 2015 to 2.0% in 2024. Europe & Central Asia began from a low base and moved from 1.2% to 0.6%. Latin America & Caribbean fell from 6.0% to 4.3%, a decline that is real but slower in proportion than those of the two regions above. The series shows the change and not its cause; commodity cycles, informal employment and the reach of cash transfers are commonly cited as context for the region, but nothing in the results tests them. North America, at 1.1% in 2015 and 0.9% in 2024, was already close to the floor of what survey-based measurement can distinguish from zero.

South Asia requires a caution. The series for the region begins in 2020, at 9.4%, and reaches 2.6% in 2024. Read at face value, this is the largest fall among the regional series, but it covers only four years (2020 to 2024), whereas the falls of the other regions cover the nine years from 2015 to 2024, so the two cannot be ranked against each other. The reading cannot be extended to 2015, because the regional value is not shown for the earlier years, and regional estimates depend on a small number of large countries with infrequent household surveys, so the aggregate may rest on interpolation as much as on fresh observation. The 2020 starting point also falls in the year of the pandemic, so part of the apparent decline may be recovery from a temporary shock rather than a sustained trend. Projected at its 2020 to 2024 rate, the region would stand at 0.4% in 2030, which the trend tool classes as on track; because the series is short and begins in the pandemic year, that classification is provisional. The figure is best taken as a sign of strong improvement of uncertain size, not as a measured change over the full period since 2015.

Two regions show no fall in the rate. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan moved in the wrong direction, from 11.3% in 2015 to 14.3% in 2024, and the trend tool classes it as regression. The grouping combines economies of very different kinds, so the rise should not be read as a uniform deterioration; armed conflict and displacement in some members are often mentioned as background, but the results do not identify the cause. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 45.4% in 2015 and 45.0% in 2024, almost no change in nine years. A flat rate in a growing population would imply a rising number of people below the line, but that number is not measured here, and only the rate is reported. How much each region contributes to the global total is likewise not measured here.

Income groups tell the same story from another side. Low-income countries recorded 50.1% in 2015 and 52.5% in 2024, a rise, so that more than half the population of the poorest group of economies lives below $3.00 a day. Lower middle income countries stood at 16.0% in 2020 and 12.4% in 2024; the series for this group, like that for South Asia, is shown from 2020 only, and the same caution applies. Upper middle income countries fell from 5.8% to 2.1%, and high-income countries from 0.7% to 0.6%. The pattern is that the decline has been concentrated where poverty was already moderate, and that it has bypassed the group where poverty is deepest.

This matters for the target. The global fall from 13.4% to 10.1% coincides with large falls in regions that started with modest rates, while the region and income group with the highest rates did not move or moved backwards. The results do not show who contributes most to the global total, but they do show that the highest rates lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. Data for the most recent years are also thinner, a limit taken up in a later part. Eradication by 2030 would require that the stagnant and regressing groups reverse course abruptly, which no part of the 2015 to 2024 record suggests.

### Country progress and the absence of convergence

Sorting countries by the pace of their progress towards a headcount of zero by 2030 shows how uneven the record is. Of 105 countries assessed on the $3.00 a day line, 18 are on track or have met the target, and together they hold 45.5% of the population of the assessed countries. The results do not show which countries account for that share. The count of countries is far less encouraging than the share of people: 18 of 105 is a small minority of national experiences.

The middle of the distribution is crowded. 41 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, and they hold 23.1% of the assessed population. A further 15 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, holding 11.3%. In neither group is the target reached at the present pace. Moderate progress means the direction is right and the speed is insufficient; marginal progress means that closing the remaining distance would require a change of pace that few countries have managed in a single decade.

The weakest classes matter most for the meaning of the target, which asks for eradication for all people everywhere. 7 countries are stagnating, with 2.2% of the assessed population. 24 countries are regressing, with 17.9%. Regression in almost a quarter of the assessed countries is a finding in its own right. The series shows the change but not its cause. As outside context, not a result of this analysis, armed conflict, state fragility, high food and energy prices and the pandemic of 2020 are commonly cited in the wider literature as reasons for setbacks. Because the classification measures movement from each country's own observations, a country can regress from a low level as well as from a high one, and the class does not by itself say how deep the deprivation is.

The convergence test addresses whether poorer countries are catching up. Across 57 countries with data from 2015 to 2022, the regression of change in the headcount on its starting level gives a beta of 0.00658 with a p-value of 0.396 and an R-squared of 0.029. A negative and significant coefficient would have shown that countries starting with higher headcounts fell faster. The coefficient is instead slightly positive, statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the starting level explains under 3% of the variation in outcomes. Starting poverty did not predict the later pace of change.

The dispersion measure points the same way. The coefficient of variation of the headcount across the 57 countries rose from 2.144 in 2015 to 2.675 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts grew relative to their mean. Two readings are open. It may reflect a true divergence in national fortunes. It may also reflect that the headcount, as it approaches zero in many countries, has a small mean, which can inflate a ratio-based dispersion measure even when absolute differences narrow. The absolute test and the relative one should be read together, and neither shows catching up.

The sample limits both results. The convergence test covers 57 countries, fewer than the 105 classified, because it needs observations close to both 2015 and 2022. Household surveys are generally less frequent in poorer and more fragile countries, which is established context rather than a result here, so the finding of no convergence may understate the divergence. For 2030, the absence of catch-up means the global target cannot be met by the average trend alone.

### A slowing decline and its limits as evidence

The pace of decline in the world headcount at $3.00 a day has not been steady. A break analysis of the annual change in the world series finds two turning points, in 2014 and in 2021. Between 2001 and 2013 the headcount fell by a mean of 1.6 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2014 to 2018 the mean annual fall was 0.9 points, and in the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 0.3 points. The three segment means all point the same way, towards a smaller annual fall, and the most recent is about a fifth of the first. The two breaks fall close to two events that shaped the period: the end of the commodity-price boom and the slowdown of growth in many low-income economies after 2014, and the pandemic shock of 2020. These are context drawn from general knowledge, not findings of the series. The data show when the pace changed; they do not isolate why. Attribution would need counterfactual modelling that the series alone cannot supply, and the timing of breaks in a short annual series is itself uncertain by a year or more.

A further reason for caution lies outside the results. As context from general experience, and not as a finding, the remaining poor when the headcount is low are often concentrated in places that are poorer, more remote, more often affected by conflict or weak states, and less able to benefit from average growth. A slowing decline may therefore be partly expected even without any change in policy effort, though the series do not test this. Yet that would not make the slowdown benign. The target requires the headcount to reach zero, or a figure close to it, and a falling rate of change moves that outcome further from 2030, not nearer.

The evidence behind the latest segment is thinner than the evidence behind the earlier ones. Poverty rates come from household surveys, which are fielded irregularly and published with a lag. The number of countries reporting a figure for the headcount was 87 in 2015, 70 in 2020 and 81 in 2021, so coverage has not moved in one direction. It fell to 60 in 2023, to 26 in 2024 and to 4 in 2025. The decline in recent years is partly a matter of surveys not yet processed or not yet conducted, so the world and regional figures for 2023 onward probably lean on estimates that carry forward earlier survey information with growth data and assumptions about distribution. The mean change for 2021-2024 should be read as a provisional estimate, likely to be revised as surveys arrive, and the 2025 figures hardly rest on observed data at all.

The coverage problem may be uneven as well as thin. Countries with infrequent surveys are plausibly those with the highest poverty and the weakest statistical systems, and so the most likely to be absent from a given year; the counts above do not themselves show which countries are missing. The world aggregate could then be least well measured where the number of poor people is largest. Anyone assessing whether 2030 is within reach should weigh the slowdown found here as a signal that is probably real in direction, since the three segment means agree, but uncertain in size.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace observed since 2015, the world will not reach zero extreme poverty by 2030. The world headcount at $3.00 a day stood at 10.1% in 2024, and the trend to the target projects 8.4% in 2030 at the compound rate since 2015, a ratio of 0.38 of the progress needed. The trend classifies the world as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. Target 1.1 can also be read as a threshold of 3%. That is this book's own choice of interpretation, and the results do not test it. On that reading the target is no more attainable, since the world headcount of 10.1% is still more than three times that level. The recent pace is slower than the pace since 2015: the segment from 2021 to 2024 shows a mean annual fall of only 0.325 points.

Even the regions that are advancing need to go faster. East Asia & Pacific, the best performer among the regions with a full series, is expected to stand at 1.0% in 2030 at its present rate, against a target of zero, and its ratio is 0.84. Europe & Central Asia is expected at 0.4%, and upper middle income countries at 1.1%. These are small residual shares, but they are the hardest to remove. As context from outside the results, the people concerned are often in remote, conflict-affected or marginalised groups that growth alone does not reach. South Asia is classed as on track, with an expected 0.4% in 2030, from a start of 9.4% in 2020. That classification is provisional: the series begins in 2020, the pandemic year, so the fall to 2.6% in 2024 covers four years and is measured from a short and unusual base. It cannot be ranked against the nine-year falls from 2015 to 2024 in other regions.

The highest rates lie where the trend is flat or reversed. Sub-Saharan Africa is in stagnation, with an expected 44.7% in 2030, and low-income countries are in regression, with 54.2% expected. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region is also in regression, with 16.7% expected. The series shows these changes but not their causes, and the contribution of each group to the world total is not measured here. Among 105 countries assessed, 24 are in regression and hold 17.9% of the assessed population.

The proposals that follow from these findings are as follows. National governments and donors should concentrate poverty-reduction effort and concessional finance on Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries. The headcount in Sub-Saharan Africa was 45.0% in 2024, almost unchanged from 45.4% in 2015, and in low-income countries it was 52.5% in 2024, up from 50.1% in 2015. National statistical offices, with the World Bank and bilateral funders, should fund household surveys at a regular and shorter interval. The interval is a proposal, not a finding, and the case for it is that 70 countries reported in 2020 against 26 for 2024 and 4 for 2025, so recent estimates rest on projection. The World Bank and national authorities should name the line and the price base whenever poverty is reported, so that the $1.25 wording of Target 1.1 is not mistaken for the current measure of $3.00 a day. The United Nations statistical system should track regression as a class of its own, since the 24 countries in that class are hidden by averages that mix them with countries that are advancing.

w-c05-2-5.text:
### Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025

Out-of-school counts at primary age are given by income group, not as a global total, and the results supply no global figure. In 2015 the four groups held 26.0 million, 52.0 million, 8.1 million and 1.3 million such children, and in 2025 they held 30.1 million, 46.4 million, 9.3 million and 2.1 million, in the order low, lower middle, upper middle and high income. The 2025 values come from only 12 reporting countries, so the answer to the question of how many children are out of school is available here only as these four group values.

The movement between the two years differs by group. Low-income countries rose from 26.0 million to 30.1 million. Lower middle income countries fell from 52.0 million to 46.4 million. Upper middle income countries rose from 8.1 million to 9.3 million, and high-income countries from 1.3 million to 2.1 million. Lower middle income countries still hold the largest group count, 46.4 million; a likely reason is the size of their school-age populations, though these series do not test it. Three of the four groups show higher counts in 2025 than in 2015 and one shows a lower count. The comparison is indicative only: with 12 reporting countries in the latest year, the country sets may differ between 2015 and 2025, and no net change on a common set of countries is measured.

The primary-age series reaches 197 countries in the rate version and 198 in the count version over its history, but the latest-year group values depend on which countries reported. The definition adds a further caution: children are counted as out of school if they are not enrolled in primary or secondary school, so those still in pre-primary education within the primary age group also count. Rises in some groups may therefore partly reflect late entry or pre-primary enrolment rather than outright exclusion.

The matter is important because Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education by 2030. A child who never enrols cannot complete, so the out-of-school count marks the first and most basic gap between the target and the present. The period after 2020 falls within the same data window. The interruption of schooling during the pandemic, conflict, displacement and population growth in the poorest countries are commonly cited pressures on enrolment, given here as context; the results do not separate these effects and cannot attribute the changes to them.

For 2030, the implication is cautious. Group counts that are higher in 2025 than in 2015 in three of four groups, on thin reporting, give no evidence of the rate of decline that ending exclusion would require. The rates in the following part show where the difficulty is concentrated.

### Low-income countries carry the highest rates and the rising counts

Income group is the sharpest dividing line in the data on exclusion from school. In 2025, 24.1% of primary-school-age children in low-income countries were out of school, against 2.5% in high-income countries. Upper middle income countries stood at 4.0% and lower middle income countries at 8.3%. Rates therefore fall as national income rises, and the poorest group sits far above the rest.

The direction of change differs by group, and the differences matter more than any single total. In low-income countries the rate eased from 25.6% in 2015 to 24.1% in 2025, yet the number of children rose from 25.99 million to 30.06 million. A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow. A plausible explanation, not tested by these series, is that fertility remains high in many low-income countries, so each year brings a larger cohort to the school gate, and classrooms, teachers and budgets must expand merely to hold the rate in place. Progress in the rate, small as it is, was outrun by the growth in the number of children.

Lower middle income countries show the one clear improvement. The rate fell from 9.7% in 2015 to 8.3% in 2025, and the count fell from 51.97 million to 46.40 million. This group still holds the largest group value for out-of-school children, because its population is so large, but it is the only group in which both measures moved the right way. The group values suggest that this gain offsets increases elsewhere, though the series do not show how far.

The movement in richer groups runs the other way. In upper middle income countries the rate rose from 3.6% to 4.0% and the count from 8.13 million to 9.28 million. In high-income countries the rate rose from 1.6% to 2.5% and the count from 1.34 million to 2.06 million. These are small shares, and the rises should be read with caution: the definition counts children in pre-primary education as out of school, and reporting changes, migration and displacement can all shift the figures. Only 12 countries reported in 2025 for each of these series, so the 2025 group values rest on a thin base and may partly reflect which countries happened to report. The data cannot show how far the rises are real.

The adolescent figures sharpen the picture. At lower secondary age, 41.7% of adolescents in low-income countries were out of school in 2025, up from 36.1% in 2015, and the share is far above the primary-age rate of 24.1% in the same group. Exclusion appears to deepen as children grow older. Likely reasons, which the data do not test, are that many enter school but few progress, and that costs, distance, early work, early marriage and a shortage of secondary places push adolescents out. Few other results in the section show so large a worsening, although it too rests on 12 reporting countries.

Other groups look very different at this level. Lower middle income countries moved from 12.7% to 11.6%, upper middle income countries from 5.7% to 5.9%, and high-income countries from 2.1% to 1.9%. Outside the low-income group, then, each group's adolescent exclusion rate changed by less than one and a half percentage points. The deterioration is concentrated where systems are weakest.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Target 4.1 asks that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education, and a low-income group in which 41.7% of lower secondary-age adolescents are out of school is far from that goal. Because the low-income count is rising, even steady gains in the rate would not shrink the number of children to be reached. The path to the target depends on expanding places and teachers in low-income countries faster than their school-age populations grow, and on retaining adolescents once they have entered.

### Girls and boys are out of school in near-equal numbers

Counts disaggregated by sex show a pattern close to parity, but the direction of the small difference depends on national income. In low-income countries, 15.71 million girls of primary school age were out of school in 2025, against 14.35 million boys, so girls are the larger group there. In 2015 the corresponding counts were 13.54 million girls and 12.45 million boys. Both counts rose over the decade, and the girls' count rose slightly more than the boys', so the gap in low-income countries appears to have widened a little in absolute terms, to the girls' disadvantage. This reading rests on sex series from only 8 reporting countries in 2025 and should be treated as indicative.

The other three income groups show the opposite ordering. In lower middle income countries, 22.14 million girls and 24.26 million boys were out of school in 2025, down from 25.27 million girls and 26.70 million boys in 2015. Girls' counts fell by more than boys' there. In upper middle income countries the counts were 4.056 million girls and 5.223 million boys in 2025, up from 3.619 million and 4.507 million in 2015. In high-income countries the counts were 984,900 girls and 1.079 million boys in 2025, up from 627,000 and 707,600. Boys outnumber girls among the excluded in these three groups, which is consistent with well-established patterns of boys leaving school early in richer systems, often for work or after repeated grade failure.

Girls are thus the larger excluded group only where overall exclusion is highest. This matters for policy, because a single global statement of parity conceals two different problems. In the poorest countries, barriers that plausibly fall hardest on girls, such as early marriage, distance to school, the cost of fees and the lack of safe facilities, may remain active, though these results do not test such causes. In better-off systems, disengagement among boys is the larger concern. The comparison after 2015 shows no sign that the sex difference has closed in low-income countries, and the period since 2020, which included school closures and economic shocks, offers no data in these results that separate the pandemic's effect from the longer trend.

The figures carry limits that bear on any reading for 2030. The sex-disaggregated series draw on 8 countries reporting in 2025, whereas the totals by income group draw on 12, so the two sets should not be compared directly. Part of each total is likely to be estimated or carried from earlier years. The counts also say nothing about disparities within countries. Children who are rural, poor, displaced or disabled are likely to be excluded at far higher rates than any national average, and a near-equal split between girls and boys can coexist with very large gaps along those lines. Target 4.1 asks for completion that is equitable, and national counts by sex cannot show whether that has been achieved. Parity between girls and boys should be read as a narrow finding, not as evidence that exclusion is evenly shared.

### Most countries are not on course to end exclusion by 2030

Between 2015 and 2025 the rate of primary-school-age children out of school barely moved in the poorest countries and rose in richer ones. In low-income countries it stood at 24.1% in 2025, against 25.6% in 2015. The trend tool classes this as stagnation: the ratio of observed to required progress is 0.09, so at the observed rate the group would still have an expected rate of 23.4% in 2030, against a target of zero. Lower middle income countries fared slightly better, falling from 9.7% to 8.3%, but the ratio of 0.21 places them in marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. The expected rate for 2030 is 7.7%.

The two richer groups moved the wrong way. High-income countries rose from 1.6% in 2015 to 2.5% in 2025, a ratio of -0.95, and upper middle income countries from 3.6% to 4.0%, a ratio of -0.17. Both are classed as regression. The levels are low, and the movement may reflect more than a real rise in exclusion. Changes in how enrolment is recorded, revisions to population estimates, and the handling of children still in pre-primary education, which the indicator counts as out of school, can all shift a small rate by a point or so. Migration and displacement, and the closures of 2020 followed by uneven returns to classrooms, are plausible pressures after the pandemic, though these are explanations the data do not test and cannot separate.

The country classes show that the pattern is general rather than the product of a few cases. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are in regression, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of the population, are on track or have met the target. A further 38 countries, with 24.2% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration, and 21 countries, with 6.1%, show marginal progress. Two countries, with 0.4%, are in stagnation. The large number of regressing countries is partly a statistical consequence of the target. When the goal is zero, any rise from a low base counts as regression, however small, so many countries with rates already near the floor are classed alongside those where exclusion is growing. Country counts and population shares therefore tell different stories: the regressing countries are the most numerous, and their 34.4% of the population is close to the 34.9% share that is on track or has met the target.

The target itself can be read in more than one way. Target 4.1 speaks of completion of free primary and secondary education, not of enrolment alone, and no tool here measures completion. A target of zero for the out-of-school rate is also stricter than the wording of the goal, which sets no numerical threshold. Read as a full elimination of exclusion, almost no group can reach it by 2030. Read as a substantial reduction, the lower middle income group has a path only with a marked change in pace, and low-income countries do not at present have one.

The reporting behind these findings is uneven. Coverage of the primary indicator reaches 197 countries, but only 178 could be assessed for trend, and the latest year, 2025, is for many countries an estimate rather than a survey result. The group levels rest on 12 reporting countries in 2025, a small base for four income groups. Where household surveys are infrequent, as in many fragile settings, changes of a point or two cannot be distinguished from noise. The classes should therefore be read as a guide to direction and scale, not as precise measurements for each country.

### Proposals for 2030 centre on data, low-income systems and adolescents

The final part of this section turns the findings into proposals, and begins with what they imply for 2030. The target, as written, is that all girls and boys complete primary and secondary education. The series on the shelf measures something narrower: enrolment at primary and lower secondary age. Reading the target as zero exclusion, which is how the trend tool reads it, no income group is close. The expected rate for 2030 is 23.4% in low-income countries and 7.7% in lower middle income countries. In upper middle income countries it is 4.2%, and in high-income countries 3.1%. Other readings of the target are possible, for example a tolerance for a small residual share, and the conclusion would change for the richer groups but not for the poorest.

The country classes show how widely the problem is spread. Of 178 countries assessed, 95 are classed as regressing, and they hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Only 22 countries, with 34.9% of that population, are on track or have met the target. The regression class is large partly because many countries start from low rates, where small rises in reporting or enrolment gaps register as movement away from zero. That is a reason to track these countries closely, not to dismiss the signal.

Adolescents show the highest observed rate. In low-income countries, 41.7% of lower secondary age adolescents were out of school in 2025, against 36.1% in 2015, while in upper middle income countries the rate moved from 5.7% to 5.9%. Only 12 countries reported the adolescent series in 2025, and the sex-disaggregated counts rest on 8, so these pictures rest on thin and uneven coverage and are indicative only. The primary and lower secondary series may also draw on different sets of countries, so a comparison across ages is a suggestion, not a finding. Fees, distance, early work and early marriage, and too few secondary places, are commonly offered as explanations for exclusion at these ages, but the data do not test these causes.

Four proposals follow. They aim at the groups where the rates are highest, and at the weaknesses of the evidence.

w-c05-6-3.text:
### Global literacy stands at 87.7 per cent among adults and 93.1 per cent among youth

Literacy, as the World Bank series defines it, is the share of people who can both read and write, with understanding, a short simple statement about their everyday life. Adults are those aged 15 and above; youth are those aged 15 to 24. The measure is a threshold of basic ability. It says nothing about fluency, about comprehension of complex texts, or about the skills needed to function in a digital economy.

On this measure the world is largely literate. The adult rate stood at 85.96 per cent in 2015 and reached 87.74 per cent in 2024. The youth rate rose from 91.4 per cent in 2015 to 93.11 per cent in 2024. Youth rates exceed adult rates in the world figures for both years. As context rather than a finding, this is consistent with younger cohorts having had more schooling than older adults, which would also lift the adult rate as cohorts replace one another; the results hold no schooling or cohort data to test that explanation.

Target 4.6 asks for more than the indicator can show. It commits countries to ensure that all youth and a substantial proportion of adults, men and women alike, achieve literacy and numeracy. The series held on the bench measures literacy only; it gives no figure for numeracy, so half of the target's wording cannot be assessed here. The phrase 'a substantial proportion of adults' also has no fixed threshold. It can be read as a majority, as most adults, or as a rate close to universal, and the reading chosen decides whether the world is already on course or far from it. For youth the wording is stricter: 'all' implies 100 per cent, and the 2024 figure of 93.11 per cent falls short of it.

The figures are global averages and conceal wide differences between regions and income groups, which the later parts of this section take up. They also rest on a limited number of surveys and censuses: only 29 countries reported an adult or youth value in 2024, so most of the figures for that year are not fresh national measurements. The results do not record how many of the aggregate values rest on earlier years or on modelled estimates, so the currency of the headline values cannot be stated precisely. The next part examines how far the headline values can be trusted given that coverage.

### Data coverage is thin and uneven, so the latest values are partly modelled or dated

Literacy data are reported by far fewer countries in any single year than the headline coverage suggests. Across all years, 155 countries have at least one adult literacy value and 160 have at least one youth value. Yet in any one year only a fraction report. Adult reporting ranged from 13 countries in 2003 to 56 in 2019, and youth reporting from 23 countries in 2003 to 62 in 2019. The latest year, 2024, holds only 29 countries in each series.

As general context, outside the results, literacy rates usually come from population censuses and household surveys, which arrive at intervals of several years rather than annually. A country then appears in the record in the year of an exercise and is absent in the years between. The counts are consistent with such a calendar: adult reporting climbed from 32 countries in 2008 to 48 in 2010 and 53 in 2011, then fell to 33 in 2013. Swings of this kind are better read as differences in which countries reported than as changes in literacy itself.

The period after 2015 shows the same unevenness. Adult reporting stood at 47 countries in 2015, reached 56 in 2019, then fell to 42 in 2020, the year the pandemic disrupted fieldwork in many places, as general context. Youth reporting went from 62 countries in 2019 to 43 in 2020. A partial recovery appeared in 2022, with 45 countries for adults and 58 for youth, before the counts dropped to 33 and 35 in 2023 and to 29 in both series in 2024.

The question of how current the data are can be answered only in part. The results show that 29 countries report a value for 2024 in each series, against 155 and 160 countries with a value in some year. They do not show how many of the remaining countries have a latest value from 2023, from 2019 or from an earlier year, nor the typical lag. The same holds for the aggregates: the world, regional and income-group values are labelled 2024 in most cases, but Europe and Central Asia is labelled 2023, North America 2022, and high income 2020 for adults and 2021 for youth. The results do not record whether any aggregate is observed, carried forward from an earlier survey or modelled, so the share of dated or modelled values is unknown. Surveys held late in the period are commonly published after a delay, so recent years may be filled in later, although the results do not show this directly.

Three cautions follow. First, regional and world values for recent years rest on few direct observations, and a country's latest value may be several years old even when labelled with a recent year. Second, year-on-year comparison is unreliable, because a change between two years may reflect a different set of countries or method rather than real movement. Third, the sparse high-income record, with a single adult value in 2020, means that the strongest literacy performers are the least visible. Comparisons are safer over longer spans, and the findings that follow are read with these limits in mind.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia hold the largest gaps, and women trail men

The widest gaps lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. In 2024 adult literacy in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 68.7 per cent and in South Asia at 78.2 per cent, against 96.6 per cent in East Asia and Pacific. Europe and Central Asia, at 98.8 per cent in 2023, and North America, at 98.8 per cent in 2022, sit close to the ceiling. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached 75.6 per cent in 2024. The adult figure covers everyone aged 15 and above, so it moves slowly. As outside context rather than a finding of these results, regions in which many older people never attended school carry that history in their totals.

The youth series shows a different and more encouraging pattern. South Asia's youth literacy rose from 89.6 per cent in 2015 to 96.9 per cent in 2024, the largest regional gain in the results. Whether schooling expansion explains the rise is not tested here; it is the usual context offered for such changes, and the results contain no schooling data. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 75.2 to 79.0 per cent over the same period, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 85.0 to 86.9 per cent. Youth literacy in East Asia and Pacific, at 99.1 per cent in 2024, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, at 98.7 per cent, has little room left to grow. By income group, low-income countries reached 75.4 per cent among youth in 2024 and 63.6 per cent among adults, while upper middle income countries stood at 99.3 and 96.2 per cent. Lower middle income countries recorded 92.0 per cent for youth and 78.3 per cent for adults.

Women trail men, and the shortfall is largest where overall literacy is lowest. Worldwide, adult female literacy was 84.6 per cent in 2024, below the adult total of 87.7 per cent. In Sub-Saharan Africa it was 62.7 per cent, in South Asia 71.6 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 67.4 per cent. In low-income countries it was 56.4 per cent. Adult female literacy in each of these groups was higher in 2024 than in 2015: Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 56.8 per cent, South Asia from 63.5 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 63.0 per cent, and low-income countries from 50.9 per cent. Starting levels were low.

The youth gender parity index, the ratio of female to male literacy, shows younger women closing the gap. It stood at 0.98 worldwide in 2024, up from 0.97 in 2015. South Asia rose from 0.96 to 0.99. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 0.90 to 0.94, and low-income countries from 0.87 to 0.93. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached only 0.92, up from 0.90, the lowest regional value in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America were at 1.00 in their latest years, as the index is reported to two decimals. Only 29 countries reported in 2024, so the latest regional values rest on a small and shifting set of observations, and part of any change may reflect which countries report. The results do not say how many of those values are modelled or carried forward, so that question stays open. Shifts after 2020 cannot be separated from this reporting pattern in these results.

### Progress is real but too slow to reach universal youth literacy by 2030, and the proposals follow

The trend-to-target results for youth literacy show progress that is real but, in every region except South Asia, too slow to reach the 2030 target on the current pace. South Asia is rated on track, but on a projection that exceeds the 100 per cent ceiling, so that rating is unreliable. The target value is 100.0 per cent, and the tool compares the observed pace since 2015 with the pace needed to reach it. The world as a whole is rated as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a ratio of 0.33 and an expected youth literacy rate of 94.3 per cent in 2030.

Even regions close to the ceiling are not rated as on track. East Asia and Pacific rose from 98.9 per cent in 2015 to 99.1 per cent in 2024 and is expected to reach 99.2 per cent in 2030, a ratio of 0.28 and a marginal rating. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 98.3 per cent to 98.7 per cent, with an expected 98.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.39. Europe and Central Asia is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.68 and an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030. High income is also moderate, with a ratio of 0.53 and an expected 99.6 per cent. North America is rated as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.07. Regions near the ceiling have little distance left to close, which is context rather than a finding, and the results give no measurement-error figure against which these small movements could be judged.

The larger shortfalls lie in regions where the starting level was lower. Low income is rated marginal and is expected to reach 77.9 per cent in 2030 on its current pace, with a ratio of 0.22. Sub-Saharan Africa is rated marginal, with an expected 81.6 per cent and a ratio of 0.26. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is rated marginal, with an expected 88.2 per cent and a ratio of 0.21. Lower middle income is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.63 and an expected 95.3 per cent. South Asia is the single region rated on track, with a ratio of 1.20. Its expected 2030 value is 102.1 per cent, which exceeds the 100 per cent ceiling and so cannot be a literal rate. The rating therefore rests on a projection that overshoots the ceiling, and on a regional value drawn from few reporting countries. South Asia's adult rate was 78.2 per cent in 2024, so the rating does not show that adult literacy is near universal.

These readings carry a caution about currency. In 2024 only 29 countries reported adult literacy and 29 reported youth literacy. The series does not record how many of the regional and world values rest on older surveys, carried-forward values or modelled estimates, so the number of dated values is unknown and cannot be stated from the results. Target 4.6 can also be read in more than one way: it asks for all youth but only a substantial proportion of adults, and it names numeracy, for which the series held here offers no measure. A projection to 100 per cent therefore addresses only part of the target. No trend-to-target result is held for adults, so the adult half of the target is left without a projected 2030 value; the adult levels, such as 87.7 per cent worldwide in 2024, show the distance but not the pace. On present evidence, every region except South Asia is rated marginal, moderate or stagnant, South Asia's on-track rating rests on a projection above 100 per cent, and no region is shown to reach universal youth literacy by 2030 on a sound projection.
