proposals: National statistical offices in countries without a recent literacy survey should run household surveys with a direct reading test, so that regional values rest on measured rather than carried-forward or modelled data.

The UNESCO Institute for Statistics and the World Bank should flag in the published series which values are modelled or dated, and cap projections at 100 per cent, so that ratings such as South Asia's are not read as proof of success.

Ministries of education and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income countries and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan should prioritise adult and youth literacy programmes, especially for women, since these groups are rated marginal for 2030.
Custodians of the indicator should add a numeracy measure to the target 4.6 series, so that the second half of the target can be tracked.
w-c05-6-3.gaps: The series does not record which values are modelled, carried forward or from surveys older than 2024, so the currency of the latest values cannot be counted. There is no numeracy measure, no adult trend-to-target result, no measurement-error figure, and country counts per year are small and change from year to year.

w-c08-2-3.text:
### Three-quarters of the world now cooks with clean fuels

Roughly three people in four now cook mainly with clean fuels and technologies. The World Bank's World Development Indicators put the share of the world's population with access at 63.9 per cent in 2015 and at 75.4 per cent in 2024. The series covers 192 countries in 2024. The indicator measures the proportion of the total population primarily using clean cooking fuels and technologies, such as electricity, gas, biogas and the cleanest stoves, as against open fires and stoves burning wood, charcoal, dung, crop residues or kerosene. Primary use is the test: a household that owns a gas ring but cooks mostly on firewood is not counted as having access.

The gain between 2015 and 2024 is real and large, but the figure carries a caveat. The series is modelled from household surveys and censuses, which are conducted at intervals of several years and are not available for every country in every year. Values for years between surveys, and the most recent years in particular, are estimates produced by statistical models rather than direct observations. The 2024 world value is therefore best read as a close approximation of the trend, and small year-to-year movements should not be treated as measured events. Nor does the indicator record how much of a household's cooking is done with clean fuels, how affordable the fuel is, or whether supply is reliable, all of which bear on the wording of target 7.1 on affordable and reliable modern energy services.

The remaining share matters because the other side of the figure is large. With 75.4 per cent having access in 2024, about one person in four still depends mainly on polluting fuels and technologies. As background outside the bench's data, smoke from such fuels is widely recognised as a cause of respiratory and cardiovascular illness, falling most heavily on women and young children, and the time spent gathering fuel and the burning of wood and charcoal are linked to schooling, paid work, forest loss and emissions. None of these links is measured in the results presented here.

The world's average conceals a wide spread between income groups, which later parts of the section take up. High-income countries stood at 98.8 per cent in 2015 and 99.5 per cent in 2024, so almost nothing remained to be gained there. Low-income countries rose only from 13.3 per cent to 15.6 per cent over the same years, while lower-middle-income countries rose from 42.7 per cent to 63.8 per cent and upper-middle-income countries from 76.9 per cent to 90.2 per cent. The global rise accompanies chiefly the middle-income groups, and the countries with the lowest access have moved the least.

For 2030, the reading is sobering. Target 7.1 calls for universal access to modern energy services, and the clean cooking series stands well short of that in 2024. The trend-to-target reading gives a world ratio of 0.56, with an expected value of 84.2 per cent in 2030, so the observed pace would not reach 100 per cent by then. The country classes show where the gap lies: 72 countries holding 61.5 per cent of the assessed population are on track or have met the target, while 46 countries with 14.9 per cent are making moderate progress, 39 with 13.8 per cent marginal progress, 29 with 8.3 per cent stagnation and 4 with 1.4 per cent regression. The point is examined further in the final part of the section.

### Regions diverge sharply, with Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Regional levels in 2024 span almost the whole range of the scale. North America stands at 100.0 per cent of the population with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking, and Europe and Central Asia at 98.3 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa stands at 22.9 per cent, up from 14.7 per cent in 2015. Fewer than one person in four in the region cooks mainly with clean fuels, while the world as a whole stands at 75.4 per cent. The income groups tell the same story: low-income economies stood at 15.6 per cent in 2024, against 99.5 per cent in high-income economies.

The regions between these poles moved at very different speeds after 2015. South Asia made the largest advance in the data, rising from 45.3 per cent to 74.3 per cent. East Asia and Pacific rose from 70.7 per cent to 87.0 per cent. Both regions are now close to or above the world level. Large national programmes to distribute gas connections and to substitute for solid fuels are well-established contributors to progress of this kind, though the indicator does not show what drove the change in any country. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 86.8 per cent to 90.5 per cent, a smaller gain from a higher base. Europe and Central Asia moved from 96.6 per cent to 98.3 per cent, as the last households switched.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved slowly, from 74.7 per cent to 77.8 per cent. The region began 2015 at a level near that of East Asia and Pacific, which has since moved well ahead. The grouping also mixes economies at very different incomes, so the regional figure conceals wide national differences that this indicator, taken at regional level, cannot display. In Sub-Saharan Africa the gain of 14.7 to 22.9 per cent is real but small against the size of the shortfall, and the region's pace needs to be read against continuing population growth, which the share alone does not capture.

The gap between rural and urban households explains much of the regional picture. Worldwide, rural access rose from 38.2 per cent in 2015 to 56.3 per cent in 2024, while urban access rose from 85.1 per cent to 89.4 per cent. Rural households therefore gained more in percentage points, yet remain far behind. Sub-Saharan Africa's rural level is the lowest in the data, at 8.6 per cent in 2024, up from 5.4 per cent in 2015. Urban Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.8 per cent, up from 29.5 per cent. Low-income economies show the same pattern, with rural access at 7.3 per cent and urban access at 31.5 per cent.

Elsewhere the contrast between rural and urban areas has narrowed. South Asia's rural level reached 61.7 per cent against an urban level of 92.0 per cent, and East Asia and Pacific's rural level reached 73.9 per cent against 94.6 per cent. In Europe and Central Asia the rural level is 95.2 per cent, and in North America 99.9 per cent. These differences matter for 2030. Where the remaining shortfall is concentrated in dispersed rural households, supply networks for fuel, stoves and finance are costlier to extend, and a regional average rising slowly leaves the poorest households for last. The data show levels and change, not the affordability of fuels, which the target also names and which the indicator does not measure.

### Gains were broad but the pace has not been steady

The global series has not risen at a steady pace. A break analysis of the annual change in the world share with access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking finds two breaks, in 2010 and in 2021. In the segment from 2001 to 2009 the mean annual change was 0.9 percentage points a year. In the segment from 2010 to 2020 it was 1.4 points a year. In the segment from 2021 to 2024 it was 1.0 point a year. Progress therefore quickened at the start of the 2010s and slowed after 2021. The 2010 break falls before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted, so the faster pace of the 2010s cannot be credited to the goals alone. The 2021 break coincides with the period after the pandemic shock of 2020, but the data show only when the pace changed, not why.

The slowdown matters for 2030. The latest segment, at 1.0 point a year from 2021 to 2024, is slightly faster than the first segment, at 0.9 points a year from 2001 to 2009, and slower than the segment from 2010 to 2020, at 1.4 points a year. The trend analysis shows that at the pace observed since 2015 the world share would reach 84.2 per cent in 2030, against a target of 100.0 per cent, with a ratio of 0.56 of the distance covered. The observed pace therefore does not reach universal access by 2030. The required annual pace is not computed here. Four years is a short window, and the 2021 break rests on few annual observations, so the estimate of its mean change is less secure than those of the longer segments. The break dates are statistical estimates and could shift with further data.

The second analysis asks whether countries drew together. Across 192 countries from 2015 to 2024, the slope of each country's annual change on its starting level is negative, at -0.0079 (p below 0.001). Countries that began with lower access therefore gained faster on average than countries that began higher, and levels moved closer. The coefficient of variation, which measures spread relative to the mean, fell from 0.57 in 2015 to 0.50 in 2024, which agrees with this reading.

The convergence is real but weak. The R2 of the regression is 0.14, so the starting level explains a small part of the variation in how fast countries gained. Many countries with similar starting points moved at very different speeds, and some low-access countries gained little. Part of the pattern is arithmetical: countries near full access have little room to rise, which pulls the slope below zero without implying that any catch-up mechanism is at work. The coefficient of variation still shows a spread that is wide, since a value near 0.50 means that the typical gap between countries remains about half the world mean.

The data do not show what drove the breaks or the uneven gains. Fuel prices, public programmes, supply chains and household incomes are commonly cited influences on the choice of cooking fuel, but none is measured in these results, and none is asserted here as the cause. The findings describe when and where access changed, and they leave open why.

### Universal access by 2030 will be missed without acceleration, and proposals follow

The trend-to-target reading sets each series against universal access, 100.0 per cent by 2030, and projects the compound annual rate observed since 2015. On that basis the world reaches an expected 84.2 per cent in 2030, from 75.4 per cent in 2024. The ratio of distance covered to distance required is 0.56, which the tool classes as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. The observed pace would therefore not reach 100.0 per cent by 2030 at the global level.

Regions differ in how near they are. East Asia and Pacific is classed as on track or target met, with an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.99. South Asia is also on track, with a ratio of 1.06, having risen from 45.3 per cent in 2015 to 74.3 per cent in 2024. Its expected value above 100 shows that the extrapolation is mechanical and cannot exceed the ceiling. Europe and Central Asia is classed as needing acceleration, with a ratio of 0.82 and an expected 99.4 per cent, a small gap in absolute terms because the region started near the top. Latin America and the Caribbean has a ratio of 0.47 and an expected 93.0 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan has a ratio of 0.20 and an expected 79.9 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.19 and an expected 30.9 per cent in 2030. Both of the last two are classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed.

By income group, upper middle income countries are on track with a ratio of 1.01, and high income countries are on track at 99.5 per cent in 2024. Lower middle income countries need acceleration, with a ratio of 0.71 and an expected 83.4 per cent. Low income countries are classed as stagnant, with a ratio of 0.05: the share moved from 13.3 per cent in 2015 to 15.6 per cent in 2024, and the expected value for 2030 is 17.4 per cent. The ratio reflects the distance still to be covered, so regions starting from a low base are penalised heavily even when their annual rate is high. Sub-Saharan Africa's rate of 0.051 is close to South Asia's 0.057, yet its starting point leaves it far from the target.

Country classes show how widely the gap is spread. Of 190 countries assessed, 72 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 61.5 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 46 countries, with 14.9 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 39 countries, with 13.8 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Twenty-nine countries, with 8.3 per cent, are stagnant, and 4 countries, with 1.4 per cent, have regressed. The classes are produced by a rule applied to each series, and they say nothing about what drives a country's change.

Two cautions apply. Target 7.1 speaks of universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services, and the text does not fix a numerical threshold for cooking. Reading it as exactly 100 per cent is the strictest reading; a reading of near-universal access would count more countries as having met it. The indicator also measures only the primary fuel or technology a household uses. It does not measure affordability or reliability of supply. The rural series shows the same pattern in sharper form: 8.6 per cent of rural people in Sub-Saharan Africa had access in 2024, against 56.3 per cent of rural people worldwide.

For 2030, the country classes show where the shortfall lies by population. The countries classed as marginal, stagnant or regressing hold 13.8, 8.3 and 1.4 per cent of the assessed population, and the 46 moderate-progress countries hold 14.9 per cent, so the unmet gap is spread across several classes and not confined to the weakest. The remoteness of rural households is often cited as a reason for the lowest levels, but this is unmeasured context that the bench's data do not test.

w-c09-2-4.text:
### World output per worker has risen by a fifth since 2015

Output per worker is the measure the bench uses for target 8.2, which asks for higher levels of economic productivity. GDP per person employed, expressed in constant 2021 purchasing power parity dollars, stood at 42,386 in 2015 and reached 50,672 in 2025. The trend tool puts the compound rate at 1.8 per cent a year over the decade and reads this pace as moderate progress, but with acceleration needed. The world figure has therefore risen by roughly a fifth, a description drawn from the two cited levels rather than from a separate result.

The result matters because productivity is the main route by which employment translates into rising living standards. An economy can raise total output by adding workers, but only gains in output per worker allow wages and public revenue to grow without more labour being drawn in. A global rate of 1.8 per cent a year is positive and sustained, yet it is a pace that would double output per worker only over roughly four decades. The target's call for diversification, technological upgrading and innovation implies a faster and broader movement than this average suggests.

The indicator has no numeric target. Target 8.2 says only that productivity should be higher, so the reading rests on direction and pace rather than a threshold. Any classification of progress, including the one used here, depends on a rule applied by the tool to the observed rate of change, and a different rule would give a different label. The finding that the world has moved in the right direction is firm; the finding that the pace is moderate is a judgement about what pace would suffice.

The period contains breaks. The break tool dates shifts in the annual change of the world series to 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The mean annual change was 967.5 dollars a year across 2010 to 2019, fell to a loss of 369.1 dollars in 2020, rebounded to a gain of 1,566.8 dollars in 2021, and averaged 815.5 dollars a year across 2022 to 2025. Because output per worker is a ratio, a shock can move it in either direction: when low-productivity jobs are lost first, the ratio can rise even as total output falls. The ten-year change reported here therefore compresses a path that was neither smooth nor driven by a single cause, and the endpoints alone do not separate lasting gains from statistical effects of the shock. Weak investment and slow trade expansion in many economies after 2015 are well-known context, though not tested here.

The limits of the series should be stated plainly. Output per worker divides GDP by total employment, so it inherits the weaknesses of both. Employment estimates in many countries rest on modelled values rather than regular labour force surveys, and informal work is imperfectly captured. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, fewer than the 177 of earlier years, so the latest values rest on a smaller set of economies and the world aggregate for 2025 is partly an estimate. Comparisons across years should be read with that in mind.

For 2030, the recent post-2022 pace of change is below the 2010 to 2019 average, so a rate of about 1.8 per cent a year is not assured. Even if it holds, the global average would rest on very uneven foundations. The sections that follow show that the world figure conceals regions where output per worker has risen quickly and others where it has fallen.

### Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker

Regional output per worker in 2025 ranges from 12,931 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa to 152,091 dollars in North America, a spread of roughly twelve times between regions. In 2025 a worker in North America produced 152,091 dollars of GDP (constant 2021 PPP), and one in Europe and Central Asia produced 103,033 dollars. South Asia stood at 24,604 dollars. The low-income group, which is an income grouping and not a region, stood at 6,041 dollars, so that the gap between North America and that group is wider still, at roughly twenty-five times. The two richest regions are close to each other by comparison. Differences of this size are commonly attributed to capital per worker, the sectoral mix of employment, the quality of institutions and the technology in use. None of these is tested here, since the bench holds no series on them for this section.

Growth since 2015 has not been even. East Asia and Pacific rose from 33,564 dollars to 49,219 dollars, a rate of 3.9 per cent a year, and the trend tool classes it as on track. South Asia rose from 17,922 dollars to 24,604 dollars, at 3.2 per cent a year, also classed on track. Shifts of labour from farming to manufacturing and services, with sustained investment, are the usual route to such gains and match what target 8.2 describes through diversification and technological upgrading, although this section does not test that explanation. East Asia and Pacific now stands close to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, which reached 50,325 dollars in 2025, up from 46,188 dollars in 2015, a pace of 0.9 per cent a year that is classed as marginal progress.

The richer regions advanced at a moderate pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 88,803 dollars to 103,033 dollars, at 1.5 per cent a year. North America rose from 132,207 dollars to 152,091 dollars, at 1.4 per cent a year. Both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Because these gains start from very high levels, a modest rate adds a large absolute amount per worker. Comparing the levels given, each of these regions added more dollars per worker than South Asia did, even though South Asia grew faster in proportion. Growth rates may therefore favour poorer regions while absolute gaps persist or widen.

Two regions stand apart for lack of progress. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 42,759 dollars to 43,303 dollars, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 13,373 dollars to 12,931 dollars, a rate of minus 0.3 per cent a year, classed as regression, and the low-income group fell from 6,401 dollars to 6,041 dollars. Possible explanations, offered as context and not tested here, include weak investment, large informal sectors and commodity dependence in Latin America, and rapid growth of a young workforce entering low-productivity work in Sub-Saharan Africa. No employment or sector result in this section confirms them.

For 2030 the implication is that no common regional pace can be assumed. Regions already growing at three per cent a year or more can keep climbing, while the two regions with stagnant or falling output per worker fall further behind the others. The target sets no numerical threshold, so classifications such as on track rest on the bench's reading of a rising trend, and a different reading would change them.

### Country outcomes split between rapid gains and decline

Beyond the world average, the bench classifies each of the 177 countries with data by the pace of its output per worker. Because target 8.2 carries no numeric threshold, the classes rest on a model-based reading of each country's trend towards 2030, and the labels should be taken as relative judgements rather than findings against a legal standard.

The result is a split. A total of 48 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 52.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. At the other end, 46 countries are in regression, meaning that output per worker has fallen over the period, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population. Between the two lie 30 countries with moderate progress that needs acceleration, 34 with marginal progress that needs significant acceleration, and 19 in stagnation. Their population shares are 17.0 per cent, 7.4 per cent and 8.1 per cent respectively.

The gap between the count of countries and the share of people is the main interpretive point. Counted by country, 48 of 177 are on track, a little over a quarter. Counted by population, the on-track group holds just over half. The tool does not say which countries drive that share, but it is consistent with populous economies, long associated with labour moving from farming into industry and services, sitting in the on-track class. A reader should therefore not conclude that most countries are advancing: by number, those regressing, 46, nearly match those on track, 48.

Regression is the most troubling class, since it means that workers in these 46 countries produce less than before. Conflict and state fragility, commodity price collapses, macroeconomic crises and, after 2020, lasting pandemic disruption are well-established causes of such declines in general. They are context only: no result here tests which applies to which country. Stagnation, in 19 countries, points to economies where output per worker has barely moved, a pattern often linked to stalled structural change, again untested here.

The classification also depends on choices that could be made differently. Without a numeric target, a different benchmark, such as a rate needed to halve a gap with richer economies, would move countries between classes. Employment estimates, which underlie the denominator, are modelled for many countries, so countries near class boundaries may be misplaced. For 2030, the implication is that the world average conceals a divergence: a group holding 52.9 per cent of the assessed population is advancing, while 46 countries are losing ground and will need a change of course, not just faster growth, to reach higher productivity by the end of the decade.

### Inequality between countries has narrowed, but convergence is weak

The spread of output per worker among countries has narrowed over the decade. Weighting each country by its population, the Gini coefficient of GDP per person employed fell from 0.449 in 2015 to 0.427 in 2020 and 0.412 in 2025. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the top and bottom of the distribution, fell from 0.347 to 0.308 and then to 0.286. Both measures point the same way. The fall was somewhat larger in the first five years than in the second, although the 2025 figures cover 168 countries against 177 earlier, so part of the comparison rests on a changed set of countries.

The narrowing is not matched by catch-up among countries as such. The convergence test regresses each country's annual change in output per worker over 2015 to 2025 on its starting level. If poorer countries were closing the gap, the coefficient would be clearly negative. It is -0.00249, with a p-value of 0.0541, so it falls just short of the conventional 5 per cent threshold, and the R2 is 0.013, meaning that the starting level explains about 1.3 per cent of the variation across the 168 countries. The unweighted coefficient of variation, which treats every country alike, moved only from 0.893 to 0.876 on this common set. The population-weighted measures fell by a larger proportion than the unweighted one. That pattern is consistent with the improvement coming mainly from where large economies stood, not from a general closing of the gap by small and poor ones, although the tools used here do not identify which countries drove it. Fast growth in a few populous economies lowers a population-weighted index even when most countries stay where they were relative to the rest.

The decomposition by region adds to this reading. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions rose from 68.3 per cent in 2015 to 71.9 per cent in 2020 and 75.2 per cent in 2025. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the remaining inequality, and the divide that persists is increasingly one between world regions. This fits the regional levels described earlier in the section, where the lowest-income groups remain a small fraction of the output per worker of the richest.

The period saw two shocks, and they affect how the figures should be read. The pandemic of 2020 cut output in many economies, including some of the richest, and a temporary fall at the top can lower measured inequality without any gain for poorer workers. The lower Gini and Theil values of 2025 show that the earlier narrowing has held rather than reversed. Even so, a weak and statistically marginal convergence coefficient gives little ground to expect that gaps between countries will close by 2030 on present trends. Target 8.2 sets no numeric threshold, and it can be read either as higher productivity everywhere or as faster productivity gains where levels are lowest. On the first reading, the world has made progress. On the second, the evidence is thin, and the narrowing seen in the weighted indices should not be mistaken for it.

### Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals

Breaks in the world series date the pace changes around 2009, 2020 and 2022, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals. The break analysis covers the world series alone, with no regional breaks tested, and its earliest segment begins in 2001. It finds change points in 2004, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. Between 2004 and 2008, output per worker rose by a mean of 1,001.2 dollars a year (constant 2021 PPP). In 2009 the mean annual change was -404.0 dollars, a year that coincides with the global financial crisis. From 2010 to 2019 gains resumed at a mean of 967.5 dollars a year, close to the 2004 to 2008 mean and not above it. There was therefore no acceleration in the dollar gain per year across that period. Because this span runs on both sides of the adoption of the Goals in 2015, it does not describe the years before them alone.

The pandemic year shows a similar pattern on a comparable scale. In 2020 the mean annual change was -369.1 dollars, and in 2021 it was 1,566.8 dollars. Part of the rebound may be a recovery of what was lost, and part may reflect the composition of employment: when low-productivity jobs disappear in a downturn, output per remaining worker can rise even where output is falling. This explanation is context and was not tested here. The link of the breaks to the crisis and the pandemic is likewise context, since the tool dates changes without attributing them. From 2022 to 2025 the mean annual gain was 815.5 dollars, below the 2010 to 2019 mean of 967.5 dollars. The recovery has thus not restored the earlier dollar gain. This suggests, without establishing, that the compound rate of 1.8 per cent a year, measured over 2015 to 2025, may not hold to 2030. The trend tool reads that rate as moderate progress, with acceleration needed.

The link between productivity and headline growth is weak. Across 168 countries for 2015 to 2025, the Spearman correlation between changes in output per worker and GDP growth is -0.048, effectively no relation. For 2025 levels the coefficient is -0.413, a moderate negative association: countries with lower output per worker tend to record higher growth rates. This is consistent with catch-up from a low base, but also with growth that comes from adding workers or hours rather than raising output per worker. Rank correlations say nothing of cause.

The country classification shows why the outlook for 2030 is uneven. Of 177 countries assessed, 46 are in regression, holding 14.6 per cent of the population assessed, while 19 are stagnating. Among regions, Sub-Saharan Africa shows falling output per worker at an annual rate of -0.3 per cent, and so does the low-income group, an income grouping and not a region, at -0.6 per cent. South Asia, at 3.2 per cent, is on track. The cause of the decline is not shown by these results and would need employment and sector series. Target 8.2 has no numeric threshold, so these classes are relative readings and not findings against a fixed standard. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, against 177 earlier.

Three proposals follow. Finance ministries and development banks in low-income and Sub-Saharan African countries, with their partners, should direct investment towards raising output per worker, since both groups show falling levels while the world average rises. National statistical offices and the World Bank should publish employment by sector and close the reporting gap between 168 and 177 countries, so that the causes of decline can be tested. The United Nations Statistical Commission should agree a numeric threshold for target 8.2, so that progress can be judged against a fixed standard.

w-c09-3-4.text:
### Vulnerable employment is the measured proxy for informality

Informal employment, the condition target 8.3 has in view, is not measured directly by any series on the shelf. The nearest measured proxy is vulnerable employment: the sum of own-account workers and contributing family workers, expressed as a percentage of total employment. The series is a modeled estimate of the International Labour Organization, and it is available for 187 economies, with 182 countries reporting in 2025. The proxy is imperfect. Some own-account workers are registered, taxed and covered by social protection, while some wage jobs are informal, with no contract and no insurance. The share of vulnerable employment therefore indicates the extent of weak job security and thin social protection, and it cannot be read as a count of informal jobs.

A second caution concerns the target itself. Target 8.3 asks for policies that encourage the formalization and growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises, but it names no numeric threshold and no year-specific level. Any statement of progress is thus a reading of direction: whether the share falls, stays flat or rises. The trend tool applies a decreasing direction by 2030 with no fixed goal, and its verdicts should be understood in that light. A different reader might judge the same movement more or less favourably.

At world level, vulnerable employment stood at 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 and at 42.4 per cent in 2025. The fall is about 0.7 percentage points over a decade. Roughly two in five workers worldwide therefore remain in own-account or contributing family work, a share that has barely moved across a period that included the adoption of the goals and the shock of 2020. The trend tool classes the world movement as stagnation, with an annual rate of change of -0.0017 on its scale.

This matters because the world figure conceals very different realities, taken up in the parts that follow. It also matters because vulnerable work is the form of employment least likely to carry a stable wage, a contract or a pension. A global share that has hardly shifted suggests that the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not, on the whole, been converted into a move towards paid employment with protection. The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring in many low-income economies probably weighed on the decade, although the series, being modeled, cannot show the timing of such effects with precision.

### Regions differ by a factor of sixteen

In 2025 the regional range in vulnerable employment is wide. South Asia stands at 69.7 per cent of total employment and Sub-Saharan Africa at 71.0 per cent. North America stands at 4.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 12.9 per cent. The highest regional figure is therefore about sixteen times the lowest (71.0 against 4.5). Two regions, both in the developing world, have roughly seven in ten workers in own-account or contributing family work. In North America the figure is below one in twenty.

The middle group lies between these poles and is more tightly bunched. East Asia and Pacific stands at 35.3 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 36.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 31.5 per cent. In each of these regions roughly one worker in three is in vulnerable employment, although their economic structures, institutions and histories are quite unlike. A region-wide average also conceals differences among countries, and the regional figures are population-weighted aggregates of modeled estimates, not direct counts.

The pattern follows the structure of production, as context rather than a result of this analysis. Where agriculture and small household enterprise employ most people and large firms offering wage contracts are few, own-account work and unpaid family work are the usual forms of employment. Where manufacturing and services are organised in larger firms and wage employment is the norm, the share is small. The income groups show the same ordering: low-income economies stand at 76.1 per cent in 2025 and high-income economies at 8.0 per cent, so income level and the share of vulnerable work move together.

The spread across countries confirms that region is the main divide: 71.9 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2025 lies between regions, and the rest within them. This shows that most of the cross-country inequality in the indicator is a difference between regional means. It does not show how many countries or workers account for the vulnerable total, and it says nothing about variation within any one region.

### Women carry more vulnerability where it is highest

In 2025 the world figure for women stands at 43.1 per cent of female employment, against 41.9 per cent of male employment for men. The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point. It conceals a division by region. Where vulnerable employment is most widespread, women are more exposed than men. Where it is rare, the order reverses.

The gap is widest in South Asia, where 76.2 per cent of employed women are in vulnerable jobs against 67.1 per cent of employed men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the figures are 79.2 per cent for women and 63.9 per cent for men, a difference of more than fifteen points. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the shares are 41.6 per cent and 34.7 per cent. These are the regions in which a large part of women's work is unpaid help in a family farm or business, or own-account activity in small trade and agriculture, with little social protection. Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work, since it can be combined with household duties.

The pattern runs the other way in the richest regions. In Europe and Central Asia the female share is 11.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent for men, and in North America 3.3 per cent against 5.4 per cent. High income economies show 6.9 per cent for women and 9.0 per cent for men. Men are more often self-employed in these economies, in trades, construction and freelance work, while women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts in services, health and education. A lower share of vulnerable employment among women here is not by itself a sign of advantage, since the series does not capture pay, hours or the quality of wage jobs.

By income group the same crossing appears. In low income countries the female share is 82.9 per cent and the male share 70.9 per cent. In lower middle income countries the figures are 74.0 per cent and 61.2 per cent. In upper middle income countries the gap narrows to 35.6 per cent against 34.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is close to parity, at 31.3 per cent for women and 31.6 per cent for men. The gender gap in vulnerability is thus largest in the poorest settings and closes as incomes rise, which bears directly on the inclusive aim of target 8.3.

### Change has been slow, uneven and not convergent

Across the 187 countries assessed, the trend to 2030 is mostly one of slow or absent progress. Only 24 countries, holding 3.7 per cent of the population of the group, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 19 countries, with 6.1 per cent of the population, show moderate progress that would need acceleration. The largest population weight lies in the 48 countries with marginal progress, which hold 51.7 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. Another 59 countries stagnate, with 25.0 per cent of the population, and 37 regress, with 13.5 per cent. Target 8.3 sets no numerical threshold, so the classes measure movement in the desired direction (a decrease) and not distance from an agreed goal; the reading is one of direction only.

The weight of population in the slower classes matters more than the count of countries. Large economies with high shares of own-account and family work move slowly, so the world average is determined by them, while many small and wealthy economies that were already low account for most of the on-track count. Progress that does occur is therefore concentrated where the problem was already smaller.

Between-country inequality in the indicator did not narrow. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.317 in 2015 across 187 countries and 0.320 in 2025 across 182. The Theil index moved from 0.178 to 0.182. The share of that inequality lying between regions, and not within them, stayed near 71 per cent: 70.8 per cent in 2015 and 71.9 per cent in 2025. The geography of vulnerability is thus still mainly a matter of which region a worker lives in. The change in country coverage, from 187 to 182, is small and does not alter the reading.

The convergence test points the same way. The coefficient on initial levels is slightly negative (beta -0.00281, p-value 0.0001), so countries with higher initial shares fell marginally faster, but the fit is weak, with an R-squared of 0.066 across 182 countries. Meanwhile the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.717 to 0.735, meaning that dispersion between countries grew. A weak tendency towards catching up coexists with a widening spread, which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved. Neither the post-2015 nor the post-2020 period can be separated by these summary measures, and the shock of 2020 is not isolated here.

Wage and salaried employment is the mirror of vulnerable employment. The rank correlation of 2025 levels is -0.994, and that of changes since 2015 is -0.920, across 182 countries. Because the two shares are close to complements, with employers forming a small remainder, this is largely definitional and gives no independent evidence that wage growth causes lower vulnerability. It does show that a fall in vulnerable work has meant a rise in paid employment, and not a shift towards other forms of work.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace of 2015 to 2025 the world would not reach a markedly lower share of vulnerable employment by 2030. The trend tool classes the world as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0017 a year, from 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 to 42.4 per cent in 2025. The calculation extends the recent line and is not a forecast. Target 8.3 sets no number for vulnerable employment, so the reading of 'on track' is the tool's: any decrease counts as movement in the right direction. Measured against the wider aim of decent work, the pace is insufficient.

Across the 187 countries assessed, 48 countries with marginal progress hold 51.7 per cent of the population of the group, and 59 countries classed as stagnating hold a further 25.0 per cent. The 37 countries classed as regressing hold 13.5 per cent. The regional trend tool gives South Asia a rate of -0.0074 a year and East Asia and Pacific a rate of -0.0074, and classes both as marginal progress. Sub-Saharan Africa has a rate of -0.0007 and is classed as stagnating. Low income countries have a rate of 0.0000 (+0.00003 a year), which is effectively flat; the tool labels the group regression, a label that rests on the sign of a very small rate and should be read as no movement. Faster movement in the regions with the highest shares would count for more than gains in Europe and Central Asia (-0.0137) or among high income countries (-0.0127), where the share is already low.

The cross-country picture shows no clear convergence. The convergence slope is negative (-0.0028), so countries that started with higher shares fell slightly faster, or rose less, each year. The fit is weak (R-squared 0.07), and the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.73 in 2025, so dispersion in relative terms widened. The tests do not show which end of the distribution drove that widening. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini was 0.32 in both 2015 and 2025, and 71.9 per cent of the Theil measure in 2025 lies between regions. Most of the inequality in vulnerable employment is therefore a difference between regions, not within them.

The link between vulnerable employment and wage employment is close: across 182 countries the Spearman correlation of 2025 levels is -0.99, and of changes since 2015 it is -0.92. This is an association, not a cause, but the two series largely mirror one another. It is consistent with a route to lower vulnerability that runs through paid jobs and firms able to employ. Whether output growth or the pandemic shaped these movements is not tested by any series used here.

Five proposals follow. The International Labour Organization and national statistical offices should monitor informal employment directly alongside the modeled proxy, using labour force surveys. Governments should set a quantified national reading of target 8.3, stating the share of vulnerable or informal work to be reached by 2030. Ministries of labour and of industry in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where shares stood at 69.7 and 71.0 per cent in 2025, should prioritise wage job creation and the formalisation of micro and small enterprises, with access to finance and simpler registration. National planners should give women's vulnerability its own targets, since women are more exposed where the share is highest. Statistical agencies and the ILO should report data gaps openly, including the modeled status of many national figures.

w-c09-6-2.text:
### The world share fell by 1.4 points, from a 2015 base, not by a substantial margin

Target 8.6 asks for a substantial reduction in the proportion of youth not in employment, education or training by 2020. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so any verdict rests on a reading chosen by the analyst. Here the reading is plain: a substantial reduction would be a fall large enough to be visible against the starting level and to change the position of most regions.

On that reading, the world record is modest. The modelled ILO estimate puts the global share at 21.2 per cent of the youth population in 2015 and at 19.8 per cent in 2025. The share therefore declined over the decade, but by a margin of well under a tenth of the 2015 level in relative terms, and the latest year available is five years after the target date. The series is a modelled estimate, not a count from a single survey. Countries with sparse labour force data receive values built from regional patterns and covariates, so small movements in the world figure should be read with caution. The estimate covers 182 countries reporting in 2025.

The pace of change did not follow a steady path. The break analysis of the annual change in the world share finds shifts in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by about 0.2 points a year on average. Between 2013 and 2019 the mean annual change was close to zero, at 0.02 points, which means that the share was essentially flat in the years just before the target date. The first five years after 2015 therefore delivered almost no reduction, and the decline recorded by 2025 was produced mainly after the pandemic year, a pattern taken up in a later part.

The income groups show why the global figure hides unequal movement. In high-income countries the share moved from 12.2 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025, and in upper middle income countries from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent. Lower middle income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The global average is thus pulled down by the middle-income and wealthier groups, while the poorest countries ended the period with a higher share than they began with.

Taken together, these results do not support a claim of substantial reduction by 2020. The 2015 base fell by a small amount over ten years, was flat before 2020, and rose in the poorest countries. Whether a stricter or looser reading of 'substantially' would change the verdict is a question the target text leaves open, but no plausible reading treats a decline of this size, reached five years late, as meeting the intent of the goal.

### Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden

Regional levels in 2025 range widely. North America holds the lowest share, at 11.8 per cent of youth, down from 12.5 per cent in 2015. East Asia and Pacific stands at 12.8 per cent, down from 14.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 13.0 per cent, down from 15.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is at 19.3 per cent, from 21.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is at 21.4 per cent, slightly above its 2015 level of 20.9 per cent. South Asia shows the largest fall among the regions, from 28.4 per cent to 23.4 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is highest at 32.1 per cent, and its share rose from 31.1 per cent. The regional picture therefore runs in two directions: most regions moved down modestly, while two did not.

Income groups show the same split. Low-income countries rose from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent, while lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent, and high-income countries from 12.2 per cent to 10.9 per cent. The poorest group is thus the one in which the share grew, and by 2025 it stands well above the others. Demographic pressure, thin labour demand and limited schooling places are well-established contexts for this pattern in low-income settings, though the series itself does not show what drives it.

Women carry the largest burden. The world female share was 30.2 per cent in 2015 and 27.1 per cent in 2025, far above the total of 19.8 per cent. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the female share was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged, so nearly half of young women are outside work and study. South Asia improved from 46.0 per cent to 37.1 per cent, yet remains high. Low-income countries moved against the trend, from 32.6 per cent to 34.4 per cent. Norms on care work and early marriage, and limits on women's mobility and employment, are the usual explanations, stated here as context only.

Among countries, the classes of the trend assessment are scattered. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the direction of the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 28 show moderate progress and 29 marginal progress, while 21 stagnate and 58 regress. The regressing group holds 18.8 per cent of the population, more than the on-track group. No numeric target exists, so the classes rest on the analyst's reading of the trend, and they should be read as direction rather than as a verdict.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, did not narrow. The Gini coefficient was 0.231 in 2015, 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for a little over half of the inequality in both years. Convergence is not shown: the beta of -0.00428 has a p-value of 0.214, not distinguishable from zero. Countries starting higher did not reliably improve faster.

### The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement

The movement of the world share is better read as a sequence of breaks in timing than as a steady trend. The break analysis of the annual change in the modelled ILO series finds breaks in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by a mean of 0.22 points a year. That is the only stretch in which the decline looks like steady progress, and it ended before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.

From 2013 to 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which is near stagnation. The share did not fall in the years when the target's clock was running towards 2020. In 2020 the annual change jumped by 1.37 points, the largest movement in the series. The timing coincides with the closure of schools and workplaces during the pandemic. That link is context drawn from well-established knowledge; the data show when the break occurred and do not test its cause. The results cited here do not give the world level for 2020, so the change from 2015 to 2020 is not stated; the 2013 to 2019 mean and the 2020 jump are the evidence on the target year.

The fall that followed was nearly as sharp. From 2021 to 2023 the share fell by a mean of 1.08 points a year, which took back much of the 2020 rise. From 2024 to 2025 the share rose again by a mean of 0.15 points a year, reversing part of the post-2020 decline. The long-run rate of change for the world, at -0.0070 on the trend tool's scale, is read by that tool as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. These classes are the tool's own categories, applied without a numeric target, and a series that rises and falls around 2020 gives a weak basis for expecting steady gains.

Sub-Saharan Africa followed a different path. Its breaks fall in 2014, 2021, 2023 and 2024. From 2006 to 2013 its mean annual change was -0.04 points. From 2014 to 2020 it rose by 0.45 points a year; that window includes the 2020 break, so the rise cannot be assigned wholly to the period before the pandemic, and no world mean for the same window is cited for comparison. A young population growing faster than jobs and school places is a common explanation, but the data do not test it. After 2020 the region eased, with a change of -0.29 points a year in 2021 and 2022 and -1.23 points in 2023, then 0.00 points a year in 2024 and 2025. The trend tool still classes the region as regression to 2030.

The breaks therefore show large swings around 2020, set against a world share that was already flat from 2013 to 2019. The fall of 2021 to 2023 is consistent with a position restored rather than advanced, though the data do not isolate the cause.

### The 2020 target was missed, and 2030 needs faster progress and a clearer definition

The target was not met in a substantial sense by 2020, and the trend to 2030 does not close the gap. The reading used here is the analyst's own, since the target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially'. The trend tool assigns its own classes, and its target is given as none, so the classes describe the direction and pace of change, not distance from a stated goal. The world is classed as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a compound annual rate of -0.7 per cent from the 2015 baseline. East Asia and Pacific stands at -1.2 per cent a year and High income at -1.2 per cent, both marginal. Latin America and the Caribbean is at -0.9 per cent, and North America at -0.6 per cent. Only Europe and Central Asia, at -1.6 per cent, and South Asia, at -1.9 per cent, reach the moderate class, and both still need acceleration.

Three groups are classed as regression: Low income, with a rate of 0.9 per cent a year, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, at 0.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.2 per cent. The country count rests on 187 countries assessed by the trend tool, whereas the levels and spread measures for 2025 rest on 182 countries reporting that year. Of the 187, 51 are on track or have met the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the assessed population. A further 28 show moderate progress, 29 marginal progress and 21 stagnation. Regression affects 58 countries, holding 18.8 per cent of the population. The largest population share, 32.1 per cent, sits in the marginal class.

The gender gap sharpens the picture. Among young women the world share fell from 30.2 per cent in 2015 to 27.1 per cent in 2025, a level above the 19.8 per cent for all youth in 2025. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan it was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged. South Asia fell from 46.0 to 37.1 per cent, a real gain from a very high base. Low income rose from 32.6 to 34.4 per cent.

Countries have not drawn together. Population-weighted Gini across countries rose from 0.231 in 2015 to 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025, and Theil's T from 0.088 to 0.096 and then 0.100. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015, 60.3 per cent in 2020 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for more than half of the inequality throughout. The convergence test gives a beta of -0.0043 with a p-value of 0.214, which cannot be told from zero, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.471 to 0.532 across 182 countries.

For 2030 the implication is that the present pace leaves the world far from any reading of substantial reduction on the reading used here. The estimates are modelled, and survey coverage behind them is thin in several low-income countries, so classes for individual countries carry uncertainty.

Several proposals follow. National statistical offices in low-income countries should run labour force surveys at least every two years, so that modelled estimates rest on measured data. Ministries of labour and education in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region should set targets for young women's transition into work or study, since their share has barely moved. The UN Statistical Commission should adopt a numeric reading of 'substantially' for target 8.6, so that future verdicts do not depend on an analyst's choice.

w-c09-10-2.text:
### Net official assistance reached US$259 billion in 2023, an imperfect proxy for Aid for Trade

The question asks how much official assistance supports trade capacity. The bench cannot answer it directly. Target 8.a calls for more Aid for Trade for developing countries, the least developed above all, including through the Enhanced Integrated Framework, but the shelf holds no Aid for Trade commitments or disbursements. It also holds no least-developed-country breakdown and no Enhanced Integrated Framework record, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The series available is net official development assistance received, which counts concessional loans, net of repayments, and grants for every purpose. It can serve only as an upper bound on the resources from which trade capacity support could be drawn, not as an estimate of that support.

Read at that level, the world total rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US$. Constant prices remove general price changes, so the rise is real. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts, so some recipients lack a figure for the latest year and any total should be read with that gap in mind. The nearest available reading for poorer recipients is by income group: low-income economies received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015. That is not a least-developed-country figure, because the groups do not coincide.

The target sets no numeric threshold and no end level. The trend tool was therefore run on direction alone, with no numeric target: a series is classed as on track when it rises at a meaningful rate, and as stagnating or marginal when it does not. On that reading the world is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.0545. The label is weak evidence. A rising total of general assistance does not show that trade capacity support has grown, that it has gone to the least developed countries, or that it has been effective. Increases may reflect emergency, humanitarian or other spending unrelated to trade.

The point matters for 2030 because the target can be read in more than one way: as a rise in the volume of Aid for Trade, as a rise in its share of assistance, or as improved support to least developed countries specifically. The bench can speak only to the first, and only through a proxy. The parts that follow take the proxy as given, examine how it differs among regions and income groups, and show what changed after 2015 and after 2020, while keeping the limits of the measure in view. In short, the amount supporting trade capacity is not measured here; US$259.5 billion in 2023 is a ceiling on the proxy, not a finding about trade.

### Assistance rose unevenly across regions and concentrated among fewer recipients

Regional totals diverged sharply between 2015 and 2023, measured in constant 2023 US dollars. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest change, from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. The trend tool classes the region as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.213. Established knowledge of the period suggests that the displacement and reconstruction needs created by war in Europe explain part of this, though the series does not show what drove the change. No target level is set in the tool, so the classification reads only the direction of travel.

Other regions moved far less. East Asia and Pacific rose from US$9.9 billion to US$10.7 billion, with a rate of 0.010, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, a rate of 0.002, classed as stagnation. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion and is classed as on track, at a rate of 0.028. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Sub-Saharan Africa remains the largest regional recipient, at US$64.8 billion in 2023, up from US$51.8 billion in 2015. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region without recipients in this series.

The pattern matters for Aid for Trade because a rise in the world total, from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, says little about where trade capacity is being built. Regions with flat inflows in real terms face rising trade-support needs without a matching rise in assistance, while this series cannot show how much of any inflow reaches trade purposes.

The spread among countries widened. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received was 0.361 in 2015, 0.370 in 2019 and 0.452 in 2023. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to large recipients, was 0.255 in 2015 and 0.256 in 2019, then rose to 0.460 in 2023. The jump came after 2019, so the concentration is a feature of the years after 2020 rather than of the first half of the period. The coefficient of variation also rose, from 0.643 in 2015 to 1.477 in 2023.

The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 38.7% in 2019 and 29.6% in 2023. Regional averages therefore explain a shrinking part of the inequality, and differences among countries within the same region now account for most of it. Regional reading alone would hide this, so country-level targeting matters more than regional envelopes.

The country count also shifted: 138 countries in 2015, 134 in 2019 and 135 in 2023. The coverage statement for 2023 elsewhere in the results gives 136 countries reporting. These small differences reflect which countries have data and pass the weighting in each tool, and they mean that part of the change in concentration could arise from changes in who is counted. The change in count is small against the size of the rise in the Gini and Theil measures, but it cannot be excluded as a contributor.

### A single surge in 2022 explains most of the recent rise, and 43 countries regressed

The break analysis of world net official development assistance, in constant 2023 US dollars, locates the recent movement in a single year. Two breaks are detected, in 2022 and 2023. In the segment from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. In 2022 alone the change averaged US$49.8 billion, several times the long-run pace. In 2023 the change turned negative, at a mean of minus US$0.7 billion. The rise in the aggregate therefore comes mainly from one year, not from a steady build-up across the period, and the following year gave back a small part of it.

The regional pattern is consistent with this reading. Europe and Central Asia shows the largest rise in the preceding part, and the timing of the 2022 break coincides with the onset of war in Europe, which prompted large emergency and reception flows. That explanation is context drawn from the history of the period. The data held here do not attribute the 2022 change to any recipient or purpose, and the break test shows only when the world series shifted, not why. A one-year surge of this kind is also a weak basis for judging whether support for trade capacity has grown, since emergency flows serve humanitarian and budget needs rather than trade facilitation.

The country classes show how little the aggregate says about most recipients. Of 138 countries assessed, 79 are on track or have met the target of an increase, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed group. Another 5 show moderate progress, with 0.4% of the population, 6 show marginal progress, with 3.1%, and 5 are stagnant, with 1.7%. The largest class by population is regression: 43 countries, holding 55.7% of the assessed population, received less assistance in real terms in 2023 than at the start of the period. The number of countries on track is larger, but the number of people living in countries with falling assistance is greater.

This divergence matters for the 2030 horizon. A world total lifted by a few exceptional recipients and a single year can rise while most of the population of recipient countries sees less support. Because the surge of 2022 was followed by a decline in 2023, there is no evidence in these results that the higher level will persist. The trend classes also carry a caveat of reading: the tool assumes a target of increase, since target 8.a sets no numeric goal, so classes such as on track describe direction of change and not the attainment of a defined threshold.

### Reaching 2030 requires better measurement and steadier, better-targeted assistance, with proposals

Reaching 2030 on target 8.a depends first on measurement. The bench cannot give an amount for official assistance that supports trade capacity. Net official development assistance received was US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US dollars, and that figure is an upper bound on what could support trade capacity, not an estimate of it. The series covers every purpose, and the shelf holds no Aid for Trade disbursements. It gives no breakdown for least developed countries and no Enhanced Integrated Framework figure, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The nearest available readings are regional and income-group totals: low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023 and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion. A recipient whose assistance grew may have received it for relief or budget support, and one whose assistance fell may still have gained trade-related help. Target 8.a also carries no numeric benchmark. The trend tool was run with no target value, so its classes rest on the direction of change alone.

The record gives little reason to assume that the 2022 jump will repeat. The mean annual change was US$6.4 billion in 2001-2021. The change in 2022 was US$49.8 billion, and in 2023 it was a fall of US$0.7 billion. The timing coincides with the war in Europe and its wider consequences, which prompted emergency flows. That is context from outside the data, and the series cannot confirm the cause or say whether the path will persist. If the rise was exceptional, a flat or falling path is one plausible reading for the years ahead, and it cannot be verified.

The distribution of recipients sharpens the concern. The trend tool classes 43 of 138 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the population assessed. This is a class of the trend rate, not a comparison of 2023 with 2015 levels. Concentration among recipients rose: the population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.361 in 2015 and 0.452 in 2023. Within-region differences now account for most of the inequality, since the between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023.
