w-c04-8-5.text:
### Service coverage has widened, but the world is far from universal

The UHC service coverage index stood at 68.0 index points for the world in 2015 and at 71.0 in 2023, the latest year, when all 193 countries report. The index is a composite of 14 tracer indicators spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health, infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases and service capacity and access. It runs from 0 to 100, and a score of 100 is the natural reading of 'universal' in target 3.8. That reading is one of several. The target also names financial risk protection and access to safe, affordable medicines, which the index does not measure directly, and a country may score high on tracer services while leaving households exposed to heavy costs. The index should therefore be read as a measure of the breadth of essential services, not as a verdict on the whole target.

On that measure, the world rose from 68.0 to 71.0 over eight years and remained well below 100 in 2023. The shortfall is large because the tracer indicators include services that are hard to extend to everyone, such as the control of hypertension and diabetes and the capacity of facilities, alongside those that are easier to scale, such as vaccination and antenatal care. A composite also moves slowly, since a gain in one area can be offset by stagnation in another. These explanations rest on general knowledge of how the index is built, not on the results shown here.

The income groups show the same ordering at both dates. Low-income countries scored 41.2 in 2015 and 43.8 in 2023. Lower-middle-income countries rose from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6, and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. High-income countries, which started closest to the ceiling, were not saturated and kept improving. The low-income rise was smaller than those of the two middle groups, so the poorest countries did not close the distance to the others in absolute terms. In 2023 they remained below the level the lower-middle-income group had reached in 2015.

The gap between countries narrowed slightly, though not by much. Among the 193 countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the index fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index fell from 0.030 to 0.024. Convergence is therefore real, but it takes place at a low overall level. Most of the inequality lies between regions: the between-region share of the Theil index was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, so the region in which a person lives accounts for more of the variation in coverage than differences within a region. Because the weighting is by population, the improvement in South Asia, whose regional score rose from 60.0 to 68.0, plausibly contributes to the narrowing, though the results do not isolate its contribution. The regional pattern is taken up in the next part.

The pace matters for 2030. The assessment was run only against a target of 100, and its sensitivity to other yardsticks was not tested. At the 2015 to 2023 pace, universality by 2030 is not reachable: the world's expected value for 2030 is 73.7, and the trend covers a ratio of 0.18 of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target. Whether the period after 2020 slowed progress cannot be judged, since the endpoints shown do not reveal change in the intervening years.

### Regions differ widely in coverage and in out-of-pocket burden

Coverage differs more between regions than any change in the world average would suggest. In 2023 North America scored 88.0 index points on the UHC service coverage index, Europe and Central Asia 82.0, East Asia and Pacific 80.0 and Latin America and the Caribbean 79.0. South Asia stood at 68.0, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 66.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa at 50.0.

The direction of travel differs as well. South Asia made the largest regional gain, from 60.0 in 2015 to 68.0 in 2023, and moved from below the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping to above it. East Asia and Pacific rose from 76.0 to 80.0, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 45.0 to 50.0. Latin America and the Caribbean did not move, at 79.0 in both years. North America, already near the top, rose from 87.0 to 88.0. Among income groups, low-income countries moved from 41.2 to 43.8, lower-middle-income countries from 56.8 to 62.4, upper-middle-income countries from 75.6 to 79.6 and high-income countries from 83.3 to 85.2. The poorest countries are improving, but from so low a base that the distance to the others has barely closed, and in 2023 the low-income group remained below the level that lower-middle-income countries held in 2015. Only the 2015 and 2023 endpoints are used here, so they do not show whether the pace changed after 2020.

Out-of-pocket spending adds a second view of the same divide. As a share of current health expenditure it was 11.1% in North America in 2023, 16.5% in Europe and Central Asia, 26.0% in East Asia and Pacific, 28.3% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 29.7% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 30.4% in Sub-Saharan Africa and 46.6% in South Asia. The world figure was 17.3%, down from 18.4% in 2015. South Asia fell from 64.3% to 46.6%, the largest fall of any region, yet it remains the highest, so households there still pay nearly half of all health spending directly. Low public funding and a large private provider sector are commonly offered as explanations, but the series do not test them. Latin America and the Caribbean and East Asia and Pacific moved the other way, from 28.2% to 29.7% and from 25.7% to 26.0%.

The share of health spending paid out of pocket and the share of people suffering hardship are related but not the same. Hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on health, affected 26.0% of the world population in 2022, against 28.0% in 2015. By region it ranged from 7.5% in North America and 13.0% in Europe and Central Asia to 20.3% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 26.5% in East Asia and Pacific, 27.5% in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, 31.7% in South Asia and 35.2% in Sub-Saharan Africa. Sub-Saharan Africa thus has the highest hardship although South Asia has the highest out-of-pocket share. Where incomes are low, even a modest payment can consume much of what remains after basic needs, though this is context and not a result. In Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, hardship rose slightly between 2015 and 2022, and in North America it was nearly flat, from 7.4% to 7.5%. Hardship estimates rest on household surveys fielded irregularly, and only 3 countries report for 2024, so the regional values carry wider uncertainty than the service index.

The spread among countries on the service index narrowed. The Gini coefficient, weighted by population, fell from 0.131 in 2015 to 0.115 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.030 to 0.024. Yet the share of the Theil index lying between regions was 69.5% in 2015 and 68.9% in 2023, essentially unchanged. About seven-tenths of the inequality in coverage is therefore associated with which region a country belongs to, and the narrowing has come with a rise across the distribution rather than a dissolving of regional divides. National averages hide this structure, and gains should be judged against the regional floor from which each country starts.

### Coverage gains were modest and financial protection moved unevenly

Financial protection improved only slightly at the global level between 2015 and 2023, and the movement was uneven. The world share of current health expenditure paid directly by households fell from 18.4% in 2015 to 17.3% in 2023. The share of people facing financial hardship, defined as spending more than 40% of the household discretionary budget on out-of-pocket health costs, fell from 28.0% in 2015 to 26.0% in 2022. Both movements are in the right direction, but they are small beside the scale of the problem. More than one person in four is still above the hardship threshold in 2022, the latest year of the world aggregate.

The out-of-pocket share fell most where it began highest. South Asia dropped from 64.3% in 2015 to 46.6% in 2023, and the lower middle income group from 58.3% to 47.0%. Low income countries moved from 53.0% to 44.5%. Sub-Saharan Africa fell to 30.4% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan to 28.3%. These reductions began from very high levels, and in South Asia nearly half of health spending is still paid at the point of care. In East Asia and Pacific the share edged up from 25.7% to 26.0%, and in Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 28.2% to 29.7%. Europe and Central Asia (17.8% to 16.5%), North America (11.9% to 11.1%) and high income countries (14.4% to 13.4%) declined modestly from low bases.

The hardship measure tells a different story from the spending share, and the difference matters. East Asia and Pacific shows a clear fall in hardship, from 30.0% to 26.5%, although its out-of-pocket share did not fall. The two measures are therefore not interchangeable: hardship depends on household budgets, prices and the burden of illness as well as on how the system is financed. Hardship rose in Europe and Central Asia from 12.6% to 13.0%, in Latin America and the Caribbean from 19.5% to 20.3%, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 27.0% to 27.5%. North America was nearly flat, moving from 7.4% to 7.5%, and high income countries moved from 9.5% to 9.7%. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the highest at 35.2% in 2022, down from 38.7%, and South Asia stood at 31.7%, down from 35.7%. Low income countries fell from 38.5% to 34.7% and lower middle income countries from 34.4% to 31.5%, while upper middle income countries moved from 26.5% to 24.9%. The pattern does not follow coverage in a uniform way: hardship fell in East Asia and Pacific, a region of relatively high coverage, and rose in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, a region of lower coverage.

The country-level classification shows the unevenness. Of 72 countries with enough hardship data for a trend assessment, 27 are on track or have met the direction, holding 34.0% of the population of those countries. A further 9 show moderate progress needing acceleration (9.5%) and 4 show marginal progress (22.7%). One country is stagnant, and 31 are regressing, holding 33.7% of the assessed population. The regressing group is thus of similar size and population weight to the on-track group. No numerical target exists for this indicator, so the classification measures only direction of travel and not distance to a defined goal; target 3.8 can be read as a call for financial risk protection for all, which leaves open what level of hardship would count as acceptable.

Public funding appears to matter. Across 21 countries with data for both series, the share of people in hardship is negatively associated with the share of health spending funded from domestic government sources. The rank correlation is -0.525 for 2022 levels and -0.258 for changes between 2015 and 2022. The level association is moderate and the association for changes is weak. This is association rather than proof of cause: richer countries tend to have both higher public shares and lower hardship, and the weaker link in changes suggests that a higher public share does not by itself reduce hardship, whose course also depends on what is covered, on prices and on who is reached.

The evidence base is uneven. Hardship has thinner coverage than the service index, with 3 countries reporting in 2024 against 22 for the out-of-pocket share, so regional aggregates rest on survey years that differ between countries. Movements of one or two points in a regional hardship figure should be read with caution.

### At the current pace, 2030 will be missed, and proposals follow

The trend assessment leaves little room for optimism about 2030. It was run against a single yardstick, a target of 100 index points, and its sensitivity to any other threshold was not tested. Target 3.8 sets no numerical threshold, and 100 index points is a convention that no health system has reached in practice, so the assessment is severe by construction. On that reading, no country is on track for the UHC service coverage index: 0 of 193 countries assessed are on track or have met the target. Only 2 countries, holding 17.3% of the population, show moderate progress that would still need acceleration. A further 102 countries, holding 64.7% of the population, show marginal progress and would need significant acceleration. Another 57 countries, holding 11.0% of the population, stagnate, and 32 countries, holding 7.0% of the population, regress. Most of the world's people therefore live in countries where coverage is rising too slowly to reach the target on the 2015 to 2023 pace. The endpoints alone do not show whether the period after 2020 slowed or quickened progress.

The projections show the scale of the shortfall, and they are conditional on the 2015 to 2023 pace continuing. The world is projected to reach 73.7 index points in 2030, covering a ratio of 0.18 of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected at 54.8 index points, with a ratio of 0.18, and low-income countries at 46.2, with a ratio of 0.09. Lower middle income countries are projected at 67.6, with a ratio of 0.25. South Asia has the highest ratio of any region, 0.40, and is projected at 75.9 index points in 2030, still short of the target. Latin America and the Caribbean is projected to stay at 79.0, a ratio of 0.00, the same as its 2023 value, so no gain on the 2015 baseline is expected. High-income countries are projected at 86.9 with a ratio of 0.21, and North America at 88.9; both remain below 100. The gap between the poorest and richest groups therefore does not close on current trends.

Financial protection tells a more divided story. The hardship indicator could be assessed for 72 countries, the number with enough data for a trend assessment; this is the sample for that series only, not a comparison with the index. Of these, 27 countries, holding 34.0% of their population, are on track or have met the target. Another 9, holding 9.5%, show moderate progress. Against this, 31 countries, holding 33.7% of their population, are regressing, and 4 more, holding 22.7%, show marginal progress. Only 1 country stagnates. The regressing group is of similar size to the on-track group in both countries and population. Coverage of services is advancing too slowly almost everywhere, while financial protection is improving in some countries and deteriorating in others, so the two cannot be assumed to move together.

Public financing is a plausible lever, though the data do not prove it. The association reported in the preceding part, across 21 countries with data for both series from 2015 to 2022, is a rank correlation of -0.52 between the level of financial hardship and the domestic government share of current health expenditure, and of -0.26 between their changes. Countries that fund more of their health spending from public sources tend to have fewer households in hardship, but a rise in public financing did not reliably accompany a fall in hardship within the period. The sample is small and the association is not proof of cause. As context outside these results, health-policy experience generally holds that pooled, prepaid funding protects households better than direct payment at the point of care.

The following proposals follow from these findings.

w-c09-1-3.text:
### World income per person has grown at under 2 per cent a year

World GDP per capita grew by 1.9 per cent in 2015 and by 2.0 per cent in 2025, according to the World Bank's World Development Indicators. A decade that opened and closed at almost the same rate, a little under 2 per cent a year, is the first finding of this section. Growth of that size doubles average income only over several decades, and it sits far below the pace that the second reading of target 8.1 asks of the least developed countries.

Target 8.1 can be read in two ways. Its first clause asks for per capita economic growth 'in accordance with national circumstances', which sets no number. Its second asks for at least 7 per cent GDP growth a year in the least developed countries, a figure for total output, not for income per person. The two measure different things: GDP growth includes the effect of a rising population, and in countries with fast population growth the gap between the two can be wide. This section uses GDP per capita growth as its main indicator, because it describes the change in output available to each resident, and turns to total GDP growth when the 7 per cent threshold is considered. Gross national income per capita is a third measure, which adds income earned abroad and subtracts income paid out; it is reported for fewer countries and is not the basis of the comparisons here.

The path of world growth over the longer run reads as a sequence of shocks rather than as a steady rise. The break analysis of the annual change in the world rate finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The mean annual change was -2.8 percentage points across 2008 and 2009, the years of the global financial crisis, and then +5.8 in 2010 as output recovered. The pattern repeated with greater force around the pandemic: the mean change was -5.4 in 2020 and +9.4 in 2021, followed by -3.1 in 2022. Between 2011 and 2019 the mean annual change was -0.2, a gentle drift downward and not a collapse, and from 2023 to 2025 it was again -0.2. These are changes in the growth rate from one year to the next, not growth rates themselves, and they should be read as the size of each swing.

The reading matters for 2030. A world economy that returns each time to roughly 2 per cent growth, after shocks that arrive about once in a decade, offers no sign of the acceleration that sustained income gains would need. The figure for 2025 rests on 186 countries reporting, against 211 in 2015, so the latest year is less complete than earlier ones and may be revised as late reports arrive.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than six

Regional growth in GDP per capita, from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, ranged widely in 2015. South Asia grew by 6.5 per cent, against 0.2 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa and 0.8 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Latin America and the Caribbean contracted, at -0.7 per cent. These figures describe a single year, not a settled order, and no ratio between regions is claimed here.

South Asia remained the fastest region throughout, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, a little below its 2015 rate. East Asia and Pacific held a similar position, at 4.0 per cent in 2015 and 3.9 per cent in 2025. The trend results cover GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars. The trend tool reads the compound annual change from 2015 and extends it to 2030. No numerical target is set for income per person, so the classes show only direction and pace, and they cannot be read as a test of any benchmark. South Asia's trend is classed as on track or target met, with an annual rate of 0.0465. East Asia and Pacific carries the same class, at 0.0357.

The wealthier regions moved the other way. Europe and Central Asia slowed from 1.6 per cent in 2015 to 1.3 per cent in 2025, and North America from 1.9 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Their trend rates, 0.0150 and 0.0167, are classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. High-income countries as a group went from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0151, in the same class. Slower growth at high income levels is often explained, as context outside these results, by the limited scope for catching up and by ageing populations; the results do not test this.

Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa show the largest rise in the annual rate between the two end years. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from -0.7 per cent to 1.6 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.2 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Both ended close to the world rate of 2.0 per cent, yet the decade-long trend in income per person is less favourable. Latin America and the Caribbean has a trend rate of 0.0054, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and Sub-Saharan Africa a rate of -0.0020, classed as regression. A single good year at the end does not alter a decade in which income per person barely rose or fell. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew by 0.8 per cent in 2015 and 0.9 per cent in 2025, with a trend rate of 0.0076, also classed as marginal progress.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after -2.9 per cent in 2015, yet their trend rate over the decade is 0.0007, classed as stagnation. Lower-middle-income countries grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025, up from 4.0 per cent in 2015, with a trend rate of 0.0292. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0371. Both of these groups are classed as on track or target met. A low-income growth rate of 2.5 per cent in 2025 is one year's reading, and the stagnation class shows that it has not yet lifted the decade's trend.

### Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015

The breaks in the annual change of world GDP per capita growth locate the large movements in the series. The break analysis of the World Development Indicators finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The segments between them are short, and several consist of one year. The breaks describe changes in the rate of growth, not its level: a mean change of -2.8 points in 2008-2009 means that the growth rate fell by that amount each year on average across those two years. The analysis does not measure what share of the movement each shock explains, so this part claims only where the breaks fall and how large they are.

The global financial crisis is the first large shock in the series, and it lies before 2015. The 2008-2009 segment has a mean annual change of -2.8 points, and 2010 follows with a rebound of 5.8 points. The long segment from 2011 to 2019 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, and it straddles the 2015 baseline. That is a slow drift downward in the growth rate across nine years, not a collapse.

The period after 2015 is dominated by the pandemic. In 2020 the annual change in world growth was -5.4 points, the largest fall in the series. The 2021 segment records a rise of 9.4 points, the largest rise. The 2022 segment then shows a change of -3.1 points. The segment from 2023 to 2025 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, so growth was drifting down again, much as in 2011-2019. These swings are why the world rate in 2025, at 2.0 per cent, can resemble the rate in 2015, at 1.9 per cent, while the path between them was violent. As context, not a result of the analysis, the 2020 fall is usually attributed to lockdowns and the collapse of travel and trade, and the 2021 gain largely to recovery from a depressed base.

Across income groups, the endpoints need the same caution. Low-income countries recorded GDP per capita growth of -2.9 per cent in 2015 and 2.5 per cent in 2025. That is a swing from contraction to modest expansion, but it compares two single years. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 4.0 per cent to 4.6 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, and high-income countries from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent. Target 8.1 sets 7 per cent for total GDP growth in the least developed countries, and these results contain neither that measure nor that group, so the target cannot be tested here. The per capita rates of every group listed are below 7 per cent, but that is not a test of the target.

A ten-year endpoint comparison therefore hides the volatility that the breaks reveal. Two years close in value say nothing about the swings between them, and a large gain between endpoints may only be recovery from a poor starting year. The comparison also depends on coverage. The number of countries reporting GDP growth was 211 in 2015, 210 in 2019 and 210 in 2021, but only 186 in 2025. The fall from 209 countries in 2022 to 204 in 2023 and 200 in 2024 suggests that data arrive late, so the 2025 values rest on fewer countries and may be revised. For 2030 this implies that the latest readings are provisional, and that any judgment on target 8.1 should wait for the revised series.

### Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence

Beyond regional averages, the trend classification sorts countries by how fast GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) has moved since 2015. No numerical 2030 target exists for this measure, and the results do not state the benchmark value behind the notional target. The tool describes only its reading rule: the compound annual rate from the baseline, and the share of the distance from baseline to target that this rate would cover by 2030. The classes are therefore relative readings of momentum, not a verdict against a legal threshold, and the benchmark cannot be reproduced from the results given.

Of 209 countries assessed, 74 are on track or have met the notional target, and they hold 56.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 36 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 16.4 per cent of the population. Another 44 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 11.8 per cent. Fifteen countries stagnate, with 5.0 per cent of the population, and 40 are in regression, with 10.3 per cent. Fewer than half of the countries assessed are therefore on track by count, though they hold a majority of the population. The results give no country-level income figures, so they do not show whether the lagging countries are the poorest.

The regional trends point the same way. South Asia has a compound rate of 0.0465, East Asia and the Pacific 0.0357, the upper middle income group 0.0371 and the lower middle income group 0.0292, and all four are classed as on track or target met. Europe and Central Asia (0.0150), high income countries (0.0151) and North America (0.0167) show moderate progress, as does the world as a whole at 0.0176. Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0054) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0076) show marginal progress. The low income group, at 0.0007, is classed as stagnating. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0020, is classed as regression, even though its annual growth rate recovered from 0.2 per cent in 2015 to 1.6 per cent in 2025.

The 7 per cent target cannot be tested with these results. Target 8.1 sets that rate for GDP growth, not per capita growth, in the least developed countries, and the results hold neither a total GDP growth series nor a group figure for those countries. What can be said is narrower: per capita growth in 2025 was below 7 per cent in every group listed. The low income group grew by 2.5 per cent after a contraction of -2.9 per cent in 2015, and South Asia, the highest, grew by 6.2 per cent. Neither is a least developed group, so these figures are a proxy and not a test.

The low income rebound from -2.9 per cent to 2.5 per cent is a sizeable swing, yet the trend classification still reads that group as stagnating, at a rate of 0.0007. As context not tested by the results, growth after a shock often restores lost ground before it adds new income, which would explain why a good year need not change the long-run class. Coverage also thins at the end of the series: 186 countries reported growth in 2025, against 211 in 2015, so the latest figures are less complete.

For 2030 the implication is measured. If present rates hold, 74 countries with 56.6 per cent of the population assessed are on track by the notional reading, while 40 countries with 10.3 per cent are in regression and 15 with 5.0 per cent stagnate. The 7 per cent goal is a different measure and remains untested.

w-c09-9-2.text:
### Account ownership reached 78.7 per cent of adults worldwide by 2024

Account ownership among adults aged 15 and over stood at 78.7 per cent worldwide in 2024, up from 69.3 per cent in 2017. The indicator counts respondents who report having an account, alone or with someone else, at a bank or another type of financial institution, or with a mobile-money-service provider. It therefore measures a person's formal link to the financial system, not the use made of the account, its cost or its quality. An account opened for a single transfer and then left dormant counts in the same way as one used daily.

Target 8.10 asks countries to strengthen the capacity of domestic financial institutions to encourage and expand access to banking, insurance and financial services for all. The target carries no numeric threshold. This book therefore reads full access as 100 per cent of adults aged 15 and over holding an account. That reading is strict and is only one of several possible; a lower benchmark, or a measure that included credit, would give a different distance to travel. Insurance, which the target names, is not measured by any of the series used here, so the book says nothing about it. On the strict reading, the world in 2024 was still short of the mark by a wide margin, though it had moved in the right direction.

The survey years need care. Account ownership is collected in periodic household surveys, not annually. For most regions the series offers two readings, 2017 and 2021, while the World aggregate and South Asia carry a 2024 reading, as do the income groups. The regional figures are therefore not all measured at the same end date, and the rise in the World figure to 2024 cannot be split into regional contributions from the 2021 values alone. The regional pictures are taken up in the next part. Here the point is that the global rise is real in the data and spans the years before and after 2020, although the gap in survey years prevents any exact reading of what the pandemic changed.

The physical infrastructure of banking moved differently. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.16 in 2015 to 11.12 in 2024, while automated teller machines per 100,000 adults rose from 36.09 to 41.91 over the same years. Accounts spread while branches thinned, so the growth in account holding cannot be attributed to a larger branch network. As context, not as a finding of these series, the period saw banks consolidate branches and customers move towards phones and digital channels; the data on branches and ATMs do not show why either count changed. Branches and machines are also a count of outlets relative to adults, not of the distance any person must travel to reach one.

These three series together suggest that account holding has become less dependent on branches, though the series do not identify the channels responsible. That matters for 2030, since the target's aim of access for all can be pursued through channels other than buildings. It also leaves open who has been reached and who has not, which the parts that follow examine by region, income group, sex and poverty.

### Regions and countries differ widely in ownership and in physical access

Regional levels of account ownership span a wide range. In 2021, North America stood at 95.5 per cent of adults aged 15 and over, Europe and Central Asia at 89.6 per cent and East Asia and Pacific at 82.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 73.6 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa 55.1 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping recorded 52.8 per cent. South Asia, whose latest reading falls in 2024, stood at 77.6 per cent. The survey years differ between South Asia and the other regions, so the South Asian figure is not strictly comparable with the 2021 readings.

The starting points in 2017 show where the movement has been fastest. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 55.2 per cent to 73.6 per cent by 2021, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 42.6 per cent to 55.1 per cent. North America moved from 93.8 per cent to 95.5 per cent, a region close to saturation. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping advanced from 47.5 per cent to 52.8 per cent, the slowest gain among the developing regions listed. Convergence is therefore under way, yet the gap between the top and bottom regions remains large.

Physical access tells a different story, and it does not line up with ownership. Commercial bank branches numbered 21.9 per 100,000 adults in North America in 2024 and 19.0 in Europe and Central Asia, against 4.0 in Sub-Saharan Africa. North America and Europe and Central Asia had fewer branches than in 2015, when the figures were 27.7 and 26.8. Branches also fell in Latin America and the Caribbean, from 13.1 to 11.6, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping, from 13.9 to 11.5. South Asia moved the other way, from 11.3 to 16.0, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 9.7 to 11.2. Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged, from 3.9 in 2015 to 4.0. The series count outlets only and do not test why counts changed. Explanations offered in the wider literature, given here as context and not as findings, include branch closures after consolidation in mature banking systems and the use of mobile channels in place of new buildings.

Automated teller machines show the same unevenness. North America had 173.8 machines per 100,000 adults in 2024, down from 222.1 in 2015, while Sub-Saharan Africa had 6.9 and South Asia 24.5. South Asia's figure was 13.2 in 2015, so the region added machines while accounts also rose. Sub-Saharan Africa began at 5.3. The densest region still has many times the provision of the sparsest, which matters for people who must withdraw cash, especially where cash remains the main means of payment.

The income groups confirm the pattern. In 2024 account ownership was 46.4 per cent in low-income economies, 70.4 per cent in lower-middle-income, 84.0 per cent in upper-middle-income and 94.9 per cent in high-income economies. Low-income economies had 2.8 branches per 100,000 adults in 2023, fewer than 3.0 in 2015, but their ATM density rose from 3.1 in 2015 to 4.0 in 2023. Lower-middle-income economies roughly doubled ATM density, from 10.6 in 2015 to 21.7 in 2024.

Country classes set against the target of universal ownership by 2030 show how uneven progress is. Of 141 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, holding 16.4 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 36 show moderate progress needing acceleration, covering 51.8 per cent of that population. A further 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, at 20.3 per cent. Three countries stagnate, at 0.7 per cent, and 36 regress, at 10.8 per cent. Because the survey is conducted in a few rounds, these classes rest on very few observations per country, and a single weak survey can place a country in regression. The classes are best read as a guide to where the pace is insufficient, not as a firm forecast. Under any reading, fewer than one-fifth of the population of assessed countries lives in a country on course for the 2030 aim.

### Mobile money and account growth outpaced branches, and the poorest and women gained

Account ownership rose fastest where it started lowest, while branch counts fell in several regions, and the poorest and women gained.

Gains in account ownership were largest where ownership started low. In Latin America and the Caribbean the share of adults with an account rose from 55.2 per cent in 2017 to 73.6 per cent in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 42.6 per cent to 55.1 per cent over the same four years. In North America, where ownership was already high, the share moved from 93.8 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Income groups show the same pattern between 2017 and 2024: low-income economies rose from 32.0 per cent to 46.4 per cent, while high-income economies moved from 93.0 per cent to 94.9 per cent. Ownership has therefore converged from below, though low-income economies remain far from the level already reached elsewhere.

The poorest 40 per cent of adults gained substantially. Worldwide their ownership rose from 61.7 per cent in 2017 to 72.4 per cent in 2024. In Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 42.9 per cent to 67.9 per cent between 2017 and 2021, a faster advance than for all adults in that region. In low-income economies the poorest 40 per cent reached 37.3 per cent in 2024, from 22.5 per cent in 2017. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.6 per cent in 2021 for this group, up from 32.0 per cent. The poorest group still trails the full adult population in every region reported.

Women's ownership also rose, from 65.9 per cent worldwide in 2017 to 76.6 per cent in 2024, against 78.7 per cent for all adults in 2024. South Asia shows a notable pattern: women stood at 75.1 per cent in 2024, from 64.0 per cent in 2017, against 77.6 per cent for all adults. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping remains the clearest case of difficulty. Women's ownership was 45.6 per cent in 2021, up from 38.0 per cent in 2017, against 52.8 per cent for all adults that year, itself up from 47.5 per cent in 2017. All-adult ownership there rose by less than in Latin America and the Caribbean or in Sub-Saharan Africa over the same years.

Physical access moved differently. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.2 in 2015 to 11.1 in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 26.8 to 19.0, and North America from 27.7 to 21.9. High-income economies fell from 22.3 to 15.5. South Asia rose from 11.3 to 16.0, and East Asia and Pacific from 9.7 to 11.2. Sub-Saharan Africa was close to unchanged, at 3.9 in 2015 and 4.0 in 2024, and low-income economies stood at 3.0 in 2015 and 2.8 in 2023. ATMs per 100,000 adults rose worldwide from 36.1 in 2015 to 41.9 in 2024, and in lower middle income economies from 10.6 to 21.7. In low-income economies they rose from 3.1 in 2015 to 4.0 in 2023. In East Asia and Pacific they fell from 52.5 to 46.5, and in North America from 222.1 to 173.8.

The contrast is that account ownership rose across the world while branches fell in many regions. Accounts therefore spread without a matching spread of branches. Mobile-money services, digital payments and the channelling of public transfers into accounts are explanations offered in the wider literature for ownership growing without bank premises, and branch consolidation and online banking have been offered for richer economies. These are context, not findings: the series measure accounts and outlets only, do not test those explanations, and cannot separate dormant accounts from active ones. Insurance and credit, which target 8.10 also names, are not measured by these series.

For 2030 the pattern implies that the post-2017 gains were broad, but that those who start lowest, including the poorest, women in some regions and residents of low-income economies, still have the furthest to go. Regional figures for 2021 and global figures for 2024 come from different survey rounds, so the years are not strictly comparable.

### Projected trends leave universal access short of 2030 outside a few regions, and proposals follow

Extrapolating the 2017 to latest-year trend towards universal access, defined here as 100 per cent of adults holding an account, shows a split picture. East Asia and Pacific and Europe and Central Asia read as on track or target met, with expected values in 2030 of 108.8 and 110.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reads the same way, with an expected 140.1 per cent. Values above 100 show that the extrapolation is mechanical: a share of adults cannot exceed 100 per cent, and the figures are not forecasts. Sub-Saharan Africa also reads as on track, with an expected 98.0 per cent in 2030. Its ratio of 0.965 is the tool's progress ratio, which compares the rate of the trend with the rate needed to reach the target; it is not the expected value divided by 100. The reading sits close to the line and is sensitive to the years chosen.

Other groups fall short. The world as a whole is in the class of moderate progress, but acceleration needed, with an expected 78.7 per cent in 2024 rising to 87.8 per cent in 2030. High income moved from 93.0 per cent in 2017 to 94.9 per cent in 2024, and projects to 96.6 per cent in 2030. The shortfall there is small in level but slow in pace, since the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach. Low income reads as marginal progress, with an expected 63.9 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping, also marginal, reaches 67.1 per cent. Lower middle income projects to 80.7 per cent and South Asia to 85.3 per cent.

Country counts confirm that the global average hides wide differences. Of 141 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, holding 16.4 per cent of the assessed population. Another 36 show moderate progress, and these hold 51.8 per cent of the population. A further 36 show marginal progress, with 20.3 per cent. Three are stagnant, and 36 are regressing, with 10.8 per cent of the population. Survey-based measures carry sampling error and rounds differ between countries, so some of these readings may reflect noise and the choice of end year, not a real fall.

Physical access does not offer a route to universal access. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.2 in 2015 to 11.1 in 2024, and in high income countries from 22.3 to 15.5. Sub-Saharan Africa stayed near 4.0, and low income countries stood at 2.8 in 2023. The series measure accounts and outlets, not channels, so they do not show how accounts were opened. As context outside the data, mobile money is one plausible route, and 2030 outcomes may depend on such channels more than on new branches.

Target 8.10 sets no number, so the reading of 100 per cent is a choice, and a different reading would change the classes above. Insurance, which the target names, is not measured by these series. The poorest 40 per cent stood at 72.4 per cent worldwide in 2024, and women at 76.6 per cent, so aggregate progress does not show who remains outside.

Three proposals follow. National governments and financial regulators in low income countries and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping should prioritise account access for the poorest and for women, since these groups are the furthest from the 2030 line. Statistical offices and survey sponsors should shorten the interval between survey rounds and report insurance and account use, so that regression readings can be told from noise.

w-c04-7-4.text:
### Adolescent fertility has fallen worldwide since 2015

The world adolescent fertility rate fell from 46.0 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 38.3 in 2024. The figure is a modelled estimate built from registration data, surveys and censuses. The series reports on all 217 countries and territories in 2024, so the global average rests on far fuller coverage than the indicators of contraceptive demand in the same section.

Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold. It calls for universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, including family planning, information and education, and offers no level of adolescent fertility that would count as success. The target can also be read in more than one way. Adolescent births are an outcome of access, schooling, marriage customs and income as much as of health services, so a fall in the rate cannot be credited to health policy alone. Any reading of progress here therefore rests on the trend classes of the bench, which compare each country's own course with the pace needed to keep falling to 2030, and not on a stated goal.

On that reading the picture is favourable in breadth. Of 217 countries assessed, 144 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of the population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. Another 26 countries, with 6.3%, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration. Eight countries, with 0.4% of the population, are stagnant, and five, with 1.0%, are regressing. The population-weighted share on track is far larger than the count of countries alone would suggest, but the results do not show which countries lie in each class by starting rate, so no claim is made here about where the laggards began.

The global decline matters because early childbearing is commonly associated with interrupted schooling, lower lifetime earnings and higher obstetric risk; this is context from established knowledge, not a finding of the bench. The world rate of 38.3 in 2024 remains well above the 8.7 recorded for high-income countries in the same year, so the average conceals a wide gap that the next parts of the section examine. As context from outside the bench, school closures and disrupted clinics after 2020 were widely expected to push adolescent births up. The bench reports only the 2015 and 2024 values of the world series, so it cannot show whether the pace faltered in particular years or places after 2020. For 2030, the trend classes indicate that gains are not secure in every country: 13 countries are stagnant or regressing. No projection of the world rate is made here.

### Demand satisfied by modern methods is poorly measured

Demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods cannot be answered at the level the question asks. The results supply no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country group, and the answer to how far demand is met is therefore limited to the direction of change in 15 countries and the population shares those countries hold. The indicator is the weakest of the series in this section. It is reported by 73 countries in at least one year between 2000 and 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. In any single year the count is small. Counts are available here for 2000, 2012, 2015 and 2019 to 2024 only, and comparison is made only within those years: 13 countries in 2000, 14 in 2012 and 8 in 2015. After 2015 the count moved unevenly. It was 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021 and 7 in 2022, then 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024. There is no steady decline and no steady recovery, and the count in 2024 remains small beside the 217 reporting on adolescent fertility. As context, not a finding of the data, household surveys are fielded at intervals of several years and were disrupted by the pandemic, so a country appears in the series only in the years after a survey has been completed and processed.

The consequence is that the indicator cannot show what happened after 2015 or after 2020 for the world. A year-on-year comparison would compare different sets of countries, and a change in the average would reflect which countries happened to report as much as any change in access to services. The shelf holds aggregates for three groups: lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The tools were not run for these groups in this section, so the level of satisfied demand is not reported for any group. Those aggregates would give a partial answer to the level question, and retrieving them is needed before it can be answered even for those three groups. No world aggregate and no aggregate for other regions is held, so regional comparison of satisfied demand is not possible on this evidence.

The definition adds a second limit. The indicator refers to married women aged 15 to 49 who have a need for family planning, and its denominator is those with demand, not all women. Unmarried women, including sexually active adolescents, fall outside it, as do women in unions not recorded as marriage in some surveys. Target 3.7 speaks of universal access to sexual and reproductive health-care services, information and education, and the indicator captures only one part of that: the use of modern methods by married women who want to space or limit births. The target also gives no numerical threshold, so no level of satisfied demand can be called the goal, and the trend assessment rests on the direction of change rather than on a fixed value. The target can be read in more than one way, and this section does not choose among the readings.

The trend classification covers only 15 countries, those with enough observations to fit a path to 2030. Of these, 2 are on track or have met the target, holding 1.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Another 5 show moderate progress needing acceleration, with 21.8 per cent. Four show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 70.3 per cent. One is stagnant, with 3.1 per cent, and 3 are regressing, with 3.3 per cent. The results do not show which countries lie in each class, so the large population share of the marginal class cannot be attributed to any particular country. Fifteen countries out of 73 reporting, and out of a world of more than 200, is too few to speak for any region, and the sample is not random. The proportions above describe the sample, not the world, and any global statement drawn from them is tentative.

### Regions differ by a factor of eight in adolescent births

Adolescent births are concentrated to a degree that the world average conceals. In 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 91.9 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19, against 50.4 in Latin America and the Caribbean and 37.8 in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. South Asia stood at 21.0, East Asia and Pacific at 14.3, North America at 11.7 and Europe and Central Asia at 11.4. The highest regional rate is therefore about eight times the lowest, and the next region down, Latin America and the Caribbean, is well above the world rate of 38.3.

The pattern follows income. Low-income countries recorded 90.7 births per 1,000 in 2024, lower-middle-income countries 42.5, upper-middle-income countries 23.6 and high-income countries 8.7. The results do not show how far income groups and regions contain the same countries, so the two views should be read as separate cuts of the data. As context rather than a finding of these results, schooling for girls, the age at first marriage, access to contraception and the reach of sexual and reproductive health education are known to differ along similar lines and to act together rather than separately.

Every region and income group named here, each with a value for both 2015 and 2024, recorded a fall between those years, but the size of the fall depends on the measure. In absolute terms Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 to 91.9 and Latin America and the Caribbean from 67.3 to 50.4. In proportional terms North America fell from 20.9 to 11.7 and East Asia and Pacific from 21.9 to 14.3, while low-income countries moved only from 103.3 to 90.7. A large absolute fall from a high starting point therefore leaves relative standing little changed: Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest rate in 2015 and remains far above every other region in 2024.

The country classification shows a similar split between breadth and depth of progress. Of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 34 countries, with 7.3 per cent of the population, show moderate progress and need acceleration. Another 26, with 6.3 per cent, show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. The population-weighted figure of 84.9 per cent should not be read as a statement about each country. The results do not show which regions the lagging classes belong to.

The target gives no numerical threshold for adolescent fertility, so the trend classification measures the pace of decline against a projected path, not against a defined goal. A different reading of what counts as sufficient progress would change the classes. The regional contrasts are nonetheless clear on any reading: the gap between Sub-Saharan Africa and the other regions remains very wide in 2024.

### Progress in family planning is moderate and uneven

Of the 15 countries for which a trend to 2030 could be computed on demand satisfied by modern methods, 2 are on track or have met the target, and these hold 1.5% of the population of the countries assessed. A further 5 countries, with 21.8% of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The weight of the picture lies in the slower classes. The 4 countries in marginal progress, which need significant acceleration, hold 70.3% of the assessed population. One country stagnates, with 3.1%, and 3 regress, with 3.3%. The population-weighted result is therefore weaker than the country count alone suggests. The trend tool shows only the share of the assessed population in each class; it does not name the countries or show which of them are the most populous.

The question of how far demand is satisfied cannot be answered at the level asked. No level of satisfied demand was retrieved for the world, for any region or for any country. The shelf holds aggregates for three groups, lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, but the tools were not run for them in this section, so the level of satisfied demand is not reported for any group. Retrieving those aggregates would give a partial answer for those three groups, and it is needed before the question can be answered for them. For now the answer is limited to the direction of change in 15 countries and the population shares they hold. The 15 countries assessed are a fraction of the 73 that have ever reported the indicator, and the survey-based series leaves most countries without enough observations to draw a trend. Annual reporting is thin and uneven: 8 countries reported in 2015, 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility in 2024. Within the years shown, the count recovered after 2019 but remained below the 14 reporting in 2012. Counts are given only for the years listed, and comparisons are made only among them. The assessment cannot be read as a global verdict. It describes a small group selected by data availability, and how far it represents other countries is not known. The target also carries no numerical threshold in this analysis, so the classes measure the pace of improvement along a path rather than attainment of a fixed level, and a different reading of the goal would sort some countries differently. The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women, including adolescents, are outside it.

The indicators do not identify why countries fall into one class or another, and no cause is asserted here. As general context, not a finding, the pace of change in contraceptive use is commonly understood to depend on the reliability of supply, the range of methods offered, the cost to users and social norms about women's choices; none of these is measured by this series. What the data do show is that regression occurs in 3 of the 15 countries, which means that gains are not automatically retained.

The adolescent fertility trend gives a firmer, though different, reading. Of 217 countries and territories, 144 are on track or have met the target, holding 84.9% of their population, and 34 show moderate progress, with 7.3%. Another 26 are in marginal progress, with 6.3%, 8 stagnate, with 0.4%, and 5 regress, with 1.0%. Progress on adolescent births is thus broad in coverage, while progress on contraceptive demand cannot be shown to be.

For 2030, progress on satisfied demand cannot be assumed to be on course. With few countries on track and most of the assessed population in the slower classes, a result consistent with universal access would require acceleration where the trend is weakest.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Adolescent fertility is expected to keep falling to 2030, but this is an expectation and not a finding, and the pace will differ between countries. Of the 217 countries and territories assessed, 144 are on track or have met the direction of travel, and they hold 84.9% of the population of the countries assessed. The remainder is the concern. A further 34 countries, with 7.3% of that population, show moderate progress and need acceleration, 26 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, 8 are stagnant and 5 are regressing. Target 3.7 sets no numerical goal for adolescent fertility, so these classes describe the pace of change in each country and do not measure distance from a value agreed in the Goals. The reading depends on the pace each country is judged against, and it should be taken as indicative.

The regional rates show where the burden lies. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 109.4 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 in 2015 to 91.9 in 2024, and low-income countries fell from 103.3 to 90.7. Both remain far above the high-income level of 8.7 in 2024, while the world rate stands at 38.3. The trend classes are computed for countries and are not shown here for regions, and the results do not name the countries that lag, so country-level lag in Sub-Saharan Africa is unknown. As context outside the evidence of this section, schooling for girls, the age at marriage and access to contraception are well-established influences on adolescent births.

The question of how far demand for family planning is satisfied cannot be answered at the level asked. The results of this section supply no level of satisfied demand for the world, for any region or for any country, and only the direction of change in 15 countries is available. The shelf holds aggregates of the indicator for three groups, lower-middle-income countries, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, but the tools were not run for those groups here, so no level is reported for them either. Retrieving those aggregates would give a partial answer for those groups and is needed before the level question can be addressed for them. Of the 15 countries, 2 are on track, 5 show moderate progress, 4 show marginal progress, 1 is stagnant and 3 are regressing. The 4 countries in marginal progress hold 70.3% of the population assessed. The results do not name those countries, so what drives that share cannot be stated. Reporting is also thin: 2 countries reported in 2019 and 7 in 2024, against 217 for adolescent fertility. The indicator covers married women only, so unmarried women and adolescents lie outside it.

The proposals that follow address both problems: the thinness of measurement and the pace of progress where rates remain highest.

w-c05-5-5.text:
### Parity at the global level, and what the index conceals

Gender parity in enrolment is measured by the gender parity index: the ratio of girls' (or women's) gross enrolment to boys' (or men's) at a given level of schooling. A value of 1.00 marks parity. Values below 1.00 indicate fewer girls than boys enrolled relative to the school-age population, and values above 1.00 indicate the reverse. The index is a ratio of two ratios, so it says nothing about how many children of either sex are in school, only how the two compare.

At the global level, primary enrolment sits very close to parity. The world index was 1.00 in 2015 (0.9993) and 0.98 in 2020 (0.9825). The movement is small and should be read with caution. In the primary series only 4 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot support a global reading, and 2020 is the last year with broad coverage. The fall is not a loss for girls: it largely reflects a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, since South Asia moved from 1.0611 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020 and lower middle income countries from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Secondary enrolment is similarly near parity at world level, at 0.99 in 2015 (0.9896) and 0.99 in 2020 (0.9887), with only 2 countries reporting in 2022. In both cases a world figure near 1.00 is an average of regions that lie on either side of it, and the average hides offsetting gaps.

Tertiary enrolment is the one level at which the world index departs clearly from parity, and it does so in favour of women. The index was 1.10 in 2015 (1.1031) and 1.12 in 2024 (1.1221). Under the plain reading of Target 4.5, an index above 1.00 is still a disparity, though one that disadvantages men. The target text speaks of eliminating gender disparities, not only those that disadvantage girls, yet policy attention and the measurement tradition have mostly concentrated on girls' exclusion. How a reader treats a tertiary index above 1.00 therefore depends on the interpretation adopted, and the data cannot settle it.

The index also conceals a good deal by construction. Gross enrolment counts all pupils at a level regardless of age, so over-age entrants and repeaters are included. A country in which boys repeat grades more often can show a different index from one in which the same numbers of boys and girls progress on time. Enrolment is also a measure of presence at the start of a school year, not of staying to the end of the cycle, still less of learning. Completion rates, taken up later in this section, and learning outcomes, treated elsewhere in the chapter, can diverge from enrolment parity in either direction. An index of 1.00 is compatible with equally poor outcomes for both sexes, and with high enrolment of girls who later leave school before finishing.

A further limit concerns the second clause of the target. Target 4.5 refers to equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. The indices used here are disaggregated only by sex, and by the country and income groupings in which the World Bank publishes them. They cannot show whether disabled girls, or girls from indigenous or displaced communities, are enrolled at the same rate as other children. The target can accordingly be read narrowly, as sex parity at each level, or broadly, as equal access for every vulnerable group. Only the narrow reading can be examined with this indicator, and a global index at or near 1.00 should not be taken as evidence that the broader aim has been met.

### Regional differences by level of schooling

Primary enrolment shows the narrowest regional spread of the three levels. In 2020 the index stood at 0.997 in East Asia and Pacific, 0.997 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.995 in North America and 0.991 in South Asia, all close to parity. Latin America and the Caribbean stood at 0.982. Two regions remained further from it. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.970 in 2015 to 0.976 in 2020, and Sub-Saharan Africa barely moved, from 0.956 to 0.958. Sub-Saharan Africa therefore ended the period with about four girls enrolled for every hundred boys fewer than parity would imply, and the change over five years was too small to alter that. The result for South Asia deserves a note: its index fell from 1.061 in 2015 to 0.991 in 2020, a drop from a ratio favouring girls to one slightly favouring boys. Gross enrolment includes over-age and repeating pupils, so a swing of this size may reflect revisions of population estimates or changes in repetition rather than a true change in who attends school.

Secondary enrolment is where the regional contrasts widen. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 0.868 in 2015 and 0.900 in 2020, the lowest regional value at this level and the widest gap to girls, though the gain of about three points was the largest among the regions at this level. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 0.952 to 0.965. The other regions lie within a few points of parity, but not all on the same side. East Asia and Pacific stood at 1.018 in 2020, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.052, so that girls are enrolled in greater proportion than boys. The data do not show why. One hypothesis, which these series cannot test, is that boys leave school early for paid work in some settings. A gap that favours girls is still a disparity under target 4.5, and it calls for different remedies from a gap that excludes them. North America fell from 1.010 to 0.982 over the period, and Europe and Central Asia was unchanged at 0.993.

At tertiary level the direction of the disparity reverses in most of the world. The global index was 1.122 in 2024, and Latin America and the Caribbean reached 1.291 and North America 1.301, so that women were enrolled well in excess of men. Europe and Central Asia, at 1.153, and East Asia and Pacific, at 1.128, follow the same pattern. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan crossed parity, rising from 0.9995 in 2015 to 1.058 in 2024, and South Asia did likewise, from 0.954 to 1.029. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception. Its index was 0.794 in 2021, the latest year the data report for the region, against 0.735 in 2015. The distance between that value and North America's 1.301 in 2024 is the widest in the whole comparison, and the two years differ, so it should be read as an indication of scale rather than a same-year gap.

Income groups reproduce the regional order. In low-income countries the index was 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Each step up the ladder of schooling therefore widens the shortfall for women and girls, from about seven points at primary to about thirty-three at tertiary. Lower-middle-income countries stood at 0.992 at primary level in 2020, 0.997 at secondary level in 2020 and 1.038 at tertiary level in 2024, close to parity at the first two levels and above it at the third. Among the groups reported here, low-income countries are below parity at all three levels. Reporting is thin for the latest year: only 4 countries reported primary data and 2 reported secondary data for 2022, so regional values for the most recent period rest on the years 2020 and 2021 rather than on a current count.

### Disparity among countries and the limits of completion data

The spread of the secondary index across countries shows how small the inequality in parity is when measured in aggregate. In 2015, across 139 countries and weighting each by population, the Gini coefficient of the secondary gender parity index was 0.048 and the Theil index was 0.006. These are low values by the standards of income or wealth, which is to be expected for a ratio that clusters around 1.00 in most countries. A low summary figure, however, does not mean that no country is far from parity. A ratio index compresses large deviations in a few countries into a small number once they are averaged against the many countries near parity, and population weighting lets large, near-parity countries dominate the result.

The more informative result is where the inequality lies. Of the Theil index in 2015, 45.5% was between regions, so that nearly half of the small disparity that exists is explained by which region a country belongs to. The remainder lies within regions, among countries that share a geography but differ in policy, income, norms about girls' schooling and the supply of schools within reach of households. This split matters for action. A regional share of this size indicates that gaps are concentrated in particular parts of the world, which supports regional programmes, while the large within-region share cautions that regional averages would hide countries in need. It also shows that the direction of the gap varies: some countries fall below parity for girls, and others, particularly at secondary level, fall below parity for boys. A single index of dispersion treats both alike, which is a further limit of the measure. The spread is also reported only for 2015, so these data cannot show whether dispersion has narrowed since.

The completion data impose a harder limit. Female primary completion rates were reported by 132 countries in 2015 and by 134 in 2020, which is a workable base for comparison. The shelf's results give no coverage counts for the male series, so the comparison of girls and boys rests on the female count alone. In 2025 only 11 countries have reported, against 110 in 2024. The 2025 count may reflect the lag with which national statistics reach the international database, but the data cannot show whether collection has stopped. Either way the consequence is the same: a comparison of completion between girls and boys at the latest date cannot yet be made across countries with confidence. Since 192 countries reported in at least one year, the series is broad over time, but the countries that report in a given year are not always the same ones, so changes in an aggregate can reflect changes in who reports.

For Target 4.5 the limits go beyond timing. The target refers to persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations, and the series on the shelf are disaggregated only by sex. No series here splits enrolment or completion by disability or indigenous status, nor by wealth, location or displacement, so it is not possible to say from these data whether girls in the most disadvantaged groups are further behind than girls overall. The target can also be read in more than one way: as parity of the index at each level, or as equal access and completion for every group. The data speak only to the first reading, and the second clause of the target is not measured. Progress to 2030 can therefore be judged only for parity between the sexes, and only to the extent that completion reporting recovers.

### What changed since 2015 and why the picture is mixed

Between 2015 and 2020 the world primary index moved from 0.9993 to 0.9825. A movement of this size looks like a loss for girls, but the regional figures show that it is largely a narrowing of a gap that favoured girls, not a loss for them. The largest fall was in South Asia, where the primary index went from 1.0611 to 0.9910. In 2015 that value lay above parity, so the region was enrolling relatively more girls than boys. The fall brought it close to 1.00 from above, and this pulled the world figure down. The lower middle income group shows the same pattern, falling from 1.0282 to 0.9919. Both movements should be read as a return towards parity rather than a deterioration, although the index alone cannot say whether girls' enrolment fell, boys' enrolment rose, or the population estimates were revised.

Elsewhere at primary level the changes were small. East Asia and Pacific rose from 0.9931 to 0.9970, Latin America and the Caribbean from 0.9792 to 0.9822, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.9561 to 0.9577. Low income countries moved from 0.9219 to 0.9263, so the persistent shortfall there narrowed only slightly. Reporting for 2022 is too thin to extend the comparison: only 4 countries reported primary values that year, and only 2 reported secondary values.

At secondary level the world index was almost unchanged, at 0.9896 in 2015 and 0.9887 in 2020. Beneath that stability the regions moved in different directions. Sub-Saharan Africa improved from 0.8678 to 0.9003, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9524 to 0.9646. These are the largest gains toward parity at this level, although both regions remain below 1.00. North America moved the other way, from 1.0102 to 0.9819, passing from a slight advantage for girls to a slight advantage for boys. The data do not identify the cause.

Tertiary enrolment shows the clearest gains for women. The world index rose from 1.1031 in 2015 to 1.1221 in 2024. South Asia passed parity, from 0.9540 to 1.0285, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 0.9995 to 1.0577. Lower middle income countries moved from 0.9593 to 1.0377. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.2253 to 1.2911, and North America from 1.2640 to 1.3008. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 0.7345 to 0.7942 by 2021, and low income countries from 0.6315 to 0.6719, yet both remain well below parity. At this level the remaining disparity favours men in the poorest settings and women almost everywhere else. East Asia and Pacific is the one region where the index slipped, from 1.1363 to 1.1275.

The data do not establish causes. The reference year 2020 coincides with school closures in most countries, and enrolment ratios for that year may reflect disrupted counts, delayed admissions or changed age structures rather than lasting shifts. Attribution to the pandemic, to policy or to longer trends is therefore cautious. The movements above describe where the index stood at two dates, not why it moved.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

Gender gaps that disadvantage girls are largest in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa, and they widen with the level of schooling. Low-income countries were below parity at all three levels: 0.926 at primary level in 2020, 0.819 at secondary level in 2020 and 0.672 at tertiary level in 2021. Other groups were also below parity in places: South Asia at tertiary level in 2015 (0.954), and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at primary level (0.976 in 2020) and secondary level (0.965 in 2020).

At secondary level, Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 0.900 in 2020, up from 0.868 in 2015. Among the regions with values for both years, this is the largest gain. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 0.952 to 0.965 over the same years and remained below parity. Low-income countries moved from 0.806 to 0.819. The direction is towards parity in each case, but no projection has been run on these series. Whether parity is reached by 2030 is therefore conjecture, and at the pace of 2015 to 2020 the low-income secondary gap would still be wide. At tertiary level the Sub-Saharan African index was 0.794 in 2021, up from 0.735 in 2015. South Asia stood at 1.029 in 2024, above parity.

At tertiary level the more common disparity now runs the other way. The world index rose from 1.103 in 2015 to 1.122 in 2024. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 1.225 to 1.291 and North America from 1.264 to 1.301, so the gap favouring women widened in those two regions; Europe and Central Asia stood at 1.153 in 2024, and East Asia and Pacific eased from 1.136 to 1.128. Target 4.5 can be read in two ways: as the elimination of gaps that disadvantage girls, or as the elimination of any gap in either direction. Under the first reading, the tertiary index is above parity in most reported regions. The second clause of the target, on equal access for the vulnerable, is not measured by these series, so the target as a whole cannot be declared met.

The evidence has limits that bear on 2030. Completion data by sex are reported by 192 countries in at least one year, but only 11 reported for 2025 and 110 for 2024. The low 2025 count may reflect the lag in release; the data cannot show whether collection has stopped. Recent completion gaps therefore cannot yet be measured. Secondary enrolment for 2022 comes from only 2 countries, too few for a global reading. The index also says nothing about disability, indigenous status or other vulnerabilities named in target 4.5, for which the shelf holds no series.

Four proposals follow, each tied to a finding.

First, national statistical offices and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should complete sex-disaggregated completion and enrolment returns within two years of the reference year, because only 11 countries reported primary completion for 2025 and 2 reported secondary enrolment for 2022. Until they do, current gaps in completion cannot be located. Progress would be monitored by the number of countries reporting each year.

Second, ministries of education and donors in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should concentrate on keeping girls in secondary school, because the secondary index was 0.900 and 0.819 in 2020. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps against girls, and would be monitored by the secondary index.

Third, ministries in low-income countries should widen access to tertiary education for women, because the low-income tertiary index was 0.672 in 2021, the lowest of any group reported.

Fourth, education ministries in Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, and Europe and Central Asia should monitor male participation at tertiary level, because the indices were 1.291, 1.301 and 1.153 in 2024. This relies on the reading of target 4.5 that counts gaps in either direction.
