w-c07-5-5.text:
### Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015

World net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, measured in constant 2023 dollars. That is a rise of more than half over eight years. In current dollars the series climbs from US$147.1 billion to US$259.5 billion. The two series meet in 2023 because the constant-price base year is 2023, so the gap between them in 2015 reflects the rise in prices since then. The constant-dollar figure is the fairer measure of change, since it removes the effect of rising prices; the current-dollar series shows a larger rise because it includes inflation.

The indicator needs careful reading before it is applied to target 6.a. It records all net official development assistance received by developing countries: grants and concessional loans, net of repayments of principal, across every sector. It does not isolate water and sanitation, nor the activities the target names, such as water harvesting, desalination, wastewater treatment, recycling and reuse. The series is therefore a proxy for the general scale of international support, and a rise in it does not show that more reached water and sanitation programmes. Spending on health, emergency relief, refugee costs or budget support can raise the total without any of it entering the sector.

The target itself adds a second limit. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building support by 2030, but it names no amount, no share of income and no baseline year. It can be read as a call for more money, for more technical assistance, or for better-targeted programmes, and a financial series speaks only to the first of these. Capacity-building, such as training, institutional support and technology transfer, is poorly captured by a measure of net disbursements. A judgement that the target is on track can therefore rest only on the direction of the aggregate, not on a threshold.

Coverage is also partial. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts in this series. The inequality analysis later in this section covers a different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023; the results do not state why the sets differ, and the use of population weights is a likely explanation rather than a finding. North America records zero in both years, which is consistent with a region of donors rather than recipients, and high-income economies receive only small amounts: US$319.3 million in 2015 and US$760.9 million in 2023 in constant dollars. Net receipts measure what arrives, not what is needed, so the series does not say whether the level is adequate against the water-stress and service gaps described elsewhere in this chapter.

With these limits stated, the direction is clear. Assistance received grew substantially after 2015 and, within the years 2015 to 2023 examined here, stood at its highest level in 2023, although the change in 2023 alone was slightly negative, at about -US$0.7 billion. Whether growth is sustained to 2030 is a separate matter, because the donor side of the ledger depends on budget decisions that recipient data cannot anticipate.

### Regions gained unevenly, and Europe and Central Asia gained most

Regional totals of net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, show that the increase since 2015 was not evenly shared. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest gain by a wide margin, rising from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023, about 4.7 times the 2015 level. In 2023 it was the second largest recipient region, behind sub-Saharan Africa (US$64.8 billion) and ahead of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region (US$35.1 billion). The series does not show what drove the rise, and it measures all official assistance, not the share spent on water.

The other regions moved much less. East Asia and Pacific received US$9.9 billion in 2015 and US$10.7 billion in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, almost no change in real terms. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion. These three regions ended the period within a narrow band of one another, near US$10.7 billion each, although their populations and water needs differ greatly. No population or per-person series is used in this section, so the totals say nothing about assistance per person; that comparison would need such a series. North America records zero in both years, as expected of a donor region rather than a recipient.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, a rise well below the world's increase. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the largest recipient, with US$51.8 billion in 2015 and US$64.8 billion in 2023. The largest absolute flows thus stayed in sub-Saharan Africa, while the fastest growth went to Europe and Central Asia.

The distribution by income group, also in constant 2023 dollars, shows a similar movement. Low-income countries received US$35.2 billion in 2015 and US$44.6 billion in 2023, and lower-middle-income countries US$54.9 billion and US$59.2 billion. Upper-middle-income countries rose from US$18.9 billion to US$57.4 billion, the fastest growth of the groups, and by 2023 they received more than the low-income group, whose receipts also rose. Target 6.a names developing countries generally rather than the poorest, so this pattern is not in itself a shortfall against it. Only a sector breakdown, which these series do not provide, could show whether water programmes followed the same path.

### A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase

The path of assistance since 2015 is not a steady climb. A structural break analysis of the annual change in world net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, places breaks in 2022 and 2023. The change in each year is treated as its own segment: from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion; in 2022 alone the change was US$49.8 billion, nearly eight times that long-run average; and in 2023 the change was about -US$0.7 billion, a single-year fall. The rise recorded between 2015 and 2023, when the world total went from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, therefore owes a large part to one year, and the gradual growth of the preceding two decades cannot be extrapolated from it. The 2022 change is large against that rise, but the series does not show a peak level in 2022: the 2023 level fell only slightly below it.

The data do not record why 2022 was exceptional. It is an inference, outside the data, that the jump reflects emergency and humanitarian flows, support to countries affected by conflict and displacement, and pandemic recovery financing. The series covers all purposes of assistance together and cannot separate such flows from spending on water and sanitation. Whether the 2023 fall marks a plateau or the start of a decline cannot be judged from one observation.

The distribution of assistance among recipient countries also changed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received rose from 0.361 in 2015, across 138 countries, to 0.452 in 2023, across 135 countries. The Theil index rose more sharply than the Gini coefficient, from 0.255 to 0.460, and the coefficient of variation rose most of the three, from 0.64 to 1.48. Assistance has thus become more unevenly spread among recipients. The country sets differ between the two years, and the 135 countries in the inequality analysis are not the same set as the 136 countries reporting in 2023 that underlie the world total, so part of the change may reflect which countries are included. The comparison should be read with that caution.

The composition of this inequality shifted too. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023. Differences among countries within the same region now account for a larger part of the disparity than differences between regions. This matters for targeting: regional averages conceal recipients that receive much more or much less than their neighbours, and allocation by region alone would miss them.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise is fragile and its distribution has become less even. Target 6.a calls for expanded cooperation and capacity-building support in water and sanitation. Total assistance, whatever its level, does not show how much reaches that sector, and a total lifted by one exceptional year is a weak guide to the sustained flows that infrastructure and capacity-building require.

### Assistance for 2030 must be tracked by sector and directed by need

The series held by the bench measures total official development assistance received, not assistance to water and sanitation. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building in water-related activities, and total flows cannot show whether that is happening. A rise in the aggregate may reflect humanitarian, budget-support or debt-related disbursements that have little to do with water supply, sewerage or wastewater treatment. For 2030, the first implication is therefore that progress on 6.a cannot be judged from the present evidence, and the headline figure of US$259.5 billion in 2023 should not be read as a measure of support for water.

The second implication concerns durability. The break analysis places breaks in 2022 and 2023. The change in 2022 alone was US$49.8 billion, against a mean annual change of US$6.4 billion over 2001 to 2021, and the change in 2023 alone was -US$0.7 billion, a small fall. A jump of that size, followed by a fall, suggests an exceptional episode, not a new trend; this reading is context, not a finding of the data. Planning that assumes the 2023 level will persist, or keep rising, risks a shortfall by 2030. The target can also be read in more than one way: it names no quantity of assistance, so expansion could mean volume, share of total aid or reach of capacity-building.

The third implication concerns distribution. Among countries, the Gini coefficient of assistance received, population-weighted and in constant 2023 dollars, rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.26 to 0.46. The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 45.3% to 29.6%, so the inequality lies increasingly within regions, among individual countries. The inequality analysis covers 135 countries in 2023, while the world total rests on 136 countries reporting, so the two sets differ slightly. In constant 2023 dollars, low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015, and sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion, yet the data do not show whether flows follow the countries with the weakest water and sanitation coverage. Upper middle income countries received US$57.4 billion in 2023, up from US$18.9 billion in 2015, a faster rise than that of low income countries, which is not a finding about need, since the target names developing countries generally and the data cannot show where water assistance went.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

claims.fact: c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015

proposals: Donors and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report water and sanitation disbursements to the World Bank's catalogue as a regular annual series by recipient country, so that progress on target 6.a can be measured directly instead of inferred from total assistance.

Ministries responsible for aid and national planners in recipient countries should base 2030 financing plans on the pre-2022 trend, not the exceptional 2022 jump, and should not assume the 2023 level will persist.

Donors should publish how water and sanitation allocations relate to service coverage gaps, so that flows can be judged against need, since the data show that assistance is increasingly unequal among countries.
w-c07-5-5.gaps: The bench holds no series of assistance to water and sanitation, so the volume, recipients and purposes of such aid are unknown. Nor does it hold capacity-building support, technology transfer or the share of commitments actually disbursed. Total assistance coverage differs between the world total and the inequality analysis, and target 6.a sets no quantity, so expansion can be read in more than one way.

w-c08-4-3.text:
### World energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured as megajoules of energy supply per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, fell from 4.8556 MJ in 2015 to 4.5449 MJ in 2021. That is a fall of 6.4 per cent, derived directly from the two levels. The direction is the one target 7.3 requires: each dollar of output needed less energy at the end of the period than at the start. The question for the section is whether the pace is the one the target asks for.

The trend tool expresses the world movement as a rate of -0.01096 per year, and classifies it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. That rate is the tool's own measure of change per year, and it is read here only as a direction and a pace relative to the tool's thresholds. The tool was run with no numerical target, so its classification rests on a generic benchmark and not on a figure derived from the wording of target 7.3. The label is a guide to the size of the gap, not a verdict on the target itself.

The target can be read in more than one way. Its wording, to double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, is commonly interpreted as doubling the rate recorded in an earlier period, which requires a baseline period to be chosen. The choice matters, because the earlier rate differs according to the years used. A second reading, used in the monitoring of the goals, sets a fixed annual rate of improvement in energy intensity for the whole period to 2030. The two readings need not give the same answer. The segment comparison in a later part tests only the first, using periods within the series; a rate for the years before 2015 is not held for the world as a whole, and the fixed-rate reading cannot be tested with the bench series.

The data also limit what can be said about the present. The world series ends in 2021, so the latest observation lies well before 2030 and says nothing about the years since. Regional series reach 2022 in some cases, and the number of countries reporting in 2022 was 116, so the final year rests on thinner coverage. Any statement that the world is or is not on course for 2030 is therefore an extrapolation from six years of change, a period that includes the sharp fall and partial rebound in economic activity around 2020. Movements in GDP affect the ratio as much as movements in energy supply, so a change in intensity does not by itself show that efficiency measures were adopted.

Why the measure matters is plain enough. Energy intensity is the broadest indicator available of how much energy an economy needs to produce its output, and a falling value lowers fuel costs, emissions and import dependence for a given level of output. It is, however, a crude proxy for efficiency, because it also reflects the structure of an economy, its climate, and the share of heavy industry in output. The following parts examine how these differences appear across regions and over time.

### Regions diverge from a 2.58 to a 6.14 MJ range by 2021 or 2022

Regional levels of energy intensity, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, span a wide range by the latest year available. Europe and Central Asia is lowest, at 2.5791 MJ in 2022, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest among regions, at 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The latest year differs between regions, 2021 for some and 2022 for others, so the comparison is approximate and the gap between regions is read as indicative rather than exact.

Europe and Central Asia fell from 4.002 MJ in 2015 to 2.5791 MJ in 2022. Its rate of change, -0.0608 per year, is the steepest of any region and the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions. Part of the decline in this region may reflect changes in economic structure and in fuel supply as well as efficiency gains; the data do not separate these.

North America and South Asia also improved substantially. North America moved from 5.0428 MJ in 2015 to 4.364 MJ in 2022, at a rate of -0.0204 per year, and South Asia from 4.5047 MJ to 3.9427 MJ in 2021, at -0.022 per year. Both are classed as on track or target met. South Asia's result is notable because it began from a level close to the world value and has since fallen below it.

The remaining regions made less headway. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5.6997 MJ in 2015 to 5.2313 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0142 per year, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 3.4822 MJ to 3.265 MJ in 2022, at -0.0092 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Its level is low, which may leave less room for further cuts, but the data do not test that.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan barely moved, from 5.3599 MJ in 2015 to 5.332 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0009 per year, classed as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa also stagnated, falling from 6.2412 MJ to 6.1403 MJ in 2021, at -0.0027 per year. Together these two regions combine high or middling levels with almost no improvement.

Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income economies stood at 7.415 MJ in 2015 and 7.1393 MJ in 2021, the highest of any group, with a rate of -0.0063 per year, classed as marginal progress. High-income economies fell from 4.3961 MJ to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, at -0.0334 per year, classed as on track or target met. Lower middle income fell from 4.644 MJ to 4.2707 MJ in 2021, and upper middle income from 5.5767 MJ to 5.2119 MJ. The poorest economies are therefore the most energy-intensive per unit of output and are improving most slowly.

Three cautions apply. First, only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the latest regional values rest on incomplete years, and regions with data only to 2021 are compared with others to 2022. Second, intensity reflects economic structure, climate, fuel mix and the share of traditional biomass in supply, and the purchasing power parity conversion of GDP, not efficiency alone. Third, the world rate of -0.011 per year is classed as marginal progress, so the regional divergence matters for 2030: the regions that are on track are not those with the highest levels, and the highest-intensity regions are those where acceleration is most needed.

### Improvement peaked before 2018 and has since slowed

The structural breaks in the annual change of world energy intensity show that the pace of improvement has not been steady. The series for the world, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, has breaks in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. These divide the record into five segments, each with its own mean annual change. A negative mean change means that intensity fell, so a larger negative figure means faster improvement.

In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ. It steepened to -0.1154 MJ in 2005-2008, the fastest pace of the early period. The break in 2009 marks a pause: in 2009-2010 the mean change was 0.0070 MJ, so intensity rose slightly instead of falling. That coincides with the global financial crisis, and a link between the two is a reasonable reading, though the data do not establish it. One possible mechanism, not tested by the data, is that output fell sharply while much of the energy supply in buildings, transport and industrial plant could not be scaled down as quickly, which tends to raise intensity in a downturn.

The break in 2011 opens the longest segment. In 2011-2017 the mean annual change was -0.1045 MJ, close to the pace of 2005-2008 and about twice that of 2001-2004. This matters for the target. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement, and the baseline year of 2015 sits inside this faster period. Any comparison of later years with the rate at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals is therefore a comparison with a stretch of unusually quick improvement, not with the slower pace of the early 2000s. Reading the target against the rate of -0.0498 MJ would make doubling look nearer than it is when set against the rate that prevailed in 2015.

The final break, in 2018, is the most consequential. In 2018-2021 the mean annual change was -0.0325 MJ, less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017, and a smaller fall than in 2001-2004 (-0.0325 against -0.0498 MJ per year). Improvement therefore peaked before 2018 and has since slowed. The segment is short, four years, and its end includes 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic disturbed both output and energy supply. A short segment with unusual years at its end warrants caution, and the mean should not be taken as a settled new trend.

The data do not identify why the slowdown occurred. Several explanations are plausible and are offered only as interpretations, not findings. The pandemic caused abrupt falls and rebounds in activity that distort a ratio of energy to output. Fuel prices affect the incentive to economise on energy, and the price changes of these years may have weakened it. Structural change in industry, including shifts in the weight of energy-intensive sectors in world output, can move intensity independently of efficiency in any single sector. The series measures energy per unit of GDP, so it blends efficiency with the composition of the economy, and none of these causes can be separated from the others using this result alone.

For 2030 the implication is conditional. If the rate of 2018-2021 persisted, the world would fall well short of doubling the rate of 2011-2017, let alone exceeding it. Meeting the target on the most demanding reading would require a pace far above any segment in the record. The target also admits more than one reading, since the earlier rate may be taken from the period before 2015 or from the baseline decade, and the choice changes the threshold. The segment comparison tests only the reading that uses periods within the series; the pre-2015 reading is not tested here. On the comparison made, the break of 2018 shows that the recent direction is away from the target, not towards it.

### Doubling the earlier rate is not met, and proposals follow

On the segment comparison, doubling the recent rate is not met. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency, but it does not say which earlier rate is to be doubled or which period is to be compared. Three readings are possible: the pace before 2015 set against the pace after it, a fixed earlier rate set against the pace to 2030, and the pace in the years of fastest improvement set against the most recent years. The bench holds no pre-2015 rate, so the first reading cannot be tested here, and the fixed-rate reading also remains untested. The comparison below tests the third reading alone: the 2011-2017 segment of the world series against the 2018-2021 segment. The verdict holds for that comparison only.

From 2011 to 2017 the mean annual change in energy intensity was -0.1045 MJ per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. From 2018 to 2021 it was -0.0325 MJ. Doubling would require a recent pace of about twice the earlier one, and the recent pace is much slower, so intensity is falling more slowly, not twice as fast. The trend tool classes the world rate of -0.01096 as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the results do not state the period of that rate. The segment from 2018 to 2021 includes the pandemic years, when output and energy supply both moved sharply, so part of the slowdown may reflect those disturbances and not a lasting change. Only four years are covered, and the data cannot separate the two explanations.

Regional results show where the world picture is made. Four groups are classed as on track or target met: Europe and Central Asia, with the steepest rate of any region at -0.06083, the high-income group at -0.03337, South Asia at -0.02197 and North America at -0.02044. The label reflects the tool's own benchmark and does not show that those groups are doubling a previous rate. The high-income group fell from 4.3961 MJ in 2015 to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 4.002 MJ to 2.5791 MJ over the same years. Efficiency gains, structural change and fuel switching are familiar possible explanations in richer economies, but the results do not establish which applies.

The regions with the least progress are, in several cases, those with high levels. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a rate of -0.00271, and its intensity moved from 6.2412 MJ in 2015 to 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is also classed as stagnating, at -0.00087, with levels of 5.3599 MJ in 2015 and 5.332 MJ in 2021. East Asia and Pacific shows moderate progress, at -0.01419, but acceleration is needed there: its intensity fell from 5.6997 MJ to 5.2313 MJ. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.00916, and the low-income group, at -0.00629, show marginal progress. The low-income group still has the highest level of any income group, at 7.1393 MJ in 2021. These readings are indicative, since end years and trend periods differ across regions.

For 2030 the implication is plain. Unless the pace rises well above the 2018 to 2021 mean, the doubling is not met on the segment comparison. The latest data point is 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, so later developments are not visible. Only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the most recent figures rest on incomplete reporting.

Intensity is also an imperfect measure of efficiency. It divides energy supply by output, so it moves with the structure of an economy, climate and trade as well as technical efficiency. A fall may come from a shift to services without any gain in equipment efficiency, and a flat series may hide improvements offset by growth in energy-heavy activity. The proposals respond to these limits and to the regional gaps, and none presumes which measures would work.

proposals: National energy ministries in Sub-Saharan Africa and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group should collect sector-level energy use data and set efficiency targets for whichever sectors that data show to dominate supply, since national intensity cannot show which sectors or measures would work.

The statistical offices and international agencies that compile energy balances should raise the number of countries reporting in the latest year, so that the pace after 2021 can be read for all regions.

Development financiers should give priority to energy-efficiency programmes in the low-income group and the stagnating regions, and should require each programme to report sector-level results, so that stagnating rates and high levels are met with evidence of what works.
The bodies responsible for monitoring target 7.3 should state which earlier rate is to be doubled and over which period, so that progress can be judged against one agreed reading.
w-c08-4-3.gaps: The bench holds no pre-2015 rate of improvement, so the reading comparing the pace before and after 2015 is untested, as is a fixed-rate reading. The latest data are for 2021 or 2022, and only 116 countries reported in 2022. Intensity cannot separate efficiency from economic structure, climate, trade and fuel mix, and no series on sector-level energy use is used here. The 2018 to 2021 segment is short and includes the pandemic years.

w-c08-3-5.text:
### The global share rose by 2.3 percentage points between 2015 and 2020

The world share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption stood at 17.4 per cent in 2015 and 19.7 per cent in 2020. The share therefore rose over the five years, and the direction is clear. Whether the magnitude meets the aim of the target is a separate question, and the data alone do not settle it. Over the period the share grew at a compound rate of 0.0255 a year, which the trend tool classes as on track or target met. That label rests on a trend tool that has no numerical target to measure against, so it should be read as a statement about the pace of change, not as a verdict on sufficiency.

Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix, and it names no threshold. Two readings are available. The first is a rise in the share: renewables supply a larger fraction of all final energy. The second is a rise in absolute use: more renewable energy is consumed, whatever the fraction. The two can diverge. Where total demand grows quickly, absolute renewable use can climb while the share stagnates or falls. The indicator reported here, renewable energy consumption as a percentage of total final energy consumption, measures only the first reading. A rise in the share is the stricter test, because it requires renewables to outpace the growth of demand as a whole.

The word 'substantial' compounds the ambiguity. No agreed numerical benchmark exists in the target text, so any judgement of sufficiency rests on a chosen standard: a doubling, a fixed number of points, or a path consistent with climate goals. Since no such standard is set in the target, this account treats the change from 17.4 to 19.7 per cent as an observed change and states plainly where a reader's own threshold would alter the verdict. By any reading, a gain of this size from a base of 17.4 per cent leaves the large majority of final energy supplied by other sources in 2020.

The composition of the indicator also matters for interpretation. Final energy consumption includes heat and transport as well as electricity, and the renewable share counts traditional biomass such as wood and charcoal burned for cooking and heating. A share can therefore be high in poor countries because of reliance on fuelwood, which is neither modern nor clean, and the aims of Goal 7 treat it differently from wind, solar or hydropower. The headline figure thus mixes two quite different kinds of renewable use, a point taken up in the regional comparisons that follow.

A limit on the evidence must be stated. The series is reported by 212 countries in every year from 2015 to 2021, but only 71 countries report a value for 2022. For most countries, therefore, the record ends in 2020 or 2021 for practical purposes, and the comparison of 2015 with 2020 is the last one that rests on near-complete coverage. Developments after 2020, including the recovery from the pandemic and the energy price shocks that followed, cannot be read from this series with confidence. For the 2030 horizon, this means the trajectory is known only for the first five of fifteen years, and the later years remain to be measured.

### Regional levels differ by a factor of ten, and nearly all regions rose

Regional levels of the renewable share span a wide range. In 2020 Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 70.3 per cent of total final energy consumption, South Asia at 36.9 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 34.2 per cent. At the other end, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded 7.5 per cent. The highest regional value is therefore about nine times the lowest, and the gap is wide in both years.

The ranking does not measure the quality of the energy system. In poorer regions a high share may reflect the burning of wood, charcoal, crop residues and dung for cooking and heating, which counts as renewable in the indicator. These fuels are often gathered unsustainably, carry serious health costs through indoor air pollution, and supply energy of low efficiency. A low share in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan may follow from large oil and gas endowments that have long dominated power generation and final use; this is context from outside the data. The indicator cannot separate traditional biomass from modern capacity such as wind, solar, hydropower or modern bioenergy, so a region can score high with little modern renewable infrastructure and low with a fast-growing one. Other series on the shelf, such as electricity output and output excluding hydropower, give a partial view of modern capacity but cover electricity only.

All six regions rose between 2015 and 2020. Latin America and the Caribbean gained from 28.2 to 34.2 per cent, the largest rise of any region. Europe and Central Asia moved from 12.9 to 15.1 per cent, East Asia and Pacific from 13.0 to 14.8 per cent, and North America from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent. The results do not test why these regions rose; falling costs of wind and solar and policy support are commonly cited in the wider literature, as context outside the data. South Asia rose more slowly, from 34.9 to 36.9 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 68.0 to 70.3 per cent. In both, a rise in the share is ambiguous: it may reflect new modern capacity, or continued reliance on biomass. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved only from 7.1 to 7.5 per cent.

The income groups show the same pattern and one reversal. The low-income group fell from 77.0 to 74.6 per cent between 2015 and 2020, the only group to decline. The fall does not necessarily signal a worsening of the energy system. As incomes rise and electricity and fossil fuels reach more households, the biomass share can fall before modern renewables replace it, so a lower share may accompany a real improvement in access. Equally, it may reflect growth in fossil-fuel use that outpaces renewables. The indicator alone cannot tell which. Lower middle income countries rose from 41.7 to 43.3 per cent, upper middle income countries from 14.9 to 16.8 per cent, and high income countries from 10.6 to 12.8 per cent.

The rise was broad across regions but small in the regions with the highest shares and absent in the low-income group, where the share fell. Reading target 7.2 as a rise in the share, the world rose; reading it as growth in modern, sustainable renewables, the aggregate hides much of what matters, because the indicator cannot show modern capacity. Coverage also limits comparison: 71 countries reported in 2022, so the latest year cannot yet confirm whether the gains held after the shock of 2020. The results do not project values for 2030.

### Country trajectories diverge: 73 on track, 85 in regression

The classification of countries separates the world into groups whose experience since 2015 has been very different. Of 202 countries assessed, 73 are classed as on track or target met, and these hold 37.5 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 11 countries show moderate progress, but acceleration is needed (3.8 per cent of population), and 14 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration (22.2 per cent). Nineteen countries are stagnating (4.8 per cent of population). The largest group by count is the 85 countries in regression, which hold 31.8 per cent of the population.

The label 'on track' needs careful reading. Target 7.2 asks for a substantial increase in the renewable share but gives no numeric value, so no threshold exists against which progress can be measured. The classification therefore rests on an extrapolated rate of change: the observed trend is projected forward to 2030, and a country is called on track when the direction is positive and the pace is adequate by the tool's own scale. 'On track' here means a positive trend only. It does not mean that a country will reach any particular share, and a country that starts from a very low share can be called on track while remaining far from a renewable-based energy system. The reading of 'substantially' is open: a rise of a few points could count under one interpretation and fall short under another.

Count and population tell different stories. The on-track group holds the largest population share of any class, 37.5 per cent, yet it has fewer countries (73) than the regression group (85), whose population share is 31.8 per cent. Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries, and the two classes hold 4.8 and 31.8 per cent of the population respectively. The data therefore show a split world: a large share of people live in countries with a positive trend, and a comparable share live in countries where the share has fallen. The world rate of 0.0255 is positive and classed as on track, but it is an aggregate and does not describe each country.

The regional rates help to explain the pattern. The rates for East Asia and Pacific (0.0267), Europe and Central Asia (0.0325), North America (0.0370) and Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0390) are all classed as on track, as are the high income (0.0381) and upper middle income (0.0240) groups. The groups under the greatest strain are the low income group, where the rate is negative at -0.0064 and classed as regression, and the lower middle income group, at 0.0079, classed as marginal. Sub-Saharan Africa (0.0065) and South Asia (0.0112) are also marginal, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0129) show moderate progress.

The indicator does not reveal why the share falls in low income settings, and the following is context, not a finding. The renewable share of final consumption in such countries is widely understood to be dominated by traditional biomass used for cooking and heating. If total consumption grows with non-renewable supply, or households shift away from biomass, the share can fall even while other goals advance. A fall is therefore not necessarily a failure of renewable policy. The gains in richer regions are commonly linked to deliberate expansion of modern renewables, but the share alone cannot confirm what was added.

For 2030 the implication is that a positive global rate can coexist with 85 regressing countries. The target will be met in substance only if the lagging groups change course, and the data cannot say whether modern renewables are replacing traditional biomass or merely sitting beside it.

### Convergence is weak and coverage thins after 2020

The convergence test asks whether countries that began with a low renewable share have gained faster than those that began high. Across 71 countries with data for both 2015 and 2022, the estimated coefficient is -0.0101 (p 0.0006, R2 0.190). The negative sign indicates that countries starting higher changed by less each year, so low-share countries gained slightly faster, and the p-value of 0.0006 indicates that the relationship is unlikely to be chance. The magnitude is small, however, and an R2 of 0.190 means that initial level explains under one fifth of the variation in change. The remainder lies elsewhere. National policy, resource endowment, the pace of electrification and the use of traditional biomass are plausible influences, but they are context only, since the results do not measure them.

The coefficient of variation points the same way. It stood at 1.040 in 2015 and at 1.039 in 2022, a change in the third decimal place. Dispersion across these countries is therefore not narrowing. A coefficient near 1.0 means that the standard deviation of national shares is about equal to their mean, which describes a very unequal distribution. Weak catch-up in the slope, combined with unchanged dispersion, means that the spread of national shares in 2022 was about what it had been in 2015.

This result needs careful reading because the renewable share in final consumption mixes two quite different things. In many low-income countries a high share reflects reliance on firewood and charcoal, not modern renewable capacity, and a fall in that share can accompany progress in clean cooking and electrification. In high-income countries a rising share usually reflects wind, solar and hydropower in the electricity system. These are well-established patterns, but the indicator cannot separate them. A convergence test that treats both as one scale cannot distinguish a desirable fall in traditional biomass from a failure to expand modern renewables. The weak convergence found here should not be read as proof that poorer countries are being left behind in modern renewable deployment.

The sample is also a limit. Reporting for this series was broad in the early years: 207 countries in 2000, 210 in 2010 and 212 in every year from 2012 to 2021. In 2022 it fell to 71 countries. The 212 countries of 2021 and the 71 of 2022 are not comparable bases, and the data do not show that the 71 are a random draw from the 212. The convergence estimate describes only those that reported, and it cannot be extended to the world or to any region without that caveat.

The drop matters for 2030 because the years after 2020 are the ones in which the pandemic recovery, the energy price shock and new policies would show. Those years are visible for only a third of countries. The series is fully covered to 2021, so the record to that year is secure, while any statement about 2022 rests on a partial group. This is a reporting lag, not a finding of decline, and it should be read as a gap in evidence.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The share has risen, from 17.4 per cent in 2015 to 19.7 per cent in 2020. Whether that is substantial cannot be settled from the data, because target 7.2 sets no number. Read as any increase, the world figure moved in the right direction. The world rate of 0.0255 a year is a pace of change only, and it is not a verdict on whether that pace suffices. The results do not project 2030, so no forecast of the 2030 share is offered here.

The countries are divided. Of the 202 countries assessed, 85 are in regression, holding 31.8 per cent of the population of the countries assessed, and 19 show stagnation, holding 4.8 per cent. A rising world average therefore conceals a large population living where the share has fallen or stood still. Set against the 37.5 per cent of the population in the 73 on-track countries, the 31.8 per cent in regression is of a similar order. Each class should be read with its own count and population share, as stated here.

The low-income group shows the problem most clearly. Its share fell from 77.0 per cent in 2015 to 74.6 per cent in 2020, yet the level remains very high. As context outside the data, such levels usually reflect reliance on firewood, charcoal and other traditional biomass, which counts as renewable in this series but is neither modern nor clean. A fall in the share can accompany welcome developments, such as grid expansion, and a high share can accompany poverty and indoor air pollution. The indicator alone cannot separate these cases, and conclusions for the poorest countries must be drawn with that caution.

For 2030, the results show where acceleration is needed. The 14 countries with marginal progress hold 22.2 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. The tools do not measure how much each group contributes to the global figure, so no claim is made about which group would move it most. Convergence is weak, and the 2022 data cover only 71 countries, so the picture after 2020 cannot be confirmed for most of the world. The data do not show whether the fall in reporting reflects a reporting lag or a change in countries' outcomes.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

w-c05-6-4.text:
### Global literacy stands at 87.7 per cent among adults and 93.1 per cent among youth

Literacy, as the World Bank series defines it, is the share of people who can both read and write, with understanding, a short simple statement about their everyday life. Adults are those aged 15 and above; youth are those aged 15 to 24. The measure is a threshold of basic ability. It says nothing about fluency, about comprehension of complex texts, or about the skills needed to function in a digital economy.

On this measure the world is largely literate. The adult rate stood at 85.96 per cent in 2015 and reached 87.74 per cent in 2024. The youth rate rose from 91.4 per cent in 2015 to 93.11 per cent in 2024. Youth rates exceed adult rates in the world figures for both years. As context rather than a finding, this is consistent with younger cohorts having had more schooling than older adults, which would also lift the adult rate as cohorts replace one another; the results hold no schooling or cohort data to test that explanation.

Target 4.6 asks for more than the indicator can show. It commits countries to ensure that all youth and a substantial proportion of adults, men and women alike, achieve literacy and numeracy. The series held on the bench measures literacy only; it gives no figure for numeracy, so half of the target's wording cannot be assessed here. The phrase 'a substantial proportion of adults' has no fixed threshold. It can be read as a majority, as most adults, or as a rate close to universal. Under the first two readings the world adult rate of 87.74 per cent in 2024 already meets the target; under the third it does not. The results do not fix which reading applies, and no trend-to-target result is held for adults, so no adult rating or expected 2030 value can be given. The adult pace can be read only from the two end points: a rise of 1.78 percentage points over nine years in the world rate is not a computed rating, and it is left to the reader. For youth the wording is stricter: 'all' implies 100 per cent, and the 2024 figure of 93.11 per cent falls short of it.

The figures are global averages and conceal wide differences between regions and income groups, which the later parts of this section take up. They also rest on a limited number of surveys and censuses: only 29 countries reported an adult value in 2024 and 29 a youth value, against 33 and 35 in 2023, so most of the figures for that year are not fresh national measurements. The results do not give the latest year of each country's value, nor how many aggregate values rest on earlier years or on modelled estimates, so the currency of the headline values cannot be stated precisely. The next part examines how far the headline values can be trusted given that coverage.

### Data coverage is thin and uneven, so the latest values are partly modelled or dated

Literacy data are reported by far fewer countries in any single year than the headline coverage suggests. Across all years, 155 countries have at least one adult literacy value and 160 have at least one youth value. Yet in any one year only a fraction report. Adult reporting ranged from 13 countries in 2003 to 56 in 2019, and youth reporting from 23 countries in 2003 to 62 in 2019. The latest year, 2024, holds only 29 countries in each series.

As general context, outside the results, literacy rates usually come from population censuses and household surveys, which arrive at intervals of several years rather than annually. A country then appears in the record in the year of an exercise and is absent in the years between. The counts are consistent with such a calendar: adult reporting climbed from 32 countries in 2008 to 48 in 2010 and 53 in 2011, then fell to 33 in 2013. Swings of this kind are better read as differences in which countries reported than as changes in literacy itself.

The period after 2015 shows the same unevenness. Adult reporting stood at 47 countries in 2015, reached 56 in 2019, then fell to 42 in 2020, the year the pandemic disrupted fieldwork in many places, as general context. Youth reporting went from 62 countries in 2019 to 43 in 2020. A partial recovery appeared in 2022, with 45 countries for adults and 58 for youth, before the counts dropped to 33 and 35 in 2023 and to 29 in both series in 2024.

The question of how current the data are can be answered only in part. The results show that 29 countries report a value for 2024 in each series, against 155 and 160 countries with a value in some year. The tools used here count reports by calendar year; they do not return each country's latest year, so the number of countries whose latest value is older than 2024, and the typical lag, could not be retrieved and are not stated. What the counts do imply is that most countries with any literacy value have no observation for 2024, and that any 2024 aggregate therefore leans on earlier surveys, on modelling, or on both. The aggregates carry different labels: the world, regional and income-group values are mostly dated 2024, but Europe and Central Asia is dated 2023, North America 2022, and high income 2020 for adults and 2021 for youth. The results do not record whether any aggregate is observed, carried forward or modelled, so the share of dated or modelled values is unknown. Surveys held late in the period are commonly published after a delay, so recent years may be filled in later, although the results do not show this directly.

Three cautions follow. First, regional and world values for recent years rest on few direct observations, and a country's latest value may be several years old even when labelled with a recent year. Second, year-on-year comparison is unreliable, because a change between two years may reflect a different set of countries or method rather than real movement. Third, the sparse high-income record, with a single adult value in 2020, means that the strongest literacy performers are the least visible. Comparisons are safer over longer spans, and the findings that follow are read with these limits in mind.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia hold the largest gaps, and women trail men

The widest gaps lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. In 2024 adult literacy in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 68.7 per cent and in South Asia at 78.2 per cent, against 96.6 per cent in East Asia and Pacific. Europe and Central Asia, at 98.8 per cent in 2023, and North America, at 98.8 per cent in 2022, sit close to the ceiling. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached 75.6 per cent in 2024. The adult figure covers everyone aged 15 and above, so it moves slowly. As outside context rather than a finding of these results, regions in which many older people never attended school carry that history in their totals.

The adult half of target 4.6 can be read only from levels, because the results hold no trend-to-target rating for adults. Target 4.6 asks for a substantial proportion of adults, and the wording sets no threshold, so it can be read in more than one way. Read against the world level, adult literacy rose from 86.0 per cent in 2015 to 87.7 per cent in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 64.3 to 68.7 per cent, South Asia from 72.0 to 78.2 per cent, and low-income countries from 59.7 to 63.6 per cent. These are gains of a few points over nine years, and none of these groups is near universal adult literacy. The results do not project adults to 2030, so the pace needed is not stated here.

The youth series shows a different and more encouraging pattern. South Asia's youth literacy rose from 89.6 per cent in 2015 to 96.9 per cent in 2024, the largest regional gain in the results. Whether schooling expansion explains the rise is not tested here; it is the usual context offered for such changes, and the results contain no schooling data. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 75.2 to 79.0 per cent over the same period, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 85.0 to 86.9 per cent. Youth literacy in East Asia and Pacific, at 99.1 per cent in 2024, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, at 98.7 per cent, has little room left to grow. By income group, low-income countries reached 75.4 per cent among youth in 2024 and 63.6 per cent among adults, while upper middle income countries stood at 99.3 and 96.2 per cent. Lower middle income countries recorded 92.0 per cent for youth and 78.3 per cent for adults.

Women trail men, and the shortfall is largest where overall literacy is lowest. Worldwide, adult female literacy was 84.6 per cent in 2024, below the adult total of 87.7 per cent. In Sub-Saharan Africa it was 62.7 per cent, in South Asia 71.6 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 67.4 per cent. In low-income countries it was 56.4 per cent. Adult female literacy in each of these groups was higher in 2024 than in 2015: Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 56.8 per cent, South Asia from 63.5 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 63.0 per cent, and low-income countries from 50.9 per cent. Starting levels were low.

The youth gender parity index, the ratio of female to male literacy, shows younger women closing the gap. It stood at 0.98 worldwide in 2024, up from 0.97 in 2015. South Asia rose from 0.96 to 0.99. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 0.90 to 0.94, and low-income countries from 0.87 to 0.93. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached only 0.92, up from 0.90, the lowest regional value in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America were at 1.00 in their latest years, as the index is reported to two decimals. Only 29 countries reported in 2024, so the latest regional values rest on a small and shifting set of observations, and part of any change may reflect which countries report. The results do not say how many of those values are modelled or carried forward, so that question stays open. Shifts after 2020 cannot be separated from this reporting pattern in these results.

### Progress is real but too slow to reach universal youth literacy by 2030, and the proposals follow

The trend-to-target results for youth literacy show progress that is real but, in every region except South Asia, too slow to reach the 2030 target on the current pace. South Asia is rated on track, but on a projection that exceeds the 100 per cent ceiling, so that rating is unreliable. The target value is 100.0 per cent, and the tool compares the observed pace since 2015 with the pace needed to reach it. The world as a whole is rated as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a ratio of 0.33 and an expected youth literacy rate of 94.3 per cent in 2030.

Even regions close to the ceiling are not rated as on track. East Asia and Pacific rose from 98.9 per cent in 2015 to 99.1 per cent in 2024 and is expected to reach 99.2 per cent in 2030, a ratio of 0.28 and a marginal rating. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 98.3 per cent to 98.7 per cent, with an expected 98.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.39. Europe and Central Asia is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.68 and an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030. High income is also moderate, with a ratio of 0.53 and an expected 99.6 per cent. North America is rated as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.07. Regions near the ceiling have little distance left to close, which is context rather than a finding, and the results give no measurement-error figure against which these small movements could be judged.

The larger shortfalls lie where the starting level was lower. Low income is rated marginal and is expected to reach 77.9 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.22. Sub-Saharan Africa is rated marginal, with an expected 81.6 per cent and a ratio of 0.26. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is rated marginal, with an expected 88.2 per cent and a ratio of 0.21. Lower middle income is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.63 and an expected 95.3 per cent. South Asia is the single region rated on track, with a ratio of 1.20, but its expected 2030 value of 102.1 per cent exceeds the ceiling and cannot be a literal rate. No region is therefore shown to reach universal youth literacy by 2030 on a sound projection.

The adult half of target 4.6 can be read only from levels, because no trend-to-target result is held for adults. The target asks for all youth but only a substantial proportion of adults, a phrase it does not define. Here it is read as a rising adult rate approaching the youth rate, and no threshold is tested. World adult literacy rose from 86.0 per cent in 2015 to 87.7 per cent in 2024. Low income moved from 59.7 per cent to 63.6 per cent, Sub-Saharan Africa from 64.3 per cent to 68.7 per cent, and South Asia from 72.0 per cent to 78.2 per cent. Adult female literacy in low-income countries was 56.4 per cent in 2024, against 50.9 per cent in 2015. These levels show the distance remaining, but the results give neither a pace nor a rating for adults, so adult progress cannot be called on or off track. The trend tool could be run on the adult series, which would settle this.

Currency also limits every reading. In 2024 only 29 countries reported adult literacy and 29 reported youth literacy. The results do not give the latest year of each country's value, so how many countries rely on values older than 2024, and by how many years, was not retrievable. The share of regional and world values resting on older surveys or modelled estimates is likewise unknown. Numeracy, which the target names, has no measure in the series held.

Proposals follow from these findings. National statistical offices in countries without recent surveys should run literacy surveys or add literacy questions to household surveys, since only 29 countries reported in 2024. The World Bank and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should publish the reference year and the source type, survey or modelled, for each country value, so that currency can be judged. Governments and donors in low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa should expand adult and second-chance programmes aimed at women, because adult female literacy there was 56.4 per cent in 2024, noting that the marginal ratings concern youth. The council should run the trend-to-target tool on adult literacy so that the adult half of target 4.6 has a pace and a rating.

w-c09-2-5.text:
### World output per worker has risen by a fifth since 2015

Output per worker is the measure the bench uses for target 8.2, which asks for higher levels of economic productivity. GDP per person employed, expressed in constant 2021 purchasing power parity dollars, stood at 42,386 in 2015 and reached 50,672 in 2025. The trend tool puts the compound rate at 1.8 per cent a year over the decade and reads this pace as moderate progress, but with acceleration needed. The world figure has therefore risen by roughly a fifth, a description drawn from the two cited levels rather than from a separate result.

The result matters because productivity is the main route by which employment translates into rising living standards. An economy can raise total output by adding workers, but only gains in output per worker allow wages and public revenue to grow without more labour being drawn in. A global rate of 1.8 per cent a year is positive and sustained, yet it is a pace that would double output per worker only over roughly four decades. The target's call for diversification, technological upgrading and innovation implies a faster and broader movement than this average suggests.

The indicator has no numeric target. Target 8.2 says only that productivity should be higher, so the reading rests on direction and pace rather than a threshold. Any classification of progress, including the one used here, depends on a rule applied by the tool to the observed rate of change, and a different rule would give a different label. The finding that the world has moved in the right direction is firm; the finding that the pace is moderate is a judgement about what pace would suffice.

The period contains breaks. The break tool dates shifts in the annual change of the world series to 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The mean annual change was 967.5 dollars a year across 2010 to 2019, fell to a loss of 369.1 dollars in 2020, rebounded to a gain of 1,566.8 dollars in 2021, and averaged 815.5 dollars a year across 2022 to 2025. Because output per worker is a ratio, a shock can move it in either direction: when low-productivity jobs are lost first, the ratio can rise even as total output falls. The ten-year change reported here therefore compresses a path that was neither smooth nor driven by a single cause, and the endpoints alone do not separate lasting gains from statistical effects of the shock. Weak investment and slow trade expansion in many economies after 2015 are well-known context, though not tested here.

The limits of the series should be stated plainly. Output per worker divides GDP by total employment, so it inherits the weaknesses of both. Employment estimates in many countries rest on modelled values rather than regular labour force surveys, and informal work is imperfectly captured. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, fewer than the 177 of earlier years, so the latest values rest on a smaller set of economies and the world aggregate for 2025 is partly an estimate. Comparisons across years should be read with that in mind.

For 2030, the recent post-2022 pace of change is below the 2010 to 2019 average, so a rate of about 1.8 per cent a year is not assured. Even if it holds, the global average would rest on very uneven foundations. The sections that follow show that the world figure conceals regions where output per worker has risen quickly and others where it has fallen.

### Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker

Regional output per worker in 2025 ranges from 12,931 dollars in Sub-Saharan Africa to 152,091 dollars in North America, a spread of roughly twelve times between the lowest and highest regions. In 2025 a worker in North America produced 152,091 dollars of GDP (constant 2021 PPP), and one in Europe and Central Asia produced 103,033 dollars. South Asia stood at 24,604 dollars, so that North America stands at roughly six times its level. The low-income group, which is an income grouping and not a region, stood at 6,041 dollars, and the gap between North America and that group is wider still, at roughly twenty-five times. Differences of this size are commonly attributed to capital per worker, the sectoral mix of employment, the quality of institutions and the technology in use. None of these is tested here, since the bench holds no series on them for this section.

Growth since 2015 has not been even. East Asia and Pacific rose from 33,564 dollars to 49,219 dollars, a rate of 3.9 per cent a year, and the trend tool classes it as on track. South Asia rose from 17,922 dollars to 24,604 dollars, at 3.2 per cent a year, also classed on track. Shifts of labour from farming to manufacturing and services, with sustained investment, are the usual route to such gains and match what target 8.2 describes through diversification and technological upgrading, although this section does not test that explanation. East Asia and Pacific now stands close to the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, which reached 50,325 dollars in 2025, up from 46,188 dollars in 2015, a pace of 0.9 per cent a year that is classed as marginal progress.

The richer regions advanced at a moderate pace. Europe and Central Asia rose from 88,803 dollars to 103,033 dollars, at 1.5 per cent a year. North America rose from 132,207 dollars to 152,091 dollars, at 1.4 per cent a year. Both are classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Because these gains start from very high levels, a modest rate adds a large absolute amount per worker. Comparing the levels given, each of these regions added more dollars per worker than South Asia did, even though South Asia grew faster in proportion. Growth rates may therefore favour poorer regions while absolute gaps persist or widen.

Two regions stand apart for lack of progress. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 42,759 dollars to 43,303 dollars, a rate of 0.1 per cent a year, which the tool classes as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 13,373 dollars to 12,931 dollars, a rate of minus 0.3 per cent a year, classed as regression, and the low-income group fell from 6,401 dollars to 6,041 dollars. Possible explanations, offered as context and not tested here, include weak investment, large informal sectors and commodity dependence in Latin America, and rapid growth of a young workforce entering low-productivity work in Sub-Saharan Africa. No employment or sector result in this section confirms them.

For 2030 the implication is that no common regional pace can be assumed. Regions already growing at three per cent a year or more can keep climbing, while the two regions with stagnant or falling output per worker fall further behind the others. The target sets no numerical threshold, so classifications such as on track rest on the bench's reading of a rising trend, and a different reading would change them.

### Country outcomes split between rapid gains and decline

Beyond the world average, the bench classifies each of the 177 countries with data by the pace of its output per worker. Because target 8.2 carries no numeric threshold, the classes rest on a model-based reading of each country's trend towards 2030, and the labels should be taken as relative judgements rather than findings against a legal standard.

The result is a split. A total of 48 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 52.9 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. At the other end, 46 countries are in regression, meaning that output per worker has fallen over the period, and they hold 14.6 per cent of the population. Between the two lie 30 countries with moderate progress that needs acceleration, 34 with marginal progress that needs significant acceleration, and 19 in stagnation. Their population shares are 17.0 per cent, 7.4 per cent and 8.1 per cent respectively.

The gap between the count of countries and the share of people is the main interpretive point. Counted by country, 48 of 177 are on track, a little over a quarter. Counted by population, the on-track group holds just over half. The tool does not say which countries drive that share, but it is consistent with populous economies, long associated with labour moving from farming into industry and services, sitting in the on-track class. A reader should therefore not conclude that most countries are advancing: by number, those regressing, 46, nearly match those on track, 48.

Regression is the most troubling class, since it means that workers in these 46 countries produce less than before. Conflict and state fragility, commodity price collapses, macroeconomic crises and, after 2020, lasting pandemic disruption are well-established causes of such declines in general. They are context only: no result here tests which applies to which country. Stagnation, in 19 countries, points to economies where output per worker has barely moved, a pattern often linked to stalled structural change, again untested here.

The classification also depends on choices that could be made differently. Without a numeric target, a different benchmark, such as a rate needed to halve a gap with richer economies, would move countries between classes. Employment estimates, which underlie the denominator, are modelled for many countries, so countries near class boundaries may be misplaced. For 2030, the implication is that the world average conceals a divergence: a group holding 52.9 per cent of the assessed population is advancing, while 46 countries are losing ground and will need a change of course, not just faster growth, to reach higher productivity by the end of the decade.

### Inequality between countries has narrowed, but convergence is weak

The spread of output per worker among countries has narrowed over the decade. Weighting each country by its population, the Gini coefficient of GDP per person employed fell from 0.449 in 2015 to 0.427 in 2020 and 0.412 in 2025. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to differences at the top and bottom of the distribution, fell from 0.347 to 0.308 and then to 0.286. Both measures point the same way. The fall was somewhat larger in the first five years than in the second, although the 2025 figures cover 168 countries against 177 earlier, so part of the comparison rests on a changed set of countries.

The narrowing is not matched by catch-up among countries as such. The convergence test regresses each country's annual change in output per worker over 2015 to 2025 on its starting level. If poorer countries were closing the gap, the coefficient would be clearly negative. It is -0.00249, with a p-value of 0.0541, so it falls just short of the conventional 5 per cent threshold, and the R2 is 0.013, meaning that the starting level explains about 1.3 per cent of the variation across the 168 countries. The unweighted coefficient of variation, which treats every country alike, moved only from 0.893 to 0.876 on this common set. The population-weighted measures fell by a larger proportion than the unweighted one. That pattern is consistent with the improvement coming mainly from where large economies stood, not from a general closing of the gap by small and poor ones, although the tools used here do not identify which countries drove it. Fast growth in a few populous economies lowers a population-weighted index even when most countries stay where they were relative to the rest.

The decomposition by region adds to this reading. The share of the Theil index attributable to differences between regions rose from 68.3 per cent in 2015 to 71.9 per cent in 2020 and 75.2 per cent in 2025. Differences within regions therefore account for a shrinking part of the remaining inequality, and the divide that persists is increasingly one between world regions. This fits the regional levels described earlier in the section, where the lowest-income groups remain a small fraction of the output per worker of the richest.

The period saw two shocks, and they affect how the figures should be read. The pandemic of 2020 cut output in many economies, including some of the richest, and a temporary fall at the top can lower measured inequality without any gain for poorer workers. The lower Gini and Theil values of 2025 show that the earlier narrowing has held rather than reversed. Even so, a weak and statistically marginal convergence coefficient gives little ground to expect that gaps between countries will close by 2030 on present trends. Target 8.2 sets no numeric threshold, and it can be read either as higher productivity everywhere or as faster productivity gains where levels are lowest. On the first reading, the world has made progress. On the second, the evidence is thin, and the narrowing seen in the weighted indices should not be mistaken for it.

### Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals

The break analysis covers the world series alone, with no regional breaks tested, and its earliest segment begins in 2001. It finds change points in 2004, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022. Between 2004 and 2008, output per worker rose by a mean of 1,001.2 dollars a year (constant 2021 PPP). In 2009 the mean annual change was -404.0 dollars, a year that coincides with the global financial crisis. From 2010 to 2019 gains resumed at a mean of 967.5 dollars a year, close to the 2004 to 2008 mean and not above it. There was therefore no acceleration in the dollar gain per year across that period. Because this span runs on both sides of the adoption of the Goals in 2015, it does not describe the years before them alone. The 2004 change point appears because the segmentation starts in 2001, and the list of six is the one used throughout this part.

The pandemic year shows a similar pattern on a comparable scale. In 2020 the mean annual change was -369.1 dollars, and in 2021 it was 1,566.8 dollars. Part of the rebound may be a recovery of what was lost, and part may reflect the composition of employment: when low-productivity jobs disappear in a downturn, output per remaining worker can rise even where output is falling. This explanation is context and was not tested here. The link of the breaks to the crisis and the pandemic is likewise context, since the tool dates changes without attributing them. From 2022 to 2025 the mean annual gain was 815.5 dollars, below the 2010 to 2019 mean of 967.5 dollars. The recovery has thus not restored the earlier dollar gain. This suggests, without establishing, that the compound rate of 1.8 per cent a year, measured over 2015 to 2025, may not hold to 2030. The trend tool reads that rate as moderate progress, with acceleration needed.

The link between productivity and headline growth is weak. Across 168 countries for 2015 to 2025, the Spearman correlation between changes in output per worker and GDP growth is -0.048, effectively no relation. For 2025 levels the coefficient is -0.413, a moderate negative association: countries with lower output per worker tend to record higher growth rates. This is consistent with catch-up from a low base, but also with growth that comes from adding workers or hours rather than raising output per worker. Rank correlations say nothing of cause.

The country classification shows why the outlook for 2030 is uneven. Of 177 countries assessed, 46 are in regression, holding 14.6 per cent of the population assessed, while 19 are stagnating. Among regions, Sub-Saharan Africa shows falling output per worker at an annual rate of -0.3 per cent, and so does the low-income group, an income grouping and not a region, at -0.6 per cent. South Asia, at 3.2 per cent, is on track. The cause of the decline is not shown by these results and would need employment and sector series. Target 8.2 has no numeric threshold, so these classes are relative readings and not findings against a fixed standard. The 2025 figures cover 168 countries, against 177 earlier.
