w-c09-3-5.text:
### Vulnerable employment is the measured proxy for informality

Informal employment, the condition target 8.3 has in view, is not measured directly by any series on the shelf. The nearest measured proxy is vulnerable employment: the sum of own-account workers and contributing family workers, expressed as a percentage of total employment. The series is a modeled estimate of the International Labour Organization, and it is available for 187 economies, with 182 countries reporting in 2025. The proxy is imperfect. Some own-account workers are registered, taxed and covered by social protection, while some wage jobs are informal, with no contract and no insurance. The share of vulnerable employment therefore indicates the extent of weak job security and thin social protection, and it cannot be read as a count of informal jobs.

A second caution concerns the target itself. Target 8.3 asks for policies that encourage the formalization and growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises, but it names no numeric threshold and no year-specific level. Any statement of progress is thus a reading of direction: whether the share falls, stays flat or rises. The trend tool applies a decreasing direction by 2030 with no fixed goal, and its verdicts should be understood in that light. A different reader might judge the same movement more or less favourably.

At world level, vulnerable employment stood at 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 and at 42.4 per cent in 2025. The fall is about 0.7 percentage points over a decade. Roughly two in five workers worldwide therefore remain in own-account or contributing family work, a share that has barely moved across a period that included the adoption of the goals and the shock of 2020. The trend tool classes the world movement as stagnation, with an annual rate of change of -0.0017 on its scale.

This matters because the world figure conceals very different realities, taken up in the parts that follow. It also matters because vulnerable work is the form of employment least likely to carry a stable wage, a contract or a pension. A global share that has hardly shifted suggests that the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not, on the whole, been converted into a move towards paid employment with protection. The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring in many low-income economies probably weighed on the decade, although the series, being modeled, cannot show the timing of such effects with precision.

### Regions differ by a factor of sixteen

In 2025 the regional range in vulnerable employment is wide. South Asia stands at 69.7 per cent of total employment and Sub-Saharan Africa at 71.0 per cent. North America stands at 4.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 12.9 per cent. The highest regional figure is therefore about sixteen times the lowest (71.0 against 4.5). Two regions, both in the developing world, have roughly seven in ten workers in own-account or contributing family work. In North America the figure is below one in twenty.

The middle group lies between these poles and is more tightly bunched. East Asia and Pacific stands at 35.3 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 36.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean at 31.5 per cent. In each of these regions roughly one worker in three is in vulnerable employment, although their economic structures, institutions and histories are quite unlike. A region-wide average also conceals differences among countries, and the regional figures are population-weighted aggregates of modeled estimates, not direct counts.

The pattern follows the structure of production, as context rather than a result of this analysis. Where agriculture and small household enterprise employ most people and large firms offering wage contracts are few, own-account work and unpaid family work are the usual forms of employment. Where manufacturing and services are organised in larger firms and wage employment is the norm, the share is small. The income groups show the same ordering: low-income economies stand at 76.1 per cent in 2025 and high-income economies at 8.0 per cent, so income level and the share of vulnerable work move together.

The spread across countries confirms that region is the main divide: 71.9 per cent of the Theil inequality in 2025 lies between regions, and the rest within them. This shows that most of the cross-country inequality in the indicator is a difference between regional means. It does not show how many countries or workers account for the vulnerable total, and it says nothing about variation within any one region.

### Women carry more vulnerability where it is highest

In 2025 the world figure for women stands at 43.1 per cent of female employment, against 41.9 per cent of male employment for men. The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point. It conceals a division by region. Where vulnerable employment is most widespread, women are more exposed than men. Where it is rare, the order reverses.

The gap is widest in South Asia, where 76.2 per cent of employed women are in vulnerable jobs against 67.1 per cent of employed men. In Sub-Saharan Africa the figures are 79.2 per cent for women and 63.9 per cent for men, a difference of more than fifteen points. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the shares are 41.6 per cent and 34.7 per cent. These are the regions in which a large part of women's work is unpaid help in a family farm or business, or own-account activity in small trade and agriculture, with little social protection. Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work, since it can be combined with household duties.

The pattern runs the other way in the richest regions. In Europe and Central Asia the female share is 11.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent for men, and in North America 3.3 per cent against 5.4 per cent. High income economies show 6.9 per cent for women and 9.0 per cent for men. Men are more often self-employed in these economies, in trades, construction and freelance work, while women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts in services, health and education. A lower share of vulnerable employment among women here is not by itself a sign of advantage, since the series does not capture pay, hours or the quality of wage jobs.

By income group the same crossing appears. In low income countries the female share is 82.9 per cent and the male share 70.9 per cent. In lower middle income countries the figures are 74.0 per cent and 61.2 per cent. In upper middle income countries the gap narrows to 35.6 per cent against 34.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is close to parity, at 31.3 per cent for women and 31.6 per cent for men. The gender gap in vulnerability is thus largest in the poorest settings and closes as incomes rise, which bears directly on the inclusive aim of target 8.3.

### Change has been slow, uneven and not convergent

Across the 187 countries assessed, the trend to 2030 is mostly one of slow or absent progress. Only 24 countries, holding 3.7 per cent of the population of the group, are on track or have met the direction of the target. A further 19 countries, with 6.1 per cent of the population, show moderate progress that would need acceleration. The largest population weight lies in the 48 countries with marginal progress, which hold 51.7 per cent of the population and need significant acceleration. Another 59 countries stagnate, with 25.0 per cent of the population, and 37 regress, with 13.5 per cent. Target 8.3 sets no numerical threshold, so the classes measure movement in the desired direction (a decrease) and not distance from an agreed goal; the reading is one of direction only.

The weight of population in the slower classes matters more than the count of countries. Large economies with high shares of own-account and family work move slowly, so the world average is determined by them, while many small and wealthy economies that were already low account for most of the on-track count. Progress that does occur is therefore concentrated where the problem was already smaller.

Between-country inequality in the indicator did not narrow. The population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.317 in 2015 across 187 countries and 0.320 in 2025 across 182. The Theil index moved from 0.178 to 0.182. The share of that inequality lying between regions, and not within them, stayed near 71 per cent: 70.8 per cent in 2015 and 71.9 per cent in 2025. The geography of vulnerability is thus still mainly a matter of which region a worker lives in. The change in country coverage, from 187 to 182, is small and does not alter the reading.

The convergence test points the same way. The coefficient on initial levels is slightly negative (beta -0.00281, p-value 0.0001), so countries with higher initial shares fell marginally faster, but the fit is weak, with an R-squared of 0.066 across 182 countries. Meanwhile the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.717 to 0.735, meaning that dispersion between countries grew. A weak tendency towards catching up coexists with a widening spread, which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved. Neither the post-2015 nor the post-2020 period can be separated by these summary measures, and the shock of 2020 is not isolated here.

Wage and salaried employment is the mirror of vulnerable employment. The rank correlation of 2025 levels is -0.994, and that of changes since 2015 is -0.920, across 182 countries. Because the two shares are close to complements, with employers forming a small remainder, this is largely definitional and gives no independent evidence that wage growth causes lower vulnerability. It does show that a fall in vulnerable work has meant a rise in paid employment, and not a shift towards other forms of work.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At the pace of 2015 to 2025 the world would not reach a markedly lower share of vulnerable employment by 2030. The trend tool classes the world as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0017 a year, from 43.1 per cent of total employment in 2015 to 42.4 per cent in 2025. The calculation extends the recent line and is not a forecast. Target 8.3 sets no number for vulnerable employment, so the reading of 'on track' is the tool's: any decrease counts as movement in the right direction. Measured against the wider aim of decent work, the pace is insufficient.

Across the 187 countries assessed, 48 countries with marginal progress hold 51.7 per cent of the population of the group, and 59 countries classed as stagnating hold a further 25.0 per cent. The 37 countries classed as regressing hold 13.5 per cent. The regional rates are small. South Asia has a rate of -0.0074 a year and East Asia and Pacific a rate of -0.0074. Sub-Saharan Africa has a rate of -0.0007, close to flat. Low income countries have a rate of 0.0000, which is no movement: their share was 76.1 per cent in 2015 and 76.1 per cent in 2025. Faster movement in the regions with the highest shares would count for more than gains in Europe and Central Asia (-0.0137) or among high income countries (-0.0127), where the share is already low.

The cross-country picture shows no clear convergence. The convergence slope is negative (-0.0028), so countries that started with higher shares fell slightly faster, or rose less, each year. The fit is weak (R-squared 0.07), and the unweighted coefficient of variation rose from 0.72 in 2015 to 0.73 in 2025, so dispersion in relative terms widened. The tests do not show which end of the distribution drove that widening. Among countries weighted by population, the Gini was 0.32 in both 2015 and 2025, and 71.9 per cent of the Theil measure in 2025 lies between regions. Most of the inequality in vulnerable employment is therefore a difference between regions, not within them.

The link between vulnerable employment and wage employment is close: across 182 countries the Spearman correlation of 2025 levels is -0.99, and of changes since 2015 it is -0.92. This is an association, not a cause, and the two series largely mirror one another by construction. It is consistent with a route to lower vulnerability that runs through paid jobs and firms able to employ. The results do not test whether output growth or the pandemic shaped these movements.

Five proposals follow. The International Labour Organization and national statistical offices should monitor informal employment directly alongside the modeled proxy, using labour force surveys. Governments should set a quantified national reading of target 8.3, stating the share of vulnerable or informal work to be reached by 2030. Ministries of labour and of industry in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where shares stood at 69.7 and 71.0 per cent in 2025, should prioritise wage job creation and the formalisation of micro and small enterprises, with access to finance and simpler registration. National planners should give women's vulnerability its own targets, since women are more exposed where the share is highest. Statistical agencies and the ILO should report data gaps openly, including the modeled status of many national figures.

w-c09-10-3.text:
### Net official assistance reached US$259 billion in 2023, an imperfect proxy for Aid for Trade

The question asks how much official assistance supports trade capacity. The bench cannot answer it directly. Target 8.a calls for more Aid for Trade for developing countries, the least developed above all, including through the Enhanced Integrated Framework, but the shelf holds no Aid for Trade commitments or disbursements. It also holds no least-developed-country breakdown and no Enhanced Integrated Framework record, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The series available is net official development assistance received, which counts concessional loans, net of repayments, and grants for every purpose. It can serve only as an upper bound on the resources from which trade capacity support could be drawn, not as an estimate of that support.

Read at that level, the world total rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US$. Constant prices remove general price changes, so the rise is real. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts, so some recipients lack a figure for the latest year and any total should be read with that gap in mind. The nearest available reading for poorer recipients is by income group: low-income economies received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015. That is not a least-developed-country figure, because the groups do not coincide.

The target sets no numeric threshold and no end level. The trend tool was therefore run on direction alone, with no numeric target: a series is classed as on track when it rises at a meaningful rate, and as stagnating or marginal when it does not. On that reading the world is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.0545. The label is weak evidence. A rising total of general assistance does not show that trade capacity support has grown, that it has gone to the least developed countries, or that it has been effective. Increases may reflect emergency, humanitarian or other spending unrelated to trade.

The point matters for 2030 because the target can be read in more than one way: as a rise in the volume of Aid for Trade, as a rise in its share of assistance, or as improved support to least developed countries specifically. The bench can speak only to the first, and only through a proxy. The parts that follow take the proxy as given, examine how it differs among regions and income groups, and show what changed after 2015 and after 2020, while keeping the limits of the measure in view. In short, the amount supporting trade capacity is not measured here; US$259.5 billion in 2023 is a ceiling on the proxy, not a finding about trade.

### Assistance rose unevenly across regions and concentrated among fewer recipients

Regional totals diverged sharply between 2015 and 2023, measured in constant 2023 US dollars. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest change, from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. The trend tool classes the region as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.213. Established knowledge of the period suggests that the displacement and reconstruction needs created by war in Europe explain part of this, though the series does not show what drove the change. No target level is set in the tool, so the classification reads only the direction of travel.

Other regions moved far less. East Asia and Pacific rose from US$9.9 billion to US$10.7 billion, with a rate of 0.010, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, a rate of 0.002, classed as stagnation. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion and is classed as on track, at a rate of 0.028. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Sub-Saharan Africa remains the largest regional recipient, at US$64.8 billion in 2023, up from US$51.8 billion in 2015. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region without recipients in this series.

The pattern matters for Aid for Trade because a rise in the world total, from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, says little about where trade capacity is being built. Regions with flat inflows in real terms face rising trade-support needs without a matching rise in assistance, while this series cannot show how much of any inflow reaches trade purposes.

The spread among countries widened. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received was 0.361 in 2015, 0.370 in 2019 and 0.452 in 2023. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to large recipients, was 0.255 in 2015 and 0.256 in 2019, then rose to 0.460 in 2023. The jump came after 2019, so the concentration is a feature of the years after 2020 rather than of the first half of the period. The coefficient of variation also rose, from 0.643 in 2015 to 1.477 in 2023.

The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 38.7% in 2019 and 29.6% in 2023. Regional averages therefore explain a shrinking part of the inequality, and differences among countries within the same region now account for most of it. Regional reading alone would hide this, so country-level targeting matters more than regional envelopes.

The country count also shifted: 138 countries in 2015, 134 in 2019 and 135 in 2023. The coverage statement for 2023 elsewhere in the results gives 136 countries reporting. These small differences reflect which countries have data and pass the weighting in each tool, and they mean that part of the change in concentration could arise from changes in who is counted. The change in count is small against the size of the rise in the Gini and Theil measures, but it cannot be excluded as a contributor.

### A single surge in 2022 explains most of the recent rise, and 43 countries regressed

The break analysis of world net official development assistance, in constant 2023 US dollars, detects breaks in 2022 and 2023. In the segment from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. The segment covering 2022 alone has a mean annual change of US$49.8 billion, which is a single-year change and is several times the long-run pace. The segment covering 2023 alone has a mean change of minus US$0.7 billion. The world total stood at US$169.7 billion in 2015 and US$259.5 billion in 2023. The break test shows when the series shifted, not why, and the results do not state what share of the 2015 to 2023 rise the 2022 change represents, so this part claims only that the movement was concentrated around 2022 and partly reversed the following year.

Context from outside these data, not tested here, points to war-related emergency and reception flows in Europe in 2022. The series does not attribute the 2022 change to any recipient or purpose. Europe and Central Asia, which rose from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023, is consistent in timing with that context, but the results do not show that it drove the world break. A one-year movement of this kind is also a weak basis for judging whether support for trade capacity has grown, since emergency flows serve humanitarian and budget needs rather than trade facilitation.

The country classes show how little the aggregate says about most recipients. Of 138 countries assessed, 79 are classed as on track or target met, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed group. Another 5 show moderate progress, with 0.4% of the population, 6 show marginal progress, with 3.1%, and 5 are stagnant, with 1.7%. The largest class by population is regression: the trend tool classes 43 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the assessed population. This is a class of the trend rate. It is not a comparison of 2023 receipts with 2015 levels, and the results do not give those country levels.

This divergence matters for the 2030 horizon. A world total can rise while the trend rate is negative for countries holding more than half of the assessed population. The tool assumes a target of increase, since target 8.a sets no numeric goal, so classes such as on track describe the direction of change and not attainment of a defined threshold. The series ends in 2023 and gives no basis for forecasting the path to 2030 in either direction.

### Reaching 2030 requires better measurement and steadier, better-targeted assistance, with proposals

Reaching 2030 on target 8.a depends first on measurement. The bench cannot give an amount for official assistance that supports trade capacity. Net official development assistance received was US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US dollars, and that figure is an upper bound on what could support trade capacity, not an estimate of it. The series covers every purpose, and the shelf holds no Aid for Trade disbursements. It gives no breakdown for least developed countries and no Enhanced Integrated Framework figure, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The nearest available readings are income-group and regional totals: low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023 and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion. A recipient whose assistance grew may have received it for relief or budget support, and one whose assistance fell may still have gained trade-related help. Target 8.a also carries no numeric benchmark. The trend tool was run with no target value, so its classes rest on the direction of change alone.

The series gives no basis for forecasting the path to 2030 in either direction. The mean annual change was US$6.4 billion in 2001-2021. The change in 2022 was US$49.8 billion, and in 2023 it was a fall of US$0.7 billion. Context from outside these data, not tested here, points to emergency flows linked to the war in Europe; the series does not show what drove the change. A series that ends in 2023 cannot say whether the 2022 level will persist, recede or be exceeded.

The distribution of recipients shows how little the aggregate says. The trend tool classes 43 of 138 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the population assessed. This is a class of the trend rate, meaning the fitted trend of their assistance is negative. It is not a comparison of 2023 with 2015 levels. Inequality among recipients rose: the population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.361 in 2015 and 0.452 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023, so the decomposition locates most of the inequality within regions. It does not show which policy would work better.

w-c09-1-4.text:
### World income per person has grown at under 2 per cent a year

World GDP per capita grew by 1.9 per cent in 2015 and by 2.0 per cent in 2025, according to the World Bank's World Development Indicators. A decade that opened and closed at almost the same rate, a little under 2 per cent a year, is the first finding of this section. Growth of that size doubles average income only over several decades, and it sits far below the pace that the second reading of target 8.1 asks of the least developed countries.

Target 8.1 can be read in two ways. Its first clause asks for per capita economic growth 'in accordance with national circumstances', which sets no number. Its second asks for at least 7 per cent GDP growth a year in the least developed countries, a figure for total output, not for income per person. The two measure different things: GDP growth includes the effect of a rising population, and in countries with fast population growth the gap between the two can be wide. This section uses GDP per capita growth as its main indicator, because it describes the change in output available to each resident, and turns to total GDP growth when the 7 per cent threshold is considered. Gross national income per capita is a third measure, which adds income earned abroad and subtracts income paid out; it is reported for fewer countries and is not the basis of the comparisons here.

The path of world growth over the longer run reads as a sequence of shocks rather than as a steady rise. The break analysis of the annual change in the world rate finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The mean annual change was -2.8 percentage points across 2008 and 2009, the years of the global financial crisis, and then +5.8 in 2010 as output recovered. The pattern repeated with greater force around the pandemic: the mean change was -5.4 in 2020 and +9.4 in 2021, followed by -3.1 in 2022. Between 2011 and 2019 the mean annual change was -0.2, a gentle drift downward and not a collapse, and from 2023 to 2025 it was again -0.2. These are changes in the growth rate from one year to the next, not growth rates themselves, and they should be read as the size of each swing.

The reading matters for 2030. A world economy that returns each time to roughly 2 per cent growth, after shocks that arrive about once in a decade, offers no sign of the acceleration that sustained income gains would need. The figure for 2025 rests on 186 countries reporting, against 211 in 2015, so the latest year is less complete than earlier ones and may be revised as late reports arrive.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than six

Regional growth in GDP per capita, from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, ranged widely in 2015. South Asia grew by 6.5 per cent, against 0.2 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa and 0.8 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Latin America and the Caribbean contracted, at -0.7 per cent. These figures describe a single year, not a settled order, and no ratio between regions is claimed here.

South Asia remained the fastest region throughout, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, a little below its 2015 rate. East Asia and Pacific held a similar position, at 4.0 per cent in 2015 and 3.9 per cent in 2025. The trend results cover GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars. The trend tool reads the compound annual change from 2015 and extends it to 2030. No numerical target is set for income per person, and the results report no benchmark value, so the classes are relative readings of momentum that cannot be reproduced from the figures given. They show direction and pace only, and they are not a test of any benchmark. South Asia's trend is classed as on track or target met, with an annual rate of 0.0465. East Asia and Pacific carries the same class, at 0.0357.

The wealthier regions moved the other way. Europe and Central Asia slowed from 1.6 per cent in 2015 to 1.3 per cent in 2025, and North America from 1.9 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Their trend rates, 0.0150 and 0.0167, are classed as moderate progress, with acceleration needed. High-income countries as a group went from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0151, in the same class. Slower growth at high income levels is often explained, as context outside these results, by the limited scope for catching up and by ageing populations; the results do not test this.

Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa show the largest rise in the annual rate between the two end years. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from -0.7 per cent to 1.6 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.2 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Both ended close to the world rate of 2.0 per cent, yet the decade-long trend in income per person is less favourable. Latin America and the Caribbean has a trend rate of 0.0054, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and Sub-Saharan Africa a rate of -0.0020, classed as regression. A single good year at the end does not alter a decade in which income per person barely rose or fell. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew by 0.8 per cent in 2015 and 0.9 per cent in 2025, with a trend rate of 0.0076, also classed as marginal progress.

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after -2.9 per cent in 2015, yet their trend rate over the decade is 0.0007, classed as stagnation. Lower-middle-income countries grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025, up from 4.0 per cent in 2015, with a trend rate of 0.0292. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0371. Both of these groups are classed as on track or target met. A low-income growth rate of 2.5 per cent in 2025 is one year's reading, and the stagnation class shows that it has not yet lifted the decade's trend.

### Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015

The breaks in the annual change of world GDP per capita growth locate the large movements in the series. The break analysis of the World Development Indicators finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The segments between them are short, and several consist of one year. The breaks describe changes in the rate of growth, not its level: a mean change of -2.8 points in 2008-2009 means that the growth rate fell by that amount each year on average across those two years. The analysis does not measure what share of the movement each shock explains, so this part claims only where the breaks fall and how large they are.

The global financial crisis is the first large shock in the series, and it lies before 2015. The 2008-2009 segment has a mean annual change of -2.8 points, and 2010 follows with a rebound of 5.8 points. The long segment from 2011 to 2019 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, and it straddles the 2015 baseline. That is a slow drift downward in the growth rate across nine years, not a collapse.

The period after 2015 is dominated by the pandemic. In 2020 the annual change in world growth was -5.4 points, the largest fall in the series. The 2021 segment records a rise of 9.4 points, the largest rise. The 2022 segment then shows a change of -3.1 points. The segment from 2023 to 2025 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, so growth was drifting down again, much as in 2011-2019. These swings are why the world rate in 2025, at 2.0 per cent, can resemble the rate in 2015, at 1.9 per cent, while the path between them was violent. As context, not a result of the analysis, the 2020 fall is usually attributed to lockdowns and the collapse of travel and trade, and the 2021 gain largely to recovery from a depressed base.

Across income groups, the endpoints need the same caution. Low-income countries recorded GDP per capita growth of -2.9 per cent in 2015 and 2.5 per cent in 2025. That is a swing from contraction to modest expansion, but it compares two single years. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 4.0 per cent to 4.6 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, and high-income countries from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent. Target 8.1 sets 7 per cent for total GDP growth in the least developed countries, and these results contain neither that measure nor that group, so the target cannot be tested here. The per capita rates of every group listed are below 7 per cent, but that is not a test of the target.

A ten-year endpoint comparison therefore hides the volatility that the breaks reveal. Two years close in value say nothing about the swings between them, and a large gain between endpoints may only be recovery from a poor starting year. The comparison also depends on coverage. The number of countries reporting GDP growth was 211 in 2015, 210 in 2019 and 210 in 2021, but only 186 in 2025. The fall from 209 countries in 2022 to 204 in 2023 and 200 in 2024 suggests that data arrive late, so the 2025 values rest on fewer countries and may be revised. For 2030 this implies that the latest readings are provisional, and that any judgment on target 8.1 should wait for the revised series.

### Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence

Beyond regional averages, the trend classification sorts countries by how fast GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) has moved since 2015. No numerical 2030 target exists for this measure, and the results do not report the benchmark value behind the notional target. The tool's reading rule is the compound annual rate from the baseline and the share of the distance from baseline to target that this rate would cover by 2030. Because the benchmark is not given, the classes are relative readings of momentum that cannot be reproduced from the results. They are not a verdict against a legal threshold.

Of 209 countries assessed, 74 are classed as on track or target met, and they hold 56.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 36 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 16.4 per cent of the population. Another 44 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 11.8 per cent. Fifteen countries stagnate, with 5.0 per cent of the population, and 40 are in regression, with 10.3 per cent. Fewer than half of the countries assessed fall in the first class by count, though they hold a majority of the population. The results give no country-level income figures, so they do not show whether the lagging countries are the poorest.

The regional readings are consistent with this. South Asia has a compound rate of 0.0465, East Asia and the Pacific 0.0357, the upper middle income group 0.0371 and the lower middle income group 0.0292, and all four are classed as on track or target met. Europe and Central Asia (0.0150), high income countries (0.0151) and North America (0.0167) show moderate progress, as does the world as a whole at 0.0176. Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0054) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0076) show marginal progress. The low income group, at 0.0007, is classed as stagnating. Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0020, is classed as regression, even though its annual growth rate recovered from 0.2 per cent in 2015 to 1.6 per cent in 2025.

The 7 per cent target cannot be tested with these results. Target 8.1 sets that rate for GDP growth, not per capita growth, in the least developed countries, and the results hold neither a total GDP growth series nor a group figure for those countries. What can be said is narrower: per capita growth in 2025 was below 7 per cent in every group listed. The low income group grew by 2.5 per cent after a contraction of -2.9 per cent in 2015, and South Asia, the highest, grew by 6.2 per cent. Neither is a least developed group, so these figures are a proxy and not a test.

The low income rebound from -2.9 per cent to 2.5 per cent is a sizeable swing, yet the trend classification still reads that group as stagnating. As context not tested by the results, growth after a shock often restores lost ground before it adds new income, which would explain why a good year need not change the long-run class. Coverage also thins at the end of the series: 186 countries reported growth in 2025, against 211 in 2015, so the latest figures are less complete.

For 2030 the implication is measured. If present rates hold, 74 countries with 56.6 per cent of the population assessed are classed as on track by the notional reading, while 40 countries with 10.3 per cent are in regression and 15 with 5.0 per cent stagnate. The 7 per cent goal is a different measure and remains untested.

w-c09-6-3.text:
### The world share fell by 1.4 points, from a 2015 base, not by a substantial margin

Target 8.6 asks for a substantial reduction in the proportion of youth not in employment, education or training by 2020. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so any verdict rests on a reading chosen by the analyst. Here the reading is plain: a substantial reduction would be a fall large enough to be visible against the starting level and to change the position of most regions.

On that reading, the world record is modest. The modelled ILO estimate puts the global share at 21.2 per cent of the youth population in 2015 and at 19.8 per cent in 2025. The share therefore declined over the decade, but by a margin of well under a tenth of the 2015 level in relative terms, and the latest year available is five years after the target date. The series is a modelled estimate, not a count from a single survey. Countries with sparse labour force data receive values built from regional patterns and covariates, so small movements in the world figure should be read with caution. The estimate covers 182 countries reporting in 2025.

The pace of change did not follow a steady path. The break analysis of the annual change in the world share finds shifts in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by about 0.2 points a year on average. Between 2013 and 2019 the mean annual change was close to zero, at 0.02 points, which means that the share was essentially flat in the years just before the target date. The first five years after 2015 therefore delivered almost no reduction, and the decline recorded by 2025 was produced mainly after the pandemic year, a pattern taken up in a later part.

The income groups show why the global figure hides unequal movement. In high-income countries the share moved from 12.2 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025, and in upper middle income countries from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent. Lower middle income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The global average is thus pulled down by the middle-income and wealthier groups, while the poorest countries ended the period with a higher share than they began with.

Taken together, these results do not support a claim of substantial reduction by 2020. The 2015 base fell by a small amount over ten years, was flat before 2020, and rose in the poorest countries. Whether a stricter or looser reading of 'substantially' would change the verdict is a question the target text leaves open, but no plausible reading treats a decline of this size, reached five years late, as meeting the intent of the goal.

### Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden

Regional levels in 2025 range widely. North America holds the lowest share, at 11.8 per cent of youth, down from 12.5 per cent in 2015. East Asia and Pacific stands at 12.8 per cent, down from 14.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 13.0 per cent, down from 15.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is at 19.3 per cent, from 21.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is at 21.4 per cent, slightly above its 2015 level of 20.9 per cent. South Asia shows the largest fall among the regions, from 28.4 per cent to 23.4 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is highest at 32.1 per cent, and its share rose from 31.1 per cent. The regional picture therefore runs in two directions: most regions moved down modestly, while two did not.

Income groups show the same split. Low-income countries rose from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent, while lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent, and high-income countries from 12.2 per cent to 10.9 per cent. The poorest group is thus the one in which the share grew, and by 2025 it stands well above the others. Demographic pressure, thin labour demand and limited schooling places are well-established contexts for this pattern in low-income settings, though the series itself does not show what drives it.

Young women have higher shares than youth as a whole. The world female share was 30.2 per cent in 2015 and 27.1 per cent in 2025, above the all-youth share of 19.8 per cent in 2025. Male shares are not among the results cited, so the comparison with young men cannot be drawn here. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the female share was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged, so nearly half of young women are outside work and study. South Asia improved from 46.0 per cent to 37.1 per cent, yet remains high. Low-income countries moved against the trend, from 32.6 per cent to 34.4 per cent. Norms on care work and early marriage, and limits on women's mobility and employment, are the usual explanations, stated here as context only.

Among countries, the classes of the trend assessment are scattered. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the direction of the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 28 show moderate progress and 29 marginal progress, while 21 stagnate and 58 regress. The regressing group holds 18.8 per cent of the population, more than the on-track group. No numeric target exists, so the classes rest on the analyst's reading of the trend, and they should be read as direction rather than as a verdict.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, did not narrow. The Gini coefficient was 0.231 in 2015, 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for a little over half of the inequality in both years. Convergence is not shown: the beta of -0.00428 has a p-value of 0.214, not distinguishable from zero. Countries starting higher did not reliably improve faster.

### The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement

The movement of the world share is better read as a sequence of breaks in timing than as a steady trend. The break analysis of the annual change in the modelled ILO series finds breaks in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by a mean of 0.2 points a year. That is the only stretch in which the decline looks like steady progress, and it ended before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.

From 2013 to 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which is near stagnation. The share did not fall in the years before the target date. In 2020 the annual change jumped by 1.37 points, the largest movement in the series. The timing coincides with the closure of schools and workplaces during the pandemic. That link is context drawn from well-established knowledge; the data show when the break occurred and do not test its cause. The results cited here give no world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be derived from them. The evidence on the target year is the 2013 to 2019 mean and the 2020 jump, and both point away from a substantial reduction by 2020.

The fall that followed was nearly as sharp. From 2021 to 2023 the share fell by a mean of 1.08 points a year, which took back much of the 2020 rise. From 2024 to 2025 the share rose again by a mean of 0.15 points a year. The long-run rate of change for the world, at -0.0070 on the trend tool's scale, is read by that tool as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. These classes are the tool's own categories, applied without a numeric target.

Sub-Saharan Africa followed a different path. Its breaks fall in 2014, 2021, 2023 and 2024. From 2006 to 2013 its mean annual change was -0.04 points. From 2014 to 2020 it rose by 0.45 points a year; that window includes the 2020 break, so the rise cannot be assigned wholly to the period before the pandemic, and no world mean for the same window is cited for comparison. A young population growing faster than jobs and school places is a common explanation, but the data do not test it. After 2020 the region eased, with a mean change of -0.29 points a year in 2021 and 2022 and -1.23 points in 2023, then 0.00 points a year in 2024 and 2025. The trend tool still classes the region as regression to 2030.

The breaks therefore cluster around 2020 and 2021, set against a world share that was already flat from 2013 to 2019. The fall of 2021 to 2023 is consistent with a position partly restored rather than advanced, though the data do not isolate the cause.

### The 2020 target was missed, and 2030 needs faster progress and a clearer definition

On the reading used here, the 2020 target was not met in a substantial sense, and the trend to 2030 does not close the gap. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so this verdict rests on the analyst's own reading. The results do not give a 2015 to 2020 net change, so the target-year answer rests on the break analysis: a mean annual change of 0.02 points between 2013 and 2019, and a jump of 1.37 points in 2020. The trend tool assigns its own classes and its target is given as none, so the classes describe the direction and pace of change, not distance from a stated goal. The world is classed as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a compound annual rate of -0.7 per cent from the 2015 baseline.

The regional rates differ. East Asia and Pacific stands at -1.2 per cent a year and High income at -1.2 per cent, both marginal. Latin America and the Caribbean is at -0.9 per cent, and North America at -0.6 per cent. Only Europe and Central Asia, at -1.6 per cent, and South Asia, at -1.9 per cent, reach the moderate class, and both still need acceleration. Three groups are classed as regression: Low income, at 0.9 per cent a year, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, at 0.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.2 per cent.

The country count rests on 187 countries assessed by the trend tool, whereas the levels and spread measures for 2025 rest on 182 countries reporting that year. Of the 187, 51 are on track or have met the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the assessed population. A further 28 show moderate progress, 29 marginal progress and 21 stagnation. Regression affects 58 countries, holding 18.8 per cent of the population. The largest population share, 32.1 per cent, sits in the marginal class.

Countries have not drawn together. The convergence test gives a beta of -0.0043 with a p-value of 0.214, which cannot be told from zero, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.471 to 0.532 across 182 countries. Population-weighted Gini rose from 0.231 in 2015 to 0.246 in 2025, so the spread among countries widened.

For 2030 the implication is that the present pace leaves the world far from any substantial reduction on the reading used here. The estimates are modelled, and survey coverage behind them is thin in several low-income countries, so classes for individual countries carry uncertainty. Male shares are not cited in this section, so the gender comparison rests on the female and all-youth figures alone.

Several proposals follow. National statistical offices in low-income countries should run labour force surveys at least every two years, so that modelled estimates rest on measured data. Ministries of labour and education in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region should set targets for young women's transition into work or study, since their share has barely moved. The UN Statistical Commission should adopt a numeric reading of 'substantially' for target 8.6, so that future verdicts do not depend on an analyst's choice.

w-c09-9-3.text:
### Account ownership reached 78.7 per cent of adults worldwide by 2024

Account ownership among adults aged 15 and over stood at 78.7 per cent worldwide in 2024, up from 69.3 per cent in 2017. The indicator counts respondents who report having an account, alone or with someone else, at a bank or another type of financial institution, or with a mobile-money-service provider. It therefore measures a person's formal link to the financial system, not the use made of the account, its cost or its quality. An account opened for a single transfer and then left dormant counts in the same way as one used daily.

Target 8.10 asks countries to strengthen the capacity of domestic financial institutions to encourage and expand access to banking, insurance and financial services for all. The target carries no numeric threshold. This book therefore reads full access as 100 per cent of adults aged 15 and over holding an account. That reading is strict and is only one of several possible; a lower benchmark, or a measure that included credit, would give a different distance to travel. Insurance, which the target names, is not measured by any of the series used here, so the book says nothing about it. On the strict reading, the world in 2024 was still short of the mark by a wide margin, though it had moved in the right direction.

The survey years need care. Account ownership is collected in periodic household surveys, not annually. For most regions the series offers two readings, 2017 and 2021, while the World aggregate and South Asia carry a 2024 reading, as do the income groups. The regional figures are therefore not all measured at the same end date, and the rise in the World figure to 2024 cannot be split into regional contributions from the 2021 values alone. The regional pictures are taken up in the next part. Here the point is that the global rise is real in the data and spans the years before and after 2020, although the gap in survey years prevents any exact reading of what the pandemic changed.

The physical infrastructure of banking moved differently. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.16 in 2015 to 11.12 in 2024, while automated teller machines per 100,000 adults rose from 36.09 to 41.91 over the same years. Accounts spread while branches thinned, so the growth in account holding cannot be attributed to a larger branch network. As context, not as a finding of these series, the period saw banks consolidate branches and customers move towards phones and digital channels; the data on branches and ATMs do not show why either count changed. Branches and machines are also a count of outlets relative to adults, not of the distance any person must travel to reach one.

These three series together suggest that account holding has become less dependent on branches, though the series do not identify the channels responsible. That matters for 2030, since the target's aim of access for all can be pursued through channels other than buildings. It also leaves open who has been reached and who has not, which the parts that follow examine by region, income group, sex and poverty.

### Regions and countries differ widely in ownership and in physical access

Regional levels of account ownership span a wide range. In 2021, North America stood at 95.5 per cent of adults aged 15 and over, Europe and Central Asia at 89.6 per cent and East Asia and Pacific at 82.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reached 73.6 per cent and Sub-Saharan Africa 55.1 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping recorded 52.8 per cent. South Asia, whose latest reading falls in 2024, stood at 77.6 per cent. The survey years differ between South Asia and the other regions, so the South Asian figure is not strictly comparable with the 2021 readings.

The starting points in 2017 show where the movement has been fastest. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 55.2 per cent to 73.6 per cent by 2021, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 42.6 per cent to 55.1 per cent. North America moved from 93.8 per cent to 95.5 per cent, a region close to saturation. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping advanced from 47.5 per cent to 52.8 per cent, the slowest gain among the developing regions listed. Convergence is therefore under way, yet the gap between the top and bottom regions remains large.

Physical access tells a different story, and it does not line up with ownership. Commercial bank branches numbered 21.9 per 100,000 adults in North America in 2024 and 19.0 in Europe and Central Asia, against 4.0 in Sub-Saharan Africa. North America and Europe and Central Asia had fewer branches than in 2015, when the figures were 27.7 and 26.8. Branches also fell in Latin America and the Caribbean, from 13.1 to 11.6, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping, from 13.9 to 11.5. South Asia moved the other way, from 11.3 to 16.0, and East Asia and Pacific rose from 9.7 to 11.2. Sub-Saharan Africa was almost unchanged, from 3.9 in 2015 to 4.0. The series count outlets only and do not test why counts changed. Explanations offered in the wider literature, given here as context and not as findings, include branch closures after consolidation in mature banking systems and the use of mobile channels in place of new buildings.

Automated teller machines show the same unevenness. North America had 173.8 machines per 100,000 adults in 2024, down from 222.1 in 2015, while Sub-Saharan Africa had 6.9 and South Asia 24.5. South Asia's figure was 13.2 in 2015, so the region added machines while accounts also rose. Sub-Saharan Africa began at 5.3. The densest region still has many times the provision of the sparsest, which matters for people who must withdraw cash, especially where cash remains the main means of payment.

The income groups confirm the pattern. In 2024 account ownership was 46.4 per cent in low-income economies, 70.4 per cent in lower-middle-income, 84.0 per cent in upper-middle-income and 94.9 per cent in high-income economies. Low-income economies had 2.8 branches per 100,000 adults in 2023, fewer than 3.0 in 2015, but their ATM density rose from 3.1 in 2015 to 4.0 in 2023. Lower-middle-income economies roughly doubled ATM density, from 10.6 in 2015 to 21.7 in 2024.

Country classes set against the target of universal ownership by 2030 show how uneven progress is. Of 141 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, holding 16.4 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 36 show moderate progress needing acceleration, covering 51.8 per cent of that population. A further 36 show marginal progress needing significant acceleration, at 20.3 per cent. Three countries stagnate, at 0.7 per cent, and 36 regress, at 10.8 per cent. Because the survey is conducted in a few rounds, these classes rest on very few observations per country, and a single weak survey can place a country in regression. The classes are best read as a guide to where the pace is insufficient, not as a firm forecast. Under any reading, fewer than one-fifth of the population of assessed countries lives in a country on course for the 2030 aim.

### Mobile money and account growth outpaced branches, and the poorest and women gained

Account ownership rose where it started low while branch counts fell in several regions, and the poorest and women gained.

Gains in account ownership were largest where ownership started low. In Latin America and the Caribbean the share of adults with an account rose from 55.2 per cent in 2017 to 73.6 per cent in 2021. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 42.6 per cent to 55.1 per cent over the same four years. In North America, where ownership was already high, the share moved from 93.8 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Income groups show the same pattern between 2017 and 2024: low-income economies rose from 32.0 per cent to 46.4 per cent, while high-income economies moved from 93.0 per cent to 94.9 per cent. Ownership has therefore converged from below, though low-income economies remain far from the level already reached elsewhere.

The poorest 40 per cent of adults gained substantially. Worldwide their ownership rose from 61.7 per cent in 2017 to 72.4 per cent in 2024. In Latin America and the Caribbean it rose from 42.9 per cent to 67.9 per cent between 2017 and 2021, a faster advance than for all adults in that region. In low-income economies the poorest 40 per cent reached 37.3 per cent in 2024, from 22.5 per cent in 2017. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 43.6 per cent in 2021 for this group, up from 32.0 per cent. The poorest group still trails the full adult population in every region reported.

Women's ownership also rose, from 65.9 per cent worldwide in 2017 to 76.6 per cent in 2024, against 78.7 per cent for all adults in 2024. South Asia shows a notable pattern: women stood at 75.1 per cent in 2024, from 64.0 per cent in 2017, against 77.6 per cent for all adults. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping remains the clearest case of difficulty. Women's ownership was 45.6 per cent in 2021, up from 38.0 per cent in 2017, against 52.8 per cent for all adults that year, itself up from 47.5 per cent in 2017. All-adult ownership there rose by less than in Latin America and the Caribbean or in Sub-Saharan Africa over the same years.

Physical access moved differently. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.2 in 2015 to 11.1 in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 26.8 to 19.0, and North America from 27.7 to 21.9. High-income economies fell from 22.3 to 15.5. South Asia rose from 11.3 to 16.0, and East Asia and Pacific from 9.7 to 11.2. Sub-Saharan Africa was close to unchanged, at 3.9 in 2015 and 4.0 in 2024, and low-income economies stood at 3.0 in 2015 and 2.8 in 2023. ATMs per 100,000 adults rose worldwide from 36.1 in 2015 to 41.9 in 2024, and in lower middle income economies from 10.6 to 21.7. In low-income economies they rose from 3.1 in 2015 to 4.0 in 2023. The low-income infrastructure series ends in 2023, while the other income groups run to 2024, so comparisons across income groups mix years. In East Asia and Pacific ATMs fell from 52.5 to 46.5, and in North America from 222.1 to 173.8.

The contrast is that account ownership rose across the world while branches fell in many regions. Accounts therefore spread without a matching spread of branches. Mobile-money services, digital payments and the channelling of public transfers into accounts are explanations offered in the wider literature for ownership growing without bank premises, and branch consolidation and online banking have been offered for richer economies. These are context, not findings: the series measure accounts and outlets only, do not test those explanations, and cannot separate dormant accounts from active ones. Insurance and credit, which target 8.10 also names, are not measured by these series.

For 2030 the pattern implies that the post-2017 gains were broad, but that those who start lowest, including the poorest, women in some regions and residents of low-income economies, still have the furthest to go. Regional figures for 2021 and global figures for 2024 come from different survey rounds, so the years are not strictly comparable.

### Projected trends leave universal access short of 2030 outside a few regions, and proposals follow

Extrapolating the 2017 to latest-year trend towards universal access, defined here as 100 per cent of adults holding an account, shows a split picture. East Asia and Pacific and Europe and Central Asia read as on track or target met, with expected values in 2030 of 108.8 and 110.8 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean reads the same way, with an expected 140.1 per cent. Values above 100 show that the extrapolation is mechanical: a share of adults cannot exceed 100 per cent, and the figures are not forecasts. Sub-Saharan Africa also reads as on track, with an expected 98.0 per cent in 2030. The on-track class rests on the tool's progress ratio, which compares the rate of the trend with the rate needed to reach the target, so a region can be classed on track with an expected value just under 100 per cent. Its ratio of 0.965 is that progress ratio; it is not the expected value divided by 100. The label therefore does not mean that the 100 per cent reading is met, and it is sensitive to the years chosen.

Other groups fall short. The world as a whole is in the class of moderate progress, but acceleration needed, with an expected 78.7 per cent in 2024 rising to 87.8 per cent in 2030. High income moved from 93.0 per cent in 2017 to 94.9 per cent in 2024, and projects to 96.6 per cent in 2030. The shortfall there is small in level but slow in pace, since the last few points of coverage are the hardest to reach. Low income reads as marginal progress, with an expected 63.9 per cent, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping, also marginal, reaches 67.1 per cent. Lower middle income projects to 80.7 per cent and South Asia to 85.3 per cent.

Country counts confirm that the global average hides wide differences. Of 141 countries assessed, 30 are on track or have met the target, holding 16.4 per cent of the assessed population. If only this class counts as on course, fewer than one-fifth of the assessed population lives in a country on course for the 2030 aim; the result does not fix what on course means, and counting other classes would change the share. Another 36 show moderate progress, and these hold 51.8 per cent of the population. A further 36 show marginal progress, with 20.3 per cent. Three are stagnant, and 36 are regressing, with 10.8 per cent of the population. Survey-based measures carry sampling error and rounds differ between countries, so some of these readings may reflect noise and the choice of end year, not a real fall.

Physical access does not offer a route to universal access. Commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults fell worldwide from 12.2 in 2015 to 11.1 in 2024, and in high income countries from 22.3 to 15.5. Sub-Saharan Africa stayed near 4.0, and low income countries stood at 2.8 in 2023. The low income branch series ends in 2023, while the other income groups run to 2024. The series measure accounts and outlets, not channels, so they do not show how accounts were opened. As context outside the data, mobile money is one plausible route, and 2030 outcomes may depend on such channels more than on new branches.

Target 8.10 sets no number, so the reading of 100 per cent is a choice, and a different reading would change the classes above. Insurance, which the target names, is not measured by these series. The poorest 40 per cent stood at 72.4 per cent worldwide in 2024, and women at 76.6 per cent, so aggregate progress does not show who remains outside.

Three proposals follow. National governments and financial regulators in low income countries and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping should prioritise account access for the poorest and for women, since these groups are the furthest from the 2030 line. Statistical offices and survey sponsors should shorten the interval between survey rounds and report insurance and account use, so that regression readings can be told from noise.

w-c08-1-5.text:
### Global access has risen, but not to universality

Access to electricity worldwide stood at 91.9 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 86.9 per cent in 2015. The gain was achieved while the world population grew, but it leaves the world short of the universal access that target 7.1 sets for 2030. The series is reported by 215 countries for 2024, so coverage is nearly complete, though some national figures rest on modelled estimates drawn from industry records and household surveys rather than a fresh count each year.

The divide between rural and urban populations explains much of the shortfall. Rural access rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a larger advance than the urban series, which moved from 96.4 per cent to 97.8 per cent. Urban access was already close to the ceiling at the start of the period, and little room remained for improvement. The remaining deficit is therefore mainly rural: 84.9 per cent rural access leaves 15.1 per cent of rural residents unserved in 2024, against 2.2 per cent of urban residents. This matters for policy, because connecting dispersed households costs more per person than extending an urban grid, and it depends on off-grid and mini-grid solutions as much as on national networks.

A headcount of people without electricity is not published in the series examined here. The scale can only be estimated by applying the 2024 deficit rates to the population series, and the result is the writer's own estimate, not a reported count. Applying 15.1 per cent to the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 gives roughly 523 million rural people; applying 2.2 per cent to the urban population of 4,750,578,960 gives roughly 105 million urban people. Three cautions apply. The access series ends in 2024 while the population series run to 2025, so the years differ. The definition of rural and urban areas is set by each national statistical office and varies between countries. The product of a percentage and a population carries the uncertainty of both inputs. Read with these limits, the estimate suggests a world total of the order of 600 million people, with rural areas holding about five in six of them, even though more people live in cities.

The period also spans two breaks, 2015 and 2020. The first marks the adoption of the goals, the second the pandemic and the economic shocks that followed, which strained public budgets and household incomes and may have slowed some connection programmes. The endpoints given here do not reveal whether progress paused after 2020. The trend projection for the world places access at 95.4 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.65 of the distance to the target covered, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. The final stretch of any access target tends to be the hardest, since the unconnected are the most remote and poorest. The sections that follow turn to where that remaining gap lies.

### Sub-Saharan Africa holds most of the remaining gap

Sub-Saharan Africa is the region furthest from universal access. Access in the region stood at 55.1 per cent of the population in 2024, up from 39.2 per cent in 2015. Every other region reported at least 96.8 per cent in 2024. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stood at 96.8 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean at 98.0 per cent and East Asia and the Pacific at 98.6 per cent. Europe and Central Asia stood at 100.0 per cent, and North America at 100.0 per cent in both years. South Asia rose from 86.5 per cent in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, and its rural access rose from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent of the rural population. The contrast shows that near-universal access is attainable at scale, and that Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception, not one case among several.

The divide between rural and urban areas is sharpest in this region. Rural access in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 35.7 per cent of the rural population in 2024, against 82.9 per cent of the urban population. In 2015 the rural figure was 18.5 per cent and the urban figure 72.7 per cent. Rural access therefore rose faster in proportion than urban access, yet the rural deficit, 100 less 35.7, was still 64.3 per cent in 2024: nearly two in three rural residents remained without electricity. The pattern follows from the economics of supply, stated here as general context outside the results, which do not measure these drivers. Grid extension to dispersed settlements costs more per household and recovers less revenue, so utilities and public programmes have tended to serve towns first. Off-grid solar and mini-grids have widened the options in recent years, although the series reports access without separating the technologies behind it.

Income groups show the same shape. Low-income economies reached 48.8 per cent access in 2024, up from 32.2 per cent in 2015. Rural access in that group stood at 37.1 per cent and urban access at 77.6 per cent. The results do not give the regional composition of the group, so no link to Sub-Saharan Africa is asserted here. Lower-middle-income economies reached 91.4 per cent, and upper-middle-income and high-income economies stood at 99.3 per cent and 100.0 per cent respectively, the latter a rounding of 99.97 per cent.

The results give no reported headcount of people without electricity, so the scale can only be indicated by derivation. Applying the 2024 rural deficit of 64.3 per cent to the 2025 rural population of 731,422,742 in Sub-Saharan Africa suggests roughly 470 million rural residents without access, an approximation. The same method with the urban deficit of 17.1 per cent and an urban population of 590,231,475 suggests a smaller number, about 101 million, in towns and cities. These are the writer's own estimates, not figures reported by the series: they mix years, and national definitions of rural and urban areas differ. They indicate that the unserved in the region are concentrated in rural areas. The results do not state the region's share of the world total, so the claim that the region holds most of the remaining gap is an inference from the gap between this region and all others, not a reported share. Rural population in the region rose from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, and urban population grew from 408,204,795 to 590,231,475. Population growth therefore works against the connection effort: every year of progress in the access rate must also cover new households.

For 2030 the implication is plain. The other regions are within a few points of universality, and their remaining gaps are small. The target will be met or missed in Sub-Saharan Africa. The trend tool classes the region as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and expects 69.2 per cent in 2030 at the pace since 2015, with a ratio of 0.49 of the distance to the target covered. That ratio implies the region is covering about half the progress required, so closing the gap would need roughly twice the pace of 2015 to 2024, concentrated on rural households that are costly to reach.

### Rural areas and South Asia account for the change since 2015

South Asia's gain moved the world average most, but not because its gain in points was the largest. Access in the region rose from 86.5 per cent of the population in 2015 to 99.8 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 13 points. Sub-Saharan Africa's overall gain was larger in points, from 39.2 per cent to 55.1 per cent, about 16 points. South Asia's rural gain was the largest of any region, from 81.4 per cent to 99.8 per cent. Because South Asia holds a very large rural population, 1,035,602,697 people in 2015 and 1,086,549,811 in 2025, closing its rural gap shifted the world average more than any other change. The region is now close to Europe and Central Asia, where access stood at 99.9989 per cent in 2024 (100.0 to one decimal place), so its contribution to further global gains is nearly exhausted.

The rural gap narrowed worldwide. Rural access in the world rose from 76.6 per cent in 2015 to 84.9 per cent in 2024, a gain of about 8 points, against about 5 points for the population as a whole. Rural areas therefore improved faster than the average, which is what a closing gap requires. Rural gains were also large in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, from 87.6 per cent to 94.0 per cent, and in low-income countries, from 17.2 per cent to 37.1 per cent. In Latin America and the Caribbean the rural rate moved from 89.1 per cent to 91.0 per cent, a smaller change, and it remains well below the region's overall rate of 98.0 per cent in 2024.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows a different pattern. Rural access rose from 18.5 per cent in 2015 to 35.7 per cent in 2024, and urban access from 72.7 per cent to 82.9 per cent. These within-area rises are the reported facts behind the regional gain. Yet the rural population of the region grew from 616,454,626 in 2015 to 731,422,742 in 2025, so a rising rate is applied to a growing base. Rural access of 35.7 per cent in 2024 means that roughly two in three rural residents of the region remained unconnected. The urban population also rose, from 408,204,795 in 2015 to 590,231,475 in 2025, and that of low-income countries from 182,500,508 to 269,862,804. Population shifts between rural and urban areas may also play a part in the regional average, but the series cannot test this and no share of the gain is attributed to it.

The question of how many people lack electricity can be answered only by derivation, since the results give shares and not headcounts. As the writer's own estimate, not a reported count, applying the world rural deficit of 15.1 per cent (100 less 84.9 per cent in 2024) to the rural population of 3,464,845,933 in 2025 gives about 523 million rural residents. Applying the urban deficit of 2.2 per cent to the urban population of 4,750,578,960 gives about 105 million. These products mix reference years, 2024 for access and 2025 for population, and rest on national definitions of rural and urban, so they indicate scale only. They also show that the unserved are overwhelmingly rural.

Causes call for restraint. The indicators show where access changed and by how much, not which policies produced it. Well-established experience points to national grid extension programmes, falling costs of solar equipment and off-grid systems, and public financing as usual drivers, but the series cannot attribute the South Asian or African gains to any one of them. Nor do the figures cited show a break after 2020, since the comparison runs between 2015 and 2024 only.

For 2030, the implication is that the world's average is now governed by one region. South Asia has largely finished its part, East Asia and the Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean are above 98 per cent, and the remaining distance lies in rural Sub-Saharan Africa, where population growth works against each point gained.

### Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030, and proposals follow

Country trajectories point to a shortfall in 2030 on the evidence of the trend classification. Of the 215 countries assessed, 154 are on track or have already met the target, and they hold 74.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 33 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, with 15.6 per cent of the population. Another 21 countries show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, with 8.0 per cent of the population. Two countries are stagnant, with 0.4 per cent, and five are regressing, with 1.4 per cent. The count of countries therefore looks reassuring, while the population shares show that about a quarter of the people in the countries assessed live where the present pace will not close the gap.

The aggregate projection agrees. Extending the 2015 to 2024 pace, the world would reach 95.4 per cent access in 2030, and the ratio of actual to required progress is 0.65, classed as moderate progress needing acceleration. Three groups have the lowest ratios, and all are classed as marginal. Latin America and the Caribbean has the lowest, at 0.47, followed by low-income countries at 0.48 and Sub-Saharan Africa at 0.49. The first differs in kind from the other two: its access was already 98.0 per cent in 2024, so the little that remains moves slowly, and the same pace would bring it to 98.6 per cent in 2030. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 69.2 per cent in 2030 and low-income countries 64.4 per cent, so these two stay far from the goal. A ratio of 0.49 means the present pace covers under half of the distance to the target, so closing the gap would need roughly twice the pace observed since 2015. South Asia, with a ratio of 1.73, and lower middle income countries, with 1.01, are on track, although the lower middle income result rests on a narrow margin.

These readings depend on how target 7.1 is interpreted. The classification treats the target as 100 per cent access by 2030, which is the plainest reading of universal access. A projection above 100, such as South Asia's 109.8 per cent, cannot occur in fact and shows only that a linear extrapolation overshoots a ceiling. As general context, not a finding of the series, the last stretch before universality is often harder than the early gains, because the remaining households tend to be more remote and poorer, so linear extrapolation may flatter regions near the ceiling. The target further names affordable and reliable energy services. The indicator measures only whether a population has access to electricity. It says nothing about the price paid, the hours of supply or the quality of the connection, so a country classed as on track may still fall short of the full wording of the target.

The implication for 2030 is that the world will not reach universal access on present trends, and that the missing people will be concentrated where the pace is slowest, in Sub-Saharan Africa and in low-income countries, particularly in rural areas, where access in the region was 35.7 per cent in 2024. Rural access in low-income countries was 37.1 per cent in the same year.

The question of how many people lack electricity can be answered only by a rough derivation, since the results hold no published headcount. Rural access for the world was 84.9 per cent in 2024, leaving a rural deficit of 15.1 per cent, and the rural population was 3,464,845,933 in 2025. Urban access was 97.8 per cent in 2024, leaving a deficit of 2.2 per cent, and the urban population was 4,750,578,960 in 2025. Applying the rates to the populations gives about 523 million rural residents and about 105 million urban residents, or roughly 628 million people in all. This is the writer's own estimate, not a reported count. It mixes years, rounds the rates and relies on national definitions of rural and urban areas, so it indicates scale only. It also shows that the rural deficit is the larger part of the world's shortfall.
