No series on tourism employment, local culture or sustainability of tourism is held, and the counts do not name the countries absent in 2020.

w-c07-5-6.text:
### Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015

World net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, measured in constant 2023 dollars. That is a rise of more than half over eight years. In current dollars the series climbs from US$147.1 billion to US$259.5 billion. The two series coincide in 2023, which is consistent with a 2023 price base; the gap between them in 2015 then reflects the rise in prices since that year. The constant-dollar figure is the fairer measure of change, since it removes the effect of rising prices; the current-dollar series shows a larger rise because it includes inflation.

The indicator needs careful reading before it is applied to target 6.a. It records all net official development assistance received by developing countries: grants and concessional loans, net of repayments of principal, across every sector. It does not isolate water and sanitation, nor the activities the target names, such as water harvesting, desalination, wastewater treatment, recycling and reuse. The series is therefore a proxy for the general scale of international support, and a rise in it does not show that more reached water and sanitation programmes. Spending on health, emergency relief, refugee costs or budget support can raise the total without any of it entering the sector.

The target itself adds a second limit. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building support by 2030, but it names no amount, no share of income and no baseline year. It can be read as a call for more money, for more technical assistance, or for better-targeted programmes, and a financial series speaks only to the first of these. Capacity-building, such as training, institutional support and technology transfer, is poorly captured by a measure of net disbursements. A judgement that the target is on track can therefore rest only on the direction of the aggregate, not on a threshold.

Coverage is also partial. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts in this series. The inequality analysis later in this section covers a different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023; the results do not state why the sets differ, and the use of population weights is a likely explanation rather than a finding. North America records zero in both years, which is consistent with a region of donors rather than recipients, and high-income economies receive only small amounts: US$319.3 million in 2015 and US$760.9 million in 2023 in constant dollars. Net receipts measure what arrives, not what is needed, so the series does not say whether the level is adequate against the water-stress and service gaps described elsewhere in this chapter.

With these limits stated, the direction is clear. Assistance received grew substantially after 2015. The annual change in 2023 was negative, at about -US$0.7 billion, so the 2023 level of US$259.5 billion lies slightly below the 2022 level, which is the highest within the years 2015 to 2023 examined here. Whether growth is sustained to 2030 is a separate matter, because the donor side of the ledger depends on budget decisions that recipient data cannot anticipate.

### Regions gained unevenly, and Europe and Central Asia gained most

Regional totals of net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, show that the increase since 2015 was not evenly shared. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest gain by a wide margin, rising from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023, about 4.7 times the 2015 level. In 2023 it was the second largest recipient region, behind sub-Saharan Africa (US$64.8 billion) and ahead of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region (US$35.1 billion). The series does not show what drove the rise, and it measures all official assistance, not the share spent on water.

The other regions moved much less. East Asia and Pacific received US$9.9 billion in 2015 and US$10.7 billion in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, almost no change in real terms. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion. These three regions ended the period within a narrow band of one another, near US$10.7 billion each, although their populations and water needs differ greatly. No population or per-person series is used in this section, so the totals say nothing about assistance per person; that comparison would need such a series. North America records zero in both years, as expected of a donor region rather than a recipient.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, a rise well below the world's increase. Sub-Saharan Africa remained the largest recipient, with US$51.8 billion in 2015 and US$64.8 billion in 2023. The largest absolute flows thus stayed in sub-Saharan Africa, while the fastest growth went to Europe and Central Asia.

The distribution by income group, also in constant 2023 dollars, shows a similar movement. Low-income countries received US$35.2 billion in 2015 and US$44.6 billion in 2023, and lower-middle-income countries US$54.9 billion and US$59.2 billion. Upper-middle-income countries rose from US$18.9 billion to US$57.4 billion, the fastest growth of the groups, and by 2023 they received more than the low-income group, whose receipts also rose. Target 6.a names developing countries generally rather than the poorest, so this pattern is not in itself a shortfall against it. Only a sector breakdown, which these series do not provide, could show whether water programmes followed the same path.

### A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase

The path of assistance since 2015 is not a steady climb. A structural break analysis of the annual change in world net official development assistance received, in constant 2023 US dollars, isolates 2022 and 2023 as single-year segments, each with its own mean change. From 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. In 2022 alone the change was US$49.8 billion, nearly eight times that long-run average. In 2023 the change was about -US$0.7 billion, which is that year's change and nothing more. The rise recorded between 2015 and 2023, when the world total went from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, therefore owes much to one year: the 2022 change of US$49.8 billion is more than half of that rise of US$89.8 billion, and the gradual growth of the preceding two decades cannot be extrapolated from it. Because the 2023 change was negative, the 2022 level was slightly higher than the 2023 level, and 2022 was the highest year of the period from 2015 to 2023.

The data do not record why 2022 was exceptional. It is an inference, outside the data, that the jump reflects emergency and humanitarian flows, support to countries affected by conflict and displacement, and pandemic recovery financing. The series covers all purposes of assistance together and cannot separate such flows from spending on water and sanitation. Whether the 2023 fall marks a plateau or the start of a decline cannot be judged from one observation.

The distribution of assistance among recipient countries also changed. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received rose from 0.361 in 2015, across 138 countries, to 0.452 in 2023, across 135 countries. The Theil index rose more sharply than the Gini coefficient, from 0.255 to 0.460, and the coefficient of variation rose most of the three, from 0.64 to 1.48. Assistance has thus become more unevenly spread among recipients. The country sets differ between the two years, and the 135 countries in the inequality analysis are not the same set as the 136 countries reporting in 2023 that underlie the world total, so part of the change may reflect which countries are included. The comparison should be read with that caution.

The composition of this inequality shifted too. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023. Differences among countries within the same region now account for a larger part of the disparity than differences between regions. This matters for targeting: regional averages conceal recipients that receive much more or much less than their neighbours, and allocation by region alone would miss them.

For 2030 the implication is that the aggregate rise is fragile and its distribution has become less even. Target 6.a calls for expanded cooperation and capacity-building support in water and sanitation. Total assistance, whatever its level, does not show how much reaches that sector, and a total lifted by one exceptional year is a weak guide to the sustained flows that infrastructure and capacity-building require.

### Assistance for 2030 must be tracked by sector and directed by need

The series held by the bench measures total official development assistance received, not assistance to water and sanitation. Target 6.a asks for expanded international cooperation and capacity-building in water-related activities, and total flows cannot show whether that is happening. A rise in the aggregate may reflect humanitarian, budget-support or debt-related disbursements that have little to do with water supply, sewerage or wastewater treatment. For 2030, the first implication is therefore that progress on 6.a cannot be judged from the present evidence, and the headline figure of US$259.5 billion in 2023 should not be read as a measure of support for water.

The second implication concerns durability. The break analysis isolates 2022 and 2023 as single-year segments, each with its own mean change. The change in 2022 alone was US$49.8 billion, against a mean annual change of US$6.4 billion over 2001 to 2021, and the change in 2023 alone was -US$0.7 billion, a small fall in that year. A jump of that size, followed by a fall, suggests an exceptional episode, not a new trend; this reading is context, not a finding of the data. Planning that assumes the 2023 level will persist, or keep rising, risks a shortfall by 2030. The target can also be read in more than one way: it names no quantity of assistance, so expansion could mean volume, share of total aid or reach of capacity-building.

The third implication concerns distribution. Among countries, the Gini coefficient of assistance received, population-weighted and in constant 2023 dollars, rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.26 to 0.46. The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 45.3% to 29.6%, so the inequality lies increasingly within regions, among individual countries. The inequality analysis covers 135 countries in 2023, while the world total rests on 136 countries reporting, so the two sets differ slightly. In constant 2023 dollars, low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015, and sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion, yet the data do not show whether flows follow the countries with the weakest water and sanitation coverage. Upper middle income countries received US$57.4 billion in 2023, up from US$18.9 billion in 2015, a faster rise than that of low income countries, which is not a finding about need, since the target names developing countries generally and the data cannot show where water assistance went.

The proposals below follow from these findings.

claims.fact: c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c07-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015

proposals: Donor governments and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report assistance to water supply, sanitation and wastewater treatment, including capacity-building, as a sector series in the World Bank's catalogue, so that progress on target 6.a can be judged.

Finance ministries and development agencies in recipient and donor countries should test 2030 financing plans against scenarios with and without the 2022 jump, and should not assume that the 2023 level will persist or keep rising.

Donors and multilateral funds should publish country-level allocations of water assistance alongside water and sanitation coverage, so that the allocation of flows to need can be checked, including among countries within the same region.
w-c07-5-6.gaps: The bench holds no series on assistance to water and sanitation, on capacity-building or on technology transfer, so target 6.a cannot be measured directly. Total assistance received does not show the sector, the purpose or the cause of the 2022 jump. The target names no quantity, so expansion can be read as volume, share or reach. Country coverage differs slightly between the world total and the inequality analysis, and the latest year in the series is 2023.

w-c08-4-4.text:
### World energy intensity fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021

World energy intensity of primary energy, measured as megajoules of energy supply per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, fell from 4.8556 MJ in 2015 to 4.5449 MJ in 2021. That is a fall of 6.4 per cent, derived directly from the two levels. The direction is the one target 7.3 requires: each dollar of output needed less energy at the end of the period than at the start. The question for the section is whether the pace is the one the target asks for.

The trend tool expresses the world movement as a rate of -0.01096 per year, and classifies it as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. That rate is the tool's own measure of change per year, and it is read here only as a direction and a pace relative to the tool's thresholds. The tool was run with no numerical target, so its classification rests on a generic benchmark and not on a figure derived from the wording of target 7.3. The label is a guide to the size of the gap, not a verdict on the target itself.

The target can be read in more than one way. Its wording, to double the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency by 2030, is commonly interpreted as doubling the rate recorded in an earlier period, which requires a baseline period to be chosen. The choice matters, because the earlier rate differs according to the years used. A second reading, used in the monitoring of the goals, sets a fixed annual rate of improvement in energy intensity for the whole period to 2030. The two readings need not give the same answer. The segment comparison in a later part tests only the first, using periods within the series; a rate for the years before 2015 is not held for the world as a whole, and the fixed-rate reading cannot be tested with the bench series.

The data also limit what can be said about the present. The world series ends in 2021, so the latest observation lies well before 2030 and says nothing about the years since. Regional series reach 2022 in some cases, and the number of countries reporting in 2022 was 116, so the final year rests on thinner coverage. Any statement that the world is or is not on course for 2030 is therefore an extrapolation from six years of change, a period that includes the sharp fall and partial rebound in economic activity around 2020. Movements in GDP affect the ratio as much as movements in energy supply, so a change in intensity does not by itself show that efficiency measures were adopted.

Why the measure matters is plain enough. Energy intensity is the broadest indicator available of how much energy an economy needs to produce its output, and a falling value lowers fuel costs, emissions and import dependence for a given level of output. It is, however, a crude proxy for efficiency, because it also reflects the structure of an economy, its climate, and the share of heavy industry in output. The following parts examine how these differences appear across regions and over time.

### Regions diverge from a 2.58 to a 6.14 MJ range by 2021 or 2022

Regional levels of energy intensity, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, span a wide range by the latest year available. Europe and Central Asia is lowest, at 2.5791 MJ in 2022, and Sub-Saharan Africa is highest among regions, at 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The latest year differs between regions, 2021 for some and 2022 for others, so the comparison is approximate and the gap between regions is read as indicative rather than exact.

Europe and Central Asia fell from 4.002 MJ in 2015 to 2.5791 MJ in 2022. Its rate of change, -0.0608 per year, is the steepest of any region and the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions. Part of the decline in this region may reflect changes in economic structure and in fuel supply as well as efficiency gains; the data do not separate these.

North America and South Asia also improved substantially. North America moved from 5.0428 MJ in 2015 to 4.364 MJ in 2022, at a rate of -0.0204 per year, and South Asia from 4.5047 MJ to 3.9427 MJ in 2021, at -0.022 per year. Both are classed as on track or target met. South Asia's result is notable because it began from a level close to the world value and has since fallen below it.

The remaining regions made less headway. East Asia and Pacific moved from 5.6997 MJ in 2015 to 5.2313 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0142 per year, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 3.4822 MJ to 3.265 MJ in 2022, at -0.0092 per year, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Its level is low, which may leave less room for further cuts, but the data do not test that.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan barely moved, from 5.3599 MJ in 2015 to 5.332 MJ in 2021, a rate of -0.0009 per year, classed as stagnation. Sub-Saharan Africa also stagnated, falling from 6.2412 MJ to 6.1403 MJ in 2021, at -0.0027 per year. Together these two regions combine high or middling levels with almost no improvement.

Income groups show the same pattern. Low-income economies stood at 7.415 MJ in 2015 and 7.1393 MJ in 2021, the highest of any group, with a rate of -0.0063 per year, classed as marginal progress. High-income economies fell from 4.3961 MJ to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, at -0.0334 per year, classed as on track or target met. Lower middle income fell from 4.644 MJ to 4.2707 MJ in 2021, and upper middle income from 5.5767 MJ to 5.2119 MJ. The poorest economies are therefore the most energy-intensive per unit of output and are improving most slowly.

Three cautions apply. First, only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the latest regional values rest on incomplete years, and regions with data only to 2021 are compared with others to 2022. Second, intensity reflects economic structure, climate, fuel mix and the share of traditional biomass in supply, and the purchasing power parity conversion of GDP, not efficiency alone. Third, the world rate of -0.011 per year is classed as marginal progress, so the regional divergence matters for 2030: the regions that are on track are not those with the highest levels, and the highest-intensity regions are those where acceleration is most needed.

### Improvement peaked before 2018 and has since slowed

The structural breaks in the annual change of world energy intensity show that the pace of improvement has not been steady. The series for the world, measured in megajoules of primary energy per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity, has breaks in 2005, 2009, 2011 and 2018. These divide the record into five segments, each with its own mean annual change. A negative mean change means that intensity fell, so a larger negative figure means faster improvement.

In 2001-2004 the mean annual change was -0.0498 MJ. It steepened to -0.1154 MJ in 2005-2008, the fastest pace of the early period. The break in 2009 marks a pause: in 2009-2010 the mean change was 0.0070 MJ, so intensity rose slightly instead of falling. That coincides with the global financial crisis, and a link between the two is a reasonable reading, though the data do not establish it. One possible mechanism, not tested by the data, is that output fell sharply while much of the energy supply in buildings, transport and industrial plant could not be scaled down as quickly, which tends to raise intensity in a downturn.

The break in 2011 opens the longest segment. In 2011-2017 the mean annual change was -0.1045 MJ, close to the pace of 2005-2008 and about twice that of 2001-2004. This matters for the target. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement, and the baseline year of 2015 sits inside this faster period. Any comparison of later years with the rate at the start of the Sustainable Development Goals is therefore a comparison with a stretch of unusually quick improvement, not with the slower pace of the early 2000s. Reading the target against the rate of -0.0498 MJ would make doubling look nearer than it is when set against the rate that prevailed in 2015.

The final break, in 2018, is the most consequential. In 2018-2021 the mean annual change was -0.0325 MJ, less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017, and a smaller fall than in 2001-2004 (-0.0325 against -0.0498 MJ per year). Improvement therefore peaked before 2018 and has since slowed. The segment is short, four years, and its end includes 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic disturbed both output and energy supply. A short segment with unusual years at its end warrants caution, and the mean should not be taken as a settled new trend.

The data do not identify why the slowdown occurred. Several explanations are plausible and are offered only as interpretations, not findings. The pandemic caused abrupt falls and rebounds in activity that distort a ratio of energy to output. Fuel prices affect the incentive to economise on energy, and the price changes of these years may have weakened it. Structural change in industry, including shifts in the weight of energy-intensive sectors in world output, can move intensity independently of efficiency in any single sector. The series measures energy per unit of GDP, so it blends efficiency with the composition of the economy, and none of these causes can be separated from the others using this result alone.

For 2030 the implication is conditional. If the rate of 2018-2021 persisted, the world would fall well short of doubling the rate of 2011-2017, let alone exceeding it. Meeting the target on the most demanding reading would require a pace far above any segment in the record. The target also admits more than one reading, since the earlier rate may be taken from the period before 2015 or from the baseline decade, and the choice changes the threshold. The segment comparison tests only the reading that uses periods within the series; the pre-2015 reading is not tested here. On the comparison made, the break of 2018 shows that the recent direction is away from the target, not towards it.

### Doubling the earlier rate is not met, and proposals follow

On the comparison of the 2011-2017 segment with the 2018-2021 segment, doubling is not met. Target 7.3 asks for a doubling of the global rate of improvement in energy efficiency, but it does not say which earlier rate is to be doubled or which period is to be compared. Three readings are possible: the pace before 2015 set against the pace after it, a fixed earlier rate set against the pace to 2030, and the pace in the years of fastest improvement set against the most recent years. The bench holds no pre-2015 rate, so the first reading cannot be tested here, and the fixed-rate reading also remains untested. The comparison below tests the third reading alone, with the 2011-2017 segment of the world series as the earlier rate and the 2018-2021 segment as the recent one. The verdict holds for that reading only.

From 2011 to 2017 the mean annual change in world energy intensity was -0.1045 MJ per dollar of GDP at 2021 purchasing power parity. From 2018 to 2021 it was -0.0325 MJ. Doubling would require a recent pace of about twice the earlier one, and the recent pace is much slower, so intensity is falling more slowly, not twice as fast. The trend tool classes the world rate of -0.0110 as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the results do not state the period of that rate. The segment from 2018 to 2021 includes the pandemic years, when output and energy supply both moved sharply, so part of the slowdown may reflect those disturbances and not a lasting change. Only four years are covered, and the data cannot separate the two explanations.

Regional results show where the world picture is made. Four groups are classed as on track or target met: Europe and Central Asia, with the steepest rate of any region at -0.0608, the high-income group at -0.0334, South Asia at -0.0220 and North America at -0.0204. The label reflects the tool's own benchmark and does not show that those groups are doubling a previous rate. The high-income group fell from 4.3961 MJ in 2015 to 3.4666 MJ in 2022, and Europe and Central Asia from 4.0020 MJ to 2.5791 MJ over the same years. Efficiency gains, structural change and fuel switching are familiar possible explanations in richer economies, but the results do not establish which applies.

Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as stagnating, with a rate of -0.0027, and its intensity moved from 6.2412 MJ in 2015 to 6.1403 MJ in 2021. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group is also classed as stagnating, at -0.0009, with levels of 5.3599 MJ in 2015 and 5.3320 MJ in 2021. East Asia and Pacific shows moderate progress, at -0.0142, but acceleration is needed there: its intensity fell from 5.6997 MJ to 5.2313 MJ. Latin America and the Caribbean, at -0.0092, and the low-income group, at -0.0063, show marginal progress. The low-income group still has the highest level of any income group, at 7.1393 MJ in 2021. These readings describe the series only; end years and trend periods differ across regions.

For 2030 the implication is limited. On the segment comparison the doubling is not met, and the latest data point is 2021 for most aggregates and 2022 for some, so later developments are not visible. Only 116 countries reported in 2022, so the most recent figures rest on incomplete reporting.

Intensity is also an imperfect measure of efficiency. It divides energy supply by output, so it moves with the structure of an economy, climate and trade as well as technical efficiency. A fall may come from a shift to services without any gain in equipment efficiency, and a flat series may hide improvements offset by growth in energy-heavy activity. The proposals respond to these limits and to the regional gaps, and none presumes which measures would work.

w-c05-6-5.text:
### Global literacy stands at 87.7 per cent among adults and 93.1 per cent among youth

Literacy, as the World Bank series defines it, is the share of people who can both read and write, with understanding, a short simple statement about their everyday life. Adults are those aged 15 and above; youth are those aged 15 to 24. The measure is a threshold of basic ability. It says nothing about fluency, about comprehension of complex texts, or about the skills needed to function in a digital economy.

On this measure the world is largely literate. The adult rate stood at 85.96 per cent in 2015 and reached 87.74 per cent in 2024. The youth rate rose from 91.4 per cent in 2015 to 93.11 per cent in 2024. Youth rates exceed adult rates in the world figures for both years. As context rather than a finding, this is consistent with younger cohorts having had more schooling than older adults, which would also lift the adult rate as cohorts replace one another; the results hold no schooling or cohort data to test that explanation.

Target 4.6 asks for more than the indicator can show. It commits countries to ensure that all youth and a substantial proportion of adults, men and women alike, achieve literacy and numeracy. The series held on the bench measures literacy only; it gives no figure for numeracy, so half of the target's wording cannot be assessed here. The phrase 'a substantial proportion of adults' has no fixed threshold. It can be read as a majority, as most adults, or as a rate close to universal. Under the first two readings the world adult rate of 87.74 per cent in 2024 already meets the target; under the third it does not. The results do not fix which reading applies. The trend-to-target tool was run on the youth series only, so the adult half of the target is answered here by levels alone: no adult rating, annual rate or expected 2030 value exists in the results, and none is claimed. The adult series is read only from its two end points, 85.96 per cent in 2015 and 87.74 per cent in 2024. For youth the wording is stricter: 'all' implies 100 per cent, and the 2024 figure of 93.11 per cent falls short of it.

The figures are global averages and conceal wide differences between regions and income groups, which the later parts of this section take up. They also rest on a limited number of surveys and censuses. The count of countries reporting an adult value was 56 in 2019, 42 in 2020, 45 in 2022, 33 in 2023 and 29 in 2024; the youth count was 62 in 2019, 43 in 2020, 58 in 2022, 35 in 2023 and 29 in 2024. Most of the 2024 figures are therefore not fresh national measurements. The results give counts of countries by reference year, but not the latest year of each country's value, so the number of countries whose latest value is older than 2024, and the typical lag, cannot be stated. The currency of the headline aggregates is thus only partly answered: the reporting counts show how thin recent years are, and the age of the underlying values stays unquantified. The next part examines how far the headline values can be trusted given that coverage.

### Data coverage is thin and uneven, so the latest values are partly modelled or dated

Literacy data are reported by far fewer countries in any single year than the headline coverage suggests. Across all years, 155 countries have at least one adult literacy value and 160 have at least one youth value. Yet in any one year only a fraction report. Adult reporting ranged from 13 countries in 2003 to 56 in 2019, and youth reporting from 23 countries in 2003 to 62 in 2019. The latest year, 2024, holds only 29 countries in each series.

As general context, outside the results, literacy rates usually come from population censuses and household surveys, which arrive at intervals of several years rather than annually. A country then appears in the record in the year of an exercise and is absent in the years between. The counts are consistent with such a calendar: adult reporting climbed from 32 countries in 2008 to 48 in 2010 and 53 in 2011, then fell to 33 in 2013. Swings of this kind are better read as differences in which countries reported than as changes in literacy itself.

The period after 2015 shows the same unevenness. Adult reporting stood at 47 countries in 2015, reached 56 in 2019, then fell to 42 in 2020, the year the pandemic disrupted fieldwork in many places, as general context. Youth reporting went from 62 countries in 2019 to 43 in 2020. A partial recovery appeared in 2022, with 45 countries for adults and 58 for youth, before the counts dropped to 33 and 35 in 2023 and to 29 in both series in 2024.

The question of how current the data are can be answered here only through these reference-year counts. The results show that 29 countries report a value for 2024 in each series, against 155 and 160 countries with a value in some year. The latest year of each country was not returned by the bench, so the number of countries whose latest value is older than 2024, and the typical lag in years, cannot be quantified; this part of the question is unanswered. What the counts do imply is that most countries with any literacy value have no observation for 2024, and that any 2024 aggregate therefore leans on earlier surveys, on modelling, or on both. The aggregates carry different labels: the world, regional and income-group values are mostly dated 2024, but Europe and Central Asia is dated 2023, North America 2022, and high income 2020 for adults and 2021 for youth. The results do not record whether any aggregate is observed, carried forward or modelled, so the share of dated or modelled values is unknown.

Three cautions follow. First, regional and world values for recent years rest on few direct observations, and a country's latest value may be several years old even when labelled with a recent year. Second, year-on-year comparison is unreliable, because a change between two years may reflect a different set of countries or method rather than real movement. Third, the sparse high-income record, with adult values labelled 2020 only, means that the strongest literacy performers are the least visible. Comparisons are safer over longer spans, and the findings that follow are read with these limits in mind.

### Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia hold the largest gaps, and women trail men

The widest gaps lie in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. In 2024 adult literacy in Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 68.7 per cent and in South Asia at 78.2 per cent, against 96.6 per cent in East Asia and Pacific. Europe and Central Asia, at 98.8 per cent in 2023, and North America, at 98.8 per cent in 2022, sit close to the ceiling. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached 75.6 per cent in 2024. The adult figure covers everyone aged 15 and above, so it moves slowly. As outside context rather than a finding of these results, regions in which many older people never attended school carry that history in their totals.

The adult half of target 4.6 can be read only from levels, because the results hold no trend-to-target rating, rate or expected 2030 value for the adult series; the rating shown below is for youth alone. Target 4.6 asks for a substantial proportion of adults, and the wording sets no threshold, so it can be read in more than one way. Read against the world level, adult literacy rose from 86.0 per cent in 2015 to 87.7 per cent in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 64.3 to 68.7 per cent, South Asia from 72.0 to 78.2 per cent, and low-income countries from 59.7 to 63.6 per cent. These are gains of a few points over nine years, and none of these groups is near universal adult literacy. The adult half of the target is therefore described, not rated, and the question of whether adults are on course for 2030 stays unanswered by these results.

The youth series shows a different and more encouraging pattern. South Asia's youth literacy rose from 89.6 per cent in 2015 to 96.9 per cent in 2024, the largest regional gain in the results, and the youth trend rating for the region is on track or target met, with an expected 2030 value above 100 per cent that is a limit of the linear projection and not a possible literacy rate. Whether schooling expansion explains the rise is not tested here; it is the usual context offered for such changes, and the results contain no schooling data. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 75.2 to 79.0 per cent over the same period, rated marginal progress with significant acceleration needed, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 85.0 to 86.9 per cent. Youth literacy in East Asia and Pacific, at 99.1 per cent in 2024, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, at 98.7 per cent, has little room left to grow. By income group, low-income countries reached 75.4 per cent among youth in 2024 and 63.6 per cent among adults, while upper middle income countries stood at 99.3 and 96.2 per cent. Lower middle income countries recorded 92.0 per cent for youth and 78.3 per cent for adults.

Women trail men, and the shortfall is largest where overall literacy is lowest. Worldwide, adult female literacy was 84.6 per cent in 2024, below the adult total of 87.7 per cent. In Sub-Saharan Africa it was 62.7 per cent, in South Asia 71.6 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan 67.4 per cent. In low-income countries it was 56.4 per cent. Adult female literacy in each of these groups was higher in 2024 than in 2015: Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 56.8 per cent, South Asia from 63.5 per cent, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan from 63.0 per cent, and low-income countries from 50.9 per cent. Starting levels were low.

The youth gender parity index, the ratio of female to male literacy, shows younger women closing the gap. It stood at 0.98 worldwide in 2024, up from 0.97 in 2015. South Asia rose from 0.96 to 0.99. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 0.90 to 0.94, and low-income countries from 0.87 to 0.93. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan reached only 0.92, up from 0.90, the lowest regional value in 2024. East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America were at 1.00 in their latest years, as the index is reported to two decimals. Only 29 countries reported in 2024, so the latest regional values rest on a small and shifting set of observations, and part of any change may reflect which countries report. The results give reporting counts by year but not each country's latest year, so how many countries rely on values older than 2024, and by how many years, is not shown. The results also do not say how many values are modelled or carried forward. Shifts after 2020 cannot be separated from this reporting pattern.

### Progress is real but too slow to reach universal youth literacy by 2030, and the proposals follow

The trend-to-target results for youth literacy show progress that is real but, in every region except South Asia, too slow to reach the 2030 target at the current pace. South Asia is rated on track, but its projection exceeds the 100 per cent ceiling, so that rating is unreliable. The target value is 100.0 per cent, and the tool compares the observed pace since 2015 with the pace needed to reach it. The world as a whole is rated as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a ratio of 0.33 and an expected youth literacy rate of 94.3 per cent in 2030.

Even regions close to the ceiling are not rated as on track. East Asia and Pacific rose from 98.9 per cent in 2015 to 99.1 per cent in 2024 and is expected to reach 99.2 per cent in 2030, a ratio of 0.28 and a marginal rating. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 98.3 per cent to 98.7 per cent, with an expected 98.9 per cent in 2030 and a ratio of 0.39. Europe and Central Asia is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.68 and an expected 99.9 per cent in 2030. High income is also moderate, with a ratio of 0.53 and an expected 99.6 per cent. North America is rated as stagnation, with a ratio of 0.07. Regions near the ceiling have little distance left to close, which is context rather than a finding, and the results give no measurement-error figure against which these small movements could be judged.

The larger shortfalls lie where the starting level was lower. Low income is rated marginal and is expected to reach 77.9 per cent in 2030, with a ratio of 0.22. Sub-Saharan Africa is rated marginal, with an expected 81.6 per cent and a ratio of 0.26. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is rated marginal, with an expected 88.2 per cent and a ratio of 0.21. Lower middle income is rated moderate, with a ratio of 0.63 and an expected 95.3 per cent. South Asia is the single region rated on track, with a ratio of 1.20, but its expected 2030 value of 102.1 per cent exceeds the ceiling and cannot be a literal rate. No region is therefore shown to reach universal youth literacy by 2030 on a sound projection.

The adult half of target 4.6 is answered here only in part. The bench returned no trend-to-target result for the adult series, so no adult pace, ratio, rating or expected 2030 value can be reported, and none is inferred. The target asks for all youth but only a substantial proportion of adults, a phrase it does not define, so no threshold is tested. Read as a rising adult rate, the levels show movement: world adult literacy rose from 86.0 per cent in 2015 to 87.7 per cent in 2024. Low income moved from 59.7 per cent to 63.6 per cent, Sub-Saharan Africa from 64.3 per cent to 68.7 per cent, and South Asia from 72.0 per cent to 78.2 per cent. Adult female literacy in low-income countries was 56.4 per cent in 2024, against 50.9 per cent in 2015. These levels show the distance remaining but do not show whether adult progress is on or off track.

Currency limits every reading, and the question of how current the data are is answered only in part. In 2024 only 29 countries reported adult literacy and 29 reported youth literacy, down from 56 adult and 62 youth reporters in 2019. The latest year of each country's value was not returned by the tools, so the number of countries relying on values older than 2024, and the size of the lag, cannot be stated. The share of regional and world values resting on older surveys or modelled estimates is likewise unknown. Numeracy, which the target names, has no measure in the series held.

Proposals follow from these findings. National statistical offices in countries without recent surveys should run literacy surveys or add literacy questions to household surveys, since only 29 countries reported in 2024. The World Bank and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should publish the reference year and the source type, survey or modelled, for each country value, so that currency can be judged. Governments and donors in low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa should expand adult and second-chance programmes aimed at women, because adult female literacy in low-income countries was 56.4 per cent in 2024, noting that the marginal ratings concern youth. The council should admit a trend-to-target computation on the adult series so that the adult half of target 4.6 has a pace and a rating.

w-c09-10-4.text:
### Net official assistance reached US$259 billion in 2023, an imperfect proxy for Aid for Trade

The question asks how much official assistance supports trade capacity. The bench cannot answer it directly. Target 8.a calls for more Aid for Trade for developing countries, the least developed above all, including through the Enhanced Integrated Framework, but the shelf holds no Aid for Trade commitments or disbursements. It also holds no least-developed-country breakdown and no Enhanced Integrated Framework record, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The series available is net official development assistance received, which counts concessional loans, net of repayments, and grants for every purpose. It can serve only as an upper bound on the resources from which trade capacity support could be drawn, not as an estimate of that support.

Read at that level, the world total rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US$. Constant prices remove general price changes, so the rise is real. In 2023, 136 countries reported receipts, so some recipients lack a figure for the latest year and any total should be read with that gap in mind. The nearest available reading for poorer recipients is by income group: low-income economies received US$44.6 billion in 2023, up from US$35.2 billion in 2015. That is not a least-developed-country figure, because the groups do not coincide.

The target sets no numeric threshold and no end level. The trend tool was therefore run on direction alone, with no numeric target: a series is classed as on track when it rises at a meaningful rate, and as stagnating or marginal when it does not. On that reading the world is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.0545. The label is weak evidence. A rising total of general assistance does not show that trade capacity support has grown, that it has gone to the least developed countries, or that it has been effective. Increases may reflect emergency, humanitarian or other spending unrelated to trade.

The point matters for 2030 because the target can be read in more than one way: as a rise in the volume of Aid for Trade, as a rise in its share of assistance, or as improved support to least developed countries specifically. The bench can speak only to the first, and only through a proxy. The parts that follow take the proxy as given, examine how it differs among regions and income groups, and show what changed after 2015 and after 2020, while keeping the limits of the measure in view. In short, the amount supporting trade capacity is not measured here; US$259.5 billion in 2023 is a ceiling on the proxy, not a finding about trade.

### Assistance rose unevenly across regions and concentrated among fewer recipients

Regional totals diverged sharply between 2015 and 2023, measured in constant 2023 US dollars. Europe and Central Asia recorded the largest change, from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023. The trend tool classes the region as on track or target met, with a rate of 0.213. Established knowledge of the period suggests that the displacement and reconstruction needs created by war in Europe explain part of this, though the series does not show what drove the change. No target level is set in the tool, so the classification reads only the direction of travel.

Other regions moved far less. East Asia and Pacific rose from US$9.9 billion to US$10.7 billion, with a rate of 0.010, classed as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. Latin America and the Caribbean went from US$10.6 billion to US$10.8 billion, a rate of 0.002, classed as stagnation. South Asia rose from US$8.5 billion to US$10.7 billion and is classed as on track, at a rate of 0.028. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan went from US$31.1 billion to US$35.1 billion, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Sub-Saharan Africa remains the largest regional recipient, at US$64.8 billion in 2023, up from US$51.8 billion in 2015. North America records zero in both years, as expected for a region without recipients in this series.

The pattern matters for Aid for Trade because a rise in the world total, from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion, says little about where trade capacity is being built. Regions with flat inflows in real terms face rising trade-support needs without a matching rise in assistance, while this series cannot show how much of any inflow reaches trade purposes.

The spread among countries widened. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of assistance received was 0.361 in 2015, 0.370 in 2019 and 0.452 in 2023. The Theil index, which is more sensitive to large recipients, was 0.255 in 2015 and 0.256 in 2019, then rose to 0.460 in 2023. The jump came after 2019, so the concentration is a feature of the years after 2020 rather than of the first half of the period. The coefficient of variation also rose, from 0.643 in 2015 to 1.477 in 2023.

The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 38.7% in 2019 and 29.6% in 2023. Regional averages therefore explain a shrinking part of the inequality, and differences among countries within the same region now account for most of it. Regional reading alone would hide this, so country-level targeting matters more than regional envelopes.

The country count also shifted: 138 countries in 2015, 134 in 2019 and 135 in 2023. The coverage statement for 2023 elsewhere in the results gives 136 countries reporting. These small differences reflect which countries have data and pass the weighting in each tool, and they mean that part of the change in concentration could arise from changes in who is counted. The change in count is small against the size of the rise in the Gini and Theil measures, but it cannot be excluded as a contributor.

### A single surge in 2022 explains most of the recent rise, and 43 countries regressed

The break analysis of world net official development assistance, in constant 2023 US dollars, detects breaks in 2022 and 2023. In the segment from 2001 to 2021 the mean annual change was US$6.4 billion. The segment covering 2022 alone has a mean annual change of US$49.8 billion, a single-year change several times the long-run pace. The segment covering 2023 alone has a mean change of minus US$0.7 billion. The world total stood at US$169.7 billion in 2015 and US$259.5 billion in 2023. The break test shows when the series shifted, not why, and the results do not state what share of the 2015 to 2023 rise the 2022 change represents. This part therefore claims only that the movement was concentrated around 2022 and eased slightly the following year.

Context from outside these data, not tested here, points to war-related emergency and reception flows in Europe in 2022. The series does not attribute the 2022 change to any recipient or purpose. Europe and Central Asia, which rose from US$10.0 billion in 2015 to US$47.0 billion in 2023, is consistent in timing with that context, but the results do not show that it drove the world break. A one-year movement of this kind is also a weak basis for judging whether support for trade capacity has grown, since emergency flows serve humanitarian and budget needs rather than trade facilitation.

The country classes show how little the aggregate says about most recipients. Of 138 countries assessed, 79 are classed as on track or target met, and they hold 39.1% of the population of the assessed group. Another 5 show moderate progress, with 0.4% of the population, 6 show marginal progress, with 3.1%, and 5 are stagnant, with 1.7%. The largest class by population is regression: the trend tool classes 43 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the assessed population. This is a class of the trend rate. It is not a comparison of 2023 receipts with 2015 levels, and the results do not give those country levels.

This divergence matters for the 2030 horizon. A world total can rise while the trend rate is negative for countries holding more than half of the assessed population. The tool was run with no numeric target, since target 8.a sets none, so the classes describe the direction of the trend rate only and not attainment of a defined threshold. The series ends in 2023 and gives no basis for forecasting the path to 2030 in either direction.

### Reaching 2030 requires better measurement and steadier, better-targeted assistance, with proposals

Reaching 2030 on target 8.a depends first on measurement. The bench cannot give an amount for official assistance that supports trade capacity. Net official development assistance received was US$259.5 billion in 2023, in constant 2023 US dollars, and that figure is an upper bound on what could support trade capacity, not an estimate of it. The series covers every purpose, and the shelf holds no Aid for Trade disbursements. It gives no breakdown for least developed countries and no Enhanced Integrated Framework figure, so those parts of the target are unanswered. The nearest available readings are income-group and regional totals: low income countries received US$44.6 billion in 2023 and Sub-Saharan Africa US$64.8 billion. Target 8.a also carries no numeric benchmark. The trend tool was run with no numeric target, so its classes describe the direction of the trend rate only.

The series gives no basis for forecasting the path to 2030. The mean annual change was US$6.4 billion in 2001-2021. The change in 2022 was US$49.8 billion, and in 2023 it was a fall of US$0.7 billion. Context from outside these data, not tested here, points to emergency flows linked to the war in Europe; the series does not show what drove the change. A series that ends in 2023 cannot say whether the 2022 level will persist, recede or be exceeded.

The distribution of recipients shows how little the aggregate says. The trend tool classes 43 of 138 countries as regressing, holding 55.7% of the population assessed. This is a class of the trend rate, meaning the fitted trend of their assistance is negative; it is not a comparison of 2023 with 2015 levels. Inequality among recipients rose: the population-weighted Gini coefficient was 0.361 in 2015 and 0.452 in 2023. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 45.3% in 2015 to 29.6% in 2023, so most of the inequality lies within regions. The decomposition does not show which allocation policy would work better.

w-c09-6-4.text:
### The world share fell by 1.4 points, from a 2015 base, not by a substantial margin

Target 8.6 asks for a substantial reduction in the proportion of youth not in employment, education or training by 2020. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so any verdict rests on a reading chosen by the analyst. Here the reading is plain: a substantial reduction would be a fall large enough to be visible against the starting level and to change the position of most regions.

The question is about 2020, yet the results do not give the world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be read directly. The verdict is therefore an inference from the available series. The modelled ILO estimate puts the global share at 21.2 per cent of the youth population in 2015 and at 19.8 per cent in 2025. The fall over the decade is 1.4 points, or about 6.8 per cent of the 2015 level. The latest year available is five years after the target date. The series is a modelled estimate, not a count from a single survey: countries with sparse labour force data receive values built from regional patterns and covariates, so small movements in the world figure should be read with caution. The estimate covers 182 countries reporting in 2025.

The pace of change did not follow a steady path. The break analysis of the annual change in the world share finds shifts in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by about 0.2 points a year on average. Between 2013 and 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which means that the share was essentially flat in the years just before the target date. In 2020 the mean annual change was 1.37 points. These windows do not coincide exactly with 2015 to 2020, so they indicate the direction of travel rather than a measured net change. The measured fall belongs to later periods, taken up in a later part, and the results do not show where within the decade most of the decline arose.

The income groups show why the global figure hides unequal movement. In high-income countries the share moved from 12.2 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025, and in upper middle income countries from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent. Lower middle income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The global average is thus pulled down by the middle-income and wealthier groups, while the poorest countries ended the period with a higher share than they began with.

On the reading used here, these results do not support a claim of substantial reduction by 2020. The share was close to flat in the years before the target date, fell by a small amount over ten years, and rose in the poorest countries. A looser reading of 'substantially' could change the verdict, and the target text leaves that question open, but on the stated reading a decline of this size, reached five years after the target date, does not meet the intent of the goal.

### Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden

Regional levels in 2025 range widely. North America holds the lowest share, at 11.8 per cent of youth, down from 12.5 per cent in 2015. East Asia and Pacific stands at 12.8 per cent, down from 14.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 13.0 per cent, down from 15.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is at 19.3 per cent, from 21.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is at 21.4 per cent, slightly above its 2015 level of 20.9 per cent. South Asia shows the largest fall among the regions, from 28.4 per cent to 23.4 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is highest at 32.1 per cent, and its share rose from 31.1 per cent. Most regions moved down modestly, while two did not.

Income groups show the same split. Low-income countries rose from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent, while lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent, and high-income countries from 12.2 per cent to 10.9 per cent. The poorest group is thus the one in which the share grew, and by 2025 it stands well above the others. Demographic pressure, thin labour demand and limited schooling places are well-established contexts for this pattern in low-income settings, though the series does not show what drives it.

Young women have higher shares than youth as a whole. The world female share was 30.2 per cent in 2015 and 27.1 per cent in 2025, above the all-youth share of 19.8 per cent in 2025. Male shares are not among the results cited, so the comparison with young men cannot be drawn here. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the female share was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged, so nearly half of young women are outside work and study. South Asia improved from 46.0 per cent to 37.1 per cent, yet remains high. Low-income countries moved against the trend, from 32.6 per cent to 34.4 per cent. Norms on care work and early marriage, and limits on women's mobility and employment, are the usual explanations, stated here as context only.

Among countries, the trend classes are scattered. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the direction of the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 28 show moderate progress and 29 marginal progress, while 21 stagnate and 58 regress. The regressing group holds 18.8 per cent of the population, more than the on-track group. No numeric target exists, so the classes rest on the analyst's reading of the trend and should be read as direction rather than as a verdict.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, did not narrow. The Gini coefficient was 0.231 in 2015, 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for a little over half of the inequality in both years. Convergence is not shown: the beta of -0.00428 has a p-value of 0.214, not distinguishable from zero. Countries starting higher did not reliably improve faster.

### The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement

The movement of the world share is better read as a sequence of breaks in timing than as a steady trend. The break analysis of the annual change in the modelled ILO series finds breaks in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by a mean of 0.2 points a year. That is the only stretch in which the decline looks like steady progress, and it ended before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.

From 2013 to 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which is near stagnation. This window does not match the 2015 to 2020 span of the target, and the results cited give no world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be derived from them. In 2020 the annual change jumped by 1.37 points, the largest movement in the series. The timing coincides with the closure of schools and workplaces during the pandemic. That link is context drawn from well-established knowledge; the data show when the break occurred and do not test its cause. The evidence bearing on the target year is therefore the 2013 to 2019 mean and the 2020 jump, and both point away from a substantial reduction by 2020. The missing 2020 level is a limit on the verdict, not a finding.

The fall that followed was nearly as sharp. From 2021 to 2023 the share fell by a mean of 1.08 points a year, a separate measured period that took back much of the 2020 rise. The results do not show where the decline recorded by 2025 was produced. From 2024 to 2025 the share rose again by a mean of 0.15 points a year. The long-run rate of change for the world, at -0.0070 on the trend tool's scale, is read by that tool as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. These classes are the tool's own categories, applied without a numeric target.

Sub-Saharan Africa followed a different path. Its breaks fall in 2014, 2021, 2023 and 2024. From 2006 to 2013 its mean annual change was -0.04 points. From 2014 to 2020 it rose by 0.45 points a year; that window includes the 2020 break, so the rise cannot be assigned wholly to the period before the pandemic, and no world mean for the same window is cited for comparison. A young population growing faster than jobs and school places is a common explanation, but the data do not test it. After 2020 the region eased, with a mean change of -0.29 points a year in 2021 and 2022 and -1.23 points in 2023, then 0.00 points a year in 2024 and 2025. The trend tool still classes the region as regression to 2030.

The breaks therefore cluster around 2020 and 2021, set against a world share that was nearly flat from 2013 to 2019. The fall of 2021 to 2023 is consistent with a position partly restored rather than advanced, though the data do not isolate the cause.

### The 2020 target was missed, and 2030 needs faster progress and a clearer definition

On the reading used here, the 2020 target was not met in a substantial sense, and a looser reading could change that verdict. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so the verdict rests on the analyst's own reading. The question of the target year cannot be answered directly, because the results give neither a 2020 world level nor a net change from 2015 to 2020. The inference rests on the break analysis: a mean annual change of 0.02 points over 2013 to 2019, followed by a rise of 1.37 points in 2020. No claim is made here about where in 2015 to 2025 the decline arose. The world share stood at 21.2 per cent of youth in 2015 and 19.8 per cent in 2025.

The trend tool assigns its own classes, and its target is given as none, so the classes describe the direction and pace of change, not distance from a stated goal. The world is classed as marginal progress, needing significant acceleration, with a compound annual rate of -0.7 per cent from the 2015 baseline. East Asia and Pacific stands at -1.2 per cent a year and High income at -1.2 per cent, both marginal. Latin America and the Caribbean is at -0.9 per cent and North America at -0.6 per cent. Only Europe and Central Asia, at -1.6 per cent, and South Asia, at -1.9 per cent, reach the moderate class, and both still need acceleration. Low income, at 0.9 per cent a year, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, at 0.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.2 per cent, are classed as regression.

The country count rests on 187 countries assessed by the trend tool, whereas the 2025 levels rest on 182 countries reporting that year. Of the 187, 51 are on track or have met the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the assessed population. A further 28 show moderate progress, 29 marginal progress and 21 stagnation. Regression affects 58 countries, holding 18.8 per cent of the population.

Countries have not drawn together. The convergence test gives a beta of -0.0043 with a p-value of 0.214, which cannot be told from zero, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.471 in 2015 to 0.532 in 2025 across 182 countries. For 2030 the implication is that the present pace leaves the world far from a substantial reduction on the reading used here. The estimates are modelled, so classes for individual countries carry uncertainty.

Several proposals follow. National statistical offices in low-income countries should run labour force surveys at least every two years, so that modelled estimates rest on measured data. Ministries of labour and education in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region should set targets for young women's transition into work or study, since their share has barely moved. The UN Statistical Commission should adopt a numeric reading of 'substantially' for target 8.6, so that future verdicts do not depend on an analyst's choice.

w-c09-1-5.text:
### World income per person has grown at under 2 per cent a year

World GDP per capita grew by 1.9 per cent in 2015 and by 2.0 per cent in 2025, according to the World Bank's World Development Indicators. A decade that opened and closed at almost the same rate, a little under 2 per cent a year, is the first finding of this section. Growth of that size doubles average income only over several decades, and it sits far below the pace that the second reading of target 8.1 asks of the least developed countries.

Target 8.1 can be read in two ways. Its first clause asks for per capita economic growth 'in accordance with national circumstances', which sets no number. Its second asks for at least 7 per cent GDP growth a year in the least developed countries, a figure for total output, not for income per person. The two measure different things: GDP growth includes the effect of a rising population, and in countries with fast population growth the gap between the two can be wide. This section uses GDP per capita growth as its main indicator, because it describes the change in output available to each resident, and turns to total GDP growth when the 7 per cent threshold is considered. Gross national income per capita is a third measure, which adds income earned abroad and subtracts income paid out; it is reported for fewer countries and is not the basis of the comparisons here.

The path of world growth over the longer run reads as a sequence of shocks rather than as a steady rise. The break analysis of the annual change in the world rate finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The mean annual change was -2.8 percentage points across 2008 and 2009, the years of the global financial crisis, and then +5.8 in 2010 as output recovered. The pattern repeated with greater force around the pandemic: the mean change was -5.4 in 2020 and +9.4 in 2021, followed by -3.1 in 2022. Between 2011 and 2019 the mean annual change was -0.2, a gentle drift downward and not a collapse, and from 2023 to 2025 it was again -0.2. These are changes in the growth rate from one year to the next, not growth rates themselves, and they should be read as the size of each swing.

The reading matters for 2030. A world economy that returns each time to roughly 2 per cent growth, after shocks that arrive about once in a decade, offers no sign of the acceleration that sustained income gains would need. The figure for 2025 rests on 186 countries reporting, against 211 in 2015, so the latest year is less complete than earlier ones and may be revised as late reports arrive.

### Regions differ by a factor of more than six

Regional growth in GDP per capita in 2015, from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, ranged from -0.7 per cent in Latin America and the Caribbean to 6.5 per cent in South Asia. Sub-Saharan Africa grew by 0.2 per cent and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan by 0.8 per cent. These figures describe a single year, not a settled order, and no ratio between regions is claimed here.

South Asia remained the fastest region throughout, at 6.2 per cent in 2025, a little below its 2015 rate. East Asia and Pacific held a similar position, at 4.0 per cent in 2015 and 3.9 per cent in 2025. The trend results cover GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars. The trend tool reads the compound annual change from 2015 and extends it to 2030. No numerical target is set for income per person, and the results report no benchmark value, so the classes are relative readings of momentum that cannot be reproduced from the figures given. They show direction and pace only, and they are not a test of any benchmark. South Asia's trend is classed as "on track or target met", with an annual rate of 0.0465. East Asia and Pacific carries the same class, at 0.0357.

The wealthier regions moved the other way. Europe and Central Asia slowed from 1.6 per cent in 2015 to 1.3 per cent in 2025, and North America from 1.9 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Their trend rates, 0.0150 and 0.0167, are classed as "moderate progress, but acceleration needed". High-income countries as a group went from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0151, in the same class. Slower growth at high income levels is often explained, as context outside these results, by the limited scope for catching up and by ageing populations; the results do not test this.

Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa show the largest rise in the annual rate between the two end years. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from -0.7 per cent to 1.6 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa from 0.2 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Both ended close to the world rate of 2.0 per cent, yet the decade-long trend in income per person is less favourable. Latin America and the Caribbean has a trend rate of 0.0054, classed as "marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed", and Sub-Saharan Africa a rate of -0.0020, classed as "regression". A single good year at the end does not alter a decade in which income per person barely rose or fell. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region grew by 0.8 per cent in 2015 and 0.9 per cent in 2025, with a trend rate of 0.0076, also classed as "marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed".

By income group the pattern is similar. Low-income countries grew by 2.5 per cent in 2025, after -2.9 per cent in 2015, yet their trend rate over the decade is 0.0007, classed as "stagnation". Lower-middle-income countries grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025, up from 4.0 per cent in 2015, with a trend rate of 0.0292. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, with a trend rate of 0.0371. Both of these groups are classed as "on track or target met". A low-income growth rate of 2.5 per cent in 2025 is one year's reading, and the "stagnation" class shows that it has not yet lifted the decade's trend.

### Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015

The breaks in the annual change of world GDP per capita growth locate the large movements in the series. The break analysis of the World Development Indicators finds breaks in 2002, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The segments between them are short, and several consist of one year. The breaks describe changes in the rate of growth, not its level: a mean change of -2.8 points in 2008-2009 means that the growth rate fell by that amount each year on average across those two years. The analysis does not measure what share of the movement each shock explains, so this part claims only where the breaks fall and how large they are.

The global financial crisis is the first large shock in the series, and it lies before 2015. The 2008-2009 segment has a mean annual change of -2.8 points, and 2010 follows with a rebound of 5.8 points. The long segment from 2011 to 2019 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, and it straddles the 2015 baseline. That is a slow drift downward in the growth rate across nine years, not a collapse.

The period after 2015 is dominated by the pandemic. In 2020 the annual change in world growth was -5.4 points, the largest fall in the series. The 2021 segment records a rise of 9.4 points, the largest rise. The 2022 segment then shows a change of -3.1 points. The segment from 2023 to 2025 has a mean annual change of -0.2 points, so growth was drifting down again, much as in 2011-2019. These swings are why the world rate in 2025, at 2.0 per cent, can resemble the rate in 2015, at 1.9 per cent, while the path between them was violent. As context, not a result of the analysis, the 2020 fall is usually attributed to lockdowns and the collapse of travel and trade, and the 2021 gain largely to recovery from a depressed base.

Across income groups, the endpoints need the same caution. Low-income countries recorded GDP per capita growth of -2.9 per cent in 2015 and 2.5 per cent in 2025. That is a swing from contraction to modest expansion, but it compares two single years. Lower-middle-income countries moved from 4.0 per cent to 4.6 per cent, upper-middle-income countries from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent, and high-income countries from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent. Target 8.1 sets 7 per cent for total GDP growth in the least developed countries, and these results contain neither that measure nor that group, so the target cannot be tested here. The per capita rates of every group listed are below 7 per cent, but that is not a test of the target.

A ten-year endpoint comparison therefore hides the volatility that the breaks reveal. Two years close in value say nothing about the swings between them, and a large gain between endpoints may only be recovery from a poor starting year. The comparison also depends on coverage. The number of countries reporting GDP growth was 211 in 2015, 210 in 2019 and 210 in 2021, but only 186 in 2025. The fall from 209 countries in 2022 to 204 in 2023 and 200 in 2024 suggests that data arrive late, so the 2025 values rest on fewer countries and may be revised. For 2030 this implies that the latest readings are provisional, and that any judgment on target 8.1 should wait for the revised series.

### Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence

Beyond regional averages, the trend classification sorts countries by how fast GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) has moved since 2015. No numerical 2030 target exists for this measure, and the results do not report the benchmark value behind the notional target. The tool's rule is the compound annual rate from the baseline and the share of the distance from baseline to target that this rate would cover by 2030. Because the benchmark is not given, the classes below are relative readings of momentum that cannot be reproduced from the results. Their labels, such as "on track or target met", are the tool's wording and are not a verdict against a legal threshold.

Of 209 countries assessed, 74 are classed "on track or target met", and they hold 56.6 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 36 countries are classed "moderate progress, but acceleration needed", with 16.4 per cent of the population. Another 44 are classed "marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed", with 11.8 per cent. Fifteen countries are classed "stagnation", with 5.0 per cent of the population, and 40 are classed "regression", with 10.3 per cent. By count, fewer than half of the countries assessed fall in the first class, though they hold a majority of the population. The results give no country-level income figures, so they do not show whether the lagging countries are the poorest.

The regional readings are consistent with this. South Asia has a compound rate of 0.0465, East Asia and the Pacific 0.0357, the upper middle income group 0.0371 and the lower middle income group 0.0292, and all four are classed "on track or target met". Europe and Central Asia (0.0150), high income countries (0.0151) and North America (0.0167) are classed "moderate progress", as is the world as a whole at 0.0176. Latin America and the Caribbean (0.0054) and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.0076) are classed "marginal progress". The low income group, at 0.0007, is classed "stagnation". Sub-Saharan Africa, at -0.0020, is classed "regression", even though its annual growth rate recovered from 0.2 per cent in 2015 to 1.6 per cent in 2025.

The 7 per cent target cannot be tested with these results. Target 8.1 sets that rate for GDP growth, not per capita growth, in the least developed countries, and the results hold neither a total GDP growth series nor a group figure for those countries. What can be said is narrower: per capita growth in 2025 was below 7 per cent in every group listed. The low income group grew by 2.5 per cent after a contraction of -2.9 per cent in 2015, and South Asia, the highest, grew by 6.2 per cent. Neither is a least developed group, so these figures are a proxy and not a test.

The low income rebound from -2.9 per cent to 2.5 per cent is a sizeable swing, yet the trend classification still reads that group as "stagnation". As context not tested by the results, growth after a shock often restores lost ground before it adds new income, which would explain why a good year need not change the long-run class. Coverage also thins at the end of the series: 186 countries reported growth in 2025, against 211 in 2015, so the latest figures are less complete.

For 2030 the implication is measured. If present rates hold, 74 countries with 56.6 per cent of the population assessed would be read as "on track or target met" on the notional benchmark, while 40 countries with 10.3 per cent are in "regression" and 15 with 5.0 per cent are in "stagnation". The 7 per cent goal is a different measure and remains untested.

Proposals follow from these findings. The World Bank and the statistical offices of the least developed countries should publish a total GDP growth series for the least developed group, so that Target 8.1 can be tested directly. National planners in the 40 countries in "regression" and the 15 in "stagnation" should set out why income per person has not risen, with attention to the low income group, where growth was 2.5 per cent in 2025.
