w-c09-6-5.text:
### The world share fell by 1.4 points, from a 2015 base, not by a substantial margin

Target 8.6 asks for a substantial reduction in the proportion of youth not in employment, education or training by 2020. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so any verdict rests on a reading chosen by the analyst. Here the reading is plain: a substantial reduction would be a fall large enough to be visible against the starting level and to change the position of most regions.

The question is about 2020, yet the results do not give the world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be read directly. The verdict is therefore an inference from the available series. The modelled ILO estimate puts the global share at 21.2 per cent of the youth population in 2015 and at 19.8 per cent in 2025. The fall over the decade is 1.4 points, or about 6.8 per cent of the 2015 level. The latest year available is five years after the target date. The series is a modelled estimate, not a count from a single survey: countries with sparse labour force data receive values built from regional patterns and covariates, so small movements in the world figure should be read with caution. The estimate covers 182 countries reporting in 2025.

The pace of change did not follow a steady path. The break analysis of the annual change in the world share finds shifts in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by about 0.2 points a year on average. Between 2013 and 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which means that the share was essentially flat in the years just before the target date. In 2020 the mean annual change was 1.37 points. These windows do not coincide exactly with 2015 to 2020, so they indicate the direction of travel rather than a measured net change. The measured fall belongs to later periods, taken up in a later part, and the results do not show where within the decade most of the decline arose.

The income groups show why the global figure hides unequal movement. In high-income countries the share moved from 12.2 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025, and in upper middle income countries from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent. Lower middle income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Low-income countries moved the other way, from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The global average is thus pulled down by the middle-income and wealthier groups, while the poorest countries ended the period with a higher share than they began with.

On the reading used here, these results do not support a claim of substantial reduction by 2020. The share was close to flat in the years before the target date, fell by a small amount over ten years, and rose in the poorest countries. A looser reading of 'substantially' could change the verdict, and the target text leaves that question open, but on the stated reading a decline of this size, reached five years after the target date, does not meet the intent of the goal.

### Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden

Regional levels in 2025 range widely. North America holds the lowest share, at 11.8 per cent of youth, down from 12.5 per cent in 2015. East Asia and Pacific stands at 12.8 per cent, down from 14.5 per cent, and Europe and Central Asia at 13.0 per cent, down from 15.3 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is at 19.3 per cent, from 21.0 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa is at 21.4 per cent, slightly above its 2015 level of 20.9 per cent. South Asia shows the largest fall among the regions in this comparison, from 28.4 per cent to 23.4 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is highest at 32.1 per cent, and its share rose from 31.1 per cent. Most regions moved down modestly, while two did not.

Income groups show the same split. Low-income countries rose from 24.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent, while lower-middle-income countries fell from 26.3 per cent to 23.3 per cent. Upper-middle-income countries moved from 18.2 per cent to 16.5 per cent, and high-income countries from 12.2 per cent to 10.9 per cent. The poorest group is thus the one in which the share grew, and by 2025 it stands above the others. Demographic pressure, thin labour demand and limited schooling places are well-established contexts for this pattern in low-income settings, though the series does not show what drives it.

Young women's shares exceed the all-youth share. The world female share was 30.2 per cent in 2015 and 27.1 per cent in 2025, against the all-youth share of 19.8 per cent in 2025. Male shares are not among the results cited, so no comparison with young men is drawn and no claim is made about which sex bears the larger burden. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the female share was 48.8 per cent in 2015 and 48.6 per cent in 2025, almost unchanged. South Asia improved from 46.0 per cent to 37.1 per cent, yet remains high. Low-income countries moved against the trend, from 32.6 per cent to 34.4 per cent. Norms on care work and early marriage, and limits on women's mobility and employment, are the usual explanations, stated here as context only.

Among countries, the trend classes are scattered. Of 187 countries assessed, 51 are on track or have met the direction of the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the population of those assessed. A further 28 show moderate progress and 29 marginal progress, while 21 stagnate and 58 regress. The regressing group holds 18.8 per cent of the population, more than the on-track group. No numeric target exists, and the results do not give the numeric thresholds that separate the classes. The classes are the trend tool's own categories, applied by the same rule to the world, regions and countries, and should be read as direction rather than as a verdict.

Inequality among countries, weighted by population, did not narrow. The Gini coefficient was 0.231 in 2015, 0.243 in 2020 and 0.246 in 2025. The between-region share of Theil's T was 56.6 per cent in 2015 and 56.7 per cent in 2025, so regional differences account for a little over half of the inequality in both years. Convergence is not shown: the beta of -0.00428 has a p-value of 0.214, not distinguishable from zero. Countries starting higher did not reliably improve faster.

### The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement

The movement of the world share is better read as a sequence of breaks in timing than as a steady trend. The break analysis of the annual change in the modelled ILO series finds breaks in 2013, 2020, 2021 and 2024. Between 2006 and 2012 the share fell by a mean of 0.2 points a year. That is the only stretch in which the decline looks like steady progress, and it ended before the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.

From 2013 to 2019 the mean annual change was 0.02 points, which is near stagnation. This window does not match the 2015 to 2020 span of the target, and the results cited give no world level for 2020, so the net change from 2015 to 2020 cannot be derived from them. In 2020 the mean annual change in that single-year segment was 1.37 points. The timing coincides with the closure of schools and workplaces during the pandemic. That link is context drawn from well-established knowledge; the data show when the break occurred and do not test its cause. The evidence bearing on the target year is therefore the 2013 to 2019 mean and the 2020 segment, and both point away from a substantial reduction by 2020. The missing 2020 level is a limit on the verdict, not a finding.

From 2021 to 2023 the share fell by a mean of 1.08 points a year, a separate measured period. The results do not show where the decline recorded by 2025 was produced, nor whether it restored the earlier position or went beyond it. From 2024 to 2025 the share rose again by a mean of 0.15 points a year. The long-run rate of change for the world, at -0.0070 on the trend tool's scale, is read by that tool as marginal progress with significant acceleration needed. These classes are the tool's own categories, applied without a numeric target, and their thresholds are not given in the results; regional and country classes rest on the same rule and are not separately tested against a target.

Sub-Saharan Africa followed a different path. Its breaks fall in 2014, 2021, 2023 and 2024. From 2006 to 2013 its mean annual change was -0.04 points. From 2014 to 2020 it rose by 0.45 points a year; that window includes the 2020 break, so the rise cannot be assigned wholly to the period before the pandemic, and no world mean for the same window is cited for comparison. A young population growing faster than jobs and school places is a common explanation, but the data do not test it. After 2020 the region eased, with a mean change of -0.29 points a year in 2021 and 2022 and -1.23 points in 2023, then 0.00 points a year in 2024 and 2025. The trend tool still classes the region as regression to 2030.

The breaks therefore cluster around 2020 and 2021, set against a world share that was nearly flat from 2013 to 2019. The pandemic link is context from outside the data, and the results isolate no cause.

### The 2020 target was missed, and 2030 needs faster progress and a clearer definition

On the reading used here, the 2020 target is unlikely to have been met in a substantial sense, and a looser reading could change that verdict. The target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially', so the verdict rests on the analyst's reading. The results give no world level for 2020 and no net change from 2015 to 2020, so the verdict is an inference, not a measurement. It rests on the break analysis already set out: a mean annual change of 0.02 points over 2013 to 2019, then a rise of 1.37 points in 2020. The world share stood at 21.2 per cent of youth in 2015 and 19.8 per cent in 2025.

The trend tool assigns its own classes, and its target is given as none, so the classes describe the direction and pace of change, not distance from a stated goal. The results do not give the numeric thresholds that separate the classes, so the placing of any region or country cannot be checked here. Regional and country classes come from the same rule as the world class, but they are not tested against a target and should not be read as verdicts on target 8.6. The world is classed as marginal progress, with a compound annual rate of -0.7 per cent from the 2015 baseline. Europe and Central Asia, at -1.6 per cent, and South Asia, at -1.9 per cent, reach the moderate class, and both still need acceleration. Low income, at 0.9 per cent a year, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region, at 0.3 per cent, and Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.2 per cent, are classed as regression.

The country count rests on 187 countries assessed by the trend tool, whereas the 2025 levels rest on 182 countries reporting that year. Of the 187, 51 are on track or have met the target, covering 12.8 per cent of the assessed population. Regression affects 58 countries, holding 18.8 per cent of the population.

Countries have not drawn together. The convergence test gives a beta of -0.0043 with a p-value of 0.214, which cannot be told from zero, and the coefficient of variation rose from 0.471 in 2015 to 0.532 in 2025. For 2030 the implication is that the present pace leaves the world far from a substantial reduction on the reading used here. The estimates are modelled, so classes for individual countries carry uncertainty.

w-c09-5-5.text:
### Unemployment and the participation gap at the global level

Between 2015 and 2025 the world picture for target 8.5 divides into two movements of very different size. Youth unemployment fell, while female participation in the labour force barely changed. The two series answer different parts of the target, and neither alone shows whether full and productive employment is being reached.

Youth unemployment, measured as the share of the labour force aged 15 to 24 without work but available for and seeking it, stood at 16.0% worldwide in 2015 and at 13.4% in 2025. For young women the rate was 17.0% in 2015 and 14.9% in 2025. Both are modelled ILO estimates. Young women therefore had a higher rate than the youth labour force as a whole at both dates, and the decline for each group was real but left a rate that is still high. A rate of 13.4% in 2025 means that between one in eight and one in seven young people in the labour force are unemployed. The target sets no numerical threshold, so this figure does not show whether the wording on young people is met.

Female labour force participation, the labour force as a share of the female population aged 15 and over, was 48.5% in 2015 and 48.9% in 2025. At the global level this is a movement of a few tenths of a percentage point over ten years. Whatever happened to women's access to work in the period, the aggregate shows no broad rise. The figure also conceals movements of opposite sign beneath it, which later parts of this section take up by region and country. These measures draw on 182 reporting countries in 2025.

The results do not give a global ratio of female to male participation, nor the ratio for 2015 and 2025 at the world level, and the male participation rate is not among the results used here. The change in the gap between women and men over the decade therefore cannot be measured globally from these results. What can be said is that the female level was almost unchanged; whether the gap narrowed depends on the male rate, which is not reported here. The regional trend results in the later parts describe the direction of the ratio, not its measured change.

The figures are modelled estimates, not direct national counts. Modelling allows countries with different survey calendars and definitions to be compared and gives a value for years in which a national survey was not run. The cost is that, where a country has few surveys, the estimate leans on patterns in similar countries and may not reflect that country's own labour market. Year-to-year movements in particular should be read with caution, and the comparison here is deliberately between two end years. The ratio of female to male participation is a national-estimate series, drawn on each country's own definitions, and it is used in the later parts on regions and countries.

Target 8.5 can be read in more than one way, and the reading changes the verdict. Read as a level of unemployment, it asks that few people who want work lack it, and the falling youth rate counts as progress. Read as parity, it asks that women and men take part in work on equal terms, and the participation rate of women, taken alone, cannot show that. The target also names equal pay, disabled persons and decent work, none of which these series measure. A fall in unemployment can occur because people leave the labour force or stop searching, so a lower rate is not by itself proof of more or better jobs.

For 2030 the global averages set the frame. At 13.4% youth unemployment is lower than a decade earlier, yet female participation at 48.9% has hardly moved. The regional and income-group figures that follow show where the global averages come from and where the gaps are widest.

### Regional differences in youth unemployment and female participation

Regional experience since 2015 departs sharply from the world averages. Youth unemployment, measured as a share of the labour force aged 15 to 24, fell most in South Asia, from 23.2 per cent in 2015 to 15.4 per cent in 2025. Europe and Central Asia recorded the next largest fall, from 19.9 per cent to 14.0 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 14.7 per cent to 12.2 per cent, and North America from 11.7 per cent to 9.8 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa began lower and ended lower, at 11.3 per cent in 2015 and 10.1 per cent in 2025. East Asia and Pacific is the exception among the regions: youth unemployment rose from 10.4 per cent to 12.5 per cent over the decade.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan stands apart for a different reason. Youth unemployment there was 20.1 per cent in 2015 and 18.7 per cent in 2025, a small improvement that leaves it the highest of the regions in the latest year. Young women in that region fare worse still: female youth unemployment was 28.5 per cent in 2015 and 28.3 per cent in 2025, essentially unchanged. By comparison, the same measure for young women in South Asia fell from 22.6 per cent to 16.3 per cent, and in Europe and Central Asia from 20.3 per cent to 14.7 per cent. In East Asia and Pacific it rose from 9.9 per cent to 11.7 per cent, in step with the rise for young people as a whole.

Female participation in the labour force, measured as a share of women aged 15 and over from modelled estimates, shows a different geography. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest rate, 64.6 per cent in 2015 and 65.2 per cent in 2025. East Asia and Pacific follows at 59.7 per cent in 2015 and 58.1 per cent in 2025, a fall. North America is nearly flat, at 56.5 per cent and then 56.8 per cent. Europe and Central Asia rose from 50.2 per cent to 51.1 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 50.8 per cent to 51.4 per cent. South Asia rose the most, from 27.5 per cent to 33.0 per cent, although the level remains low. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the rate fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent, the lowest of any region in both years. A high participation rate is not in itself a sign of decent work. As context rather than finding, women in low-income settings often work because household incomes leave no alternative, so the rate must be read beside the section on informal and vulnerable employment.

The results do not give the ratio of female to male participation for 2015 or 2025, and no male participation rate is among them, so the change in the gap over the decade cannot be measured directly. What the results give is the expected ratio for 2030, with 100.0 as parity, and the class of each regional path. In Europe and Central Asia the trend is classed as stagnation, with 80.3 expected in 2030. High-income economies are classed as marginal progress needing significant acceleration, with 83.2 expected. Latin America and the Caribbean is under the same classification, with 71.9 expected. North America is expected to reach 86.0 on its present path, again with significant acceleration needed. South Asia is expected to reach 60.5 and is also classed as marginal progress. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is the one region in regression, with an expected ratio of 29.8. These are extrapolations of past rates, not forecasts, and say nothing of policy changes that might alter them.

One result calls for caution. The lower-middle-income group is classed as on track or target met, with 99.6 expected in 2030. That path covers a shorter period than the others and rests on national estimates, whose coverage and definitions can differ between survey rounds. The classification should not be read as parity within reach.

The regional list in the trend results is also cut short. East Asia and Pacific and Sub-Saharan Africa are not reported there, and the figures for them in this part come only from the participation and unemployment levels. Their ratios of female to male participation are therefore not stated, and no judgement about their path to parity is made.

### How countries are distributed along the path to parity

The classification of 166 countries on the ratio of female to male labour force participation (a national estimate) shows how uneven the path to parity is. The target value is 100.0 per cent by 2030. Each country is placed by the compound annual rate of change from its 2015 baseline, or from the first year after it, and by the share of the distance to the target that this rate would cover by 2030. The results classify countries by trend and give projected values; they do not report a global ratio or a ratio for each region at 2015 and 2025, so the change in the gap over the decade is read here from the direction and pace of the trends, not from measured end-year ratios.

Only 13 countries are on track or have met the target, and they hold 7.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. A further 19 countries, with 2.8 per cent of that population, show moderate progress but need acceleration. The largest class is the 71 countries making marginal progress and needing significant acceleration. They hold 61.7 per cent of the population, so most people in the countries assessed live where the gap is narrowing too slowly to close by 2030.

The two classes that show no gain are reported separately. In 13 countries, with 10.4 per cent of the population, the ratio is stagnating. In 50 countries, with 17.9 per cent of the population, it is regressing, which means it has moved away from parity. A fall in the ratio can arise in two ways: women's participation may have fallen, or men's may have risen faster. The classification does not distinguish between them and does not show causes. As context only, and not as a finding of these results, the pace of structural change in economies, the availability of care services, legal and social norms on women's work, and the 2020 pandemic's effects on sectors that employ many women are commonly discussed influences.

The regional results show why the population shares look as they do. The lower middle income group is classed as on track, with a rate of 0.103 and an expected ratio of 99.6 in 2030. Its series is shorter than the others and rests on fewer observations, so its trend should be treated with caution. South Asia has a rate of 0.065 and an expected ratio of 60.5 in 2030, covering 0.45 of the distance to the target. This is the largest share among the regions not classed as on track, yet the ratio stays low. Europe and Central Asia is classed as stagnating, with an expected ratio of 80.3 in 2030, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan as regressing, with an expected ratio of 29.8.

The rate has limits as a reading. It is a compound annual change measured from a baseline, so it favours countries that start low, where a small absolute gain is a large proportional one, and it penalises those that start near parity. High income economies, at an expected 83.2 in 2030, and North America, at 86.0, are classed as marginal because the remaining distance is covered too slowly, not because they are far from parity. Reaching exactly 100.0 is also only one reading of the target: a ratio above 100.0 would mean women participate more than men, and the target text speaks of equality, not of a particular value. Finally, the classification covers 166 countries, because a trend needs observations at both ends of the period.

### What changed and what may explain it

The measured change in the gap between female and male participation cannot be stated from these results. They give no ratio of female to male participation for 2015 or 2025, no world ratio and no male rate. What they give are female participation levels, trend classes for the ratio and expected values for 2030. The question on the gap is therefore only partly answered, and what follows separates what is measured from what is context.

The movements recorded since 2015 are of two kinds. Youth unemployment is sensitive to the business cycle. Its fall in several regions may be consistent with recovery after the shock of 2020, when hiring stopped and young people, often on temporary contracts, were among the first to lose work; this is context, not a finding. Female participation is commonly thought to move more slowly, because it is tied to household arrangements, schooling, the availability of care, legal restrictions and social norms that change over decades. This too is context. The two series should be read at different speeds.

The female participation rates differ by region beneath a flat world figure. Female participation in South Asia rose from 27.5 per cent of women aged 15 and over in 2015 to 33.0 per cent in 2025. In East Asia and Pacific it fell from 59.7 per cent to 58.1 per cent. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan it fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent, the lowest level of any region in both years. The world rate was 48.5 per cent in 2015 and 48.9 per cent in 2025. One possible reading is that regional rises and falls offset each other, but no decomposition of the world figure is among the results, so this is not a finding. Sub-Saharan Africa stayed highest, at 64.6 per cent in 2015 and 65.2 per cent in 2025.

Income groups show a similar split. Female participation rose in lower middle income countries, from 35.5 per cent to 39.2 per cent, and in high income countries, from 52.8 per cent to 54.3 per cent. It fell in low income countries, from 56.6 per cent to 54.7 per cent, and in upper middle income countries, from 55.0 per cent to 53.4 per cent. Youth unemployment among young women moved differently by group: in upper middle income countries it rose from 16.4 per cent to 17.3 per cent, while in high income countries it fell from 16.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

The direction of the gap can be given only as the trend class that the results assign to the ratio. Regression is recorded in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, stagnation in Europe and Central Asia, and marginal progress in high income countries, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America and South Asia. These classes describe the pace of the ratio against the target, not its change between two stated years.

These indicators cannot identify causes. A fall in participation may reflect women withdrawing from work, women staying longer in education, or discouragement that removes them from the count of the unemployed; the series does not distinguish them. A rise may reflect new opportunity or economic necessity. Explanations drawn from expanding schooling, changing norms or legal barriers to women's work remain context.

The second half of target 8.5, equal pay for work of equal value, is not measured by any of these results. Unemployment and participation describe access to work, not its reward, so progress on pay cannot be judged from this section.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

The change in the gap between female and male labour force participation cannot be measured from these results, and the question is therefore only partly answered. They give no ratio of female to male participation for 2015 or 2025, no world ratio and no male rate. What they give are trend classes for the ratio (a national estimate), expected values for 2030 and female participation levels. The target value for the ratio is 100.0 per cent by 2030, and the implications below rest on those classes and expected values alone.

On present trends, the classified paths do not reach parity by 2030. In Europe and Central Asia the ratio was stagnant, and the expected value for 2030 is 80.3 per cent. In high-income countries, where progress was marginal and significant acceleration is needed, the expected value is 83.2 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean is expected to reach 71.9 per cent, and North America 86.0 per cent. South Asia is expected to reach 60.5 per cent, and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan the series regressed and is expected to stand at 29.8 per cent.

The share of the distance to the target already covered is 0.057 in Europe and Central Asia, 0.218 in high-income countries, 0.165 in Latin America and the Caribbean, 0.2 in North America and 0.448 in South Asia. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan it is negative, at -0.019. Female participation levels give a partial view: South Asia rose from 27.5 per cent of women aged 15 and over in 2015 to 33.0 per cent in 2025, while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan fell from 21.1 per cent to 19.7 per cent. Without a male rate, these levels do not yield a ratio.

Only one group in the regional table projects to parity. The lower-middle-income group is expected to reach 99.6 per cent, but its series covers a shorter period than the others and rests on a short run of national estimates, so this result should be treated with caution. The target can also be read in more than one way: a ratio of 100.0 per cent means equal participation rates, not equal pay or equal quality of work, and the section's series do not measure pay or disability.

The country classification points the same way. Of 166 countries assessed, 13 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 7.2 per cent of the population of the countries assessed. Thirteen countries stagnate, holding 10.4 per cent of that population, and 50 regressed, holding 17.9 per cent. Most people live in the group of 71 countries with marginal progress, which holds 61.7 per cent. On present trends the classification implies that faster acceleration is needed to reach parity by 2030.

Several proposals follow. National statistical offices and the International Labour Organization should publish participation rates for men and women side by side, so that the ratio can be tracked from 2015 onward. Governments in countries where the series regressed or stagnated should address the legal, care and mobility barriers to women's work and report against the 2030 target. Donors and development banks should fund labour force surveys in countries with short or interrupted national series.

w-c05-1-5.text:
### Primary completion has barely moved since 2015

The world primary completion rate stood at 87.9% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 88.0% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The change over nine years is too small to register as progress. The period spans the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals, the school closures of 2020 and the uneven recovery since, and the aggregate shows no surge after 2015 and no visible collapse after 2020. A flat global line can conceal movement in both directions, and the regional and income-group figures show that it does.

The indicator needs careful reading. Primary completion here is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of primary education: new entrants in the last grade, whatever their age, divided by the population at the entrance age for that grade. Because late entrants and early starters are counted in the numerator but not in the denominator, the ratio can exceed 100, and it is not the share of a birth cohort that finishes primary school. The target can be read in more than one way: as universal completion, meaning every child finishes, or as a rate of 100 or more, which the ratio can reach while some children remain outside school. The trend assessment in this chapter takes the second, arithmetical reading, with 100.0 as the threshold.

The movement beneath the flat world line is large in places. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% to 83.7%, a gain of nearly ten points. East Asia and Pacific rose from 94.1% to 95.4% by 2022, its latest value. Sub-Saharan Africa moved only from 66.3% to 68.9%, and low-income countries from 60.5% in 2015 to 62.9% in 2023, so the poorest groups remain furthest from the target and gained little. Against these gains, South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4%, Latin America and the Caribbean from 98.4% to 96.5%, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% by 2023. Lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% and then 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% by 2023 and high income countries stayed near 98.1% and 97.8%. Gains in one region are therefore offset by losses in others, which is why the world figure does not move.

Under the arithmetical reading, the country classification is sobering. Of 173 countries assessed, 50 are on track or have met the target, holding 19.6% of the assessed population. A further 14 show moderate progress, with 13.0% of the assessed population, and 14 show marginal progress, with 5.7%. Three stagnate, with 0.5%. Regression is the largest class: 92 countries, holding 61.3% of the assessed population. The results do not show how much of this reflects real deterioration. Some of it may arise where ratios above 100 drift back towards 100 as late entry and repetition decline, which the classification counts as movement away from the target. The count alone cannot separate the two.

Reporting is a further limit. Only 11 countries had reported a value for 2025 at the time of access, so the most recent global figure rests on 2024. The finding of near stagnation is firm for the period to 2024 but says little about the last years before the target date.

### Lower secondary completion shows slow, uneven gains

The world lower secondary completion rate stood at 74.8% of the relevant age group in 2015 and at 77.9% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The measure is a gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education, so it counts new entrants in that grade regardless of age. A ratio can therefore exceed 100.0%, and the rate indicates intake to the last grade rather than certified completion. The trend tool gives the world a ratio of 0.21 of the distance from baseline to target, and an expected value of 80.0% in 2030.

Set beside primary completion, which was 88.0% in 2024, the world figure for lower secondary shows that intake falls between the two cycles. Because the indicator is a ratio and not a count of a single cohort, this gap should not be converted into a number of adolescents. Research on education systems points to rising costs, scarcer and more distant schools, and the demands of household labour after primary school. This is context that the series themselves do not test, and they do not isolate these causes.

The regional series show where the shortfall lies. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 42.3% in 2015 and 44.4% in 2023, and remains far below the world rate; the trend ratio is 0.07. Low-income countries moved from 37.0% in 2015 to 38.6% in 2023, with a ratio of 0.05, and are the group furthest from the target. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 57.1% to 66.7% in 2024, a faster pace than most regions, with a trend ratio of 0.39, yet it remains well below the world rate. South Asia advanced from 83.7% to 86.6%, with a ratio of 0.30.

East Asia and Pacific rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, the largest gain among the regional aggregates, with a trend ratio of 1.39. The results do not show what drives the world rise, but this gain is the largest of any regional series. Europe and Central Asia moved from 90.9% to 91.9%, with a ratio of 0.19, and Latin America and the Caribbean from 81.3% to 81.5%, with a ratio of 0.02. By income group, upper-middle-income countries rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 93.0% in 2023, with a ratio of 0.95. High-income countries moved from 94.0% to 95.6% in 2024, with a ratio of 0.44, and lower-middle-income countries from 71.0% to 73.7%, with a ratio of 0.16. Low-income countries have closed little of the distance.

Several series do not cover the full period. The North American series begins in 2016, not 2015, at 104.3%, and ends in 2023 at 100.8%. Both values lie above 100.0% because the ratio counts older entrants, so the decline does not indicate a fall below universal completion. The Sub-Saharan Africa, low-income and upper-middle-income series end in 2023, one year before the world and several other groups, so comparisons across aggregates mix periods of different length. Only 11 countries reported a value for 2025, too few to support any statement about that year.

The aggregates show no break that can be attributed to the school closures of 2020. Projected to 2030 at the observed pace, the world rate reaches about 80.0%, far short of the target. Sub-Saharan Africa reaches about 46.2% and low-income countries about 40.1%, while East Asia and Pacific passes 100.0% on the same method. The country classes for this indicator are set out in the section on divergence and are not repeated here.

### Regions and countries diverge sharply

Regional averages conceal a wide spread in how far children travel through school. In Sub-Saharan Africa the primary completion rate was 68.9% of the relevant age group in 2024, up from 66.3% in 2015. Lower secondary completion in the same region was 44.4% in 2023, up from 42.3% in 2015. Fewer than half of the children in the region reach the last grade of lower secondary, and the small gain leaves the region far from the target of 100.0%. The trend tool gives the region a ratio of 0.07 of the distance to the target, with an expected value of 46.2% in 2030. Low-income countries are further from the target than any region: 62.9% at primary in 2023 and 38.6% at lower secondary in 2023, up from 37.0% in 2015, with an expected 2030 value of 40.1% at lower secondary and a ratio of 0.05.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region shows the largest gain in primary completion, from 73.8% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2024. At lower secondary the region rose from 57.1% to 66.7%. The tool gives it a ratio of 0.39 and an expected value of 73.9% in 2030, still well short of 100.0%. East Asia and Pacific has a ratio of 1.39. The region's figures combine countries in very different circumstances, and measurement may be uncertain where conflict and displacement are present. The gain should be read as a regional average, not as a uniform improvement.

East Asia and Pacific is the clearest success. Lower secondary completion rose from 86.3% in 2015 to 97.3% in 2024, with an expected 105.4% in 2030. A value above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio, so it does not signal that every child completes on time. Primary completion in the region reached 95.4% in 2022, from 94.1% in 2015. Upper middle income countries have a ratio of 0.95 at lower secondary, rising from 86.3% to 93.0% in 2023. Lower middle income countries moved from 71.0% to 73.7% in 2024, with a ratio of 0.16. At primary level lower middle income countries were flat, at 88.2% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, while upper middle income countries rose from 94.4% to 95.2% in 2023.

Several regions went backwards at primary level. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 98.4% in 2015 to 96.5% in 2024. South Asia fell from 98.5% to 94.4% over the same years, and North America from 98.9% to 96.0% in 2023. These regions began near universal completion, so the declines differ in kind from the shortfalls in Africa. The data do not show why they fell; the 2020 disruption and changes in enrolment and repetition are possible contributors, and because the measure counts new entrants in the last grade, shifts in repetition or age at entry can move it without any change in the number of children finishing. Primary completion in Europe and Central Asia rose from 97.2% to 98.1%. At lower secondary, Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 81.3% in 2015 to 81.5% in 2024, a ratio of 0.02, and South Asia improved from 83.7% to 86.6%. North America stood at 100.8% in 2023, down from 104.3% in 2016; the series already sits above the target, so its ratio is not a measure of progress.

Country classes confirm that the global average hides a divide. Of 173 countries assessed on primary completion, 50 are on track or have met the target, and 92 are in regression, holding 61.3% of the assessed population. The tool does not separate countries that fell from near-universal levels from those that fell from low ones, so the size of the regression class should be read with care. At lower secondary 49 countries are on track and 66 are in regression, holding 21.1% of the assessed population, while the 32 countries in marginal progress hold 38.4%. Many people therefore live in countries advancing too slowly to arrive by 2030.

### Learning lags behind completion, and the data are thin

Completion measures how many children reach the last grade; it does not show what they have learned. The indicator of pupils below the minimum reading proficiency level at the end of primary schooling addresses that gap. Worldwide, 45.9% of assessed pupils at the end of primary were below the minimum level in 2015, and 49.6% in 2019. This is a share of assessed pupils, not of those who completed school, and it refers to years different from the 2024 completion rate of 88.0%, so the two measures are not directly comparable. Read together, they suggest that reaching the last grade does not by itself secure basic reading, which Target 4.1 requires. The series covers reading at the end of primary only. Minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not measured by any series on the shelf, so that part of the question cannot be answered here.

The regional contrasts are wide. Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest share below the threshold, at 80.7% in 2015 and 83.3% in 2019. Low income countries stood at 83.5% in 2015 and 87.4% in 2019, and lower middle income countries at 52.9% and 57.4%. South Asia was nearly unchanged, at 55.8% and then 56.0%, and the region of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan moved from 57.7% to 57.5%. Latin America and the Caribbean rose from 49.1% to 51.0%. The results do not identify why additional years in school have not translated into basic skills in these regions. As context only, explanations often offered include rapid expansion of enrolment, large classes and limited teacher training, but the data in hand do not test them.

At the other end, Europe and Central Asia fell from 6.8% to 5.5%, and high income countries from 6.4% to 6.2%. North America was flat, at 3.9% in both years. Low shares in these regions leave little room for movement, so the near absence of change there differs in kind from the stagnation seen in South Asia. Upper middle income countries were close to unchanged, at 28.0% in 2015 and 28.6% in 2019.

The largest movement was in East Asia and Pacific, where the share below the threshold rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019. A rise of that size in a region with strong education systems calls for caution. It may partly reflect a change in which countries and pupils were assessed between the two waves, not only a decline in learning. The data in hand cannot separate the two explanations. The trend calculation for the region extrapolates to 124.3% in 2030, which is impossible as a share and shows only that two points cannot support a projection.

The coverage of the series explains the difficulty. Data come in survey waves, not as annual observations. Countries reporting numbered 46 in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, with an isolated report in 2023 from 1 country. In all, 125 countries reported in at least one year, so the aggregates in any single year rest on fewer countries. The aggregates end in 2019, so they do not capture the effect of the school closures of 2020 and after, which is a serious omission for a question about what changed after 2020. The 2021 wave exists at country level but has no regional aggregate in the results here.

For 2030 the evidence supports only a statement of direction. Extrapolating the 2015 to 2019 movement gives 61.3% of pupils below the threshold worldwide, against a target of zero. Sub-Saharan Africa would reach 91.0% and low income countries 99.1% on the same arithmetic. Europe and Central Asia would reach 3.0%, from a low base. The extrapolations are mechanical, rest on two points and should be read as the observed direction of change from 2015 to 2019, not as a forecast.

### Implications for 2030 and proposals

At present rates the world will miss target 4.1. The lower secondary trend to target puts the world on course for an expected completion rate of 80.0% of the relevant age group in 2030, against a target of 100.0%. The trend ratio for the world is 0.21, the share of the distance from the 2015 baseline to the target that the trend would cover. Among 173 countries assessed, 49 are on track or have met the target for lower secondary completion, covering 22.1% of the assessed population, while 66 are regressing, covering 21.1% of the assessed population. For primary completion, 50 countries are on track, covering 19.6% of the assessed population, and 92 are regressing, covering 61.3%. Regression is therefore the most common class at primary level. The classes come from a trend to target, so a country that has already reached a high rate and slipped slightly may be recorded as regressing; the reading needs care, and the target can be read as universal completion or as a rate near it.

Completing school is not the same as learning. The learning trend for the world gives an expected share below minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary of 61.3% in 2030, against a target of 0.0%, with a ratio of -0.34. This figure is a projected share of assessed pupils and is distinct from the share of the assessed population in regressing countries at primary completion. In Low income countries the expected share is 99.1% in 2030, and in Sub-Saharan Africa 91.0%. These projections extend a change between 2015 and 2019 mechanically, from two points in time, so they indicate direction rather than forecast. High completion does not guarantee learning: in East Asia & Pacific the share of pupils below the minimum reading level rose from 19.2% in 2015 to 31.6% in 2019, while lower secondary completion reached 97.3% in 2024, with an expected rate of 105.4% in 2030 and a ratio of 1.39. A rate above 100.0% is possible because the measure is a gross intake ratio. Completion gains not matched by learning gains deliver the certificate without the skills. The learning series ends in 2019 for these trends. Across all years, 125 countries reported in at least one year, but each survey wave is far smaller: 46 countries in 2016, 41 in 2019 and 53 in 2021, and the aggregates rest on fewer countries in each year. The series therefore cannot show whether recovery after 2020 has changed this. It also addresses reading at the end of primary only; minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not covered, and the learning shares cannot be compared directly with completion rates of other years.

The regional picture shows where acceleration matters most. Low income countries have a lower secondary trend ratio of 0.05 and an expected rate of 40.1% in 2030, the furthest of any group from the target. Sub-Saharan Africa has a ratio of 0.07 and an expected rate of 46.2% in 2030. The same groups have the worst learning outcomes: 87.4% of assessed pupils in Low income countries and 83.3% in Sub-Saharan Africa were below minimum reading proficiency in 2019, and their learning data are among the thinnest. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region has a ratio of 0.39 and an expected rate of 73.9% in 2030, still short of what the target requires.

Proposals follow from these findings. Governments of low-income countries and of countries with the weakest completion trends, with their development partners, should fund the transition to lower secondary and tie that funding to measured learning outcomes, since completion alone does not show what pupils have learned. Targeting should rest on the level of completion and learning, not on the regression class alone, because that class can reflect rates above 100.0% drifting back towards 100.0%. National education ministries and international assessment bodies should run reading assessments at the end of primary at regular intervals in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, so that the post-2020 position is known.

w-c06-1-3.text:
### The legal record covers almost every economy, but the bench has computed only its frame

Target 5.1 asks for an end to all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere, and its formal indicator asks whether legal frameworks are in place to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis of sex. Of all the commitments in Goal 5, this is the one most directly in the hands of legislators. A statute that bars a married woman from registering a business, that forbids her from working at night, that sets her pensionable age earlier and so shortens her contribution record, or that leaves dismissal for pregnancy unpunished can be amended by a vote. The measurement of law therefore records choices that governments make, rather than outcomes that depend on markets, households and custom, and this gives it a particular place in an account of the Goals.

The instrument on the shelf is the Legal Framework Index of the World Bank's Women, Business and the Law project. It scores each economy on whether its laws treat women and men equally across the domains that shape a working life, among them safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. The topic scores are averaged on a scale from 0 to 100, so an economy that has reformed its labour code thoroughly but left property and inheritance law untouched cannot reach the top of the scale. The equal weighting of topics is a choice of method rather than a finding about which laws matter most for women's economic lives.

The bench's coverage tool shows that the index reports a value for 189 economies in 2025, and that 189 economies report in at least one year. The equality of the two counts means that every economy ever scored is scored in the latest year. It does not establish that each economy has been scored in every year, and it says nothing about how far back the series runs. For a measure of national law, read from statute books rather than gathered through household surveys, near-universal coverage is what one would expect. It contrasts with the uneven coverage of the outcome indicators treated elsewhere in this chapter, several of which rest on surveys conducted irregularly and in only part of the world.

Coverage is all the bench has computed for this series. No level, no regional or income-group average and no change since 2015 or 2020 has been drawn from the shelf, so the direction and size of change in laws affecting women's economic opportunity cannot be stated here. The sections that follow therefore set out what the instrument measures, how its readings should be interpreted, and what a computed record would have to show. None of the general expectations about legal reform that appear there is a measured finding.

### A second generation of measurement changes what counts as equality

The series on the shelf belongs to a revised generation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology. The earlier index scored a narrower set of legal questions and awarded high marks to many economies once the most overt forms of discrimination had been removed. The revised framework adds domains such as safety and childcare, which the earlier one largely omitted. It is accompanied on the shelf by two companion series: a Supportive Framework Index, which asks whether the policies, budgets and institutions needed to implement a law exist, and an Enforcement Perceptions Index, which records how experts judge the law to operate in practice.

Three consequences follow for interpretation. First, scores under the revised framework are not comparable with the headline figures of the earlier index. A reader who remembers older, higher numbers should not set the new ones beside them; an apparent fall between the two would be an artefact of method, not a retreat in law. Second, the wider scope tends to lower the standing of economies that looked close to parity on the narrower questions. Comprehensive protection against harassment, criminalisation of domestic abuse and legal provision for childcare are demanding tests, and an economy can have abolished every explicit restriction on women's employment and still sit well below the top of the scale. Third, because the revised series is recent, its history may be short. Whether the shelf holds comparable values back to 2015, the baseline used throughout this book, has not been verified. If it does not, change since the adoption of the Goals cannot be measured with this index, and no statement about the period after 2015 or after 2020 can rest on it.

The only result computed for this index is its coverage. In 2025 the Legal Framework Index was reported by 189 countries, and the same number reported in at least one year, so the frame is complete for the economies it covers. Regional and income-group aggregates are also held, but no level, trend or comparison has been calculated, and this part draws no conclusion about direction of change.

The pairing of the three indices matters most for target 5.1, because the target's indicator speaks not only of laws but of their enforcement and monitoring. The legal score records what the statute book says; the supportive score records whether institutions exist to give the law effect; the enforcement score records whether the law is believed to bite. The distance between the first and the other two is the distance between a promise and its delivery. That distance has not been computed here.

According to the World Bank's documentation of the Women, Business and the Law methodology, the index scores the formal law that applies in the main business city of each economy. In federal states or plural legal systems it may therefore not describe the rules that govern most women, particularly where customary or religious law determines marriage, land and inheritance. The index also measures whether the state has removed its own barriers and erected protections; it does not measure whether women can use them. Both cautions argue for reading the legal index together with its companions on support and enforcement and with the outcome indicators, never alone.

With those cautions, the legal framework index is well suited to a global account. The coverage tool shows 189 economies reporting in 2025, the same number as in any year, as stated in the opening part of this section. That count is the number in the series; it has not been checked against the total number of economies in the world, so it should not be read as a census of every one. A measured answer, once computed, would rest on nearly all the economies the series holds rather than on a sample.

The question of how laws affecting women's economic opportunity have changed is therefore unanswered in this section, and the answer is stated plainly as missing. The coverage result gives no level, change since 2015 or 2020, count of economies rising or falling, income-group value or topic score, and none is claimed here. Whether the index can be computed back to 2015 on a comparable basis has not been established by the bench, and that is the first thing to settle; if the earliest comparable year is later, it must be stated and used in place of 2015. The task left to the bench is to turn coverage into levels, changes, distributions and topic scores, and to set the legal score beside the measures of support and enforcement so that the distance between promise and practice can be seen for each economy. Until then, any statement about direction, or about how the revised scope affects country standings, remains an untested expectation drawn from the design of the index, and no verdict on target 5.1 for 2030 can be given.

w-c01-1-1.text:
## Overview

### The book reads the goals through one source and states its limits

This book examines progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals using a single body of evidence, the World Bank's World Development Indicators. Each section sets a target's wording against the nearest series the bench holds, states the value for the world in 2015 and in the latest year available, and records how many countries report. The adopted sections reach from poverty and hunger through health, education, gender, water, energy and the economy. Their findings fall into three groups: a set of indicators moving clearly in the right direction, a larger set that is flat or moving too slowly, and a set of targets that the data cannot measure at all. This overview follows that order after a short tour of the goals.

### Poverty measures are wide in reach but thin in time

National poverty lines give the measure closest to target 1.2, yet reporting is irregular. Across all years 161 countries report a national-line headcount, but in any single year far fewer do: 16 in 2000, 15 in 2001, 36 in 2004, 41 in 2005 and 40 in 2008. No continuous world trend can be built from such a series. Social protection and labour programmes reached 56.3% of the world's population in 2021, a single reading that describes a position rather than a change; only 1 country reports for 2023, and 121 countries report in any year. Exposure to climate-related disasters, the subject of target 1.5, is recorded only through new displacement: 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 in 2023, a rise of a little more than a third, with a mean annual change of about 789,790 cases between 2009 and 2023. The unit is cases, not persons. Education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in the world in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023; East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 to 13.0 per cent over the same years, while Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 16.4 per cent in 2015 to 16.6 per cent in 2024. A budget share measures priority, not sufficiency.

### Hunger has not fallen and food insecurity has risen

The prevalence of undernourishment stood at 8.0 per cent of the world's population in 2015 and 8.1 per cent in 2024, with 165 countries reporting in 2024. The prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity rose from 21.4 per cent to 28.0 per cent over the same period, on reports from 135 countries. Stunting among children under five eased from 24.6% in 2015 to 23.2% in 2024, and wasting from 7.1% to 6.6%; the trend tool expects stunting of 22.3% in 2030, well short of the agreed targets. Agricultural value added per worker rose from 3,491 to 4,264 constant 2015 US dollars between 2015 and 2025, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year, far below the pace a doubling would need; East Asia and Pacific rose from 4,087 to 6,991 dollars, at 5.5 per cent a year. The doubling in target 2.3 is defined for small-scale producers and names no baseline year, so whole-economy figures read it only indirectly. Agricultural land held at 36.8 per cent of land area in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023, while the companion fertiliser series moved from 132.9 to 136.5. Food price volatility under target 2.c is not measured directly; consumer price inflation stands in for it, and the number of reporting countries fell from 189 in 2015 to 169 in 2025.

### Health shows the clearest gains and the widest gaps

The world maternal mortality ratio fell from 228.0 per 100,000 live births in 2015 to 197.0 in 2023, against a target below 70. The trend tool expects 173.4 in 2030, with a ratio of progress to required pace of 0.35; Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 448 in 2023. HIV incidence fell from 0.26 to 0.16 new infections per 1,000 uninfected population between 2015 and 2024, and tuberculosis incidence from 150.0 to 131.0 per 100,000 people. Alcohol consumption fell from 5.9 to 4.9 litres of pure alcohol per adult between 2015 and 2020. Adolescent fertility fell from 46.0 to 38.3 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 between 2015 and 2024; of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9% of the relevant population, are on track or have met the target. Adult tobacco use fell from 24.5 per cent to 20.3 per cent between 2015 and 2024, though it remained at 24.9 per cent in Europe and Central Asia and 23.6 per cent in South Asia, against 8.9 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa. The universal health coverage service index rose from 68.0 to 71.0 points between 2015 and 2023; low-income countries moved only from 41.2 to 43.8. Reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health coverage, the nearest measure for immunisation, is flat: the world annual rate is -0.0017, and several regions and income groups show a rate of 0.

### Education is expanding at the edges while primary completion stalls

The world primary completion rate was 87.9% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024, against a target of 100.0% by 2030. The flat line conceals movement: the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% to 83.7%, and East Asia and Pacific from 94.1% in 2015 to 95.4% in 2022. Pre-primary gross enrolment rose from 56.0 per cent in 2015 to 60.9 per cent in 2020, but reporting collapses after that year, from 71 countries in 2021 to 4 in 2022. Gross tertiary enrolment rose from 36.6 to 43.6 per cent between 2015 and 2024, an annualised rate of 0.0196, classed as moderate progress with acceleration needed. Public spending on education fell from 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023; of 186 countries assessed, 98 show regression on the trend tool.

### Gender equality advances slowly and is measured unevenly

In 2022, 19.5% of women aged 20 to 24 had been married by age 18, against a target of elimination; East Asia and Pacific stood at 5.6% and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan at 17.7%. Women held 27.2 per cent of seats in national parliaments in 2025, up from 22.8 per cent in 2015, with 184 countries reporting; management data are thinner, with 77 countries reporting in 2015. Account ownership among women rose from 65.9% in 2017 to 76.6% in 2024, and among men from 72.8% to 80.9%, so the gap narrowed. Internet use among women rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024, and among men from 56.0 per cent in 2019 to 76.6 per cent in 2025; the bench holds no series on mobile phone ownership by sex, nor on women's ownership of land.

### Water, sanitation and clean cooking are on the clearest upward paths

Safely managed drinking water reached 73.7% of the world's population in 2024, up from 67.7% in 2015. Basic sanitation rose from 72.6 per cent to 82.2 per cent, and open defecation fell from 10.6 per cent to 4.3 per cent, between 2015 and 2024. Safely managed sanitation, a proxy for wastewater treatment, rose from 48.4 per cent to 58.5 per cent. Wastewater treatment and ecosystem condition under targets 6.3 and 6.6 are not measured directly. Net official development assistance received rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023 in constant 2023 dollars; the series is not specific to water. Clean cooking fuels reached 75.4 per cent of the world's population in 2024, up from 63.9 per cent in 2015, though low-income countries began from 13.3 per cent against 98.8 per cent in high-income countries.

### The economy decarbonises and banks more people

Carbon intensity of world output fell from 0.26 to 0.22 kg CO2e per 2021 PPP dollar between 2015 and 2024. A structural break falls in 2012: the mean annual change was -0.00217 kg per dollar in 2001 to 2011 and -0.00531 from 2012 to 2024, so the acceleration predates the goals. Adult account ownership rose from 69.3 per cent in 2017 to 78.7 per cent in 2024. Child labour cannot be quantified: the results give only counts of reporting countries, 97 across all years and as few as 4 in 2002, and no world aggregate exists.

### Across goals, the world is on track in access and off track in outcomes

Where progress is measured as access to a service or facility, the world is moving: water, sanitation, clean cooking, accounts, internet use, tertiary enrolment and adolescent fertility all show sustained gains. Where progress depends on deeper outcomes, the world is off track: undernourishment is unchanged, food insecurity has risen, primary completion is flat, maternal mortality will remain far above its target, and child nutrition targets will be missed on current trends. Public commitment has not grown with need; education's share of budgets and of GDP has held or fallen. Disaster displacement is rising.

### The data leave large parts of the agenda unmeasured

Several targets have no direct series: food price anomalies, wastewater treatment, ecosystem condition, mobile ownership by sex, women's land ownership and child labour shares. Others rest on single readings, as with social protection, or on reporting that collapses after 2020. Several targets set no numerical threshold or can be read in more than one way, and the book states each reading it adopts.

The adopted sections cover goals 1 to 6 and parts of goals 7 and 8. Goal 7 is read through clean cooking alone. Goal 8 is read through carbon intensity and account ownership, and child labour is named but cannot be quantified. Goal 9 and goals 10 to 17 are not covered by any adopted section, because the bench holds no section on them, and no verdict is passed on them. Series end in different years, from 2020 to 2025, so comparisons across sections are comparisons of direction, not of like periods. The verdicts below apply only to the goals and targets that were measured.

### Goal 1: poverty measures are wide in reach but thin in time

National poverty lines give the measure closest to target 1.2, yet reporting is irregular. Across all years 161 countries report a national-line headcount, but in 2000, 2001, 2004, 2005 and 2008 the counts were 16, 15, 36, 41 and 40. No continuous world trend can be built from such a series. Social protection and labour programmes reached 56.3% of the world's population in 2021. That single reading describes a position, not a change, and only 1 country reports for 2023 on that series. A separate coverage series has 121 countries reporting in any year. Exposure to climate-related disasters under target 1.5 is recorded only through new displacement: 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 in 2023, a rise of a little more than a third. The unit is cases, not persons. A mean annual change of about 789,790 cases over 2009 to 2023 covers a different period and is set aside here. Public budgets are read under this goal as well: education took 14.1 per cent of general government expenditure in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023. East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 to 13.0 per cent over those years, while Latin America and the Caribbean moved from 16.4 per cent in 2015 to 16.6 per cent in 2024. A budget share measures priority, not sufficiency.

### Goal 2: hunger has not fallen and food insecurity has risen

The prevalence of undernourishment stood at 8.0 per cent of the world's population in 2015 and 8.1 per cent in 2024, with 165 countries reporting in 2024. The prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity rose from 21.4 per cent to 28.0 per cent over the same period, on reports from 135 countries. Stunting among children under five eased from 24.6% in 2015 to 23.2% in 2024, and wasting from 7.1% to 6.6%. The trend tool projects stunting of 22.3% in 2030; this is a projection, not a target. Agricultural value added per worker rose from 3,491 to 4,264 constant 2015 US dollars between 2015 and 2025, a rate of 2.0 per cent a year. East Asia and Pacific rose from 4,087 to 6,991 dollars, at 5.5 per cent a year. The doubling in target 2.3 is defined for small-scale producers and names no baseline year, so whole-economy figures read it only indirectly. Agricultural land held at 36.8 per cent of land area in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023, reported by 208 countries in 2024. A fertiliser series exists, but its unit is not stated in the material available, so it is listed among the gaps. Food price volatility under target 2.c is not measured directly. Consumer price inflation is the indirect proxy: it records general prices, not food price swings. The number of countries reporting that series is a coverage figure, not a price measure, and it fell from 189 in 2015 to 169 in 2025.

### Goal 3: health shows clear gains and wide gaps

The world maternal mortality ratio fell from 228.0 per 100,000 live births in 2015 to 197.0 in 2023, against a target of below 70. The trend tool expects 173.4 in 2030, and its ratio of progress to required pace is 0.35. Sub-Saharan Africa stood at 448 in 2023. Adolescent fertility fell from 46.0 to 38.3 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 between 2015 and 2024. Of 217 countries assessed, 144, holding 84.9% of the relevant population, are on track or have met the target. Target 3.7 sets no numerical threshold. Adult tobacco use fell from 24.5 per cent to 20.3 per cent between 2015 and 2024, though it stood at 24.9 per cent in Europe and Central Asia and 23.6 per cent in South Asia in 2024, against 8.9 per cent in Sub-Saharan Africa. ### Goal 4: education expands at the edges while primary completion stalls

### Goal 5: gender equality advances slowly and is measured unevenly

### Goals 6 and 7: water, sanitation and clean cooking rise

Wastewater treatment and ecosystem condition under targets 6.3 and 6.6 are not measured directly. For goal 7 only clean cooking is assessed: it reached 75.4 per cent of the world's population in 2024, up from 63.9 per cent in 2015. Low-income countries stood at 13.3 per cent in 2015, against 98.8 per cent in high-income countries.

### Goal 8: carbon intensity falls and account ownership rises

The results give only counts of reporting countries, 97 across all years, and no world aggregate exists.

### Measured goals show gains in most series and none in several

This verdict covers only goals 1 to 6 and the assessed parts of goals 7 and 8. Water, sanitation, clean cooking, accounts, internet use and tertiary enrolment rose. HIV incidence, tuberculosis incidence, tobacco use and adolescent fertility fell. Undernourishment is unchanged, food insecurity has risen, and primary completion is flat. Maternal mortality remains far above its target of 70 and is projected at 173.4 in 2030. Disaster displacement rose between 2015 and 2023. r-w-c03-4-1-orchard/reviewer.comments: Numbers match the facts after rounding, but several statements go beyond them. (1) The text says cereal yields in East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, and the Middle East group are 2023 values, which is correct, but the Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income yields are 2024, and the section says 'over the same period' without stating years for the comparison. (2) 'Less than a third of the yield of North America' is wrong for 2015-24 in part: 1,453/8,414 is 17%, so it holds, but the comparison mixes 2024 with 2015 values; state the year. (3) The claim 'no region has sustained' a doubling pace over the decade is contradicted by 5.5% in East Asia and Pacific, which would nearly double over fifteen years (1.055^15 is about 2.2). Value added in that region rose 71% in ten years, so the 'only regional rate approaching' and 'would need to match' wording is fine, but the sentence that the pace is 'far below' is fine only for the world. Rewrite this. (4) The claim that the high-to-low-income gap has not narrowed is not computed from a result; the gap was 32 times in 2015 and 40 times in 2025, so give those figures. (5) The causes of the stagnation (conflict, droughts, the war in Ukraine) are asserted without a cited result; mark them as context. (6) The closing 'Proposals' heading introduces nothing; the proposals are absent from the text.

r-w-c03-4-1-quarry/reviewer.comments: S1: the cited numbers match their facts after rounding. Some text numbers are not facts of any result: 'close to five per cent a year' for a doubling over fifteen years (about 4.7) and 'less than a third of the yield of North America' (1,453 against 8,414 is under a fifth, and the 2015 pair is also well under a third). Ten of fifteen years elapsed is acceptable. The South Asia cereal yield year is 2024 and is correct. S3: the claim that a decade shows low-income productivity 'shrunk' fits, but the upper-middle-income cereal yield comparison and the high-income one say 'both in 2023', which is fine. The unsupported items are causal: the region paragraphs on irrigation, no-till and 'conflict, droughts' are asserted without results, and the proposals on research cuts after price shocks and on women's tenure rest on no finding. 'The market and the existing policy mix are not closing gaps' goes beyond a null convergence result. The claim that the 2.0 per cent rate is 'generous' is sound. Mark the causal claims as background, or cut them, and tie each proposal to a finding. The proposals section lists only an introductory line in the text; present the proposals.

r-w-c06-1-1-elm/reviewer.comments:
S1: the only figures are 189 (2025) and 189 (any year), both matching the facts. The 'no economy has dropped out' inference is slightly stronger than equal counts support; reword it.

S2: The question is how laws have changed. The section gives no score, level or change, and answers only from uncited 'literature' and 'project publications'. Most of the section is unsupported assertion, not a finding. Compute the index for 2015 and the latest year, by income group, before adopting.

S3: Many findings do not follow from the bench results: reform direction, pandemic effects, enforcement gaps larger than legal gaps, regional ordering, reversals. Proposals such as the back-cast and the side-by-side reporting follow from the stated gaps, but the family-law proposal rests on uncited claims. Mark or remove the uncomputed claims.

S4: Limits are stated well: coverage only, series start unverified, the earlier index not comparable, main-city scope, and two readings of the target.

S5: Clear and well ordered, but long. Much of the text is background, and the headings sometimes promise findings the section does not deliver (for example 'direction of reform is clear'). Shorten it.

r-w-c06-1-1-fernhill/reviewer.comments: S1: the only figures are 189 (2025) and 189 (any year), both matching the facts. S2: the question is how laws have changed, yet the section computes no level, change or regional value; the direction of reform is asserted from outside literature rather than from the bench, so the question is left unanswered for target 5.1. S3: many findings (reforms outnumber reversals, implementation shortfall exceeds legal shortfall, the gap is large almost everywhere, most remaining discrimination lies in family law) rest on recollected publications, not on results. Proposals on family codes, social-insurance leave and childcare follow from those unsupported claims, not from a finding. The back-cast proposal does follow from the stated gap. r-w-c03-3-1-bao/reviewer.comments: S1: Most figures match the facts after rounding. r-w-c02-4-1-chidi/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c03-1-1-amara/reviewer.comments: S1: Most figures match their facts after rounding. r-w-c04-1-1-fernhill/reviewer.comments: S1: Several figures differ from their facts. The lower-middle-income ratio is given as 0.44, but the fact is 0.435 (0.43 in the claims). r-w-c04-5-1-saltmarsh/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c04-10-1-birchwood/reviewer.comments: S1: Theil 2024 is given as 0.081, but the fact is 0.0806, which rounds to 0.081, so that is acceptable. Real errors: the ratio 24.9/8.9 is 2.79 (24.88/8.92 = 2.79), which is fine. The 'about 4.3 percentage points' figure is wrong; 24.5355 minus 20.2755 is 4.26, which rounds to 4.3, so it stands. The coefficient of variation values 0.444 and 0.507 come from r5, but r4 gives 0.352 and 0.377 for the same years. The text uses r5 without noting the discrepancy, which may confuse readers. The heading 'more than two' is loose against the 2.79 ratio. S3: 'Regions differ by a factor of more than two' is correct, but 'nearly half of the population is in countries not moving quickly enough' follows from 46.6 per cent, which is acceptable. The proposal that the male and female series move 'only moderately' together rests on a Spearman of 0.567, which is reasonable. The line 'both a large-country problem and a problem of many small ones' is an overreach. The marginal group's 23.5 per cent does not make the 63 countries a large-country problem. The proposal to prioritise the largest-population countries is weakly tied to the findings. S5: the three section headings state findings, as the house style requires. Some repetition between the sections on country counts, rates and convergence could be trimmed. The 'Gini rose' claim cites 2020 without giving its values.

r-w-c04-10-1-birch/reviewer.comments: S1: The Theil 2024 figure is wrong. The text gives 0.081 but the fact is 0.0806, which rounds to 0.081, so that one is fine. The error is the Theil 2015 value, where 0.070 is a correct rounding of 0.0704. However, 'the problem is both a large-country and a many-small-countries problem' is not supported, since the shares do not show country size. The proposal 'changes in the two move together only moderately' contradicts the text's wording of shared drivers and a correlation of 0.567; reconcile the two. The proposal to prioritise the largest populations among the 37 stagnating and regressing countries rests on no population figure by country. S5: Resolve the two coefficient-of-variation series and the heading wording; the text is otherwise clear.

r-w-c04-1-1-idris/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c04-5-1-juno/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c04-10-1-rowan/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c04-5-1-bao/reviewer.comments: S1: Most figures match the facts after rounding. Faults: 'roughly one sixth' is correct (0.994/5.887 = 16.9%). r-w-c04-10-1-chidi/reviewer.comments: S1: Theil 2024 is given as 0.081, but the fact is 0.0806, which rounds to 0.081, so that is fine. The ratio of 2.79 is correct (24.88/8.92). r-w-c06-3-1-orchard/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c03-7-1-goran/reviewer.comments:

r-w-c06-3-1-birch/reviewer.comments: S1: The numbers match the facts after rounding, but ratios 5.60 and 2.89 appear in no cited result. 31.1/5.6 gives 5.55 (31.0909/5.5504 gives 5.60, so acceptable), but 2.89 is a derived figure, so cite it or remove it.
