r-w-c02-6-1-farah/reviewer.comments: S1: Most numbers match their facts. Faults: the South Asia education figure of 11.3 per cent is for 2025, with 2015 at 13.9, but the text says 'latest year' without a year. East Asia and Pacific 13.0 is 2023, again unstated. The education fall of 14.1 to 14.0 is 0.145 points, so 'under a fifth' is fine. 'Roughly three to one' is loose, since 17.9 against 5.4 and 4.8 gives about 3.3 to 3.7. 'Under a quarter' is acceptable. The Theil increase 'more than half' is fine. S2: Social protection is not answered, and this is disclosed. The text also says the 'Spearman correlation between 2022 levels', but the fact has no year. S3: The claim that poorer regions put more into education than health is fine, but the claim that health spending after 2020 'reflects emergency responses' is asserted without data. 'A few budget decisions shape the outcome for most of the world's children' goes beyond the results. The claim that the aggregate 'hides little movement because regional shifts offset' is not shown, since the regions fell. The proposal on fast reporting within two years has no finding behind it. S5: The health and education trend findings are repeated in two sections. The opening text says the education series 'rests on partial reporting' for 2025, and the next sentence repeats this point.

r-w-c05-4-1-farah/reviewer.comments: S1: the text says the rise is 'over nine years' and '7.0 points'; both are correct (43.6151-36.6131=7.0). Several numbers are not backed by cited facts: the Europe and Central Asia 2015 figure is fine, but the 'about seven percentage points' for South Asia is correct (7.4) and acceptable. The Lower middle income rate 0.0264 is classed on track in the facts, yet the text lumps it with 'middle-income groups' without issue. The real faults are in S3. (1) The text says the region of Sub-Saharan Africa's gap with Europe has 'widened in absolute terms'; this is plausible but rests on a 2021 versus 2024 mismatch and should be stated with numbers. (2) 'Forty regress' in the heading versus 'most countries advancing' is fine. (3) Causes for North America (tuition, labour market, two-year institutions) and East Asia (public and private funding) are not in the results and should be removed or flagged as unsupported. (4) 'The poorest regions are not' advancing is too strong given positive rates; say 'advancing slowly'. (5) The high-income group is classed marginal (0.0083) but is not mentioned. (6) The proposal to prioritise financing for ratios below 10 per cent rests on an inference about the binding constraint (secondary completion), which the data do not show. Remove it or soften it.

r-w-c05-1-1-bao/reviewer.comments:
S1: Several figures differ from their facts. Primary completion in Sub-Saharan Africa (66.3% to 68.9%) is correct, but the lower middle income lower secondary series is given as 71.0% to 73.7% 'in 2024' where the text elsewhere implies otherwise; check periods. The 'nearly ten points' MENA primary rise is right (9.8). The 'about 10 percentage points' gap and 'one adolescent in four' are derived, not facts; 'about 0.017 a year' mixes a rate with a point change. Note that the text lacks the primary figures for income groups, which are in the facts. 'Upper middle income countries classed on-track' is correct. The claim that Europe and Central Asia 'shows moderate progress' on learning is correct but its 2030 value is omitted.
S2: Minimum proficiency at the end of lower secondary is not addressed, only primary reading. State this limit.
S3: Reading the primary-completion class 'regression' as an artefact of ceilings is asserted, not shown. Statements that the poorest have 'scarcely closed any distance' and reasons for out-of-school (fees, early marriage) and for learning gaps have no result behind them. Proposal 1 omits low-income countries by name, though the findings single them out.
S5: Country classifications and the 2030 projections are repeated three times; condense. The statement that the world primary rate 'does not approach universal' wording is fine. The section should cut the repeated gross-intake caveat.

r-w-c02-2-1-chidi/reviewer.comments: S1: most figures match the facts, but several statements are not supported. 'Held between 40 and 50 through 2008 to 2014' is fine (2008 is 40, 2012 is 50, 2014 is 46). 'Passed 0.39 in 2015' is wrong, as the fact is 0.3912, which is acceptable. The 2019 Gini is 0.6269, so 0.63 is fine. The text says the 2020 Theil index is unavailable, which matches the facts. Explanations such as 'some surveys collected in 2020 are dated to the following income reference year' and 'the lag in EU-SILC dating is one reason' for the 2021 peak are not backed by any result. S2: the question is about how rates have moved, yet no national poverty rate level or change is reported anywhere. The answer rests on trend classes, reporting counts and dispersion statistics. S3: the dispersion section asserts that national lines are higher in richer regions and that regional location explains most of the gap, without any result. The statement that 'a few countries hold very large populations' is likewise unsupported. The proposal on annual publication follows only loosely from the findings. S5: the section is long and repeats the reporting counts and trend-class figures in several places. It could be condensed, and the first-person-free style is good.

r-w-c05-4-1-chidi/reviewer.comments: S1: Lower middle income is classed on track in the facts, but the text lumps it as advancing (acceptable). The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region is called 'marginal', which matches. Most figures check out. Faults: 'Sub-Saharan Africa sits at 9.3 per cent' is correctly dated 2021, but the heading calls it 2024-wide. High income is classed marginal (0.0083) and is never mentioned, though the text says the poorest regions alone are not advancing. S3: 'At this pace the region will remain far from levels reached elsewhere in 2015' is fine, but 'the gap with Europe and Central Asia has widened' is unstated, though derivable (58.1 to ~75.6 points; ok). The claim that East Asia's gain stems from funded university systems and near-universal secondary completion, and the North America causes (labour market, tuition, pandemic), are not supported by any result; cut them or flag them as conjecture. 'Growth spread across starting points' and 'led by populous countries' go beyond the regression. Proposal 1 sets a 10 per cent threshold not found in a finding stated as such. S1 also: 'moderate progress' for the world is quoted correctly. Remove the repeated gross ratio explanation and repeated convergence figures to tighten.

r-w-c02-6-1-dagny/reviewer.comments: S1: The education figures for World (14.1, 14.0) are correct, but 'a fall of under a fifth of a percentage point' is wrong: the fall is 0.145, which is under 0.15, so the wording holds only loosely. The education text says South Asia fell to 11.3 per cent without a year, and that year is 2025, which should be stated. East Asia and Pacific's 13.0 is for 2023, not 'the latest year'. The claim that the world aggregate 'hides little movement because large regional shifts offset one another' is unsupported. 'Roughly three to one' for the rich-poor health gap compares 18.5 with 5.3 across different years. 'Most populous countries' regressing is asserted, not shown. 'A fifth of the population lives where they are falling' is fair. The 'Theil rose by more than half' is correct (0.065 to 0.101). S2: Social protection is unanswered, which is disclosed; the question is only two-thirds answered. S3: Causal claims (pandemic raising health priority; emergency expansion after 2020) go beyond the data. The 'Poorer regions put more into schooling' claim compares across regions and years loosely. The proposal to protect the education share is reasonable. S5: The text repeats the health and education class counts across sections, and 'Gini 0.18/0.22' then '0.181/0.223' is inconsistent presentation.

r-w-c05-7-1-dagny/reviewer.comments:
S1: Most figures match the facts after rounding. Faults: 'a world ratio of 0.15' is fine, but 'the Theil index fell from 0.026 to 0.011' is correct. The claim that Europe and Central Asia fell 'from 94.1% in 2015 to 91.6% in 2020' is correct. The text calls South Asia 'second-lowest' in 2015, which no cited result supports: Sub-Saharan Africa 66.2% and low income 65.8% are lower, but other regions' 2015 values are not given. 'Second-highest' in 2024 is supported. The 'roughly one in five' claim is fine. Slope to 83.4% is described as 'continuing the slope', which is acceptable. Gap 'larger than any two of the other regions' is unsupported for those not cited.
S2: Pupil-teacher ratios are unanswered; the section says so honestly. Target 4.a is named but not answered in the section body, only in gaps. State this in the text.
S3: Several causal claims (policy certification, refugees, pandemic halting convergence) go beyond the results. The 4.a proposal does not follow from any finding. The 'pupil-teacher ratio' proposal is tied to a gap, not a finding. Soften the causal wording and tie each proposal to a numbered finding.

r-w-c04-11-1-amara/reviewer.comments: S1: Most figures match their facts. Three do not. Stagnation in the 2015 to 2023 index is described with 'a rate of zero' correctly, but the index values (73, 72, 85, 78, 82, 66, 68, 72, 69, 51, 49, 53) have no cited fact, so they cannot be checked. The 2015 to 2023 gain for North America, 'roughly 2,372', follows from the facts (6,959.0 minus 4,587.0 is 2,372.0), so it is acceptable. The spending-share sentence calls 2015 to 2023 'eight years', which is correct. S3: 'Nearly four in five live in flat or sliding countries' is right (48.1 plus 29.5 is 77.6), but 'the financing half of 3.c is being met' overreaches, since 142 countries on a direction-of-travel test is not a substantial increase. Later claims that spending 'has plainly not translated into coverage' and that causes are 'well established' (weak tax collection, debt service) are not drawn from the results. The proposal on annual immunisation reporting rests on a composite index only. S5: The same country-class figures are repeated three times, and the 'Regions and countries' and 'Implications' sections restate earlier text. Condense the repetition. Also, the section headings need to reflect their sections' findings more precisely.

r-w-c04-2-1-orchard/reviewer.comments: [minor, S1] Counting countries section: 'Together these 53 countries hold 19.7% of the population by the shares given, 7.8% and 11.9%': The facts give 7.84% and 11.87%, which sum to 19.7%, so this is correct. However the earlier statement that the 66 remaining countries hold 27.6% is wrong: 7.8+11.9+2.1+5.7 = 27.5 (0.0784+0.1187+0.0212+0.0572 = 0.2755). Correction: Change 27.6% to 27.5% (or 27.6% only if exact sum is checked; the facts give 27.55%, so state about 27.5%).; [minor, S1] Regions section: 'South Asia ... ratio of 0.96, just short of fully matching the neonatal pace needed' and 'The pace of decline, -0.0502 a year ... ratio of 1.30': The neonatal expected 2030 value is 12.5, above the threshold 12.0, which fits a ratio below 1. This is consistent. However the claim that 'Sub-Saharan Africa moved slowest on the neonatal measure' and 'roughly twice the pace of the world' is fine. The heading claims a factor of seven, yet the under-five ratio is 11.12 and the neonatal 7.39, so the heading mixes the two. Correction: Make the heading state that neonatal rates differ by a factor of about seven and under-five rates by about eleven.; [major, S3] Counting countries: 'three countries carry nearly as much population as the 39 moderate countries carry per country on average in neonatal terms': The comparison is incoherent and unsupported. It mixes indicators and per-country averages, and the data do not support it. Three countries hold 4.9% against 16.1% for the 39 moderate countries. Correction: Rewrite: the three stagnating countries hold 4.9% of the population, about 1.6% each, against about 0.4% each for the 39 moderate countries.; [major, S3] Proposal 3: shift funding from the under-five agenda to neonatal care: The findings show under-five mortality is also far above the threshold in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries (71.2 and 68.8 against 25.0). They do not support moving funds away from it, and the text itself says both need acceleration. Correction: Propose adding or targeting funding for neonatal care alongside the under-five agenda, without reducing it.; [minor, S3] Proposal 2: 'the 13 that are stagnating or regressing': The 13 (4+9) refers to neonatal only; stated without that qualification it may be read as covering both indicators. Correction: Say 'the 13 that stagnate or regress on neonatal mortality'.; [major, S2] Whole section; ques | Keep the clear separation of country counts, population shares and the world average, and the open statement that the on-track class merges achievement with projection. The regional and income tables with expected 2030 values are strong, as are the caution on modelled data and the note about truncated output. Strengthen by answering the headline question directly.

r-w-c06-5-1-elm/reviewer.comments: [minor, S1] Section 'Reporting has changed little since 2015', first paragraph: 'The count rose to 10 in 2016 and reached a peak of 15 in 2018'; also earlier 'The series has been reported by 81 countries in any year since 2006': The sentence 'reported by 81 countries in any year since 2006' is awkward but matches the fact. However, the heading's claim that reporting 'has changed little' conflicts with the counts, which swing from 4 to 15. This is a heading/number mismatch rather than a figure error. Correction: Retitle the section to 'Reporting has fluctuated since 2015 without a trend'.; [minor, S1] Section 'Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data', second paragraph: 'A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2019 and 2020': The sentence implies 2019 and 2020 are the pair of a 15-country year and a 4-country year, but both had 4 countries; 15 was 2018. The pairing misattributes the years. Correction: Write 'A year with 15 reporting countries (2018) and a year with 4 (2019) cannot be set side by side.'; [minor, S3] Section 'Reporting has changed little since 2015': 'The fall to 4 countries in 2019 and 2020 coincides with the onset of the pandemic': 2019 precedes the pandemic, so the coincidence claim is only half true; the text partly corrects this later, but the opening assertion is not supported by the results. Correction: Say that the 2020 count of 4 coincides with the pandemic's onset, while the 2019 count of 4 precedes it, and the series cannot separate the causes.; [minor, S3] Section 'Thin coverage limits any global picture': 'a measure that most countries report only once in a decade': The results give counts of reporters per year and a total of 81 ever reporting; they do not show how often individual countries report, so the 'once in a decade' frequency is unsupported. Correction: Replace with 'a measure reported by only 3 to 15 countries in any year'.; [major, S2] Whole section: The question asks what share of women make their own decisions. The section gives no share for any country, even for the 5 reporting in 2024, although the shelf holds a levels result. It answers only that no aggregate exists and never reports the available national values or their range, nor separates decisions on health care from contraception. Correction: Add the 2024 country values with their survey years and units from the levels resul | The treatment of coverage is the section's strength: it is candid that survey timing, not behaviour, drives the yearly counts, and it keeps the composite definition and the married-or-in-union limit in view throughout. Keep the refusal to average five countries and the proposals tied to these limits. Strengthen it by showing the actual country readings available, and by checking years against counts.

r-w-c06-7-1-saltmarsh/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Global section: 'The 2019 figures are on a common footing... Whatever the true gap in 2024, it is therefore unlikely to have vanished, and the figures give no sign that it has widened': The 2019 gap says nothing about 2024. The claim that the gap has not widened contradicts the section's own warning that the 2024/2025 mismatch cannot be read as a gap. The regional 2024 gaps and the 8.4-point upper bound do not support it. Correction: Rewrite the paragraph. State the 2019 gap (4.2 points, ratio about 0.93) as a 2019 fact only, and say the world gap in 2024 cannot be measured from these results.; [major, S3] Regional section: 'the gap... is widest where overall connectivity is at a middle level'; and 'Income groups show the same pattern in sharper form': The regional numbers contradict the pattern claimed. South Asia and the Middle East have gaps of about 12.6 to 12.8 points, while Sub-Saharan Africa, at a lower level, has 8.5. Low-income countries are said to show it 'in sharper form' on 7-country data. Correction: Say the point gap is largest in the middle-level regions (12.6 and 12.8 points) and smaller at the lowest level (8.5 in Sub-Saharan Africa). Drop 'sharper form' and note that income-group figures are indicative.; [major, S3] Implications: 'If current trends continue, the regions with the lowest female use are unlikely to reach parity by 2030'; and the regional paragraph 'tens of millions of women online': No projection or population figure is in the results, so both statements are unsupported. Correction: Remove the projection and the 'tens of millions' claim, or state that the data support only the observed gaps in 2024.; [minor, S1] 'Fewer than one woman in five... the male share was more than half as large again': 28.6/18.3 is about 1.56, so 'more than half as large again' is correct; but 'about 10.6 points in 2019' for South Asia is a gap of 10.6, and 'stayed within a narrow band' is loose against the 12.8 figure for 2024. Moreover Europe, Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa all fell, while only the Middle East/North Africa rose and others were flat, so the claim that most regions did not cut is unsupported. The attribution is a causal inference not in the results. Correction: Remove the causal explanation and state that the world figure fell alongside declines in Latin America, Europe and Central Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and lower middle income countries, with rises in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan and in South Asia.; [minor, S3] Section 1: 'The decline is not a matter of a few outliers alone, since the world figure is an aggregate across many reporting countries.': The fact that the figure is an aggregate does not show that the decline is broad-based; the inference does not follow. Correction: Delete the sentence or cite the country classification (98 of 186 regressed).; [minor, S3] Section 3, paragraph 2: 'several very populous countries lost ground' and 'the population share of regression exceeds the country share on both measures': Regression population share 62.3 per cent against country share 52.7 per cent supports it, but 'weighs heavily on any global reading' is an overreach. Also the fall in sub-groups described as 'largest school-age populations' is not in the results. Correction: Soften to 'larger countries are over-represented among those regressing'; remove the unsupported claim about school-age populations.; [minor, S3] Section 4, paragraph 1: 'depend mainly on wages, which make up most current spending in education': The results contain no w | Keep the clear two-measure framing, the explicit statement that no numerical target exists, and the frank reporting-coverage caution. Strengthen by removing unsupported causal claims about regions, wages and school-age populations, and by stating years whenever regional figures are compared across measures.

r-w-c04-8-1-hana/reviewer.comments: [minor, S1] Para on income groups: 'High-income countries ... added 1.9 points' and 'The lower-middle-income group gained most, 5.5 points': High income rose 83.2933 to 85.1777, which is 1.88, so 1.9 is fine. Lower middle rose 56.8317 to 62.3619, which is 5.53, so 5.5 is fine. The statement that the low-income gain (2.6) was smaller than the gains of 'the other three groups' is wrong, because high income gained only 1.9. Correction: Say the low-income gain of 2.6 points was smaller than those of lower-middle and upper-middle income countries (5.5 and 4.0), and larger than that of high-income countries (1.9).; [major, S3] Opening section: 'The poorest group ... gained least in absolute terms': Low income gained 2.6 points, but high income gained only 1.9, so the poorest group did not gain least. The conclusion about the poorest falling behind the others on absolute gains is not supported. Correction: Rewrite to say that low-income countries gained more than high-income countries in absolute terms but less than the two middle groups, and that they remain below the 2015 level of lower-middle income countries.; [minor, S3] Regions section: 'Latin America ... overtaken in pace by regions that started lower' and 'a distance that no region other than Sub-Saharan Africa comes close to approaching from below': The second phrase is garbled and unsupported by the figures. The gap of 38.0 is correct (88-50), but the claim about other regions is not a finding. Correction: Delete the clause and state only the 38.0-point gap between North America and Sub-Saharan Africa.; [minor, S3] Hardship passage: 'In three regions ... hardship rose slightly'; 'Households there still pay nearly half ... consequence of low public funding and a large private provider sector': The causal explanation for South Asia has no support in the results. 'Reflects the rising cost of care for chronic conditions' is likewise unsupported. Correction: Remove the causal explanations or mark them as hypotheses beyond the data.; [major, S3] Final section: 'South Asia has the fastest pace of any region' and the proposal on Latin America being blocked by 'capacity and access rather than by funding': The proposal for Latin America rests on no finding about capacity or funding, so it does not follow from the results. The claim that Latin America 'stagnates' is also loosely applied. Correction: Ground the propo | Keep the clear separation of service coverage from financial protection, the explicit warning that the 100-point reading of target 3.8 is a convention, and the candid account of thin hardship data and small samples. Keep the pairing of both trend assessments. Strengthen the regional and income-group comparisons by checking each ranking against the figures, and mark every causal explanation as a hypothesis.}

r-w-c06-5-1-dagny/reviewer.comments: [minor, S1] Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data, second paragraph: 'A year with 15 reporting countries and a year with 4, as in 2019 and 2020': The results give 4 countries in 2019, not 15. The 15-country year is 2018, so the example misstates the count it relies on. Correction: Change to 'as in 2018 and 2019', with 15 in 2018 and 4 in 2019, which matches the series.; [minor, S1] Regions and countries cannot be compared on current data, third paragraph: 'The series has been reported by 81 countries in any year since 2006': The figure of 81 is the number of countries reporting at least once across all years, not the number reporting in any one year. The sentence misreads the fact. Correction: Rewrite as 'Across all years from 2006 to 2024, 81 countries have reported at least once, yet in 2024 only 5 of them reported.'; [minor, S3] Thin coverage limits any global picture: 'a measure that most countries report only once in a decade': The results give the number of countries reporting per year and the total of 81 countries over 19 years. They do not show how often each country reports, so the claim about reporting once a decade is not supported. Correction: Delete the clause or replace it with the observed figures: 'a measure reported by 81 countries across 2006 to 2024, but by at most 15 in any single year'.; [major, S2] Opening question and the whole section: the question asks what share of women make their own decisions: The section never states a share for any country or year. It gives only the count of reporting countries, although result c06-5.r1 is a levels result for 2024. The question is therefore answered only by the statement that no global share exists, and the national readings are left unreported and unexplained. Correction: State the 2024 values for the five reporting countries, each with its country, year and unit (% of women aged 15 to 49), or state explicitly that the results file holds no such values and that the question is unanswered for 2024. | The section is clear and well ordered, and its treatment of survey timing, the composite definition and the thin coverage is careful and sound. Keep the caveats on comparability and the refusal to average five countries. Strengthen the answer to the question itself by stating what the 2024 readings are, or by saying plainly that they are not in the data. Correct the count and the 81-country wording so every figure matches its result exactly.

r-w-c03-2-1-quarry/reviewer.comments: [minor, S1] Income groups paragraph: 'Low-income countries began at 37.9% stunting in 2015': The cited fact for low-income stunting in 2015 is 37.95 in one result and 38.0 in the citation, and the text gives 37.9% in one place and 38.0% in another. 37.95 rounds to 38.0 (or 37.9 when truncated), so the text is inconsistent. Correction: Use 38.0% for low-income stunting in 2015 in both places.; [minor, S1] Regional section: 'The regional trend calculation shows it on track for the 5.0% reference level by 2030, with an expected value of 3.8%' and the preceding wasting values for Europe and Central Asia: The 5.0% target in the trend result is applied to stunting; the sentence follows wasting figures and is ambiguous about which indicator it concerns. The 5.0% reference level is also presented as the stunting target, though the text says no stunting threshold is given. Correction: State that the 3.8% expected value is for stunting and that 5.0% is the ceiling used by the trend tool, not the agreed stunting benchmark.; [major, S1] Gradient paragraph: 'about nine times that of high-income countries in 2015 and about nine times in 2024': The ratios are 37.95/3.9 ≈ 9.7 in 2015 and 35.79/4.04 ≈ 8.9 in 2024. These are not the same, and 'has not narrowed in relative terms' is contradicted: the ratio narrowed slightly. Correction: State about 9.7 times in 2015 and about 8.9 times in 2024, and drop the claim that the gradient has not narrowed.; [minor, S1] Stunting benchmark: 'agreed global nutrition benchmarks ... set a wasting level of 5.0% by 2030'; and later 'the 2030 goal is a prevalence of 3%': The two statements contradict each other: 5.0% is called the agreed 2030 level and 3% is then called the 2030 goal. The 3% and the 'below 5% by 2025' claims are not facts from the results. Correction: Say the trend tool uses 5.0% by 2030 and that other readings of the benchmark exist, without quoting 3% as a result.; [major, S3] Projection section: 'At the observed rates, the world will not reach the stunting target of 5.0% by 2030 ... a ratio of 0.12' and 'Only two groups are on track': Ratio 2.13 for Europe and Central Asia is called the fastest pace, but the text then lists North America and high income as on track as well, making three groups. Calling the 5.0% ceiling the stunting target contradicts the earlier statement that no stunting threshold is given. Correction: Sa | Keep the clear separation of chronic and acute malnutrition, the population-weighted reading of the wasting classes, the frank treatment of survey coverage and the convergence statistics. Strengthen consistency between the stated target readings and make every derived figure traceable to a result.

r-w-c02-3-1-elm/reviewer.comments: [minor, S1] Section 1, data limits paragraph: 'Coverage of 130 countries is substantial but not complete': The figure of 130 countries is not among the cited facts or results. The only country count for the series is 121 countries reporting in any year, and that count is for the poorest-quintile series, not the world aggregate. Correction: Delete the 130-country claim, or replace it with a figure the results hold and say which series it describes.; [minor, S1] Section 2, first paragraph: 'a range of about twenty-two percentage points': The span between the highest (72.5%) and lowest (50.6%) regions is 21.9 points, so 'about twenty-two' is a rounding of a derived figure that is not a cited fact. The same paragraph also gives a 7.1-point gap for the step from lower-middle to upper-middle income, which is again not a cited fact. Correction: Give the figures as 'about 22 points' only if marked as derived from the cited values, or drop the derived numbers and let the cited percentages carry the comparison.; [major, S3] Section 2: 'Only South Asia and the two best-placed regions lie above the world figure of 56.3%; the other two regions fall below it.': The count is wrong. South Asia, Europe and Central Asia, and East Asia and Pacific are the three regions above 56.3%. Latin America and the Caribbean (54.5%) and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (50.6%) are below. The wording 'South Asia and the two best-placed regions' double-counts South Asia as separate from the best-placed regions. Correction: Write: 'South Asia, Europe and Central Asia, and East Asia and Pacific lie above the world figure of 56.3%; the other two regions fall below it.'; [major, S3] Section 3 heading and opening: 'Coverage of the poorest quintile has regressed in many countries'; 'coverage of the poorest fifth fell in nearly half of the assessed countries, weighted by people'; and 'Regression is the largest single class by country count': The trend classification tests direction against a target with no numeric value. It cannot be read as an observed fall, and the text later concedes this. Saying coverage 'fell' for 48.9% of the assessed population contradicts the section's own caveat about measurement. Also, 26 of 55 countries is 47%, so 'nearly half' by country count is acceptable, but the population weighting is of the assessed countries, not of the world. Correction: Rewo | Keep the clear separation between whole-population coverage and the poorest quintile, the open statement that target 1.3 has no numeric threshold, and the year-by-year account of reporting counts. The caveats on participation versus adequacy are strong. Correct the regional count and the unsupported inferences, and keep every number tied to a cited fact.

r-w-c06-2-1-fernhill/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Heading 'Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap' and the paragraph on the decomposition: The heading and text say regions 'explain' most of the gap and speak of 'where a country sits in the world'. A between-region Theil share of 66.2% in one year among 35 non-random countries is only a descriptive decomposition and does not support 'explain'. The heading also says 'differ widely' while the text calls the Gini of 0.29 'not extreme'. Correction: Rewrite the heading and paragraph so the 66.2% is described as the share of measured inequality lying between regions in 2012 among 35 reporting countries, without causal language, and make 'widely' agree with the moderate Gini.; [minor, S1] Section 2, 'The coefficient of variation, at 0.66, points the same way, with country values spread widely': The coefficient of variation is read as pointing the same way as a 'real but not extreme' gap, yet described as 'widely' spread. This is inconsistent and unsupported by the figure. Correction: State only that the coefficient of variation is 0.66 in 2012, and do not say it points the same way or that values are spread widely.; [minor, S1] Section 4, 'The series holds 106 countries in any year' and 'with 72 countries reporting in any year': The facts are the number of countries reporting in at least one year, not in any single year. As worded, they suggest 106 and 72 countries report in a given year. Correction: Write '106 countries report in at least one year' and '72 countries report in at least one year'.; [minor, S3] Section 3, 'The drop around 2019 and 2020 coincides with the period in which field surveys were interrupted': The results show only the counts of reporting countries. The interruption of surveys is an outside claim and is not supported by the results. Similarly, 'Demographic and Health Surveys programme' and 'chiefly lower-income countries' are not in the results. Correction: Say that the counts fall in 2019 and 2020, and flag the survey-interruption explanation and the DHS coverage as outside the bench data, or remove them.; [minor, S3] Section 2, 'The 2012 estimates ... reflect a coordinated modelled estimation exercise' and 'rest on estimation rather than direct survey': The results do not show that the 2012 values are modelled estimates. This is asserted without support. Correction: Remove the claim or mar | The section states its coverage limits clearly: the narrow indicator, the thin years, the missing post-2017 data and the empty trend classes. Keep the explicit link between measurement gaps and the proposals, and the caution that attitudes are not experience. Strengthen the discipline of tying every explanation to the results.

faults.where: Heading 'Where data exist, countries differ widely and regions explain most of the gap' and the paragraph on the decomposition
faults.problem: The heading and text say regions 'explain' most of the gap and speak of 'where a country sits in the world'. A between-region Theil share of 66.2% in one year among 35 non-random countries is only a descriptive decomposition and does not support 'explain'. The heading also says 'differ widely' while the text calls the Gini of 0.29 'not extreme'.
faults.correction: Rewrite the heading and paragraph so the 66.2% is described as the share of measured inequality lying between regions in 2012 among 35 reporting countries, without causal language, and make 'widely' agree with the moderate Gini.

faults.where: Section 2, 'The coefficient of variation, at 0.66, points the same way, with country values spread widely'
faults.problem: The coefficient of variation is read as pointing the same way as a 'real but not extreme' gap, yet described as 'widely' spread. This is inconsistent and unsupported by the figure.
faults.correction: State only that the coefficient of variation is 0.66 in 2012, and do not say it points the same way or that values are spread widely.

faults.where: Section 4, 'The series holds 106 countries in any year' and 'with 72 countries reporting in any year'
faults.problem: The facts are the number of countries reporting in at least one year, not in any single year. As worded, they suggest 106 and 72 countries report in a given year.
faults.correction: Write '106 countries report in at least one year' and '72 countries report in at least one year'.

faults.where: Section 3, 'The drop around 2019 and 2020 coincides with the period in which field surveys were interrupted'
faults.problem: The results show only the counts of reporting countries. The interruption of surveys is an outside claim and is not supported by the results. Similarly, 'Demographic and Health Surveys programme' and 'chiefly lower-income countries' are not in the results.
faults.correction: Say that the counts fall in 2019 and 2020, and flag the survey-interruption explanation and the DHS coverage as outside the bench data, or remove them.

faults.where: Section 2, 'The 2012 estimates ... reflect a coordinated modelled estimation exercise' and 'rest on estimation rather than direct survey'
faults.problem: The results do not show that the 2012 values are modelled estimates. This is asserted without support.
faults.correction: Remove the claim or mark it as unverified from the data; say only that 35 countries report in 2012, far more than in other years.

r-w-c07-1-1-quarry/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Section 'Regions differ...': 'gap ... has changed little since 2015' and 'The gap between the top and bottom regions is 65.0 percentage points': 97.4 minus 32.4 is 65.0, but in 2015 the gap was 96.3 minus 26.4 = 69.9, so it narrowed by about five points. 'Changed little' misstates the result; the 'more than sixty' heading is fine. Correction: State that the gap narrowed from 69.9 to 65.0 points between 2015 and 2024, and revise the claim that it has changed little.; [minor, S1] Third section: 'South Asia ... a gain of 14.4 percentage points': 77.6 minus 63.1 is 14.5 (77.5515 minus 63.1086 = 14.44), so 14.4 is right from the facts, but the text says East Asia gained 10.1 (75.2336-65.139=10.09), which is also right. No error here; however the text says 'The gain of about six percentage points' for the world, which is correct (6.0). Correction: No change needed.; [major, S3] Third section: 'Sub-Saharan Africa ... pace ... close to that of South Asia' and fourth section 'pace of Sub-Saharan Africa, at 0.02 a year': South Asia gained 14.4 points against about 6 for Sub-Saharan Africa, so its pace is more than twice as fast. The figure of 0.02 a year is not a cited result and is inconsistent with the rest of the text. Correction: Remove the claim of a pace close to South Asia's and the 0.02 figure; say Sub-Saharan Africa gained about 0.7 points a year against about 1.6 for South Asia, computed from cited levels.; [major, S3] Third section: 'the regions with the largest deficits gained least in relative terms'; 'Gains ... middling starting points': Sub-Saharan Africa rose 6.0 points from 26.4%, a relative gain of about 23%, larger than most regions, so the relative claim is unsupported. The claim that South Asia's progress came from middling starting points is fine. Correction: Say the regions with the largest deficits gained less in points than South Asia and East Asia and Pacific, and remove 'in relative terms'.; [minor, S3] Regions section: 'the data do not separate these causes' versus 'well-established reasons'; also 'The Middle East ... began the period level with South Asia': Causes (conflict, scarcity, utilities, investment, population growth) are asserted without any result. MENAP started at 64.7% against South Asia 63.1% and East Asia 65.1%, which is roughly level, but the causal explanations are unsupported. Correction: Present causes as poss | Keep the explicit statement of how 'universal' can be read, the candid treatment of the weak convergence fit, the coverage caveats and the link between basic and safely managed service. The projection section is well structured. Tie every comparison to cited numbers and avoid causal explanations the data cannot carry.

r-w-c03-3-2-elm/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Section 3, regional anaemia paragraph: 'Europe and Central Asia, at 0.0202, also rises faster than South Asia, at 0.0070... concentrated among regions with lower prevalence': The rates are cited correctly, but the interpretation overreaches: the claim that rises are concentrated in low-prevalence regions rests on a few regions and ignores that every region regresses, and the text says 'Rates are highest in North America... lowest in East Asia'. Mostly supported, though 'lower prevalence' is not shown for Europe and Central Asia, whose level is not cited. Correction: Cite the Europe and Central Asia anaemia level or soften the claim to say that South Asia, the highest-prevalence region, rises more slowly than North America and Europe and Central Asia.; [major, S3] Section 1 and 4: 'Both series worsened after 2015' and 'anaemia has risen almost everywhere'; heading 'Regions differ most on anaemia, and overweight is highest where hunger is lower': The heading brings in 'hunger', which no result measures, and the trend classes are said to show anaemia 'risen almost everywhere' although the classes use a no-target direction test and 18 countries are stagnant, 9 marginal. Also 'the direction of travel does not depend on the line' is unsupported, since no sensitivity test was run. Correction: Replace 'where hunger is lower' with 'where anaemia is lower', and delete or support the claim that the direction does not depend on the benchmark line.; [major, S3] Proposals 2 and 3: Proposal 2 rests on overweight rising in Sub-Saharan Africa, but the Sub-Saharan trend figures are only partly given; proposal 3 relies on a benchmark of 3.0 per cent that is the authors' own and on projections. Neither proposal follows from a finding about programme effectiveness or causes, which the text says it cannot identify. Correction: Tie each proposal to a stated finding with its number and say the benchmark is a working one, or reword them as monitoring proposals.; [minor, S1] Section 3: 'Sub-Saharan Africa... classed as regressing' and ratio of regional gaps 'more than three times the lowest, at a ratio of 3.43': The ratios 3.43 and 2.92 are not in the cited facts; computed from the cited levels 51.1/14.9 gives 3.43 but 9.9/3.4 gives 2.92, which are derived, not cited results. Correction: Cite the ratios as derived from the regional levels, or state the levels and omit the | Keep the explicit statement that the 3.0 per cent benchmark is the book's own and that anaemia has no target. The caution about modelled estimates and the separation of level association from change are strong. Keep the numbers with years and units, and the open acknowledgement of what the data cannot show.

r-w-c04-9-1-goran/reviewer.comments: [major, S2] Whole section; the question asks how many deaths are attributed to air pollution and unsafe water and sanitation: The section gives no count of deaths and no air pollution result. Only the inequality of one water, sanitation and hygiene rate in 2019 is analysed, so the question is largely unanswered. Correction: Retrieve and analyse the air pollution mortality series, the water rate itself (level, not only inequality) and a death count or population figures, then state the totals, or rewrite the section to answer only what the data support.; [major, S3] Implications section: 'Progress on the target depends on the regions where rates are highest' and 'conceal the places where most of the avoidable deaths occur': The decomposition does not name regions, give rates by region or give counts. Correction: Remove the causal claim and state only that low-income countries (24.8 per cent) exceed lower-middle-income ones (23.6 per cent), without explanation.; [major, S3] Regions paragraph: 'Reserved seats and candidate quotas explain much of the progress elsewhere, and the regions that rose most are those where such rules are widespread.'; also the South Asia explanation about suspended assemblies: No result measures quotas, reserved seats or suspended assemblies. Correction: Delete the claims or mark them as outside the data, and the proposal on quotas should be presented as a general policy view, not as following from a finding.; [major, S3] 'a count of countries suggests regression is the second most common outcome, while the population view shows stagnation touches twice as many people. The 2015 values are 0.2438 and 0.707, so the region was already below and the gap narrowed because low-income fell. The sentence is muddled, and the contrast with 'a different story' is weak. Correction: State that the region started below low-income countries and still does, with the gap closing only because the low-income rate halved.; [major, S3] Malaria paragraph in regional section: 'consistent with the weight of Sub-Saharan Africa in the population at risk': Sub-Saharan Africa's rate fell slightly (232.5 to 229.3) and low-income stayed flat, so its weight cannot explain a rise in the world rate from 59.0 to 64.0. Correction: Remove the claim, or say that the series do not show which groups drive the rise in the world rate.; [major, S3] Proposal 1 on malaria in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries: Proposal 1 rests on 'barely moved', but the data also show the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rising from 4.3 to 10.0, a regression, which gets no proposal. The one genuine mismatch is the world gain of 3.0 and shortfall of 29.0, which are derived and correct. Correction: No change needed to these figures; check only the derived values against the cited results.; [major, S3] Final section, paragraph on 2030 projections: 'Latin America and the Caribbean ... ratio of 0.00, which the assessment classes as stagnation' and 'low-income countries ... ratio of 0.09 that the assessment classes as stagnation': The cited results give no classification for these groups, so the 'stagnation' label for each group is not supported. The text also says the assessment 'classes' them, which attributes a finding to results that do not contain it. Correction: Remove the classification wording, or state only the projected value and the ratio the results give.; [major, S3] Final section, opening: 'the direction of the finding holds under a gentler yardstick, because the projected 2030 values sit well below any plausible aspiration': No gentler target was tested, and 'any plausible aspiration' is an assertion not drawn from the results. The inference is unsupported. Correction: State that the assessment was run only against 100 and that its sensitivity to other yardsticks was not tested.; [major, S3] Coverage paragraph: 'universality by 2030 was not within reach' and 'Whether the period after 2020 slowed progress cannot be judged': The first sentence uses the past tense about a future date and states a certainty. Correction: Say that 2030 universality is not reachable on the 2015–2023 pace and that the endpoints do not show intervening change.; [minor, S3] Hardship paragraph in the section on coverage and protection: 'protection improved where out-of-pocket reliance was highest, and it stalled or revers | Keep the explicit caveats on the reading of target 3.8, the data gaps for hardship, and the careful wording of association against cause. The paired view of service coverage and out-of-pocket burden is useful. Strengthen by removing unsupported classifications and repetition, and by keeping every inference tied to a cited result.

r-w-c06-5-2-ewan/reviewer.comments: [minor, S3] Section 'Reporting has changed little since 2015', heading and opening paragraph: The heading says reporting 'has changed little', but the body says it 'has swung widely' with no trend. The heading contradicts the evidence it introduces and would mislead a skimming reader. Correction: Change the heading to a declarative statement that matches the body, for example 'Reporting has swung widely since 2015 without a trend'.; [minor, S3] Section 'Reporting has changed little since 2015', second paragraph on the 2020 count: The text attributes the count of 4 in 2020 to the pandemic's interruption of fieldwork. That cause is not in the retrieved results, which give only counts of reporting countries, so the link is an unsupported inference. Correction: State that the cause of the 2020 count is not in the results, or remove the causal link and say only that the series cannot show why the count fell.; [minor, S3] Section 'The indicator and what it measures', paragraph on the composite: The text says the composite's level 'is bound to be lower than the level for any single component'. Correction: Replace 'is bound to be lower than' with 'cannot exceed'.; [minor, S5] Throughout, especially 'Thin coverage', 'Regions and countries cannot be compared' and 'Implications for 2030': The figures 5, 81, 3 to 15 and the absence of share values are restated in nearly every section, often in the same paragraph. Correction: State each count once in its place in the argument and refer back to it briefly elsewhere, cutting repeated sentences in the implications section. | The section keeps its strongest feature: it states plainly that the results hold counts of reporting countries and no share values, and it explains why the years and countries cannot be compared. It should keep that candour and the link from each finding to a proposal. It should strengthen the separation of what the data show from what is inferred, and trim repeated figures so the argument reads in order.

r-w-c03-7-3-chidi/reviewer.comments: [minor, S3] Dispersion section: 'The fall in the between-region share from 2022 to 2024, while the index itself rose, indicates that the rise in dispersion after 2022 came mainly from differences among countries of the same region': The earlier reviewer's fault is not mended. Within-region inequality was already the majority in every year, so one 3-point shift does not establish that the post-2022 rise came mainly from within-region differences. Four years cannot show the path. Correction: Label both passages as context from outside this book's data, or cut them, and state that the series do not identify which countries or shocks account for the movements.

r-w-c09-7-1-amara/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Section 'Country values differ widely', final paragraph: 'For 2030, the only safe inference is that where child employment persists, it is concentrated by region': The spread results stop at 2012 and describe inequality among reporting countries in those years only. They cannot show where child employment persists in 2030, so this projection is an inference the results do not support. Correction: Delete the 2030 inference, or restate it as a limit: the spread results cover 2000 to 2012 only and say nothing about the position in 2030 or whether employment is persisting.; [minor, S1] Section 'Country values differ widely', second paragraph: 'In five of the six years shown, more than four-fifths of the difference among countries': All six between-region shares exceed 80%, including 85.4% in 2006 and 77.0% in 2011 is the only one below 80%, so the count is wrong: five of six is not the correct reading of 77.0% and 85.4% together. The 2011 value of 77.0% falls below four-fifths, so only five of six exceed it, but the sentence then calls 77.0% the lowest share and says it still leaves regional position largest; the count should be stated exactly. Correction: State that five of the six years exceed four-fifths (2011, at 77.0%, is the exception), and keep the statement that regions remain the largest component in every year.; [minor, S3] Section 'Country values differ widely', first paragraph: 'the 2012 figure indicates a distribution in which a few populous countries sit far from the rest': The Gini and Theil values do not identify which countries are populous or distant; this description goes beyond the measure, which the same section later admits does not identify which countries drive the figures. Correction: Replace with a description of the measure alone: the 2012 Gini of 0.625 indicates a highly unequal distribution of country values among the 24 reporting countries, with the drivers not identified. | The section answers its question clearly: 97 countries reporting at least once, 2 in 2016, and the 2016 limit on the age and sex splits. It separates the 7-to-14 measure from the target's wording well. Strengthen the link between the coverage counts and each reading, and keep the explicit labelling of context as separate from findings.

r-w-c08-1-2-quarry/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Country trajectories: 'Europe and Central Asia reached 100.0 per cent'; 'High-income economies stood at 100.0 per cent': High income 2024 is 99.968, which rounds to 100.0 at one decimal, so this is acceptable; but 'South Asia ... overall 13 points' and 'urban population... 2.2 per cent' are fine. Correction: Cut the claim, or reword it as a possibility that the data cannot test, without asserting that part of the gain comes from migration.; [major, S2] Section question: how many people lack electricity, and where: The section still gives no headcount of people without electricity, whether derived and labelled or otherwise. r-w-c08-4-1-goran/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Heading and first paragraph: 'fell by 6.4 per cent between 2015 and 2021': The heading states 6.4 per cent, which the text itself says is not in the results and is not relied on. The two levels (4.8556 to 4.5449) give 6.399 per cent, so the figure is correct, but the text disclaims it, contradicting its own heading. This is an inconsistent presentation of a derived number. Correction: Either state that the 6.4 per cent is calculated from the two cited levels, or retitle the part without the percentage. Remove the sentence saying the figure is not relied on.; [major, S3] Third part: 'Improvement peaked before 2018'; 2011-2017 'about twice that of 2001-2004'; 2018-2021 'below even the 2001-2004 rate': The 2018-2021 mean (-0.0325) is not below the 2001-2004 mean (-0.0498); it is smaller in magnitude, so improvement was slower, which is the opposite of 'below' in the sense of faster. The wording is ambiguous but the claim 'below even the 2001-2004 rate' is read as slower, which is true. However, 'less than a third of the pace of 2011-2017' is wrong: 0.0325/0.1045 is 31 per cent, so it is just under a third and is acceptable. The real error is that 2011-2017 is said to be 'close to the pace of 2005-2008' (-0.1154), a reasonable reading, so the finding stands. Correction: Say 'slower than the 2001-2004 pace' to remove ambiguity.; [major, S3] Regions part: 'the only one the trend tool classes as on track or target met among regions': The text then says North America and South Asia are also classed as on track or target met, so Europe and Central Asia is not the only region so classed. Correction: Say Europe and Central Asia has the steepest rate; North America and South Asia are also classed as on track.; [minor, S3] Fourth part: 'the world series gives no sign of doubling' under either reading, and the title 'Doubling the earlier rate is not met': The text admits the earlier rate cannot be tested because no pre-2015 rate is held, yet states a firm verdict under both readings. The segment comparison tests only one reading. Correction: Label the verdict as holding on the segment comparison, and state that the pre-2015 reading is untested.; [minor, S3] First paragraph and fourth part: 'rate of -0.01096 ... from a longer baseline': The trend rate is described as a longer baseline although its period is not stated in the results. Correction: Omit 'from a lo | Keep the explicit caveats on readings of target 7.3, the short final segment and the pandemic, and the regional comparison with years and units. Strengthen consistency of rates and wording, and tie the verdict to what was actually tested.

r-w-c04-7-2-idris/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Family planning section, paragraph on country counts reporting demand satisfied by modern methods: 'Since 2019 the count has fallen further, to 2 in 2019, 3 in 2020, 6 in 2021, 7 in 2022, 4 in 2023 and 7 in 2024.': The cited counts rise from 2 in 2019 to 7 in 2024, so 'fallen further' misreads the series and states a direction the figures contradict. Correction: Replace 'fallen further' with a plain statement that the count was 2 in 2019 and 7 in 2024, noting the year-to-year rise and fall (3, 6, 7, 4, 7 in 2020 to 2024) without implying a steady decline.; [minor, S2] Family planning section and Implications: 'no level of satisfied demand is reported here': The question asks how far demand is satisfied and the section gives only trend classes and population shares. The gap is acknowledged, but the answer to the level question is still not stated as unavailable in the data itself, so the reader cannot tell whether the level is missing from the bench or was not sought. Correction: State once, in the opening of the section, that the bench supplies no level of satisfied demand for any country group or the world, and that the answer to 'how far' is therefore limited to direction and population share in 15 countries.; [minor, S3] Adolescent fertility section, income paragraph: 'Income groups and regions overlap heavily, so the two views largely describe the same countries.': No overlap of countries between income groups and regions is reported by the results, so the claim is unsupported. Correction: Remove the claim or label it as an assumption, for example: 'The results do not show how far income groups and regions contain the same countries.' | The section keeps its disciplined labelling of context, its population-weighted reporting and its candid limits on the trend classes, and these should be kept. Strengthen the answer to the question on satisfied demand by stating plainly what the bench cannot supply, and correct the description of the reporting counts so that the direction of the series matches its figures.

r-w-c07-4-2-juno/reviewer.comments: [minor, S3] Ecosystem section, final paragraph: 'no region combines gains in forest, protected land and sanitation': Regional protected-area results are not cited, so the claim that no region combines gains across the three measures is unsupported. The forest sentence, 'stagnant in most regions', is also loosely stated. Correction: Cite the regional protected-land results or delete the claim. State forest changes region by region with their years and units.; [minor, S1] Regions section (CV 0.484 to 0.382) and Implications (CV 0.549 to 0.501): Two coefficient-of-variation pairs for the same indicator are given without saying that they rest on different country sets (145 and 141 countries in one case, 2015 and 2024 on a common set in the other). Correction: Label each pair with its country set and years, and state which pair the convergence result uses.; [minor, S1] Coverage paragraph: 'Five countries that reported at the peak therefore no longer report in the latest year': The fall from 146 to 141 is a net change. It does not show that five specific countries stopped reporting, since some may have started or stopped in other combinations. Correction: Write that the number of reporting countries fell by five, from 146 in 2016 to 141 in 2024, net of entries and exits.; [minor, S3] Regions section: 'Near-stagnation at a high level is partly a ceiling effect': A cause for the high-level stagnation is asserted as fact without a cited result. It is an interpretation. Correction: Label the ceiling effect as a possible explanation and not a finding.; [minor, S3] Implications: 'stagnation in sanitation is also stagnation in the protection of freshwater': The link from sanitation classes to freshwater protection is an inference the results do not test, since no freshwater series is held. Correction: Present the link as a plausible route to pollution and say that no freshwater series confirms it.; [minor, S5] Proposals paragraph: 'Three proposals follow... Finally, reports on the goals': The text announces three proposals and then gives four, with the fourth introduced as 'Finally'. Correction: Change 'Three proposals follow' to 'Four proposals follow' and number the fourth explicitly. | The revision mends the coverage contradiction, the unsupported 2030 projections and the Asian-gainers claim. Keep the explicit statements of what the proxies cannot measure and the direct reading of the trend classes. Strengthen the link between each proposal and its specific finding, and state the country set and year for every coefficient of variation.

r-w-c03-3-4-quarry/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Section 3 heading: 'The two burdens are not linked by change, and 2030 will be missed without a shift in course': The heading, which the prior review flagged, still states as a forecast that 2030 will be missed. No anaemia benchmark exists and the overweight benchmark of 3.0 per cent is a working one the bench never tested. The projections are straight-line extrapolations. Correction: Reword to a finding the data support, e.g. 'The two burdens are not linked by change, and on current trends overweight stays above the working benchmark'.; [major, S3] Section 2 opening: 'Most countries have moved away from the overweight target and anaemia has risen almost everywhere'; and the section 1 line 'it runs against the direction the reference value implies': Only 92 of 163 countries are regressing, with 33 on track. 'Most countries' is true by count, but 'moved away from the target' rests on a working benchmark of 3.0 per cent that is not in Target 2.2. The earlier fault on loose inference is only partly mended. Correction: Say 'against a working benchmark' in the heading and keep the benchmark label wherever 'target' is used.; [minor, S1] Regional overweight paragraph: 'regression is the most common class, with two exceptions' and the list of regressing groups: The text lists six regions as regressing and two exceptions, but it names only the lower-income groups, not the high-income group's status clearly. The 0.0518 for South Asia is later given as 0.052 and the world rate 0.0115 appears next to 0.115 style rounding. The mix of precisions is inconsistent, though not wrong. Correction: Use one precision for each repeated figure.; [minor, S3] Section 1: 'Even so, the direction of both world figures is adverse' and 'Overweight is highest where hunger is lower': Heading claims overweight is highest where hunger is lower, but hunger is not measured in this section, so the claim goes beyond the results. Correction: Say 'where anaemia is lower'. | Keep the explicit labelling of the 3.0 per cent figure as a working benchmark, the separation of level and change correlations, and the repeated statement that no causes are identified. The modelled-estimate caveats and the gaps paragraph are strong.

r-w-c09-10-1-elm/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Section 'A single surge in 2022 explains most of the recent rise' (heading and first paragraph): The claim that one year explains most of the rise is not supported. The 2022 change of US$49.8 billion is a mean change in a break segment, but the 2015-2023 rise is US$89.8 billion, so 2022 does not clearly account for most of it. Correction: Say the break analysis places a large one-year increase in 2022, about US$49.8 billion, and soften the heading; do not say it explains most of the rise.; [minor, S3] Regional section: 'Regional averages therefore explain a shrinking part... so country-level targeting matters more than regional envelopes': The policy inference about targeting does not follow from the Theil decomposition alone. Correction: Present it as a proposal or cut it; keep only that within-region differences now account for most of the inequality.; [minor, S3] Proposals: priority to the 43 regressing recipients: This does not follow from findings about Aid for Trade, since the regression is in total assistance, which the text says is not a measure of trade support. Correction: Link the proposal to trade-related support or label it as concerning general assistance.; [minor, S1] Section 3: 'In 2022 alone the change averaged US$49.8 billion' and 'The country count also shifted': Wording of 'averaged' for a single year is loose, and the 136 versus 135 countries discrepancy is noted but the 150-country coverage figure is not in the cited facts. Correction: Say 'the change was US$49.8 billion' and remove the unsupported 150-country coverage figure.; [minor, S3] Section 3: 'timing of the 2022 break coincides with the onset of war... which prompted large emergency flows': Causal context stated about the data, though it is outside the results. Correction: Label it clearly as outside context, as in the earlier paragraph, or cut it.; [minor, S5] Final line: 'Four proposals follow from these findings, and each names its actor.': The section ends with an announcement and the argument repeats the country-class figures a second time. Correction: Cut the sentence and remove the repeated country-class passage. | Keep the candid treatment of the proxy limits, the explicit labelling of context versus data, and the clear statement of what the bench cannot show. The Theil decomposition and country-class population shares are strong. Reduce repetition between sections.

r-w-c04-1-4-hana/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] First section, paragraph 2: 'the world has covered 0.35 of the distance from its 2015 value to the target': Not mended. The 0.35 (0.346) is the tool's ratio of progress to required pace, not the share of distance covered. The distance covered is (228.0-197.0)/(228.0-70) = 31/158, about 0.20, so the sentence is false. Correction: Say that the ratio of progress to required pace is 0.35, or give the share of distance covered as about 0.20, computed from 228.0, 197.0 and 70.; [minor, S3] Regions section, paragraph 3: 'The trend tool classes several regions as on track or as having met the target' for Europe and Central Asia, North America, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan; repeated in the projections section: Not mended. No cited result gives these classes, only 2015 and 2023 values and 2030 projections. The explanation 'the ratio is already so low that further gains are small' is also speculative. Correction: State only the cited values and projections, and note that the classes are not among the cited results, or cite the class results. Cut or label the explanation as context.; [minor, S5] Sections 'Progress slowed after 2008' and 'At the present pace the 2030 target will be missed'; closing stub 'The proposals follow from these findings.': Not mended. Country classes, regional projections, Gini, Theil and convergence figures are repeated almost verbatim. The 2015 between-region Theil share appears as 70.9% in one place and 71.0% in another (the fact is 0.7095). The section ends on a stub sentence. Correction: Give the repeated figures once and use one rounding of the 2015 Theil share. Remove the stub line or lead into the proposals.; [minor, S1] Pandemic paragraph and projections section: 'The 2022 fall' and the 4.0 increase in 2020: The text calls the 2020 change an increase of 4 points. The cited fact is a mean annual change of 4 for 2020, which is acceptable. The 2023 fall of 6 is given without its sign convention. Correction: Check the sign and unit wording for each annual change. | Keep the plain statement of the modelled nature of the series, the careful limits on country-by-country readings, and the clear regional and income-group figures with projections. Strengthen the opening by stating the tool's ratio correctly, and cut the repetition.

Correction: State that counts are given for named years only, and qualify the lowest and highest counts as the lowest and highest among the years with a count.; [minor, S5] Throughout, especially 'Thin coverage', 'Regions and countries cannot be compared' and 'Implications for 2030 and proposals': The fault was not mended. The figures 5 in 2024, 81 countries in total, 3 to 15 and the absence of share values are restated in nearly every section, often within one paragraph, which weakens readability and the order of the argument. Correction: State the coverage figures once, in the opening section, and refer back to them elsewhere without repeating the numbers. | The section is careful about what the counts cannot show, and its definition of the indicator is clearly labelled as background. Keep that discipline. Strengthen it by making the headings match the evidence, stating each coverage figure once, and removing the contradiction about which years have counts. The proposals follow sensibly from the gaps.

r-w-c08-2-2-juno/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Section 'Gains were broad but the pace has not been steady', slowdown paragraph: 'the latest segment is the slowest since the early 2000s': The results give 0.9 points a year for 2001-2009 and 1.0 point a year for 2021-2024, so the latest segment is faster than the first decade, not the slowest since the early 2000s. This reverses the reading of the result. Correction: Replace with: the latest segment (1.0 point a year, 2021-2024) is slightly faster than 2001-2009 (0.9 points a year) and slower than 2010-2020 (1.4 points a year).; [minor, S3] Slowdown paragraph: 'Universal access requires a pace above any of the three segments': The required annual pace is asserted, not computed from the results; the text gives only the ratio of 0.56. Correction: State the required pace explicitly (about 4.1 points a year from 75.4 per cent in 2024 to 100 per cent in 2030) and compare it with the segment means, or label the claim as a calculation the reader can check.; [minor, S3] Regions section: 'Both regions are now close to or above the world level' and 'The gap between rural and urban households explains much of the regional picture': South Asia (74.3 per cent in 2024) is below the world level of 75.4 per cent, so 'above' is loose for one region. The rural-urban gap is described descriptively, yet 'explains' implies a causal or decomposed role the results do not show. Correction: Write: East Asia and Pacific (87.0 per cent) is above the world level and South Asia (74.3 per cent) is just below it; the rural-urban gap accompanies the regional differences, without claiming it explains them. | The chapter's numbers are carefully sourced and rounded correctly, and the caveats on modelled data, primary-fuel measurement and the reading of target 7.1 are strong. Keep these. Strengthen the trend analysis by checking every comparison of segment pace against the figures, and keep causal explanations clearly labelled as context.

r-w-c05-2-4-rowan/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Opening heading: 'Out-of-school children number about 88 million at primary age in 2025': Not mended. The headline gives a global total of about 88 million, which is a sum of four group values from 12 reporting countries and is not a cited fact. The body says no global figure is given, so the headline contradicts the text and answers the section's question with a derived number the results do not support. Correction: Replace the heading with one that states the finding the results support, for example 'Out-of-school counts are given only by income group, for 12 reporting countries in 2025', and remove 88 million from the heading.; [major, S3] Lower middle income paragraph: 'The group values suggest that this gain offsets increases elsewhere, though the series do not show how far.': The claim is contradicted by the group values. The falls in lower middle income countries (5.57 million) are smaller than the rises elsewhere (4.07 + 1.15 + 0.72 = 5.94 million), so the net change across groups is an increase of about 0.37 million, not an offset. Correction: Delete the offsetting claim and state the facts: the lower middle income count fell by 5.57 million (52.0 to 46.4 million, 2015 to 2025), while the other three groups rose by 5.94 million together, from reporters that may differ between years.; [minor, S3] Low-income paragraph: 'A falling rate with a rising count is the signature of a school-age population growing faster than enrolment can follow.': The population explanation is stated as a general signature, though the series do not test it; the sentence then offers a hedged cause, so the firmer wording overstates the inference. Correction: Reword as 'A falling rate with a rising count is consistent with a school-age population growing faster than enrolment', and keep the explanation labelled as untested.; [minor, S3] Lower middle income paragraph: 'which reflects very large school-age populations even where the rate is moderate.': An unsupported causal claim: the results give the group count but not the population sizes that would explain it. Correction: Label the explanation as a likely reason not tested by these series, or cut the clause.; [minor, S4] Low-income section: 'The years after 2020 ... are well-established pressures that tend to hold counts up.': Pandemic, conflict and population pressures are presented as established effects on thes | The revision mends most earlier faults: the reporter-set caveats, the hedged sex and adolescent readings, the bounded adolescent change and the target readings are now clear. Keep the country-class arithmetic, which checks against its facts, and the explicit statements of what the data do not cover. The section must still drop the 88 million headline and the offsetting claim before it is adopted.

r-w-c09-2-3-ewan/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Regions section heading: 'Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker', and the paragraph citing North America at roughly twelve times Sub-Saharan Africa: Not mended. Among regions the largest ratio is about 12-fold (North America to Sub-Saharan Africa) and about 6-fold to South Asia; the 25-fold gap is to the low-income group, which is an income grouping, not a region. The heading therefore overstates the regional spread. Correction: Rewrite the heading to state the regional ratio exactly, for example 'Regional output per worker differs by up to twelvefold', and keep the 25-fold low-income comparison separate and labelled as an income group.; [major, S3] Final section heading: 'Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals', and the opening of that section: Not mended. r-w-c02-4-5-idris/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Section heading 'Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East trail every other region' and the Middle East paragraph: Not mended. The 211-country, 161-country and 77.4% electricity figures are national access classes, yet the text still calls them a rural series and a rural population share. The heading also presents a cross-series ranking ('advanced fastest') that the text itself says is not measured. Correction: Relabel the classes as national electricity access covering the whole population, remove 'rural' from the heading and the paragraph, and drop 'advanced fastest' in favour of a statement of the class shares alone.; [minor, S1] Paragraph on the disruption of 2020: 'did not reverse any of the three global trends in these series': Not mended. Correction: Replace with a statement that the series do not show annual values around 2020, so whether the pandemic reversed any trend cannot be tested here. | The section keeps a clear structure, careful caveats on measures, and correct arithmetic for the shortfalls and the account gain. It should strengthen its handling of the poor: state plainly that the water, sanitation and electricity series cover whole populations, and separate measured results from context. r-w-c07-5-4-idris/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Section 'Regions gained unevenly', paragraph 1: 'lifted the region ... to the third largest, behind sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region': The 2023 figures contradict this ranking. Sub-Saharan Africa had US$64.8 billion, Europe and Central Asia US$47.0 billion, and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region US$35.1 billion, so Europe and Central Asia was second, not third, and ahead of the latter region. Correction: State that Europe and Central Asia became the second largest recipient region in 2023, behind sub-Saharan Africa (US$64.8 billion) and ahead of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan region (US$35.1 billion).; [minor, S4] Section 'Coverage is also partial': 'The inequality analysis ... covers a different set of countries, 138 in 2015 and 135 in 2023, because it requires population weights': The stated reason for the difference in country sets is asserted as fact, but the data do not show it; it is an unsupported claim of cause. Correction: Label the reason as a likely explanation, or remove it, and state only that the inequality analysis covers different countries from the world total.; [minor, S1] Section 'The aggregate path of assistance' / first section, 'the annual change in 2023 was slightly negative, at a mean of about -US$0.7 billion': A mean is taken over several years, but 2023 is a single observation, so 'mean' misdescribes the figure. Correction: Replace 'at a mean of about -US$0.7 billion' with 'of about -US$0.7 billion' (a single-year change, 2023).; [minor, S1] Section 'The distribution of assistance among recipient countries': 'The Theil index rose more sharply, from 0.255 to 0.460': The comparison is with the Gini coefficient only, and the coefficient of variation rose more sharply still (0.64 to 1.48). The sentence reads as though the Theil index had the largest rise. Correction: Say that the Theil index rose more sharply than the Gini coefficient, and note that the coefficient of variation rose most of the three. | The section's measurement caveats are careful and its inequality figures match their facts. Keep the explicit statement that total assistance cannot answer the water question, and keep the labelled inferences about 2022. Strengthen the regional ranking, checking every ordering against the 2023 totals, and make clear which statements are context rather than findings.
