The rising coefficient of variation shows wider dispersion but not which end moved more, and the implications section admits the tests do not show this, so the two passages contradict each other.
faults.correction: Delete the low-end and top-end inference. State only that the beta is negative (higher initial shares fell marginally faster), that dispersion widened (CV 0.717 to 0.735), and that the tests do not show which part of the distribution drove the widening.

faults.where: Implications for 2030 and proposals, second paragraph: 'classes both as marginal progress', 'Sub-Saharan Africa... classed as stagnating', and low income countries 'the tool labels the group regression'
faults.problem: Not mended. The cited results give the regional and income-group rates but no class labels, so these class assertions are unsupported and are presented as tool outputs. The low-income 'regression' label rests on a rate of 0.0000 (+0.00003), which is effectively flat.
faults.correction: Report only the rates, with their years and units, and state that the class labels are not in the cited results. Either cite the tool's class output for each group or remove the labels and describe the movement as flat, slow or fast from the rates alone.

faults.where: Vulnerable employment proxy section, final paragraph: 'the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not... been converted' and 'The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring... probably weighed on the decade'; repeated in the Change section
faults.problem: Not mended. No cited result measures output growth or the pandemic's effect on hiring, and the gaps note says these are untested. The sentences are causal readings presented as explanation.
faults.correction: Label these as hypotheses outside the data, or cut them. For example: 'The results do not test whether output growth or the pandemic affected this movement.'

faults.where: Women carry more vulnerability section, third and fourth paragraphs: 'Men are more often self-employed... women are concentrated in wage and salaried posts' and 'Low participation in wage employment, restrictions on women's mobility and ownership of assets, and the burden of unpaid care all push women toward such work'
faults.problem: Not mended. These mechanisms are asserted as settled causes, but the series cannot test them, and the section itself notes that the proxy does not capture pay or job quality.
faults.correction: Mark the mechanisms as context from outside this analysis, not as findings, and state that the series does not test them.

faults.where: Women carry more vulnerability section, first paragraph: 'The global gap is therefore small, at about one percentage point'
faults.problem: Not mended. The figures 43.1 and 41.9 per cent give a gap of 1.2 points (1.24 from the unrounded values), so 'about one' understates the figure.
faults.correction: Replace 'about one percentage point' with 'about 1.2 percentage points'.

Correction: Retitle the section to state the timing of the breaks, for example 'The breaks cluster around 2020 and 2021', and state that the cause is not tested by the data.; [major, S3] Opening section: 'The first five years after 2015 therefore delivered almost no reduction': The claim rests on the 2013 to 2019 mean of 0.02 points, a window that does not match 2015 to 2020. No 2015 to 2020 net change is cited, so the claim about the first five years after 2015 is not supported by the figure given. Correction: Replace with the cited window: 'The mean annual change from 2013 to 2019 was 0.02 points, so the share was essentially flat in the years before the target date; the 2015 to 2020 net change is not cited.'; [minor, S3] Heading 'Regions and countries diverge, and women carry the largest burden': The largest-burden claim compares the female share with the all-youth total, not with the male share, and no male figures are cited, so the heading claims more than the results show. Correction: Change the heading to 'Young women have higher shares than all youth', and state that male shares are not cited.; [minor, S3] Opening section: 'no plausible reading treats a decline of this size, reached five years late, as meeting the intent of the goal': This is stronger than the open-reading caveat in the same paragraph allows, since the target sets no numeric threshold for 'substantially'. Correction: Replace with: 'On the reading used here, and on the stricter readings tested, a decline of this size does not meet the intent of the goal.'; [minor, S1] Opening section: 'by a margin of well under a tenth of the 2015 level in relative terms': The relative fall is about 6.8 per cent (1.45 of 21.24 points), so the vague phrase gives the reader no checkable number. Strengthen the link between each finding and its figures by removing causal headings, stating every window used, and cutting repeated passages so that the verdict on 2020 rests on one stated comparison.

The rising coefficient of variation shows only wider dispersion, not a sharper fall at the low end, and the Implications section says the tests do not show which end moved more. Correction: Replace 'about one percentage point' with 'about 1.2 percentage points'.; [minor, S3] Vulnerable employment proxy section, final paragraph: 'the growth of output recorded elsewhere in this chapter has not... been converted' and 'The pandemic and the slow recovery of formal hiring... probably weighed on the decade': Not mended. r-w-c09-6-2-juno/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Section heading 'The pandemic shock and recovery explain most of the movement': The heading still asserts a causal explanation, although the body says the break analysis shows only the timing of breaks and cannot isolate their cause. The fault from the previous version is not mended. Correction: Retitle the section to state the timing of the breaks, for example 'The share broke sharply around 2020, and the cause is not isolated by the data', and remove any claim that the pandemic explains the movement.; [major, S3] Opening section: 'The first five years after 2015 therefore delivered almost no reduction, and the decline recorded by 2025 was produced mainly after the pandemic year': No 2015-to-2020 net change is cited. The 2013-2019 mean of 0.02 points is a different window, and the +1.37 point jump in 2020 means the 2020 level was higher than before. The claim that the decline was 'produced mainly after the pandemic year' is therefore not supported by a cited figure. Correction: State that the 2015-to-2020 change is not given by the results, and report only the 2013-2019 mean of 0.02 points and the 2020 jump of 1.37 points, without the claim that the decline was produced after 2020.; [minor, S3] Opening section: 'no plausible reading treats a decline of this size, reached five years late, as meeting the intent of the goal': This claim is stronger than the caveat before it, which says the target admits more than one reading of 'substantially'. The previous fault was not mended. Correction: Replace with 'on the reading used here, a decline of this size, reached five years late, does not meet the intent of the goal', so that the verdict is labelled as resting on the chosen reading.; [minor, S3] Section heading 'Women carry the largest burden' and the sentence 'far above the total of 19.8 per cent': The claim that women carry the largest burden compares the female share with the total, but no male share is cited, so the comparison that defines the largest burden is missing. The previous fault was not mended. Correction: Either cite the male share for 2015 and 2025 and compare it with the female share, or change the heading to 'The female share is above the total' and state that male figures are not in the results. | The writer has handled the 182 and 187 country bases, the Sub-Saharan Africa window and the target-reading caveats well, and these should be kept. The main work left is to align the headings and the opening verdict with what the break analysis can show, separating the timing of the 2020 break from any claim about its cause, and to state the 2015-to-2020 change as not available.

r-w-c09-1-3-juno/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Heading 'Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence': Not mended. Only 74 of 209 countries (about 35 per cent by count) are on track or have met the notional target, so 'most countries' is false. The 'quarter' figure is a count of 55 countries (26 per cent), while the population share in stagnation and regression is 15.3 per cent. The heading also asserts that the 7 per cent target is out of reach, which the results cannot show because the target is untested. Correction: Rewrite the heading to state the count and population shares: 74 of 209 countries (35 per cent), holding 56.6 per cent of the population, are on track or have met the notional target; drop the claim that the 7 per cent target is out of reach and say it is untested.; [major, S3] Section heading 'Regions differ by a factor of more than six' and its opening paragraph: Not mended. No result gives a factor of six. South Asia's 6.5 against Sub-Saharan Africa's 0.2 is about thirty, and against the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan's 0.8 it is about eight. The body disclaims any ratio, so the heading contradicts the text. Correction: Replace the heading with a factual statement, for example 'Regional GDP per capita growth in 2015 ranged from -0.7 to 6.5 per cent', and delete the factor.; [minor, S3] Heading 'Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015': Not mended. The heading claims that shocks explain most of the movement, a share the text itself says the analysis does not measure. Correction: Retitle as 'Break years locate the largest swings in world income growth since 2008', which states only what the analysis measures.; [minor, S4] Trend classification paragraph, 'notional target' and 'share of the distance... that this rate would cover by 2030': Partly mended. The notional target is described only as a share of distance to be covered by 2030, with no benchmark value or formula, so the classes cannot be reproduced or read exactly. Correction: State explicitly that no benchmark value is given in the results, and give the formula for the share of distance covered by 2030 as the tool applies it, or label the classes as unreproducible. | The section is clear and its figures match their facts. Keep the careful labelling of context, the separation of per capita growth from the untested 7 per cent GDP target, and the coverage caveats. Strengthen the headings so each states only what the results show, since the headings are where the remaining faults sit.

r-w-c09-9-2-farah/reviewer.comments: [minor, S3] Heading of the second part: 'Mobile money and account growth outpaced branches, and the poorest and women gained': The heading presents mobile money as the cause of account growth. The body says the series do not measure channels and that mobile money is an explanation from the wider literature, so the heading states an unmeasured cause as a finding. This fault was not mended. Correction: Reword the heading to state only the measured pattern, for example 'Account ownership grew faster than branches, and the poorest and women gained', and keep mobile money in the body as labelled context.; [minor, S4] Country-class paragraph of the projections section: 'Under any reading, fewer than one-fifth of the population of assessed countries lives in a country on course for the 2030 aim.': The phrase 'under any reading' overstates the case. Only the on-track class (16.4 per cent) is below one-fifth; if moderate progress (51.8 per cent) counts as on course, the share is well above one-fifth. The definition of 'on course' is not fixed in the text. This fault was not mended. Correction: Replace 'Under any reading' with a statement of the definition used, for example 'If only the on-track and target-met class (16.4 per cent of the population) counts as on course, fewer than one-fifth of the population of assessed countries is on course for the 2030 aim.'; [minor, S4] Projections paragraph on Sub-Saharan Africa: 'Sub-Saharan Africa also reads as on track, with an expected 98.0 per cent in 2030.': The region is labelled on track although its expected 2030 value (98.0 per cent) is below the 100 per cent reading of target 8.10. The text gives the ratio 0.965 but does not state the rule that places it in the on-track class, so the label can be read as target met. This fault was only partly mended. Correction: State the classification rule the tool applies and say that the region is on track on that rule while its expected 2030 value of 98.0 per cent falls short of 100 per cent. | The section is well grounded: its figures match the cited facts after rounding, and the survey-year gaps, the strict reading of target 8.10 and the missing insurance and credit data are stated openly. Keep that discipline. Strengthen it by removing causal headings and by stating the classification rule behind every on-track label.

r-w-c07-5-5-juno/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Section 'A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase', paragraph 1: 'the series does not show a peak level in 2022: the 2023 level fell only slightly below it': A fall in the 2023 level below the 2022 level, with the 2023 change at -US$0.7 billion, makes 2022 the highest level of the 2022 to 2023 pair, so the sentence contradicts the data it describes and conflicts with the proposal to base plans on the pre-2022 trend. Correction: Replace with 'stood at its highest level in 2022 and fell slightly in 2023, to US$259.5 billion' and give the 2022 level.; [minor, S1] Heading 'Official assistance received worldwide has risen by half since 2015': The constant-dollar rise from US$169.7 billion to US$259.5 billion is 52.9%, which is more than half; 'by half' understates the body text's own wording. Correction: Change the heading to 'has risen by more than half since 2015'.; [minor, S3] Heading 'A single jump in 2022 explains much of the recent increase' and the sentence 'owes a large part to one year': The claim is not quantified. The 2022 change of US$49.8 billion is about 55% of the US$89.8 billion rise from 2015 to 2023, and the text does not give this share. It also says breaks fall in 2022 and 2023 without stating which test or segment places each break. Correction: Give the share (about 55%) in the body text and state the break test and the segments that place breaks in both 2022 and 2023. | The section now answers its question with accurate regional and income figures, and it states its data limits clearly, including the target's ambiguity and the missing sector series. Keep that structure. Strengthen the treatment of the 2022 peak so the level series and the annual changes are described consistently, and quantify the share attributed to 2022.

The later paragraph says the data do not show whether the fall reflects reporting lag or change in outcomes, so the two statements contradict each other.
faults.correction: Replace the sentence with: 'The drop from 212 to 71 countries may reflect a reporting lag or other changes in reporting; the data do not show which, so it is a gap in evidence rather than a finding of decline.'

r-w-c08-3-5-amara/reviewer.comments: [major, S1] Heading of the regional section: 'Regional levels differ by a factor of ten, and nearly all regions rose': Not mended. The 2020 values 70.3 and 7.5 per cent give a ratio of about 9.3, and the body says 'a factor of nine', so 'ten' misstates the gap. 'Nearly all regions rose' contradicts the text, which states that all six regions rose between 2015 and 2020. Correction: Change the heading to 'Regional levels differ by a factor of nine, and all regions rose' (or give the ratio as about 9.3) so that it matches the 2020 values and the 2015 to 2020 changes.; [major, S1] Country trajectories paragraph: 'Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries, and the two classes hold 4.8 and 31.8 per cent of the population respectively.': Not mended. The order is reversed: regression holds 31.8 per cent and stagnation 4.8 per cent, so 'respectively' assigns the wrong share to each class. The combined population share of 36.6 per cent is never stated. Correction: Replace with 'Regression and stagnation together cover 104 countries: regression holds 31.8 per cent of the population and stagnation 4.8 per cent, 36.6 per cent in all.'; [major, S3] Opening section: 'which the trend tool classes as on track or target met': Not mended. The label is still reported as a result for the world rate, although the target sets no number and so the label has no basis. The hedge that follows does not remove the claim. Correction: State that the tool's label reflects only the direction and pace of the trend and carries no judgement against a target, or remove the label from the text.; [minor, S5] Convergence and coverage paragraph: 'This is a reporting lag, not a finding of decline, and it should be read as a gap in evidence.': The text asserts as fact that the post-2020 drop in reporting is a reporting lag, a cause the data do not establish; the drop could reflect other changes in reporting or in countries' outcomes. Correction: Replace with 'The drop may reflect a reporting lag or other changes in reporting; the data do not show which, so it is a gap in evidence rather than a finding of decline.' | The chapter's structure is clear, and its handling of the target's ambiguity, the biomass problem and the coverage gap is strong; keep these. Mend the regional heading and the reversed population shares first, since they state false facts. Make the trend-tool label carry its own limit, and label the reporting-lag reading as one possible cause rather than a finding.

r-w-c09-2-5-orchard/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Final section heading: 'Shocks explain the pace, and the 2030 outlook calls for proposals': Not mended. The heading asserts that shocks explain the pace, but the break tool only dates changes in the world series, and the body labels the shock explanations as context that was not tested. Correction: Use a descriptive heading, for example 'Breaks in the world series date the shocks, and the 2030 outlook is uneven'.; [major, S1] Regions heading: 'Regions differ by an order of magnitude in output per worker': Not mended. The regional spread is about twelve-fold, and North America to South Asia is about six-fold. Only the low-income group, which is not a region, reaches about twenty-five-fold. The heading overstates the regional gap. Correction: Say 'Regional output per worker differs about twelve-fold' or similar.; [minor, S3] Inequality section: 'The lower Gini and Theil values of 2025 show that the earlier narrowing has held rather than reversed.': Not mended. The 2025 values cover 168 countries against 177 in 2020, so the comparison is not on a common set, and 'show' and 'held' claim more than the data allow. Correction: Say the 2025 values are lower but rest on a smaller set of countries, so the comparison is indicative only.; [minor, S3] Opening section 2030 paragraph: 'the recent post-2022 pace of change is below the 2010 to 2019 average, so a rate of about 1.8 per cent a year is not assured': Not mended. It compares mean dollar changes (815.5 and 967.5 dollars a year) and then draws a conclusion about a per cent compound rate, which mixes units and periods. Correction: Compare dollar changes with dollar changes and state that this only suggests the 1.8 per cent rate may not hold.; [minor, S4] Opening breaks paragraph (2009, 2010, 2020, 2021, 2022) against the Shocks section (2004 added): Partly mended. The opening list omits the 2004 break and does not say why the two lists differ. Correction: Add 2004 to the opening list, or note that it arises from the segmentation starting in 2001. | Keep the explicit labelling of untested explanations as context, the clear reporting of the missing numeric threshold, and the careful contrast between population-weighted and unweighted inequality measures. The regional and country sections are exact and readable.

r-w-c09-3-5-orchard/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Change section, convergence paragraph: 'which implies that countries at the low end fell proportionally further while many at the top barely moved': Not mended. The negative beta (-0.00281) means countries with higher initial shares fell faster, the opposite of this claim. The rising coefficient of variation shows only wider dispersion, and the Implications section admits the tests do not show which end moved more. Correction: Cut the inference and state that higher-share countries fell marginally faster while dispersion widened, with the tests unable to show which end drove the widening.; [minor, S3] Opening section, final paragraph: output growth 'has not... been converted'; pandemic and slow formal hiring 'probably weighed on the decade': Not mended. The gap is 1.2 points (43.1 against 41.9; 1.24 unrounded), so 'about one' understates it. Correction: Write 'about 1.2 percentage points'.; [minor, S4] Women section, third and fourth paragraphs: mechanisms for women's work (mobility restrictions, asset ownership, unpaid care) and men's self-employment in rich regions: Not mended. Correction: Label them as context outside the data, or cut them, and state that the series does not test them. | Keep the clear treatment of vulnerable employment as a proxy, the plain statement that target 8.3 has no numeric threshold, and the regional and gender contrasts with year and unit. r-w-c09-1-4-fernhill/reviewer.comments: [major, S3] Heading 'Most countries are on course for income growth, but a quarter are not, and the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence': Not mended. Only 74 of 209 countries (about 35 per cent) are on track, so 'most countries' is false by count, and the body says fewer than half are. The 'quarter' is a count share (55 of 209), while the population share in stagnation and regression is 15.3 per cent. Correction: Rewrite the heading to match the counts, e.g. 'Roughly a third of countries are on track on the notional reading; 40 are in regression'.; [major, S2] Same heading, clause 'the 7 per cent target is out of reach on present evidence'; closing paragraphs: Not mended. The 7 per cent target is for total GDP growth in least developed countries, and the results contain neither that series nor that group. The heading gives a verdict the body says cannot be reached. Correction: Cut the clause or say that the 7 per cent target cannot be tested with these results.; [major, S3] Heading 'Regions differ by a factor of more than six' and its opening paragraph: Not mended. No result gives a factor of six. South Asia (6.5) against Sub-Saharan Africa (0.2) is about thirty, and against the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (0.8) about eight. The body says no ratio is claimed, so the heading contradicts it. Correction: Replace with a heading stating the range, e.g. 'Regional growth in 2015 ranged from -0.7 to 6.5 per cent'.; [minor, S3] Heading 'Single-year shocks explain most of the movement since 2015': Not mended. The heading claims a share explained, which the text says the analysis does not measure. The 2008-2011 breaks also lie before 2015. Correction: Retitle, e.g. 'Breaks in the world growth rate cluster around 2008-2011 and 2020-2023'.; [minor, S4] Trend classification paragraphs, 'notional target' and 'on track': Partly mended. The text admits the benchmark and formula are not given, but it still labels countries and regions 'on track' as if the classes were meaningful. Correction: Use the class labels in quotation marks as relative momentum readings, and drop 'on course' wording. | Keep the clear separation of GDP growth from GDP per capita growth, the explicit coverage warnings (211 countries in 2015, 186 in 2025) and the labelling of causal remarks as context. The honest statement that the 7 per cent target is untested is the strongest part; make the headings match it.

Correction: Give the full list of on-track groups (adding Europe & Central Asia, North America and high income) so that it matches the Implications section, and note that the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan show moderate progress.; [minor, S3] Regions and income groups, third paragraph: 'A falling share there can even accompany a shift to commercial fuels': Not mended. Correction: Write the figure as a fall of about 789,790 cases a year (-789,790), or leave the figure out and say the 2009 to 2023 trend runs the other way from the 2015 to 2023 rise.; [minor, S1] Education section: 'classed by the trend tool as moderate progress with acceleration needed': This classification is not among the cited facts, so it is a statement with no source. Correction: Delete the classification or cite the result that gives it; keep the annualised rate of 0.0196.; [minor, S4] Hunger section: fertiliser series 'moved from 132.9 to 136.5'; its unit 'is not restated in the abstract and is not given here': The unit is missing, so the finding is not exact. The sentence admits the gap but does not label it clearly as a data gap. Correction: Give the unit from the series metadata, or drop the figures and list the fertiliser series among the gaps.; [minor, S4] Health section: 'the nearest measure for immunisation'; hunger section: consumer price inflation 'stands in' for food price volatility: Both proxies are named, but neither is flagged with its limits. The inflation proxy has no figure for the period. Correction: State that these series are proxies and say what they do not capture; give the inflation figures or note that none are reported.; [minor, S3] Water section: net official development assistance placed among the water findings: The text says the series is not specific to water, so it does not support a finding about the water targets, although the sentence is labelled as context. Correction: Move it to the gaps section or the context notes, or cut it. | Keep the explicit limits on scope: goals 10 to 17 are left unjudged, sampled years are named, and the stunting projection is not compared with an invented target. Keep the plain statement of years and units, and the open reading of the carbon break. Strengthen the sign of every rate of change.

compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-chose.name: compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-chose
compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-chose.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params['start_year'])
    y1 = int(params['end_year'])
    min_cov = params.get('min_countries', 10)
    s = data[code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    n = y1 - y0
    rates = {}
    skipped = 0
    for unit in s:
        ser = s[unit]
        if unit not in regions:
            continue
        a = ser.get(y0)
        b = ser.get(y1)
        if a is None or b is None:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        if a <= 0 or b <= 0 or n <= 0:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        rates[unit] = ((b / a) ** (1.0 / n) - 1.0) * 100.0
    facts = {}
    count = len(rates)
    facts['countries_with_both_years'] = count
    facts['countries_skipped'] = skipped
    facts['years_spanned'] = n
    if count < min_cov:
        facts['coverage_met'] = 'no'
        return {'facts': facts, 'summary': 'Coverage is below the minimum of ' + str(min_cov) + ' countries: only ' + str(count) + ' have values in both ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ' for ' + code + '. No growth rate is reported.'}
    facts['coverage_met'] = 'yes'
    vals = list(rates.values())
    med = statistics.median(vals)
    facts['median_cagr_pct'] = round(med, 2)
    facts['mean_cagr_pct'] = round(statistics.mean(vals), 2)
    best = max(rates, key=lambda k: rates[k])
    worst = min(rates, key=lambda k: rates[k])
    facts['fastest_country'] = names.get(best, best)
    facts['fastest_cagr_pct'] = round(rates[best], 2)
    facts['slowest_country'] = names.get(worst, worst)
    facts['slowest_cagr_pct'] = round(rates[worst], 2)
    groups = {}
    for k in rates:
        groups.setdefault(regions[k], []).append(rates[k])
    for g in groups:
        if len(groups[g]) >= 3:
            facts['median_cagr_pct_region_' + str(g)] = round(statistics.median(groups[g]), 2)
    summary = 'Between ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ', the median compound annual growth rate of ' + code + ' across ' + str(count) + ' countries was ' + str(round(med, 2)) + ' per cent a year. ' + str(skipped) + ' countries lacked a positive value in one of the two years and are excluded. The rate is computed from end points only and ignores movement between them.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}
compound-annual-growth-rate-over-a-chose.about: Computes the compound annual growth rate, in per cent a year, of a level series between two chosen years for each country, then the median, mean, extremes and regional medians, with a minimum-coverage rule that withholds results when too few countries have both years.

params.series: World Bank indicator code to analyse, which must also be listed in series_params
params.end_year: Last year of the interval, later than start_year
params.min_countries: Minimum number of countries with both years required to report results; default 10

fixed-panel-national-poverty-comparison.name: fixed-panel-national-poverty-comparison
fixed-panel-national-poverty-comparison.about: Compares national poverty headcount ratios for a fixed panel of countries that report in both chosen years, avoiding composition effects from changing country coverage. Reports panel size, unweighted mean and median change, count of decliners and the extreme movers.

params.series: World Bank series code of the national-line headcount ratio, e.g. SI.POV.NAHC

required-pace-comparison.name: required-pace-comparison
required-pace-comparison.about: Computes the annual change needed from the latest observed year to reach a target by a target year, the observed annual change since a base year (2015 by default, using the nearest earlier observation), and the ratio of required to observed change, for one series and one unit of a single aggregate or country entry.

params.series: World Development Indicators series code, also named in series_params
params.unit: Key in the series data for the country or aggregate whose values are used
params.target: Target value in the series' own unit
params.target_year: Year by which the target is to be reached; default 2030
params.base_year: Year from which the observed pace is measured; default 2015

commons.text:
## The commons: proposals for the shelf of evidence

The commons keeps the book's shelf of data. For each section, one gatherer chose series from the World Bank's catalogue and a second, of a different origin, checked them. That work shows where the shelf is full and where it is thin. The proposals below follow from what the adopted sections found about the record itself: how many countries report, in which years, under which definitions. A target cannot be judged before 2030 if the series that would judge it ends in 2021 or reaches only a few countries. Each proposal names who should act and what the action would make measurable.

### The record thins in the latest years

The most common finding across the book is that country coverage falls sharply in the most recent years, the years that matter most for a 2030 judgement. Pre-primary participation was reported by 71 countries in 2021 and by 4 in 2022. Tertiary enrolment had 9 reporting countries in 2025, against 147 in 2015 and 94 in 2024. Child marriage, with a world share of 19.5% in 2022, had 3 reporting countries in 2025. Social protection coverage stood at 56.3% of the world population in 2021, with one country reporting for 2023. Inflation, the proxy used for food prices, fell from 189 reporting countries in 2015 and 2016 to 185 in 2017 and 179 in 2020.

Part of this thinning is a reporting lag and will close as late submissions arrive. Part of it is not: some series stop because surveys are not fielded. The book cannot tell the two apart from the catalogue alone, so a fall in the count of reporting countries may mean late data, absent data, or both.

Proposal 1. The World Bank, with the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and the other custodian agencies, should publish with each catalogue release a register of which countries are missing for each Goal series in each of the latest five years. For each gap the register should say whether data are expected later, whether a survey is scheduled or whether none is planned. This would let readers of pre-primary, tertiary and inflation series separate regression from missing data before 2030.

Proposal 2. National statistical offices in countries with no reading since 2020 for pre-primary participation, tertiary enrolment or social protection coverage should resume annual submissions by 2027. Development partners should fund the offices that cannot meet that date. A reading in 2027 or 2028 is the last that can inform a 2030 assessment.

### Survey-based indicators arrive unevenly

Indicators drawn from household surveys reach the shelf in scattered years, so in any one year only a small, shifting set of countries reports. National poverty rates have been reported by 161 countries in some year, but by 16 in 2000, 15 in 2001 and 36 in 2004. Child labour has been reported by 97 countries in some year, with 24 in 2000, 4 in 2002 and 31 in 2006. Women in management were reported by 40 countries in 2000, and by 184 in 2025 for women in parliaments. A world average built from a few countries in one year and different countries in the next describes the sample as much as the world.

Proposal 3. Survey programmes should coordinate the timing of their modules so that a large share of countries report poverty, child labour, contraceptive demand and food insecurity within a common window of two or three years before 2030. A window centred on 2027 to 2029 would allow one comparison across a stable set of countries at the end of the period. The World Bank, national statistical offices and the agencies that sponsor household surveys should agree this schedule by 2026.

Proposal 4. Whenever the catalogue publishes a regional or global aggregate from survey data, it should also publish the number of countries and the share of population behind that aggregate, and the span of survey years it draws on. This applies first to child labour and to the satisfied-demand indicator for family planning, where the book could not form a reliable aggregate. Without this information a reader cannot tell whether a change in the world share reflects a change in the world or a change in who reported.

### Some targets have no series on the shelf

Several sections had to leave part of their target unmeasured because the catalogue holds no comparable series. Public spending on essential services lacked a comparable series on social protection spending. Water quality lacked the share of wastewater treated and the extent of freshwater ecosystems. The section on 2.c read food prices through general inflation because the catalogue holds no food-price anomaly series. The section on 3.b rested on a composite proxy rather than direct immunisation coverage and access to medicines. Women's ownership under 5.a could be tracked only through financial accounts. In each case the book followed its own rule and said that the data were missing; it did not estimate the gap.

Proposal 5. The United Nations custodian agencies and the World Bank should add to the catalogue, before 2028, the series already defined in the global indicator framework but absent from it: food price anomalies (2.c.1), the share of wastewater safely treated (6.3.1), change in freshwater ecosystems (6.6.1), women's ownership of land in their own name (5.a.1), and a comparable social protection spending share. Each is needed to judge a target that the book could address only in part.

Proposal 6. Donor governments and the OECD Development Assistance Committee should report water and sanitation assistance as a separate sector series in the catalogue. The book's section on support for water found a world series that rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, but that series is not specific to water and sanitation. Target 6.a cannot be judged until a sector series exists.

### Definitions leave targets open to more than one reading

Several sections found that a target, as written, can be read in more than one way, so a country's trend cannot be classed against a fixed end point. Target 1.3 does not give a number for "substantial coverage". Target 2.3 does not give a baseline or a numeric reading of "doubling". Target 3.8 has no threshold for the service coverage index; the world value was 71.0 in 2023, against 68.0 in 2015. Target 3.5 does not say whether it requires a quantitative cut in alcohol consumption; the world level fell from 5.9 in 2015 to 4.9 in 2020. Tobacco has no numeric prevalence goal; the world rate was 24.5 in 2015 and 20.3 in 2024. Undernourishment is reported with a floor of 2.5 per cent that coincides with the practical target, so the world rate of 8.0 in 2015 and 8.1 in 2024 cannot show progress below the floor.

Proposal 7. The Inter-agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators should publish, before 2027, a stated numeric reading for each target where the book found none: the coverage threshold under 1.3, the baseline and doubling path under 2.3, the coverage threshold under 3.8, the quantitative intent under 3.5 and a prevalence end point for tobacco. Where a body declines to fix a number, it should say so. Publishing the reading does not change the targets. It fixes the yardstick against which every report, this book included, classes progress.

Proposal 8. FAO should publish undernourishment values below the 2.5 per cent floor, with uncertainty ranges, or state plainly that the series cannot show attainment of zero hunger. The agencies that produce modelled maternal mortality estimates should publish uncertainty ranges beside each national ratio. The world ratio was 228.0 per 100,000 live births in 2015 and 197.0 in 2023, with an expected 173.4 in 2030 against a target below 70. Class assignments near a boundary cannot be judged without these ranges.

### Revisions and carried-forward values hide change

Two further weaknesses hide change inside series that look complete. National poverty lines are revised without a published bridge, so a fall in a national rate may reflect a new line rather than fewer poor people. Some agricultural water withdrawal series appear carried forward. Arable land, at 36.8 in 2015 and 36.9 in 2023 with 208 countries reporting in 2024, looks complete; withdrawal series of similar apparent completeness may hold repeated values rather than new measurement. A series that repeats its last value reads as stagnation when in fact nothing was measured.

Proposal 9. National statistical offices should publish the date and reason of each poverty line revision, together with an overlap series computed on the old and new lines. FAO and the World Bank should flag in the catalogue every value that is carried forward, imputed or modelled rather than observed. Both measures would let a reader tell measured change from an artefact of method.

### Disaggregation is needed where averages mask gaps

Several targets are framed for groups that the catalogue does not separate. Agricultural productivity under 2.3 concerns small-scale producers, women and other groups, yet the series are national: world value added per worker was 3,491 in 2015 and 4,264 in 2025. Mobile phone ownership by sex is not measured, although internet use by women rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024. Water and sanitation are published as national totals, which can hide off-network communities.

Proposal 10. The ILO, FAO, the ITU and national statistical offices should publish by sex and farm size the series that targets 2.3, 5.b and 6.1 address to particular groups, and should publish rural and urban splits for water, sanitation and clean cooking. The first releases should come before 2028, so that at least one disaggregated reading exists before the 2030 assessment.

### A standing check of origin and provenance

The commons' own method is to have each series chosen by one gatherer and checked by another of a different origin. That double check caught carried-forward values, missing aggregates and proxy series that a single reader could have taken at face value. The same discipline can be applied at the source.

Proposal 11. The World Bank should attach to each Goal series in its catalogue a short provenance note giving the custodian agency, whether the value is observed or modelled, the year of the latest underlying measurement and the date of last revision. Custodian agencies should review one another's notes every two years until 2030. Reports on the Goals, including this one, should state where data are missing and not fill gaps with unsupported estimates, as the section on water quality also proposed.

### Order of priority

The commons ranks these proposals by what they unlock before 2030. First come the missing-country register and the resumption of reporting (Proposals 1 and 2), because without them the latest years cannot be read at all. Second is the common survey window (Proposal 3), which must be scheduled now for fieldwork in 2027 to 2029. Third are the numeric readings of targets (Proposal 7), which cost little and settle disputes over classification. The new series, the disaggregation and the provenance notes (Proposals 5, 10 and 11) are larger tasks. Their value lies in the assessment after 2030 as much as in the one at 2030.

c09-7.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: The World Bank and custodian agencies should publish with each catalogue release a register of missing countries per Goal series for the latest five years, stating whether data are expected, scheduled or not planned.
National statistical offices without a reading since 2020 for pre-primary, tertiary or social protection coverage should resume submissions by 2027, with partner funding where needed.
Survey programmes should coordinate poverty, child labour, contraceptive demand and food insecurity modules in a common 2027-2029 window agreed by 2026.
Every survey-based aggregate should carry the number of countries, population share and span of survey years behind it.

Custodian agencies and the World Bank should add food price anomalies, wastewater treated, freshwater ecosystem change, women's land ownership and a social protection spending share to the catalogue before 2028.
Donors and the OECD DAC should report water and sanitation assistance as a sector series in the catalogue.
The IAEG-SDGs should publish numeric readings for targets 1.3, 2.3, 3.5, 3.8 and a tobacco end point before 2027, or state that none will be fixed.
FAO should publish undernourishment below the 2.5 per cent floor with uncertainty, and maternal mortality estimates should carry uncertainty ranges.
Statistical offices should publish poverty line revisions with overlap series, and the catalogue should flag carried-forward, imputed or modelled values.
ILO, FAO, ITU and statistical offices should publish group-targeted series by sex, farm size and rural-urban location before 2028.
The World Bank should attach provenance notes to each Goal series, reviewed across custodian agencies every two years.
commons.gaps: The catalogue does not reveal whether recent falls in reporting counts are lags or absent surveys; no fact key was available for the count of carried-forward values, so that weakness is stated qualitatively. Several sections (c02-5, c03-2, c09-4) gave no proposals and were not drawn on. The water assistance series cited from c07-5 may not be water-specific, as noted in the text.

cooperative.text:
## The cooperative's proposals: measure what is promised, then fund where the gap is widest

The cooperative writes only from analyses its guild has replicated, and it revises until a section is adopted. Its proposals follow that discipline. They come in three groups. The first concerns the records on which every judgement of the Goals depends, because several adopted sections found that the record thins just as 2030 approaches. The second concerns targets that cannot be judged because their wording carries no number. The third concerns where money and effort should go, and the cooperative proposes direction of finance only where the adopted findings support it, and no further. Each proposal names who should act and what should be done before 2030.

### The record is thinning where it matters most, and must be restored first

A trend cannot be judged from countries that have stopped reporting. The adopted sections show this repeatedly.

On poverty at national lines, 161 countries have reported a national rate in some year, but the record is uneven across time: 16 countries reported in 2000, 15 in 2001 and 36 in 2004 (c02-2). The section warned that the post-2020 record is too thin to judge the halving of poverty by 2030. The World Bank and national statistical offices should sustain survey cycles so that the count of countries reporting after 2021 recovers. National statistical offices should also publish the date and reason of each revision to a national poverty line, with linked series for the overlap years.

On social protection, the world coverage stood at 56.3% in 2021, yet only 1 country reported in 2023, against 121 that have reported in some year (c02-3). A world figure resting on one country's recent report cannot show direction. National governments and statistical offices should keep poorest-quintile survey reporting continuous after 2020.

On pre-primary education, 71 countries reported in 2021 and 4 in 2022 (c05-3). A fall of that size makes regression indistinguishable from silence. Ministries of education and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should restore national reporting, so that a fall in participation can be told apart from missing data. On tertiary education, the count of reporting countries fell from 147 in 2015 to 94 in 2024, and 9 countries had reported for 2025 (c05-4). National statistical offices and the Institute should report enrolment promptly.

On child marriage, the world share stood at 19.5% in 2022, with 145 countries reporting in some year but 3 reporting for 2025 (c06-3). On child labour, 97 countries have reported in some year; 24 reported in 2000, 4 in 2002 and 31 in 2006 (c09-7). Both indicators rest on household surveys fielded at irregular intervals. National statistical offices and survey sponsors should schedule these modules so that many countries report in the same few years, and the international bodies that compile them should publish each aggregate with its survey year and the countries behind it. The child labour series covers ages 7 to 14 only; statistical agencies and labour ministries should extend measurement to children aged 15 to 17 in hazardous work and to forced labour, since the existing indicator cannot show whether the worst forms have ended.

On food prices, the count of countries reporting inflation fell from 189 in 2015 and 2016 to 185 in 2017 and 179 in 2020 (c03-7). Statistical offices that stopped reporting should resume annual submissions, and the World Bank should state each year which countries are missing and why. National statistical offices should also publish a food-specific consumer price series beside general inflation, so that target 2.c is read from food prices rather than a general proxy.

On spending, the reporting lag is itself the problem. Public spending on education fell from 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023 at world level, and 98 of 186 countries assessed were classed as regressing (c05-8). The spending series of low-income countries often end years before the latest reporting year (c02-6). The World Bank, the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and national statistical offices should shorten these lags, so that the latest years are not left thin. Ministries of finance and statistical offices should also report social protection spending as a comparable series, which the adopted section could not find.

On water, 146 countries have reported the relevant ecosystem series in some year, 141 in 2024 (c07-4); coverage is steady there, but the indicator set lacks the share of wastewater treated and the extent of freshwater ecosystems. The custodian agencies and the World Bank should add both to the core set. Reports on the Goals, this one included, should state where data are missing and not fill gaps with unsupported estimates.

Several adopted sections found that a target was measured only in part. The cooperative endorses their requests: a comparable survey item on women's land and dwelling ownership in their own name (c06-6), where world account ownership among women rose from 65.9% in 2017 to 76.6% in 2024 but land is unmeasured; mobile phone ownership by sex in household surveys (c06-7), where women's internet use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024; the female share of management reported every year, with regional aggregates, since 184 countries reported the parliamentary share in 2025 and world representation stood at 27.2 per cent against 22.8 in 2015 (c06-4); community health worker counts reported annually, and immunisation and essential medicines reported directly, so that targets 3.b and 3.c do not rest on proxies (c04-11); agricultural productivity reported by sex and farm size so that target 2.3 can be read for small-scale producers (c03-4); and agricultural water withdrawals measured afresh each year where series appear carried forward (c03-5).

### Targets without numbers cannot be judged, and must be given readings

Several adopted sections could judge direction but not distance, because the target sets no threshold. The bodies that maintain the global indicator framework should fix numeric readings before 2030, publish them, and state the baseline year each assumes.

- Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of social protection. With world coverage at 56.3% in 2021 (c02-3), the word substantial must be given a number so that countries are judged against one threshold.
- Target 2.3 asks for a doubling of productivity. World agricultural value added per worker rose from 3,491 in 2015 to 4,264 in 2025, at a world rate of 2.0 per cent a year (c03-4); whether that is on the path to doubling depends on a baseline the target does not state.
- Target 2.1 is read through undernourishment, which stood at 8.0 per cent in 2015 and 8.1 per cent in 2024 at world level, with 165 countries reporting in 2024 (c03-1). The reporting floor of 2.5 per cent coincides with any plausible end point. The statistical community should publish values below that floor, or agree a target that does not coincide with the reporting limit, and set a benchmark for moderate or severe food insecurity, which stood at 21.4 per cent in 2015.
- Target 3.5 carries no stated quantitative reduction for alcohol. World consumption fell from 5.9 litres per head in 2015 to 4.9 in 2020, with 185 countries reporting in 2020 (c04-5). The bodies that set Goal 3 indicators should state whether a reduction is intended. The World Health Organization should also publish observed, not only projected, estimates for the 54 countries classed as regressing.
- Target 3.8 is judged by the convention of a service coverage index of 100. The world index rose from 68.0 in 2015 to 71.0 in 2023 (c04-8). The World Health Organization and the World Bank should agree and publish a numerical reading.
- Tobacco use fell from 24.5 per cent in 2015 to 20.3 per cent in 2024 at world level (c04-10), but there is no 2030 end point. Countries and the Framework Convention secretariat should set one.
- For maternal mortality the target of 70 per 100,000 live births is numeric, yet class assignments rest on modelled estimates (c04-1). The producing agencies should publish uncertainty ranges beside each national ratio.

### Finance should follow the widest gaps, and the findings bound how far

The cooperative proposes direction of finance only where an adopted finding locates the gap.

Maternal mortality fell from 228.0 per 100,000 live births in 2015 to 197.0 in 2023, and the world value expected in 2030 is 173.4, with a progress ratio of 0.35 (c04-1). The target of 70 will not be met at world level on this path. Donors and development banks should direct health financing to low-income and lower-middle-income countries, and ministries of health in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia should prioritise skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care and civil registration of deaths.

Service coverage in low-income countries stood at 41.2 in 2015 (c04-8). Ministries of health and finance in low-income and lower-middle-income countries should raise the share of health spending from pooled domestic public sources. Where domestic government health spending per head is falling, finance ministries should publish medium-term health budgets (c04-11); the world rate of change was −0.0017, and rates for several regions rounded to zero.

HIV incidence fell from 0.26 to 0.16 per 1,000 uninfected people between 2015 and 2024, with 139 countries reporting in 2024 (c04-3). Donors should keep HIV financing in Sub-Saharan Africa, where incidence remains highest, and governments and funders should give priority to malaria control in the countries in regression, which hold 27.5 per cent of the assessed population.

On learning, world primary completion stood at 87.9% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024 (c05-1): almost no change. Governments of low-income countries and their partners should fund the transition to lower secondary and tie it to measured learning, with reading assessments at the end of primary run at regular intervals in Sub-Saharan Africa. Tertiary enrolment grew at a world rate of 0.0196 a year, from 36.6 in 2015 to 43.6 in 2024, but at 0.0077 in low-income countries and 0.0080 in Sub-Saharan Africa (c05-4); support for tertiary systems should go there. Finance and education ministries should treat the education share of GDP as a monitored quantity and publish plans that halt its fall (c05-8).

On water, the world share using safely managed drinking water rose from 67.7% in 2015 to 73.7% in 2024, with 150 and 148 countries reporting in those years (c07-1). Investment should go first to the 79 stagnating or regressing countries, which hold 34.4% of the assessed population. Basic sanitation rose from 72.6 per cent to 82.2 per cent over the same years, while open defecation stood at 10.6 per cent in 2015 (c07-2); sanitation finance should concentrate in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries, where open defecation is projected to remain highest in 2030. Assistance for water and sanitation, in the series the section examined, rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023, largely through a jump in 2022 (c07-5). Finance ministries and development agencies should test 2030 plans with and without that jump, and donors should publish country-level allocations beside coverage so that the match of flows to need can be checked.

Access to clean cooking fuels rose from 63.9 per cent in 2015 to 75.4 per cent in 2024 at world level, against 98.8 per cent in high-income countries in 2015 (c08-2). Governments in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should prioritise clean fuels for rural households, with concessional finance from development partners.

In agriculture, the world average masks stagnation. East Asia and Pacific value added per worker stood at 4,087 in 2015 (c03-4), while low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa saw value added per worker fall and cereal yield stand still. Agriculture ministries and partners should direct productivity programmes there and finance crop research and extension suited to low-yield regions. Fertiliser change tracks yield change only weakly (c03-5), so any rise in fertiliser supply in those regions should be paired with seed, extension and water control; the agricultural land share stood at 36.8 per cent in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023.

Account ownership rose from 69.3 per cent in 2017 to 78.7 per cent in 2024 (c09-9). Regulators in low-income countries and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan should prioritise account access for the poorest and for women, and in the 33 countries where women's ownership regressed, providers should report account data by sex (c06-6).

### Where the cooperative stops

Four adopted sections offered no proposals, and the cooperative adds none it cannot ground. Disaster exposure rose in the world series from 19,188,817 people in 2015 to 26,393,278 in 2023, a mean annual change of about 789,790 over 2009 to 2023, with 80 countries reporting in 2008 (c02-5); the finding establishes direction, not cause. Stunting fell from 24.6% to 23.2% and wasting from 7.1% to 6.6% between 2015 and 2024 (c03-2). Material use per unit of output fell from 0.26 to 0.22 between 2015 and 2024, with a structural break in 2012 (c09-4). The cooperative records these findings and asks only that the series be kept continuous, so that the next edition can say what should be done.

The World Bank, the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and national statistical offices should shorten reporting lags for spending series in low-income countries.
The bodies maintaining the global indicator framework should fix numeric readings and baselines for targets 1.3, 2.1, 2.3, 3.5, 3.8 and a 2030 tobacco end point.
Donors and development banks should direct health, education, water, sanitation and clean cooking finance to low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa where adopted findings locate the widest gaps.

guild.text:
## The guild's proposals: measurement that can be replicated before 2030

The guild analyses by one method: every plan of analyses runs on the shared bench and is replicated by an analyst of another origin before any writer may use it. Its proposals follow from that order. A finding that cannot be replicated cannot carry a proposal, and the book's adopted sections show repeatedly that the binding constraint on judging the Goals in 2030 is not the absence of policy ideas but the thinness, lateness and ambiguity of the record. The proposals below therefore give first place to the conditions under which progress can be measured and checked, and second place to the substantive actions that the findings already support. Each states who should act and what should be done before 2030, and each rests on a finding cited by its fact key.

### The reporting base is eroding where the Goals are judged

Several series are dense in 2015 and thin in the latest years. Pre-primary participation, which stood at 60.9 per cent of the relevant age group worldwide in 2020 against 56.0 per cent in 2015, was reported by 71 countries in 2021 and by 4 in 2022 (c05-3.r6). Social protection coverage of the poorest quintile, 56.3 per cent worldwide in 2021, rests on a single reporting country in 2023 (c02-3.r1), although 121 countries have reported in some year (c02-3.r3). Child marriage, 19.5 per cent worldwide in 2022, has 3 reporting countries in 2025 (c06-3.r1). Tertiary enrolment counts fell from 147 reporting countries in 2015 to 94 in 2024, with 9 in 2025 (c05-4.r1). National poverty rates were reported by 161 countries in some year, but by only 16 in 2000 and 15 in 2001 (c02-2.r2), a pattern of uneven cycles that recurs after 2020.

A trend computed across such gaps reflects which countries report as much as what happens in them. The guild cannot replicate a global trend whose country set changes from year to year, and neither can any other reader.

The guild proposes that national statistical offices, with the UNESCO Institute for Statistics, the World Bank and the survey programmes that support them, adopt a reporting floor for the final review: for each indicator, a fixed panel of countries that commit to report in 2026 and again in 2029. Without such a panel the 2030 assessment will compare different sets of countries. The floor matters most for pre-primary participation, social protection coverage and tertiary enrolment, where the collapse in reporting is sharpest.

The guild further proposes that every published aggregate carry the count of countries behind it and the share of the population they cover, year by year. Child labour shows why: 97 countries have reported in some year, but 24 in 2000, 4 in 2002 and 31 in 2006 (c09-7.r1). An aggregate built on 4 countries and one built on 31 are not the same quantity and should not be printed as if they were.

### Constant-panel trends should be published beside headline trends

Inflation reporting fell from 189 countries in 2015 and 2016 to 185 in 2017 and 179 in 2020 (c03-7.r3). The fall is modest, but it is not random: countries that stop reporting are often those under strain. Water quality and ecosystem series show 137 reporting countries in 2000, 146 in 2016 and 141 in 2024 (c07-4.r8).

The guild proposes that the World Bank, when it publishes regional and global aggregates, publish beside each a constant-panel series computed only on countries reporting in both 2015 and the latest year, and state the difference between the two. Where the two diverge, the divergence is itself a finding about who has dropped out. This is the form in which the guild's own analyses are replicated, and it costs the producing agencies little.

### Targets without numbers cannot be scored the same way twice

A replicated analysis requires that two analysts reach the same class from the same data. Many targets do not allow this, because they lack a numerical reading. The adopted sections record target 1.3 on substantial coverage of social protection, target 2.3 on doubling agricultural productivity, target 3.5 on alcohol, target 3.8 on universal health coverage and the absence of a 2030 prevalence goal for tobacco.

The numbers show the cost. The service coverage index rose from 68.0 in 2015 to 71.0 in 2023 worldwide (c04-8.r1), against 41.2 for low-income countries in 2015; whether this is adequate depends wholly on whether the target is read as 100 points or some lower threshold. Agricultural value added per worker rose from 3,491 in 2015 to 4,264 in 2025 worldwide in constant US dollars (c03-4.r1), an annualised rate of 2.0 per cent (c03-4.r4); a doubling over fifteen years would require roughly 4.7 per cent a year, but the target names neither a baseline year nor whether it means labour productivity, so a second analyst may legitimately choose otherwise. Tobacco use fell from 24.5 per cent of adults in 2015 to 20.3 per cent in 2024 (c04-10.r1), a clear direction with no end point to measure it against. Total alcohol consumption fell from 5.9 to 4.9 litres per person between 2015 and 2020 (c04-5.r1), yet the target carries no quantitative reduction.

The guild proposes that the UN Statistical Commission and the custodian agencies (the International Labour Organization for 1.3, the FAO for 2.3, the WHO for 3.5, 3.8 and tobacco) publish, before the 2027 review, a single numerical reading for each target that lacks one, with a baseline year. These readings should be stated as conventions, open to revision, and applied to all countries alike. The guild does not propose the numbers themselves; its point is that one stated number, however chosen, makes every assessment reproducible, while none makes every assessment arguable.

The undernourishment indicator shows a related defect. The prevalence was 8.0 per cent worldwide in 2015 and 8.1 per cent in 2024 (c03-1.r1), and 165 countries reported in 2024. But the series is floored at 2.5 per cent, so countries below the floor cannot show further progress and the target of ending hunger coincides with the reporting limit. The guild endorses the proposal of section c03-1 that the series be published below the floor or the target be reinterpreted.

### Modelled estimates should carry their uncertainty

The maternal mortality ratio fell from 228.0 to 197.0 deaths per 100,000 live births between 2015 and 2023 worldwide (c04-1.r1), and the projected 2030 value is 173.4 (c04-1.r2) against a target of 70; the ratio of achieved to required progress is 0.35. These are modelled values, and the class a country receives depends on estimates whose ranges are not published in the catalogue. Alcohol projections for the 54 countries classed as regressing raise the same difficulty.

The guild proposes that the WHO and the inter-agency groups that produce modelled health estimates publish lower and upper bounds beside every national value in the World Bank's catalogue by 2027. Two analysts given the same point estimate and no range cannot tell a regression from noise; given the range, they can test whether a class assignment survives it.

### Revisions and breaks should be dated

National poverty lines are revised, and a rate before and after a revision is not comparable. Material use per unit of output fell from 0.26 to 0.22 kilograms per US dollar between 2015 and 2024 worldwide (c09-4.r1), but the series shows a structural break in 2012 (c09-4.r5), which a trend computed across it absorbs without notice.

The guild proposes that national statistical offices publish the date and reason for every revision to a national poverty line, with a linked series over the overlap years, as section c02-2 recommends, and that the World Bank flag structural breaks in its catalogue metadata. A replicating analyst must know where a series changes its meaning.

### Carried-forward values should be marked

Agricultural land has stood near 36.8 per cent of land area in 2015 and 36.9 per cent in 2023 (c03-5.r2), with 208 countries reporting in 2024. Near-constant series can be real or carried forward from an old measurement; section c03-5 found water withdrawal series that appear carried forward. The guild proposes that the FAO and national offices mark every value that repeats an earlier measurement rather than records a new one, so that analysts can exclude it from trend estimation.

### Financing figures should be tested against their volatility

The water and sanitation support series rose from US$169.7 billion in 2015 to US$259.5 billion in 2023 (c07-5.r1), with a jump in 2022. A plan that extrapolates from 2023 builds on a single unusual year. The guild endorses the proposal of section c07-5 that finance ministries and development agencies test 2030 financing plans under scenarios with and without the 2022 jump, and adds that the test should be published so that a second analyst can rerun it.

Education spending fell from 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023 worldwide (c05-8.r1); of 186 countries assessed, 98 were classed as regressing (c05-8.r3). The share of government spending devoted to education and health stood at 14.1 per cent in 2015 and 14.0 per cent in 2023 worldwide, while East Asia and Pacific fell from 15.1 to 13.0 (c02-6.r2). The guild proposes that ministries of finance publish these shares each budget cycle with a stated reference year, so that the fall can be checked against the budget that caused it rather than inferred years later from a lagged series.

### Where the findings support action, act on the regions they name

The guild's emphasis on measurement does not defer action where the record is adequate. Several findings are dense, consistent and replicated, and they point to the same places.

Maternal mortality, with a projected 2030 world value of 173.4 against a target of 70 (c04-1.r2), supports the proposal that donors and development banks direct health financing to low-income and lower-middle-income countries, and that health ministries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia prioritise skilled attendance, emergency obstetric care and the civil registration of deaths. Registration serves both ends: it saves lives through accountability and it replaces modelled estimates with counts.

Stunting fell only from 24.6 to 23.2 per cent of children under five between 2015 and 2024, and wasting from 7.1 to 6.6 per cent (c03-2.r1, c03-2.r2). At that pace the 2030 targets will not be met. The guild proposes that governments in the countries with the highest prevalence, with UNICEF and development partners, link nutrition programmes to the social protection and food reserves that section c03-1 recommends, and that survey programmes measure stunting at least every three years in those countries so that the effect can be read before 2030.

Safely managed drinking water reached 73.7 per cent of the world population in 2024, up from 67.7 per cent in 2015 (c07-1.r1), but the 79 stagnating or regressing countries hold 34.4 per cent of the assessed population. Basic sanitation rose from 72.6 to 82.2 per cent (c07-2.r1). Clean cooking rose from 63.9 to 75.4 per cent of the population (c08-2.r1) against 98.8 per cent in high-income countries in 2015. In each case the guild supports concessional finance directed to low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa, and adds one condition from its method: every programme so financed should report the indicator it is meant to move at a fixed interval, so that its effect enters the record by 2029.

Malaria, where countries in regression hold 27.5 per cent of the assessed population, and HIV, whose world incidence fell from 0.26 to 0.16 per 1,000 uninfected people between 2015 and 2024 (c04-3.r1), support continued financing for Sub-Saharan Africa. The guild endorses the request in section c04-3 that health ministries in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan report whether rising malaria incidence reflects transmission or detection; until that is known, the rise is not a finding on which spending should turn.

Adolescent births fell from 46.0 to 38.3 per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 between 2015 and 2024 (c04-7.r2), with 217 countries reporting. The guild supports funding for keeping girls in school and for contraceptive services reaching adolescents in the countries with the highest rates.

Account ownership among women rose from 65.9 to 76.6 per cent between 2017 and 2024 worldwide (c06-6.r1), and overall account ownership from 69.3 to 78.7 per cent (c09-9.r1). The guild supports the call on financial regulators in the 33 countries where women's ownership regressed to require providers to report account data by sex, which serves measurement and policy alike.

### A replication standard for the 2030 review

The guild's final proposal concerns the review itself. The custodian agencies and the High-level Political Forum should require that every headline classification in the 2030 assessment be accompanied by the code, the data vintage and the country panel used, and that each be reproduced by a team independent of the one that produced it before publication. The book's five communities have worked under this rule, and it has repeatedly caught readings that a single analyst would have let stand: aggregates built on a handful of countries, trends that cross a break, classes that do not survive a stated uncertainty. The cost is modest; the benefit is that the 2030 judgement can be trusted by those it judges.

### Where the data leave the question open

Some questions cannot be closed before 2030 on the present record. Disaster exposure rose from 19,188,817 people in 2015 to 26,393,278 in 2023 worldwide (c02-5.r3), a mean annual change of about 789,790 (c02-5.r4), but only 80 countries reported in 2008 (c02-5.r1), and annual counts are dominated by single events; the guild does not treat this series as a trend on which to allocate resources. Domestic government health spending per head shows a world annualised rate of -0.0017 and rates of 0 for several regions (c04-11.r1); a rate of exactly zero more likely reflects a missing or carried value than true stagnation, and the guild proposes that this be investigated before any conclusion is drawn. Completion rates moved from 87.9 to 88.0 per cent worldwide between 2015 and 2024 (c05-1.r1), while the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8 to 83.7 per cent; whether the world figure reflects stagnation or a shifting country set should be tested on a constant panel before it is cited as the former.
