proposals: National statistical offices, UNESCO Institute for Statistics, the World Bank and survey programmes should commit a fixed panel of countries to report each indicator in 2026 and 2029, starting with pre-primary participation, social protection coverage and tertiary enrolment.
Every published aggregate should carry the count of reporting countries and the population share they cover, year by year.
The World Bank should publish a constant-panel series (countries reporting in 2015 and the latest year) beside each headline regional and global aggregate, stating the difference.

The UN Statistical Commission and custodian agencies should publish before the 2027 review a single numerical reading and baseline year for targets 1.3, 2.3, 3.5, 3.8 and a 2030 tobacco prevalence goal.
The WHO and inter-agency estimation groups should publish uncertainty bounds beside every modelled national value in the World Bank catalogue by 2027.
National statistical offices should date and explain every poverty line revision with linked overlap series, and the World Bank should flag structural breaks in catalogue metadata.
The FAO and national offices should mark values carried forward from earlier measurements so they can be excluded from trend estimation.

Finance ministries and development agencies should publish tests of 2030 water financing plans with and without the 2022 jump, and publish education and health spending shares each budget cycle with a reference year.

Donors and development banks should direct maternal health, water, sanitation and clean cooking finance to low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa, with each financed programme reporting its target indicator at fixed intervals.
Governments with the highest stunting, with UNICEF and partners, should link nutrition programmes to social protection and food reserves, with stunting surveys at least every three years.

The custodian agencies and the High-level Political Forum should require every headline 2030 classification to be published with code, data vintage and country panel, and reproduced by an independent team before release.
guild.gaps: Disaster exposure counts are event-driven and thinly reported (80 countries in 2008), so no trend-based allocation is proposed. Zero annualised rates in government health spending per head likely reflect missing or carried values and need checking. The near-flat world completion rate has not been tested on a constant panel. Several targets lack a numerical reading, so classifications against them depend on conventions; the guild proposes that numbers be fixed but does not choose them.

forum.text:
## The forum's proposals: those the goals concern

The forum speaks for the people whom the goals name: the poor, the hungry, mothers, children, girls, and households without water, sanitation or clean fuel. Its proposals are therefore ordered by a single test: whether what is written, and what is measured, reaches those people before 2030. Three convictions run through what follows. First, a world average can hide the people furthest behind, so action must be directed to the places where they live. Second, a person who is not counted cannot be served, so the gaps in reporting are themselves a harm and must be closed. Third, where a target can be read in more than one way, those it concerns are entitled to know which reading is used against them. Each proposal below follows from a finding of the book's adopted sections, and the figures are those of the World Bank's World Development Indicators as reported there.

### Hunger has not fallen, and those who carry it must come first

The prevalence of undernourishment in the world stood at 8.0 per cent in 2015 and 8.1 per cent in 2024. Nine years of the goals have left the share of hungry people where it began. For a family that cannot eat enough, the stability of an average is no comfort, and the section on undernourishment records that the trend in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa is regression.

Donors and development banks should direct hunger financing first to low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa before 2030, and should tie it to social protection and food reserves that cushion households against price shocks. The forum adds a condition from its mission: that financing should be judged by whether hunger falls among those reached, and its results reported each year in the same series used here.

Children bear hunger in their bodies. Stunting among children under five fell from 24.6% in 2015 to 23.2% in 2024, and wasting from 7.1% to 6.6%. These are slow declines; nearly a quarter of young children remained stunted in the latest year. The section offered no proposals of its own. The forum proposes that national health and agriculture ministries in the countries with the highest stunting combine the hunger financing above with nutrition for mothers and young children, and that the stunting and wasting series be reported alongside the hunger figures so that the two can be read together.

Prices matter as much as harvests. The number of countries reporting inflation fell from 189 in 2015 to 179 in 2020. Those who spend most of their income on food cannot be protected if food prices are not watched. National statistical offices and the World Bank should publish a food-specific consumer price series beside general inflation for every reporting country, and governments of the countries with the highest inflation should publish information on food reserves and market conditions promptly, as target 2.c asks.

### Social protection must reach the poorest countries first

In 2021, 56.3% of the world's population was covered by at least one social protection measure, by the reading of the adopted section. The section records 18.3% coverage in low-income countries against 77.8% in high-income countries. Those least able to absorb a lost harvest, an illness or a price shock are the least protected.

Donors should direct support for social protection to low-income countries before 2030; the data support this targeting and no more. The bodies responsible for the goals should also fix a numeric reading of "substantial coverage" under target 1.3. Without such a reading a government can claim success at any level, and the people left outside the system have no standard by which to hold it to account. The record also thins: one country reported poorest-quintile coverage in 2023. National governments and statistical offices should keep this reporting continuous, because the poorest quintile is precisely the group whose position is otherwise inferred.

Poverty itself is counted in ways that people cannot easily follow. Of 161 countries that have reported a national poverty rate in any year, few report in a given year; 16 did so in 2000 and 36 in 2004. National statistical offices should publish the date and reason of every revision to a national poverty line, with a linked series for the overlap years, and countries should assess target 1.2 against each country's own 2015 rate while reading the national line together with an international one. A person moved across a poverty line by a revision has not changed their circumstances, and the public is owed that distinction.

### Mothers and young women need services, not averages

The maternal mortality ratio fell from 228.0 to 197.0 deaths per 100,000 live births between 2015 and 2023. At that pace the world reaches an expected 173.4 in 2030, far above the target of 70. The section's ratio of 0.35 measures how small a share of the required progress the current path delivers. For women in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where the ratios are highest, this is the most direct measure of whether the goals serve them.

Ministries of health in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia should prioritise skilled attendance at birth, emergency obstetric care and the civil registration of deaths before 2030, and donors and development banks should direct health financing to low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Registration is not an administrative nicety: a woman whose death is not recorded leaves no trace in the evidence on which policy rests. Health authorities in Latin America and the Caribbean should investigate the rise in that region's ratio from 74 to 77 and act on its causes.

Adolescent fertility fell from 46.0 to 38.3 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19 between 2015 and 2024, across 217 countries assessed. Early births and early marriage are linked; child marriage stood at 19.5% of young women in 2022, and only three countries reported in 2025. Ministries of health and education in the countries with the highest adolescent fertility should concentrate funding on keeping girls in school and on contraceptive services that reach adolescents and unmarried women. The forum adds that the child marriage series, for which the section offered no proposal, needs regular surveys: national statistical offices should field marriage questions in household surveys at least every five years, so that girls married in the years after 2020 are counted before 2030.

### Health coverage must protect households from ruin

The service coverage index rose from 68.0 in 2015 to 71.0 in 2023 for the world, with low-income countries starting at 41.2 in 2015. Coverage that comes with ruinous payment is not coverage in the sense that matters to a household. Ministries of health and finance in low-income and lower-middle-income countries should raise the share of health spending funded from pooled domestic public sources, and national health authorities where financial hardship is rising should publish annual hardship figures and review user fees and benefit packages. The World Health Organization and the World Bank should publish a numerical reading of target 3.8, so that people can know what universal coverage is meant to mean.

Disease burdens fall unevenly. HIV incidence fell from 0.26 to 0.16 per 1,000 uninfected people between 2015 and 2024, yet Sub-Saharan Africa still carries the highest incidence; donors should keep HIV financing there. The section on malaria found countries in regression holding 27.5 per cent of the assessed population; governments and funders should give priority to malaria control there, with Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries first.

### Water, sanitation and clean fuel are matters of daily dignity

Safely managed drinking water reached 73.7% of the world's population in 2024, up from 67.7% in 2015. The section found 79 countries stagnating or regressing, holding 34.4% of the assessed population. National governments and utilities in those countries should be the first priority for investment and monitoring, and donors should direct concessional finance to low-income countries and Sub-Saharan Africa. The forum endorses the section's further point that averages near 96.2% in rich regions can hide off-network and marginalised communities; statistical offices there should report on them.

Basic sanitation rose from 72.6 per cent in 2015 to 82.2 per cent in 2024, while open defecation stood at 10.6 per cent in 2015. Sanitation finance in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should go where open defecation is projected to remain highest in 2030. The burden of its absence falls hardest on women and girls, for safety and privacy; the forum therefore asks that rural and urban series, and data on the overlap of deprivations, be published so that the number of people lacking at least one service is known.

Aid for water rose sharply: the section records US$169.7 billion in 2015 and US$259.5 billion in 2023 in the series used. Money is not service. Donors and multilateral funds should publish country-level allocations of water assistance alongside coverage, so that those without water can see whether the money follows their need, and finance ministries should not assume the 2023 level will persist.

Clean cooking reached 75.4 per cent of the world's population in 2024, up from 63.9 per cent in 2015, against 98.8 per cent in high-income countries in 2015. Smoke from dirty fuels harms women and children above all. National governments in Sub-Saharan Africa and low-income countries should prioritise clean cooking for rural households, and statistical offices should report affordability and reliability, because a stove that a family cannot afford to fuel does not serve it.

### Children's schooling and work must be seen together

Primary completion stood at 87.9% in 2015 and 88.0% in 2024: almost no change for the world, though the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan rose from 73.8% to 83.7%. Public spending on education fell from 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2015 to 3.6 per cent in 2023, with 98 of 186 countries assessed in regression. A child's chance of finishing school should not depend on a budget line silently shrinking. Ministries of finance and education should treat the education share of GDP as a monitored quantity and publish plans that halt its fall, first in low-income and lower-middle-income countries, and governments should fund the transition to lower secondary tied to measured learning.

Pre-primary participation rose from 56.0 in 2015 to 60.9 in 2020, but the reporting record collapsed from 71 countries in 2021 to 4 in 2022. Children in the years since cannot be counted. Ministries of education and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics should restore reporting, and donors should direct support for early childhood places to low-income countries and to Sub-Saharan Africa.

Child labour is the other side of schooling. Only 97 countries have ever reported it, and few in the same year. Statistical agencies should schedule child labour modules so that many countries report in the same years, and should extend measurement to children aged 15 to 17 in hazardous work and to forced labour, since the worst forms are not visible in the present indicator.

### Women's voice and assets must be counted

Women's share of parliamentary seats rose from 22.8 in 2015 to 27.2 in 2025, with 184 countries reporting. Where the regional share has fallen, in South Asia and in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, parliaments and electoral bodies should review nomination rules and consider reserved seats or party quotas. Representation is the means by which women judge, in public, whether what is written serves them.

Women's account ownership rose from 65.9% in 2017 to 76.6% in 2024, with 139 countries reporting. Regulators in the 33 countries where it regressed should require providers to report account data by sex. Women's internet use rose from 51.8 per cent in 2019 to 68.2 per cent in 2024. Regulators in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa should lower the cost of data and handsets and publish internet use by sex each year. Ownership of land and dwellings, central to target 5.a, is not measured in the series available; a comparable survey item should be added.

### Exposure to disaster is rising for the vulnerable

The number of people affected by disasters in the world series rose from 19,188,817 in 2015 to 26,393,278 in 2023, a mean annual change of about 789,790 over 2009 to 2023. The section made no proposals. The forum proposes that national disaster authorities report affected people by income group and by sex, and that the social protection coverage proposed above be designed to scale up after a disaster, so that those already poor are not pushed further behind. The year-to-year volatility of the series means this rise should be read with caution.

### What is written must be readable by those it concerns

Across the book, many targets lack a numeric reading: substantial coverage under 1.3, the doubling under 2.3, universal health coverage under 3.8, a tobacco prevalence goal, a quantitative reduction for alcohol. The forum's mission asks whether what is written serves the people concerned. A target that cannot be read cannot be claimed by them. The bodies that maintain the global framework should, before 2030, publish one stated reading for each such target, and reports on the goals should state plainly where data are missing rather than fill gaps with unsupported estimates, as the section on water quality urges.

The forum notes the limits of these proposals. Many findings rest on world and regional aggregates; the people furthest behind are often in countries with the thinnest records, and the post-2020 years are the least observed. Where this is so, the proposals ask first for measurement, because a commitment to leave no one behind cannot be honoured for people who remain uncounted.
